Title: Introductory remarks, End-of-year press conference
text: Year-end press conference, Zurich, 12 December 1997 Introductory remarks by Bruno Gehrig, Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank The events that have shaken the financial markets in recent months - especially in recent weeks - have caused concern around the world. The crisis originated in Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia, in economies facing difficulties. In the meantime, it has spread to other Southeast Asian countries, particularly South Korea. Let us briefly see, taking the case of Thailand, what are the main causes of this crisis. With the Thai baht pegged to a basket of currencies in which the US dollar plays a dominant role, its real rate has reached an excessive level in the wake of the dollar's firmness. As a result, exports have declined, economic growth has slowed, and financing the large current account deficit has become more difficult. Macroeconomic problems have been further exacerbated by the obvious weaknesses of the financial system. The baht exchange rate regime has encouraged financial institutions to take on debt, apparently risk-free, abroad and to lend in local currency, at higher interest rates, the funds thus raised. In the middle of the year, the Thai government had to float the baht under pressure from the markets. The wave of depreciation affected almost all Southeast Asian currencies and led to substantial declines in local equity markets. The tremors that disrupted the financial markets of Southeast Asia have led to turbulence in all other stock exchanges, but also corrections in the exchange rate relations between the currencies of the industrialized countries. The Japanese yen then weakened sharply against the US dollar and European currencies. The problems that the Japanese financial sector has been experiencing for years have worsened. What lessons can be drawn from these events? I will mention three that I think are important. We have seen - firstly - how strong globalisation is in the financial field. Globalization has enabled many countries to make very good economic progress, but has also significantly increased dependence, both regionally and even globally. Shocks  usually caused by erroneous policy decisions that are made in one country  quickly spread to other countries and markets. Chain reactions, with very serious consequences, can result since the fall in the value of a currency leads to downward pressure on the currencies of neighbouring countries. Protecting the stability and security of the financial system has become even more important. The behaviour of key players in the financial markets - the second lesson - has been ambivalent. On the one hand, these speakers have adopted an attitude encouraging countries to be more disciplined and triggered economically justified adaptations. On the other hand, after having greatly underestimated the risks related to their operations, they suddenly fled them. By moving from one extreme to the other, at the same time and from one bloc, they have accentuated the shocks and, consequently, caused damage, especially to emerging economies outside Asia which have seen their interest charges increase massively. Many market participants have an important lesson to learn from this. The International Monetary Fund (IMF)  the third lesson  has an irreplaceable role to play in protecting the global financial system. The focus must be even more on prevention than on crisis management. The IMF, which had issued warnings - to Thailand in particular long before the outbreak of the crisis , does not have the instruments to ensure that its recommendations to sovereign states are actually implemented. An important reform must aim to ensure greater transparency. Financial markets can only play their role effectively if they continuously receive key information about national economies. The IMF must therefore be able to impose the publication of such information. It is also necessary to act as a matter of priority to ensure that the banking and financial sectors are efficient and subject to effective supervision. While infrastructure remains underdeveloped in the financial and regulatory fields, the liberalization of capital movements leads to serious problems. In addition, increased flexibility margins should be provided for in fixed exchange rate regimes. For countries that do not have a tradition of stability, fixed exchange rates certainly offer decisive advantages in terms of inflation and financing opportunities. When, for whatever reason, currencies in a fixed exchange rate regime become fundamentally overvalued, however, they must be able to be devalued in time, i.e. before the markets impose a sudden adjustment. The more successfully the IMF can carry out its preventive tasks, the lower the moral risk that governments and market participants will rely on the Fund's helping hand and operate with the knowledge that capital provided by third parties will remedy the damage. Crises requiring the establishment of aid will always exist. It is important, however, that IMF assistance is systematically linked to strict conditions and that these conditions are not circumvented by bilateral or regional agreements. The turbulence on the financial markets has had repercussions in Switzerland as well. As we have seen, the franc has come under upward pressure due to short-term capital inflows. We then generously supplied the market with liquidity, given the undesirable trend towards a strengthening of the Swiss franc, but also because liquidity needs generally increase in phases of increased uncertainty. In the money market, remuneration has thus fallen. It is difficult to estimate the impact that the slowdown in growth in Southeast Asia will have on the Swiss economy. Today, we can say that we should expect a slight reduction in our economic growth. The fear of falling into a generalized deflationary process is in our view unfounded. Developments in the financial markets in recent months have been a bad experience for several economies and many stakeholders. However, they also represent an opportunity if lessons can be learned and put into practice.

Title: Introductory remarks, End-of-year press conference
text: End-of-year press conference, Zurich, 12 December 1997 Introductory Remarks by Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank The Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank, in agreement with the Federal Government, does not plan to tighten monetary policy in 1998. It currently considers the inflation risks in Switzerland to be low. The supply of money will be expanded as required to permit continued economic recovery without threatening price stability. Monetary policy will also duly take the uncertainties emanating from European monetary integration into account. As usual, the Governing Board will retain the option of deviating from its monetary course in the event of disruptions in the financial markets. The Swiss National Bank's task is to pursue a monetary policy serving the interests of the country as a whole. This task needs to be described in more detail. A monetary policy that ensures an adequate supply of money in relation to the needs of the real economy tends to guarantee price stability in the long term. Price stability is not an end in itself. It helps to create a favourable framework for balanced economic development. More particularly, price stability is an important social concern since the weakest members of society suffer most from inflation. As the year went by, the prospects for a gradual economic recovery began to improve. The long stagnation, which has taken its sad toll in terms of human suffering and material loss of substance, may well be behind us. Before discussing our monetary policy intentions for the coming year, I should like once more to look back on past developments. A year ago we planned to continue implementing a generous monetary policy. At that time, we had to take into account the unfavourable economic situation as well as the possible implications of European monetary integration. We expected a gradual economic recovery and at first only a minor danger of inflation. Nevertheless, we drew attention to the strong expansion of the monetary base and emphasised the associated medium-term risks. However, we also pointed out that a change in monetary policy would only enter into consideration once the economy was clearly on an uptrend. Today we are able to say that economic developments in Switzerland have largely come up to our expectations. Real gross domestic product rose markedly in the second and third quarters of 1997. Its growth rate is expected to be 0.5% on an annual average. With an inflation rate on a similar level, it is possible to speak of price stability. In the implementation of an adequate monetary course, however, considerable difficulties were encountered in the course of the year. We had already pointed out at the end of 1996 that the demand for base money had exceeded expectations and that this falsified the indicator value of our target aggregate. In 1997 new problems arose. Notably, the demand for one thousand franc banknotes increased excessively. It therefore seemed to us beyond doubt that the vigorous expansion of the monetary base, which is likely to surpass the previous year's level by approximately 3% in the fourth quarter, overstated the degree of monetary expansion (cf. chart). In view of these imponderables, we set our sights increasingly on other money supply aggregates, notably on M3. Our investigations show that there is a fairly close correlation between the development of the money supply M3 and the price level. At the end of 1995, the growth of M3 accelerated markedly, reflecting our generous monetary policy. The comparatively strong expansion of M3 by and large continued in the first half of 1997. We were therefore of the opinion that monetary policy would have to be considerably tightened sooner or later. Until late summer our aim was to supply the money market with abundant liquidity. Given the clear signs of economic revival, we permitted money market rates to rise moderately in October, in line with interest rate developments in other European countries. We found it necessary to tighten monetary policy somewhat in order to contain money supply growth and thus maintain price stability in the long term. A renewed review of the situation, however, leads to the conclusion that the excess money supply which existed at the beginning of 1997 already seems to have been reduced substantially. The growth in the money supply M3 amounted to 4% at the end of October. It therefore tends to lie in a range consistent with price stability in the long term. The monetary base shows a similar development if the said shifts in demand are disregarded as far as possible. Without these shifts the monetary base is likely to come close to its medium-term target path. As stated earlier on, we intend to expand the money supply in 1998 so as to permit the economic recovery to continue without threatening price stability. This implies that we will adjust the supply of money to the increase in demand resulting from the development of the Swiss economy forecast for 1998. We are expecting an increase in the real gross domestic product of 2% and a rise in consumer prices of 1%. Under these circumstances, the growth trend of the money supply M3 is likely to remain at the present level in 1998. Temporary deviations from the growth trend cannot, however, be ruled out even for M3. Due to the said distortions and possible future shifts in demand it is difficult to predict how the monetary base will develop. Should no further shifts occur, the monetary base is likely to rise from its present level on a line parallel to the medium-term target path. From this follows that for the time being there is no need for another increase in Swiss interest rates. As in 1997, we shall not orient our monetary policy solely to the monetary aggregates but will also take the economic and exchange rate situation as well as interest rate developments into account. If real growth should fall considerably short of expectations, then the expansion of the money supply is also likely to decrease markedly. Under these circumstances, interest rates would have to fall. An unexpectedly pronounced economic upswing, on the other hand, would probably put upward pressure on interest rates. The course we are aiming at will in any case support the economic revival from the monetary side. Next spring the European Union will decide on the beginning of the third stage of the Economic and Monetary Union. The markets are expecting a timely start at the beginning of 1999. This expectation is already reflected in the development of the exchange rates of the Swiss franc vis-a-vis the European currencies. It is nevertheless conceivable that the transition to the third stage will trigger fluctuations of the Swiss franc exchange rate that are both unexpected and undesirable. To end with, I should like to reiterate that we shall certainly use the monetary means at our disposal to counter an exchange rate development that is undesirable from the point of view of the economy as a whole.

Title: Introductory remarks, End-of-year press conference
text: Year-end press conference, Zurich, 12 December 1997 Introductory remarks by Jean-Pierre Roth, Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank On 1 November, a partial revision of the National Bank Act entered into force. The aim of this revision was to give the SNB additional flexibility in the management of its currencies and gold cash in order to improve its profitability. In the gold sector, it has been given the power to repurchase gold, i.e. to carry out "gold lending" operations (until now Article 14(9) of the NBA only mentioned the possibility of selling or buying gold). At the same time, the gold hedging rate of banknotes in circulation was reduced from 40 per cent to 25 per cent. Although the SNB has always had the competence to sell or buy gold, we have not been able to carry out such operations for many years and we will not be able to do so until there is a fundamental reform of our legal framework, which will have to demonetize gold. Indeed, we are still bound by the official parity of the franc which allows us to operate on the market only at the price of 4,595.74 per kilo of gold. We hope that the forthcoming revision of the Constitution and then of the SNB Act will enable us to gain greater freedom in this area. That said, we do not intend to quickly divest our cash position because we are convinced that gold will continue to play a role as a foreign exchange reserve instrument, especially in the event of a crisis. In addition, in the eyes of many, gold is synonymous with stability and security, so our intention is to keep significant metal reserves. Those who expect massive sales from us will be disappointed. The SNB's last gold transactions were in 1976. At the time, we had acquired 2.4 tons of gold, against dollars, at an average price of 9,752 francs per kilo, as part of an auction of part of the IMF's metal cash. At that time, the General Management considered that a purchase for dollars - although it was carried out at a price other than the parity value - was in conformity with the SNB Act. His argument was that the SNB was only required to respect parity for its operations of buying or selling gold against Swiss francs, not against foreign currencies. Since then, this view of things has been the subject of much criticism from legal experts. They considered that operating in foreign currencies does not relieve the SNB of the obligation to respect parity. The gold purchases of 1976 were therefore made in the context of an interpretation of the SNB Act to which we believe that we can no longer adhere to today. As soon as the recent revision of the law came into force, the SNB carried out its first gold lending operations. These operations consist in making physical gold available to a counterparty for a fixed period of time and in return for remuneration. During the duration of the transaction, this counterparty freely disposes of the gold it has received on loan. For this service, it pays an interest rate calculated on the market value of the metal at its disposal. These lending operations can also be pledged, with the counterparty receiving the gold providing collateral securities, usually government debt securities. Pledged gold loans carry lower counterparty risk, but also show a lower return. They are not the usual form of "gold lending". The SNB intends to repurchase only a small part of its gold stock. This prudent policy is explained by the narrowness of the market and the risks entailed by this type of operation. The SNB's partners for gold lending operations are leading financial institutions that play an active role in the gold market. For these institutions, limits have been defined internally. The big Swiss banks belong to this circle. Our annual report will inform the public about our gold lending operations. We will then clearly distinguish the part of the gold that is lent ("claims on gold transactions"), from that which we freely dispose ("gold") and which is included in the calculation of the gold hedging. In the situations we publish every ten days, these two positions are consolidated. Revenue from gold lending operations is - in relation to the amounts committed - modest. In the eighties, the yield on gold loans was less than 1% per year because gold producers did little to hedge against the risk of a price decline. In the nineties, rates were observed above 1%. Today, they are of the order of 2%. Currently, 100 tonnes of gold loaned corresponds to an advance of 1.4 billion francs and an additional revenue of around 30 million francs. * * * On December 1st, the Independent Commission of Experts: Switzerland - Second World War made a first assessment of its research, its final report on gold to be tabled next January. The SNB draws two conclusions from this interim document: The figures for the SNB's gold transactions, published by the Commission on the basis of its consultation of the archives, particularly in Germany, correspond to those we have already had. the opportunity to introduce yourself last December and March. We are pleased that full clarity now exists on this subject. The report refers to the discussions within the SNB as early as 1941 on the origin of the gold delivered by the Reichsbank. We have repeatedly criticised the attitude of the General Directorate at the time, when it accepted without further assurances that the gold delivered by the Reichsbank came from its pre-war reserves. The final report of the Committee of Experts should establish why the SNB was willing to take so many moral and political risks by agreeing to acquire gold whose origin could be doubtful. The Gold Conference held in London at the beginning of December placed Switzerland's operations in a broader context. Nothing fundamentally new has emerged with regard to the SNB's gold transactions. On the other hand, new indications have emerged that private gold has been mixed with monetary gold. Moreover - as we already told you last December - it is now confirmed that the Allies already had at their disposal most of the relevant information concerning the nature of the Reichsbank's operations at the end of the war. There can therefore be no doubt that the Washington Agreement was signed with full knowledge of the facts.

On ne peut donc douter que l'Accord de Washington ait t sign en connaissance de cause.

Title: On monetary policy in the new year
text: Monetary policy in the new year Dr. Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank, University of St. Gallen, St. Gallen, 14 January 1998 Introduction Almost a quarter of a century ago to the day, on 23 January 1973, the Swiss National Bank, in agreement with the Federal Council, stopped its massive foreign exchange purchases to support the dollar. The renewed waves of speculation that began against the dollar and European currencies in early 1973 left no doubt that the Bretton Woods fixed rate system had outlived itself. With the transition to flexible exchange rates, we were given the opportunity to conduct an independent monetary policy for the first time in the post-war period. Their goal was undisputed. The aim was to contain high inflation and deep-rooted inflation expectations and thus to create stable monetary conditions again. The development of the money supply served as a guideline for monetary policy, for which we set targets almost continuously from 1975 onwards - first for the money supply M1 and from 1980 for the banknote amount. In the following years, not all the hopes that had been placed in the flexible exchange rates were fulfilled. The real exchange rates of the various currencies were at times subject to strong fluctuations. Switzerland felt these fluctuations particularly strongly. Financial innovations then undermined the validity of monetary aggregates in some countries. Other strategies and solutions were introduced, which replaced the previous money supply control in many countries. One constant, however, remained, namely the recognition that a high degree of price stability is an essential prerequisite for balanced economic growth. For this reason, the objective of price stability was subsequently enshrined in many central bank laws, not least in the statute of the future European Central Bank. However monetary policy is designed in concrete terms, the central bank needs indicators, i.e. benchmarks that show it in the long term and with foresight where the journey is going, how the price level will develop. It must disclose these indicators and make their importance understandable. Communication takes place via various channels. In Switzerland, our press conferences, which take place twice a year, play an important role in this. The press conference at the end of each year gives us the opportunity to look back on the past year and compare what we have achieved with our expectations. Above all, however, it serves to explain our monetary policy intentions for the coming year. I would like to take this opportunity today to present the monetary policy that we envisage for this year, while at the same time giving you an insight into the monetary policy decision-making process. Our press conference in December focused on conveying three main messages: Firstly, we announced that we did not intend to tighten monetary policy in 1998. Secondly, we pointed out that in the future we would like to attach greater weight to the broader monetary aggregate M3. Thirdly, we announced that we intend to continue to use other indicators to assess monetary policy. Let me elaborate on these three points. 1. Monetary policy in 1998 What are the reasons behind the decision not to tighten monetary policy in 1998? The starting point is the assessment of the economic situation and price developments as well as an assessment of our previous monetary policy. Over the past year, the economic recovery has finally begun. The most significant impetus came from exports, which were increasingly gaining momentum. Domestic demand picked up tentatively; recessive tendencies continued, especially in one important sector - the construction industry. In the course of the year, the number of unemployed also began to fall slightly. This decline was largely due to the employment programmes offered by the cantons on the basis of the revised Unemployment Act. However, other indicators indicated that the trough had been reached. However, it was clear that the reduction in unemployment would be slow. With average inflation of 0.5% at the consumer level and unchanged producer and import prices, price stability prevailed in Switzerland last year. A risk of inflation could not be identified. On the contrary, liberalisation measures and increased competition are putting pressure on prices in some areas, such as the communications sector. The outlook for 1998 was favourable. Admittedly, no one expected a brilliant growth spurt. However, the continued good international economic situation pointed to robust demand for Swiss export goods. Domestic demand should take hold and the construction industry in particular should gradually gain ground. Under these circumstances, the economic research centres expected an increase in real gross domestic product of just under 2%. This is roughly in line with longer-term trend growth. After the long-term stagnation, however, the Swiss economy is below the long-term growth path. With growth of 2%, the output gap would therefore only partially close. Nevertheless, the forecasts suggested that we would find the connection to the international growth train again. As a central bank, the next step is to ask ourselves how our monetary policy of recent months and years will affect future economic and price developments. Due to the delay with which monetary policy affects prices, it is important to assess whether any corrective measures may be necessary. The assessment of monetary policy - the degree of monetary policy restriction - was more difficult at the end of 1997 than in previous years. The central bank money supply, our main indicator, grew very rapidly at the beginning of 1997. Above all, the demand for thousand-franc notes suddenly increased sharply, a phenomenon that could not be explained by either income or interest rate developments. We had to assume that this was a shift in demand. For this reason, we supported the additional demand for banknotes by expanding the money supply accordingly, otherwise it would have triggered an undesirable increase in interest rates. In any case, it was clear that the central bank money supply greatly overstated the degree of monetary policy expansion in 1997 and had thus lost its significance as a monetary policy indicator, at least temporarily. In this situation, we increasingly focused our attention on the broader monetary aggregates. The focus was on the M3 money supply, which has a reliable connection to the development of the price level. Since the end of 1995, the growth of M3 has accelerated. This reflected our loose monetary policy. In the first half of 1997, M3 continued to grow strongly. We therefore felt that a tightening of monetary policy would be imperative sooner or later. As the signs of an economic recovery intensified, we allowed a limited increase in money market rates last October. This was not an isolated rise in interest rates, but a movement in line with interest rate developments in other European countries, especially Germany. We considered the slight tightening of monetary policy to be necessary in order to moderate monetary growth and thus maintain price stability in the longer term. However, this assessment of the situation changed during the fourth quarter. The crisis in Southeast Asia led to price swings on the financial markets worldwide and thus impressively demonstrated the increasing interconnectedness of the global economy. The Swiss franc came under upward pressure and thus tightened the degree of restriction of monetary policy. At the end of November, we made it clear that we would not allow an appreciation boost. We added additional liquidity to the money market to counteract the appreciation of the Swiss franc. At the end of October, as in September, M3 growth of 4% was again in a range that should be in line with price stability. This led us to the conclusion that the money overhang that still existed at the beginning of 1997 had now been largely reduced. An in-depth analysis of the central bank money supply confirmed this assessment: Taking into account the above-mentioned shifts in demand, the central bank money supply was close to the medium-term target path of 1%. The normalisation of money supply growth initially left room to take account of the exchange rate without jeopardising price stability in the medium term. Above all, it meant that there was no need to tighten the monetary policy reins in 1998. Indeed, if real economic growth developed as expected, monetary growth would remain in a range compatible with balanced economic growth and price stability. As you can see, the definition of monetary policy is largely based on forecasts. This in turn means that the course must be deviated from if things develop significantly differently than expected. More recently, the crisis in Southeast Asia has prompted the International Monetary Fund and the OECD to revise their growth forecasts for developed countries slightly downwards. The consequences of such crises are extremely difficult to assess. Of course, we have to be on our guard. Should real growth will be much weaker this year, monetary growth is also likely to decline significantly. In order to prevent such an undesirable decline, a further decline in interest rates would be necessary. If, on the other hand, the economic upswing were to be strong above expectations, we would have to allow interest rates to rise in principle. However, this is not the case before other indicators, in particular the development of exchange rates, the foreign economy, long-term interest rates and inflation expectations - would be subjected to a reassessment. 2. The money supply M3 as a monetary policy indicator This brings me to the second point of our press conference - the increased consideration of the broader monetary aggregate M3. As is well known, monetary policy impulses first have an effect on macroeconomic production and, with a considerable delay, finally on price levels. A central bank therefore needs preliminary indicators that provide information on the future development of production and prices, in short the nominal gross domestic product. Only if it has such indicators will it be able to conduct monetary policy properly and in a timely manner. Monetary aggregates are among the most important leading indicators. They therefore have an important role to play in all monetary policy strategies. This does not always mean that the central bank also publishes targets for the monetary aggregates. In recent years, some central banks have moved away from announcing money supply targets. The reason was the instability of money demand - mostly caused by financial innovation. These central banks - a prominent example is the Bank of England - instead use a variety of indicators to forecast the future development of production and prices. If the forecasts deviate from the desired development, the central bank will take appropriate measures. Monetary aggregates are no longer at the forefront of monetary policy communication. However, they continue to occupy an important place among the various monetary policy indicators. In Switzerland, as I said, the central bank money supply has served as the main indicator since 1980. This is a very narrow aggregate that corresponds to the sum of the banknotes in circulation and the current account balances of the banks at the National Bank. Until 1989, we set annual growth targets for this aggregate. In 1990, we moved to a medium-term growth path. The central bank money supply has advantages over other monetary aggregates. It is, in principle, a reliable monetary policy indicator. Also advantageous are its good controllability, the daily availability of the data and, last but not least, the fact that it is subject to much lower fluctuations in the short term compared to the broader monetary aggregates. This makes it comparatively easy to interpret. As mentioned, however, problems arose with the central bank money supply in 1996 and 1997, which were exacerbated at the beginning of 1997 by the massive increase in demand for thousands of notes. We were able to filter out these distortions to some extent and thus continue to extract useful information from the central bank money supply. However, the distortions made it considerably more difficult for monetary policy to communicate. We therefore decided to increase the use of other indicators in addition to the central bank money supply, at least temporarily. We are still in the comfortable position in Switzerland that the broader monetary aggregates still have a fairly stable relationship with price levels over the longer term. Econometric models of Swiss price developments explain the long-term inflation trend primarily with the growth of monetary aggregates. Nevertheless, not all monetary aggregates are equally well suited as monetary policy indicators. The main reason, as I have already indicated, is their different interest rate volatility. What does this mean? Interest rates show a pronounced cyclical pattern. In times of boom, the monetary dress that the central bank has tailored for medium-term price stability is becoming increasingly tighter. Liquidity is becoming scarcer and interest rates are rising. Conversely, if the economy flattens out, the demand for money also falls with the declining economic activity. This is reflected in falling interest rates. Such pro-cyclical interest rate movements are quite desirable. By triggering such interest rate movements, monetary policy also acts as an economic stabiliser. As is well known, however, the demand for money is not only influenced by income, but also by interest rate developments - in the opposite sense. If, for example, interest rates rise in the course of the economy, the demand for money decreases, as holding non-interest-bearing or low-interest means of payment causes costs in the form of lost interest. Economic agents try to keep these opportunity costs as low as possible by reducing the holding of money at the expense of higher-interest investments. Conversely, the demand for money increases again as soon as interest rates fall and opportunity costs become less significant. In the case of the monetary aggregates M1 and M2, which include non-interest-bearing or rather low-interest forms of money with sight and savings deposits, the opportunity costs are particularly noticeable. Interest rate increases therefore regularly trigger shifts to higher-interest investments such as time deposits, which are not included in the two aggregates. This results in a high volatility of M1 and M2. It is therefore often difficult to identify a trend from their development and to gain clues as to the degree of restriction of monetary policy. That is why our attention has recently been increasingly focused on the M3 money supply, which includes time deposits and is therefore less sensitive to interest-related shifts. As I have already explained, there is a stable correlation between the growth of M3 and the development of inflation around three years later. M3 thus fulfils the main requirement for a monetary policy indicator. Research shows that average growth of M3 of the order of 4% is consistent with price stability over the longer term. This growth is high compared to that of the central bank money supply of 1%. How does this value come about? We assume that potential growth in Switzerland is around 2% per year and that price stability has been achieved with an increase in the consumer price index of the order of 1% per year. This results in a longer-term growth of nominal gross domestic product of 3% per year. However, it must now be taken into account that the orbital velocity of M3 decreases slightly over time. The reason is that an important component of M3 - time deposits - increases much more than nominal gross domestic product over time. This is because the time deposits do not serve as a transaction medium, but as an investment. M3 also has a certain sensitivity to interest rates. Even with this aggregate, the inflation development cannot be mechanically extrapolated. In 1982 and 1993/94, for example, the growth of M3 temporarily accelerated significantly without triggering an increase in inflation three years later. With a higher growth of M3, therefore, an inflation potential is not necessarily built. The reason lies in the aforementioned cyclical movement of interest rates. In 1982 and 1993/94, domestic interest rates fell in the wake of the economic downturn. As a result, the demand for money increased significantly, and the growth of M3 accelerated. There was no risk of inflation. The acceleration of M3 growth was merely a side effect of the decline in interest rates. These fluctuations triggered by interest rate movements may make it difficult for monetary policy to communicate. There is also another problem. The money supply M3 reacts mainly to long-term interest rates. However, these depend not only on the development of domestic money market rates, but also on other influencing factors such as interest rate movements abroad and inflation expectations. If long-term interest rates rise abroad, M3 growth may weaken. This may unnecessarily tighten the degree of restriction of monetary policy. If, on the other hand, the rise in long-term interest rates reflects increasing inflation expectations, then the associated tightening of monetary policy may even be desirable. This brings me to the last point of our press conference, namely the importance of further monetary policy indicators. 3. The role of other indicators The money supply M3 - as well as the other meaningful monetary aggregates - are indicators that provide information about the development of inflation in the longer term. On the other hand, they are not suitable for forecasting price developments over the short term of up to three years. However, a central bank must also be able to get an idea of this period, i.e. the intermediate stages of the monetary policy transmission mechanism. For this reason, it must use further indicators to assess monetary policy. Economic dynamism has a decisive influence on inflation. A fairly reliable indicator of short-term price developments in many countries is the output gap. This measures the positive or negative deviation between the actual production and the long-term growth path and thus allows conclusions to be drawn about the available capacity margin. If actual production rapidly approaches the long-term growth path or even threatens to grow beyond it, this heralds price-driving shortages. The central bank will then have to consider tightening monetary policy. Conversely, a large output gap points to existing overcapacity, which makes the risk of an increase in inflation appear low in the foreseeable future. In practice, however, measuring the output gap is a difficult undertaking. The result depends crucially on which trend growth is assumed. For example, Switzerland now has a high output gap of more than 4%, assuming that the long-term potential growth in the nineties remained unchanged at just under 2%. However, it is quite possible that the long period of stagnation together with the rapid structural change temporarily lowered trend growth. The available production reserves would then be smaller than the output gap suggests. A number of other indicators must therefore be used to complement the output gap. These include, for example, the supply and demand conditions on the labour market, which give an indication of the future development of wage costs. Here, too, however, we are faced with the problem that the level of unemployment alone does not say everything. In particular, we must try to assess which part of unemployment has structural causes and is therefore independent of the economic situation. In an open economy like Switzerland, exchange rate fluctuations also have a strong influence on inflation. In addition to the output gap and the analysis of the labour market, the development of the real exchange rate is therefore also an important indicator of inflation in the short term. A weakening of the real exchange rate entails the risk of an imported increase in inflation, a sharp increase can lead to deflationary tendencies. How quickly exchange-rate-related price increases are reflected in the price level depends on how demand conditions develop. Given the still sluggish domestic demand, it was not surprising that prices for imported goods barely rose last year, even though the real Swiss franc had fallen significantly by the beginning of 1997. Finally, certain conclusions about the development of inflation can also be drawn from the course of long-term interest rates. An increase may indicate that inflation expectations in the economy are increasing and therefore caution is advised. However, long-term interest rates can also rise for other reasons, such as higher interest rates abroad. Moreover, it can never be ruled out that the real return on capital has changed because of the relative scarcity on the capital markets or the development of productivity. As you can see, before conclusions for monetary policy can be drawn from the course of the short-term indicators, an in-depth analysis is required. The indicators must not be considered in isolation, but must be seen in the overall context. Above all, however, they are not a substitute, but an important addition to the monetary aggregates. This is due to the long delay with which monetary policy affects price developments. If, for example, the rapidly closing output gap signals a risk of inflation, then it is usually too late to avoid the price increase. In the best case, the central bank can mitigate it. It therefore cannot do without indicators which, like monetary aggregates, provide information on longer-term price developments. 4. Summary and outlook That brings me to the end. I began my remarks by saying that we do not intend to tighten monetary policy this year. I went on to say that we consider inflation risks to be low at the moment. This statement can be justified both on the basis of the development of monetary aggregates and short-term indicators. In other words, we are currently in the fortunate position that all the major indicators point in the same direction. This is not always the case be. Central banks usually walk delicate tightropes. Under certain circumstances, they may even be forced to deviate from the stability-oriented course. Disruptions in the financial markets can be one reason for this. Strong fluctuations in the Swiss franc exchange rate - triggered by the transition to the third stage of monetary union - are a scenario that we have to reckon with today. At our press conference, we therefore made it clear that we will use our monetary policy resources to counter undesirable exchange rate developments for the economy as a whole. Overall, our monetary policy intentions for the new year have been well received. We are happy to take note of this. For our monetary policy, we need the support of the economy and society. However, we do not only need it today, when we can promise a continued generous monetary policy and low interest rates. We will also need it at a time when monetary policy reins need to be tightened in order to safeguard price stability in the longer term. In other words, it is the social consensus on price stability that forms the basis for a stability-oriented monetary policy. This consensus must include three elements. It must include, firstly, recognising the economic benefits of price stability and not simply displacing the significant costs of inflation because of temporary benefits. The consensus must then include the limits of the possibilities of monetary policy. Monetary policy is indeed an effective economic policy instrument. However, its use is anything but easy in view of the long delays in its effects to which it is exposed. It can only influence price developments in terms of length. By ensuring a stable monetary environment, monetary policy prepares the ground for a dynamic development of the economy. Finally, the consensus must include a healthy distrust of simple recipes, such as the often overly superficial demand for a flexible, short-term oriented monetary policy. In Switzerland, we have been able to count on such a consensus until now. This was the precondition for a high degree of price stability to be achieved after the collapse of the Bretton Woods fixed price system a quarter of a century ago, despite some setbacks. I hope that such a social consensus will also be further consolidated in Europe and that the future European Central Bank will thus receive the necessary support among the population to conduct a stability-oriented monetary policy. If this is the case, there is a good chance that the gains hoped for by the European Monetary Union will materialise for the European Community.

Januar 1998 Einleitung Fast auf den Tag genau vor einem Vierteljahrhundert, am 23. In der Schweiz kommt dabei unseren Pressegesprchen, die zweimal jhrlich stattfinden, eine bedeutende Rolle zu. Wir gaben drittens bekannt, dass wir weiterhin auch andere Indikatoren zur Beurteilung der Geldpolitik heranziehen wollen. Lassen sie mich auf diese drei Punkte nher eingehen. 1. Zur Geldpolitik im Jahre 1998 Welche berlegungen stehen hinter dem Entscheid, die Geldpolitik im Jahre 1998 nicht zu straffen?
