Die Normalisierung des Geldmengenwachstums liess zunchst Spielraum, um auf den Wechselkurs Rcksicht zu nehmen, ohne die Preisstabilitt mittelfristig zu gefhrden. Vor allem aber bedeutete sie, dass keine Notwendigkeit bestand, die geldpolitischen Zgel im Jahre 1998 zu straffen. Entwickelte sich nmlich das reale Wirtschaftswachstum wie erwartet, so wrde das Geldmengenwachstum weiterhin in einem Bereich bleiben, der mit einem ausgeglichenen Wirtschaftswachstum und Preisstabilitt vereinbar wre. Wie Sie sehen, beruht die Festlegung der Geldpolitik in hohem Masse auf Prognosen. Dies hat wiederum zur Folge, dass vom Kurs abgewichen werden muss, falls sich die Dinge deutlich anders entwickeln als erwartet. In jngster Zeit veranlasste die Krise in Sdostasien den Internationalen Whrungsfonds und die OECD, ihre Wachstumsprognosen fr die Industrielnder leicht nach unten zu revidieren. Die Folgen solcher Krisen sind usserst schwierig abzuschtzen. Sicher mssen wir auf der Hut sein. Sollte das Realwachstum in diesem Jahr wesentlich schwcher ausfallen, drfte auch das Geldmengenwachstum der Tendenz nach deutlich sinken. Um ein solches unerwnschtes Absinken zu verhindern, wre ein weiterer Zinsrckgang erforderlich. Wrde dagegen der Konjunkturaufschwung ber Erwarten stark ausfallen, mssten wir grundstzlich einen Anstieg der Zinsstze zulassen. Dies allerdings nicht, bevor auch andere Indikatoren insbesondere die Entwicklung der Wechselkurse, der Auslandkonjunktur, der langfristigen Zinsstze und der Inflationserwartungen - einer erneuten Beurteilung unterzogen wrden Ich werde auf diesen Punkt nochmals zurckkommen. 2. Die Geldmenge M3 als geldpolitischer Indikator Damit komme ich zum zweiten Punkt unseres Pressegesprchs - die vermehrte Bercksichtigung des breiteren Geldaggregates M3. Geldpolitische Impulse wirken bekanntlich zuerst auf die gesamtwirtschaftliche Produktion und mit einer erheblichen Verzgerung schliesslich auf das Preisniveau. Eine Notenbank braucht deshalb vorlaufende Indikatoren, die ber die knftige Entwicklung der Produktion und der Preise, kurz des nominellen Bruttoinlandproduktes, Auskunft geben. Nur wenn sie ber solche Indikatoren verfgt, ist sie in der Lage, die Geldpolitik sach- und zeitgerecht zu fhren. Zu den wichtigsten vorlaufenden Indikatoren gehren die Geldaggregate. Ihnen kommt deshalb in allen geldpolitischen Strategien eine bedeutende Rolle zu. Dies muss nicht immer bedeuten, dass die Notenbank fr die Geldaggregate auch Ziele verffentlicht. In den letzten Jahren kamen einige Zentralbanken davon ab, Geldmengenziele bekanntzugeben. Der Grund lag in der Instabilitt der Geldnachfrage - meist verursacht durch Finanzinnovationen. Diese Notenbanken - ein prominentes Beispiel ist die Bank of England - ziehen statt dessen eine Vielzahl von Indikatoren heran, um die knftige Entwicklung von Produktion und Preisen zu prognostizieren. Weichen die Prognosen von der angestrebten Entwicklung ab, ergreift die Notenbank entsprechende Massnahmen. Die Geldaggregate stehen zwar bei der Kommunikation der Geldpolitik nicht mehr im Vordergrund. Sie nehmen aber unter den verschiedenen geldpolitischen Indikatoren weiterhin einen wichtigen Platz ein. In der Schweiz diente wie gesagt seit 1980 die Notenbankgeldmenge als Hauptindikator. Es handelt sich dabei um ein sehr enges Aggregat, das der Summe aus dem Notenumlauf und den Giroguthaben der Banken bei der Nationalbank entspricht. Bis 1989 legten wir fr dieses Aggregat Jahreswachstumsziele fest. 1990 gingen wir zu einem mittelfristigen Wachstumspfad ber. Die Notenbankgeldmenge hat gegenber anderen Geldaggregaten Vorzge. Sie ist grundstzlich ein zuverlssiger geldpolitischer Indikator. Von Vorteil sind auch ihre gute Steuerbarkeit, die tgliche Verfgbarkeit der Daten und nicht zuletzt die Tatsache, dass sie im Vergleich zu den breiteren Geldaggregaten kurzfristig weit geringeren Schwankungen unterworfen ist. Sie lsst sich dadurch vergleichsweise leicht interpretieren. Wie erwhnt, traten aber bei der Notenbankgeldmenge in den Jahren 1996 und 1997 Probleme auf, die sich Anfang 1997 durch die massive Zunahme der Nachfrage nach Tausendernoten zuspitzten. Zwar gelang es uns, diese Verzerrungen einigermassen herauszufiltern und dadurch weiterhin ntzliche Informationen aus der Notenbankgeldmenge zu ziehen. Die Verzerrungen erschwerten aber die Kommunikation der Geldpolitik erheblich. Wir beschlossen deshalb, neben der Notenbankgeldmenge zumindest vorbergehend noch vermehrt andere Indikatoren heranzuziehen. Wir befinden uns in der Schweiz nach wie vor in der komfortablen Lage, dass die breiteren Geldaggregate lngerfristig immer noch eine ziemlich stabile Beziehung zum Preisniveau aufweisen. konometrische Modelle der schweizerischen Preisentwicklung erklren denn auch den langfristigen Inflationstrend vor allem mit dem Wachstum der Geldaggregate. Dennoch eignen sich nicht alle Geldaggregate gleich gut als geldpolitische Indikatoren. Der Hauptgrund liegt - wie ich bereits angetnt habe - in ihrer unterschiedlichen Zinsvolatilitt. Was bedeutet dies? Die Zinsstze weisen ein ausgeprgtes zyklisches Muster auf. In Zeiten der Hochkonjunktur wird das Geldkleid, das die Zentralbank im Hinblick auf die mittelfristige Preisstabilitt geschneidert hat, zunehmend enger. Die Liquiditt wird knapper, und die Zinsen steigen. Flacht umgekehrt die Konjunktur ab, sinkt auch die Geldnachfrage mit der rcklufigen wirtschaftlichen Aktivitt. Dies ussert sich in sinkenden Zinsstzen. Solche prozyklischen Zinsbewegungen sind durchaus erwnscht. Indem die Geldpolitik solche Zinsbewegungen auslst, wirkt sie auch als Konjunkturstabilisator. Die Geldnachfrage wird aber bekanntlich nicht nur durch das Einkommen, sondern auch durch die Zinsentwicklung beeinflusst - und zwar im gegenlufigen Sinn. Steigen die Zinsen zum Beispiel im Konjunkturverlauf, so sinkt die Geldnachfrage, da das Halten von unverzinsten oder tiefverzinsten Zahlungsmitteln Kosten in Form entgangener Zinsen verursacht. Die Wirtschaftssubjekte versuchen, diese Opportunittskosten mglichst gering zu halten, indem sie die Geldhaltung zulasten hher verzinslicher Anlagen vermindern. Umgekehrt nimmt die Geldnachfrage wieder zu, sobald die Zinsstze sinken und die Opportunittskosten nicht mehr so stark ins Gewicht fallen. Bei den Geldaggregaten M1 und M2, welche mit den Sicht- und Spareinlagen unverzinsliche oder eher tief verzinste Geldformen umfassen, sind die Opportunittskosten besonders stark sprbar. Zinserhhungen lsen deshalb regelmssig Umschichtungen in hher verzinsliche Anlagen wie Termineinlagen aus, die in den beiden Aggregaten nicht enthalten sind. Dies fhrt zu einer hohen Volatilitt von M1 und M2. Es ist daher oft schwierig, aus deren Entwicklung einen Trend herauszulesen und Anhaltspunkte fr den Restriktionsgrad der Geldpolitik zu gewinnen. Deshalb hat sich unsere Aufmerksamkeit in der letzten Zeit vermehrt auf die Geldmenge M3 gerichtet, welche die Termineinlagen mitumfasst und damit gegenber zinsbedingten Umschichtungen weniger empfindlich ist. Wie ich bereits dargelegt habe, besteht zwischen dem Wachstum von M3 und der Inflationsentwicklung rund drei Jahre spter ein stabiler Zusammenhang. Damit erfllt M3 die Hauptanforderung an einen geldpolitischen Indikator. Untersuchungen zeigen, dass ein durchschnittliches Wachstum von M3 in der Grssenordnung von 4% lngerfristig mit Preisstabilitt in Einklang steht. Dieses Wachstum ist im Vergleich zu jenem der Notenbankgeldmenge von 1% hoch. Wie kommt dieser Wert zustande? Wir gehen davon aus, dass das Potentialwachstum in der Schweiz etwa 2% pro Jahr betrgt und Preisstabilitt mit einem Anstieg des Konsumentenpreisindexes in der Grssenordnung von 1% pro Jahr erreicht ist. Dies ergibt ein lngerfristiges Wachstum des nominellen Bruttoinlandproduktes von 3% pro Jahr. Es gilt nun aber zu bercksichtigen, dass die Umlaufgeschwindigkeit von M3 im Zeitverlauf leicht sinkt. Der Grund liegt darin, dass eine wichtige Komponente von M3 - die Termineinlagen - ber die Zeit hinweg wesentlich strker steigt als das nominale Bruttoinlandprodukt. Dies deshalb, weil die Termineinlagen nicht als Transaktionsmittel, sondern als Vermgensanlage dienen. Auch M3 weist eine gewisse Zinsempfindlichkeit auf. Auch bei diesem Aggregat kann deshalb die Inflationsentwicklung nicht mechanisch extrapoliert werden. In den Jahren 1982 und 1993/94 beschleunigte sich beispielsweise das Wachstum von M3 vorbergehend deutlich, ohne dass dies drei Jahre spter einen Inflationsanstieg ausgelst htte. Mit einem hheren Wachstum von M3 wird somit nicht unbedingt ein Inflationspotential aufgebaut. Der Grund liegt in der erwhnten zyklischen Bewegung der Zinsstze. In der Jahren 1982 und 1993/94 gingen die inlndischen Zinsstze im Gefolge des Konjunktureinbruchs zurck. Deshalb stieg die Geldnachfrage markant, und das Wachstum von M3 beschleunigte sich. Eine Inflationsgefahr war damit nicht verbunden. Die Wachstumsbeschleunigung von M3 war lediglich eine Begleiterscheinung des Zinsrckgangs. Diese durch die Zinsbewegungen ausgelsten Schwankungen knnen unter Umstnden die Kommunikation der Geldpolitik erschweren. Dazu kommt ein weiteres Problem. Die Geldmenge M3 reagiert vor allem auf die langfristigen Zinsstze. Diese hngen aber nicht nur von der Entwicklung der inlndischen Geldmarktstze, sondern auch von anderen Einflussfaktoren wie den Zinsbewegungen im Ausland und den Inflationserwartungen ab. Steigen die langfristigen Zinsstze im Ausland, so kann dies eine Wachstumsabschwchung von M3 zur Folge haben. Damit wird der Restriktionsgrad der Geldpolitik unter Umstnden unntig verschrft. Widerspiegelt der Anstieg der langfristigen Zinsstze dagegen zunehmende Inflationserwartungen, dann kann die damit verbundene Verschrfung der Geldpolitik sogar erwnscht sein. Damit komme ich zum letzten Punkt unseres Pressegesprchs, nmlich die Bedeutung weiterer geldpolitischer Indikatoren. 3. Die Rolle weiterer Indikatoren Die Geldmenge M3 - wie auch die anderen aussagekrftigen Geldaggregate - sind Indikatoren, die Aufschlsse ber die Inflationsentwicklung in der lngeren Frist geben. Fr Prognosen der Preisentwicklung ber die kurze Frist bis zu drei Jahren sind sie dagegen nicht geeignet. Eine Notenbank muss sich aber auch ber diesen Zeitraum, d.h. die Zwischenstadien des geldpolitischen Transmissionsmechanismus, ein Bild machen knnen. Aus diesem Grund muss sie weitere Indikatoren zur Beurteilung der Geldpolitik heranziehen. Die wirtschaftliche Dynamik bt einen entscheidenden Einfluss auf die Inflation aus. Ein recht zuverlssiger Indikator fr die kurzfristige Preisentwicklung ist in vielen Lndern die Produktionslcke. Diese misst die positive oder negative Abweichung zwischen der tatschlichen Produktion und dem langfristigen Wachstumspfad und lsst damit Rckschlsse ber den vorhandenen Kapazittsspielraum zu. Nhert sich die tatschliche Produktion rasch dem langfristigen Wachstumspfad oder droht sie gar darber hinaus zu wachsen, so kndigt dies preistreibende Verknappungen an. Die Notenbank wird dann eine Straffung der Geldpolitik ins Auge fassen mssen. Umgekehrt deutet eine grosse Produktionslcke auf bestehende berkapazitten hin, die in absehbarer Zeit das Risiko eines Teuerungsanstieges als gering erscheinen lassen. In der Praxis ist die Messung der Produktionslcke allerdings ein schwieriges Unterfangen. Das Ergebnis hngt entscheidend davon ab, von welchem Trendwachstum man ausgeht. So weist die Schweiz beispielsweise heute eine hohe Produktionslcke von mehr als 4% auf, wenn wir davon ausgehen, dass das langfristige Potentialwachstum in den neunziger Jahren unverndert bei knapp 2% blieb. Es ist aber durchaus mglich, dass die lange Stagnationsphase zusammen mit dem raschen Strukturwandel vorbergehend das Trendwachstum senkte. Die verfgbaren Produktionsreserven wren dann kleiner, als die Produktionslcke vermuten lsst. Als Ergnzung zur Produktionslcke mssen daher eine Reihe weiterer Indikatoren herangezogen werden. Dazu gehren beispielsweise die Angebots- und Nachfrageverhltnisse am Arbeitsmarkt, die einen Hinweis auf die knftige Entwicklung der Lohnkosten geben. Auch hier stehen wir allerdings vor dem Problem, dass die Hhe der Arbeitslosigkeit allein noch nicht alles besagt. Wir mssen insbesondere abzuschtzen versuchen, welcher Teil der Arbeitslosigkeit strukturelle Ursachen hat und damit von der Konjunkturlage unabhngig ist. In einer offenen Volkswirtschaft wie der Schweiz ben auch Wechselkursausschlge einen starken Einfluss auf die Inflationsentwicklung aus. Neben der Produktionslcke und der Analyse des Arbeitsmarktes ist daher auch die Entwicklung des realen Wechselkurses ein wichtiger Indikator fr die Inflation in der kurzen Frist. Eine Abschwchung des realen Wechselkurses bringt die Gefahr eines importierten Inflationsanstieges, ein starker Anstieg kann deflationre Tendenzen zur Folge haben. Wie rasch sich wechselkursbedingte Preissteigerungen auf das Preisniveau niederschlagen, hngt wiederum davon ab, wie sich die Nachfrageverhltnisse entwickeln. So war es angesichts der immer noch flauen Binnennachfrage nicht berraschend, dass die Preise fr importierte Gter im letzten Jahr kaum anzogen, obschon der reale Frankenkurs bis Anfang 1997 deutlich gesunken war. Gewisse Rckschlsse auf die Inflationsentwicklung lassen sich schliesslich auch aus dem Verlauf der langfristigen Zinsstze ziehen. Ein Anstieg kann darauf hinweisen, dass die Inflationserwartungen in der Wirtschaft zunehmen und deshalb Vorsicht geboten ist. Die langfristigen Zinsstze knnen aber auch aus anderen Grnden steigen, zum Beispiel infolge hherer Zinsstze im Ausland. Es ist ausserdem nie auszuschliessen, dass sich wegen der relativen Knappheit auf den Kapitalmrkten oder der Produktivittsentwicklung die reale Rendite des Kapitals verndert hat. Sie sehen: Bevor aus dem Verlauf der kurzfristigen Indikatoren Folgerungen fr die Geldpolitik gezogen werden knnen, bedarf es einer eingehenden Analyse. Die Indikatoren drfen nicht isoliert betrachtet, sondern mssen im Gesamtzusammenhang gesehen werden. Vor allem aber sind sie kein Ersatz, sondern eine wichtige Ergnzung zu den Geldaggregaten. Dies aufgrund der langen Verzgerung, mit der sich die Geldpolitik auf die Preisentwicklung auswirkt. Signalisiert beispielsweise die sich rasch schliessende Produktionslcke eine Inflationsgefahr, dann ist es zumeist zu spt, um den Preisanstieg zu vermeiden. Die Notenbank kann ihn im besten Fall noch mildern. Sie kommt daher nicht ohne Indikatoren aus, die wie die Geldaggregate ber die lngerfristige Preisentwicklung Aufschluss geben. 4. Zusammenfassung und Ausblick Damit komme ich zum Schluss. Ich habe meine Ausfhrungen mit der Aussage eingeleitet, dass wir in diesem Jahr keine Straffung der Geldpolitik beabsichtigen. Ich sagte weiter, dass wir die Inflationsrisiken derzeit als gering erachten. Diese Aussage lsst sich sowohl aufgrund der Entwicklung der Geldaggregate als auch der kurzfristigen Indikatoren begrnden. Wir befinden uns mit anderen Worten momentan in der glcklichen Lage, dass alle wichtigen Indikatoren in die gleiche Richtung weisen. Dies wird nicht immer so sein. Die Notenbanken befinden sich in der Regel auf heiklen Gratwanderungen. Unter Umstnden sind sie sogar gezwungen, vom stabilittsgerechten Kurs abzuweichen. Strungen an den Finanzmrkten knnen dafr ein Grund sein. Starke Schwankungen des Frankenkurses - ausgelst durch den bergang in die dritte Stufe der Whrungsunion - sind ein Szenario, mit dem wir heute konkret rechnen mssen. Wir haben deshalb an unserem Pressegesprch klar darauf hingewiesen, dass wir einer gesamtwirtschaftlich unerwnschten Wechselkursentwicklung mit unseren geldpolitischen Mitteln entgegentreten werden. Unsere geldpolitischen Absichten fr das neue Jahr wurden alles in allem gut aufgenommen. Wir nehmen das gerne zur Kenntnis. Fr unsere Geldpolitik brauchen wir den Rckhalt von Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft. Wir brauchen ihn aber nicht nur heute, wo wir eine weiterhin grosszgige Geldpolitik und tiefe Zinsstze in Aussicht stellen knnen. Wir werden ihn auch in Zeiten bentigen, in denen die geldpolitischen Zgel gestrafft werden mssen, um die Preisstabilitt lngerfristig zu sichern. Es ist mit anderen Worten der gesellschaftliche Konsens bezglich der Preisstabilitt, der die Grundlage fr eine stabilittsorientierte Geldpolitik bildet. Dieser Konsens muss drei Elemente umfassen. Er muss erstens beinhalten, dass der volkswirtschaftliche Nutzen der Preisstabilitt erkannt und die erheblichen Kosten der Inflation vorbergehender Vorteile wegen nicht einfach verdrngt werden. Der Konsens muss sodann die Grenzen der Mglichkeiten der Geldpolitik einschliessen. Die Geldpolitik ist zwar ein wirkungsvolles wirtschaftspolitisches Instrument. Ihr Einsatz ist aber angesichts der langen Wirkungsverzgerungen, denen sie ausgesetzt ist, alles andere als einfach. Sie kann auf die Lnge nur die Preisentwicklung beeinflussen. Durch die Gewhrleistung stabiler monetrer Rahmenbedingungen bereitet die Geldpolitik den Boden fr eine dynamische Entfaltung der Wirtschaft. Der Konsens muss schliesslich ein gesundes Misstrauen gegenber einfachen Rezepten, wie der oft allzu vordergrndigen Forderung nach einer flexiblen, kurzfristig orientierten Geldpolitik beinhalten. In der Schweiz konnten wir bis anhin auf einen solchen Konsens zhlen. Dies war die Voraussetzung, dass nach dem Zusammenbruch des Fixkurssystems von Bretton Woods vor einem Vierteljahrhundert trotz mancher Rckschlge ein hoher Grad an Preisstabili tt erreichte wurde. Ich hoffe, dass sich ein solcher gesellschaftlicher Konsens auch in Europa weiter festigen wird und die knftige Europische Zentralbank damit den ntigen Rckhalt in der Bevlkerung erhlt, um eine stabilittsorientierte Geldpolitik zu fhren. Ist dies der Fall, so stehen die Chancen gut, dass sich die von der Europischen Whrungsunion erhofften Gewinne fr die europische Gemeinschaft einstellen werden.

Title: Aspects of competitiveness
text: Aspects of competitiveness Dr. Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank General Assembly of the Swiss Association of International Trading Companies Zurich, 19 January 1998 1 1. Introduction Our country can look back on a prolonged period of modest economic development. As expected, growth remained weak at half a percentage point in the past year. In the new year, we can finally expect a somewhat more pronounced development again. For the past seven years, our economy has had one of the weakest performances in the developed world, with a growth rate of less than one percent; it recorded growth only half as high as the OECD average. Against the background of this unsatisfactory development, the question arises as to the economic future of our country. In view of the globalization of markets and the possible shift in the focus of the global economy towards new growth regions, the key concept of the competitiveness of our economy has once again become the focus of the economic policy discussion. One of the reasons for the strong public interest in competitiveness and competitiveness certainly lies in the close international interdependence of our national economy: foreign trade accounts for around one third of Switzerland's gross domestic product. Another reason is Switzerland's increasingly poor performance in international competitive studies in recent years. The internationalization of large corporations with their cross-border and cross-market production structures and the greatly increased mobility of capital are leading to an intensification of global competition for investors and jobs. Like other industrialised nations, Switzerland is therefore under increasing pressure to optimise its economic framework conditions in order to ensure international competitiveness. What about the international competitiveness of our country? At what level are we operating in the global environment? Is our competitiveness seriously endangered or can we continue with peace of mind as 2 hitherto? How will Switzerland position itself in the future? I would like to explore these questions in the second part of my presentation. First, however, I would like to take a closer look at the concept of competitiveness. As diverse as the interpretations of the term are, the answers to the questions about the situation of our country are just as different. 2. What is competitiveness? As buzzwords, competitiveness or competitiveness are so much on everyone's lips that one might think that everyone knows exactly what he has to understand by it. This shows that the strong dissemination of a term does not guarantee conceptual clarity and conciseness. As early as 1982, a study by eth Zurich's Economic Research Centre stated that there was hardly an economic term that was used as much, but at the same time was as questionable and problematic in its concrete application as the concept of competitiveness. This has not changed much to this day. This situation is reflected in the different ideas about the competitiveness of the Swiss economy. Differences arise above all from the fact that in the economic policy debate competitiveness at different levels - at the company, the industry and the economic level - is considered and also often a different time horizon is taken as a basis. While in the short term the competitiveness of the individual companies is more in the foreground, the economic policy interest in the longer term concentrates on the entire economy, where concepts such as productivity and location attractiveness are at the center. I would like to discuss some of these concepts below. Let me anticipate the following: achieving competitiveness is 3 not an end in itself. Ultimately, it is about the ability of an economy to increase the prosperity of its population. An economy is not a company It is problematic to equate the competitiveness of a nation with that of a company. From this point of view, the focus is on the "ability to sell", the exportability of a country: From this point of view, a country is competitive if it succeeds in selling products and services on the global markets under competitive conditions. However, an important aspect is omitted, namely the "ability to earn", the ability to earn an income from export activity. This is a fundamental difference between an economy and a company. If the real income and the achievable standard of living of an economy are disregarded, then insufficient productivity can be compensated for with a low wage level or with a corresponding adjustment of the exchange rate and competitiveness can be restored at any time. For an economy, in contrast to companies or industries, the question never arises as to whether it is competitive or not, but actually only under what conditions, i.e. at what income level or at what standard of living. When a company is no longer competitive, it goes bankrupt and ceases to exist. A country cannot go bankrupt, nor does it cease to exist for economic reasons. On the one hand, the standard of living - as we see in a frightening way in Third World countries - can fall to almost arbitrarily low levels, on the other hand, the international community usually helps a country with loans. An economy is not a company: another misunderstanding in assessing a country's competitiveness is that often - 4 analogous to the income statement of a company - the current account is used as a benchmark for the assessment of competitiveness. It is believed that a competitive country is characterized by the fact that it can sell a lot, i.e. exports more than it imports, and therefore has a current account surplus. However, a country's current account is a poor indicator of economic competitiveness. The problem with such an approach is that it ignores capital movements, which are the main counterparts to transactions in goods and services. A current account surplus is offset by net capital exports and a current account deficit by net capital imports. Such capital movements are primarily determined by the savings and investment ratio in a country and by return considerations. In the case of Switzerland, therefore, the massive current account surplus does not reflect a high level of competitiveness, but only the fact that more is being saved than invested in our country. I will come back to this issue when we talk about direct investment. How is competitiveness measured? The competitiveness of an economy is determined less by the "ability to sell", the ability to sell goods and services in different markets, but rather by the level of macroeconomic productivity. A measure of productivity, labour productivity, corresponds to the value added per hour worked and is influenced by the amount of capital employed, the state of the art and the know-how of the workforce. Put simply, an economy is competitive if it has the ability to sell goods and services on domestic and foreign markets without having to accept losses in real wage levels. The gross national product per capita achieved in real terms is therefore a greatly simplified measure of a nation's competitiveness. 5 This equation of productivity and efficiency with competitiveness may elegantly avoid further substantive issues. However, it falls short if one seeks an economic policy orientation with the study of competitiveness or if one wants to compare the performance of different economies more closely with each other. Also, the gross national product per capita, since it only provides information about the status quo, does not provide a basis for forecasts about the development of competitiveness in the future. I would therefore like to discuss further determinants of competitiveness in the following. Competitiveness in an international comparison If one wants to compare the economic performance of individual countries with each other and also to make statements about the future performance of a country, one must examine the individual determinants of the performance of an economy in more detail. Productivity and thus the growth and prosperity of a country depend on a wealth of variables. The growth process is extremely complex and represents an interplay of various economic, institutional, political and legal factors. I would like to mention here only the main determinants of economic growth: the investment and savings rates, the level of education of the population, the role and position of the state, the infrastructure, the market structure and the openness of the economy, and the quality of economic policy. Later we will see what other factors are also relevant for our country. By quantifying these most important growth factors and including other influencing factors, important statements can be made about the relative competitiveness of a country and also its future opportunities can be predicted. This method, also called benchmarking method, 6 is now used by various international and private institutions, the results of which are regularly published. These studies, for all their shortcomings in the selection criteria of the individual determinants and their measurability, are an important complement to the assessment of a country's competitiveness. Important in the benchmarking method is not only the absolute placement of the individual economies. Of particular interest is the clear identification of the key factors. This makes it possible to define more precisely the framework conditions that are indispensable for growth and thus for competitiveness. A single important aspect of measuring the competitiveness of an economy is, for example, determining the degree of economic freedom of the country concerned. Economic freedom increases the room for manoeuvre of economic agents. The studies published on this topic show that freedom and growth go hand in hand and that countries with high levels of economic freedom usually also achieve significantly higher economic growth. With the knowledge of the framework conditions of growth, statements can also be made regarding the potential of the competitiveness of the individual nations. With this broader view, this could be defined as the ability of a country to sustainably support value creation by creating suitable framework conditions and to achieve high economic growth in the medium term. The concept of location attractiveness The increasing mobility of the production factors capital and technological know-how give the concept of competitiveness a further dimension. This interpretation is dynamic in nature and assumes that: 7 that the individual economies compete with each other for these mobile factors of production. A country can only create sustainable prosperity in the competition between locations if it is able to attract capital and know-how in the form of qualified workers. Against this background, the role of governments in influencing the framework conditions of production sites is becoming increasingly important. Modern economies are increasingly feeling the pressure exerted from outside - namely from the world market - to optimize their economic framework conditions and to look for strategies for success in order to be able to assert themselves within the framework of a new global division of labour. The relative attractiveness of a location must be promoted if we want to prevent industries that have mobile factors from migrating. For this reason, the attractiveness of the location plays a special role in the competitiveness of a country. Location attractiveness is not to be equated with competitiveness, but represents an important determining factor of the same. While until a few years ago the framework conditions were not yet an issue, today they have become the focus of interest. It should be borne in mind that economic policy could never be conducted independently of constraints. The extraordinary growth phase of the post-war period may have led to illusions in this regard. Today's globalization and interdependence of the economy has led to the fact that economic policy is also increasingly exposed to competition. The attractiveness of today's location determines to a large extent the competitiveness of our country of tomorrow. In addition to the factors of competitiveness already mentioned, legal certainty with clearly defined property and liability rights and the tax system should be mentioned as determining factors of location quality. 8 The importance of the attractiveness of the location has also been recognized in our country, and questions about location competition are increasingly influencing the economic policy agenda and political debates. 3. Where does Switzerland stand? I would now like to turn to the question of Switzerland's international competitiveness. The main objective of participation in the international competition is to increase the prosperity of the population. For this reason, the simplest indicator of prosperity is the real value added per capita of the population. This can be seen as a rough overall indicator of the international competitiveness achieved, as it reflects not only the performance of a country's companies, but also, to a certain extent, the overall economic environment. If one takes the gross national product per capita adjusted according to purchasing power parities as an indicator of the competitiveness of our country, a pleasing picture emerges: In 1996, Switzerland was in third place in a global comparison with a gross national product per capita of US 26,000, behind Luxembourg and the USA, ahead of Hong Kong and Singapore. If another macroeconomic indicator, labour productivity, is taken into account, Switzerland ranks second in the world with a gross domestic product per person employed of US 77,000. However, we must not forget that, as already mentioned, this macroeconomic indicator is a result-oriented parameter that measures Switzerland's competitive position in the past. In this static view, we only look at the level achieved, not the growth of our economy. As we saw in the introduction, it is precisely this dynamic aspect that gives us cause for concern. That is why we have to add other greats to our super-member states. 9 That is why we have tabled a motion for a resolution calling on the Commission and the Member States to take the necessary steps to ensure that the European Union is fully involved in the implementation of the acquis communautaire. Switzerland in the mirror of international competitive studies We have seen that the benchmarking method can provide us with certain insights. It is worth mentioning the regular reports of the World Economic Forum and the Lausanne Management Institute IMD, which are certainly known to you. In the most recent study by the World Economic Forum in 1997, Switzerland was able to maintain its sixth place from last year, and in that of the IMD it even moved up from 9th to 7th place. As a result, the decline in Switzerland's competitiveness seems to have come to a standstill in an international comparison over the last few years. Until a few years ago, our country regularly occupied medal ranks in the competition for international competitiveness. In both studies, Switzerland achieves top international rankings in the areas of the cost of capital, the performance of the financial centre, social, political and legislative stability, the level and distribution of tax burdens, the intensity of research and development, the education system and, last but not least, the efficiency of management. Switzerland is also in the top ranks in terms of low unemployment, the ability and motivation of the workforce and the number of hours worked per week. According to these studies, the factors that affect Swiss competitiveness are not unknown to us. These include the foreclosure of the internal market - both for goods and labour - and a lack of flexibility and adaptability. As I have also mentioned, another criterion for measuring international competitiveness is the degree of economic freedom. According to the latest studies, here too, un- 10 This country is similar to that of the two reports already cited. In a Canadian study, the "Economic Freedom of the World Annual Report", Switzerland ranks sixth in Europe, ahead of the UK as the second best European country. With such a result, Switzerland's competitiveness is once again given a good, if not outstanding, certificate. According to this study, independent monetary policy, the guarantee of property rights, the free movement of finance and the absence of black markets contribute to economic freedom in Switzerland. Freedom is adversely affected by state interventions in the economy, such as excessive government spending, administered prices, subsidies and, associated with this, relatively high taxes. The low share of trade in total value added was also criticised. With the exception of a few deviations, the individual studies paint a uniformly positive picture of the competitiveness of the Swiss economy. The general improvement compared to previous years is an indication that Switzerland has reached the end of the tunnel and that structural adjustments to the globalised economy are yielding initial successes. Switzerland knows and knew how to assert itself in international competition and still has a robust competitive position and a healthy basis for future economic development. The relationship between weak growth and competitiveness In the introduction, I painted a rather gloomy picture of Swiss economic development in the nineties. If in recent years the impression has arisen that our country is losing more and more competitiveness, then this is less related to the level of what has been achieved so far than to this weak growth. 11 Can the weak growth in Switzerland now also lead to a low level of competitiveness? I believe that such a conclusion would be wrong. The weak economic growth of recent years is basically due to two causes: On the one hand, Swiss economic growth was at a very low level, because our country, like most other industrialized countries, was going through a recession. On the other hand, our country also had to undergo a profound structural change and the need to clean up contaminated sites. The combination of these effects had a strong dampening effect on the Swiss growth rate. Although the process of structural adjustment and adjustment had a negative impact on growth in the short term due to the associated costs, it also laid the foundation for future economic development and ultimately makes our country more competitive again. For this reason alone, low growth must not in principle be inferred from low competitiveness. But even after overcoming these structural and economic difficulties, Switzerland will still have a lower growth rate than other countries. The reason for this is that the individual economies have different levels of development. Today's emerging market economies are achieving high growth rates in part because they are catching up: "catching up is easier than running in front". Backward countries are growing faster than developed ones, among other things, because they can adopt existing technologies. However, as growth progresses, this advantage diminishes more and more, so that the growth dynamics will automatically slow down. With the transition from imitation to innovation competition, research and development costs and thus also unit labour costs are increasing. In the long term, convergence, i.e. a convergence of growth rates between Switzerland and the countries with high growth rates, is to be expected. 12 From the rapid catching-up process of various emerging economies in recent times, it is not possible to conclude in principle that the Swiss economy is weak in its competition. Our country has a comparatively dynamic development potential. The openness of the economy as an important determinant Of all the factors already mentioned for the competitiveness of an economy - investment, human capital, the political framework conditions, infrastructure, market structure and openness as well as the quality of economic policy - I would like to single out the element of openness of an economy in this particular context. A fundamental source of competitiveness lies in foreign trade itself. Only free trade makes it possible to actually exploit comparative advantages in production. International specialization allows a country to produce only those goods for which there is a comparative advantage, i.e. which are produced more efficiently domestically than elsewhere. International specialization and free trade also make it possible - through production for large international markets - to reduce average production costs through positive economies of scale. Lower production costs lead to lower final prices and thus increase competitiveness. International trade also promotes the dissemination of technical know-how and knowledge through the exchange of goods and services. Knowledge and innovation play an essential role in increasing the competitiveness of companies; international competition also exerts pressure on a country's companies to innovate. This increases technical progress and thus productivity, which is ultimately reflected in competitiveness. This fact is also shown by a recent study by the Bank of England. Between international openness - measured by the degree of free flow of 13 there is a clear empirical correlation between international goods, services, factors of production and know-how and economic growth. On average, open sectors have higher growth rates of factor productivity than less open ones. Increasing international openness increases productivity growth and thus competitiveness by primarily increasing the speed of productivity convergence with the respective technological world market leader. Even if this study is primarily based on Anglo-Saxon figures, the findings gained in it are likely to have international validity and also apply to our country. The role of direct investment In addition to strong foreign trade, Switzerland's international integration is also reflected in direct investment. Swiss direct investment abroad has increased sharply in recent years. In 1996, Swiss companies invested CHF 20 billion, almost twice as much as five years ago abroad. On the one hand, as I have already mentioned, the high capital exports are due to the fact that more is being saved than invested in Switzerland. On the other hand, foreign direct investment is also an expression of successful participation in the growth opportunities associated with globalisation. Participation in international know-how through the establishment of foreign bases is of eminent importance for the competitiveness and strength of Switzerland as a business location. Conversely, it would also be important for foreign companies to invest in Switzerland to the same extent. Due to the spill-over effects that have already been announced, the Swiss economy would be in a position to benefit from knowledge and know-how transfers by foreign companies. With an investment volume of 3.3 billion for 1996 and a low 14 However, foreign direct investment in Switzerland has been extremely modest in recent years. This fact points to one of the weak points of the company location. The reasons for this are manifold: certainly these include the smallness of our country, the relatively high cost and price level, the weak domestic economy, but also the high regulatory density and the European policy going it alone. It is true that Switzerland is experiencing a boost in liberalisation through membership of GATT and the WTO and, apart from the agricultural sector, is one of the more open economies. However, free trade is still hampered by countless non-tariff barriers, most of which are hidden forms of protectionism. In Switzerland, however, the greatest obstacles are less in the mobility of products than in the mobility of the factors of production, in particular the workforce. There is still a need for action in this area in our country. 4. Outlook Despite the historically long period of stagnation, Switzerland has managed to maintain its once excellent competitiveness at a fairly high level. This shows that our country has initiated the necessary reform measures for structural change and is on the right track. However, although we are still among the ten most competitive countries in the world, we must not let up in our efforts to promote competitiveness. You don't acquire them once and for all, but you have to constantly rework them. The prerequisite for this is the ability to adapt to new markets through structural change, to exploit comparative advantages and thus to find and defend a position in the international division of labour. 15 As a small open economy, Switzerland cannot escape globalisation and the compulsion to compete. However, it still has the necessary potential to remain one of the most competitive countries in the world in the next millennium.

Internationale Spitzenrnge erreicht die Schweiz in beiden Studien im Bereich der Kapitalkosten, bei der Leistungsfhigkeit des Finanzplatzes, bei der sozialen, politischen und gesetzgeberischen Stabilitt, bei der Hhe und der Verteilung der Steuerlasten, bei der Intensitt von Forschung und Entwicklung, beim Bildungssystem und nicht zuletzt bei der Effizienz des Managements. Die einzelnen Studien zeichnen, mit Ausnahme einiger Abweichungen, ein einheitlich positives Bild der Konkurrenzfhigkeit der schweizerischen Wirtschaft. Die allgemeine Verbesserung gegenber den Vorjahren ist ein Indiz dafr, dass die Schweiz am Ende des Tunnels angelangt ist und die Strukturanpassungen an die globalisierte Wirtschaft erste Erfolge zeitigen. Der Zusammenhang zwischen Wachstumsschwche und Konkurrenzfhigkeit In der Einleitung habe ich ein eher dsteres Bild der schweizerischen Wirtschaftsentwicklung in den neunziger Jahren gezeichnet. Wenn sich in den letzten Jahren der Eindruck ergeben hat, unser Land verliere mehr und mehr an Konkurrenzfhigkeit, dann hngt dies weniger mit dem Niveau des bisher Erreichten zusammen, als eben mit dieser Wachstumsschwche. 11 Lsst sich nun aus der schweizerischen Wachstumsschwche auch auf eine geringe Konkurrenzfhigkeit schliessen? Die Offenheit der Volkswirtschaft als wichtige Determinante Von all den schon erwhnten Bestimmungsfaktoren fr die Konkurrenzfhigkeit einer Volkswirtschaft - die Investitionsttigkeit, das Humankapital, die politischen Rahmenbedingungen, die Infrastruktur, die Marktstruktur und Offenheit sowie die Qualitt der Wirtschaftspolitik - mchte ich gerade in diesem Kreise das Element der Offenheit einer Volkswirtschaft herausgreifen. Zwischen internationaler Offenheit - gemessen am Grad des freien Flusses von 13 internationalen Gtern, Dienstleistungen, Produktionsfaktoren und Know-how und Wirtschaftswachstum besteht ein klarer empirischer Zusammenhang. Auch wenn diese Studie sich in erster Linie auf angelschsisches Zahlenmaterial sttzt, drften die darin gewonnenen Erkenntnisse international Gltigkeit besitzen und auch fr unser Land gelten. Die Rolle der Direktinvestitionen Ausdruck der internationalen Verflechtung der Schweiz sind neben dem starken Aussenhandel auch die Direktinvestitionen. Die schweizerischen Direktinvestitionen im Ausland haben in den letzten Jahren stark zugenommen. 1996 investierten schweizerische Unternehmen mit 20 Milliarden Franken fast doppelt so viel wie noch vor fnf Jahren im Ausland. Die hohen Kapitalexporte sind einerseits - wie ich schon erwhnt habe - darauf zurckzufhren, dass in der Schweiz mehr gespart als investiert wird. Andererseits sind die Direktinvestitionen im Ausland auch Ausdruck einer erfolgreichen Beteiligung an den mit der Globalisierung verbundenen Wachstumschancen. Die Schweiz erfhrt zwar durch die Mitgliedschaft im GATT und in der WTO einen Liberalisierungsschub und gehrt, abgesehen vom Agrarsektor, zu den offeneren Volkswirtschaften. In diesem Bereich herrscht in unserem Land nach wie vor Handlungsbedarf. 4. Ausblick Trotz der historisch langen Phase der Stagnation ist es der Schweiz gelungen, ihre einstmals ausgezeichnete Konkurrenzfhigkeit auf recht hohem Niveau aufrechtzuerhalten. Title: Basic aspects of monetary policy
text: Fundamental aspects of monetary policy Dr. Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Association of Basel Economists Basel, 22 January 1998 We know that the quality of economic policy depends on various factors. Probably the most important decisions are made in monetary policy, fiscal policy and competition policy. Of course, all measures taken within the framework of economic policy are closely interdependent: they jointly determine the overall economic framework conditions. In my remarks today, I will focus on monetary policy and mention the other central areas of economic policy at most in passing. Unfortunately, the SNB's monetary policy is too often judged by the public from a rather short-term perspective. The monetary policy discussion is shaped by the current economic and monetary situation; for example, the current strength of the Swiss franc and the still tentative economic upswing. Although these questions are very important, there is a risk that the dialogue on the fundamental direction of monetary policy will either be neglected or influenced too much by short-term aspects. Given the importance of monetary policy for the overall economic environment, I consider this to be problematic. I am therefore happy to take the opportunity to explain to an expert audience the principles that I believe should guide an optimal monetary policy in the long term. In my remarks, I will first discuss the orientation of monetary policy towards maintaining price stability and then outline the possibilities of monetary policy in stabilising the economy. I will then talk about the options that will exist for the National Bank after the formation of the European Monetary Union. Finally, I will talk about the operational implementation of monetary policy, i.e. the question of the optimal indicators and intermediate targets. 2 1. Price stability as an objective of monetary policy The SNB tends to focus its policy on maintaining price stability in the longer term, equating price stability with an inflation rate of the order of one percent. We are repeatedly criticised for this objective from various quarters. I would therefore like to state at the outset of my remarks that the objective of maintaining price stability is, of course, not our invention. Rather, it is about putting into practice the clear findings of the national economy of the last three decades. Today, the central banks of most of the leading industrial nations are pursuing the same goal. In the following, I will mention the most important reasons why a central bank should focus its policy on price stability in the aforementioned sense: Contrary to the prevailing opinion in the fifties and sixties, an expansionary monetary policy cannot permanently increase employment and national income. An expansionary monetary policy is likely to have a positive impact on output and employment in the short term. However, this is lost over time. What remains is a permanently higher inflation rate. Monetary policy is therefore an unsuitable means of solving the structural problems of an economy and permanently reducing unemployment. An increased inflation rate does not have a neutral effect on the economy in the longer term. Rather, it leads to massive losses in prosperity and can also have a negative impact on the growth of the national economy. There are several reasons for these negative effects of increased inflation, although quantifying the individual costs is not always easy: Inflation significantly distorts the tax system. Tax rates are either not adjusted at all or only with a delay to inflation. As a result, pro- 3 Aggressive and percentage taxes, such as income tax, are strongly measured in real terms by increased inflation, while nominally fixed taxes, such as fuel levies, are becoming smaller in real terms. It is important to note that inflation also places an additional tax burden on companies for two reasons. On the one hand, the nominally increased corporate profits as a result of inflation are taxed higher in real terms as a result of the progression. On the other hand, inflation leads to nominal appreciation gains on assets, although the real value of these assets remains unchanged. This will further increase the real tax burden on companies. These distortions also cause the real net return  i.e. the return after deduction of taxes  on savings and investments to shrink with higher inflation. On the one hand, this reduces the total savings and investment volume of an economy. On the other hand, investments are increasingly being diverted from the production sector to the residential construction sector, as these investments are not additionally taxed by increased inflation. Both mechanisms reduce the long-term growth of an economy. As mentioned, in periods of high inflation, too large resources are channelled into the construction industry from an economic point of view. However, this also applies to the financial sector, as households and companies are forced to have their liquid assets managed more by the financial sector in the event of higher inflation. Sooner or later, this misallocation of economic resources will have to be paid for by costly structural adjustments. Increased inflation creates further economic costs by forcing economic operators to hold less cash and spend more time optimising their spot holdings. Companies have to constantly adjust their prices. This is also economically costly and often distorts relative prices because not all goods can be adapted to inflation at the same time. This distortion of the 4 Relative prices generally lead to a non-optimal use of resources, as the price signals do not reflect the correct scarcity ratios between the goods. High inflation is usually also associated with variable inflation. This means that economic operators are surprised by changes in the rate of inflation. Uncertainty about the level of inflation fundamentally impairs the willingness to invest in the longer term and thus further reduces the growth prospects of the economy. However, it is also very important that inflation surprises result in redistributions between debtors and creditors. Since small savers are less able to hedge against these inflation surprises than large investors, high and variable inflation leads to disadvantages for the financially weaker members of an economy. However, the socially disadvantaged groups in society are not only disadvantaged by higher inflation on the asset side. Rather, inflation also directly affects the income situation of these groups: pensions are often not or only belatedly adjusted to inflation. Inflation is also not always compensated for in wages. These remarks show that the orientation of monetary policy towards price stability is not an end in itself, but is a prerequisite for optimal framework conditions for macroeconomic development. However, the focus on price stability means that we also want to prevent deflationary conditions. Deflation also entails high costs for the economy. Prolonged deflation, however, was never a significant problem in the post-war period. In Switzerland, there was a threat of deflation in 1995 as a result of the strong appreciation of the Swiss franc at the time and the economic slowdown in Western Europe. We averted these dangers with a significant easing of monetary policy. 5 A clear distinction must be made between deflation and a phase of inflation reduction, the so-called disinflation. Experience shows that economies are subject to inflationary shocks from time to time. These are triggered either by an overly expansionary monetary policy or by external influences, such as an oil shock. An overly expansionary monetary policy can, on the one hand, be the result of a forecast error by the central bank about the actual demand for money or, on the other hand, the result of an intended attempt to explicitly stimulate the economy. It is important to note that it is always worth fighting inflation once it has occurred, regardless of what was the cause of the inflationary surge. A reduction in inflation is associated with costs: it leads to a recession and thus to increased unemployment. However, this recessive effect is of a short-term nature; it usually does not last long. The costs of this disinflation must be compared with the long-term benefits that become apparent when disinflation is complete and price stability returns. To refrain from disinflation because it incurs costs in the short term would be equivalent to refraining from the long-term optimisation of the monetary policy framework. As a number of scientific research shows, the short-term costs of disinflation are usually higher when a country has a low inflation rate on average. These costs are often recorded with the so-called victim quota. This measures the temporary reduction of the national product, which must be accepted per percentage point of disinflation. Probably the most important reason for this connection is the fact that with average low inflation, wages and prices are adjusted less quickly than with average high inflation, thus prolonging the adjustment process to the new inflation level. 6 On the basis of this finding, the public sometimes demands that the SNB should allow inflation to be higher on average so that the respective adjustment costs are lower after an inflationary shock. This is a questionable demand. It disregards the overall long-term benefits of a policy geared to price stability. A country with a monetary policy geared to price stability has to live with the fact that the costs of disinflation after an inflationary surge are at best slightly higher than in countries with average high inflation. The consequence should not be to aim for higher inflation, but rather to focus monetary policy strictly on preventing unnecessary inflationary shocks. I take this opportunity to clear up another misunderstanding. It is argued on several occasions that by trying to prevent the occurrence of inflation, the SNB fundamentally inhibits the development of the real economy. It is, so to speak, on the brake pedal of economic development. Of course, this is not the case. As I have already mentioned, the reduction in inflation has a negative impact on the economy in the short term. However, as soon as price stability is achieved, monetary policy no longer has an inhibiting effect on economic development. On the contrary, in the sense of what I have said so far, it has a long-term growth-promoting effect because it improves the monetary framework conditions. 2. Possibilities of monetary policy in stabilising the economy What about the possibility of using monetary policy to stabilise the economy? Monetary policy can influence the national product in the short term. This provides an instrument to dampen economic fluctuations. However, in the context of the question of the use of monetary policy to stabilise the economy, the following considerations must be taken into account: 7 By orienting the money supply towards the potential growth of the economy, the SNB is already having a stabilising effect on the course of the economy without explicitly pursuing an activist policy. In this context, one speaks of the automatic stabiliser effect of monetary policy. Since the demand for money depends on the volume of production, a money supply oriented towards potential economic growth during a recession is greater than the demand for money. This increases the demand for goods and thus has a stimulating effect on the economy. During a recessionary phase in which price stability already prevails, the SNB can also make the money supply to the economy additionally generous. The main aim is to ensure that no unnecessary deflationary effects arise during the recession that would inhibit the economic upswing. In this sense, we have been providing the economy with sufficient liquidity for some time now, thereby supporting the economic recovery. An additional commitment to economic stabilisation is associated with risks and is counterproductive in the long run, as it endangers long-term price stability. There are three valid reasons for using monetary policy only very cautiously to stabilise the economy beyond the aforementioned extent: 1. Monetary policy affects production only with a certain time lag. This time delay can vary in length. This makes it very difficult to use monetary policy specifically to stabilise the economy. 2. Various studies suggest that an expansionary monetary policy has only a weak effect on the national product and manifests itself above all in an increase in inflation. A restrictive monetary policy, on the other hand, e.g. during a period of disinflation, has a very strong influence on production. In this context, an asymmetric 8 The impact of monetary policy has been discussed. This asymmetry underscores the fact that monetary policy is not necessarily the appropriate means of stabilizing the economy: a strongly expansionary monetary policy during a recession would primarily increase the inflation rate, but not production. However, the subsequent restrictive monetary policy, which is necessary to reduce the inflation rate again, would have a strong negative impact on production and employment. 3. In order to use monetary policy to stabilise the economy, it is necessary for the SNB to have precise knowledge of the causes of the economic weakness or of the nature of the shocks that have occurred. This is important because monetary policy can, at best, compensate for a general weakness in demand. When monetary policy is used in the event of structural problems, it only produces inflation and increases the adjustment pressure of the sectors concerned even more. In reality, however, it is hardly possible to neatly separate structural from purely cyclical shocks. An activist monetary policy therefore runs the risk of being too expansionary. In doing so, it worsens the monetary policy environment instead of improving it. In my remarks so far, I have shown that the SNB can make the greatest possible contribution to balanced macroeconomic development if it fundamentally focuses its policy on price stability and consistently combats inflationary shocks that have occurred. This also means that the SNB is doing everything in its power to prevent unnecessary inflationary but also deflationary spurts and the resulting adjustment costs. 9 3. Independence of the SNB and monetary policy mandate The SNB can best achieve its objective of maintaining price stability if it has a clear mandate and can fulfil it with a high degree of independence. The planned reform of the monetary constitution therefore represents a further step towards a long-term optimisation of Swiss monetary policy: the SNB's mandate and independence will be formulated more precisely and thus help to further increase the credibility of monetary policy. With regard to the current debate on constitutional reform, I would like to emphasise that the independence of the National Bank is, of course, not an absolute one. The mandate is a clear guideline according to which it must be guided. It will be guided by teaching and experience. The mandate must be formulated in an economically sensible way and be fulfilled with the resources available to the SNB. My remarks clearly show that, on behalf of the SNB, price stability must be given a special assessment, as it represents the central contribution of the SNB and monetary policy to Switzerland's economic prosperity in the long term. An institutional framework with an independent National Bank, which must fulfil a clear mandate, has the advantage that the population, parliament and government agree, so to speak, in advance on a policy that they consider to be optimal in the long term. By delegating the implementation of monetary policy to the SNB, short-term special interests are prevented from being put before the long-term interests of the whole country in critical situations, such as a recession and large budget deficits. This is the mechanism that increases the credibility of the monetary policy of an independent central bank. In most developed countries, this view has prevailed, and many countries, such as the United States. 10 Kingdoms, where the government used to directly determine monetary policy, now have independent central banks. Of course, the issuing of an order to the SNB presupposes that there is a broad social consensus on the long-term objective of monetary policy. I am convinced that this consensus exists in Switzerland and that the fundamental orientation of monetary policy towards price stability is strongly supported by the population. However, the delegation of monetary policy to an independent central bank also means that it must make its policies transparent and account for its activities, as is already the case in practice today. This is the only way to achieve a long-term optimisation of the monetary policy framework. 4. Monetary policy after the establishment of the European Monetary Union: Autonomous monetary policy versus pegging of the Swiss franc to the euro My comments so far have focused on the SNB's monetary policy objective of price stability. Achieving price stability is not an easy task in reality. The uncertainty about the nature of the economic shocks, the various influences from abroad and the limited knowledge about the way in which monetary impulses are transferred to the real economy make our work considerably more difficult. A few years ago, a well-known Swiss economist aptly stated that monetary policy was ultimately an art. In the following, I would like to address two problems that the SNB is currently facing in the implementation of monetary policy. The first is the forthcoming implementation of The European Monetary Union. The second concerns the question of whether the SNB will continue to work with an official 11 Interim target or directly oriented towards an inflation target. Let us first turn to the forthcoming European Monetary Union. On 1 January 1999, most members of the European Union will probably abandon their own currency and adopt the euro as a means of payment. The European Central Bank will then determine the single monetary policy of the European Monetary Union. The Maastricht Treaty and the subsequent supplementary treaties grant the European Central Bank a high degree of independence and give it the mandate to ensure first and foremost the maintenance of price stability. Participation in monetary union is subject to the well-known convergence conditions. All this suggests that the monetary policy of the European Central Bank will not differ, or at least not a priori, from the previous policies of the major countries, which were decisively shaped by German monetary policy. Nevertheless, we must expect increased uncertainties in the first phase of monetary union. There are several reasons for this. The European Central Bank will first have to build its own reputation. At the beginning, it will be in uncharted territory, as the experience for a comprehensive European monetary policy is still lacking. Mistakes can easily happen. The credibility of the European Central Bank would suffer serious damage if the representatives of the various states tried to represent country-specific interests instead of clearly adhering to the mandate. For Switzerland, a policy of the European Central Bank consistently focused on price stability - and thus a strong euro - would clearly be the most comfortable situation. However, we must assume that currency turbulence can occur at the beginning of the monetary union and that the Swiss franc may appreciate because international investors still distrust the quality of European monetary policy. 12 Basically, we have three options to respond to such a situation: 1. We can fix the exchange rate against the euro from the outset and aim for a fixed exchange rate in the longer term. 2. We can continue to pursue an autonomous monetary policy with the aim of maintaining price stability. In doing so, we would take into account disturbances in the foreign exchange market to the extent compatible with the objective of price stability. 3. We can pursue a pragmatic policy and temporarily fix the Swiss franc exchange rate against the euro in the event of extreme fluctuations in exchange rates. All these variants have advantages and disadvantages. With the first possibility, we would fully follow European monetary policy and thus renounce an independent policy. For the export industry, this variant would eliminate the exchange rate risks. However, such a policy is only unproblematic in the long term if it is compatible with price stability. At least at the beginning of monetary union, it is not yet clear at what level European inflation will level off on average. In addition, we would also have to expect substantial interest rate hikes if the exchange rate were fixed against the euro. This option is therefore not a viable alternative for the SNB at the moment. The second option guarantees that the fundamental direction of monetary policy does not have to be changed due to current currency turbulence. The export industry of our country is sufficiently flexible in most of the disturbances in the foreign exchange markets to adapt to the new conditions. In addition, the SNB can try to mitigate the disturbances up to 13 to a certain extent, as long as this does not jeopardise price stability in the long term. This variant therefore represents a more attractive solution than pegging the Swiss franc to the euro. With this policy, Switzerland would also be able to retain its interest rate advantage for the time being. However, there may be a massive and disproportionate appreciation of the Swiss franc, so that even the most flexible companies in the export industry run into great difficulties. In such a situation, it is conceivable that the third variant, namely the temporary fixation of the Swiss franc exchange rate, would be the best solution. However, I would like to emphasise that this variant must be reserved for exceptional cases and must not be used for minor faults. The risk of this variant lies in the fact that the additional liquidity supply as a result of exchange rate fixation is not compatible with the long-term objective of price stability. The SNB would therefore have to return the money supply to its original equilibrium path as quickly as possible after the exchange rate fixation was lifted. I underline once again that the euro is very likely to be relatively stable. In this case, we will hardly have to intervene in the foreign exchange market. The real and economically relevant exchange rate is determined in the long term by market conditions. The SNB can thus correct excessive movements in the foreign exchange market in the short term; however, it cannot influence the real Swiss franc exchange rate in the long run. 14 5. Money supply target versus inflation target As I have already indicated, there are two main difficulties in conducting monetary policy: on the one hand, there is a large and variable period of time between a monetary stimulus and its consequences for production and price levels. On the other hand, the velocity of circulation or the demand for money can change unexpectedly. As a result, the SNB operates in an environment in which it cannot always accurately predict the impact of its policies. To alleviate these problems, central banks have traditionally used monetary aggregates as indicators or as intermediate targets. Monetary aggregates are particularly well suited as an intermediate target because they are easily controllable by the central bank and also closely correlate with the ultimate goal of price stability. Therefore, if a central bank controls the growth rate of a monetary aggregate, it also indirectly controls the inflation rate. However, the prerequisite for this mechanism is that the velocity of circulation or the demand for money is sufficiently stable in the medium and long term. The SNB has been using the monetary base as an interim target for around two decades. All in all, the experience with this has been positive. Since the end of the eighties, however, it has become apparent that the demand for base money is subject to additional fluctuations. Changes in banks' liquidity management, such as the savings in current account balances as a result of Swiss Interbank Clearing and the substitution of postal cheque balances by current balances, play a major role in this. In addition, the demand for notes is subject to strong fluctuations due to their high interest elasticity. A few years ago, we therefore set a medium-term target path for the central bank money supply instead of annual targets. This makes it possible to 15 to deviate from the target path in the short term and to take into account indicators other than the central bank money supply when determining monetary policy. Various countries, especially in the Anglo-Saxon region, have abandoned their money supply targets in recent years and are now directly targeting inflation. This change was necessary because there was no longer a stable demand for money in these countries. If the stability of demand for central bank money in Switzerland were to deteriorate dramatically, the transition to a direct inflation target would also be a possible monetary policy alternative for us. I would therefore like to point out the differences between these two monetary policy strategies, i.e. between the money supply target strategy and the inflation target strategy, referring in particular to Swiss conditions. In a monetary policy with a direct inflation target, the central bank refrains from formulating an interim target and tries to achieve the final target directly. In doing so, it must prepare an inflation forecast and change its monetary policy instruments in such a way that the projected inflation is in line with its inflation target. Compared to a monetary policy with a money supply target, this policy has the advantage that the target orientation becomes more transparent for a broad layer of the population. An inflation target is easier to understand than a money supply target. In the event of a missed target, however, it is more difficult for the public to determine whether this can be blamed on the central bank or whether it has come about as a result of a surprising change in the velocity of circulation that cannot be compensated for immediately by the SNB. However, the less the public can verify the actual actions of the central bank, the more difficult it can be for them to build credibility and reputation. The SNB's pragmatic implementation of the money supply target strategy already has many aspects in common with a policy of 16 direct inflation targeting. The differences between the SNB's money supply strategy and the inflation target strategy are relatively small for two reasons: First, we set our money supply target with an inflation target in mind, so that in a world without disruption, both strategies would be congruent. On the other hand, the SNB can already deviate from its money supply target today if it is convinced that it can better achieve the objective of price stability or if there are other valid reasons for doing so. So we are pursuing a conditional money supply target. The medium-term formulation of the money supply target allows us to deviate from the target path in the short term in the interest of maintaining price stability and to also take other economic indicators into account in the analysis of the situation. The main difference between the two strategies is therefore that the inflation target strategy generally uses a wider range of monetary policy indicators and that communication between the central bank and the public is no longer primarily based on the explanation of monetary developments, but on a broader basis in the form of an inflation report. However, it is important to note that a change of strategy would neither significantly simplify the SNB's task nor solve the current problems of the operational implementation of monetary policy without further ado. This is not because the predictability of the short- and medium-term inflation rate is not easy. Forecast errors would probably be relatively common, as foreign shocks in particular also influence the domestic inflation rate. In addition, economic knowledge of the necessary quantitative change in short-term interest rates to bring the inflation forecast back to the inflation target is limited. However, there would be one advantage to the inflation target strategy: the SNB would be more flexible in the choice and evaluation of its monetary policy indicators and could emphasise the importance of taking into account the indicators. 17 That is why we have tabled a motion for a resolution calling on the Commission and the Council to take the necessary steps to ensure that the European Parliament is fully involved in the work of the Committee on Agriculture, Fisheries and Rural Development. In summary, the differences between money supply management, as we operate it, and an inflation target strategy are relatively small. A change of strategy would be imperative above all if the information content of the money supply would become very low in the future. However, a change of strategy presupposes that the inflation rate can be forecast with sufficient precision over the medium term and that the quantitative effect of interest rate changes on inflation rates in subsequent periods is sufficiently known. Both requirements are currently only fulfilled to a limited extent. 6. Schlussbemerkungen I will conclude by summarising the main statements: n Maintaining price stability is the SNB's key contribution to shaping the best possible environment for the Swiss economy. The SNB can best maintain price stability in the long term if it has a clear mandate and can fulfil it with appropriate independence. The SNB can stabilise the economy and exchange rates in the short term, provided that this is compatible with the objective of price stability. But this is a very risky undertaking; it should therefore be reserved for exceptional situations. Overall, the SNB probably makes the best contribution to economic stabilisation if it prevents unnecessary inflation and deflation. 18 n A weak euro is unlikely to be expected in the transition to the European Monetary Union. The SNB will therefore be able to continue its autonomous monetary policy with the primary objective of price stability. Should the Swiss franc unexpectedly appreciate excessively, we would try to prevent an overshoot. n The SNB has to operate in an environment characterised by great uncertainty about the shocks that will occur. In addition, our knowledge of many interdependencies in the monetary transmission mechanism is limited and we are exposed to strong foreign influences. This makes the assessment of the situation considerably more difficult. We are therefore pursuing a pragmatic strategy with a medium-term target for the central bank money supply. In the future, in addition to the central bank money supply, we will increasingly use indicators for situation analysis. Already today, our policy is very similar in the essential aspects of an inflation target strategy. It is important that we continue to complete the knowledge about the exact transmission mechanisms in order to be able to further optimize our policy in the future. 19
