Die Europische Zentralbank wird alsdann die einheitliche Geldpolitik der Europischen Whrungsunion bestimmen. Der Vertrag von Maastricht und die nachfolgenden Ergnzungsvertrge gestehen der Europischen Zentralbank eine grosse Unabhngigkeit zu und erteilen ihr den Auftrag, in erster Linie fr die Erhaltung der Preisstabilitt zu sorgen. Die Teilnahme an der Whrungsunion ist an die bekannten Konvergenzbedingungen geknpft. Dies alles lsst erwarten, dass die Geldpolitik der Europischen Zentralbank sich nicht oder zumindest nicht a priori von der bisherigen Politik der wichtigen Lnder, die massgeblich von der deutschen Geldpolitik geprgt wurde, unterscheiden wird. Trotzdem mssen wir in der ersten Phase der Whrungsunion mit erhhten Unsicherheiten rechnen. Dafr gibt es verschiedene Grnde. Die Europische Zentralbank wird sich ihre eigene Reputation erst erarbeiten mssen. Sie wird sich am Anfang in Neuland bewegen, da die Erfahrungen fr eine gesamthafte europische Geldpolitik noch fehlen. Dabei knnen leicht Fehler passieren. Schweren Schaden wrde die Glaubwrdigkeit der Europischen Zentralbank dann erleiden, wenn die Vertreter der verschiedenen Staaten versuchen wrden, lnderspezifische Interessen zu vertreten, statt sich klar an den Auftrag zu halten. Fr die Schweiz wrde eine konsequent auf Preisstabilitt ausgerichtete Politik der Europischen Zentralbank - und damit ein starker Euro - eindeutig die komfortabelste Situation darstellen. Wir mssen aber davon ausgehen, dass zu Beginn der Whrungsunion Whrungsturbulenzen auftreten knnen und dass es zu einer Aufwertung des Schweizer Frankens kommen kann, weil die internationalen Investoren der Qualitt der europischen Geldpolitik noch misstrauen. 12 Grundstzlich haben wir drei Mglichkeiten, um auf eine solche Situation zu reagieren: 1. Wir knnen den Wechselkurs gegenber dem Euro von vornherein fixieren und auf lngere Frist einen festen Wechselkurs anstreben. 2. Wir knnen wie bisher eine autonome Geldpolitik mit dem Ziel der Erhaltung der Preisstabilitt verfolgen. Dabei wrden wir, soweit mit dem Ziel der Preisstabilitt vereinbar, auf Strungen im Devisenmarkt Rcksicht nehmen. 3. Wir knnen eine pragmatische Politik verfolgen und bei extremen Schwankungen der Wechselkurse den Frankenkurs vorbergehend gegenber dem Euro fixieren. Alle diese Varianten haben Vor- und Nachteile. Bei der ersten Mglichkeit wrden wir vollstndig der europischen Geldpolitik folgen und damit auf eine eigenstndige Politik verzichten. Fr die Exportwirtschaft wrden bei dieser Variante die Wechselkursrisiken wegfallen. Eine solche Politik ist aber langfristig nur dann unproblematisch, wenn sie mit Preisstabilitt vereinbar ist. Zumindest zu Beginn der Whrungsunion ist noch nicht klar, auf welchem Niveau sich die europische Inflation durchschnittlich einpendeln wird. Zudem mssten wir auch mit substantiellen Zinserhhungen rechnen, wenn der Wechselkurs gegenber dem Euro fixiert wrde. Diese Mglichkeit stellt deshalb fr die Nationalbank im Moment keine valable Alternative dar. Die zweite Mglichkeit garantiert, dass die fundamentale Ausrichtung der Geldpolitik nicht wegen momentanen Whrungsturbulenzen gendert werden muss. Die Exportindustrie unseres Landes ist bei den meisten Strungen auf den Devisenmrkten gengend flexibel, um sich den neuen Verhltnissen anzupassen. Zudem kann die Nationalbank versuchen, die Strungen bis zu 13 einem gewissen Grad zu dmpfen, solange dies nicht die Preisstabilitt langfristig gefhrdet. Diese Variante stellt daher eine attraktivere Lsung dar als die Bindung des Frankens an den Euro. Bei dieser Politik wrde die Schweiz vorderhand auch ihren Zinsvorteil behalten knnen. Es kann jedoch unter Umstnden zu einer massiven und unverhltnismssigen Aufwertung des Frankens kommen, so dass auch die flexibelsten Unternehmen der Exportwirtschaft in grosse Schwierigkeiten geraten. In einer derartigen Situation ist es denkbar, dass die dritte Variante, nmlich die vorbergehende Fixierung des Frankenkurses, die beste Lsung darstellen wrde. Ich mchte jedoch betonen, dass diese Variante fr Ausnahmeflle reserviert bleiben muss und nicht bereits bei kleineren Strungen verwendet werden darf. Das Risiko dieser Variante liegt nmlich darin, dass die zustzliche Liquidittsversorgung als Folge der Wechselkursfixierung nicht mit dem langfristigen Ziel der Preisstabilitt vereinbar ist. Die Nationalbank msste daher nach der Aufhebung der Wechselkursfixierung die Geldmenge mglichst rasch wieder auf ihren ursprnglichen Gleichgewichtspfad zurckbringen. Ich unterstreiche nochmals, dass der Euro mit grosser Wahrscheinlichkeit relativ stabil sein wird. In diesem Fall werden wir kaum in den Devisenmarkt eingreifen mssen. Sollte es trotzdem zu einer Situation kommen, in der die Nationalbank den Franken-Eurokurs beeinflusst, muss man sich klar vor Augen halten, dass nur der nominelle Wechselkurs langfristig durch die Notenbanken bestimmt werden kann. Der reale und wirtschaftlich relevante Wechselkurs wird in der langen Frist durch die Marktverhltnisse bestimmt. Die Nationalbank kann somit kurzfristig bermssige Bewegungen am Devisenmarkt korrigieren; sie kann aber den realen Frankenkurs auf die Dauer nicht beeinflussen. 14 5. Geldmengenziel versus Inflationsziel Wie ich bereits angetnt habe, bestehen bei der Durchfhrung der Geldpolitik zwei Hauptschwierigkeiten: Einerseits liegt zwischen einem monetren Impuls und seinen Folgen fr Produktion und Preisniveau eine grosse und variable Zeitspanne. Andererseits knnen sich die Umlaufsgeschwindigkeit oder die Geldnachfrage unerwartet verndern. Dadurch operiert die Nationalbank in einem Umfeld, in dem sie die Wirkung ihrer Politik nicht immer exakt prognostizieren kann. Um diese Probleme zu verringern, haben die Notenbanken traditionell Geldmengenaggregate als Indikatoren oder als Zwischenziele verwendet. Geldmengenaggregate eignen sich besonders gut als Zwischenziel, weil sie durch die Notenbank gut kontrollierbar sind und berdies eng mit dem Endziel der Preisstabilitt korrelieren. Kontrolliert eine Zentralbank daher die Wachstumsrate eines Geldmengenaggregates, so kontrolliert sie indirekt auch die Inflationsrate. Die Voraussetzung fr diesen Mechanismus ist allerdings, dass die Umlaufsgeschwindigkeit oder die Geldnachfrage mittel- und langfristig hinreichend stabil sind. Die Nationalbank verwendet seit rund zwei Jahrzehnten die monetre Basis als Zwischenziel. Die Erfahrungen damit sind alles in allem genommen positiv ausgefallen. Seit dem Ende der achtziger Jahre hat sich jedoch gezeigt, dass die Nachfrage nach Basisgeld zustzlichen Schwankungen unterworfen ist. Dabei spielen Vernderungen beim Liquidittsmanagement der Banken, wie beispielsweise die Einsparungen an Giroguthaben als Folge des Swiss Interbank Clearing und die Substitution von Postcheckguthaben durch Giroguthaben, eine grosse Rolle. Zudem ist die Nachfrage nach Noten wegen ihrer grossen Zinselastizitt starken Schwankungen unterworfen. Wir haben daher vor einigen Jahren anstelle von jhrlichen Zielvorgaben einen mittelfristigen Zielpfad fr die Notenbankgeldmenge festgelegt. Dadurch ist es mglich, in der 15 kurzen Frist vom Zielpfad abzuweichen und bei der Festlegung der Geldpolitik auch andere Indikatoren als die Notenbankgeldmenge zu bercksichtigen. Verschiedene Lnder, vor allem im angelschsischen Raum, haben in den letzten Jahren ihre Geldmengenziele aufgegeben und visieren nun direkt ein Inflationsziel an. Dieser Wechsel war ntig, weil in diesen Lndern keine stabile Geldnachfrage mehr vorhanden war. Wrde sich die Stabilitt der Nachfrage nach Notenbankgeld in der Schweiz dramatisch verschlechtern, wre der bergang zu einem direkten Inflationsziel auch fr uns eine mgliche geldpolitische Alternative. Ich mchte deshalb die Unterschiede zwischen diesen beiden geldpolitischen Strategien, d.h. zwischen Geldmengenzielstrategie und Inflationszielstrategie, aufzeigen und dabei vor allem auf die schweizerischen Verhltnisse Bezug nehmen. Bei einer Geldpolitik mit einem direkten Inflationsziel verzichtet die Notenbank auf die Formulierung eines Zwischenzieles und versucht, das Endziel direkt zu erreichen. Dabei muss sie eine Inflationsprognose erstellen und ihre geldpolitischen Instrumente so verndern, dass die prognostizierte Inflation mit ihrem Inflationsziel in bereinstimmung kommt. Gegenber einer Geldpolitik mit einem Geldmengenziel hat diese Politik den Vorteil, dass die Zielausrichtung fr eine breite Schicht der Bevlkerung transparenter wird. Ein Inflationsziel ist einfacher zu verstehen als ein Geldmengenziel. Bei einer Zielverfehlung ist es allerdings fr das Publikum schwieriger festzustellen, ob diese der Notenbank angelastet werden kann oder ob sie durch eine berraschende und daher fr die Nationalbank nicht sofort kompensierbare Vernderung der Umlaufsgeschwindigkeit zustanden gekommen ist. Je weniger aber die ffentlichkeit die tatschlichen Handlungen der Notenbank berprfen kann, desto schwieriger kann es fr diese sein, Glaubwrdigkeit und Reputation aufzubauen. Die pragmatische Umsetzung der Geldmengenzielstrategie durch die Nationalbank hat bereits heute viele gemeinsame Aspekte mit einer Politik der 16 direkten Inflationssteuerung. Die Unterschiede zwischen der Geldmengenstrategie der Nationalbank und der Inflationszielstrategie sind aus zwei Grnden relativ gering: Zum einen legen wir unser Geldmengenziel im Hinblick auf ein Inflationsziel fest, so dass in einer Welt ohne Strungen beide Strategien deckungsgleich wren. Zum anderen kann die Nationalbank von ihrem Geldmengenziel bereits heute abweichen, falls sie berzeugt ist, damit das Ziel der Preisstabilitt besser zu erreichen oder falls andere triftige Grnde dafr sprechen. Wir verfolgen also ein bedingtes Geldmengenziel. Die mittelfristige Formulierung des Geldmengenzieles erlaubt es uns, im Interesse der Erhaltung der Preisstabilitt kurzfristig vom Zielpfad abzuweichen und andere konomische Indikatoren bei der Lageanalyse ebenfalls zu bercksichtigen. Der Hauptunterschied zwischen beiden Strategien liegt somit darin, dass bei der Inflationszielstrategie generell eine breitere Palette von geldpolitischen Indikatoren verwendet wird und dass die Kommunikation zwischen Notenbank und ffentlichkeit nicht mehr in erster Linie ber die Erluterung der Geldmengenentwicklung, sondern dass sie breiter abgesttzt in Form eines Inflationsberichtes erfolgt. Es ist jedoch wichtig festzuhalten, dass ein Strategiewechsel weder die Aufgabe der Nationalbank wesentlich vereinfachen noch die gegenwrtigen Probleme der operativen Umsetzung der Geldpolitik ohne weiteres lsen wrde. Dies deshalb nicht, weil einmal die Prognostizierbarkeit der kurz- und mittelfristigen Inflationsrate nicht einfach ist. Prognosefehler wren wohl relativ hufig, da insbesondere auch auslndische Schocks die inlndische Inflationsrate beeinflussen. Zudem sind die konomischen Kenntnisse ber die notwendige quantitative Vernderung der kurzfristigen Zinsstze, um die Inflationsprognose zurck auf das Inflationsziel zu bringen, nur beschrnkt vorhanden. Ein Vorteil wrde bei der Inflationszielstrategie allerdings bestehen: Die Nationalbank wre bei der Wahl und der Auswertung ihrer geldpolitischen Indikatoren flexibler und knnte die Akzentsetzung bei der Bercksichtigung der Indikato- 17 ren verndern, ohne dass in der ffentlichkeit jedesmal der Eindruck einer eigentlichen Strategienderung entstehen wrde. Zusammenfassend kann gesagt werden, dass die Unterschiede zwischen der Geldmengensteuerung, wie wir sie betreiben, und einer Inflationszielstrategie relativ klein sind. Ein Wechsel der Strategie wrde sich vor allem dann aufdrngen, wenn der Informationsgehalt der Geldmengen zuknftig sehr gering werden wrde. Ein Wechsel der Strategie setzt aber voraus, dass die Inflationsrate auf mittlere Frist ausreichend przise prognostiziert werden kann und die quantitative Wirkung von Zinsvernderungen auf die Inflationsraten in den nachfolgenen Zeitperioden gengend bekannt ist. Beide Voraussetzungen sind zur Zeit nur begrenzt erfllt. 6. Schlussbemerkungen Ich komme zum Schluss meiner Ausfhrungen und mchte die Hauptaussagen noch einmal zusammenfassen: n Die Erhaltung der Preisstabilitt stellt den zentralen Beitrag der Nationalbank zur Gestaltung von optimalen Rahmenbedingung fr die schweizerische Wirtschaft dar. Preisstabilitt kann die Nationalbank langfristig am besten erhalten, wenn sie einen klaren Auftrag hat und diesen in angemessener Unabhngigkeit erfllen kann. Die Nationalbank kann in der kurzen Frist - sofern dies mit dem Ziel der Preisstabilitt vereinbar ist - Konjunktur und Wechselkurse stabilisieren. Dies ist aber ein sehr riskantes Unterfangen; es sollte deshalb fr Ausnahmesituationen reserviert bleiben. Insgesamt leistet die Nationalbank wohl den besten Beitrag zur wirtschaftlichen Stabilisierung, wenn sie unntige Inflations- und Deflationsschbe verhindert. 18 n Beim bergang zur Europischen Whrungsunion ist mit grosser Wahrscheinlichkeit nicht mit einem schwachen Euro zu rechnen. Die Nationalbank wird deshalb ihre autonome Geldpolitik mit dem vorrangigen Ziel der Preisstabilitt fortsetzen knnen. Sollte es unerwarteterweise zu einer bermssigen Aufwertung des Frankens kommen, wrden wir versuchen, ein berschiessen zu verhindern. n Die Nationalbank hat in einem Umfeld zu operieren, das von grossen Unsicherheiten bezglich der auftretenden Schocks geprgt ist. Dazu kommt, dass unser Wissen ber viele Wirkungszusammenhnge im monetren Transmissionsmechanismus beschrnkt ist und dass wir starken Auslandeinflssen ausgesetzt sind. Dies erschwert die Lagebeurteilung erheblich. Wir verfolgen deshalb eine pragmatische Strategie mit einem mittelfristigen Ziel fr die Notenbankgeldmenge. In Zukunft werden wir in einem vermehrten Ausmass neben der Notenbankgeldmenge zustzlich Indikatoren zur Lageanalyse heranziehen. Bereits heute ist unsere Politik in den wesentlichen Aspekten einer Inflationszielstrategie sehr hnlich. Wichtig ist, dass wir das Wissen ber die exakten bertragungsmechanismen weiter vervollstndigen, um so unsere Politik in Zukunft weiter optimieren zu knnen. 19

Title: The Swiss National Bank facing new challenges
text: The Swiss National Bank faces new challenges Speech by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-President of the Swiss National Bank at the University of St. Gallen 5 February 1998 1. Introduction First of all, I would like to thank you for the invitation to give a lecture here in St. Gallen. Obviously, NATIONAL Bank representatives are welcome speakers at the University of St. Gallen, as my colleague Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Governing Board, was also a guest here just three weeks ago. In December, we announced our monetary policy intentions for 1998. Hans Meyer dealt with this topic in detail in his lecture. In my presentation today, I myself would first like to address the rapidly changing environment in which monetary policy takes place and then outline the SNB's response to these changes. To meet these new challenges, the SNB needs, in particular, a modern institutional framework and a flexible monetary policy approach. 2. A changing environment The environment in which the Swiss National Bank conducts its policy is in a state of upheaval. The main features of this upheaval can be summed up in three key words: progressive globalisation, the dynamics of the financial markets and the European Monetary Union. 2.1 Advancing globalisation The roots of today's globalization go back to the 60s and 70s, when a gradual departure from interventionism and protectionism took place. In the 80s, deregulation and liberalization became more and more prevalent and were extended to other areas, such as services and capital movements. Visible signs of this development were, for example, the Uruguay Round of the then GATT (now WTO), the signing of the Single European Act and later the preparations for the European internal market. 1 The ongoing deregulation and liberalisation affected both the goods and financial markets. Protectionist restrictions on product markets were further reduced, increasing international trade and strengthening the international division of labour. In many places, intensified competition forced a profound structural change with negative short-term effects on output and employment. In the end, however, deregulation and liberalisation result in a more efficient allocation of scarce resources, which ultimately benefits the economy as a whole. Internationalisation on the financial markets was even more pronounced than on the goods markets. The enormous advances in computer science have contributed significantly to this development. Today's telecommunications enable the rapid and cheap procurement and processing of enormous amounts of information. This created the conditions for worldwide arbitrage and increased international competition. Intense competition for mobile capital forced the dismantling of regulations and restrictions and promoted the unification of rules and the standardization of products. At the same time, numerous new financial instruments and forms of risk hedging have been developed. The resulate of advancing globalization is an ever-increasing interdependence of national markets. Through flows of goods and capital, economic impulses are transmitted more intensively than ever from one country to another. For national economic policy and also for monetary policy, this means that its ability to influence events is becoming even more limited; this is all the more true for a small open country like Switzerland. Economic and monetary policy should therefore realistically be limited to the creation of favourable framework conditions for strengthening competitiveness in international competition. These favourable conditions also include a stable currency, accompanied by low inflation and correspondingly low interest rates. 2 2.2 The free movement of capital as an opportunity and a risk In the wake of liberalisation, deregulation and IT support, the volume of sales on the international financial and foreign exchange markets has skyrocketed. The free movement of international capital is a necessary condition for an efficient allocation of savings and investments. At the same time, however, with the scale of capital flows and the increasing interconnectedness of markets, the risk of cross-border financial crises has also increased. Financial crises, on the other hand, can have serious consequences for the development of the real economy. With the outbreak of the financial crisis in Asia, international capital flows have once again come under heavy fire. The crisis was partly blamed on malicious speculators, and the demand for restrictions on the movement of capital became loud. It is true that the not always rational behaviour of global market participants plays a certain role in the markets. However, it would be a mistake to fall back into a regime with restrictions on capital movements. What role did international capital flows actually play in the Asian crisis? For several years, Asia has been an attractive destination for international capital flows with its high growth rates. Asia experienced huge capital inflows. The rather loose monetary conditions worldwide had expanded global liquidity, so that large sums of capital were in search of profitable investment opportunities. These capital inflows led to an excessive inflation of assets, both on the stock market and in the real estate market. The abundance of liquidity and rising assets led banks and financial institutions to lend too freely. We now know that too much, too unproductive and too risky has been invested in Asia as a whole. The extensive neglect of risks by the banks is due, among other things, to the fact that the interdependence between the state and the banking system was sometimes so close that an implicit state guarantee was assumed. In addition, there was only one in the countries concerned. 3 insufficient control of banking, credit and capital markets, and the financial sector in general suffered from a lack of transparency and legal certainty. The structural adjustment programmes mandated by the International Monetary Fund therefore focus on a comprehensive reform of the banking and financial sector and the capital markets. Important elements of these reforms are the establishment of independent banking supervision, compliance with the capital requirements recommended by the BIS, the application of uniform and transparent accounting standards and auditing by internationally recognised companies. At the same time, the financial sector is to be further liberalised and increasingly exposed to international competition. The crisis in Asia has shown once again that the violation of fundamental financial principles sooner or later leads to problems. It is therefore not necessary to look for new theories; the tried and tested only has to be applied. In my opinion, it would therefore be wrong to try to counter the Asian crisis by restricting international capital mobility. It is much more important that these capital flows and their use take place within a transparent and orderly framework, that the banking system plays its role as an efficient hub for capital and that the central bank pursues a realistic strategy. These measures can minimize the risk of systemic crises. Central banks in particular have a great interest in this, as in the event of impending systemic crises, they are faced with the dilemma of being able to defuse the crisis by supplying liquidity, but thus jeopardizing price stability in the longer term. 2.3 European monetary integration Parallel to the changes triggered by advancing globalisation and the free movement of capital, a veritable monetary revolution is emerging in Europe: the introduction of a European single currency. In just three months, the EU will determine the countries participating in monetary union from the outset, and in less than a year the European Central Bank will take over the monetary policy sceptre. From January 1999 onwards, the national European currencies will no longer be used as separate monetary units, but only as 4 Subunits of the euro exist. Finally, by 1 July 2002, national currencies will disappear completely; from that date, the euro will be the only legal tender in the monetary union. The monetary policy merger creates the world's largest economic area with a single currency. The European Monetary Union will also have a significant impact on Switzerland. Although not a member of the EU, Switzerland belongs geographically, historically and culturally to Europe. Switzerland is also closely linked to the EU economically: around 80% of our imports come from the EU, which in turn takes 62% of our exports. With the introduction of monetary union, the nature of our economic relations with the EU and the role of the Swiss franc will change. For the first time in our history, Switzerland will be surrounded by countries that all use the same means of payment. This gives our export industry the hope of being able to operate in a stable environment. At the same time, however, European monetary integration also increases our dependence on an environment that we can hardly influence. As a result, Switzerland will find itself even more than before in an economic community of destiny with the EU. The future exchange rate ratio between the Swiss franc and the euro will therefore be even more important than the current Sfr./DM exchange rate. The focus on the euro presents both opportunities and risks for Swiss foreign trade. With a stable price ratio in line with fundamentals, Switzerland could benefit greatly from the advantages of the euro. The introduction of a single currency leads to a radical simplification of foreign exchange transactions, increases transparency and increases competition and integration in the goods and financial markets. Conversely, a weak and volatile euro would pose major problems for the Swiss economy. In this situation, the Swiss National Bank would use all the means at its disposal to counteract an unrealistic appreciation of the Swiss franc. 5 Personally, however, I am optimistic that the euro will become a stable currency. The guarantor of a strong euro is the European Central Bank (ECB), which was modelled on the Deutsche Bundesbank. The ECB's primary objective is to maintain price stability. In carrying out its task, the ECB shall be independent of political authorities and shall not seek or take instructions from them. Furthermore, the ECB is expressly prohibited from contributing in any way to government deficit financing. Additional barriers to undisciplined fiscal policy are the convergence criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty and the Stability Pact. The Stability Pact is intended to ensure that member states continue to pursue fiscal policies that are compatible with the ECB's price stability policy in the long term. The institutional framework for a strong euro is therefore favourable. Nevertheless, the ECB will also have to earn its monetary policy spurs first. It cannot be ruled out that the initial phase of monetary union will be marked by increased uncertainty until the markets have gained confidence in the ECB. In addition, the heterogeneity of EU countries can lead to difficulties in implementing the common monetary policy. In the long run, however, the parallelism of the stability policy principles of the Swiss National Bank and the future European Central Bank should lead to a stable exchange rate relationship between the Swiss franc and the euro, similar to the relationship with the Deutsche Bundesbank. 3. The reform of the institutional framework Globalisation and European monetary integration pose significant challenges for the Swiss National Bank. In order to succeed in this dynamic new environment, the SNB needs a modern institutional framework. This is the direction of the reform of the monetary constitution that is currently underway. In the following, I would like to discuss what I consider to be three central elements of the new currency constitution: the detachment of the Swiss franc from gold, the explicit anchoring of price stability and the independence of the SNB, and the question of the necessary currency reserves. 6 3.1 The detachment of the Swiss franc from gold The gold peg of the Swiss franc is a relic from the time of the gold standard. Under the gold standard, a country fixed the price of gold in its currency (gold parity). The central bank was obliged to cover the notes with gold and to maintain parity by buying and selling gold. A permanent expansion of the money supply was only possible through gold purchases by the central bank; the natural scarcity of gold and the high production costs set tight limits on the growth of the money supply. Despite short-term fluctuations, the gold standard guaranteed a stable price level on a longer-term average. The gold standard in its classic form came to an end with the outbreak of the First World War. In the subsequent monetary systems, especially in the dollar-gold standard of Bretton Woods, the gold peg was reintroduced only in a greatly loosened form. Under the Bretton Woods fixed rate system, gold no longer had the function of a means of payment, but only served as a means of determining the external value of a currency. With the abolition of the dollar's gold parity in 1971 and the transition to flexible exchange rates, gold has lost its key monetary policy role. Nevertheless, the Swiss monetary constitution still contains the corresponding earlier rules. The legal system still in force today is based on three pillars: the fixation of gold parity, the obligation to redeem banknotes and the guarantee requirement for banknotes. Together, these three elements form a logical whole. For example, the coverage requirement requires that the banknote circulation is sufficiently covered by gold. The obligation to redeem the banknotes gives them the character of gold substitutes. Gold parity, in turn, is the benchmark for the external value of the currency or for the SNB's gold holdings. The obligation to redeem banknotes was only effectively applied for a few years. The Constitution allows the suspension of the obligation to redeem in times of war or in the case of "disturbed currency conditions"; on this basis 7 The Federal Council abolished the obligation to redeem it in 1936. We have been living permanently in disturbed conditions for more than sixty years! Despite a suspended redemption obligation, there is still a coverage requirement for the banknote circulation. The extent of gold backing is laid down in the Central Bank Act; until recently, the coverage ratio was 40%. With the entry into force of the revised Central Bank Act in November last year, the coverage rate was reduced to 25%. After the abolition of the redemption obligation and after the transition to floating, the gold parity in turn only has the function as a valuation criterion for the gold reserves. The parity in force today was set in 1971 and, at CHF 4,595/kg, is far below the current market price. Since the SNB is only allowed to buy or sell gold at official parity, the bank's gold holdings are de facto immobilized. Today it is time to close the gap between the monetary constitution and lived currency reality. At constitutional level, Articles 38 and 39 should therefore be amended. However, care must be taken to ensure that the old regulations, the original purpose of which was to safeguard the value of the Swiss franc, are replaced by modern rules with the same effect. This includes, above all, the establishment in the constitution of the independence of the SNB and its priority objective of price stability. In addition, confidence in the Swiss franc is to be strengthened by holding high currency reserves. 3.2 The new foundations: price stability and independence Under the gold standard, monetary policy was almost automatically determined by gold flows. Under this regime, the question of the independence of the central bank was of no importance, as it only had to conduct a policy that ensured the maintenance of official gold parity. In the context of the detachment of the Swiss franc from gold, the framework within which 8 monetary policy is being redefined. Two points are of central importance: the clear definition of the central bank's mandate and the independence of the monetary policy authority in fulfilling its mandate. The discussion about the SNB's mandate over the past few months has partly slipped into the emotional. This is understandable in view of today's problems of the Swiss economy. In the context of formulating the SNB's mandate, however, the long-term overall interest of the Swiss economy must be in the foreground, and a realistic distinction must be made between what is politically desirable and what is feasible in monetary policy. Thus, no one denies that price stability, growth and full employment are, as it were, desirable economic policy objectives. With monetary policy, however, only the first objective, price stability, can be achieved in the long term. The central bank has only a temporary and uncertain influence on growth and employment. In a situation like the current one, where there is virtually no inflation, there is a certain tendency to take price stability for granted. At the beginning of the 90s, however, inflation rates in Switzerland were still close to 6%; under these circumstances, awareness of the harmfulness of inflation was much more present than it is today. It is therefore useful to briefly recall the cost of inflation at this point. Inflation acts like a tax on cash holdings. A high inflation rate therefore leads to the maintenance of an inefficiently deep real cash register and causes unnecessary transaction and coordination costs. Second, with the level of inflation, inflation also increases inflation volatility. A volatile inflation rate reinforces the uncertainty associated with longer-term fixed prices of all kinds (prices in the narrower sense, wages, interest rates, rents). This leads to costly but incomplete protective measures against inflation uncertainty, such as shortening the duration of contracts or indexing contracts. Furthermore, inflation uncertainty can lead to the incorporation of risk premiums, e.g. on interest rates, but also on other prices. 9 After all, unanticipated inflation fluctuations cause an arbitrary redistribution of income and wealth, which usually hits the socially weaker particularly hard. Thirdly, a high inflation rate triggers fundamentally unjustified shifts in price relations between different products or product groups. These distortions in the pricing system reduce the efficiency of markets and lead to the misallocation of scarce resources. Overall, the enumerated costs of inflation have negative consequences for economic growth. Empirical studies have shown that countries with high inflation rates have lower growth rates on a longer-term average than countries with a low inflation rate. Although trade-offs between price stability on the one hand and growth or employment on the other may arise in the short term, a monetary policy geared to price stability thus makes a positive contribution to long-term economic growth. What is the best way to achieve the objective of price stability? There is a consensus in economics that price stability can best be ensured if monetary policy is placed in the hands of an independent central bank. By delegating monetary policy to an independent body, short-term particular interests are prevented from being put before the long-term interests of the economy as a whole in difficult situations. The positive relationship between the independence of a central bank and the stability of a currency is confirmed by numerous empirical studies. In practice, it is argued that independent central banks pursue the goal of price stability too stubbornly and react too little to economic fluctuations. According to this criticism, independent central banks produce a low inflation rate, but only at the price of increased cyclical instability. Empirical studies cannot support this accusation. In an international comparison, countries with an independent central bank do not have a higher output variability than countries in which the central bank is subordinate to the government. 10 These results can also be explained theoretically. For example, an independent central bank may be less anxious to actively smooth out economic fluctuations. Conversely, however, a stability-oriented, steady monetary policy itself becomes less the cause of economic fluctuations than an activist policy with its numerous information and lag problems. By compensating for each other, an independent central bank does not lead to higher output variability. However, the autonomy of the central bank is not to be understood absolutely; rather, it relates to the freedom of decision and action in relation to a particular objective. In a democracy, the aim of this goal lies in the competence of politics and ultimately of the people. The central bank depends on a broad social consensus on its ultimate goal; in the long run, it cannot conduct its policy without the fundamental support of the population. An independent central bank is therefore not a foreign body in democracy. Back to the reform of the monetary constitution. Central bank independence and the objective of price stability are not explicitly anchored in today's legal foundations. Nevertheless, in practice, the Swiss National Bank enjoyed a high degree of autonomy and pursued the primary objective of price stability. In this respect, the planned establishment of independence and the objective of price stability is essentially an adaptation of the monetary constitution to the prevailing monetary reality. At the same time, Switzerland is also adapting its central bank legislation to the standards required by the Maastricht Treaty, which are now common throughout Europe. 3.3. Securing confidence through high currency reserves The current constitution stipulates that the banknote circulation must be covered by gold and short-term balances. Under the gold standard and under the system of fixed exchange rates, this provision served to curb money supply growth. Under flexible exchange rates, this braking mechanism is overridden. If the exchange rate is flexible, the central bank can reduce the money supply in the 11 Increase the principle arbitrarily by buying foreign currency against Swiss francs. The consequence of an excessive expansion of the money supply compared to other countries is a devaluation of the Swiss franc. In today's monetary system, currency reserves therefore have different tasks than under fixed exchange rates. Currency reserves serve to prevent and overcome any crises and thus provide a stabilisation contribution. In general, high currency reserves increase confidence in a currency without being able to quantify this influence exactly. For this reason, the new currency constitution will also require the holding of sufficient currency reserves. The amount of the necessary reserves is measured above all by the size and degree of foreign integration of a country. As a small, open economy, Switzerland will continue to hold higher reserves in relation to its gross domestic product than large, domestically oriented countries. The international importance of the Swiss financial centre is, of course, another argument in favour of holding extensive reserves. 4. Monetary policy under scrutiny In addition to a favourable institutional framework, the SNB also needs a functioning operational concept in order to successfully fulfil its task. As you know, for some time now the SNB has had certain difficulties with its strategy based on the management of the base money supply. My colleague Hans Meyer spoke in detail about this topic in his recent presentation here in St. Gallen. I myself will therefore be brief on this point. 4.1 Problems of traditional monetary policy and possible alternatives After the collapse of the fixed-rate system, many countries, including Switzerland, adopted a monetary policy based on the management of the money supply. This policy is based on the relationship between the money supply and nominal gross national product. In concrete terms, price stability is ensured if the money supply is in step with the productive potential of the economy in the medium term. 12 grows, if necessary corrected by an increase or decrease in the orbital velocity. A policy of money supply control delivers good results as long as the relationship described above is relatively stable and predictable. Steady, trending changes in money demand can also be easily taken into account by monetary policy. However, difficulties arise when the demand for money changes frequently, substantially and unpredictably. Such fluctuations are mainly caused by financial innovations, but also legal changes or changes in the payment and investment habits of the public, whereby these elements are often interdependent. Towards the mid-80s, the onset of deregulation and liberalization of the financial markets and the associated financial innovations, especially in the Anglo-Saxon countries, led to a far-reaching collapse of the relationship between the growth of the money supply and the inflation rate. As a result, many countries abandoned monetary policy and turned to other monetary policy concepts. In Switzerland, and incidentally also in Germany, there still seems to be a relatively stable relationship between money supply and inflation in the medium term. Recently, however, the Swiss National Bank has also had to contend with difficulties with the central bank money supply it controls. The existence of certain problems with a monetary policy approach does not automatically lead to its abandonment. Rather, it must be carefully examined whether alternatives exist that lead to better results. Of the various alternatives, I would like to discuss here only the two that seem most relevant to me: namely, the fixing of the exchange rate and the pursuit of a direct inflation target. By pegging one's own currency to that of a reserve currency country, the question of the monetary policy concept is transferred to the reserve currency country. Depending on the monetary policy success of the reserve currency country, price stability is thus imported via the exchange rate. A fixed exchange rate can be beneficial for countries 13 who have difficulty controlling inflation for structural-technical reasons or lack of credibility. The main disadvantage of an exchange rate peg is the loss of monetary autonomy, which manifests itself in an alignment of interest rates with foreign levels. In the specific case of Switzerland, a significant increase in interest rates would very likely be expected. The central question in any exchange rate peg is its credibility. Given the openness and dynamism of the financial markets, a peg of the Swiss franc to a reserve currency would only lead to the desired exchange rate stability if this peg were considered permanent. The experience of recent years with the EMS has shown that a fixation of the exchange rate can only succeed if it is accompanied by a coherent monetary policy integration strategy. Since there is no clear development in Switzerland towards EU accession and thus towards adopting the euro, the peg to the European single currency remains a problematic option. The second alternative, the direct pursuit of an inflation target, has gained popularity, especially since the early 90s. When pursuing an inflation target, the central bank forecasts future inflation and compares the forecast with the target. The difference between forecast and target determines the necessary adjustment of monetary policy instruments. The problems of an inflation-targeted policy lie first in predictability and then in the short-term control of inflation. The forecast of inflation is associated with great uncertainty, because no one, not even the central bank, knows the "true model" of the economy. This is all the more true in a small open economy like Switzerland, where external influences play an important role. At the same time, the central bank cannot control inflation in the short term and with complete precision, but only in the medium-term trend. Thus, the inflation rate is temporarily influenced by various factors that are not under the control of the central bank. The strategy of directly pursuing an inflation target has so far proved particularly effective in countries where the central bank has struggled to get the markets off its will. 14 to combat inflation. In this environment, the announcement of an inflation target sent a signal that indicated a change in policy. The Swiss National Bank, on the other hand, enjoys the confidence of the markets, so that an explicit inflation target would have little signal effect. A closer look also reveals that monetary policy strategies with inflation or money supply targets are not as fundamentally different from each other in practice as one might spontaneously think. Central banks with a direct inflation target take into account, among other variables, the development of the money supply when preparing their forecasts of price developments. Conversely, the SNB does not pursue its money supply objective as an end in itself, but as an intermediate objective on the way to price stability. In addition to the money supply, the SNB also pays attention to other variables. If these indicators clearly suggest a deviation from the monetary objective with regard to the final objective of price stability, the SNB is prepared to allow these deviations. The discussion of the different strategies shows the complexity of the current monetary policy environment. There is no simple solution that gives a clear answer in every situation. Rather, monetary policy calls for a global approach in which indicators of market liquidity play a priority role, but which at the same time also includes other variables such as exchange rates or interest rate structures in assessing the situation. 4.2 The strategy of the Swiss National Bank Undoubtedly, monetary aggregates have played and continue to play a central role in Swiss monetary policy, although there are certain problems of interpretation. For example, the validity of our traditional indicator, the central bank money supply M0, is currently being affected by various shocks. The exact demarcation and explanation of the shocks is difficult and associated with great uncertainty. Nevertheless, we are trying to estimate the extent of these shocks and to clean up the central bank money supply accordingly. If we look at the adjusted central bank money supply, it becomes clear that our current policy does not pose a threat to future price developments. 15 In addition to M0, we are seeing more M3. The M3 unit has a particularly close medium-term relationship with the price level. Thus, a strong expansion of M3 is followed by an increase in inflation after about three years. Compared to M0, M3 has the disadvantage that we can control it less directly and precisely than M0. The current pace of growth of M3 is also in line with a stable price level over the medium term. The volatility of the financial markets is a reality that we live with permanently and that we must take into account. That is why we are watching the development of exchange rates and the interest rate structure with great attention. It would be fatal for the Swiss economy if we were to commit ourselves through a stubborn concept. Today's situation requires flexibility. 5. Schlussbemerkungen As we have seen, in today's rapidly changing world, there is no shortage of challenges for a central bank. Today, the environment in which the Swiss National Bank operates is characterised by liberalisation, deregulation, strong global networking and, in some cases, breathtaking dynamics of the financial markets. In addition, the ambitious project of the European Monetary Union will soon enter its third and final phase - right on Switzerland's doorstep. I am confident that we are well prepared for these challenges. The new legal framework, which guarantees the Bank independence in the conduct of monetary policy and gives it the primary objective of price stability, is a favourable precondition for the continuation of our stability policy, which is generally quite successful by international standards. In the future, we will continue to apply our monetary policy concept, which is based on the management of the central bank money supply, pragmatically and flexibly. In doing so, we always have the overall interest of the economy in mind. The stability of the monetary framework that the SNB is striving for ultimately serves the country's overall interest. 16
