Dazu gehren vor allem die Festschreibung der Unabhngigkeit der Nationalbank und ihres prioritren Zieles, der Preisstabilitt, in der Verfassung. Zustzlich soll das Vertrauen in den Schweizer Franken durch das Halten von hohen Whrungsreserven gestrkt werden. 3.2 Die neuen Fundamente: Preisstabilitt und Unabhngigkeit Unter dem Goldstandard wurde die Geldpolitik quasi automatisch durch die Goldflsse bestimmt. Unter diesem Regime war die Frage der Unabhngigkeit der Notenbank nicht von Bedeutung, da diese lediglich eine Politik zu fhren hatte, die die Aufrechterhaltung der offiziellen Goldparitt gewhrleistete. Im Zusammenhang mit der Loslsung des Frankens vom Gold muss der Rahmen, innerhalb dessen sich 8 die Geldpolitik abspielt, neu definiert werden. Dabei sind zwei Punkte von zentraler Bedeutung: die klare Definition des Auftrags der Notenbank und die Unabhngigkeit der geldpolitischen Behrde bei der Erfllung ihres Auftrags. Die Diskussion um den Auftrag der Nationalbank whrend der vergangenen Monate ist teilweise ins Emotionale abgeglitten. Dies ist angesichts der heutigen Probleme der schweizerischen Wirtschaft verstndlich. Im Zusammenhang mit der Formulierung des Auftrag der SNB muss jedoch das langfristige Gesamtinteresse der schweizerischen Volkswirtschaft im Vordergrund stehen, und es muss realistisch zwischen dem politisch Wnschbaren und dem geldpolitisch Machbaren unterschieden werden. So bestreitet niemand, dass Preisstabilitt, Wachstum und Vollbeschftigung gleichsam wnschenswerte wirtschaftspolitische Ziele sind. Mit der Geldpolitik lsst sich aber nur das erste Ziel, die Preisstabilitt, dauerhaft erreichen. Auf Wachstum und Beschftigung hat die Notenbank nur einen vorbergehenden und unsicheren Einfluss. In einer Situation wie der gegenwrtigen, in der praktisch keine Teuerung existiert, besteht eine gewisse Tendenz, Preisstabilitt als etwas Selbstverstndliches zu betrachten. Noch Anfang der 90er Jahre herrschten in der Schweiz jedoch Inflationsraten von beinahe 6%; unter diesen Umstnden war das Bewusstsein um die Schdlichkeit der Inflation viel strker prsent als heute. Es ist deshalb ntzlich, an dieser Stelle kurz an die Kosten der Inflation zu erinnern. Inflation wirkt wie eine Steuer auf Bargeldbestnde. Eine hohe Inflationsrate fhrt daher zur Haltung einer ineffizient tiefen Realkassa und verursacht unntige Transaktions- und Koordinationskosten. Zweitens erhht sich mit der Hhe der Inflation auch gleichzeitig die Inflationsvolatilitt. Eine volatile Inflationsrate verstrkt die Unsicherheit, die mit lngerfristig festgesetzten Preisen aller Art (Preise im engeren Sinne, Lhne, Zinsen, Mieten) zusammenhngt. Dies fhrt zu kostspieligen, aber unvollstndigen Schutzmassnahmen gegen die Inflationsunsicherheit wie die Verkrzung der Vertragsdauer oder die Indexierung von Vertrgen. Weiter kann Inflationsunsicherheit zum Einbau von Risikoprmien fhren, z.B. auf den Zinsen, aber auch auf anderen Preisen. 9 Schliesslich bewirken unantizipierte Inflationsschwankungen eine willkrliche Umverteilung von Einkommen und Vermgen, die meist die sozial Schwcheren besonders hart trifft. Drittens lst eine hohe Inflationsrate fundamental nicht gerechtfertigte Verschiebungen in den Preisrelationen zwischen verschiedenen Produkten oder Produktegruppen aus. Diese Verzerrungen im Preissystem verringern die Effizienz der Mrkte und fhren zur Fehlallokation von knappen Ressourcen. Insgesamt haben die aufgezhlten Kosten der Inflation negative Konsequenzen fr das Wirtschaftswachstum. So haben empirische Untersuchungen gezeigt, dass Lnder mit hohen Inflationsraten im lngerfristigen Durchschnitt tiefere Wachstumsraten aufweisen als Lnder mit einer niedrigen Inflationsrate. Obwohl in der kurzen Frist Zielkonflikte zwischen Preisstabilitt einerseits und Wachstum bzw. Beschftigung andererseits auftreten knnen, leistet eine auf Preisstabilitt ausgerichtete Geldpolitik somit einen positiven Beitrag zum langfristigen Wirtschaftswachstum. Wie kann das Ziel der Preisstabilitt am besten erreicht werden? In der Wirtschaftswissenschaft besteht Einigkeit darber, dass Preisstabilitt am besten gewhrleistet werden kann, wenn die Geldpolitik in die Hnde einer unabhngigen Zentralbank gelegt wird. Durch die Delegation der Geldpolitik an eine unabhngige Instanz wird verhindert, dass in schwierigen Situationen kurzfristige Partikularinteressen vor die langfristigen Interessen der Volkswirtschaft als ganzer gestellt werden. Die positive Beziehung zwischen der Unabhngigkeit einer Notenbank und der Stabilitt einer Whrung wird durch zahlreiche empirische Untersuchungen besttigt. In der Praxis wird verschiedentlich argumentiert, unabhngige Notenbanken verfolgten das Ziel der Preisstabilitt zu stur und reagierten zu wenig auf konjunkturelle Schwankungen. Gemss dieser Kritik produzieren unabhngige Zentralbanken zwar eine niedrige Inflationsrate, aber nur um den Preis einer verstrkten zyklischen Instabilitt. Empirische Untersuchungen knnen diesen Vorwurf nicht sttzen. So weisen im internationalen Vergleich Lnder mit unabhngigen Zentralbank keine hhere Outputvariabilitt auf als Lnder, in denen die Notenbank der Regierung unterstellt ist. 10 Diese Ergebnisse lassen sich auch theoretisch erklren. So ist eine unabhngige Notenbank mglicherweise weniger bestrebt, konjunkturelle Schwankungen aktiv zu gltten. Umgekehrt wird aber eine auf Stabilitt ausgerichtete, stetige Geldpolitik selbst weniger zur Ursache von Konjunkturschwankungen als eine aktivistische Politik mit ihren zahlreichen Informations- und Lagproblemen. Indem sich diese beiden Effekte gegenseitig kompensieren, fhrt eine unabhngige Zentralbank nicht zu einer hheren Outputvariabilitt. Die Autonomie der Notenbank ist jedoch nicht absolut zu verstehen; sie bezieht sich vielmehr auf die Entscheidungs- und Handlungsfreiheit in bezug auf ein bestimmtes Ziel. Die Vorgabe dieses Zieles liegt in einer Demokratie in der Kompetenz der Politik und letztlich beim Volk. Die Notenbank ist auf einen breiten gesellschaftlichen Konsens ber ihres oberstes Ziel angewiesen; auf die Dauer kann sie ihre Politik nicht ohne grundstzliche Untersttzung durch die Bevlkerung fhren. Eine unabhngige Notenbank ist somit kein Fremdkrper in der Demokratie. Zurck zur Reform der Whrungsverfassung. Notenbankunabhngigkeit und Preisstabilittsziel sind in den heutigen gesetzlichen Grundlagen nicht explizit verankert. Dennoch besass die Schweizerische Nationalbank in der Praxis ein hohes Mass an Autonomie und verfolgte das vorrangige Ziel der Preisstabilitt. Insofern handelt es sich bei der geplanten Festschreibung von Unabhngigkeit und Preisstabilittsziel im wesentlichen um eine Anpassung der Whrungsverfassung an die praktizierte Whrungsrealitt. Gleichzeitig passt die Schweiz ihre Notenbankgesetzgebung auch den im Vertrag von Maastricht geforderten und inzwischen in ganz Europa gngigen Standards an. 3.3. Sicherung des Vertrauens durch hohe Whrungsreserven Die geltende Verfassung schreibt vor, dass der Notenumlauf durch Gold und kurzfristige Guthaben gedeckt sein msse. Unter dem Goldstandard und unter dem System fixer Wechselkurse diente diese Vorschrift der Eindmmung des Geldmengenwachstums. Unter flexiblen Wechselkursen ist dieser Bremsmechanismus ausser Kraft gesetzt. Ist der Wechselkurs flexibel, so kann die Notenbank die Geldmenge im 11 Prinzip beliebig erhhen, indem sie Devisen gegen Franken kauft. Folge einer im Vergleich zum Ausland bermssigen Geldmengenexpansion ist eine Abwertung des Frankens. Im heutigen Whrungssystem kommen den Whrungsreserven daher andere Aufgaben zu als unter fixen Wechselkursen. Whrungsreserven dienen der Vorbeugung und berwindung allflliger Krisen und liefern damit einen Stabilisierungsbeitrag. Ganz allgemein verstrken hohe Whrungsreserven das Vertrauen in eine Whrung, ohne dass man diesen Einfluss genau beziffern knnte. Aus diesem Grund wird auch die neue Whrungsverfassung das Halten von ausreichenden Whrungsreserven vorschreiben. Die Hhe der notwendigen Reserven bemisst sich vor allem an der Grsse und am Grad der Auslandverflechtung eines Landes. Als kleine, offene Volkswirtschaften wird die Schweiz auch in Zukunft im Verhltnis zu ihrem Bruttoinlandprodukt hhere Reserven halten als grosse, binnenorientierte Lnder. Die internationale Bedeutung des Finanzplatzes Schweiz ist natrlich ein weiteres Argument fr das Halten umfangreicher Reserven. 4. Die Geldpolitik auf dem Prfstand Neben einem gnstigen institutionellen Rahmen braucht die Nationalbank fr ein erfolgreiches Erfllen ihrer Aufgabe auch ein funktionierendes operatives Konzept. Wie Sie wissen, hat die Nationalbank seit einiger Zeit gewisse Schwierigkeiten mit ihrer auf der Steuerung der Basisgeldmenge beruhenden Strategie. Mein Kollege Hans Meyer hat sich in seinem krzlichen Referat hier in St. Gallen ausfhrlich zu diesem Thema geussert. Ich selbst werde mich in diesem Punkt daher kurz fassen. 4.1 Probleme der traditionellen Geldmengenpolitik und mgliche Alternativen Nach dem Zusammenbruch des Fixkurssystems gingen viele Lnder, unter anderem auch die Schweiz, zu einer auf der Steuerung der Geldmenge basierenden Geldpolitik ber. Diese Politik beruht auf dem Zusammenhang zwischen Geldmenge und nominalem Bruttosozialprodukt. Konkret wird Preisstabilitt gewhrleistet, wenn die Geldmenge mittelfristig im Gleichschritt mit dem Produktionspotential der Wirtschaft 12 wchst, gegebenenfalls korrigiert um eine Zu- oder Abnahme der Umlaufgeschwindigkeit. Eine Politik der Geldmengensteuerung liefert solange gute Ergebnisse, als der oben beschriebene Zusammenhang relativ stabil und vorhersehbar ist. Stete, trendmssige Vernderungen der Geldnachfrage knnen von der Geldpolitik ebenfalls problemlos bercksichtigt werden. Schwierigkeiten entstehen jedoch, wenn die Geldnachfrage sich hufig, wesentlich und unvorhersehbar verndert. Ursache solcher Schwankungen sind vor allem Finanzinnovationen, aber auch gesetzliche Vernderungen oder nderungen in den Zahlungs- und Anlagegewohnheiten des Publikums, wobei diese Elemente oft interdependent sind. Gegen Mitte der 80er Jahre fhrten die einsetzende Deregulierung und Liberalisierung der Finanzmrkte und die damit einhergehenden Finanzinnovationen besonders in den angelschsischen Lndern zu einem weitgehenden Zusammenbruch der Beziehung zwischen dem Wachstum der Geldmenge und der Inflationsrate. In der Folge gaben viele Lnder die Geldmengenpolitik auf und wandten sich anderen geldpolitischen Konzepten zu. In der Schweiz, und brigens auch in Deutschland, scheint mittelfristig noch eine relativ stabile Beziehung zwischen Geldmenge und Inflation zu bestehen. In jngster Zeit hatte jedoch auch die Schweizerische Nationalbank mit Schwierigkeiten bei der von ihr gesteuerten Notenbankgeldmenge zu kmpfen. Das Vorliegen gewisser Probleme bei einem geldpolitischen Konzept muss nicht automatisch zu dessen Aufgabe fhren. Vielmehr muss sorgfltig geprft werden, ob Alternativen existieren, die zu besseren Resultaten fhren. Von den verschiedenen Alternativen mchte ich hier nur die zwei diskutieren, die mir am relevantesten erscheinen: nmlich die Fixierung des Wechselkurses und die Verfolgung eines direkten Inflationsziels. Durch die Bindung der eigenen Whrung an diejenige eines Leitwhrungslandes wird die Frage des geldpolitischen Konzepts auf das Leitwhrungsland bertragen. Je nach geldpolitischem Erfolg des Leitwhrungslandes wird Preisstabilitt somit ber den Wechselkurs importiert. Ein fester Wechselkurs kann fr Lnder von Vorteil 13 sein, die aus strukturell-technischen Grnden oder aufgrund mangelnder Glaubwrdigkeit Mhe mit der Inflationskontrolle haben. Der hauptschliche Nachteil einer Wechselkurs bindung ist der Verlust an geldpolitischer Autonomie, der sich in einer Angleichung der Zinsen an das auslndische Niveau ussert. Im konkreten Fall der Schweiz wre sehr wahrscheinlich mit einem deutlichen Anstieg des Zinsniveaus zu rechnen. Die zentrale Frage bei jeder Wechselkursbindung ist deren Glaubwrdigkeit. Angesichts der Offenheit und der Dynamik der Finanzmrkte wrde eine Anbindung des Frankens an eine Leitwhrung nur dann zur gewnschten Wechselkursstabilitt fhren, wenn diese Bindung als dauerhaft angesehen wrde. Die Erfahrungen der letzten Jahre mit dem EWS haben gezeigt, dass eine Fixierung des Wechselkurses nur Erfolg hat, wenn sie von einer koherenten geldpolitischen Integrationsstrategie begleitet wird. Da sich in der Schweiz keine klare Entwicklung in Richtung EU-Beitritt und somit zur bernahme des Euros abzeichnet, bleibt die Anbindung an die europische Einheitswhrung eine problematische Option. Die zweite Alternative, die direkte Verfolgung eines Inflationsziels, hat vor allem seit Anfang der 90er Jahre an Beliebtheit gewonnen. Bei der Verfolgung eines Inflationszieles prognostiziert die Notenbank die zuknftige Inflation und vergleicht die Prognose mit dem Ziel. Die Differenz zwischen Prognose und Ziel bestimmt die notwendige Anpassung der geldpolitischen Instrumente. Die Probleme einer auf ein Inflationsziel ausgerichteten Politik liegen zuerst in der Prognostizierbarkeit und dann in der kurzfristigen Kontrolle der Inflation. Die Prognose der Inflation ist mit grosser Unsicherheit verbunden, weil niemand, auch die Notenbank nicht, das wahre Modell der Volkswirtschaft kennt. Dies gilt umso mehr in einer kleinen offenen Volkswirtschaft wie der Schweiz, wo externe Einflsse eine bedeutende Rolle spielen. Gleichzeitig kann die Notenbank die Inflation nicht kurzfristig und vollkommen przise, sondern nur im mittelfristigen Trend kontrollieren. So wird die Inflationsrate vorbergehend von verschiedenen Faktoren beeinflusst, die nicht unter der Kontrolle der Notenbank stehen. Die Strategie der direkten Verfolgung eines Inflationsziels hat sich bisher vor allem in Lndern bewhrt, in denen die Notenbank Mhe hatte, die Mrkte von ihrem Willen 14 zur Inflationsbekmpfung zu berzeugen. In diesem Umfeld ging von der Ankndigung eines Inflationsziels eine Signalwirkung aus, die einen Politikwechsel anzeigte. Die Schweizeische Nationalbank hingegen geniesst das Vertrauen der Mrkte, so dass ein explizites Inflationsziel kaum Signalwirkung htte. Bei nherem Hinschauen erweist sich zudem, dass sich geldpolitische Strategien mit Inflations- bzw. Geldmengenziel in der Praxis nicht so grundstzlich von einander unterscheiden, wie man spontan meinen knnte. Notenbanken mit einem direkten Inflationsziel bercksichtigen neben anderen Variablen auch die Entwicklung der Geldmenge bei der Erstellung ihrer Prognosen der Preisentwicklung. Umgekehrt verfolgt die Nationalbank ihr Geldmengenziel nicht als Selbstzweck, sondern als Zwischenziel auf dem Weg zur Preisstabilitt. Neben der Geldmenge schenkt die Nationalbank auch noch anderen Variablen Beachtung. Falls diese Indikatoren im Hinblick auf das Endziel der Preisstabilitt ein Abweichen vom Geldmengenziel deutlich nahelegen, so ist die Nationalbank bereit, diese Abweichungen zuzulassen. Die Diskussion der verschiedenen Strategien zeigt die Komplexitt des gegenwrtigen Umfelds der Geldpolitik auf. Es existiert keine einfache Lsung, die in jeder Situation eine klare Antwort gibt. Vielmehr verlangt die Geldpolitik nach einem globalen Ansatz, innerhalb dessen Indikatoren der Marktliquiditt eine prioritre Rolle spielen, der aber gleichzeitig auch andere Variablen wie die Wechselkurse oder die Zinsstruktur zur Beurteilung der Lage beizieht. 4.2 Die Strategie der Schweizeischen Nationalbank Zweifellos spielten und spielen auch heute noch die monetren Aggregate in der schweizerischen Geldpolitik eine zentrale Rolle, obwohl gewisse Interpretationsprobleme bestehen. So wird die Aussagekraft unseres traditionellen Indikators, der Notenbankgeldmenge M0, gegenwrtig durch verschiedene Schocks beeintrchtigt. Die genaue Abgrenzung und Erklrung der Schocks ist schwierig und mit grosser Unsicherheit verbunden. Dennoch versuchen wir, das Ausmass dieser Schocks abzuschtzen und die Notenbankgeldmenge entsprechend zu bereinigen. Betrachten wir die bereinigte Notenbankgeldmenge, so zeigt sich, dass unsere gegenwrtige Politik keine Gefahr fr die zuknftige Preisentwicklung darstellt. 15 Zustzlich zu M0 beobachten wir vermehrt M3. Das Aggregat M3 weist eine besonders enge mittelfristige Beziehung zum Preisniveau auf. So folgt auf eine starke Ausdehnung von M3 nach etwa drei Jahren ein Anstieg der Teuerung. Im Vergleich zu M0 hat M3 den Nachteil, dass wir es weniger direkt und przise steuern knnen als M0. Auch das heutige Wachstumstempo von M3 steht im Einklang mit einem auf mittlere Sicht stabilen Preisniveau. Die Volatilitt der Finanzmrkte ist eine Realitt, mit der wir permanent leben und die wir bercksichtigen mssen. Deshalb beobachten wir die Entwicklung der Wechselkurse und der Zinsstruktur mit grosser Aufmerksamkeit. Es wre fatal fr die schweizerische Wirtschaft, wenn wir uns durch ein stures Konzept binden wrden. Die heutige Lage verlangt Flexibilitt. 5. Schlussbemerkungen Wie wir gesehen haben, fehlt es in der heutigen, durch rasche Vernderungen geprgten Welt nicht an Herausforderungen fr eine Zentralbank. Das Umfeld, in dem die Schweizerische Nationalbank operiert, ist heute geprgt durch Liberalisierung, Deregulierung, eine starke globale Vernetzung und eine teilweise atemberaubende Dynamik der Finanzmrkte. Zustzlich tritt demnchst -direkt vor der schweizerischen Haustr- das ehrgeizige Projekt der Europischen Whrungsunion in seine dritte und letzte Phase. Ich bin zuversichtlich, dass wir fr diese Herausforderungen gut vorbereitet sind. Der neue gesetzliche Rahmen, der der Bank Unabhngigkeit bei der Durchfhrung der Geldpolitik garantiert und ihr das vorrangige Ziel der Preisstabilitt vorgibt, bildet eine gnstige Voraussetzung fr die Weiterfhrung unserer im internationalen Vergleich insgesamt recht erfolgreichen Stabilittspolitik. Auch in Zukunft werden wir unser auf der Steuerung der Notenbankgeldmenge basierendes geldpolitisches Konzept pragmatisch und flexibel handhaben. Dabei haben wir stets das Gesamtinteresse der Wirtschaft im Visier. Die von der Nationalbank angestrebte Stabilitt der monetren Rahmenbedingungen dient schlussendlich dem Gesamtinteresse des Landes. 16

Title: Swiss economy in global change
text: Swiss economy undergoing global change An assessment of economic policy Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Presentation at the General Assembly of the Association of Bernese Economists on 25 March 1998 in Bern Bern, 25 March 1998 2 I was very happy to accept the invitation to today's presentation. The AGM of the alumni is a fitting occasion to symbolically say thank you to our Bernese alma mater for the longer or less long training semesters that we were able to spend at Hochschulstrasse 4. I know that this opening of the presentation is unspectacular at a time when demands and accusations against the state seem much more contemporary than a word of thanks to one of its institutions. But that is precisely why this sign is important to me, especially in our circle, which we were allowed to participate in the privilege of a university education. In terms of content, the choice fell on a topic of Swiss economic policy. Not only because I work in this field today. Also because in my memory of my studies, the confrontation with economic policy has remained particularly vivid. It is inextricably linked to Paul Stocker's committed, exciting and even infectious performances, first in lecture hall 31. Five months before the 25th anniversary of his death on August 28, all those who were able to experience him will remember him gratefully. Swiss economy in global change - an economic policy assessment. The topic requires a holistic view of change and its consequences. The attempt to look at the spheres of life of society, the economy and the political system in isolation seems unsuitable, as is all too often the practice. The specialist's narrow view of the problems of changing trade and investment flows, processes of social disintegration or questions of legitimacy of international organizations may lead to useful insights, but not to viable concepts and useful answers to the question of what to do. In addition, it should be clear that the way we react to change, try to master it, must be far more than the effort of technocrats to do what is supposedly right. It is also and imperatively about goals and values, about balancing interests, fairness and credibility. Moreover, we must respectfully accept that we think and decide under uncertainty and do not know much that we should know. To use Paul Stocker's formulation: Even in the corps material of economic policy, there is no "futurometer" complete by budget. Always 3 again we are surprised and forced to revise our assessment of the situation and the use of measures. Economic policy is also and essentially an attempt to take the right steps on a steep and bumpy learning curve. After a few remarks on the causes of globalisation, I would like to reflect on its consequences, with a focus on the labour market and the social consequences therein. In the second part of the presentation, I turn to the question of what we should do in terms of economic policy to improve our chances of successful adjustment and to resist imminent undesirable developments. Globalization Globalization is the central concept of any reflection on change in the arsenal of fears and hopes. A dazzling word, certainly. Abused for the devoted bow to the relentless penetrating power of the market, from which any attempt at political design bounces off ineffectively. Also abused as a stimulant of fear to generate feelings of political powerlessness and being at the mercy of others. What globalization means is certainly not radically new, if only because the view that everything about history is unique is a fallacy. Equally erroneous is the opposite idea that history always repeats itself. Globalisation is something more far-reaching than just the continuation of trade liberalisation, even if it is true that globalisation and deregulation reinforce each other, thus creating economic, social and political constraints. Globalization is not a politically desired program that has ever been voted on anywhere. Globalization is - similar to a natural event - simply there, decisive as a result of technical development. In particular, advances in information and communication technology have three immediate consequences, which are new in scope: (a) Firstly, a growing number of products and debt and equity are entering larger, in extreme cases global markets. This means more competition, especially since the field of competitors has become much more heterogeneous. Increasingly, the chances of hiding in this world are dwindling. 4 b) Secondly, the new technologies allow a rigorous optimization and control of production with a high degree of transparency of success. This leads in particular to vertical specialization at different locations. The location-based exporter is supplemented and partly replaced by the transnational company. c) Thirdly, progress in information technology is enabling productivity gains in the service sector as never before in history. This results in an impressive efficiency potential. At the same time, however, a substitution process that has facilitated structural change in recent decades threatens to weaken, namely the absorption of released industrial resources by the service sector. Globalization is not a state of affairs, but a process that has begun and will continue - with new processes, in additional production areas and other regions that have so far been little affected. Certainly, nothing can avoid two insights. Firstly, that globalisation is an irreversible process as long as we do not abolish the premise of the peaceful coexistence of peoples. And secondly, that globalization opens up an undreamt-of potential for prosperity for the world as a whole. There can be no doubt about this: it opens up unprecedented opportunities for prosperity, security and development for countless people. Setbacks, as we have experienced in recent months, fundamentally do not change this finding. Values and institutions under stress But globalization creates adjustment constraints, in emerging countries no less than in mature industrialized and service countries, for companies no less than for workers, also for the state and its institutions. Tried and tested and familiar things are coming under pressure, even in our country. Thus, the market, this historically powerful manifestation of the idea of freedom, is increasingly becoming the source of adjustment constraints, the justification for renunciation and restriction in the service of competitiveness. 5 And the social partnership, once a proven vehicle for the consensual reconciliation of interests, is threatened by superimposed conflicts of interest. If mobility means power, the balance of power between capital and labour must change to the detriment of labour, because labour is and remains less mobile than capital. Under the regime of open location competition, a competitive relationship between workers at different locations arises for the favor of capital that is always ready for allocation. This creates new conditions when Swiss employers talk to Swiss employees about wages and social benefits. Our dual economic structure, characterised by the coexistence of a competitive international sector with a largely protected domestic economy governed by consensus, is urgently called into question. This subtle combination of openness with internal economic-social stability, also favored by state-building, proves to be a fair-weather structure that presupposes scope for distribution that hardly exists today, at least no longer at the collectively scheduled level of the economy as a whole or entire industries. Finally, globalized competition leads to a loss of significance of the nation as a mental category and unit of action. The nation  once a key concept of national economy  is no longer a central unit under the condition of open product and capital markets. Market boundaries result from the characteristics of goods and demand, as illustrated by the comparison between a neighborhood bistro and a car manufacturer. And Ricardo's famous theory of comparative cost advantages no longer has much to do with the new world: for it examines the advantageousness of commodity trade under the obsolete condition of the geographical immobility of capital. The strength of an economy is no longer determined by the strength of its national enterprises. Global actors are homeless, they are hardly standard bearers of the country in which they originated and incorporated. They are more likely to be guests staying in the country, as long as they find the best possible conditions. Instead, the strength of the national economy is shaped by its 6 Attractiveness of the location and the added value that - by whatever kind of company is provided at the location. As a result, national politics suffers a conspicuous loss of sovereign agency. The constraints of locational competition require in many areas the renunciation of one's own path - for example in tax law, trade policy or competition law. The relationship between the state and transnational corporations is undergoing a qualitative change, because these actors are no longer dependent on a national legal order for better or for worse, because - much more concretely than before - the option of leaving is open to them. Rather exaggerated, but not without an accurate core, are the images of the "comprehensible legislation through the photocopier" or even the formula of the "economy that eats politics". Such allusions generate widespread fear, because obviously vested interests are in danger. What threatens is a demonization of the globalization process with suggestive buzzwords such as "turbo-capitalism", "social ice age" and "dehumanised competition". This easily leads to disastrous wrong reactions. Avoiding them is a difficult communicative challenge. Competition and structural change - such terms are difficult to translate into populist slogans. And the ritualistic formula that change entails not only risks but also opportunities, proves to be an inadequate sedative, because adjustment losses can usually be estimated more concretely and occur faster than restructuring advantages, and because different groups are affected by the advantages and disadvantages. What is needed is factual and comprehensible information and the renunciation of opinion makers to play with fears, to instrumentalize them in the service of special interests or out of greed for publicity. Focus on the labour market and social coherence In general, but especially for a highly developed economy, the consequences of globalization on the labor market are of central importance. Simply because they affect people most directly and questions 7 to the continued existence of our free, coherent society. In contrast to the dispositive of optimizing companies, there are no surplus personnel units in democratically constituted companies. Unemployment is becoming a serious challenge and a critical test for the democracies of the West and their social market economy order. Now, unemployment is certainly not primarily the result of globalization. It has its roots in cyclical upheavals and structural weaknesses, skills shortages and institutional incentives that have always played a role. It is difficult to assess the impact of globalised competition on the labour market and how this factor is shaping the employment problem. Two partial effects are likely to be in the foreground. On the one hand, the requirements for flexibility are increasing. Not only, but reinforced by globalization, the model of the life profession and the place of life loses its economic basis. This has implications for training on the supply side, but above all on the demand side in the sense of personal willingness to devote time and energy to learning. The individual planning of gainful employment, training time and other activities is becoming more diverse and changeable. The more this combinatorial diversity becomes established, the more inadequate institutional rules become that bind rights and demands to a profession or even to a workplace. Occupational flexibility requires institutional mobility, otherwise it becomes unfair. Flexibility entails opportunities and risks. The chance for a more comprehensive realization of personal life plans. The risk of not meeting the increased demands on the ability to learn and the reorientation suffers from uncertainties with stressful consequences for family and community. Certainly, flexibility is a contrast to rigidity, but also to protection and security. If Manpower is the largest employer in the USA today, this certainly demonstrates a high degree of flexibility. But aren't we at the same time reminded of the sad image of just-in-time workers, of modern day labourers? Secondly, the thesis that - shaped by the qualification structure - the differences in labour income will increase is largely undisputed. Indicative of this are the experiences of the USA in the 90s. Admittedly, the 8 registered disparity increases are not huge, but they refer to cyclically very good years and will certainly increase as economic activity slows. Now, income differences are not a bad thing and by no means incompatible with the idea of a civil society, to name Ralf Dahrendorf. However, the problem - and incompatible with the idea of a civil society - would be a development which, at the lower end of the qualification spectrum, excludes an entire middle class from working life, because it is simply no longer needed, because GNP can grow without it. It would be excluded from our society, with no prospect of advancement and participation. Despite all the uncertainties surrounding the labour market consequences of technical progress and globalised competition, it is clear that politics and business will be tested most sustainably in dealing with the weakest and least qualified, the actual losers of adaptation. Not an easy test for a society that wants to secure prosperity opportunities for all, social coherence and personal freedom in the future. Selected fields of action In these circumstances, it is appropriate to think about strategies and measures that can improve the development opportunities of our country. I would like to do this - incompletely and selectively - from the four perspectives of the attractiveness of the location, competition at home, the labour market and the need for political adjustment. 1. Attractiveness of the location The globalization of markets and production is taking place. It is a date, whether you like it or not. It is certainly not threatened by a referendum. It is unrealistic, even dishonest, to fight in public with more politically pleasing options that no longer exist and will no longer exist in the foreseeable future. A small, world-integrated country like Switzerland has no alternative to rapidly adapting to the changed competitive conditions except that of the 9 Impoverishment. This leads to a massaging of constraints in business and politics, again and again to decision-making situations with few variants, often only one. Key players in the adaptation process are the companies that carry out value-added activities in Switzerland. Without their success, the adaptation cannot succeed. As a necessary condition, this presupposes a high degree of attractiveness as a location, which calls for the political process. No one will complain about a lack of concepts and recipes. But writing and speaking are easier than acting. Nothing illustrates this more impressively than the in principle hardly disputed and urgent effort to bring the federal budget and social services into financial balance. Part of the difficulties lies in the fact that measures for the attractiveness of the location often amount to relief of the capital factor and therefore fall into the wake of crippling distribution discussions. In Switzerland, this effect should be somewhat moderated by the fact that broader sections of the population receive capital income via the cover capital of the second pillar than in countries with pay-as-you-go systems. But many citizens lack any understanding of the connections, because in this country the economy has largely taken place outside the classrooms: that increased investments can create and maintain jobs, and that high labor incomes are only possible with high labor productivity, and these are only possible with high capital investment. All too easily, the attempt at consensus fails because the public dispute is much more interested in zero-sum games, in the question of how a given cake is distributed than in the more complex task of baking a bigger and better cake. More relentlessly than in the past, prosperity is a question of relative attractiveness as a location - an economic policy that ignores this realization is certain to fail. 2. Domestic competition In my opinion, the most important, most urgent level of action relates to the market-based renewal at home. The goods and services of the so-called domestic sector are also included as cost factors in the 10 International competition is sensitive: prices for food, craft services, consulting services and public infrastructure services. In an international comparison, we perform poorly here - many things are much more expensive than elsewhere. Our consumer goods prices are top worldwide. Compared to the EU average, the gap is close to 50%. Even if food is not taken into account as a kind of special case, the price differences to the detriment of Switzerland remain very large, as the WTO pointed out in 1996 in the Policy Review on Switzerland. Almost without exception, our country is substantially more expensive in the product groups studied. In part, this is due to the comparatively high per capita income, but for the greater part it manifests competitive shortcomings and regulations that have led to inefficient, too costly structures. Moreover, sector analyses  and this is the other half of our domestic problem  show that our public sector is very complex by OECD standards. Further reform energy is essential in this area. The revitalisation programme brings some important progress, but the process of internal reforms is slower and less far-reaching than the liberalisation of product markets, which would have been effective in our country by joining the European Economic Area. Certainly, much is in motion, in the public and private sectors. The Internal Market Act must also be implemented in the cantons and communes by this summer at the latest. The consequences of the decree are probably underestimated. With the monitoring commission at the BAWI and the right of appeal for discriminated providers, he certainly has teeth, and that's a good thing. Alone, the revitalization takes time. For the time being, the dismantling of commercial cartels leads to overcapacities that only erode viscously. The same applies to the numerous import cartels in whose shadow inefficient distribution structures have formed - for example, a world record-breaking car garage density. After all, it will probably only be possible under the pressure of the free movement of persons with the EU to 11 to achieve competitive, reasonably Euro-compatible price structures in the so-called liberal professions. It is revenge that our relationship to competition in the post-war period was very ambivalent. Economic freedom as a right to free private-sector gainful employment has a rich expression in our country, which in its exaggerated form even included the option of partial or complete collective renunciation of competition. A much less important role - compared to Anglo-Saxon countries, for example - has traditionally been played by competition as a guarantor of the lowest possible prices for the benefit of consumers: the obligation to compete as a correlate to the right to free commercial activity. This peculiarity of our economic cultural history may explain why we have lived for so long with competitive deficits that reduce prosperity, have not eliminated them out of our own conviction and now have to take action on many fronts and very quickly because of our international competitiveness - and justified by this. Competition at home - this also has a connection to the question of the control of companies, to the problem of corporate governance. History has produced two models. The Anglo-Saxon type, characterized by lively trading and the ongoing valuation of property rights in the open capital market, structurally characterized by the existence of many, often active but only exceptionally dominant shareholders. Their value-driven behaviour represents a permanent risk of dismissal and takeover for the company's management. This model is preceded by the more corporate type of corporate management on the European continent and in Japan, characterized by large fixed participations and a high bank influence, at least a structure of property rights that minimizes the risk of takeover. Is globalization causing the advance of the Anglo-Saxon model? The question should be answered in the affirmative. In the fight for scarce, internationally mobile risk capital, locations will suffer from disadvantages if they hinder or even override the control processes of the capital market through legal or private regulations. From this perspective 12 Our country could very well benefit from the fact that capital market-related corporate control has reached a much stronger extent in this country than in the major continental European economies. With a market capitalization of Swiss equities that far exceeds gross domestic product, our capital market clearly assumes Anglo-Saxon proportions. In any case, it is much more important than in our neighbouring countries. This structural feature and the fact that the legislator has implemented renewal steps with the new stock corporation law and the Stock Exchange Act that sustainably strengthen corporate governance via the capital market should facilitate the adjustment process, at least accelerate it. 3. Labour market and training From an economic, social and political point of view, further developments in the labour market and training are crucial. Anyone who argues in a completely understandable way that the low wage level in distant countries cannot be regarded as a guideline for desirable competitive fitness in this country must also accept that this is only possible under the condition of high labour productivity. This requires an above-average degree of labour market flexibility and an efficient, actively used training system. No one will deny that there are weaknesses here, for example in the enforcement of unemployment insurance, but also - despite impressive improvements in services - in the field of training. Not everywhere has the insight prevailed that with increased demands on occupational mobility, the responsibility for further training and professional skills lies primarily and decisively with the employees themselves. The responsibility for what you do, but also for what you don't do. If, as a result of change, the chances of getting a "job for life" disappear, which they undoubtedly do, employability becomes the decisive occupational quality and the dominant determinant of individual unemployment risk. This requires self-responsible care, commitment and sacrifice. Education is rarely to have with pleasurable play, usually only with effort. 13 Such reservations, however, do not change the general finding that our country is well equipped in these areas. This applies to the education system, which has a major strength in the widespread vocational training system, which makes it much easier to enter employment than in other systems. The measures taken to promote horizontal mobility between training courses and the effort initiated to set up universities of applied sciences are also proving to be beneficial. With regard to the efficiency of the labour market, an OECD study published last year even gives Switzerland top marks. In fact, any comparison between countries leads to the conclusion that our labour market is much closer to the Anglo-Saxon model in terms of flexibility than to the far more rigid labour market structures of the large continental European countries. Our starting conditions are therefore good, but at a time of increased job risks, in which about 1/5 of the working population have now experienced unemployment themselves, setbacks and undesirable developments triggered by the motive of securing the acquis cannot be ruled out. All the more so since such initiatives cannot be denied the populist appeal. Precisely because our labour market generally functions efficiently, I am not pessimistic about the future of the Swiss employment problem. With all the well-founded indications of structural weaknesses that have not yet been overcome - first of all in the domestic sector - we should not overlook the fact that we have the longest economic weakness phase of the post-war period behind us. You have to keep that in mind when dealing with country comparisons. If we manage to achieve positive growth of just over 2% in our country for a few years, the chances are intact that unemployment will decrease and recede in the direction of the structural unemployment rate of about 3%. 3% - this is certainly not the perfect world. But this figure compares to an IMF estimate of non-cyclical unemployment in the EU of around 9%. Here our country has an important relative strength and an element of competitive fitness that others will have to fight for for a long time to come. 14 Our core problem is the rapid rise in long-term unemployment since 1993, which has now reached the OECD average at around one third. There are several reasons for this. One is of an institutional nature. At 520 days, the maximum duration of unemployment benefits in our country is very long, as the OECD has also critically pointed out. This regime can lead to the unemployed remaining unemployed for too long and thus largely losing touch with employment, thereby increasing structural unemployment and the adjustment rate. The main reason, however, lies in the obvious educational, professional and linguistic skills deficits in this area. Here, too, the long-term consequences of the seasonal workers' statute with entitlement to establishment, which is already disadvantageous from a structural point of view, have a negative effect. Statistical surveys and the experience of the regional placement offices confirm with convincing clarity: both the risk of becoming unemployed and the average duration of unemployment increase sharply with decreasing qualifications. Therefore, the priority for action must lie in training and integration efforts. Only in this way will it be possible to limit the economically and socially very stressful problem of long-term unemployment. However, it cannot be completely solved. Because there must be no illusions about this. The combination of global competition with labour market flexibility creates a socio-political compulsion to act in the segment of the disadvantaged for some reason and the least qualified. It is important to react to it in a meaningful way. Not by trying to eliminate the market here, but by correcting unacceptable market results with redistributive measures. 4. Required political system Even a selective sketch of the implications of global economic changes cannot avoid questions of general political reach. A rapidly growing part of economic processes takes place globally, unimpressed by national borders, indeed quite mobile enough, national 15 To avoid or seek spaces with their social, fiscal and legal characteristics. This creates and increases tensions. Global mobility undermines the sphere of influence of sovereign nation states and thus the credibility of the Contrat Social, which by its very nature is based on a national consensus. It easily leads to fears and feelings of powerlessness in the less mobile factors. Globalization is a process in the large space that can provide little evidence of identification, hardly a framework for social integration and certainly no basis for the lived and experienced homeland. The world society is at best a vision - the chances are low that it will ever be able to perform the functions that fall to the traditional states. To believe that the political vacuum can be entrusted to the ordering hand of unregulated global competition is a fallacy. Human coexistence can be shaped in important areas, but not integrally with the principles of competition. Too important, indeed increasingly important under the influence of globalization, are glaring areas of market failure: externalities to the detriment of uninvolved third parties, public goods and the protection of minimum human rights and social standards. In view of these problems, international organisations in particular are called upon. Their roles and responsibilities must be strengthened if globalisation is not to suffer serious setbacks, for example in protectionist defensive reflexes. Three functions are in the foreground. Firstly, there are internationally enforceable rules of fair competition - access to the market and prevention of abuse of market power. In addition, this includes minimum standards with regard to the protection of human rights and - if global competition is to be sustainable - measures to safeguard our ecological foundations. Second, international organizations should support countries in building those political and economic conditions without which inclusion in the global division of labor becomes an irresponsible adventure. The International Monetary Fund and the Bank for International Settlements operate with such objectives in mind, with a solid track record so far, as we all know. And thirdly, there is a need for a 16 institutional crisis management mechanism that limits the external costs of shocks without incentivizing excessive risk preference. Indeed, successful participation in global competition presupposes a generally underestimated degree of political and regulatory convergence between states. Similar strategies are urgently needed, especially in the areas of monetary policy, public debt control, the design and regulation of the national financial sector and corporate governance. International organisations can and must play an increasingly important role in building these national conditions and coping with inevitable crisis setbacks: advisory, helpful, enforcing and controlling with performance requirements. Against the background of such changes, the question of Switzerland's ability to act politically also arises for the small state of Switzerland. Especially in an environment of accelerated change that eliminates and creates jobs, the need for an integrating, identity-creating and in a certain sense protective force is increasing. This task must fall decisively to the state. Its institutions must be able to involve our country more closely in international decision-making processes. Even a small player plays along and has well-known chances to represent his own interests with skill and expertise. Abstinence, on the other hand, is abstinence. It amounts to the passive and incapacitating reproduction of constraints that others have set. The question of whether and in what respect direct democracy stands in the way of the state's ability to act is controversial. To answer this only with yes or no would be too shortened. If numerous indications are not deceiving, in many countries - undoubtedly also in the European Union - the increase in importance of the supranational is followed by the demand for increased democratic legitimacy and the development of local competence. Sustainable foreign policy capacity cannot be achieved anywhere without a democratic balance that prevents the incapacitation of the citizen and the emergence of a distinct classe politique. The diverse 17 Complaints about the outdated sluggishness of our decision-making processes must not obscure the fact that a large part of the criticism of direct democracy amounts to a criticism of democracy. What is needed, however, are serious steps towards the essentialisation of direct democracy, at least a substantial increase in the number of signatures required for initiatives and referendums. Today, it is too easy to use the threat of a referendum to complicate the process of finding a solution and to block the government and parliament. The reform proposals based in the dispatch on the total revision point in the right direction. Whether they will be stronger than the waves of populist profiling manoeuvres and - even more critically - whether they will suffice in the long term is an open question. Concluding remark Ladies and gentlemen, I shall conclude. For our country and our economy, the starting position is much better than its reputation, which has suffered to an unrealistic extent after years of stagnation. Even if the economic situation has - finally and thank God - changed for the better, much remains to be done. Not only for politicians and officials, but for all those who bear responsibility in this country and have to stand up for solutions. In the portfolio of efforts necessary to successfully meet the challenges, the contribution of economics plays an indispensable role. This applies equally to their micro- and macroeconomic research and teaching areas. Although I have taught business administration myself, I do not want to hide the fact that I am concerned about the relative loss of importance of macroeconomics and economic policy, which is unmistakable throughout Switzerland. As important and right as it was to expand management teaching and finance in recent years, it would be unfortunate to let the pendulum swing too far now and in the future. It is therefore all the more grateful to note that our Bernese Faculty is very committed to the areas of expertise that are particularly important for economic policy. This will continue to suit her in the future in the service of the Public Service in the Federal Capital.

Title: Repurchase agreements (repos) - an innovation in the Swiss financial centre
text: Repurchase Agreements (repos) - An Innovation in the Swiss Financial Centre by Bruno Gehrig, Member of the Governing Board, Swiss National Bank Ladies and Gentlemen On behalf of the Swiss National Bank - and also of Swiss Securities Clearing Corporation (SEGA) and the Swiss Bankers' Association - I should like to welcome you to today's press conference. The focus of this gathering is on repurchase agreements (repos) - an innovation in the Swiss franc money market. In cooperation with the banks and the Swiss National Bank, SEGA has worked out a solution which we would like to present to you today. After my opening remarks, Mr Sporndli of the National Bank will introduce you to repos as a monetary policy instrument. Mr Fuglister, representing the Swiss Bankers' Association, will then explain the significance of the repo as a financial market instrument. Finally, Mr Haberli will sketch the services which SEGA will provide based on the existing infrastructure. The various contributions also include legal and technical aspects as these are considered to be valuable additional information. At the end of the presentation, we and a number of other experts will answer any questions you may have. What exactly is meant by a repurchase agreement? In a money market transaction known as repo the cash taker sells his own or borrowed securities to the cash provider. At the same time, it is agreed that the cash taker will repurchase paper of the same type and quantity from the cash provider at a later date. From an economic point of view, a repo is considered to be a secured loan, and the cash taker thus pays repo interest to the cash provider during the term of the agreement. To ensure cover in the event of price fluctuations, any deviations are compensated by daily margin transfers. Repos thus replace unsecured money market advances by secured forms of financing. Repurchase Agreements (repos) - An Innovation in the Swiss Financial Centre B. Gehrig, 17 April 1998 The introduction of repurchase agreements fulfils a common need of the banks and the National Bank. The advantage to the banks is that unsecured money market investments are replaced by an attractive securities-backed operation. And for the Swiss National Bank repos are an ideal addition to the existing range of monetary policy instruments. The institutional framework is conducive to a successful launching of the new financial instrument: fiscal aspects, capital adequacy requirements, the technical processing infrastructure and the amendments to the National Bank Law.  At the beginning of 1997 the Federal Department of Finance clarified the scope of federal stamp duty by confirming that repos are in principle not subject to this tax. The reason is that - economically speaking - repos are to be regarded as secured loans and not as purchases or sales of securities.  Capital adequacy rules are another aspect that make repos attractive from a cost point of view. As secured loans repos are not subject to capital adequacy requirements. The lender is only required to provide adequate capital for that part of the loan which may not be covered. This helps to save on equity costs, notably when compared with traditional unsecured interbank advances.  As far as processing is concerned, SEGA has provided an infrastructure which represents a safe and efficient solution with a minimum of processing risks. Moreover, the Swiss Stock Exchange has decided to provide a platform for repos on the basis of its electronic trading infrastructure.  Finally, a further precondition was fulfilled when the revised National Bank Law became effective in November 1997. Article 14 now explicitly authorises the National Bank to enter into repurchase agreements. 2 Repurchase Agreements (repos) - An Innovation in the Swiss Financial Centre B. Gehrig, 17 April 1998 While favourable conditions are of the essence for the success of the venture, they are not sufficient in themselves. The attractiveness of the new instrument depends very much on how it is structured. In a combined effort a marketable product has been developed. Let me briefly describe three main features:  The trading concept provides for standardised and non-standardised agreements. In over-the-phone trading both types of transactions may be concluded. Standardised agreements have the advantage of being more liquid, which in turn renders pricing more transparent. An electronic trading platform at the Swiss Stock Exchange would further enhance the efficiency of this instrument.  A second important prerequisite for success, in view of the size of our securities markets, is to be seen in the structure of repos, which is designed to conserve market liquidity. The securities lodged with the cash provider as collateral are not blocked in a closed custody account and thus withheld from the market for the entire duration of the repo. The opposite is the case: the cash provider can dispose of the securities at any time. While the possibility thus provided for a multiple use of the securities enhances market liquidity, it also makes higher demands on portfolio management by cash providers. The technical prerequisites for efficacious risk control, however, fully exist. We are convinced that the liquidity of the Swiss franc bond market will not be adversely affected by repo operations but, on the contrary, will probably be improved by them.  Repos, moreover, require a secure legal basis, making it possible, in the event of disruptions, to claim ownership rights with respect to the securities. The Swiss standard agreement on a multilateral basis adequately meets this requirement. 3 Repurchase Agreements (repos) - An Innovation in the Swiss Financial Centre B. Gehrig, 17 April 1998 Given the favourable environment, the attractive structuring and the cost-effective processing mode, we are confident that interbank trading will establish itself on a broad basis, which will also permit smaller banks to participate. Not only the individual participants stand to benefit from this new instrument. The replacement of unsecured credit relationships by secured loans as well as the step-by-step processing guaranteed by SEGA will heighten the safety of the entire system and thus strengthen the financial sector as a whole. The new financial market instrument is to be introduced gradually. On 20 April we will start with RepoLight, a simplified preliminary version with a limited circle of participants, which will replace our traditional swaps with federal money market debt register claims (MMDRCs). The full project is to be launched at the end of September 1998. 4

Title: The repurchase agreement (repo) as a monetary policy instrument
text: The Repurchase Agreement (Repo) as a Monetary Policy Instrument by Erich Sporndli, Director, Swiss National Bank As Mr Gehrig has already pointed out, the repo is an ideal addition to our range of monetary policy instruments. Before entering into the characteristic features of the new tool, I should briefly like to describe the instruments we are currently using for steering the money market. In longer-term steering of the market we fulfil the basic liquidity requirements of the banking system by means of foreign exchange swaps. To this end, we buy US dollars in exchange for Swiss francs while at the same time selling the dollars forward. These contracts, limited in time, are usually renewed by us after expiry. While the market for foreign exchange swaps is an extremely liquid market this instrument has the drawbacks that it exposes us to counterparty risks and that the circle of participants is limited. For the short-term steering of liquidity - fine-tuning we resort to swaps with money market debt register claims or the onward placing in the market of investments held with us by the Confederation. The limited liquidity potential is a disadvantage in the use of these two domestic instruments of the Swiss National Bank (SNB). What benefits do repos offer the SNB? Repo agreements are a versatile monetary policy instrument suitable both for creating and siphoning off liquidity. They can be used for longer-term and short-term steering of bank liquidity. Moreover, repos offer two considerable advantages, notably compared with foreign exchange swaps:  The circle of counterparties engaging in money market operations with the National Bank will become larger. The prescribed minimum transaction amount for repo agreements will be Sfr 1 million, also giving smaller banks direct access to the SNB. The Repurchase Agreement (Repo) as a Monetary Policy Instrument E. Sporndli, 17 April 1998  Repos are also an ideal monetary policy instrument for risk considerations: the delivery-versus-payment transaction guaranteed by SEGA eliminates the performance risk, to which we are particularly exposed in the case of foreign exchange swaps. Moreover, the market price risk attaching to the securities serving as collateral is averted by daily margin transfers. Repos thus meet high demands as regards their possible application, circle of participants and risk. In order to enter into a repo agreement with the National Bank, the counterparty must have securities eligible as collateral at the SNB. Naturally, the National Bank must require such securities to meet certain standards as regards quality. This leads to a conflict of aims: on the one hand, we are interested in a maximum market potential of securities eligible as collateral at the SNB and, on the other hand, the risks incurred must be minimised to the greatest extent possible. The present solution fulfils both requirements. The basket of securities has been designed to be broad. We also expect it to be suitable for repo agreements between the banks. This should help to prevent a segmentation of the market in the interest of liquidity. Debtor categories in the SNB's basket of securities Foreign banks (22%) International organisations (11%) Foreign governments (8%) Confederation (31%) Other Swiss debtors (28%) 2 The Repurchase Agreement (Repo) as a Monetary Policy Instrument E. Sporndli, 17 April 1998 What then are our criteria for securities eligible as collateral for a repo agreement with the National Bank? The basic requirement is that the securities must be denominated in Swiss francs. In addition, certain restrictions apply as regards liquidity, type of security and category of debtor. Since customer holdings may be included the market potential can be widened substantially. A commercial bank can employ securities borrowed from customers for repurchase agreements with the National Bank. The advantage for the customer lies in the fact that he can increase his earnings through securities lending. The market potential, i.e. the available volume of securities eligible for repurchase agreements should therefore not represent a major restriction. I come to the end of my remarks. The advantages of repos are self-evident. We are therefore confident that repos will also prove their worth as a major monetary policy instrument in Switzerland. This assessment is supported by the experience gained in other countries. Most European central banks are already using repos as their chief monetary policy instrument today. Repurchase agreements will also play a prominent part at the European Central Bank. 3

Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the President of the Bank Council
text: Opening address by Mr Jakob Schonenberger, Chairman of the Bank Council, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 24 April 1998 Introduction In the banking sector, structural changes have marked a further acceleration in Switzerland with the announcement of the merger of the Union of Swiss Banks and the Swiss Bank Corporation. Unlike the upheavals observed in the early nineties, this merger has a dimension that goes beyond the borders of our country. Fierce competition on international markets encourages not only industrial companies but also large Swiss banks to continuously adapt their structures. The effects of market globalization are the subject of intense discussion. It is obvious that wanting to rest on one's laurels is not a guarantee of success either for companies or for economic policy. Structural changes in the Swiss banking sector - A retrospective We are too often inclined to overestimate the importance of the present and the near future. A brief look at the past can help us keep the right proportions when it comes to structural changes in Swiss banks. Despite all the upheavals, the tasks that banks perform for the economy have remained fundamentally the same: to provide investment opportunities, to provide funds to businesses and households, and to provide services in payment transactions and wealth management. The close relations that Swiss banks have with foreign countries are also a constant. The first private bankers were already operating abroad and not in the domestic credit market, which offered little fertile ground for banks because of the abundance of capital in the former Confederation. The successes achieved by private bankers today show that Switzerland has long been the home of banks aspiring to further expand their activities internationally. Industrialization in the 19th century created a strong demand for capital. It has also led to an increase in incomes, hence the need for safe, liquid and well-paid forms of investment on the part of the population. This constellation has fostered the development of many financial institutions that, even today, make their mark on the Swiss banking sector. Already at the time, small and medium-sized enterprises complained of a lack of 2 credits. The good results achieved by cantonal, mortgage, cooperative and people's banks prove that transactions with the general public can be quite profitable in Switzerland. If the situation is different today, the cause must be sought rather on the side of an imbalance due to overcapacity. I do not see why the traditional banking operations of deposits and loans should not, in the long run, be profitable in one of the richest industrial nations in the world. A real break was observed in the thirties. Many banks did not withstand the shocks of the Great Depression, and the state then put in place new framework conditions for the financial sector. The Liberal strategy on banking supervision has proved beneficial; combined with the good economic situation of the fifties and sixties, it was the basis of a period of strong growth for Swiss banks. The establishment in our country at that time of many foreign banks shows the attractiveness of the Swiss financial centre. At the same time, the major banks began a phase of expansion of their international operations, a phase which, despite sometimes setbacks, continues to this day. In the Swiss market, the expansion of banks came to an abrupt end in the late eighties. The dismantling of cartel practices and the weakening of the economic situation have exposed unhealthy structures that had formed within the economy and the banking sector. The credit system in Switzerland, which is based like no other in the world on the mortgage guarantee, has been hit hard by the fall in real estate prices. After the closure of the Guichets de la Caisse d'Epargne and Prets de Thun, a wave of restructuring led to the disappearance of nearly a hundred banking institutions. With rare exceptions, these restructurings have taken place without recourse to public funds. Between 1991 and 1996, the banks, mainly on their own, amortized their loans to Swiss customers amounting to a considerable amount of 42 billion francs. Among the institutions most affected are, of course, those whose activity focuses mainly on loans to Swiss customers and whose product structure is not very diversified. Adapting to market conditions has required painful corrections in trade policy. Thanks to these adaptations, most cantonal and regional banks can also look to the future with some optimism today. The restructuring has also had a heavy impact on banking staff. After years of strong expansion, many banks have had to significantly reduce their staff. These downsizing have largely been achieved through natural departures and early retirements, with the result that redundancies have been relatively few. Staff, who had benefited for years from the strong growth in this sector, felt deeply the effects of this reversal of trend. 3 Perspectives In the future, the financial system will be further transformed under the influence of economic, technological, legal and regulatory changes. The merger of two major banks does not mean the end of structural changes for the Swiss financial centre. New forms of distribution for financial services, the growing role of the capital market in raising and investing funds and many other, partly unpredictable, developments will force Swiss banks to adapt their activities to the ever-changing market conditions. Institutions that are able to meet the ever-changing needs of their clientele, without neglecting the issue of costs and risks, will do best. For large banks in particular, this may imply an increased trend towards the internationalisation of activities. For other banking institutions, a policy focused on a good knowledge of local particularities and proximity will perhaps be the most promising. The high pace of change in the financial sector presents banks and their supervisory authorities with great challenges. In the future too, these authorities will have the task of ensuring competition between institutions, protecting banks' creditors and safeguarding the stability of the banking system. Ensuring the solvency of each institution is of fundamental importance here. The task of the Federal Banking Commission and other supervisory authorities has become more demanding, particularly as a result of the increasing internationalisation of financial operations and the emergence of new financial instruments. The Banking Commission's plan to mobilise more resources for the supervision of large financial institutions established in Switzerland takes into account the complexity of the risks of these companies and therefore deserves support. It is also in the interest of the SNB that the large banks are subject to effective supervision. The main contribution of the issuing institution to the soundness of the financial system is to conduct a stability-oriented monetary policy. The SNB also acts as the lender of last resort. Fortunately, its experience in this area is modest, and the SNB is happy to do without acquiring more. That is why it has a clear interest in the fact that the big banks do not put their solvency and soundness at stake through their global operations. The contrast between the international importance of the large Swiss banks and the narrowness of their internal market is likely to create difficulties from the point of view of system protection that should not be overlooked. The SNB therefore supports measures to help reduce risks in the international financial system. Economic change should not be used as a pretext to mix the tasks of market participants and those of public authorities. The responsibility of the latter relates to the adjustment of the framework conditions, within which economic agents can develop their activities. Within the framework defined by the State, these actors must assume the responsibility involved in carrying out their tasks. Recently, the Asian financial crisis has once again highlighted the price to be paid for confusing responsibilities. 4 of the State and individuals, in particular when large loans are granted on the basis of political criteria. When the State adjusts the framework conditions, a sufficiently large margin must be left to market forces so that they can encourage greater self-discipline. Only a financial sector where market forces play their part can make a lasting contribution to prosperity.
