Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the Chairman of the Governing Board
text: Presentation by Mr. Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Executive Board, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 24 April 1998 A year ago, the end of a long period of stagnation was emerging in Switzerland. Cautious optimism was noticeable. We now know that the hopes of that time have largely been realized. Our economy has returned to growth. The recovery, which started from foreign trade, strengthened its foothold during the year and gained elements of domestic demand. The financial crisis in East Asia, however, has tarnished the outlook somewhat. The developments in the area of monetary union that the EU countries are preparing have confronted us with additional challenges. Other tasks have also absorbed us a lot. I am thinking above all of the reform of the constitutional provisions on money and, in terms of exploitation, the reorganization of cash movements. Finally, a new rule for the distribution of the SNB's profits has been established in agreement with the Federal Council. 1. The economic situation and monetary policy In the fourth quarter of 1997, real gross domestic product was 2% higher than in the last three months of the previous year. In this growth, the most remarkable fact is the expansion of an unexpected strength in exports. Favourable monetary framework conditions, the marked recovery of the economic situation in our European trading partners and the resolute adaptation of our companies to structural changes have given a new impetus to our external trade. Gradually, the domestic economy has also regained dynamism. Private consumption regained strength, while the propensity to invest was maintained. The unfavourable situation that persisted in construction slowed down the economy. This branch has suffered from demand always 2 low, both for housing and for buildings for industry, crafts and services, but also for excess capacity on the supply side. Although recessionary trends have eased in recent months, the painful adaptation of structures will still last for some time. In the labour market, the first glimmers of hope have appeared on the horizon. In the fourth quarter, employment rose quarter-over-quarter for the first time in nearly two years. The more vacancies and the more optimistic assessment of companies in terms of employment also show that the demand for labour is gradually on the rise. However, unemployment will decline only slowly. It will always be difficult to find a job quickly, especially for low-skilled workers. Companies remain subject to strong constraints that push them to rationalize. In the meantime, these constraints have extended to wholesale and retail trade, i.e. to branches important for employment. However, the outlook is good, and employment in Switzerland is expected to increase again in the coming years. Recent efforts to liberalize and revitalize our economy are beginning to bear fruit. It is highly desirable that they be prosecuted. Let me now comment on our monetary policy. In 1997, we continued to pursue a broad policy. In view of the still weak economic situation, exchange rate developments have been our main concern. We have tried to counteract the trend towards an excessive revaluation of the Swiss franc. In October, we allowed short-term interest rates to rise, as the recovery in the economy had strengthened at that time. The Asian financial crisis d0 it erupted last summer in Thailand and then spread rapidly to other East Asian countries d0 has, however, changed our assessment of the situation. In the autumn, the Swiss franc came under greater upward pressure, which led us to strengthen the liquidity endowment of the market. The overnight silver rate fell until the end of the year and fell below the 1% mark. The further easing of our policy seemed reasonable to us in view of the evolution of monetary aggregates. Growth 3 of M3 in particular, i.e. the aggregate which meets the broadest definition, had indeed slowed down to find an appropriate rhythm. As we announced last December, we maintained the course of our monetary policy in 1998, above all to counter a revaluation of the franc, which was undesirable from the point of view of economic developments. Our policy has thus led to a further decline in the remuneration paid on the money market. On a monthly average basis, short-term interest rates fell in January and February to levels not seen since 1978. Long-term rates have also fallen sharply. In the meantime, they have increased somewhat again. The risks associated with a generous supply of money appear to be low at the moment, given the still modest economic growth, the production capacity that is not fully utilized and the favourable outlook for higher prices. In the first quarter, consumer prices were unchanged on an annual basis. It is even possible that they will decline somewhat in the coming months. The recent decline in mortgage rates is expected to result in a slight decrease in housing rents. In other areas, notably telecommunications, increased competition leads to price reductions. Similarly, the fall in oil prices moderates the evolution of consumer prices. In our view, however, the fear of deflation is unfounded. Economic growth accelerated in 1997 and, in terms of the continued growth this year, the outlook is good. Price stability, as our economy is currently experiencing, is a considerable advantage. 2. The international monetary situation The economic and financial crisis in East Asia caused more and more waves in international financial markets last year. The Asian crisis has multiple origins. Significant flows of funds have been observed in recent years from industrialized countries to the emerging economies of East Asia. These funds were generally not intended for direct investment. It was indeed short-term capital, which was 4 nevertheless invested in long-term projects, which are also not very productive for many of them. In addition, exchange rate risks were underestimated, because the currencies of several Asian countries were pegged to the dollar. As a result of the revaluation of the dollar, Asian countries whose currencies were pegged to the greenback have suffered a deterioration in their competitiveness, especially against Japan. As a result, export growth and hence the growth of economies as a whole weakened, resulting in a collapse in the real estate and stock markets, which had recorded strong increases. Investors, realizing then that fixed exchange rate relations were threatened, sought refuge outside local currencies. The subsequent depreciations increased pressure on heavily indebted industrial firms and banks. Faced with massive capital outflows, Thailand, then Indonesia and South Korea had to resort to the help of the International Monetary Fund. The Philippines has extended a credit agreement. In addition to the Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank have also made capital available. Finally, several countries have expressed their readiness to form a second line of defence through bilateral appropriations. The Swiss National Bank has opened a loan of approximately 312 million to South Korea, which is guaranteed by the Confederation. These bilateral credits are subject to conditions that require recipient countries to undergo comprehensive reform programmes. The International Monetary Fund's reform programmes take into account the particularities of the crisis. They provide for the implementation of the usual macroeconomic measures, but also other measures aimed at restructuring banks and industrial enterprises. In particular, it is a question of strengthening banks' capital endowment and improving banking supervision. Foreign investors, who had clearly underestimated the risks of their investments in East Asia, are also being called upon to participate in the consolidation efforts. The measures I have just briefly described have already had their first effects. In particular, they made it possible to stabilize currencies which, caught in the whirlwind of events, had lost more than 50% of their value. Countries 5 however, they will suffer temporary declines in production and employment. Events in East Asia confirm that, regionally and globally, sustainable economic development is possible only on the basis of economically and socially stable states. Flawed economic developments, corruption, fragile financial systems and inadequate supervision of financial markets are only symptoms of an imbalance between the economic and the social. It is primarily up to the community formed by the inhabitants of each country to correct such an imbalance. No one can, however, ignore the difficulties of this task. The repercussions of the Asian crisis will also be felt in North America and Europe. Most forecasters, however, do not expect a sharp slowdown in economic growth in real terms. Their estimate also applies to Switzerland. It is true that the growth of our exports to East Asia has marked a sharp decline. For our economy as a whole, however, these countries are not of such importance that their difficulties would pose a serious threat to the development of the swiss economy. So far, the Asian turbulence has resulted above all in a further revaluation of the Swiss franc. The uncertainties that have persisted in the run-up to the transition to monetary union in Europe have increased upward pressure on the franc. The expected decisions, which the European Union will take in about ten days' time, have already helped to calm the situation on the foreign exchange market. We will continue to follow very closely the efforts towards the creation of the single European currency d0 the euro d0 and will take this into account when setting the course for our monetary policy. 3. Reform of the monetary regime In 1997, important steps were taken towards the reform of the constitutional provisions on the currency. At the end of October, a group of experts presented its draft constitutional article on the currency. In December 1997, the Federal Council submitted for consultation a version which deviates slightly from that of the 6 of the expert group. The cantons, political parties, as well as economic and trade union circles overwhelmingly welcomed this text. In the article on money, as proposed by the Federal Council, the franc is no longer legally pegged to gold, which, de facto, has already been the case for a long time. In addition, the mandate of the central bank and its independence are specified in the constitution. The article also requires the SNB to hold sufficient monetary reserves to fulfil its mandate. It thus creates a modern monetary regime that also takes appropriate account of international developments. Compared to the version provided for in the pure update of the Constitution, a task that the Federal Chambers have been working on since the beginning of 1998, the draft article on currency, as revised by the Federal Department of Finance, has several advantages. This text unambiguously defines the mandate of the central bank since it assigns it to serve the general interests of the country, while giving priority to the objective of price stability. A mandate formulated in this way adequately counterbalances the abandonment of the attachment of the franc to gold. It is therefore likely to strengthen confidence in the stability of the franc. A clear definition of the mandate is also necessary given the anchoring in the constitution of the independence of the central bank. Independence linked to a specific mandate integrates the SNB into the public authorities and allows it to report clearly on its activities to the Confederation and to the public. As a result of the abolition of the peg of the franc to gold, a decision will have to be taken as to the allocation of the part of gold reserves that is not necessary for the conduct of monetary policy. This share represents approximately half of the approximately 2600 tonnes of gold currently held by the SNB. Contrary to the text provided for in the pure update of the Constitution, the article on currency, in the version proposed by the Federal Department of Finance, calls on the SNB not only to build up but also to hold sufficient monetary reserves. It therefore also implies that monetary reserves that the SNB does not need to fulfil its monetary mandate are made available for other public purposes. The Federal Council intends to make a levy on this national heritage which has 7 was constituted for many years. He wants to get off the balance sheet of the National Gold Bank for a counter-value of 7 billion francs. The sum must be used for the endowment of the Swiss Solidarity Foundation, which is planned to be set up. The other part of the metal reserves not essential for the conduct of monetary policy would continue to be held by the SNB and would be managed according to commercial principles. This task must be carried out without creating conflicts of interest between the management of assets belonging to the country and the conduct of monetary policy. Consideration could be given to entrusting the management of these assets to third parties; the SNB would appoint the managers, impose directives on them and control management. These issues will, however, be the subject of a revision of the National Bank Act, which will be undertaken after the reform of the constitutional provisions on currency. The grooming of the SNB Act should not be limited to those aspects related to the demonetisation of gold. Indeed, other areas also need modernisation. I am thinking in particular of the SNB's organisational structures d0 they have become a little outdated over the years d0 and the means of action which, in part, are no longer adapted to our times. 8 4. Reorganization of cash movements Last year, I told you that we would be reviewing our structures. This has now been done with respect to cash movements. In this area, our environment has changed significantly in recent years. Our main partners d0 banks, Swiss Post and large retail chains d0 are increasingly refocusing, for cost reasons in particular, on their core activities. They therefore entrust third parties with a significant part of the sorting and transport of banknotes and coins, resulting in a concentration of cash movements. Our strategy so far has been to decentralize as much as possible the sorting and control of banknotes and coins. In the medium term, only deviations in cash flows and, consequently, undesirable interventions in the organisation of the market would enable us to ensure full use of our network of counters, which consists of two headquarters and eight branches. We have therefore carried out an in-depth examination and looked at how to adapt our cash activities in order to find a sensible solution for all parties involved, i.e. for the SNB as well as for banks, Swiss Post, large distribution chains and companies specialising in cash transport and sorting. The result of these reflections was presented to the Bank Committee in February this year. We intend to concentrate cash sorting and control in four locations: Bern, Zurich, Geneva and Lugano. Our network of agencies and correspondents will be maintained and even expanded. Our agencies and correspondents receive cash deliveries, but do not take care of sorting or checking. After consulting the cantons concerned, we will submit a concrete proposal to the Bank Council this summer. If approved by this body, we will still have cash register services at our headquarters in Bern and Zurich as well as at our branches in Geneva and Lugano. The branches in Basel, Lausanne, Lucerne and St. Gallen will continue to perform an important task, namely to explain the policy pursued by the issuing institute and to inform the Directorate-General of the economic situation. They will thus play, as before, the role 9 a link between the SNB and regional representatives of political and economic circles. For the Aarau and Neuch89tel departments, this task will be carried out from the headquarters in Zurich and Bern. Some eighty employees will be directly affected by these reorganization measures. We will offer them a job at another counter or early retirement. We believe that there will be no need for redundancies. 5. Distribution of the SNB's profits At the beginning of 1992, the Federal Council and the SNB agreed to distribute an additional share of the issuing institution's products. Previously, distributions were limited to the dividend to be paid to shareholders and the compensation per capita of population that the law allocates to the cantons. The additional amount was to be returned, as required by the Constitution and the law, one third to the Confederation and two thirds to the cantons. It was necessary, as no one disputed, to allow the SNB to retain part of its proceeds and thus to increase its foreign exchange reserves without foreign exchange guarantees. For this reason, it was planned to increase the SNB's provisions at the same rate as the nominal gross national product. To avoid fluctuations in the additional distribution, a maximum amount of CHF 600 million per year was set. The products of the issuing institution recorded significant variations, mainly due to strong movements in the dollar rate. The first distribution of 600 million francs was made for the 1991 financial year. An identical amount was also distributed in the following years, and the same will apply to the 1997 financial year. On average from 1991 to 1997, the increase to be given to provisions amounted to about one billion francs per year. For the coming years, we plan to significantly increase the amounts distributed and stabilize them even better. Under the new agreement between the Federal Council and the SNB, the distribution for the years 1998 to 2002 was determined in advance on the basis of a forecast of 10 our products. We have thus committed ourselves to paying an amount of CHF 1.5 billion per year for a period of five years. Only considerable losses would reduce or even interrupt this distribution. In setting future distributions, we have relied on an improvement in our revenues, which we expect to achieve with the increased investment flexibility we have since the partial revision of the National Bank Act came into force in November 1997. We have also taken into account the fact that, thanks to the favourable development of the proceeds of our foreign currency investments and the extraordinary income resulting in 1996 from the change in our valuation principles, our provisions are now well above the target level. Under the new agreement, the shares accruing to the Confederation and the cantons for the past financial year will be paid after the General Meeting. Until now, I remind you, the distribution did not take place until the beginning of the following year. This adaptation will be introduced without further delay. We therefore plan to pay the distribution for the 1997 financial year, i.e. 600 million francs, immediately after this General Assembly. Taking into account the distribution for the 1996 financial year, which was improved in January, the Confederation and the cantons will therefore receive CHF 1.2 billion in 1998. 6. Gold operations during World War II Let me return again to the issue of gold operations by the Swiss National Bank during the Second World War. I would like to stress once again that we fully understand the need, expressed by many individuals and associations, to shed light on this important chapter of our past. The Swiss National Bank is a public institution. His attitude during the Second World War must be examined in the light of Swiss politics at the time. The gold transactions that the issuing institution carried out during these years were the subject, with the Washington agreement of 1946, of a settlement under international law. 11 The measures taken so far by our authorities are, we are convinced, likely to contribute to serious work on our past. They will make it possible, when the time comes, to make a final political assessment. We will oppose, by all legal means at our disposal, a collective complaint in the United States. We see no legal basis on which such a claim could be based and believe that the U.S. courts do not have jurisdiction over us. * * * * * During the past year, we have faced many challenges, both exciting and difficult to overcome. Today I would like to reiterate my sincerest thanks to all our employees for their valuable support. I also thank you for being here, which demonstrates your interest in our Institute.

Title: Reform and reconstruction of the Swiss economy
text: The Swiss economy under restructuring Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Presentation at the General Assembly of the Lucerne Industry Association on 30 April 1998 in Malters 2 The Swiss economy has overcome the seven-year recession and stagnation. For this year, we expect real economic growth of around 2%. The Asian crisis that alarmed us last autumn will also leave its mark on Switzerland. However, there are now enough forces from Germany and abroad to effectively support the economy. The nineties were a time of disappointment and uncertainty for many employers and employees. And yet developments have begun that give cause for optimism for the future. The internationally oriented industry has impressively increased its competitiveness, and the structural change towards services, which is unavoidable in the old industrial countries such as Switzerland, has made further progress. There are also signs that the location-based and so far too uncompetitive domestic economy has become more flexible and innovative. The main impetus for change came from technological progress, European integration and globalisation. Important impulses also came from economic policy. Under the pressure of the changed circumstances, certain regulatory framework conditions have been improved. These include innovations such as the Internal Market Act, which strengthens domestic competition, the revised Antitrust Act, which is intended to protect it more effectively, and the deregulation in telecommunications, energy supply and agriculture that has entered into force or is planned. In addition, there are the measures taken at cantonal level to make the economy more flexible. I am thinking, for example, of the liberalisation of shop opening hours and deregulation in the hospitality industry. All these innovations contribute to sustainably increasing the long-term performance of the Swiss economy. A lot has been done and has been set in motion d0 but the restructuring of the Swiss economy has not yet been completed. Further efforts are needed to strengthen the economy for the benefit of all. The increase in material prosperity is certainly not the measure of all things. Factors that are not taken into account in the national product, as they can hardly ever be measured in Swiss francs, are at least as important for the quality of life. This includes collective goods such as the quality of our environment and social peace. The Crux 3 Lies in the fact that we demand payments from the economy in francs and centimes for these achievements. This is particularly evident in the increasing entitlement to a high level of social security. These demands have to be worked out on a daily basis. In order to meet these requirements alone, the economy must significantly increase its performance in the coming years. Economic efficiency and productivity advances do not fall from the sky. Rather, they result from the interaction of certain factors that can also be influenced by economic policy. The performance of the economy is thus also a measure of the quality and success of economic policy. Four determinants are in the foreground, namely - firstly, a stable macroeconomic environment, i.e. sound public finances and a high degree of price stability, secondly, high investment in physical capital as well as in education, i.e. Human capital - thirdly, competition in all areas - and fourthly, the ability to respond rapidly to a changing environment, to react to changing market conditions, technologies and institutional circumstances. In the following, I would like to shed some light on these four areas. I'll start with education and the labor market. After that, I will deal with the formation of physical capital. The third section deals with competition, the fourth section with the ability to change and the fifth part with public finances. I shall conclude by referring to the importance of monetary stability, also in connection with the creation of European Monetary Union. 1. Education and the labour market No one denies that an efficient economy needs a well-educated and motivated workforce. However, education also contributes to personal development and tends to reduce social inequalities. This is mainly for two reasons: firstly, well-educated workers earn a higher income and secondly, they bear a smaller risk of becoming unemployed. 4 However, the acquisition of education is not a Sunday walk, but often a strenuous mountain tour that requires tenacious will. Incentives are therefore needed so that a young person strives for the best possible initial training and that someone later spends time and money to improve their professional qualifications through further training and to adapt to changing circumstances. The incentives to invest in education depend on various factors. Two seem to me to be particularly important. a5 On the one hand, the material incentives. The chance of a higher income is an indispensable driving force for effort for education and further education. This requires a pronounced permeability of the income pyramid - the chance of income improvements, but also the risk of downgrades. This concept, known as income mobility, strengthens self-reliance on professional skills and personal employability. a5 A second factor is the labour market. If the chances are great to find a suitable and satisfying job later, this promotes the willingness to invest in education. On the other hand, high permanent unemployment has a deterrent and paralyzing effect. Unemployment in Switzerland is low by European standards. We owe this essentially to the flexible labour market. We have the most liberal labour law on the European continent, which sensibly regulates central areas such as protection against dismissal. Non-wage labour costs are lower than in the EU, and unemployment insurance is organised in such a way that abuse is limited. Finally, a largely decentralised wage formation process ensures that wages develop in line with the economic performance of companies. 5 These favourable conditions are reflected in a high willingness of employers to create jobs and in the willingness of employees to reintegrate quickly into the labour market. In the course of the economic upswing that has now begun, unemployment will decline significantly. But it will no longer sink to those paradisiacal low values of the eighties. How high the base will be is difficult to estimate. Most research suggests a structural unemployment rate of around 3%. Even if this is deep by European standards, we should fight against it. Apart from the fact that unemployment is often a difficult personal fate, other aspects seem to me to be worth considering. Older workers are disproportionately affected by long-term unemployment. This can promote the general prejudice that further training is no longer worthwhile for a middle-aged person in the first place. This leads to resignation and the waste of professional experience at a time when our country needs the productive commitment of all those capable of working in view of the inevitable demographic shifts. In the case of Switzerland, basic unemployment is favoured by structural change and the design of unemployment insurance. a5 Structural change is leading to a decline in the demand for low-skilled workers. It is partly substituted by the use of technologies and by outsourcing production to low-wage countries. Poorly educated workers are therefore particularly affected by unemployment today, and this will not change in the future. a5 The very long duration of unemployment benefits, even by international standards, increases the risk that an unemployed person will postpone re-entry into working life. Skills are lost, and training devalues. This reduces his future chances on the labour market. The Unemployment Insurance Act contains a certain corrective with the mandatory employment programmes of the cantons in order to prevent the emergence of long-term unemployment. Whether this provision is sufficient, however, seems questionable. 6 The best way to reduce structural unemployment is to promote employment. This must be based on both labour demand and labour supply. On the demand side d0 on the employers' side d0 we must first prevent anything that makes the labour factor even more expensive. Non-wage labour costs in Switzerland are still significantly lower than in most European countries, mainly because health insurance is not financed by wage percentages. However, there is a clear tendency to jeopardise this important advantage of the Swiss workplace. In addition, all those measures will promote employment that aim to make the economy more dynamic and create entrepreneurial freedom. Such measures are unfortunately unspectacular, have little original effect and hardly ever lead to headlines. Miracle cures for increasing employment such as the reduction of statutory working hours have it much easier. They lead to the impression that we are running out of work and that we should therefore distribute the remaining work to more heads and hands. This view is misguided. The service sector as well as the new technologies represent a huge employment potential, which will be exploited under suitable conditions. Nevertheless, the already long-standing trend towards shorter working hours will continue d0 for the simple reason that leisure time increases in value as prosperity increases. On the supply side, i.e. in the case of workers, we need to address existing weaknesses. The duration of unemployment benefits should be shortened as soon as the labour market situation improves considerably. Above all, however, we must ensure that training keeps pace with the demands of the labour market. The Swiss education system enjoys a very good reputation. Its dual structure, namely practical vocational training geared to the needs of the labour market on the one hand and education at the university of applied sciences and higher education level on the other, has proved its worth. It is considered the main reason for the low youth unemployment in Switzerland. 7 However, the Swiss school and education system is also under great challenge at all levels due to rapid structural change and new technologies. In recent years, new paths have been taken in many areas. Are there any weaknesses? The OECD refers to the foreign workforce. Their education is often poor, and often their language skills are also inadequate. There is no doubt that there is a need for action here. In particular, the educational shortcoming must not be transferred to the second generation, which often has unfavorable starting conditions. Technical innovation is the key factor for the performance of a modern economy. There is an important employment potential in the technologically leading, innovative areas. The OECD's recent report on education indicators points to a weakness in the Swiss education system: the proportion of graduates with a doctorate in the field of technical and natural sciences is very low internationally, at 400 graduates per 100,000 people in working age between the ages of 25 and 34. This puts Switzerland in fourth last place within the OECD. The proportion of women is also alarmingly low. The reasons for this development should be investigated. All the more so as the international location comparison study recently published by the BAK shows that companies rate the highly qualified workforce in Switzerland worse than those in most Western European locations and in the USA. I would like to conclude my remarks on education and the labour market with a perhaps sobering but necessary point. Despite all the training efforts, there will be long-term unemployment in the weakest area of the labour market and the phenomenon of the "working poor", where people are employed but very poor. In this segment, solidarity and socio-political commitment are needed as an indispensable correlate to the flexibility of the labour market. This brings me to the importance of investment, the formation of physical capital. 8 2. Sachkapital In addition to human capital, physical capital plays a central role in economic growth. It is only in combination with modern equipment and technology that human capital achieves the productivity gains that increase prosperity. By international standards, Switzerland has a very modern and large capital stock. This reflects the above-average investment rate, through which new technologies are quickly introduced and the economy remains technologically on the ball. Even in the past economically difficult years, the modernization of the capital stock was pushed forward. In principle, this is a good testimony to the economic conditions in Switzerland. The basis of the high level of investment activity is the abundant savings available, which are channelled to investors via an efficient banking system and a modern capital market. In recent difficult years, the function of banks as financial intermediaries has come under heavy fire. In particular, small and medium-sized enterprises, which do not have access to the capital market, complained about the restrictive credit policy of the banks. In particular, the lack of risk financing was also criticized. A reversal to a risk-appropriate credit policy of the banks was inevitable after the exaggerations of the eighties. Also with regard to a balanced economic development, one must not wish back the sometimes reckless credit policy of the banks. In other words, companies will basically have to live with the fact that investment projects will be examined according to stricter criteria than just a few years ago. However, this does not mean that the relationship between banks and companies cannot be improved. The initiative of the bankers' association, trade association and suburb to set up a kind of financial advice for small and medium-sized enterprises should contribute to this. Ultimately, the concentration process in the banking system could work in the same direction. The reduction in domestic capacity initiated by the major banks increases the business opportunities for the other banking groups. They can match their undeniable strength of customer-oriented 9 Increasingly use anchoring in the regions. Efforts to refinance existing credit relationships on the capital market promise particularly attractive potential. In this way, which has long been tried and tested in Anglo-Saxon countries, bank balance sheets can be relieved and additional credit leeway can be opened up without any disadvantages for the traditional credit customers. This brings me to the importance of competition. 3. Competition Competition is a cornerstone of the market economy. However, even those who are fundamentally liberal and market-oriented often have considerable difficulty in accepting competition in their own area as a rule of the game. Switzerland is a special case in so far as the export industry, which is accustomed to competition, and the location-based sector, which has long been isolated from anti-competitive rules by a scrub, have been facing each other. Regulations that make market access more difficult lead to structural rigidities in the form of inefficient production, outdated and expensive distribution systems and poor product quality. This reduces the performance of an economy and represents a considerable competitive disadvantage for the export industry, which is dependent on location-specific services. The International Monetary Fund sees the structurally weak domestic sector as the main reason why the Swiss economy achieved lower productivity progress than other European countries and the USA between 1975 and 1997. The Basel Working Group for Economic Research also does not give the domestic economy a good testimony in its already mentioned location comparison study. Productivity clearly lags behind that at other locations and has even deteriorated in recent years. We should take these analyses seriously and continue efforts to increase efficiency and dynamism in the location-based industries. This applies to the 10 affected private actors no less than for the state, which has taken important first steps with the Internal Market Act and the new Antitrust Act. 4. Ability to change As a fourth determinant of a country's performance, I would like to mention the ability to change, the determination to adapt quickly to changing circumstances. This refers to the willingness to adopt innovative technologies, to learn new things and to take risks. Fortunately, the last few years have shown that this ability is present in the economy and, to a certain extent, in politics. Nevertheless, the ability to change d0 made even more important by globalization and new technologies d0 is a buzzword in certain circles. It is feared that globalization will require the old industrialized countries to adapt in advance, which threatens to undermine the foundations of our coexistence. Alone, be warned against illusions. All too often, globalization merely exposes incrustations and omissions that sooner or later can be remedied. This also applies to economic policy. Globalization and modern communication technology give companies and consumers much better opportunities to look for alternatives and make comparisons. Unlike the economy, politics is not very familiar with such an environment. It means that political actors can no longer concentrate only on getting the best out of their interest and voter groups, but must also increasingly include backlash in their calculations. All in all, I am sure that the compulsion to face competition d0 the competition between locations d0 also holds opportunities for the political system. 11 5. Public finances Stable macroeconomic conditions are a central basis for the long-term prosperity of the economy. In a broad sense, this includes legal certainty, political stability and social peace. Where arbitrariness, corruption and social tensions prevail, no economy thrives in the long run. Innovations are drying up, the willingness to invest in physical capital and in one's own training is weakening. This removes the foundation of economic growth and prosperity. A stable macroeconomic environment requires balanced public finances. Switzerland's public finances have deteriorated massively in recent years at all levels of government, but especially at the federal level. With a general government deficit ratio of more than 3% this year, Switzerland occupies one of the lower places in Europe. With a debt ratio of more than 50% of GDP, we are on track to soon miss the second Maastricht criterion. The massive deterioration of public finances is partly of an economic nature, caused by the long stagnation that led to tax losses and high social costs. However, more than half of the deficit is structural in nature. The deterioration had been looming for a long time. It is mainly due to the financing gaps in social security, AHV/IV and unemployment insurance. There is a consensus that the persistent deficits are intolerable because they trigger a debt dynamic that undermines confidence in the state's ability to act. In the meantime, the restructuring of federal finances has been taken by the hand. In June, we will vote on the 2001 budget target, an article of the Constitution which is intended to emphasise the fundamental obligation to balance the budget. The Stability Package 98, on which the parties involved in the restructuring process agreed at the round table at the beginning of April, is intended to make it clear to voters how the budget correction is to be achieved by 2001. 12 As expected, the compromise reached, which is intended to relieve the federal budget of more than CHF 2 billion over the next three years, provokes mixed feelings. Relief that the restructuring process has finally got underway, regret that it provides for not insignificant tax increases. Savings were also made d0 especially in the politically unproblematic military sector and in transfer payments to the cantons. The latter quickly agreed, not least because they will receive considerable additional income as a result of higher income distributions from the SNB. In the politically sensitive area of social benefits, the corrections remained moderate as expected. In order to finance social services, VAT is to be increased. At 6.5%, the rate is currently only about a third as high as in the rest of Europe. If things go according to plan, it will rise by almost 4 percent over the next six years. Even then, however, it is only just over 10%. Compared to wage percentages, VAT has the advantage of not unilaterally taxing the added value created by labour. Nevertheless, the promising, labour-intensive service sector will clearly feel the effects of the VAT-related increase in the price of its services. Just like high non-wage labour costs, VAT also favours the informal economy. The desire to improve social protection entails the risk of promoting that sector of the economy in which there is no social security. Such effects would be highly counterproductive. They signal limits to the VAT burden. You can turn what you have achieved at the round table as you like: Budgetary restructuring efforts never find the harmonious applause of those involved and affected with contradictory interests. The decisive positive aspect of the compromise outlined above is the correction of an ominous deficit dynamic, which is far more important in economic terms than individual unpleasant annual results. But one must not be under any illusions about the sustainability of what has been achieved. The critical examination of the limits of state redistribution, supported by long-term fiscal concerns, is in our country 13 far from complete. Other popular requests will continue to test the will to discipline responsible for fiscal policy in the future. This brings me to the last part of what I said today, namely monetary policy and the challenges of European monetary union. 6. Stable monetary conditions In the area of tension in the political process, monetary policy in Switzerland benefits from the fact that there is a fairly broad consensus on two things in this country. First, there is little denying the insight that price stability is a fundamental prerequisite for economic growth and prosperity, but also for the fairness of income and wealth distribution. Opinions certainly differ on whether price stability has now been achieved at zero, one or two percent, but this does not detract from the agreement in principle. Second, there is an almost equally broad consensus that monetary policy instruments cannot generate lasting gains in employment and prosperity. The historical experience is clear: the attempt to flood structural weaknesses and often painful restructuring constraints with a flood of liquidity ends in a fiasco. This two-part consensus - on the importance of price stability and the limits of what can be achieved in monetary policy - is the foundation of a political culture of stability, which makes an essential contribution to the economic and social quality of our country as a location. Fortunately, we are currently seeing price stability, and most indicators justify the expectation that the powerful export stimulus will have a positive impact on domestic demand. In recent quarters, our policy has been geared towards improving the monetary conditions for an economic recovery within the framework of what is responsible for the long term. We are convinced that we have not exaggerated and, in particular, have not laid an inflationary liquidity base, which we would have to withdraw as soon as possible by means of a restrictive braking manoeuvre. For Switzerland, the chances of a sustained period of non-inflationary growth are good. That 14 will also have a positive impact on the situation on the labour market. In this environment, it should be possible to gradually reduce cyclical unemployment. As a monetary authority, we are faced with the challenge of managing a mid-range course that does not stifle the forces of growth, but on the other hand does not lead to a longer-term inflation problem. In this task, the development of the euro is a priority. This most important monetary event of the post-war period since the collapse of the Bretton Woods fixed price regulation in the 70s will enter its actual implementation phase tomorrow with the three-day conference of heads of state and government. Even though the financial markets have taken up the venture with a remarkable degree of confidence, uncertainty and the resulting exchange rate turbulence cannot be ruled out. In an effort to do what best serves the overall interest of our country, we will follow developments very closely and, if necessary, respond with measures. However, the monetary conditions for a successful restructuring of the European monetary system are good. The European Central Bank will pursue a stability-oriented gel policy. In doing so, it can rely on a solid consensus on the paramount importance of price stability. Its formal mandate binds it decisively to this objective, and its leadership enjoys a maximum of independence from ongoing, often opportunistic influences of the political process. The risks of the euro project are hardly in the monetary sphere, but rather in the real economic adjustment constraints, which are reinforced by the transition to a currency area. Because appreciation and depreciation are eliminated in order to adapt to development divergences, other market processes must provide greater adaptation performance. The focus is on the labour markets, which - with double-digit unemployment rates in the large countries - require far-reaching flexibilisation reforms. In this regard, and in addition to the indispensable continuation of public fiscal consolidation efforts, governments and parliaments will be called upon. The fact that they meet these challenges is the most important condition for the success of the Euro project in the long run. In your circle I do not need 15 to further justify that its success is crucial for the interests of our economy, which is inextricably linked to Europe. Schlussbemerkungen I would like to conclude with three observations: 1. For our economy, the 90s were a time of lethargy and many disappointed expectations. But also a period of intensive restructuring efforts at all levels. There is much to suggest that in this country, under the pressure of comparatively prolonged stagnation and favored by a high degree of flexibility in the labor market, efforts to restructure have progressed further than in various other countries. This finding, which is favourable to our growth prospects, does not apply to individual domestic sectors and parts of the public sector, where further reform energy seems essential. 2. The economic environment and the development of demand in Switzerland have changed for the better in recent quarters and months. Overheating is difficult to discern, and the risk of a relapse into stagnation seems narrowly limited. In the near future, it will be crucial to rigorously continue the efforts for structural fitness in the more favorable economic climate. 3. Even convinced euro optimists will admit that, despite its promising launch, the euro project is associated with risks that could weigh on our economy. This does not mean smaller and short-term exchange rate fluctuations, but larger, longer-lasting distortions that shift the price ratios sustainably. This risk scenario should be thought of with attentive serenity. It's not very likely, in my opinion. And besides, as a central bank, we are not entirely without such an aberration in terms of such an undesirable development. 16 Defenses. Finally, in this case too, the experience is that the more competitive and structurally fit the companies that operate productively in it, the better an economy copes with shocks.
text_original: Die schweizerische Wirtschaft im Umbau Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Mitglied des Direktoriums Schweizerische Nationalbank Referat an der Generalversammlung der Luzerner Industrie Vereinigung am 30. April 1998 in Malters 2 Die schweizerische Wirtschaft hat die siebenjhrige Rezession und Stagnation berwunden. Fr dieses Jahr rechnen wir mit einem realen Wirtschaftswachstum von rund 2%. Die Asien-Krise, die uns im letzten Herbst aufgeschreckt hat, wird zwar auch in der Schweiz ihre Spuren hinterlassen. Es gibt aber inzwischen gengend Krfte aus dem In- und Ausland, welche die Konjunktur wirksam sttzen. Die neunziger Jahre waren fr viele Arbeitgeber und Arbeitnehmer eine Zeit der Enttuschungen und der Unsicherheit. Und dennoch sind Entwicklungen in Gang gekommen, die fr die Zukunft optimistisch stimmen. Die international ausgerichtete Industrie hat ihre Wettbewerbsfhigkeit eindrcklich gesteigert, und der in den alten Industrielndern wie der Schweiz unumgngliche Strukturwandel in Richtung Dienstleistungen, ist weiter vorangekommen. Auch gibt es Anzeichen, dass die standortgebundene und bisher zu wenig wettbewerbsorientierte Binnenwirtschaft flexibler und innovativer geworden ist . Die hauptschlichen Impulse fr den Wandel gingen vom technischen Fortschritt, von der europischen Integration und von der Globalisierung aus. Wichtige Anstsse kamen auch von der Wirtschaftspolitik. Unter dem Druck der genderten Verhltnisse wurden gewisse ordnungspolitische Rahmenbedingungen verbessert. Dazu gehren Neuerungen wie das Binnenmarktgesetz, das den Wettbewerb im Inland strkt, das revidierte Kartellgesetz, das ihn wirksamer schtzen soll sowie die in Kraft getretene oder geplante Deregulierung in der Telekommunikation, der Energieversorgung und der Landwirtschaft. Dazu kommen die auf kantonaler Stufe getroffenen Massnahmen zur Flexibilisierung der Wirtschaft. Ich denke beispielsweise an die Liberalisierung der Ladenffnungszeiten und die Deregulierung im Gastgewerbe. All diese Neuerungen tragen dazu bei, die langfristige Leistungskraft der schweizerischen Wirtschaft nachhaltig zu steigern. Title: Euro, Swiss monetary policy and interest rates
text: Euro, Swiss monetary policy and interest rates Georg Rich Swiss National Bank Presentation at the conference "EURO and Capital Markets", organized by Management Circle, Zurich, 12 May 1998. That is why we have tabled a motion for a resolution calling on the Commission and the Member States to take the necessary steps to ensure that the European Parliament is fully involved in the work The euro will pose a number of challenges for the Swiss economy. In my presentation, I would like to highlight three questions that concern the Swiss public: How will the euro affect the level and volatility of the Swiss franc exchange rate on the foreign exchange market? What options does the Swiss National Bank have to counter undesirable fluctuations in the exchange rate? Will the interest bonus on the Swiss franc disappear? I will conclude my presentation with a few remarks on the future of the Swiss financial centre. The imminent transition to the third stage of EMU is likely to have a lasting impact on the Swiss economy. At the beginning of 1999, the euro will see the light of day as the new European single currency. The European Central Bank, which is responsible for issuing the new currency, will conduct a single monetary policy across the euro area. The start of the third stage of EMU will also create a single money and capital market for the whole euro area. Money markets across the euro area will henceforth be subject to identical interest rates, and the differences between national capital market rates that still exist today will also largely disappear. Switzerland is not part of the European Union. That is why we are not directly affected by the introduction of the euro. Nevertheless, the Swiss economy will be able to cope with the euro. 1 Influence of the euro on the exchange rate of the Swiss franc In Switzerland, there is widespread fear that the completion of EMU will drive up the exchange rate of the Swiss franc and thus undermine the competitiveness of the domestic export industry. The economic upswing that began in Switzerland in the spring of 1997 and has now affected large areas of our economy could be nipped in the bud by an exaggerated strength of the Swiss franc. Indeed, many investors doubt the stability of the euro and are keen to partially convert their assets into safe alternative currencies. One of these is the Swiss franc. As a result of these relocations, our currency appreciated above all in 1994 Index November 1977 100 Figure 1: Real exchange rates of the Swiss franc 130 125 DM 120 115 110 105 100 95 handelsgewichtet 90 85 80 1974 1976 1978 1980 1982 1984 1986 1988 1990 1992 1994 1996 1998 2000 SNB 1 Economic Affairs 1998 and in 1995. In 1996, the situation on the foreign exchange market calmed down again. Despite the widespread doubts about the stability of the euro, I consider the risk of a renewed flight into the Swiss franc to be low, at least for the immediate future. There are two reasons against such a development, which is harmful to the Swiss economy: On the one hand, it must be emphasized again and again that the markets for foreign exchange and financial assets do not only react to current events. They are also strongly focused on the future. If expectations about future developments change, this is immediately reflected in price formation on the foreign exchange and financial markets. The doubts about the euro have long been contained in the swiss franc's exchange rates against the DMark and the other currencies of the future euro area. We do not have to wait for the start of the third stage of EMU until these doubts will have an impact on what is happening in the foreign exchange market. On the other hand, almost all EU countries meet the Maastricht convergence criteria. For individual countries, the sustainability of compliance still seems to raise questions. But the conditions for a successful transition to the euro are much more favourable than could have been expected just a short time ago. This strengthens confidence in the future European single currency. The recent weakening of the Swiss franc against European currencies shows that the euro is not only a source of concern. He also seems to have a considerable leap of faith among many investors. In addition, there are often fears that the volatility of Swiss franc exchange rates will increase after the introduction of the euro. The inhabitants of Franconian Island in the future Euro-Sea would have to accept higher waves in the form of volatile exchange rates. This fear is exaggerated. The transition to the euro is likely to trigger impulses that will both increase and reduce the volatility of Swiss franc exchange rates. On the one hand, capital inflows from the huge euro area are expected to hit the small and narrow swiss franc foreign exchange market with greater force than before. Depending on the liquidity situation of our foreign exchange market, this is likely to lead to strong fluctuations in the Swiss franc exchange rate. On the other hand, the introduction of the euro could also lead to a reduction in exchange rate volatility. Should the euro develop into a currency as stable as the Deutschmark, the future exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the euro should not fluctuate much more than the current exchange rate against the German currency. However, this would reduce the volatility of the Swiss franc's exchange rate against the euro area as a whole. In 1994 and 1995, for example, the Swiss export industry suffered mainly from the high volatility of the Swiss franc against the Italian lira, while fluctuations against the Deutschmark were limited. The monetary policy stance that the SNB has been pursuing for three years clearly shows that Switzerland is not powerless at the mercy of undesirable exchange rate fluctuations. The real appreciation of the Swiss franc that began in 1994 (Figure 1), which partly reflected the uncertainties arising from EMU, led to a renewed economic slump in our country towards the end of the year. The Swiss economy was in danger of plunging into a real deflation. This would no longer have been in line with our mandate to ensure price stability. A monetary policy correction was imperative. This caused domestic money market rates to fall below 2% by the end of 1995. In mid-1996, money market rates rose temporarily again, but then returned to the level reached at the end of 1995. In 1997, they tended to fall further, especially after the outbreak of the financial crisis in East Asia. Towards the end of March 1998, they began to rise again after the Swiss franc had weakened slightly in the foreign exchange market. Swiss interest rates also fell relative to those in Germany and other major partner countries (Figure 2). With the decline in interest rates, the attractiveness of portfolio transfers to the Swiss franc declined. Our currency therefore began to weaken again at the beginning of 1996. The decline accelerated in the autumn of 1996 following a further easing of Swiss monetary policy, aided by the strong recovery of the dollar. Apart from a temporary appreciation of the Swiss franc following the outbreak of the Asian crisis, exchange rates have been at a level since the beginning of 1997 that no longer hinders the economic recovery of the Swiss economy (Figure 1). Real growth reacted to the change in monetary policy with the usual delay of about 1 1/2 years in Switzerland. At the end of 1996, the Swiss economy reached its economic low point. Since then, the economy has picked up significantly. Initially, the upswing was mainly driven by strong growth in exports. Subsequently, the recovery also spread to the domestic economy. Only the construction industry, which has been particularly badly hit by the recession, is still struggling with difficulties. The reduced attractiveness of the Swiss franc as an investment currency led to a "diversification" of the portfolio shifts fuelled by doubts about the euro. Investors increasingly looked for stable alternatives for the Swiss franc and sought refuge in the American dollar and, since the UK's rapid accession to the third stage is not under discussion, in the British pound. This development also helped to alleviate the problems that arose for the Swiss economy as a result of the monetary integration of Europe. Of course, we are anxious not to jeopardise price stability in Switzerland in the longer term. To this end, we follow the development of monetary aggregates, which provide information on future inflation developments. Figure 3 shows that central bank money supply growth accelerated sharply after the transition to expansionary monetary policy. For some time now, the central bank money supply has been well above the medium-term target path set by the SNB. However, Figure 3 is not very meaningful, as the development of the central bank money supply overstates the degree of expansion of Swiss monetary policy due to various distortions. For this reason, we have been increasingly focusing on the growth of the M3 money supply for some time now. Figure 4, which is based on smoothed data for M3 and the price level, shows that a sharp acceleration in money supply growth after about three years regularly triggers an increase in inflation. M3 growth also picked up as a result of monetary easing, but has been declining markedly since the beginning of 1997, which is not yet fully apparent from Figure 4. It is currently at a comparatively low level, so that there is no immediate risk of inflation. However, we expect M3 to accelerate growth again in the wake of the economic recovery. Should this aggregate soar too much, the question of a renewed tightening of our monetary policy would arise. After all, we must do everything in our power to maintain price stability in Switzerland. However, we will continue to seek to protect the Swiss economy from harmful exchange rate fluctuations, insofar as this is consistent with the objective of price stability. Even if a strong appreciation of the Swiss franc is unlikely in the foreseeable future, various dangers still lurk in the longer term. It is true that, as I have already said, the euro enjoys a considerable leap of faith. But confidence in the euro is still on shaky ground. The European Central Bank must first acquire its credibility by proving that it can fulfil the stability mandate of the Maastricht Treaty. As long as the proof is outstanding, the possibility of exchange rate turbulence is to be expected at any time. It is to be hoped that the discord in the election of the first president of the European Central Bank will not detract from its credibility. I would like to mention in particular two cliffs that the European Central Bank must overcome, for better or worse. On the one hand, the new monetary authority must set its course in a financial environment that will change fundamentally with the introduction of the euro. It will only be able to rely on past experience to a limited extent in the use of its monetary policy instruments. The task of the European Central Bank to dose its monetary policy correctly will therefore be anything but easy. On the other hand, the European Central Bank will have to conduct a single monetary policy for the entire euro area. It is possible that the rate followed by the new monetary authority will not be equally appropriate for all euro area countries. Unemployment could also worsen in individual countries or regions. As multiple rigidities hamper the functioning of European labour markets, the question remains as to how economic imbalances in the euro area will be addressed in the future. 3 Interest bonus on the Swiss franc Swiss interest rates have been at a lower level than anywhere else in Europe for a long time. In this context, there is often talk of an interest bonus on Swiss francs. The interest bonus is particularly pronounced in the case of long-term contracts. Figure 5 shows that the average yield on swiss bonds over the past forty years has tended to be 2-4 percentage points below the interest rate on corresponding German securities. This does not only apply to the nominal interest rate differential. The real interest rate differential, i.e. the nominal difference adjusted for changes in the Deutschmark/Swiss franc exchange rate and German and Swiss consumer prices, developed similarly. However, Figure 6 shows that the real interest rate differential over the last forty years has fallen from more than 3% to an average of 2.3% in the period 1985-1997. walked. The comparatively low interest rates form a locational advantage that benefits the Swiss economy in international competition. It goes without saying that the interest rate bonus quickly disappeared as Switzerland approached EMU by irrevocably fixing the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the euro. In this case, the SNB would lose all autonomy in monetary policy. Swiss monetary policy and the Swiss interest rate level would henceforth be determined by the European Central Bank. Domestic interest rates, first in the short term, would climb completely to euro area levels. This would run counter to the interests of the Swiss economy. The permanent peg of the Swiss franc to the euro would therefore not be a tempting alternative, at least at the present time. Sometimes the opinion is expressed that the Swiss interest bonus will melt away in the long run anyway. The interest rate bonus can only be maintained if the SNB pursues a more successful stability policy than the European Central Bank. If the European Central Bank acts in accordance with the monetary policy mandate of the Maastricht Treaty, EMU will in future be as stable as Switzerland. However, the opinion that the existence of the interest rate bonus presupposes a better stability policy in Switzerland than in the euro area contradicts the findings of the past. So far, the interest bonus has not been due to the fact that the SNB tended to provide greater stability in Switzerland than the Bundesbank in Germany. On average, the inflation rate in Switzerland over the last 40 years has been similar to that of German. Percent Figure 5: Real and nominal differences in long-term Interest rates (Switzerland-Germany) 7 7 6 real 6 5 5 4 4 3 3 2 2 nominally 1 1 0 0 -1 -1 1956 1958 1960 1962 1964 1966 1968 1970 1972 1974 1976 1978 1980 1982 1984 1986 1988 1990 1992 1994 1996 1998 2000 SNB 5 Economic Affairs 1998 land. Nevertheless, nominal and real interest rates in Switzerland tended to be lower than in our neighbouring country. How can this inconsistency be explained? The opinion that the interest bonus can only be preserved if the SNB performs better than the European Central Bank is based on a misunderstanding. I am convinced that both the SNB and the European Central Bank will seek to fulfil their stability mandate as well as possible. Despite all efforts to ensure good monetary policy, they will not always be able to avoid making wrong decisions. Risk-averse market participants will try to protect themselves against such wrong decisions by diversifying their investments in terms of currency. If they live in the euro area, they will invest their assets not only in euros, but also in Swiss francs and other stable currencies. Diversification into the Swiss franc is imperative even if the SNB and the European Central Bank are to come up with services that tend to be equivalent. However, in order for diversification to reduce risk while maintaining the same return, an important additional condition must be met: should the two central banks ever be mistaken, the unintended deviations of inflation from the stability objective in Switzerland and the euro area must follow different patterns. The two central banks may be wrong from time to time, but not in the same way. The deviations from the stability objective must either be negatively correlated in the two currency areas, in technical terms, or the correlation, if positive, must be only moderately high. Otherwise, diversification does not reduce risk. As long as these conditions are met, risk-averse investors in the euro area will continue to seek to hold part of their assets in Swiss francs and similarly stable alternative currencies even after the start of the third stage. Of course, the same considerations also apply to Swiss investors who are seeking an analogous diversification of their assets. The additional demand for Swiss francs from the euro area, however, more than outweighs the decline resulting from the diversification of Swiss assets. Given the size and economic potency of the euro area, huge assets are crowding into the investment there. This means that there is a high demand for Swiss francs from the euro area. Switzerland, on the other hand, is a small country that can only boast a limited supply of assets in its own currency. The high demand for Swiss francs, which is hitting the scarce supply, is putting pressure on the Swiss interest rate level and explains the interest bonus on our currency. Switzerland takes advantage of the fact that foreign investors have an interest in using the Swiss franc, which it can only provide with a scarce supply, for diversification purposes. My remarks make it clear that I justify the existence of the interest bonus in a different way than is usually done. Most analysts attribute the interest bonus to the high Swiss current account surplus. This reflects the fact that savings in Switzerland are significantly higher than investments. The part of the savings that is not invested domestically flows into foreign investments. The current account surplus is therefore financed by capital exports. In order for capital to flow abroad, Swiss real interest rates must fall below the level prevailing abroad. The high current account surplus undoubtedly contributes to keeping Swiss real interest rates comparatively low. However, the statement based on the current account leaves an important question unanswered. Why does arbitrage on the international financial markets not compensate for the real interest rate differentials between Switzerland and abroad? My analysis provides the answer to this question. Arbitrage would only make real interest rate differentials disappear if the Swiss franc and foreign currencies were perfect substitutes. However, in the real world, where investors have to live with uncertainties of all kinds, this condition is not met. As I have already pointed out, among other uncertainties, there is no guarantee that the SNB and the European Central Bank will provide completely identical services, even if both institutions have the same monetary policy mandate. As long as the possibility remains that the SNB and the European Central Bank will achieve different results, intentionally or unintentionally, investors will not regard the franc and the euro as perfect substitutes. They will have an interest in not putting all their eggs in the same basket of currencies. Diversification is worthwhile, even if real interest rates in Switzerland remain consistently lower than in the euro area. The interest bonus will therefore only disappear once the Swiss franc loses its usefulness as a diversification instrument. Whether this will ever happen is difficult to predict. It is conceivable that, over time, the Swiss economy will become more and more closely intertwined with that of other European countries, even if our country continues to rule out accession to the European Union. If Switzerland were to become an appendage of the European Union even without membership, the development of inflation is likely to change. and the real economy in our country are becoming more and more similar to those in the euro area. This would remove the incentive for diversification into the Swiss franc and arbitrage would henceforth compensate for real interest rate differentials. The Swiss franc would also lose its attractiveness as a diversification instrument if our authorities decided to fix the exchange rate of our currency against the euro. However, I would like to emphasise that the fixation of the Swiss franc exchange rate alone was not enough to make the interest bonus disappear. As Figures 5 and 6 show, the interest rate bonus already existed under the fixed price system prevailing before 1973. The authorities would not only have to fix the exchange rate, but also announce that they would irrevocably leave the franc at the level once set in the future. They would also have to follow up their words with deeds. As I have already pointed out, the price fixation in the sense outlined above meant that the SNB would lose all autonomy in monetary policy. From now on, it would have to understand the monetary policy stance defined by the European Central Bank. For investors, diversification into the Swiss franc would lose its purpose, as our country would become part of the euro area, at least informally. The demand for Swiss francs caused by diversification would be eliminated and thus also the main reason for the interest bonus. 4 Schlussbemerkungen The transition to the euro will pose considerable challenges for the Swiss financial centre and Swiss monetary policy. I have tried to show what options the SNB has if the introduction of the new European single currency were to damage the Swiss economy. SNB 7 Economic Affairs 1998 That is why we have tabled a number of amendments. Both the European Union and Switzerland are interested in the euro becoming a strong and stable currency. If the European Central Bank succeeds in maintaining price stability, This would also benefit Switzerland. A strong and stable euro would significantly reduce the risk of undesirable exchange rate fluctuations. With a successful European monetary policy geared to price stability, the Swiss interest rate bonus would by no means disappear. If the SNB continues to pursue a stability-conscious monetary policy, the Swiss franc is likely to continue to play an important role as an instrument of diversification for risk-averse euro area investors in the future. If the Swiss franc remains an attractive investment currency, the Swiss financial centre will continue to be able to hold its own on the international stage. The However, competition is likely to become even tougher, because the transition to the euro is likely to trigger a surge in innovation on the European financial markets. Swiss banks are well prepared for increasingly fierce competition. Structural change is already in full swing at our banks, while it is only in its infancy for financial institutions in our neighbouring countries. Nevertheless, great efforts will be required to maintain the clout of the Swiss financial centre. It goes without saying that Swiss industry, commerce and consumers are also interested in a strong domestic financial centre. Only with a strong financial centre will they be able to benefit from comparatively low domestic interest rates in the future. SNB 8 Economic Affairs 1998
