Title: International aspects of monetary policy
text: International aspects of monetary policy Hans Meyer Chairman of the Executive Board Swiss National Bank France-Switzerland Chamber of Commerce and Industry Geneva, 20 May 1998 2 On 1st January next the single European currency will appear in eleven countries of the European Union. The advent of this new currency goes hand in hand with the sharing of the exercise of monetary sovereignty. This sharing will expose the countries of the euro area to a fundamentally new situation. For Switzerland, the single European currency, important as it may be, will not create an entirely new situation. The consequences that the euro could have, if any, on the Swiss economy are not unknown to us in principle. Fundamentally, they are just another expression of a traditional difficulty in implementing monetary policy in a small, open economy, namely that of judiciously accounting for foreign influences. So my objective today is to talk to you in general about these international aspects of monetary policy. I will end my presentation with a few remarks on the specificities of the single European currency, as well as the consequences for Switzerland and its monetary policy. First, and in order to put this discussion into perspective, I will first briefly look at the mandate of the SNB, then at the concept behind the application of monetary policy and finally at the main difficulties that arise in applying this concept. These main difficulties relate, in addition to foreign influences, to the use of a monetary aggregate as an intermediate target, the assessment of the economic situation and the links between money and inflation. The general framework Let us start with the mandate of the SNB, as set out in the Constitution. According to this mandate, we must adopt a monetary policy that serves the general interests of the country. In view of the other legal provisions relating to economic policy, this means, in principle, that the SNB must give priority to price stability. I would like to stress that a policy aimed at price stability is not in all circumstances synonymous with a restrictive monetary policy. It is, if inflationary pressures threaten price stability. On the other hand, if the pressure on prices is 3 Weak or no monetary policy may be appropriate to combat possible deflationary trends. The implementation of such a mandate requires a concept. The concept currently used by the SNB is based on an intermediate monetary objective. It is based on the idea that inflation is essentially a monetary phenomenon. Therefore, by controlling the growth of the money supply, we control inflation. It is called an intermediary because the monetary objective is not an end in itself, but a means to achieve price stability. This monetary objective is defined over the medium term. It gives us the direction in which our action should be taken, but it gives us room for manoeuvre to take account of the economic situation. Because of the medium-term nature of this objective, we do not seek to ensure that the actual growth of the money supply corresponds to the objective each year. If we did, we would strangle the expansion at the beginning of the business cycle. But it also means that at some point in cyclical development, we need to pull on the reins of monetary policy. Tightening is necessary if we are to avoid a runaway economy with the corollary of excessive price pressure. In its application, this simple concept in its essential principle encounters several difficulties. Let me dwell on a few of them. A first difficulty relates to the choice of a particular monetary aggregate as an intermediate target. There are indeed several ways to define money. Among the various possible definitions, the SNB favours the central currency. The latter consists of banknotes and bank transfer account assets with the issuing institution. However, sometimes, as was the case last year, the evolution of the central currency is dictated by autonomous movements unrelated to the evolution of the economy. In this case, we have to resort to other aggregates. Thus, since last year, we have been paying close attention to the evolution of the monetary aggregate M3, which is an aggregate of broad definition. A second difficulty in applying our concept of monetary policy relates to the assessment of the economic situation. Our medium-term goal means that we do not have to follow month after month, or year after year, 4 obediently a pre-fixed monetary line. Not only can we, but we must take into account the state of the cyclical situation as a leading indicator of inflation when determining the course we intend to give to monetary policy in the short term. Assessing the state of the economic situation is not always an easy task. Conflicting signals can emerge from the various regions that make up our country. The various branches of economic affairs are not all in the same situation. Currently, for example, construction is more exposed than exporting branches. However, it is not possible to conduct a differentiated monetary policy: we can only conduct one monetary policy for our country as a whole. A third type of difficulty lies in the complex links and mechanisms between monetary growth and the rate of inflation. On the one hand, we know that exaggerated monetary growth only has an effect on prices after a certain period of time, usually three years. On the other hand, we also observe that, before prices are affected, the exchange rate and interest rates, first, and then economic activity are affected by the increase in the money supply. From these observations, we see that the positive effects of an expansive monetary policy d0 lower exchange rates and interest rates and stimulation of economic activity d0 are felt well before its possible negative effects d0 higher inflation. Such a constellation can be an incentive to pursue an expansive policy for too long. This means that, if inflation is to be avoided, monetary reins must be drawn well before it appears. We cannot wait for inflation to appear before adopting a tighter monetary policy. Finally, it should be noted that the three-year period between the increase in the supply of money and the appearance of inflation is an average magnitude. Depending on the circumstances, this value may be different. This uncertainty further increases the difficulty of the task. For example, a rapid economic recovery helps shorten this time frame. Let me explain. Monetary impulses only turn into inflation through the recovery of economic activity. It is only when economic activity picks up d0 that is, turnover increases and unemployment decreases d0 that one is tempted to increase one's income through price and wage increases. Therefore, if the 5 Economic recovery had to happen quickly, we would have to imagine being able to tighten the monetary floodgates even before the economic recovery was really started. This is not easy. External influences I now come to the fourth type of difficulty we encounter in the exercise of monetary policy, namely those resulting from foreign influences. In general, these influences can be said to be a challenge for monetary policy when they jeopardize the stability of exchange rate relations. This endangerment is fundamentally the result of a divergence in economic developments in Switzerland and abroad. Monetary policies play a key role in this regard. Fundamentally, a relatively more expansive monetary policy abroad than in Switzerland results in a depreciation of the foreign currency and thus an appreciation of the franc. However, the exchange rate reacts not only to the realization of certain facts d0 which may influence the exchange rate d0 but also and above all to the anticipation of these same facts. Thus, both the current and the expected rate of monetary policy are important. Forecasting means uncertainty. Uncertainty about monetary policy also plays a role, and not least. In the presence of uncertainties, exchange rate volatility will increase. Uncertainty about monetary policy is fuelled in particular by significant public debt. It is also due to high unemployment. The lessons of history show that it is essentially these two factors that have led some central banks to adopt overly lax policies. Conversely, exchange rate stability is based on the convergence of economic developments between Switzerland and abroad. Similar monetary policies are the source of exchange rate stability. Economic conditions that allow economic agents to believe that these monetary policies will remain similar contribute to this. 6 This stability is certainly not absolute. Small changes in the exchange rate, which are likely to respond to cyclical differences, do not only have negative effects. On the contrary, a slight loss in the external value of the currency during a cyclical downturn is likely to contribute to reviving growth. Conversely, a slight rise in the exchange rate during a recovery helps to curb any inflationary pressures that may develop in the future. Such fluctuations do not have consequences. On the contrary, they are beneficial, they help to restore economic balance. The influence on the exchange rate, and in particular that coming from divergent monetary policies, is not the only channel through which the foreigner acts on our economy. In a small open economy like ours, the influence of the outside world is still felt in other ways. Two factors, both positively and negatively, are worth mentioning. These are, firstly, the consequences of cyclical variations abroad and, secondly, the effects of changes in the prices of the main imported products. Economic activity abroad influences economic developments in our country. For example, a slowdown in economic activity abroad is slowing down the economic boom at home. This effect is mainly transmitted by a decline in exports. The slowdown we have recently seen in Southeast Asia has had a much smaller effect than a similar slowdown in Europe would have had due to the relative weakness of our trade ties with these countries. Conversely, an acceleration of growth abroad favours our exports and therefore growth in Switzerland. Developments abroad, insofar as they influence the Swiss economic situation, must be taken into account when determining the course of our monetary policy. Changes in the prices of imported goods can have effects that are more difficult to cope with. For example, the oil price increases we have seen in the past have dampened growth and simultaneously helped fuel inflation. For inflation to appear, it was certainly necessary that the money supply was sufficient. Had it not been, inflation could have remained under control, but then price reductions would have had to be applied in other sectors of the economy. This would not have been accomplished immediately and easily. Conversely, the drop in oil prices that we have seen in recent times has certainly 7 had a positive effect on both price developments and the level of activity in Switzerland. The single European currency After these general considerations on the mandate of the SNB, the concept of monetary policy that we use and the four major categories of difficulties we face in applying this concept, I come to European monetary integration, before discussing the possible consequences for Switzerland. European monetary integration corresponds, in my view, to a fundamental movement in European history. It responds to a trend that goes back far beyond the first sketches of monetary unification and even beyond the founding of the first European Community in 1951 d0 the European Coal and Steel Community. In other words, European monetary integration is a step in the direction of history. I will not try to trace the origin of this idea. I shall confine myself to drawing the conclusion that we must essentially count on the success of this project. While European integration, and in particular monetary integration, is in line with history, this does not mean that it will necessarily go smoothly. For it to be achieved without major shocks, there must be clear political will and an adequate social climate. In concrete terms, this means that the countries of the European Union must create the conditions, firstly, for the European System of Central Banks to be able to pursue a monetary policy geared towards price stability and, secondly, for such a policy to be maintained over time. With regard to the first condition, relating to the European System of Central Banks, it can legitimately be considered that the countries of the European Union have done their utmost to ensure that it can conduct a monetary policy geared towards price stability. They have included in the Treaty establishing the European Communities the institutional provisions necessary for this to be the case. I will mention only two elements. The objective of price stability is explicitly mentioned in this Treaty as the main objective of the European 8 central banks. In my view, this is fundamentally based on the support that the population as a whole gives to the objective of price stability. In turn, this support is determined in particular by public debt and unemployment. This support will be all the higher the lower the public debt and the lower the unemployment. The excessive government deficit procedure laid down in the Treaty establishing the European Communities and the Stability and Growth Pact should be able to reduce or maintain public debt at a reasonable level. In doing so, euro area countries prevent the need to service the debt from resulting in an excessively heavy tax burden. Excessive taxation could give rise, if historical experience is to be believed, to inflationary temptations. Thus, by keeping public debt at a reasonable level, the European Union is helping to maintain the support of the population as a whole for the objective of price stability. Against unemployment, on the other hand, the European Union has been less effective. However, the flexibilisation of labour markets appears to be a necessary complement to monetary integration. Indeed, it cannot be ruled out that the current unemployment in the countries of the future euro area, which is already high, will rise temporarily in the monetary union. However, too high an unemployment rate could contribute to undermining public support for the objective of price stability. Of course, no one believes that an expansive monetary policy can sustainably improve the employment situation. In the short term, however, an easing of monetary conditions is generally favourable to employment. An overly expansive monetary policy on the part of the European System of Central Banks, if indeed to be adopted, would threaten price stability within the euro area. It would exert downward pressure on the euro exchange rate. In addition, exchange rate uncertainty could fuel the volatility of the external value of the euro. 9 Consequences for Switzerland Under these conditions, what are the opportunities and risks that the euro brings to our economy? The chances are those of a positive repercussion of an increase in economic growth in the euro area. This increase would be fuelled by lower transaction costs and increased competition within the area. Both of these factors should ultimately be beneficial for growth. What are the risks? The major risk we run with the euro is an exaggerated appreciation of the franc against this currency. Such a revaluation would not in itself constitute a new phenomenon for the Swiss economy and monetary policy. We have experienced many times in the past an exaggerated revaluation of our currency in the event of divergences in monetary policies. I hasten to point out that if the nature of the phenomenon is the same, I am aware that its dimension may be different. Indeed, an appreciation of a given percentage against the euro could have a much deeper impact on the economy than an appreciation of the same percentage against only one of the currencies of our trading partners. The reason is that the eurozone countries absorb more than half of our exports, which was not the case for either the United States or Germany. As clear as the nature of this risk posed by the euro to the Swiss economy, this does not mean that it will be realized. If this were to be the case anyway, what should we do, what could we do? Faced with an exaggerated appreciation of the Swiss franc, the SNB essentially has two monetary policy options to choose from. It can, first, ease monetary policy to take appropriate account of the exchange rate. The appreciation of a currency's exchange rate is a sign of an unmet increase in its demand. To avoid exchange rate appreciation, it is sufficient for the central bank to offer money in sufficient quantities to appease demand. There is no limit, per se, to such an action. The only limitations are those imposed by the reasonable consideration of the disadvantages of such a policy. 10 Indeed, if there were only advantages to this solution, we would not have to discuss it today. The fact is that such a policy also has a major drawback. In particular, it increases the risk of inflation in the future. The expansive monetary policy needed to combat exaggerated exchange rate appreciation creates excess liquidity in the economy that, once economic activity is underway, can translate into inflationary pressures. The challenge is to withdraw this liquidity before it can be translated into excessive stimulation of economic activity and thus inflation. So what would be the alternative? It would consist in letting the appreciation of the franc follow its course. Any risk of inflation would thus be eliminated. However, economic activity would also be unduly jeopardized. The conditions for deflation to possibly develop would thus be established. This would not be compatible with our objective of price stability: deflation, like inflation, is at odds with price stability. The practical difficulty is therefore to weigh these two disadvantages: the decrease in economic activity, which is due to an exaggerated appreciation of the franc; and the risk of inflation due to exaggerated monetary growth. This difficulty is reinforced by the fact that the decline in activity is felt rapidly, while inflation does not appear until much later. The second monetary policy option available to the SNB in response to an exaggerated appreciation of the swiss franc would be to peg the franc to the euro. Anchoring does not offer a substitute for expansive monetary policy. Rather, it complements such a policy. Indeed, anchoring does not eliminate inflationary risk. It only aligns the national inflation rate with the external inflation rate. In addition, as in any fixed exchange rate regime, it removes the possibility of small-scale exchange rate adjustments. These changes in the exchange rate facilitate the absorption of differences in the business cycle between Switzerland and abroad. Finally, it is worth mentioning that, as a result of the exchange rate peg, some of our advantage in terms of long-term interest rates could disappear. The monetary policy option of pegging the franc to the euro also has advantages. The main of these is to make people understand unequivocally the 11 intentions of the central bank. In some situations, this can be helpful. It also has the effect of reducing the short- and medium-term volatility of the Swiss franc. In the longer term, however, no central bank can defend an exchange rate that would be incompatible with the inflation rate desired by the majority of the population. Given the disadvantages and advantages of pegging the franc, it seems clear to me that such a monetary policy option can only be adopted as a last resort. Conclusion I hope I have been able to show you that for Switzerland the single European currency, important as it may be, will not create an entirely new situation. The consequences that the euro could have, if any, on the Swiss economy are not unknown to us in principle. They are just another expression of a traditional difficulty in implementing monetary policy in a small, open economy, namely that of judiciously accounting for foreign influences. Such a consideration is always possible, although it is not easy because of the dilemma it often puts the monetary authorities in front of.

La politique montaire expansive ncessaire pour lutter contre une apprciation exagre du taux de change cre des liquidits excdentaires dans lconomie qui, une fois lactivit conomique en route, pourront se traduire par des pressions inflationnistes. La difficult consiste  retirer ces liquidits avant quelles naient pu se traduire par une stimulation excessive de lactivit conomique et donc par de linflation. Quelle serait donc lalternative ? Elle consisterait  laisser lapprciation du franc suivre son cours. Tout risque dinflation serait ainsi cart. Cependant, lactivit conomique serait aussi indment mise en pril. Les conditions pour quune dflation puisse ventuellement se dvelopper seraient ainsi tablies. Or ceci ne serait pas compatible avec notre objectif de stabilit des prix : la dflation, tout comme linflation, tant en contradiction avec la stabilit des prix. La difficult pratique consiste donc  pondrer ces deux inconvnients : la diminution de lactivit conomique qui est due  une apprciation exagre du franc ; et le risque dinflation qui est d  une croissance montaire exagre. Cette difficult est renforce du fait que la diminution de lactivit se fait sentir rapidement, alors que linflation napparat que bien plus tardivement. La deuxime option de politique montaire  disposition de la Banque nationale pour rpondre  une apprciation exagre du franc consisterait  ancrer le franc  leuro. Lancrage noffre pas un substitut  une politique montaire expansive. Il constitue plutt un complment  une telle politique. En effet, lancrage nlimine pas le risque inflationniste. Il ne fait qualigner le taux dinflation national sur le taux dinflation prvalant  lextrieur. En outre, comme dans tout rgime de changes fixes, il supprime la possibilit dajustement de faible ampleur du taux de change. Ces modifications du cours du change facilitent labsorption des divergences de cycle conomique entre la Suisse et ltranger. Enfin, il convient de mentionner que, par suite de lancrage du change, une partie de notre avantage en termes de taux dintrt  long terme pourrait disparatre. Loption de politique montaire consistant  ancrer le franc  leuro comporte certes aussi des avantages. Le principal dentre eux est de faire comprendre de faon univoque les 11 intentions de la banque centrale. Dans certaines situations, cela peut tre utile. Il a aussi pour effet de rduire la volatilit  court et moyen terme du franc. A plus long terme cependant, aucune banque centrale ne peut dfendre un taux de change qui serait incompatible avec le taux dinflation souhait par la majorit de la population. Au vu des inconvnients et des avantages de lancrage du franc, il me semble clair quune telle option de politique montaire ne saurait tre adopte quen dernier ressort. Conclusion J'espre avoir pu vous montrer que pour la Suisse la monnaie unique europenne, pour importante quelle puisse tre, ne crera pas une situation entirement nouvelle. Les consquences que leuro pourrait avoir, le cas chant, sur lconomie suisse ne nous sont pas inconnues en principe. Elles ne constituent quune nouvelle expression dune difficult traditionnelle de lapplication de la politique montaire dans une petite conomie ouverte,  savoir celle qui a trait  la prise en compte judicieuse des influences de ltranger. Une telle prise en compte est toujours possible, bien quelle ne soit gure aise en raison du dilemme devant lequel elle place souvent les autorits montaires.

Title: The Swiss economy facing the challenges of Europe under construction
text: The Swiss economy facing Europe's challenges under construction Lecture given by Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank on the occasion of the Salon des Industries de l'Automation, de la Mecanique and Subcontracting (SIAMS), held in Moutier, on 27 May 1998 * * * 2 The decisions taken at the beginning of May by the Heads of State and Government of the European Union open a new chapter in European monetary history. Early next year, eleven countries will complete their currency mergers. The euro will appear as the common European currency, first at the level of financial transactions, then at the level of the public two years later. In a few months' time, the national central banks will give up their monetary sovereignty and the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) will lead the common policy. The exchange rate risk between European currencies will have disappeared and the financial market will be unified: the framework in which European companies operate will have been profoundly changed. Switzerland is not a member of the European Union and - even if membership is the strategic objective of the Federal Council's policy - it is unlikely to be part of it in the coming years. Nevertheless, our country is affected by the decisions taken in Brussels at the beginning of May. The appearance of the euro cannot leave us indifferent. Far from it. This is a profound change in our environment: for the first time in our history, all the countries around us will have the same currency. Fundamentally, the monetary integration efforts of our neighbours are good news. The good news is the fact that monetary regimes that have so far had very different performances have been placed under one roof- solidly. I am thinking above all of the integration of the currencies of southern Europe, which tomorrow will be managed with the same rigour as currencies with a more proven tradition of stability. Switzerland, with its geographical position adjoining Germany and Italy, can only welcome any progress in the monetary management of its neighbours. Our companies have often suffered from distortions of competition caused by volatile currencies. If, tomorrow, such situations were to no longer occur, we could only note a clear improvement in the conditions under which we access external markets. 1. Weakened role of the Swiss franc as a settlement currency Beyond this general assessment, it should also be noted that the single currency will have important repercussions on the Swiss economy because the framework in which we operate will be profoundly changed: we will move from a situation characterised by multiple currencies to a much more uniform situation; what in the past was a monetary mosaic will soon become a monocolored whole. For the Swiss franc, such a change is more profound than simply reducing the number of currencies in circulation or eliminating a number of arbitrage possibilities from our exchange rooms. Indeed, it can be expected that the euro will quickly become the reference and accounting currency for European Union companies that trade with each other. Why would they keep the franc, the lira or the mark when they could simplify their mutual payments by using the euro? Until 2002 they will certainly still carry out transactions in national currency for the payment of wages or domestic resources, but the use of the old 3 Currencies will soon be limited to current public expenditure. Faster than we think, the euro will become the reference currency for European companies. What can we expect for Switzerland? The establishment of a European monetary bloc will not be without effect on our export companies. Increasingly, our partners in the European Union will be reluctant to accept payments in Swiss francs. As we know, a significant part of our exports to the European area are denominated in Swiss francs. With monetary integration, this position of the Swiss franc as a transaction currency will be compromised, all the more so if the euro were to show signs of weakness against our currency. It is not a great "Realpolitik" to note that European monetary unification will make Switzerland a somewhat exotic and somewhat marginal market. The great unified market that is being set up on our doorstep will have its rules, its conditions and its currency. We will have to adapt to its particularities and needs, including its payment habits. The euro will thus become a currency with which our companies trading with Europe will have to rely more widely than in the past. 2. The growing use of the euro The increased use of the euro in our external payments will expose our companies to a wider exchange rate risk. How to consider this question? Swiss exporters are already experiencing the difficulties arising from an unstable monetary environment. The whole history of our foreign trade is marked by this. In the recent past, the most violent tremors occurred in the seventies, when the Swiss franc ceased to be pegged to the dollar and became a floating currency. When we consider that at the time of the collapse of the fixed exchange rate regime the dollar was worth 3.70 francs and the German mark 1.16 francs, we realize the difficult path that had to be traveled by our companies. The seventies were years of almost chaotic exchange rate adjustment to the new international monetary order or, more precisely, to the new situation of absence of a monetary regime. We remember in particular 1978 and the overvaluation of the franc which caused the German mark to fall below 80 cents. Then things stabilized and even developed in a relatively harmonious way. If we look at the last fifteen years, we see that the relationship between the Swiss franc and the German mark, if measured in real terms, has not developed irrationally. Over these fifteen years, the franc has appreciated at an average annual rate of 0.5% and it has oscillated around this trend in a band of /- 5%. Bearing in mind that, in the background of these developments, the SNB has implemented an autonomous monetary policy, not based on stabilizing exchange rates through intervention, it must be recognized that the markets have not behaved irrationally. They have, in fact, assessed in a comparable way the currencies - the franc and the mark - of two countries with often very similar cyclical situations, aimed at 4 similar stability objectives and applying identical monetary strategies. This convergence of fundamentals has led to the relative stability of exchange rates. This is not to say that the franc-mark relationship has been risk-free for our export sector. On the contrary, there have been rapid changes in the situation, with the mark price being able to move from one limit of the fluctuation band to another - i.e. vary by 10% - in the space of a few months. These sudden movements are particularly painful for our companies because they cannot be neutralized in the short term by productivity gains, but must be absorbed by margins, to the detriment of cash flow. The presence of currency risk has therefore been a permanent component of the problem of our exports for many years. In the mosaic of post-war European currencies, bilateral risk management was complicated by the multiplicity of currencies. Thus, most generally the reference currency has been the dollar or the DM. Obviously, the ideal solution for us has always been to aim for a settlement in Swiss francs in order to completely eliminate currency risk. In addition, our companies have sought, through an adequate distribution of their place of production or supply, to distribute as much as possible the risks incurred. The emergence of the euro will change the conditions for managing foreign exchange risk in two ways: Firstly, the arrival of the euro will be a welcome simplification. For our exporters, there will no longer be a lira or French franc risk, but a single risk against the euro. For those who until now had to hedge against different risks, things will be simpler. For those who source and resell in the European Union, the risks will be neutralised. In terms of foreign exchange risk management, the euro will therefore be a source of simplification and increased clearing. Secondly, and beyond these positive aspects, we must not hide the difficulties that the single currency could entail. Monolithic Europe will manifest imperialist tendencies, seeking to impose its currency on us in order to be able to trade with it. The marginalization of the franc as a transaction currency will thus carry a greater exchange rate risk for our companies. Is this risk serious? Should we fear monetary turbulence? 5 3. The uncertainties of the euro There is no easy answer to this question. We simply have a set of elements that allow us to judge how the European monetary landscape will look in the coming years. Much has been done to make the euro the worthy successor to the German mark. The Maastricht Treaty established the principle that only the most financially stable countries will participate in the first phase of integration. In this way, we wanted to ensure that the foundations of the euro were solid, free from any discussion. No one will deny the efforts of European countries to fulfil the convergence criteria. When it comes to inflation, interest rates and public deficits, we are now in a much more harmonised situation than we were just five years ago. The most spectacular progress has been made in the area of inflation with the restoration of price stability in continental Europe. Interest rates followed. The situation is much more precarious in the area of public finances. While deficits have fallen below the 3% mark, many countries still have debt-to-GNP ratios that make current account deficits very sensitive to rising interest rates. Despite these reservations, it should be pointed out that few would have imagined, a year ago, that eleven countries would be able to qualify for the first phase of integration. The question that arises at this stage is that of the continuity of this effort. The members of the European Union themselves are wondering about this, since they have planned to guarantee their common discipline through a Stability Pact. The document exists, the commitments are made, but how will it be implemented? Here we must hope that the constraints will be exercised without any political considerations, for the sake of the common well-being and the credibility of the common policy. Indeed, without well-controlled public finances, conflicts of interest between monetary policy and fiscal policy become so important that the application of a policy of price stability is hindered. The European Central Bank (ECB) will already have enough problems managing the monetary system to do without conflicts with the finance ministers! The ECB's challenges are enormous both technically and politically. At the technical level, it will have to define a strategy and instruments to enable it to maintain inflation control. From the point of view of monetary technology, the ambition is already great to want to manage in parallel eleven countries with different monetary structures. The task of interconnected markets will be to ensure that Europe has only one capital market and one money market. So there will be only one interest rate from Hamburg to Lisbon. The merging of markets and the unification of monetary intervention techniques are very ambitious chapters in the single currency project. Experts have been working this for years. For all operators, the most visible part is the establishment of a European system of electronic payments, the system that will allow German and Portuguese banks to exchange funds without wasting time and that will give the ECB the means to regulate market liquidity, and therefore to implement its policy. If it can be accepted that, from 1.1.1999, the technical infrastructure will enable payments to be made in euro and the ECB to implement its policy, 6 questions still remain about how the new monetary regime will operate over time. Let us have no illusions, the European monetary institutions will still have to be honed; they are a masterpiece of political balance but they lack the patina of time. Let me illustrate this with some analog examples: First of all, these institutions have no history, therefore no acquired reputation. The model of the vehicle is known but it is not known exactly how its driver - even if he is aware of the rules of the road - will behave once seated in front of his steering wheel. Here the continuity with the existing central banks gives the assurance that the search for stability will be the objective of the common action. Nevertheless, the fact that the policy will be set to eleven creates uncertainty about the dynamics of the group. Secondly, there is much to fear that the first stages of the monetary journey will be marked by a thick fog. Indeed, at the beginning of its activity the ECB will not be able to observe reliable monetary indicators. These simply do not exist at the moment at European level and when they do exist it will still take time to understand their characteristics. The launch period of the common currency will therefore be full of uncertainties in the conduct of the common monetary policy. Secondly, it is not known whether or not the driver will be sensitive to the injunctions he will receive from the outside. Will it follow its monetary path without being influenced by political pressure from its member countries? It will be necessary to see it in use. In any case, the discussions surrounding the appointment of the first President of the ECB have shown that politics will not refrain from reacting to the common monetary policy. Moreover, it is likely that the national parliaments, which are responsible for national social policies, will not remain indifferent to the supranational decisions that will be taken in the monetary field. Will the common currency become "unmanageable" in the event of a cyclical setback? I do not think so. However, the absence of a European government leaves the ECB alone in the face of criticism of short-term economic policy. Finally, and from a Swiss point of view, it should already be realised that, over time, a "Fortress Europe" mentality will develop - as it exists in the United States - which will tend to bagatellize exchange rate problems, which are not of great importance for the functioning of the internal market. If this were to be the case, countries outside the euro area could suffer the consequences of the volatility of the European currency. 7 4. Controlling exchange rate risk We are therefore entering uncertain waters, in an environment where the functioning of the European institutions, or even the policy followed, can lead to significant exchange rate risks for external countries. This issue is of great interest to us given the importance of our trade relations with the eleven of the Monetary Union. How to approach it? Some will think from the outset that the responsibility for ensuring the stability of the link between the euro and the Swiss franc lies with the SNB. These people misunderstand our mandate and overestimate our possibilities for action. Our mandate is to conduct monetary policy in the general interest of the country, which is understood as price stability. Our mandate is not to ensure exchange rate stability, although this parameter is important for the development of our exports. To want to ensure the stability of the exchange rate is to put monetary policy at the service of a specific objective that can conflict - in extreme situations - with that of internal monetary control, all the more so if the world around us is troubled. In the event of currency turbulence, the SNB cannot fight on two fronts. This was not possible in the 1970s, it is even less possible today with globalized markets. Even if we wanted to prioritize neutralizing external monetary turmoil, we could have great difficulty in achieving it. As long as Switzerland is not part of the EU, it is illusory to think that the Swiss franc-euro relationship can be stabilized, with a wave of a magic wand, by the SNB. It is sometimes suggested that we set a parity between the franc and the future euro autonomously in order to eliminate exchange rate uncertainties. A unilateral peg of the franc to the euro would be perceived by the markets as a very attractive speculative objective. Markets would test parity. This would recreate the speculative atmosphere of the fixed exchange period when our currency was always a candidate for revaluation. We would blow on the embers instead of easing tensions. We are convinced that the answer to monetary uncertainty is not the setting of artificial lines of defence  unsustainable and benefiting only speculators  ; the only adequate answer is uncertainty, and therefore exchange rate flexibility. The economy cannot therefore expect the SNB to eliminate the problem of foreign exchange risk management. As I indicated at the beginning of my presentation, the need to hedge exchange rate risks is not a new problem for our export companies. This question will simply take on a new intensity tomorrow. The problem of hedging exchange rate risks is well known: to the extent that companies have revenues in euros that are not covered by costs denominated in euros, they run a currency risk. In a way, hedging residual risk will be easier tomorrow than in the past because a single currency will exist and no longer a whole set of currencies of various qualities. Companies will always tend to hedge part of their risks through an appropriate diversification of their sources of supply in the euro area. This is an understandable reaction and it is clear at a time that there will be a great deal of pressure on domestic producers, in particular. 8 SMEs, so that they produce on terms comparable to those of the euro area. Increased competition is always legitimate and in the interest of low production costs. However, in my view, that competition would go too far if it were intended solely to transfer exporters' costs of hedging exporters' foreign exchange risks to Swiss subcontracting. The limits of deferring the costs of hedging foreign exchange risks are obvious anyway. Some production costs fall in Swiss francs, including wage costs. With regard to these, only a policy of financial hedging of risks by exporters will be appropriate. Any attempt to shift exchange rate uncertainties onto wages would be counterproductive over time because of the social tensions it would trigger. In the end, it makes good sense that the costs of hedging exchange rate risks should be borne by those who export and not transferred to the elements upstream of the production process, which are by nature less well equipped to deal with this problem. 5. Let's remain vigilant In a few months' time, the Europe around us will begin a process of monetary transformation. The project is very ambitious. The elements put in place are intended to promote lasting stability. Monetary union is a stage in the construction of Europe. It will complement and consolidate what has already been achieved in terms of market integration. In this respect, it gives an irrevocable character to the company. Monetary union is also an ambitious project from a technical and political point of view. For the first time in history, national currencies will disappear in favor of a supranational currency without a political revolution taking place in the background. Ambitious project also means risky project and source of uncertainty. Many questions will remain in the coming months about the quality of the future European currency. These uncertainties will also affect us. It is up to us to do everything we can to protect ourselves from their negative consequences. The SNB is aware of this. For almost two years, it has been pursuing a policy that seeks to prevent the Swiss franc from being put under pressure due to uncertainties about the euro. This preventive strategy has worked well so far, the markets have remained remarkably calm. These calm waters do not mean that we are immune to disturbances. Once the euro is installed, these could become all the more damaging as the Swiss franc can be used more difficult as a means of settlement. Our economy will thus become more fragile in the face of exchange rate fluctuations. Exporting companies must remain vigilant in this regard. They cannot hope that monetary policy will be able to ensure the stability of the relationship between the franc and the euro. Distortions cannot be excluded, distortions that 9 could be very damaging to our export sector if it was not careful to hedge its exchange rate risks. In the end, it is only through concerted action by the monetary authorities and businesses that our economy will be able to protect itself against the disruptions caused by the uncertainties of monetary union.

Title: Height and significance of the currency reserves of the Swiss National Bank
text: by Dr. Peter Klauser Director of the Swiss National Bank (SVP Delegates' Assembly of 30 May 1998 in Aarau) Introduction "Gold - Gold Reserves - Golden Times for Public Finances", this idea some people seem to associate with the reform of the monetary constitution. In fact, the Swiss franc's dissolution of the legal obligation to gold allows the SNB's gold holdings to be revalued. However, it also requires an assessment of the amount and importance of currency reserves as a whole. Only then can one talk about the management and use of so-called surplus reserves. I would like to introduce you to my topic in three steps: 1. What are currency reserves? 2. How high are the SNB's foreign exchange reserves today? 3. How high should the SNB's foreign exchange reserves be in the future? 1. What are currency reserves? Currency reserves are assets of a central bank, namely those that can be used for international payment purposes. Currency reserves mainly include gold, foreign exchange and assets with the International Monetary Fund. Foreign exchange reserves do not include the SNB's domestic assets, such as domestic securities. Currency reserves can be used to influence the exchange rate, for international monetary cooperation and - not unimportant - for crisis preparedness and management. 2 In systems with fixed exchange rates, currency reserves are needed to defend the exchange rate limits; this compensates for temporary balance-of-payments imbalances. Freely fluctuating exchange rates, on the other hand, automatically compensate for any balance of payments inequalities. Nevertheless, after the transition to flexible exchange rates at the beginning of the seventies, the need for short-term currency reserves worldwide did not diminish. On the contrary, currency reserves increased in many industrialised countries- including Switzerland. In order to counteract undesirable exchange rate movements, relatively high foreign exchange reserves are particularly useful for interventions in the foreign exchange market. They help smooth out unforeseen capital flows and maintain confidence in one's own currency. High currency reserves serve to prevent and overcome any crises. The financial crisis in Southeast Asia has shown us drastically how quickly the credibility of a currency can be shaken by the dwindling of a central bank's reserves. Such a provision has its price. The central bank's reserves required for monetary policy must be kept in a liquid, secure form. Yield considerations play a subordinate role in their investment and management - in contrast to the so-called surplus reserves. 2. What are the SNB's current currency reserves? At the end of December 1997, the SNB's foreign exchange reserves amounted to around CHF 68.5 billion. The lion's share of this is accounted for by unsecured foreign exchange, i.e. investments in foreign currency (40.8 billion euros). Franconia); about three quarters were invested in dollars, the rest in DM, yen and some other currencies. In second place are the exchange rate hedged currencies (12.5 billion). Franconia); these are dollar investments that have already been sold against Swiss francs on a future date (liquidity swaps). In third place figure with 11.9 billion. Swiss francs the gold holdings. They 3 amount to 2,590 tonnes and have been valued at the official parity price of CHF 4,595/kg since 1971. The reserve position at the IMF and the other international means of payment amount to 3.2 billion. Swiss franc accounts for only 4.7% of foreign exchange reserves. The composition of Switzerland's currency reserves has changed considerably in the last 30 years: in the mid-sixties, foreign exchange reserves with a stock of CHF 1 billion did not yet account for 10 percent of the gold stock. The high dollar purchases before and after the collapse of the system of fixed exchange rates at the beginning of the seventies caused the SNB's dollar holdings to rise sharply. These dollar investments also yielded income that was retained until 1991, i.e. not distributed to the Confederation and the cantons. At the end of 1997, the total foreign exchange portfolio amounted to CHF 53.3 billion. about 41/2 times as high as the gold stock. If the gold reserves were valued at the market price of December 1997 (CHF 13,500/kg), this would result in an amount of at least 35 billion. Swiss francs or almost as much as the unsecured foreign exchange. What functions do the individual components of currency reserves fulfil? In a very simplified way, the following can be said: The unsecured foreign exchange reserves allow the SNB to intervene in the foreign exchange market in the event of exchange rate turbulence and to ensure orderly currency conditions. It is undisputed that a small country like Switzerland, which is closely intertwined with the global economy and has a major international financial centre, must have sufficient unsecured foreign exchange reserves. The need for unsecured foreign exchange reserves is increasing with the growth of foreign trade and capital movements. From this derives the rule of thumb that the unsecured foreign exchange reserves should be increased at least in step with the nominal gross national product. The profit distribution concept agreed by the SNB with the Federal Council at the beginning of 1992 is based on this rule - as is the new 4 Profit distribution agreement concluded by the Federal Council and the SNB in April 1998. The exchange rate-hedged foreign exchange reserves held by the SNB in the form of liquidity swaps are nominally denominated in dollars, but are in fact investments in Swiss francs. They perform a completely different function than the unsecured foreign exchange investments. The SNB uses them as an instrument to manage the money supply. In this sense, they cannot be regarded as actual currency reserves. With the increased use of securities repo transactions for money supply management, the holdings of secured foreign exchange reserves are likely to decrease in the future anyway. With the reform of the monetary constitution, gold takes on a different significance: the SNB's obligation to redeem banknotes in gold, which has already been suspended for decades, the minimum gold coverage of banknotes in circulation and the gold parity of the franc are abolished. Nevertheless, gold will remain a special reserve medium. In contrast to foreign exchange investments, gold is the only state-independent international means of payment; Gold reserves stored domestically cannot be blocked by decisions of authorities or their availability restricted. A second reason in favor of keeping gold is the way its value develops: while in normal times gold incurs costs from warehousing and lost interest rates, its value increases in times of financial crises and unstable conditions. Thus, the value of gold behaves just opposite to the value of foreign exchange investments. This makes gold a valuable means of portfolio diversification for central banks. Finally, the presence of a well-known gold stock increases the credibility of monetary policy for emotional reasons. The reserve position at the IMF could indeed be held by Switzerland in the event of Zahlungsbilanzschwierigkeiten claim. For However, these balances are not available for exchange rate interventions. 5 Decree. Nor can the IMF's Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) be acquired through the market or used for exchange rate interventions. Finally, the ECU balances also result from international monetary cooperation and cannot be planned in advance. These central bank assets therefore hardly play a role in the discussion about the future level of the SNB's foreign exchange reserves. 3. How high should the SNB's currency reserves be in the future? How much currency reserves a central bank needs to conduct a successful monetary policy cannot be scientifically determined exactly. What is certain is that the necessary amount of currency reserves depends above all on the size of the country's economy and its international ties. The size of the economy can be measured by gross domestic product by annual national income. A simple measure for determining the openness of an economy is the volume of imports or exports. If one compares gross domestic product and import volume - the current currency reserves of the SNB with those of other central banks - on the basis of these figures, the desirable amount of foreign exchange reserves can be estimated. At the end of 1997, the SNB's foreign exchange reserves - which value gold at the market price - amounted to 23% of Switzerland's gross domestic product. This puts us by far at the top of the Western industrialised countries. Countries with a similar structure and size to Switzerland - such as Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden - have to make do with significantly fewer foreign exchange reserves, usually with less than 10% of the gross domestic product. It is easy to see that smaller countries with strong foreign ties tend to hold higher foreign exchange reserves in relation to their gross domestic product than larger industrialised countries (USA, Great Britain). Today, gold's share of currency reserves is still an average of 29% in western industrialized countries, and almost half in Switzerland (excluding secured foreign exchange). 6 Measured in terms of annual imports, Switzerland's foreign exchange reserves amounted to around 90% at the end of 1997. Only Japan is on a similar scale among the western industrialized countries. The International Monetary Fund recommends in its programmes for developing and transition countries that a country's foreign exchange reserves should allow all imports to be financed for three months. For developed countries with good access to international capital markets, this ratio may be lower. As our comparison shows, it is not or only narrowly achieved by various countries in the group of ten. An international cross-comparison of the reserve quotation, broken down according to the components of unsecured foreign exchange and gold, is now meaningful. Foreign exchange reserves in relation to gross domestic product and imports show that Switzerland - with 11.3% and 42.5% respectively - is in a similar order of magnitude to Austria. It is confirmed that smaller countries hold higher reserves in relation to gross domestic product than larger countries. As a percentage of imports, Japan has a significantly higher foreign exchange allocation than Switzerland. When comparing gold reserves, it is first noticeable that most central banks in western industrialized countries have stuck to gold as a currency reserve. Gold sales have been made in recent years in the USA, Canada, Belgium and the Netherlands. As the overview shows, the USA holds by far the most gold with over 8,000 tons. Germany follows in second place with 2,960 tonnes, ahead of Switzerland (2,590 tonnes), France (2,547 tonnes) and Italy (2,074 tonnes). In terms of gross domestic product and imports, Switzerland is the lone leader here. In summary, these comparisons show us that the SNB does not have unusually high unsecured foreign exchange reserves. On the other hand, the extremely well-endowed gold reserves fall out of the frame. With the reform of the monetary order, the gold stock is now gaining its function 7 back as a normally usable currency reserve; it is no longer immobilized due to legal gold parity. This raises the question: Does the SNB need a gold stock of just under 2,600 tonnes to fulfil its monetary policy mandate? The Expert Group on "Reform of the Monetary Order" saw two reasons why the SNB should not be content with holding similarly high foreign exchange reserves as the central banks of comparable European economies: Firstly, Switzerland has an important international financial centre. A strong central bank with well-endowed currency reserves helps to secure the confidence of foreign investors. This promotes the stability of the Swiss financial system. A high level of confidence on the part of foreign investors also helps to keep interest rates in Switzerland low. This, in turn, is in the interest of the entire economy. Secondly, at the beginning of 1999, Switzerland will not adopt the European single currency, the euro, but will continue to conduct an independent monetary policy. This is another reason why the SNB must hold generously endowed currency reserves compared to other European countries. In the event of financial crises and other turbulence, it cannot automatically count on the assistance of its foreign colleagues. Rather, it is on its own. The amount of additional foreign exchange reserves that the SNB should have at its disposal in addition to the foreign exchange reserves is not easy to determine. The expert group estimated him at 10 billion. Franconia, and the Federal Council followed suit. The SNB would hold these additional reserves in gold. Gold should be valued cautiously. With a valuation of 60% of the market price (of CHF 13,500/kg in December 1997), a gold stock of just under 1,300 tonnes is necessary to build on additional reserves of a good 10 billion tonnes. Franconia. 8 Conclusion What does this mean in concrete terms? In addition to foreign exchange reserves and balances with the International Monetary Fund, the SNB still needs around 1,300 tonnes of gold for monetary policy purposes. As a result, it will be able to conduct a stability-oriented monetary policy even after the Swiss franc's gold peg has been abandoned and will be able to provide the banking system with the necessary support. Half of today's gold stock - 1,300 tons or at today's market price (14,000 Fr./kg) around 18 billion. Swiss francs are available for other public purposes. For what purposes does politics, not the National Bank, have to decide?
