Stark vereinfacht lsst sich folgendes sagen: Die ungesicherten Devisenreserven erlauben der SNB, bei Wechselkursturbulenzen am Devisenmarkt zu intervenieren und fr geordnete Whrungverhltnisse zu sorgen. Es ist unbestritten, dass ein kleines Land wie die Schweiz, das eng mit der Weltwirtschaft verflochten ist und einen bedeutenden internationalen Finanzplatz besitzt, ber gengend ungesicherte Devisenreserven verfgen muss. Der Bedarf an ungesicherten Devisenreserven nimmt mit dem Wachstum des Aussenhandels und des Kapitalverkehrs zu. Daraus leitet sich die Faustregel ab, dass die ungesicherten Devisenreserven mindestens im Gleichschritt mit dem nominalen Bruttosozialprodukt aufgestockt werden sollten. Das Gewinnausschttungskonzept, das die SNB Anfang 1992 mit dem Bundesrat vereinbarte, beruht auf dieser Regel - ebenso wie die neue 4 Gewinnausschttungsvereinbarung, die Bundesrat und Nationalbank im April 1998 abschlossen. Die kursgesicherten Devisenreserven, welche die SNB in Form von Liquiditts-swaps hlt, lauten zwar nominell auf Dollar, sind aber faktisch Anlagen in Schweizerfranken. Sie erfllen eine vllig andere Funktion als die ungesicherten Devisenanlagen. Die SNB verwendet sie als Instrument zur Steuerung der Geldmenge. In diesem Sinne knnen sie nicht als eigentliche Whrungsreserven gelten. Mit dem vermehrten Einsatz von WertpapierRepogeschften fr die Geldmengensteuerung drften die Bestnde an gesicherten Devisenreserven in Zukunft ohnehin abnehmen. Das Gold erhlt mit der Reform der Whrungsverfassung einen anderen Stellenwert: Die Pflicht der SNB zur Einlsung von Banknoten in Gold, die ohnehin schon seit Jahrzehnten suspendiert ist, die Mindestgolddeckung des Notenumlaufs sowie die Goldparitt des Frankens werden aufgehoben. Trotzdem wird das Gold ein spezielles Reservemedium bleiben. Im Gegensatz zu den Devisenanlagen ist Gold das einzige staatenunabhngige internationale Zahlungsmittel; im Inland aufbewahrte Goldreserven lassen sich weder durch Entscheide von Behrden blockieren noch in ihrer Verfgbarkeit einschrnken. Ein zweiter Grund, der fr die Goldhaltung spricht, ist die Art und Weise, wie sich sein Wert entwickelt: Whrend Gold in normalen Zeiten Kosten durch Lagerhaltung und entgangene Zinsen verursacht, steigt sein Wert in Zeiten von Finanzkrisen und instabilen Verhltnissen. Damit verhlt sich der Wert des Goldes gerade gegenstzlich zum Wert von Devisenanlagen. Das lsst Gold zu einem wertvollen Mittel der Portfoliodiversifikation fr Zentralbanken werden. Schliesslich steigert das Vorhandensein eines namhaften Goldbestandes aus emotionellen Grnden die Glaubwrdigkeit der Geldpolitik. Die Reserveposition beim IWF knnte die Schweiz zwar im Fall von Zahlungsbilanzschwierigkeiten beanspruchen. Fr Wechselkursinterventionen stehen diese Guthaben jedoch nicht zur 5 Verfgung. Auch die Sonderziehungsrechte (SZR) des IWF lassen sich weder ber den Markt erwerben noch fr Wechselkursinterventionen einsetzen. Die ECU-Guthaben schliesslich ergeben sich ebenfalls aus der internationalen Whrungskooperation und sind nicht im voraus planbar. Diese Aktiven der Notenbank spielen daher in der Diskussion um die zuknftige Hhe der Whrungsreserven der SNB kaum eine Rolle. 3. Wie hoch sollten die Whrungsreserven der SNB insknftig sein? Wie viel Whrungsreserven eine Notenbank braucht, um eine erfolgreiche Geld- und Whrungspolitik zu fhren, lsst sich nicht wissenschaftlich exakt festlegen. Sicher ist, dass der notwendige Umfang an Whrungsreserven vor allem von der Grsse der Wirtschaft und der Auslandverflechtung des Landes abhngt. Die Grsse der Wirtschaft kann am Bruttoinlandprodukt am jhrlichen Volkseinkommen - gemessen werden. Ein einfaches Mass fr die Bestimmung der Offenheit einer Volkswirtschaft ist das Volumen der Importe oder Exporte. Vergleicht man anhand dieser Grssen Bruttoinlandprodukt und Importvolumen - die aktuellen Whrungsreserven der SNB mit jenen anderer Zentralbanken, so lsst sich die wnschbare Hhe der Whrungsreserven abschtzen. Ende 1997 beliefen sich die Whrungsreserven der Nationalbank - das Gold zum Marktpreis bewertet - auf 23% des Bruttoinlandprodukts der Schweiz. Wir liegen damit bei weitem an der Spitze der westlichen Industrielnder. Lnder mit hnlicher Struktur und Grsse wie die Schweiz - etwa Oesterreich, Belgien, Niederlande, Schweden - mssen mit deutlich weniger Whrungsreserven auskommen, zumeist mit weniger als 10% des Bruttoinlandprodukts. Leicht erkennbar ist, dass kleinere Lnder mit einer starken Auslandverflechtung im Verhltnis zu ihrem Bruttoinlandprodukt eher hhere Whrungsreserven halten als grssere Industrielnder (USA, Grossbritannien). Der Anteil des Goldes an den Whrungsreserven betrgt heute in den westlichen Industrielndern noch durchschnittlich 29%, in der Schweiz nahezu die Hlfte (ohne gesicherte Devisen). 6 Gemessen an den jhrlichen Importen, beliefen sich die Whrungsreserven der Schweiz Ende 1997 auf gegen 90%. Nur Japan bewegt sich hier unter den westlichen Industrielndern in einer hnlichen Grssenordnung. Der internationale Whrungsfonds empfiehlt in seinen Programmen fr Entwicklungs- und Transitionslnder, dass die Whrungsreserven eines Landes whrend drei Monaten eine Finanzierung smtlicher Importe ermglichen sollten. Fr Industrielnder mit gutem Zugang zu den internationalen Kapitalmrkten kann diese Quote tiefer sein. Sie wird denn auch - wie unser Vergleich zeigt - von verschiedenen Lndern der Zehnergruppe nicht oder nur knapp erreicht. Aussagekrftig ist nun ein internationaler Quervergleich der Reservedotierung, aufgegliedert nach den Komponenten ungesicherte Devisen und Gold. Bei den Devisenreserven im Verhltnis zum Bruttoinlandprodukt und zu den Importen zeigt sich, dass die Schweiz - mit 11,3% bzw. 42,5% - in einer hnlichen Grssenordnung liegt wie sterreich. Es besttigt sich, dass kleinere Lnder im Verhltnis zum Bruttoinlandprodukt hhere Reserven halten als grssere Lnder. In Prozenten der Importe verfgt Japan ber eine deutlich hhere Devisenausstattung als die Schweiz. Beim Vergleich der Goldreserven fllt zunchst auf, dass die meisten Notenbanken der westlichen Industrielnder am Gold als Whrungsreserve festgehalten haben. Goldverkufe ttigten in den letzten Jahren die USA, Kanada, Belgien und die Niederlande. Wie aus der bersicht hervorgeht, halten die USA mit ber 8'000 Tonnen mit Abstand am meisten Gold. Deutschland folgt an zweiter Stelle mit 2'960 Tonnen, vor der Schweiz (2'590 Tonnen), Frankreich (2'547 Tonnen) und Italien (2'074 Tonnen). Gemessen am Bruttoinlandprodukt und an den Importen ist die Schweiz hier einsame Spitze. Zusammenfassend zeigen uns diese Vergleiche: Die Nationalbank verfgt nicht ber ungewhnlich hohe ungesicherte Devisenreserven. Aus dem Rahmen fallen dagegen die beraus gut dotierten Goldreserven. Mit der Reform der Whrungsordnung gewinnt nun der Goldbestand seine Funktion 7 als normal verwendbare Whrungsreserve zurck; er ist nicht lnger aufgrund der gesetzlichen Goldparitt immobilisiert. Deshalb stellt sich die Frage: Bentigt die SNB einen Goldbestand von knapp 2'600 Tonnen, um ihren geld- und whrungspolitischen Auftrag zu erfllen? Die Expertengruppe "Reform der Whrungsordnung" sah zwei Grnde, weshalb die Nationalbank sich nicht damit begngen sollte, hnlich hohe Whrungsreserven zu halten wie die Zentralbanken von vergleichbaren europischen Volkswirtschaften: Erstens verfgt die Schweiz ber einen bedeutenden internationalen Finanzplatz. Eine starke Zentralbank mit gut dotierten Whrungsreserven trgt dazu bei, das Vertrauen der auslndischen Anleger zu sichern. Dadurch wird die Stabilitt des schweizerischen Finanzsystems gefrdert. Ein hohes Vertrauen der auslndischen Anleger hilft zudem mit, die Zinsen in der Schweiz tief zu halten. Das wiederum liegt im Interesse der ganzen Volkswirtschaft. Zweitens wird die Schweiz anfangs 1999 nicht die europische Einheitswhrung, den Euro, bernehmen, sondern weiterhin eine eigenstndige Geld- und Whrungspolitik fhren. Auch deshalb muss die SNB im Vergleich zu anderen europischen Lndern grosszgig dotierte Whrungsreserven halten. Sie kann nmlich bei Finanzkrisen und anderen Turbulenzen nicht automatisch mit dem Beistand ihrer auslndischen Kolleginnen rechnen. Sie ist vielmehr auf sich selbst gestellt. Der Betrag an zustzlichen Whrungsreserven, ber den die Nationalbank nebst den Devisenreserven verfgen sollte, ist nicht einfach zu bestimmen. Die Expertengruppe schtzte ihn auf 10 Mia. Franken, und der Bundesrat ist ihr gefolgt. Die Nationalbank wrde diese zustzlichen Reserven in Gold halten. Dabei ist das Gold vorsichtig zu bewerten. Bei einer Bewertung von 60% des Marktpreises (von 13'500 Fr./kg im Dezember 1997) ist ein Goldbestand von knapp 1'300 Tonnen ntig, um auf zustzliche Reserven von gut 10 Mia. Franken zu kommen. 8 Schlussfolgerung Was bedeutet dies konkret? Die Nationalbank braucht fr geld- und whrungspolitische Zwecke neben den Devisenreserven und den Guthaben beim Internationalen Whrungsfonds noch etwa 1'300 Tonnen Gold. Damit wird sie auch nach Aufgabe der Goldbindung des Frankens eine stabilittsorientierte Geldpolitik fhren und dem Bankensystem den ntigen Rckhalt geben knnen. Die Hlfte des heutigen Goldbestandes - 1'300 Tonnen oder zum heutigen Marktpreis (14'000 Fr./kg) rund 18 Mia. Franken stehen fr andere ffentliche Zwecke zur Verfgung. Fr welche Zwecke, hat die Politik, nicht die Nationalbank, zu entscheiden.

Title: Introductory remarks, half-yearly press conference
text: Biannual press conference, Geneva, 18 June 1998 Introductory remarks by Bruno Gehrig In the run-up to the changeover to the euro On 1 January 1999, eleven of the fifteen Member States of the European Union will introduce the euro. This will open a new chapter in international monetary history. Within the zone, conversion rates will be set irrevocably. In all eleven countries, the euro will become a common value standard and means of payment. Initially exclusively scriptural, the new currency will be extended to cash payments in 2002, after the exchange of all banknotes and coins. The financial markets welcomed the delimitation of the euro currency area. The conditions are good for the new currency to be stable. Thus, the euro should follow in the footsteps of the German mark and become the main currency, after the US dollar. The European Central Bank (ECB) - the new monetary authority will determine and implement the monetary policy of the entire area. An undeniably delicate task, but one that is not insurmountable. Compared to what was generally imagined a few years ago, the framework conditions necessary for the success of monetary policy are now more favourable. In anticipation of the euro, the interest rate differentials of the countries of the zone have already largely closed. On the economic side, significant discrepancies are still observed; however, they should show a downward trend. Moreover, there have been no signs of easing so far in efforts to consolidate public finances, which remain an ongoing task. Perhaps the toughest problem is unemployment. However, the ECB will only be able to make a marginal contribution to resolving it. As a result of the changeover to the euro, the Swiss economy will face many challenges. The main one is exchange rates. We may see increased volatility in exchange rates, at least in the first instance. 2 phase. Such volatility is not worrisome, as long as it is short-term fluctuations and not too strong. However, this problem will not only arise from 1999 onwards. It is indeed already current - and has been for some time - since expectations play a dominant role in the evolution of exchange rate relations. Retroactively, it can be seen that, contrary to the fears of many market specialists, prices have not suffered strong shocks. Let us not forget that the evolution of exchange rate relations between the currencies of the future euro area and the franc has not jeopardised the recovery of the economic situation in Switzerland, which, it must be stressed, is part of exports. Exchange rates, however, are a risk that always requires sustained attention from all concerned. However, with regard to the impact of the euro on payment transactions, we do not currently have a reliable benchmark. For cross-border trade, the disappearance of several currencies in favour of a single one will be an advantage. Hedging of foreign exchange risk will be simpler, especially as the costs inherent in this hedging will decrease thanks to market liquidity, which is likely to be stronger, and easier access to financial instruments. In addition, part of the trade flows that are invoiced today in Swiss francs should in the long run be denominated in euros. The fear that the euro will gradually supplant the franc in Switzerland is unfounded. Large payments will of course be made in euros between banks, in corporate financial services and on the stock exchange. In addition, the European currency is likely to play a certain role in transactions with Swiss suppliers. Swiss exporters with substantial revenues in euros may attempt to impose on their suppliers invoicing in euros or, if they fail to do so, a discount on prices in francs, which will correspond approximately to the cost of hedging the exchange rate risk. However, the bulk of payments in our country will continue to be made in Swiss francs. Thus, wages and, consequently, consumer expenditure, as well as the flow of payments relating to pension provision and the public sector, will remain in Swiss francs, probably almost without exception. Salaries will probably not be paid in euros, apart from a few cases. This estimate is based less on legal aspects than on considerations relating to the ability to take risks and the cost of hedging the risk of 3 exchange. An average household is neither willing nor able to bear a foreign exchange risk on the income used to maintain it. For reasons of profitability, it is clear that businesses  not households  will make the necessary arrangements to hedge against currency risk. Conclusion: The euro will increasingly affect economic life in Switzerland. However, it should not impose itself as a parallel currency, at least not in the areas of wages and consumption. Increased margin in the SNB's investment policy A revision of the National Bank Act entered into force on 1 November. It has created the legal basis for a more cost-effective management of foreign exchange reserves. Since then, the SNB has had more room for manoeuvre for its investments. It must no longer confine itself to investments whose duration does not exceed twelve months, i.e. in investments on the money markets, but can also acquire bonds, whatever the duration. We therefore have the opportunity to further diversify our foreign exchange reserves and invest in currencies for which only the medium- or long-term bond markets offer the liquidity that meets our needs. After the revision came into effect, we started to revamp our portfolio to around CHF 40 billion (see table). We have increased the share of the German mark, to the detriment of that of the UNITED States dollar, and invested in three new currencies, namely the pound sterling, the Dutch guilder and the Danish krone. These currencies have one thing in common: their bond markets enjoy good liquidity. Investments in pounds sterling and, to a lesser extent, guilders have been made for the purpose of diversification in particular. Today, 60% of our foreign exchange reserves are still in US dollars. The share of the German mark is almost 30%. Other foreign exchange reserves are denominated in yen and the three new investment currencies. The UNITED States dollar will continue to play a dominant role. As a result of these realignments, we have significantly reduced the monetary risk on our portfolio. We have also gradually increased the average duration of our investments. Since November 1st, we have reduced the share of investments on 4 money markets in total foreign exchange reserves (see chart). We are aiming for an average duration of about three years. Foreign currency holdings that arise from swaps - i.e. are sold forward - do not enter foreign exchange reserves because they are not fully available. At the SNB, dollar-to-franc swaps have a long tradition as an instrument of monetary policy. Last week, we passed swaps for German marks against francs for the first time in order to strengthen the possibilities we have for the implementation of our monetary policy. These reshuffles were able to take place at a steady pace and without any adverse repercussions on the markets. As our investment opportunities expanded, we strengthened risk management. Market and credit risks are monitored on a daily basis, in accordance with the relevant rules. Experience in recent months shows that it must be possible, thanks to the new provisions governing our investments, to obtain generally higher and less fluctuating returns. Our investment policy, it should be recalled, remains subordinated to monetary objectives. Above all, we focus on highly liquid investments with minimal credit risk. Bonds issued by states and those with an explicit or implicit state guarantee meet these strict requirements. 5 Foreign exchange reserves - Breakdown by duration of investments Part 100% 80% 60% 40% 20% Money Market Investments (up to one year) Bonds (more than one year old) 0% Nov. 97 Dec 97 Jan. 98 Feb. 98 Mar 98 Apr 98 May 98 Foreign exchange reserves - Breakdown by currency United States dollar German mark Yen Dutch guilder Pound sterling Danish krone Dec. 96 79% 16% 5% - Dec. 97 72% May 98 60% 22% 5% 1% - 28% 6% 4% 2% less than 1%
text_original: Confrence de presse semestrielle, Genve, le 18 juin 1998 Remarques introductives de Bruno Gehrig A l'approche du passage  l'euro Le 1er janvier 1999, onze des quinze Etats de l'Union europenne introduiront l'euro. Ainsi s'ouvrira un nouveau chapitre de l'histoire montaire internationale. Au sein de la zone, les cours de conversion seront fixs irrvocablement. Dans les onze pays, l'euro deviendra un talon de valeur et un moyen de paiement communs. D'abord exclusivement scripturale, la nouvelle monnaie sera tendue aux paiements en numraire, en 2002, aprs l'change de tous les billets et de toutes les pices. Les marchs financiers ont bien accueilli la dlimitation de la zone montaire de l'euro. Les conditions sont bonnes pour que la nouvelle monnaie soit stable. Ainsi, l'euro devrait marcher sur les traces du mark allemand et devenir la principale monnaie, aprs le dollar des Etats-Unis. La Banque centrale europenne (BCE) - la nouvelle autorit montaire dterminera et mettra en uvre la politique montaire de l'ensemble de la zone. Une tche incontestablement dlicate, mais qui n'est pas insurmontable. Par rapport  ce qu'on imaginait gnralement il y a quelques annes, les conditions-cadres ncessaires au succs de la politique montaire sont aujourd'hui plus favorables. Dans l'attente de l'euro, les carts entre taux d'intrt des pays de la zone se sont dj en grande partie combls. Du ct de la conjoncture conomique, de sensibles dcalages sont encore observs; ils devraient toutefois marquer une tendance au repli. En outre, aucun signe de relchement n'est apparu jusqu'ici dans les efforts en vue d'assainir les finances publiques, qui restent une tche permanente. Le problme le plus coriace est sans doute celui du chmage. La BCE ne pourra cependant contribuer que marginalement  le rsoudre. Du fait du passage  l'euro, l'conomie suisse devra relever de nombreux dfis. Le principal d'entre eux porte sur les cours de change. Nous observerons peuttre une volatilit accrue des cours de change, au moins dans une premire 2 phase. Une telle volatilit n'est pas inquitante, tant qu'il s'agit de fluctuations  court terme et pas trop fortes. Toutefois, ce problme ne se posera pas seulement  partir de 1999. Il est en effet dj actuel - et depuis un certain temps - puisque les anticipations jouent un rle dominant dans l'volution des relations de change. Rtroactivement, on peut constater que, contrairement aux craintes de nombreux spcialistes des marchs, les cours n'ont pas subi de fortes secousses. N'oublions pas que l'volution des relations de change entre les monnaies de la future zone de l'euro et le franc n'a pas mis en danger la reprise de la conjoncture en Suisse, reprise qui, il faut le souligner, est partie des exportations. Les cours de change constituent cependant un risque qui requiert toujours une attention soutenue de la part de tous les concerns. Par contre, pour ce qui a trait aux rpercussions de l'euro sur les oprations de paiement, nous n'avons pour le moment aucun point de repre fiable. Pour le commerce transfrontire, la disparition de plusieurs monnaies au profit d'une seule constituera un avantage. La couverture du risque de change sera plus simple, d'autant que les cots inhrents  cette couverture diminueront grce  la liquidit du march, qui sera sans doute plus forte, et  un accs plus ais aux instruments financiers. En outre, une partie des flux commerciaux qui sont facturs aujourd'hui en francs devrait  la longue tre libelle en euros. La crainte de voir l'euro supplanter peu  peu le franc en Suisse n'est gure fonde. D'importants paiements se feront bien sr en euros entre les banques, dans les services financiers d'entreprises et  la Bourse. De plus, la monnaie europenne jouera probablement un certain rle dans les oprations avec des fournisseurs suisses. Les exportateurs suisses disposant de substantielles recettes en euros pourront tenter d'imposer  leurs fournisseurs une facturation en euros ou, s'ils n'y parviennent pas, un rabais sur les prix en francs, rabais qui correspondra approximativement au cot de la couverture du risque de change. Le gros des paiements dans notre pays continuera toutefois  se drouler en francs. Ainsi, les salaires et, partant, les dpenses de consommation, ainsi que les flux de paiements affrents  la prvoyance et au secteur public resteront en francs, probablement presque sans exceptions. Les salaires ne seront sans doute pas pays en euros, abstraction faite de quelques cas. Cette estimation repose moins sur des aspects juridiques que sur des considrations ayant trait  la capacit  prendre des risques et au cot de la couverture du risque de 3 change. Un mnage moyen n'est ni dispos ni en mesure de supporter un risque de change sur le revenu servant  son entretien. Pour des raisons de rentabilit, il est clair que les entreprises - et non les mnages - prendront les dispositions ncessaires pour se couvrir contre le risque de change. Conclusion: L'euro influera de plus en plus sur la vie conomique en Suisse. Il ne devrait toutefois pas s'imposer en tant que monnaie parallle, en tout cas pas dans les domaines des salaires et de la consommation. Marge accrue dans la politique de placement de la BNS Une rvision de la loi sur la Banque nationale est entre en vigueur le 1er novembre dernier. Elle a cr les bases juridiques en vue d'une gestion plus rentable des rserves de devises. Depuis, la Banque nationale dispose d'une marge de manoeuvre accrue pour ses placements. Elle ne doit plus se cantonner dans des placements dont la dure n'excde pas douze mois, donc dans des placements sur les marchs montaires, mais peut aussi acqurir des obligations, quelle qu'en soit la dure. Nous avons par consquent la possibilit de diversifier davantage nos rserves de devises et d'investir dans des monnaies pour lesquelles seuls les marchs des obligations  moyen ou long terme offrent la liquidit rpondant  nos besoins. Aprs l'entre en vigueur de la rvision, nous avons commenc  remanier notre portefeuille qui atteint environ 40 milliards de francs (voir tableau). Nous avons augment la part du mark allemand, au dtriment de celle du dollar des EtatsUnis, et opr des placements dans trois nouvelles monnaies,  savoir la livre sterling, le florin nerlandais et la couronne danoise. Ces monnaies ont un point commun: leurs marchs des obligations bnficient d'une bonne liquidit. Les placements en livres sterling et, dans une moindre mesure, en florins ont t accomplis dans un but de diversification notamment. Aujourd'hui, 60% de nos rserves de devises sont encore en dollars des Etats-Unis. La part du mark allemand s'inscrit  prs de 30%. Les autres rserves de devises sont libelles en yens et dans les trois nouvelles monnaies de placement. Le dollar des EtatsUnis continuera  jouer un rle dominant. Grce  ces remaniements, nous avons sensiblement rduit le risque montaire sur notre portefeuille. Nous avons aussi augment graduellement la dure moyenne de nos placements. Depuis le 1er novembre, nous avons ramen de 100%  30% la part des placements sur 4 les marchs montaires au total des rserves de devises (voir graphique). Nous visons une dure moyenne de trois ans environ. Les avoirs en monnaies trangres qui dcoulent de swaps - donc qui sont vendus  terme - n'entrent pas dans les rserves de devises parce qu'ils ne sont pas entirement disponibles. A la BNS, les swaps dollars contre francs ont une longue tradition en tant qu'instrument de la politique montaire. La semaine dernire, nous avons pass pour la premire fois des swaps marks allemands contre francs afin de renforcer les possibilits dont nous disposons pour la mise en uvre de notre politique montaire. Ces remaniements ont pu se faire  un rythme soutenu et sans rpercussions fcheuses sur les marchs. Au fur et  mesure de l'extension de nos possibilits de placements, nous avons renforc la gestion des risques. Les risques de march et de crdit font l'objet d'une surveillance quotidienne, selon les rgles en la matire. Les expriences faites ces derniers mois montrent qu'il doit tre possible, grce aux nouvelles dispositions rgissant nos placements, d'obtenir des rendements gnralement plus levs et moins fluctuants. Notre politique de placement, il convient de le rappeler, reste subordonne  des objectifs montaires. Nous nous concentrons avant tout sur des placements trs liquides et prsentant un risque minimal de crdit. Les obligations mises par des Etats et celles qui bnficient d'une garantie tatique explicite ou implicite satisfont  ces exigences strictes. 5 Rserves de devises - Rpartition selon la dure des placements Part 100% 80% 60% 40% 20% Placements sur les marchs montaires (jusqu' un an) Obligations ( plus d'un an) 0% Nov. 97 Dc. 97 Jan. 98 Fv. 98 Mars 98 Avr. 98 Mai 98 Rserves de devises - Rpartition selon la monnaie Dollar des tatsUnis Mark allemand Yen Florin nerlandais Livre sterling Couronne danoise Dc. 96 79% 16% 5% - Dc. 97 72% Mai 98 60% 22% 5% 1% - 28% 6% 4% 2% moins de 1%

Title: Introductory remarks, Media News Conference
text: Half-yearly press conference, Geneva, 18 June 1998 Introductory remarks by Jean-Pierre Roth The Swiss National Bank's gold transactions during the Second World War The interim report of the Independent Commission of Experts Switzerland - Second World War (ICE) on Switzerland's gold transactions between 1939 and 1945 has given rise to a new tide of commentaries on the National Bank's policy during this period. In its comments of 25 May, the Bank's Governing Board welcomed the extensive research conducted by the Commission of Experts under the chairmanship of Professor Bergier and once more expressed its profound regret that the SNB may have unwittingly acquired gold originating from concentration camps. The second report of the U.S. Under Secretary of State Stuart Eizenstat was published on 2 June. This report deals mainly with the economic relations between the other neutral countries and Germany during the War. The introduction presents a more realistic picture of the constraints facing Switzerland and thus corrects the general impression created by the first report published last year. The report of the Bergier Commission is very critical of the National Bank's policy during the War. It blames the Governing Board of the time for having maintained the free convertibility of the Swiss franc into gold without taking into account the political and moral consequences of such a policy. The ICE in particular evaluates the arguments put forward by the SNB at the end of the War justifying its transactions with the Reichsbank. It concludes that neither good faith nor the policy of neutrality nor the dissuasive effects of the gold transactions are convincing arguments. The report shows that the members of the Governing Board knew about the seizures of gold in German-occupied countries, but they considered these seizures to be covered by the Hague Convention. Moreover, they believed to be acting in good faith for as long as they were not provided with formal evidence that stolen gold had been delivered to Berne. We share the opinion expressed by the ICE that the Governing Board of the time had a limited conception of good faith and that its interpretation of international law was too narrow. It did not show enough sensitivity to the moral dimension of a possible acquisition of stolen gold. 2 The ICE holds the view that the argument of neutrality was only put forward later on by the National Bank in order to justify its transactions with the Reichsbank. A more subtle view is called for. The ICE should have taken into account that the National Bank's Governing Board unintentionally underestimated its room for manoeuvre in this field. During the second half of the War it would probably have been difficult for the National Bank to break off its relations with Germany while continuing to purchase ever larger quantities of gold from the Allies. Nevertheless, our predecessors undoubtedly showed a certain bookkeepers' mentality in their approach to neutrality, particularly since the two sides involved in the War could not be considered on a par in moral respects. In our opinion, the interim report has a shortcoming: it lacks an in-depth analysis of the economic policies implemented during the War. The report does not enter into the question of whether the National Bank could have chosen another course of action ensuring monetary stability - an element of Switzerland's defence capacity. While the report elaborates on the monetary framework of the gold transactions, it does not sufficiently explain to what extent this framework formed part of the economic policy of that time. By maintaining the convertibility of the Swiss franc into gold, the National Bank did not pursue its policy as a simple matter of routine. Rather, it tried to secure the country's monetary stability and solvency in an extremely unstable environment. In this connection, it considered it important to continue the gold transactions with the Reichsbank because, after Swiss assets had been frozen in the United States, Germany remained Switzerland's single source of gold which could be used unrestrictedly for financing imports from countries that accepted only gold as a means of payment. Furthermore, gold was also used by the SNB for siphoning off excessive liquidity in Switzerland itself. The report quite rightly states that the blocking of Swiss assets in the United States placed limits on the development of exchanges between Switzerland and the Allies while the clearing mechanism did not hinder more pragmatic trade relations with Germany. The fact that the National Bank adopted a relatively restrictive stance towards the Allies while showing itself more liberal towards Germany was not the result of a political decision but an expression of its concern for internal stability. Thus the National Bank tried to restrict the conversion of dollars deriving from Swiss exports to the United States into Swiss francs. Its aim was to put a brake on the expansion of liquidity in the Swiss market and thus to prevent inflation from being fuelled. The report overlooks the fact that the Swiss francs created by the conversion 3 of dollars caused the domestic money supply to expand. This did not apply to Swiss francs that were sold for gold to the Reichsbank as these were used by Germany mainly in foreign markets. Despite extremely difficult conditions, the National Bank did not fail in the fulfilment of its task of maintaining monetary stability during the War. However, irrespective of the success of its efforts in this field, it misjudged the political and moral implications of its actions. Is the conclusion therefore to be that the National Bank pursued a shortsighted policy of "business as usual" during the Second World War? Minutes in our archive show that the Governing Board was, at the time, aware of the complexity of its task. The false assessment arose mainly from the wrong approach concerning the legitimacy of German seizures in occupied territories, an excessive confidence in the Reichsbank and a narrow understanding of the constraints of neutrality. Despite these misjudgements, doubts relating to the willingness of the Governing Board of that time to serve the interests of the country do not seem called for. According to the report of the Bergier Commission, the Reichsbank transferred more gold from concentration camps to its deposit at the National Bank than had previously been assumed. These figures, too, support the evidence that only a small part of the gold from the so-called Melmer account reached Switzerland. The report also confirms that at that time the Governing Board had no means of knowing the origins of this gold. Nevertheless, we regret most profoundly that the National Bank became involved in the horrors of the Holocaust in this way by the confusions of the War. The memory of the Holocaust imposes a duty on everybody to show solidarity with all persons still suffering from the after-effects of the crimes committed under the National Socialist regime. We have expressed our sympathy and our support by contributing an amount of Sfr 100 million to the fund in favour of needy victims of the Holocaust/Shoah. This fund is exemplary on an international level. The amount of the contribution seems appropriate to us, particularly in view of the initiatives recently introduced abroad in support of survivors of the Holocaust. For some weeks now the National Bank has been threatened with a class action in the United States in connection with its gold transactions in the Second World War. We hold the view that it is not a matter for a court in the United States to pass judgement on the monetary policy conducted by the Swiss National Bank, the central bank of a sovereign state. We therefore deny the jurisdiction of the American courts 4 in this matter and are resolved to oppose any such action vigorously. We shall not enter into negotiations concerning an out-of-court settlement.

Title: Introductory remarks, mid-year media briefing
text: Biannual press conference, Geneva, 18 June 1998 Introductory remarks by Hans Meyer A positive interim assessment can be drawn up at the end of the first half of 1998 with regard to economic developments and monetary policy. Consumer prices have remained stable, and the economic recovery has strengthened. As expected, the Asian crisis has dampened export expansion. Domestic demand has gradually regained strength, which has offset the impact of the Asian crisis on the growth of the Swiss economy. In the first quarter, real gross domestic product was 2.4% higher than in the corresponding period of 1997. Employment increased slightly, and unemployment fell in all regions of the country. Broadly speaking, our monetary policy has been in line with what we announced at the end of December 1997. At that time, we were considering not tightening monetary reins, given that inflationary risks were low. In addition, we stressed that we would take into account the uncertainties that might arise from European monetary integration. At the beginning of the year, we were concerned about the strength of the franc. To counteract a surge in revaluation that threatened the Swiss franc, we increased the liquidity endowment of the money market in February. On the Euro-Franc market, the three-month deposit rate then fell temporarily below 1%. Our strategy has paid off. In March, the franc weakened against all major currencies. The liquidity thus injected into the market was quickly absorbed. Short-term interest rates then rose slightly. Long-term rates, which averaged 2.7% in February, or their lowest level in about twenty years, also rose, but less pronouncedly. In May, both short-term and long-term earnings returned to their end-1997 levels. On the monetary front, however, conditions were somewhat more expansionary than in December 1997, as the franc fell in export-weighted and real terms. The increase in liquidity in February led to a sharp increase in the seasonally adjusted central currency. The gap between the aggregate and its path of 2 Growth of 1% then widened to nearly 6%. In March, it declined rapidly to 3.6%. Over the next two months, the central currency recorded annual growth rates of more than 1%. The stronger growth of banknotes in circulation - these form about 90% of the central currency - reflects the decline in the remuneration paid on savings funds and the recovery in consumption. Central money does not lend itself unreservedly to the role of monetary policy indicator, because the demand for banknotes and the demand for transfer accounts - the two components of central money - are at times unstable. For this reason, in judging our monetary policy, we are making greater use of broadly defined aggregates, in particular M3. We already pointed this out at our press conference in December 1997. At the end of 1997, we estimated that M3 growth would average around 4% in 1998. However, the increase in this aggregate during the first four months of the year was significantly lower. Given the fall in interest rates at the beginning of 1998 and the recovery of the economy, we expect the growth of M3 to accelerate significantly by the end of the year. For the time being, however, a tightening of the monetary reins is not necessary either from the point of view of the growth of monetary aggregates or from that of the expected evolution of the economic situation. Over the next few months, real gross domestic product is likely to continue to grow at a rate of about 2%. Domestic demand will be stimulated by low interest rates and a slight increase in real household disposable income. In the construction sector, demand will take off slowly and thus leave its low level. Exports, the engine of growth last year, on the other hand, are expected to lose some of their strength, mainly because of the sharp decline in exports to East Asia and the weakening of the impulses resulting from the significant fall in the franc in 1996. Several indicators suggest that businesses will create more jobs. The number of unemployed, it is hoped, could fall more sharply than expected. For 1999, we do not expect economic growth to accelerate. Compared to previous business cycles, the economic recovery is somewhat slower, due in part to the 3 construction that struggles to restart. In addition, the inevitable consolidation of federal finances temporarily has effects that thwart rapid economic growth. A moderate but sustained recovery in the economy, however, is preferable for the economy. It prevents the remaining capacity from being exhausted too quickly and from resulting in new inflationary pressures. The consumer price index showed no annual change in the first four months of the year, and inflation is expected to remain at a low level in 1998. This high degree of price stability is not the result of particular factors, such as a decline in oil prices. This is due to the very moderate evolution of prices in all groups of goods, a development in which the remaining spare capacity in the economy is reflected; such a situation restricts the margin available for price increases. Fierce competition, both domestically and internationally, and higher productivity, achieved through the use of new manufacturing processes, also temper price developments. For the economy as a whole, a high degree of price stability is an asset. The absence of distortions due to inflation - such distortions are a brake on the growth of economic activity - promotes long-term growth. However, price stability can be maintained only if the supply of money to the economy remains focused on the objective of inflation-free economic growth. This will also be the objective of the European Central Bank. Thus, an important condition will be met if the European currency, the euro, is to gain public confidence from the outset and for disruptions not to shake the foreign exchange markets. However, uncertainties cannot be completely eliminated. For us, this means that we will have to continue to follow the evolution of exchange rates very closely. As before, we reserve the right to react vigorously if upward pressure on the Swiss franc threatens the recovery of the economy.

Title: A view from Switzerland
text: A view from Switzerland Address by Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board Swiss National Bank Swiss Chamber of Commerce and Industry Tokyo, July 14, 1998 2 1. Introduction These days, you find yourselves in the eye of the hurricane. Naturally, you know well what the world looks like from a Japanese perspective. I shall therefore refrain from speaking about things that you are already familiar with. It seems more attractive to me to present a few thoughts from a Swiss point of view in order to give you an idea of what concerns us at home. In keeping with the occasion, I shall essentially limit my comments to economic problems in a wider sense. You should not, however, conclude from this that I overestimate the significance of economic performance. While a balanced development of the economy is a necessary condition for achieving common goals, it is not sufficient in itself. General well-being in a comprehensive sense not only has economic aspects, it also has social and cultural dimensions. It is important to understand that promoting the public welfare must be a concern of all citizens. They have a twofold contribution to make: as citizens and as economic subjects. A question of central importance is therefore to what extent it will be possible to deal with the underlying tension between individualistic inclinations and communal spirit. This is not a new challenge; it is one that comes up time and again. In a narrow economic context, the challenge lies in the creation of human and material conditions for adequate and sustainable growth with moderate inflation and low unemployment. As you know, these are fairly classic demands. In keeping with the present state of our economic and social development, the issues of social equilibrium and environmental compatibility have for good reasons become added concerns in recent times. As regards people, it is imperative to pay constant attention to qualification and motivation. While skills are primarily acquired through education and training, the will to act is the result of upbringing and the influence of the economic environment. 3 2. Where do we stand? At the end of the twentieth century, Switzerland is once again at a turning-point of its economic and social development. In the past decades, both the economy and society have undergone profound changes. Prosperity and welfare have increased to a remarkable extent. Never before has such a large section of the Swiss population been so well off in material terms as today. At the same time, and probably related to this achievement, social ties have become looser. Even though our age likes to call itself the era of communication, contact between individual human beings in all its facets has not become any easier. The pollution of the environment has become a problem which, in a climate of economic stagnation, has been pushed into the background in recent years. Moreover, the awareness is increasingly gaining ground that the growing international involvement not only offers opportunities, but also bears risks. Many fellow citizens thus feel that the gratification at what has been achieved is overshadowed by insecurity and fears with respect to the future. Nevertheless, there are clear rays of hope. After an unusually long period of stagnation in the nineties, which took its toll in terms of personal and material sacrifices - a fact that naturally affected the general mood - we are now at the beginning of a new upswing. Both the favourable monetary framework - interest rates, inflation rate, exchange rate - as well as the adjustment of outdated structures have created a sound basis for such a development. As usual, the improvement in the economic situation of our neighbouring countries then provided the decisive stimulus. To my mind, it is quite remarkable that economic difficulties, taken overall, are typical neither of individual branches nor of certain parts of the country. Instead, the dividing line between light and shade runs right across the entire economic landscape. It is the superior performance characterised by innovation, flexibility and 4 productivity that is decisive for a sustained success. An increase in value creation must be the guiding principle of our economic performance. Re-establishing sound public finances remains important. The public sector was gradually expanded in the course of the economic and social developments of the postwar years. Originally, the aim was to meet an obvious backlog of demand. The development, however, became more and more critical. Given the limited resources, all questions pertaining to the type and extent of state activity as well as to the consistency and efficiency of the performance of the public sector have become more urgent. For some time now, an intensive debate on these questions has been under way, which will certainly lead to concrete results. Above and beyond the financial domain, the efforts to create favourable competitive conditions must be continued. Experience shows that this is a never ending story. However, some progress has been made in recent time. This is remarkable in so far as large sections of the public remain sceptical with regard to the principle of free competition. Quite obviously, people still need to be convinced that the free play of market forces provides the best conditions for a meaningful use of production factors, thereby creating both prosperity and welfare. It must, however, be pointed out that this positive effect of competition will only make itself felt in a stable economic environment. Other important factors are increased flexibility with respect to conditions of employment and greater mobility. On a human level, education and training need to be further promoted. As a matter of fact, the imbalance still existing in the labour market is primarily a question of qualification. It seems striking that even in a period of stagnation with a relatively high level of unemployment, at least by Swiss standards, the lack of suitably qualified staff was always deplored. All in all, care must be taken to achieve a healthy balance between market-related incentives and social cohesion. 5 Maintaining an equilibrium between economic and social development is, to my mind, of crucial importance, a fact that has been impressively demonstrated by recent events in Asia. The countries concerned are quite obviously communities that are very different in type and size. Nevertheless, it is possible to make a few statements of general significance. An unbalanced economic development, weak financial systems and insufficient supervision of the financial markets are merely symptoms of deeper-lying causes. Today's difficulties show clearly that a sustained development is only possible on the basis of stable social conditions. The experience of past decades has taught us that such conditions must first and foremost be created by individual countries themselves. Only in this way can a solid basis for lasting international cooperation be created. 3. Where are we heading? What is happening today has its roots in the past and, at the same time, has effects on future events. Contrary to a widespread belief, development has been remarkably constant from a long-term point of view. There are valid reasons for this, both on a human and a material scale. Since human beings are at the centre of the world's happenings, it is an experience of some consequence that they are by nature capable of changing and adapting, while at the same time instinctively seeking stability, continuity and security. If, in the final analysis, we want to maintain the prosperity we have achieved as a precondition for more comprehensive social objectives, adjustments will continue to be indispensable. These must, however, take place in a way that will not threaten the social cohesion. Such a highly balanced development requires a rhythm that will make it possible to maintain an equilibrium - precarious by its very nature - between persistence and flexibility, circumspection and daring, cautiousness and boldness. 6 Finding a balance between prosperity, social cohesion and political freedom will be one of the major tasks in the coming years. Only such a balance will lead to selfconfidence, confidence in the opportunities offered by the environment and confidence that the community will be in a position to guarantee certain basic rules of co-existence. We have seen that a favourable framework for the economy as a whole is an important condition for organic development. I have already mentioned the significance of sound public finances and competition policy. Naturally, I neither can nor wish to deny the significance attaching to monetary policy in this connection. The central role of monetary policy is formulated in the mandate of the Swiss National Bank, namely to pursue a monetary policy in the general interest of the country. With a supply of money that is adequate in relation to real economic development, monetary policy can ensure a stable long-term price trend. Price stability, however, is not an end in itself. Rather, it represents the best contribution which monetary policy is able to make in the long term to creating favourable conditions for a balanced overall economic development. Moreover, price stability is also an eminently social issue, since the weakest members of society suffer the most from inflation. Occasionally, the question arises whether price stability is, in fact, still seriously threatened. To my mind, such a question reveals a rather poor historical awareness. Admittedly, impressive results have been achieved in fighting inflation in the last few years. It is also true that price stability is hardly jeopardised in the current economic environment. But to conclude that this will remain so in future does seem to me somewhat daring. 7 Finally, monetary policy represents a social as well as an economic challenge. Numerous examples show that neither the results of scientific research nor the endeavours of the central bank in themselves suffice. Of decisive importance is a basic and widespread understanding of the significance of a stability-oriented policy. Such insight must continually influence the attitudes of the people, parliament and the government. This includes a willingness to take account of the experience that a central bank which is an independent institution within the limits of its mandate is in the best position to pursue a successful monetary policy with due regard to scientific teaching and experience. Such a policy is, of course, in large measure dependent on the international environment. In the coming years, the efforts to create a European Monetary Union will be of primary interest to us too. If the present concepts can be successfully realised, the conditions for economic development in Europe will be significantly improved. What is of decisive importance is whether the participating countries will succeed in pursuing a consistently convergent stability policy. In this connection, the fact may not be overlooked that there will be increasing demands of flexibility on the markets - particularly the labour markets - in a single monetary area. Switzerland's prime task in the coming years will be to keep her own house in order. Of primary importance is the desire to find a sustainable balance between economic flexibility and social cohesion and thus to bring stability and change in harmony with each other. Beyond this, we must preserve and strengthen our traditional openness towards other countries. It is not for the first time that our relations with our neighbours, both near and far, must be renewed and adapted to a changing environment. The conditions for this, however, must first be created, especially within the country. In this way we can make the best contribution to international solidarity.

Title: Where are we going?
text: Where are we going? Dr. Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Chamber of Industry and Commerce St. Gallen-Appenzell in the auditorium of the KV-Zentrum Kreuzbleiche, St. Gallen 9. September 1998 2 1. Introduction You know the classic question: Where do we come from? Where do we stand? Where are we going? It expresses, in my view, a fact that is of central importance. As contemporaries, we stand in a continuous flow of events. The past shapes the present and this in turn influences future events. Of course, we are inclined to focus our attention on the period of time that is of particular importance to us because we are actively experiencing it. As a rule, the question of how things could develop further is also of interest. One is tempted to say that this is especially true in uncertain times. However, we should not overlook the fact that from the point of view of the contemporary, every epoch seems to be uncertain. As a rule, only a minority deals with the past and its influences on current events. Under special circumstances, however, the interest in the origin moves wider circles, as we have experienced in recent years. In my remarks today, I would like to start from current events and, following on from this, I would like to make a few observations on the possible further development. The focus is therefore on the questions "Where do we stand? and where are we going? 3 2. Where do we stand? Slowly but surely, we are approaching the turn of the century. Similar to the much more frequent end of the year, but of course to a more pronounced extent, such a striking milestone in the flow of events encourages thoughtful assessment of the situation. In the history of the economic and social development of our country, the past half century will one day occupy an important place. At the beginning of this century, the still young industrialization was about to draw further circles when it was interrupted by two world wars and a worldwide economic crisis. In the second half of the century, economic development prevailed in large parts of the world. Especially in the industrialized countries, prosperity and welfare have been sustainably increased. However, this pleasing event was increasingly accompanied by tendencies that we must regard as the other side of the coin. In the course of economic development, Community cohesion has been loosened. Despite impressive progress in terms of mobility and communication, people-to-people contacts have obviously not become easier. The burden on the environment has developed into a problem that we unjustly like to suppress. Especially in recent times, we have been reminded with all desirable clarity that international economic integration probably brings with it great opportunities, but also considerable risks. The development briefly outlined here has obviously led to the fact that we as contemporaries are in a somewhat ambivalent mood. The satisfaction of what has been achieved is associated with a discomfort about the associated negative side effects. It is obviously not easy to decide how to set accents in an assessment of the overall picture. This mood is typical of a turning point. Today, however, there is no lack of positive signs. After an unusually long period of stagnation, the negative effects of which have had a negative impact on the atmosphere in the human and factual sphere, we are at the beginning of a new upswing according to human judgement. In my opinion, the fact that the trend has changed for the better is more important than the extent of the recovery, which can only be speculated about anyway. 4 As always, different influences have brought about the trend reversal. The monetary framework had a positive effect. Price stability, low interest rates and reasonable exchange rates have created a favourable environment. Impressive adjustments in the public sector also contributed to improving the framework conditions. Significant progress has been made in financial policy, competition policy and the promotion of education and training. As always, opinions differ on the nature and scope of the reforms. With a balanced view, however, they should not be overlooked. As a rule, the real or even apparent difficulties associated with the current state of our international relations receive broad attention. On the other hand, our cooperation within the framework of the Bretton Woods institutions - the Monetary Fund and the World Bank - and the World Trade Organisation (WTO), for example, is not sufficiently noticed. In view of the economic recovery, the structural adjustments that our economy has made in recent years under the pressure of events then play an essential role. With the necessary restraint, it can be stated that an impressive achievement has been achieved here, even by international standards. It gives a good testimony to the flexibility, innovative strength and motivation of the people working in our economy. After all, it was once again the economic recovery of our most important economic partners that contributed the spark. 3. Where are we going? Let us now turn to the question of how things could develop further. After what has been said, it makes sense to build on the existing. If we want to maintain the achieved level of economic development - or the associated prosperity - not least with regard to further social objectives, then sustainable efforts remain indispensable. In the case of economic policy, it is less about questions of the conceptual approach, are 5 but all in all, the broad lines of responsible economic policy are largely undisputed. For this reason, the call for a so-called third way does not seem to me to be very convincing. It is sufficient to reflect fully on the well-known principles of the balanced concept of a social market economy. Emphasis must therefore be placed on the implementation of the necessary measures. This is a challenge that is as social as it is economic. Good policy in this area of Community design also presupposes the willingness of an appropriate number of fellow citizens to participate actively. However, this is only possible on the basis of sufficient identification with the community. Necessary adjustments must therefore be made in such a way that Community cohesion is not called into question. What is needed is therefore a rhythm of action that reconciles and maintains flexibility and perseverance, daring and prudence, boldness and care. Looking at current events, I think it is remarkable that difficulties are not typical for individual sectors of the economy or for specific regions. Light and shadow can obviously be found across the economic landscape. Demanding performance, characterized by innovation and flexibility, as well as efficient service provision remain decisive. The guideline for our economic activities must remain the increase in added value. Of course, the economic people must make the decisive contribution to this. Favourable framework conditions should support their efforts and at the same time ensure organic development. Let us not overlook the fact that these framework conditions must be created by the same people - now in their capacity as citizens! In a democratic society, the individual must therefore meet a demanding and exciting double challenge. The restructuring of public budgets remains important. In the course of the development of the past decades outlined in the introduction, the public sector was gradually expanded. This was unproblematic as long as there was an obvious need to catch up. As a result, the development became increasingly critical. Questions about type and 6 The extent of government activity and the efficiency of the provision of services in the public sector became more important. These are fundamental questions of community design. Answering them will be a challenging task in the coming years. A lean but strong state should serve as a model. Efforts to create favourable competitive conditions must then be continued. As already indicated, considerable progress has been made here in recent times. This is all the more remarkable since the idea of competition is still met with scepticism in large circles. We must make even greater efforts to convince our fellow citizens that free competition can very well ensure a sensible use of the factors of production. However, it must not be concealed that this is only possible in a stable environment. Finally, it is important to promote training and further education in the human sphere. In a rapidly changing environment, it is particularly difficult for those workers who do not have sufficient qualifications or who are unable to adapt to new requirements properly and in a timely manner. It is essential to recognise that improving conditions in these areas - fiscal policy, competition policy and training - is a permanent challenge. The idea that there are quick, simple and even cheap solutions to the problems mentioned is therefore wrong and harmful. First and foremost, what is needed is bone work that is as determined as it is persistent. What I believe to be the central importance of the balance between economic and social development is currently being demonstrated to us by what is happening in parts of Asia and also in Russia with a clarity that leaves nothing to be desired. The countries in question appear to be very different in nature and size. Nevertheless, it is possible to make findings that are of general validity. Today's difficulties confirm that sustainable development is only possible on the basis of stable social conditions. Of central importance is the guarantee of "ordre public". It is clear that things are often intertwined. They 7 maintaining a state of appropriate balance remains primarily a national challenge. But this means that help from outside, if it is now provided by individual states or by multinational institutions, can only ever be help for self-help. Anyone who closes himself to this insight risks squandering valuable funds purposelessly. It is also not wrong to conclude from such considerations that any assistance should be provided primarily in the sense of advice and less in the form of credit assistance. The emphasis on the importance of national action also highlights the possibilities and limits of inter-state integration. In principle, there is no doubt about the desirability of an international division of labour. However, it should be noted that each chain is only as strong as its weakest link. It is therefore in the interest of sustainable development if recent events lead to a more realistic assessment of things. It has hardly escaped you that I have not yet spoken of monetary policy in connection with the framework conditions. Let me conclude by saying a few words about this. The central importance is expressed in the mandate to conduct a monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. With an adequate supply of money compared to real economic developments, monetary policy can tend to ensure price stability in the longer term. However, price stability is not an end in itself. It is the contribution of monetary policy to creating the conditions for balanced macroeconomic development. Unfortunately, it is often overlooked that price stability is an eminently social concern. It is precisely the weaker members of the Community that suffer most from inflation. The conduct of monetary policy is not only an economic challenge, but also a social one. Essential is the fundamental insight of broad circles into the importance of a stability-oriented policy. Such insight must be reflected in the behaviour of the people, parliament and government. This includes a willingness to take into account the experience that a central bank that is independent within its mandate is best placed to conduct a successful monetary policy, taking into account doctrine and experience. 8 4. Summary My remarks can be summarised as follows: By referring to a period of change, I wanted above all to draw attention to the fact that, with regard to economic and social development, we have reached a point where both the advantages and the disadvantages of this development are becoming known in many ways. Prosperity and welfare have reached a remarkable level. At the same time, however, the development that made this possible has also exacerbated social and ecological problems and in some cases created new ones. The resulting challenge can be described by stating that we, as citizens and as economic agents, must learn even better to live with prosperity. Ultimately, it is about balancing economic and social development. Both are mutually dependent. However, it requires the permanent striving to keep them in a precarious balance. That is the challenge we face in our dual capacity. The way we manage them will shape the further events to a large extent.

Dr. Hans Meyer Prsident des Direktoriums der Schweizerischen Nationalbank Industrie- und Handelskammer St. Gallen-Appenzell in der Aula des KV-Zentrums Kreuzbleiche, St. Gallen 9. September 1998 2 1. Wollen wir den erreichten Stand der wirtschaftlichen Entwicklung - beziehungsweise den damit verbundenen Wohlstand - nicht zuletzt im Blick auf weiterfhrende gesellschaftliche Zielsetzungen wahren, dann bleiben nachhaltige Anstrengungen weiterhin unerlsslich. Dabei geht es im Falle der Wirtschaftspolitik weniger um Fragen des konzeptionellen Ansatzes, sind 5 doch die Grundzge einer verantwortungsvollen Wirtschaftspolitik alles in allem genommen weitgehend unbestritten. Aus diesem Grunde scheint mir auch der Ruf nach einem sogenannten dritten Weg wenig berzeugend. Es gengt vollstndig, sich auf die altbekannten Grundstze des ausgewogenen Konzeptes einer sozialen Marktwirtschaft zu besinnen. Der Akzent ist somit auf die Umsetzung der gebotenen Massnahmen zu legen. Dabei handelt es sich um eine Herausforderung, die ebenso gesellschaftlicher wie wirtschaftlicher Natur ist. Gute Politik setzt auch in diesem Bereich gemeinschaftlichen Gestaltens die Bereitschaft einer angemessenen Zahl von Mitbrgerinnen und Mitbrgern zur aktiven Mitwirkung voraus. Entscheidend bleiben die anspruchsvolle Leistung, geprgt durch Innovation und Flexibilitt, sowie eine effiziente Leistungserstellung. Leitlinie fr unser wirtschaftliches Handeln muss die Erhhung der Wertschpfung bleiben. Dazu mssen natrlich die wirtschaftenden Menschen den entscheidenden Beitrag leisten. Im Zuge der einleitend skizzierten Entwicklung der vergangenen Jahrzehnte wurde der ffentliche Sektor schrittweise ausgebaut. Es darf allerdings nicht verschwiegen werden, dass dies nur in einem stabilen Umfeld mglich ist. Schliesslich gilt es, im menschlichen Bereich die Aus- und Weiterbildung zu frdern. In einem sich rasch wandelnden Umfeld haben vor allem diejenigen Arbeitnehmer Schwierigkeiten, die nicht ber ausreichende Qualifikationen verfgen, bzw. nicht in der Lage sind, sich neuen Anforderungen sach- und zeitgerecht anzupassen. Wesentlich ist die Erkenntnis, dass es sich bei der Verbesserung der Bedingungen in den genannten Bereichen - Finanzpolitik, Wettbewerbspolitik sowie Ausbildung - um eine dauerhafte Herausforderung handelt. Die heutigen Schwierigkeiten besttigen, dass eine nachhaltige Entwicklung nur auf der Grundlage stabiler gesellschaftlicher Verhltnisse mglich ist. Von zentraler Bedeutung ist die Gewhrleistung des "ordre public". Dabei ist klar, dass die Dinge vielfach verflochten sind. Sie 7 in einem Zustand angemessener Ausgewogenheit zu halten, bleibt in erster Linie eine einzelstaatliche Herausforderung. Das aber bedeutet, dass Hilfe von aussen, werde sie nun von Einzelstaaten oder von multinationalen Institutionen gewhrt, immer nur Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe sein kann. Wer sich dieser Einsicht verschliesst, der riskiert, wertvolle Mittel zwecklos zu verschleudern. Es ist auch nicht falsch, aus solchen berlegungen zu schliessen, dass eine allfllige Hilfeleistung in erster Linie im Sinne der Beratung und weniger in der Form der Kredithilfe erfolgen sollte. Mit dem Hinweis auf die Bedeutung einzelstaatlichen Handelns werden auch die Mglichkeiten und Grenzen zwischenstaatlicher Verflechtung ins richtige Licht gerckt. Grundstzlich ist an der Wnschbarkeit einer internationalen Arbeitsteilung nicht zu zweifeln. Allerdings bleibt zu beachten, dass jede Kette nur so stark ist wie ihr schwchstes Glied. Es liegt denn auch durchaus im Interesse einer nachhaltigen Entwicklung, wenn die jngsten Ereignisse zu einer realistischeren Einschtzung der Dinge fhren. Es ist Ihnen kaum entgangen, dass ich bisher im Zusammenhang mit den Rahmenbedingungen nicht von der Geldpolitik gesprochen habe. Lassen Sie mich dazu abschliessend noch einige Worte sagen.
