Preisstabilitt ist allerdings kein Selbstzweck. Sie ist der Beitrag der Geldpolitik zur Schaffung der Voraussetzungen fr eine ausgewogene gesamtwirtschaftliche Entwicklung. Leider wird oft bersehen, dass Preisstabilitt ein eminent soziales Anliegen ist. Gerade die schwcheren Glieder der Gemeinschaft leiden am strksten unter der Teuerung. Auch die Fhrung der Geldpolitik ist nicht nur eine wirtschaftliche, sondern ebenso eine gesellschaftliche Herausforderung. Wesentlich ist die grundlegende Einsicht weiter Kreise in die Bedeutung einer stabilittsgerechten Politik. Solche Einsicht muss sich im Verhalten von Volk, Parlament und Regierung niederschlagen. Dazu gehrt auch die Bereitschaft, der Erfahrung Rechnung zu tragen, dass eine im Rahmen ihres Auftrages unabhngige Notenbank am besten in der Lage ist, unter Bercksichtigung von Lehre und Erfahrung eine erfolgreiche Geldpolitik zu fhren. 8 4. Zusammenfassung Meine Ausfhrungen lassen sich wie folgt zusammenfassen: Mit dem Hinweis auf eine Zeit der Wende wollte ich vor allem darauf aufmerksam machen, dass wir in bezug auf die wirtschaftliche und gesellschaftliche Entwicklung an einem Punkte angelangt sind, an dem sowohl die Vorteile als auch die Nachteile dieser Entwicklung vielfltig bewusst werden. Wohlstand und Wohlfahrt haben einen bemerkenswerten Stand erreicht. Die Entwicklung, die das mglich gemacht hat, hat aber gleichzeitig auch soziale und kologische Probleme verschrft und teilweise neu geschaffen. Die sich daraus ergebende Herausforderung kann mit der Feststellung umschrieben werden, dass wir als Staatsbrger und als Wirtschaftssubjekte noch besser lernen mssen, mit dem Wohlstand zu leben. Letztlich geht es um die Ausgewogenheit von wirtschaftlicher und gesellschaftlicher Entwicklung. Beide bedingen sich gegenseitig. Es bedarf aber des dauerhaften Strebens, sie in einem wenn auch prekren Gleichgewicht zu halten. Das ist die Herausforderung, vor die wir in unserer doppelten Eigenschaft gestellt sind. Von der Art, wie wir sie bewltigen, wird das weitere Geschehen in hohem Masse geprgt sein.

Title: The Euro: Impact on Swiss small and medium-sized enterprises
text: The euro: influence on Swiss Small and medium-sized enterprises Dr. Hans Theiler Director of the Swiss National Bank Bern Public event of the University of Applied Sciences Aargau, Windisch 10. September 1998 1 In 112 days, that's exactly 16 weeks, the euro starts. This creates a currency area with less than 300 million inhabitants. First of all, the currencies of the participating countries are fixed among themselves, irrevocably. This creates the common currency. Monetary policy is no longer conducted by the national central banks, but by the European Central Bank in the common currency. Similarly, transactions on the financial markets are settled in euros. However, it is not yet time for everyone to calculate and pay in euros. Companies and private individuals can also conduct their business in euros, but they do not have to. National cash remains in circulation for the time being, and bank accounts continue to be denominated in national currencies. Only in the first half of 2002 - in about four years - will monetary union become visible to everyone. Then the banknotes and coins of the individual countries will be replaced by the euro. According to the timetable, the euro will be the sole means of payment on 1 July 2002. When the influence on small and medium-sized enterprises is examined below, I am not thinking of administrative changes. They are always annoying, but unique. Rather, it is about things that influence competitiveness. These are in particular the exchange rate and interest rate developments and the influence of a large market area with extensive price transparency. The question of whether euros received in intra-Swiss traffic are passed on to the downstream bodies and thus the franc is displaced by the euro is also of interest in this context. Now, it's not that the impact on our currency and our economy can simply be predicted so easily and accurately. If the euro is a strong currency, the effects are different than if it is a weak currency. Much therefore depends on the quality of the new currency and its assessment by the financial markets. However, there are no reliable forecasts about this. A distinction must then be made between short-term and long-term effects. Strong links with the new currency area It is a trivial observation that the introduction of the euro not only sets a lot in motion in the participating countries, but also has an impact on third countries. This is particularly true for Switzerland, with its strong economic links with the future euro area. A good 50 percent of our exports go to the countries of the monetary union and 70 percent of our imports come from there. In the case of services, the shares are also at the 50 percent mark. 2 In the future, an appreciation of the Swiss franc will affect all exporters to the euro area equally. Until now, the influence has been different depending on which country someone has delivered to, as the individual currencies in Europe have often moved in opposite directions. Those who delivered to several countries had a certain risk compensation. With the creation of the euro, this risk compensation no longer exists; rather, the exporter faces a kind of cluster risk. Given the EU's high share of our exports, this entails considerable risks for the economy as a whole. Multinationals may be better able to tackle such problems than small and medium-sized enterprises; the big ones are everywhere and usually have a lower depth of value added domestically. SMEs operate primarily from here and are feeling the brunt of a possible appreciation of the Swiss franc more strongly. The crucial question: strong or weak euro? As mentioned earlier, backed-up forecasts of the future currency are difficult to make. Scenarios are therefore used to discuss the impact on our currency and economy. Scenarios are a tool. They are conditional statements by making a certain assumption and thinking about what happens when that assumption comes true. In the case of the introduction of the euro, two alternative basic assumptions can be made: the euro will be a strong currency or vice versa, the euro will be a weak currency. Depending on this, the effects on the Swiss franc and the Swiss economy vary. First, let's look at the case that the euro will be a strong currency. This is the ideal state for us. In such a case, there will be no flight from the euro into the Swiss franc and thus no unbearable upward pressure. The SNB can look at what is happening with serenity, at least as far as monetary policy is concerned, and the export industry and tourism can offer their services in Europe on competitive terms. The expectation that the euro will be a strong currency is quite realistic. The European Central Bank's primary objective is price stability. It will probably conduct a policy similar to that of Europe's leading central banks today, among which the Deutsche Bundesbank sets the tone. The European Central Bank is therefore tasked with pursuing a policy of stability, it has the will to do so and it also has the necessary resources. Actually, nothing should go wrong. But if, for whatever reason, the euro is not a strong currency, but a weak one? Then the Swiss franc would be put in the spotlight as a currency of refuge and would be exposed to upward pressure. The export industry and tourism would be the victims. In such a case, the SNB would limit the rise of the Swiss franc with a high supply of Swiss francs. 3 In extreme cases - it should be emphasized: in extreme cases - even a temporary peg to the euro would have to be considered. In doing so, the SNB would abandon its own policy and delegate it to the European Central Bank. However, such a measure would be associated with disadvantages. On the one hand, this would jeopardise our price stability and, since the weak euro would be accompanied by a high level of interest rates, higher European interest rates would also have to be accepted. That might be no less painful for our economy than a high exchange rate. Incidentally, it would be strange to cede autonomy to the institution that is judged negatively by the public and the financial markets. But even if the euro does not turn out to be a strong currency or is not initially perceived as such by the financial markets, this does not necessarily have to have catastrophic consequences for the Swiss franc. It is not the case that in such a scenario only the euro and the franc existed. Holders of euro balances who want to switch to another currency would have other strong currencies at their disposal: the dollar, the English pound and, who knows, perhaps the yen again. Switzerland would therefore by no means be the only "euro asylum country". It would therefore be possible for the Swiss franc to appreciate strongly against the euro, but to have an acceptable exchange rate level against other major currencies. The test will come later Let's assume the cheapest option for all conceivable scenarios and assume that the euro is a strong currency at the beginning and has no teething problems. In short: a picture book start. This is a very realistic scenario. Now, as the old saying goes, one should not praise the day before the evening. The test of the single currency and the monetary system is only to come after some time. The euro does not encounter a trouble-free environment, neither in terms of the real economy nor in terms of economic policy. It will not eliminate the real problems; in the short term, he will even accentuate them more. Where are these problems to be located? Monetary union will increase competitive pressure in the countries of the Community. The euro creates price transparency from Sicily to Scandinavia. It will hardly be possible for companies to make spatial price differentiations for identical products. For example, pharmaceutical products, cars and other consumer durables will cost the same  apart from marginal differences. This creates pressure to rationalise and innovate and leads to accelerated structural change and, at least temporarily, to higher unemployment among enterprises in the countries of the Community. 4 It should be noted, by the way, that price transparency and, as a result, tougher competitive pressure will not only challenge EU entrepreneurs. Swiss providers - insofar as they have so far been able to enforce spatial price differentiations - will also be affected. It is not possible to say exactly what the effective effects are. Depending on where, what, how much, at what prices or price differences were sold, the effects will be different for each company. But let us return to the countries of the monetary union and remember that three important participating countries - Germany, France and Italy - today have unemployment of around 10 percent. In Spain, Portugal and Finland it is even higher and only in some smaller countries below. People hardly accept unemployment in the long run as a God-given fate. You want work. If the single currency initially even leads to higher unemployment, the objective of stability could be compromised - not formally, but in fact. Stability policy is not limited to monetary policy; fiscal policy is also involved. The pressure from the streets on the politicians could then lead to a renaissance of deficit policy, despite all assurances to the contrary. This danger is all the greater because the central central bank does not face a central government, but there are still eleven national governments. Only the harsh reality will show whether he is worth his paper. If you put Germany equal to 100, only France has comparable productivity with 95. Italy and the Netherlands are already significantly lower at 85 points. Again, let's start from the two variants according to which the euro will be either a weak or a strong currency. If the euro is a weak currency, people prefer a strong currency, such as the Swiss franc. No economically minded person in Switzerland will want to keep their savings in euros or have their wages paid out in euros if this currency is weak. He would constantly lose substance. It is not the case that an employer could simply decide to pay wages in euros because he also receives euros for his exported goods. There is no obligation to accept the euro in Switzerland; anyone can insist on having their credit paid out in Swiss francs. That depends on which of the two currencies tends to strengthen or weaken. If the euro is under appreciation pressure - i.e. it is strong - the customer will be burdened in Swiss francs; this may result in a currency gain until the account is debited. In principle, in order to answer the question of its role as an investment currency, two main scenarios must be distinguished, namely the euro as a strong currency and the euro as a weak currency. Let's start with the second scenario and assume that the euro is a weak currency. The answer is simple; it coincides with what was said at the beginning in general terms for this case. The euro is less attractive as an investment currency. Investors are looking for alternatives in strong currencies, and the Swiss franc is also suitable for this. A strong Franc is even more sought after as an investment currency and thus even stronger. As a result, Swiss franc interest rates will be low. This is all the more so since in this scenario the SNB will try to dampen the appreciation of the Swiss franc by means of an additional supply of Swiss francs. 8 Less obvious are the consequences in the other case, namely when the euro is a strong currency. Prima vista one is inclined to say that then the franc will be less sought after as an investment currency. What does less mean? Compared to the scenario of a weak euro, this is undoubtedly true. But that is not the comparison to be made. Another question is of interest here: Does the Swiss franc lose its attractiveness as an investment currency compared to today - i.e. the pre-euro period - if the euro is a strong currency? To give an answer, one has to be aware that with the introduction of the euro - whether strong or weak - various investment currencies will disappear. Think of the D-Mark, the French franc or the guilder. However, the investor has the need to diversify the investment funds, not only by form of investment, but also by currency. Not only investors in Switzerland and in the countries of the future monetary union should be considered, but investors all over the world. The need for diversification will prompt investors not to simply convert the capital invested today in the various European currencies into euros, but to redistribute them among the world's existing investment currencies. The Swiss franc will benefit from this, even if the euro is strong. And since the Swiss franc is still sought after as an investment currency - probably stronger than before - Swiss franc interest rates are also likely to be lower than euro interest rates for the time being. In the scenario "Swiss franc as an investment currency in a strong euro environment" - as I have just outlined - two sub-scenarios would actually have to be underwritten. It is important to distinguish whether our country will move closer to the EU in such a case or whether it will remain at a distance. In the event of an approximation, the real interest rate differential with euro interest rates is likely to narrow sharply until disappear completely. A similar development was observed in 1992, after the Federal Council had submitted an application for accession negotiations. However, if Switzerland remains at a distance from the EU, a certain interest rate differential with the euro will also remain. And that - as I said - even if the euro is a strong currency. Result Around our country - as I said at the beginning - a single currency area with less than 300 million inhabitants will be created in 16 weeks. The conditions for a good functioning of the euro in the sense of a stable currency are good for the beginning. In the longer term, however, there are significant risks, in particular in connection with financial, labour market and social policies. The euro cannot cover up the problems in these areas. The "enterprise" euro is therefore doomed to success. 9 Even if any euro turbulence does not have to be about the existence or non-existence of the new currency, but only a noticeable weakness of the euro, this would affect the Swiss economy considerably more than the participating countries. After the changeover, European companies will largely operate in a domestic market; the proportion of foreign countries is low compared to Switzerland. Whether the euro is strong or weak does not have the same meaning for them as it does for a Swiss entrepreneur. In this respect, the euro risk for the Swiss economy - and this applies above all to small and medium-sized entrepreneurs - is greater than for the euro countries themselves.

Geschfte und Gastwirtschaftsbetriebe in Grenzregionen sowie in Tourismuszentren werden mit dem Euro konfrontiert sein. Doch sind sie es heute schon gewohnt, mit Fremdwhrungen umzugehen, zu rechnen und die Preise in anderen Whrungen anzuschreiben. Der Kunde zahlt vermutlich mit der Kreditkarte und kann entscheiden, ob er in Franken oder Euro belastet werden will. Welche Whrung wird er whlen? Ist hingegen der Euro schwach und der Franken steht unter Aufwertungsdruck, wird der auslndische Kunde - vielleicht auch der schweizerische - sich lieber in Euro belasten lassen. 7 Stellt ein Geschftsinhaber fest, dass auch die schweizerische Kundschaft von der Wahlmglichkeit Gebrauch macht und durchwegs die fr sie gnstigere - und somit fr den Verkufer ungnstigere - Variante whlt, verschwinden die Doppelpreisschilder vermutlich sehr rasch. Man knnte die Beispiele endlos verlngern. Tatsache ist, dass die Schweiz als kleines, aber wirtschaftlich stark mit dem Ausland verbundenes Land schon bisher mit Fremdwhrungen gelebt hat. In Zukunft knnte diese Bereitschaft schwinden. Wieso soll man fr den "kleinen Exoten" eine Ausnahme machen? Was passiert mit dem Franken als Anlagewhrung und den Franken-Zinsen? Der Franken spielt international vor allem als Anlagewhrung eine Rolle. Wird seine Rolle als Anlagewhrung in Frage gestellt, wenn rund um uns herum eine gemeinsame Whrung entsteht? Title: The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy
text: The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy Georg Rich Swiss National Bank Presented at the Norwegian-Swiss Euro Seminar, organized by the Royal Norwegian Embassy and Credit Swiss Group, Lugano, 18 September, 1998. The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 2 The Swiss public is deeply divided about the question of joining the European Union. Although the Swiss government applied for membership in the spring of 1992, Switzerland will unlikely enter the European Union in the near future. The ambivalent attitude of the Swiss public also comes to the fore in the internal discussions on European monetary unification and the euro. Many Swiss are concerned that the transition to the euro will create various problems for the Swiss economy. A frequently voiced fear is that after the adoption of the common currency, the exchange rate of the Swiss franc vis-a-vis the euro might fluctuate too much. Are these concerns justified? In my contribution to this conference, I will first look at the likely developments in the European Monetary Union after the introduction of the euro at the beginning of 1999. I will then examine the possible effects of the euro on the Swiss economy and conclude with a discussion of how the Swiss National Bank (SNB), if necessary, might respond to excessive turbulences in the exchange rate. 1. European Monetary Union: What is Likely to Happen? The introduction of the euro will entail both economic benefits and costs. The benefits arise from the elimination of transactions costs and exchange rate uncertainty once the need to exchange national currencies within the euro area disappears. Moreover, the introduction of a common currency will promote competition by improving the transparency of prices charged by firms within the euro area. Another benefit is the clear mandate conferred upon the European Central Bank (ECB), which will issue the common currency and conduct monetary policy in the euro area. According to the Maastricht Treaty, the ECBs main task is to achieve and maintain price stability. In view of the ECBs mandate, there is a good chance that the euro will be a stable currency and will thus contribute to fostering economic growth in the European Union. Moreover, the introduction of the common currency implies that unified money and capital markets will emerge within the The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 3 euro area. On 1 January, 1999, short-term money market rates will become identical throughout that area. In the capital market, interest rate differentials between the various countries will also largely disappear. As a matter of fact, they have already narrowed substantially within the euro area. Thus, the fragmented national capital markets will be replaced by a large and liquid market for fixed-income securities and equity. As a result, the cost to European enterprises of financing their business activities is likely to fall. In the public debate about European monetary integration, it is frequently forgotten that the introduction of the euro will not only convey economic benefits. There are also economic costs. The main cost of introducing a common currency lies in the loss of national monetary autonomy incurred by the countries in the euro area. After the transition to the common currency, it will no longer be possible to tailor monetary policy to the needs of individual countries or regions of the euro area. As indicated above, uniform short-term interest rates will rule throughout the euro area. Therefore, the ECB cannot take into account the needs of individual countries or regions in setting interest rates. The loss of national monetary autonomy would not matter much if economic developments of individual countries within the euro area were highly synchronized. The ECBs uniform monetary policy would then be suitable for all the countries of the euro area. While the economies of Germany, France and their smaller neighbors tend to move together, economic developments in the southern part of the euro area have often been out of step with those further north. Thus, the uniform monetary policy  even if appropriate for the euro area as a whole  may create problems in individual countries or regions in the form of high unemployment or inflationary overheating of the economy. Needless to say, exchange rate adjustments within the euro area will be ruled out as a means for relieving regional imbalances. In the event of serious imbalances, the question arises whether other methods of adjustment are available. Two possibilities come to mind. The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 4 First, the authorities at the European and national levels could attempt to deal with local problems by making more vigorous use of fiscal policy in lieu of adjustments in the exchange rate. However, greater reliance on fiscal policy may run up against a major obstacle. The member countries of the European Union have concluded a Stability and Growth Pact, designed to ensure that national authorities will continue to pursue sound fiscal policies after the introduction of the euro. While that pact does not preclude use of fiscal policy to stimulate local economic activity, it clearly limits the national governments room for maneuver in the budgetary area. Moreover, the European Union does not intend to expand its modest existent programs for financial support of its low-income regions. Therefore, it is likely that regional imbalances will have to be corrected in another way. In the United States, flexible labor markets play an important role in leveling regional disparities. In regions with high unemployment, wages tend to rise less than elsewhere, inducing new firms to enter and to create jobs. Furthermore, people are prepared to move to regions with better job prospects. In many member countries of the European Union, by contrast, labor markets are inflexible. Wage structures are too egalitarian and do not take sufficient account of labor supply and demand conditions in individual occupations, industries and regions. In addition, people are reluctant to move, not only across national borders, but also within their own countries. European Union officials recognize that greater flexibility of labor markets is required if the euro is to enhance economic welfare. However, while some modest reforms of labor markets have been implemented, efforts to tackle the rigidities head on tend to run up against fierce political resistance in most countries of the European Union. Consequently, it is an open question whether the shift to the euro will help the European Union to promote its economic welfare. The uncertainties surrounding the economic effects of the euro must be kept in mind if we try to assess the consequences of the common currency for the Swiss economy. The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 5 2. Consequences for the Swiss Economy European monetary integration may affect the Swiss economy in various ways. During the planning phase of the euro project, monetary integration already began to cast shadows on our economy. In 1994 and 1995, the Swiss franc appreciated strongly in nominal and real terms against most currencies, including those of our key European trading partners. The upsurge of the Swiss franc was attributable in large measure to the uncertainties arising from European monetary integration. Many investors  both inside and outside the European Union  appeared to place little confidence in the stability of the future euro. They viewed the Swiss franc as a safe currency providing a hedge against the vagaries of the euro project. The rise of the Swiss franc magnified the pain felt by the domestic economy, which was just about to recover from a severe recession. A shift in Swiss monetary policy in the spring of 1995  to be discussed later  and a significant strengthening of the US dollar in 1996 served to rectify the exchange rate misalignment. More recently, our currency has again tended to strengthen to some extent. However, that modest rise in the real exchange rate of the Swiss franc does not reflect concerns about the stability of the euro. It is due rather to save-haven effects emanating from the crises in East Asia and Russia. As a matter of fact, investor sentiment turned strongly in favor of the euro after the decision to introduce the common currency. Before that decision was taken, many Swiss had been concerned that the shift to the euro might trigger an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc. These anxieties proved to be unfounded. On the contrary, markets became convinced that the euro would be a stable currency. They recognized the efforts made by the member countries of the European Union to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria. They were also impressed by the highly competent professionals appointed to manage the ECB. The euro certainly stands a good chance of becoming a stable currency, as currently anticipated by market participants. I am convinced that the management The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 6 of the ECB will make every effort to fulfill the mandate of the Maastricht Treaty and to conduct monetary policies aimed at price stability. A stable euro would also be in the interest of our economy as it would contribute to restrain exchange rate movements of the Swiss franc vis-a-vis our neighbor countries. Nevertheless, I believe that markets right now are too optimistic about the prospects of the euro. They are underestimating the technical difficulties faced by the ECB in setting monetary policy. The ECB will operate in a radically different policy environment, characterized by unified financial markets within the euro area. This is likely to distort the indicators central banks require to spot impending threats to price stability. Central banks cannot wait until an inflation or deflation problem actually occurs because monetary policy tends to affect the price level with a long lag. Therefore, central banks, if at all possible, must detect such problems well in advance if they are to maintain price stability. Without reliable indicators of future inflation or deflation, the conduct of monetary policy is akin to steering a ship in uncharted waters. Furthermore, markets, in my opinion, take an overly benign view of the economic costs that are likely to arise after the transition to the euro. Since these costs  as indicated earlier  may be significant, I would not be surprised to see the current wave of optimism give way again to a more sober assessment of the euro once it dawns on market participants that the common currency is unlikely to lead to economic paradise. For these reasons, one cannot rule out the possibility that shifts in market expectations about the stability of the euro will elicit renewed exchange rate turbulences even if the ECB strives to stick to the mandate of the Maastricht Treaty. Some analysts fear that the fluctuations of our currency vis-a-vis the euro will far exceed those observed in the past for the Swiss franc/Deutsche mark exchange rate. In their view, the highly unequal size of the euro and Swiss franc areas will exacerbate exchange rate volatility. Should the euro giant sneeze, the Swiss franc dwarf will likely be tossed about in the air. However, I am not aware of any research pointing to a relationship between exchange rate volatility and the The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 7 relative size of currency areas. Moreover, I can also think of forces that will help to curtail exchange rate volatility after the introduction of the euro. In 1994 and 1995, the Swiss economy was hurt, above all, by a sharp appreciation of the Swiss franc in relation to the Italian lira. Since the Italian currency will soon be replaced by the euro, an important source of exchange rate instability will disappear. Thus, I am unable to predict whether, on balance, the introduction of the euro will increase or decrease the volatility of the Swiss franc exchange rate vis-a-vis our neighbor countries. Aside from possible effects on exchange rate volatility, some analysts assert that the shift to the euro, sooner or later, will cause Swiss interest rates to rise to the levels prevailing in the euro area. Swiss interest rates, especially longterm rates, have traditionally been lower than anywhere else in Europe. In the 1950s and 1960s, the average yield on German government bonds, adjusted for exchange rate gains or losses, was typically more than 3 percentage points higher than the corresponding Swiss average. Over the years, this interest differential has tended to shrink, but it still amounts to close to two percentage points. In my view, it is unclear why the introduction of the euro should remove the interest bonus on Swiss-franc assets. Even after the shift to the euro, our currency will continue to be used by foreign investors as an attractive means of diversifying the asset composition of their portfolios. So long as the Swiss franc remains an stable investment instrument, the interest bonus will continue to stay with us. Thus, the chief threat to the Swiss economy arising from the shift to the euro lies in a possible increase in exchange rate volatility. In particular, a loss of confidence in the euro might trigger an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc. What could the SNB do in the face of adverse exchange rate shocks? The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 8 3. How Could the Swiss National Bank React? If confronted with an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc, the SNB could react in two possible ways. First, it could continue to stick to its traditional policy approach of controlling money growth in an effort to achieve and maintain price stability. But it would relax its policy stance in response to the exchange rate shock. By shifting to a more expansionary course, the SNB would lower domestic interest rates and make Swiss franc assets less attractive to foreign investors. In this way, it could counter the appreciation of the Swiss franc. This is exactly the approach the SNB adopted three and a half years ago, when it relaxed substantially its monetary policy. At the beginning of 1995, the sharp appreciation of the Swiss franc, mentioned earlier, started to choke the modest cyclical recovery that had set in two years earlier. The SNB tried to perform a delicate balancing act in order to reconcile its desire to shield the domestic economy from the ill-effects of the strong Swiss franc with its obligation to preserve price stability in the longer run. Even though the SNB loosened considerably its monetary reins, it was unable to soothe entirely the pain inflicted by the strong Swiss franc because the exchange rate did not react instantaneously to its policy shift. Nevertheless, SNB was reluctant to adopt an even more expansionary stance. It was concerned that an overly expansionary policy might fuel inflation at a future point in time. However, in 1996 it became clear that the shift to an expansionary stance had been fully justified as the main problem at that time was a threat of deflation, rather than inflation By relaxing its policy course, the SNB set the monetary pre-conditions for a sustained recovery of the Swiss economy. Thanks to the lower real exchange rate of the Swiss franc and a parallel recovery of Western European economies, Swiss real GDP has been growing again since the beginning of 1997. At present, the SNB is still pursuing its relaxed policy course. As the Swiss economy continues to expand, though, the SNB, at some future point in time, will have to tighten policy again in The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 9 order to preserve price stability. However, considering the shadows cast by the East Asian and Russian crises on the cyclical recovery of the European economies, the SNB does not believe that the time has come for tightening its monetary reins. Thus, recent experience indicates that the SNB, through shifts in monetary policy, is able to offset to a large extent the ill-effects of adverse exchange rate shocks. A second possibility would be to peg the exchange rate of the Swiss franc to the euro. The peg could either be temporary or Swiss authorities could decide to link the Swiss franc permanently to the euro through a fixed exchange rate. In the present environment, a permanent peg does not seem to be an attractive alternative to the SNBs traditional policy approach. With a permanent peg, the SNB would give up voluntarily its monetary autonomy. Thereafter, Swiss monetary conditions would be determined entirely by the ECB. Switzerland would forego the benefits of its past attempts to maintain price stability on the strength of its own efforts. In particular, we would have to accept a rise in domestic interest rates to euro-area levels since the Swiss franc, for all practical purposes, would become equivalent to the euro. It would clearly be odd to link the Swiss franc to an anchor currency whose stability record would still need to be established. Of course, the question of linking the Swiss franc permanently to the euro is closely related to the more general issue of how Switzerland will arrange itself with the European Union in the coming years. Should the Swiss decide to join the European Union, they will likely be drawn into the euros orbit. A temporary peg, by contrast, would not entail a loss of monetary autonomy. However, by placing a temporary ceiling on the Swiss franc exchange rate, the SNB would lose control over the money supply and, thus, run the risk of setting the stage for a subsequent rise in inflation. The SNB would regard a temporary peg only as a measure of last resort in the event of extreme exchange rate disturbances. In conclusion, the SNB is certainly able to smooth excessive fluctuations in the exchange rate arising from portfolio shifts into Swiss francs, induced by doubts about the stability of the euro. But in the presence of extreme exchange The Euro and Swiss Monetary Policy SNB 10 rate shocks, the SNB would be caught in a dilemma: If it tried to shield the domestic economy entirely from these shocks, it would probably jeopardize price stability in the medium and long runs.

Title: Swiss Franc - Options for the SNB
text: Island currency Franc Options for the SNB Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Presentation at the conference of the Economics Center (WWZ) of the University of Basel, on the occasion of the anniversary event 10 years WWZ/VBo Basel, 19 September 1998 2 1. Initial situation The introduction of the euro will change the international monetary system and financial structure. The euro is likely to follow in the footsteps of the Deutschmark, but surpass its international significance. The euro has a high potential, particularly in the area of investment and issuance. However, the success story of the euro has not yet been written. Important tests lie ahead. In the past, member countries had different economic and monetary policy preferences and track records. They are in different phases in the economic cycle. The European Central Bank (ECB) must prove that it can permanently bring the various interests under the hat of stability orientation, which is relentlessly clearly defined in its statutes. There are also practical monetary policy problems: which monetary policy strategy will the ECB choose? Will it be based primarily on a money supply target or directly on an inflation target? Either way, it relies on reliable monetary policy indicators. The significance of the previous indicators in the new context is open. This brings an additional moment of uncertainty to the design and implementation of monetary policy. Regardless of how these challenges are mastered in detail, Switzerland is particularly challenged - as an island surrounded by "euro country", with densely woven economic interdependence. Around 60 percent of our exports go to the EMU region. Over 70 percent of imports come from this region. Of course, this will make the euro more important for Switzerland than any of the previous currencies. Compared to their European competitors, Swiss companies will have to live with currency fluctuations on larger shares, even if the absorption of historically soft European currencies by the euro promises significant relief for individual groups of exporters. The EMU area will be less affected by exchange rate fluctuations overall. The share of foreign trade in EMU GDP will fall to just over 10 percent. The structure of the EMU economic area is approaching that of a closed economy. 3 2. The flexible exchange rate Switzerland, on the other hand, is one of the most open economies of all. The exchange rate of the Swiss franc is therefore a key economic parameter. Major exchange rate changes leave a clear mark on our economy. The special importance of the Swiss franc on the international financial markets favours the occurrence of exchange rate disturbances. Nevertheless, since 1973 - when the Bretton Woods system collapsed - Switzerland has not chosen the path of permanent exchange rate fixation. Why? Let's take a quick look back: The largely autonomous monetary policy, geared to price stability and economic needs, has so far brought advantages to the country. The Swiss interest rate advantage is the most obvious fruit. The upward pressure on the Swiss franc is, to a certain extent, the reflection of this. The long-term price development against the D-Mark can be roughly divided into two phases. The significant appreciation between 1973 and 1983 brought about the - perhaps excessive - correction of a previous undervaluation of the Swiss franc. Since 1983, there has been only a moderate appreciation trend of the Swiss franc; both against the D-Mark and export-weighted. By contrast, the export-weighted exchange rate index fluctuated much more. This is primarily due to the movements of the US dollar. An assessment must distinguish between fluctuations and trend. The constant competitive pressure resulting from a moderate upward trend is unlikely to have harmed the Swiss economy as a whole. Productivity increases were encouraged. On the other hand, the repeated appreciation spurts clearly had a negative impact. For example, the strong, sustained appreciation between 1992 and 1995 weighed heavily on the Swiss economy. The economy was severely slowed down. Switzerland's interest rate bonus is inextricably linked to the continuous appreciation of the Swiss franc. The same phases can also be distinguished for the interest rate differential as for the exchange rate. Up to approx. In the mid-eighties, i.e. at the time of the significant appreciation of the Swiss franc, the 4 nominal interest rate differential with Germany between three and four percent. From 1985, when the upward pressure against the D-Mark subsided, the difference levelled off at around two percent. Recently, the real interest rate differential has narrowed again. There are various reasons for the stability of the Swiss franc and the lower level of interest rates in the past.  Firstly, the fact that Switzerland has had a very high propensity to save by international standards for generations. On the one hand, this led to regular current account surpluses. Record levels of foreign assets relative to GDP are a consequence of this. On the other hand, investors' risk aversion means that a higher interest rate is required for investments in foreign currencies. This risk premium is reflected in the lower interest rates on Swiss franc investments.  Secondly, Switzerland was characterised by political continuity, a largely healthy state budget and monetary stability. Until the end of the eighties, the inflation rate was well below that of most European countries. On the other hand, Switzerland does not have lower average inflation than Germany over the period under review.  The stable framework conditions and the well-developed financial centre favoured - thirdly - the role of the Swiss franc as an international investment currency. The Swiss franc offered attractive diversification opportunities for international investors. From the point of view of European investors, it was particularly suitable as a hedge against dollar exchange rate fluctuations. A weakness of the dollar was quite regularly accompanied by a strengthening of the Swiss franc against the European currencies. This characteristic led to constant international investment requirements in Swiss francs and thus contributed to the interest bonus. In these areas, there were clear differences between Switzerland and most EMU countries in the seventies and eighties. The different stability preferences and the interest rate advantage legitimized an autonomous monetary policy. 5 3. Options for the SNB The SNB is called upon to position the Swiss franc in the changed currency environment. We need to assess the conditions under which an autonomous monetary policy is possible and sensible. We must also consider under what circumstances closer cooperation with EMU would make sense. There are three main adjustment strategies for Swiss monetary policy: - Continuation of the previous policy - Unilateral pegging of the Swiss franc to the euro - Accession to the euro area. (a) Continuation of the existing policy Under the heading "Continuation of existing policy", there can and must not be any talk of a monetary policy concept that is characterized by complete abstinence from exchange rate policy. This view, which has never been practiced in the history of the SNB, has its roots in rule-based money supply models that have not gained empirical significance even in relatively closed economies. Rather, it refers to a policy that responds to serious exchange rate distortions as part of its objective of price stability, but without - and this is crucial - pursuing explicit exchange rate targets. The exchange rate is an indicator in this understanding - no more and no less. In an open economy, its movements form an essential component in the field of tension between the forces that determine the economy. They must therefore be taken into account when it comes to the ongoing dosage of the policy. However, this does not mean that every price movement should be reacted to. The arguments against those who confuse the monetary policymaker's environment with the job of a precision mechanic weigh far too heavily. Despite all the tolerance towards the diversity of opinion among economists, the concept of macroeconomic fine-tuning, which was still relevant for auditing in the sixties, can be regarded as discarded. Only serious exchange rate fluctuations can be relevant in terms of action, which as exogenous shocks affect the economic development in the country 6 endanger.
