Die Europische Whrungsunion hat einen ziemlich detailliert ausgestalteten Check-in, aber keinen Check-out. Daher ist es ein Gebot vernnftiger Entscheidungsfindung, diesen Schritt nur zu tun, wenn er durch klar berwiegende Interessen gerechtfertigt ist. Unter diesen Voraussetzungen steht die Beitrittsvariante jetzt nicht zur Diskussion. Aber sie wird mit Sicherheit zu einem zentralen wirtschaftspolitischen Thema, wenn sich der Euro so entwickelt, wie sich das seine Architekten erhoffen. Als Alternative scheint die einseitige Bindung des Frankens an den Euro auf den ersten Blick attraktiv. Zwar wrde die Schweiz  so die Argumentation  einen Teil des Zinsunterschieds verlieren, dafr aber das fr das Wohlergehen unserer Wirtschaft gewichtige Wechselkursproblem wesentlich entschrfen. Ntigenfalls knnte man ja in lngeren Intervallen mit Parittsnderungen Korrekturen vornehmen. Allein, mehrere berlegungen lassen diese Lsung als wenig ratsamen Weg erscheinen. Mit der Anbindung soll primr eine Aufwertungstendenz gebrochen werden. Was wre die Folge? Ein wirklich schwerwiegendes Aufwertungsproblem drfte sich nur einstellen, falls die Europische Zentralbank eine destabilisierende Geldpolitik betreibt. Ein Anbindung wrde dann nichts anderes bedeuten, als dass wir diese schlechte Geldpolitik importieren wrden. Eine Anbindung des Wechselkurses mit dem Vorbehalt, die Paritt gegebenenfalls zu ndern, vermag ausserdem aller Erfahrung nach die Erwartungen der Devisenmrkte nicht hinreichend zu stabilisieren. Wir wrden bei auftretenden Zweifeln den Franken - aber auch unseren realen Sektor schwerwiegenden spekulativen Schocks aussetzen. Im Vergleich mit einem grundstzlich freien Kursregime schliesst die Anbindungsvariante die Mglichkeit einer graduellen Anpassung zum vornherein aus. Das sollten wir nicht tun in einer Phase, die reich an Vernderungen und Unsicherheiten ist. So bleibt als dritte Variante die Fortfhrung der bisherigen Politik, die man als Floating mit Reaktionsvorbehalt bezeichnen kann. Damit ist eine Politik gemeint, die im Rahmen ihres Ziels der Preisstabilitt auf schwerwiegende Kursverzerrungen nach oben und nach unten - reagiert, ohne aber - und das ist entscheidend - explizite 10 Wechselkursziele anzustreben. Diese Politik trgt dem Umstand Rechnung, dass im Spannungsfeld der konjunkturbestimmenden Krfte dem Wechselkurs ein wichtiger Stellenwert zukommt. Deren Identifikation ist ein schwieriges und gewiss risikoreiches Unterfangen, weil in der konkreten Situation verschiedenen Aspekten Rechnung zu tragen ist: den konjunkturellen Perspektiven, der monetren Marktsituation, den Ursachen und der mutmasslichen Dauer einer Verwerfung. Ermessen und Intuition spielen in diesem Prozess eine wichtige Rolle. Simple und den Marktteilnehmern transparente Reaktionskriterien wren fundamental kontraproduktiv. Es ist vielmehr sachdienlich, wenn die aktiven Marktteilnehmer zwar damit rechnen mssen, dass Korrekturen drohen, aber ber alles Weitere unsicher sind. Zur dieser Politik gehrt auch die ultima ratio der vorbergehenden Festlegung einer Obergrenze. Bei allen Risiken und den zugegebenermassen gemischten Erfahrungen drfen und wollen wir ein derartiges Manver im Blick auf die Zukunft nicht ausschliessen. Es bleibt allerdings vernnftigerweise beschrnkt auf den Fall einer schwerwiegenden Vertrauenserosion in den Euro, eine Konstellation die ich fr wenig wahrscheinlich halte. Es gibt im Blick auf die Herausforderung Euro fr die absehbare Zukunft realistischerweise keine bessere Alternative als eine eher pragmatische Politik des eigenen, umsichtig begangenen Weges. Wir wollen sie mit hoher Lernbereitschaft in Bezug auf Vernderungen, flexibel, aber doch fest verankert in unserem Stabilittsauftrag umsetzen. 4. Konjunkturausblick Lassen Sie mich mit einigen Ausfhrungen zur Konjunktur zum Schluss kommen. Nach einer enttuschend langen, sechsjhrigen Stagnationsphase brachte 1997 die langersehnte konjunkturelle Wende. Im Zug eines starken aussenwirtschaftlichen Impulses mit einem Exportanstieg von fast 9% erreichte unser Bruttoinlandprodukt 11 ein Wachstum von 1,7%. Vorbergehend registrierten wir gar Wachstumsraten von rund 3%. Der Aussenimpuls hat mittlerweile einen guten Teil seiner Schubkraft eingebsst. Aber dieser Effekt wird kompensiert durch eine schon 1997 eingetretene Belebung der Inlandnachfrage, insbesondere des Konsums und der Ausrstungsinvestitionen. Die Bauwirtschaft drfte dank der anhaltenden Zunahme der ffentlichen Bauttigkeit in diesem Jahr etwa stagnieren. Fr 1998 sollten wir insgesamt ein Wachstum des Bruttoinlandproduktes von etwa 2% erreichen. Dabei scheint dreierlei bemerkenswert. Erstens kann man feststellen, dass die anfnglich sehr exportlastige Belebung an Breite gewonnen hat. Die konjunkturelle Aktivitt ist heute besser abgesttzt und damit solider geworden. Zweitens haben sich die Verhltnisse am Arbeitsmarkt sprbar verbessert. Zugegeben, der Rckgang der Arbeitslosenquote von ber 5,5% anfangs 1997 auf 3,2% diesen September berzeichnet die erreichten Fortschritte. Aber am Befund einer deutlichen Verbesserung ndern die notwendigen statistischen Korrekturen nichts: die Gesamtbeschftigung nimmt zu, und die Zahl der Stellensuchenden bildet sich zurck. Das sind berzeugende Hinweise darauf, dass unser Arbeitsmarkt - trotz gelegentlicher bler Nachrede - gut funktioniert. Drittens mssen wir aber feststellen, dass sich das Wachstumstempo im Jahresverlauf abschwcht. Der Aufschwung wird moderater, aber er ist breiter abgesttzt. So weit, so gut. Interessanter als die Gegenwart ist indessen die Zukunft. Wie werden sich die Verhltnisse weiter entwickeln? Die Antwort fllt nicht leicht, denn unter verschiedenen Blickwinkeln gewinnt man ein widersprchliches Bild. Die aussenwirtschaftlichen Perspektiven stehen im Zeichen belastender Unsicherheiten an den Finanzmrkten. Die brske Korrektur von Fehlentwicklungen konfrontiert zahllose private und ffentliche Schuldner mit markanten Zinserhhungen und Finanzierungsengpssen. Dies hat reale Konsequenzen, leider auch fr Kreise und Sektoren, die mit den Fehlentwicklungen nie etwas zu tun hatten. Auf dem Hintergrund einer zwar auch beeintrchtigten aber trotzdem recht robusten Konjunkturperspektive fr unser europisches Umfeld rechne ich mit einem weiteren Nachlassen der Exportdynamik, aber nicht mit einem Einbruch. Weniger wahrscheinlich, aber als Risikoszenario nicht auszuschliessen, ist ein deutlicheres 12 Abflachen der EU-Konjunktur. Mit einer solchen Entwicklung msste man wohl rechnen, wenn - wie dies einige Pessimisten glauben - die Konjunktur in den USA in eine rezessive Phase eintreten wrde. Unter diesen Umstnden wren Europa und die Schweiz von einem deutlich restriktiveren Aussenimpuls betroffen. Die Inlandnachfrage in der Schweiz sollte vor allem dank des Konsums weiterhin massvoll wachsen. Sie profitiert von einer gnstigen Entwicklung der Haushaltseinkommen und dem wohl weiterhin tiefen Zinsniveau. Eine zustzliche Untersttzung drfte der Konsum durch die anhaltenden Verbesserungen am Arbeitsmarkt erfahren. Wenn nicht alles tuscht, wird die Arbeitslosigkeit im Jahr 1999 die Marke von 3% unterschreiten, was sich auf das Konsumentenvertrauen gnstig auswirken wird. Von den tiefen Zinsstzen sollte auch die Bauttigkeit etwas profitieren, aber ihre Wachstumsrate drfte nur leicht positiv ausfallen. Wenn diese Einschtzung in den groben Zgen zutrifft, werden wir in den kommenden ein bis zwei Jahren ein moderates Wachstum des Bruttoinlandprodukts von 1-2% erreichen. Damit verbindet sich kein nennenswertes Inflationsrisiko, so dass uns nichts daran hindern sollte, unsere massvoll stimulierende Geldpolitik fortzusetzen. Allein, der Risiken sind viele, insbesondere im internationalen Kontext. Zu ihnen gehren die noch schwer fassbaren realen Konsequenzen der Turbulenzen im Finanzsystem und gewiss auch der Start zur Europischen Whrungsunion. Diese Unwgbarkeiten verlangen von allen - auch von der Nationalbank - Umsichtigkeit und ntigenfalls den Mut zu entschlossenem Handeln.

Title: Thoughts on current monetary and currency policy issues
text: Thoughts on current monetary policy issues Dr. Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Bank and Corporate Evening '98 Munich, 27.10.98 In accordance with the chosen topic, I will primarily comment on monetary policy in my remarks today. Naturally, I will do this from a Swiss perspective. However, as a representative of the central bank of a small, open economy, I am aware that foreign influences have always been of great importance for both the Swiss real economy and Swiss monetary policy. The start of European Monetary Union on 1 January 1999 will change our monetary policy environment and bring us additional uncertainty, at least in the early stages. For this reason, the discussion of the impact of the euro on Swiss monetary policy will be a focus of my remarks. In addition to the introduction of the euro, we are currently facing further uncertainty: our interim monetary target, the central bank money supply, has been exposed to various shocks for some time. In our monetary policy decisions, we can no longer rely on the course of the central bank money supply to the extent it has done so far, so we are increasingly taking additional indicators into account. A further focus of my remarks will therefore be a comparison of our flexible money supply target strategy with the inflation target strategy that has recently been applied in various countries. Finally, I will also talk about the fundamental orientation of our monetary policy and the current monetary policy situation. 1. Economic development in Switzerland Let me start with a review of the economic development in Switzerland this year. Phase of growth After a long period of stagnation, Switzerland is likely to have returned to a growth phase. Growth in real gross domestic product began to pick up significantly in the second half of 1997. In the 1st half of 1998, however, it declined somewhat as a result of the flattening of exports to East Asia. 2 The upswing began with a strong expansion of exports, which had already begun in the first quarter of 1997. However, the upswing was not limited to exports. Since the second half of 1997, domestic consumption has also been growing more strongly. Since the beginning of the year, the economy has also been supported by investments. It is pleasing that not only is investment in equipment increasing, but that the construction industry is now also recovering. After a long period of contraction, construction returned to positive growth rates in 1998. The development on the labour market is also positive. Unemployment is currently about 3.5%, compared with just over 5% in 1997. However, we are aware that the decline is somewhat exaggerated as a result of government employment programs. Crises in emerging economies At the moment, many emerging economies are experiencing a deep economic, but also political and social crisis. Until recently, we assumed that the crises in Asia, Russia and Latin America would have little impact on Switzerland. In the meantime, we have become a little more cautious in our assessment, as the regional crises accumulate in their negative effects. As a result of the crisis in East Asia, all Western industrialized countries have suffered losses in their exports. For the time being, most countries were able to compensate for the export losses with strong domestic consumption and investment demand. Overall, however, we must expect growth in the industrialised countries to slow down in the medium term. This would also further dampen demand for goods from Switzerland. However, the relatively good economic outlook in the European Community suggests that the weakening of demand for Swiss export goods will be limited. In any case, it is important for the upswing in Switzerland that domestic demand growth now remains robust. 3 Not all regional crises are due to the same causes. The Russian crisis is first and foremost a political crisis. As a result of the lack of "public policy", the transformation of the Soviet planned economy into a functioning market economy has come to a standstill for the time being. However, since the Russian economy is small compared to the global economy, the direct consequences of the Russian crisis for the economy in the western industrialized countries are relatively limited. By contrast, the consequences of the Asian crisis, in particular the crisis in Japan, are much more noticeable for the global economy and also for Switzerland. It is true that Switzerland's economic ties with East Asia and Japan are also limited, so that the direct impact of the crisis does not have to lead to a recession in Switzerland. The main risk of this crisis, however, is that Asia is of great importance to the American economy. The US would inevitably be affected by a sharp economic slump in Japan. This would also have a negative impact on Switzerland and the countries of the European Union. Price collapse on the stock exchanges In addition to the crises in the emerging markets, the situation on the stock exchanges has recently come to a head. The price collapse in recent months is striking and affects all stock exchanges in the world. The Swiss stock exchange also lost over 25% of its value after rising to an all-time high in July this year. How is this decline in value to be assessed on the financial markets? A massive and rapid decline in stock market prices can have significant consequences, especially for the financial sector. The financial stability of banks and financial institutions can be affected if banks suffer large losses on their securities holdings. However, the solvency of the banks can also be affected if their loan debtors get into trouble due to the collapse of share prices and can no longer repay their loans. In extreme cases, certain banks could become insolvent and illiquid. Since the banks provide liquidity and capital to the other sectors of the economy through their lending, this would have had drastic consequences. 4 Impact on the other sectors of the economy. A chain reaction could develop that would lead to the stagnation and deflation of an economy. However, a sober look at the stock market situation shows that we are far from an actual collapse of stock prices in the USA and Europe. The strong bear market on the stock markets in Europe and the USA is above all a correction of the pronounced price development of recent years. The share prices have hardly reflected the possible profit developments of the companies. Sooner or later, an adjustment became inevitable. The price correction is also useful in that it again leads to a healthier perception of risks in the equity and financial markets. This correct perception of risks is essential for an efficient distribution of capital. We assume that the price correction of the stock exchange will not have too much of an impact on the economy in Switzerland to the current extent. On the one hand, our shareholdings are not excessively broadly diversified. On the other hand, the strong bull market of recent years has not had a major positive effect on consumption. Gains and losses from equity investments do not seem to influence the short-term consumer behaviour of economic agents too much. Economic outlook for Switzerland I come back to the economic development in Switzerland. I am still confident that we are currently at the beginning of an upswing, albeit a modest one. An important reason for this assessment is that the competitiveness of many Swiss companies has improved considerably in recent years. The long stagnation has caused pressure to adapt, which has led to a significant improvement in the flexibility and innovative strength of our economy. In addition to the efforts of the economic partners, a number of liberalisations of government regulations have also contributed to increasing this flexibility and improving the framework conditions. Examples include the new bin- 5 Market Act and the revised Antitrust Act, which increase competition in Switzerland. The forecasts for the future course of business and for the order intake of the companies also point to a still quite robust domestic economy. I therefore assume that this will increasingly emerge as an engine of economic development. However, in order not to jeopardise the recovery unnecessarily, we must continue our own efforts. For me, the focus is on further improving competitive and labour market conditions, restructuring public finances and ensuring a high level of training. 2. The fundamental orientation of Swiss monetary policy I would now like to turn to the monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank. Let me start with some basic thoughts on the direction of this policy. In the long term, we focus our policy on maintaining price stability, equating price stability with an inflation rate of one to two percent. The orientation of monetary policy towards maintaining price stability is, of course, not an end in itself, but reflects the clear findings of national economic research over the last thirty years, according to which an unstable monetary environment can lead to significant losses in prosperity and growth and also place an excessive burden on the socially vulnerable groups in the population. Scientific studies have then shown that fluctuations in the inflation rate lead to short-term production losses. A central bank therefore makes the best contribution to a balanced macroeconomic development if it aligns its policy towards price stability in the long term and consistently combats inflationary shocks that have occurred. It must also do everything in its power to prevent unnecessary inflationary but also deflationary flare-ups and the resulting adjustment costs. It is gratifying to note that our 6 Assessment of a reasonable orientation of monetary policy practically coincides with that of the Bundesbank and also of the new European Central Bank. As the crises in Asia and Russia show, a stable monetary environment is a prerequisite for the functioning of money and capital markets. A stable currency and a transparent monetary policy make it easier to assess risks and opportunities. Through a stability-oriented policy, the SNB can therefore also help to limit systemic risks on the Swiss financial markets. Despite the clear theoretical and empirical findings on the value of a stability-oriented monetary policy, the Swiss National Bank and other central banks are repeatedly criticized by various sides for their objectives. Various groups try to influence the policies of central banks for their own, mostly short-term interests. However, this is highly undesirable. Science has been able to clearly demonstrate that monetary policy is most successful when it can fulfil its tasks in a largely independent manner. Since its foundation, the Swiss National Bank has enjoyed great independence from the political authorities in the exercise of monetary policy. This is remarkable in that the legal structure was created as early as 1905. The legislature and the voters obviously acted far-sightedly at that time without the latest scientific findings on the importance of an independent central bank and decided against a pure state bank. Since the national bank was founded at the beginning of this century, the economic and legal situation has changed considerably. We would therefore like to revise the articles of the Swiss Federal Constitution concerning the SNB in order to ensure an optimal orientation of Swiss monetary policy in the long term. The primary aim is to define the independence of the SNB more precisely and to formulate the monetary policy mandate more precisely. 7 Of course, the independence of the central bank cannot be absolute in a democratic state. Independence requires a clear mandate and an accountability obligation. The mandate is a clear guideline that the SNB must follow when defining its monetary policy. It must be formulated in an economically sensible way and be achieved with the resources available to the SNB. As I have explained above, maintaining price stability is the SNB's central contribution to the economic environment in Switzerland. The maintenance of price stability must therefore be given a special assessment on behalf of the SNB to conduct a monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. With the creation of an independent central bank with a clear mandate, the population, parliament and government agree, so to speak, in advance on a monetary policy that they consider optimal in the long term. By delegating the implementation of monetary policy to the central bank, short-term special interests are prevented from being placed before the long-term overall interest of the entire country in critical situations, such as a recession and large budget deficits. This is the mechanism that so greatly increases the credibility of an independent central bank's monetary policy. In most developed countries, this view has prevailed and many countries, such as the UK, where the government used to directly determine monetary policy, now have independent central banks. However, it is also important to us that the European Monetary Union has followed this path and created an independent central bank with the aim of maintaining price stability. Of course, the issuance of an order to the central bank presupposes that there is a broad consensus on the long-term goal of monetary policy. I am pleased to note that this consensus exists in Switzerland and that the orientation of monetary policy towards price stability is widely supported by the population. This consensus obviously also exists in Germany and I hope that it will spread to the other European countries in the transition to monetary union over time. 8 3. The introduction of the euro Let me move from my reflections on the fundamental aspects of monetary policy to questions of the current implementation of monetary policy. Since mid-1996, we have had inflation of less than one percent in Switzerland. Our forecasts point to continued favourable price developments, so that inflation will be close to our target for the foreseeable future. Nevertheless, we do not currently operate in a problem-free environment. There are two aspects that are critical to our monetary policy. One concerns the introduction of European Monetary Union at the beginning of next year, the other a certain degree of uncertainty in the indicators available to us for assessing the degree of expansion of monetary policy in the short term. I will first talk about the introduction of The European Monetary Union and later turn to the indicators. Most members of the European Union will abandon their own currency on 1 January 1999 and adopt the euro as a means of payment. The previous de facto dominance of the Deutsche Bundesbank with regard to European monetary relations will cease to exist and the European Central Bank will henceforth determine the single monetary policy of the European Union. The importance of the introduction of the euro for the economic environment in the European Union is great. Monetary union will complete the internal market and bring a number of benefits to intergovernmental transport within the Union: transaction costs will be lower and exchange rate risks will be eliminated altogether. In addition, there is a great increase in transparency through the use of a uniform unit of account throughout the European Union, which will increase competition between providers. However, economic advantages can also result from the newly emerging uniform money and capital markets. This large single financial market should contribute to a more efficient allocation of savings and capital. All this suggests that monetary union 9 will fundamentally improve the economic environment in the European Union. In addition to these advantages, however, the risks of monetary union must not be overlooked. The question to be discussed is how stability-oriented the monetary policy of the European Central Bank will be. Clear structures have been put in place for monetary union. The Maastricht Treaty and the subsequent supplementary treaties have granted the European Central Bank a high degree of independence and given it the mandate to ensure the maintenance of price stability as a matter of priority. Participation in monetary union is also linked to the well-known convergence conditions. In addition, the key positions in the European Central Bank were convincingly filled. All this suggests that the monetary policy of the European Central Bank will not differ, or at least not a priori, from the previous policy of the Deutsche Bundesbank. An additional problem for the participating countries lies in the disappearance of the national autonomy of monetary policy. Member states will no longer be able to adjust their monetary policy to the state of their own economies. This is not a major problem in and of itself, as long as the cycles of national economies in the EU are similar. If this is not the case, imbalances between member states can in future only be compensated for by fiscal means or by a flexible labour market. However, with its Stability Pact, the EU sets certain limits on national fiscal policy and there is no EU-wide fiscal equalisation between the member states for the time being. In addition, the flexibility of the workforce is not very great. This means that the economic benefits of monetary union may be less than is generally assumed. Let me outline below the impact of the introduction of the European Monetary Union on the monetary environment of the Swiss National Bank. For Switzerland, it is important that the euro becomes a stable currency. I am confident about this because, as I said earlier, the institutional framework is good. 10 Nevertheless, in my view, there are two risks for Switzerland: On the one hand, we must expect increased uncertainties in the first phase of monetary union, as the European Central Bank does not yet have reliable and meaningful monetary policy indicators. It will have to break new ground at the beginning, as it still lacks the experience for a comprehensive European monetary policy. The European Central Bank will not automatically be able to take over the credibility of the Deutsche Bundesbank, for example; rather, it must create its own reputation over time. On the other hand, despite the good legal framework conditions, there is a medium-term risk that the representatives of individual states will be tempted to represent country-specific interests and thus not fully support the mandate. This would severely damage the credibility of the European Central Bank. Alternatives for Switzerland A stable euro would clearly be the best situation for Switzerland's monetary environment. However, we have to assume that currency turbulence could occur at the beginning of the monetary union and that there is a risk of an appreciation of the Swiss franc, because international investors are not yet convinced of the quality of European monetary policy. In principle, the SNB has three options for reacting to such a situation: 1. It can fix the exchange rate against the euro from the outset and focus on A fixed exchange rate is aimed at a longer period of time. 2. It may continue to pursue an autonomous monetary policy with the aim of maintaining price - Track stability. In doing so, it would take into account disturbances in the foreign exchange market, to the extent compatible with that objective. 3. It can pursue a pragmatic policy and temporarily fix the Swiss franc exchange rate against the euro in the event of extreme fluctuations in exchange rates. 11 Each of these variants has advantages and disadvantages. By permanently fixing the Swiss franc against the euro, the SNB would dispense with an independent policy and fully follow European monetary policy. For the export industry, this variant would eliminate the exchange rate risks. In the long term, however, this exchange rate fixation is only unproblematic if it is compatible with price stability. At least at the beginning of monetary union, it is not yet clear at what level European inflation will level off on average. In addition, we would have to expect substantial interest rate hikes if the exchange rate were fixed against the euro. The permanent fixation of the Swiss franc against the euro is therefore not a viable alternative for the SNB at the moment. The pursuit of an autonomous monetary policy - i.e. our second alternative - has the advantage that we can maintain the fundamental orientation of monetary policy and do not have to change it because of individual currency turbulences. In the face of most disruptions in the foreign exchange markets, our country's export industry is sufficiently flexible to adapt quickly to the new conditions. In addition, the SNB can try to dampen the disturbances to a certain extent. This variant therefore represents a more attractive solution for us than pegging the Swiss franc to the euro. With this policy, Switzerland would be able to retain its interest rate advantage for the time being. Under certain circumstances, however, there could be a disproportionate appreciation of the Swiss franc, so that even the most flexible companies in the export industry would run into great difficulties. In such a situation, it is conceivable that the third variant, namely the temporary fixation of the Swiss franc exchange rate, would be the best solution. However, I must emphasise that this variant must be reserved for real exceptional cases and must not be used for minor disturbances. The risk of this variant lies in the fact that the additional liquidity supply as a result of exchange rate fixation is not compatible with the long-term objective of price stability. The SNB must therefore return the money supply to its original equilibrium path as quickly as possible after the exchange rate fixation has been lifted. 12 I stress once again that I most likely expect a stable and hard euro. In this case, the SNB will hardly have to intervene in the foreign exchange market and will be able to successfully continue its autonomous policy. 4. Money supply target versus inflation target Let me now move on to issues of the operational implementation of an autonomous monetary policy. There are long and variable time intervals between monetary impulses and their effects on price levels and production. For this reason, central banks have traditionally used money supply as indicators or as intermediate targets to implement their monetary policy operationally and to assess the degree of expansion of their policies. Money supplies are suitable as an intermediate target if they are easily controllable by the central bank and also closely correlate with the ultimate goal of price stability. If a central bank controls the growth of a monetary aggregate under these conditions, it also indirectly controls the inflation rate. The condition for this mechanism, however, is that the velocity of circulation or the demand for money is sufficiently stable in the medium and long term. In various countries, especially in the Anglo-Saxon world, the link between monetary developments and the inflation rate has become questionable as a result of strong innovations in the financial sector. These countries have therefore abandoned their money supply targets and are now pursuing a so-called inflation target strategy, in which they directly target an inflation target. As you know, the European Central Bank has recently fleshed out its view of price stability. However, it refrains from formulating a direct inflation target and stresses the important role of the money supply in its future monetary policy. The Swiss National Bank has been pursuing a money supply strategy since the transition to flexible exchange rates. Since 1980, we have been using the monetary base as an interim target. Until 1990, we formulated annual targets for the monetary base, and since then we have been setting a medium-term target path for the central bank money supply for a period of about five years. The experience with this intermediate goal is generally positive. With the formulation of a medium-term target path, we have today 13 a flexible strategy that allows us to deviate from the target path in the short term and to take into account indicators other than the central bank money supply when setting monetary policy. Since last year, disruptions in the demand for central bank money have increased sharply. Changes in banks' liquidity policies, in particular increased volatility in banks' demand for sight deposits, play a major role in this. Public demand for 1000-franc music sections has also risen sharply. The question therefore arises to what extent the inflation target strategy would represent an alternative to our monetary policy. In the following, I would like to show the differences between a money supply target strategy and an inflation target strategy, referring in particular to Swiss conditions. In a monetary policy with a direct inflation target, the central bank refrains from formulating an interim target and tries to achieve the final target directly. In doing so, it must prepare an inflation forecast and design its monetary policy in such a way that the inflation forecast is in line with its inflation target. Compared to a monetary policy with a money supply target, this policy may have the advantage that the target orientation is more understandable for a broader layer of the population. An inflation target is at best easier to understand than a money supply target. In the event of a missed target, however, it is more difficult for the public to determine whether the central bank's missed target can be blamed for or whether it has come about through a surprising change in the velocity of circulation that cannot be compensated for immediately by the central bank. The less the public can check the actual actions of the central bank, the more difficult it can be to build credibility and thus reputation. The operational implementation of monetary policy is more difficult with an inflation target strategy than with a money supply strategy: forecasts of the short- and medium-term inflation rate are generally associated with a great deal of uncertainty. Inflation forecasts in a small, open economy like Switzerland are particularly delicate because foreign shocks often have a strong impact on the domestic inflation rate. It is also difficult to determine the exact change in the short-term 14 To determine the interest rates necessary to achieve the inflation target in each case. For this, the economic knowledge is only available to a limited extent. However, it seems important to me to note that our pragmatic money supply target strategy already has common aspects with a policy of direct inflation targeting. The differences between our money supply strategy and the inflation target strategy are relatively small for two reasons: On the one hand, the Swiss National Bank sets its money supply target with regard to its vision of price stability. It therefore pursues a conditional money supply objective. In a world without disruption, both strategies would thus be congruent. On the other hand, the SNB has a very flexible money supply target with its medium-term target path for the central bank money supply. It may deviate from the trajectory and may also take into account indicators other than the central bank money supply if it is convinced that it will better achieve the objective of price stability or if there are other valid reasons for doing so. An important difference between the two strategies, however, is that in a money supply strategy, a central bank commits itself not only to achieving price stability but also to an operational framework for achieving its objectives. Setting an operational framework - that is, formulating a target for a monetary aggregate - has, in our view, a positive effect on credibility. This gives market participants the opportunity to assess the central bank's policy at an early stage before its effect on inflation becomes apparent. In summary, we can conclude that the differences between the Swiss National Bank's money supply management and an inflation target strategy are relatively small. Our flexible money supply strategy includes essential elements of an inflation target strategy. However, we continue to attach great importance to the development of the money supply, as the operational framework thus established can contribute to the credibility of the SNB. A transition to a pure inflation target strategy would only be an option for us if the link between the development of the money supply and the price level were to collapse completely. 15 5. Our current monetary policy I would now like to make a few comments on our current monetary policy. As a result of the aforementioned disruptions in the demand for central bank money in the last two years, we have been forced to make use of our flexible monetary policy strategy and to increasingly use additional indicators in addition to the central bank money supply for our monetary policy decisions. For us, the money supply M3 currently plays an important role as an additional monetary policy indicator. This unit has a close relationship to price developments in the long term and is less sensitive to interest rates in the short term than the narrower aggregates M1 and M2. In the short term, however, the development of M3 and the price level do not necessarily have to be parallel. We therefore also observe other meaningful indicators such as the exchange rate, the discrepancy between actual and potential production, and the different interest rates. As a result of the increased consideration of additional indicators, we have been publishing so-called "monetary policy conclusions" on a quarterly basis since the beginning of this year, in which we present our assessment of the monetary environment to market participants and formulate our monetary policy intentions for the coming quarter. This increases the transparency of our monetary policy decisions and thus enables the public to get a good picture of the monetary policy situation. At the moment, we are conducting a relatively expansionary monetary policy, which is reflected in low money and capital market interest rates. In this way, we want to continue to support the upswing in the Swiss economy that has begun. Our indicators suggest that we are not building up inflation potential as a result: on the one hand, the growth of the large monetary aggregates is not excessively strong, and on the other hand, economic production is still far from its potential. However, we are closely monitoring developments in order to withdraw liquidity from the market at an early stage if an increase in inflation were to become apparent. We are also closely following the crises in Asia, Russia and Latin America as well as the development of the stock markets. The SNB cannot resolve these crises or 16 Stabilize stock market prices. However, it must assess the effects of this turbulence on production and prices in Switzerland and react to deflationary or inflationary developments by means of appropriate monetary policy measures. Switzerland can also help resolve regional crises within the framework of the International Monetary Fund. However, I would like to emphasise once again that the solution must first and foremost come from the countries concerned themselves. In Switzerland, with a stable monetary environment, the SNB can help to minimise the systemic risks of undesirable developments in the equity and financial markets. 5. Schlussbemerkungen I will conclude my remarks and would like to highlight once again the main statements of my presentation: n After a long recession, Switzerland has returned to a phase of modest growth, albeit for the time being. In order to continue the upswing, further efforts are needed to improve the framework conditions. The SNB supports the upswing as long as it does not build up inflation potential. n The fundamental orientation of monetary policy towards maintaining price stability represents the SNB's greatest contribution to balanced macroeconomic development. Constitutionally guaranteed independence, combined with a clear mandate, offers the greatest guarantee that the SNB will be able to maintain price stability in the long term in the overall interest of the country. n Our flexible money supply strategy has many similarities with an inflation target strategy. However, it has the advantage that it also defines the operational framework of monetary policy and can thus increase the credibility of the SNB. The strategy is flexible enough to react adequately to disruptions in the short term. n We expect a stable euro in the transition to The European Monetary Union. The Swiss National Bank will therefore implement its autonomous monetary policy with 17 continue to pursue the primary objective of price stability. We would counter an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc with the means at our disposal. 18
