Wir mssen aber davon ausgehen, dass zu Beginn der Whrungsunion Whrungs-turbulenzen auftreten knnten und dass das Risiko einer Aufwertung des Schweizerfrankens besteht, weil die internationalen Investoren von der Qualitt der europischen Geldpolitik noch nicht berzeugt sind. Die Nationalbank hat im Prinzip drei Mglichkeiten, auf eine solche Situation zu reagieren: 1. Sie kann den Wechselkurs gegenber dem Euro von vornherein fixieren und auf ln- gere Frist einen festen Wechselkurs anstreben. 2. Sie kann wie bisher eine autonome Geldpolitik mit dem Ziel der Erhaltung der Preis - stabilitt verfolgen. Dabei wrde sie - soweit mit diesem Ziel vereinbar - auf Strungen im Devisenmarkt Rcksicht nehmen. 3. Sie kann eine pragmatische Politik verfolgen und bei extremen Schwankungen der Wechselkurse den Frankenkurs vorbergehend gegenber dem Euro fixieren. 11 Jede dieser Varianten hat Vor- und Nachteile. Mit einer permanenten Fixierung des Frankens gegenber dem Euro wrde die Nationalbank auf eine eigenstndige Politik verzichten und vollstndig der europischen Geldpolitik folgen. Fr die Exportwirtschaft wrden bei dieser Variante die Wechselkursrisiken wegfallen. Langfristig ist diese Wechselkursfixierung aber nur dann unproblematisch, wenn sie mit Preisstabilitt vereinbar ist. Zumindest zu Beginn der Whrungsunion ist noch nicht klar, auf welchem Niveau sich die europische Inflation durchschnittlich einpendeln wird. Zudem mssten wir mit substantiellen Zinserhhungen rechnen, wenn der Wechselkurs gegenber dem Euro fixiert wrde. Die permanente Fixierung des Frankens gegenber dem Euro stellt deshalb fr die Nationalbank im Moment keine valable Alternative dar. Die Weiterverfolgung einer autonomen Geldpolitik - also unsere zweite Alternative hat den Vorteil, dass wir die fundamentale Ausrichtung der Geldpolitik beibehalten knnen und nicht wegen einzelnen Whrungsturbulenzen ndern mssen. Die Exportindustrie unseres Landes ist bei den meisten Strungen auf den Devisenmrkten gengend flexibel, um sich den neuen Verhltnissen rasch anzupassen. Zudem kann die Nationalbank versuchen, die Strungen bis zu einem gewissen Grad zu dmpfen. Diese Variante stellt daher fr uns eine attraktivere Lsung dar als die Bindung des Frankens an den Euro. Bei dieser Politik wrde die Schweiz vorderhand ihren Zinsvorteil behalten knnen. Unter bestimmten Umstnden knnte es jedoch zu einer unverhltnismssigen Aufwertung des Frankens kommen, so dass auch die flexibelsten Unternehmen der Exportwirtschaft in grosse Schwierigkeiten geraten wrden. In einer derartigen Situation ist es denkbar, dass die dritte Variante, nmlich die vorbergehende Fixierung des Frankenkurses, die beste Lsung darstellen wrde. Ich muss jedoch betonen, dass diese Variante fr wirkliche Ausnahmeflle vorbehalten bleiben muss und nicht bei kleineren Strungen verwendet werden darf. Das Risiko dieser Variante liegt darin, dass die zustzliche Liquidittsversorgung als Folge der Wechselkursfixierung nicht mit dem langfristigen Ziel der Preisstabilitt vereinbar ist. Die Nationalbank muss daher nach Aufhebung der Wechselkursfixierung die Geldmenge mglichst rasch wieder auf ihren ursprnglichen Gleichgewichtspfad zurckbringen. 12 Ich betone nochmals, dass ich mit grosser Wahrscheinlichkeit einen stabilen und harten Euro erwarte. In diesem Fall wird die Nationalbank kaum in den Devisenmarkt eingreifen mssen und ihre autonome Politik erfolgreich weiterfhren knnen. 4. Geldmengenziel versus Inflationsziel Lassen Sie mich nun zu Fragen der operativen Umsetzung einer autonomen Geldpolitik bergehen. Zwischen monetren Impulsen und deren Wirkungen auf das Preisniveau und die Produktion bestehen lange und zudem variable Zeitabstnde. Notenbanken haben aus diesem Grund traditionell Geldmengen als Indikatoren oder als Zwischenziele verwendet, um ihre Geldpolitik operativ umzusetzen und den Expansionsgrad ihrer Politik zu beurteilen. Geldmengen eignen sich dann als Zwischenziel, wenn sie durch die Notenbank gut kontrollierbar sind und berdies eng mit dem Endziel der Preisstabilitt korrelieren. Kontrolliert eine Notenbank unter diesen Voraussetzungen das Wachstum eines Geldaggregates, dann kontrolliert sie indirekt auch die Inflationsrate. Die Bedingung fr diesen Mechanismus ist allerdings, dass die Umlaufsgeschwindigkeit oder die Geldnachfrage mittel- und langfristig hinreichend stabil ist. In verschiedenen Lndern, vor allem im angelschsischen Raum, ist die Verbindung zwischen der Geldmengenentwicklung und der Inflationsrate als Folge der starken Innovationen im Finanzsektor fragwrdig geworden. Diese Lnder haben daher ihre Geldmengenziele aufgegeben und verfolgen jetzt eine sogenannte Inflationszielstrategie, bei der sie direkt ein Inflationsziel anvisieren. Die Europische Zentralbank hat bekanntlich vor kurzem ihre Auffassung von Preisstabilitt konkretisiert. Sie verzichtet aber auf die Formulierung eines direkten Inflationszieles und betont die wichtige Rolle der Geldmenge bei ihrer zuknftigen Geldpolitik. Die Schweizerische Nationalbank verfolgt seit dem bergang zu flexiblen Wechselkursen eine Geldmengenstrategie. Seit 1980 verwenden wir die monetre Basis als Zwischenziel. Bis 1990 formulierten wir jhrliche Ziele fr die monetre Basis und seither legen wir einen mittelfristigen Zielpfad fr die Notenbankgeldmenge jeweils fr eine Periode von etwa fnf Jahren fest. Die Erfahrungen mit diesem Zwischenziel sind allgemein positiv. Mit der Formulierung eines mittelfristigen Zielpfades haben wir heute 13 eine flexible Strategie, die es uns ermglicht, in der kurzen Frist vom Zielpfad abzuweichen und bei der Festlegung der Geldpolitik auch andere Indikatoren als die Notenbankgeldmenge zu bercksichtigen. Seit dem letzten Jahr haben Strungen bei der Nachfrage nach Notenbankgeld stark zugenommen. Dabei spielen Vernderungen bei der Liquidittspolitik der Banken, insbesondere eine erhhte Volatilitt bei der Nachfrage der Banken nach Giroguthaben, eine grosse Rolle. Auch die Nachfrage des Publikums nach 1000-Franken Notenabschnitten ist stark angestiegen. Es stellt sich daher die Frage, inwiefern die Inflationszielstrategie eine Alternative fr unsere Geldpolitik darstellen wrde. Ich mchte im folgenden die Unterschiede zwischen einer Geldmengenzielstrategie und einer Inflationszielstrategie aufzeigen und dabei vor allem auf die schweizerischen Verhltnisse Bezug nehmen. Bei einer Geldpolitik mit einem direkten Inflationsziel verzichtet die Notenbank auf die Formulierung eines Zwischenzieles und versucht das Endziel direkt zu erreichen. Dabei muss sie eine Inflationsprognose erstellen und ihre Geldpolitik so gestalten, dass die Inflationsprognose mit ihrem Inflationsziel in bereinstimmung kommt. Gegenber einer Geldpolitik mit einem Geldmengenziel hat diese Politik mglicherweise den Vorteil, dass die Zielausrichtung fr eine breitere Schicht der Bevlkerung verstndlicher ist. Ein Inflationsziel ist allenfalls einfacher zu verstehen als ein Geldmengenziel. Bei einer Zielverfehlung ist es allerdings fr das Publikum schwieriger, festzustellen, ob die Zielverfehlung der Notenbank angelastet werden kann oder ob sie durch eine berraschende und daher fr die Notenbank nicht sofort kompensierbare Vernderung der Umlaufsgeschwindigkeit zustande gekommen ist. Je weniger die ffentlichkeit die tatschlichen Handlungen der Notenbank berprfen kann, desto schwieriger kann es sein, Glaubwrdigkeit und damit auch Reputation aufzubauen. Die operative Umsetzung der Geldpolitik ist mit einer Inflationszielstrategie eher schwieriger als mit einer Geldmengenstrategie: Prognosen der kurz- und mittelfristigen Inflationsrate sind allgemein mit einer grossen Unsicherheit verbunden. Inflationsprognosen in einer kleinen, offenen Volkswirtschaft wie der Schweiz sind speziell heikel, weil oft auslndische Schocks einen starken Einfluss auf die inlndische Inflationsrate haben. Schwierig ist es auch, die exakte Vernderung der kurzfristigen 14 Zinsstze zu bestimmen, die ntig ist, um jeweils das Inflationsziel zu erreichen. Dafr sind die konomischen Kenntnisse nur beschrnkt vorhanden. Es scheint mir aber wichtig festzuhalten, dass unsere pragmatische Geldmengenzielstrategie bereits heute gemeinsame Aspekte mit einer Politik der direkten Inflationssteuerung hat. Die Unterschiede zwischen unserer Geldmengenstrategie und der Inflationszielstrategie sind aus zwei Grnden relativ gering: Zum einen legt die Schweizerische Nationalbank ihr Geldmengenziel im Hinblick auf ihre Vorstellung von Preisstabilitt fest. Sie verfolgt also ein bedingtes Geldmengenziel. In einer Welt ohne Strungen wren beide Strategien somit deckungsgleich. Zum anderen hat die Nationalbank mit ihrem mittelfristigen Zielpfad fr die Notenbankgeldmenge ein sehr flexibles Geldmengenziel. Sie kann vom Zielpfad abweichen und auch andere Indikatoren als die Notenbankgeldmenge bercksichtigen, falls sie berzeugt ist, damit das Ziel der Preisstabilitt besser zu erreichen oder falls andere triftige Grnde dafr sprechen. Ein wichtiger Unterschied zwischen beiden Strategien liegt aber darin, dass sich eine Notenbank bei einer Geldmengenstrategie neben der Erreichung der Preisstabilitt auch auf einen operationellen Rahmen fr die Zielerreichung festlegt. Das Festlegen auf einen operationellen Rahmen - also die Formulierung einer Zielgrsse fr ein monetres Aggregat - hat unserer Ansicht nach eine positive Wirkung auf die Glaubwrdigkeit. Die Marktteilnehmer erhalten damit die Mglichkeit, die Politik der Notenbank in einem frhen Stadium zu beurteilen, bevor deren Wirkung auf die Inflation sichtbar wird. Zusammenfassend knnen wir feststellen, dass die Unterschiede zwischen der Geldmengensteuerung der Schweizerischen Nationalbank und einer Inflationszielstrategie relativ klein sind. Unsere flexible Geldmengenstrategie umfasst wesentliche Elemente einer Inflationszielstrategie. Wir legen aber weiterhin einen grossen Wert auf die Geldmengenentwicklung, da der dadurch festgelegte operationelle Rahmen zur Glaubwrdigkeit der Nationalbank beitragen kann. Ein bergang zu einer reinen Inflationzielstrategie wrde fr uns nur dann in Frage kommen, wenn der Zusammenhang zwischen der Geldmengenentwicklung und dem Preisniveau vllig zusammenbrechen wrde. 15 5. Unsere aktuelle Geldpolitik Nun noch einige Bemerkungen zu unserer aktuellen Geldpolitik. Als Folge der erwhnten Strungen bei der Nachfrage nach Notenbankgeld in den letzten beiden Jahren waren wir gezwungen, von unserer flexiblen geldpolitischen Strategie Gebrauch zu machen und neben der Notenbankgeldmenge fr unsere geldpolitischen Entscheidungen vermehrt zustzliche Indikatoren zu Hilfe zu nehmen. Fr uns spielt zur Zeit die Geldmenge M3 als zustzlicher geldpolitischer Indikator eine wichtige Rolle. Dieses Aggregat besitzt in der langen Frist einen engen Zusammenhang zur Preisentwicklung und ist in der kurzen Frist weniger zinsempfindlich als die engeren Aggregate M1 und M2. In der kurzen Frist mssen jedoch die Entwicklung von M3 und des Preisniveaus nicht unbedingt parallel verlaufen. Wir beobachten daher auch andere aussagekrftige Indikatoren wie den Wechselkurs, die Diskrepanz zwischen tatschlicher und potentieller Produktion und die verschiedenen Zinsstze. Als Folge der vermehrten Bercksichtigung von zustzlichen Indikatoren publizieren wir seit Beginn dieses Jahres quartalsweise sogenannte "Geldpolitische Schlussfolgerungen", in denen wir den Marktteilnehmern unsere Einschtzung des monetren Umfeldes darlegen und unsere geldpolitischen Absichten fr das kommende Quartal formulieren. Dies erhht die Transparenz unserer geldpolitischen Entscheide und ermglicht es damit dem Publikum, sich ein gutes Bild der geldpolitischen Lage zu machen. Im Moment fhren wir eine relativ expansive Geldpolitik, was sich in tiefen Geld- und Kapitalmarktzinsen ausdrckt. Damit wollen wir den begonnenen Aufschwung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft weiterhin untersttzen. Unserer Indikatoren deuten darauf hin, dass wir dadurch kein Inflationspotential aufbauen: Einerseits ist das Wachstum der grossen Geldaggregate nicht bermssig stark und andererseits ist die Wirtschaftsproduktion immer noch von ihrem Potential entfernt. Wir beobachten jedoch die Entwicklungen genau, um frhzeitig dem Markt Liquiditt zu entziehen, falls sich eine Erhhung der Inflation abzeichnen wrde. Wir verfolgen auch die Krisen in Asien, Russland und Lateinamerika sowie die Brsenentwicklung aufmerksam. Die Nationalbank kann weder diese Krisen lsen noch die 16 Brsenkurse stabilisieren. Sie muss aber die Wirkungen dieser Turbulenzen auf Produktion und Preise in der Schweiz abschtzen und auf deflatorische oder inflatorische Entwicklungen durch entsprechende geldpolitische Massnahmen reagieren. Die Schweiz kann berdies im Rahmen des Internationalen Whrungsfonds mithelfen, regionale Krisen zu lsen. Ich betone aber nochmals, dass die Lsung in erster Linie von den betroffenen Lndern selber kommen muss. In der Schweiz kann die Nationalbank mit einem stabilen monetren Umfeld dazu beitragen, dass die Systemrisiken fr Fehlentwicklungen in den Aktien- und Finanzmrkten mglichst gering sind. 5. Schlussbemerkungen Ich komme zum Schluss meiner Ausfhrungen und mchte die Hauptaussagen meines Vortrages noch einmal hervorheben: n Nach einer langen Rezession ist die Schweiz wieder in eine Phase des wenn auch wohl vorerst bescheidenen Wachstums eingetreten. Um den Aufschwung fortzusetzen, bedarf es weiterer Anstrengungen bei der Verbesserung der Rahmenbedingungen. Die Nationalbank untersttzt den Aufschwung, solange dadurch kein Inflationspotential aufgebaut wird. n Die fundamentale Ausrichtung der Geldpolitik auf die Erhaltung der Preisstabilitt stellt den grssten Beitrag der Nationalbank zu einer ausgewogenen gesamtwirtschaftlichen Entwicklung dar. Eine verfassungsmssig abgesicherte Unabhngigkeit, verbunden mit einem klaren Auftrag, bietet die grsste Gewhr, dass die Nationalbank langfristig im Gesamtinteresse des Landes Preisstabilitt aufrechterhalten kann. n Unsere flexible Geldmengenstrategie hat viele Gemeinsamkeiten mit einer Inflationszielstrategie. Sie hat aber den Vorteil, dass sie auch den operationellen Rahmen der Geldpolitik festlegt und somit die Glaubwrdigkeit der Nationalbank erhhen kann. Die Strategie ist gengend flexibel, um in der kurzen Frist adquat auf Strungen zu reagieren. n Beim bergang zur Europischen Whrungsunion rechnen wir mit einem stabilen Euro. Die Schweizerische Nationalbank wird deshalb ihre autonome Geldpolitik mit 17 dem vorrangigen Ziel der Preisstabilitt fortsetzen. Einer bermssigen Aufwertung des Frankens wrden wir mit den uns zur Verfgung stehenden Mitteln entgegentreten. 18

Title: The construction industry in the overall economy
text: The construction industry in the overall economy Dr. Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Plenary Assembly of the Swiss Construction Industry Conference Bern, 12.11.1998 2 In the nineties, our construction industry fell into a deep crisis. Construction activity did not collapse as much as after the oil crisis in the seventies. On the other hand, the recessive tendencies lasted unusually long. Since the end of last year, there have been slight signs of recovery. However, it is not yet possible to speak of a clear trend reversal. Even today, one and a half years after the onset of the economic upswing, the construction sector is providing little impetus. This means that an important driving force for the overall economic development is missing. In my speech, I would like to address the causes of this intractable crisis. First of all, I will make a few comments on the importance of the construction sector. In a second part, I come to the development of this sector in the boom of the late eighties, where today's problems are rooted to a large extent. Later came structural changes in the economy and the environment, which exacerbated the difficulties of the construction industry. This will be the subject of the third part. In a fourth part, I would like to raise the question of what lessons can be learned from the crisis and how monetary policy can improve the framework conditions for the construction industry. Finally, I will try to give an outlook on the future of the construction industry. 1. The construction sector as a key sector The great interest in the well-being of the construction industry is no coincidence, as it is the most important of the domestically oriented industries and thus a key sector of the Swiss economy. The share of total construction activity in gross domestic product has averaged around 13% in recent years. During the late eighties it reached 16% at times. As a result, the construction sector in Switzerland was also above average by international standards. The proportion of employees in the construction industry reflects their importance: At the beginning of the nineties, more than 11% of the full-time employees were employed in the main construction and finishing industries. If you include the industries, 3 which provide direct inputs for the construction, then the share was almost 20%. Due to its interdependence with other sectors, construction activity also has a strong multiplier effect: construction investments lead to follow-up orders, for example in horticulture, the furniture industry or the textile industry. The situation of the construction industry thus spreads to the entire national economy. Apart from its large share of value creation, construction also influences our economic performance. Together with investment in equipment, investment in construction forms the capital stock of our economy. A good half of the investments made annually are construction investments. They are therefore an important factor for the production of goods and services. The capital stock of an economy is built up through investment. Only a small part of it is replaced per year. Thus, the capital stock influences economic activity over a long period of time. A high-quality construction capital stock  in the form of infrastructure, commercial and industrial buildings, but also residential buildings  is of great importance for the productivity of the national economy. The formation of such a capital stock requires an efficient construction industry. 2. The boom phase of the late eighties The crisis in the construction sector has its roots partly in the boom phase of the late eighties. At that time, the economy showed clear signs of overheating. Experience has shown that construction activity reacts above average to fluctuations in economic growth. The share of construction investment in GDP  the construction ratio  increased significantly during this period. At the same time, real estate prices rose to exorbitant levels. The question arises as to how this overflowing could have happened. A closer look reveals that both monetary and real influencing factors played a role. Let me first look at the monetary factors and then at some real factors. 4 At the beginning of 1986, the Swiss franc began to appreciate significantly, a trend that lasted until mid-1987. The real export-weighted Swiss franc rose by 10%, well above its long-term trend. This did not remain without consequences for the export industry. Export growth weakened sharply. At the end of 1986, real exports were well below the previous year's level and overall economic growth came to a near standstill. The SNB was faced with a dilemma. Given the strong money supply growth at the time, it should have tightened the monetary policy reins. Against the background of the strong Swiss franc and the slowing economy, however, higher interest rates seemed undesirable, even dangerous. Added to this was the stock market crash in the autumn of 1987, which startled the world. The central banks of the industrialised countries, including the National Bank, generously supplied the economy with liquidity, as they had to reckon with a recession in view of the massive price losses. In our case, a further boost in appreciation also spoke in favour of an easing of monetary policy. In retrospect, the monetary policy stance was too loose from 1986 to 1988. This is not altered by the fact that in 1988 the changes in the institutional framework  in particular the revision of the banks' liquidity requirements  made it very difficult to assess the degree of monetary restrictions. The overly favourable monetary conditions initially benefited the economy. Together with the sudden strengthening of export demand, they formed the basis for the rapid economic upswing. On the other hand, they created the basis for the signs of overheating that were soon to be visible everywhere. Gross domestic product grew by more than 3% per year in real terms between 1988 and 1990. At over 7% in 1988 and 1989, real construction investment increased more than twice as much. However, the monetary environment was not solely responsible for the construction boom. Demographic developments and the development of incomes  two equally important determinants of construction demand  further fuelled it. The rapidly growing economy called for additional workers. Towards the end of the eighties, the immigration of foreign workers and their families increased significantly. Population growth increased the demand for 5 Housing. At the same time, household incomes, which grew with rising employment, stimulated consumer demand. Among other things, the demand for living space per capita also increased significantly. The creation of jobs also increased the demand for commercial-industrial space. Construction activity in this sector was most strongly influenced by the boom. It expanded annually at double-digit rates at the end of the eighties. The pronounced excess demand in the real estate sector triggered the price explosion that I hardly need to remind you of. In the Canton of Zurich, prices per square metre for building land increased by around 30% per year between 1986 and 1990. Rent inflation in the same period was significantly higher than general consumer inflation. The strong reaction of real estate and rental prices was based on a sector-specific peculiarity  namely the short-term inelastic supply. The supply of new buildings reacts to changes in demand only with a strong delay. The reason for this lies first in the long planning and approval phases for construction projects, but then also in the actual construction period. In the case of consumer goods  and to a lesser extent also in investment in equipment  supply is reacting more quickly. Often an increased demand can also be covered by imports. In the construction sector, this is practically impossible. If one also takes into account the fact that a large part of the annual construction investments serve as a substitute for depreciation, the construction capital stock increased by only around 1.5% in 1990. In comparison, the capital stock of machinery and other equipment increased by around 15%. Despite the exorbitant price increase, the strong demand for real estate continued. This initially reflected the increase in demand as a result of demographic developments and income increases. Another reason for the continued strong demand was also the changes in the assessment of the risks of real estate. In view of rising inflation, investments in real estate seemed particularly attractive: fixed-income investments do not offer a hedge against unexpected inflation, and investments in equities do not promise a particularly good return in inflationary times. For the comparatively slow growth of rental income, the expected 6 Increases in real value on real estate. Steadily rising prices for building land and real estate became a matter of course. Since the soil factor was particularly scarce in Switzerland, no one expected prices to collapse. Real estate was thus regarded as practically risk-free investments. This gave demand a strong speculative element: it reflected not only the need of households and companies for housing and commercial space, but also the demand of investors for the asset real estate. The  supposedly  low risk combined with high returns drove prices even higher. The banks shared the market's assessment. Financing construction projects with bank loans became easier. The optimistic valuation of investments in real estate led to a higher loan-to-value ratio of such properties. The share of equity required by the banks fell. The approved construction loans expanded annually by around 10% in the second half of the eighties. This expansion of the volume of loans supported demand in the construction sector. A little later, however, it had serious consequences. From the autumn of 1988, the SNB began to gradually tighten its monetary policy. The now clear signs of overheating of the economy and the associated inflationary tendencies made such a step inevitable. Interest rates rose, and the economy began to cool down significantly with a certain delay. Mirroring the upswing, the construction sector also reacted above average in the ensuing recession. The inertia of the offer led to an oversupply and to a marked price collapse on the real estate market. 3. The causes of the construction crisis The recession in the construction sector was initially a normal, unavoidable consequence of the economic slowdown. However, the scale of the crisis and the difficulties of the construction sector in finding its way out suggest that it was not only the change in the monetary environment that played a role. I would like to discuss three important structural causes in more detail below. Firstly, the changing risk behaviour of the market towards real estate, secondly, the 7 Structural change in industry and the service sector and thirdly to the changes in the regulatory environment of the construction sector. The rise in interest rates burst the speculative bubble in the real estate market. The often extremely high loan-to-value of real estate resulted in over-indebtedness for many borrowers, which in many cases forced the sale of the properties. This further exacerbated the price decline triggered by higher interest rates and led to sensitive losses for real estate dealers, entrepreneurs and, last but not least, banks. The prices for houses, apartments and offices are today between a quarter and a third lower than at the beginning of the nineties! As a result of this development, construction investment has been viewed much more cautiously for a few years now; they are now considered an investment with considerable risk. Bank lending has become correspondingly more restrained, and the loan-to-value ratio remains well below the levels of the late eighties. As project-specific risks are given greater weighting, financing conditions for companies and households have tightened in recent years despite low interest rates. In the commercial-industrial sector, a property no longer automatically serves as collateral for business loans. This fact is particularly difficult for small and medium-sized enterprises, which cannot offer other collateral. Not only the tightening of financing conditions dampened the demand for real estate. The construction industry  especially commercial-industrial construction  also felt the strong structural changes in our economy. The difficult economic situation and fierce international competition forced companies to increase their productivity. These efforts manifested themselves in various respects. In the industrial sector, production processes have been streamlined and optimized. Part of the production was relocated abroad. Warehousing is less important today than it used to be. It was replaced by more flexible, order-related production. All these developments had essentially the same effect: the demand for workshops and production facilities decreased significantly. The many industrial wastelands are a clear testimony to this development. 8 A little later than industry, the service sector was affected by structural change. It continues today, as the economic recovery has begun. The noticeable concentration process reduces the number of activities. In the retail trade, new forms of distribution are gaining in importance. The demand for retail space is increasing only slightly. Reorganizations in the banking sector lead to the closure of branches. In the financial sector, too, workflows have been  and are still being  streamlined. The associated staff reductions are reducing the demand for office space. The past few years have also brought changes in the regulatory environment. Overall, the framework conditions in the construction industry have become more competitive. In its 1994 report on Switzerland, the OECD pointed to the excessive construction costs in our country. They result from the combination of high price and wage levels and low productivity. A major reason for the relatively low productivity of many domestically oriented industries compared to the export sector is weak competitive pressure. In the construction industry, the proliferation of regulations over the years favoured weak competition. In the course of the deregulation and revitalization of Switzerland as a business location, however, some of the provisions that contributed to the isolation from competition have recently disappeared. The Internal Market Act and the revision of the Antitrust Act force more competitive behaviour. Price fixing and cartel practices are assessed more rigorously by the Cartel Commission. Standards and regulations that protected local suppliers from non-resident competitors were abolished under the Internal Market Act. Likewise, the submission system of the public sector has been made closer to the market due to adjustments to the requirements of international agreements in the field of trade. The revision of Lex Friedrich is also of essential importance for the development of more market. Prior to their revision, foreigners were only able to acquire land or real estate in Switzerland to a very limited extent. This made it impossible for foreign general contractors to carry out large-scale projects in Switzerland, as they would have had to be the owners of the country. With the revision, these restrictions were at least partially lifted. 9 At the same time, the easing meant that part of the lack of domestic demand for office and commercial space can be compensated for by the demand of foreign companies. More intense competition requires construction companies to increase productivity. Overcapacities, which could be maintained for a long time due to high construction prices, must be reduced. This necessary reduction in capacities has so far been slow. The measures taken by the public sector to stimulate the economy are likely to have had an unintended effect on preserving the structure. In the spring of 1993, Parliament adopted an economic recovery programme. Two thirds of the approved funds of around CHF 300 million were allocated to the so-called investment bonus, which was used to financially support public construction projects. One third went to the promotion of housing construction. Due to the strong multiplier effect of construction activity, the programme was expected to have a lasting effect on the economy as a whole. The construction industry actually experienced an upswing in 1994. Housing construction reacted particularly strongly to the programme  the number of newly built apartments increased by more than 30% in 1994 compared to the previous year and increased again by around 9% in 1995. In the case of public construction, the impact was somewhat less pronounced. However, the upswing was short-lived. Already in 1995, construction activity as a whole was declining again. The large number of newly built apartments increased the existing oversupply. 4. Lessons from the crisis  Contribution of monetary policy to improving the framework conditions in the construction sector What lessons can we learn from the developments of the eighties and nineties? I believe that the experience of the late eighties clearly underlines the importance of an appropriate monetary environment, or the preservation of price stability. In all industrialised countries, price stability  synonymous with a low inflation rate  is now regarded as the most important objective of monetary policy. The SNB also focuses on maintaining price stability. The reason for this 10 Prioritization is the costs of inflation. Inflation leads to an arbitrary redistribution between different groups within society  between creditors and debtors, employees and employers, but also between taxpayers and the public sector. Inflation forces prices to be adjusted on an ongoing basis, which is not only costly, but also carries the risk of incorrect adjustments. Finally, the precautions taken by households and businesses to protect their assets from inflation tie up time and resources. They lead to the dangerous price distortions already mentioned in certain markets  especially in the real estate market. At the same time, they are driving up nominal and real interest rates. Creditors want to be compensated for the expected inflation-related loss of purchasing power. They demand a corresponding inflation premium on the return on their investments and, if necessary, an additional premium for the future inflation risk. If inflation is difficult to predict, this risk premium increases. Empirical studies show that the level and volatility of the inflation rate are positively correlated. In other words, when inflation is high, uncertainty about future price developments increases; the risk premium is increasing. Low, constant inflation rates, on the other hand, simplify the formation of expectations and lower risk premiums for unforeseen inflation. Thus, a monetary policy geared to price stability contributes to a low level and a stabilization of long-term interest rates. Predictable, favorable financing conditions are undeniable advantages both for investors and for the construction industry as the creator of capital goods. Experience in Switzerland has shown that the population is aware of the benefits of price stability or, in other words, the costs of inflation. This includes the insight that inflation cannot generate lasting employment gains. Once households and businesses have included higher inflation in their calculations, its stimulating effect on economic growth will fizzle out. Applied to the construction industry, this means that an inflationary boom is not worthwhile in the long term. What is built in such a phase due to hasty investment decisions has long weighed on the market as a pressing oversupply. Given the dominant importance of the 11 Banks are also regularly involved in the vortex when financing construction projects. Both are responsible for the fact that the damage of speculative exaggerations is felt for a long time and the recovery phase is lengthy. This explains to a large extent why the fight against inflation inevitably entails considerable costs in the form of low economic growth and unemployment. A central bank would therefore do well to prevent the emergence of an inflation potential. A major difficulty, however, is to recognize the risk of inflation at an early stage. As is well known, two to three years pass between monetary policy measures and their effect on prices in Switzerland. We must therefore recognise the danger of future inflation at a time when everything still seems to be in perfect order. This is not easy, especially in an open economy such as the Swiss economy, which is also heavily dependent on economic developments abroad and in which exchange rate fluctuations can be a major burden. In the mid-eighties, we had underestimated the risk of inflation. But we have learned lessons from this. In order to assess the long-term risk of inflation, monetary aggregates continue to perform a useful function in Switzerland. In the shorter and medium term, however, further indicators must be used. Among other things, an in-depth analysis of price developments in the various sectors and at various stages of the economy helps to identify signs of inflationary pressure from the outset. In this context, the question arises as to how much the SNB should take into account the prices of assets, including in particular real estate prices, in its analysis. The experience of the eighties suggests that price developments on the real estate market in particular could be a leading indicator of a future risk of inflation. In Switzerland, inflation is measured by the national consumer price index. This shows the price development of the average basket of goods of consumers and thus measures the purchasing power of households. When analysing price developments, the first step is to 12 take into account that the consumer price index may not adequately reflect the prevailing inflationary pressure in the economy. On the one hand, it is strongly influenced by the prices of foreign goods  for example, oil prices. Abstracting from the price development of foreign goods, it is important to keep in mind that a considerable proportion of the prices of domestic goods and services only adapt to the prevailing market conditions with a considerable delay. This applies above all to the most important component of the domestic basket of goods  namely apartment rents. With a share of a good 20%, these have a strong influence on the course of inflation. To a large extent, however, they do not represent market prices, but adapt to changing demand conditions only late and often only incompletely due to tenant protection legislation. This can lead to dangerous misjudgements of the prevailing pressure on inflation. The development of consumer prices is even less suitable for assessing future inflation. As already mentioned, this must be based on a large number of indicators that are as forward-looking as possible. This also includes the prices of real estate. While the official rent index is slow to reflect rising or falling demand pressures, a sharp change in demand for housing is having a rapid impact on property prices. The price development on the real estate market therefore helps to assess the future course of rents and thus also of general inflation. However, the prices of investments also provide useful information for monetary policy because they indirectly influence price developments on the goods and services markets. Rising prices for investments mean an increase in assets. Less is saved as households feel richer and increase consumption. Since certain assets, especially real estate, serve as collateral for loans, the loan volume of an economy also tends to increase as assets increase. Conversely, a price collapse on the stock or real estate markets reduces wealth and thus dampens domestic demand. In Switzerland, the wealth effect on equities is likely to be small, as share ownership is still not very broadly diversified. It is likely to play a greater role in real estate. The development of real estate prices can thus indicate imminent 13 Overheating or recession risks and thus also on the future development of inflation. 5. A look into the future The economic development in Switzerland today gives rise to cautious optimism. This is despite the major economic difficulties in Asia and Eastern Europe and the price corrections on the financial markets in recent months. It is optimistic that domestic demand in Europe will continue to gain momentum. This also applies to our country. The easing of monetary policy, which began in early 1995, initiated the recovery of domestic demand at the beginning of 1997 with the usual delay. The gradual improvement in the situation on the labour market strengthened consumer confidence. In the meantime, wages are rising again, which, together with increasing employment, has a positive effect on the overall development of income and purchasing power. Thanks to the improved earnings situation and low interest rates, investment activity also began to regain its footing. In the construction industry, the multi-year decline came to a halt last year, and a modest recovery began. It can be expected that construction activity will continue to revive in the coming years and that the construction quota will increase again somewhat. But there is no going back to the values reached in the unhealthy boom of the late eighties. The changed  and more realistic  risk assessment of investments in real estate, the ongoing structural change in the economy and, finally, demographic developments will keep demand for construction services within limits. For a long time, the construction rate in Switzerland was significantly higher than in the other European countries. In the meantime, it has fallen below the long-term average and is even lower than in some European countries. In the future, it is likely to operate within an internationally comparable framework. Structural changes are still to be expected within the construction industry. Due to the relatively high average age of our capital stock, conversions and renovations will gain in importance in the future in favor of new construction. The share of these sectors in total construction activity has increased between 14 In 1990 and 1996 already increased significantly  from 24% to 37%. This development particularly affects residential construction and commercial-industrial construction. In civil engineering, demand will be shaped by major infrastructure projects in connection with the NEAT and Bahn 2000. Contractors will not be unemployed in the next few years. However, they need to adapt even more to changing demand. In view of more intense competition, they will have to further increase their productivity and reduce the overcapacity that still exists. Today, the monetary framework conditions are a good prerequisite for the recovery of the construction industry and the shift towards a long-term sustainable growth trend. Price stability has prevailed for three years and the outlook for inflation is favourable. This is an important reason why interest rates are low and a favourable interest rate environment can still be expected. The SNB's task is to continue to ensure appropriate monetary conditions in the future. To this end, it must ensure that the high degree of price stability is maintained. In this way, it creates optimal conditions for investment activity within the scope of its possibilities and thus contributes to a balanced development of the construction industry.

Ich meine, dass die Erfahrungen der spten achtziger Jahre klar die Bedeutung eines angemessenen monetren Umfeldes, bzw. der Bewahrung der Preisstabilitt, unterstreichen. In allen Industrielndern wird heute Preisstabilitt  gleichbedeutend mit einer tiefen Inflationsrate  als wichtigstes Ziel der Geldpolitik betrachtet. Teuerung fhrt zu einer willkrlichen Umverteilung zwischen verschiedenen Gruppen innerhalb der Gesellschaft  zwischen Glubigern und Schuldnern, Angestellten und Arbeitgebern, aber auch zwischen Steuerzahlern und der ffentlichen Hand. Teuerung zwingt zur laufenden Anpassung der Preise, was nicht nur kostspielig ist, sondern auch die Gefahr von fehlerhaften Anpassungen birgt. Schliesslich binden die von den Haushalten und Unternehmen gettigten Vorkehrungen, um ihr Vermgen vor Inflation zu schtzen, Zeit und Ressourcen. Sie fhren auf gewissen Mrkten  insbesondere auf dem Immobilienmarkt  zu den bereits erwhnten gefhrlichen Preisverzerrungen. Gleichzeitig treiben sie die nominellen und realen Zinsstze in die Hhe. Glubiger wollen fr den erwarteten inflationsbedingten Verlust an Kaufkraft entschdigt werden. Sie verlangen auf der Rendite ihrer Anlagen eine entsprechende Inflationsprmie und allenfalls eine Zusatzprmie fr das knftige Inflationsrisiko. Ist die Teuerung schwierig zu prognostizieren, steigt diese Risikoprmie. Empirische Untersuchungen zeigen, dass Hhe und Volatilitt der Teuerungsrate positiv korreliert sind. Bei hoher Inflation steigt mit anderen Worten die Unsicherheit bezglich der zuknftigen Preisentwicklung; die Risikoprmie nimmt zu. Tiefe, konstante Teuerungsraten vereinfachen dagegen die Erwartungsbildung und senken die Risikoprmien fr unvorhergesehene Inflation. Damit trgt eine auf Preisstabilitt ausgerichtete Geldpolitik zu einem tiefen Niveau und einer Verstetigung der langfristigen Zinsstze bei. Abschtzbare, gnstige Finanzierungsbedingungen sind sowohl fr die Investoren wie auch fr die Bauwirtschaft als Erstellerin der Kapitalgter von unbestreitbarem Vorteil. Die Erfahrungen in der Schweiz haben gezeigt, dass sich die Bevlkerung ber den Nutzen der Preisstabilitt oder  anders ausgedrckt  ber die Kosten der Inflation im Klaren ist. Dies schliesst die Einsicht ein, dass sich mit Inflation keine dauernden Beschftigungsgewinne erzielen lassen. Haben die Haushalte und die Unternehmen die hhere Inflation einmal in ihr Kalkl einbezogen, verpufft deren stimulierende Wirkung auf das Wirtschaftswachstum. Auf die Bauwirtschaft bertragen heisst dies, dass sich ein inflationrer Boom langfristig nicht lohnt. Was in einer solchen Phase aufgrund bereilter Investitionsentscheidungen gebaut wird, lastet auf dem Markt lange als drckendes berangebot. Angesichts der dominierenden Bedeutung der 11 Banken bei der Finanzierung von Bauvorhaben werden auch sie regelmssig in den Strudel miteinbezogen. Beides ist dafr verantwortlich, dass die Schden spekulativer bertreibungen lange Zeit sprbar sind und die Genesungsphase langwierig ist. Dies erklrt zu einem guten Teil, weshalb die Teuerungsbekmpfung unweigerlich mit erheblichen Kosten in Form von geringem Wirtschaftswachstum und Arbeitslosigkeit verbunden ist. Eine Notenbank tut deshalb gut daran, die Entstehung eines Inflationspotentials zu verhindern. Eine Hauptschwierigkeit besteht dabei allerdings darin, die Teuerungsgefahr frhzeitig zu erkennen. Zwischen geldpolitischen Massnahmen und ihrer Wirkung auf die Preise vergehen in der Schweiz bekanntlich zwei bis drei Jahre. Wir mssen deshalb die Gefahr einer zuknftigen Teuerung zu einem Zeitpunkt erkennen, in dem noch alles in bester Ordnung zu sein scheint. Dies ist gerade in einer offenen Volkswirtschaft wie der schweizerischen, die stark auch von der Konjunkturentwicklung im Ausland abhngt und in der Wechselkursfluktuationen eine grosse Belastung darstellen knnen, nicht einfach. Mitte der achtziger Jahren hatten wir die Teuerungsgefahr unterschtzt. Wir haben aber daraus Lehren gezogen. Um die langfristige Teuerungsgefahr abzuschtzen, erfllen in der Schweiz die Geldaggregate nach wie vor eine ntzliche Funktion. In der krzeren und mittleren Frist mssen aber weitere Indikatoren herangezogen werden. Unter anderem trgt eine vertiefte Analyse der Preisentwicklung in den verschiedenen Sektoren und auf verschiedenen Stufen der Wirtschaft dazu bei, Anzeichen eines Teuerungsdruckes bereits in den Anfngen zu erkennen. In diesem Zusammenhang stellt sich die Frage, wie stark die Nationalbank die Preise von Vermgensanlagen, darunter insbesondere die Immobilienpreise, in ihrer Analyse mitbercksichtigen soll. Die Erfahrung der achtziger Jahre deutet darauf hin, dass gerade die Preisentwicklung am Immobilienmarkt ein Frhindikator fr eine knftige Teuerungsgefahr sein knnte. In der Schweiz wird die Teuerung anhand des Landesindexes der Konsumentenpreise gemessen. Dieser zeigt die Preisentwicklung des durchschnittlichen Gterkorbes der Konsumenten und misst damit die Kaufkraft der Haushalte. Bei der Analyse der Preisentwicklung gilt es zunchst zu 12 bercksichtigen, dass der Konsumentenpreisindex den herrschenden Teuerungsdruck in der Wirtschaft unter Umstnden nicht adquat wiedergibt. Einmal wird er stark von den Preisen auslndischer Gter  zum Beispiel den Erdlpreisen  beeinflusst. Abstrahiert man von der Preisentwicklung der auslndischen Gter, so gilt es weiter im Auge zu behalten, dass sich ein betrchtlicher Teil der Preise inlndischer Gter und Dienstleistungen erst mit erheblicher Verzgerung an die herrschenden Marktverhltnisse anpasst. Dies gilt vor allem fr die wichtigste Komponente des inlndischen Gterkorbes  nmlich die Wohnungsmieten. Mit einem Anteil von gut 20% prgen diese den Teuerungsverlauf zwar stark. Sie stellen aber zu einem grossen Teil keine Marktpreise dar, sondern passen sich aufgrund der Mieterschutzgesetzgebung erst spt und oft nur unvollstndig an vernderte Nachfragebedingungen an. Dies kann zu gefhrlichen Fehleinschtzungen des herrschenden Teuerungsdruckes fhren. Noch weniger taugt die Entwicklung der Konsumentenpreise zur Beurteilung der knftigen Teuerung. Wie bereits erwhnt, muss hierzu auf eine Vielzahl mglichst zukunftsweisender Indikatoren abgestellt werden. Dazu gehren auch die Preise von Immobilien. Whrend der offizielle Mietpreisindex einen steigenden oder fallenden Nachfragedruck nur langsam zum Ausdruck kommen lsst, wirkt sich eine starke Vernderung der Nachfrage nach Wohnraum rasch auf die Immobilienpreise aus. Die Preisentwicklung am Immobilienmarkt hilft daher, den knftigen Verlauf der Mieten und damit auch der generellen Teuerung einzuschtzen. Die Preise von Vermgensanlagen geben fr die Geldpolitik aber auch deshalb ntzliche Hinweise, weil sie indirekt die Preisentwicklung auf den Gter- und Dienstleistungsmrkten beeinflussen. Steigende Preise fr Vermgensanlagen bedeuten eine Erhhung des Vermgens. Es wird weniger gespart, da sich die Haushalte reicher fhlen und den Konsum steigern. Da gewisse Vermgenswerte, insbesondere Immobilien, als Sicherheiten fr Kredite dienen, nimmt bei steigenden Vermgenswerten auch das Kreditvolumen einer Volkswirtschaft tendenziell zu. Umgekehrt vermindert ein Preiszerfall auf den Aktien- oder Immobilienmrkten das Vermgen und dmpft damit die inlndische Nachfrage. In der Schweiz drfte der Vermgenseffekt bei den Aktien gering sein, da der Aktienbesitz immer noch wenig breit gestreut ist. Bei den Immobilien drfte er eine grssere Rolle spielen. Die Entwicklung der Immobilienpreise kann damit Hinweise auf bevorstehende 13 berhitzungs- oder Rezessionsgefahren und damit auch auf die knftige Teuerungsentwicklung geben. 5. Ein Blick in die Zukunft Die konjunkturelle Entwicklung in der Schweiz gibt heute Anlass zu einem vorsichtigen Optimismus. Dies trotz der grossen wirtschaftlichen Schwierigkeiten in Asien und Osteuropa und der in den letzten Monaten erfolgten Kurskorrekturen an den Finanzmrkten. Optimistisch stimmt, dass die Binnennachfrage in Europa weiter Tritt fasst. Dies gilt auch fr unser Land. Die Lockerung der Geldpolitik, die Anfang 1995 einsetzte, leitete Anfang 1997 mit der blichen Verzgerung die Erholung der Binnennachfrage ein. Die allmhliche Verbesserung der Lage am Arbeitsmarkt strkte das Vertrauen der Konsumenten. Inzwischen sind die Lhne wieder im Steigen begriffen, was sich zusammen mit der zunehmenden Beschftigung auf die gesamtwirtschaftliche Einkommens- und Kaufkraftentwicklung positiv auswirkt. Dank der verbesserten Ertragslage und der tiefen Zinsstze begann auch die Investitionsttigkeit wieder Tritt zu fassen. In der Bauwirtschaft kam der mehrjhrige Rckgang im letzten Jahr zum Stillstand, und eine bescheidene Erholung setzte ein. Es kann damit gerechnet werden, dass sich die Bauttigkeit in den nchsten Jahren weiter beleben und dass damit die Bauquote wieder etwas zunehmen wird. Es gibt aber kein zurck zu den Werten, die im ungesunden Boom der spten achtziger Jahre erreicht wurden. Die vernderte  und realistischere  Risikoeinschtzung bezglich Anlagen in Immobilien, der anhaltende Strukturwandel der Wirtschaft sowie schliesslich die demographische Entwicklung werden die Nachfrage nach Bauleistungen in Grenzen halten. Die Bauquote war in der Schweiz lange Zeit markant hher als in den anderen europischen Lndern. Inzwischen ist sie unter das langfristige Mittel gesunken und liegt sogar tiefer als in einigen europischen Lndern. Sie drfte sich knftig in einem international vergleichbaren Rahmen bewegen. Innerhalb der Baubranche ist weiterhin mit strukturellen nderungen zu rechnen. Aufgrund des relativ hohen Durchschnittsalters unseres Kapitalstockes werden Umbau und Renovationen in Zukunft zugunsten des Neubaus an Bedeutung gewinnen. Der Anteil dieser Sparten an der gesamten Bauttigkeit hat zwischen 14 1990 und 1996 bereits markant  von 24% auf 37%  zugenommen. Diese Entwicklung betrifft besonders den Wohnungsbau und den gewerblich-industriellen Bau. Im Tiefbau werden grosse Infrastrukturvorhaben im Zusammenhang mit der NEAT und der Bahn 2000 die Nachfrage prgen. Die Bauunternehmer werden in den nchsten Jahren nicht arbeitslos sein. Sie mssen sich jedoch noch strker an die vernderte Nachfrage anpassen. Im Hinblick auf den intensiveren Wettbewerb werden sie ihre Produktivitt weiter steigern und die nach wie vor bestehenden berkapazitten abbauen mssen. Die monetren Rahmenbedingungen bilden heute eine gute Voraussetzung fr die Erholung der Bauwirtschaft und das Einschwenken auf einen langfristig tragbaren Wachstumstrend. Seit drei Jahren herrscht Preisstabilitt, und die Teuerungsaussichten sind gnstig. Dies ist ein wichtiger Grund dafr, dass die Zinsstze tief sind und weiterhin mit einem gnstigen Zinsumfeld gerechnet werden kann. Die Aufgabe der Nationalbank besteht darin, auch knftig fr angemessene monetre Rahmenbedingungen zu sorgen. Sie muss zu diesem Zwecke sicherstellen, dass der hohe Grad an Preisstabilitt erhalten bleibt. Damit schafft sie im Rahmen ihrer Mglichkeiten optimale Voraussetzungen fr die Investitionsttigkeit und trgt so zu einer ausgewogenen Entwicklung der Bauwirtschaft bei.

Title: Swiss franc: European currency
text: Swiss franc: European currency Message from Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank on the occasion of the 20th anniversary of the Jean Monnet Foundation for Europe Dorigny, 20 November 1998 2 At the beginning of next year, the European continent will experience a real revolution. This revolution, like any shock of this nature, will trigger waves whose consequences we do not yet appreciate. The mosaic of national currencies that we have always known will be followed by the homogeneous whole of the euro. After centuries of asserting monetary power at regional level, the single European currency will replace national currency symbols. The euro will crown and cement the achievements of post-war economic integration and become the symbol of the community with a shared future for Europeans. The present generation, that of the workers of the last hour, must pay tribute here to the visionaries, to the precursors, to those who, horrified by the battlefields of the First and then of the Second World War, set themselves the ambition of building ever wider and stronger bridges between the european peoples, so often in conflict. Jean Monnet played a prominent role in this regard. The single currency will represent that solidarity, that sense of common interest that he so hoped he would see triumph on our continent. As we know, Switzerland stands on the sidelines of the integration process. It has not followed the same path as the countries around us. Even today, she feels comfortable only on the steep paths of her mountains, observing from a distance the great maneuvers that take place in the plains. The analysis would be too quick to say that our current isolation is a mere reflection of an inability to share the ideals of our neighbours by seeking only our short-term interests. If it is thus isolated, it is because our country has sought, in the ravaged Europe of the 20th century, to protect its identity and independence, to avoid the battlefields. Could he do anything other than take the steep paths while the major European roads were ravaged by bloody conflicts? This solitary march has also left its mark on our monetary regime. The Swiss franc has had a different history than the currencies around us. The franc has become an extraordinary symbol of historical continuity and independence: are we not the only country in Europe whose coins have remained virtually unchanged since their introduction in the 19th century? 3 Isn't the autonomy of our action reflected in the sometimes excessive rate of the franc on the markets? Originally, however, the Swiss authorities could not imagine that the currency of this small country could have had a destiny other than European. Indeed, when the Swiss franc was created in 1850, our Parliament decided to introduce on our soil the French monetary regime, which was thought to serve as a catalyst for the continental monetary regime. A new step in this direction was taken in 1865 by the conclusion by the France, Belgium, Italy and Switzerland of the Treaty establishing the Latin Monetary Union, a union which provided for the standardization of the monetary regimes of its participants. The preamble to the Treaty stated that "the Swiss Confederation, His Majesty the King of the Belgians, His Majesty the Emperor of the French and His Majesty the King of Italy, also motivated by the desire to establish greater harmony between their monetary legislation, to remedy the inconveniences resulting [...] of the diversity [...] of their currencies ... and to contribute [...] to the progress of the standardization of weights, measures and currencies, have resolved to conclude a convention to that effect'. This first attempt at monetary unification of our continent did not withstand the political and financial turmoil. The union faltered very quickly and became practically inoperative by the Franco-German War of 1870. Political rivalries led to monetary disorder. More than 130 years have passed since the creation of the Latin Monetary Union. European countries are once again ready to unite their monetary destiny. Even though today's world is more complex than that of the 19th century, the chances of their business encountering failure are limited because their preparation for monetary fusion has been very careful. By applying strict stability criteria, their economies have been placed in a phase of macroeconomic convergence and the Maastricht Treaty has given the European Central Bank the powers and autonomy necessary for sound monetary management. In addition, Europeans have the ambition to gradually strengthen their political ties, which should include the common currency in a coherent whole. 4 1. The stakes for the European economy As I said in the introduction, the single currency will represent a revolution for Europe. It will affect the functioning of its economy at all levels, at the level of citizens, by the disappearance of national monetary signs, at the level of companies, which will operate in a new environment of stability, at the level of the Authorities, finally, since the management of affairs will become common in an area of traditionally national competences. For the citizens, however, nothing spectacular will happen on 1 January 1999. Of course, savers will be offered banking products denominated in euros or will be able to subscribe for securities in this currency, but the substitution of traditional means of payment will not take place until three years later, when the denominations and national coins are replaced by European monetary signs. Even if francs or marks will still circulate in the coming years, citizens will still benefit from the advantages of introducing the euro at company level from the outset. Indeed, for European businesses, the euro will be an extraordinary source of simplification and transparency. The multiplicity of prices denominated in different currencies - more or less stable between them - will be followed by the uniqueness of prices in euros and the absence of exchange rate risk. The instrument of the single currency will then become a whip in the service of competition. The borders of national markets will disappear in favour of new borders, this time European. Consumers and businesses will thus have access to a market of nearly 300 million inhabitants, which is larger and more competitive than the one they have experienced so far. For businesses, the euro revolution will not only be one of increased transparency and competition, but also of the creation of a vast market for financial resources denominated in euros. The European financial market, which is still highly compartmentalised today, will become a financial market with American dimensions where capital will circulate freely, without obstacles due to exchange rate risks. From Lisbon to Helsinki, the conditions of credit will be the same, the markets will be open to the investment and borrowing of everyone. This is to be expected to increase the effectiveness of the 5 Vestments, an optimization of localization decisions and, over time, the emergence of pan-European companies that we will no longer know if they are French or German, especially since they will, unfortunately for us, have an increasing tendency to communicate in English. With the single currency, the "large European market" that the European Union has been developing since the 1980s will thus take on its full dimension, it will not only be the place where goods, services and factors of production will circulate freely, but it will also be a framework for the efficient allocation of resources. The complete disappearance of national barriers will obviously pose an extraordinary challenge to the European authorities in charge of economic policy. 2. What is at stake for European monetary policy The European Central Bank (ECB) embodies this challenge. On the first of January next year, the ECB will have sole responsibility for defining the course of European monetary policy; the Bank of France, the Bundesbank and the central banks of the other countries of the Monetary Union will join the ranks or, more precisely, integrate into the European System of Central Banks. The transfer of monetary competence to the ECB is certainly the most important act since until now the right to mint money and define the monetary regime has always been considered a privilege of national sovereignty. It is true that in our world of globalization and the necessary coordination of national policies, the effective room for manoeuvre in the monetary field is more limited than some imagine. The members of the European Union have experience of the constraints of common monetary management since they have been linked since 1979 by the rules of operation of the European Monetary System. The collective exercise of monetary responsibility will, however, take a new turn because the functioning of the EMS was strongly marked by the action of the Bundesbank. The "one man one vote" in the ECB Council will place Europe's monetary destiny in different hands than we have known so far. 6 On the other hand, we must be aware that the centralised conduct of European affairs will not be easy. Indeed, the euro will be the currency of an area where regional differences are still very much in the spotlight. It will be the currency of the Netherlands, a country with a high technological level, where the workforce is highly educated, and that of Portugal, where the development of the economy is at a less advanced stage. It will be the currency of Ireland and Finland, countries whose geopolitical situations are very far apart. It will also be the currency of Italy - with its diversities - and of Germany. Many of the regional realities that hitherto could be expressed in local financial markets will tomorrow be placed under the extraordinarily unifying effect of the common currency. The management of this contrasting set will therefore not be without difficulty. At the heart of the problem will be employment policy, what economist jargon calls the "functioning of the labour market". Two points are necessary in this context. The first is that if monetary union can lead to a gradual standardisation of prices on the European goods market, it would be dangerous for it to push for the hasty unification of wages. As productivity differences are still very large between European countries, any attempt to level wages would lead to regional losses in competitiveness that are contrary to growth and employment. Thus, the benefits of the new European monetary order could be undermined by excessive rigidity of national labour markets or by unjustified standardisation of remuneration. The "wage adventures" which in the past led to devaluations can only lead to local unemployment or emigration tomorrow. The second point relates to the necessary flexibility of economic structures in the event of regional difficulties. The size of the European monetary area may be subject to shocks that will affect only one of its regions depending on the geographical position of the latter or its type of production. Take the example of the impact on Finland of a crisis in the timber market or the effect on Ireland of a depreciation of the pound sterling, the currency of a country still outside the Union. To these local shocks, the common currency will not be able to provide any remedy. The euro is an instrument for managing the area as a whole, so regional problems will require regional responses, first of all a strong capacity 7 the adaptation of local economic structures, followed by Community financial aid under the heading of solidarity. From all this, we must draw two conclusions that reveal the European challenges of tomorrow:  the first is to stress that, beyond its technical aspects, monetary union will entail social consequences which Europeans will have to learn to manage jointly. Much will be required of the social partners to ensure the success of the enterprise. But will it be possible - in a pan-European whole - to apply more rigorously the rules of discipline and good management that we have tried to follow at national level?  the second, which is somewhat a consequence of the first, stems from an intuition: the common currency will change so profoundly the conditions for the functioning of the European economy and the implementation of economic policy that a new institutional dynamic will be created, which will push for the establishment of a European economic government, or even the creation of new mechanisms to support the regions. The introduction of a common currency will inevitably trigger centralizing forces. These forces will manifest themselves in the organization of markets, as well as in the architecture of institutions. 3. Implications for Switzerland If we can use the term "revolution" when we talk about the consequences for the surrounding Europe of the introduction of the euro, we must immediately note that the single currency will also have very important repercussions on non-member European countries, and particularly on Switzerland, which will be placed in the unique situation of being totally surrounded by the new monetary zone. For our country, the appearance of the euro will not lead to a revolution because our monetary sovereignty, even if it is relative, will continue to be exercised by the National Bank. Nevertheless, for the first time in our history, we will be surrounded by a unified monetary zone. This change is not only symbolic, it will have 8 some will have important consequences, some will be positive, others will have disadvantages. Let's review these elements. Positive is necessarily the fact that our exporters will, in future, operate in a limited number of European currencies. The result will be a more homogeneous market, in which our companies can act more simply and freely. If the ECB's objectives are met, the euro will become a quality currency like the German mark was in the post-war period. Switzerland will then be located in the heart of a stable monetary zone and the fate of a number of European currencies that were, in the past, a source of disruption for our economy, will be definitively fixed. No more break between strong and weak currencies, no more exotic or "Mediterranean" currencies. We will benefit from a less volatile European environment, and therefore more favourable to the development of our exports. Contrary to a simplistic picture of our situation, Switzerland suffers more than it benefits from currency crises. As our history shows, our economy has always borne high adjustment costs in the event of external monetary instability. Whether we remember the fall of the dollar in the seventies or the collapse of the Italian lira in the early nineties. In each of these cases, we had to hastily adapt our productive structures to the new constellation of exchange rates. If the external monetary regime had been able to promote more discipline, such adjustments would not have been necessary or, at least, would not have been so brutal. Positive is also the fact that the euro will gradually lead to a unification of the European market. On our doorstep will be created a market of the size of the American market, in which only one means of payment will circulate. Our exporting companies, like those of the Union itself, will see their horizons broaden and their operational framework simplified. But the creation of a large European market also entails risks for those who, like us, will remain on the margins of the Union. Indeed, we must expect the large European market to turn into a vast internal market since the external trade of the Eleven will not represent 9 than 10% of their GDP. This new reality will inevitably lead to a gradual change in the commercial vision of Europeans. They will gradually develop an internal market mentality, asking their trading partners to adapt to their internal rules and accept the euro more widely as a means of payment. It is therefore likely that the franc will be used less than at present in the settlement of our exports. In addition, we are likely to see an increased use of the euro on Swiss territory. Already today it is possible to use foreign currencies to make payments in tourist places. Tomorrow, these possibilities will probably have to be extended. However, the use of the euro within our borders and the dual display of prices in areas with high tourist traffic should only develop when neighbouring countries have completely abandoned their national currencies. The increased use of the euro as a billing currency and as a means of payment on our territory will result in a certain weakening of our economy because it will have a greater exposure to exchange rate risks. 4. Challenges for the Swiss National Bank's policy In this way, we naturally come to ask ourselves the question that concerns the export community, and of course also the SNB: what relations will be established between the franc and the euro and what will be the means of the Swiss National Bank to avoid any difficulties? To want to make a forecast of the future relationship between the franc and the euro today is necessarily highly speculative because we have little evidence of appreciation. On the one hand, we do not know what the course of the ECB's policy will be and, on the other hand, we realise that the conduct of monetary policy in the new European whole may run into difficulties. In addition, with the conclusion of the bilateral negotiations, we will also see closer ties between Switzerland and the European Union. 10 In the face of these uncertainties, however, we have two important elements of assessment. In the first place, there will be a strong convergence of the macroeconomic objectives set by the European Authorities and the Swiss Authorities. On both sides, price stability is seen as the goal of monetary action. This objective is explicitly reflected in the ECB's mandate, and it is the traditional aim of monetary policy in our country. Moreover, based on the information available, there is every reason to believe that the strategies for implementing monetary policy by the ECB and the SNB will be very similar. In both cases, attention will be paid to the development of monetary aggregates consistent with price stability in the medium term. In both cases too, this approach will be applied with the flexibility imposed by often very changing situations on the financial markets. Secondly, experience shows that countries with similar macroeconomic objectives and close cyclical developments benefit from relatively stable exchange rates. Here we must bear in mind the relationship that has developed between the franc and the German mark over the last fifteen years. Considered in real terms, this relationship has changed little, contrary to what has been observed between the franc and the lira or the franc and the dollar. If, tomorrow, the euro were to be the worthy successor to the mark, we have every reason to believe that the exchange rate relationship between the Swiss franc and the European currency will not develop chaotically. To conclude this point, I will simply say that Switzerland's increasingly European behaviour and the increasingly disciplined and Swiss attitude of our neighbours should create favourable conditions for stability. This similarity of situation should convince the markets that the franc and the euro are currencies with very similar fundamental characteristics. But it is undeniable that the monetary revolution that the euro represents involves new uncertainties because the European currency will not simply be the heir to the current national currencies. It will be a new value, the fate of which will depend greatly on the policy followed by the new European Authorities and the perception that the markets will have of it. 11 We are therefore entering little-known waters and must stand ready to take all necessary measures to protect the Swiss franc from negative spillovers. In fact, we did not wait for the arrival of the euro to develop a strategy in this regard. We started to worry about possible disruptions two years ago because the implementation phase of the euro involved risks of destabilizing the markets. Our action was to conduct a flexible liquidity policy, generously supplying the market when the demand for Swiss francs was particularly strong. We have endeavoured to recall the European characteristics of our currency rather than to emphasise its aspects of safe haven money. It is obvious that in terms of economic fundamentals, the Swiss franc, the mark or the French franc have such similarities that a different assessment by the markets would be unjustified. Our strategy has therefore been essentially preventive. Market experience has taught us that tensions on the Swiss franc can hardly be eased by direct action and that it is therefore wiser to take prior action to avoid imbalances that are too deep. This strategy seems to us to have borne the expected results. The franc, which was thought to be doomed to appreciate against European currencies, remained remarkably stable. This success has, of course, greatly benefited from the orderly and credible progress of the European monetary integration process. Had this not been the case, market tensions would have been much stronger. Some of the staunchest supporters of European integration often ask us whether, in the end, a unilateral pegging of the franc to a European standard would not be the most elegant and effective response to the challenges posed by the euro. Would this not be proof, by our actions, that the Swiss economy can only prosper in a European environment and that the Swiss franc belongs to the family of European currencies? Those who propose it forget that monetary decisions can only be sustainable and stabilizing if they are well rooted in reality. 12 Indeed, a unilateral peg of the franc to the euro - by declaring parity between the two currencies - would not be perceived today, by the markets, as a definitive solution. As long as Switzerland is not part of the European Union and its institutions, any unilateral "clash" of the franc would appear to be a decision that could be subject to subsequent revision, in particular during accession negotiations. As the markets hate half-measures, the declared parity would not fail to entice speculation always looking for weak lines of defense. Instead of calming the situation, parity would only fuel speculative zeal. It therefore seems to us contraindicated to want to definitively set the monetary rules of our country while the timetable for our integration into the European political environment is still uncertain. That would put the cart before the horse. But, on the other hand, should we not also recognize that between the Swiss and European realities, there are still gaps in the financial field that do not allow things to be precipitated on the monetary level. Although they have come very close in recent years, the paths of monetary convergence between Europe and Switzerland have not yet come together. Its currency, created one hundred and fifty years ago to ensure its development and integration into continental trade, has often reflected the difficulties of its neighbors. Tomorrow, with the establishment of a European area of monetary stability, the Swiss franc, naturally following in the wake of the euro, will allow our country to participate fully in the economic development of our Continent.
