Title: Introductory Remarks, End-of-year Media News Conference
text: End-of-year Media , Zurich, 11 December 1998 Introductory Remarks by Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Introductory Remarks by Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank We intend, in agreement with the Federal Government, to continue conducting a basically generous monetary policy in 1999. The Swiss economy will thus be granted the monetary leeway necessary for an enduring economic recovery. The problems in East Asia and the slowdown in growth in the United States are likely to lead to a weakening of economic activity in western Europe. The Swiss economy should, however, achieve further satisfactory growth. The intentions of the Governing Board duly take into account the uncertainties associated with the forthcoming launch of the euro. The Swiss National Bank - as is known - has the task of pursuing a monetary policy serving the interests of the country as a whole. Within the scope of monetary policy, the National Bank must help to create conditions that facilitate balanced - and also sustained - economic development. The best contribution monetary policy can make is to guarantee price stability. The National Bank considers this to be achieved with an annual inflation rate of 1% - 2%. Once more it must be emphasised that for the National Bank price stability is a means to an end rather than an end in itself. Economic theory shows convincingly that the absence of price stability can lead to a considerable loss of growth, and consequently a loss of welfare. To this must be added that notably the weaker members of the community suffer from inflation. Price stability is therefore an important social issue. The economic recovery, which got under way in 1997 and was initially supported mainly by exports, spread to every sector of the economy in the current year. Despite the slowdown triggered by the problems in various parts of the world, the real rate of growth of Switzerland's gross domestic product in 1998 is expected to be approximately 2%, in line with the National Bank's forecast. Exports to East Asia contracted considerably. Nevertheless, these losses were offset by a vigorous expansion of exports into the countries of the European Union and the United States and by the revival of domestic demand. Inflation, at 0.1%, is below original expectations. In the coming year, economic growth is likely to weaken somewhat both in Switzerland and in other countries in continental Europe. In Switzerland, real gross domestic product is still expected to expand by approximately 1.5%. The export sector will come to feel the results of the external disturbances, while domestic demand should continue to act as a welcome pillar of the economy. In view of the moderate real growth, unused production capacities are unlikely to be reduced any further. The pressure on consumer prices will therefore remain insignificant. Inflation will probably rise to 1%, with about half this amount being attributable to the increase in value-added tax. In the year now drawing to a close the development of the Swiss franc rate was only affected to a minor degree by preparations for the European Monetary Union. Of decisive importance, however, were the turbulences in the international financial markets, which boosted the demand for Swiss francs. The National Bank countered the effects on the exchange rate by repeatedly supplying the money market with generous liquidity. Currently the exchange rate is on an adequate level. Should the introduction of the euro pass without a hitch, no particular difficulties are to be expected for Switzerland. The National Bank and the European Central Bank will pursue similar policies. There is considerable agreement both as regards the goals and the operational framework of monetary policy. This will be conducive to exchange rate stability. As early as a year ago, we pointed out that the development of the monetary base is becoming more and more difficult to interpret. While the circulation of one-thousand-franc banknotes, which had risen considerably in the previous years, seems to have returned to normal the development of sight deposits exceeded the National Bank's forecasts. In the wake of international financial problems several banks increased their liquid funds. The already mentioned additional supplies of liquidity also contributed to the growth of sight deposits. The problems of interpretation referred to induced the National Bank to pay closer attention to the course of the broader money stock M3. After having risen markedly in 1996 and at the beginning of 1997, its growth has since levelled off considerably. The moderate development does not point to inflationary risks. In the implementation of the monetary policy intentions for 1999 no marked change in money market rates is to be expected. There are no indications of an immediate danger of inflation. Nevertheless, it is necessary to be on the alert. It is a well-known fact that monetary policy decisions only have an influence on developments with a time lag of approximately two years. In future, too, we will watch a number of other indicators. Particular attention is paid to factors pointing to the cyclical development of economic activity and the exchange rate. In the present environment it is difficult to gauge the future economic development. Should it deviate considerably from present perceptions, the Governing Board would, of course, reassess the situation.

Title: The overall interest of the country
text: The overall interest of the country Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Albisg9fetli Conference Zurich, Friday, 15 January 1999 2 As a public institution, the Swiss National Bank fulfils an important task. It has the mandate to conduct monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. Dealing with the question of what is to be understood by this overall interest and how to act in its sense is therefore one of my daily duties. I am pleased to have the opportunity to express some thoughts on this today. The overall interest of a community is basically identical to the sum of the individual wishes and hopes that the members of this community want to realize. The focus is on three concerns: welfare, security and freedom. They are intrinsically related, which does not rule out the possibility that their meaning is weighted differently. In today's complex world, the individual can usually only realize his concerns within the framework of a community. As an individual, as an employed person and as a citizen, he is often connected to this community. This can lead to tensions. The result depends on the way we deal with them. Successful joint cooperation is only possible if a large number of fellow citizens rise to the challenge of active participation. This presupposes that one can identify sufficiently with the community. This, in turn, will be the case if it is characterized by qualities such as balance, justice, humanity, but also performance. Only then will the individual feel at home in her and also be convinced that she can support him in the realization of his concerns. Of course, we must be aware that these characteristics of the community are also shaped by our own actions and omissions. Because every member of the community is fundamentally equal, success depends not least on the willingness to respect others - even if they are different and think differently. The limit of tolerance must not be drawn in the case of being and thinking differently, but only in the case of non-solidarity behaviour. 3 Such considerations also apply to nationals of other States who live with us. Throughout its history, our country has been enriched in some ways by its traditionally hospitable attitude. There is therefore no reason to deviate from this openness. Of course, it can be expected that the law as well as the customs and customs of the host country will be respected in the usual way. Experience has shown that this is true in the vast majority of cases. Excesses must be countered calmly and decisively in the interest of all in the matter, but also in perfect form. Quite a few contemporaries are currently in a strange mood. Probably the proximity of the turn of the century gives the impression that one is at a turning point in economic and social development. Such feelings become understandable when we recall what has happened in recent decades. All in all, we can look back on an impressive economic development. In the immediate post-war period, the need to catch up at home and abroad created a special spirit of optimism. Later, economic output has constantly improved in terms of type and scope. It is often overlooked that we have largely transformed into a service society. In the course of this remarkably steady development, material prosperity has increased and spread to an unimagined extent. However, this coin also has its downside. Numerous contemporaries were overwhelmed by the rhythm of events, which led to new exclusions. Community cohesion has loosened. Interpersonal relationships have not become easier in all areas of life. Pollution of the environment has become a problem that we like to suppress. After all, we have recently learned again that the increasing economic interdependence between individual states brings both opportunities and risks. 4 In the context of Community cooperation, economic activity is certainly not the only concern, but it is nevertheless a central concern. Only an efficient economy can create the conditions for achieving the common goals of welfare, security and freedom. Ultimately, the decisive factor for economic success in the sense of steady growth with price stability and good employment is the actions and omissions of individuals. Within the framework of the Community, they should be given the opportunity to develop their talents and to develop them under favourable conditions. Such framework conditions must be created primarily with a stability-conscious monetary policy, a sound fiscal policy, an effective competition policy and- last but not least - an efficient education policy. Even today, many still doubt the important role of free competition. Experience has shown that, under stable conditions, it is best placed to stimulate and control the diverse economic situation. Experience has shown that undesirable developments are not due to the principle of free competition, but to the lack of stability of the environment. Monetary policy, which is particularly close to my heart, is an important but only an instrument of economic policy. It is their task to provide the economy with adequate money, taking into account real developments. Teaching and experience confirm that it tends to be the best way to ensure price stability in the longer term. However, it is important to be aware that price stability is not an end in itself, but only a means to an end. It is an important contribution to creating the framework conditions that enable balanced economic development. Last but not least, price stability is also an important social concern, since it is precisely the weaker members of the Community that suffer most from inflation. 5 There is now broad agreement on the importance of the abovementioned framework conditions. However, the implementation of the well-known and proven rules of conduct proves to be difficult again and again. This is mainly due to the demanding dual role of the individual as an employed person and as a citizen. Here, too, there is the claim that the individual interests, which are quite legitimate in themselves, must be reconciled with those of other contemporaries. This is possible if individual inclinations and a sense of community - i.e. the recognition of shared responsibility for the community - are kept in a reasonable balance. This is particularly difficult today because we have already reached a high level of development. One could almost say that we still have to learn how to deal with prosperity. When it is possible to appreciate what has been achieved, it is easy to forget what it took to get this far and what is still necessary to preserve and increase what already exists. Adjustments will continue to be essential in the future. However, they must be carried out in a way that does not jeopardise Community cohesion. This presupposes a rhythm of development in which perseverance and flexibility, prudence and daring, care and boldness can be maintained in a balance, albeit uncertain. An organic development is therefore to be strived for. Only it is appropriate for a society on a human scale. Of course, difficulties also arise from different ideological views, which lead to different accents being set differently. Such differences relate to issues such as the appropriate relationship between self-responsibility and care, isolation and competition, perseverance and change, independence and openness to the outside world. 6 Depending on how we deal with these tensions, they can be fruitful or destructive to the community. It is important that the discussions are conducted with the necessary fundamentality, but also with the required serenity. Such serenity arises from the insight that different views are normal and legitimate, as well as from the willingness to respect the dissenter. We are dependent on the Community precisely because we alone have no prospect of realizing our concerns to the desired extent. But the community can only fulfil its task if we support it humanely and objectively. Respect and tolerance must not stop at other opinions. Many of you will understand these considerations particularly well because you are fortunate to be rooted in uncluttered communities. They therefore also have a special understanding of the importance of small groups, which play an important role in the area between the individual and the state organs in the sense of maintaining interpersonal relationships. Such groups are suitable for giving the individual the feeling of connectedness and security that is essential for him. They counteract individualisation and can relieve the public sector of claims. Last but not least, they have a special meaning for contemporaries who are on the dark side of life. Their promotion is therefore of particular concern in all areas of life. Community cooperation has never stopped at national borders. Our country in particular has an old tradition and a corresponding experience in intergovernmental cooperation in the economic, social and cultural fields. 7 There are also areas of tension in these relationships. They result from the experience that successful international cooperation is only possible if it can be based on economically and politically stable individual states. For the foreseeable future, the individual state will provide the best framework for joint cooperation in the economy, society and culture. Without stable individual states, it is impossible to think of a smooth free movement of goods, services, people and capital. In the positive case, however, all parties involved will benefit from the international division of labour. The correctness of such considerations is confirmed not least by the experiences in the Third World. They impressively show that even in these cases it is essential that each country first and foremost keeps its own house in order. Only then can external aid make an effective contribution to further development. Of course, ordering one's own house is also the first order in the case of the developed industrial countries. However, the willingness to open up must not be lost. Especially contemporaries who are particularly attached to their own house run the risk of focusing too much on the inside and thus also their own efforts. The willingness to open up is not only an economic imperative, it must rather encompass all areas of society and, last but not least, cultural concerns. Here, too, sustainable, fruitful cooperation is only possible on the basis of joint action, mutual respect, the balance of performance and consideration, of living and letting live. In this sense, we maintain relations above all with our European neighbours. With a Europe in the middle of which we live and whose inhabitants today harbor desires and hopes that are quite similar to our own. The recently concluded negotiations with the European Union have led to a result that allows us to develop our relations in a tried and tested way - committed to coming here, but also openly beyond borders. 8 In my view, it is useless to worry today about where and when to follow this step. For the foreseeable future, the bilateral agreements will provide us with a solid basis for fruitful cooperation with our most important partners. Certainly, the world will not stand still. How things will develop further can be waited for attentively, but confidently. Finally, I would like to summarize my thoughts. Acting in the overall interest of a country means helping people to live in a community with the highest levels of welfare, security and freedom. It is an ideal destination to which we are always on the way, without ever reaching it. Everyone is challenged. Only if a large number participate in the shaping of communal coexistence will the approach to the goal succeed. In view of this challenge, three things are particularly important. First and foremost, the self-responsibility of the individual must be emphasized. Within the scope of their possibilities, everyone must feel responsible for their own way of life. The aim is to recognize and develop one's own abilities and interests. Not everyone is able to do this to the same extent. We have also seen that in today's complex world, no one can realize their wishes and hopes only on their own. We therefore need a legal, economic and social framework to be created and maintained by the Community. This is the task of a lean but efficient state in every respect. But let us remember that it is we ourselves who have to support this state. Self-responsibility must therefore be supplemented by a sense of community. This is the recognition of a responsibility towards one's fellow human beings and the willingness to work together in mutual respect. 9 Finally, we must account for the fact that there is not only the need for interaction between individuals. Rather, they also exist between the individual communities. Other communities are more or less similar to us in nature and scope, so the relationships are different. Essential is the fundamental willingness to open up. In the intergovernmental field, too, cooperation will succeed best if we combine an awareness of one's own value with a willingness to know and acknowledge others. This is not only about economic, but also about social and cultural contacts. In the interaction of self-responsibility, community spirit and openness to the outside world, it will best succeed in realizing welfare, security and freedom to a high degree in the overall interest of the country.

Januar 1999 2 Die Schweizerische Nationalbank erfllt als ffentliche Institution eine wichtige Aufgabe. Sie hat den Auftrag, die Geldpolitik im Gesamtinteresse des Landes zu fhren. Die Beschftigung mit der Frage, was unter diesem Gesamtinteresse zu verstehen und wie in seinem Sinne zu handeln sei, gehrt deshalb zu meinen tglichen Pflichten. Ich freue mich ber die Gelegenheit, heute dazu einige Gedanken zu ussern. Das Gesamtinteresse einer Gemeinschaft ist grundstzlich identisch mit der Summe der individuellen Wnsche und Hoffnungen, die die Angehrigen dieser Gemeinschaft verwirklichen mchten. Im Vordergrund stehen dabei drei Anliegen: Wohlfahrt, Sicherheit und Freiheit. Sie stehen in einem inneren Zusammenhang, was nicht ausschliesst, dass ihre Bedeutung unterschiedlich gewichtet wird. Der Einzelne kann in der heutigen komplexen Welt seine Anliegen in der Regel nur noch im Rahmen einer Gemeinschaft verwirklichen. Als Individuum, als Erwerbsttiger und als Staatsbrger ist er mit dieser Gemeinschaft vielfach verbunden. Daraus knnen sich Spannungen ergeben. Von der Art und Weise, wie wir mit ihnen umgehen, hngt das Ergebnis ab. Ein erfolgreiches gemeinschaftliches Zusammenwirken ist nur mglich, wenn sich eine grosse Zahl von Mitbrgerinnen und Mitbrgern der Herausforderung zur aktiven Mitgestaltung stellt. Das setzt voraus, dass man sich in ausreichendem Masse mit der Gemeinschaft identifizieren kann. Dies wiederum wird dann der Fall sein, wenn sie durch Eigenschaften wie Ausgewogenheit, Gerechtigkeit, Menschlichkeit, aber auch Leistungsfhigkeit, geprgt ist. Nur dann wird sich der Einzelne in ihr aufgehoben fhlen und auch berzeugt sein, dass sie ihn bei der Verwirklichung seiner Anliegen zu untersttzen vermag. Dabei mssen wir uns natrlich bewusst sein, dass diese Eigenschaften der Gemeinschaft auch durch unser eigenes Tun und Lassen geprgt werden. Weil jeder Angehrige der Gemeinschaft grundstzlich gleichberechtigt ist, hngt der Erfolg nicht zuletzt auch von der Bereitschaft ab, die Anderen zu respektieren - selbst dann, wenn sie anders sind und anders denken. Nicht beim anders Sein und Denken, sondern erst bei unsolidarischem Verhalten ist die Grenze der Toleranz zu ziehen. 3 Solche berlegungen gelten auch fr die Angehrigen anderer Staaten, die bei uns leben. Im Laufe seiner Geschichte wurde unser Land durch seine traditionell gastfreundliche Haltung in mancher Hinsicht bereichert. Es gibt deshalb keinen Grund, von dieser Offenheit abzuweichen. Selbstverstndlich darf erwartet werden, dass das Recht ebenso wie die Sitten und Gebruche des Gastlandes in blicher Weise respektiert werden. Erfahrungsgemss trifft das in der grossen Mehrheit der Flle zu. Auswchsen ist im Interesse aller in der Sache ruhig und bestimmt, aber auch in einwandfreier Form entgegenzutreten. Nicht wenige Zeitgenossen befinden sich gegenwrtig in einer eigenartigen Stimmungslage. Wahrscheinlich frdert die Nhe der Jahrhundertwende den Eindruck, dass man sich an einem Wendepunkt der wirtschaftlichen und gesellschaftlichen Entwicklung befinde. Solche Empfindungen werden dann verstndlich, wenn wir uns das Geschehen der letzten Jahrzehnte in Erinnerung rufen. Alles in allem genommen blicken wir vor allem auf eine eindrckliche wirtschaftliche Entwicklung zurck. In der unmittelbaren Nachkriegszeit schuf der Nachholbedarf im In- und Ausland eine besondere Aufbruchstimmung. Spter hat sich die Wirtschaftsleistung nach Art und Umfang stndig verbessert. Hufig wird dabei bersehen, dass wir uns weitgehend zu einer Dienstleistungsgesellschaft gewandelt haben. Der materielle Wohlstand hat sich im Zuge dieser bemerkenswert stetigen Entwicklung in ungeahntem Masse erhht und verbreitet. Allerdings hat auch diese Medaille ihre Kehrseite. Zahlreiche Zeitgenossen wurden vom Rhythmus des Geschehens berfordert, was zu neuen Ausgrenzungen fhrte. Der gemeinschaftliche Zusammenhalt hat sich gelockert. Die zwischenmenschlichen Beziehungen sind in allen Lebensbereichen nicht einfacher geworden. Die Belastung der Umwelt hat sich zu einem Problem entwickelt, das wir gerne verdrngen. Schliesslich haben wir gerade in jngster Zeit wieder erfahren, dass die zunehmende wirtschaftliche Verflechtung zwischen einzelnen Staaten sowohl Chancen als auch Risiken mit sich bringt. 4 Im Rahmen der gemeinschaftlichen Zusammenarbeit ist die Wirtschaftsttigkeit sicher nicht das einzige, aber doch ein zentrales Anliegen. Nur eine leistungsfhige Wirtschaft kann die Voraussetzungen dafr schaffen, dass die gemeinsamen Ziele - Wohlfahrt, Sicherheit und Freiheit - erreicht werden knnen. Entscheidend fr den wirtschaftlichen Erfolg im Sinne eines stetigen Wachstums bei Preisstabilitt und guter Beschftigung ist letztlich das Tun und Lassen der einzelnen Menschen. Ihnen soll im Rahmen der Gemeinschaft Gelegenheit gegeben werden, ihre Talente zu entwickeln und unter gnstigen Rahmenbedingungen zu entfalten. Solche Rahmenbedingungen sind in erster Linie mit einer stabilittsbewussten Geldpolitik, einer soliden Finanzpolitik, einer wirksamen Wettbewerbspolitik und - nicht zuletzt - einer leistungsfhigen Bildungspolitik zu schaffen. Viele zweifeln auch heute noch an der wichtigen Rolle des freien Wettbewerbes. Dabei lehrt die Erfahrung, dass dieser bei stabilen Verhltnissen am besten in der Lage ist, das vielfltige Wirtschaftsgeschehen zu stimulieren und zu steuern. Erfahrungsgemss sind Fehlentwicklungen nicht auf den Grundsatz des freien Wettbewerbes, sondern auf die mangelnde Stabilitt des Umfeldes zurckzufhren. Die Geldpolitik, die mir besonders am Herzen liegt, ist ein wichtiges, aber doch nur ein Instrument der Wirtschaftspolitik. Es ist ihre Aufgabe, die Wirtschaft unter Bercksichtigung der realen Entwicklung angemessen mit Geld zu versorgen. Lehre und Erfahrung besttigen, dass sie damit tendenziell und lngerfristig am besten die Preisstabilitt zu gewhrleisten vermag. Es ist aber wichtig, sich bewusst zu sein, dass Preisstabilitt kein Selbstzweck, sondern nur ein Mittel zum Zweck ist. Sie ist ein wichtiger Beitrag zur Schaffung der Rahmenbedingungen, die eine ausgeglichene wirtschaftliche Entwicklung ermglichen. Nicht zuletzt ist Preisstabilitt auch ein wichtiges soziales Anliegen, leiden doch gerade die schwcheren Glieder der Gemeinschaft am strksten unter der Teuerung. 5 In bezug auf die Bedeutung der erwhnten Rahmenbedingungen besteht heute weitgehende Einigkeit. Als schwierig erweist sich allerdings immer wieder die Umsetzung der altbekannten und auch bewhrten Verhaltensregeln. Das hngt vor allem mit der anspruchsvollen Doppelrolle des Einzelnen als Erwerbsttiger und als Staatsbrger zusammen. Auch hier besteht der Anspruch, dass die an sich durchaus legitimen Einzelinteressen mit denjenigen der anderen Zeitgenossen in Einklang zu bringen sind. Das ist dann mglich, wenn individuelle Neigungen und Gemeinsinn - d.h. die Anerkennung einer Mitverantwortung fr die Gemeinschaft - in einem vernnftigen Gleichgewicht gehalten werden. Dies ist heute deshalb besonders schwierig, weil wir bereits einen hohen Stand der Entwicklung erreicht haben. Man knnte beinahe sagen, dass wir noch immer lernen mssen, mit dem Wohlstand umzugehen. Bei der Genugtuung ber das Erreichte wird leicht vergessen, was es brauchte, um so weit zu kommen und was weiterhin notwendig ist zur Wahrung und Mehrung des Bestehenden. Anpassungen werden auch in Zukunft unerlsslich sein. Sie mssen aber in einer Art und Weise vollzogen werden, die den gemeinschaftlichen Zusammenhalt nicht gefhrdet. Das setzt einen Rhythmus der Entwicklung voraus, bei dem Beharrungsvermgen und Flexibilitt, Besonnenheit und Wagemut, Sorgfalt und Khnheit in einem wenn auch unsicheren Gleichgewicht gehalten werden knnen. Anzustreben ist somit eine organische Entwicklung. Nur sie ist einer Gesellschaft nach menschlichem Mass angemessen. Schwierigkeiten ergeben sich natrlich auch aus unterschiedlichen weltanschaulichen Auffassungen, die dazu fhren, dass Akzente verschieden gesetzt werden. Solche Unterschiede beziehen sich auf Fragen wie das angemessene Verhltnis zwischen Selbstverantwortung und Frsorge, Abschottung und Wettbewerb, Beharrung und Wandel, Eigenstndigkeit und Offenheit nach aussen. 6 Je nachdem, wie wir auch mit diesen Spannungen umgehen, knnen sie fr die Gemeinschaft fruchtbar oder aber zerstrerisch sein. Wichtig ist, dass die Auseinandersetzungen mit der notwendigen Grundstzlichkeit, aber auch mit der gebotenen Gelassenheit gefhrt werden. Solche Gelassenheit entsteht aus der Einsicht, dass unterschiedliche Auffassungen normal und legitim sind sowie aus der Bereitschaft, den Andersdenkenden zu respektieren. Wir sind ja gerade deshalb auf die Gemeinschaft angewiesen, weil wir allein keine Aussicht haben, unsere Anliegen in erwnschtem Masse zu verwirklichen. Die Gemeinschaft aber vermag ihre Aufgabe nur zu erfllen, wenn wir sie menschlich und sachlich mittragen. Respekt und Toleranz drfen nicht vor anderen Meinungen Halt machen. Viele von Ihnen werden diese berlegungen besonders gut verstehen, weil sie das Glck haben, in bersichtlichen Gemeinschaften verwurzelt zu sein. Sie haben deshalb auch ein besonderes Verstndnis fr die Bedeutung von kleinen Gruppen, die im Bereich zwischen dem Einzelnen und den staatlichen Organen eine wichtige Rolle im Sinne der Pflege zwischenmenschlicher Beziehungen spielen. Solche Gruppen sind geeignet, dem Einzelnen das fr ihn unerlssliche Gefhl der Verbundenheit und Geborgenheit zu geben. Sie wirken der Individualisierung entgegen und knnen den ffentlichen Sektor von Ansprchen entlasten. Nicht zuletzt haben sie eine besondere Bedeutung fr Zeitgenossen, die sich auf der Schattenseite des Lebens befinden. Ihre Frderung ist deshalb in allen Lebensbereichen ein besonderes Anliegen. Gemeinschaftliches Zusammenwirken hat nie an den Landesgrenzen Halt gemacht. Gerade unser Land hat eine alte Tradition und eine entsprechende Erfahrung in der zwischenstaatlichen Zusammenarbeit im wirtschaftlichen, gesellschaftlichen und kulturellen Bereich. 7 Auch bei diesen Beziehungen bestehen Spannungsfelder. Sie ergeben sich aus der Erfahrung, dass eine erfolgreiche internationale Zusammenarbeit nur dann mglich ist, wenn sie sich auf wirtschaftlich und politisch stabile Einzelstaaten absttzen kann. Noch auf absehbare Zeit wird der einzelne Staat den besten Rahmen fr gemeinschaftliches Zusammenwirken in Wirtschaft, Gesellschaft und Kultur bilden. Ohne stabile Einzelstaaten ist nicht an eine reibungslose Freizgigkeit von Gtern, Dienstleistungen, Menschen und Kapital zu denken. Im positiven Falle aber werden alle Beteiligten von der internationalen Arbeitsteilung profitieren. Die Richtigkeit solcher berlegungen wird nicht zuletzt durch die Erfahrungen in der dritten Welt besttigt. Sie zeigen eindrcklich, dass es auch in diesen Fllen unerlsslich ist, dass jedes Land zuerst und vor allem das eigene Haus in Ordnung hlt. Nur dann kann Hilfe von aussen wirksam zur weiteren Entwicklung beitragen. Die Bestellung des eigenen Hauses ist natrlich auch im Falle der entwickelten Industriestaaten erstes Gebot. Die Bereitschaft zur ffnung darf dabei allerdings nicht verloren gehen. Gerade Zeitgenossen, die dem eigenen Hause in besonderem Masse verbunden sind, laufen Gefahr, den Blick und damit auch die eigenen Anstrengungen zu sehr nach innen zu richten. Die Bereitschaft zur ffnung ist nicht nur wirtschaftliches Gebot, sie muss vielmehr alle gesellschaftlichen Bereiche und nicht zuletzt die kulturellen Belange umfassen. Auch hier gilt, dass nachhaltige, fruchtbare Zusammenarbeit nur auf der Grundlage des gemeinsamen Handelns, des gegenseitigen Respektes, der Ausgewogenheit von Leistung und Gegenleistung, des Lebens und Lebenlassens, mglich ist. In diesem Sinne pflegen wir die Beziehungen vor allem mit unseren europischen Nachbarn. Mit einem Europa, in dessen Mitte wir leben und dessen Bewohner gerade heute Wnsche und Hoffnungen hegen, die unseren eigenen durchaus hnlich sind. Die jngst abgeschlossenen Verhandlungen mit der Europischen Union haben zu einem Ergebnis gefhrt, das es uns ermglicht, unsere Beziehungen in bewhrter Weise weiterzuentwickeln - dem Herkommen verpflichtet, aber auch offen ber die Grenzen hinaus. 8 Es ist meines Erachtens mssig, sich heute darber den Kopf zu zerbrechen, wo und wann diesem Schritt weitere folgen sollen. Fr die absehbare Zukunft werden wir mit den bilateralen Vertrgen eine tragfhige Grundlage fr die fruchtbare Zusammenarbeit mit unseren wichtigsten Partnern erhalten. Mit Sicherheit wird die Welt nicht stillstehen. Wie sich die Dinge weiter entwickeln werden, kann aufmerksam, aber getrost abgewartet werden. Ich mchte zum Schluss meine Gedanken zusammenfassen. Im Gesamtinteresse eines Landes zu handeln heisst, dazu beizutragen, dass Menschen in einer Gemeinschaft mit einem Hchstmass an Wohlfahrt, Sicherheit und Freiheit leben knnen. Es ist dies ein ideales Ziel, zu dem wir uns immer auf dem Weg befinden, ohne es je zu erreichen. Alle sind dabei gefordert. Nur dann, wenn sich eine grosse Zahl an der Gestaltung gemeinschaftlichen Zusammenlebens beteiligt, gelingt die Annherung an das Ziel. Im Blick auf diese Herausforderung sind vor allem drei Dinge wichtig. In erster Linie ist die Selbstverantwortung des Einzelnen zu betonen. Im Rahmen seiner Mglichkeiten muss sich jeder selbst fr seine Lebensgestaltung verantwortlich fhlen. Dabei geht es darum, die eigenen Fhigkeiten und Interessen zu erkennen und zu entwickeln. Nicht jeder ist dazu in gleichem Masse in der Lage. Wir haben auch gesehen, dass in der heutigen komplexen Welt berhaupt niemand seine Wnsche und Hoffnungen nur auf sich selbst gestellt verwirklichen kann. Wir brauchen deshalb einen rechtlichen, wirtschaftlichen und gesellschaftlichen Rahmen, der durch die Gemeinschaft zu schaffen und zu bewahren ist. Dies ist die Aufgabe eines schlanken, aber in jeder Hinsicht leistungsfhigen Staates. Erinnern wir uns aber daran, dass wir selbst es sind, die diesen Staat tragen mssen. Die Selbstverantwortung muss deshalb durch den Gemeinsinn ergnzt werden. Dies ist die Anerkennung einer Verantwortung gegenber dem Mitmenschen und die Bereitschaft, im gegenseitigen Respekt zusammen zu arbeiten. 9 Schliesslich mssen wir uns darber Rechenschaft geben, dass es nicht nur die Notwendigkeit des Zusammenwirkens zwischen Einzelnen gibt. Es gibt sie vielmehr auch zwischen den einzelnen Gemeinschaften. Andere Gemeinschaften sind uns nach Art und Umfang mehr oder weniger hnlich, so dass sich die Beziehungen unterschiedlich gestalten. Wesentlich ist die grundstzliche Bereitschaft zur ffnung. Auch im zwischenstaatlichen Bereich wird die Zusammenarbeit am besten gelingen, wenn wir das Bewusstsein des eigenen Wertes mit der Bereitschaft verbinden, andere zu kennen und anzuerkennen. Dabei geht es nicht nur um wirtschaftliche, sondern auch um gesellschaftliche und kulturelle Kontakte. Im Zusammenwirken von Selbstverantwortung, Gemeinsinn und Offenheit nach aussen wird es am besten gelingen, im Gesamtinteresse des Landes Wohlfahrt, Sicherheit und Freiheit in hohem Masse zu verwirklichen.

Title: On monetary policy in the new year
text: Monetary policy in the new year Dr. Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank University of St. Gallen St. Gallen, 21 January 1999 2 For the second time d0 almost establishing a tradition d0 I am using your university's invitation as a welcome opportunity to explain our monetary policy in more detail to a critical audience. I'll start with a look back at 1998, which will be remembered as one of the more turbulent of the recent past. In the second part of my remarks, I will explain what led us to once again announce a monetary policy that tended to be generous. In the third part, I would like to address some fundamental questions of our monetary policy, a monetary policy that I myself described as pragmatic at the media conference last December. The fourth and final part deals with the mandate of the National Bank. In the December session, the National Council was the first of the two chambers to approve the new currency article in the constitution; the vote in the Council of States is scheduled for March. 1 Review The year 1998 was a pleasing year for the Swiss economy as a whole. The economic recovery continued despite the deterioration of the global economic environment. The favourable monetary conditions contributed to this. Short-term interest rates were slight, while long-term interest rates were significantly lower than in the previous year. With an average of 2.8%, the yield on federal bonds reached its lowest level since the end of the fifties. At the same time, the rise in consumer prices came to a standstill, not least under the influence of the sharp decline in oil prices. This led to a significant increase in real incomes and a revival in domestic demand. From abroad, however, a rough wind blew. The crisis in East Asia, which erupted in mid-1997, proved to be more lasting than initially assumed. The export industry clearly felt the marked drop in demand from this once dynamic region. Exports, which in 1997 were still the main pillar of the economy, lost momentum. 3 Massive disruptions also emanated from the financial markets. Despite the ongoing crisis in East Asia and the growing problems in other emerging countries, the bull market in the industrialised countries initially continued. In Switzerland, too, stock market listings reached new record levels in the summer. However, there are increasing signs that the crisis in large parts of the world will not leave the industrialized countries untouched. As a result, earnings expectations were revised downwards. The outbreak of the Russian crisis and the unilateral debt moratorium ultimately formed the impetus for a massive price correction on all major stock exchanges. In Switzerland, the Swiss Performance Index lost almost 40% of its value by the beginning of October. This abrupt correction in the stock market also led to turbulence in other markets. In Switzerland, the strong demand for federal bonds caused their yields to fall significantly, while the interest rate on the bonds of private debtors rose slightly. Even more pronounced were the shifts to safe government securities in the United States. The nervousness came to a head when, in September, a renowned institute specializing in derivatives trading got into a tailspin and had to be rescued by a large-scale action coordinated by the US Federal Reserve. Many began to fear that it might be the tip of an iceberg. In this tense situation, the US Federal Reserve lowered its key interest rate by 0.25% to 5.25% at the end of September. This contributed significantly to the calming of the financial markets and subsequently to the recovery of the equity markets. The Fed's intervention highlighted the difficult question of how central banks should behave in the face of financial market developments. Basically, it is certainly right if they do not care too much about the price movements on the stock markets. Such price movements are strongly influenced by expectations d0 also with regard to monetary policy. Central banks must avoid their monetary policy becoming the plaything of such expectations. 4 The situation is different when turbulence causes financial institutions into difficulties and there is a risk of chain reactions that could endanger a country's financial system. In the case of such systemic risks, it may be appropriate to provide the financial system with additional liquidity. The INTEREST rate hike by the US Federal Reserve, which was followed by two more in mid-October and mid-November, was also appropriate for economic reasons. The massive decline in the share price on the stock markets threatened to cool down the American economy, which was already feeling the consequences of the Asian crisis, too much. In Europe, and especially in Switzerland, this was less the case. Share ownership is not excessively widely distributed in this country; Gains and losses from equity investments do not seem to have a strong influence on short-term consumer behavior. In addition, the high household savings rate compared to the US provides an effective buffer to absorb such losses. Perhaps even more dangerous than the impact of the financial crisis on developed countries was the possibility that the crisis would spread to the emerging countries of Latin America. For some time now, these countries have had to cope with rising risk premia and growing pressure on their currencies. The outbreak of the financial crisis in the summer triggered further redeployments to safer plants in the industrialized countries. In order to avert the acute danger of destabilization of Brazil, this country was granted extensive international financial assistance, in which the National Bank also participated. Our contribution to measures in favour of countries with balance of payments difficulties or in favour of the IMF today amounts to a total of CHF 2.6 billion. This includes our bilateral aid operations within the framework of the currency decision, the ceiling of which of one billion francs has now been exhausted. The Federal Council and Parliament will therefore have to envisage an increase if Switzerland is not to be sidelined. The rapid spread of the Asian and Russian crises to other emerging economies once again drew attention to the supposedly harmful effects of high capital mobility. The debate is as old as the experience that financial market crises can quickly spread widely. Sealing off countries through financial market controls may mitigate the transmission of shocks. But this is only at the price that the 5 The development of their economy must be managed largely without foreign capital. A better solution for these countries would be to put the domestic financial sector on a solid footing, including by increasing banks' capital adequacy and strengthening financial market supervision. Switzerland was affected by the turbulence on the financial markets, not least because the upward pressure on the Swiss franc increased. In order not to jeopardize the economic recovery, we counteracted this pressure by providing generous money. In doing so, we had to take into account the fact that the banks temporarily held more current balances as a precautionary fund. The current account, which was above CHF 5 billion on individual days, therefore oversubscribed the degree of monetary policy expansion. The approaching introduction of the euro caused few problems last year. After certain uncertainties had led to higher demand for the Swiss franc at the beginning of the year, the situation calmed down quickly. The establishment of bilateral parities at the beginning of May and the determined expansion of the European Central Bank strengthened confidence in the new currency. Their launch at the beginning of this year went smoothly. To date, the Swiss franc exchange rate against the euro has developed within a reasonable framework. 2 Monetary policy in 1999 If, for the third time in a row, a generally generous monetary policy is announced, the impression may arise that nothing is actually decided anymore, but automatically everything is left as it is. This impression is deceptive. Even if in the end monetary policy actually remains the same, this decision is based on a detailed decision-making process. It can essentially be divided into four steps. 6 a5 Based on the current economic situation, the real economic development in the following year must first be estimated. An economic analysis gives us an idea of the future development of capacity utilisation or, in other words, of the output gap. This leads to initial conclusions about the presumed development of the price level. a5 In a second step, this assessment is supplemented with information on short-term price developments. These include special factors such as changes in indirect taxes or foreseeable influences from import prices. a5 Subsequently, it must be examined whether the previously gained idea of the appropriate monetary policy stance is also justifiable from a longer-term perspective. To assess this, we mainly use monetary aggregates. In Switzerland, there is still a sufficient link between the development of the price level and monetary aggregates in the longer term. Monetary aggregates therefore remain useful indicators for assessing the longer-term price trend. a5 Finally, it is a question of drawing conclusions for monetary policy from the course of all the indicators examined. Essentially, we need to consider whether the money supply trend is in line with a balanced economic development and the objective of longer-term price stability. If this is not the case, then a tightening or a loosening of monetary policy must be envisaged, depending on the case. This brings me to the concrete reflections on monetary policy in 1999. I will start with an assessment of the economic situation. 7 2.1 Economic situation Most economic forecasts, as well as our own calculations, point to a slowdown in economic growth in 1999. First of all, this reflects the Asian crisis, which is also likely to lead to a slowdown in growth in our important trading partners. We must therefore expect weaker export growth. On the other hand, domestic demand, especially private consumption, is likely to act as an economic stimulus. According to our assessment, real economic growth will be in the order of 1.5% and thus will not exceed the long-term trend or potential growth this year. This leaves room for manoeuvre. This is also reflected in the labour market. The number of registered unemployed fell pleasingly sharply last year. However, the decline is overestimated by two factors, namely the active labour market measures such as the cantonal employment programmes and the management of the long-term unemployed. So there is still considerable unemployment. This does not preclude the labour market from being largely dried up for certain categories of workers. However, productivity gains and, above all, fierce competition should prevent the higher wages paid in these cases from leading to a general increase in the price level. Like inflation risks, we currently consider the risk that the recovery of the economy will stall and thus deflationary tendencies could be triggered as low. Growth prospects have been revised downwards in most industrialised countries. However, low inflation and low interest rates point to a continuation of the economic recovery in Europe and to a continued good economy in the United States. There is therefore no reason to fear a slump in exports. 8 All in all, the basic economic and labour market indicators speak in favour of maintaining our generally generous monetary policy. Unfortunately, these indicators are not always reliable. The concept of the production gap is struggling with measurement problems. On the one hand, the estimated output gap depends on what potential growth is assumed. On the other hand, the data on the effective development of macroeconomic production is also fraught with uncertainty. An example was provided last year by the substantial revision of the national accounts for 1997. In retrospect, this shows a much more favorable development of the gross domestic product than the quarterly estimates suggested. Similar reservations apply to the labour market. Our research shows that estimates of base unemployment are so inaccurate that they are of little use to monetary policy. For these reasons, further indicators need to be examined in order to clarify the picture. Mention should be made of the effects of VAT, the influences from abroad on the price level and other special factors that are likely to shape price developments. 2.2 Further influences on inflation In 1998, the consumer price index remained unchanged for the first time since the end of the fifties. In November and December, it was even slightly below the previous year's level. This result, which was also unexpected for us, was mainly a consequence of the collapse of oil prices. By contrast, the prices of other goods, in particular those of private services, rose slightly in view of the revival in demand. For this year, we expect inflation to rise by an average of 1%. At the beginning of the year, the increase in VAT from 6.5% to 7.5% came into force. We assume that this general adjustment will be largely passed on to consumer prices. It is likely to account for around half of the expected rise in inflation. 9 The remaining price pressure is likely to remain low. In addition to the moderate economic development, this is initially due to international influences. Against the backdrop of weaker global economic growth, commodity prices, especially oil prices, are likely to remain depressed. The exchange rate development also hardly threatens to boost inflation. Assuming that the real, export-weighted Swiss franc will remain roughly at the level of the end of the year, this side will have a slight dampening effect on prices. In the domestic sector, deregulation and increased competition then limit the scope for price increases. The best example is the telecommunications sector. In the same direction, the transformation of agriculture away from price subsidies towards direct payments or the liberalisation of the hospitality industry that has already taken place in some cantons is having an effect. The increased price transparency in neighbouring countries created by the introduction of the euro is also likely to have a dampening effect on prices. However, this does not mean that the phenomenon of inflation would be a thing of the past. However, these are special factors that can contain the risk of inflation over some time. Monetary developments remain an important indicator for assessing price developments over the longer term. 2.3 Considerations on monetary developments Monetary aggregates are known to provide reliable information on the longer-term inflation trend as long as the demand for money is stable. Where there is a close and stable link between a given monetary supply and the objective of price stability, it can be used as an intermediate monetary policy objective. Until 1996, the central bank money supply, which includes banknotes in circulation and banks' sight deposits with the SNB, fulfilled this requirement. For this reason, we defined a medium-term target path for this size in the sense of an orientation aid. 10 Since 1997, disruptions in the demand for central bank money have increased sharply. Changes in banks' liquidity policies, in particular increased volatility in banks' demand for sight deposits, play a major role in this. The audience's demand for thousands of notes has also increased sharply for reasons that are still unclear. The development of the central bank money supply therefore lost its significance and therefore receded into the background as a guide. This prompted us to pay more attention to the course of the broader money supply M3. Long-term demand for M3 tends to be stable and there is a reliable correlation to price developments in the longer term. However, M3 is less controllable than the central bank money supply. The aggregate reacts significantly to changes in long-term interest rates, which can lead to interpretation problems. The expected development of M3 this year does not suggest any risks to price stability. 2.4 Monetary policy conclusions The analysis of the indicators carried out in autumn 1998 showed us that monetary policy, which continues to be generous, is in the interests of a balanced economic development and should not pose a threat to price stability. There was therefore no reason to change the monetary policy stance. Decision-making was simple in that virtually all indicators pointed in the same direction. However, our considerations are based to a large extent on forecasts and thus on an uncertain basis. We therefore have to review the monetary policy stance on the basis of new information and, if necessary, correct it. We communicate our ongoing assessment in the monetary policy conclusions, which we publish quarterly in the Quarterly Bulletin. 11 The monetary policy announcements at the end of the year, as well as our quarterly monetary policy conclusions, usually end with the indication that we would respond to serious disruptions in the foreign exchange and financial markets. This reservation is almost self-evident this year in view of the introduction of the euro. The creation of the euro is a turning point. It also affects the Swiss economy and will require changes and adjustments. The new European currency has basically good prospects of becoming a stable currency. Nevertheless, surprises cannot be ruled out. We must therefore regularly include the development of the euro exchange rate in our monetary policy calculations. Let me move on to the third part of my presentation, on monetary policy strategy. How can it be characterized? To what extent is it pragmatic? 3 The monetary policy strategy Our monetary policy is based on a flexible strategy. We are trying to achieve the objective of price stability by probably following the development of monetary aggregates, while at the same time taking other indicators into account. Our interim targets for the central bank money supply have always been tied to certain conditions. They applied insofar as the underlying assumptions about functional relationships and key economic variables remained valid and did not have to be adjusted on the basis of new information. I am thinking in particular of the demand for money and the exchange rate. The flexibility of our strategy is reflected in the fact that the money supply targets were often not achieved, even though the central bank money supply would have been fairly controllable. 12 In the last two years, as I said, the difficulties in assessing the central bank money supply have led us to increasingly use the M3 money supply and to point out the other indicators even more explicitly than before. At the last media conference, we described our monetary policy as pragmatic. In doing so, we expressed that the number of indicators used is not exhaustive and that the weight we attach to individuals is not fixed from the outset. A pragmatic monetary policy, however, is not an opportunistic monetary policy based on the least resistance. Such a monetary policy would be doomed to failure. It would most likely lead to a destabilisation of the price level and a growing uncertainty in the economy and households. The credibility of the central bank would be quickly lost and a return to stable conditions would only be possible at high social costs. Our monetary policy is fundamentally geared towards maintaining price stability. Inflation rates of up to 2% can be tolerated. If higher inflation tends to develop, then the situation must be reassessed and, if necessary, countermeasures must be taken. The same applies, of course, in the event that a risk of generally falling prices, i.e. deflation, becomes apparent. It would have to be counteracted with an expansive monetary policy. A one-off fall in prices marked by special factors is irrelevant; however, a tendency towards a decrease in the price level is dangerous. As an alternative to a flexible d0 or pragmatic d0 money supply strategy, the direct inflation target strategy has received increasing attention in recent years. Such a strategy is particularly suitable if the monetary aggregates have largely lost their significance due to financial market innovations, for example. It was mainly chosen by countries where the inflation rate had to be lowered from a high level or an earlier exchange rate peg had to be abandoned. The formulation of an explicit inflation target is intended to quickly give a central bank credibility and thus reduce the costs of fighting inflation. 13 At the heart of an inflation target strategy is the central bank's inflation forecast. If this deviates from the inflation target, monetary policy must be adjusted. However, this strategy also has its pitfalls. Making an inflation forecast over a longer period of time is difficult. In a small, open economy, it is anything but easy, even in the short term, because disruptions from abroad often have a strong impact on domestic price levels. Whatever strategy a central bank chooses, it will always face uncertainty. It must trust information and forecasts that may turn out to be wrong. If a price adjustment appears necessary, it has only one means, namely the influence on the money supply. In addition, there is only the possibility of pegging the exchange rate firmly to another currency and thus transferring responsibility for monetary policy to another central bank. Of course, this is confronted with the same fundamental problems, but will have little understanding for the special needs of accessible places. Monetary policy decisions can never do justice to all ideas. They are to a considerable extent and unavoidably discretionary decisions. If a central bank wants to avoid undesirable developments, it must act in good time. It has to make its decisions at a moment when the problems are not yet virulent and many see no danger. In such a situation, it will try to create as much transparency as possible and to disclose the reasons for its actions. Even then, it is not immune to criticism, as indicators can often be interpreted differently. Precisely because the central bank has to act under uncertainty and make discretionary decisions, it is important that there is clarity about its mandate. Let me move on to the last part of my speech, the mandate of the National Bank. 14 4 The mandate of the Swiss National Bank As mentioned in the introduction, the National Council approved the new currency article with a clear majority in the last December session. This first loosens the outdated peg of the franc to gold. It instructs the SNB to conduct monetary policy in the overall interest of the country, with the objective of price stability as a priority. It then enshrines the independence of the SNB and at the same time obliges it to be accountable to the Federal Council, the Federal Assembly and the public. Finally, the new currency article states that part of the currency reserves necessary for the fulfillment of the order must continue to be held in gold. Federal legislation is intended to regulate the use of currency reserves that are no longer needed for monetary policy purposes. As is well known, the SNB has today formulated its mandate to conduct monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. It is noteworthy that the question of what is meant by the overall interest in this context has remained unanswered for decades. Only the inclusion of the economic article in the constitution brought the desired clarification. Accordingly, the Confederation is obliged to take precautions for balanced economic development, in particular to prevent and combat unemployment and inflation. It is obvious that the SNB should also be guided by this objective. The mandate contained in the economic article relates to the entire economic policy. Monetary policy is only one of the instruments at its disposal. It must first and foremost be supported and complemented by fiscal policy and competition policy. In the interest of an optimal overall effect, each instrument must be used according to its special properties. 15 In conducting monetary policy, it must be assumed that there is a tendency and longer-term link between the money supply and price stability. This is confirmed by teaching and experience. Ultimately, therefore, it is a matter of adapting the money supply appropriately to the real economic development. This ensures price stability in the best possible way. However, price stability is not an end in itself, but an essential contribution to creating the conditions for balanced economic development. Last but not least, it is an essential social concern, since the weakest members of the Community suffer most from inflation. The intention to formulate the mandate of monetary policy more concisely is based on these considerations. This is also desirable because the clear mandate appears to be a correlate to the relative independence of the SNB. Corresponding considerations were also decisive for the formulation of the mandate of the new European Central Bank. As a traditionally stability-conscious country, Switzerland must not lag behind European development for objective and psychological reasons. It is clear that the precise order is probably a necessary, but not a sufficient prerequisite for success. Ultimately, the decisive factor is consistent and persistent efforts. 5 Outlook 1998 was a difficult year. We have seen how disturbances in individual regions of the world can quickly spread to other areas. Financial market turbulence has unsettled investors and savers. In this situation, the central banks helped to calm the situation. The low inflation rates and the credibility they had gained with their monetary policy geared to price stability were favourable conditions for this. They made it possible to increase liquidity without raising inflation expectations. The cheap 16 Monetary conditions in Europe and the USA prevented the industrialised countries from falling into recession and thus destabilising the global economic situation even more. In Switzerland, the economic recovery has strengthened despite the difficult environment. Special factors such as the renewed sharp decline in oil prices led to a stable price level as measured by the consumer price index. The expected economic and price developments as well as the forecast course of monetary indicators speak in favour of a continued generous monetary policy. This decision has met with broad approval. However, this should not obscure the fact that in times of high price stability it will be more difficult to find understanding for the continuation of a stability-oriented monetary policy. Nevertheless, I am confident. The future will show that price stability and solid growth are compatible in the longer term. This will make the benefits of stable monetary conditions visible.
