In autumn 1977, for instance, international demand for our currency was so strong that the appreciation of the Swiss franc was getting out of control. The exchange rate was seriously jeopardising the balanced growth of the Swiss economy. In an attempt to reduce the demand for Swiss francs in foreign exchange markets, the Swiss National Bank saw no other way but to introduce a series of regulatory measures such as negative interest rates on Swiss franc deposits held by foreigners. Over time, Switzerland's comparative advantages based on its tradition of stability became fewer. Several countries had pushed down their inflation rate to levels similar to that of Switzerland. In this changed environment, the financial sector had to make new efforts in order to remain successful. One of these efforts was directed at developing an efficient and safe infrastructure for trading stocks, settling securities transactions and for interbank payments, and it has - as we can see today - achieved its aims to a large extent. These market developments and technological advances did not fail to have an influence on the Swiss National Bank. They concerned us most immediately in the following three areas: First, the risk of an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc - like that experienced in 1977 - has become much smaller. While at times the overvaluation of the franc may still be a problem, it no longer poses the same existential threat to our economy. In the last few years we have been able to avoid exchange rate distortions by means of purely market-oriented measures without building up inflation. We are confident that we will succeed in continuing this flexible policy. Our policy approach is clearly based on the view that we will best achieve our targets if we rely on truly open markets, a sound infrastructure and instruments that utilise rather than restrict - market processes. 5 The second example to demonstrate how internationalisation and technology have affected the Swiss National Bank is the implementation of monetary policy. Last year, we switched from foreign exchange swaps to repos as the main form of liquidity provision. Thanks to a new technological platform at the central securities depository SEGA, repos can now be settled in a safe, fast and inexpensive way. The implementation of monetary policy by means of repos instead of foreign exchange swaps has two decided advantages: a) repos bear fewer credit and settlement risks, and b) we are able to transact this form of business with more counterparties. Instead of just three or four, we now deal with some twenty partners. Starting this summer, our range of counterparties will include banks abroad, which underlines our willingness to operate as broadly as possible. Third, we support the financial sector in developing competitive, state-of-the-art trading, payment and settlement systems. Our main payment system, the twelveyear old Swiss Interbank Clearing system (SIC), was one of the first Real-Time Gross Settlement systems to be developed. Later, we were among the first to implement a Delivery-versus-Payment scheme that settled both the money and the securities leg on a transaction-by-transaction basis. Just recently, we added a new and also unique feature to our settlement infrastructure. Today, Switzerland offers a direct link between the stock exchange, securities settlement and the payment system. At the same time, we provide remote access to all three institutions, which, of course, includes a National Bank account. We thereby invite as many market players as possible to participate directly in our markets. We are convinced that the promotion of direct access enhances system stability. Thanks to these efforts and to the modern financial infrastructure they have produced, I am confident that the financial industry has good prospects for the future. But we know that innovation and flexibility are the key to success in today's dynamic markets. They have to be the industry's guiding principles independent of any future developments in the relationship between our country and the European Union, and also independent of the question of whether or not the Swiss franc will be replaced by the euro some day.

Title: The Swiss franc in the heart of Euroland
text: The Swiss franc at the heart of Euroland Message from Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank at lunch - debate of the Centre for European Policy Studies Brussels, 20 April 1999 2 At the beginning of this year, Europe entered a new phase in its monetary history. The mosaic of national currencies that we inherited from the 19th century is followed by the homogeneous whole of the euro. The single currency crowns and cements the achievements of economic integration and becomes the symbol of the community of destinies of the European nations. Switzerland stands on the sidelines of the common integration process. It develops its relations with its neighbours on a bilateral basis, thus choosing a slower, more difficult path, which is explained by its history and its present reality. Even if it is still lagging behind the integration process, my country is nevertheless very directly affected by the decisions of the European Union. This is the case in the field of trade in goods and services but also in that of money. The emergence of the euro is indeed a fundamental change in its financial environment, a change which cannot remain without effect on the conditions for the implementation of monetary policy. My presentation will address three points: - the likely consequences - for the Swiss economy - of the appearance of the euro, - the prospects for the cohabitation of the franc and the euro, - the implications of these changes for the monetary strategy of the Swiss National Bank. 1. The likely consequences for the Swiss economy of the emergence of the euro With the introduction of the euro, Switzerland is, for the first time, surrounded by a unified currency area. Until now, our monetary history has been marked by more or less harmonious relations between the franc and the currencies of our neighbours. In recent years, the increasing convergence brought about by the Maastricht Treaty had already led to a gradual standardisation of the monetary landscape. However, a decisive step was taken on 1 January with the final welding of the currencies of eleven countries of the European Union. This environmental change has both positives and negatives. Positive is necessarily the fact that our exporting companies can, from now on, operate in euros and that the exchange rate risk between the currencies of the Eleven has disappeared. The result is more efficient management of their liquidity and risks. Since the beginning of this year, several thousand euro-denominated accounts have been opened by Swiss banks for their customers, mainly export-oriented companies. Many companies now intend to offset their external revenue in euro with expenditure denominated in euros, or intend to ask their local suppliers to apply "euro" conditions to them. 3 Monetary unification is therefore a source of efficiency for a country largely open to European trade like Switzerland. That in itself is good news. It would indeed be a misunderstanding of the Swiss situation to imagine a Switzerland benefiting - on a net basis - from external monetary disorders. What is true of a few exchange rooms is not true for the entire economy. By way of example, I would simply point out that the fall of the Italian lira in the mid-nineties led to hasty and very painful adjustments in our textile industry and deeply depressed the Italian-speaking part of the country. If, at the time, the European monetary regime had been able to promote more discipline, such adjustments would not have been necessary or, at least, would not have been so brutal. Another consequence of monetary unification is the likely diminishing role of the Swiss franc as the settlement currency for our exports. This will be the natural consequence of the rise of the euro in Europe, a region where only 10 to 15% of GDP will now be gained outside Euroland. It is likely that Europe will thus be less and less willing to trade in other currencies, so that the role of the Swiss franc could become more modest. On the other hand - but this should only become very concrete from 2002 onwards - we will certainly see an increasing use of the euro as a settlement currency on Swiss territory itself. In mind, of course, we are tourists, European or otherwise, reluctant to change currency if they come to pass through the cramped territory of the Confederation. The acceptance of payments in euros and the dual display of prices could thus become the rule in border and tourist areas. The increased use of the euro as the invoicing currency for Swiss exports and as a means of payment within the country will result in an increasing exposure of our economy to exchange rate risk, which will make the exchange rate of the euro against the Swiss franc an essential parameter for the smooth running of business in Switzerland. Thus, the development of the euro market will gradually increase Switzerland's dependence on its immediate monetary environment. It is true that our freedom of manoeuvre in this area was already limited given the close commercial ties that traditionally unite Switzerland and the surrounding Europe. Tomorrow, surrounded by the single currency, our autonomy will be even more relative. 2. The prospects for the cohabitation of the franc and the euro As Switzerland becomes more fragile in the face of exchange rate risks, we need to ask ourselves about the prospects for the relationship between the franc and the euro, and then about the consequences for the SNB's policy of the uncertainties surrounding the future value of the euro against the Swiss franc. To want to make a forecast of the future relationship between the franc and the euro today is necessarily highly speculative because we have little evidence of appreciation. On the one hand, the history of the ECB is still very short; moreover 4 we realise that the conduct of monetary policy in a still heterogeneous European whole could run into difficulties. In view of these uncertainties, we can place important sources of convergence. Firstly, the macroeconomic objectives set by the European authorities and the Swiss authorities largely coincide. On both sides, price stability is seen as the goal of monetary action. This objective is explicitly reflected in the ECB's mandate, and it is the traditional aim of monetary policy in our country. Moreover, based on the experiences of recent months, there is every reason to believe that the strategies for implementing monetary policy by the ECB and the SNB will largely overlap. In both cases, attention will be paid to the development of monetary aggregates consistent with price stability in the medium term. In both cases too, this approach will be applied with the flexibility imposed by the constraints of the economic situation and often very changing situations on the financial markets. Secondly, experience shows that countries with similar macroeconomic objectives and close cyclical developments benefit from relatively stable exchange rates. Here, we must bear in mind the relationship that has developed between the franc and the German mark over the last fifteen years. Considered in real terms, this relationship has changed little, contrary to what has been observed between the franc and the lira or the franc and the dollar. If, tomorrow, the euro were to be the worthy successor to the mark, we have every reason to believe that the exchange rate relationship between the Swiss franc and the European currency will develop in an orderly manner. In this respect, the experience of the first three months of operation of the euro area is very encouraging for us. The relationship between the franc and the euro has been extraordinarily stable, with the value of the single currency fluctuating between 1.61 francs and 1.59 francs, i.e. within a very narrow fluctuation band. The volatility of the franc-euro relationship has so far been lower than that observed in 1998 in the franc-mark relationship. Interesting is also to note that our currency has not behaved in recent months as it traditionally did against a strong dollar. In the past, a certain correlation could be observed between the movements of the dollar and the mark against the franc. In the event of a strong dollar, the mark was also strengthened against the franc. This situation was simply due to the fact that our currency, whose market is narrower than that of the German currency, reacted more strongly than the latter against the dollar. 5 However, it is striking to note that nothing like this has manifested itself since the beginning of the year. The dollar appreciated against the euro by about 8%, while the euro-Swiss franc relationship remained virtually unchanged. It would therefore seem that our currency is now less affected by transfers between the euro and the dollar than previously by those between the dollar and European currencies. It is too early to draw any definitive conclusions, but this unusual calm must nevertheless be emphasized. The serene situation of recent months is perhaps only fortuitous. Since it is undeniable that European monetary unification involves uncertainties that lead us into little-known waters, particular vigilance is required. Let us now turn to the SNB's strategy in the new environment created by the euro. 3. The SNB's strategy in the environment created by the euro It is natural that the SNB did not wait until 1 January this year to draw up a strategy for the euro. We began to be concerned about the change in the monetary environment two years ago because the implementation phase of the single currency involved risks of destabilising the markets. Our action was to conduct a flexible liquidity policy, generously supplying the market when the demand for Swiss francs was particularly strong. We have also endeavoured to recall the European characteristics of our currency because it is obvious that, in terms of economic fundamental factors, the Swiss franc, the mark or the French franc today have such similarities that a different assessment by the markets would hardly be justified. This strategy has led to a significant fall in interest rates in Switzerland, which has not, however, led to an acceleration in monetary growth that is contrary to monetary stability in the medium term. Currently, the M3 money supply is growing at a trend rate of less than 2%, which remains modest compared to monetary growth in Euroland. Our policy in recent years has therefore been aimed at prevention rather than cure. Market experience has clearly taught us that tensions on the Swiss franc can hardly be eased by direct action. Prevention was therefore a natural necessity. This strategy seems to us to have borne the expected results. The franc, which was thought to be doomed to appreciate against European currencies, remained relatively stable. This success has, of course, greatly benefited from the orderly and credible progress of the European monetary integration process. 6 We are often asked whether, in the end, rather than operating autonomously, a unilateral pegging of the franc to a European standard - now to the euro - would not be the most elegant and effective response to the challenges posed by monetary integration. Would this not be proof, by our actions, that the Swiss economy will only prosper in a European environment and that the Swiss franc belongs to the family of European currencies? Those who propose it forget that monetary decisions can only be sustainable and stabilizing if they are well anchored in reality. Indeed, a unilateral peg of the franc to the euro - by fixing a parity between the two currencies - would not be perceived, today, by the markets as an irrevocable decision. As long as Switzerland is not part of the European Union and its institutions, any "clash" of the franc could be revised at a later date and any parity unilaterally declared by Switzerland could be the subject of discussions, in particular during accession negotiations. As the markets hate half-measures, the declared parity would not fail to entice speculation always looking for weak lines of defense. Instead of calming the situation, such a measure would only encourage speculative zeal. It therefore seems to us contraindicated to want to definitively set the monetary rules of our country, while the timetable for our integration into the European political environment is still uncertain. That would be putting the plow in front of the eggs. But, on the other hand, should we not also recognise that, between the Swiss and European realities, there are still gaps in the financial field that do not make it possible to precipitate things on the monetary level? Although they have come very close in recent years, the paths of monetary convergence between Europe and Switzerland have not yet come together. Our country lives in an environment of lower interest rates than its neighbours. To want to force monetary adjustment would inevitably force that of rates, a strategy that would be very painful in terms of the economy. In this respect, Switzerland's position is different from that of all the countries - with the exception of Germany - that have participated in monetary union. For the latter, the prospect of the single currency was also that of lower, German-level interest rates, which was seen as a future incentive for investment and a welcome reduction in public budgets. In our case, the monetary merger would mean, in the current environment, a recovery in interest rates of the order of 1.5%, in the short and long term. Such an adjustment would result in a rapid increase in the mortgage debt burden (a significant burden for Swiss households) and an additional - albeit gradual - burden on public budgets. Two structural changes that would lead to a deterioration in disposable income, and therefore to a decline in aggregate demand. 7 At present, therefore, the convergence between the monetary situations of Switzerland and the European Union - measured by the interest differential - has not been achieved. Will this situation change or will it remain an obstacle to our integration into the surrounding Europe? It is not possible to give a definitive answer to this question, which is so important for the assessment of the consequences of accession. Indeed, the difference in interest rates between the franc and the euro will reflect the perception that the markets will have of the fundamental characteristics of these two currencies. In this respect, we are likely to see a gradual change in the environment. Two factors will be essential: firstly, our economy will become increasingly dependent on the European environment because the single market will play an increasingly important role in the running of our business. Even more integrated into the European area, our country will see its economic cycle coincide closely with that of its major neighbours. Secondly, both faced with very similar situations, the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank are likely to apply policies that are similar to each other. These common foundations will naturally lead to converging monetary developments. As Europe asserts itself as a zone of stability, the pay gap between the euro and that of the Swiss franc will narrow. This process may take time, but as accession will only take place in the long term, markets and the economy will have the opportunity to adapt to the new monetary realities. In the end, if everything goes according to the plans drawn up in Maastricht, the Swiss franc will follow the path of the single currency ever closer. * * * The emergence of the euro has profoundly changed the context in which Swiss monetary policy is defined. The franc, which was already moving in the wake of the mark, has placed itself in line with the euro. While one could fear increased volatility due to the uncertainties of the moment, the stability of its price against the European currency was surprising. Although in monetary matters, markets take their time before being convinced of the sustainability of a situation, the developments of recent months are encouraging. They confirm the hopes that, with converging fundamentals and policies, the euro and the franc will evolve harmoniously. If this were to be the case, a convergence process will exist, which will allow Switzerland, at the time chosen for its accession to the European Union, to integrate into Euroland without difficulty.

Pour ces derniers, la perspective de la monnaie unique tait aussi celle de taux d'intrt plus bas, de niveau allemand, ce qui tait peru comme un encouragement futur  l'investissement et un allgement bienvenu des budgets publics. Dans notre cas, la fusion montaire signifierait, dans l'environnement actuel, un redressement des taux d'intrt de l'ordre de 1,5 %, sur le court comme sur le long terme. D'un tel ajustement rsulterait un alourdissement rapide de la charge des dettes hypothcaires (une charge importante pour les mnages suisses) et un poids supplmentaire - quoique progressif - pour les budgets publics. Deux modifications structurelles qui conduiraient  une dgradation du revenu disponible, donc  un flchissement de la demande globale. 7 Actuellement donc, la convergence entre les situations montaires de la Suisse et de l'Union europenne - mesure au diffrentiel d'intrt - n'est pas ralise. Cette situation voluera-t-elle ou restera-t-elle un obstacle  notre intgration  l'Europe environnante ? Il n'est pas possible d'apporter de rponse dfinitive  cette question si importante pour l'apprciation des consquences d'une adhsion. En effet, la diffrence des taux d'intrt entre le franc et l'euro va reflter la perception que les marchs auront des caractristiques fondamentales de ces deux monnaies. A cet gard, nous allons probablement assister  une modification progressive de l'environnement. Deux facteurs seront essentiels : en premier lieu, notre conomie deviendra de plus en plus dpendante de l'environnement europen car le grand march jouera un rle toujours plus important pour la marche de nos affaires. Plus intgr encore dans l'espace europen, notre pays verra son cycle conomique concider troitement avec celui de ses grands voisins. En second lieu, confrontes toutes deux  des situations fort semblables, la Banque centrale europenne et la Banque nationale suisse appliqueront probablement des politiques proches l'une de l'autre. Ces fondements communs conduiront naturellement  des dveloppements montaires convergents. Au fur et  mesure que l'Europe s'affirmera comme une zone de stabilit, l'cart entre la rmunration de l'euro et celle du franc suisse diminuera. Ce processus pourra prendre du temps, mais comme une adhsion n'interviendra que dans le long terme, les marchs et l'conomie auront le loisir de s'adapter aux nouvelles ralits montaires. En fin de compte, si tout se droule selon les plans dresss  Maastricht, le franc suisse suivra de toujours plus prs la trajectoire de la monnaie unique. * * * L'apparition de l'euro a profondment modifi le contexte dans lequel se dfinit la politique montaire suisse. Le franc, qui voluait dj dans le sillage du mark, s'est plac dans la ligne de l'euro. Alors que l'on pouvait craindre une volatilit accrue due aux incertitudes du moment, la stabilit de son cours face  la devise europenne a surpris. Bien qu'en matire montaire, les marchs prennent leur temps avant d'tre convaincus de la prennit d'une situation, les dveloppements de ces derniers mois sont encourageants. Ils confirment les espoirs que, disposant d'lments fondamentaux et de politiques convergents, l'euro et le franc volueront harmonieusement. Si tel devait tre le cas, un processus de convergence existera, qui permettra  la Suisse, au moment choisi pour son adhsion  l'Union europenne, de s'intgrer sans difficults dans l'Euroland.

Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the President of the Bank Council
text: Opening address by Mr Jakob Schonenberger, Chairman of the Bank Council, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 23 April 1999 Introduction As President of the General Assembly for the last time today, I would like to present a retrospective of the six years I spent at the head of the National Bank's Banking Board. What were the highlights of this period for the world economy in general and for Switzerland in particular? What were the issues that occupied the SNB? What problems did the issuing institute face? Finally, what were the main novelties? The year 1993 Let us briefly go back to 1993. In many respects, the economic situation was then in a gloomy light. In OECD member states, economic growth was around 1%, and cyclical disparities between these countries were widening. In Western Europe, unemployment was rising sharply. Both Germany and Japan were in recession. Only the United States and the United Kingdom were in a recovery phase. The increase in prices, which had already declined in previous years, continued its downward trend at the global level. In 1993, the European Monetary System (EMS) suffered its most serious crisis. Several currencies participating in the EMS exchange rate mechanism were in turn under severe pressure. In the end, the permissible fluctuation band had to be widened. Central banks in most industrialized countries have eased monetary policy. During that year, the SNB reduced its discount rate five times, from 6% to 4%. The sluggish economic situation has revived protectionist tendencies in several countries. 2 The Maastricht Treaty, which laid the foundations for the creation of the European Union (EU), entered into force in November 1993. It has also significantly strengthened the role of the European Parliament. In the second half of 1993, the Swiss economy began to show signs of improvement. Over the year as a whole, however, real gross domestic product fell by 0.5%. The labor market remained depressed, and the unemployment rate reached 4.5%. In Switzerland, the banking sector was already undergoing structural change. The number of banking institutions continued to decline as a result of mergers and takeovers. In this area, the most important event of 1993 was the takeover of Banque Populaire Suisse (BPS) by Credit Suisse Holding. In addition, several cantons have decided, as the National Bank wishes, to submit their cantonal banks to the supervision of the Federal Banking Commission. The years 1994 to 1997 The global economy The next four years were marked by generally strong growth in the world economy, although growth slowed in many countries in 1995. This loss of dynamism is attributable to the restrictive fiscal policy pursued at the time by many industrialized nations. In Germany, Japan and Switzerland, countries whose currencies had risen sharply, foreign trade also slowed the economic recovery. However, the real gross domestic product of OECD countries increased by 2.8% on average from 1994 to 1997. Fluctuations in growth rates have been particularly strong in Anglo-Saxon countries. On the European continent, the economic situation has somehow followed the trends observed in the United States and the United Kingdom. As for Japan, it has not managed to make a lasting recovery. It has even gotten worse. Southeast Asia first benefited from very high growth rates, then signs of overheating appeared. Also in Latin America, activity 3 economic has accelerated. In OECD countries, the restoration of price stability, the easing of monetary policy and, consequently, the decline in interest rates have contributed to the recovery of the economy. On average for the OECD area, the unemployment rate rose again slightly, mainly due to developments in continental Europe. In many countries, inflation has retreated to levels not seen since the mid-sixties. In several East Asian States, structural imbalances, which are early warning signs of the crisis that has meanwhile erupted in Asia, increased during 1997. The rise of the dollar in the foreign exchange markets has also aggravated the situation. The Asian financial crisis has also drawn attention to the structural problems of Latin American countries. The economic situation in Switzerland In Switzerland, the improvement in the economic situation from 1993 onwards has been strengthened, and then a weakening has been observed in our country since the autumn of 1994. Our real gross domestic product growth remained well below the OECD average. The difference is mainly due to the persistent problems of the real estate and construction markets, the savings efforts of public authorities, structural adjustments in industry and services, but also to the revaluation that the Franc has suffered as a result of the currency turbulence. In 1996, the economic situation in Switzerland continued to deteriorate, while the world economy was already restarting. As a result, our gross domestic product has declined. This recession was the result of both cyclical and structural factors. For the Swiss economy, the horizon did not begin to brighten significantly until 1997. The recovery was mainly based on exports, which rose sharply thanks to the acceleration of economic growth abroad and the weakening of the franc in 1996. In addition, private consumption regained some strength during the year, and investment in capital goods expanded further. On the other hand, 4 investment in construction and public consumption have once again declined. At the beginning of the period from 1994 to 1997, long-term interest rates rose sharply in the wake of the rise in yields served on capital markets abroad. Subsequently, they showed a downward trend, which continued until the end of 1997. Taking this movement into account, the SNB reduced its discount rate from 4% to 1% in six stages. Throughout this period, the increase in prices remained below 2%. In 1997, it fell to its lowest level since the end of the fifties, i.e. at 0.5%. Initially, the situation stabilized in our labour market. After reaching a record high of 5% in January 1994, the unemployment rate fell continuously until the end of 1995 and then rose again to a significant 5% in 1997. However, since 1997, the cantonal employment programmes and the economic recovery have led to a reduction in the number of unemployed in the statistics. Economic and financial milestones What events have particularly marked the economy and financial markets? Let me remind you of a few of them. The Treaty on the European Economic Area (EEA) entered into force on 1 January 1994. It established between the twelve States of the European Community (EC) and five States of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) a situation similar to that of an internal market as regards the movement of goods, services, capital and persons. As Switzerland has not joined the EEA and has sought through bilateral negotiations to create an appropriate framework for its trade with the EU. Also at the beginning of 1994, the second stage of economic and monetary union began, during which the European Monetary Institute (EMI) took office. The main tasks of the EMI were to lay the foundations for the common monetary policy of the Central Bank. 5 to strengthen cooperation between national central banks, to monitor the functioning of the European Monetary System and to make cross-border payment systems more efficient. While there was general calm in the EMS EXCHANGE rate mechanism, the dollar attracted attention in 1994 as it weakened sharply in the foreign exchange markets. Between January and December, it lost nearly 10% against the Swiss franc. On 1 January 1995, Austria, Finland and Sweden, three EFTA States, joined the EU. For example, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland remained members of EFTA. In early 1995, a financial crisis erupted in Mexico. The SNB also participated in the financial aid set up by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). This crisis temporarily shook confidence in the rapidly expanding financial markets of emerging economies and led to a fall in the dollar. To support the U.S. currency, the central banks of the major industrialized countries have repeatedly made concerted interventions in foreign exchange markets. Between December 1994 and December 1995, however, the dollar fell by more than 14% against the Swiss franc. In addition, tensions have arisen more than once in the EMS exchange rate mechanism. Within the EU, work on the introduction of the single European currency has continued. The ECB's monetary policy strategy has been defined. It is based on the combination of an inflation target and a monetary aggregate target. For the ECB, price stability prevails when the consumer price index does not increase by more than 2% per year. The ECB also sets a reference value for the growth of the monetary aggregate M3. In implementing its monetary policy, it uses primarily open market operations, mainly short-term repurchase agreements. I cannot fail to mention developments in the equity markets. In most countries, share prices rose throughout the period under review, with the exception of 1994. The lowering of interest rates from 6 1995 had a positive impact on prices. The Swiss Performance Index has recorded double-digit growth rates for several years in a row. However, the Asian crisis caused a global fall in prices in 1997. Structural change in Switzerland In recent years, the Swiss banking sector has been marked by major structural changes. The big banks, in particular, have announced restructurings in their operations in the Swiss market and the closure of many branches. The result has been a substantial decrease in jobs in this sector. The merger process continued with the consolidation of several banking institutions. In this connection, I would like to recall the takeover in 1994 of the majority of the shares of the Solothurn Kantonalbank by Bank Solothurn, a subsidiary of the former Swiss Bank Corporation. For the first time, a cantonal bank has thus passed into private hands. The status of the cantonal banks, in an environment characterised by increased competition, was then the subject of heated discussions. In a 1995 report on the situation of cantonal banks in the banking sector, the Cartel Commission considered that the guarantee given by the cantons for their banks' liabilities leads to unjustified distortions of competition and should therefore be abolished or at least restricted. Subsequently, other cantonal banks were fully or partially privatized. The New Bank of Aargau, which at the time was the largest regional bank in Switzerland, was taken over in November 1994 by CS Holding. In addition, the Swiss regional banks founded the RBA-Holding. Two-thirds of the establishments in this category have joined it. The others have for the most part secured the participation or cooperation of institutions of some importance. In addition, several banks have opted to strengthen their collaboration with life insurance companies, and others, for cooperation with foreign banks. Mergers of major financial sector companies reached their peak with the merger of Credit Suisse Group and Winterthur Swiss Company 7 insurance, then that announced in 1997 by the Union of Swiss Banks and the Swiss Bank Corporation. This latest merger created UBS, one of the world's largest financial institutions. The rationalization process also affected the equity market, since the Swiss Electronic Stock Exchange (BES) began operations at the end of 1995 and shortly thereafter auction trading was abandoned in favour of an electronic system. 8 Events in the immediate environment of the SNB Many events also took place in the immediate environment of the SNB. The launch of a new series of banknotes began in October 1995 and ended last year with the introduction of the 100-franc note. As a result, Switzerland now has arguably the most modern banknotes in the world in terms of security features. Discussions on Switzerland's financial relations during the Second World War were of great importance to the SNB and to our country as a whole. They focused on the volume and fate of the assets deposited in Switzerland before and during the Second World War by the victims of the National Socialist regime, on the gold transactions carried out by the National Bank during the war years and on the question of Nazi funds placed in Switzerland. These discussions generated many reactions. I would remind you in particular of the establishment of a Committee to clarify the question of assets whose holders have no longer been in contact with their bank, but also of a Commission of Historians to investigate the fate of assets that ended up in Switzerland following the advent of the National Socialist regime. In addition, a Fund for Victims of the Holocaust/Shoah in Need was established and the SNB contributed to its endowment. Internationally, the SNB has remained in the spotlight because of the collective complaint filed against it in the United States by victims of the Holocaust. After the agreement reached between the complainants and the major banks, the discussions have clearly lost their intensity. In the legislative field, work on the revision of the Federal Constitution, including the provisions governing money and the bank of issue, has been well under way. At the end of 1996, the Federal Council approved the revised draft of the new constitution and the related dispatch. However, the tabling of two parliamentary initiatives prompted the Federal Council to also launch a separate revision of the articles on money and on the bank of issue. 9 Thus, work on the two reform projects was conducted in parallel. With the 1997 partial revision of the National Bank Act, the maximum maturity of twelve months for investments that can be easily marketed abroad was abolished. Since then, the SNB has had the opportunity to invest its currencies for a longer term and thus obtain a better return. It may also use derivatives to manage market risks on foreign exchange reserves and to switch to gold repo operations with a view to more active management of its gold cash. As a result, it has been able to generate increased revenues. Conclusion It is time to close this retrospective. I have chosen, as you have no doubt noticed, not to address the most recent developments, knowing that the President of the Directorate-General will comment on them in his presentation. Overall, the last six years have been a turbulent period dominated by themes such as globalization, interdependence, rationalization, bancassurance, the replacement of old structures with new ones, but also the rereading of the past. For our part, we have been able to contribute directly to the resolution of a large number of problems, but - and this is inherent in the nature of things - many others have not yet found solutions. For both Switzerland and the SNB, the road ahead has not become easier in the new European environment. The policy of the issuing institution certainly remains a major challenge.

Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the Chairman of the Governing Board
text: Presentation by Mr. Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Executive Board, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 23 April 1999 Last year, the Swiss economy continued on the road to recovery, despite a difficult international environment. The favourable monetary framework conditions contributed decisively to this welcome development. After an overview of the economic situation in our country and our monetary policy, I will look at the economic and social problems that shook several regions of the world and had a profound impact on 1998. Next, I will return to two themes that I already commented on a year ago, namely the reform of the constitutional provisions on currency and the controversy over our past. 1. The economic situation in Switzerland According to the estimates available to us, Switzerland's real gross domestic product increased by more than 2% in 1998. From one year to the next, the growth of our economy has accelerated. However, the crises facing several regions of the world have had a significant impact, also in Switzerland. Exports, which had recovered strongly in 1997, stopped growing towards the end of 1998. These negative effects were, however, offset by favourable developments in domestic demand. The latter has benefited from decisive impulses from low interest rates, price stability and a return to an increase in household income. Private consumption provided important support to the economy. Thanks to the improvement in the labour market situation, consumer sentiment has recovered further. The turbulence that erupted in the summer in the financial markets has hardly tarnished this renewed confidence. In addition, business investment remained 2 remarkably vigorous. In this area, the impulses came mainly from the services sector, as momentum in the industrial sector weakened following a less favourable outlook. On the construction side, the recessionary trend has ended, but the recovery has still been modest. In private construction, demand increased slightly. On the other hand, civil engineering has slowed down, after benefiting in 1997 from the recovery programme adopted by Parliament. Stronger domestic demand has led to a strong expansion of imports, leading to a widening of the foreign trade deficit. A similar trend was observed in most other industrialized countries. On the other hand, many newly industrialized countries, whose currencies had lost much of their value, recorded growing trade surpluses. These divergent trends reflect the adjustment mechanisms under way at the international level, which enable the newly industrialized countries to overcome their economic crisis and return to the path of balanced growth. In industrialized countries, however, they cause temporary losses in growth. In the wake of the economic recovery, the unemployment rate in Switzerland has fallen from 5% at the end of 1997 to just over 3% today. Its decline, which surprised by its magnitude, is partly explained by statistical factors. Unemployed persons taking part in a cantonal employment programme or having an intermediate earnings do not enter the unemployment statistics. In addition, the unemployed at the end of their entitlements - there were about 40 000 in 1998, almost double the figure of the previous year - are also excluded from the statistics. Nevertheless, a turning point has clearly been observed in the labour market. Employment increased for the first time in this decade, and the number of vacancies increased. This encouraging development attests to the flexibility of our labour market and its actors, both for employees and employers. However, structural changes remain perceptible. Above all, they affect the 3 least skilled workforce. Labour market and, above all, training policies must take this into account. 2. Monetary policy For 1998, we announced the continuation of our broad monetary policy. We planned to adapt the supply of money to the increase in demand and thus keep money market interest rates low. On an annual average, economic growth has met our expectations. However, cyclical risks increased during the year. As I have already pointed out, the impact of the Asian crisis on exports has become increasingly apparent. In addition, the Swiss franc began to appreciate sharply from the middle of the year onwards as a result of the turbulence on the financial markets. Between July and October, the franc rose by 5%, in real terms and after weighting by exports. To ensure that the economic recovery is not threatened, we have counteracted this trend towards a firm franc by strengthening the supply of money to the market. We also took into account the fact that the banks, in a more uncertain environment, wanted to hold, in the form of central money, a higher precautionary cash. In the fourth quarter, the situation in the financial markets calmed down significantly, thanks in particular to the fall in official interest rates in the United States. The upward pressure on the franc then also faded. On an annual average, short-term interest rates have fallen only slightly, in contrast to long-term rates, which have fallen sharply. The average yield on federal bonds fell to 2.8%, a level not seen since the late fifties. This decline was largely due to increased investor preference for safer government securities. It was also supported by falling inflation expectations and continued efforts to consolidate federal finances. Despite the trend towards revaluation 4 observed in the second half of the year, the Swiss franc rose only slightly from one year to the next, in real terms and after weighting by exports. As a result, monetary framework conditions were generally slightly more favourable than in 1997. After rising by about 0.5% in 1997, the consumer price index remained stable in 1998. The prices of petroleum products, which have fallen sharply, have contributed significantly to this stability. The continued decline in telecommunications prices has also played a moderating role. It offset a slight increase in private sector services. The increase in VAT at the beginning of 1999 led as expected to an increase in consumer prices. So far, however, these impacts have remained moderate. For the current year, we plan to maintain our broad monetary policy. We thus take into account the expected slowdown in the economic situation. We expect real growth of 1.5%. Available production capacity should be moderately stretched; therefore, there will be no further upward pressure on prices. Similarly, the evolution of monetary indicators is in line with the direction we intend to give to our policy; the growth of M3 in particular is not expected to accelerate sharply. Recently, we have allowed interest rates to fall in the money market and, in the wake of the European Central Bank, cut our discount rate by half a point to 0.5%. The changeover to the euro at the beginning of 1999 went remarkably well. Since then, the exchange rate relationship between the euro and the franc has fluctuated within a narrow margin. There is good reason to believe that it will continue to evolve in this way for the rest of the year. This confidence is based above all on the fact that the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank pursue a similar monetary policy in terms of both objectives and operational strategies. Both institutes aim for a degree 5 high price level stability, in the interest of balanced economic growth. For both the European Union and Switzerland, the achievement of monetary union has fundamentally changed the monetary landscape. Even if the euro has a high chance of becoming a stable currency, surprises cannot be ruled out. We will therefore closely follow developments in this area and take them into account in the regular reviews of the situation. 3. International developments In 1998, there were also economic and social crises in various parts of the world. These crises have had repercussions, particularly on the financial markets. Leaving Thailand in 1997, we remember, they then reached South Korea, Indonesia and Malaysia, then reached, in 1998, above all Russia and Brazil. In both Russia and Brazil, public finances have been the main cause of the difficulties. In recent years, Russia has failed, in its social context, to put the state's finances in order. Due to a complex and poorly applied tax system, state revenues have consistently fallen short of budgeted amounts. The latest consolidation programme of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has also not brought any improvement. Established last summer, it was financed largely through the use of general arrangements to borrow. Switzerland, as a member of the Group of Ten, contributed CHF 750 million. In mid-August, the link between the ruble and the dollar was eased, and then completely abolished. The Russian currency then fell, and the government declared a moratorium on the repayment of Russian private sector debts to foreign private creditors. In the second half of 1998, the crisis worsened in Brazil. The substantial public expenditure surplus and the large current account deficit have brought many observers to the country. 6 as abroad, to analyze with a more critical eye the situation in Brazil, hence downward pressure on the Brazilian currency. A financial package was then put together, at international level, to help clean up the situation and prevent a fall in the real. Switzerland participated in this with loans granted on the basis of the Federal Decree on Switzerland's cooperation in international measures and the IMF's new arrangements to borrow. However, this aid was only a short-lived success. At the beginning of 1999, the real had to be floated, which led to a sharp depreciation of the Brazilian currency. The countries of East Asia, to which I have already referred, have also experienced difficult times. Those who have concluded a consolidation programme with the IMF and have begun to implement it systematically, however, seem to have crossed the trough of the wave. Their currencies have regained much of the ground they had ceded, and financial markets have stabilized. Reforms are progressing in the financial sector. As a result, the outlook is not unfavourable today. One of the questions raised by the crises of recent years concerns the functioning of the international monetary and financial system. Critical voices have been heard, in particular, on the overly rapid opening of hitherto protected national economies to international capital movements, the behaviour of international investors in the face of risks, and the programmes, considered unsuited to the situation, drawn up by the IMF. These criticisms are not without any basis. Thus, within the framework of the IMF, we have repeatedly warned of the dangers of opening up capital markets too precipitously. Liberalization is fundamentally desirable, but it can only succeed if macroeconomic conditions, particularly with regard to financial markets, are stable. International investors frequently underestimate the risks arising from their holdings in newly industrialized countries. Often 7 they neglect the importance to be attached to an appropriate balance between economic and social developments. In addition, they tend to rely too easily on the guarantees, official or unofficial, of the debtor countries. On the subject of the IMF, they believe that the IMF will provide support in all cases. Recent experiences will lead to the necessary lessons. Criticism of IMF policy is not incomprehensible, but often appears to be exaggerated. Since its foundation half a century ago, this institution has been torn between two requirements, namely to strengthen the individual responsibility of the Member States, on the one hand, and to make funds available to facilitate adjustment processes, on the other. In addition, it should be remembered that the IMF is ultimately unable to enforce its recommendations and that its resources are still too low to meet the needs. Sufficiently stable exchange rate relations are essential for international economic collaboration. It is sometimes forgotten that it is primarily up to each country to create the necessary conditions by pursuing a sound long-term economic policy. Administrative regulations do not offer an alternative. This is why the proposal to introduce target zones for the exchange rates of the main currencies leaves one sceptical. For a state, the best way to serve international collaboration is first and foremost to put its own house in order. 4. The reform of the constitutional provisions on currency The adaptation of the constitutional provisions on money to the requirements of our time is on track. An important step was taken with the approval by the people and the cantons of the updating of the federal constitution. It contains an article on money that reflects our monetary regime as it is applied in reality. The outdated attachment of the Swiss franc to gold has disappeared from the constitution. A 8 new legal basis to create the conditions to change the valuation of gold on our balance sheet and to better manage our gold cash. The separate reform of the constitutional article on the currency, submitted to Parliament by the Federal Council's dispatch of May 1998, has also made good progress in recent months. The clarification proposed by the Federal Council of the SNB's mandate gave rise to discussion. However, in both the National Council and the Council of States, a majority considered the proposed version to be balanced. According to this text, the SNB must conduct monetary policy in the general interest of the country, while giving priority to price stability. The formulation chosen emphasizes the general interest. It also implies that a monetary policy based on price stability provides the best possible contribution to balanced economic developments. By price stability, we mean an increase in prices of less than 2%. Once again, I would like to stress that the objective of price stability is also in the interests of the weakest sections of society. The draft separate reform also incorporates the rule governing the distribution of profits. As we know, this rule requires the SNB to pay two thirds of its net profit to the cantons and one third to the Confederation. The Federal Chambers also approved the provision requiring the SNB to hold the monetary reserves, partly in the form of gold, which are necessary for its mission. Part of the current monetary reserves, which corresponds to approximately half of the gold cash of 2600 tonnes, will be available for other public purposes in the future. The National Council and the Council of States considered that, for the future use of these assets, a special constitutional basis must be created, which would allow derogation from the ordinary rule governing the distribution of profit. While the National Council supplemented the draft constitutional article on the currency with an additional paragraph, the Council of States preferred to add a transitional provision to the constitution. The solution adopted by the Council of States 9 refers explicitly to the monetary reserves which the SNB will no longer need, at the time of entry into force of that Article, for the conduct of its monetary policy. It thus rightly emphasises the uniqueness of the allocation of surplus monetary reserves for other public purposes. 5. The controversy over the past The controversy over our past continued to occupy us during the year 1998. In the spring, the Independent Commission of Experts Switzerland- World War II published its interim report on Switzerland's gold operations during the Second World War. The report confirms in all the data that were already known. But it also focuses on two aspects. First, he considers that the argument of the good faith of the leaders of the time is not defensible. Secondly, he estimated that about 120 kilograms of gold from the concentration camps had in the 336 tons transferred by the Reichsbank of Germany in the deposit it had at the National Bank. There is nothing, however, the report expressly points out, that the leaders of the time were aware of the real origin of this gold. We have taken a public position on the interim report and consider that it does not lead to a significant change in the assessment of the SNB's policy during the Second World War. Therefore, we considered that the measures taken so far are appropriate. We also reaffirmed our commitment to continue to support efforts to clarify this chapter in the history of the SNB. Over the past year, we have also had to carefully manage the situation following the filing of a collective complaint against the Swiss National Bank in the United States. 10 From a legal point of view, we have held that the National Bank, as the central bank of a sovereign State, enjoys immunity in the United States and fundamentally challenged the jurisdiction of an American court in this matter. We have therefore announced our determination to oppose, by all available legal means, this collective complaint. Subsequently, the major banks against which collective complaints had been filed reached an agreement. We have always had understanding for the banks' efforts to find an out-of-court solution. We therefore welcomed this result and were pleased to note that the agreement also includes the complaint against us. As we did not take part in the negotiations that led to the conclusion of this agreement, we rejected any participation in the financing of the sum to be paid. A financial contribution from the SNB would have made the agreement official, which, in my view, would not have served the general interests of the country. We have stressed on several occasions - including last year, when the controversy was in full swing - that we regret the grey areas surrounding the attitude of the SNB during the difficult period of the war. For us, the official efforts underway are likely to shed light, and convincingly, on our past. When the time comes, the Government, Parliament and the people will have the opportunity to make a definitive assessment and decide on possible follow-up. Perspectives The past year has also brought us a mix of continuity and change. Overall, our economy has evolved in line with expectations. After years of stagnation and profound structural changes, it has regained momentum. However, the difficult international environment has contributed to the weakening of the recovery. It is a question of continuing to improve the conditions that, on the human and material levels, lead to economic success. In this respect, it is not necessary to 11 not to lose sight of the imperatives of economic competitiveness and social balance. This is the only way to ensure cohesion within society. International events, near and far, compel us to draw the necessary conclusions. International collaboration, which is fundamentally desirable, can only be ensured in the long term if each country manages to put its own house in order as a matter of priority. In many cases, outside help is needed. However, it can only be effective if it complements measures taken within the country itself. The implementation of these principles is a long and difficult process. However, it would be illusory to believe that they could be replaced by a simple, and even less expensive, alternative. I cannot conclude my briefing without thanking all those who have supported us, by their words and deeds, in the accomplishment of our mission. To you, dear shareholders, I would like to express my gratitude for the interest you have in our work and which you are once again demonstrating through your presence here.
