L'application de standards internationaux de scurit et de transparence vise  mettre en place une infrastructure institutionnelle capable de rendre plus stable et plus fiable le processus d'allocation des ressources dans le monde. 15 Conclusions Le chemin vers la consolidation du systme financier international sera long et, sur bien des points, controvers. Assurment, aucune formule magique ne permettra de rsoudre rapidement les problmes. Pour relever efficacement le dfi, nous avons davantage besoin dartisans engags et comptents que d'architectes appels  redessiner les plans de ldifice financier international. Il serait trs fcheux que le retour  un certain calme sur les marchs financiers, tel que nous lobservons aujourdhui, ralentisse les travaux en cours. Les cots sociaux des crises financires sont en effet si levs quil vaut la peine de fournir de grands efforts pour accomplir des progrs, mme modestes, dans le renforcement de la stabilit du systme financier international. Je vous remercie de votre attention.

Title: The euro: a first assessment
text: The euro: first assessments Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-President of the Executive Board of the Swiss National Bank General Assembly of the Jura Chamber of Commerce and Industry Saignelegier, May 18, 1999 2 The euro was born just five months ago. As it normally takes years until a new currency builds a character, or more precisely a reputation on the markets, the establishment of a first balance sheet, after such a short time, can only be temporary. Similarly, forecasts based on such a short experience are necessarily largely speculative. With these reservations in mind, let me give you my assessment of these first months of the single currency's existence. No appreciation of the Swiss franc The introduction of the euro began to preoccupy the financial markets well before January 1999. Investors, commercial banks, central banks, international financial institutions, all had been training their expectations and strategies for the new European currency for two years already. The SNB, too, had been thinking about the likely impact of the euro on the Swiss economy and the monetary response it could give to possible market disturbances. During the implementation phase of the single currency, the scenario considered most likely by observers was that the introduction of the euro would be linked to a great deal of uncertainty that could cause turbulence. The initial phase would therefore be characterized by relatively high volatility in exchange rate relations. After this first uncertain period, the euro would establish itself as a strong and stable currency, due to the institutional provisions of the Maastricht Treaty and the large current account surplus of the euro area. This scenario did not come true, the introduction of the euro went smoothly and did not lead to any particular turbulence in the markets. In fact, the nervousness observed last year in the financial markets was not due to the euro but to the financial difficulties of some emerging countries. The phase of introduction of the single currency has therefore proceeded better than expected. 3 When it comes to market development in recent months, things have also taken an unexpected turn. The forecast of a strong euro against the dollar has not yet been verified. On the contrary, the euro has shown weakness against the US currency, falling by about 9% since the beginning of the year. This decline is not inexplicable, it can be attributed to the cyclical differences between the United States and the euro zone. While America has entered the ninth year of still remarkably strong growth, a significant slowdown in the economy has been felt since last autumn in Europe. The outlook was thus for rising interest rates in the United States while a downside potential existed in Europe. For Europeans, however, the cyclical weakness of the euro against the dollar is perceived as a problem because it does not facilitate the establishment of the reputation of the new currency on the markets. Whatever the origin of the euro's weakening, the European Central Bank has been placed in an environment that has not allowed it to convincingly deploy its monetary strategy. The best proof that the markets are first and foremost under the influence of a strong dollar is the extraordinary stability that has emerged between the euro and the Swiss franc, a traditionally strong currency and even a safe haven currency. Since the beginning of the year, the relationship between the euro and the franc has fluctuated between 1.5877 and 1.6185. This is an extremely narrow fluctuation band, since the difference between the highest and lowest prices is only 1.9%. To better illustrate the degree of stability between the two currencies, it should be recalled that the maximum fluctuation band allowed between the Danish krone and the euro under EMS II is 4.5%. It should also be noted that the volatility of the exchange rate between the franc and the euro during the first five months of this year was only two-thirds of that observed between the franc and the mark during 1998. The high degree of stability between the franc and the euro has come as a surprise, but there is no shortage of reasons for this phenomenon. The Swiss economy is so heavily integrated into the European economy that our business cycle practically coincides with that of the euro area, and more particularly with that of the "core" of the euro area, Germany and France. Like these countries, the economic recovery in Switzerland has 4 started in 1997 and was initially driven by exports. Then, in 1998, growth strengthened while relying more on domestic demand. Currently, there is a slowdown in growth both in Switzerland and in the surrounding Europe. A slight cyclical improvement is expected only in the second half of the year. Just as cyclical divergences with the United States have caused a depreciation of the euro and the Swiss franc against the dollar, the parallelism of the economic situation between Switzerland and its neighbours reinforces the stability of the franc/euro exchange rate. In my opinion, however, cyclical parallelism alone is not enough to explain the degree of exchange rate stability. Equally important is the convergence of Swiss and European monetary policies. Indeed, the policy of the two central banks is similar in both objectives and strategy. Both banks aim for price stability. In the case of the European Central Bank (ECB), this aim is explicitly set out in the Maastricht Treaty. The SNB's mandate is not as explicit, but it has always been interpreted in such a way as to give priority to price stability. In addition, the institutional framework allows the two central banks to conduct their policies independently. At the strategic level, both banks focus on the development of monetary aggregates while taking into account other indicators such as the state of the economy and the situation on the financial markets. A convergence in action and in situations has led the markets to consider the franc and the euro as close currencies. The use of the euro in Switzerland: the first steps If the first experiences with the euro are particularly positive from the point of view of Swiss monetary policy, what about the use of the euro in our country? Is the single currency being established as a parallel currency? According to the observations made so far and according to a survey of enterprises, this is not 5 not the case. The euro seems to be gaining ground only - and still modestly - in outward-looking sectors. However, there is an increasing number of euro accounts with banks. These accounts are useful in the context of asset management because they allow the subsidy of interest or repayments from the euro area by avoiding fees when reinvesting in euros. They also have the advantage, unlike the old foreign currency accounts, of being remunerated. Many euro accounts have also been opened by exporting companies. Given the close economic relations between Switzerland and the euro area, Swiss exports to European countries will increasingly be charged in euros. In addition, some exporting companies want to source more and more from Euroland or pay their suppliers in euros as well. Thus, the effects of possible exchange rate movements on margins are neutralised, at least partially, because the possibilities for exporting companies to pay their expenses in euros are not unlimited. In particular, wage costs form a hardly compressible share of production costs denominated in Swiss francs. To our knowledge, nothing has changed in this area despite often shattering statements before the arrival of the euro. This is good because our exporting companies must actively manage the exchange rate risk and not seek to push it down the production process. Finally, the European currency cannot be expected to become a widely accepted means of payment until the euro exists in cash form. This will not be the case until 2002. The dual display of prices in some hotels, restaurants and shops in tourist areas may then become commonplace. Things are moving slowly in Switzerland, but they are moving just as slowly in the Euroland countries. The euro is still largely unknown to the public. It will only start operating in euros when national currencies are disappearing. 6 The hesitant functioning of the European Central Bank Let us now return to the European Central Bank and its policy. For us Swiss, the experience of these first months of activity of the European Central Bank has been positive. But it must be acknowledged that this period was not easy for the new authorities in Frankfurt and that some question marks remain. First, the ECB took over the monetary torch at a time when the economy in Europe was beginning to weaken. The European unemployment rate remains very high and fell only slightly during the previous short phase of growth. In many areas, the structural reforms needed to create jobs have only been partially undertaken or have remained wishful thinking. Under these conditions, there was a risk of political pressure on the new European Central Bank to adopt a pro-cyclical policy. Yet, in an effort to prevent such pressure, the last act of the eurozone's national central banks was to lower interest rates last December. Despite this, political pressure has not failed to manifest itself. The interventions of the former German finance minister, Lafontaine, have largely paralyzed the new central bank anxious to establish its reputation. Since the reshuffle of the German government, however, relations between the ECB and the political authorities have normalised. The fact that the ECB has been the object of political attacks is not surprising because of the imbalance that the European institutions present today. Indeed, at European level, the ECB has the responsibility to conduct the common monetary policy but, in front of it, there is no European government in charge of macroeconomic policy. This institutional imbalance - unique in the organisation of the industrialised countries - places, and will always place, the ECB in a difficult political situation unless there is very strong support from national governments. This support is likely to be lacking when the economic situation is difficult. Beyond these difficulties inherent in the construction of the ECB, it is quite normal for a newly created institution to go through a learning phase. 7 This is all the more understandable when it comes to an international institution formed by eleven member countries, with "external posts" (the national central banks) in each country and with collaborators from all these different countries. Moreover, the ECB carries out its functions in particularly difficult circumstances. It must conduct monetary policy for the eleven members of the Monetary Union using new instruments and without having experience on the macroeconomic mechanisms of operation of the zone. Moreover, with the introduction of a single currency, economic relations that were valid only yesterday may no longer be valid today. In these circumstances, flexibility and pragmatism are required because previously acquired knowledge must be continually questioned. This is a necessity and has nothing to do with a lack of principles, but it is necessarily a handicap in gaining credibility with regard to the markets. The authority of the ECB is not yet firmly established. This is understandable but should encourage us to be cautious even if, on the trend, there are many factors of convergence. Encouraging prospects Let us now turn our gaze to the future. What are the prospects for the European Central Bank and the euro, and more specifically, what to expect from the exchange rate between the Swiss franc and the euro? As regards the functioning of the European Central Bank, increased cooperation within the euro area will lead to greater convergence of economic situations. In this process, the emergence of conflicts of interest and friction cannot be ruled out, but over time greater cohesion is to be expected. On the technical side, the Bank will continue to gain experience and knowledge on monetary policy in the euro area. With the possible enlargement of the euro area to other members of the European Union or to other members, new 8 difficulties will arise that will have to be overcome by existing institutions or by their adaptation. Let us not forget that all national monetary regimes have evolved over time and experience. Relations between the ECB and the political authorities will depend largely on economic developments. Some expect monetary policy to put Europe back on the path to growth. The capacity of the monetary authorities is limited in this respect because the creation of new jobs today requires more the creation of a climate of confidence, the flexibilization of the labour market, sound fiscal policies, than monetary stimulus. The recent rate cut in Europe has also created very favourable conditions in this respect. If the relay of structural adjustments does not intervene, the benefit of the rate cut will be greatly diluted. A lack of momentum in the efforts to make European economies more flexible could therefore remain a burden on the value of the euro, even if Euroland is able to generate a significant external surplus. The euro's ability to establish itself as a reference currency will ultimately depend on the success of structural reforms and European growth prospects. As far as the franc/euro relationship - so important for our economy - is concerned, I do not expect any abrupt changes. While there is no guarantee that the value of the euro will always fluctuate in a narrow band as it has so far, the convergence of the fundamental factors of Switzerland and the euro area should ensure relative exchange rate stability. It must also be recognised that we face the same problems as our neighbours and that we often have the same difficulties as they do in providing adequate solutions to our difficulties. This community of destiny leads to monetary convergence. Conclusion: trust and vigilance The introduction of the euro went smoothly. Markets remained calm, and the relationship between the franc and the euro showed remarkable stability. 9 The initial euphoria was somewhat dampened by the euro's decline against the dollar and by the public debate on the ECB's interest rate policy. Things have now stabilized. The relationship between the euro and the dollar has adapted to the different economic outlook on both sides of the Atlantic and the recent cut in European rates has put an end to speculation about the ECB's policy. From a Swiss point of view, the first experiences with the euro are positive. The single currency is beginning to be used as a unit of account. Developments in this area will be little marked as long as the euro is not a means of payment used by the general public. The use of the euro in Switzerland seems to be growing at the same slow pace as in the Euroland countries themselves. The positive experience of recent months contributes to strengthening our confidence in the future stability of the relationship between the franc and the euro. In this respect, it is first and foremost the fundamental elements of the economies concerned that will play an essential role. The broad convergence of economic situations and prospects between Switzerland and its neighbours is the best guarantee of maintaining a situation of relative stability. The experience of a few months, however, is too short to draw definitive conclusions. The conduct of monetary policy in the euro area is a delicate undertaking due to regional economic differences and the ECB's action remains under the critical attention of markets and politics. In these circumstances, vigilance is required at all levels. At the level of companies, which must guard against the illusion that the exchange rate risk between the franc and the euro has now disappeared. At the level of the National Bank, of course, for whom the uncertainty of the European environment remains an important component of its assessment of the situation.

Il convient aussi de reconnatre que nous sommes confronts aux mmes problmes que nos voisins et que nous avons souvent les mmes difficults qu'eux  apporter  nos difficults des solutions adquates. Cette communaut de destin conduit  la convergence montaire. Conclusion: confiance et vigilance L'introduction de l'euro s'est droule en douceur. Les marchs sont demeurs calmes, la relation entre le franc et l'euro a fait preuve d'une remarquable stabilit. 9 L'euphorie initiale a quelque peu t attnue par la baisse de l'euro face au dollar et par le dbat public sur la politique des taux d'intrt de la BCE. Les choses se sont maintenant stabilises. La relation entre l'euro et le dollar s'est adapte aux perspectives conomiques diffrentes de part et d'autre de l'Atlantique et la rcente baisse des taux europens a mis un terme aux spculations sur la politique de la BCE. D'un point de vue suisse, les premires expriences avec l'euro sont positives. La monnaie unique commence  tre utilise comme unit de compte. Les dveloppements dans ce domaine seront peu marqus tant que l'euro ne sera pas un moyen de paiement utilis par le grand public. L'utilisation de l'euro en Suisse semble se dvelopper au mme rythme lent que dans les pays de l'Euroland eux-mes. L'exprience positive de ces derniers mois contribue  renforcer notre confiance dans la stabilit future de la relation entre le franc et l'euro. A cet gard, ce sont d'abord les lments fondamentaux des conomies concernes qui joueront un rle essentiel. La large convergence des situations et des perspectives conomiques entre la Suisse et ses voisins est la meilleure garantie du maintien d'une situation de relative stabilit. L'exprience de quelques mois est toutefois trop courte pour tirer des conclusions dfinitives. La conduite de la politique montaire dans la zone euro est une entreprise dlicate en raison des diffrences conomiques rgionales et l'action de la BCE reste sous l'attention critique des marchs et de la politique. Dans ces conditions, la vigilance s'impose  tous niveaux. Au niveau des entreprises, qui doivent se garder de l'illusion que le risque de change entre le franc et l'euro a maintenant disparu. Au niveau de la Banque nationale, videmment, pour qui l'incertitude de l'environnement europen reste une composante importante de son apprciation de situation.

Title: Swiss monetary policy in the midst of the euro area: An illusive independence?
text: Swiss monetary policy in the middle of the eurozone, an illusory independence? Georg Rich Director of the Swiss National Bank Centre d'etudes bancaires et Association Bancaire Tessinoise Vezia, 19 May 1999 2 1 Introduction The introduction of the euro at the beginning of 1999 proceeded without major problems. In the run-up to the changeover to the single currency, there was often talk in Switzerland of the fear that the franc would become a safe haven, hence a revaluation of our currency and, therefore, a threat to the competitiveness of our industry. This fear, as we see today, was exaggerated. Indeed, the advent of the single currency did not trigger big waves on the foreign exchange markets. The relatively quiet changeover to the euro is not in itself a surprise. Even before the introduction of the single currency, the markets had become convinced that the euro would be a safe and stable currency. Of course, it cannot be ruled out that they will one day revise their judgment. After the reshaping of the European monetary landscape, what is the likelihood of fluctuations that are detrimental to our economy? The European Central Bank (ECB), which is responsible for conducting monetary policy in the euro area, has been given a specific task as it must give priority to price stability. I have no doubt that the ECB will do its utmost to fulfil its mandate in the best possible way. If it preserves price stability in the euro area, the exchange rate relationship between the euro and the Swiss franc should remain within reasonable limits. However, the ECB will not have an easy task. Several obstacles could indeed stand in its way:  The ECB must conduct its monetary policy in a completely new environment, characterised by a single money market and capital market for the entire euro area. The transformation of European financial markets due to the changeover to the euro is likely to weaken the reliability of the indicators the ECB needs to set the course for its monetary policy. Properly balancing monetary policy could then become a delicate problem, a source of breakdowns.  Second, the ECB must conduct a uniform monetary policy for the entire euro area. Unlike the national central banks before 1999, it can no longer take account of the specific characteristics of each country. Since 3 At the beginning of the year, it is no longer possible to compensate for regional disparities within the euro area by exchange rate adjustments. Compensation for these inequalities must be done through other channels. While flexible, labour and goods markets play a particularly important regulatory role. However, in most euro area countries, labour markets, especially labour markets, are characterised by many rigidities. It is therefore not excluded that regional disparities and, consequently, unemployment problems will worsen within the euro area. The ECB, under increasing pressure, could then turn away from its original mission and pay more attention to the fight against unemployment.  Finally, sound public finances are an important condition for the success of a monetary policy based on price stability. In recent years, EU countries have made efforts to meet the criteria for participation in the euro and thus made great strides in consolidating their finances. To enable the ECB to effectively fulfil its stability mandate, these states should not relax their fiscal policy after the introduction of the euro. As we can see, considerable challenges await the European Central Bank. They could, sooner or later, erode the confidence that the markets currently have in the euro. What means would the SNB be available if a loss of confidence in the euro were to lead to an undesirable rise in the Swiss franc? 2 Means of action of the SNB As we have often said, we are not helpless in the face of undesirable fluctuations in exchange rates. Fundamentally, we can counteract too much of a swiss franc revaluation by easing our monetary policy. However, this is a delicate balancing act: if we let go of too much ballast, we run the risk of fuelling inflation in the medium term. In the past, it has been clear to us on several occasions that the stability of 4 Change, desired by the economy, was not necessarily reconcilable with our mandate to ensure, also in the medium term, price stability. The monetary policy we have pursued in recent years clearly illustrates our possibilities and the limits of exchange rate action. The sharp acceleration of inflation in Switzerland in 1989 and 1990 led the SNB to tighten the monetary reins. Swiss short-term interest rates then rose to over 9% at the beginning of 1990. They then remained between 8% and 9% for the next two and a half years (Chart 1). The rise in interest rates has plunged Switzerland into a recession that has deepened with the profound structural changes in our economy and the need to consolidate public finances. Towards the end of 1991, inflation began to decline, first timidly, frankly then frankly. This allowed the SNB to ease its monetary policy. From the summer of 1992, Swiss short-term interest rates began to fall and then stabilised at around 4% at the end of 1993. At the beginning of 1994, signs of a recovery of the Swiss economy multiplied. However, the recovery was short-lived. Already in the second half of 1994, growth began to slow down once again. The reason for this disappointing business situation in Switzerland can be found in the evolution of exchange rates. In both nominal and real terms, the Swiss franc appreciated significantly between 1993 and 1995, after weakening for several phases in previous years (Figure 2). The firmness of the franc essentially reflected the then widespread doubts about the stability of the future euro, doubts that made our currency a safe haven. In 1995, the franc reached heights that seriously threatened the competitiveness of Swiss industry. Its surge caused, especially in 1996, a new sharp fall in the economic situation and posed a real danger of deflation in Switzerland. As a result, the SNB further eased its monetary policy in the spring of 1995. As a result, growth in monetary aggregates accelerated markedly (Graph 3), and shortterm interest rates fell below 2% at the end of 1995. Since then, the SNB has, in several stages, further loosened the bridle; currently, short-term interest rates are slightly below 1%. 5 The change in monetary course did not immediately affect exchange rates. The franc did not weaken until the end of 1995, first timidly and then more frankly, between August 1996 and January 1997, after a further easing of monetary policy. At the beginning of 1997, the Swiss economy restarted. In 1997 and 1998, it reached respectable growth rates, and unemployment fell. Despite the recovery in the economy, prices remained stable in Switzerland. However, the crisis in East Asia, Russia and South America has cast a shadow over this pleasing picture. Even today, it weighs on economic growth in Switzerland and neighbouring countries. However, it is difficult to make a reliable prognosis on the repercussions of the international crisis on the Swiss economy, as domestic demand, which is still robust, mitigates the effects of the significant weakening of exports. For our part, we still expect real gross domestic product growth of 1.5% in 1999, i.e. a slowdown compared to the performance of more than 2% observed for 1998. It is interesting to note that the Asian crisis and the introduction of the euro had little influence on the exchange rate of the Swiss franc. The latter is, in real terms, at a level only slightly higher than at the beginning of 1997 (Graph 2). The remarkable stability of the Swiss franc in this phase of international turbulence is to the credit of the SNB's generous monetary policy. Thanks to the low level of short-term interest rates, the SNB has contributed and is helping to reduce the attractiveness of the Swiss franc as an international safe haven currency. The above considerations show that the SNB has the possibility of combating an undesirable revaluation of the Swiss franc. However, I would like to warn against overestimating this possibility. The SNB can conduct a monetary policy based on exchange rate stability at any time. Thus, since 1996, we have repeatedly curbed an undesirable rise in the Franc by generously supplying the money market with liquidity. If the upward pressure on the franc were to become extremely strong, we could even go one step further and, as we did in the autumn of 1978, temporarily peg our currency to another. Such a measure would, however, have an unfortunate consequence: the SNB would lose control of the evolution of the money supply. If the money supply were to swell disproportionately, the SNB 6 would create a new inflationary potential. It would achieve exchange rate stabilization at the cost of a subsequent acceleration of inflation. For this reason, the SNB must not lose sight of maintaining price stability - its main task - when it intervenes in the foreign exchange market. In recent decades, it has not always managed to reconcile exchange rate stability - a wish of many economic circles - with the objective of price stability. Does such a conflict of objectives threaten us today? The current situation is very different from what we have experienced at certain times. Indeed, the danger of a return of inflation is low. Indicators that provide information on future price developments - the growth of money supply, for example - do not suggest any danger on this side. The relatively convenient position in which the SNB finds itself is primarily to the credit of the coherent monetary policy of the early nineties, which was resolutely focused on price stability. By curbing inflation, the SNB has increased its room for manoeuvre to combat undesirable exchange rate fluctuations. The SNB is often criticised for having pursued an overly rigorous policy during the first half of the nineties. The authors of such criticisms forget that the restrictive monetary policy of the time and the return to price stability created precisely the conditions that today allow the SNB to protect the Swiss economy largely from undesirable exchange rate fluctuations. The SNB must therefore make every effort to preserve price stability in Switzerland, also in the medium term. Some believe that a little inflation would be beneficial to the economy, because it would mitigate the damaging consequences of large exchange rate fluctuations and other undesirable shocks. Such recommendations make no sense. The price level is not a variable that the SNB can manage accurately. If the SNB succumbed to the temptation to tolerate "a little" inflation, it would run the risk of ending up with much higher inflation. It would also reduce the room for manoeuvre that allows it to absorb shocks. The SNB can therefore do no other than ensure price stability in the first place. 7 The SNB is therefore perfectly able to counter undesirable fluctuations in exchange rates. Yet some wonder whether, for Switzerland as for other small countries, it makes sense to conduct an autonomous monetary policy. Would Switzerland not be better advised to peg the franc to the euro in the long term, instead of seeking to conduct an autonomous monetary policy? In the remainder of my presentation, I will try to answer that question. I will first look at the advantages of pegging the franc to the euro, and then I will move on to the disadvantages. 3 The advantages of pegging to the euro The advantages of pegging to the euro are obvious: if the exchange rate is fixed, exporting and importing companies have an easier task. They have a high degree of certainty about the prices at which they can sell or buy their products abroad. As a result, they can better plan their production and investments and reduce the risk of making bad decisions. However, the conversion of euros into Swiss francs and swiss francs into euros will continue to incur costs. Only the introduction of the euro instead of the franc, as a legal tender means of payment, would make it possible to eliminate conversion costs. The pegging of the franc to the euro would obviously not completely eliminate exchange rate fluctuations. These fluctuations would continue to persist, in two forms. Firstly, only the exchange rate relationship between the euro and the franc would be stabilised. However, a preponderant part of Switzerland's foreign trade would benefit from the advantages of a fixed rate: in 1998, 55% of Swiss exports of goods went to the euro area and at least 70% of our imports came from it. Secondly, the Swiss authorities could set the nominal rate of the euro, but not its real rate, which is decisive for the competitiveness of the Swiss economy. The question that arises is therefore whether the fixing of a nominal rate would also ensure the stability of the real price. 8 As can be seen from the experience of many countries with floating exchange rates, the deviations of the real rate in the short and medium term from its long-term trend are mainly due to nominal fluctuations. Real price volatility should therefore decrease significantly in the event of a changeover to fixed exchange rates. Even after the franc is pegged to the euro, real changes could still occur, but to a limited extent, if prices in Switzerland do not move in parallel with those in the euro area. Moreover, the example of Canada shows that, even within a single currency area, inflation can vary significantly from one region to another, resulting in changes in "real prices". While the fixing of a parity - a nominal rate - is likely to help stabilize, in the short and medium term, the external value of our currency, other rules apply for the long term. In this case, there is only a loose link between the nominal price and the real price. Thus, since the mid-seventies, both the nominal and real rates of the franc have been on an upward trend. However, the nominal price has risen much more than the real price. This is due to the fact that inflation in Switzerland has generally been lower than abroad. The revaluation of the Swiss franc in nominal terms has therefore largely reflected the differences between inflation rates abroad and in Switzerland. In the seventies, especially, it went beyond the difference between inflation rates. In this regard, it should be recalled that the long-term rise in the real exchange rate of the Swiss franc (Chart 2) depends little on monetary policy and other monetary influences. It has its origins more in the evolution of the relative prices of goods and services produced and sold only on the Swiss market. These prices, compared to those of products entering international trade, rose more sharply in Switzerland than in the euro area. The relatively strong increase in the price of products not entering international trade in Switzerland is probably due, above all, to the rather low supply of housing and the lack of competition on the domestic market. Thus, the long-term rise in the real exchange rate of the Swiss franc does not mean that the competitiveness of the Swiss export industry has tended to deteriorate over the past two decades. 9 4 The disadvantages of pegging to the euro The positive element, namely greater stability in real prices, must be weighed against the two major disadvantages that would result from pegging the franc to the euro. First, the peg of the Franc would eliminate the advantages of our lower interest rates than abroad. Secondly, it would completely deprive the SNB of the possibility of conducting an autonomous monetary policy. In Switzerland, as you know, interest rates are usually lower than the levels observed in all other European countries. The spread is wider for long-term rates than for short-term rates, which are highly dependent on the SNB's monetary policy and the economic situation in Switzerland. Returns on long-term investments in Swiss francs are lower than anywhere else in Europe, even if the comparison takes into account capital gains and losses resulting from changes in prices and exchange rates. Figure 4 shows the evolution of the gap between real long-term interest rates in Germany and Switzerland. This gap, measured in real terms, has tended to decrease over the last three decades, but it still rises today to a level varying between 1 and 2 points. The reasons behind this asset for our economy divide experts. The large surplus in our current account is likely to help keep Swiss interest rates low. In my opinion, however, the main explanation lies in the traditional stability of the Swiss franc, which makes our currency an attractive diversification instrument for international investors. If Switzerland were to set a parity for the exchange rate relationship between the euro and the franc, the advantage of low interest rates would melt over time. International investors would consider the euro and the Swiss franc as two perfectly interchangeable currencies. The incentive to diversify into our currency would disappear. Investments in euros and Swiss francs of the same quality and duration would yield the same returns. Swiss interest rates would be in line with those of the euro area and would be determined mainly by the European Central Bank. The SNB would no longer be able to influence 10 the evolution of rates in Switzerland and to ensure, by its own means, the stability of the Swiss franc. For the Swiss economy, rising interest rates would entail adjustments that would not be cost-effective. The Swiss economy would lose an international competitive advantage. The higher level of interest rates would lead Swiss companies to reduce the capital factor in the production apparatus. Swiss wages, which are high in real terms, would come under downward pressure. The Confederation, the cantons and the communes would see an increase in their expenditure on debt servicing. Homeowners would feel the increase in interest charges on their mortgages. The adjustment costs that the Swiss economy would have to bear as a result of rising interest rates should not be underestimated. They should be compared with the advantages that would result from pegging the franc to the euro. The total loss of autonomy in the conduct of monetary policy  the second major drawback  is often downplayed in discussions. The SNB puts forward as an argument - follows the ECB, after having aligned itself closely with the German central bank. In addition, the economic situation in Switzerland generally evolves in line with the economic situation in Germany. Thus, the SNB would not even be forced to conduct a monetary policy that deviates significantly from that of the German central bank or, now, the ECB. Those who question the need for Switzerland to be able to conduct an autonomous monetary policy, however, forget an important point: in the discussion of the relevance of an autonomous monetary policy, the devil hides in the details, as is so often the case. It is true that a great deal of similarity can generally be observed in economic developments on both sides of the Rhine. Scientific studies confirm this state of affairs. Moreover, the ECB  like the German central bank before it  assigns to its monetary policy the same objectives as the SNB. Given this similarity in monetary policy objectives and economic developments, it is not surprising that the SNB frequently gives its monetary policy the same stance as the ECB or, previously, the German central bank. 11 However, this finding should not lead to the conclusion that the SNB is merely copying the decisions taken in Frankfurt. If we look at Swiss monetary policy in recent years, we see that the SNB has also made use of its room for manoeuvre on several occasions and thus operated autonomously. Thus, between the summer of 1992 and the summer of 1993, the SNB eased its monetary policy more quickly than the German central bank. For this reason, money market interest rates have fallen faster in Switzerland than in Germany; during this period, the spread between German and Swiss interest rates reached at times 3 points (Chart 1). The German central bank was forced to pursue a more restrictive policy than the SNB, since the rise in prices in Germany had not fallen as quickly and as sustainably as in Switzerland. As a result of the temporary economic boom triggered by reunification, inflation in Germany rose to more than 4% in 1993, while it continued to decline in Switzerland. The gap between German and Swiss interest rates remained stable for the following years. Even today, short-term interest rates in Switzerland are lower than in Germany and the euro area. As I have already pointed out, the SNB pursues a rather expansionary monetary policy that takes account of economic developments in Switzerland. It thus takes into account the specific economic difficulties that Switzerland has been facing for several years, difficulties that manifest themselves in the form of structural changes that are more painful than in other European countries. If the franc were pegged to the euro, Swiss interest rates would rise on the money market to the level of the euro area. The SNB could no longer change them on its own. I do not need to stress that such a rate hike would be extremely unfortunate in the current economic landscape. It can of course be objected that Switzerland, by pegging the franc to the euro, would be integrated even more closely into the euro area economically, which would reduce the need for it to conduct an autonomous monetary policy. However, it is unlikely that the economic conditions for a complete surrender of our monetary policy autonomy will be met quickly. For this reason, the SNB would do well not to sacrifice its autonomy lightly. 12 5 Conclusions The SNB, by conducting an autonomous monetary policy, most effectively serves the general interests of the country. If it maintains its own course, it is also able to take into account, in setting its monetary policy, the special needs of the Swiss population and economy. But the SNB can only conduct an autonomous and effective monetary policy if it allows the franc to fluctuate freely. It is then possible that the Swiss franc will revalue in undesirable proportions and thus cause damage to the Swiss economy. As I have tried to show, the SNB is not helpless in the face of such developments. If it focuses its monetary policy on stabilizing exchange rates, it must be careful not to loosen the monetary reins too strongly so as not to create a new inflationary potential. The pegging of the franc to the euro would considerably reduce the risk of adverse exchange rate fluctuations. But the greater stability of prices would have a price, namely the loss of autonomy in the conduct of monetary policy. Swiss monetary policy would no longer be defined by the SNB, but by the European Central Bank. The advantage that comes to us from lower interest rates on the Swiss franc would disappear. The attractiveness of the Swiss franc as an investment currency would no longer depend on the SNB's credibility and reputation. The quality of monetary policy conducted in Frankfurt would henceforth be the only determining factor. How long will Switzerland maintain an autonomous monetary policy? This issue is often the subject of speculation. For my part, I renounce to make a prognosis. In my opinion, as long as Switzerland remains outside the European Union, there is no reason to abandon our autonomous monetary policy. Our country's accession to the European Union would naturally change the situation. If Switzerland were to join the European Union, it would probably take back the euro and lose its monetary autonomy at the same time. However, Switzerland's rapid accession to the European Union remains, for the time being, an unlikely one. Depuis, la BNS a, en plusieurs tapes, relch encore davantage la bride; actuellement, les taux d'intrt  court terme sont lgrement infrieurs  1%. 5 Le changement de cap montaire n'a pas influ immdiatement sur les cours de change. Le franc n'a faibli qu' partir de la fin de 1995, d'abord timidement, puis de manire plus franche, entre aot 1996 et janvier 1997, aprs un nouvel assouplissement de la politique montaire. Au dbut de 1997, l'conomie suisse a redmarr. En 1997 et 1998, elle a atteint des taux de croissance respectables, et le chmage s'est repli. Malgr la reprise de la conjoncture, les prix sont rests stables en Suisse. La crise en Asie orientale, en Russie et en Amrique du Sud est toutefois venue jeter une ombre  ce tableau rjouissant. Aujourd'hui encore, elle pse sur la croissance conomique en Suisse et dans les pays voisins. Il est nanmoins difficile de faire un pronostic fiable sur les rpercussions de la crise internationale sur l'conomie suisse, dans la mesure o la demande intrieure, toujours robuste, attnue les effets de l'affaiblissement sensible des exportations. Pour notre part, nous tablons toujours sur une croissance du produit intrieur brut rel de 1,5% en 1999, donc sur un ralentissement par rapport  la performance de plus de 2% observe pour 1998. Il est intressant de noter que la crise asiatique et l'introduction de l'euro ont peu influ sur le cours du franc suisse. Ce dernier est, en termes rels,  un niveau  peine suprieur  celui du dbut de 1997 (graphique 2). La remarquable stabilit du franc dans cette phase de turbulences internationales est  mettre au crdit de la politique montaire gnreuse de la BNS. Grce au bas niveau des taux  court terme, la BNS a contribu et contribue  diminuer l'attrait du franc en tant que monnaie refuge sur le plan international. Les considrations qui prcdent montrent que la BNS a la possibilit de lutter contre une revalorisation indsirable du franc. J'aimerais cependant mettre en garde contre une surestimation de cette possibilit. La BNS peut en tout temps mener une politique montaire axe sur la stabilit des cours de change. Ainsi, depuis 1996, nous avons  plusieurs reprises frein une hausse indsirable du franc en approvisionnant gnreusement le march montaire en liquidits. Si les pressions  la hausse sur le franc devaient devenir extrmement fortes, nous pourrions mme franchir un pas de plus et, comme nous l'avons fait en automne 1978, rattacher temporairement notre monnaie  une autre. Une telle mesure aurait toutefois une consquence fcheuse: la BNS perdrait le contrle de l'volution de la masse montaire. Si la masse montaire devait gonfler dmesurment, la BNS 6 crerait un nouveau potentiel inflationniste. Elle obtiendrait la stabilisation des cours de change au prix d'une acclration ultrieure de l'inflation. Pour cette raison, la BNS ne doit pas perdre de vue le maintien de la stabilit des prix - sa mission principale - quand elle intervient sur le march des changes. Ces dernires dcennies, elle n'est pas toujours parvenue  concilier la stabilit des cours de change - un souhait de nombreux milieux conomiques - avec l'objectif de la stabilit des prix. Un tel conflit d'objectifs nous menace-t-il aujourd'hui? La situation actuelle est trs diffrente de ce que nous avons connu  certaines poques. En effet, le danger d'un retour de l'inflation est faible. Les indicateurs qui renseignent sur l'volution future des prix - la croissance des masses montaires par exemple - ne laissent entrevoir aucun danger de ce ct-l. La position relativement commode dans laquelle se trouve la BNS est  mettre avant tout au crdit de la politique montaire cohrente du dbut des annes nonante, politique montaire qui tait rsolument axe sur la stabilit des prix. En jugulant l'inflation, la BNS a accru sa marge de man uvre pour lutter contre des variations indsirables des cours de change. On reproche souvent  la BNS d'avoir men une politique trop rigoureuse pendant la premire moiti des annes nonante. Les auteurs de telles critiques oublient que la politique montaire restrictive d'alors et le retour  la stabilit des prix ont prcisment cr les conditions qui permettent aujourd'hui  la BNS de mettre l'conomie suisse largement  l'abri de fluctuations indsirables des cours de change. En consquence, la BNS doit tout mettre en  uvre pour prserver la stabilit des prix en Suisse,  moyen terme galement. Certains pensent qu'un peu d'inflation serait bnfique pour l'conomie, parce que cela permettrait d'attnuer les consquences dommageables de fortes variations des cours de change et d'autres chocs indsirables. De telles recommandations n'ont pas de sens. Le niveau des prix n'est pas une variable que la BNS peut grer avec prcision. Si la BNS succombait  la tentation de tolrer "un peu" de renchrissement, elle courrait le risque de se retrouver avec une inflation bien plus forte. Elle rduirait galement la marge de man uvre qui lui permet d'amortir des chocs. Aussi la BNS ne peut-elle faire autrement que de veiller en premier lieu  la stabilit des prix. 7 La BNS est donc parfaitement en mesure de contrer des fluctuations indsirables des cours de change. Pourtant, d'aucuns se demandent si, pour la Suisse comme pour d'autres petits pays, mener une politique montaire autonome a un sens. La Suisse ne serait-elle pas mieux avise de rattacher durablement le franc  l'euro, au lieu de chercher  mener une politique montaire autonome? Dans la suite de mon expos, je vais tenter de rpondre  cette question. J'examinerai dans un premier temps les avantages d'un rattachement du franc  l'euro, puis je passerai aux inconvnients. 3 Les avantages d'un rattachement  l'euro Les avantages d'un rattachement  l'euro sautent aux yeux: si le cours de change est fixe, les entreprises exportatrices et importatrices ont la tche facilite. Elles bnficient d'une grande certitude pour ce qui a trait aux prix auxquels elles peuvent vendre ou acheter leurs produits  l'tranger. Elles peuvent par consquent mieux planifier leur production et leurs investissements et rduire le risque de prendre de mauvaises dcisions. Toutefois, la conversion d'euros en francs suisses et de francs suisses en euros continuera  leur engendrer des cots. Seule l'introduction de l'euro  la place du franc, comme moyen de paiement ayant cours lgal, permettrait de faire disparatre les cots de conversion. Le rattachement du franc  l'euro n'liminerait videmment pas intgralement les fluctuations des changes. Ces fluctuations continueraient  subsister, sous deux formes. Premirement, seule la relation de change entre l'euro et le franc serait stabilise. Une partie prpondrante du commerce extrieur de la Suisse bnficierait toutefois des avantages d'un cours fixe: en 1998, 55% des exportations suisses de biens taient destines  la zone euro et au moins 70% de nos importations en provenaient. Deuximement, les autorits suisses pourraient fixer le cours nominal de l'euro, mais non son cours rel, lequel est dterminant pour la comptitivit de l'conomie suisse. La question qui se pose est donc de savoir si la fixation d'un cours nominal permettrait aussi d'assurer la stabilit du cours rel. 8 Comme il ressort des expriences faites dans de nombreux pays ayant des cours de change flottants, les carts que le cours rel enregistre  court et  moyen terme par rapport  sa tendance  long terme dcoulent avant tout des fluctuations nominales. La volatilit du cours rel devrait par consquent sensiblement diminuer en cas de passage  des changes fixes. Mme aprs le rattachement du franc  l'euro, des variations relles pourraient encore survenir, mais dans une mesure limite, si les prix en Suisse n'voluaient pas paralllement  ceux de la zone euro. En outre, l'exemple du Canada montre que, mme  l'intrieur d'une zone montaire unique, l'inflation peut varier sensiblement d'une rgion  l'autre, d'o des variations des "cours rels". Si la fixation d'une parit - d'un cours nominal - est susceptible de contribuer  stabiliser,  court et  moyen terme, la valeur extrieure de notre monnaie, d'autres rgles s'appliquent pour le long terme. Dans ce cas-l, il n'y a qu'un lien lche entre le cours nominal et le cours rel. Ainsi, depuis le milieu des annes septante, le cours nominal et le cours rel du franc marquent tous deux une tendance  la hausse. Le cours nominal a cependant beaucoup plus augment que le cours rel. Ce phnomne s'explique par le fait que l'inflation en Suisse a t gnralement plus basse qu' l'tranger. La revalorisation du franc en termes nominaux a par consquent reflt, en grande partie, les carts entre les taux d'inflation  l'tranger et en Suisse. Dans les annes septante, surtout, elle est alle au-del de la diffrence entre les taux d'inflation. Il convient  ce propos de rappeler que la hausse  long terme du cours rel du franc (graphique 2) dpend peu de la politique montaire et d'autres influences montaires. Elle trouve davantage son origine dans l'volution des prix relatifs des biens et services produits et vendus uniquement sur le march suisse. Ces prix, compars  ceux des produits entrant dans le commerce international, ont augment plus fortement en Suisse que dans la zone euro. Le renchrissement relativement fort qui a t observ, en Suisse, pour les produits n'entrant pas dans le commerce international est probablement d, avant tout,  l'offre de logements plutt faible et  l'absence de concurrence sur le march intrieur. Ainsi, la hausse  long terme du cours rel du franc ne signifie pas que la comptitivit de l'industrie suisse d'exportation a eu tendance  se dgrader durant les deux dernires dcennies. 9 4 Les inconvnients d'un rattachement  l'euro L'lment positif, soit une plus grande stabilit des cours rels, est  mettre en balance avec les deux inconvnients majeurs qu'engendrerait un rattachement du franc  l'euro. D'abord, le rattachement du franc ferait disparatre les avantages dcoulant de nos taux d'intrt plus bas qu' l'tranger. Ensuite, il priverait totalement la BNS de la possibilit de mener une politique montaire autonome. En Suisse, vous le savez, les taux d'intrt sont habituellement infrieurs aux niveaux observs dans tous les autres pays europens. L'cart est plus marqu pour les taux  long terme que pour les taux  court terme, lesquels dpendent trs fortement de la politique montaire de la BNS et de la conjoncture conomique en Suisse. Les rendements sur les placements  long terme en francs sont plus bas que partout ailleurs en Europe, mme si l'on tient compte, dans la comparaison, des gains et pertes en capital conscutifs aux variations des prix et des cours de change. Le graphique 4 montre l'volution de l'cart entre les taux d'intrt rels  long terme en Allemagne et en Suisse. Cet cart, mesur en termes rels je le rappelle, a eu tendance  diminuer durant les trois dernires dcennies, mais il s'lve aujourd'hui encore  un niveau variant entre 1 et 2 points. Les raisons qui sont  l'origine de cet atout pour notre conomie divisent les experts. Il est probable que le fort excdent de notre balance des transactions courantes contribue  maintenir les taux d'intrt suisses  un bas niveau. A mon avis, la principale explication rside toutefois dans la stabilit traditionnelle du franc suisse, qui fait de notre monnaie un instrument de diversification attrayant pour les investisseurs internationaux. Si la Suisse fixait une parit pour la relation de change entre l'euro et le franc, l'atout dcoulant des taux d'intrt bas fondrait avec le temps. Les investisseurs internationaux considreraient l'euro et le franc suisse comme deux monnaies parfaitement interchangeables. L'incitation  se diversifier dans notre monnaie disparatrait. Les placements en euros et en francs suisses de mme qualit et de mme dure donneraient les mmes rendements. Les taux d'intrt suisses s'aligneraient sur ceux de la zone euro et seraient dtermins essentiellement par la Banque centrale europenne. La BNS ne serait plus en mesure d'influer sur 10 l'volution des taux en Suisse et de veiller, par ses propres moyens,  la stabilit du franc suisse. Pour l'conomie suisse, la hausse des taux d'intrt impliquerait des ajustements qui ne se feraient pas sans cots. L'conomie suisse perdrait un avantage concurrentiel sur le plan international. Le niveau plus lev des taux d'intrt amnerait les entreprises suisses  rduire le facteur capital dans l'appareil de production. Les salaires suisses, levs en termes rels, subiraient des pressions  la baisse. La Confdration, les cantons et les communes verraient s'accrotre leurs dpenses au titre du service de la dette. Les propritaires ressentiraient l'alourdissement des charges d'intrts sur leurs hypothques. Les cots d'ajustement que l'conomie suisse aurait  supporter  la suite de la hausse des taux d'intrt ne doivent pas tre sous-estims. Ils devraient tre compars aux avantages qui dcouleraient du rattachement du franc  l'euro. La perte totale d'autonomie dans la conduite de la politique montaire - le second inconvnient majeur - est souvent minimise dans les discussions. La BNS avance-t-on comme argument - suit la BCE, aprs s'tre aligne troitement sur la banque centrale allemande. En outre, la conjoncture en Suisse volue, en rgle gnrale, paralllement  la conjoncture en Allemagne. Ainsi, la BNS ne serait mme pas contrainte de mener une politique montaire s'cartant sensiblement de celle de la banque centrale allemande ou, maintenant, de la BCE. Ceux qui mettent en question la ncessit pour la Suisse de pouvoir mener une politique montaire autonome oublient toutefois un point important: dans la discussion sur la pertinence d'une politique montaire autonome, le diable se cache dans les dtails, comme cela est si souvent le cas. Il est vrai qu'une grande similitude peut gnralement tre observe dans l'volution conjoncturelle de part et d'autre du Rhin. Des tudes scientifiques confirment cet tat de fait. De plus, la BCE - comme la banque centrale allemande avant elle - assigne  sa politique montaire les mmes objectifs que la BNS. Etant donn cette similitude des objectifs de politique montaire et de l'volution conomique, il n'est pas tonnant que la BNS donne frquemment  sa politique montaire la mme orientation que la BCE ou, prcdemment, la banque centrale allemande. 11 Ce constat ne doit cependant pas dboucher sur la conclusion que la BNS se contente de copier les dcisions prises  Francfort. Si l'on examine la politique montaire suisse des dernires annes, on s'aperoit que la BNS a aussi mis  profit,  plusieurs reprises, sa marge de man uvre et, partant, opr de manire autonome. Ainsi, entre l't 1992 et l't 1993, la BNS a assoupli sa politique montaire plus rapidement que la banque centrale allemande. C'est pour cette raison que les taux d'intrt sur le march montaire ont baiss plus vite en Suisse qu'en Allemagne; durant cette priode, l'cart entre les taux d'intrt allemands et suisses a atteint par moments 3 points (graphique 1). La banque centrale allemande tait contrainte de mener une politique plus restrictive que la BNS, tant donn que le renchrissement outre-Rhin ne s'tait pas repli aussi rapidement et aussi durablement qu'en Suisse. A la suite de l'essor conomique passager qu'avait dclench la runification, l'inflation en Allemagne a pass  plus de 4% en 1993, alors qu'elle continuait  reculer en Suisse. L'cart entre les taux d'intrt allemands et suisses s'est maintenu pendant les annes suivantes. Aujourd'hui encore, les taux d'intrt  court terme sont en Suisse plus bas qu'en Allemagne et que dans la zone euro. Comme je l'ai dj soulign, la BNS poursuit une politique montaire plutt expansionniste qui tient compte de l'volution de la conjoncture en Suisse. Elle prend ainsi en considration les difficults conomiques spcifiques que la Suisse affronte depuis plusieurs annes, difficults qui se manifestent sous forme de mutations structurelles plus douloureuses que dans les autres pays europens. En cas de rattachement du franc  l'euro, les taux d'intrt suisses augmenteraient sur le march montaire pour rejoindre le niveau de la zone euro. La BNS ne pourrait plus les modifier de son propre chef. Je n'ai pas besoin d'insister sur le fait qu'une telle hausse des taux serait extrmement fcheuse dans le paysage conjoncturel actuel. On peut naturellement objecter que la Suisse, en rattachant le franc  l'euro, serait intgre encore plus troitement  la zone euro sur le plan conomique, ce qui rduirait la ncessit pour elle de mener une politique montaire autonome. Il est toutefois improbable que les conditions conomiques pour un abandon total de notre autonomie en matire de politique montaire soient rapidement remplies. Pour cette raison, la BNS ferait bien de ne pas sacrifier  la lgre son autonomie. 12 5 Conclusions La BNS, en menant une politique montaire autonome, sert le plus efficacement les intrts gnraux du pays. Si elle maintient son propre cap, elle est galement en mesure de tenir compte, dans la fixation de sa politique montaire, des besoins particuliers de la population et de l'conomie suisses. Mais la BNS ne peut conduire une politique montaire autonome et efficace que si elle laisse fluctuer librement le cours du franc. Il est alors possible que le franc suisse se revalorise dans des proportions indsirables et, partant, qu'il cause des dommages  l'conomie suisse. Comme j'ai tent de le montrer, la BNS n'est pas dsarme face  ce genre d'volutions. Si elle axe sa politique montaire sur la stabilisation des cours de change, elle doit veiller  ne pas relcher trop fortement les rnes montaires pour ne pas crer un nouveau potentiel inflationniste. Le rattachement du franc  l'euro rduirait considrablement le risque de variations prjudiciables des cours de change. Mais la plus grande stabilit des cours aurait un prix,  savoir la perte d'autonomie dans la conduite de la politique montaire. La politique montaire suisse serait dfinie non plus par la BNS, mais par la Banque centrale europenne. L'atout qui nous vient des taux d'intrt plus bas sur le franc suisse disparatrait. L'attrait du franc comme monnaie de placement ne dpendrait plus de la crdibilit et du renom de la BNS. La qualit de la politique montaire mene  Francfort serait dornavant seule dterminante. Pendant combien de temps la Suisse maintiendra-t-elle une politique montaire autonome? Cette question fait souvent l'objet de spculations. Je renonce pour ma part  mettre un pronostic. A mon avis, tant que la Suisse reste en dehors de l'Union europenne, il n'existe aucune raison d'abandonner notre politique montaire autonome. Une adhsion de notre pays  l'Union europenne changerait naturellement la donne. Si la Suisse entrait dans l'Union europenne, elle reprendrait probablement l'euro et perdrait du mme coup son autonomie montaire. Toutefois, une adhsion rapide de la Suisse  l'Union europenne reste, pour l'instant, du domaine de l'improbable.
