Title: Economic perspectives and the policy of the Swiss National Bank
text: Economic and political outlook of the Swiss National Bank Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-President of the Executive Board of the Swiss National Bank Annual General Meeting of the Council for economic Development of the Canton of Vaud (DEV) Lausanne, 25 May 1999 2 After many years of economic stagnation, Switzerland returned to growth a little over two years ago. The economic situation was first driven by exports and then, at the end of 1997, as external demand gradually lost momentum, domestic demand took over. Growth peaked in early 1998. Since then, the pace of expansion of the Swiss economy has gradually slowed down. Was the economic upturn only temporary? Let me address this issue by first presenting to you the reasons for the cyclical downturn of the last twelve months. I will then remind you of the contribution of monetary policy in supporting economic activity and, finally, I will ask myself about the outlook for the economic situation. The economic diagnosis: Switzerland victim of the general cooling From a cyclical point of view, 1998 had started very encouragingly. Economic growth exceeded 3%, a figure we had not seen in almost ten years. Our country thus seemed to emerge from the tunnel of stagnation in which it had been walking since 1991. But clouds of bad conjuncture were already visible on the horizon. A financial crisis was shaking the emerging countries of Asia. It began in Thailand in the summer of 1997 and then spread to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. Soon after, it hit South Korea, the world's tenth largest economy. Japan, for its part, was still not emerging from the stagnation in which it had found itself for two years. Thus, an entire region, so previously spoiled by exceptional growth rates, was facing significant difficulties. Weakening of the world economy At first it was thought that the Asian crisis would have little effect on the economic situation of the industrialized countries. It should be remembered that for Switzerland exports to the 3 Emerging Asian economies accounted for only 9% of total exports in 1997. This underestimated the contagion effects and the increased weakening of the world economy, particularly in financial terms, caused by the crisis in these countries. Last August, the Russian crisis followed the Asian difficulties. Here clearly, it was not the prospect of a deterioration in trade relations that worried - our exports to Russia are of the order of magnitude of those we sell to Portugal - but the new shake-up of the international financial edifice that would not fail to trigger the suspension of payments from a great political power. The financial markets were indeed deeply shaken by the Russian crisis. They quickly showed a strong distrust of risky investments: stock markets fell sharply, interest rates on second-grade bonds soared. Fears began for the stability of the international financial system, which led to a sharp decline in the dollar on all fronts. In the autumn, the atmosphere continued to grow as Brazil was in turn affected by the crisis of investor confidence. The mobilization was then general to avoid an extension of the crisis. The International Monetary Fund and the industrialized countries provided massive financial assistance to this country. The situation seemed so fragile that the Federal Reserve cut its key rates three times even though the economy on the other side of the Atlantic was still very strong. IMF action and lower U.S. rates helped calm the situation, risk premia fell, stock markets recovered, but market volatility remained relatively high. Adding up, the difficulties of emerging economies and Japan increasingly weighed on Swiss exports. Our deliveries to these markets, which together account for one-sixth of our foreign trade, fell by almost 17% in one year. Moreover, as most European countries were facing the same phenomenon, demand from our neighbours also declined. 4 In my opinion, if the crisis in emerging countries has played a direct role in the slowdown of the economic situation in Switzerland, we must realize that the degree of activity in our country depends above all on the economic situation of the countries around us, which are themselves also affected by the global economy. When we know that Germany, France and Italy absorb roughly 40% of our exports and are responsible for half of our imports, it is not surprising that our economic cycle is closely linked to theirs. However, 1998 was marked by a marked downturn in the economic situation in Germany, due not only to the slowdown in exports due to the deterioration of the international scene but also to problems specific to that country, in particular a marked loss of investor confidence, a loss of confidence caused both by the uncertainties surrounding the German tax reform and by the lack of progress in the necessary structural reforms. to stimulate employment. On the French side, a slowdown in activity occurred but the scale of the movement was less pronounced than in Germany. In Italy, on the other hand, the trend reversal was much more abrupt. In fact, only the United States played the role of economic locomotive last year. On the other side of the Atlantic, growth and employment remained at a high level. Unfortunately for us, even though the growth of our exports to North America was still strongly positive at the beginning of 1998, it was less and less positive and even became negative at the end of the year. Overall, the deteriorating economic situation in our trading partners is increasingly weighing on our exports. The growth of the latter continued to decline throughout 1998 and even became negative at the end of the year. Sustained domestic demand While the slowdown and then the fall in exports gradually hampered growth in Switzerland, domestic demand developed in a welcome way that mitigated the effects of the slowdown in activity at the international level. Indeed, private consumption became the strongest support of our 5 conjuncture. It has its roots in a favourable trend in household income and in a climate of confidence created by the fall in unemployment. This has resulted in particularly strong demand for consumer durables. Clearly, there was a need to catch up with previous lean years. In contrast to private consumption, public consumption contributed only slightly to growth, as the necessary consolidation of public finances precluded higher growth in public spending. This situation is not unfavourable as it helps to reassure investors about future financial stability. The high degree of confidence of economic actors is confirmed by the lack of momentum in the field of investment. The stagnation of investment in construction is more than offset by the marked growth in investment in equipment. It seems that the momentum of investment in equipment can be attributed mainly to the services sector, while the industrial sector is showing restraint. In construction, the often announced recovery is still awaited. Information on this sector is contradictory; the only thing that can be said is that a clear and clear trend change has not yet taken place. Overall, therefore, the swiss economy is relatively good. Domestic demand is strong, supported by the high level of confidence shown by consumers and investors. Cyclical weakness is of external origin, a phenomenon that is not the consequence of a loss of competitiveness of the Swiss economy, but the result of weak global demand. Falling unemployment and stable prices This positive diagnosis can be supplemented by information on the evolution of unemployment and prices. 6 In April, statisticians surprised us with the good news that unemployment in Switzerland had fallen below 3% to its lowest level since 1992. With 106,000 people, the number of unemployed has almost halved since the peak of 200,000 registered in February 1997. However, these figures tend to overestimate the improvement in the labour market situation. Indeed, it is not enough to look at the number of unemployed, we must bear in mind that the statistics are embellished by the fact that unemployed people have reached the end of their entitlements. In addition, account must also be taken of persons seeking employment without being classified as unemployed because they are in an employment or training programme, or have an intermediate job. The total number of jobseekers and unemployed then reached more than 180,000 people, but the trend is fortunately decreasing. As regards the composition of the unemployed, it would appear that the labour market has practically absorbed skilled labour, while the low-skilled unemployed have more difficulty finding a job. The second positive factor I would like to address is price stability. The current pace of price increases is around 0.5% despite the recent VAT increase of 1 percentage point. Price stability is a strange good: when you do not have it, it is what you want more, and when you have it, you consider it unimportant. We then tend to quickly forget the vicious effects of inflation, the distortions it causes and the mesallocations it causes. In the long run, excessive price increases hamper growth and employment and causes an unjustified redistribution of income between debtors and creditors, and hits especially the socially disadvantaged classes. There is concern that price stability will turn into a general fall in the price level, i.e. deflation. Deflation is just as dangerous, if not more so, than inflation. In addition to the price-distorting and redistributive effects it causes, deflation can truly cripple an economy. Given the current strength of domestic demand, I believe that fears of a deflationary spiral are unfounded. 7 The stabilizing role of monetary policy The SNB's action aims to maintain monetary stability while promoting economic growth as much as possible. That is why, convinced of the imminent return of price stability, we began in 1995 to relax the monetary reins. This policy was even reinforced in 1996 when the prospects for cyclical warming were slow to materialize. During all these years, we have generously supplied the market with liquidity, which was reflected in a fall in short-term interest rates from almost 4% in early 1995 to 1.5% in early 1997. At that time, the first signs of an export-led economic recovery appeared. Our feeling, however, was that this development was still too uncertain to justify a change in our policy. Moreover, the situation on the foreign exchange market, which at the time was characterised by a pronounced weakness of the German mark against the Swiss franc, did not make a change in strategy seem appropriate either. Signs of recovery multiplied during the summer of 1997. For the SNB, therefore, the question arose as to whether the time had come to slowly tighten its policy. At the same time, the Asian crisis broke out. Although the scale and consequences of this crisis were not yet measurable, a weakening of orders from these countries could be expected. With a more uncertain export outlook and still fragile domestic demand, we could afford to maintain our generous policy without fear of inflationary pressures; all the more so since the strength of the franc against the DM mitigated the development of the price of imported goods. 1998 brought a new change of scenery. The year was turbulent due to the weakening of financial markets and great uncertainty surrounded the process of monetary integration in Europe. The Swiss franc was thus brought to play from time to time a role of safe haven. In January and February, a first wave of speculation led to strong demand for Swiss francs on the market. To counteract the move, the SNB supplied the market with additional liquidity. The rate 8 of interest at three months temporarily fell to 1%. In March, as the situation on the foreign exchange market normalized, the excess liquidity was absorbed. On the cyclical side, annual growth exceeded the 3% threshold in the first quarter of 1998, but growth was forecast to slow down towards the end of the year, making it inappropriate to change monetary conditions. In August, the Russian debacle, followed by the worst crisis in the financial markets since the stock market crash of 1987, asked us to once again satisfy the markets' appetite for liquidity, which redirected interest rates downwards. Unlike the previous situation, it would have been contraindicated, once calm had returned, to quickly withdraw liquidity from the market because the crisis was much more serious than the turbulence of the spring. In addition, growth forecasts were continually revised downwards and risks of deflation were even mentioned. Finally, we considered it preferable to maintain a generous supply of liquidity to the market at a time when the uncertainties surrounding the introduction of the euro could be disruptive. With our decision last April to follow the european Central Bank's reduction in the key interest rates with an adjustment to our discount rate, we confirmed our desire to see the franc-euro relationship remain stable while the inflationary outlook is converging strongly between Switzerland and its neighbours. Overall, monetary policy over the past three years has been marked by remarkable continuity. We have endeavoured to maintain favourable monetary conditions for the development of the Swiss economy without, however, taking the risk of a monetary runaway, and therefore of a destabilization of prices. The relative stability of the franc against the currencies of neighbouring countries and then against the resulting euro has given our economy the best chance of adapting to changes in the international situation. It has certainly been a factor in strengthening investor and consumer confidence, whose stable behaviour has been decisive in preventing the economy from taking a sharper turn. 9 Encouraging prospects Despite the slowdown in mid-1998, last year's growth was still 2.1%. For 1999, the autumn forecasts of the specialized institutes still amounted to a growth rate of 1.7%. In the meantime, these figures have been revised downwards to retain only 1.3% growth. The downward revision does not affect all components of demand to the same extent. Forecasts for domestic demand (consumption and investment) were only slightly corrected, while exports underwent a more pronounced revision. Once again, we realise how much the Swiss economy is linked to the state of the European economy around us. Switzerland directs more than half of its exports to euro area countries. The current weakness of the economic situation in this large economic area cannot therefore remain without consequences for our country. A certain optimism is now taking hold in Europe and a cyclical warming is announced. Recent figures published by the OECD are encouraging in this regard. The euro area is expected to experience more sustained growth as early as this summer. We can expect a boost in our exports and renewed growth for the Swiss economy. Thus, forecasting institutes now expect the economy to accelerate from the second half of the year. For next year, they forecast a growth rate of 1.8%. On the monetary side, the conditions for a recovery are favourable. Prices are stable and interest rates are low in both the short and long term. The exchange rate against the euro is not a handicap for our competitiveness and its stability is encouraging. Another point that inspires optimism is the outcome of the bilateral agreements between Switzerland and the European Union. The conclusion of the negotiations puts an end to a phase of uncertainty regarding the Swiss-European relationship, a phase that began with the rejection of Switzerland's participation in the EEA in 1992. Bilateral agreements give a new basis for our relations with our most important partner 10 commercial; they contribute significantly to the improvement of the framework conditions for the Swiss economy. It remains to be hoped that the process of ratifying the agreements will be swift and friction-free. In some other areas, however, the framework conditions could still be improved. I am thinking, for example, of the continuation of structural reforms, in particular the removal of barriers to competition in our internal market and the restoration of the balance of public finances. Such reforms are necessary not only for the advancement of our well-being but also for the preservation of our future competitiveness. Conclusions The recent downturn in the Swiss economy does not herald a new phase of economic stagnation. The weakness in growth, noted over the past year, has been driven by the general cooling of global business following the crisis in emerging countries. The normalization of the financial market situation and the prospects for economic recovery in Europe will soon put the Swiss economy on the path to better growth. The swiss National Bank's policy in recent years has been aimed at price stability while seeking to create the best possible monetary conditions for the expansion of the Swiss economy. Today, with low interest rates and a high degree of stability of the Franc against the euro, an optimal framework exists that will allow our companies to take full advantage of the expected recovery of the global economy.
text_original: Perspectives conomiques et politique de la Banque nationale suisse Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-prsident de la Direction gnrale de la Banque nationale suisse Assemble gnrale annuelle du Conseil pour le Dveloppement Economique du Canton de Vaud (DEV) Lausanne, le 25 mai 1999 2 Aprs de nombreuses annes de stagnation conomique, la Suisse a retrouv le chemin de la croissance il y a un peu plus de deux ans. La croissance conomique dpassait les 3%, chiffre que nous n'avions plus connu depuis prs de dix ans. Notre pays semblait ainsi sortir du tunnel de la stagnation dans lequel il cheminait depuis 1991. Mais des nuages de mauvaise augure conjoncturelle taient dj visibles  l'horizon. Une crise financire secouait les pays mergents d'Asie. Ainsi, toute une rgion, si gte antrieurement par des taux de croissance exceptionnels, rencontrait d'importantes difficults. C'tait sous-estimer les effets de contagion et la fragilisation accrue de l'conomie mondiale, notamment sur le plan financier, entrans par la crise de ces pays. En aot dernier, la crise russe succda aux difficults asiatiques. Ici clairement, ce ne fut pas la perspective d'une dgradation des relations commerciales qui inquita - nos exportations vers la Russie sont de l'ordre de grandeur de celles que nous coulons au Portugal - mais le nouvel branlement de l'difice financier international que ne manquerait pas de dclencher la suspension des paiements d'une grande puissance politique. Les marchs financiers furent effectivement profondment branls par la crise russe. Ils manifestrent rapidement une forte mfiance  l'gard de placements risqus: les bourses chutrent brusquement, les taux d'intrt sur les obligations de seconde qualit montrent en flche. On commena  craindre pour la stabilit du systme financier international, ce qui entrana une baisse marque du dollar sur tous les fronts. A l'automne, l'atmosphre continua de s'alourdir car le Brsil fut touch  son tour par la crise de confiance des investisseurs. La mobilisation fut alors gnrale pour viter une extension de la crise. Le Fonds montaire international et les pays industrialiss apportrent une aide financire massive  ce pays. Nos livraisons sur ces marchs, qui reprsentent globalement un sixime de notre commerce extrieur, baissrent de prs de 17% en un an. Or, l'anne 1998 a t marque par un flchissement marqu de la conjoncture en Allemagne en raison non seulement du ralentissement des exportations d  la dtrioration de la scne internationale mais aussi du fait de problmes propres  ce pays, en particulier une perte de confiance marque des investisseurs, perte de confiance provoque  la fois par les incertitudes entourant la rforme fiscale allemande et par l'absence de progrs dans les rformes structurelles indispensables  stimuler l'emploi. Du ct franais, un ralentissement d'activit est intervenu mais l'ampleur du mouvement a t moins prononc qu'en Allemagne. En Italie, en revanche, le renversement de tendance a t beaucoup plus abrupt. Malheureusement pour nous, mme si la croissance de nos exportations en direction de l'Amrique du Nord tait encore fortement positive au dbut de 1998, elle le fut de moins en moins et devint mme ngative en fin d'anne. Demande intrieure soutenue Si le ralentissement puis la baisse des exportations entravrent progressivement la croissance en Suisse, la demande intrieure connut une volution rjouissante qui attnua les effets du tassement de l'activit au niveau international. Elle trouve ses racines dans une volution favorable du revenu des mnages et dans un climat de confiance cr par la baisse du chmage. Cette situation n'est pas dfavorable car elle contribue  rassurer les investisseurs sur la stabilit financire future. Dans son ensemble donc, l'tat de sant de l'conomie suisse est relativement bon. La demande intrieure est solide, elle est soutenue par le haut degr de confiance que manifestent les consommateurs et les investisseurs. Baisse du chmage et stabilit des prix Ce diagnostic positif peut tre complt par les informations relatives  l'volution du chmage et des prix. 6 En avril, les statisticiens nous ont surpris avec la bonne nouvelle que le chmage, en Suisse, tait tomb sous la barre des 3 % pour atteindre son niveau le plus bas depuis 1992. Ces chiffres tendent cependant  surestimer l'amlioration de la situation sur le march du travail. En effet, il ne suffit pas d'observer le nombre de chmeurs, nous devons garder  l'esprit que la statistique est enjolive par le fait que des chmeurs sont arrivs en fin de droits. Par ailleurs, il faut galement tenir compte des personnes cherchant un emploi sans tre classes chmeurs car elles suivent un programme d'occupation ou de formation, ou ont un emploi intermdiaire. Le nombre total de demandeurs d'emploi et de chmeurs atteint alors plus de 180'000 personnes, mais le trend est heureusement  la baisse. En ce qui concerne la composition des chmeurs, il semblerait que le march du travail ait pratiquement absorb la main-d' uvre qualifie, tandis que les chmeurs faiblement qualifis ont plus de difficults  retrouver un emploi. Le deuxime facteur positif que j'aimerais aborder est la stabilit des prix. Le rythme actuel de la hausse des prix est de l'ordre de 0,5% en dpit de la rcente hausse de TVA de 1 point de pourcentage. La stabilit des prix est un bien trange: quand on ne l'a pas, elle est ce qu'on dsire de plus, et lorsqu'on l'a, on la considre comme sans importance. On tend alors  oublier rapidement les effets vicieux de l'inflation, les distorsions qu'elle entrane et les mesallocations qu'elle provoque. A long terme, une hausse excessive des prix entrave la croissance et l'emploi et provoque une redistribution injustifie de revenus entre dbiteurs et crditeurs, et frappe surtout les classes socialement dfavorises. Certains s'inquitent que la stabilit des prix ne tourne  une baisse gnrale du niveau des prix, c'est--dire  une dflation. La dflation est tout aussi dangereuse, si ce n'est plus, que l'inflation. Outre les effets de distorsion des prix et de redistribution qu'elle provoque, la dflation peut vritablement paralyser une conomie. Etant donn la vigueur actuelle de la demande interne, je crois que les craintes d'une spirale dflationniste sont sans fondement. 7 Le rle stabilisateur de la politique montaire L'action de la Banque nationale vise au maintien de la stabilit montaire tout en favorisant autant que possible la croissance conomique. C'est pourquoi, convaincus du retour prochain de la stabilit des prix, nous avons commenc, ds 1995,  relcher les rnes montaires. Cette politique fut mme renforce en 1996 alors que les perspectives d'un rchauffement conjoncturel tardaient  se concrtiser. Pendant toutes ces annes, nous avons approvisionn gnreusement le march en liquidits, ce qui se reflta dans une baisse des taux d'intrt  court terme, qui passrent de prs de 4% au dbut de 1995  1,5% au dbut de 1997. A ce moment-l, se manifestrent les premiers signes d'une reprise conomique base sur les exportations. Notre sentiment tait toutefois que cette volution tait encore trop incertaine pour justifier une modification de notre politique. En outre, la situation sur le march des changes, caractrise  l'poque par une faiblesse prononce du mark allemand par rapport au franc suisse, ne laissait pas non plus paratre opportun un changement de stratgie. Les signes de reprise se multiplirent au courant de l't 1997. Pour la BNS, se posait ds lors la question de savoir si le moment tait venu de resserrer lentement sa politique. Au mme moment clata la crise asiatique. Bien que la dimension et les consquences de cette crise n'taient pas encore mesurables, on pouvait s'attendre  un affaiblissement des commandes en provenance de ces pays. Avec des perspectives d'exportation plus incertaines et une demande intrieure encore fragile, nous pouvions nous permettre de maintenir notre politique gnreuse sans craindre des pressions inflationnistes; ceci d'autant plus que la force du franc par rapport au DM attnuait le dveloppement du prix des biens imports. 1998 entrana un nouveau changement de dcor. L'anne fut mouvemente en raison de la fragilisation des marchs financiers et une grande incertitude entoura le processus d'intgration montaire en Europe. Le franc suisse fut ainsi amen  jouer de temps  autre un rle de monnaie de refuge. En janvier et fvrier, une premire vague de spculation mena  une forte demande de francs sur le march. Pour contrecarrer le mouvement, la BNS alimenta le march en liquidits supplmentaires. Le taux 8 d'intrt  trois mois tomba temporairement  1%. En mars, la situation sur le march des changes s'tant normalise, la liquidit excdentaire fut rsorbe. Ct conjoncture, la croissance annuelle dpassa le seuil de 3% pendant le premier trimestre de 1998, mais les prvisions taient au ralentissement de la croissance vers la fin de l'anne, ce qui rendait inopportune une ventuelle modification des conditions montaires. En aot, la dbcle russe, suivie par la plus grave crise sur les marchs financiers depuis le crash boursier de 1987, nous demanda de satisfaire une nouvelle fois l'apptit des marchs pour les liquidits, ce qui rorienta les taux d'intrt vers le bas. Contrairement  la situation prcdente, il aurait t contre-indiqu, une fois le calme revenu, de retirer rapidement les liquidits du march car la crise tait beaucoup plus srieuse que les turbulences du printemps. De plus, les prvisions de croissance taient continuellement rvises  la baisse et des risques de dflation taient mme voqus. Enfin, nous jugions prfrable de conserver une alimentation gnreuse du march en liquidits alors que les incertitudes entourant l'introduction de l'euro pouvaient tre sources de perturbations. Par notre dcision d'avril dernier de suivre par un ajustement de notre taux d'escompte la baisse des taux directeurs de la Banque Centrale Europenne, nous avons confirm notre volont de voir la relation franc-euro demeurer stable alors que les perspectives inflationnistes convergent fortement entre la Suisse et ses voisins. Dans l'ensemble, la politique montaire de ces trois dernires annes a t marque par une remarquable continuit. Nous nous sommes efforcs de maintenir des conditions montaires favorables au dveloppement de l'conomie suisse sans toutefois prendre le risque d'un emballement montaire, donc d'une dstabilisation des prix. La relative stabilit du franc par rapport aux monnaies des pays voisins, puis par rapport  l'euro qui en est dcoule a donn  notre conomie les meilleures chances de s'adapter  l'volution de la conjoncture internationale. Elle a certainement t un lment renforant la confiance des investisseurs et des consommateurs, dont la stabilit du comportement a t dcisive pour empcher que la conjoncture ne pique plus fortement du nez. 9 Des perspectives encourageantes Malgr le ralentissement survenu  la mi-1998, la croissance de l'anne passe s'est encore inscrite  2,1%. Pour 1999, les prvisions d'automne des instituts spcialiss s'levaient encore  un taux de croissance de 1,7%. Entre-temps, ces chiffres ont t rviss  la baisse pour ne retenir qu'une croissance de 1,3%. La rvision  la baisse ne touche pas toutes les composantes de la demande dans la mme mesure. Les prvisions concernant la demande interne (consommation et investissements) ne furent que lgrement corriges, tandis que les exportations ont subit une rvision plus prononce. Une fois de plus, nous nous rendons compte  quel point la conjoncture suisse est lie  l'tat de l'conomie europenne qui nous entoure. La Suisse dirige plus de la moiti de ses exportations vers les pays de la zone euro. La faiblesse actuelle de la conjoncture dans ce grand espace conomique ne peut donc rester sans consquence pour notre pays. Un certain optimisme s'installe maintenant en Europe et un rchauffement conjoncturel est annonc. Les chiffres rcents publis par l'OCDE sont encourageants  cet gard. La zone euro devrait connatre une croissance plus soutenue ds cet t. Nous pouvons en attendre une stimulation de nos exportations et un regain de croissance pour l'conomie suisse. Ainsi, les instituts de prvision s'attendent maintenant  ce que la conjoncture s'acclre  partir de la deuxime moiti de l'anne. Pour l'anne prochaine, ils prvoient un taux de croissance de 1,8%. Du ct montaire, les conditions pour une reprise sont favorables. Les prix sont stables et les taux d'intrt sont bas aussi bien sur le court que sur le long terme. Le taux de change par rapport  l'euro n'est pas un handicap pour notre comptitivit et sa stabilit est rjouissante. Un autre point qui m'inspire de l'optimisme est l'aboutissement des accords bilatraux entre la Suisse et l'Union europenne. La conclusion des ngociations met fin  une phase d'incertitude concernant le rapport Suisse-Europe, phase qui avait dbut avec le rejet de la participation de la Suisse  l'EEE en 1992. Les accords bilatraux donnent une nouvelle base  nos relations avec notre plus important partenaire 10 commercial; ils contribuent sensiblement  l'amlioration des conditions cadre pour l'conomie suisse. Il reste  esprer que le processus de ratification des accords soit rapide et libre de frictions. Dans certains autres domaines par contre, les conditions cadre pourraient encore tre amliores. Je pense, par exemple,  la poursuite des rformes structurelles, notamment  l'limination de barrires entravant la concurrence sur notre march intrieur et  la restauration de l'quilibre des finances publiques. De telles rformes sont ncessaires non seulement au progrs de notre bien-tre mais aussi  la prservation de notre future comptitivit. Conclusions Le rcent flchissement de la conjoncture en Suisse n'est pas annonciateur d'une nouvelle phase de stagnation conomique. La faiblesse de la croissance, note depuis un an, a t entrane par le refroidissement gnral de la marche des affaires au niveau mondial  la suite de la crise des pays mergents. La normalisation de la situation des marchs financiers et les perspectives de redressement conjoncturel en Europe placeront prochainement l'conomie suisse sur le chemin d'une meilleure croissance. La politique mene par la Banque nationale suisse ces dernires annes a vis la stabilit des prix tout en cherchant  crer les meilleures conditions montaires possibles pour l'expansion de l'conomie suisse. Aujourd'hui, avec des taux d'intrt bas et une grande stabilit du franc par rapport  l'euro, un cadre optimal existe, qui permettra  nos entreprises de profiter pleinement du redressement attendu de l'conomie mondiale.

Title: Introductory Remarks, Half-yearly Media News Conference
text: Half-yearly Media , Berne, 17 June 1999 Introductory remarks by Bruno Gehrig, Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Introductory remarks by Bruno Gehrig, Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Mastering the challenge of the millennium transition requires careful preparation and considerable resources. Malfunctions in electronic elements caused by the century date change can occur in all areas of the economy and life and cause havoc. The banking and financial sectors are particularly vulnerable, because they not only rely heavily on information technology but are also very sensitive to information. Secure processing of transactions and the integrity of data are a crucial element of trust in the modern banking and financial world. If there are serious technical problems with transactions that financial institutions conduct with their customers, or if parts of the financial centre's infrastructure are disrupted for any length of time, this jeopardises customers' trust and might lead to reactions with disastrous consequences. In an effort to take precautions, the Swiss Bankers' Association is therefore called upon to play a key role. Each financial organisation ought to have every interest in assuring its Year 2000 readiness. Since mid-1997, the Federal Banking Commission (FBC), for its part, has been monitoring the efforts undertaken by each individual bank and issues general guidelines on the topic. Interbank service providers for stock exchange trading (SWX), securities clearing (SECOM), and payment transactions (SIC) are also being scrutinised, however. At the moment, nothing points to any significant risk of malfunctions in the financial sector at the end of the year. The interbank test, which comprised nearly all the common IT systems, the joint ventures, and Postfinance did not uncover any deficiencies. Co-ordination among the financial market participants during this interbank test was efficient as well. By international standards, Switzerland is addressing the Year 2000 issue with the utmost care, not only with regard to the financial centre but also including the other sectors of the economy. The international co-ordination group, Global 2000, has confirmed this fact. Furthermore, surveys conducted by this forum, which is composed of private and public institutions, show that compared with other sectors worldwide, the financial sector (banks, stock exchanges and clearing houses) is well advanced in is preparations. The National Bank, in its efforts to cope with the Year 2000 problem, takes a three-prong approach:  Firstly, assuring the smooth functioning of its own banking operations;  Secondly, guaranteeing that the banking system is supplied with cash and sight deposits;  Thirdly, carrying out co-ordination and communication efforts in Switzerland as a financial centre We have reviewed our IT systems and tested the communication channels with our business partners. Of course, we also participated in the interbank test mentioned previously. In accordance with the results available, as far as our own operations are concerned, we can count on a smooth transition into the next millennium. Toward the end of the year, we expect increased demand for cash by the business community. This normally happens as a result of a seasonally induced peak in transaction volume. The widespread awareness with regard to the Year 2000 problem and the resultant precaution mentality might further stimulate the demand for cash. This is rather unnecessary, however, given the fact that preparations are well under way. We will, of course, meet any additional demand for banknotes. Our 60-million-franc supply of banknotes is considerable, both in absolute terms and in relation to the situation in other countries. We could easily cover the usual additional demand for banknotes at the end of year many times over. In addition, we do not foresee any bottlenecks or technical difficulties in the distribution of cash. Banks, the post office, manufacturers of automated teller machines as well as network providers have tested the cash dispensers of banks and the post office and found them to be Year 2000 compatible. In view of increased banknote circulation and taking into account their own liquidity requirements, the banks' requirements for sight deposits with the National Bank may well exceed seasonal demand. We can easily cover the additional need by taking appropriate liquidity measures. In so doing, we rely on our proven monetary instruments: repo transactions, foreign exchange swaps, and onward placement of time deposits of the Confederation. We focus on repo transactions, which combine the advantages of high volume potential, broad access to the market, collateral against advances, and efficient settlement. Smaller banks or foreign institutes can refinance themselves with repos directly with the National Bank. Should there be - contrary to expectations - technical problems at the turn of the year, we can conclude repos over the phone and process them manually. Together with the Federal Banking Commission, we ask that banks do two things in view of liquidity management at the end of the year. Firstly, they must plan their liquidity needs carefully and also take into account friction scenarios, however unlikely they may be. Secondly, based on their planning, they must make arrangements to secure liquidity consisting of three elements: maintaining liquidity, securing interbank limits, and making available bonds admitted for repo transactions. It is important to have sufficient holdings of such securities both for the procurement of liquidity on the money market and with the National Bank. Beyond that, we give banks the opportunity to temporarily increase their lombard loan limit with us. It is imperative that we have emergency plans in place so that we are not caught off guard even in the unlikely event of malfunctions. The Federal Banking Commission and the National Bank must play a coordination and communication role. For this purpose, both public institutions are represented in the steering committee of the banks, which is in charge of emergency planning for Switzerland as a financial centre. This committee will be operational around the clock from 31 December 1999 to 5 January 2000. Owing to this package of measures, ranging from prevention, recommendations, controls, tests and action plans, we are confident that the millennium transition will go without a hitch. There is no reason to be apprehensive as to the stability of our financial centre.

Title: Introductory Remarks, Half-yearly Media News Conference, Berne
text: Biannual press conference, Bern, 17 June 1999 Introductory remarks by Jean-Pierre Roth, Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Despite intense preparatory work, the introduction of the single currency entailed many uncertainties not only for the countries concerned, but also for the international financial markets. Disruptions in the financial markets were unlikely, but there were fears that the new European currency would lead to significant capital transfers. After a little less than six months of experience, we can see that this introduction has not led to the feared imbalances. In Switzerland too, the money, capital and foreign exchange markets have not been disturbed by the emergence of the euro. The movements of the euro against the franc were relatively narrow. So far, the relationship between the franc and the euro has been more stable than what we used to see between the franc and the German mark. Against the dollar, however, the euro has weakened clearly, losing more than 10% of its value since its introduction. This can be explained by the difference in business cycles and divergent interest rate expectations on both sides of the Atlantic. Moreover, as Latin America's financial situation has consolidated, the dollar has tended to regain the ground it lost in the fourth quarter of last year. These various elements, to which must be added questions about the role of the exchange rate in the monetary strategy of the European Central Bank, have combined to place the new European currency in a less favourable light than hoped. This development has weighed on the euro, which has not yet been able to establish itself as a solid pole and competitor of the dollar. Proof of this is the fact that, despite different business cycles, interest rates on the euro have been clearly influenced by the rise in long-term rates in the United States. Admittedly, the movements of European rates have been less marked than those of American rates, but this kind of attenuated reaction is a phenomenon already observed in the past. On the technical side, the emergence of the euro has advanced the integration of financial markets within the eleven countries of the Monetary Union. The money markets, which had largely converged during 1998, are now perfectly under the control of the European Central Bank. On the capital market, the euro has enabled the creation of a vast European market that is in second place, after that of the United States and ahead of the Japanese, British and Swiss markets. The volume of issues in the euro area has increased very positively from the outset. Its growth reached nearly 45% in the first quarter, while the US market saw only a 20% increase. However, its level remains below that of dollar issues. In terms of existing debt, the volume of the "euro" capital market represents nearly 60% of the US market. While papers issued by private debtors occupy a relatively small place in Europe compared to the situation on the other side of the Atlantic, the public debt securities of the eleven countries of the Union form a mass comparable to that of the US federal debt. However, this vast market is far from having reached the degree of integration of that of US Treasuries because of the partitions still present between European markets. In addition, there is some heterogeneity in the market for sovereign debt securities. For example, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and Finnish government bonds come with interest rates 30 basis points higher than the rates on Germany's ten-year public debt, which now serves as a benchmark on the eurozone capital market. These spreads have remained relatively stable since the beginning of the year. With regard to the impact of monetary unification on the Swiss capital market, the pace of issuance in the first half of the year did not reveal any atypical developments. The volume of swiss franc issues remained stable (CHF 21 billion for the first quarter), a stability that has been evident for more than a year now. As regards the distribution between Swiss and foreign debtor issuances, the doubling of the latter compared to the fourth quarter of 1998 is the result of a normalisation caused by the lull in the international financial markets. The spread between German and Swiss interest rates is a parameter that could react to the introduction of the single currency. For ten-year rates, this gap is currently 1.5 percentage points, compared to about two percentage points on average from 1985 to 1997. The narrowing of the gap is not a recent phenomenon. He had already manifested itself in the first half of 1998, when uncertainties about monetary integration dissipated, European long-term rates fell sharply. On the short-term rate side (3 months), the spread averaged only 1 percentage point during the years 1985 to 1997. It has always varied according to the accents of monetary policy in Switzerland and the surrounding Europe. It had virtually disappeared in the early nineties and had widened sharply in the two years before the introduction of the euro, a period during which German monetary policy had maintained a restrictive stance. Things have changed since then; European rates have fallen by 1 percentage point since last December, while ours have fallen by only about half a percentage point. The emergence of the euro thus coincided with a relaxation of the previous European monetary policy and led to a normalization of the gap between short rates. Before the advent of the single currency, there were also questions about the competition that the euro could make to the franc as a means of payment. In recent months, many euro-denominated accounts have been opened in Swiss banks, but the use of the European currency has grown only slowly. The euro is emerging as a means of payment in companies linked to foreign trade and in portfolio management. The slow pace of developments in recent months is not surprising, as monetary integration is still in its infancy. An acceleration of the process will certainly take place when the time comes closer to exchanging the old European denominations with the new euro denominations. On the whole, therefore, the appearance of the euro did not create the shock wave that some had expected. We are happy about that. However, the European currency is struggling to assert itself as a solid investment alternative against the dollar. We have never hidden that the introduction of the single currency would be surrounded by uncertainties and that the start-up phase of the new monetary regime would take time.

Title: Introductory Remarks, Half-yearly Media News Conference, Berne
text: Biannual press conference, Bern, 17 June 1999 Introductory remarks by Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank As expected, growth in the Swiss economy has been weak in recent months. In the first quarter, real gross domestic product was 0.7% higher than in the corresponding period of 1998. No impetus came from exports, and domestic demand lost some of its dynamism. Poor weather conditions, another factor that has weighed on developments, have had a significant impact on tourism and construction. The slowdown in growth has also affected the labour market. Since mid-1998, employment has been growing at a slower pace. However, unemployment continued to fall. Its decrease, it should be pointed out, has been amplified by the high number of unemployed at the end of their entitlements. Nevertheless, a positive turning point was clearly observed. It attests to the flexibility of our labour market. Other glimmers of hope have emerged in recent months. For example, for the global economy, the outlook is more favourable today than it was six months ago. The U.S. economy, which is still growing strongly, is providing welcome support to the global economy. In addition, the economic situation has stabilized in several East Asian countries. On the eurozone side, several indicators suggest that countries are gradually emerging from the phase of low growth. These developments have contributed decisively to the improvement of the climate in the Swiss economy. Based on a series of leading indicators, we can expect the economic situation in Switzerland to regain strength towards the end of the year. The calmer international environment is likely to have a positive impact on exports. Together with favourable consumption developments and the slow recovery in construction activity, these effects should stimulate economic growth. The hypothesis of an increase of about 1.5% in real gross domestic product in 1999 still seems plausible to us. As we announced last December, we continued to pursue a generous monetary policy. Short-term interest rates remained at a low level, at around 1%. On 9th April we reduced our discount rate from 1% to 0.5%, after the european Central Bank's key interest rate was cut. The remuneration paid on the Swiss money market then fell sharply, falling below 1%. As for long-term interest rates, they have done little to react to the reduction in the discount rate. In real and export-weighted terms, the exchange rate of the Franc fell slightly between January and April, so that monetary conditions in the first quarter were somewhat more expansionary than in the previous period. In April, we lowered our discount rate primarily to avoid a revaluation of the franc against the euro, which would have been contraindicated in view of the economic situation. Since the introduction of the euro at the beginning of the year, the exchange rate relationship between the new European currency and the franc has hardly fluctuated. This great stability reflects in particular the similarity in the evolution of the economic situation in Switzerland and in the countries of the euro zone, but also the broad concordance between the monetary policies pursued by the two central banks. The evolution of the M3 aggregate, which provides useful information on the medium-term trend of inflation, indicates that consumer prices in Switzerland are expected to remain stable in the near future. On average from January to April, M3 was only 0.8% above its level in the corresponding period of 1998. Such an increase shows that no inflationary danger threatens. As for the central currency, it has declined since December 1998. But, for known reasons, we can give little importance to its evolution. In the first months of this year, inflation accelerated slightly, as expected. On average from January to May, the consumer price index was 0.4% higher than in the same period of 1998. The increase in VAT, which entered into force at the beginning of 1999, has so far only been partially passed on to prices, according to estimates by the Federal Statistical Office. For goods in particular, it is clearly difficult to impose price increases. Moderate developments in commodity prices, global excess capacity in industry and strong international competition leave little room for such increases. In addition, the dismantling of measures supporting the prices of agricultural products is weighing on prices in the field of food. Apart from the liberalised telecommunications market, where there is intense competition, the services sector is much less affected by these developments. As a result, domestic demand, which is still robust, has led to significant but not worrying price increases for certain services provided by the private sector. In addition, none Inflationary pressure does not stem from wages, although a scarcity of supply can be observed in several segments of the labour market. For 1999 as a whole, we expect consumer prices to rise by less than 1%. Thus, price stability will continue to prevail in Switzerland. Low inflation is not incompatible with price stability, as the Swiss consumer price index slightly increases the price increase. In a recently published study on the measurement problems associated with the consumer price index, the Federal Statistical Office estimates that the distortion is about half a point. We welcome the Agency's intention to eliminate this distortion in the medium term. Overall, the environment in which we operated in the first half of the year was what we expected. The outlook, as always, remains uncertain. Trust, however, seems to be well-founded. Through our monetary policy, we are helping to ensure that the Swiss economy can overcome its phase of low growth, without jeopardizing price stability in the medium term.
