Title: International Monetary Developments
text: International Monetary Developments Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board Swiss National Bank Edinburgh Finance & Investment Seminar Glasgow Discussion Group on Finance & Investment, Edinburgh Tuesday, June 22, 1999 2 1. Premise The fact that close international cooperation in the economic and social as well as in the cultural sphere is a worthy pursuit does not have to be emphasised on this occasion. If, however, we are convinced that this endeavour is in fact important, there must be clarity as to what it takes to succeed. My following remarks are intended to make a contribution to this end. For obvious reasons, the main focus will be on international monetary developments. Reasonably stable currency relations are a decisive precondition for successful economic cooperation beyond one's own borders. Such relations are ultimately the result of a sustained convergence of solid economic policies implemented by individual countries. Unfortunately, the push toward globalisation often clouds the perception that at least for the foreseeable future, each country must take responsibility for its own actions and failures to act. Guaranteeing reasonably stable currency relations is, in the final analysis, a social challenge. It is vital that individual countries muster the necessary discipline for a sustained effort. This cannot be achieved with institutional means alone. The respective rules and regulations are a necessary, but not a sufficient basis for success. 2. Possible solutions Looking back over the past hundred years, three different models for shaping international monetary relations can be distinguished: the Gold Standard, the Bretton Woods agreements and a flexible exchange rate system. With the Gold Standard, the value of different currencies was defined in terms of gold, which also established the parity between individual currencies. This regulation severely curtailed the individual central banks' room for manoeuvre. Defending the gold parity of their own currency was the primary concern. Imbalances in international economic relations led to gold movements. These movements subsequently triggered either expansive or restrictive monetary impulses in the countries affected, which tended to restore the balance. 3 The Gold Standard was in its prime during the decades before and after the turn of the last century, a period characterised by widespread economic stability in individual countries. International economic relations and overall economic growth developed at a correspondingly favourable pace. The term "globalisation" applies to this past period as much as it does to the present time. However, in evaluating the Gold Standard, a distinction must be made between fact and fiction. It was, after all, not gold itself that paved the way for a favourable development, but rather the willingness of individual countries to subordinate their national economic policy interests to the requirements of foreign trade. Gold merely had the function of indicating a need for adjustments. When countries began to set priorities differently in pursuing their economic policy goals, these signals were increasingly ignored. By then, the sands were running out for the Gold Standard. While the Gold Standard had developed rather informally, the Bretton Woods regulations were the result of concrete international agreements which were already negotiated during the Second World War and finalised immediately after it was over. The idea behind these agreements was to regulate international monetary relations in an attempt to strike a balance between flexibility and pegging. While exchange rates were to be fixed, they should nevertheless be adjustable in the event of fundamental imbalances. The possibility of taking corrective action was introduced in order to facilitate the adjustment process. Individual countries were granted the right to limit the free flow of capital. These regulations, of course, reflect a change in attitude with respect to the priorities of economic policy. Even though close economic integration between individual countries basically remained a desirable goal, it was not necessarily considered an economic priority. In the final analysis, it was a question of attempting to find an optimal compromise between conflicting interests of policies focused on domestic and international objectives. With a view to implementing the intentions contained in the Bretton Woods agreements, the International Monetary Fund was assigned the task of promoting international monetary cooperation. Economic policy counselling, specialist technical 4 support and financial assistance in the form of loans to help ease adaptation processes have become the main elements of its activities. Experience has subsequently shown that institutional regulations are a necessary, but insufficient requirement for success. It is indispensable for individual countries to make their own contributions. In the course of time, finding a proper balance between stressing the self-reliance of a member country and support from the international community represented in the IMF has become the true leitmotiv. Around the mid-seventies, the transition was made to a floating exchange rate system, which, at the time, gave rise to high hopes. It was believed that with exchange rates becoming more flexible, the conflicting interests between autonomous action and cooperation would largely become non-existent. A quarter of a century later, the experience gained presents a mixed picture. Positively, flexible exchange rates have proved to be a suitable instrument for overcoming imbalances. Despite sizeable differences in the economic development of individual countries, economic interchange has become considerably more pronounced. If, however, the need for adjustment goes beyond a certain level both in manner and scope, even flexible exchange rates can no longer provide a remedy. Again, the assertion that it is imperative for individual countries to keep their own house in order has shown itself to be correct. This insight has also proved to be true in times when greater freedom of capital movements resulted in more sensitive reactions to wrong developments. Occasionally, attempts have been made to counteract extraordinary exchange rate developments with official market interventions. Economics and experience have shown, however, that such interventions only make sense when they are coupled with a change in the course of monetary policy. 3. Current situation In recent times, international monetary relations around the world have been influenced by the well-known developments in Asia, Russia and Latin America. 5 These developments may have their characteristic features in individual cases; they nevertheless give rise to a number of comments of a more general nature. In my opinion, it is essential to recognise that imbalances in economic development, weak financial systems and insufficient supervision of financial markets are merely symptoms of deeper-lying causes. Our most recent experiences serve to confirm the opinion that sustained economic development is only possible on the basis of social and economic stability. First and foremost, however, individual countries themselves bear the responsibility for creating this stability. In so doing, they ultimately make the best contribution toward international cooperation. In the course of developments in recent years, the International Monetary Fund has increasingly been in the limelight and, at the same time, also under attack. This is a fairly normal development. Even though criticism of the institution with prime responsibility for international monetary cooperation is nothing unusual, it nevertheless frequently seems to be exaggerated. As mentioned earlier, since its inception, the IMF has had to strike a balance between stressing the self-reliance of individual countries and a readiness to facilitate adjustment processes. This will not change much in the future either. Walking this tightrope is not made any easier by the fact that even this multinational institution is not immune to political influences. In this respect, too, things will hardly change. The situation is further complicated because the Monetary Fund is only able to enforce its recommendations to a limited degree. Moreover, it is obvious that the means at its disposal for granting financial assistance in the form of loans will always be limited. Such situations cannot be mastered with institutional means alone. The regularly recurring call for reform of the international monetary order can change little in this respect. Naturally, this does not rule out improvements. However, in my opinion, conceptual questions are not the main issue. The primary need is actually to implement what has been recognised as basically right. Improved transparency of financial market transactions is an essential goal. This will enable both official authorities and private market participants to make a more accurate assessment of the situation. At the same time, it cannot be overlooked that 6 errors and failures are frequently due to the inappropriate evaluation of actually available information rather than to a lack of transparency. Another urgent matter is improved supervision of national financial markets. Again, conceptual questions are hardly the issue, since these have been dealt with by various bodies in recent years. The emphasis is now on the consistent application of the insights gained. Yet another difficult chapter is the question of participation by the private sector in preparing for, and overcoming, crisis situations. The basic principle should be to hold the private sector responsible for its own actions and failures to act. Official financial aid in the form of credits may not extend to the point of relieving it of its responsibility. This, of course, applies to both the domestic and foreign private sectors. 4. European Monetary Union The European Monetary Union must be included in any consideration of developments in the international monetary sphere. Its formal realisation at the beginning of this year represents a significant turning point both for the countries immediately affected as well as for the remaining European countries. If the European Monetary Union develops according to plan, the preconditions for productive economic development in Europe will undoubtedly improve markedly. It is not, however, the single currency as such that is of decisive importance, but rather what lies behind, namely a sustained convergence of stability-oriented policies, at least in the major countries. In the context of the run-up to monetary union, significant progress has been made in this respect in the participating countries. Inflation has been contained and government budgets have been brought in line with lasting effect. In view of the challenges that lie ahead, one must bear in mind that with the fixing of exchange rates, individual countries have forfeited an element of flexibility in their economic policies. Imbalances in economic development could formerly be 7 compensated with flexible exchange rates. Losing this possibility is significant since flexibility is already lacking in numerous countries today. The European Central Bank has clearly stated its position on the question of its strategy. It has offered a concrete definition of its view of price stability: the consumer price index is not to exceed 2% p.a. However, an inflation target was not formulated. At the same time, the significance of the development of the money stocks is emphasised. I note with satisfaction that these ideas are largely in conformity with our own thinking. The chances are thus good that this will result in a sustained convergence of stability-oriented policies and, as a consequence, basically stable currency relations between Switzerland and the new monetary area. With this scenario, we would not have to contend with undue repercussions on the Swiss franc. Should, however, difficulties arise when the present goals are implemented, we would have to expect some turbulence. This is likely to result in upward pressures on the Swiss franc. The National Bank would have the possibility of relaxing monetary policy to counteract such a trend. This might, however, conflict with its policy's orientation towards stability. All this implies that a small and open country such as Switzerland only has limited room for manoeuvre in conducting its monetary relations. There are basically two options. The country's currency can be pegged to the currency of another country. That, however, means having to relinquish an independent monetary policy. A previously existing favourable interest rate differential would at least be significantly reduced. Our economy would be burdened with substantial adjustment costs. The other possibility would be to keep currency relations flexible, thereby preserving a greater measure of autonomy. There is obviously no ideal solution. There would be no objection to a fixed link if the policy of the partner matched one's own ideas and if this could be assumed to remain the case also in the future. This second precondition is rarely ever met, which seems to favour the option providing for more autonomy in the conduct of monetary policy. After a good start, the euro has now entered more turbulent waters. As far as I can see, there are various reasons for this. Diverging economic developments in the United States and in Europe are an important factor. Secondly, the implications of the 8 revived economic policy debate in Europe must be mentioned. Finally, a certain euphoria, which made itself felt in the preparatory phase and when the euro was launched, has given way to a more sober attitude. The development has not reached a critical point as yet. However, the responsible persons and bodies are well advised to give their full attention to the further course of events. When all is said and done, the experience gained during this short period already serves to confirm the prediction that success will depend on the ability of participants to muster the discipline necessary for a sustained stability-oriented policy. 5. Outlook In the past decades, the quality and scope of the economic and social environment have changed considerably. The experience gained in the course of this development has, however, also shown that a number of basic insights must be taken into account. In particular, I would like to point out once more that even in the economic sphere, sustained international cooperation is only possible among countries that have achieved economic and social stability. The demand made on any individual country is therefore first and foremost to keep its own house in order. This will in all circumstances be a difficult and onerous task. Moreover, it is obvious that the preconditions for success vary from one country to another. Outside help is therefore indispensable in many cases. Such assistance can, however, only be effective if it is provided in the form of help towards self-help. International financial relations are supported mainly by the private sector. Basic conditions must be designed so as to be conducive to the stability and integrity of such relations. Good use should be made of market forces in creating these conditions. If the difficult circumstances in which the International Monetary Fund has to perform its task are taken into account, its activity can be rated as mainly positive. The 9 institution's mandate and self-image have changed in line with the changing environment in the course of time. That will also be the case in the future. What is important, in the final analysis, is to take due care to maintain a balance between conceptual adjustments and their consistent implementation.

Title: The Swiss franc in an international environment
text: The Swiss franc in the international currency concert Georg Rich Swiss National Bank Presentation at the Capital Markets Symposium of WGZ-Bank Luxembourg S.A., Luxembourg, 10 September 1999 1. Introduction The debate about the introduction of the euro also made waves in Switzerland, even though our country is not part of the European Union. Many Swiss believe that European monetary integration will have a strong impact on monetary developments in our country. Especially before the changeover to the euro, there was widespread fear that the creation of the European Monetary Union would lead to an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc on the foreign exchange market and thus undermine the competitiveness of the Swiss export industry. Many observers of European monetary integration - inside and outside Switzerland - also believe that with the introduction of the euro, the Swiss National Bank (SNB), the central bank of Switzerland, will sooner or later feel compelled to abandon its autonomous monetary policy and lean closely on the European Central Bank. The loss of monetary policy autonomy will also deal the death blow to the "interest rate island of Switzerland". Rather, the comparatively low interest rates in our country would climb to the level in the euro area. Some observers even go a step further and predict that the euro will establish itself as a parallel currency in Switzerland and displace the franc over time. Switzerland will nolens volens be dragged into the spell of the euro. These sometimes dramatic predictions have not yet materialized. Of course, the euro does not leave the Swiss economy and Swiss monetary policy untouched. But the developments triggered by the euro in Switzerland lack the revolutionary veneer. For example, the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the euro is within narrow limits. There is no sign of the upward pressure on the Swiss franc feared in many places. The Swiss economy has been undergoing a profound and painful structural change for some time now. However, these upheavals have little to do with European monetary integration. Rather, they reflect the globalization of the economy and the associated intensification of the international competitive climate. This raises the question of whether the euro is likely to have such a dramatic impact on the Swiss economy and monetary policy, as is often claimed. I would like to look into this question below. I will start with the relationship between European monetary integration and the Swiss franc exchange rate. I will then discuss the prospects for the continuation of an independent Swiss monetary policy and for the preservation of the interest rate island of Switzerland. I will conclude with a few comments on the possible role of the euro as a parallel currency. 2. Euro and Swiss franc exchange rate The fear of an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc is understandable when one thinks back to the exchange rate turbulence of 1993 to 1995. At that time, the Swiss franc exchange rate rose - both nominally and in real terms - to a level that seriously affected the international competitiveness of Swiss industry. This development seemed to be mainly related to European monetary integration. Many investors doubted the stability of the planned common currency and were anxious to reallocate part of their assets into Swiss francs. The soaring of our currency was contrary to the economic condition of the Swiss economy at the time. After a recession that had already lasted three years, an economic recovery became apparent in Switzerland at the beginning of 1994. However, the upswing turned out to be short-lived. As early as the second half of 1994, Swiss economic growth began to flatten out again. The main reason for the disappointing performance of the Swiss economy was the massive appreciation of the Swiss franc. The rise in the share price led to a renewed economic slump in 1996 and conjured up a real risk of deflation in Switzerland. In the spring of 1995, the SNB began to gradually loosen its monetary policy, having already switched to an expansionary monetary policy in the summer of 1992. This was expressed in a sharp decline in Swiss short-term interest rates and an acceleration in growth in monetary aggregates. The change in monetary policy did not immediately affect the exchange rate. The Swiss franc did not weaken until 1995 - at first only modestly and accelerated from August 1996 to January 1997 after a further easing of the monetary policy reins. At the beginning of 1997, the Swiss economy also picked up speed again. The Swiss economy achieved respectable growth rates in both 1997 and 1998, and unemployment declined. However, this favourable picture is clouded by the crisis in East Asia, which has been affecting economic growth in Switzerland and our neighbouring countries since the 2nd half of 1998. Various signs, however, indicate that the Swiss economy is reviving. We expect higher real growth again in the 2nd half of 1999. Overall, Switzerland's real gross domestic product is expected to increase by about 1.5% in 1999, after having risen by a good 2% in the previous year. The unemployment rate in July 1999 was 2.7% seasonally adjusted. In 1997 it had climbed over 5%. In view of these developments, fears that the changeover to the euro could excessively raise the exchange rate of the Swiss franc were justified. However, my remarks also make it clear that we are not powerless at the mercy of such developments. The SNB is in a position to counteract an undesirable appreciation of the Swiss franc. The monetary policy stance that we have been steering for four years shows the extent to which we can protect the Swiss economy from harmful exchange rate fluctuations. Nevertheless, the limits of an exchange-rate-based monetary policy should not be overlooked. The SNB can focus its monetary policy on stabilising the exchange rate at any time. It can loosen monetary policy in the event of an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc and, in extreme cases, even go one step further by temporarily fixing the exchange rate. However, the temporary fixation of the exchange rate would have a serious consequence: the SNB would lose control of the Money supply. If it expands the money supply too much, it would create a new inflation potential. It would have to buy the stabilization of the exchange rate at the price of a later rise in inflation. For this reason, the SNB must not lose sight of its main mandate to keep the price level stable in its actions on the foreign exchange market. In the past, the SNB has not always succeeded in reconciling the wishes of wider economic circles for a stable exchange rate with the objective of price stability. In the last three years, however, the SNB has been in a comparatively pleasant position, as there has been no conflict of objectives between price and exchange rate stability. In the mid-nineties, as I have already explained, the Swiss economy was burdened by a real deflationary pressure, which the SNB had to counter with an expansive monetary policy. It was clear to us that neither inflationary nor deflationary absenteeism was consistent with the objective of price stability. The strong appreciation of the Swiss franc in 1993 and 1994 exacerbated deflationary pressures in Switzerland. The Asian crisis also fuelled fears of deflation once again. Therefore, the SNB's efforts to prevent the Swiss franc from appreciating excessively have helped to maintain price stability. As the SNB pays close attention to exchange rate developments, the stability of the euro/franc ratio is no surprise. However, I do not want to give the impression that the SNB alone ensured that the Swiss franc did not appreciate significantly against the euro - contrary to widespread fears. The European Central Bank's consistent monetary policy, aimed at maintaining price stability, also helped to avoid serious disturbances in the foreign exchange market. The weakness of the euro against the dollar, which was particularly pronounced last summer, was often attributed to a lack of confidence in the ECB. In my opinion, however, the reason for the weakness of the euro at that time lay in a different place: as a result of the different developments in the European and American economies, a temporary lower valuation of the euro against the dollar was almost imperative. The The Swiss franc weakened against the dollar in step with the euro, as the Swiss economy developed in a similar way to that of the euro area. There are therefore good economic reasons for the recent movements in the euro and franc exchange rates against the dollar. This had nothing to do with a lack of confidence in the ECB. Otherwise, the weakness of the euro would also have triggered flight movements into the Swiss franc. I would also like to warn against interpreting a paradigm shift in Swiss monetary policy into the stability of the franc/euro ratio. Market participants sometimes argue that the swiss franc's stable stance against the euro reflects a departure by the SNB from its autonomous monetary policy: it has informally linked the franc to the euro and is more or less adopting the monetary policy pursued by the ECB. However, there can be no question of a paradigm shift. As I have already stressed, our exchange-rate-related monetary policy was in line with our objective of maintaining price stability. I would not rule out the possibility that we will have to allow greater fluctuations against the euro again in the future if we want to remain true to our main monetary policy objective. With these remarks, I come to the more general question of whether it makes sense at all for a small country like Switzerland to pursue an independent monetary policy. Wouldn't Switzerland be better advised to permanently peg the franc to the euro and thus give up its monetary policy autonomy? Let me respond briefly to this question. 3. Autonomous monetary policy and Switzerland as the island of interest rates The advantages of linking the Swiss franc to the euro are obvious: the fixed exchange rate makes it easier for companies involved in export and import to do so. They have a higher degree of certainty about the prices at which they can sell or purchase their products abroad. You can use it better plan their production and investments and reduce the risk of business mistakes. However, there are still costs involved in exchanging foreign currencies for Swiss francs and vice versa. Transaction costs in foreign exchange trading would only be eliminated if Switzerland not only tied the franc to the euro, but also introduced the euro as legal tender instead of the franc. With the peg of the Swiss franc to the euro, of course, the exchange rate fluctuations did not disappear completely. Only the exchange rate against the euro area would be stabilised. However, the vast majority of Switzerland's total foreign trade would be conducted via a fixed exchange rate: in 1998, 55% of Swiss exports of goods and a good 70% of the corresponding imports accounted for the euro area. Foreign trade vis-e0-vis the dollar area, on the other hand, would not be affected by the peg. The advantage of greater exchange rate stability would be offset by two major disadvantages of pegging the Swiss franc to the euro. On the one hand, the interest bonus on the Swiss franc disappeared with the connection. On the other hand, the SNB would completely lose its ability to conduct an independent monetary policy. As is well known, interest rates in Switzerland tend to be lower than in all other European countries. This pattern is more pronounced for long-term interest rates than for short-term ones, which are particularly dependent on the SNB's monetary policy and the respective economic condition of the Swiss economy. Returns on long-term Swiss franc investments are lower than elsewhere in Europe, even if the comparison takes into account the real capital gains and losses incurred as a result of exchange rate and price changes. The real interest rate differential is still 1-2 percentage points, even though it has tended to recede over the past three decades. The experts argue about the reasons for the interest bonus on the Swiss franc. The high current account surplus is likely to help keep interest rates in Switzerland low. In my opinion, however, the main reason lies in the traditional stability of the Swiss franc, which makes our currency an attractive diversification tool for international investors. If Switzerland fixed the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the euro, the interest bonus would be lost over time. International investors would henceforth regard the euro and the Swiss franc as perfect substitutes; the incentive to diversify into our currency would be eliminated. Investments in euros and Swiss francs of the same quality and the same maturity would also have to yield the same returns. Swiss interest rates would align with those in the euro area and would essentially be determined by the ECB. The SNB would no longer be in a position to influence domestic interest rate developments and to ensure the stability of the Swiss franc on its own. The adjustment of the Swiss economy to a higher level of interest rates would not be free of charge. The Swiss economy would lose an international competitive advantage. The higher interest rates would prompt Swiss companies to reduce the use of capital in their production. As a result, the high Swiss real wages came under pressure. The Swiss Confederation, the cantons and the communes would have to accept an increase in their expenditure in the form of interest on their debts, while the homeowners would feel the higher interest burden on their mortgages. The adjustment costs that the Swiss economy would have to bear as a result of the interest rate hike should not be underestimated. They would have to be contrasted with the advantages of pegging to the euro. The second major drawback, the complete loss of monetary policy autonomy, is often downplayed in public debate. For example, one hears the argument that the SNB has already leaned closely on the Deutsche Bundesbank and is now in the shadow of the ECB. Furthermore, the economic development in Switzerland usually runs parallel to that in Germany. Thus, the SNB is not forced to conduct a monetary policy that differs significantly from that of the Bundesbank or the ECB. However, commentators who question the need for an independent Swiss monetary policy overlook an important point: in the discussion about the sense and nonsense of an independent monetary policy, the devil is - as so often - in the detail. It is true that there is usually a great deal of agreement between the economic development in Germany and Switzerland. Scientific studies confirm this fact. Furthermore, like the Deutsche Bundesbank in the past, the ECB pursues the same monetary policy objectives as the SNB. Given the similarity of monetary policy objectives and the economic environment, it is not surprising that the SNB often follows the same course as the ECB or the Deutsche Bundesbank. However, this fact must not lead to the SNB merely imitating the policy of our sister institutions in the north. If we look at Swiss monetary policy in recent years, it becomes clear that the SNB - despite all the similarities in principle - has repeatedly exhausted its scope for an independent course. From the summer of 1992 to the end of 1993, it eased its monetary policy more quickly than the Deutsche Bundesbank. As a result, money market interest rates in Switzerland fell faster than in Germany; in this period, the interest rate differential with Germany temporarily reached 3 percentage points. The Bundesbank was forced to steer a more restrictive course than the SNB, as inflation in Germany did not decline as quickly and sustainably as in Switzerland. As a result of the temporary economic boom triggered by reunification, inflation in Germany rose again to over 4% in 1993, while in Switzerland it continued to decline. The interest rate differential with Germany remained in the following years. At present, money market interest rates in Switzerland are still below those in Germany and the euro area. As I have already pointed out, the SNB continues to pursue an expansionary monetary policy in view of the rather subdued economic recovery of the Swiss economy. In doing so, it takes into account the specific economic difficulties of Switzerland, which has been undergoing a particularly painful structural change compared to other European countries for several years. With the Swiss franc pegging to the euro, Swiss money market interest rates would have to rise to the level in the euro area and could no longer be changed autonomously by the SNB. I do not need to point out specifically that such a surge in interest rates would be completely wrong in the current economic landscape. Of course, one can argue that the connection would integrate Switzerland even more closely into the euro area economically. This would also reduce the need for an independent Swiss monetary policy. However, it is unlikely that the economic conditions for a complete abandonment of our monetary autonomy would set in immediately. For this reason, the SNB is well advised not to give up its independence lightly. 4. The euro as a Swiss parallel currency Some observers of European monetary integration go so far as to claim that the decision on the peg of the Swiss franc to the euro will ultimately be made by the market, even if the authorities insist on an autonomous monetary policy. Market forces would ensure that the euro will spread in Switzerland over time as a parallel currency to the Swiss franc. Once the euro has established itself in Switzerland, it will sooner or later displace the franc. The SNB thus loses its ability to manage the Swiss money supply, as the Swiss public will no longer hold the money it has spent. Regardless of the will of the Swiss authorities, the market will thus force the "peg" of the franc to the euro. What is to be made of this claim? To answer this question, we must first clarify the concept of the parallel currency. This refers to two different phenomena. On the one hand, it can be assumed that the euro will increasingly serve as an invoice currency for cross-border transactions. Many foreign customers are likely to insist that Swiss producers invoice their exports in euros instead of francs. In Swiss Tourist centres and border towns are already very willing to accept the euro as a means of payment. It is also conceivable that Swiss companies will accommodate foreign investors by issuing more euro-denominated securities. The euro will undoubtedly play an important role as an international transaction currency. For example, an ECB study1 published in August suggests that the new common currency accounts for a larger share of international bond issuances in the euro area than the corresponding national currencies before 1999. Thus, the euro seems to be establishing itself on the capital market as a transaction currency. For Swiss monetary policy, however, the question of whether the euro or the swiss franc serves as the unit of account for cross-border transactions is of secondary importance. In principle, every payment linked to a cross-border transaction consists of a foreign currency and a Swiss franc part. If Swiss hotels accept euros instead of francs in payment, little will change for Swiss monetary policy. The use of the euro as a transaction currency only means that the hotel establishments - instead of the guests - have to exchange euros into francs. Of course, the hotel companies take an exchange rate risk. It is also conceivable that Swiss companies active in international trade will feel compelled to keep their bank balances increasingly in euros and less in swiss francs in order to process their payment transactions. The SNB would have to take these shifts in money demand into account when determining its monetary policy. The SNB would only face serious problems if the euro displaced the franc as a domestic means of payment and store of value. However, there are no signs of such a development. True parallel currency systems - under which both domestic and one foreign currency are optionally used for domestic payments - only dive in countries with extremely high 1 Europe4ische Zentralbank, "The international role of the euro", ECB Monthly Bulletin, August 1999, S. 34. Inflation. On the other hand, I know of no examples of countries with moderate or low inflation in which parallel currencies have ever played a significant role. Sometimes it is claimed that in Canada the American dollar is used to a large extent as a parallel currency. Anyone familiar with Canadian conditions knows that the American dollar does not circulate there as a parallel currency any more than the euro does in Switzerland. The fear that the euro will prevail in Switzerland as the actual parallel currency is therefore exaggerated. 5. Schlussbetrachtung As I have shown, there is no reason for the SNB to move away from an independent monetary policy. If the SNB pursues an independent course, it is in a position to take account of the special needs of the Swiss population and economy when defining monetary policy. However, the SNB can only conduct an effective independent monetary policy if it allows the exchange rate of the Swiss franc to fluctuate freely in principle. It is possible that the Swiss franc will appreciate to an undesirable extent and cause damage to the Swiss economy. However, the SNB is not powerless in the face of such developments. If it focuses its monetary policy on stabilising the exchange rate, it must ensure that it does not loosen monetary policy too much and thus creates new inflation potential. The pegging of the Swiss franc to the euro would significantly reduce the risk of harmful exchange rate fluctuations. However, higher exchange rate stability would have to be bought at the price of a loss of monetary policy autonomy. Swiss monetary policy would no longer be determined by the SNB, but by the ECB. The interest bonus on the Swiss franc would disappear. The attractiveness of the Swiss franc as an investment currency no longer depends on the credibility and good reputation of the SNB; the quality of the monetary policy conducted in Frankfurt would henceforth be the only decisive factor. There is occasional speculation about how long Switzerland will stick to an independent monetary policy. I refrain from making my own forecast. In my opinion, there is no reason to abandon our independent monetary policy as long as Switzerland remains outside the European Union. Our country's accession to the European Union would, of course, change the situation. If Switzerland joined the European Union, it would probably also adopt the euro and thus lose its monetary autonomy. However, Switzerland's rapid accession to the European Union is still unlikely.

Euro und Frankenkurs Die Furcht vor einer bermssigen Frankenaufwertung ist verstndlich, wenn man an die Wechselkursturbulenzen von 1993 bis 1995 zurckdenkt. Damals stieg der Frankenkurs - sowohl nominell als auch real - auf ein Niveau, das die internationale Konkurrenzfhigkeit der schweizerischen Industrie ernsthaft beeintrchtigte. Anfang 1997 kam auch die schweizerische Konjunktur erneut in Fahrt. Die schweizerische Wirtschaft erreichte sowohl 1997 als auch 1998 ansehnliche Wachstumsraten, und die Arbeitslosigkeit bildete sich zurck. Dieses gnstige Bild wird allerdings durch die Krise in Ostasien getrbt, die seit dem 2. Halbjahr 1998 das Wirtschaftswachstum in der Schweiz und in unseren Nachbarlndern beeintrchtigt. Verschiedene Anzeichen deuten indessen darauf hin, dass die schweizerische Konjunktur zu neuem Leben erwacht. Wir rechnen fr das 2. Halbjahr 1999 wieder mit einem hheren Realwachstum. Insgesamt drfte das reale schweizerische Bruttoinlandprodukt im Jahre 1999 um etwa 1,5% zunehmen, nachdem es im Vorjahr noch um gut 2% gestiegen war. Die Arbeitslosenquote betrug im Juli 1999 saisonbereinigt 2,7%. Im Jahre 1997 war sie ber 5% geklettert. Angesichts dieser Entwicklungen waren die Befrchtungen, der bergang zum Euro knnte den Wechselkurs des Schweizer Frankens bermssig in die Hhe treiben, angebracht. Meine Ausfhrungen machen aber auch deutlich, dass wir solchen Entwicklungen nicht machtlos ausgeliefert sind. Die SNB ist in der Lage, einer unerwnschten Frankenaufwertung entgegenzuwirken. Der geldpolitische Kurs, den wir seit vier Jahren steuern, zeigt, inwieweit wir die schweizerische Wirtschaft vor schdlichen Wechselkursschwankungen schtzen knnen. Dennoch sollten die Grenzen einer am Wechselkurs ausgerichteten Geldpolitik nicht bersehen werden. Die SNB kann zwar ihre Geldpolitik jederzeit auf die Stabilisierung des Wechselkurses ausrichten. Sie kann bei einer bermssigen Frankenaufwertung die Geldpolitik lockern und im Extremfall sogar noch einen Schritt weitergehen, indem sie den Wechselkurs vorbergehend fixiert. Die vorbergehende Fixierung des Wechselkurses htte aber eine schwer wiegende Konsequenz: Die SNB verlre die Kontrolle ber die Geldmenge. Weitete sie die Geldmenge allzu stark aus, schfe sie ein neues Inflationspotenzial. Sie msste die Stabilisierung des Wechselkurses um den Preis eines spteren Inflationsanstiegs erkaufen. Aus diesem Grunde darf die SNB bei ihren Aktionen am Devisenmarkt ihren Hauptauftrag, das Preisniveau stabil zu halten, nicht aus den Augen verlieren. In der Vergangenheit gelang es der SNB nicht immer, die Wnsche weiter Kreise der Wirtschaft nach einem stabilen Wechselkurs mit dem Ziel der Preisstabilitt in Einklang zu bringen. In den letzten drei Jahren befand sich die SNB freilich in einer vergleichsweise angenehmen Lage, da kein Zielkonflikt zwischen Preis- und Wechselkursstabilitt auftrat. Mitte der neunziger Jahre lastete auf der schweizerischen Wirtschaft - wie ich schon ausfhrte - ein eigentlicher Deflationsdruck, dem die SNB mit einer expansiven Geldpolitik begegnen musste. Denn es war fr uns klar, dass weder inflationre noch deflationre Fehlent wicklungen mit dem Ziel der Preisstabilitt in Einklang stehen. Die starke Frankenaufwertung von 1993 und 1994 verschlimmerte den Deflationsdruck in der Schweiz. Auch die Asienkrise schrte noch einmal die Deflationsngste. Deshalb trugen die Bemhungen der SNB, eine allzu starke Aufwertung des Schweizer Frankens zu verhindern, zur Bewahrung der Preisstabilitt bei. Da die SNB der Wechselkursentwicklung grosse Aufmerksamkeit schenkt, stellt die Stabilitt der Euro/Franken-Relation keine berraschung dar. Ich mchte aber nicht den Eindruck erwecken, die SNB allein habe dafr gesorgt, dass sich der Schweizer Franken gegenber dem Euro - entgegen den weit verbreiteten Befrchtungen - nicht wesentlich aufwertete. Die konsequente, auf die Bewahrung der Preisstabilitt ausgerichtete Geldpolitik der Europischen Zentralbank trug ebenfalls dazu bei, schwer wiegende Strungen am Devisenmarkt zu vermeiden. Die vor allem im vergangenen Sommer ausgeprgte Schwche des Euro gegenber dem Dollar wurde zwar hufig auf einen Mangel an Vertrauen in die EZB zurckgefhrt. Der Grund fr die damalige Euroschwche lag aber nach meiner Meinung an einem anderen Ort: Als Folge der unterschiedlichen Entwicklungen der europischen und amerikanischen Konjunktur drngte sich eine vorbergehende Tieferbewertung des Euro gegenber dem Dollar geradezu auf. Der Schweizer Franken schwchte sich im Verhltnis zum Dollar im Gleichschritt mit dem Euro ab, da sich die schweizerische Konjunktur hnlich entwickelte wie jene des Eurogebiets. Es gibt somit gute wirtschaftliche Grnde fr die jngsten Bewegungen des Euro- und Frankenkurses gegenber dem Dollar. Mit einem Mangel an Vertrauen in die EZB hatte dies nichts zu tun. Sonst htte die Euroschwche auch Fluchtbewegungen in den Schweizer Franken ausgelst. Ich mchte ebenfalls davor warnen, in die Stabilitt der Franken/Euro-Relation einen Paradigmawechsel in der schweizerischen Geldpolitik hinein zu interpretieren. Marktteilnehmer vertreten manchmal die Meinung, der stabile Kurs des Frankens gegenber dem Euro widerspiegle eine Abkehr der SNB von ihrer autonomen Geldpolitik: Sie habe den Franken informell an den Euro angebunden und bernehme mehr oder weniger die von der EZB verfolgte Geldpolitik. Von einem Paradigmawechsel kann indessen keine Rede sein. Wie ich schon betonte, stand unsere wechselkursbezogene Geldpolitik im Einklang mit unserem Ziel, die Preisstabilitt zu bewahren. Ich wrde die Mglichkeit nicht ausschliessen, dass wir in Zukunft wieder grssere Kursschwankungen gegenber dem Euro zulassen mssen, wenn wir unserem geldpolitischen Hauptziel treu bleiben wollen. Mit diesen Ausfhrungen komme ich zu der allgemeineren Frage, ob es fr ein kleines Land wie die Schweiz berhaupt Sinn macht, eine eigenstndige Geldpolitik zu verfolgen. Wre die Schweiz nicht besser beraten, den Franken dauernd an den Euro zu binden und damit ihre geldpolitische Autonomie aufzugeben? Lassen Sie mich kurz auf diese Frage eingehen. 3. Autonome Geldpolitik und Zinsinsel Schweiz Die Vorteile einer Anbindung des Frankens an den Euro liegen auf der Hand: Der fixe Wechselkurs erleichtert die Aufgabe der im Export und Import ttigen Unternehmen. Diese verfgen ber eine hhere Gewissheit in Bezug auf die Preise, zu denen sie ihre Produkte im Ausland absetzen bzw. erwerben knnen. Sie knnen damit ihre Produktion und ihre Investitionen besser planen und das Risiko unternehmerischer Fehlentscheide verringern. Allerdings entstehen immer noch Kosten beim Tausch von auslndischen Whrungen in Schweizer Franken und umgekehrt. Die Transaktionskosten im Devisenhandel entfielen nur, wenn die Schweiz nicht nur den Franken an den Euro bnde, sondern den Euro an Stelle des Frankes als gesetzliches Zahlungsmittel einfhrte. Mit der Anbindung des Frankens an den Euro verschwnden die Wechselkursschwankungen natrlich nicht vollstndig. Nur der Wechselkurs gegenber dem Eurogebiet wrde stabilisiert. Der berwiegende Teil des gesamten schweizerischen Aussenhandels wrde indessen ber einen fixen Wechselkurs abgewickelt: Im Jahre 1998 ent fielen 55% der schweizerischen Gterexporte und gut 70% der entsprechenden Importe auf das Eurogebiet. Der Aussenhandel gegenber dem Dollarraum wre von der Anbindung dagegen nicht betroffen. Dem Vorteil der grsseren Wechselkursstabilitt stnden zwei gewichtige Nachteile einer Anbindung des Frankens an den Euro gegenber. Zum einen verschwnde mit der Anbindung der Zinsbonus auf dem Schweizer Franken. Zum anderen verlre die SNB vollstndig ihre Fhigkeit, eine eigenstndige Geldpolitik zu fhren. Die Zinsstze liegen in der Schweiz bekanntlich auf einem tendenziell tieferen Niveau als in allen anderen europischen Lndern. Dabei ist dieses Muster bei den langfristigen Zinsstzen ausgeprgter als bei den kurzfristigen, die besonders stark von der Geldpolitik der SNB und von der jeweiligen konjunkturellen Verfassung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft abhngen. Die Ertrge auf langfristigen Frankenanlagen sind tiefer als anderswo in Europa, selbst wenn beim Vergleich die realen Kapitalgewinne und -verluste, die als Folge von Wechselkurs- und Preisnderungen anfallen, bercksichtigt werden. Die reale Zinsdifferenz betrgt immer noch 1-2 Prozentpunkte, auch wenn sie sich ber die letzten drei Jahrzehnte hinweg tendenziell zurckgebildet hat. ber die Grnde fr den Zinsbonus auf dem Schweizer Franken streiten sich die Experten. Wahrscheinlich trgt der hohe Ertragsbilanzberschuss dazu bei, die Zinsen in der Schweiz tief zu halten. Nach meiner Meinung liegt der Hauptgrund aber in der traditionellen Stabilitt des Schweizer Frankens, die unsere Whrung zu einem attraktiven Diversifikationsinstrument fr die internationalen Anleger macht. Fixierte die Schweiz den Wechselkurs des Schweizer Frankens gegenber dem Euro, ginge der Zinsbonus mit der Zeit verloren. Die internationalen Anleger wrden den Euro und den Schweizer Franken fortan als perfekte Substitute betrachten; der Anreiz, in unsere Whrung zu diversifizieren, entfiele. Anlagen in Euro und Schweizer Franken von gleicher Qualitt und gleicher Laufzeit mssten auch die gleichen Ertrge abwerfen. Die schweizerischen Zinsen wrden sich an jene im Eurogebiet angleichen und wrden im Wesent lichen durch die EZB bestimmt. Die SNB wre nicht mehr in der Lage, die inlndische Zinsentwicklung zu beeinflussen und aus eigener Kraft fr die Stabilitt des Schweizer Frankens zu sorgen. Die Anpassung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft an ein hheres Zinsniveau wre nicht kostenlos. Die schweizerische Wirtschaft verlre einen internationalen Konkurrenzvorteil. Die hheren Zinsen wrden die schweizerischen Unternehmen dazu veranlassen, den Kapitaleinsatz in ihrer Produktion zu verringern. Dadurch gerieten die hohen schweizerischen Reallhne unter Druck. Die schweizerische Eidgenossenschaft, die Kantone und die Gemeinden mssten einen Anstieg ihrer Ausgaben in der Form von Zinsen auf ihren Schulden hinnehmen, whrend die Hausbesitzer die hhere Zinsenlast auf ihren Hypotheken zu spren bekmen. Die Anpassungskosten, die die schweizerische Wirtschaft als Folge der Zinserhhung tragen msste, drfen nicht unterschtzt werden. Sie mssten den Vorteilen, die aus der Anbindung an den Euro erwachsen, gegenbergestellt werden. Der zweite wesentliche Nachteil, der vllige Verlust der geldpolitischen Autonomie, wird in der ffentlichen Diskussion hufig heruntergespielt. So hrt man etwa das Argument, die SNB habe sich schon bisher eng an die Deutsche Bundesbank angelehnt und stehe heute im Schatten der EZB. Ferner verlaufe die Konjunkturentwicklung in der Schweiz in der Regel parallel zu jener in Deutschland. Damit sei die SNB auch nicht gezwungen, eine Geldpolitik zu fhren, die wesentlich von jener der Bundesbank bzw. der EZB abweiche. Die Kommentatoren, die die Notwendigkeit einer eigenstndigen schweizerischen Geldpolitik in Frage stellen, bersehe n allerdings einen wichtigen Punkt: Bei der Diskussion um den Sinn und Unsinn einer eigenstndigen Geldpolitik liegt der Teufel - wie so oft - im Detail. Es ist zwar richtig, dass zwischen der konjunkturellen Entwicklung in Deutschland und der Schweiz in der Regel eine grosse bereinstimmung besteht. Wissenschaftliche Untersuchungen besttigen diesen Sachverhalt. Ferner verfolgt die EZB wie schon frher die Deutsche Bundesbank die gleichen geldpolitischen Ziele wie die SNB. Angesichts der hnlichkeit der geldpolitischen Ziele und des wirtschaftlichen Umfelds erstaunt es nicht, dass die SNB hufig den gleichen Kurs steuert wie die EZB bzw. die Deutsche Bundesbank. Dieser Tatbestand darf aber nicht zum Schluss verleiten, die SNB ahme lediglich die Politik unserer Schwesterinstitute im Norden nach. Betrachten wir die schweizerische Geldpolitik der letzten Jahre, wird ersichtlich, dass die SNB - trotz aller hnlichkeit im Grundstzlichen - wiederholt ihren Spielraum fr einen eigenstndigen Kurs ausschpf te. So lockerte sie ihre Geldpolitik vom Sommer 1992 bis Ende 1993 rascher als die Deutsche Bundesbank. Deshalb sanken auch die Geldmarktzinsen in der Schweiz schneller als in Deutschland; in dieser Periode erreichte der Zinsunterschied zu Deutschland zeitweise 3 Prozentpunkte. Die Bundesbank war gezwungen, einen restriktiveren Kurs zu steuern als die SNB, da sich die Teuerung in Deutschland nicht so rasch und nachhaltig zurckbildete wie in der Schweiz. Als Folge des vorbergehenden Wirtschaftsbooms, den die Wiedervereinigung ausgelst hatte, stieg die Inflation in Deutschland im Jahre 1993 erneut auf ber 4%, whrend sie sich in der Schweiz weiter zurckbildete. Der Zinsunterschied zu Deutschland blieb in den Folgejahren erhalten. Auch gegenwrtig liegen die Geldmarktzinsen in der Schweiz immer noch unter jenen in Deutschland bzw. im Eurogebiet. Wie ich schon ausfhrte, verfolgt die SNB angesichts der eher verhaltenen konjunkturellen Erholung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft weiterhin eine expansive Geldpolitik. Sie trgt damit den spezifischen wirtschaftlichen Schwierigkeiten der Schweiz, die seit einigen Jahren einen im Vergleich zu anderen europischen Lndern besonders schmerzvollen Strukturwandel durchluft, Rechnung. Mit der Bindung des Frankens an den Euro mssten die schweizerischen Geldmarktzinsen auf das Niveau im Eurogebiet steigen und knnten von der SNB nicht mehr autonom verndert werden. Ich brauche nicht speziell darauf hinzuweisen, dass ein solcher Zinsschub vllig verkehrt in der gegenwrtigen konjunkturellen Landschaft lge. Man kann natrlich einwenden, dass mit der Anbindung die Schweiz wirtschaftlich noch enger in das Eurogebiet integriert wrde. Damit wrde auch die Notwendigkeit einer eigenstndigen schweizerischen Geldpolitik schwinden. Es ist allerdings unwahr scheinlich, dass sich die wirtschaftlichen Voraussetzungen fr eine vllige Aufgabe unserer geldpolitischen Autonomie sofort einstellen wrden. Aus diesem Grunde ist die SNB wohl beraten, ihre Eigenstndigkeit nicht leichtfertig aus der Hand zu geben. 4. Der Euro als schweizerische Parallelwhrung Einige Beobachter der europischen Whrungsintegration gehen so weit zu behaupten, der Entscheid ber die Anbindung des Frankens an den Euro werde letztlich durch den Markt gefllt, selbst wenn die Behrden auf einer autonomen Geldpolitik beharrten. Die Marktkrfte wrden dafr sorgen, dass sich der Euro in der Schweiz mit der Zeit als Parallelwhrung zum Franken ausbreiten werden. Habe sich der Euro in der Schweiz einmal etabliert, werde er den Franken frher oder spter verdrngen. Die SNB verliere damit ihre Fhigkeit, die schweizerische Geldmenge zu steuern, da die schweizerische ffentlichkeit das von ihr ausgegebene Geld gar nicht mehr halten werde. Unabhngig vom Willen der schweizerischen Behrden werde der Markt damit die "Anbindung" des Frankens an den Euro erzwingen. Was ist von dieser Behauptung zu halten? Um diese Frage zu beantworten, mssen wir zuerst den Begriff der Parallelwhrung klren. Damit werden nmlich zwei unterschiedliche Phnomene bezeichnet. Zum einen ist davon auszugehen, dass der Euro vermehrt als Rechnungswhrung fr grenzberschreitende Transaktionen dienen wird. Viele auslndische Abnehmer drften darauf bestehen, dass schweizerische Produzenten ihre Exporte in Euro anstatt in Franken fakturieren. In schweizerischen Fremdenverkehrszentren und Grenzorten besteht auch schon heute eine grosse Bereitschaft, den Euro als Zahlungsmittel zu akzeptieren. Es ist ferner denkbar, dass schweizerische Unternehmen den auslndischen Anlegern entgegenkommen, indem sie vermehrt auf Euro lautende Wertpapiere ausgeben. Der Euro wird ohne Zweifel eine wichtige Rolle als internationale Transaktionswhrung spielen. So deutet eine im August erschienene Studie der EZB1 darauf hin, dass bei internationalen Emissionen von Schuldverschreibungen im Eurogebiet ein grsserer Anteil auf die neue gemeinsame Whrung entfllt als vor 1999 auf die entsprechenden nationalen Whrungen. Damit scheint sich der Euro am Kapitalmarkt als Transaktionswhrung durchzusetzen. Fr die schweizerische Geldpolitik ist indessen die Frage, ob bei grenzberschreitenden Transaktionen der Euro oder der Franken als Rechnungseinheit dient, von untergeordneter Bedeutung. Grundstzlich besteht jede Zahlung, die mit einer grenzberschreitenden Transaktion verknpft ist, aus einem Fremdwhrungs- und einem Frankenteil. Nehmen schweizerische Hotelbetriebe Euro statt Franken an Zahlung an, ndert sich fr die schweizerische Geldpolitik wenig. Die Verwendung des Euro als Transaktionswhrung bedeutet lediglich, dass die Hotelbetriebe - an Stelle der Gste Euro in Franken umtauschen mssen. Die Hotelbetriebe gehen dabei natrlich ein Wechselkursrisiko ein. Es ist auch denkbar, dass sich die im internationalen Handel ttigen schweizerischen Unternehmen veranlasst sehen, zur Abwicklung ihres Zahlungsverkehrs ihre Bankguthaben vermehrt in Euro und weniger in Franken zu halten. Die SNB msste diese Verschiebungen in der Geldnachfrage bei der Festlegung ihrer Geldpolitik bercksichtigen. Die SNB she sich nur dann vor ernsthafte Probleme gestellt, wenn der Euro den Franken als inlndisches Zahlungs- und Wertaufbewahrungsmittel verdrngen wrde. Es gibt indessen keine Anzeichen einer solchen Entwicklung. Echte Parallelwhrungssysteme - unter denen sowohl die inlndische als auch eine auslndische Whrung wahlweise fr inlndische Zahlungen verwendet werden - tauchen nur in Lndern mit extrem hoher 1 Europische Zentralbank, "The international role of the euro", ECB Monthly Bulletin, August 1999, S. 34. Inflation auf. Dagegen kenne ich keine Beispiele von Lndern mit moderater oder tiefer Inflation, in denen Parallelwhrungen je eine bedeutende Rolle spielten. Manchmal wird behauptet, in Kanada werde der werde der amerikanische Dollar in grossem Ausmass als Parallelwhrung verwendet. Wer die kanadischen Verhltnisse kennt, weiss, dass dort der amerikanische Dollar ebenso wenig als Parallelwhrung zirkuliert wie der Euro in der Schweiz. Die Befrchtung, der Euro werde sich in der Schweiz als eigentliche Parallelwhrung durchsetzen, ist deshalb bertrieben. 5. Schlussbetrachtung Wie ich gezeigt habe, besteht fr die SNB kein Anlass, von einer eigenstndigen Geldpolitik abzurcken. Fhrt die SNB einen eigenstndigen Kurs, ist sie in der Lage, bei der Festlegung der Geldpolitik auf die besonderen Bedrfnisse der schweizerischen Bevlkerung und Wirtschaft Rcksicht zu nehmen. Die SNB kann aber nur dann eine wirksame eigenstndige Geldpolitik fhren, wenn sie den Wechselkurs des Schweizer Frankens grundstzlich frei schwanken lsst. Dabei ist es mglich, dass sich der Schweizer Franken in einem unerwnschten Ausmass aufwertet und der schweizerischen Wirtschaft Schaden zufgt. Die SNB steht solchen Entwicklungen indessen nicht machtlos gegenber. Richtet sie ihre Geldpolitik auf die Stabilisierung des Wechselkurses aus, muss sie darauf achten, dass sie die Geldpolitik nicht zu stark lockert und damit ein neues Inflationspotenzial schafft. Mit der Anbindung des Frankens an den Euro wrde die Gefahr von schdlichen Wechselkursausschlgen wesentlich verringert. Die hhere Wechselkursstabilitt msste aber um den Preis eines Verlustes der geldpolitischen Autonomie erkauft werden. Die schweizerische Geldpolitik wrde nicht mehr durch die SNB, sondern durch die EZB bestimmt. Der Zinsbonus auf dem Schweizer Franken wrde verschwinden. Die Attraktivitt des Frankens als Anlagewhrung hinge nicht mehr von der Glaubwrdigkeit und vom guten Ruf der SNB ab; die Qualitt der in Frankfurt gefhrten Geldpolitik wre fortan allein massgebend. Gelegentlich wird darber spekuliert, wie lange die Schweiz noch an einer eigenstndigen Geldpolitik festhalten werde. Ich verzichte auf eine eigene Prognose. Nach meiner Meinung gibt es keinen Grund, unsere eigenstndige Geldpolitik aufzugeben, solange die Schweiz ausserhalb der Europischen Union bleibt. Ein Beitritt unseres Landes zur Europischen Union wrde die Lage natrlich ndern. Schlsse sich die Schweiz der Europischen Union an, bernhme sie wahrscheinlich auch den Euro und verlre damit ihre geldpolitische Autonomie. Ein rascher Beitritt der Schweiz zur Europischen Union ist allerdings nach wie vor unwahrscheinlich.

Title: The Liechtenstein financial centre on the threshold to the third millennium - a neighbour's reflections
text: The Liechtenstein Financial Centre on the Threshold of the 3rd Millennium - Reflections of a Neighbour Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig, Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Lecture on the occasion of the thirty-year anniversary of the Liechtenstein Banking Association, Vaduz, 30 September 1999 2 Above all, I would like to thank others for the honour of speaking to you on the thirtieth birthday of the Liechtenstein Banking Association. I enjoy your hospitality. Not only because, as a St. Gallen resident, I feel particularly connected to their country. Moreover, because of the close and in many ways unique relations with the Principality, we are highly interested in you being able to continue your prosperous development. Their problems could easily affect us - but the inverted is also true. So it is in the relationship between neighbors who interact every day and whose properties are not even separated by a fence. As a representative of the Swiss National Bank, I would also like to congratulate you on your thirtieth anniversary. I thank you for your constructive cooperation and look forward to continuing it. On the stock market, one speaks of a 'triple witching hour' when three futures and options contracts mature at the same time on the same date. As a rule, such an event is associated with large sales and some nervousness in the market. The Principality of Liechtenstein is also experiencing a 'triple witch hour' this year, albeit noticeably less hectic than the corresponding stock market event. This year marks not only the thirtieth anniversary of the Liechtenstein Banking Association. From a Swiss point of view, there are two other important anniversaries to celebrate. On the one hand, the Swiss franc has been an official means of payment in your country for exactly 75 years. On the other hand, it will soon be 20 years since the currency treaty between Liechtenstein and Switzerland was signed. I would like to take this multiple anniversary as an opportunity to take a cautious look into the future of the Liechtenstein financial centre - especially that of the banking sector. My remarks focus on the profound change in the competitive environment and the opportunities and threats that arise from these changed framework conditions for the Principality. 3 Almost 20 years of the Monetary Treaty The fact that the conclusion of the Monetary Treaty will mark the twentieth anniversary next June gives me a welcome opportunity to begin by making a few brief remarks on this subject. Without going up to a boring history lesson, it can be said in retrospect from our point of view and - in my opinion - also from your point of view that our monetary union has proven itself well. Against the background of Liechtenstein's experience during the monetary turbulence in the 70s, the most important innovation for the Principality was that it was henceforth regarded as a Swiss domestic in terms of capital movements. This eliminated the risk that Liechtenstein would once again be cut off from the Swiss financial centre in the event of a future currency crisis. Together with the SNB's official recognition of the Swiss franc as a means of payment in the Principality, this has led to a further increase in Liechtenstein's stability and international reputation. Last but not least, the formal extension of our role as "Lender of Last Resort" to the Liechtenstein banks contributes to this assessment. The concerns that were still expressed at the time of the contract negotiations have not been fulfilled. For example, the fear of a loss of independence if such a loss existed at all due to the de facto links with Switzerland in this area - soon proved to be unfounded. And the obligation to provide information to the SNB has not proved to be an unreasonable burden. On the contrary. Overall, the Liechtenstein financial centre has benefited more from the transparency generated by the reporting and has gained international trust and reputation. Of course, the contract was not concluded without certain reservations on the part of the National Bank. Many of you will certainly remember the sometimes critical statements made by representatives of the National Bank. The lack of official banking supervision has repeatedly been criticised as the biggest weakness. It is therefore with great satisfaction that the SNB has taken note of the creation of the 'Banking Supervision Service', which has only recently been transformed into the 'Office for Financial Services'. In accordance with its ideas at the time, the SNB thus received an independent, competent and well-informed contact person. 4 Beyond this important step, the 90s were a remarkably intense time for Liechtenstein legislation. These include the new decrees on investment companies, mutual legal assistance, due diligence, money laundering and insider trading. In addition, the implementation of the EEA obligations provided further legal impetus for revision. In one under the chairmanship of the Swiss Federal Government. The report, which was completed in 1990, pointed out - and rightly so, in my view - a considerable regulatory gap and some legislative constraints. The gaps located there can now be considered eliminated. We have already expressed this assessment appreciatively in our 1997 Annual Report. The only significant material difference relates to the offence of tax fraud, for which legal assistance is still not possible in the Principality. Whether this regulation will prove itself in the long term must be shown by their own experience. Part of the Swiss franc area As a currency contractual partner, you are part of the franc currency area. You benefit from what we succeed in monetary policy, but you are also affected if we make a mistake. To the best of our knowledge, we strive for a successful stability policy that results in low inflation and the smallest possible economic cycles. This endeavor is fraught with all sorts of risks and uncertainties. We approach our task undogmatically, willing to learn and with the necessary flexibility. In doing so, we are following developments in the euro area with the utmost attention and taking them into account appropriately. But we are going our own way, which is clearly focused on the stability of economic development in our - and yours - country. On the basis of the regular reporting of our St. Gallen-based Director Dr. Jetzer, we on the Board of Directors are well informed about the situation and trends at Liechtenstein's more important companies. This information is systematically incorporated into our assessment of the situation. 5 Actually, in the past nine months we have learned to live and deal quite well with the euro - our new big monetary brother. The fluctuation range of the SFR/Euro exchange rate has remained surprisingly narrow, although we have not once become active in the foreign exchange market. The parallel economic development has led to a similar monetary policy in both areas, so that there were no reasons for significant exchange rate corrections on the markets. Nevertheless, the occasionally drawn picture of the Franc as the backpack currency of the euro is incorrect. This can be demonstrated more convincingly than with long-term declarations of intent with the continuing considerable interest rate differentials on the markets. Not only in the money market, where we influence events, but also - and there without our intervention - in the long-term area, a significant interest rate bonus in favor of the Swiss franc indicates that the markets do not understand and value our currency as a clone of the euro. For the real sector, its competitiveness and its growth and employment prospects, the interest rate bonus is a significant locational advantage. Not in the orientation, but in the implementation of our policy, we have shifted the accents somewhat in the recent past. We have abandoned the traditional control of a monetary aggregate and replaced it with the control of SFR money market interest rates. Not out of pure desire for fashion change, but because the rapid technological, structural and institutional changes of recent years have made the demand for SFR more unstable. Der Finanzplatz Liechtenstein hat in dieser Hinsicht in den letzten Jahren bemerkenswert erfolgreich operiert. Er ist weniger als andere in die negativen Schlagzeilen geraten. Ob und in welchem Masse diese Selbstdisziplinierung durch die ffnung, den damit verbundenen Wettbewerbsdruck und wahrscheinlich auch eine gewisse Anonymisierung relativiert wird, ist eine offene, jedoch naheliegende Frage. Schlussbemerkung Ich komme zum Schluss. Das Bankgeschft war schon immer gekennzeichnet durch das oft ziemlich verwobene Nebeneinander von Chancen und Risiken.
