Title: Theory and practice of the financial markets - a fruitful alliance
text: Theory and practice of Financial Markets  a fruitful liaison Bruno Gehrig, Member of the Executive Board of the Swiss National Bank Speech on the occasion of the presentation of the "Bank and Finance" Prize of the Banque Cantonale de Geneve, in cooperation with the Universities of Lausanne and Geneva. Geneva, 24 November 1999 2 I would like to begin by thanking the organizers for inviting them to today's ceremony. It is an honour for me to be able to attend and share some thoughts. This event of course pays tribute to students who, with the support of their professors and assistants, presented remarkable works. I would also like to congratulate the Banque Cantonale de Geneve for sponsoring this prize, as it builds a bridge between academics and practitioners. My reflections will be at the meeting point between these two worlds, whose exchanges benefit everyone. Application on a large scale The contributions of economics have influenced and changed practice in the field of finance and financial markets much more strongly and much more sustainably than in many others. In the regulation of an investment fund, in a wealth management contract or in the place of work of any operator on the bond market, one inevitably comes across notions and theories developed in scientific circles. These notions and theories have sometimes taken time to establish themselves. Thus, Markowitz's article, "Portfolio Selection", remained unknown for a long time. Considered revolutionary today, this article appeared in 1952 already in the Journal of Finance. In 1973, more than twenty years later, Black and Scholes published "The pricing of options and corporate liabilities" in the Journal of Political Economy, an article that stimulated academic circles in an exceptional way. In Switzerland, it was at least another ten years before theory in the field of finance and financial markets finally met with growing interest, first in a few universities and then in practice. In this respect, Heinz Zimmermann of the University of St. Gallen and  a little later  Rajna Gibson of the University of Lausanne, played a pioneering role, both as a researcher and as a teacher. When you consider that the Swiss financial centre has always been at the forefront of wealth management, you can only be surprised at the slow start of this start. Since then, it is true, the situation has changed radically. Today, the Swiss financial centre has highly sophisticated integrated trading systems and offers a choice of modern instruments that can satisfy all 3 expectations or almost. The credit for this goes to economists from universities, but also and above all to committed practitioners who have launched and carried out, with the support of the major banks mainly, projects mainly related to the stock market. Today, the Swiss financial centre deserves a good rating for the implementation of modern theories and techniques; I am thinking here of the quality of services provided to our financial centre in general, but also of areas such as regulation, technology and know-how. Among the tools that contribute to the dissemination of knowledge and training, I would mention the Swiss journal "Financial Market and Portfolio Management", in which scientists and practitioners deal with topics that are common to them. Thanks to the commitment of authors, readers and a few banks, the journal continues to have an appointment with success, thirteen years after its launch. In this case, all the conditions are in place in Switzerland to continue and even deepen the dialogue between theorists and practitioners. We live in a time when financial markets around the world are experiencing rapid development, which is not without disruptions or setbacks. The issue of the stability of the financial system is becoming increasingly important for both market participants and authorities. Those who have followed the not very fruitful discussion on the new architecture of the international financial system will have quickly realized how much research needs to be done in this area. In recent years, we have been surprised on several occasions and have had to recognize that our knowledge of essential mechanisms is, at best, fragmentary. I cannot change this frustrating observation, but I hope, this evening, to at least be able to give you some elements that will encourage you to continue this reflection. Increased risks due to interdependence The nineties brought a fundamental change: financial markets and the participants in those markets became much more interdependent. On both sides of a bank's balance sheet, as well as in off-balance sheet activities, positions have acquired a more global dimension. Due to the range of derivative financial instruments available to operators, the effect of 4 leverage has tended to increase sharply with, it is true, phases marked by a return to a more moderate scale. As never before, the financial community today is dependent on a common technological and institutional infrastructure. We live in a world where externalities are far greater than they were a generation ago. As a result, the risk of chain reactions has increased significantly. The spectacular case from this point of view of the Long Term Capital Management (LTCM) fund has shown us, along with others, how extremely difficult it is, due to the degree of interconnection and leverage, to isolate an institution at risk and solve the problem. This finding is important for the regulatory framework in particular. Does the individual pursuit of profit by many operators sufficiently generate the collective good of "system stability"? In any case, the issue seriously concerns the authorities in charge of the financial markets. Should there be regulatory consequences? Several studies and reflections are underway on this subject. In particular, we need to gain a better understanding of the behaviour of operators on the financial markets. This is a topic of interest to university economists as well. In addition, this topic should also occupy a greater place in the risk management of private sector operators. The various risk management models are criticized for giving too little weight to the behaviour of other stakeholders. In this regard, recent events inspire me with two observations. Gregarious behaviours First of all, it is necessary to note the importance of gregarious behaviour. In many situations, financial market participants do not act independently of each other at all. They often recall the story of the sheep of Panurge. However, their reactions are not always irrational. In times of uncertainty, it may be strategically wise to follow the opinion of one or more leaders. Imitating great or famous figures in the market can be perfectly profitable. A second rational explanation for the gregarious behaviour of stakeholders is that many of them rely on similar benchmarks. When uncertainty increases 5 It may be appropriate to leave original positions and seek salvation in a middle way, in other words in the heart of the flock. In such situations, wealth management operates in a market that seems risk-averse: it honors the minimization of possible losses more than the chances of a higher return. Finally, third explanation, gregarious behaviors are also a question of mood. Markets are indeed crossed by waves of optimism or pessimism against which most participants are not at all immune. Look for example at investments in real estate or Internet stocks. It may seem irrational, but the irrational is part of our life in the same way as the rational. The phenomenon of gregarious behaviour is important for two reasons. At the individual level, the market participant must know that his reaction will most likely come at a time when the majority of operators want to make the same decision. At the market level, excessive movements are therefore to be expected. Financial markets occasionally generate distortions, deviations from the long-term trend in prices. These gaps can be destabilizing, including for the real economy. Reactions to a shock A second phenomenon came to light - in the autumn of 1998 - when Russia unilaterally - and to everyone's surprise - decreed a moratorium on the repayment of private sector debts. This announcement caused a shock to the entire financial community and triggered a massive movement towards low-risk investments that are as liquid as possible. One cannot help but think that the still little proven value-at-risk (VAR) models have amplified the shock. Three thoughts lead us to believe this. First, VAR makes it possible to measure the risk of an entire portfolio, often very complex, in the form of a simple figure. A shock then inevitably has repercussions on the entire portfolio and, therefore, on all the financial markets concerned. Almost automatically, the shock develops chain reactions and is absorbed by a multitude of markets. It therefore also extends to 6 markets that have, fundamentally, nothing to do with what was causing the shock. Then, in the wake of this shock, many stakeholders had to realize that they had greatly overestimated market liquidity. A shock immediately increases the expected risks. In such a case, var can only be maintained at a constant level if the risk limits are brutally reduced. As most of the players wanted to operate at the same time, the liquidity of the markets became totally insufficient, even for the usually most liquid markets. As a result, many establishments have found themselves stuck in delicate and very dangerous situations. The liquidity hypothesis, one of the assumptions on which VAR models are based, has been a costly illusion. Markets do not function well when all participants want the same thing at the same time. Market liquidity is an extremely fragile feature, and it has not yet been possible to integrate it satisfactorily into portfolio management. Finally, the shock has shown us how the effects of diversification can erode, how quickly correlation coefficients can converge to one, and how, under certain circumstances, credit, market and liquidity risks can combine. In most participants, these experiments resulted in a reduction in risk appetite, a reduction that took place not gradually, but abruptly. And it's definitely better that way. These considerations, ladies and gentlemen, demonstrate the need for emphasis on critical analysis of the behaviour of market participants. Knowing and understanding their behaviour better is essential to success in business, but also to the formulation of rules and regulations that bring maximum stability and efficiency to the system. Conclusions Let me conclude by mentioning two current developments designed to reduce systemic risk. A year and a half ago, we launched the securities repo project, together with banks and companies created in 7 common for the Swiss financial centre. In the meantime, rest has become our main instrument of monetary policy. Most of these transactions are placed on the stock exchange, which ensures good transparency and also allows smaller institutions to access them. A few weeks ago, we started offering intraday rest. Between midnight and 3 p.m., we provide free intraday liquidity to the system. Although few banks have made use of this possibility so far, we have seen a very positive impact on payment transactions through the Swiss Interbank Clearing System. In the CIS, payments are now better distributed throughout the day. The risks associated with the accumulation of payment orders before the clearing stop have significantly decreased. It is regrettable, however, that rest periods are still too little used in interbank transactions. It may take time for unsecured interbank transactions - and therefore presenting certain risks - to be replaced by repos on the money market, which are accompanied by collateral. For the stability of the system, such an extension of rests is in any case desirable. In a year's time, an important step will probably be taken towards greater stability of the system. If all goes according to plan, the "Continuous Linked Settlement" project  or CLS  will be implemented. This system, developed by the international banking community on the initiative of central banks, will almost completely eliminate settlement risk in foreign exchange transactions, the Herstatt risk in our jargon. The bank that delivered the currency sold will no longer run the risk of not receiving the purchased currency from its counterparty. Thanks to the CLS project, the principle of "payment against payment" at international level will be realized. For those of you who are not familiar with the practice in this area, this novelty may seem like a simple administrative modality. This is not the case. The only settlement risk in foreign exchange transactions is considerable. Every business day, many banks are exposed to this risk alone for an amount exceeding the volume of their own funds. By eliminating such a risk through organizational measures, we are therefore taking a big step towards greater stability of the system. With this change- 8 a significant part of the volume of payments in Swiss francs will no longer be executed by the SIC but by the CLS system. The newly introduced intraday rest periods are also intended to effectively address the problem of cash flow in Swiss francs to the CLS et vice versa system. Ladies and gentlemen, let me go back to the beginning of my presentation and to the brilliant students whose work has been selected. I congratulate you once again on the remarkable results you have achieved and hope that your success will inspire many young people to enter the fascinating world of financial markets and to participate in the fruitful dialogue between theorists and practitioners.

Leurs ractions ne sont toutefois pas toujours irrationnels. En priode d'incertitude, il peut tre stratgiquement judicieux de suivre l'opinion d'un ou de plusieurs leaders. Imiter de grandes ou de clbres figures du march peut tre parfaitement profitable. Une deuxime explication rationnelle du comportement grgaire des intervenants tient au fait que nombre d'entre eux se fondent sur des repres  ou benchmarks - semblables. Lorsque l'incertitude aug- 5 mente, il peut tre opportun de quitter des positions originales et de chercher son salut dans une voie mdiane, en d'autres termes au cur du troupeau. Dans de telles situations, la gestion de fortune opre sur un march qui semble craindre les risques: il honore davantage la minimisation des pertes possibles que les chances d'un rendement plus lev. Enfin, troisime explication, les comportements grgaires sont aussi une question d'humeur. Les marchs sont en effet traverss par des vagues d'optimisme ou de pessimisme contre lesquelles la plupart des participants ne sont pas du tout immuniss. Voyez par exemple les investissements dans l'immobilier ou les actions Internet. Cela peut paratre irrationnel, mais l'irrationnel fait partie de notre vie au mme titre que le rationnel. Le phnomne des comportements grgaires est important pour deux raisons. Sur le plan individuel, l'intervenant sur un march doit savoir que sa raction interviendra trs probablement  un moment o la majorit des oprateurs souhaiteront prendre la mme dcision. Au niveau du march, il faut donc s'attendre  des mouvements excessifs. Les marchs financiers gnrent occasionnellement des distorsions, des carts par rapport  la tendance  long terme des cours. Ces carts peuvent se rvler dstabilisants, y compris pour l'conomie relle. Ractions  un choc Un deuxime phnomne est apparu au grand jour - en automne 1998 - quand la Russie dcrta unilatralement - et  la surprise gnrale - un moratoire sur le remboursement des dettes du secteur priv. Cette annonce a provoqu un choc frappant l'ensemble de la communaut financire et dclench un mouvement massif vers des placements peu risqus et aussi liquides que possible. On ne peut s'empcher de penser que les modles, encore peu prouvs, de value-at-risk (VAR) ont amplifi le choc. Trois rflexions portent  le croire. D'abord, la VAR permet de mesurer le risque de tout un portefeuille, souvent trs complexe, sous la forme d'un simple chiffre. Un choc entrane alors forcment des rpercussions sur l'ensemble du portefeuille et, partant, sur tous les marchs financiers concerns. Presque automatiquement, le choc dveloppe des ractions en chane et est absorb par une multitude de marchs. Il s'tend par consquent aussi  des 6 marchs qui n'ont, fondamentalement, rien  voir avec ce qui tait  l'origine du choc. Ensuite, dans le sillage de ce choc, de nombreux intervenants ont d raliser qu'ils ont largement surestim la liquidit des marchs. Un choc fait immdiatement augmenter les risques attendus. Dans un pareil cas, la VAR ne peut tre maintenue  un niveau constant que si les limites de risque sont rduites brutalement. Comme la plupart des intervenants ont voulu oprer en mme temps, la liquidit des marchs est devenue totalement insuffisante, mme pour les marchs habituellement les plus liquides. En consquence, de nombreux tablissements se sont retrouvs bloqus dans des situations dlicates et fort dangereuses. L'hypothse de liquidit une des hypothses sur lesquelles reposent les modles VAR - a t une coteuse illusion. Les marchs fonctionnent en effet mal quand tous les participants veulent la mme chose au mme moment. La liquidit des marchs est une caractristique extrmement fragile, et il n'a pas encore t possible de l'intgrer de manire satisfaisante dans la gestion de portefeuille. Enfin, le choc nous a montr  quel point les effets de la diversification peuvent s'roder, combien les coefficients de corrlation peuvent rapidement converger vers un et combien, dans certaines circonstances, les risques de crdit, de march et de liquidit peuvent se conjuguer. Chez la plupart des participants, ces expriences ont eu pour consquence de rduire le got du risque, rduction qui a eu lieu non pas graduellement, mais brutalement. Et c'est incontestablement mieux ainsi. Ces considrations, Mesdames et Messieurs, prouvent qu'il faut mettre l'accent sur l'analyse critique du comportement des intervenants sur les marchs. Mieux connatre et mieux comprendre leur comportement est indispensable au succs dans les affaires, mais aussi  la formulation de rgles et de rglementations apportant au systme un maximum de stabilit et d'efficacit. Conclusions Permettez-moi de conclure en mentionnant deux faits d'actualit destins  rduire le risque systmique. Il y a un an et demi, nous avons lanc le projet pensions de titres, ou "repo", conjointement avec les banques et des entreprises cres en 7 commun pour la place financire suisse. Entre-temps, les repos sont devenus notre principal instrument de politique montaire. Ces oprations sont passes en majeure partie en Bourse, ce qui assure une bonne transparence et permet aussi  des tablissements de plus petite taille d'y accder. Il y a quelques semaines, nous avons commenc  offrir des repos intrajournaliers. Entre minuit et 15 heures, nous fournissons ainsi gratuitement des liquidits intrajournalires au systme. Mme si peu de banques ont recouru  cette possibilit jusqu' prsent, nous avons observ des rpercussions trs positives sur le trafic des paiements passant par le "Swiss Interbank Clearing System". Dans le SIC, les paiements sont maintenant mieux rpartis sur l'ensemble de la journe. Les risques lis  l'accumulation des ordres de paiement avant l'arrt de clearing ont nettement diminu. On peut toutefois regretter que les repos soient encore trop peu utiliss dans les oprations interbancaires. Il est possible qu'il faille du temps pour que, sur le march montaire, les oprations interbancaires non garanties - donc prsentant certains risques - soient remplaces par des repos qui, eux, sont assorties d'une garantie. Pour la stabilit du systme, une telle extension des repos est en tout cas souhaitable. Dans un an, un pas important sera vraisemblablement franchi vers une plus grande stabilit du systme. Si tout se droule comme prvu, le projet "Continuous Linked Settlement" - ou CLS - sera mis en uvre. Ce systme, dvelopp par la communaut bancaire internationale sur l'initiative des banques centrales, liminera presque intgralement le risque de rglement dans les oprations de change, le risque Herstatt dans notre jargon. La banque qui a livr la monnaie vendue ne courra plus le risque de ne pas recevoir, de sa contrepartie, la monnaie achete. Grce au projet CLS, le principe du "paiement contre paiement" au niveau international sera ralis. Pour ceux d'entre vous qui ne sont pas familiariss avec la pratique en la matire, cette nouveaut peut paratre une simple modalit administrative. Il n'en est rien. Le seul risque de rglement dans les oprations de change est considrable. Chaque jour ouvrable, de nombreuses banques sont exposes  ce seul risque pour un montant dpassant le volume de leurs fonds propres. En liminant un tel risque grce  des mesures sur le plan organisationnel, nous faisons donc un grand pas vers une stabilit accrue du systme. Avec ce change- 8 ment, une partie importante du volume des paiements en francs suisses sera excute non plus par le SIC, mais par le systme CLS. Les repos intrajournaliers, nouvellement introduits, ont galement pour but de rgler de manire efficace le problme du flux des liquidits en francs suisses vers le systme CLS et viceversa. Title: Introductory Remarks, End-of-year Media News Conference
text: End-of-year Media , Zurich, 10 December 1999 Introductory remarks by Bruno Gehrig, Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Steering concept The change of concept will also bear on the operations area. In implementing monetary policy, we will henceforth target the interest rate level on the money market rather than the amount of liquidity. Our steering concept consists of three elements:  The first element is a clearly defined reference interest rate: we will use the 3-month LIBOR (London Interbank Offered Rate), the economically most important money market rate for Swiss franc investments. We will publish it daily in the major financial data services and on our website.  The second element of monetary control is the target range for the 3-month LIBOR, which establishes the guidelines for practical monetary policy and - supplementing the long-term inflation forecast - serves the market as an orientation framework. The target range has a spread of one percentage point (corresponding to 100 basis points). We publish the location of the target range and check it on an ongoing basis.  Thirdly, we will also announce in what area within the target range we expect the 3-month LIBOR to be. It is not our intention to exercise precise control over the LIBOR. We will continue to tolerate certain market-induced fluctuations. We will, however, take action should any development of the LIBOR have an undesirable monetary policy effect. The LIBOR target range will lie between 1.25% and 2.25% in the near term. We plan to allow a moderate increase in the LIBOR towards the middle of the target range. This intention refers to the development after the transition to the new year. Current interest rates exhibiting a strong upward distortion due to the end-ofmonth effect will settle in at a normal level after the turn of the year. We are convinced that this steering concept promotes transparency and thus the efficiency of monetary policy without compromising the indispensable room for manoeuvre. Why the LIBOR? The LIBOR, the interest rate for three-month investments in the interbank market, is the most frequently used Swiss franc money market rate. It is fixed and published daily in the London market according to a transparent mechanism. The LIBOR reflects money market conditions and is a central parameter for the refinancing of first-rate banks and companies. It is more important economically than the short-term repo rates which we use for daily monetary transactions. There are two additional qualities which favour the LIBOR as a monetary policy reference interest rate. Firstly, it does not react too violently to short-term imbalances on the money market, is thus less prone to incidental fluctuations and as such is well-suited as a monetary bellwether. Secondly, it reacts more quickly than the repo rate to economically relevant interest rate effects influencing our money market from abroad or from the capital market, thus enhancing its role as an indicator. Experience has shown that the LIBOR is more closely interconnected to the entire interest rate and economic structure and fluctuates to a much lesser degree than, for example, the call money rate (graph in annex). When interpreting the LIBOR it must be borne in mind that it cannot be compared directly with the repo rates. It tends to be higher for two reasons. One aspect is that it applies to the longer maturity of three months. The second is that it refers to unsecured interbank loans and therefore includes a risk premium. Repo rates, by contrast, are zero-risk interest rates with underlying loans secured by securities. It is impossible to determine the risk premium exactly since no instruments with similar liquidity are available for the zero-risk money market rate (yet). Our experience with repo transactions this year has shown that depending on maturity and market conditions, repo rates can be up to one half percentage point lower than the three-month LIBOR. Steering technique and signalling effect We will take a flexible approach in steering the LIBOR and not react to short-term swings. As a general rule, we will chart the course of the LIBOR indirectly, i.e. via short-term repo transactions. Any undesirable upturns in interest rates can be corrected by injecting more liquidity or, conversely, by draining liquidity, we can induce an upward movement of interest rates. While we communicate our long-term monetary stance with the inflation forecast, the target range serves as an indicator for our intentions in the shorter term. As a rule, we will assess this indicator every quarter and justify any changes. Moreover, we will make a statement as to the position of the reference rate within the target range. Short-term repo rates, by contrast, do not serve as a monetary indicator. Contrary to the practice of the ECB, we will in principle act daily in the market and take a flexible approach in setting the repo rates. More often than not, they vary not because of the monetary course but due to liquidity distribution aspects within the system or due to short-term distortions. In supplying the market with liquidity, we rely on the proven monetary policy instruments, centring on repo transactions with maturities ranging from one day to several weeks. At currently approximately 20 billion Swiss francs, they correspond to roughly half the monetary base. In addition, we can place federal government funds with the banks or conclude foreign exchange swaps should the need arise. In case of unforeseen liquidity bottlenecks, advances against securities (lombard loans) are still available. Furthermore, since October, banks have been able to use intraday liquidity on a repo basis to speed up payment transactions. This new facility serves to facilitate the settlement of payments within the Swiss Interbank Clearing system (SIC). Monetary policy is not affected, however. Discount rate no longer used Discount business - a classical instrument of the National Bank - has become increasingly insignificant over the last decades. The National Bank has not concluded a single discount transaction since 1993. The discount rate still had a certain significance as a monetary indicator, however. In the new steering concept the target range for the LIBOR will assume this role, rendering the discount rate obsolete also in this respect. Consequently, starting in January 2000, we will no longer fix and publish a discount rate. There are no provisions in the National Bank Law which would prohibit such a step. The rules governing the lombard rate remain unchanged. Ready for the millennium change The Swiss financial centre is very well prepared for the millennium change. Everything reasonably feasible has been done. The relevant systems have been successfully tested and the necessary preparations made. Even in the most unlikely event of a crisis there is a plan of action in place for the whole financial centre. In spite of the well-founded confidence all the parties concerned are still called upon to stand ready to take action at any time during the turn of the year and to carry out the numerous test and control jobs with the utmost care. With regard to supplying the market with liquidity, we plan to have a regular presence in the market also in the coming weeks and to make our contribution to a century rollover without disruptions. Annex LIBOR The London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) is the rate fixed every business day at 11:00 o'clock (London time) by the British Bankers' Association. It is the rate at which major banks are prepared to grant unsecured money market loans to each other. The LIBOR is fixed according to a clearly defined procedure for different currencies and maturities. The Swiss franc LIBOR corresponds to the average of the current interest rates of six leading banks. Repo rate The repo rate is the interest rate used for repo transactions. In a repo (repurchase agreement) the cash taker sells securities to the cash provider with the understanding to repurchase securities of the same type and quantity at a later date. The repo rate is owed for the amount loaned and is generally lower than the interest rate for unsecured money market loans. The National Bank uses this instrument for the steering of liquidity. In principle, it is willing to purchase any securities from the "SNB basket" and the "German GC basket".

Title: Introductory Remarks, End-of-year Media News Conference
text: End-of-year Media , Zurich, 10 December 1999 Introductory Remarks by Jean-Pierre Roth, Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank In the course of the past twelve months significant changes have taken place in the domain of banknotes and the provision of currency. In autumn 1998 the old "Borromini" 100 franc banknote was replaced by the new "Giacometti" banknote. This was the last banknote of the new series to be put into circulation. In retrospect, the introduction of the new series proceeded without a hitch: currently 80% of banknotes in circulation are accounted for by the new series; in each case, 50%-60% of the banknotes were replaced within three months from the time the exchange began. The new banknotes were well received by the public, in particular the 200 franc banknote, which - in terms of value - already occupies a position similar to that of the old 500 franc banknote. The success of the new banknotes is not merely ascribable to the close cooperation between the National Bank, the commercial banks and the manufacturers of ATMs and vending machines, but also to the adaptability of the public, which rapidly accepted the personalities depicted on the banknotes. In technological respects, Switzerland with its new banknotes is leading among the industrialised countries. The banknotes are well equipped to meet the challenges posed by modern reproduction techniques: copies are easily identified and can be detected quickly. The characteristic identifying features of the banknotes make life even more difficult for counterfeiters than the preceding series. By international standards, Swiss banknotes are considered to be among the safest. Since modern reproduction techniques are constantly being improved, the head start in the fight against counterfeiting can only be maintained if the public pays careful attention to the security features on the banknotes. A brief glance at the kinegram, the glittering number and the coloured number will allow a counterfeit banknote to be quickly identified. In order to make it even easier for the public to check the banknotes, we have introduced a perforated number on the 100, 200 and 1000 franc banknotes. When the banknote is held up to the light, the face value is seen as a perforated surface. In due course, this new security feature will also be used on all other denominations. Last September we issued the final recall of the last but one series of banknotes, the series with the portraits of Gottfried Keller and Henri Dufour. At the time of the recall there were still banknotes of this series to the value of Sfr 260 million in circulation. To date, the return flow has been modest. I should like to point out once more that these outdated banknotes will be valueless after 1 May 2000 and that according to Article 24 of the National Bank Law their countervalue will be remitted to the Swiss fund for aid in case of uninsurable damage by the forces of nature. In 1978, when the previous series (the Hodler series) was recalled, an amount of Sfr 39 million was transferred to this fund. At the moment we are not yet anywhere near this figure. We should therefore like to encourage the public to check their safes and piggy banks for longforgotten old banknotes and to have these exchanged before the deadline expires. In the past twelve months we have also brought the distribution of currency in our country in line with modern requirements. In 1998, the Swiss National Bank still maintained a presence throughout the country in the form of cash counters at its two head offices, eight branch offices and 18 agencies at cantonal banks. The changes in the banking sector and the increasingly professional money transport services have convinced us of the need to streamline our network of cash counters. Since the beginning of the year, the activities of our branch offices in Neuchatel and Aarau have been transferred to our head offices in Berne and Zurich respectively. As from the start of next year, the branch offices in Basel, Lausanne, Lucerne and St Gallen will no longer provide cash distribution services. Only the Geneva and Lugano branches and the head offices in Berne and Zurich will maintain their cash distribution services in their present form. We will, however, continue to have the full support of our network of agencies at the cantonal banks. The closure of our cash counters in six locations should not be interpreted as a centralisation reflex of the National Bank. In Basel and Lucerne, the cantonal banks have agreed to provide the cash counter services formerly performed by the National Bank. Moreover, our representatives will continue to be present in the various regions and to devote themselves even more intensively than in the past to following economic developments and maintaining contacts with the business commmunity and political circles. The streamlining of our cash counter network will therefore not weaken our regional presence. The structural changes referred to have, of course, also had a certain impact on the head count. Of the 71 staff members affected by the restructuring, 40 were taken over by other SNB offices, 14 took early retirement, and 17 left the SNB of their own volition. The reintegration of persons transferred within the Bank was facilitated by the early retirement of 26 staff members in Zurich, Berne and Geneva. A suitable solution was thus found for every staff member concerned. The bank buildings of the branches that were closed have all been sold or are about to be sold. At the beginning of the new year, the National Bank will thus be better equipped to deal with the challenges posed by modern payment transactions; at the same time, it will be closer to the pulse of regional economic developments. In the past twelve months, numerous developments - some of them spectacular - have also been seen in another area, namely gold. The process of the demonetisation of gold is well under way in Switzerland. Last April both the Swiss people and the cantons adopted the total revision of the Federal Constitution. This will release the National Bank (as from 1.1.2000) from the obligation of providing partial gold cover for banknote circulation. This marks the end of a regulation dating from the time of the gold standard which had lost its practical significance after the breakdown of the Bretton Woods system. In our day and age it is no longer the gold cover that secures public confidence in a currency, but rather the ability of the central bank to ensure price stability. Furthermore, the Coinage Law, which fixes the gold parity of the Swiss franc, is soon due to be replaced by the new Federal law on currency and payment instruments. Under this new law, the Swiss franc will no longer be linked to gold. If the law is passed by parliament before Christmas - and we hope this deadline will be met - the severance of the Swiss franc from gold could enter into force next spring, when the three-month referendum deadline expires. From that time onwards, the National Bank will value gold at the market price and become active on the market, free from the shackles of legal regulations. It will be possible for us gradually to convert a part of our gold holdings into financial assets. This will apply to that part of our gold stock which may be set aside for other purposes than monetary aims (1,300 tonnes of the total holdings of 2,600 tonnes). It will be for the Swiss people to decide, when the time comes, to what use the proceeds of these gold sales are to be put. We cannot, as yet, name the exact time when gold sales are to begin, nor the specific form they will take. As you know, we shall effect our gold sales within the framework of the gold agreement which was concluded between the European central banks (the European Central Bank, the 11 central banks of the euro zone, the Bank of England, the Bank of Sweden and the Swiss National Bank) and which is, moreover, supported by the US Federal Reserve Bank and the Bank of Japan. These banks jointly hold 85% of the official gold reserves. The participating central banks undertake to limit their gold sales to 2,000 tonnes during the next five years. This figure includes the planned gold sales of the SNB totalling 1,300 tonnes. With the gold agreement the central banks have given the market a clear indication of their medium-term plans with respect to gold. The amount of gold which they intend to sell in the next five years (400 tonnes per year) is less than two-thirds of the total sales by the official sector during the past five years. We are thus confident that the sales provided for in the agreement will not depress the gold price.

Title: Introductory Remarks, End-of-year Media News Conference
text: End-of-year Media , Zurich, 10 December 1999 Introductory Remarks by Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Monetary policy The Swiss National Bank, in agreement with the Federal Government, plans to tighten monetary policy somewhat in the coming year 2000. Already this past autumn it permitted money market rates to rise after having pursued a generous monetary policy for an extended period. The National Bank continues to support the economic upswing with its policy, without jeopardising price stability in the long term. At the start of the year 2000, the National Bank will adapt its monetary concept in various respects. It will no longer fix growth targets for the money supply. Monetary policy decisions will, in future, be based mainly on an inflation forecast, which will take all relevant indicators into account. The money stock M3, will continue to play an important role as a monetary indicator. As in the past, the National Bank will primarily orient its monetary policy to the preservation of price stability. Price stability is considered to have been achieved with an inflation rate, measured by the national consumer price index, of less than 2% per annum. Finally, an innovation will be introduced in the field of money market steering by the fixing of a target range for the three-month Swiss franc money market rate. For the time being, the National Bank will aim at keeping the three-month rate within a range of 1.25% - 2.25%. It is generally known that in the past years the seasonally-adjusted monetary base was used as a target variable for monetary policy. Originally, annual growth targets were set. Since the beginning of the nineties, we have been applying medium-term growth targets in order to enable us to take better account of the fact that the development of the money supply influences the course of inflation notably in the medium term. The medium-term orientation of monetary policy created the necessary leeway for also taking into account other indicators in decision-making processes, such as real economic development, the situation on the labour market and the exchange rate. The deviations from the target path make it clear that the medium-term target was always considered to be a guideline only. In recent years, this has particularly been the case as the monetary base increasingly forfeited its informative value. For this reason, we have decided no longer to announce a growth target for the monetary base in future. The broad foundation on which our policy rests and which takes all significant indicators into account must become even clearer. In future, we shall provide a forecast at year-end for the development of inflation in the three ensuing years. The period of three years takes account of the time required for the transmission of monetary stimuli. It is, of course, not easy to predict inflation for such a long period. Our prognosis will therefore be fraught with uncertainties. By publishing a forecast for the following three years, however, we wish to emphasise the need to adopt a forward-looking stance and to react at an early stage to any threats to price stability. In general and in the longer term, inflation depends largely on the development of the money supply. Notably the money stock M3 thus remains a useful indicator. In the shorter term, however, other indicators of inflationary development must be considered. The main focus is on general economic development, the situation on the labour market, and exchange rates. The National Bank will comment the development of the indicators on which the inflation forecast is based on a quarterly basis. By ensuring price stability, monetary policy makes the best contribution to a balanced macroeconomic development. Price stability is considered to be an inflation rate of less than 2%. This takes account, among other things, of the fact that inflation cannot ever be measured with complete accuracy. Measuring problems may, for example, arise from qualitative changes in goods and services. Once more, it must be emphasised that price stability is not an end in itself. Stable prices are conducive to sustained economic growth and prevent socially undesirable developments. The National Bank must expect frequent price movements in the short term, which it can only influence to a limited extent. As a rule, these result from unexpected strong fluctuations in the oil price and other import prices and from exchange rate changes. Persistent inflationary and also deflationary developments must, however, be firmly countered. If the inflation forecast deviates from price stability as defined by us, this has implications for monetary policy. Should inflation exceed its forecast, the monetary reins must be tightened, and vice versa. For the purpose of implementing its monetary policy intentions, the National Bank will, in future, fix a target range for the three-month Swiss franc money market rate. At the same time, we shall provide information on the area we aim at within this target range. The target range will be reviewed periodically and be adjusted, if necessary. In this way, the implementation of monetary policy will become transparent. In return, the discount rate can be abolished. In his remarks, Mr Gehrig will deal in some detail with the ways and means of implementing monetary policy. Against this background, what then are our concrete intentions for the coming year? Generally speaking, a sustained upswing is to be expected. Following an expansion of just under 1.5% in 1999, real gross domestic product is likely to increase by 1.8% next year. Inflation, which amounted to approximately 1% in the current year, should rise to 1.5%. Employment will probably grow somewhat. This development is due to three main causes: the efforts undertaken by the Swiss economy itself, the improved international economic situation and the favourable monetary conditions. The price development forecast for the coming year will not depend significantly on our future monetary policy. This policy will only have an influence on price developments in the succeeding years. As is generally known, we already adjusted our generous monetary policy moderately last autumn. In order to guarantee price stability in the medium term, we will probably again have to tighten the monetary reins slightly in the coming year. In this case, inflation up to the year 2002 is likely to develop as shown in the graph. Given Switzerland's favourable economic performance, inflation will probably lie in the upper part of the range we equate with price stability. We shall continue to respond flexibly to extraordinary developments such as in the field of exchange rates. In the year 2000 notably the sustained economic upswing is likely to exert a certain upward pressure on consumer prices. The upward price movement should, however, be dampened by continuing intense competition and falling prices in telecommunications and in the agricultural sector. The predicted course of inflation is in conformity with the expected development of the monetary indicators watched by us. During the recession of the nineties, the growth of M3 had accelerated considerably in the wake of the National Bank's increasingly expansionary monetary policy. In spring 1997, it began to level off again as the National Bank further relaxed its monetary policy, but to a limited extent only. In October 1999, growth in M3 was at a comparatively low level of 1.0%. No inflationary stimuli of note are therefore likely to emanate from the expansionary monetary policy which the National Bank conducted until recently. We shall closely observe the development of the principal indicators and review the analyses which form the basis of the inflation forecast every three months. We shall also continue to publish the results of our monetary policy assessment in our Quarterly Bulletin.

Title: Continuity and radical change: the Swiss monetary policy and its environment
text: Continuity and upheaval: Swiss monetary policy and its environment Presentation by Dr. Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-President of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank at the Economic Forum of the Zurich University of Applied Sciences Winterthur January 20, 2000 Introduction First of all, I would like to thank you for the invitation to give a lecture here at the Zurich University of Applied Sciences in Winterthur. I am pleased with the obvious interest shown in the Swiss National Bank and its tasks. The general public usually perceives SNB policy in a very topical manner. The discussion will focus on the current course of monetary policy and on the SNB's reaction to specific events. At the beginning of December, public interest was focused on the announcement of monetary policy in 2000. Subsequently, attention turned to the millennium problem on the financial markets and the possible intervention of the central banks. I have no doubt that market developments - be it exchange rate or interest rate developments - will soon put the SNB back at the centre of its topicality. There will be no shortage of opportunities. In my talk today, I would like to counterbalance this widespread but all too short-term perspective. I would like to address the question of how the SNB can contribute to the prosperity of the Swiss economy in the medium to long term, and this in a world in which the only constant is change. Continuity and upheaval characterize Swiss monetary policy and its environment. 1. An environment in transition The keywords globalization, deregulation and liberalization are probably among the most frequently used words of the nineties and seem almost a bit worn. Nevertheless, it is these characteristics that most aptly characterize today's time. From an economic point of view, deregulation and liberalisation lead to a more efficient allocation of scarce resources and thus increase overall prosperity. However, this general positive effect is offset by concrete disadvantages for certain population groups or economic sectors. In addition, the advantages of stronger competition usually only become apparent in the medium term, while the costs of structural change in the form of production declines and unemployment are immediately noticeable. Liberalisation and deregulation therefore cause uncertainty and rejection among those affected, while advocates often find it difficult to put their advantages in the right light. For this reason, periods of liberalization and deregulation alternate in history with periods of interventionism and protectionism. The current liberal phase began after the turbulent 70s, at the beginning of the 80s. Product markets were given new liberalisation impulses, which increased international trade and promoted the international division of labour. Milestones for these efforts were the Uruguay Round of the then GATT (now WTO), the signing of the Single European Act and later the preparations for the European single market. In the meantime, this large common market has become a reality in Europe. For companies, the abolition of trade barriers brings on the one hand a broadening and standardization of the sales market, but on the other hand also intensified competition with foreign companies. The numerous major mergers in recent years are an expression of this competition on the global market. Internationalisation on the financial markets was even more pronounced than on the goods markets. The enormous technical advances have contributed significantly to this development. Computer science and modern telecommunications enable the rapid and cheap procurement and processing of enormous amounts of information. This created the conditions for worldwide arbitrage and increased international competition. The dismantling of regulations and restrictions has been forced by competition for mobile capital. Here, too, the free movement of international capital leads to an efficient allocation of savings and investments and thus promotes prosperity. At the same time, however, the risk of cross-border financial crises has increased with the increasing interconnectedness of markets. We had to experience this with the Asian crisis. In Europe, the integration of financial markets has taken a decisive step forward through the introduction of the euro. The replacement of ten currencies by a single one and the emergence of a broad and liquid euro capital market have fundamentally changed the conditions on the foreign exchange market and the international capital market. Although the dominant position of the US dollar as an international investment currency remains undisputed, new issues in euros show impressive growth rates. From Switzerland's point of view, the introduction of the European single currency represents a monetary challenge. For a year now, our currency and our economy have been operating in a completely new European environment. In the recent past, global globalization has been further accelerated by the rapid spread of the Internet. Under these circumstances, the step back is hardly conceivable. In contrast to the past, efforts to seal off from the outside world are unlikely to be successful today. In other words, the current state of the world as a global village will last. What consequences does the described change have for economic policy? For economic policy, the increasing international interdependence means that the short-term development of an economy can be controlled even less than in the past. Especially in a small, open country like Switzerland, the economic situation is significantly influenced by foreign economic impulses; the possibilities of an active domestic economic policy are correspondingly limited. This makes the framework conditions with which a country faces international competition all the more important. This is the challenge for economic policy: to provide the economy with a framework in which it can develop optimally. Monetary policy is part of economic policy. I would therefore like to show how the SNB contributes to favourable macroeconomic conditions in its field. 2. Continuity on behalf of the company Ensuring monetary stability is the SNB's most important contribution to the above-mentioned framework conditions for the Swiss economy. The law assigns the NATIONAL Bank the task of conducting a monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. The SNB has always interpreted this mandate in such a way that it best serves the overall interest by maintaining price stability. By maintaining price stability, the SNB understands the avoidance of both inflation and deflation, as both have a negative impact on the real economy. Empirical studies have shown that a low inflation rate makes a positive contribution to the economic development of a country in the long term. This connection can be explained by the central importance of the price system in the economy. In the economy, prices have the function of signals for the efficient allocation of scarce resources. The more stable the prices are over time, the better they can fulfil their steering function. It follows that both inflation and deflation are harmful; Inflationary or deflationary distorted prices lead equally to wrong decisions by the actors and thus to the misallocation of resources. Furthermore, inflation and deflation also have undesirable distributional effects. Inflation causes redistribution from creditor to debtor by reducing the real value of the outstanding debt; Deflation does the opposite. After all, inflation is considered anti-social, as it hits the recipients of fixed pensions particularly hard. Deflation, on the other hand, would favour the recipients of fixed pensions. To the extent that monetary policy should not be used to pursue a policy of distribution, inflation and deflation should therefore be avoided equally. Is inflation "passe9"? Some observers believe that the phenomenon of inflation is now a thing of the past. It is true that we in Switzerland have had remarkable price stability for several years now. The American economy is also growing strongly, without tensions on the price front. Have the basic economic laws changed? Do the more pronounced structural flexibility of the economy and productivity gains definitely protect us from inflation risks? The greatest caution must be exercised in answering these questions. Inflation is a long-term phenomenon whose causes are monetary. At present, we are still drawing on the stability-oriented environment of the second half of the 90s. However, since there is again largely full employment, it cannot be ruled out that earlier price increase reflexes will reappear. Productivity gains can absorb cost pressure. Such productivity gains appear to play a role in the strong yet price-stable growth of the American economy. In Europe, on the other hand, a trend towards accelerating productivity is not yet noticeable, despite the rapid spread of computer science. For this reason, vigilance is the order of the day. In a situation such as the present one, a central bank would be well advised to refrain from inflationary developments at an early stage. References If it allows inflation expectations to arise and solidify, then there is a risk that a dynamic process will be set in motion that is difficult to break and with high social costs. That is why we have recently decided to revise our relatively generous monetary policy stance somewhat. What exactly does the SNB mean by "price stability"? Last December, we announced that we equate price stability with an inflation rate of less than 2%. The reason why we are not aiming for an inflation rate of 0% is that the consumer price index slightly overestimates inflation. Among other things, the index does not take into account quality improvements and new products. The exact extent of the inaccuracy in the consumer price index is difficult to estimate. However, we assume that an increase in prices of less than 2% does not pose a threat to price stability. At the same time, I would like to emphasise that the SNB seeks to avoid not only inflation but also deflation. A decline in the general price level is incompatible with the objective of price stability. 3. Upheaval in the European environment - Continuity in the SNB strategy Will the new currency architecture in Europe lead to a change in the SNB's monetary policy strategy? In the past, the SNB has been advised on several occasions to abandon its autonomous policy in favour of an exchange rate-based strategy. Specifically, a stabilization of the Swiss franc against the German mark as the currency of our most important trading partner was usually considered. With the advent of the euro as the single European currency just over a year ago, this discussion has become more topical again. In fact, the exchange rate between the Swiss franc and the euro is even more important for our country than the previous relationship between the franc and the Deutschmark. The Swiss economy is closely intertwined with the European economy: around 52% of our exports go to the monetary union, while around 70% of our imports come from the eurozone. Doesn't this strong economic ties with a Europe in which there is only one currency suggest that the Swiss franc should be linked to the euro? First of all, it must be emphasized that a stable price level and a stable exchange rate are not a priori mutually exclusive. Last year, for example, there was price stability in Switzerland, with an extremely stable exchange rate between the Swiss franc and the euro. This favourable constellation can be attributed, firstly, to the stability efforts of the EU countries and, secondly, to the similar monetary policy and the broad economic convergence in Switzerland and the euro area. There is a good chance that this monetary and cyclical similarity will continue to contribute to a stable exchange rate in the future. In this case, price and exchange rate stability should continue to be compatible. You may now wonder why the SNB does not immediately switch to an explicit exchange rate peg when there is a prospect that the exchange rate between the Swiss franc and the euro will continue to move in a relatively narrow range in the future with price stability. I would like to say that the future is never exactly foreshadowed. References We have had very good experiences with the euro so far. Last year, for example, the volatility of the euro vis-e0-vis the Swiss franc was significantly lower than the previous volatility of the franc/DM exchange rate. This positive development surprised us somewhat, as the monetary integration process in Europe is still characterized by uncertainties. There are still open questions, for example around the tension between economic and political agreement. Switzerland's future relationship with Europe also remains in limbo. Switzerland is not yet fully integrated into the EU. In these circumstances, would it be wise to dispense with the exchange rate as an adjustment instrument in the event of asymmetric shocks? Thus, before the transition to the single currency, Europeans accepted the principle of labour mobility, which is a prerequisite for the success of monetary union. We cannot yet assess whether labour mobility in the EU will be effectively sufficient. However, we know that the requirement for labour mobility between Switzerland and the EU has not yet been met. A peg of the Swiss franc to the euro therefore seems premature and little considered at present. In today's situation, abandoning autonomous monetary policy and fixing the Swiss franc against the euro would also entail significant disadvantages. Swiss interest rates would approach the European level and the interest rate bonus, if not necessarily completely, would disappear for the most part. A permanently higher level of interest rates would certainly have profound consequences for the Swiss economy. A rise in interest rates would first of all result in an adjustment recession, with the interest-rate-sensitive financial and real estate sectors being particularly hard hit. It is uncertain to what extent the long-term growth path of the Swiss economy would be adversely affected by a permanently higher level of interest rates. Furthermore, an increase in the price of the capital factor would have the same effect as a brake on investment. Lower capitalization would reduce labor productivity, which would not be without consequences for wage levels. Finally, higher interest rates lead to a redistribution from debtors to creditors. Mortgage debtors in particular and the state as the largest debtor would suffer as a result. Our monetary policy has always operated in an environment of uncertainty. This is also the case today, although markets have been less volatile in recent months. This uncertainty and the reality of the Swiss economy suggest that we should continue with our cautious monetary policy strategy and not simply operate in the shadow of the European Central Bank. 4. Unchanged relationship between monetary policy and the economy A demand that is also often brought to the attention of the National Bank is for active support for the economy. Here, however, the SNB's possibilities are usually overestimated. Thus, the concrete course of monetary policy can only influence the economy temporarily. The long-term growth path of an economy, on the other hand, is determined by other factors. Again, the framework That is why we have tabled a motion for a resolution calling on the Commission and the Member States to take the necessary steps to ensure that the European Parliament is given the opportunity to express its views on this matter. With a monetary policy geared towards price stability, the SNB makes the best contribution to promoting long-term economic growth. The SNB's options for short-term economic stabilisation are also limited. First of all, economic development in a small, open economy such as Switzerland depends to a large extent on impulses from abroad. Apart from that, targeted economic influence or even control requires information that a central bank normally does not have at its disposal. When deciding on the use of monetary policy to stabilise the economy, difficult diagnostic and forecasting problems arise. In addition, the real economy only reacts to the use of monetary policy instruments with a delay of more or less a long time. This can lead to a policy geared towards "fine tuning" ultimately endangering monetary stability. An activist stop-and-go policy must therefore be clearly rejected. What is needed much more is a steady monetary policy that focuses on the goal that it can actually achieve: the medium-term stabilization of the price level. With such a policy, the central bank contributes best to the stabilization of economic development. 5. A stable and transparent monetary policy framework An essential prerequisite for the long-term prosperity of the financial markets are favourable economic, political, legal and technological framework conditions. Here, too, the SNB's central contribution lies in the management of a transparent and consistent policy. This creates a stable and predictable environment within which banks and other players in the financial markets can plan, calculate and plan. The years of consistency of the basic monetary policy orientation are likely to be particularly helpful in times of change. While our ultimate goal, price stability, and our strategy of achieving this goal through an independent policy, have not changed since the beginning of the 70s, we have introduced some innovations in the concrete implementation of monetary policy since the beginning of the year. Among other things, these innovations are intended to increase the transparency of our policy and to communicate our assessments and intentions to the markets even better. For example, we are now publishing an inflation forecast that reflects the inflation rate we expect for the coming years. At the same time, we have announced a target range for the money market interest rate we are targeting. If the value of the projected inflation approaches the upper limit of 2%, which for us is just about compatible with price stability, then this triggers a rethinking of the monetary policy stance. Depending on the result of this process, there may be a shift in interest within the target band or a change in the band itself. However, it may also be that we come to the conclusion that there is no need for action. Our new strategy does not imply automatic interest rates. Rather, it defines a framework that should help us to make our decisions systematically and rationally. As in the past, our assessment will be based on a bouquet of indicators. Our assessment of future price developments will be at the heart of the process. In justifying our decisions, we will use our Present assessments and considerations openly and thus provide the market with important clues about our assessment of the economic and monetary situation. With this new way of presenting its policy, the SNB has also taken certain risks: First, the publication of an operating interest rate can expose us to market pressures, all the more so since short-term movements of this size are often determined by external factors. To mitigate this problem, we define our goal within a range for the 3-month rate and not as an absolute level target. The range should protect us from short-term activism in case market conditions come under the influence of external shocks. Defining a range for the operating interest rate is an imperative of flexibility for a small economy. Second, the increased transparency of our policies will increasingly put monetary policy decision-making in the public spotlight. We have committed ourselves to publishing our assessment of the situation. This makes the debate on monetary policy decisions transparent and public. One should not be under any illusions here, the management of monetary policy will become more difficult under these circumstances compared to the past. In delicate situations, there will be no lack of criticism or counter-expertise. It will then be important to strictly uphold the principle of monetary policy autonomy, as the independence of the central bank is an essential prerequisite for monetary stability. However, the new procedure forces us to communicate our decisions in even more detail, which should contribute to the stability of the markets. In summary, I would like to say that monetary policy has never been an easy business. We always decide under imperfect information. There is no method that can guarantee the "right" decisions. Monetary policy requires expertise, tact and a certain amount of luck. This will continue to be the case in the future and under the new concept. 6. Schlussbemerkungen The environment in which the Swiss National Bank operates has changed profoundly in recent years. It is characterized by liberalization, deregulation and an ever stronger global network. The upheavals caused by this affect both the product and financial markets, with the financial markets outperforming the product markets in terms of dynamism. There is much to suggest that this process will continue and even intensify in the coming years. In addition to this general development, a significant change has also taken place in the concrete monetary environment in Switzerland. For more than a year now, the euro has been in the countries around us. The ambitious project of the European Monetary Union has thus entered its third and final phase. Acting in this new environment is a challenge for authorities, companies and private individuals. Favourable framework conditions are now more important than ever for a country to survive in the face of increased global competition. With a policy geared towards monetary stability, the SNB makes the best contribution to the long-term prosperity of our country. Monetary policy actions to stimulate the economy may present themselves as a seductively simple solution in difficult economic situations; however, experience teaches that economic growth depends on real factors in the long term. It is therefore crucial that the central bank pursues a steady, medium-term strategy. At the same time, the change in the monetary policy environment requires certain adjustments in the concrete implementation of the latter. In our new monetary policy concept, the increase in transparency stands out above all. With the publication of an inflation forecast and the definition of an interest rate band, we are breaking new ground. In doing so, we are fulfilling the market's desire for more information about our assessments and intentions. At the same time, we are also taking a certain risk with these innovations. It remains to be seen how the market will deal with the new information situation. However, I am confident that the new concept will prove itself in practice.

Diese gnstige Konstellation kann erstens auf die Stabilittsbemhungen der EULnder und, zweitens, auf die hnliche Geldpolitik und die weitgehende konjunkturelle bereinstimmung in der Schweiz und im Eurogebiet zurckgefhrt werden. In diesem Fall drften Preis- und Wechselkursstabilitt auch weiterhin miteinander kompatibel sein. Sie mgen sich nun fragen, warum die Nationalbank nicht gleich zu einer expliziten Wechselkursbindung bergeht, wenn doch Aussicht besteht, dass sich der Wechselkurs zwischen Franken und Euro bei Preisstabilitt auch in Zukunft in einem relativ engen Band bewegen wird. Dazu mchte ich sagen, dass die Zukunft sich nie genau voraussehen lsst. Wir haben bisher sehr gute Erfahrungen mit dem Euro gemacht. So war die Volatilitt des Euros vis--vis des Frankens im letzten Jahr deutlich tiefer als die frhere Volatilitt des Franken/DM-Kurses. Diese positive Entwicklung hat uns etwas berrascht, da der monetre Integrationsprozess in Europa immer noch von Unsicherheiten geprgt ist. Es bestehen nach wie vor offene Fragen, zum Beispiel rund um das Spannungsfeld wirtschaftliche versus politische Einigung. Auch das zuknftige Verhltnis der Schweiz zu Europa bleibt weiterhin in der Schwebe. Die Schweiz ist im EU-Raum noch nicht vollstndig integriert. Wre es unter diesen Umstnden weise, auf den Wechselkurs als Anpassungsinstrument bei asymmetrischen Schocks zu verzichten? So haben die Europer vor dem bergang zur Einheitswhrung das Prinzip der Arbeitskrftemobilitt akzeptiert, das eine Voraussetzung fr den Erfolg der Whrungsunion darstellt. Ob die Mobilitt der Arbeitskrfte in der EU effektiv ausreichend sein wird, knnen wir noch nicht beurteilen. Wir wissen aber, dass die Voraussetzung der Arbeitskrftemobilitt zwischen der Schweiz und der EU heute noch nicht erfllt ist. Eine Bindung des Frankens an den Euro scheint daher gegenwrtig vorschnell und wenig berlegt. In der heutigen Lage wrden eine Aufgabe der autonomen Geldpolitik und eine Fixierung des Frankens gegenber dem Euro auch gewichtige Nachteile mit sich bringen. Die schweizerischen Zinsen wrden sich dem europischen Niveau annhern und der Zinsbonus wrde, wenn auch nicht unbedingt vollstndig, so doch grsstenteils verschwinden. Ein permanent hheres Zinsniveau htte sicher tiefgreifende Konsequenzen fr die schweizerische Volkswirtschaft. Ein Zinsanstieg htte zuerst einmal eine Anpassungsrezession zur Folge, wobei der zinssensible Finanz- und Immobiliensektor besonders stark betroffen wre. Ungewiss ist, inwiefern der langfristige Wachstumspfad der schweizerischen Volkswirtschaft durch ein dauerhaft hheres Zinsniveau beeintrchtigt wrde. Weiter wrde sich eine Verteuerung des Faktors Kapital wie eine Investitionsbremse auswirken. Durch die geringere Kapitalausstattung wrde die Arbeitsproduktivitt sinken, was nicht ohne Folgen fr die Lohnniveau bleiben wrde. Schliesslich fhren hhere Zinsen zu einer Umverteilung von den Schuldnern zu den Glubigern. Darunter htten insbesondere die Hypothekarschuldner und der Staat als grsster Schuldner zu leiden. Unsere Geldpolitik hat sich stets in einem von Unsicherheit geprgten Umfeld bewegt. Dies ist auch gegenwrtig der Fall, obwohl die Mrkte in den letzten Monaten weniger volatil waren. Diese Unsicherheit und die Realitt der Schweizer Wirtschaft legen uns nahe, mit unserer vorsichtigen geldpolitischen Strategie weiterzufahren und nicht einfach im Schatten der Europischen Zentralbank zu operieren. 4. Unvernderte Beziehung zwischen Geldpolitik und Konjunktur Eine Forderung, die ebenfalls oft an die Nationalbank heran getragen wird, lautet auf eine aktive Untersttzung der Konjunktur. Hier werden allerdings die Mglichkeiten der Nationalbank meist berschtzt. So kann der konkrete Kurs der Geldpolitik die Konjunktur nur vorbergehend beeinflussen. Der langfristige Wachstumspfad einer Volkswirtschaft hingegen wird durch andere Faktoren bestimmt. Angesprochen sind hier wieder die Rahmenbe- dingungen, zu denen wie bereits gesagt auch die Preisstabilitt gehrt. Mit einer auf Preisstabilitt ausgerichteten Geldpolitik leistet die Nationalbank den besten Beitrag zur Frderung des langfristigen Wirtschaftswachstums. Auch in bezug auf die kurzfristige Konjunkturstabilisierung sind die Mglichkeiten der Nationalbank beschrnkt. Zuerst hngt die konjunkturelle Entwicklung in einer kleinen, offenen Volkswirtschaft wie der Schweiz zu einem grossen Teil von den Impulsen aus dem Ausland ab. Davon einmal abgesehen setzt eine gezielte Konjunkturbeeinflussung oder gar -steuerung Informationen voraus, ber die eine Zentralbank im Normalfall gar nicht verfgt. Bei der Entscheidung ber den Einsatz der Geldpolitik zur Konjunkturstabilisierung stellen sich schwierige Diagnose- und Prognoseprobleme. Ausserdem reagiert die Realwirtschaft erst mit einer mehr oder weniger langen Verzgerung auf den Einsatz der geldpolitischen Instrumente. Dies kann dazu fhren, dass eine auf "fine tuning" ausgerichtete Politik im Endeffekt die Geldwertstabilitt gefhrdet. Einer aktivistischen stop-and-go Politik ist daher eine klare Absage zu erteilen. Gefordert ist viel mehr eine stetige Geldpolitik, die sich auf das Ziel konzentriert, das sie auch tatschlich erreichen kann: auf die mittelfristige Stabilisierung des Preisniveaus. Mit einer solchen Politik trgt die Notenbank am besten zur Verstetigung der Wirtschaftsentwicklung bei. 5. Ein stabiler und transparenter Rahmen fr die Geldpolitik Wesentliche Voraussetzung fr das langfristige Gedeihen der Finanzmrkte sind gnstige wirtschaftliche, politische, rechtliche und technologische Rahmenbedingungen. Der zentrale Beitrag der Nationalbank liegt auch hier wieder in der Fhrung einer transparenten und stetigen Politik. Dadurch entsteht ein stabiles und berechenbares Umfeld, innerhalb dessen die Banken und die brigen Akteure an den Finanzmrkten planen, kalkulieren und disponieren knnen. Die jahrelange Konstanz der geldpolitischen Grundausrichtung drfte gerade in Zeiten des Wandels besonders hilfreich sein. Whrend sich an unserem obersten Ziel, der Preisstabilitt, und unserer Strategie, dieses Ziel durch eine selbstndige Politik zu erreichen, seit Beginn der 70er Jahre nichts gendert hat, so haben wir hingegen in der konkreten Durchfhrung der Geldpolitik seit Anfang Jahr einige Neuerungen eingefhrt.
