So publizieren wir neu eine Inflationsprognose, die die von uns fr die kommenden Jahre erwartete Inflationsrate widerspiegelt. Gleichzeitig haben wir ein Zielband fr den von uns anvisierten Geldmarktzins bekannt gegeben. Nhert sich der Wert der prognostizierten Inflation der Obergrenze von 2%, die fr uns gerade noch mit Preisstabilitt vereinbar ist, dann lst dies ein berdenken des geldpolitischen Kurses aus. Je nach Resultat dieses Prozesses kann es zu einer Verschiebung des Zinses innerhalb des Zielbandes oder zu einer nderung des Bandes selbst kommen. Es kann aber auch sein, dass wir zum Schluss kommen, dass kein Handlungsbedarf vorliegt. Unsere neue Strategie impliziert keinen Zins-Automatismus. Vielmehr steckt sie einen Rahmen ab, der uns helfen soll, unsere Entscheide systematisch und rational zu treffen. Wie in der Vergangenheit wird sich unsere Lagebeurteilung auf einen Strauss von Indikatoren sttzen. Unsere Einschtzung der zuknftigen Preisentwicklung wird dabei im Zentrum des Verfahrens stehen. Bei der Begrndung unserer Entscheide werden wir unsere Einschtzungen und berlegungen offen darlegen und dem Markt damit wichtige Anhaltspunkte ber unsere Beurteilung der wirtschaftlichen und monetren Lage vermitteln. Mit dieser neuen Darstellungsart ihrer Politik ist die SNB auch gewisse Risiken eingegangen: Erstens kann die Verffentlichung eines operativen Zinssatzes uns dem Druck der Mrkte aussetzen, und zwar umso mehr, als die kurzfristigen Bewegungen dieser Grsse oft von externen Faktoren bestimmt werden. Um dieses Problem zu entschrfen definieren wir unser Ziel im Rahmen einer Bandbreite fr den 3-Monatssatz und nicht als absolutes Niveauziel. Die Bandbreite sollte uns vor kurzfristigem Aktivismus bewahren, falls die Marktkonditionen unter den Einfluss von externen Schocks geraten. Die Definition einer Bandbreite fr den operativen Zins ist fr eine kleine Volkswirtschaft geradezu ein Gebot der Flexibilitt. Zweitens wird die erhhte Transparenz unserer Politik die geldpolitische Entscheidungsfindung vermehrt ins Rampenlicht der ffentlichkeit stellen. Wir haben uns dazu verpflichtet, unsere Lagebeurteilung zu publizieren. Dadurch wird die Debatte ber die geldpolitischen Entscheidungen transparent und ffentlich. Man sollte sich hier keine Illusionen machen, die Fhrung der Geldpolitik wird unter diesen Umstnden im Vergleich zu frher schwieriger. In heiklen Situationen wird es weder an Kritik noch an Gegenexpertisen fehlen. Es wird dann darauf ankommen, das Prinzip der geldpolitischen Autonomie strikte aufrecht zu erhalten, ist die Unabhngigkeit der Notenbank doch eine wesentliche Voraussetzung fr die Geldwertstabilitt. Das neue Verfahren zwingt uns aber, unsere Entscheide noch ausfhrlicher zu kommunizieren, was zur Stabilitt der Mrkte beitragen sollte. Zusammenfassend mchte ich sagen, dass Geldpolitik nie ein einfaches Geschft war. Wir entscheiden immer unter unvollkommener Information. Es gibt keine Methode, die die "richtigen" Entscheide garantieren kann. Geldpolitik verlangt nach Fachwissen, Fingerspitzengefhl und einer gewissen Portion Glck. Dies wird auch in Zukunft und unter dem neuen Konzept so bleiben. 6. Schlussbemerkungen Das Umfeld, in dem die Schweizerische Nationalbank operiert, hat sich in den letzten Jahren tiefgreifend verndert. Es ist geprgt von Liberalisierung, Deregulierung und einer immer strkeren globalen Vernetzung. Die dadurch verursachten Umwlzungen betreffen sowohl die Gter- als auch die Finanzmrkte, wobei die Finanzmrkte die Gtermrkte an Dynamik noch bertreffen. Vieles spricht dafr, dass dieser Prozess in den nchsten Jahren weiter andauern, ja sich sogar noch verstrken wird. Neben dieser allgemeinen Entwicklung hat auch im konkreten monetren Umfeld der Schweiz eine bedeutende Vernderung stattgefunden. Seit gut einem Jahr ist der Euro in den uns umgebenden Lndern eingefhrt worden. Das ehrgeizige Projekt der Europischen Whrungsunion ist somit in seine dritte und letzte Phase getreten. Das Agieren in diesem neuen Umfeld stellt fr Behrden, Unternehmen und Private eine Herausforderung dar. Gnstige Rahmenbedingungen sind heute wichtiger denn je, damit ein Land im verstrkten globalen Wettbewerb bestehen kann. Mit einer auf Geldwertstabilitt ausgerichteten Politik leistet die Nationalbank den besten Beitrag zum langfristigen Gedeihen unseres Landes. Geldpolitische Aktionen zur Konjunkturankurbelung mgen sich in wirtschaftlich schwierigen Situationen als verfhrerisch einfache Lsung prsentieren; die Erfahrung lehrt jedoch, dass das Wirtschaftswachstum langfristig von realen Faktoren abhngig ist. Es ist daher zentral, dass die Notenbank eine stetige, mittelfristig orientierte Strategie verfolgt. Gleichzeitig verlangt der Wandel im Umfeld der Geldpolitik nach gewissen Anpassungen bei der konkreten Umsetzung der letzteren. Bei unserem neuen geldpolitischen Konzept sticht vor allem die Erhhung der Transparenz heraus. Mit der Publikation einer Inflationsprognose und der Festlegung eines Zinsbandes beschreiten wir neue Wege. Wir erfllen damit den Wunsch des Marktes nach vermehrter Information ber unsere Einschtzungen und Absichten. Gleichzeitig gehen wir mit diesen Neuerungen auch ein gewisses Risiko ein. So wird sich erst noch zeigen, wie der Markt mit der neuen Informationslage umgeht. Ich bin aber zuversichtlich, dass sich das neue Konzept in der Praxis bewhren wird.

Title: On monetary policy in the new year
text: Monetary policy in the new year Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Research Institute for Empirical Economics and Economic Policy University of St. Gallen Thursday, 20 January 2000 For the third time, the University of St. Gallen and its Research Institute for Empirical Economics and Economic Policy are giving me the opportunity to explain the SNB's monetary policy intentions for the new year. Today, however, I will not limit myself to the planned monetary policy alone. As you have seen from the media, the SNB made an adjustment to its monetary policy approach at the beginning of this year. I am looking forward to delving deeper into this concept in front of an expert audience. First of all, in the first part of my remarks, I would like to take a look back at the economic events of the past year. After explaining our approach, I will discuss the economic outlook and monetary policy intentions for the current year in a third part. I will conclude my presentation with a few basic remarks. 1. Review International development The international economic situation brightened significantly in the course of 1999 after the global economy had been shaken by the crises in East Asia, Russia and South America in the two previous years. The emerging economies of East Asia recovered faster than expected from the sharp economic slump and Japan also overcame its recession thanks to massive government stimulus measures. The situation also improved in South America after a financial crisis was averted in Brazil. In Russia, the situation remains extremely difficult, which has a negative impact not least on the development of many countries in Eastern Europe. Overcoming the crisis in East Asia led to a noticeable revival of world trade in the course of 1999. The industrialised countries also benefited from this favourable development. Exports and investment grew strongly, so that the real growth of the OECD countries in 1999 was more than half a percentage point higher than in the previous year. However, the dynamics in the OECD region are still different. The United States continued its economic recovery. For the third consecutive year, real growth reached around 4%. This strong growth was not least due to the continued rise in share prices, which opened up additional consumption opportunities for American households. Growth has also increased sustainably in Japan. The Japanese economy returned to positive development in 1999, having shrunk by almost 3% in 1998. On the other hand, events in Europe were much more restrained. In the first half of the year, many countries still suffered from weak exports as a result of the Asian crisis. It was not until the second half of the year that an improvement began to emerge. However, the economic upswing in the two important countries of Germany and Italy was delayed as a result of persistent, profound structural problems. The different developments are also visible in employment. The United States again recorded a strong increase in employment, while demand for labour in Germany and Italy developed only modestly. The change in the economic outlook in the course of 1999 has had an impact on monetary policy. In the first half of the year, the US monetary authorities and the European Central Bank continued the loose monetary policy initiated to avoid a global economic slump as a result of the international financial crisis in autumn 1998. As recently as April 1999, the ECB cut its key interest rate by 50 basis points. As the economic environment began to improve in the middle of the year, central banks tightened their monetary policy. The US Federal Reserve increased the rate for overnight money from 4.75% to 5.5% in three steps between June and November. The European Central Bank raised its key interest rate by 0.5 percentage points in November. At the end of November 1999, key interest rates were thus at a level comparable to those before the outbreak of the international financial crisis in autumn 1998. With the increase, the central banks reacted to the renewed danger of a rise in inflation. Situation in Switzerland In the first half of the year, economic activity in Switzerland was still influenced by the consequences of the Asian crisis. Only when they were overcome was the economy able to gain significant momentum in the second half of the year. The most important impulses came from the export industry, which benefited from the strong increase in world trade. In addition to exports, private consumption continued to provide significant economic support, as in the previous year. However, due to weak growth in the first half of the year, real growth in 1999 was around 1.5% below that of 1998. Fortunately, unemployment continued to fall last year. Employment grew less strongly in 1999 than in the previous year. This is mainly a consequence of the economic downturn in the second half of 1998, with employment in industry continuing to fall slightly, while it is rising steadily in the services sector. The demand for labour is currently growing most strongly in the IT sector and insurance companies. The improvement in the labour market can also be seen in the development of the number of jobseekers, which includes not only the unemployed but also people who earn an interim income or in an employment respite. Retraining program are involved. The number of job seekers has practically fallen by a quarter. On a positive note, regional disparities in unemployment have decreased. Inflation, as measured by the national consumer price index, again remained moderate last year, averaging 0.8%. This is slightly higher than in the two previous years, with around 0.3 percentage points likely to be attributable to the increase in VAT. However, inflation picked up noticeably towards the end of the year. The main reason for this increase is the imported goods, which rose sharply as a result of the sharp rise in oil prices. At the time, we envisaged a continuation of our generally generous monetary policy for 1999. This reflected our assessment at the time that the Swiss economy would weaken as a result of the crises in East Asia and on the financial markets. We also indicated that we wanted to take account of the uncertainties associated with the introduction of the euro at the beginning of 1999. We had to prevent any speculation against the euro from leading to an economically unjustified appreciation of the Swiss franc in this difficult phase. After the uncertainties had eased in the course of the year, we were again able to pay less attention to the euro exchange rate and continue our autonomous monetary policy. Nevertheless, the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the euro moved in narrow ranges. However, this had nothing to do with our policy, but with the similar economic situation in which Switzerland and the countries of the euro area found themselves. In the second half of September, we tightened our share price because the now pick-up economy had tended to intensify the risk of inflation again. Introduction of the euro To conclude my review, I would like to add a few fundamental remarks on the new European currency. The introduction of the euro at the beginning of last year went smoothly. The European Central Bank and its predecessor, the European Monetary Institute, together with the national central banks, have done a good job. The technical processes for supplying the banking system with liquidity and the TARGET clearing system are working perfectly. The euro quickly established itself as an investment currency on the financial markets and achieved a considerable market share on the money and capital markets in the first year of its existence. The European Central Bank bases its monetary policy decisions on a reference value for the M3 money supply and on a broad-based assessment of the inflation outlook. This "two-pillar" strategy has been criticized from various quarters. I believe that this criticism falls short. Within a very short period of time, the ECB had to develop a monetary policy concept for a monetary policy concept of the size of the United States. For which virtually no data and studies on the monetary policy transmission mechanism have been available up to that point. In this environment of great uncertainty, it has opted for a cautious strategy that combines proven elements of the Deutsche Bundesbank's money supply management with new elements of an inflation target strategy. The ECB has done quite well with this strategy so far; it has successfully fulfilled its mission of maintaining price stability. However, the euro lost around 15% of its value against the dollar. Contrary to an often held opinion, however, this loss of value is not attributable to a wrong monetary policy. Rather, the reason for the appreciation of the dollar lies primarily in the different economic developments in the USA and Europe. However, the success of monetary union depends not only on the monetary policy concept, but also on its consistent implementation. As a new central bank, the ECB has yet to acquire the reputation of an independent institution committed to maintaining price stability. Already in the first year of the existence of the monetary union, those responsible have contributed to building the credibility of the ECB through their actions by resisting attempts at pressure from politicians. However, a deeper assessment of monetary union will only be possible in a few years' time. Last but not least, it will depend on whether the individual member states of the monetary union will have the discipline that is essential for a sustainably convergent stability policy. 2. Adjustment of the monetary policy approach Last December, we announced an adjustment to our monetary policy approach. I deliberately use the term adjustment to underline that the fundamental orientation of the Swiss National Bank's monetary policy remains unchanged and continues to be primarily aimed at maintaining price stability. At the same time, however, I would like to emphasise that this is the most important change in concept since the transition to a flexible Swiss franc exchange rate in 1973. The SNB's future monetary policy concept consists essentially of three elements: the first element concerns the definition of price stability. The second element involves the use of a broad-based inflation forecast as the main indicator for monetary policy decision-making. From now on, we refrain from setting targets for the growth of the money supply. However, the development of the money supply will play a decisive role in the preparation of the inflation forecast. The third element is a target range for the three-month rate on the Swiss franc money market as an operational requirement for the implementation of monetary policy. We then strive to further improve the transparency of our monetary policy. Previous strategy Before turning to these three elements, I would like to briefly discuss our monetary policy strategy to date. After a lengthy period of annual targets  first for the M1 money supply and later for the central bank money supply  the SNB decided at the beginning of the nineties to orient monetary policy towards a medium-term target path for the seasonally adjusted central bank money supply. This target path was set for a period of five years. The solution impressed above all with two properties. On the one hand, it created a more effective anchor for medium-term price developments than in the case of annual targets. It required that deviations from the target path were corrected again in the medium term. The SNB was obliged to exercise greater monetary policy discipline, as the monetary developments of recent years have not been could simply be forgotten. On the other hand, however, it made it possible to conduct monetary policy flexibly. With the medium-term target path, it was possible to react pragmatically to exchange rate disturbances and economic fluctuations, since monetary policy was not tied to a specific money supply target in the short term. The medium-term trajectory solution thus combined the benefits of a longer-term commitment to maintain price stability with a large margin for monetary policy in the short term. Like any other concept based on a monetary aggregate, however, it depended crucially on whether the demand for central bank money was sufficiently stable and predictable. In the course of 1997, we found that the demand for central bank money was severely disrupted. These disturbances affected both the circulation of banknotes and the current account balances of the banks. Public demand for thousand-franc notes rose sharply for reasons that have never been clarified before, and banks' demand for sight deposits became increasingly volatile. The deviations of the central bank money supply from the target path were therefore no longer meaningful. In December 1997, the SNB relativised the importance of the trajectory and from then on increasingly emphasised the M3 money supply as an important indicator. However, the solution with the medium-term target path has not yet been completely abandoned, as at that time it was unclear whether the disturbances were permanent or only temporary. Towards the end of 1998, it became apparent that demand for central bank money would not normalise in the foreseeable future. A continuation of the concept with a medium-term target path for the central bank money supply was therefore no longer conceivable. Let me now go into a little more detail about the three main elements of the adapted concept. First element: Definition of price stability The first element of the concept concerns an explicit definition of price stability. By price stability, we mean inflation of less than 2% per year as measured by the national consumer price index. The SNB's mission is to conduct monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. With the means at its disposal, it can primarily ensure price stability. Price stability facilitates a balanced macroeconomic development and reduces undesirable undesirable undesirable developments. We chose this definition of price stability for two reasons. Firstly, we must take into account the fact that inflation can never be measured accurately. On the other hand, it is practically impossible for the SNB to control inflation exactly. The first element anchors the medium-term orientation of monetary policy. Although the definition of price stability does not provide for a floor, the intention to ensure price stability implies that we must also prevent deflation. We want to keep inflation within the defined price stability range in the medium term. However, it is important to underline that we are not pursuing an actual inflation target. We make no commitment to keep inflation in line with price stability at all times. In a small, open economy like Switzerland, inflation is often affected by unexpected swings in oil and other import prices, as well as significant changes in the exchange rate. The SNB is therefore hardly in a position to prevent these price movements that occur in the short term. In many cases, it would also make no economic sense to suppress these short-term price movements, even if we were able to do so. As long as these price movements do not lead to persistent inflation or deflation, they are manageable for the economy. On the other hand, combating temporary inflation shocks too rigorously can lead to an excessive increase in economic fluctuations and thus be associated with high real economic costs. In the fight against temporary inflation shocks, the SNB will therefore also be responsible for the real economy. That is why we have tabled a number of amendments. However, it will resolutely oppose any persistent inflationary or deflationary development. Second element: inflation forecast Let me now move on to the second element of our concept. In the future, the SNB's monetary policy decisions will be based primarily on an inflation forecast. As is well known, monetary policy has an effect on inflation with a delay of around two to three years. We are forced to take a forward-looking stance and to react early to inflation risks. The inflation forecast is therefore becoming the central indicator for monetary policy. We will make our monetary policy decisions in such a way that expected inflation tends to be in the realm of price stability. For example, we will tighten monetary policy if projected inflation rises beyond the realm of price stability. Conversely, we will ease monetary policy if the forecast points to deflation. The published forecast will take into account the impact of the intended monetary policy stance. Our inflation forecast is a so-called consensus forecast. A consensus forecast is the product of an economic weighting of information from various important indicator groups. We base our assessment of future price developments primarily on three types of indicators. Firstly, we consider the course of monetary aggregates, especially M3. The price development in the longer term depends crucially on the course of the money supply. The medium-term inflation forecast must therefore rely heavily on the development of monetary aggregates. Second, we use a number of econometric predictive models. This includes both structural models and statistical time series models. The structural models predict inflation based on a specific theoretical model of the economy. The time series models, on the other hand, exploit the historical correlation between inflation and certain variables to make forecasts. Both types of models also take into account factors such as the economic situation and the exchange rate, which influence inflation, especially in the short term. influence. Finally, thirdly, we take into account other factors that cannot be directly integrated into the forecast models. These include special items such as an increase in VAT, a change in the price of crude oil or the liberalisation of a market segment. An economic assessment and consideration of the information from the various indicator groups finally results in the consensus forecast for the development of inflation over the following three years. The consensus forecast is thus a broad-based forecast. Forecasting inflation over three years is difficult and fraught with uncertainty. Many factors that ultimately influence inflation in the following years are still unknown when the forecast is drawn up. Irrespective of these difficulties, however, the inflation forecast must be used as the basis for monetary policy decision-making and used to explain monetary policy decisions. As I have already stressed, we must pursue a forward-looking policy if we are to maintain price stability. Third element: Target band for Libor The third element of our strategy concerns the operational implementation of monetary policy. From now on, the SNB will set a target range of 100 basis points for the three-month rate on the Swiss franc money market as an operational target. The three-month Libor ("London Interbank Offered Rate") serves as the reference interest rate. The target range is set in such a way that the projected inflation remains in the range that we equate with price stability. The operational implementation of our monetary policy to date has been based on a quantitative target for supplying the banking system with current account balances. Interest rate formation on the money market was largely left to market participants. However, the strong fluctuations in banks' demand for sight deposits have made it impossible for some time to implement monetary policy operationally, which was based solely on a volume requirement for sight deposits. At strong fluctuations in banks' demand for current account balances lead to a purely quantity requirement to an economically undesirable high volatility of money market rates. The adjustment of the concept that has now been made takes this fact into account. We could also have made the operational target for the implementation of monetary policy by setting the interest rate for a short-term repo transaction. This repo interest rate would be very easy to control by the National Bank. However, we have adopted a different solution for the following two reasons: firstly, the SNB wants to remain flexible in its day-to-day monetary operations without every small change in interest rates in its money market operations being interpreted by the markets as a monetary policy signal. In the short term, imbalances in the liquidity supply of the banking system and other disturbances in the money and foreign exchange market often occur, which manifest themselves in strong fluctuations in the overnight money rate. Under these circumstances, the interest rate for very short-term repo transactions is not suitable as a signal carrier for the direction of our monetary policy. By Swiss standards, a slightly longer-term rate in an economically important segment of the money market is much better suited for this. The three-month Libor interest rate is one of the most important interest rates in the Swiss franc money market. It is regarded as a central factor for the refinancing of first-class banks and companies and is determined and published daily in a transparent procedure. This rate reacts relatively little to short-term imbalances and random fluctuations in the money market. The three-month Libor is therefore very well suited as a reference rate for signalling our shorter-term monetary policy intentions. Second, the SNB does not intend interest rate activism. The idea of setting a target range and not a target value is to continue to allow fluctuations to a certain extent and to leave the market to fine-tune. The use of a target band for the Libor as a monetary policy signal carrier also means that we can henceforth dispense with the setting of a discount rate. In recent decades, the discount business has improved its monetary policy Meaning lost. The SNB has not carried out any discount transactions for years. At best, the determination of the discount rate still had a certain signal effect. With the introduction of an interest rate band, it has become superfluous. Transparency The monetary policy of an independent central bank in particular must be transparent to the public. A transparent monetary policy contributes significantly to the efficient design of economic processes in a modern market economy. Both the International Monetary Fund and the Bank for International Settlements have been working for some time to develop guidelines for the transparency of central banks. As is repeatedly emphasised by the aforementioned international institutions, the Swiss National Bank has already been a pioneer in a transparent monetary policy. The adjustment of the monetary policy approach will further improve transparency. By presenting our concept, we are announcing to the audience the framework for the course of monetary policy decisions. We regularly publish the key data of our decisions, such as the inflation forecast and the target range for Libor, in various media. With the quarterly publication of the "Monetary Policy Decisions", we explain our monetary policy decisions in detail so that the audience also has clarity about their background. Some misconceptions To conclude my remarks on the monetary policy approach, let me briefly address two points. They concern aspects that were partly misinterpreted following our press conference last December. I take this opportunity to clear up these misunderstandings. The first point concerns interest rate management. The introduction of a target band for Libor led some commentators to say that the SNB had switched to an interest rate policy. The term interest rate policy is understood to mean a monetary policy that strives for a certain nominal or even real interest rate in the medium term, so that the interest rate becomes the actual goal of monetary policy. But that is not our intention. The target band for Libor is an operational guideline for money market governance. This gives it the character of a signal carrier for the SNB's shorter-term intentions on the money market. In the medium term, however, we are not guided by an interest rate expectation, but by the inflation forecast. The interest rate band reflects the necessary monetary policy measures to maintain price stability in the medium term. Its introduction is not a substitute for monetary objectives. Rather, the inflation forecast takes over their previous role. The second point concerns the designation of our strategy. In various comments, our strategy has been referred to as the so-called "inflation target strategy". Such a strategy, such as that used in the United Kingdom, Canada or New Zealand, is aimed at the permanent achievement of an explicit inflation target. We do not see our concept as an inflation target strategy. It is true that our monetary policy decisions are primarily based on an inflation forecast. However, we do not pursue an explicit inflation target. As I have already mentioned, inflation in Switzerland in the short term is strongly influenced by factors that are not directly under the control of the SNB. We cannot, therefore, make a commitment to stabilise inflation at a certain level at a permanent level. Our strategy aims to maintain price stability in the medium term. To achieve this, we use a number of important indicators, especially the money supply. We therefore see our monetary policy concept as a broad-based strategy for maintaining price stability. 3. Economic outlook and monetary policy in 2000 Economic outlook The economic outlook for the current year is favourable for the Swiss economy. In line with the relevant forecasts, we expect real growth of the order of 2%. The economy will be driven by both domestic demand and exports. We expect a further significant revival in world trade. However, certain risks come from Japan, where structural adjustment urgently needs to continue, and from the United States, where the economy could slowly run out. Nevertheless, Swiss exports should grow strongly in the current year and support the economy strongly. The domestic economy will continue to be an important pillar of the economy. Private consumption should increase in the order of magnitude of the previous year. Fixed investment is likely to grow more strongly again. Fortunately, for the first time in a long time, construction investment could also provide impetus. The output gap will continue to close in the course of 2000 and employment should continue to increase. This development, which is favourable to the Swiss economy, can be attributed to three main causes. Firstly, our economy has made great efforts in recent years to solve its structural problems. Second, the global economic climate has improved significantly over the past year. And thirdly, our economy has benefited from the favourable monetary conditions. Monetary policy intentions We published an inflation forecast for the first time last December. Inflation this year will not depend significantly on our current monetary policy. As a result of the delay in action, our Current monetary policy will only influence inflation for the next year and the year after next. The target range for the three-month Libor is 1.25% - 2.25%, with us initially aiming for the middle range of the band. The position of the target range is in line with our inflation forecast. According to our current state of knowledge, inflation over the next three years will remain in the range we equate with price stability if we keep the three-month rate roughly in the middle of the target range. However, inflation is likely to rise slightly. Our inflation forecast for 2000 is 1.5% and for 2001 and 2002 1.7% and 1.8% respectively. The projected course of inflation is consistent with the evolution of the monetary aggregates we observe. During the recession of the nineties, the growth of M3 had increased sharply as a result of the SNB's increasingly expansionary monetary policy. Since the spring of 1997, growth has slowed again as we continued to loosen monetary policy only to a limited extent and it has now reached a comparatively low level. The expansionary monetary policy that we conducted until recently is therefore unlikely to provide any significant impetus for inflation. The SNB will closely monitor the development of the relevant indicators and periodically review the analyses on which the inflation forecast is based. The pronounced dynamism of recent economic development prompts us to be particularly cautious. A further increase in economic growth could potentially increase the risks of inflation. 4. Outlook I would like to conclude with a few fundamental remarks. The Federal Constitution, which came into force at the beginning of the year, also instructs the SNB to conduct monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. lead. Together with fiscal policy and competition policy, it is intended to help create a framework that enables steady growth with high employment and low inflation. Monetary policy focuses on ensuring price stability. Once again, it should be emphasised that price stability is not an end in itself. Stable prices enable sustainable economic growth and prevent undesirable undesirable undesirable developments. The adjustment of our monetary policy concept, which takes account of the changes that have occurred on the financial markets, creates the necessary conditions for us to continue to fulfil our mission in the future. However, a good concept alone is no guarantee for a successful monetary policy. The decisive factor is the implementation of the concept and the quality of monetary policy decisions. The concept can provide a clear framework for monetary policy decision-making. Often, however, it is not so much the details of a concept that matter, but rather the willingness of those responsible to make consistent decisions  possibly also unpopular decisions. However, monetary policy decisions must also be supported by a social consensus. In the longer term, the SNB will only be able to fulfil its mandate if the political will to stabilise monetary conditions in Switzerland remains broadly based.
