Par rapport  l'euro, n'oublions pas que notre conomie a atteint une situation de quasi-plein emploi, alors que les grands pays de l'Union europenne sont toujours confronts  un chmage lev. La conduite de la politique montaire est et reste un exercice dlicat d'quilibriste. Aujourd'hui, il s'agit dj pour nous de trouver le juste milieu afin d'viter  notre conomie de tomber dans deux volutions regrettables. Si nous menons une politique trop restrictive, nous empcherons notre conomie dutiliser son potentiel de croissance accru, aprs les restructurations et les investissements quelle a oprs. Dun autre ct, si nous pratiquons une politique trop laxiste, nous favoriserons la sur- 11 chauffe et, fatalement, attiserons linflation. Force est donc de constater que dans notre activit - comme cela est si souvent le cas dans la vie - la voie moyenne est celle qui conduit au rsultat optimal. Je vous remercie de votre attention.

Title: Swiss Monetary Policy: Autonomy or Adaptation to Europe?
text: Swiss monetary policy: autonomy or adaptation to Europe? Georg Rich Swiss National Bank Lecture at the Seminar on the Monetary Policy of Central Banks, Institute for European Studies, University of Basel, 3 April 2000 2 The introduction of the euro at the beginning of 1999 marked the beginning of a new chapter in European monetary history. The transition to the euro fundamentally changed the environment for European monetary policy. The European Central Bank assumed responsibility for monetary policy in the euro area from the national central banks. The centralisation of the monetary system has a far-reaching consequence: the European Central Bank must conduct a single monetary policy for the entire euro area. Since the transition to the new single currency, the same money market rates have prevailed throughout the euro area. Interest rates on the capital market have also largely converged. Under these conditions, the European Central Bank has no choice but to focus its monetary policy on the overall interest of the euro area. It can no longer take the needs of individual countries into account, as it used to take the national music institutes into account. Despite the upheavals brought about by the transition to the new single currency, the introduction of the euro went smoothly. The turbulence on the money and foreign exchange markets, which had been predicted by some observers at the beginning of 1999, did not occur. Nevertheless, it is premature to make a final judgement on the success or failure of European monetary integration. That is why I would first like to make a few comments on the experience with the euro so far. I will then discuss the consequences of the euro for the Swiss economy. Finally, I would like to compare the monetary policy strategy and the economic environment of the Swiss National Bank with that of the European Central Bank. 1. Previous experience with the euro The smooth transition at the beginning of 1999 served many observers as proof of the thesis put forward by the official EU authorities that the euro would prove to be a strong and stable currency. In the meantime, disillusionment has spread: the massive fall in the euro's exchange rate against the dollar is unsettling the public and gnawing away at the credibility of the European Central Bank. Despite the current tendency of the euro to weaken, I would like to warn against hasty judgments about the expediency of European monetary union and the credibility of the European Central Bank. The expediency and credibility of a monetary order can only be assessed on the basis of a long period of observation. As is well known, monetary policy is slow: the results of the monetary policy currently being pursued will only become fully apparent in two to three years' time. In addition, as a young institution, the European Central Bank has no history. Therefore, some time must first elapse before their performance can be evaluated. For example, the current favourable state of the euro area economy still has little to do with the monetary policy of the European Central Bank. Rather, the historically low inflation in Europe is mainly due to the stability-oriented course pursued by the national central banks before 1999. We will not be able to assess the appropriateness of the European Central Bank's monetary policy until next year and in the following period. For the time being, it also makes little sense to use the exchange rate development of the euro against the dollar as an indicator of the credibility of the European Central Bank. In general, it can be assumed that nominal exchange rate movements will compensate for the differences in purchasing power between the various currencies in the long term. In the short and medium term, however, substantial and sustained 3 Deviations from purchasing power parity occur. These deviations  even if they last for a long time  are often not convincingly explainable. Since the euro is a new currency, it is difficult to say whether and to what extent its current exchange rate against the dollar deviates from purchasing power parity. The only thing that is clear is that the recent weakening of the euro came as a surprise to many observers. In the event of unexpected changes in the exchange rate, legions of analysts who can explain the price movements retrospectively always appear on the scene. Initially, the disparities in economic development  rapid economic growth in the United States and faltering business in key euro area countries  are likely to have contributed to the weakness of the euro. In recent months, however, the European economy has picked up significantly. Nevertheless, the euro did not recover, but continued to depreciate. In view of this development, many analysts are looking for new explanations. They criticise the European Central Bank's monetary policy concept and accuse it of a lack of transparency. They claim that the European Central Bank is jeopardising its credibility and contributing to the weakness of the euro. As I will show in the last part of my presentation, I consider the frequently expressed criticism of the European Central Bank to be exaggerated. Above all, I doubt that such arguments can explain the current weakness of the euro. As I have already emphasised, the time has not yet come for a comprehensive assessment of the performance of the European Central Bank. 2. Consequences for the Swiss economy Before the transition to the new single currency, there was widespread fear in Switzerland that the introduction of the euro would trigger turbulence on the foreign exchange markets. Many observers expected a strong appreciation of the Swiss franc against the new common currency, which could undermine the international competitiveness of domestic industry. These fears were fuelled by the events of 1994 and 1995, when the Swiss franc appreciated significantly against major currencies (Chart 1). The appreciation against the Italian lira was particularly dramatic. The rise of the Swiss franc was generally attributed to a lack of confidence in the future common currency. Many investors were therefore forced to convert part of their assets into Swiss francs and other stable currencies that would not be absorbed into the euro. The SNB reacted to this flight into the Swiss franc by easing monetary policy in the spring of 1995. As a result, it further relaxed its reins and led a very expansive course, especially in 1997 and 1998. For this reason, the three-month rate on the Swiss money market fell from around 4% at the end of 1994 to 2% at the end of 1995 and to well below 2% in the course of 1997. Since the late summer of 1999, it has been on the rise again, for reasons I will come back to (Figure 2). Over time, the easing of monetary policy had an impact on the exchange rate and economic development. The rise of the Swiss franc came to a standstill at the end of 1995 and again gave way to a lower valuation. The Swiss economy began to pick up at the beginning of 1997. Although the initially strong upswing came to a temporary halt in the second half of 1998 as a result of the Asian crisis, it has been going on for a few months now. 4 However, there are increasing signs that the Swiss economy has entered a real boom phase. Some observers regarded the easing of Swiss monetary policy as a real paradigm shift for the SNB. They took the view that the SNB was increasingly focusing its policy on stabilising the exchange rate with a view to the introduction of the euro. It has also often been claimed that after the introduction of the euro, the SNB will have no choice but to closely align itself with the European Central Bank in terms of monetary policy. These views were fed by statements by important exponents of the National Bank that the Swiss central bank would pull out all the stops to prevent an undesirable appreciation of the Swiss franc. It has often been overlooked that the SNB does not regard exchange rate stability as an end in itself. Rather, the need to counter the appreciation trend of the Swiss franc arose from the SNB's mandate to ensure price stability. At that time, the Swiss economy was under pressure from deflation, which the SNB had to resolutely oppose. Because, as we keep stressing, maintaining price stability means preventing inflation and deflation. In recent months, however, the constitution of the Swiss economy has changed dramatically. Deflationary pressures have not only given way, but the strong economic upswing is resurrecting fears of inflation. The current strengthening of the dollar is also contributing to the revival of the Swiss economy. In these circumstances, a monetary policy aimed at preventing the appreciation of the Swiss franc is no longer appropriate. Such a policy would inevitably trigger an increase in inflation in today's economic environment. Thus, exchange rate stability no longer plays the same role for Swiss monetary policy as it did in the second half of the nineties, when our economy was under deflationary pressures. Nor do we pursue an exchange rate target. Rather, our aim is to prevent the current economic upswing from leading to a marked rise in inflation. The SNB clearly expressed its intentions in adjusting its monetary policy approach at the end of 1999. It continues to focus its monetary policy on maintaining price stability, which it equates with inflation below 2%. In doing so, it strives to avoid both an increase in inflation to over 2% and a decline in the price level. In order to achieve the objective of price stability, it regularly prepares inflation forecasts. If the forecasts suggest that inflation threatens to leave the realm of price stability, it adjusts monetary policy accordingly. It dresses its monetary policy decisions in the form of an interest rate band for the three-month Libor rate on the money market for Swiss francs. This band is decisive for their operations on the money market. The SNB also pursues a number of indicators which, according to experience, influence future price developments and thus feed into its inflation forecasts. In the shorter term, price developments depend primarily on the economic situation and exchange rate movements. At present, the sharp rise in the price of oil is also having an inflationary effect. In the longer term, price developments are largely determined by the growth of monetary aggregates, in particular the M3 money supply. This is how the SNB reacted to the marked recovery of the Swiss 5 Economy since the second half of 1999, when it tightened its monetary policy in several steps. As a result, the Libor rate for Swiss francs rose again towards 3%. Despite the tightening of Swiss monetary policy, the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the euro remained surprisingly stable. The fear of an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc, which was often expressed in the run-up to the changeover to the euro, did not come true. However, immediately after the European Union's decision in May 1998 to introduce the euro on time, a relatively smooth transition to the new monetary regime could be expected. European monetary integration had gained considerable credibility. All the countries that adopted the euro met the convergence criteria of the Maastricht Treaty, with the exception of a few embellishments of fiscal data. Furthermore, there was little doubt that the European Central Bank would conduct a consistent monetary policy aimed at maintaining price stability. This was guaranteed both by the institutionally anchored, high degree of independence of the future common monetary authority and the quality of its newly elected leaders. After the introduction of the euro, the SNB also helped to keep the Swiss franc exchange rate stable against the new common currency for a while. In the spring of 1999, when the Swiss economy was still suffering from the consequences of the Asian crisis, it preceded an imminent appreciation of the Swiss franc with a further easing of monetary policy. In the meantime, however, as I have already said, the economic situation in Switzerland has changed fundamentally. That is why the SNB is no longer endeavouring to prevent our currency from appreciating on the foreign exchange market. However, the Swiss franc exchange rate of the euro remained stable despite the change in monetary policy. How can this stability be explained? I do not want to claim that I can answer this question convincingly. The stability of the euro/franc relationship poses as many mysteries as the recent weakness of the euro against the American dollar. One possible explanation lies in the expectations of market participants. Obviously, many assume that although Switzerland is not part of the European Union, it is de facto part of the euro area. They believe that the SNB is in the same environment as the European Central Bank and must therefore nolens volens steer the same monetary policy stance as its sister institution in Frankfurt. Under these circumstances, there was no need for major changes in the euro/franc ratio. Is it right to regard the National Bank as an appendage of the European Central Bank? I would like to address this question below and compare both the monetary policy concepts and the economic environment of the two central banks. 3. Swiss and European monetary policy: a comparison 3.1 Monetary policy strategy The monetary policy strategies of the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank have many similarities, but also some differences. Both central banks regard price stability, which they equate to an inflation rate below 2%, as the main objective of monetary policy. However, they do not set an actual inflation target. Neither the European Central Bank nor the SNB undertake to keep inflation within a pre-announced and precisely defined corridor. Rather, their intention is to maintain the inflation trend in what they equate with price stability. In doing so, they allow the possibility that the 6 Inflation temporarily deviates from the stable range. Such deviations can occur, for example, as a result of sharp changes in the price of oil or exchange rates. As long as they are only temporary, they do not cause significant economic damage and do not require a monetary policy response. However, both the European Central Bank and the SNB are prepared to react to developments that could permanently jeopardise price stability by adjusting monetary policy. Both central banks also take a similar approach when setting the monetary policy stance they deem necessary to maintain price stability. They rely primarily on inflation forecasts to assess the appropriateness of their monetary policy. In doing so, they take into account the now generally accepted fact that central banks must act with foresight. However, there are also some differences in the conceptual area. While both central banks stress the importance of the money supply for the development of inflation, they explain this fact to the public in different ways. The European Central Bank explains its monetary policy on the basis of the two-pillar strategy it has developed: when setting its course, it bases both inflation forecasts and the growth of the M3 money supply in relation to a reference value it has announced in advance. The two-pillar principle, however, raises problems of interpretation. If the two pillars send out contradictory monetary policy signals, the question arises as to the weighting of the different information. The European Central Bank has not yet answered this question. Nor does it publish comprehensive inflation forecasts that would allow the public itself to assess the relative importance of the two pillars. It justifies this approach with the convincing argument that, as a new institution, it can only consider publishing comprehensive forecasts once it has gained sufficient experience with its forecasting activities. For the SNB, there are no mitigating circumstances that would allow it to refrain from publishing inflation forecasts. At the end of 1999, it therefore published a forecast of inflation over the following three years as part of the adjustment of its monetary policy approach. With its broad forecast horizon, the SNB takes account of the fact that the transfer of monetary policy impulses to the price level in Switzerland takes around three years. In contrast to the European Central Bank, the SNB also dispensed with a two-pillar strategy. Rather, it made it clear that it bases its monetary policy decisions exclusively on its inflation forecasts. As I have already said, it tracks monetary policy indicators such as the M3 money supply, economic developments and the exchange rate, which play a central role in forecasting inflation. The money supply M3 does not rest on a separate pillar as with the European Central Bank, but is an important building block in the inflation forecast. From an operational point of view, there are also differences between the European Central Bank and the National Bank. Both monetary institutions control inflation through interest rates on the money market. They set them at the level that they consider to ensure price stability in the longer term. The European Central Bank fixes the interest rate for the repo transactions it concludes with the banks, while the SNB announces a target corridor for the three-month Libor rate. 7 In this comparison, we should not forget that most central banks, both inside and outside Europe, today pursue similar monetary policy objectives and strategies. Therefore, the similarities between the European Central Bank and the National Bank itself are not surprising. Where differences occur, they lie less in the substance of monetary policy concepts than in the methods by which central banks communicate and explain their monetary policy decisions to the public. With regard to the communication of monetary policy decisions, the European Central Bank currently seems to be facing stronger criticism than the National Bank. In the case of the European Central Bank, the two-pillar concept in particular is causing controversy. Critical questions are also addressed to the SNB. But these questions concern all central banks that rely on inflation forecasts. The public rightly demands that the considerations on which inflation forecasts are based should be presented transparently, a wish that cannot be fulfilled by simple means. The often raised accusation that the European Central Bank behaves in a non-transparent manner is, in my opinion, exaggerated. Although the two-pillar strategy raises questions, the European Central Bank is prepared to provide comprehensive information on its monetary policy decisions. What bothers me anyway about the critical discussion about the transparency of the European Central Bank is that it is moving in the wrong direction. For example, there is a dispute as to whether the European Central Bank should publish the minutes and voting results of its decision-making bodies. The discussion revolves around the instruments with which transparency is to be created. Debates on instruments, however, are pointless unless it is made clear what transparency is intended to achieve. In my view, transparency should encourage central banks to disclose their monetary policy objectives and strategies. In doing so, one can argue in good faith about which instruments are best suited to creating transparency. No central bank has yet invented a patent method. 3.2 Monetary policy environment Although the European Central Bank and the SNB pursue similar monetary policy objectives and strategies, this need not mean that they always follow the same course. The correct dosage of monetary policy depends crucially on the economic environment in which the central bank is embedded. If, for example, Switzerland's economic conditions differ from those of the euro area, it would not be appropriate for the SNB to steer the same monetary policy stance as the European Central Bank, even if it pursues similar objectives and strategies as its sister institution in Frankfurt. As Switzerland is closely intertwined economically with the euro area, the SNB is likely to pursue a similar monetary policy to that of the European Central Bank. Even before the introduction of the euro, the similarity of the economic environment meant that there was often a great deal of agreement between the monetary policy of the SNB and the Deutsche Bundesbank. This repeatedly leads analysts to claim that the SNB does not in fact pursue an autonomous monetary policy, but leans closely on the European Central Bank or the Bundesbank. Switzerland would lose little if it completely gave up its monetary policy autonomy by permanently fixing the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the euro. After being linked to the euro, the SNB would hardly control a significantly different exchange rate than under an autonomous approach. The peg to the euro would also lead to a greater 8 Exchange rate stability, which would facilitate the planning of export and import companies. What is to be made of this claim? Although the SNB is likely to often steer a similar course to that of the European Central Bank, the importance of our monetary policy autonomy should not be downplayed. If Switzerland were to fix the Swiss franc exchange rate against the euro, this would have two important consequences for our economy: On the one hand, Swiss money market interest rates would be fully aligned with those of the euro area. From now on, they would no longer be determined by the National Bank, but exclusively by the European Central Bank. It must be guided by the overall interests of the euro area when defining monetary policy and could therefore not take Switzerland's specific needs into account. On the other hand, after the connection, Swiss capital market and mortgage interest rates, which are low compared to other countries, would rise permanently and approach the usual level in the euro area. Swiss companies, households and public bodies would thus have to accept a permanent increase in their debt interest rates. Even though there is often a great deal of agreement between Swiss and European monetary policy, the SNB should not forego the possibility of autonomously changing domestic money market interest rates. From time to time, it could feel compelled to steer a course that deviates from the European Central Bank. This has already been the case in the past with regard to the Deutsche Bundesbank. In the second half of the nineties, for example, the SNB conducted a more expansionary monetary policy than the Bundesbank and later the European Central Bank. It reacted to the fact that the recession in Switzerland left deeper traces than in our neighbouring countries, thus creating a real risk of deflation. The comparatively deep economic slump in Switzerland is not only explained by the exchange rate turbulence of 1994 and 1995. It also arose from the structural upheavals in the economy that began earlier in Switzerland than in our neighbouring countries. Thanks to its ability to change domestic money market interest rates autonomously, the SNB has been able to take account of specific economic developments in Switzerland. Conversely, in the recent past it has been able to tighten monetary policy more than the European Central Bank. It thus took into account the stronger than expected economic recovery in Switzerland. The comparatively low level of interest rates gives Switzerland a competitive advantage that it should not give up lightly. However, analysts repeatedly predict the demise of the interest rate island of Switzerland. They claim that swiss interest rates will sooner or later adapt to those in the euro area, regardless of whether the SNB maintains its monetary policy autonomy. Despite such forecasts, however, there is little sign of a levelling of interest rate differentials between Switzerland and the euro area. The gap with the euro area has narrowed somewhat since the transition to the single currency. However, this development mainly reflects temporary influences on the Swiss interest rate level. As I have already said, the SNB has tightened monetary policy more than the European Central Bank in recent months. It is therefore not surprising that the interest rate differential with the euro area narrowed. There are therefore no signs that the interest island will disappear. Rather, investors still see the Swiss franc as an attractive alternative to the euro and other major currencies. Of course, they will only use the franc for diversification purposes as long as they consider it a currency in its own right. The franc would be its independence 9 if the authorities permanently fixed its exchange rate against the euro. With a fixed exchange rate, the Franc and the Euro would be transformed into virtually identical currencies. In order for the Swiss franc to retain its autonomy, its exchange rate against the euro must be able to fluctuate freely. However, the independence of the Swiss franc does not presuppose a high variability of the exchange rate. Some analysts are of the opinion that the stability of the euro/franc ratio observed since the beginning of 1999 will make the interest rate island of Switzerland disappear over time. The more stable the exchange rate, the lower the probability that investors will still see the Swiss franc as a currency in its own right. However, the independence of the Swiss franc will only be called into question if the SNB deliberately strives for a stable exchange rate. If, on the other hand, market forces are primarily responsible for stability, the interest rate island of Switzerland does not need to disappear. With exchange rates that are generally flexible, investors must always expect the euro/franc ratio to adjust, even if it has remained stable over a longer period of time. Longer periods of stable exchange rates have already occurred in the past without heralding the end of the interest island of Switzerland. Chart 1 shows that the Swiss franc's exchange rate against the Deutschmark moved only slightly from 1983 to 1987, despite a massive temporary appreciation of the dollar. Furthermore, from 1985 to 1987, Swiss money market interest rates were roughly at the German level (Chart 2). Nevertheless, the interest rate differential with Germany, which tended to be 2-3 percentage points in the long-term range in the eighties, was maintained. Even then, numerous analysts claimed that the SNB was pursuing an exchange rate target. This was not true. Rather, the stable price development was due to market forces. These considerations indicate that the interest island of Switzerland is not yet doomed. 4. Conclusion With the introduction of the new single currency, the monetary policy framework in the euro area changed fundamentally. The national central banks, which had hitherto been responsible for conducting monetary policy, transferred their powers to a new monetary authority. The European Central Bank, which is responsible for issuing the euro, has been pursuing a single monetary policy for the euro area since the beginning of 1999. Although the European integration process took a major step forward with the transition to the euro, the impact on the Swiss economy was less than expected. The often expressed fear that the Swiss franc would start to soar after the introduction of the euro did not come true. The framework conditions for Swiss monetary policy also remained largely unchanged. As long as Switzerland is not part of the European Union, it would be well advised to stick to its autonomous monetary policy and refrain from pegging the swiss franc to the euro. Sie behaupten, die Europische Zentralbank setze damit ihre Glaubwrdigkeit aufs Spiel und trage zur Schwcheneigung des Euro bei. Konsequenzen fr die schweizerische Wirtschaft Vor dem bergang zur neuen gemeinsamen Whrung war in der Schweiz die Befrchtung weit verbreitet, die Einfhrung des Euro werde Turbulenzen an den Devisenmrkten auslsen. Viele Beobachter rechneten mit einer starken Aufwertung des Schweizer Frankens gegenber der neuen gemeinsamen Whrung, welche die internationale Wettbewerbsfhigkeit der inlndischen Industrie untergraben knnte. Diese Befrchtungen wurden durch die Ereignisse von 1994 und 1995 genhrt, als sich der Schweizer Franken gegenber wichtigen Whrungen deutlich aufwertete (Grafik 1). Viele Anleger sahen sich deshalb veranlasst, einen Teil ihrer Vermgen in Schweizer Franken und andere stabile Whrungen, die nicht im Euro aufgehen wrden, umzuwandeln. Die Nationalbank reagierte auf diese Flucht in den Schweizer Franken mit einer Lockerung der Geldpolitik im Frhjahr 1995. In der Folge entspannte sie ihre Zgel weiter und fhrte vor allem in den Jahren 1997 und 1998 einen sehr expansiven Kurs. Aus diesem Grunde fiel der Dreimonatssatz am schweizerischen Geldmarkt von etwa 4% Ende 1994 auf tendenziell 2% Ende 1995 und auf deutlich unter 2% im Laufe des Jahres 1997. Seit dem Sptsommer 1999 ist er wieder im Steigen begriffen, aus Grnden, auf die ich noch zurckkommen werde (Grafik 2). Die Lockerung der Geldpolitik wirkte sich mit der Zeit auf den Wechselkurs und die Konjunkturentwicklung aus. Der Hhenflug des Frankens kam Ende 1995 zum Stillstand und machte wieder einer Tieferbewertung Platz. Die schweizerische Konjunktur begann sich Anfang 1997 zu beleben. Der anfnglich krftige Aufschwung kam zwar in der zweiten Hlfte 1998 als Folge der Asienkrise vorbergehend ins Stocken, seit einigen Monaten 4 mehren sich aber die Zeichen, dass die schweizerische Wirtschaft in eine eigentliche Boomphase eingetreten ist. Manche Beobachter betrachteten die Lockerung der schweizerischen Geldpolitik als einen eigentlichen Paradigmawechsel der Nationalbank. Sie vertraten die Meinung, die Nationalbank richte ihre Politik, im Hinblick auf die Einfhrung des Euro, vermehrt auf die Stabilisierung des Wechselkurses aus. Hufig wurde auch behauptet, die Nationalbank werde nach der Einfhrung des Euro keine andere Wahl haben, als sich geldpolitisch eng an die Europische Zentralbank anzulehnen. Diese Auffassungen erhielten Nahrung durch Aussagen wichtiger Exponenten der Nationalbank, das schweizerische Noteninstitut werde alle Hebel in Bewegung setzen, um eine unerwnschte Aufwertung des Schweizer Frankens zu unterbinden. Dabei wurde hufig bersehen, dass die Nationalbank die Wechselkursstabilitt nicht als Selbstzweck betrachtet. Die Notwendigkeit, der Aufwertungstendenz des Frankens entgegenzutreten, ergab sich vielmehr aus dem Auftrag der Nationalbank, die Preisstabilitt zu gewhrleisten. Damals lastete ein eigentlicher Deflationsdruck auf der schweizerischen Wirtschaft, dem die Nationalbank entschieden entgegentreten musste. Denn wie wir immer wieder betonen, bedeutet die Gewhrleistung von Preisstabilitt Verhinderung von Inflation und Deflation. In den letzten Monaten hat sich indessen die Verfassung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft dramatisch gewandelt. Der Deflationsdruck ist nicht nur gewichen, sondern der krftige Konjunkturaufschwung lsst wieder Inflationsngste aufkeimen. Die gegenwrtige Strkeneigung des Dollar trgt ebenfalls zur Belebung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft bei. Unter diesen Umstnden ist eine Geldpolitik, die auf die Verhinderung einer Frankenaufwertung abzielt, nicht mehr angebracht. Eine solche Politik wrde im heutigen wirtschaftlichen Umfeld unweigerlich einen Inflationsanstieg auslsen. Somit spielt die Wechselkursstabilitt fr die schweizerische Geldpolitik nicht mehr die gleiche Rolle wie in der zweiten Hlfte der Neunzigerjahre, als unsere Wirtschaft unter einem Deflationsdruck stand. Wir verfolgen auch nicht ein Wechselkursziel. Uns geht es vielmehr darum zu verhindern, dass der gegenwrtige Konjunkturaufschwung in einen markanten Teuerungsanstieg ausmndet. Die Nationalbank hat ihre Absichten im Rahmen einer Anpassung ihres geldpolitischen Konzepts Ende 1999 klar zum Ausdruck gebracht. Sie richtet ihre Geldpolitik nach wie vor auf die Gewhrleistung der Preisstabilitt aus, die sie mit einer Teuerung von unter 2% gleichsetzt. Dabei ist sie bestrebt, sowohl einen Anstieg der Teuerung auf ber 2% als auch einen Rckgang des Preisniveaus zu vermeiden. Um das Ziel der Preisstabilitt zu erreichen, stellt sie regelmssig Inflationsprognosen auf. Deuten die Prognosen darauf hin, dass die Inflation den Bereich der Preisstabilitt zu verlassen droht, passt sie die Geldpolitik entsprechend an. Sie kleidet ihre geldpolitischen Entscheide in die Form eines Zinsbandes fr den dreimonatigen Liborsatz am Geldmarkt fr Schweizer Franken. Dieses Band ist fr ihre Operationen am Geldmarkt massgebend. Die Nationalbank verfolgt ferner eine Reihe von Indikatoren, die erfahrungsgemss die knftige Preisentwicklung beeinflussen und damit in ihre Inflationsprognosen einfliessen. In der krzeren Frist hngt die Preisentwicklung vor allem von der Konjunkturlage und von den Wechselkursbewegungen ab. Gegenwrtig bt auch der sprunghafte Anstieg des Erdlpreises eine inflationstreibende Wirkung aus. Lngerfristig wird die Preisentwicklung massgeblich durch das Wachstum der Geldaggregate, insbesondere der Geldmenge M3, bestimmt. So reagierte die Nationalbank auf die markante Erholung der schweizerischen 5 Konjunktur seit dem zweiten Halbjahr 1999, in dem sie ihre Geldpolitik in mehreren Schritten straffte. Als Folge davon stieg der Liborsatz fr Schweizer Franken wieder gegen 3%. Trotz der Verschrfung der schweizerischen Geldpolitik blieb der Wechselkurs des Schweizer Frankens gegenber dem Euro erstaunlich stabil. Die im Vorfeld des bergangs zum Euro hufig geusserte Befrchtung einer bermssigen Frankenaufwertung wurde nicht wahr. Allerdings konnte schon unmittelbar nach dem Entscheid der Europischen Union im Mai 1998, den Euro termingerecht einzufhren, mit einem verhltnismssig reibungslosen bergang zum neuen Whrungsregime gerechnet werden. Die europische Whrungsintegration hatte nmlich betrchtlich an Glaubwrdigkeit gewonnen. Alle Lnder, die den Euro bernahmen, erfllten  abgesehen von einigen Schnungen der Fiskaldaten  die Konvergenzkriterien des Unionsvertrags von Maastricht. Ferner bestand kaum ein Zweifel, dass die Europische Zentralbank eine konsequente, auf die Gewhrleistung der Preisstabilitt ausgerichtete Geldpolitik fhren wrde. Dafr brgten sowohl der institutionell verankerte, hohe Grad an Unabhngigkeit der knftigen gemeinsamen Whrungsbehrde als auch die Qualitt ihrer neu gewhlten leitenden Persnlichkeiten. Nach der Einfhrung des Euro trug die Nationalbank fr eine Weile ebenfalls dazu bei, den Frankenkurs gegenber der neuen gemeinsamen Whrung stabil zu halten. Sie kam im Frhjahr 1999  als die schweizerische Wirtschaft immer noch unter den Folgen der Asienkrise litt  einer drohenden Frankenaufwertung mit einer weiteren Lockerung der Geldpolitik zuvor. In der Zwischenzeit hat sich die wirtschaftliche Lage in der Schweiz indessen  wie ich schon ausfhrte  grundlegend gewandelt. Deshalb ist die Nationalbank nicht mehr bestrebt, eine Aufwertung unserer Whrung am Devisenmarkt zu unterbinden. Der Frankenkurs des Euro blieb aber trotz der geldpolitischen Kursnderung weiterhin stabil. Wie erklrt sich diese Stabilitt? Ich mchte nicht behaupten, dass ich diese Frage berzeugend beantworten kann. Denn die Stabilitt der Euro/Franken-Relation gibt ebenso viele Rtsel auf wie die jngste Schwche des Euro gegenber dem amerikanischen Dollar. Eine mgliche Erklrung liegt in den Erwartungen der Marktteilnehmer. Offensichtlich gehen viele davon aus, dass die Schweiz zwar nicht zur Europischen Union gehrt, aber de facto einen Bestandteil des Eurogebiets bildet. Sie glauben, die Nationalbank befinde sich im gleichen Umfeld wie die Europische Zentralbank und msse deshalb nolens volens den selben geldpolitischen Kurs steuern wie ihr Schwesterinstitut in Frankfurt. Unter diesen Umstnden erbrigten sich grssere nderungen der Euro/Franken-Relation. Ist es richtig, die Nationalbank als Anhngsel der Europischen Zentralbank zu betrachten? Ich mchte im Folgenden auf diese Frage eingehen und sowohl die geldpolitischen Konzepte als auch die wirtschaftlichen Rahmenbedingungen der beiden Zentralbanken vergleichen. 3. Schweizerische und europische Geldpolitik: ein Vergleich 3.1 Geldpolitische Strategie Die geldpolitischen Strategien der Europischen Zentralbank und der Schweizerischen Nationalbank weisen viele hnlichkeiten, aber auch einige Unterschiede auf. Beide Zentralbanken betrachten Preisstabilitt, die sie einer Inflationsrate von unter 2% gleichsetzen, als das Hauptziel der Geldpolitik. Sie legen allerdings nicht ein eigentliches Inflationsziel fest. Weder die Europische Zentralbank noch die Nationalbank gehen eine Verpflichtung ein, die Inflation innerhalb eines zum Voraus angekndigten und przise definierten Korridors zu halten. Ihre Absicht besteht vielmehr darin, den Inflationstrend in jenem Bereich zu halten, den sie mit Preisstabilitt gleichsetzen. Dabei lassen sie die Mglichkeit zu, dass die 6 Inflation zeitweise vom stabilen Bereich abweicht. Solche Abweichungen knnen beispielsweise als Folge von starken Vernderungen des Erdlpreises oder der Wechselkurse auftreten. Solange sie nur vorbergehender Natur sind, verursachen sie keine nennenswerten volkswirtschaftlichen Schden und erfordern auch keine geldpolitische Reaktion. Sowohl die Europische Zentralbank als auch die Nationalbank sind aber bereit, auf Entwicklungen, welche die Preisstabilitt anhaltend gefhrden knnten, mit einer Anpassung der Geldpolitik zu reagieren. Beide Zentralbanken gehen auch hnlich vor, wenn sie den geldpolitischen Kurs festlegen, den sie fr die Gewhrleistung der Preisstabilitt als notwendig erachten. Sie sttzen sich vor allem auf Inflationsprognosen, um die Zweckmssigkeit ihrer Geldpolitik zu beurteilen. Damit bercksichtigen sie die heute allgemein akzeptierte Tatsache, dass die Zentralbanken vorausschauend handeln mssen. Allerdings bestehen im konzeptuellen Bereich auch einige Unterschiede. Whrend beide Zentralbanken die Bedeutung der Geldmenge fr die Inflationsentwicklung betonen, erklren sie diesen Tatbestand der ffentlichkeit auf unterschiedliche Weise. Die Europische Zentralbank erlutert ihre Geldpolitik anhand der von ihr entwickelten Zwei-Sulen-Strategie: Bei der Festlegung ihres Kurses stellt sie sowohl auf Inflationsprognosen als auch auf das Wachstum der Geldmenge M3 im Verhltnis zu einem von ihr zum Voraus angekndigten Referenzwert ab. Das Zwei-Sulen-Prinzip wirft indessen Interpretationsprobleme auf. Senden die beiden Sulen widersprchliche geldpolitische Signale aus, stellt sich die Frage nach der Gewichtung der unterschiedlichen Informationen. Die Europische Zentralbank hat diese Frage bisher nicht beantwortet. Sie publiziert auch keine umfassenden Inflationsprognosen, die der ffentlichkeit selber gestatten wrden, die relative Bedeutung der beiden Sulen zu beurteilen. Sie rechtfertigt dieses Vorgehen mit dem an sich berzeugenden Argument, dass sie als neue Institution eine Publikation umfassender Voraussagen erst dann in Betracht ziehen kann, wenn sie mit ihrer Prognosettigkeit ausreichende Erfahrungen gesammelt hat. Fr die Nationalbank existieren keine mildernden Umstnde, die ihr erlauben wrden, auf die Publikation von Inflationsprognosen zu verzichten. Sie verffentlichte deshalb  im Zuge der Anpassung ihres geldpolitischen Konzepts  Ende 1999 eine Voraussage der Inflationsentwicklung ber die folgenden drei Jahre. Mit dem weit gesteckten Prognosehorizont trgt die Nationalbank der Tatsache Rechnung, dass die bertragung geldpolitischer Impulse auf das Preisniveau in der Schweiz ungefhr drei Jahre dauert. Im Unterschied zur Europischen Zentralbank verzichtete die Nationalbank ferner auf eine Zwei-Sulen-Strategie. Sie stellte vielmehr klar, dass sie ihre geldpolitischen Entscheide ausschliesslich auf ihre Inflationsprognosen absttzt. Wie ich schon ausfhrte, verfolgt sie dabei geldpolitische Indikatoren wie die Geldmenge M3, die Konjunkturentwicklung und den Wechselkurs, die fr die Inflationsprognose eine zentrale Rolle spielen. Die Geldmenge M3 ruht nicht wie bei der Europischen Zentralbank auf einer separaten Sule, sondern geht als wichtiger Baustein in die Inflationsprognose ein. In operationaler Hinsicht bestehen zwischen der Europischen Zentralbank und der Nationalbank ebenfalls Unterschiede. Beide Whrungsinstitute steuern die Inflation ber die Zinsstze am Geldmarkt. Sie legen diese auf jenem Niveau fest, das nach ihrer Ansicht die Preisstabilitt lngerfristig gewhrleistet. Die Europische Zentralbank fixiert dabei den Zinssatz fr die Repogeschfte, die sie mit den Banken abschliesst, whrend die Nationalbank einen Zielkorridor fr den Dreimonats-Liborsatz bekannt gibt. 7 Beim diesem Vergleich sollten wir nicht vergessen, dass die meisten Zentralbanken sowohl innerhalb als auch ausserhalb Europas heute hnliche geldpolitische Ziele und Strategien verfolgen. Daher sind die hnlichkeiten zwischen der Europischen Zentralbank und der Nationalbank an sich nicht berraschend. Sofern Unterschiede auftreten, liegen sie weniger in der Substanz der geldpolitischen Konzepte, als in den Methoden, mit denen die Zentralbanken ihre geldpolitischen Entscheide der ffentlichkeit mitteilen und erklren. In Bezug auf die Kommunikation geldpolitischer Entscheide scheint die Europische Zentralbank gegenwrtig auf strkere Kritik zu stossen als die Nationalbank. Im Falle der Europischen Zentralbank lst vor allem das Zwei-Sulen-Konzept Kontroversen aus. An die Nationalbank werden zwar ebenfalls kritische Fragen gerichtet. Aber diese Fragen beschftigen alle Zentralbanken, die sich auf Inflationsprognosen sttzen. Die ffentlichkeit fordert zurecht, dass die berlegungen, auf denen die Inflationsprognosen beruhen, transparent dargestellt werden sollten, ein Wunsch, der indessen nicht mit einfachen Mitteln zu erfllen ist. Der oft erhobene Vorwurf, die Europische Zentralbank verhalte sich intransparent, ist nach meiner Meinung berrissen. Obwohl die Zwei-Sulen-Strategie zu Fragen Anlass gibt, ist die Europische Zentralbank bereit, ber ihre geldpolitischen Beschlsse umfassend Auskunft zu geben. An der kritischen Diskussion ber die Transparenz der Europischen Zentralbank strt mich ohnehin, dass sie sich auf falschen Bahnen bewegt. So wird darber gestritten, ob die Europische Zentralbank die Protokolle und Abstimmungsresultate ihrer Entscheidungsgremien publizieren sollte. Dabei dreht sich die Diskussion um die Instrumente, mit denen Transparenz geschaffen werden soll. Debatten ber Instrumente sind indessen sinnlos, wenn nicht klar gestellt wird, was mit der Transparenz erreicht werden soll. Nach meiner Auffassung sollte die Transparenz die Zentralbanken dazu veranlassen, ihre geldpolitischen Ziele und Strategien offen zu legen. Dabei kann man sich in guten Treuen darber streiten, welche Instrumente zur Schaffung von Transparenz am besten geeignet sind. Noch keine Zentralbank hat eine Patentmethode erfunden. 3.2 Geldpolitisches Umfeld Obwohl die Europische Zentralbank und die Nationalbank hnliche geldpolitische Ziele und Strategien verfolgen, braucht dies nicht zu bedeuten, dass sie stets den gleichen Kurs steuern. Denn die richtige Dosierung der Geldpolitik hngt entscheidend vom wirtschaftlichen Umfeld ab, in das die Zentralbank eingebettet ist. Unterscheiden sich beispielsweise die konjunkturellen Verhltnisse der Schweiz von jenen des Eurogebiets, wre es fr die Nationalbank nicht zweckmssig, den gleichen geldpolitischen Kurs wie die Europische Zentralbank zu steuern, selbst wenn sie hnliche Ziele und Strategien wie ihr Schwesterinstitut in Frankfurt verfolgt. Da die Schweiz wirtschaftlich eng mit dem Eurogebiet verflochten ist, drfte die Nationalbank hufig eine hnliche Geldpolitik verfolgen wie die Europische Zentralbank. Die hnlichkeit des wirtschaftlichen Umfelds hatte schon vor der Einfhrung des Euro zur Folge, dass zwischen der Geldpolitik der Nationalbank und der Deutschen Bundesbank oft eine grosse bereinstimmung bestand. Dies verleitet Analysten immer wieder zur Behauptung, die Nationalbank betreibe in Wirklichkeit keine autonome Geldpolitik, sondern lehne sich eng an die Europische Zentralbank bzw. die Bundesbank an. Die Schweiz verlre wenig, wenn sie ihre geldpolitische Autonomie gnzlich aufgbe, indem sie den Wechselkurs des Frankens gegenber dem Euro dauerhaft fixierte. Die Nationalbank wrde nach der Anbindung an den Euro kaum einen wesentlich anderen Kurs als unter einem autonomen Vorgehen steuern. Die Anbindung an den Euro wrde ferner zu einer grsseren 8 Wechselkursstabilitt fhren, welche die Planung der im Export und Import ttigen Unternehmen erleichtern wrde. Was ist von dieser Behauptung zu halten? Obwohl die Nationalbank wahrscheinlich hufig einen hnlichen Kurs wie die Europische Zentralbank steuern wird, sollte die Bedeutung unserer geldpolitischen Autonomie nicht heruntergespielt werden. Fixierte die Schweiz den Frankenkurs gegenber dem Euro, ergben sich daraus zwei wichtige Konsequenzen fr unsere Wirtschaft: Zum einen wrden sich die schweizerischen Geldmarktzinsen vollstndig an jene des Eurogebiets angleichen. Sie wrden fortan nicht mehr von der Nationalbank, sondern ausschliesslich von der Europischen Zentralbank bestimmt. Diese muss sich bei der Festlegung der Geldpolitik von den Gesamtinteressen des Eurogebiets leiten lassen und knnte deshalb nicht auf die spezifischen Bedrfnisse der Schweiz Rcksicht nehmen. Zum anderen wrden nach der Anbindung die im Vergleich zum Ausland tiefen schweizerischen Kapitalmarkt- und Hypothekarzinsen dauerhaft ansteigen und sich dem im Eurogebiet gngigen Niveau annhern. Die schweizerischen Unternehmen, Haushalte und ffentlichen Krperschaften mssten damit einen permanenten Anstieg ihrer Schuldzinsen hinnehmen. Auch wenn zwischen schweizerischer und europischer Geldpolitik hufig eine grosse bereinstimmung bestehen drfte, sollte die Nationalbank auf die Mglichkeit, die inlndischen Geldmarktzinsen autonom zu verndern, nicht verzichten. Denn sie knnte sich von Zeit zu Zeit veranlasst sehen, einen von der Europischen Zentralbank abweichenden Kurs zu steuern. Dies war schon in der Vergangenheit in Bezug auf die Deutsche Bundesbank der Fall. So fhrte die Nationalbank in der zweiten Hlfte der Neunzigerjahre eine expansivere Geldpolitik als die Bundesbank und spter die Europische Zentralbank. Sie reagierte auf die Tatsache, dass die Rezession in der Schweiz tiefere Spuren als in unseren Nachbarlndern hinterliess und damit eine eigentliche Deflationsgefahr heraufbeschwor. Der vergleichsweise tiefe wirtschaftliche Einbruch in der Schweiz erklrt sich nicht nur aus den Wechselkursturbulenzen von 1994 und 1995. Er entsprang auch den strukturellen Umwlzungen in der Wirtschaft, die in der Schweiz frher einsetzten als in unseren Nachbarlndern. Dank ihrer Fhigkeit, die inlndischen Geldmarktzinsen autonom zu verndern, konnte die Nationalbank auf die spezifischen wirtschaftlichen Entwicklungen in der Schweiz Rcksicht nehmen. Umgekehrt war sie in der jngsten Vergangenheit in der Lage, die Geldpolitik strker als die Europische Zentralbank zu straffen. Sie trug damit der ber Erwarten krftigen Konjunkturerholung in der Schweiz Rechnung. Das vergleichsweise niedrige Zinsniveau verschafft der Schweiz einen Wettbewerbsvorteil, auf den sie nicht leichtfertig verzichten sollte. Allerdings sagen Analysten immer wieder den Untergang der Zinsinsel Schweiz voraus. Sie behaupten, das schweizerische Zinsniveau werde sich frher oder spter an jenes im Eurogebiet anpassen und zwar unabhngig davon, ob die Nationalbank an ihrer geldpolitischen Autonomie festhalte. Von einer Nivellierung der Zinsunterschiede zwischen der Schweiz und dem Eurogebiet ist trotz solcher Voraussagen indessen wenig zu verspren. Der Abstand zum Eurogebiet hat sich zwar seit dem bergang zur gemeinsamen Whrung etwas verringert. Diese Entwicklung widerspiegelt aber vor allem temporre Einflsse auf das schweizerische Zinsniveau. Wie ich schon ausfhrte, straffte die Nationalbank die Geldpolitik in den letzten Monaten strker als die Europische Zentralbank. Deshalb ist es nicht erstaunlich, dass sich der Zinsabstand zum Eurogebiet verengte. Es bestehen somit keine Anzeichen, dass die Zinsinsel verschwinden wird. Vielmehr betrachten die Anleger den Schweizer Franken nach wie vor als attraktive Alternative zum Euro und anderen wichtigen Whrungen. Natrlich werden sie den Franken nur solange fr Diversifikationszwecke verwenden, als sie ihn fr eine eigenstndige Whrung halten. Der Franken wrde seine Eigenstndigkeit 9 verlieren, wenn die Behrden seinen Kurs gegenber dem Euro dauerhaft fixierten. Mit einem fixen Wechselkurs wrden der Franken und der Euro in faktisch identische Whrungen verwandelt. Damit der Franken seine Eigenstndigkeit bewahren kann, muss sein Wechselkurs gegenber dem Euro frei schwanken knnen. Die Eigenstndigkeit des Frankens setzt aber nicht eine hohe Variabilitt des Wechselkurses voraus. Manche Analysten vertreten die Meinung, die seit Anfang 1999 beobachtete Stabilitt der Euro/Franken-Relation werde die Zinsinsel Schweiz mit der Zeit zum Verschwinden bringen. Je stabiler sich der Wechselkurs verhalte, umso geringer sei die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass die Anleger den Franken noch als eigenstndige Whrung anschauten. Die Eigenstndigkeit des Frankens wird indessen nur in Frage gestellt, wenn die Nationalbank bewusst einen stabilen Wechselkurs anstrebt. Sind dagegen die Marktkrfte vornehmlich fr die Stabilitt verantwortlich, braucht die Zinsinsel Schweiz nicht zu verschwinden. Denn bei grundstzlich flexiblen Wechselkursen mssen die Anleger stets mit einer Anpassung der Euro/Franken-Relation rechnen, selbst wenn sich diese ber lngere Zeit hinweg stabil verhalten hat. Lngere Phasen stabiler Wechselkurse traten schon in der Vergangenheit auf, ohne dass das Ende der Zinsinsel Schweiz eingelutet wurde. Aus der Grafik 1 ist ersichtlich, dass sich der Kurs des Frankens gegenber der D-Mark von 1983 bis 1987  trotz einer massiven temporren Aufwertung des Dollars  nur geringfgig bewegte. Ferner befanden sich die schweizerischen Geldmarktzinsen von 1985 bis 1987 ungefhr auf dem deutschen Niveau (Grafik 2). Dennoch blieb der Zinsabstand zu Deutschland, der im langfristigen Bereich in den Achtzigerjahren tendenziell 2-3 Prozentpunkte betrug, erhalten. Schon damals behaupteten zahlreiche Analysten, die Nationalbank verfolge ein Wechselkursziel. Dies entsprach nicht den Tatsachen. Der stabile Kursverlauf war vielmehr den Marktkrften zu verdanken. Diese berlegungen deuten darauf hin, dass die Zinsinsel Schweiz noch nicht dem Untergang geweiht ist. 4. Schlussbemerkung Mit der Einfhrung der neuen gemeinsamen Whrung nderten sich die geldpolitischen Rahmenbedingungen im Eurogebiet grundlegend. Die nationalen Noteninstitute, die bis anhin fr die Fhrung der Geldpolitik zustndig gewesen waren, bertrugen ihre Kompetenzen an eine neue Whrungsbehrde. Die Europische Zentralbank, welche die Verantwortung fr die Ausgabe des Euro trgt, betreibt seit Anfang 1999 eine fr das gesamte Eurogebiet einheitliche Geldpolitik. Obwohl der europische Integrationsprozess mit dem bergang zum Euro einen grossen Schritt vorwrts machte, waren die Auswirkungen auf die schweizerische Wirtschaft geringer als erwartet. Die oft geusserte Befrchtung, der Schweizer Franken werde nach der Einfhrung des Euro zu einem fr unsere Wirtschaft schdlichen Hhenflug ansetzen, bewahrheitete sich nicht. Auch die Rahmenbedingungen fr die schweizerische Geldpolitik blieben weitgehend unverndert. Solange die Schweiz nicht zur Europischen Union gehrt, ist sie gut beraten, an ihrer autonomen Geldpolitik festzuhalten und von einer Anbindung des Frankens an den Euro abzusehen. Title: The policy of the Swiss National Bank in the new international environment
text: The SNB's policy in the new environment international monetary Presentation by Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-President of the Swiss National Bank University of Fribourg Seminar in International Economics 11 April 2000 2 Globalization, trade liberalization and deregulation are key words that characterize the atmosphere in which economic policy is currently articulated. These terms have traditionally applied to trade in goods, increasingly to trade in services, but it is mainly in the capital markets that they have taken on a symbolic appearance. Capital now flows freely between the main financial centres and most countries have dismantled their control systems. In terms of capital exchange, the world economy is now largely integrated. This development has been made possible by the spectacular advances made in the field of electronics. Indeed, modern computers and telecommunications means allow for fast, easy and inexpensive management of an enormous amount of information. The result is optimal arbitrage conditions and increased competition on the capital market. A more efficient allocation of resources is beneficial, over time, to the growth of the world economy. But advances in communication have also strengthened the dissemination of information and the interdependence - technical and psychological - of financial markets. By screens and computers interposed the funds move according to the appreciations of the moment. The danger of a financial "monoculture" with ripple and contagion effects is obvious. We experienced this fragility during the Asian crisis of 1997 and 1998. The uncertainties currently created by the volatility of the stock markets are a second expression of this. In Europe, the phenomena of globalization and deregulation have been reinforced by monetary unification. The substitution of ten national currencies by a single one has given rise to a large and liquid capital market in euro, which has changed the conditions for the functioning of financial markets. Financing conditions have become unified on the common currency market and there has been a rapid development of euro-denominated issues. In addition, the integration of financial markets calls into question traditional banking and stock market structures. We are only at the beginning of a process that should remove national borders and promote the emergence of a pan-European market. At the international level, the appearance of the euro has not overshadowed, for the time being, the predominant role of the US dollar as an investment currency. The greenback remains the vehicle currency par excellence. Since the fall of the Iron Curtain, the American economy has dominated the world economic scene, both in power and technology. For Switzerland, the phenomena of market globalization, to which have now been added the effects of monetary unification in Europe, have inevitably changed the environment in which the SNB operates. We have recently updated the way we conduct monetary policy and we have now accumulated some experience of cohabitation with the euro. Let me take stock of the impact of globalisation and monetary unification on the SNB's activities. What about the objective of our policy in a globalised economy? Is this new environment changing the way money is conducted? 3 1. Monetary policy: objective unchanged... The law assumes that the SNB conducts a monetary policy in the general interest of the country. We believe that this general interest is best served if our action is aimed at maintaining price stability. The globalization of markets has not changed our conviction in this regard. Why this commitment to the objective of price stability? First, inflation is an impediment to long-term economic growth because it prevents the price system from fulfilling its natural function of allocating resources. This results in efficiency losses contrary to the development of the economy. In addition, inflation has undesirable redistributive effects, favouring debtors at the expense of creditors. In combination with a progressive tax system, it gradually increases the tax burden. Finally, inflation has harmful social consequences because it particularly disadvantages those who do not have the means to protect themselves from it. The globalization of the economy does not alter the need to focus central bank action on price stability. Indeed, even in a situation of globalization, inflation stems from a liquidity supply to the economy that is too generous in relation to the possibilities of real growth. As long as Switzerland has not taken the step towards monetary integration, the management of market liquidity remains the responsibility of the SNB. The issue obviously takes a fundamentally different turn in countries  such as eurozone members who have transferred their monetary competences to an external authority, or in countries that have decided to tie their currency to an external standard. Maintaining price stability is understood as a long-term monetary objective. Over the short period of time, other factors can affect the rate of inflation, such as a change in the prices of imported goods or a change in indirect taxation. From a macroeconomic point of view, these are not inflationary pressures but changes in relative prices. Immediate monetary action carries the risk of a deflationary impact over time. Essential in such a case is to prevent a sectoral rise in prices from turning into a lasting phenomenon. With the globalization of markets - and the close interreaction of economic conditions - the ability of central banks to stimulate economic development is even more limited than in the past. Admittedly, expansive monetary policy can temporarily fuel growth and reduce unemployment. After a certain period of time, however, this effect fades with the only lasting result being a higher price level. By focusing on the objective of price stability, the SNB is therefore in no way denying the seriousness of the problem of unemployment; on the other hand, it is not convinced that monetary policy is the right instrument to combat it. Its real contribution to growth is the maintenance of stable monetary conditions so that the economy can make the most of its development opportunities. 4 2. ... but reformed strategy While the final objective of monetary policy remains unchanged, the new financial environment has led the SNB to adapt the conditions for implementing its policy, technically known as its strategy. Let me first briefly describe our old modus operandi and the problems that led us to abandon it. I will then come to the new concept in force since the beginning of this year. Since the end of the seventies, the SNB's action has been aimed at controlling the growth of the M0 money supply (banknotes in circulation and transfer accounts). This strategy was based on the existence of a stable link between the growth of the money supply, that of the real PIK and the price level. Put another way, this approach recognized the existence of a demand for stable money. Under these conditions, the Bank could hope to control inflation over the medium term by pursuing an objective of adequate money supply growth. In practice, we had set ourselves a medium-term growth path of M0 compatible with price stability. The trend growth rate was set at 1%. At the end of the 1980s, we preferred a medium-term growth path to annual targets in order to have more flexibility in the event of external shocks, in particular from the foreign exchange market. Over the years, many difficulties of application have accumulated. First, central money grew at a slower pace than its trend rate, even though our monetary policy was frankly expansive. Then, as early as 1996, MO's growth suddenly accelerated at a time when the domestic economic situation did not allow a more restrictive price. We have thus come to the conclusion that the development of central money is no longer an operating variable reliable enough to serve as a guide to our action. The demand for money responded to factors that escaped us. The demand for transfer accounts was a reaction to structural changes affecting interbank payment mechanisms in Switzerland; as for the demand for banknotes, it may have been stimulated by external factors. Drawing on this negative experience, the SNB has defined a new policy framework that clearly departs from the traditional approach to controlling monetary growth. This strategy - implemented since the beginning of this year - aims to promote a coherent and transparent decision-making process. It is based on three pillars: First, the Bank has achieved its objective of price stability. We believe that this goal is achieved when growth in the consumer price index remains below 2%. With this definition, we take into account the fact that the consumer price index tends to slightly overestimate the increase. The objective of our action is thus quantified and known. The second element of our strategy is an estimate of future inflation. With the help of various econometric models, also by analysing monetary developments, we try to predict the future evolution of inflation, a three-year horizon serving as a reference here. Why three years? To take into account 5 delays between monetary policy decisions and price developments. This forecasting exercise is essential because it asks us to judge whether our action is appropriate in relation to the objective we are pursuing. The fact that we regularly publish our assessment of the inflationary outlook provides the transparency necessary to understand the course of our policy. Finally, we defined a new modus operandi by choosing the three-month LIBOR interest rate as an indicator of the degree of restriction of our policy in the short term. To this end, we set a fluctuation band for the three-month rate and conduct the necessary market operations to stabilize it within the chosen fluctuation band. Here, too, the progress in transparency is considerable compared to the previous mode of action. Inflation forecasting is at the heart of the new monetary policy concept. If the expected price increase crosses the 2% mark, our policy must aim for a higher LIBOR rate, which may also require a move up the announced fluctuation band. However, there is no mechanical link because the importance of the rate adjustment is also based on an assessment of the risks associated with the future course of the economy. Our new strategy therefore does not imply any automatism; however, it helps us to form our decisions in a systematic and rational way within a clear and predefined framework. Transparency is an important part of our new concept. We regularly conduct an analysis of the economic situation and inflationary outlook and publish the conclusions. This communication effort aims to provide the market with the main elements on which our decisions are based so that it understands the motivations. In this way, we hope to contribute to the stability of the financial markets. We want to prevent misunderstood decisions from causing erratic or excessive movements in exchange rates or interest rates. The globalization of financial markets requires operators to understand the meaning and motivation of our measures. The transparency of our action is increased, but it cannot be total. Our new concept of monetary policy is not a "black box" from which the decisions to be taken mechanically emerge. It must be understood as an aid to monetary decision-making. The latter will always have to appeal to an element of judgment that may necessarily depend on the conditions of the moment. It was then up to the SNB to convince the market that "the day and time" were correctly chosen. Its degree of credibility plays a key role in this regard. The new concept of monetary policy also carries risks. First, the success of monetary policy depends on the quality of inflation forecasts. As you know, forecasting is not an exact science. Their quality depends on the degree of sophistication of the simulations, but also on the information collected. Models that appear to be effective at some point are not necessarily effective in the future. Second, the publication of an interest rate target can put us under pressure from the markets, especially since short-term movements in rates can be influenced by external factors. The adoption of a target band and not a target level is intended to provide us with the necessary flexibility in the event of external shocks. 6 dull on rates. For a small open economy such as Switzerland, this flexibility is a necessity. Finally, our transparency efforts put us more at the centre of the public interest. In difficult situations or unpopular decisions, criticism and counter-expertise will surely not be lacking. These spotlight effects will not make monetary policy any easier. There is no doubt that globalization makes the exercise of monetary authority more complex than in the past. Let us now turn to the second factor that has changed the Swiss monetary policy environment: the emergence of a single currency - the euro - on the European front. 3. The difficult birth of the euro The launch of the euro was accompanied by high ambitions. It was expected that the euro would become a solid currency, capable of competing with the dollar. This strength was to stem first of all from a monetary policy geared to price stability - since this is the explicit objective of the European Central Bank's action - and from a comfortable situation for European external payments. These assets were supposed to carry their full weight in the face of a US situation characterized by potential inflationary pressures and a growing external deficit. Moreover, the integration of European financial markets, under the aegis of the euro, would give European securities a completely new liquidity attraction that would whet the appetite of international underwriters. These positive expectations have not been realized, or at least not yet realized. On the contrary, the euro has lost 18% of its value against the dollar since its introduction in January 1999. What are the reasons for this development? First, we must mention the brilliant performance of the US economy, which is experiencing high growth rates without generating inflationary pressures. In this respect, progress in productivity and great flexibility in job creation and in the functioning of the labour market play an important role. However, the question remains open as to whether these are transient effects or truly lasting effects. The Eurozone, on the other hand, is struggling to inspire confidence in the markets despite the improvement in its economic situation and better growth prospects. Its members still experience significant structural handicaps that hinder their ability to fully benefit from the globalization of markets. Moreover, the functioning of the monetary union itself still has important grey areas: First, the convergence of financial stability conditions within the euro area appears to be weakening. Thus, over the past twelve months, the differences in the cyclical development of the Member States have tended to increase: Ireland, Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands are almost overheating, while the economic situation is only starting in Germany and Italy. This disparity gives rise to uncertainty about the future course of the common monetary policy: Should we follow the 7 realities of large countries? But how then can we curb small economies where price stability is threatened? Secondly, the ECB's decision-making process seems cumbersome. Before each decision, the internal debate seems difficult; the search for consensus inevitably runs counter to certain national interests. In addition, the ECB's external communication suffers from a proliferation of spokespersons. The fact that differences of opinion arise between the members of the ECB Council does not contribute to the perception of a clear strategy. Finally, there are currently many uncertainties about the future of the European institutions. The enlargement of the European Union to the East seems to be a foregone conclusion, but it is still difficult to measure the political and monetary consequences. Is it possible to imagine that the eurozone will expand beyond the well-known candidates like Greece, Sweden, Denmark and, possibly, the United Kingdom? Will it be necessary to make room for other countries, which are monetarily behind European standards? And even if this is not the case, what will be the consequences of enlargement to the East for national budgets? In a word, will the 'greater Europe' of tomorrow be able to compare - in terms of stability - to the Rhine Europe resulting from the Franco-German Alliance? All these different elements weigh on the European currency and have prevented it, for the moment, from asserting itself as an attractive alternative to the dollar. 4. The effects of the euro on the Swiss franc During the first sixteen months of the existence of the new European currency, the Swiss franc-euro relationship was marked by unexpected stability. Previous fears that bouts of weakness in the euro would inevitably trigger speculative waves on the Swiss franc have not materialized. This in itself is good news and it is not entirely a surprise considering that the relationship between two currencies depends first and foremost on the convergence of their fundamental elements. For most of 1999, the cyclical parallelism between Switzerland and the surrounding Europe, especially Germany, was evident. The SNB and the European Central Bank were thus called upon to act together. But the situation changed in the last quarter of last year when it became clear that the very expansive course of our policy had to be gradually corrected due to the improvement in the economic situation in Switzerland. The desynchronization of policies has increased in recent weeks due to the now fully proven observation that the intensity of the economic recovery in our country exceeds that of the euro area. The fundamental elements are therefore less convergent today than sixteen months ago, the tones of monetary policies are no longer the same, which has led the franc to strengthen against the European currency. The existence of the euro represents a profound change in the environment in which our monetary policy operates. For the first time in its history, Switzerland is surrounded by countries with the same currency. It is obvious that the exchange rate relationship between the franc and this common currency is of a very special nature. 8 given the intensity of our trade relations with our neighbours. Today, more than 70% of our imports come from the euro area, while more than 50% of our exports are sold there. These figures speak for themselves: a high volatility of the franc-euro relationship would be painful for the Swiss economy. Two factors lead us to believe that this relationship should not develop irrationally: In the first place, the experience of the last fifteen years shows us that the relationship between the franc and the European standard is relatively stable on the trend - when measured in real terms - because the realities of the Swiss economy never deviate very strongly from those of its neighbours. This is due to economic structures, social and cultural factors. Phases of strength or weakness of our currency against the German mark have been observed in the past, they have been painful at times but they have remained of a bearable intensity. It would have been quite different if the volatility between the franc and the mark had been comparable to that between the franc and the dollar. Floating exchange rates are therefore not erratic: converging economies experience relative stability in their exchange rate relationship. That is an encouraging message. Secondly, the strong stability noted between the franc and the euro since last year may also be the consequence of the change in the structural environment in which the franc operates. Indeed, with the arrival of the euro, the international monetary scene has changed significantly. Ten currencies came together and formed a new bloc that was supposed to compete with the dollar. In the previous monetary landscape, the franc was sought after as a means of diversification. Alongside the DM, it was an element that was supposed to counterbalance the risks borne by other currencies that did not have such a proven tradition of stability. Faced with the current monetary blocs, the franc no longer plays the same role as in the past. Losing part of its financial profile, it should therefore evolve in greater harmony with the fundamental realities of the Swiss economy. Fears that changes in the European environment would paralyse Swiss monetary policy have not materialised. The relationship between the franc and the euro evolves largely according to the economic fundamentals of the economies under consideration. There is no indication that the market is now operating irrationally. We therefore remain in a position to pursue the appropriate policy to maintain monetary stability in Switzerland. 5. Monetary policy in a globalised environment: a provisional balance sheet The globalisation of the financial markets and the emergence of a single currency in Europe pose challenges for the SNB's policy. Capital today circulates freely, the flow of information is global and electronic means allow continuous trade-offs. In Europe, the consolidation of the monetary landscape has created a unique situation in which Switzerland is at the heart of a currency area to which the franc is not attached. More than in the past, markets are now able to sanction - through their reaction - inappropriate or perceived policies. 9 The SNB is responding to these challenges through transparency, consistency and communication. It is in this direction that the reform of the way monetary policy is conducted that it carried out at the beginning of the year. The effort at transparency has led us to quantify the objective of price stability and to concretize the price of our share by setting a fluctuation band for the three-month interest rate. Monetary policy measures must not only be coherent, they must also be understandable. For this reason, we regularly publish our assessments of the economic and monetary situation and the conclusions we draw from them for monetary policy. In this way, we give the public the means to judge the course of our action. We expect this to increase efficiency in the conduct of our policy, to react more rationally from the markets, and therefore to strengthen our ability to take the necessary measures to preserve monetary stability in Switzerland. Despite our efforts, the transparency of our action can never be complete. There is no model for determining which monetary policy measures are "right" to take. We are simply looking to create a framework for consistent decision-making. Nevertheless, there remains a margin of appreciation which is the responsibility of the Monetary Authorities. Systematically organized decision-making tends to diminish it. Our experiences of conducting monetary policy in a globalized environment are encouraging. Despite fully integrated markets and total freedom of capital movements, the Franc does not move erratically. Its price tends to reflect the relative evolution of the fundamentals of the Swiss economy. This is particularly the case on the European front. Fears that Swiss monetary policy would be paralysed by the effects of financial globalisation and European monetary integration have therefore not materialised.

Cependant, la question reste ouverte de savoir s'il s'agit l d'effets passagers ou d'effets vraiment durables. La zone Euro, par contre, peine  inspirer confiance aux marchs en dpit de l'amlioration de sa situation conomique et de meilleures perspectives de croissance. De plus, le fonctionnement de l'union montaire elle-mme comporte encore des zones d'ombre importantes: En premier lieu, la convergence des conditions de stabilit financire au sein de la zone euro semble s'affaiblir. De cette disparit nat une incertitude sur le cours futur de la politique montaire commune: Faut-il suivre les 7 ralits des grands pays? Mais comment alors freiner les petites conomies o la stabilit des prix est menace? En second lieu, le processus de dcision de la BCE semble lourd. Avant chaque dcision, le dbat interne parat difficile; la recherche du consensus s'achoppe forcment  certains intrts nationaux. Par ailleurs, la communication extrieure de la BCE souffre d'une multiplication de porte-parole. Le fait que des divergences d'apprciation apparaissent entre les membres du Conseil de la BCE ne contribue pas  la perception d'une stratgie claire. Enfin, de nombreuses incertitudes se manifestent actuellement quant au futur des institutions europennes. L'largissement de l'Union Europenne  l'Est semble une dcision acquise mais on en mesure encore mal les consquences politiques et montaires. Est-il possible d'imaginer que la zone euro s'largisse au-del des candidats connus comme la Grce, la Sude, le Danemark et, ventuellement, le Royaume-Uni?
