En un mot, la "grande Europe" de demain pourra-t-elle se comparer - en terme de stabilit -  l'Europe Rhnane issue de l'Alliance franco-allemande? Tous ces diffrents lments psent sur la monnaie europenne et l'ont empch, pour l'instant, de s'affirmer comme une alternative attrayante face au dollar. 4. Les effets de l'euro sur le franc suisse Au cours des seize premiers mois d'existence de la nouvelle monnaie europenne, la relation franc suisse - euro a t marque par une stabilit inattendue. Les craintes antrieures selon lesquelles des accs de faiblesse de l'euro dclencheraient immanquablement des vagues spculatives sur le franc suisse ne se sont pas ralises. C'est en soi une bonne nouvelle et ce n'est pas tout  fait une surprise si l'on songe que les relations entre deux monnaies dpendent d'abord de la convergence de leurs lments fondamentaux. Au cours de la majeure partie de 1999, le paralllisme conjoncturel entre la Suisse et l'Europe environnante, surtout l'Allemagne, tait vident. La Banque nationale et la Banque centrale europenne ont ainsi t amenes  agir de concert. Mais la situation s'est modifie au cours du dernier trimestre de l'an dernier lorsqu'il est devenu clair que le cours trs expansif de notre politique devait tre progressivement corrig en raison de l'amlioration de la conjoncture en Suisse. La dsynchronisation des politiques s'est accentue ces dernires semaines en raison de la constatation, maintenant pleinement avre, que l'intensit de la reprise conomique dans notre pays dpasse celle de la zone euro. Les lments fondamentaux sont donc aujourd'hui moins convergents qu'il y a seize mois, les tonalits des politiques montaires ne sont plus les mmes, ce qui a conduit le franc  se renforcer par rapport  la monnaie europenne. L'existence de l'euro constitue une modification profonde de l'environnement dans lequel opre notre politique montaire. Pour la premire fois de son histoire, la Suisse est entoure de pays disposant d'une mme monnaie. Il est vident que la relation de change entre le franc et cette monnaie commune est d'une nature toute particulire 8 tant donn l'intensit de nos relations commerciales avec nos voisins. Aujourd'hui, plus du 70 % de nos importations proviennent de la zone euro, alors que plus de 50 % de nos exportations y sont coules. Ces chiffres sont parlants: une forte volatilit de la relation franc - euro serait douloureuse pour l'conomie suisse. Deux facteurs nous incitent  penser que cette relation ne devrait pas se dvelopper de faon irrationnelle: En premier lieu, l'exprience des quinze dernires annes nous montre que la relation entre le franc et l'talon europen est relativement stable sur la tendance - lorsqu'on la mesure en termes rels - car les ralits de l'conomie suisse ne s'loignent jamais trs fortement de celles de ses voisins. Ceci tient aux structures conomiques, aux facteurs sociaux et culturels. Des phases de force ou de faiblesse de notre monnaie par rapport au mark allemand ont t observes par le pass, elles ont t douloureuses par moment mais elles sont restes d'une intensit supportable. Il en aurait t tout autrement si la volatilit entre le franc et le mark avait t comparable  celle qui s'est faite jour entre le franc et le dollar. Les changes flottants ne sont donc pas erratiques: des conomies convergentes connaissent une relative stabilit de leur relation de change. C'est un message encourageant. En second lieu, la forte stabilit note entre le franc et l'euro depuis l'an dernier peut aussi tre la consquence du changement de l'environnement structurel dans lequel opre le franc. En effet, avec l'arrive de l'euro, la scne montaire internationale s'est sensiblement modifie. Dix monnaies se sont soudes et ont constitu un nouveau bloc sens concurrencer le dollar. Dans le paysage montaire prcdent, le franc tait recherch comme moyen de diversification. Aux cts du DM, il tait un lment sens contrebalancer les risques supports par d'autres monnaies n'ayant pas une tradition de stabilit aussi avre. Face aux blocs montaires actuels, le franc ne joue plus le mme rle que par le pass. Perdant une partie de son profil financier, il devrait donc voluer en plus grande harmonie avec les ralits fondamentales de l'conomie suisse. Les craintes que l'on pouvait avoir que les modifications de l'environnement europen paralyseraient la politique montaire suisse ne se sont pas concrtises. Les relations entre le franc et l'euro voluent largement en fonction des lments conomiques fondamentaux des conomies considres. Rien n'indique que le march opre maintenant de manire irrationnelle. Nous restons donc en mesure de mener la politique qui convient au maintien de la stabilit montaire en Suisse. 5. Politique montaire dans un environnement globalis: un bilan provisoire La globalisation des marchs financiers et l'apparition d'une monnaie unique en Europe constituent des dfis pour la politique de la Banque nationale. Les capitaux circulent aujourd'hui librement, le flux des informations est global et les moyens lectroniques permettent des arbitrages continus. En Europe, la consolidation du paysage montaire a cr une situation unique qui voit la Suisse se situer au cur d'une zone montaire  laquelle le franc n'est pas rattach. Plus que par le pass, les marchs sont maintenant en mesure de sanctionner - par leur raction - des politiques inappropries ou perues comme telles. 9 La Banque nationale relve ces dfis par un effort de transparence, de cohrence et de communication. C'est dans ce sens que va la rforme du mode de conduite de la politique montaire  laquelle elle a procd en dbut d'anne. L'effort de transparence nous a conduits  chiffrer l'objectif de stabilit des prix et  concrtiser le cours de notre action par la fixation d'une bande de fluctuation pour le taux d'intrt  trois mois. Les mesures de politique montaire doivent tre non seulement cohrentes, elles doivent aussi tre comprhensibles. C'est pourquoi, nous publions rgulirement nos lments d'apprciation de la situation conomique et montaire et les conclusions que nous en tirons pour la politique montaire. Nous donnons ainsi au public les moyens de juger le cours de notre action. Nous en attendons un gain d'efficacit dans la conduite de notre politique, une raction plus rationnelle des marchs, donc un renforcement de notre capacit  prendre les mesures ncessaires  la prservation de la stabilit montaire en Suisse. Malgr nos efforts, la transparence de notre action ne pourra jamais tre totale. Il n'existe pas de modle permettant de dterminer quelles sont les "bonnes" mesures de politique montaire  prendre. Nous cherchons simplement  crer un cadre permettant une prise de dcision cohrente. Il reste nanmoins une marge d'apprciation qui relve de la responsabilit des Autorits montaires. Une prise de dcision organise de manire systmatique tend  la diminuer. Nos expriences de conduite de la politique montaire dans un environnement globalis sont encourageantes. En dpit de marchs pleinement intgrs et d'une libert totale des mouvements des capitaux, le franc n'volue pas de manire erratique. Son cours tend  reflter l'volution relative des lments fondamentaux de l'conomie suisse. C'est notamment le cas sur le front europen. Les craintes de voir la politique montaire suisse tre paralyse par les effets de la globalisation financire et de l'intgration montaire europenne ne se sont donc pas concrtises.

Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the President of the Bank Council
text: Opening address by Mr Eduard Belser, Chairman of the Bank Council, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 28 April 2000 Security and stability in a changing world Security, freedom and prosperity are the main goals to which the community aspires. As a public institution, the SNB must also make its contribution to their implementation. As you know, its task is to conduct a monetary policy that serves the general interests of the country. For monetary policy, maintaining price level stability is paramount. The SNB, with its resources, thus makes the best contribution to balanced macroeconomic developments. Security and stability are not only objectives assigned to monetary policy. They are also the conditions for the success of the SNB's action. Security and stability, however, are not taken for granted once and for all. The work must be constantly put back on the job, which naturally implies uncertainties and risks. The Bank Council - in particular its Committee - is responsible for supervising the conduct and conduct of the affairs of the issuing institution. He is therefore co-responsible for the solidity of the company. With this in mind, I would like to discuss some of the Bank's activities, but also several challenges it faces. The reorganization of cash movements was successfully completed at the end of 1999. In the field of cash, the tasks relate to everything that surrounds the manufacture of banknotes, but mainly to storage, transport and sorting. In relation to the resources committed to exploitation, cash remains the main area of activity of the SNB. I would remind you that the Commission had to carry out this 2 reorganization so that its services are adapted to demand. Cash control and sorting were thus centralized at counters in Bern, Zurich, Geneva and Lugano. However, the SNB remains present in all regions of the country to ensure its traditional contacts with economic and social circles. This reorganisation also reflects the SNB's desire to focus on the key tasks arising from its mandate. A light but effective structure must make it possible to provide the services. Today, IT is strongly present in everything related to operations. The SNB is not an exception in this respect. Developments in this area are extremely rapid. For years, significant human and financial resources have been engaged in the development of information technology. The services responsible for payment transactions, banking and scientific work are among the main users. In all areas, applications must meet high requirements for safety and reliability. The transition to the year 2000 was a particular challenge for the SNB as well; the preventive measures it has taken in coordination with the main operators on the financial markets have been, as you have seen, successful. The requirements for security and stability arise not only at the operational level, but also and above all in the financial field. New conditions result from the amendment in November 1997 of the Law on the National Bank - extension of authorized operations - the new constitutional article and the entry into force, on 1 May next, of the Law on the monetary unit and means of payment. The abolition of the swiss franc's peg to gold will enable the SNB to value its cash balance at market prices. After the revaluation of its gold cash, the issuing institution will hold monetary reserves in excess of what is necessary for the conduct of monetary policy. However, it is not for it to decide on the allocation of these excess reserves. Parliament and the people will be called upon to give their opinion on this issue. In the long term, the management of excess reserves cannot be entrusted to the SNB either. It makes more sense for the beneficiaries themselves to make the decisions regarding the investment of this wealth. 3 The updated constitution expressly requires the SNB to hold sufficient monetary reserves. These are primarily foreign currency assets, which are liquid, not accompanied by an exchange rate guarantee and therefore available for monetary purposes. Such assets are exposed to currency, interest rate and credit risks. In order for these risks to be contained, the relevant departments within the Bank must, in their operations, comply with guidelines and constraints. The Risk Management Directorate is responsible for ensuring that decision-making and enforcement processes are followed. Risks are therefore systematically identified, limited and controlled. The Risk Management Directorate has been gradually expanded in recent years. It is placed under the high supervision of the Bank Council. A delegation from the Banking Committee is particularly responsible for this task. The financial statements for the financial year 1999 clearly show the risks associated with the management of our assets. Rising interest rates have led to price losses on fixed income investments. However, these losses were more than offset by foreign exchange gains on investments in foreign currencies. A 10% fluctuation in the value of the dollar generates a gain or loss of almost CHF 2 billion for the SNB. This clearly indicates the high volatility of the results of the issuing institution. Every business ultimately relies on its human resources. With its 600 employees, the SNB has had a stable workforce for years. In the labour market, it competes primarily with other financial institutions. Continuous efforts are needed to ensure that staff meet the requirements qualitatively and quantitatively. Training and assistance remain ongoing concerns. Training in the technical field and in staff conduct, language courses and personality development were continued and deepened last year. The work to revise the regulations governing salaries will enable us to establish a salary policy in accordance with our charter and taking into account both the functions, the benefits and the market, but also the characteristics of the SNB. 4 Throughout its almost century-old history, the SNB has had to continually adapt its activities to an ever-changing environment. Of course, this will be the case in the future. Some prophets even go so far as to dream of an Internet currency that would make issuing institutes obsolete as we know them today. In addition, depending on the solution that our country adopts to settle its relations with Europe, this will have a profound impact on the National Bank. We all know that. In the meantime and more concretely, a total revision of the SNB Act is approaching. The issuing institution needs a legal framework that is better suited to our time. Despite all the uncertainties of the future, let us not forget that a safe and stable company is better able to face the challenges that will arise. The Bank's Senior Management and authorities will continue to work in this direction in the future as well.

Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the Chairman of the Governing Board
text: Presentation by Mr Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Executive Board, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 28 April 2000 The Swiss economy gained strength in 1999. For a long time, we have not been so close to the goal of balanced macroeconomic developments: appropriate growth, high employment and price stability. Three factors above all are at the root of this situation: the efforts made by our economy, the improvement in the global economy and the favourable monetary framework conditions. Changes in our critical environment have led us to re-examine the foundations of our monetary policy. Our tailored strategy will enable us to continue, in a changing environment, to fulfil our mandate to conduct a monetary policy that serves the general interests of the country. Ensuring the stability of the price level is our primary task. A stable price level facilitates balanced economic growth and prevents undesirable social developments. In my briefing, I will focus, as I do in every General Assembly, on the issues that have received our particular attention over the past year. 1. Economic situation According to available estimates, our economy grew by 1.7% in 1999. This rate is a little lower than the previous year, but higher than what was expected a year ago. The marked acceleration in growth in the second half of 1999 was broad-based and led to a further reduction in unemployment. The main impulses came from exports, which surprised by their strength. Favourable economic developments in our largest trading partners and the weakness of the Swiss franc against the dollar have both boosted our exports. Sales in the United States and countries 2 of Southeast Asia have marked a remarkable expansion. Faced with this boom, demand from European countries has remained moderate until now. The internal market has also contributed significantly to the economic recovery. Private consumption remained an important support for the economy. In January 2000, the consumer sentiment index reached its highest level in the last ten years. After breaking through the trough of the wave in 1998, construction has gradually returned to the path of recovery. In 1999, investment in construction thus contributed to economic growth, which had not been the case for the previous four years. Demand recovered not only in housing and civil engineering, but also, and above all, in construction for industry, crafts and services, in a segment that had suffered particularly from the recession. Investment in capital goods did not increase as much as in 1998, but its level remained high. In this area, demand from the services sector has been strong, while the propensity to invest has remained moderate in industry. The labour market has also developed positively. Thanks to the economic recovery, the unemployment rate has fallen from 3.2% at the end of 1998 to 2.3% today. Employment has increased in all branches of our economy. With the outlook good, we are approaching full employment. However, we must not forget the complexity of the labour market, which makes it difficult to make a nuanced assessment. The lack of qualified personnel remains a major problem. In this regard, signs of tension have undeniably increased. Another important problem is that of all those who, for one reason or another, have difficulty finding their place in a very dynamic economy. In the wake of the economic recovery, inflation  measured at consumer prices  accelerated last year, as expected. It reached 1.7% at the end of 1999, while a level close to zero had still been observed a year earlier. Its sharp acceleration is largely due to the massive rise in oil prices. The increase in VAT - the rate was raised from 6.5% to 7.5% in 1999 - also contributed, but to a small extent, to the increase in prices. On the other hand, the opposite effects continued to result from the intense competition. This has led to price reductions, particularly in the field of telecommunications. 3 2. Monetary policy We had announced our intention to continue our broad monetary policy in 1999. We were then trying to ensure that the Swiss economy, which was still suffering from the repercussions of the Asian crisis, had the necessary monetary room for manoeuvre for recovery. We also had to take account of the uncertainties arising from the introduction of the euro. In this phase, the aim was to prevent any movement against the euro from leading to an economically unjustified revaluation of the Swiss franc. At the beginning of April 1999, we reduced the discount rate to 0.5%. After this adjustment, the remuneration paid on the Swiss money market, which was already at a low level, fell further. As the real export-weighted rate of the franc had also declined, monetary framework conditions in the first half of 1999 were more favourable than in the previous year. After the introduction of the European currency, the exchange rate relationship between the euro and the franc showed great stability. This stability and the ever-increasing economic recovery have changed the environment. We have therefore decided to tighten monetary controls slightly, which has resulted in higher short-term interest rates in the money market. Given the similarity of developments in the euro area and Switzerland, it is not surprising that the exchange rate relationship between the euro and the franc has continued to remain within a narrow margin. If we consider the first year after the introduction of the euro, an ambivalent judgment can be made about the new currency. The domestic value of the euro was able to be maintained to a pleasing extent. On the other hand, its external value has, for several reasons, tended to weaken. It should be noted, however, that the euro area's economic relations with the rest of the world are relatively small. A weak currency stimulates economic recovery. But, on the other hand, it increases the risk of higher import prices. Finally, a weak currency presents the danger of developing a downward dynamic, which can be difficult to control. For many years, as you know, central money has served as an aggregate for our monetary policy. In a first phase, we set 4 annual growth targets. Then, in the nineties, we moved to medium-term growth targets to take into account the fact that the supply of money has a major impact on inflation in the medium term. By focusing our policy on the medium term, we have given ourselves the flexibility to take into account other indicators, such as the evolution of the real economy, the situation on the labour market and exchange rates, in our decisions. We have always considered our medium-term objective as a guideline. Experience has shown us that the central currency has lost its reliability in recent years. This has led us to re-examine the foundations of our monetary policy. We then decided not to publish a growth target in terms of central money. The broad foundation of our policy, which is based on all the main indicators - is reflected and will be reflected more visibly in practice. Since its adaptation, our monetary policy strategy has been based on three elements. The first is an explicit definition of price level stability. By price level stability we mean an increase in prices - measured at consumer prices - of less than 2% per year. In this way, we take into account, among other things, the fact that the increase can never be measured accurately. Our efforts have always been focused on maintaining price stability. Only the explicit definition is new. The second element of our strategy is a three-year inflation forecast. We thus take into account the approximately three-year lag with which monetary policy measures operate. The inflation forecast is based on all the information we can derive from an analysis of the determining factors. The evolution of monetary aggregates, in particular M3, still plays an important role. It is valuable above all for assessing the medium-term trend. The results of econometric forecasting models also come into play, as do factors such as the evolution of the real economy and exchange rates. Finally, we also take into account particular factors, for example passenger shocks. 5 This method ensures a decision-making process based on a broad base. Of course, even such a broadly substantiated process cannot change the fact that monetary policy decisions ultimately remain a matter of appreciation. If the inflation forecast shows that the upward trend deviates from the definition of price level stability, then action is needed. The inflation forecast we publish takes into account possible monetary policy decisions. The third element of our strategy concerns the implementation of monetary policy. We assign a fluctuation margin of 100 basis points to the main interest rate on three-month deposits in Swiss francs. To influence this rate, we generally trade short-term on the money market. The setting of a fluctuation band leaves the market some latitude for fine management. This pragmatic strategy will allow us to fulfill our mission even if conditions change. Monetary policy, let us not forget, is ultimately a challenge for the economy, but also for society. The implementation, with determination, of the knowledge that comes to us from theory and research is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for success. It is indeed essential that society as a whole be well aware of the importance of stability for sustainable macroeconomic development. At the end of 1999, we had forecast an average increase in prices of 1.5% for 2000, then of 1.7% and 1.8% for the following two years. We started from real economic growth of about 2%. Initially, we set the three-month interest rate fluctuation band at 1.25% - 2.25%. But we quickly realized that economic developments were going to be stronger than expected. So we let the three-month rate in January be at the top of the fluctuation band. In early February, we raised the margin by 50 basis points. Finally, about a month ago, we decided, after a thorough analysis of the situation, to tighten the monetary reins further and increase the fluctuation band to 2.5% - 3.5%. Published data on economic developments in Switzerland and abroad confirmed the impression we had. The boom, according to these data, will be more vigorous than what was expected until recently. Today 6 it is estimated that real growth is expected to be well above 2% in 2000. The countries that are important to us are experiencing very favourable economic developments. In addition, the high exchange rate of the dollar against the franc strengthens the competitiveness of our economy. Domestic demand, in particular private consumption and investment in construction, is also experiencing dynamic developments. On the labour market, as I have already pointed out, there are signs of drying up, which will not remain without effects on wages. The evolution of the price increase is not worrying at the moment. Given the significant lag in monetary policy measures, we need to operate preventively. By tightening the monetary reins in time, we have reacted in accordance with our mandate, namely to ensure, above all, the stability of the price level in the interests of balanced macroeconomic developments. Our assessment of macroeconomic developments and, consequently, of the prospects for inflation is not intangible. We will closely monitor future developments and periodically review the analyses on which our inflation forecast is based. We will regularly inform the public of the outcome of our reviews of the situation. 3. Financial sector stability and integrity The SNB has co-responsibility for the stability and integrity of the financial sector. In this context, it is first necessary to recall the individual responsibility of operators on the markets. Through a solid business policy and an adequate organizational system, these operators must ensure their solvency at all times. Governing bodies must be able to make the right decisions, at the right time, and act accordingly. It is then desirable that, even in a dynamic environment, evolution should take place in a certain continuity on the material and human levels. The public authorities must first contribute to the establishment of appropriate framework conditions. Economic and social, but also legal and technical conditions must constitute a favourable framework for the activity of each 7 economic agent. A stability-oriented monetary policy is the best contribution that the SNB can make to the balance of the system. The incessant structural changes of recent years have left deep traces in our financial sector in particular. The latter has gained in competitiveness and, today, it benefits from it in a favourable economic environment. Structural changes are of course never complete. Economic, social and, above all, technological developments will continually require new adaptations. Efficiency or competitiveness is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for sustainable success. The latter also requires the presence of another factor, an adequate endowment of equity. The question of the appropriate level of own funds concerns above all the bodies which, in the various countries, are responsible for supervision. At the international level, the discussion is conducted mainly in the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision at the Bank for International Settlements. The Committee, which brings together representatives of central banks and supervisory bodies from major countries, is currently developing standards to make capital requirements more responsive to actual risks. Finally, these are questions of appreciation that must be decided with foresight. In other words, it is necessary to take into account the undeniable costs of holding own funds, but also the clear usefulness of own funds for safeguarding sustainable development. Ultimately, it is up to the oversight bodies to ensure that emphasis is appropriately emphasized. With respect to integrity, careful choice of business relationships is one of the things to consider. This is particularly relevant to the financial sector, which has traditionally been customer-oriented from all regions of the world. Political and economic stability, an efficient infrastructure, a clear legal order and the quality of the services provided by employees are rightly regarded as conditions for sustainable success. To this must be added reputation, which presupposes a solid business ethic. The practice of banking secrecy also comes into play in this context. I will distinguish three aspects. There is no dispute that the private sphere is protected from 8 Appropriately. The link between banking secrecy and unlawful conduct is the second aspect I would like to highlight. The acceleration of mutual legal assistance and the extension of the anti-money-laundering framework have made it possible to erect effective barriers in the recent period. It is to be welcomed that financial market supervision has been extended beyond the narrow circle of banking institutions. Finally, there is the link between banking secrecy and tax evasion. Under Swiss law, tax evasion is a criminal offence, but not tax evasion. As a result, our banking secrecy is perceived abroad as an instrument to evade taxation. In the recent period, the European Union has sought a solution to tax income from capital invested outside the tax domicile. The discussion focuses on two possibilities, namely a withholding tax and an obligation to report. An agreement is not in sight at the moment. In this area, for a solution to be convincing, it must apply to all major financial centres. If the EU countries succeed, we will hardly be able to avoid cooperation on withholding taxes. 4. New constitutional and legal provisions on currency In force since the beginning of 2000, the new federal constitution contains an article on monetary policy, which is an update of the articles on money and bank of issue of the old constitution. The pegging of the Swiss franc to gold was thus abolished. Last year, the Federal Chambers approved the new law on the monetary unit and means of payment. This law is already based on the updated constitution and eliminates the provisions that, in federal legislation, still linked the franc to gold. Thus, it abolishes the obligation for the National Bank to reimburse gold banknotes, the minimum gold hedging of banknotes in circulation and the gold parity of the franc. As the referendum deadline has ended without having been used, the Federal Act on the Monetary Unit and Means of Payment will enter into force on 1 May. The abolition of the gold parity of the franc expands our possibilities in terms of valuation and use of our gold cash. As soon as the gold stock is valued at the market price, the SNB will hold many more assets than it needs for monetary purposes. About half of the current gold cash - a share of 9 1300 tons - will therefore be available for other public purposes. The constitutional basis for removing these assets from the SNB's balance sheet and giving them another allocation will be created in the near future. As soon as possible, we will start selling the portion of the gold cash that can be used for other public purposes. Last autumn, the main European central banks agreed, I would remind you, to limit their gold sales to 2000 tonnes over the next five years. Our sales will take place within the framework of this agreement. Until the constitutional basis for removing these assets from the SNB's balance sheet and using them for another use has been established, we will place the proceeds of gold sales in accordance with the legal provisions governing our operations. 5. International monetary relations The countries of East Asia and Latin America have overcome their economic difficulties of recent years with remarkable speed. However, this applies more to the symptoms than to the deep origins of the crisis. It should not be forgotten that economic and social problems remain and that these problems still stand in the way of sustainable growth. Sustainable growth, as experience has confirmed, is only possible on the basis of economic and social stability. The required conditions must be created in the first place by each of the countries concerned. Any help from outside must be designed to support the country in its own efforts. These aspects are also decisive in judging the activities of the International Monetary Fund. As a member country, Switzerland participates in the activities of this institution, which is the most important for international monetary cooperation. That is why I think some thoughts on the current debate are useful here. The Monetary Fund must remember that its main task is to support member countries in formulating and implementing an adequate macroeconomic economic policy. Only secondly, an aid credit may be envisaged in order to facilitate the necessary adaptation measures. These credits must be granted in the short term and subject to conditions ensuring that they are indeed aid to support the efforts to be made by the countries themselves. 10 The idea of opening up credit lines for healthy countries for preventive purposes is not convincing. Never has an important country encountered persistent difficulties without it itself causing them. The World Bank's main task is to facilitate structural adjustments and to promote the implementation of specific medium-term economic projects. By refocusing on their core competencies, these two institutions will provide the best contribution to balanced economic development. The Monetary Fund is constantly torn between advice and adjustment aid. His task is all the more difficult because he is ultimately unable to enforce his recommendations. In addition, the various member countries seek to put the activities of the Monetary Fund at the service of their own interests. International monetary relations are also constantly changing. When difficulties arise from time to time, voices are quickly raised to demand fundamental reforms. Experience shows, however, that major reforms are unlikely to succeed. On the other hand, moving forward in small steps, but with perseverance and without losing sight of the goal to be achieved, often gives better results. Beyond these fundamental principles, I would like to make the following few remarks: The experiences of recent years have confirmed, in particular, the importance of stable financial markets. It would therefore be appropriate for the MONETARY Fund to place particular emphasis on this area, primarily through advisory and training activities. I believe that it is essential to implement the knowledge acquired in recent years in various bodies. It is also important to improve the transparency of developments in the financial markets. Both market operators and official bodies will thus be able to make a relevant judgment on the situation. However, poor decisions and lack of reaction are often due not to a lack of information but rather to an overly superficial analysis of the existing literature. 11 The Monetary Fund must also strive to achieve greater transparency. A simple way to contribute to this would be to publish periodic analyses of country situations. In particular, it is the countries concerned that oppose such publication. Several proposals deserve support. They concern the definition of leading supervisory indicators, the reduction of incentives for short-term capital movements and the renunciation of implicit guarantees given to creditors. In addition, the idea of introducing clauses in debt contracts to facilitate decision-making in the event of a crisis merits consideration. The impact of such clauses on the conduct of contracting parties and on fundraising is unclear. Authorising the Monetary Fund to temporarily suspend the rights of certain creditors seems to me to be problematic. International financial relations derive largely from the private economy. It is therefore necessary and logical to involve the private sector in efforts to prevent and resolve crises. I am thinking here above all of the creation of market economy incentives. The provision of official assistance must again be made more conditional on the participation of the private sector. Under no circumstances can private sector operators on the market be released from any liability. The necessary collaboration presupposes an ongoing dialogue. The more cooperative the private sector is, the less restrictive regulations will be required. Perspectives In conclusion, I would like to emphasize once again that the situation and prospects for our economy are currently encouraging. This year, we are likely to achieve substantial economic growth, in a context of almost full employment and low inflation. But the coin also has its flip side. Indeed, risks to macroeconomic stability are increasing tendentially. Moreover, this generally positive picture contains the danger of obscuring the need to constantly improve, and in a socially bearable manner, the macroeconomic framework conditions. 12 I would also like to thank the employees of the National Bank for their support during a not simple but interesting year. I would also like to thank the members of the Bank's authorities for their support. Finally, I thank you all, ladies and gentlemen, for the interest you have shown us by participating in our General Assembly today.

Nouvelles dispositions constitutionnelles et lgales sur la monnaie En vigueur depuis le dbut de 2000, la nouvelle constitution fdrale contient un article sur la politique montaire, qui est une mise  jour des articles sur la monnaie et la banque d'mission de l'ancienne constitution. Relations montaires internationales Les pays d'Asie orientale et d'Amrique latine ont surmont avec une remarquable rapidit leurs difficults conomiques de ces dernires annes. Cette constatation s'applique toutefois plus aux symptmes qu'aux origines profondes de la crise. Une croissance durable, l'exprience l'a confirm, n'est possible que sur la base d'une stabilit conomique et sociale. Les conditions requises doivent tre cres en premier lieu par chacun des pays concerns. Toute aide venant de l'extrieur doit tre conue pour soutenir le pays dans ses propres efforts. En second lieu seulement, un crdit d'aide peut tre envisag afin de faciliter les mesures d'adaptations qui s'imposent. Ces crdits doivent tre accords  court terme et assortis de conditions garantissant qu'il s'agit bien d'aides pour soutenir les efforts  accomplir par les pays eux-mmes. 10 L'ide d'ouvrir,  des fins prventives, des lignes de crdit en faveur de pays sains ne convainc pas. La Banque mondiale a, quant  elle, pour tche essentielle de faciliter les adaptations structurelles ainsi que de favoriser la ralisation de projets conomiques particuliers  moyen terme. En se concentrant de nouveau sur leurs attributions fondamentales, ces deux institutions fourniront la meilleure des contributions  une volution conomique quilibre. En outre, les divers pays membres cherchent  mettre les activits du Fonds montaire au service de leurs propres intrts. Les relations montaires internationales sont elles aussi en mutation permanente. Quand des difficults surgissent de temps  autre, des voix s'lvent rapidement pour exiger des rformes fondamentales. L'exprience nous montre cependant que les grandes rformes n'ont que peu de chances d'aboutir. En revanche, avancer  petits pas, mais avec persvrance et sans perdre de vue le but  atteindre, donne souvent de meilleurs rsultats. Au-del de ces principes fondamentaux, je voudrais formuler les quelques remarques suivantes: Les expriences de ces dernires annes ont confirm notamment l'importance que revtent des marchs financiers stables. Il importe en outre d'amliorer la transparence des dveloppements sur les marchs financiers. Toutefois, les mauvaises dcisions et les absences de raction sont dues souvent non pas  un manque d'informations mais plutt  une analyse trop superficielle de la documentation existante. 11 Le Fonds montaire doit lui aussi s'efforcer de parvenir  une plus grande transparence. Une manire simple d'y contribuer consisterait  publier les analyses priodiques de la situation des pays. Ce sont notamment les pays concerns qui s'opposent  une telle publication. En outre, l'ide d'introduire dans les contrats d'emprunt des clauses facilitant la prise de dcisions en cas de crise mrite d'tre examine. Autoriser le Fonds montaire  suspendre temporairement les droits de certains cranciers me semble par contre problmatique. Les relations financires internationales dcoulent en majeure partie de l'conomie prive. Il est par consquent ncessaire et logique d'associer le secteur priv aux efforts pour prvenir et rsoudre les crises. Je pense ici avant tout  la cration d'incitations relevant de l'conomie de march. En aucun cas, les oprateurs du secteur priv sur le march ne peuvent tre dgags de toute responsabilit. La collaboration ncessaire suppose un dialogue permanent. Plus le secteur priv se montrera coopratif, moins il faudra recourir  des rglementations contraignantes. Perspectives Pour conclure, j'aimerais souligner une fois encore que la situation et les perspectives de notre conomie sont actuellement rjouissantes. Cette anne, nous atteindrons vraisemblablement une croissance conomique substantielle, dans un contexte de quasiplein emploi et de faible renchrissement. Mais la mdaille a aussi son revers. En effet, les risques pesant sur la stabilit macroconomique augmentent tendanciellement. Title: The SNB's policy in the current environment
text: SNB policy in today's environment Presentation by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank at the Annual General Meeting of the Association of Bernese Regional Banks Sumiswald, 12 May 2000 2 1. An environment in transition The keywords globalization, deregulation and liberalization are probably among the most frequently used words of the nineties and seem almost a bit worn. Nevertheless, it is these characteristics that most aptly characterize today's time. These developments shape both the markets for goods and services and the financial markets. Banks, as providers of services and as a hinge between the real economy and the financial markets, are particularly affected by this upheaval. The Swiss banking sector in particular has undergone a profound structural change in recent years. The merger of two major banks was only the most spectacular expression of this change; however, this cannot hide the fact that the consolidation of regional banks has changed the Swiss banking landscape just as substantially. From an economic point of view, globalization, deregulation and liberalization lead to a more efficient use of scarce resources and thus increase overall prosperity. However, this general positive effect is offset by concrete, albeit usually temporary, disadvantages for certain population groups or economic sectors. In addition, the advantages of stronger competition usually only become apparent in the medium term, while the costs of structural change in the form of production declines and unemployment are immediately noticeable. The Swiss banks also had to endure a certain dry spell after the numerous takeovers, restructurings and mergers. However, the recently published annual financial statements again show consistently positive results. This is especially true for many smaller banks, which have obviously managed to put their specific advantages in the right light. Internationalisation on the financial markets was even more pronounced than in the markets for goods and services. The enormous technical advances have contributed significantly to this development. Computer science and modern telecommunications enable the rapid and cheap procurement and processing of enormous amounts of information. This created the conditions for worldwide arbitrage and increased international competition. The dismantling of regulations and restrictions has been forced by competition for mobile capital. Here, too, the free movement of international capital leads to an efficient use of savings and thus promotes prosperity. At the same time, however, the risk of cross-border financial crises has increased with the increasing interconnectedness of markets. We had to experience this with the Asian crisis. In Europe, the integration of financial markets has taken a decisive step forward through the introduction of the euro. The replacement of ten currencies by a single one and the emergence of a broad and liquid euro capital market have fundamentally changed the conditions on the foreign exchange market and the international capital market. The structures of the European banking and stock exchange landscape are also increasingly being called into question. Globalisation and the introduction of the European single currency pose significant challenges for banks and the entire Swiss economy. The Swiss National Bank is also facing a new environment. In the following, I would like to explain how the SNB has adapted its monetary policy to this new environment characterised by globalisation and the euro. 3 2. Monetary policy: an unchanged objective ... The law assigns the NATIONAL Bank the task of conducting a monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. The SNB has always interpreted this mandate in such a way that it best serves the overall interest by maintaining price stability. Globalisation has not changed our convictions in this regard. Why do we place so much emphasis on maintaining price stability? First, we do this because inflation hinders economic growth in the longer term. If inflation prevails, the price system can no longer fulfil its natural control function. Relative prices are distorted because not all goods can be adapted to inflation at the same time. Since the price signals do not indicate the correct scarcity ratios between the goods, inefficiencies arise that inhibit economic development. Furthermore, inflation also has undesirable distributional effects by causing a redistribution from creditors to debtors. In a tax system with progressive tax rates, inflation also leads to a creeping increase in the tax burden. After all, inflation is considered anti-social, as it hits those who are least able to protect themselves against it the most; these are usually the socially weaker. Globalisation does not change our task of ensuring price stability. Even in a globalized economy, an abundant supply of liquidity compared to the real growth potential of the economy sooner or later leads to rising prices. As long as Switzerland commits itself to an independent monetary policy free from exchange rate constraints, the Swiss National Bank will remain responsible for providing liquidity. This would only change if Switzerland were to peg the franc to the euro in one form or another or even join the monetary union. Focusing on the objective of price stability does not mean that the SNB ignores problems such as weak growth and unemployment. However, it is convinced that monetary policy is not the appropriate instrument for combating it. Monetary policy has real economic effects only in the short term. Thus, an expansionary monetary policy can only stimulate growth temporarily. After a short time, the economic flash in the pan goes out again, and the only thing that remains permanent is a higher price level. In addition, in the age of the globalization of markets and the associated stronger economic interdependence of international economic cycles, the possibilities of a single central bank are even more limited than before. This is a further argument for the SNB's abstinence from economic policy and for the priority of price stability. 3. ... but a new strategy While our ultimate objective, price stability, has not changed, the changed environment in which we operate has led to some innovations in the actual conduct of monetary policy. The transition to a direct inflation target was 4 because the demand for money became increasingly unstable. As a result, the relationship between the intermediate objective of the monetary aggregate and the ultimate objective of price stability became less and less reliable. With our new strategy, which has been in force since the beginning of the year, we have given ourselves a clear and coherent decision-making framework. At the same time, this increases the transparency of our policy and allows us to communicate our assessments and intentions to the markets even better. Let me briefly explain the elements of our new concept. First, the SNB specified and quantified its price stability objective. For us, price stability is achieved when the inflation rate measured by the consumer price index is below 2%. With this definition, we take into account the fact that the consumer price index slightly overstates inflation. The second element of our new strategy is an estimate or forecast of future inflation. For example, we are now publishing an inflation forecast that reflects the inflation rate we expect for the coming years. At the same time, we have announced a target range for the money market interest rate we are targeting. If the value of the projected inflation approaches the upper limit of 2%, which for us is just about compatible with price stability, then this triggers a rethinking of the monetary policy stance. Depending on the result of this process, there may be a shift in interest within the target band or a change in the band itself. However, it may also be that we come to the conclusion that there is no need for action. Our new strategy does not imply automatic interest rates. Rather, it defines a framework that should help us to make our decisions systematically and rationally. Our decisions are based on a wide range of indicators, with our assessment of future price developments at the heart of the process. In justifying our decisions, we disclose our assessments and considerations, which provides the market with important clues about our assessment of the economic and monetary situation. With this new way of presenting its policy, the SNB has also taken certain risks: First, the publication of an interest rate target can expose us to market pressure, all the more so since the short-term movements of our target are often determined by external factors. To mitigate this problem, we define our target within a range of 100 basis points for the 3-month rate and not as an absolute level target. The range should protect us from short-term activism in case market conditions come under the influence of external shocks. Defining the interest rate target within a range is an imperative of flexibility for a small, open economy like Switzerland. Second, the increased transparency of our policies will increasingly put monetary policy decision-making in the public spotlight. We have committed ourselves to publishing our assessment of the situation. This makes the debate on monetary policy decisions transparent and public. One should not be under any illusions here, the management of monetary policy will become more difficult under these circumstances compared to the past. In delicate situations, there will be no lack of criticism or counter-expertise. It will then be important to strictly uphold the principle of monetary policy autonomy, as the independence of the central bank is an essential prerequisite for monetary stability. 5 Let me now turn to the second innovation that has permanently changed the environment of our monetary policy, namely the introduction of the euro. 4. The difficult first year of the euro Just over 16 months ago, the common European currency became a reality. The expectations originally placed in the euro were high, as they hoped for a strong euro as a real alternative to the US dollar. Both the stability-oriented monetary policy of the European Central Bank and the comfortable surplus of the European current account should give the euro the hoped-for strength and solidity. The emergence of a broad and liquid European capital market should make the euro even more attractive as an investment currency. As is now known, the euro has not yet been able to meet the expectations placed in it. On the contrary, the European currency has lost around 20% of its value against the US dollar since its introduction. What are the reasons for this disappointing development? The most frequently cited argument for the weakness of the euro is the phenomenal state of the American economy, which shines with high growth rates while inflation remains very moderate. In the recent past, however, the European economy has also strengthened significantly, and growth rates in the two currency areas are expected to converge gradually in the current and next years. Nevertheless, the euro continues to depreciate. As a result, structural arguments for the weakness of the euro have now increasingly come to the fore. European economies continue to suffer from significant structural deficiencies, e.g. in the areas of labour market, social policy and taxation. These shortcomings prevent the economic potential of the euro area from fully unfolding. It is also striking that the weakening of the euro over the past year has not led to an increase in the surplus in the European current account; this is in contrast to the situation in Switzerland, where exports of goods and services have gained significant momentum. However, the euro is also burdened by problems relating to the functioning of monetary union itself. The economic differences between the individual member countries make it difficult to conduct a monetary policy that is adjusted for all members and lead to uncertainties about their future course. The ECB's external communication does not always help to clarify the situation, and the bank's internal decision-making process seems cumbersome and not very transparent. This negatively affects market psychology and leads to corresponding behavior of market participants. All these different points have so far prevented the euro from establishing itself as an attractive alternative to the dollar. 5. The relationship between the euro and the Swiss franc The exchange rate between the euro and the Swiss franc has remained surprisingly stable throughout 1999. This pronounced stability can be attributed to the extensive cyclical synchronisation between Switzerland and the euro zone, 6 in particular Germany, can be repatriated. Due to the similar economic situation, the Swiss National Bank and the European Central Bank have pursued virtually identical policies. Towards the end of last year, the economic parallelism between Switzerland and the euro zone weakened somewhat. In Switzerland, there were increasing signs of an imminent upswing, and the SNB felt compelled to correct the very expansionary course of its policy somewhat. In the meantime, expectations of picking up growth have been confirmed and even exceeded; the upswing in Switzerland also seems to be stronger at present than in the large countries of the euro zone. The SNB responded by further tightening its policy last March. The increased degree of restriction of monetary policy compared to Europe led to a certain strengthening of the Swiss franc against the euro. The slight appreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro thus corresponds to the underlying economic conditions, the so-called fundamentals. If the exchange rate continues to largely follow the fundamentals in the future - and the experience of the last 15 years with the DM suggests this - then the relationship between the franc and the euro should continue to develop in an orderly manner. The economic development of the Swiss economy is usually not too different from that in Europe. Switzerland is too closely intertwined economically with Europe for this: more than 50% of our exports go to the euro zone, while we source more than 70% of our imports from Europe. For the future, therefore, absolute exchange rate stability in the style of last year should not be expected; However, erratic fluctuations in the exchange rate are also unlikely. The ability of the ECB and the European authorities to maintain confidence in the euro will be central to further events in the foreign exchange market. 6. Monetary policy in a global environment: a provisional balance sheet The globalisation of financial markets and the emergence of a single currency in Europe pose significant challenges for the Policy of the Swiss National Bank. The free, cross-border movement of capital is a reality, the flow of information is global and electronic media enable permanent arbitrage. In Europe, the unification of the monetary landscape has led to a new, unique situation in which Switzerland is at the heart of a currency zone in which it does not participate. Markets are now even more able than in the past to punish inappropriate or seemingly inappropriate policies through appropriate responses. The SNB is meeting these challenges by stepping up its efforts to ensure transparency. This is also the direction of the innovations in the conduct of monetary policy introduced at the beginning of this year. The quest for greater transparency has led us to quantify the objective of price stability and to present our monetary policy stance by announcing a target range for the 3-month interest rate. We also regularly publish our assessment of the economic and monetary situation and the conclusions we draw from it for monetary policy. In this way, we give the public the means to understand and assess our measures. We expect this to increase efficiency in the conduct of our policy and a more rational reaction of the markets, 7 i.e. a strengthening of our ability to take the necessary measures to maintain price stability in Switzerland. Our monetary policy experience to date in a global environment is encouraging. Despite fully integrated markets and completely free movement of capital, the Swiss franc fluctuates to a reasonable extent. The exchange rate reflects the relative development of the fundamentals of the Swiss economy. This applies in particular to the exchange rate between the Swiss franc and the euro. Fears that the effects of financial globalisation and European integration could lead to a paralysis of Swiss monetary policy have therefore not come true.

Mai 2000 2 1. Eine Umwelt im Umbruch Die Stichworte Globalisierung, Deregulierung und Liberalisierung gehren wohl zu den meist gebrauchten Wrtern der neunziger Jahre und wirken schon beinahe etwas abgegriffen. Auch die schweizerische Nationalbank sieht sich einem neuen Umfeld gegenber. Im folgenden mchte ich erlutern, wie die Nationalbank ihre Geldpolitik an dieses neue, von Globalisierung und Euro geprgte Umfeld angepasst hat. 3 2. Geldpolitik: ein unverndertes Ziel ... Das Gesetz weist der Nationalbank die Aufgabe zu, eine Geldpolitik im Gesamtinteresse des Landes zu fhren.
