Title: Globalization and the Euro: The Future Role of the Swiss National Bank
text: Globalisation and the euro: the future role of the Swiss National Bank Georg Rich Swiss National Bank Lecture at the 2nd International Banking Forum 2000, Zurich, organizer EUROFORUM HandelsZeitung Konferenz AG, Zurich 2 1. Introduction Both in Switzerland and in other countries, the economic environment has changed fundamentally in the last ten to twenty years. The manifold efforts to integrate the national economies are showing their effects: A rapidly growing number of companies are no longer exclusively active in the national markets, but operate in a global environment. The introduction of the euro is an important milestone in the process of globalisation. The new single currency created a single money and capital market in the euro area. As a result, the same money market interest rates now prevail throughout the euro area and rates on the capital market have largely converged. The unification of the money and capital markets has been accompanied by the centralisation of monetary policy. The European Central Bank (ECB), which is responsible for issuing the single currency, has no choice but to conduct a single monetary policy for the whole euro area. In contrast to the formerly competent national central banks, the ECB can no longer take the needs of individual countries into account. The centralisation of the monetary policy decision-making process associated with the euro raises both hopes and fears. On the one hand, many people expect the euro to prove to be a catalyst for a sustainable economic revival of Europe. Some hope that the euro will also provide impetus for promoting and deepening political integration. On the other hand, the centralization of the monetary system is met with mistrust. It feeds the fear that the interests of individual countries will be 3 could get under the wheels. Of course, it is still too early to judge the advantages and disadvantages of the euro. However, I will return to individual aspects of this discussion in the course of my presentation. Compared to other forms of globalisation, the introduction of the euro is characterised by the fact that it is based on a political decision and thus reflects the will of the political authorities. Often, however, there are market forces behind globalization that steer national economies in international channels. At most, politics plays an indirect role in setting framework conditions that promote globalization or at least do not prevent it. The dismantling of tariffs and other trade barriers, the liberation of international capital movements from state shackles, the promotion of competition and other measures helped to promote the globalization of the economy. If globalization takes place within reasonable state framework conditions, it strengthens the efficiency of the economy and thus contributes to the welfare of the population. However, many people are struggling to see the economic benefits of globalization. They doubt that the market forces that promote globalization will help them to live a better life. In the face of such fears, the frequently expressed demand that the economy must subordinate itself to politics, and not politics to the economy, falls on fertile ground. Those who demand the supremacy of politics, however, should be aware that in a market economy companies have freedom that they are allowed to exploit, even if they do so national borders. 4 exceed. The demand that the economy must subordinate itself to politics cannot therefore be correct in this shortened form. Basically, the task of politics is to set framework conditions for the economic activities of companies and thus to clearly define the freedom open to private economic actors. Within the limits set by politics, market forces determine economic events. In today's globalised environment, it is of course possible that decisions that have a profound influence on economic events in Switzerland are made by foreign companies. Conversely, decisions by Swiss companies can have an impact on economic activity abroad. Decisions made by foreign companies need not contradict Swiss interests. After all, both foreign and Swiss companies are primarily oriented towards the global market; they do not act as stooges of their respective governments. Rather, the global market forces them to behave in a similar way, which is in the overall interest of our country, provided that the companies are in effective competition with each other and comply with the legal regulations issued by the Swiss authorities. Framework conditions that are set exclusively by nation states can of course cause problems in a global economic environment. Globally active companies take into account the different national regulations when choosing a location and settle where they want to do so for 5 they find the most favourable environment. It is often believed that globalisation requires harmonisation of national framework conditions. Companies should be able to struggle with equally long spikes in all countries. In the EU, the belief that the harmonisation of national government regulations is essential in a global economy is widespread. The centralisation of the monetary system within the EU is not least an expression of such harmonisation efforts. For example, with the introduction of the new common currency within the euro area, the exchange rate fluctuations that had repeatedly led to distortions of competition were made to disappear. Switzerland is also feeling the pressure to harmonise, both from the EU in particular and from globalisation in general. It often makes sense for Switzerland to seek to harmonise its state regulations with those of other countries. However, there is no need to harmonise everything and everything. Where independent regulations and institutions protect Switzerland's vital interests, harmonisation  globalisation and European integration or not  has no place. An independent approach need not impair Switzerland's competitiveness. If Switzerland offers more liberal and attractive solutions than abroad, an independent approach improves its locational qualities. After all, what good are Switzerland's equally long spikes if they are all dull? Globalization also arouses fears in many people for other reasons. Companies operating in global markets are feeling the effects of structural change 6 much more intense than those who can decouple themselves from undesirable international developments  at least to a certain extent. The restructuring, closures and mergers and acquisitions of companies testify to the severity of international competition. However, it is highly problematic to avoid these challenges by nurturing and caring for national gardens and protecting them from foreign competition. In the past, Switzerland always performed best when it fully faced international economic challenges. Sectors of the economy that tried to escape competition with the help of cartel agreements or state crutches weakened their competitive position in the long run. Just think of the current state of agriculture, the construction industry, the electricity industry and other previously protected sectors. The role of the state must not be to inhibit or even prevent structural change. It should limit itself to cushioning this  as far as possible  socially. Let me now flesh out these considerations on the basis of two specific issues. In the following, I will discuss the benefits of an autonomous Swiss monetary policy and the role of the Swiss financial centre in a globalised environment. 2. Benefits of an autonomous Swiss monetary policy A small country like Switzerland can basically choose between two monetary policy strategies: either Switzerland fixes the Swiss franc exchange rate against an important currency  such as the euro  or it controls an autonomous rate. If it opts for an autonomous strategy, it has no other way to 7 than to allow the exchange rate of the Swiss franc to fluctuate freely on the foreign exchange market. Fixing the exchange rate against the euro would mean that the SNB would lose its autonomy in monetary policy. If the exchange rate were to remain fixed forever at the level once fixed, interest rates on the Swiss money market would align with those of the euro area. There would no longer be any valid reasons for interest rate differentials  at least on the money market  as investors would regard the euro and the Swiss franc as perfect substitutes. The Swiss interest rate level would henceforth be determined by the ECB. It could not take Switzerland's needs into account when defining its monetary policy any more than it could take into account the interests of the individual euro area countries. The SNB became a shadow member of the ECB without being able to influence European monetary policy. Flexible exchange rates are therefore a prerequisite for monetary policy autonomy. Both strategies have advantages and disadvantages. If the SNB chooses the autonomous strategy, it can in principle tailor its monetary policy to Swiss needs. However, with the autonomous strategy, it runs the risk of increasing the exchange rate fluctuations of the Swiss franc. This reduces the international competitiveness of Swiss companies, as the uncertainties associated with price volatility increase the risk of business mistakes. If price fluctuations are eliminated, this facilitates entrepreneurial planning, but  as I have already explained  the SNB loses its monetary policy autonomy. 8 However, attempts are repeatedly made to eliminate the disadvantages of fixed and flexible exchange rates within the framework of mixed systems. For example, there are many countries that keep the exchange rate of their currency as stable as possible, but are willing to adjust it if necessary. Other countries are trying to maintain their monetary autonomy despite fixed exchange rates by controlling international capital movements, thereby driving a wedge between interest rates at home and abroad. For Switzerland, however, such mixing systems are not a reasonable alternative. They fit poorly into a world of global financial markets. Such markets can only function satisfactorily if there are clear rules of the game. If the authorities accept the globalisation of their national financial markets, they must also allow the free movement of capital and refrain from returning to controls if necessary. This is because suddenly introduced controls cause high economic costs once the providers and consumers of financial services have adapted to the global orientation of these markets. The free movement of capital has another consequence. It also means that a mix of fixed and flexible exchange rates works poorly in practice. Under such a system, the authorities often strive to keep the exchange rate stable for as long as possible. If they cling to the fixed price, they run the risk of causing speculative capital movements. If they delay the adjustment for too long, investors usually know that the exchange rate can only change in one direction. Speculation on the foreign exchange market thus becomes almost risk-free. The speculative capital movements triggered by investors can take on massive proportions, which 9 usually force the authorities to release the exchange rate. For Switzerland, the choice is therefore clear. Against the background of global financial markets, it must clearly opt for fixed or flexible exchange rates. With mixing systems, it only charges itself with problems. Switzerland opted for flexible exchange rates as early as the beginning of 1973. Since then, the Swiss franc has generally been determined by market forces (Figure 1). The SNB is thus in a position to conduct an autonomous monetary policy. However, this need not mean that the SNB steers a course that is always different from that of its important sister institution, the ECB. The correct dosage of monetary policy depends to a large extent on the economic environment in which the SNB is embedded. Only if the economic situation in Switzerland differs from that of the euro area is it appropriate for the SNB to steer a different monetary policy stance than the ECB. As Switzerland is closely intertwined economically with the euro area, the SNB is likely to pursue a similar monetary policy to the ECB. Even before the introduction of the euro, the similarity of the economic environment meant that there was often a great deal of agreement between the snb's monetary policy and that of the Deutsche Bundesbank. This repeatedly leads analysts to claim that the SNB does not in fact pursue an autonomous monetary policy, but leans closely on the ECB or the Bundesbank. Switzerland would lose little if it completely gave up its monetary policy autonomy by changing the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against 10 the euro permanently fixed. After being linked to the euro, the SNB would hardly control a significantly different exchange rate than under an autonomous approach. The peg to the euro would also lead to greater exchange rate stability, which would facilitate the planning of export and import companies. What is to be made of this claim? Although the SNB is likely to often steer a similar course to the ECB, the benefits of our monetary policy autonomy should not be downplayed. If Switzerland fixed the Swiss franc exchange rate against the euro, this would have two important consequences for our economy: On the one hand, as I have already explained, Swiss monetary policy would be set in Frankfurt and would no longer take into account Switzerland's specific needs. On the other hand, after the connection, Swiss capital market and mortgage interest rates, which are low compared to other countries, would rise permanently and approach the usual level in the euro area. Swiss companies, households and public bodies would thus have to accept a permanent increase in their debt interest rates. Even though there is often a great deal of agreement between Swiss and European monetary policy, the SNB should not forego the possibility of autonomously changing domestic money market interest rates. From time to time, it could feel compelled to steer a course that deviates from the ECB. This has already been the case in the past with regard to the Deutsche Bundesbank. In the second half of the nineties, for example, the SNB conducted a more expansionary monetary policy than the Bundesbank. 11 and later the ECB. It reacted to the fact that the recession in Switzerland left deeper traces than in our neighbouring countries, thus creating a real risk of deflation. Thanks to its ability to change domestic money market interest rates autonomously, the SNB has been able to take account of specific economic developments in Switzerland. Conversely, in the recent past it has been able to tighten monetary policy more than the European Central Bank. It thus took into account the stronger economic recovery than expected and the growing risk of inflation in Switzerland (Figure 2). The comparatively low level of interest rates gives Switzerland a competitive advantage that it should not give up lightly. However, analysts repeatedly predict the demise of the interest rate island of Switzerland. They claim that swiss interest rates will sooner or later adapt to those in the euro area, regardless of whether the SNB maintains its monetary policy autonomy. Despite such forecasts, however, there is little sign of a levelling of interest rate differentials between Switzerland and the euro area. Although the gap with Germany and the euro area has narrowed somewhat, at least nominally since the transition to the single currency (Figure 3).1 However.dem, this development mainly reflects temporary influences on the 1 The figure shows the difference between nominal and real returns on German and Swiss federal bonds. For 1999, the real interest rate differential was reduced by the Euro/Franc exchange rate and the harmonised consumer price index for the euro area calculated. 12 Swiss interest rate level. As I have already said, the SNB has tightened monetary policy more than the European Central Bank in recent months. It is therefore not surprising that the interest rate differential with the euro area narrowed somewhat. There are therefore no signs that the interest island will disappear. Rather, investors still see the Swiss franc as an attractive alternative to the euro and other major currencies. I will come back to this point in the last part of my presentation. Of course, investors will only use the franc for diversification purposes as long as they consider it a currency in its own right. The Swiss franc would lose its autonomy if the authorities permanently fixed its exchange rate against the euro. However, the independence of the Swiss franc does not presuppose a high variability of the exchange rate. Some analysts were influenced by the strong appreciation of the Swiss franc from 1983 to 1985 and were surprised by the remarkable stability of the euro/franc ratio, which lasted until spring 2000. They believed that the high degree of price stability would make the interest rate island of Switzerland disappear over time. The more stable the exchange rate, the lower the probability that investors will still see the Swiss franc as a currency in its own right. However, the independence of the Swiss franc will only be called into question if the SNB deliberately strives for a stable exchange rate. If, on the other hand, market forces are primarily responsible for stability, the interest rate island of Switzerland does not need to disappear. Because with fundamentally flexible exchange rates 13 investors must always expect an adjustment of the euro/franc ratio, even if it has remained stable over a longer period of time. Longer periods of stable exchange rates have already occurred in the past without heralding the end of the interest island of Switzerland. Figure 1 shows that the Swiss franc's exchange rate against the Deutschmark moved only slightly from 1983 to 1987, despite a massive temporary appreciation of the dollar. Furthermore, from 1985 to 1987, Swiss money market interest rates were roughly at the German level (Figure 2). Nevertheless, the interest rate differential with Germany, which tended to be 2-3 percentage points in the long-term range in the eighties, was maintained (Figure 3). Even then, numerous analysts claimed that the SNB was pursuing an exchange rate target. This was not true. Rather, the stable price development was due to market forces. These considerations indicate that the interest island of Switzerland is not yet doomed. Thus, there are no convincing reasons to abandon Switzerland's monetary policy autonomy. Despite globalisation and the euro, the benefits that Switzerland could derive from monetary alignment with the euro area are not obvious. 3. Impact of globalisation and the euro on the Swiss financial market As already mentioned, the transition to the single currency created a single money and capital market in the euro area. Most analysts expected the introduction of the euro to affect European bonds and 14 Stock markets will be boosted. The removal of barriers between national capital markets would create uniform and highly liquid European markets for bonds and equities. This will strengthen Europe's importance as a credit intermediary and push the dollar's role as an international transaction and reserve currency into the background. Some analysts went so far as to claim that the euro would displace the dollar as an international reserve currency. Furthermore, it was expected that with the emergence of a highly liquid capital market, the importance of banks as credit intermediaries  as in the United States  would decrease. Different opinions were expressed on the impact of the euro on the Swiss financial centre. Some analysts believed that the emergence of liquid and efficient money and capital markets in the euro area would lead to a marginalisation of the Swiss financial centre over time. The Swiss franc will lose interest for international investors and will hardly be able to hold its own against the euro. Other analysts still saw opportunities for the Swiss financial centre. They were of the opinion that the Swiss franc would continue to play a useful role in the future for investors who want to diversify their portfolios in terms of currency. With regard to euro area financial markets, these predictions turned out to be at least partially correct. For example, the euro area bond market exploded as a result of the introduction of the single currency. The euro bond market proved to be particularly attractive for private debtors. Both debtors within and 15 outside the euro area, the euro bond market was actively used. In the period from July 1998 to December 1999, non-euro area debtors issued one fifth of their bonds in euro, i.e. almost twice as much as they had issued in previous currencies.2 By contrast, the impact of the euro was limited on equity markets, which continue to be characterised by strong segmentation along national borders. Nor was the euro able to break the dominance of the American dollar as a reserve currency. The Swiss franc also held its own despite competition from the euro. As I have already explained, the continued existence of the interest rate island of Switzerland indicates that international investors continue to use our currency for diversification purposes. New figures compiled by the SNB on the monetary composition of securities custody accounts managed by Swiss banks confirm this fact. Figure 4 shows the currency breakdown of securities custody accounts held by domestic and foreign clients. At the end of 1999, domestic clients held 62% of their securities holdings in Swiss francs, while the share of our currency among foreign clients was 35%. The opinion is often expressed that foreign customers hold only a small proportion of their securities holdings in Swiss francs. This view is obviously refuted by the SNB's figures. It is also interesting to note that the monetary breakdown of the 2 See Bank for International Settlements, 70th Annual Report, Basel 2000, p. 144. 16 Securities holdings of nationals and foreigners have hardly changed since the end of 1998 (Figure 5). The shares attributable to Swiss francs fell slightly, while the dollar, the euro and the other currencies gained. It is possible that these shifts in shares partly reflect the sharp rise in the dollar's exchange rate against the euro and the Swiss franc. There can therefore be no question of the franc being displaced by the euro. Rather, Figures 4 and 5 lead to the opposite conclusion. They suggest that our currency still has significant significance for international investors. That is why the SNB's offer of an independent and stable currency not only serves the Swiss economy as a whole, but also strengthens the international competitiveness of the domestic financial centre. As a result of its small size, the Swiss capital market does not have the liquidity of its counterpart in the euro area. Since the introduction of the single currency, the euro bond market in particular has become more attractive to debtors in a similar way to that of the fixed-income dollar bond market. However, this need not mean that the euro will banish the Swiss capital market to complete insignificance. The swiss franc fixed-income bond market is likely to continue to play a useful niche role in the future. Of course, banks can issue bonds denominated in euros or dollars on the Swiss capital market. In the past, such transactions were severely hampered by stamp duty; the urgent measures taken by the Swiss 17 However, the authorities of March 1999 in the area of the turnover tax have greatly loosened these shackles. Nevertheless, I do not believe that bond issuance in dollars or euros will play a major role on the domestic capital market. The major Swiss banks are already heavily involved in this business through their subsidiaries in London and other places. In any case, it is remarkable that local financial institutions in the euro area have so far benefited only to a limited extent from the creation of the single European capital market. Their strengths lay above all in their knowledge of the national characteristics of the capital markets. This know-how is no longer in demand today within the framework of the single euro capital market. On the other hand, those institutions that have already had a global orientation have a competitive advantage. These include above all the major American securities houses, the major Swiss banks and a few globally oriented banks in the euro area. They also have a good knowledge of the market for private debtor bonds, which, as I have already said, is developing particularly dynamically in the euro area. Many local banks in the euro area, on the other hand, specialise mainly in the issuance of sovereign bonds. The impact of the single currency on the equity markets of the euro area and Switzerland is still hardly foreseeable. The press repeatedly reports on projects of stock exchange mergers or cooperation agreements under stock exchanges. There is no doubt that there are too many stock exchanges in Europe. Consolidation in the stock exchange sector is imperative not only in view of the euro, but also in view of the globalisation of the financial markets. However, this consolidation encounters several obstacles: 18  Centralization of exchange trading is not appropriate in all circumstances. It makes sense for "blue chips" stocks, but not for local stocks, which are likely to be traded on local stock exchanges in the future.  Centralization of trading platforms is not enough. A particularly thorny task is the standardization of the very different systems for securities settlement.  In the case of supranational stock exchanges, the question arises as to how they should be supervised by the national authorities.  Finally, reform efforts in the area of corporate governance must continue in Europe so that the stock market can play its proper economic role. The Swiss stock exchange certainly has a chance of holding its own in the upcoming consolidation process. Its strengths include securities settlement and the progressive conditions of corporate governance in Switzerland compared to our neighbouring countries. The future development of European equity markets is likely to raise fascinating questions. 4. Conclusion The introduction of the single currency has fundamentally changed the monetary policy framework in the euro area. Today, there is a single money and capital market in the euro area. This also means that the ECB must conduct a single monetary policy across the euro area. And 19 the euro and globalisation pose a variety of challenges for the Swiss economy. The SNB benefits the Swiss economy most if it continues to adhere to its monetary policy aimed at ensuring price stability and tries to fulfil its stability mandate autonomously. Beliesse sie den Wechselkurs fr immer auf dem einmal fixierten Niveau, wrden sich die Zinsen am schweizerischen Geldmarkt an jene des Eurogebiets anpassen. Fr Zinsunterschiede  zumindest am Geldmarkt  gbe es keine stichhaltigen Grnde mehr, da die Anleger den Euro und den Franken als vollkommene Substitute betrachten wrden. Das schweizerische Zinsniveau wrde fortan von der EZB bestimmt. Diese knnte bei der Festlegung ihrer Geldpolitik ebenso wenig die Bedrfnisse der Schweiz bercksichtigen, wie sie den Interessen der einzelnen Lnder des Eurogebiets Rechnung tragen kann. Die Nationalbank wandelte sich zu einem Schattenmitglied der EZB, ohne indessen die europische Geldpolitik beeinflussen zu knnen. Flexible Wechselkurse bilden somit die Voraussetzung fr geldpolitische Autonomie. Beide Strategien besitzen Vor- und Nachteile. Whlt die Nationalbank die autonome Strategie, kann sie ihre Geldpolitik grundstzlich massgeschneidert auf die schweizerischen Bedrfnisse ausrichten. Allerdings luft sie mit der autonomen Strategie Gefahr, die Wechselkursschwankungen des Schweizer Frankens zu verstrken. Dies vermindert die internationale Konkurrenzfhigkeit der schweizerischen Unternehmen, da die mit der Kursvolatilitt verbundenen Unsicherheiten die Gefahr unternehmerischer Fehlentscheide erhhen. Werden die Kursschwankungen ausgeschaltet, erleichtert dies zwar die unternehmerische Planung, aber die Nationalbank verliert  wie ich schon ausfhrte  ihre geldpolitische Autonomie. 8 Allerdings wird immer wieder versucht, im Rahmen von Mischsystemen, die Nachteile fixer und flexibler Wechselkurse zu beseitigen. So gibt es viele Lnder, die den Kurs ihrer Whrung soweit als mglich stabil halten, aber bereit sind, ihn bei Bedarf anzupassen. Andere Lnder versuchen, ihre geldpolitische Autonomie trotz fixer Wechselkurse zu bewahren, indem sie die internationalen Kapitalbewegungen kontrollieren und damit einen Keil zwischen die Zinsen im Inund Ausland treiben. Fr die Schweiz stellen solche Mischsysteme indessen keine vernnftige Alternative dar. Sie passen schlecht in eine Welt globaler Finanzmrkte. Solche Mrkte knnen nur befriedigend funktionieren, wenn klare Spielregeln bestehen. Akzeptieren die Behrden die Globalisierung ihrer nationalen Finanzmrkte, mssen sie auch die Freiheit des internationalen Kapitalverkehrs zulassen und darauf verzichten, bei Bedarf zu Kontrollen zurckzukehren. Denn pltzlich eingefhrte Kontrollen verursachen hohe volkswirtschaftliche Kosten, wenn sich die Anbieter und Konsumenten von Finanzdienstleistungen einmal der globalen Ausrichtung dieser Mrkte angepasst haben. Der freie Kapitalverkehr hat eine weitere Konsequenz. Er fhrt auch dazu, dass ein Mix von fixen und flexiblen Wechselkursen in der Praxis schlecht funktioniert. Unter einem solchen System sind die Behrden hufig bestrebt, den Wechselkurs mglichst lange stabil zu halten. Klammern sie sich an den fixen Kurs, laufen sie Gefahr, spekulative Kapitalbewegungen zu verursachen. Zgern sie die Anpassung zu lange hinaus, wissen die Anleger in der Regel, dass sich der Wechselkurs nur in die eine Richtung verndern kann. Die Spekulation am Devisenmarkt wird damit nahezu risikolos. Die von den Anlegern ausgelsten spekulativen Kapitalbewegungen knnen massive Proportionen annehmen, welche 9 die Behrden zumeist zu einer Freigabe des Wechselkurses zwingen. Fr die Schweiz ist die Wahl somit eindeutig. Vor dem Hintergrund globaler Finanzmrkte muss sie sich klar fr fixe oder flexible Wechselkurse entscheiden. Mit Mischsystemen ldt sie sich nur Probleme auf. Die Schweiz entschied sich schon Anfang 1973 fr flexible Wechselkurse. Seither wird der Kurs des Schweizer Frankens grundstzlich durch die Marktkrfte bestimmt (Abbildung 1). Die Nationalbank ist damit in der Lage, eine autonome Geldpolitik zu fhren. Dies braucht indessen nicht zu bedeuten, dass die Nationalbank einen Kurs steuert, der sich stets von jenem ihres wichtigen Schwesterinstituts, der EZB, unterscheidet. Die richtige Dosierung der Geldpolitik hngt nmlich wesentlich vom wirtschaftlichen Umfeld ab, in das die Nationalbank eingebettet ist. Nur wenn sich die konjunkturellen Verhltnisse der Schweiz von jenen des Eurogebiets unterscheiden, ist es fr die Nationalbank zweckmssig, einen anderen geldpolitischen Kurs als die EZB zu steuern. Da die Schweiz wirtschaftlich eng mit dem Eurogebiet verflochten ist, drfte die Nationalbank hufig eine hnliche Geldpolitik verfolgen wie die EZB. Die hnlichkeit des wirtschaftlichen Umfelds hatte schon vor der Einfhrung des Euro zur Folge, dass zwischen der Geldpolitik der Nationalbank und jener der Deutschen Bundesbank oft eine grosse bereinstimmung bestand. Dies verleitet Analysten immer wieder zur Behauptung, die Nationalbank betreibe in Wirklichkeit keine autonome Geldpolitik, sondern lehne sich eng an die EZB bzw. die Bundesbank an. Die Schweiz verlre wenig, wenn sie ihre geldpolitische Autonomie gnzlich aufgbe, indem sie den Wechselkurs des Frankens gegenber 10 dem Euro dauerhaft fixierte. Die Nationalbank wrde nach der Anbindung an den Euro kaum einen wesentlich anderen Kurs als unter einem autonomen Vorgehen steuern. Die Anbindung an den Euro wrde ferner zu einer grsseren Wechselkursstabilitt fhren, welche die Planung der im Export und Import ttigen Unternehmen erleichtern wrde. Was ist von dieser Behauptung zu halten? Obwohl die Nationalbank wahrscheinlich hufig einen hnlichen Kurs wie die EZB steuern wird, sollte der Nutzen unserer geldpolitischen Autonomie nicht heruntergespielt werden. Fixierte die Schweiz den Frankenkurs gegenber dem Euro, ergben sich daraus zwei wichtige Konsequenzen fr unsere Wirtschaft: Zum einen wrde die schweizerische Geldpolitik  wie ich schon ausfhrte  in Frankfurt festgelegt und trge den spezifischen Bedrfnissen der Schweiz nicht mehr Rechnung. Zum anderen wrden nach der Anbindung die im Vergleich zum Ausland tiefen schweizerischen Kapitalmarkt- und Hypothekarzinsen dauerhaft ansteigen und sich dem im Eurogebiet gngigen Niveau annhern. Die schweizerischen Unternehmen, Haushalte und ffentlichen Krperschaften mssten damit einen permanenten Anstieg ihrer Schuldzinsen hinnehmen. Auch wenn zwischen schweizerischer und europischer Geldpolitik hufig eine grosse bereinstimmung bestehen drfte, sollte die Nationalbank auf die Mglichkeit, die inlndischen Geldmarktzinsen autonom zu verndern, nicht verzichten. Denn sie knnte sich von Zeit zu Zeit veranlasst sehen, einen von der EZB abweichenden Kurs zu steuern. Dies war schon in der Vergangenheit in Bezug auf die Deutsche Bundesbank der Fall. So fhrte die Nationalbank in der zweiten Hlfte der Neunzigerjahre eine expansivere Geldpolitik als die Bundesbank 11 und spter die EZB. Sie reagierte auf die Tatsache, dass die Rezession in der Schweiz tiefere Spuren als in unseren Nachbarlndern hinterliess und damit eine eigentliche Deflationsgefahr heraufbeschwor. Dank ihrer Fhigkeit, die inlndischen Geldmarktzinsen autonom zu verndern, konnte die Nationalbank auf die spezifischen wirtschaftlichen Entwicklungen in der Schweiz Rcksicht nehmen. Umgekehrt war sie in der jngsten Vergangenheit in der Lage, die Geldpolitik strker als die Europische Zentralbank zu straffen. Sie trug damit der ber Erwarten krftigen Konjunkturerholung und der wachsenden Inflationsgefahr in der Schweiz Rechnung (Abbildung 2). Das vergleichsweise niedrige Zinsniveau verschafft der Schweiz einen Wettbewerbsvorteil, auf den sie nicht leichtfertig verzichten sollte. Allerdings sagen Analysten immer wieder den Untergang der Zinsinsel Schweiz voraus. Sie behaupten, das schweizerische Zinsniveau werde sich frher oder spter an jenes im Eurogebiet anpassen und zwar unabhngig davon, ob die Nationalbank an ihrer geldpolitischen Autonomie festhalte. Von einer Nivellierung der Zinsunterschiede zwischen der Schweiz und dem Eurogebiet ist trotz solcher Voraussagen indessen wenig zu verspren. Der Abstand zu Deutschland bzw. dem Eurogebiet hat sich zwar seit dem bergang zur gemeinsamen Whrung zumindest nominell etwas verringert (Abbildung 3).1 Diese Entwicklung widerspiegelt aber vor allem temporre Einflsse auf das 1 Die Abbildung zeigt den Unterschied der nominellen und realen Renditen auf deutschen und schweizerischen Bundesobligationen. Fr 1999 wurde die reale Zinsdifferenz aufgrund des Euro/Franken-Kurses und des harmonisierten Konsumentenpreisindexes fr das Eurogebiet berechnet. 12 schweizerische Zinsniveau. Wie ich schon ausfhrte, straffte die Nationalbank die Geldpolitik in den letzten Monaten strker als die Europische Zentralbank. Deshalb ist es nicht erstaunlich, dass sich der Zinsabstand zum Eurogebiet etwas verengte. Es bestehen somit keine Anzeichen, dass die Zinsinsel verschwinden wird. Vielmehr betrachten die Anleger den Schweizer Franken nach wie vor als attraktive Alternative zum Euro und anderen wichtigen Whrungen. Ich werde auf diesen Punkt im letzten Teil meines Referates nochmals zu sprechen kommen. Natrlich werden die Anleger den Franken nur solange fr Diversifikationszwecke verwenden, als sie ihn fr eine eigenstndige Whrung halten. Der Franken wrde seine Eigenstndigkeit verlieren, wenn die Behrden seinen Kurs gegenber dem Euro dauerhaft fixierten. Die Eigenstndigkeit des Frankens setzt aber nicht eine hohe Variabilitt des Wechselkurses voraus. Manche Analysten standen unter dem Eindruck der starken Frankenaufwertung von 1983 bis 1985 und waren von der bemerkenswerten Stabilitt der Euro/Franken-Relation, die bis zum Frhjahr 2000 anhielt, berrascht. Sie glaubten, der hohe Grad an Kursstabilitt werde die Zinsinsel Schweiz mit der Zeit zum Verschwinden bringen. Je stabiler sich der Wechselkurs verhalte, umso geringer sei die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass die Anleger den Franken noch als eigenstndige Whrung anschauten. Die Eigenstndigkeit des Frankens wird indessen nur in Frage gestellt, wenn die Nationalbank bewusst einen stabilen Wechselkurs anstrebt. Sind dagegen die Marktkrfte vornehmlich fr die Stabilitt verantwortlich, braucht die Zinsinsel Schweiz nicht zu verschwinden. Denn bei grundstzlich flexiblen Wechselkursen 13 mssen die Anleger stets mit einer Anpassung der Euro/Franken-Relation rechnen, selbst wenn sich diese ber lngere Zeit hinweg stabil verhalten hat. Lngere Phasen stabiler Wechselkurse traten schon in der Vergangenheit auf, ohne dass das Ende der Zinsinsel Schweiz eingelutet wurde. Aus der Abbildung 1 ist ersichtlich, dass sich der Kurs des Frankens gegenber der D-Mark von 1983 bis 1987  trotz einer massiven temporren Aufwertung des Dollars  nur geringfgig bewegte. Ferner befanden sich die schweizerischen Geldmarktzinsen von 1985 bis 1987 ungefhr auf dem deutschen Niveau (Abbildung 2). Dennoch blieb der Zinsabstand zu Deutschland, der im langfristigen Bereich in den Achtzigerjahren tendenziell 2-3 Prozentpunkte betrug, erhalten (Abbildung 3). Schon damals behaupteten zahlreiche Analysten, die Nationalbank verfolge ein Wechselkursziel. Dies entsprach nicht den Tatsachen. Der stabile Kursverlauf war vielmehr den Marktkrften zu verdanken. Diese berlegungen deuten darauf hin, dass die Zinsinsel Schweiz noch nicht dem Untergang geweiht ist. Somit gibt es keine berzeugenden Grnde, die fr eine Aufgabe der schweizerischen geldpolitischen Autonomie sprechen. Trotz Globalisierung und Euro liegt der Nutzen, den die Schweiz aus einer monetren Angleichung an das Eurogebiet ziehen knnte, nicht auf der Hand. 3. Wirkung von Globalisierung und Euro auf den schweizerischen Finanzmarkt Mit dem bergang zur gemeinsamen Whrung entstand im Eurogebiet  wie schon erwhnt  ein einheitlicher Geld- und Kapitalmarkt. Die meisten Analysten erwarteten, dass die Einfhrung des Euro die europischen Obligationen- und 14 Aktienmrkte beflgeln werde. Mit dem Wegfall der Schranken zwischen den nationalen Kapitalmrkten wrden einheitliche und hoch liquide europische Mrkte fr Obligationen und Aktien entstehen. Dies werde die Bedeutung Europas als Kreditvermittler strken und die Rolle des Dollars als internationale Transaktionsund Reservewhrung in den Hintergrund drngen. Einige Analysten gingen so weit zu behaupten, der Euro werde den Dollar als internationale Reservewhrung verdrngen. Ferner wurde erwartet, dass mit dem Entstehen eines hoch liquiden Kapitalmarktes die Bedeutung der Banken als Kreditvermittler  wie in den Vereinigten Staaten  sinken werde. ber die Auswirkungen des Euro auf den schweizerischen Finanzplatz wurden unterschiedliche Meinungen geussert. Einige Analysten glaubten, die Entstehung liquider und leistungsfhiger Geld- und Kapitalmrkte im Eurogebiet werde mit der Zeit zu einer Marginalisierung des Finanzplatzes Schweiz fhren. Der Schweizer Franken werde fr die internationalen Anleger an Interesse verlieren und sich gegenber dem Euro kaum behaupten knnen. Andere Analysten sahen immer noch Chancen fr den Finanzplatz Schweiz. Sie waren der Auffassung, der Franken werde fr Anleger, die ihre Portefeuilles whrungsmssig diversifizieren mchten, auch insknftig eine ntzliche Rolle spielen knnen. In Bezug auf die Finanzmrkte des Eurogebiets entpuppten sich diese Voraussagen zumindest teilweise als richtig. So entwickelte sich der Obligationenmarkt des Eurogebiets als Folge der Einfhrung der gemeinsamen Whrung explosionsartig. Besonders attraktiv erwies sich der EuroObligationenmarkt fr private Schuldner. Sowohl Schuldner innerhalb als auch 15 ausserhalb des Eurogebiets nahmen den Euro-Obligationenmarkt rege in Anspruch. In der Periode Juli 1998 bis Dezember 1999 begaben die ausserhalb des Eurogebiets ansssigen Schuldner einen Fnftel ihrer Obligationen in Euro, d.h. fast doppelt so viel, wie sie in den Vorgngerwhrungen emittiert hatten.2 Dagegen wirkte sich der Euro nur beschrnkt auf die Aktienmrkte aus, die sich nach wie vor durch eine starke Segmentierung entlang der Landesgrenzen auszeichnen. Der Euro vermochte auch nicht die Dominanz des amerikanischen Dollars als Reservewhrung zu brechen. Der Schweizer Franken konnte sich trotz der Konkurrenz des Euro ebenfalls gut behaupten. Wie ich schon ausfhrte, deutet der Fortbestand der Zinsinsel Schweiz darauf hin, dass internationale Anleger unsere Whrung nach wie vor fr Diversifikationszwecke verwenden. Neue von der Nationalbank erhobene Zahlen ber die whrungsmssige Zusammensetzung der Wertschriftendepots, die von den Schweizer Banken verwaltet werden, besttigen diesen Sachverhalt. Die Abbildung 4 zeigt die whrungsmssige Gliederung der von inlndischen und auslndischen Kunden gehaltenen Wertschriftendepots. Ende 1999 hielten die inlndischen Kunden 62% ihrer Wertpapierbestnde in Schweizer Franken, whrend der Anteil unserer Whrung bei den auslndischen Kunden 35% betrug. Hufig wird die Meinung geussert, auslndische Kunden hielten nur einen geringen Anteil ihrer Wertpapierbestnde in Schweizer Franken. Diese Auffassung wird durch die Zahlen der Nationalbank offensichtlich widerlegt. Interessant ist auch die Tatsache, dass sich die whrungsmssige Gliederung der 2 Vgl. Die auf Franken entfallenden Anteile nahmen etwas ab, whrend der Dollar, der Euro und die brigen Whrungen hinzu gewannen. Es ist mglich, dass diese Verschiebungen in den Anteilen teilweise den krftigen Anstieg des Dollarkurses gegenber dem Euro und dem Franken widerspiegeln. Von einer Verdrngung des Frankens durch den Euro kann somit keine Rede sein. Die Abbildungen 4 und 5 fhren vielmehr zum gegenteiligen Schluss. Sie deuten darauf hin, dass unsere Whrung fr die internationalen Anleger immer noch eine erhebliche Bedeutung besitzt. Deshalb leistet die Nationalbank mit ihrem Angebot einer eigenstndigen und stabilen Whrung nicht nur der schweizerischen Wirtschaft insgesamt einen Dienst, sondern sie strkt auch die internationale Konkurrenzfhigkeit des inlndischen Finanzplatzes. Der schweizerische Kapitalmarkt verfgt  als Folge seiner geringen Grsse  nicht ber die Liquiditt seines Gegenspielers im Eurogebiet. Seit der Einfhrung der gemeinsamen Whrung hat insbesondere der Euro-Obligationenmarkt fr die Schuldner eine hnliche Attraktivitt erlangt wie der Markt fr festverzinsliche Dollaranleihen. Dies braucht indessen nicht zu bedeuten, dass der Euro den schweizerischen Kapitalmarkt in die vllige Bedeutungslosigkeit verbannen wird. Der Markt fr festverzinsliche Schweizer Franken-Anleihen drfte auch in Zukunft eine ntzliche Nischenfunktion erfllen. Natrlich knnen die Banken am schweizerischen Kapitalmarkt Anleihen, die auf Euro oder Dollar lauten, begeben. Frher wurden solche Geschfte durch die Stempelsteuer stark behindert; die dringlichen Massnahmen der schweizerischen 17 Behrden von Mrz 1999 im Bereich der Umsatzabgabe haben indessen diese Fesseln stark gelockert. Dennoch glaube ich nicht, dass Obligationenemissionen in Dollar oder Euro am inlndischen Kapitalmarkt eine grosse Rolle spielen werden. Die schweizerischen Grossbanken sind an diesem Geschft schon ber ihre Tchter in London und anderen Orten stark beteiligt. Es ist ohnehin bemerkenswert, dass die lokalen Finanzinstitute im Eurogebiet von der Schaffung des einheitlichen europischen Kapitalmarktes bis jetzt nur beschrnkt profitiert haben. Ihre Strken bestanden vor allem in ihrer Kenntnis der nationalen Eigenheiten der Kapitalmrkte. Dieses Know-how ist heute im Rahmen des einheitlichen Euro-Kapitalmarktes nicht mehr gefragt. Dagegen verfgen jene Institute ber einen Wettbewerbsvorteil, die schon bisher global ausgerichtet waren. Dazu gehren vor allem die grossen amerikanischen Wertschriftenhuser, die schweizerischen Grossbanken sowie einige wenige global orientierte Banken des Eurogebiets. Sie besitzen auch gute Kenntnisse des Marktes fr Obligationen privater Schuldner, der sich im Eurogebiet  wie ich schon ausfhrte  besonders dynamisch entwickelt. Viele lokale Banken des Eurogebiets sind dagegen vor allem auf die Emission staatlicher Schuldverschreibungen spezialisiert. Noch wenig absehbar sind die Auswirkungen der gemeinsamen Whrung auf die Aktienmrkte des Eurogebiets und der Schweiz. Die Presse berichtet immer wieder ber Projekte von Brsenzusammenschlssen oder Kooperationsabkommen unter Brsen. In Europa existieren zweifelsohne zu viele Brsen. Eine Konsolidierung im Brsenbereich drngt sich nicht nur angesichts des Euro, sondern auch aufgrund der Globalisierung der Finanzmrkte auf. Allerdings stsst diese Konsolidierung auf verschiedene Hindernisse: 18  Eine Zentralisierung des Brsenhandels ist nicht unter allen Umstnden angebracht. Sie macht fr "blue chips"-Aktien Sinn, aber nicht fr lokale Werte, die auch insknftig an lokalen Brsen gehandelt werden drften.  Die Zentralisierung der Handelsplattformen gengt nicht. Eine besonders dornige Aufgabe besteht in der Vereinheitlichung der hchst unterschiedlichen Systeme fr die Wertschriftenabwicklung.  Bei supranationalen Brsen stellt sich die Frage, wie sie von den nationalen Behrden beaufsichtigt werden sollten.  Schliesslich mssen in Europa die Reformbestrebungen im Bereich der "corporate governance" fortgesetzt werden, damit der Aktienmarkt die ihm gebhrende volkswirtschaftliche Rolle spielen kann. Die Schweizer Brse hat durchaus Chancen, sich im bevorstehenden Konsolidierungsprozess behaupten zu knnen. Zu ihren Strken zhlt die Wertschriftenabwicklung und die in der Schweiz im Vergleich zu unseren Nachbarlndern fortschrittlichen Verhltnisse der "corporate governance". Die knftige Entwicklung der europischen Aktienmrkte drfte faszinierende Fragen aufwerfen. 4. Schlussbemerkung Die Einfhrung der gemeinsamen Whrung hat die geldpolitischen Rahmenbedingungen im Eurogebiet grundlegend gendert. Heute besteht im Eurogebiet ein einheitlicher Geld- und Kapitalmarkt. Dies bedeutet auch, dass die EZB eine fr das gesamte Eurogebiet einheitliche Geldpolitik fhren muss. Sowohl 19 der Euro als auch die Globalisierung stellen die schweizerische Wirtschaft vor vielfltige Herausforderungen. Die Nationalbank ntzt der schweizerischen Wirtschaft am meisten, wenn sie weiterhin an ihrer auf die Gewhrleistung der Preisstabilitt ausgerichteten Geldpolitik festhlt und versucht, ihren Stabilittsauftrag autonom zu erfllen. Title: The Swiss banking industry in the midst of profound changes
text: The Swiss banking industry in upheaval Prof. Bruno Gehrig Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Lecture at the Swiss Banking School Zurich, 26 September 2000 Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Swiss Banking School Alumni, the quality of a school can be recognized on the one hand by the knowledge of its graduates, on the other hand by its cohesion as a sign of its - fashionably expressed social competence. You have already sufficiently demonstrated your professional competence in your work; Your social skills are demonstrated by your numerous appearances on this social occasion. I would like to thank you very much for letting me be in your round and giving me the opportunity to present a few thoughts on "Swiss Banking". 15 eventful years The Swiss Banking School was founded 15 years ago - measured by the pulse of the banking business an eternity ago. Just a few keywords as a reminder. 1987: The Berlin Wall still divides Europe into East and West. Today, the Eastern European countries are integrated into the European economy and are pushing into the EU and NATO. 1987: the first PCs conquer the desks. Today: No children's room without Internet. At that time: dawn of marketable financial derivatives; today: no bank without sophisticated risk management. 1987: intensive, not to say bitter, discussions on the question: cantonal stock exchanges or pan-Swiss stock exchange? Today, we are at best still proud of the fact that in the Darwinian struggle for survival on a pan-European level in the form of virt-x a stock exchange with Swiss genes on the maternal side prevails. No wonder the banking landscape has also changed in these fast-paced 15 years. In 1987, of the ten largest banks in the international Champions League, no less than seven came from Japan. Today, Japanese banks are still suffering from the longest banking crisis in post-war history. At the Swiss level, five major banks have become two. Of the 29 cantonal banks, 24 have survived, some with financial injections from their sponsoring cantons. Half of the regional banks have lost their independence after the collapse of SL Thun, and the survivors have moved closer together. In return, the number of foreign institutions established in Switzerland has increased. Swiss banks have coped well with the structural change of the last 15 years. Real collapses were virtually absent, and shocks to the real economy or government bailouts were avoided  crucially thanks to cooperation among the banks. The high degree of concentration achieved - two banking groups account for almost two-thirds of the banking system - is not without its problems. However, countries with lower bank concentrations, above all the USA and Germany, still have some of the structural change already survived in Switzerland and the resulting surge in concentration ahead of them. Refinanzierungsprobleme This does not mean that structural change has been completed in Switzerland. Various banks are increasingly struggling to manage their lending business at an acceptable cost 2 Refinance. 15 years ago, the mortgage business could still be financed by 120 percent of the industry average with savings and similar deposits. Financing gap in mortgage business (1988  2000) All banks 1.4 Regional and cantonal banks 1.3 1.2 1.1 1 0.9 0.8 0.7 1988 1990 1992 1994 1996 1998 2000 Today, there is a gap of - again on average - around ten percent. For individual banks, it is significantly larger. This financing gap is only partly due to the economic situation. Essentially, it highlights a structural problem. It is true that consumers are more likely to save more than in previous years: on the one hand, net capital accumulation in the context of occupational pensions is still in progress; on the other hand, there are many doubts about the performance promises of the first pillar. Private pension provision is thus gaining in importance. At the same time, the competition for the money saved is increasing. Savers are also demanding their share of the "Securitisation and Globalisation Dividend". They are less and less willing to subsidize mortgage borrowers through low interest rates. Since it was not easy to find an alternative to the traditional savings book, it is now rather difficult for the customer to find his way through the jungle of account forms (up to two dozen at some banks). In addition, there are countless competing offers from insurance companies and investment funds. What are the consequences? In the short term, the financing gap will mainly be filled with funds from the interbank market. Such funds, if you look at the Swiss banking system as a whole, can only come from abroad. The obligations of Swiss banks vis-a-vis foreign banks have increased sharply. Their long-stable balance sheet share has doubled from 13 to 26 percent within five years. 3 Obligations gg. foreign banks (as % of total assets) 30% 25% 20% 15% 10% 5% 0% 1990 1991 1992 1993 1994 1995 1996 1997 1998 1999 2000 Even banks that do not have access to the international interbank market themselves rely on it indirectly today. This way out is not without risks to liquidity and profitability. As a longer-term way out, the capital market offers itself as a source of finance. However, it is precisely the capital marketable, i.e. larger, banks that have the least problems with mortgage refinancing. The smaller ones, on the other hand, are not capital marketable, at least not on their own. Capital market capability will only be achievable for different banks through mergers or other forms of cooperation. However, it is difficult to raise money together; it is likely to be limited, especially after the failure of the emission centre of the Swiss municipalities. If you want to borrow collectively, you must be able to prove at least strict supervision of your members. Tougher times for mortgage borrowers The closest remedy for a worse refinancing ratio to a bank is an increase in passive interest rates. However, this is at the expense of profitability if active interest rates cannot be raised to the same extent. The consequence is twofold: On the one hand, banks that already generate tight interest margins on a risk-adjusted basis are facing difficult times. Here, too, the signs point to consolidation. On the other hand, mortgages in Switzerland tend to become more expensive. Even the various capital market solutions cannot prevent this effect. 4 Compared to other countries, lower debt in the longer term would not be a national disaster, but rather a turn to normality. The Swiss are quite lonely at the top internationally in terms of debt: the Americans have debt amounting to 50 percent of GDP. In Japan and Europe, the corresponding values are 100 percent; in Switzerland, on the other hand, debt reaches a staggering 270 percent of GDP. Leverage (private sector bank debt as % of GDP, 1999) USA 47 Japan Euroland 107 102 Switzerland 269 0 50 100 150 200 250 300 A natural way to reduce mortgage debt would be increased amortization. Today, the repayment of debts is not popular with debtors. The tax reform under discussion - the simultaneous abolition of imputed rental value and deductibility of mortgage interest - could effectively defuse the conflict between bank and debtor regarding amortisation. I know that opinions on the question of debt interest and imputed rental value are divided. But do you know an example of a tax-related distortion that has not produced significant negative side effects in the long run? Even the supposed beneficiaries are often affected by the non-optimal use of their funds for the economy as a whole. Away from the retail business? In view of tighter margins and under the impression of unexpected losses in the lending business, various banks have for the first time rigorously considered what is still worthwhile and what is not. Clear differences can be observed: Fifteen years ago, the share of lending business on the balance sheet of the big banks was still over 50 percent. Today it is a good half as high. Conversely, the regional banks and cantonal banks, which have already slightly increased their lending business from 75 and 85 percent respectively. There is still room in Switzerland for disintermediation, in the sense of displacing the credit intermediation of banks by securities markets. The banks always mediate 5 still a multiple of money compared to the capital market. Switzerland has a well-developed capital market: the ratio between market capitalisation and gross domestic product (GDP), for example, is a good 3:1 in Switzerland, just under 2:1 in the USA and Japan and 1:1 in the eurozone. More disintermediation does not have to harm the banks. It does not necessarily mean less, but primarily different business. There would be an opportunity for various banks to diversify their sources of income more. Compared to German banks, for example, Swiss banks are less diversified or more specialised individually; the banking system as a whole, on the other hand, is more diversified than the German one. However, disintermediation means that the cards are reshuffled in competition. Anyone who is successful in the lending business does not necessarily have to be in the securities business. Traditional banks in particular face a difficult task here. It comes at the same time as the challenge of e-banking. Internet: "new economy" or flash in the pan? Will e-banking and e-finance bring a revolution in banking or just an electronic "twist" to a basically unchanged business? On the one hand, e-banking and the hopes and fears attached to it are reminiscent of the advent of mail order a hundred years ago. At the beginning, "catalogue retailing" experienced considerable growth rates, which for many were alarming. The traditional retail business was predicted to die soon. A century later, an estimated four percent of goods are ordered by catalogue. Direct customer contact, and thus a real branch network, are much more important than assumed at the time. Is ebanking threatened with a similar fate? Such skepticism, combined with noticeable listlessness, is quite common in the industry. The argument is something like this: So far, e-banking has only brought us additional costs. Far from replacing the physical business, the Internet presence devours high funds. These voices rightly point out that customers only trust a bank's virtual business if physical, i.e. living, contact persons are also available if necessary. Only - so one hears - the Internet window is unfortunately an indispensable part of a modern appearance. Anyone who argues in this way is probably making a mistake. E-banking is not simply a presence arm attached to the existing one. The Internet is fundamentally turning the banking business upside down in the longer term. A few keywords. Information: The Internet gives a bank the opportunity to inform its customers - and those of the competition - much better about its products. Products: It will be much easier to offer targeted product bundles and even to include third-party products in your own range. Competition: Customers are better informed and thus receive longer spikes. Market entry for providers of relatively standardised services such as brokerage will become easier; marge erosion has already started here. The power of the Internet, however, is likely to extend even further. Experience in the USA shows that not all, but a majority of customers would prefer to entrust their entire financial transactions to the same bank  a house bank, so to speak. But this only under two conditions. Firstly, access to the classic, frequently used on-line services, in particular payment transactions and brokerage, must be convenient and secure. Secondly, the 6 Be open to bank details for access to competing products, especially in the investment sector. The customer wants his priority bank, but he does not want to be exclusively dependent on it. At the same time, it demands the comfort of a solid, intimate relationship and easy access to the advantages of competition. A convincing Internet presence not only visually, but above all in terms of service quality, thus becomes the backbone of a successful banking strategy. The physical activities are then grouped around this. In other words, anyone who thinks that the Internet window of their bank is simply an additional sales channel, the Surferswil branch, so to speak, is probably wrong. Success factors: trust and attention This does not mean that the physical presence of a bank becomes superfluous. The root of banking is trust. This has been the case for centuries and remains so in the Internet age. Trust requires, among other things, that the customer can turn to a contact person with an open ear if necessary. It is probably human nature that trust thrives best in personal contact. A purely virtual bank should therefore not be an option as a house bank for the majority of customers. However, personal contacts are time-consuming and not possible between a bank and its large number of customers. What is important is the good reputation of a business partner, his reputation. On the Internet, where the path to the local regional bank is as far as to a bank in California, the reputation of a bank, its "brand name", is even more important than before. Competition on the Internet is therefore also a competition between brand names. Again, the little ones are particularly challenged here. A good name does not necessarily require size, but the list of first (Internet) addresses in the Swiss banking business will certainly not have 300 entries. A prerequisite for success on the Internet is to bring potential customers to your own website in the first place. However, it is known that only a very small percentage of Internet addresses are visited by a large number of customers. The vast majority of Internet sites are those that few non-specialists get lost on. In addition, man is sluggish. Once you have installed your bank details with accounts, passwords and everything that goes with it, you tend to stay. The banks that can first establish a successful Internet presence gain a difficult advantage over the competition. The Internet also shakes taboos. In the past, a ticket corner and a stand with bank-owned brochures had the "magnet function" to bring people into the counter hall. In the Internet business, such is no longer enough. It's not just about colorful decoys that turn a bank's website into an experience space. But the potential customer is most likely to visit the homepage of a bank if it is worthwhile for him, even if he does not  or not yet  think about changing his bank details. A first-class range of information - also about offers from the competition - should be the minimum requirement. Winners and losers E-banking is more than just an Internet presence. Electronization not only simplifies processing, but also enables the storage and evaluation of immense data sets. It allows the development, the offer and nota bene also the pricing of products, 7 that are precisely tailored to a customer profile. McKinsey estimates that optimal customer segmentation creates revenue potentials of up to 200 basis points. Conversely, e-banking also brings risks. Even before e-banking, most banks knew how to sing a song about growing IT budgets. Now additional investments are coming to the banks. Realistically, it is to be expected that individuals will be among the big winners, but many will never get their money's worth. The bank, which defines its strategy early and decisively - especially if it does so free of illusions - has the best chance of prevailing in the competition. Traditional customer bases and undisputed revenue niches can prove to be dangerous mirages. Cooperation with competitors Another prerequisite for success is the ability to cooperate. Increasingly, this includes cooperation with competitors. With the new technologies, the infrastructure of banking has become a key factor of success. The Swiss banks have very successfully created a common infrastructure platform: 1. the SIC as a reliable and efficient payment system linked to the European TARGET; 2. the fully electronic exchange SWX, both connected by 3. a world-leading "delivery-versus-payment" securities settlement system (SECOM/SIS), and supplemented by 4th Repo SWX as a trading platform for secured money market loans. In the last five years alone, it has been possible to reduce every franc of transaction costs to 20 centimes. SWX therefore has a good chance of successfully placing itself in European equity trading in conjunction with tradepoint. The infrastructure remains a success factor of Swiss Banking, and the ability to cooperate with competitors forms the basis for their further development. This cooperation is not always easy, as the example of the non-existent transaction bank shows. There is much to suggest that in the infrastructural, but also in the product area, the specific forms of cooperation between the poles of the comprehensive joint work and the contractual, market-based reference to a partner bank are becoming more diverse and colorful. At this level, market participants are confronted with difficult, even vital, decisions about their structure. In the ability to identify stable, mutually beneficial partnerships, to establish them legally optimally and to maintain and further develop them with skill, there is a condition for success that will probably be much more important in the coming years than in the past. Concluding remarks This brings me to a few concluding remarks. The selection of problems mentioned is certainly incomplete. One would also have to talk about private banking, regulatory risks, the project of a Postbank and concrete all-financial trends. With my emphasis, I wanted to focus on two problem areas which, in my opinion, have the highest places in the hierarchy of challenges. 8 The worsening refinancing and disintermediation problems force creative reflection and decisive action. The obvious trends have a crucial structural component that remains effective regardless of ongoing interest rate and capital market fluctuations. Against this background, it is a good sign that we are registering a moderate development of loans despite favorable economic prospects. The success of the strategic response to the tendency towards disintermediation is as much in your interest as it is in the interest of the security and efficiency of Switzerland as a banking centre. Even though I am not a particular technology freak, I share the view of those who believe that e-banking is the biggest challenge of the post-war period for the traditional banking structure. Like hardly any other event before, the spread of e-banking accelerates Schumpeter's process of creative destruction, a process in which we suspect that it will also shake the foundations without knowing exactly where it will lead. When I think of the early 80s, the time of my first experiences in a bank, and look at the financial landscape today, I register one thing above all: changes. Our banks have proven that they are able to adapt to new circumstances and circumstances. That makes us confident. Stronger than in the last 15 years, this ability for successful change will be important in the future. Regardless of whether a bank sees itself as global, regional, universal, specialized, traditional or virtual, this ability is based on two main prerequisites: On the one hand, strategic impartiality. What may have been a taboo in the past - such as a merger with the sharpest competitor to date or the admission that it is no longer competitive in a business area - must be openly addressed and analyzed. The more tolerance, openness and willingness to engage in dialogue characterize the corporate communication climate, the better the self-critical, searching reflection will succeed. In a time of rapid and fundamental change, corporate correctness and subservience to preconceived notions can prove disastrous tranquilizers. On the other hand, adaptability is essentially a question of willingness to learn and train. Any entrepreneurial reorientation makes professional experience and skills obsolete, but at the same time creates the need to create new human capital. As a graduate of the Swiss Banking School, you have long since made your commitment to lifelong learning. With this basic attitude, you make a significant contribution to the commercial flourishing and security of our financial centre. Obviously, the SNB is also highly interested in both. I would like to thank you for listening and the directors and lecturers of the Swiss Banking School for your tireless, successful commitment. 9

Ein erstklassiges Informationsangebot - auch ber Angebote der Konkurrenz - drfte das Minimalerfordernis sein. Gewinner und Verlierer E-banking ist mehr als ein Internet-Auftritt. Die Elektronisierung vereinfacht nicht nur die Verarbeitung, sondern ermglicht die Speicherung und Auswertung immenser Datenstze. Sie erlaubt die Entwicklung, das Angebot und nota bene auch das Pricing von Produkten, 7 die genau auf ein Kundenprofil zugeschnitten sind. McKinsey schtzt, dass eine optimale Kundensegmentierung Ertragspotentiale von bis zu 200 Basispunkten schafft. Umgekehrt bringt das e-banking auch Risiken. Die meisten Banken wussten schon vor dem e-banking ein Lied ber wachsende Informatikbudgets zu singen. Jetzt kommen zustzliche Investitionen auf die Banken zu. Realistischerweise ist zu erwarten, dass einzelne zu den grossen Gewinnern gehren, Viele aber nie auf ihre Kosten kommen werden. Die besten Chancen, sich im Wettbewerb durchzusetzen, hat die Bank, die frh und dezidiert ihre Strategie definiert - vor allem, wenn sie dies frei von Illusionen tut. Traditionelle Kundenstmme und unangefochtene Ertragsnischen knnen sich als gefhrliche Trugbilder erweisen. Kooperation mit Konkurrenten Eine weitere Voraussetzung des Erfolgs ist die Fhigkeit zu kooperieren. Zunehmend gehrt dazu die Zusammenarbeit mit Konkurrenten. Mit den neuen Technologien ist die Infrastruktur des Bankwesens zu einem Schlsselfaktor des Erfolgs geworden. Die Schweizer Banken haben sich sehr erfolgreich eine gemeinsame Infrastrukturplattform geschaffen: 1. das SIC als zuverlssiges und effizientes Zahlungssystem mit Verbindung zum europischen TARGET, 2. die vollelektronische Brse SWX, beides verbunden durch 3. ein weltweit fhrendes "delivery-versus-payment"-Wertpapierabwicklungssystem (SECOM/SIS), und ergnzt durch 4. Repo SWX als Handelsplattform fr gesicherte Geldmarktkredite. Allein in den letzten fnf Jahren ist es gelungen, jeden Franken Transaktionskosten auf 20 Rappen zu drcken. SWX hat deshalb gute Chancen, sich in der Verbindung mit tradepoint erfolgreich im europischen Aktienhandel zu plazieren. Die Infrastruktur bleibt ein Erfolgsfaktor des Swiss Banking, und die Fhigkeit zur Kooperation mit Konkurrenten bildet die Basis zu deren Weiterentwicklung. Diese Zusammenarbeit ist nicht immer einfach, wie das Beispiel der nicht zustande gekommenen Transaktionsbank zeigt. Vieles spricht dafr, dass im infrastrukturellen, aber auch im Produktebereich die spezifischen Kooperationsformen zwischen den Polen des umfassenden Gemeinschaftswerks und der vertraglichen, marktmssigen Anlehnung an eine Partnerbank vielfltiger und bunter werden. Auf dieser Ebene sind die Marktteilnehmer mit schwierigen, ja berlebenswichtigen Entscheiden ber ihre Struktur konfrontiert. In der Fhigkeit, stabile, gegenseitig vorteilhafte Partnerschaften zu identifizieren, rechtlich optimal zu begrnden und mit Geschick zu unterhalten und weiterzuentwickeln, liegt eine Erfolgsbedingung, auf die es wohl in den kommenden Jahren viel strker ankommen wird als in der Vergangenheit. Abschliessende Bemerkungen Ich komme damit zu einigen abschliessenden Bemerkungen. Die angesprochene Auswahl von Problemen ist gewiss unvollstndig. Man msste auch ber Private Banking reden, ber regulatorische Risiken, das Projekt einer Postbank und sich konkretisierende Allfinanztrends. Ich wollte mit meiner Akzentuierung zwei Problembereiche in den Vordergrund stellen, denen meines Erachtens in der Hierarchie der Herausforderungen die obersten Pltze zukommen. 8 Die sich verschrfenden Refinanzierungs- und Disintermediationsprobleme zwingen zu kreativem Nachdenken und entschlossenem Handeln. Die augenflligen Trends haben eine entscheidende strukturelle Komponente, die unabhngig von laufenden Zins- und Kapitalmarktschwankungen wirksam bleibt. Es ist auf diesem Hintergrund ein gutes Zeichen, dass wir trotz gnstiger konjunktureller Perspektiven eine massvolle Entwicklung der Kredite registrieren. Dass die strategische Reaktion auf die Disintermediationstendenz gelingt, liegt ebenso in Ihrem wie im Interesse der Sicherheit und Effizienz des Bankplatzes Schweiz. Auch wenn ich kein besonderer Technologiefreak bin, teile ich die Auffassung derjenigen, die im e-banking die fr die hergebrachte Bankenstruktur grsste Herausforderung der Nachkriegszeit vermuten. Wie kaum ein Ereignis zuvor beschleunigt die Verbreitung des e-banking den Schumpeter'schen Prozess der kreativen Zerstrung, einen Vorgang, bei dem wir erahnen, dass er auch die Fundamente erschttert, ohne zu wissen, wohin er genau fhren wird. Wenn ich an die frhen 80er Jahre denke, die Zeit meiner ersten Erfahrungen in einer Bank, und mir die Finanzlandschaft heute anschaue, registriere ich vor allem eines: Vernderungen. Unsere Banken haben den Tatbeweis erbracht, dass sie fhig sind, sich an neue Umstnde und Gegebenheiten anzupassen. Das stimmt zuversichtlich. Strker als in den letzten 15 Jahren, wird es in Zukunft auf diese Fhigkeit zum erfolgreichen Wandel ankommen. Unabhngig davon, ob sich eine Bank als global, regional, universal, spezialisiert, traditionell oder virtuell versteht, beruht diese Fhigkeit vor allem auf zwei Voraussetzungen: Zum einen auf strategischer Unvoreingenommenheit. Was in der Vergangenheit vielleicht ein Tabu war - etwa ein Zusammengehen mit dem bisher schrfsten Konkurrenten oder das Eingestndnis, in einem Geschftsfeld nicht mehr konkurrenzfhig zu sein - muss offen angesprochen und analysiert werden. Die selbstkritisch-suchende Reflexion wird umso besser gelingen, je mehr Toleranz, Offenheit und Dialogbereitschaft das betriebliche Kommunikationsklima prgen. In einer Zeit rascher und grundlegender Vernderungen knnen sich betriebspolitische Korrektheit und Unterwrfigkeit in Bezug auf vorgefasste Meinungen als verhngnisvolle Tranquilizers erweisen. Zum anderen ist Anpassungsfhigkeit wesentlich eine Frage der Lern- und Ausbildungsbereitschaft. Jede unternehmerische Umorientierung lsst berufliche Erfahrungen und Fertigkeiten obsolet werden, schafft aber gleichzeitig die Notwendigkeit, neues Humankapital zu schaffen. Als Absolventen der Swiss Banking School haben Sie Ihr Bekenntnis zur lebenslangen Weiterbildung lngst abgelegt. Mit dieser Grundhaltung leisten Sie einen wesentlichen Beitrag zum kommerziellen Gedeihen und zur Sicherheit unseres Finanzplatzes. An beidem ist naheliegenderweise auch die Nationalbank in hohem Masse interessiert.
