Title: Introductory Remarks, End-of-year Media News Conference
text: End-of-year Media , Zurich, 8 December 2000 Introductory remarks by Bruno Gehrig, Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Interest rate and monetary situation The year 2000 saw ambivalent interest rate and monetary developments. On the interest rate front, short-term rates rose while long-term rates remained stable or were on the decline. In view of robust and dynamic growth, the central banks, including the National Bank, had to raise their key rates markedly in the first half-year. This had the gratifying effect of very slightly dampening long-term interest rates, a development also supported by significant improvements in government budget prospects. Given the remarkable economic growth in Switzerland and in other countries, current interest rates are, by historical standards, at a conspicuously low level. The chances of a continued positive economic development accompanied by low inflation risks therefore seem to be good. During the current year, the Swiss franc underwent a sometimes marked decline vis-a-vis the US dollar, while appreciating against the euro. In the wake of this contrary development, the export-weighted price index remained fairly stable. In other words, positive and negative exchange rate effects on the economy as a whole more or less balanced each other out. Such shifts in the exchange rate can, of course, have considerable implications for individual sectors and enterprises, depending on the currency distribution of income and expenditure. The high US dollar rate stimulates exports and makes imports more expensive, while the low euro exchange rate is a handicap for exports to the euro area and facilitates imports. Given the exceedingly dynamic pace of economic activity and renewed full employment in our country, the disengagement of the Swiss franc from the weakening trend of the euro at the end of March was an altogether desirable development. This supported the National Bank's efforts to tighten monetary conditions somewhat by gradually raising interest rates. The financial markets interpreted this development as confirmation of the independent monetary policy course. The interest rate bonus, which has risen since then, goes hand in hand with the renewed significance of the Swiss franc as a diversification currency. On the foreign exchange markets, however, the enduring weak trend of the euro was the central event of the year now drawing to a close. The growth differential between the United States and the countries of the European Monetary Union, which is narrowing in line with expectations, has succeeded in stabilising the euro in the past few weeks. To what extent interventions by the central banks have contributed to this is open to question. In principle, the chances of success of sterilised interventions, i.e. interventions with neutralised effects on liquidity, are limited. Experience with the euro has taught us that we have an imperfect understanding of the determinants of short- and medium-term exchange rate movements. In cross-border business, it is therefore of vital importance to assess exchange rate risks consistently and to steer them in such a way that even unexpected changes can still be coped with economically. Steering of the interest rate - a first assessment With the monetary policy concept presented a year ago - and which rests on three pillars: definition of price stability, inflation forecast and Libor target range - the National Bank has switched, on the operational level, to steering the interest rate after previously having primarily steered the money supply. What is our experience with this new policy? Let me first reiterate the principles of the steering method applied today: the target range for the three-month Libor rate reflects our monetary policy intentions. Within the target range, a band of one percentage point, we allow for a controlled fluctuation of the Libor rate. As a rule, we keep this interest rate around the middle of the target range. If this is necessary from a monetary policy point of view, we can let it rise or fall to the upper or the lower part of the band respectively. We steer the Libor rate indirectly by means of repo transactions with maturities of a few days or weeks, while the Libor rate applies to three-month investments. This distinguishes our steering method from the key interest rate regime of other central banks, which aim at a very short-term interest rate and transact business directly at this rate. We have opted for the three-month rate because, on the one hand, it is less susceptible to technical market disruptions and, on the other hand, it is more sensitive to economically relevant changes impacting on the Swiss franc money market from abroad or from the capital market. In retrospect, the new steering regime has so far stood the test (cf. enclosed graph). The target range and the Libor rate as a reference rate are already firmly entrenched in the monetary policy discussion. As was to be expected, all parties concerned had to become accustomed in practice to the new steering concept. Thus numerous market participants at first concentrated on repo rates as the transmitters of signals, which led to increased movements of the Libor rate within the target range. In the meantime, the insight has gained ground that monetary policy signals emanate from shifts in the interest rate band - or possibly from the new positioning of the Libor rate within the target range. Despite the misgivings expressed by a few persons in the early stage, there were never any serious doubts that the Libor could be steered. By and large, we were quite successful in steering it to the desired level, or to keep it there. This also applies to the first half-year, when we had to adjust the target range and the Libor position upward at relatively short intervals. Precisely in such phases, the Libor rate is a better transmitter of monetary policy signals than the repo rate. To some extent, the repo rate is subject to purely technically induced fluctuations whose stabilisation would be counterproductive from a monetary policy point of view. We also do not intend to adjust the width of the target range. It provides us with the necessary interest rate flexibility without undermining the significance of the target range as a signal for the market. A narrower target range would have obliged us to announce interest rate steps at intervals that would have diminished the credibility and transparency of the new concept. Repo business made a major contribution to the positive results of interest rate steering. The fully automated repo trading and settlement platform gives us a maximum of operational flexibility. At the beginning of the year, we therefore switched to repos for steering the entire money market and are now holding the traditional instruments (foreign exchange swaps, placement of Confederation funds) in reserve for special cases only. We can transact and settle repo business on a continuous basis at variable conditions and in varying amounts with all counterparties linked to the system practically at any time during the day. Thanks to the efficiency of the repo system, the circle of participants has widened to currently 90 banks, which conclude transactions among themselves or with the National Bank. Approximately 40 of these banks participate in our repo auctions including, in the meantime, renowned institutions from abroad. The direct link to the National Bank gives the participating banks advantages in liquidity management, but most of all it strengthens competition on the Swiss franc money market, thus enhancing the efficiency of price formation, which, in the final analysis, benefits all participants. With this opening, the influence of the big banks on conditions on the money market was reduced. Their share in total outstanding liquidity transactions has declined from more than 80% to now approximately 50%. For just over a year now the SNB has, moreover, offered the banks interest-free intraday liquidity. Every day funds totalling approximately Sfr two billion are drawn. This transaction is intended to facilitate cashless payment transactions. Since the introduction of intraday credit, payment flows in SIC have become more regular in the course of the day. In particular, the accumulation of unsettled payment transactions in the runup to daily clearing settlement has declined markedly. Title: Introductory Remarks, End-of-year Media News Conference
text: End-of-year Media , Zurich, 8 December 2000 Introductory Remarks by Jean-Pierre Roth, Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Situation on the capital markets Since our last media in June, the financial markets have been subject to the combined effects of rising oil prices and a gradual slowdown in economic growth. Despite the general acceleration in inflation, long-term interest rates for prime borrowers have remained relatively stable or have even declined slightly. This development indicates that the markets do not expect the oil shock to become a lasting inflationary phenomenon. In Switzerland, the yield on ten-year Confederation bonds has thus fallen from 4% in June to currently 3.75%. On the different markets, the trend in yields on government bonds has also been influenced by special circumstances. In the United States, the federal budget surplus has accelerated the decline in the yield on federal bonds; in the euro area, stagnating long-term interest rates are probably due to the markets' lack of confidence in the European currency. The generally expected slowdown in economic growth nevertheless had a stronger impact on the financial markets than might have been expected given the weak volatility of long-term government bonds. In fact, it is evident today that the less favourable economic prospects induce investors to adopt a more cautious attitude with respect to risk. On the stock markets, enthusiasm for technology paper has evaporated across the board. In the United States, where the signs of a slowdown are now evident at the end of a period of strong growth, the Nasdaq index has fallen by more than 30% from its summer peak, back to the level in the autumn of 1999. On the other exchanges, the indexes of the new markets have reacted in a similar way. The development on the traditional stock exchanges depended largely on the relative weighting of technology paper in their indexes. In Japan, the steady decline of the Nikkei index mainly reflects the difficulties connected with the recovery of the country's economy. Investors' reluctance to assume risks also resulted in a considerable widening of spreads between the yield on government securities and that on bonds of private borrowers. On the other side of the Atlantic, in particular a marked deterioration in the financing conditions of enterprises with a poor rating has become observable. The spread to their detriment has reached a record level which surpasses the one witnessed during the financial crisis of 1998. In the eyes of investors, it is also imperative to be more prudent in the assessment of country risks. Certain emerging economies with a still unsound basis stand to suffer more from a likely slowdown in world growth and an increase in oil prices. The most fragile among them face a deterioration in their financing conditions and attract greater international attention. Compared with events in the past, the financial markets thus seem to react more quickly and with greater perception to changes in the economic landscape. The extent of the adjustments observed is revealing in this respect. The fact that this volatility has not disturbed investors shows that previous extreme fluctuations could be corrected and that market conditions can be explained by the new assessment of risks. Gold sales and administration of free assets The entry into force, at the beginning of May 2000, of the Federal Law on Currency and Payment Instruments has permitted us to start our sales programme for 1,300 tonnes of gold. To date, 160 tonnes have been put on the market, and we intend to sell the same quantity between now and the end of September 2001. Our sales activities are coordinated with those of the central banks which signed the agreement of 26 September 1999. The Bank for International Settlements has been commissioned to effect the sale of the first 220 tonnes. As our periodic bank returns show, the gold is sold regularly, in small tranches, in order to avoid exerting an undue influence on prices. This procedure has borne fruit: the market has been able to absorb the additional supply without any problems. The average price of our sales amounted to 275.9 /oz, which is slightly higher than the London fixing, the reference price on the gold market, during this period. The dollar amounts generated by the gold sales are invested in different financial instruments authorised by the National Bank Law. In this way, a portfolio will gradually be built up which will ultimately be allocated to the objectives to be established by parliament. The final size of the portfolio will depend on two main parameters, i.e. (1) the development of the gold price in Swiss francs, and (2) the yield on investments. When the sales are completed, and based on the current gold price, the portfolio of free assets should amount to approximately Sfr 20 billion. The possibilities of protecting ourselves against an unfavourable development of the gold price in Swiss francs are limited by the agreement of 26 September 1999, which prohibits us from hedging transactions with respect to the future gold price (expressed in dollars) on the market. We can, however, limit the uncertainties associated with the fluctuations of the dollar against the Swiss franc. Yet, a complete hedge is not warranted for experience has shown that there is a negative correlation between the development of the dollar against the Swiss franc and that of the gold price in dollars; a fall in the dollar price for gold is generally associated with a rise in the dollar against the Swiss franc. The existence of this "natural hedge" has led us to adopt a strategy of a partial hedge for the dollar risk by engaging in forward sales of dollars against Swiss francs in an amount corresponding to approximately a third of the proceeds from gold sales. In this way, we can limit the adverse effects which a depreciation of the dollar would have on future earnings from the sale of gold. The proceeds from the sale of gold are invested in a bond portfolio with a considerably different composition from that of our foreign exchange reserves. The main reasons for this are twofold. First, even if we do not yet know the future beneficiaries of the free assets, we may nevertheless assume that they will be primarily interested in a portfolio which generates a regular flow of Swiss franc denominated yields. Second, these future beneficiaries will come into possession of their assets within two to three years, and it is essential that, at the time of transfer, the value of the accumulated portfolio will be sufficient to cover the amount to be remitted by the SNB. This is because up to that point in time the SNB must bear all the risks associated with the investments of the proceeds from the gold sales. Safeguarding the interests of the recipients of the ordinary profits of the SNB - the Confederation and the cantons thus requires that we adopt an investment strategy that is not too aggressive. Approximately 60% of the portfolio is hedged against the exchange rate risk and thus corresponds to an investment in Swiss franc bonds. The balance is invested in Eurobonds (20%), in US dollars (10%) and in bonds denominated in other currencies (10%). The average duration of the portfolio is approximately three years. The investment profile of the free assets has thus been defined so as to take into account, as far as possible, the needs of future beneficiaries and the probable date on which they will take possession of their assets. Besides, we have taken all the necessary administrative steps to ensure efficient portfolio management:  The free assets are managed like a separate portfolio whose market value, yield and risk profile are known to us at any time. Nevertheless, since this portfolio does not yet constitute separate assets in the legal sense, it does not figure as such in our balance sheet. The investments are included under various positions on the assets side.  We have defined reference portfolios with a reference index for every form of investment of free assets. Performance may thus be evaluated continually based on objective criteria. With these measures, we ensure transparency in the management of the assets not required for the conduct of monetary policy, and this will facilitate their transfer to the future beneficiaries once the legal framework is in place.

Title: Introductory Remarks, End-of-year Media News Conference
text: End-of-year Media , Zurich, 8 December 2000 Introductory Remarks by Hans Meyer, Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank The Swiss National Bank, in agreement with the Federal Government, has decided to adhere to its current monetary policy. It will leave the target range for the three-month Libor rate, which has stood at 3.0% - 4.0% since 15 June 2000, unchanged. For the time being, the three-month Libor rate is to be kept in the middle of the target range. Since there are no discernible signs of a long-term threat to price stability, the National Bank will refrain from another tightening of monetary policy. The latest inflation forecast shown in the graph still gives a favourable picture of the future inflation trend. In essence, it corresponds to the inflation development forecast in June 2000. The adjustment to the national consumer price index made a few days ago has not influenced our forecast significantly. At an unchanged target range for the threemonth Libor, inflation is likely to increase to slightly above 2% by the middle of 2001 and to fall below this level again in the course of the year 2002. On average, we expect inflation to rise from 1.6% in 2000 to 2.1% in 2001 and to drop again to 1.7% by 2003. As is known, a rate of inflation of 2% per annum is considered to be the upper limit of the range which we equate with price stability. The expected temporary deviation from this target can be explained by the vigorous development of economic activity during the current year and, above all, by the massive rise in oil prices. We anticipate that they will fall again during the course of 2001 or will at least stabilise on the current, albeit high level. It may come as a surprise that the upward pressure on prices has remained moderate in spite of the favourable economic situation in Switzerland. Nevertheless, the continued strong real growth we have been experiencing since the middle of 1999 manifests itself in a shortage of skilled labour and rising labour costs. Partly as a result of the latest increase in mortgage rates, housing rents are going up as well. Despite this, there is no inflationary push on the horizon. In the short term, inflation will presumably depend largely on economic and exchange rate movements as well as on the further development of oil prices. We expect that the economy will continue to expand, though at a slower pace. After a growth rate of 3.3% during the current year, we forecast an increase in real gross domestic product of approximately 2.2% in 2001. In 2002, real growth is expected to continue levelling off to 1.6%. This corresponds approximately to the average of the forecasts by the Swiss forecasting institutes. With the anticipated slowdown in growth, the threat of inflationary overheating of the Swiss economy is likely to pass. The projected development of real growth is mainly the consequence of an expected loss of momentum of economic activity in the United States and the European Union, which will in all likelihood put a damper on the dynamic Swiss export industry. The gradual tightening of Swiss monetary policy between autumn 1999 and summer 2000 will also help to prevent economic overheating. A similar effect emanates from the export-weighted real exchange rate of the Swiss franc, which has firmed since the spring of 2000, notably vis-a-vis the euro. In the long term, the course of Swiss inflation depends to a large degree on the development of the monetary aggregates. The course of the money stock M3 also gives no indication of any future threats to price stability. Bank loans, which tend to go up only insignificantly, convey the same message. A year ago, on the occasion of our , we presented various adjustments to our monetary policy concept. What is fundamentally new is that our monetary policy decisions are based on an inflation forecast. The experience gained with the adjusted monetary policy concept has been positive so far. The obligation to make an inflation forecast on a regular basis provides an incentive to examine all the relevant factors affecting future price developments carefully. Furthermore, it leads to greater transparency of monetary policy. It is our desire to disclose, as much as possible, the analyses on which we base our inflation forecast. Consequently, we intend to publish various studies in the near future which will explain our forecasting activities in some detail. We use several methods to forecast inflation and real growth. The results are discussed internally and are subsequently integrated in a consensus forecast. Forecasting inflation for the ensuing three years is a difficult undertaking. It is inevitable, therefore, that occasional forecast errors occur. We do not claim to be infallible when we make forecasts. The purpose of our inflation forecasts is to explain to the public what the considerations are on which we base our monetary policy decisions. Forecast errors can serve as valuable indicators for economic developments requiring an adjustment of monetary policy. Each central bank is confronted with the same basic problem: the monetary transmission mechanism entails considerable time lags. If we are to preserve price stability, therefore, we must act in a forward-looking manner.

Title: On monetary policy in the new year
text: Monetary policy in the new year Hans Meyer Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Research Institute for Empirical Economics and Economic Policy University of St. Gallen Thursday, December 21, 2000 2 In the course of my studies at the former University of St. Gallen, I was increasingly fascinated by the Swiss National Bank. I saw it as a venerable institution, independent and yet firmly anchored in the state structure, with the beautiful mission of conducting monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. Today, more than three decades later, I can say that this fascination has never diminished. Working in the field of tension between business, science and politics, primarily related to my own country and yet internationally oriented, has always been a challenge for me. I would like to take the opportunity to explain monetary policy for the coming year in more detail here. One last time I participated in the decision-making. It is now up to the successors to implement the intentions taking into account the changing environment. I wish them all the best. I'll start with some reflections on the mission. I would then like to recall the essential elements of the adapted monetary policy approach. I will then outline the economic development over the past year and discuss initial experiences with the adapted monetary policy concept. Following an digression into monetary policy, I would like to turn to the economic outlook and our monetary policy intentions. 3 1. The order The Swiss National Bank's mission is to conduct monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. Together with fiscal policy and competition policy, it is intended to help create a favourable framework for balanced and thus sustainable macroeconomic development. Such a development is characterized by steady growth, low unemployment and modest inflation. Monetary policy focuses on ensuring price stability. Doctrine and experience leave no doubt about the connection between money supply and price stability. Monetary policy makes an optimal contribution in line with its mandate if it succeeds in adjusting the money supply to the real growth of the economy in the longer term. It is clear that price stability is not an end in itself. Stable prices facilitate balanced macroeconomic development and prevent undesirable undesirable undesirable developments. In my experience, there are three main problems in the conduct of monetary policy: the difficulty of assessing the respective economic situation, the limited knowledge of the macroeconomic contexts and the influences from abroad. 2. The adjusted monetary policy approach In recent decades, we have famously used the central bank money supply as the target of monetary policy. Originally, annual growth rates were set. At the beginning of the nineties, we moved to medium-term growth targets. We wanted to take greater account of the fact that the development of inflation in the medium term depends primarily on the money supply. The medium-term orientation of our policy has created a margin of manoeuvre which 4 made it possible to take into account other indicators such as real economic developments, the situation on the labour market and the exchange rate in the decision-making process. However, the medium-term objective has always been understood only as a guideline. In the second half of the nineties, we experienced that the central bank money supply was no longer sufficiently stable and thus predictable. The medium-term target path therefore lost importance as a guideline for monetary policy. This prompted us to rethink the fundamentals of our monetary policy. As a result, we have decided not to announce a growth target for the central bank money supply in the future. The broad support of our policy on all relevant indicators should be increasingly expressed. This is how the adapted monetary policy concept was born, which, as is well known, rests on three pillars. The first pillar is an explicit definition of price stability. By this we mean an inflation of less than 2% per year, measured by the development of consumer prices. This definition is not least intended to take into account the fact that inflation can never be measured accurately. Our efforts to date have been focused on maintaining price stability. Only the explicit definition is new. This definition should not be confused with an inflation target. It is not a question of keeping inflation within the defined framework in every case. In a small, open economy, it is repeatedly influenced by external impulses that are difficult to control. As a rule, it would make little sense for the economy as a whole to suppress such impulses. It is essential that sustainable inflationary and deflationary tendencies are decisively opposed. The second pillar of the concept is an inflation forecast. This is drawn up every six months for the following three years. In this way, we contribute to the 5 Experience calculates that monetary policy measures only have an effect with a delay of around three years. When preparing the inflation forecast, all findings resulting from an analysis of the relevant factors are taken into account. The course of the money supply  especially of M3  continues to play an important role. It is important for estimating longer-term developments. The results of econometric model calculations are then taken into account. The corresponding forecast models also take into account factors such as real economic development and the development of exchange rates. Last but not least, special factors such as temporary shocks should also be taken into account, the effects of which are not covered by the other indicators. This approach ensures a broad support for decision-making. However, even broad-based decision-making cannot change the fact that monetary policy decisions are ultimately a matter of discretion. If the analysis reveals a trend in inflation that is not in line with our definition of price stability, then there is a need for action. The forecast ultimately published is based on the assumption that the relevant three-month rate will not be changed during the period of the forecast. The third pillar of the concept relates to the implementation of monetary policy. It consists of the target range set for the relevant three-month rate for Swiss francs. The SNB can influence this rate with short-term money market transactions without engaging in undesirable fine-tuning. Monetary policy is ultimately not only an economic challenge, but also a social one. The consistent consideration of 6 Teaching and experience is a necessary, but not sufficient, prerequisite for success. What is crucial is a fundamental insight into the importance of macroeconomic stability for balanced and thus sustainable development, which is broadly anchored in society. 3. Economic development and monetary policy in 2000 As the year draws to a close, economic development has unfolded a force that has surprised us all. This is true for both the global economy and the Swiss economy. With regard to the global economy, the fact remains worrying that around 20% of the world's population still provides and consumes around 80% of the world's economic output. The imbalance expressed in these orders of magnitude is accentuated by demographic and ecological tendencies. With regard to Switzerland, it can be stated without reservation that our economy is in an excellent, remarkably balanced state. With the new upswing, an unusually long period of stagnation has been completed. It was preceded by a period of strong expansion in the second half of the eighties. As a result, quite a few contaminated sites  especially in the construction industry, agriculture and tourism  had to be managed. In addition, there were problems of a cyclical nature. In the economic field, the economic situation in the partner countries, public finances, the development of exchange rates and, last but not least, intense competition should be mentioned. In the structural area, the consequences of a structurally preserving labour market policy, insufficient competition in parts of the domestic economy, technological progress and increasing inter-state interdependence had an impact. The economic recovery abroad, sustainable structural adjustments, the flexibility of both the 7 Employers as well as the employees give a good certificate, as well as favorable monetary conditions subsequently brought about a new upswing. For the year that is coming to an end, we expect real growth of just over 3%, which corresponds to a doubling compared to the previous year. The unemployment rate has fallen surprisingly quickly to below 2%. This means that there is practically full employment again. The shortage of qualified workers is particularly pronounced. At the same time, however, there are also people who have trouble finding their way in a dynamic working world. It remains remarkable that Switzerland's economic problems are neither sector- nor region-specific. Rather, the dividing line between positive and negative developments runs right through the economic landscape. Performance in terms of innovation, flexibility and productivity remains crucial. Ensuring favourable framework conditions through economic policy and their sensible use by the people involved are constant challenges. In this way, efforts to ensure healthy public budgets must be continued. This also applies to the promotion of competition. However, this concern is complicated by the fact that large circles are still sceptical about the idea of competition. Obviously, it has not yet been possible to make it sufficiently understandable that the free play of market forces in the use of the means of production is quite suitable for creating prosperity and thus also welfare. However, this requires a stable macroeconomic environment. Inflation, as measured by the national consumer price index, will amount to a good 1.5% in the current year. It thus remains in the area that we have with 8 To equate price stability. This year, inflation was mainly influenced by the rise in the price of oil. The so-called core inflation adjusted for special items will be less than 1%. A year ago, we promised to tighten the monetary policy reins. As a result, the outlined development has prompted us to react more quickly and sustainably than originally planned. With the intention of maintaining price stability in the medium term, we raised the target range for the relevant three-month rate to 3  4% in three steps in the first half of the year. With slight fluctuations, the movement moves in the middle of the volume. This means that it has roughly doubled within a year. Initial experience with the adjusted monetary policy approach has been positive. I would like to highlight two aspects in particular. On the one hand, the internal process of forming opinions has deepened. It has then become easier to communicate the fact that decision-making is very broad, taking into account all the relevant facts and considerations. In the foreseeable future, we will publish studies that provide more information about our forecasting activities. However, exaggerated expectations should be warned. A broad-based approach, taking into account different models and indicators, will hardly ever make it possible to fully understand the forecasts. Of course, this also applies to other central banks that publish forecasts. For the transparency of monetary policy, it is therefore particularly important that the decisions and the considerations on which they are based are clearly explained. 9 4. Monetary policy Monetary conditions have become somewhat more restrictive, not only as a result of the rise in interest rates, but also as a result of the strengthening of the Swiss franc. This accentuation is not undesirable in the current circumstances. In the currency sector, we have also been particularly concerned with the development of the euro in the current year. Looking back, it should be noted that the transition to the European Monetary Union has all in all been a good success. Cooperation has been well established both in the formulation and implementation of Community monetary policy. This is remarkable, not least because the political and economic environment has not facilitated the beginning. Above all, it has succeeded in preserving the domestic value of the new European currency. This positive finding is not altered by the impression that in recent times factual and mentality-related differences between the individual countries have become increasingly noticeable. As is well known, the external value of the euro has increasingly tended to weaken. One reason for this is the different economic development in the USA and in the countries affiliated to the monetary union. Even more important, however, is the latent mistrust in the ability of the relevant European countries to adapt their framework conditions to the requirements of balanced macroeconomic development. It will be significant for further events that the individual states have renounced an element of flexibility in their economic policies by fixing exchange rates. In the past, differences in economic development could be compensated to a certain extent by flexible exchange rates. The loss of this possibility is therefore 10 because many of the countries in question are already suffering from a lack of flexibility. When assessing the development of the euro, one must ultimately be aware that the external interdependence of the euro area is relatively low. In addition, a weak currency facilitates economic recovery to some extent. However, it also increases the risk of imported inflation. Last but not least, there is a risk that a weak currency will develop a momentum of its own that can become difficult to control. For Switzerland, the introduction of the euro has so far resulted in a gradual but not yet a fundamental change in the environment. First and foremost, the effort to keep your own house in order remains important. In monetary policy decision-making, the consideration of exchange rates remains an important concern. The exchange rate influences price developments directly through the prices of imported goods and indirectly through its impact on production and employment. However, we have never based our policy solely on this indicator and will not do so in the future. The prospects are good for a convergence of sustainable stability between Switzerland and the euro area in the medium term. This is the decisive prerequisite for exchange rates that tend to be stable. However, if difficulties arise in the implementation of the European Monetary Union, turbulence would have to be expected. In this case, we would have the opportunity to counteract an appreciation pressure on the Swiss franc by easing monetary policy. However, we could come into conflict with the stability policy orientation of the monetary policy stance. This is in line with our old experience that we probably have a certain amount of room for manoeuvre with regard to our international monetary relations, but this is not unlimited. 11 5. Economic outlook and monetary policy in the coming year The economic growth of the industrialized countries is likely to flatten out in the coming years. In the United States, we are seeing signs of a pronounced dampening of dynamics. In the European Union, too, growth is unlikely to reach the level recorded this year. The slowdown is due to both the tightening of monetary policy and the increase in the price of oil. Real growth in these economic areas will approach potential growth, so that the risk of economic overheating and thus an undesirable rise in inflation will be reduced. For the Swiss economy, we expect weaker but still broad-based growth in the coming years. It should be a good 2% next year and around 1.5% in 2002. Since there are no signs of a threat to price stability in the foreseeable future, we have decided to continue our previous monetary policy and thus leave the target range for the relevant three-month rate unchanged for the time being. This gives us sufficient freedom of action to be able to react appropriately and in a timely manner to all conceivable developments. Our latest inflation forecast essentially confirms the course of inflation as we had already predicted in the middle of the year. With an unchanged target range for the three-month rate, inflation is expected to rise slightly above 2% next year and fall back below this mark in the course of 2002. This forecast takes into account the recent correction of the national consumer price index, which, however, has hardly influenced our considerations. 12 As I said, our inflation forecast is based on the assumption of an unchanged three-month rate for the forecast period. It thus differs from the forecasts of most forecasting institutes, which also estimate the future course of monetary policy and take its effects into account in the forecast. Predicting inflation for three years is not easy. Many influences that will influence events during this period are not yet known in terms of type and scope. It is therefore inevitable that forecast errors will be made. However, it is precisely such mistakes that can provide indications of economic developments that are important for decision-making. 6. Outlook As contemporaries, it is not easy for us to classify current events in the larger context. We tend to overlook the fact that it is just an episode between the past and the future. In recent decades, we have experienced enormous economic and social development. Prosperity and welfare have increased and spread to a previously unimagined extent. Obviously, however, not all problems were solved. Quite a few fellow human beings express difficulty with the rhythm of development. Community cohesion has become looser. Pollution of the environment remains an important problem. Last but not least, experience has shown that the international integration of states not only brings opportunities, but also risks. For the foreseeable future, we will be confronted with the problems of a mature society. We still have to learn to live with prosperity. Whether we are satisfied with what has been achieved, we must not forget what it took, 13 to get this far and what will continue to be necessary to preserve and increase the stock. In the overall interest of the country, it is about striving for a development that guarantees freedom, security and welfare to a high degree. In the economic field, we need adequate growth with high employment and low inflation. Monetary policy, fiscal policy, competition policy and, last but not least, education policy must create favourable framework conditions for the people involved. Innovation, flexibility and productivity remain crucial for the performance of the economy. However, the necessary ongoing adjustments must be made in a way that does not jeopardise Community cohesion. Today, there is broad agreement on the principles of a market-oriented economic policy that also takes social and ecological concerns into account. There are fewer problems in the conceptual area than in the implementation. In principle, both in the design and in the implementation of policy, an active participation of the widest possible circles of the Community should be sought. Only in this way are appropriate but also consensual solutions possible: in the overall interest of the country!

text: Wahrungspolitischer Overview Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Chamber of Industry and Commerce Southern Upper Rhine and Chamber of Commerce basel Freiburg im Breisgau Tuesday, March 27, 2001 2 Dear Sir or Madam, It is a special honour for me to be able to speak as a representative of the Swiss National Bank here in the Zahringer city of Freiburg im Breisgau, i.e. abroad. This applies to a greater extent to today's event, where I am allowed to do so in front of a very knowledgeable, economically and politically committed audience. I thank you for your right to hospitality and would like to invite you to a short monetary policy tour d'horizon. Alone, the term "abroad" actually fits badly with the atmosphere that I am now allowed to feel in your circle. Even though I don't come from northwestern Switzerland and almost have to admit a bit ashamed that I'm stopping in Fribourg for the first time today, I don't feel like I'm in a foreign country here at all. The similarities and networks with Switzerland are too pronounced and diverse. Thus, the trinational region of the Upper Rhine is not only a geographical entity, but also an economic, political and social living space with its own identity  a living piece of European integration. Unspectacular, but tangible for the people here; not an abstract vision, but a concrete and useful reality. This reality today and will undoubtedly include the coexistence of two currencies for the foreseeable future. One may regret this or find it good. In any case, we can assume that the regime of an independent Swiss monetary policy will only change, if at all, in the distant future. In view of this initial situation, I will divide my Tour d'horizon into three stages: I will start with some references to the networking of the Swiss economy with that of the European Union and the fundamental consequences that this has for monetary policy. Then, in the sense of a preliminary interim assessment, I will turn to the experiences we have had so far in living together with the euro as an outstanding monetary brother. And finally, I would like to deal with the current global economic trends and contours of presumed future developments. Switzerland is integrated into the European economy Economic integration in the sense of inclusion in the cross-border division of labour and functions has many faces: labour and capital markets, flows of traded goods and services, or direct investment. Among these and many other criteria, the Swiss economy is intimately linked to its European environment and thus obviously also dependent on this environment. This striking exposure is reflected above all in the importance of Swiss foreign trade with the EU. 3 Switzerland exports more goods to the EU than an average member state. Growth in Germany from 1991 to 1997 was clearly higher than growth in Switzerland. Whether and to what extent this synchronicity will continue remains to be seen. What has been said in the retrospective for the economic context between Germany and Switzerland is likely to apply even more strongly to our current and future economic dependence on the EU. Cyclical developments in the euro area are the dominant determinants of economic activity in Switzerland. But there will also be phases of divergence in the future, in which independent monetary policy corrections are necessary in terms of stability policy. Secondly, the close networking leads to the obvious recognition that the exchange rate against the euro plays a key role in Switzerland's economic prosperity. It is worth taking a closer look at this fact against the background of the long-term development of the Swiss franc exchange rate. 5 3FBMFS 8FDITFMLVSTJOEFY EFT 4DIXFJ[FS 'SBOLFOT &YQPSUHFXJDIUFUFS 8FDITFMLVSTJOEFY -OEFS BO BO BO BO BO BO BO BO BO BO BO BO BO BO Decisive is above all the real, trade-weighted franc price development, shown here since 1973, when the order of Bretton Woods broke up and was replaced by floating. For this period, it initially shows a trend towards appreciation to the extent of an average of about 0.6% p.a. It is likely to be due to several factors, including the traditionally very high current account surpluses of more than 10% of gross domestic product (GDP) in phases. Such surpluses, which result to a significant extent from the country's international net creditor position, contribute to the currency's reputation and continuously generate additional demand for Swiss franc assets. The appreciation trend, which was accompanied by a real interest rate bonus, is not a problem in economic policy. On the contrary, it made imported goods cheaper and thus increased the purchasing power of given Swiss franc incomes. The export industry has also generally coped well with this upward trend. Indications of this are the trend increase in our export rate of goods and services to 45% of GDP and the continuous improvements in the terms of trade, i.e. the relationship between average export prices achieved and import prices paid. Instead, the massive fluctuations in the real Swiss franc exchange rate around the trend in phases are problematic. In several periods, most recently from 1994 to 1996, they have destabilised the economy and led to severe adjustment constraints. With the arrival of the euro, the economy's exposure to exchange rate risk has changed. Traditionally particularly volatile currencies, whose periodic devaluations have repeatedly confronted individual sectors of our economy  such as tourism  with difficult challenges, have been replaced by the more stable euro. This is an important advantage  for example for the economy in Ticino  6 part. At the same time, currency risk is concentrated to a decisive extent on a price relation, the exchange rate between the euro and the SFR. Bankers would speak here of a cluster risk, which is also likely to be further accentuated under the influence of the bilateral agreements. Swiss economic actors must adapt to this, while for competitors domiciled in the European currency area, exposure to currency risks has declined substantially. There is no doubt that this is a detrimental effect of going it alone in monetary policy and at the same time the strongest economic argument of those who want to replace the franc with the euro as soon as possible. Coexistence with the euro: an interim assessment After these remarks on the embedding of the Swiss economy in its European environment, I would like to turn to the experiences and insights that we have gained in our coexistence with the euro, which has now lasted two and a quarter of a year. I do this in the sense of an interim assessment, i.e. in the knowledge that although we have learned something valuable and valid, the future can very well confront us with new, possibly surprising constellations and decision-making situations. In the run-up to the launch of the European Monetary Union, two fears in particular were expressed and discussed with understandable concern. On the one hand, there were those who estimated the risk of serious exchange rate shocks to be very high and held out the prospect of serious disruptions that would be disastrous for the economy. This scenario was justified by supposedly inevitable withdrawals of confidence in the new, as yet untested currency and the resulting capital flows into the Swiss franc, this monetary dwarf with its disproportionate importance as an investment currency. And on the other hand, there were those who, in view of the magnitude of the magnitudes, no longer saw any room for an independent Swiss monetary policy and reasoned that the SNB had no choice but to follow European policy as faithfully as possible. These two perspectives have not come true over the past two years. Instead, those who have adjusted with serenity and without excitement to a scenario that would gradually but not fundamentally differ from the conditions before the introduction of the euro were proved right. This insight can be illustrated by looking at the monetary policy stance we have taken since 1999. It is reflected in the course of the three-month interest rate, LIBOR, which we steer as the operational target of our price stability policy. At the beginning of last year, we began to announce this control with the help of a one-percentage-point target range. 7 -*#03 . POBUF ""Oh, "Oh!" Always &63 ! We wanted to define the monetary framework generously with very low money market rates of around 1% and were not unhappy that during this period the Swiss franc remained very stable against the euro and  like the euro  weakened against the USD. The interest rate hump in the fourth quarter of 1999 had nothing to do with our policy. It built up as a millennium premium and later dismantled it again. With the surprisingly strong recovery that began in winter, we increased the three-month rate in several steps from around 1% to 3.5% in June 2000. At this stage, our course was much more restrictive than the policy of the European Central Bank. We considered this correction to be appropriate because our economy quickly reached full employment status and the risks of overheating with all their consequences had to be limited. After June 2000, we did not change interest rates until last Thursday. In retrospect, that was an appropriate course. Although there was still widespread talk of overheating in August and September and the majority of the markets expected a further interest rate hike, we did not take action. It seemed plausible to us that the signs of a slowdown at home and abroad would soon become clear. This attitude was not without risks, but has since proven to be correct. In monetary policy, too, you occasionally need a bit of luck. The fluctuations remained in a narrow range of only about plus/minus one percent around the price level of SFR 1.60 per euro. This pattern is almost reminiscent of the regime of a course fixation. It was the result of a policy and an economic scene that was characterized by striking similarities in Switzerland and Euroland. We have implemented our monetary policy  focused on the needs of the Swiss economy  on the SFR money market and have not once appeared on the foreign exchange market. But we have repeatedly said in advance that we would resist excessive price distortion if necessary through intervention in the foreign exchange market. This signal probably also contributed to the stabilisation of expectations and the calm development of the financial markets. In March 2000, initialized by our interest rate hikes, the SFR started to appreciate by around six percent. Since October of last year, it has been at about this level, but with larger short-term ups and downs than was the case in the course of 1999. The correction that has been made has probably also convinced the sceptics that we have the will and the means to pursue an independent monetary policy. Thus, after a good two years of coexistence with the euro, the interim balance is not unfavorable. Three aspects seem remarkable. First, and contrary to widespread fears, it can be noted that the floating exchange rate mechanism has not thwarted our monetary policy, but rather supported it. When we wanted to be expansionary in 1999, the franc remained weak. It depreciated significantly against the USD  on a par with the euro. And when we started a restrictive correction in the spring of 2000, it appreciated against the euro without overshooting. Without these supportive effects of the floating exchange rate, we would undoubtedly have had to make stronger interest rate hikes. Secondly, the significant weakening of the dollar against the euro a few months ago did not lead to any unpleasant shocks. The effect, which used to be registered with some regularity, that a weakening of the USD against the DM led to an appreciation of the Franc against the DM, has no longer materialised. Whether this undesirable, because destabilizing "mocha cups effect" has disappeared forever with the euro remains to be seen. 9 Finally, it is worth taking a look at the long-term interest rates, the interest rate differential for ten-year government bonds of Germany and the Swiss Confederation. For a large part of the population, this interest bonus is the most important economic argument against participation in monetary union. It reached its minimum of 110 basis points at the beginning of 1999, when doubts about our monetary policy autonomy spread in the market. With the correction of March 2000, which came as a surprise to many, the difference has widened again. This probably has less to do with changed inflation expectations than with presumably regained diversification properties of Swiss franc investments. Only if investors believe in a different Swiss franc development from the euro do they attest to the diversification characteristics of Swiss franc investments in a multi-currency portfolio. Only then are they willing to hold debt securities despite a slightly lower yield. Well, defending the interest rate bonus is certainly not a monetary policy objective. But the interest rate differential is a welcome companion of our independent currency regime and as such must be taken into account when thinking about alternatives. Coexistence with the euro: In summary, the finding is obvious that the monetary policy regime has proven itself quite well as a dwarf next to the giant. No monetary system can ever function to everyone's complete satisfaction. Primarily, it is important to achieve a reasonable degree of price stability and to contribute to the cyclically balanced development at full employment. This has not been done badly so far. 10 Current assessment of the situation and outlook Experience has shown that whether, when and how this favourable development will change depends not only on monetary policy, but also on a bundle of different influencing factors. In the final part of my presentation, let me make some reflections on current trends and the outlook. The global economic scene has undoubtedly deteriorated in the recent past. But under the impression of these changes, one must not overlook the fact that price stability, which is well secured widely, is an essential element of robustness and strength achieved. Whatever the problems we face, their solution will not, as so often in the past, be overshadowed by the painful task of substantially reducing inflation. In the headlines are above all the USA, whose long-standing economic boom has given way to an unexpectedly significant setback. To be sure, there are still good reasons to hope that this slowdown won't lead to a recession and won't last very long, especially since the Federal Reserve has responded with swift and significant rate cuts. However, it should be borne in mind that such cyclical changes of scenery are difficult to grasp in their determinants and therefore their exact course is difficult to estimate. Three aspects weigh on the outlook: First, the suspicion that after the long, massive investment boom a capital overhang has to be absorbed, which will curb investment demand for a long time. Second, the concern that the huge wealth losses that have occurred on the stock markets over the past twelve months will have a significant impact on consumer spending, especially as they hit households that have barely saved and incurred ample debt in the recent past. Thirdly, no economic forecast can ignore the fact that the current account development has been strongly deficit for a long time, even reaching a post-war record in the 4th quarter of last year. In a global comparison, however, these burdensome factors are offset by very favorable medium- and long-term growth prospects that overshadow the current setback. With sustained growth potential estimated at around 4%, the chances of a cyclical correction without recession are more intact than for a country with lower growth power. In any case, the cyclically remarkably high exchange rate of the USD signals a largely unbroken belief of international investors in the qualities of the USA as an investment country. Certainly, this is an element of strength, but at the same time a circumstance that weakens, if not prevents, a cyclically welcome devaluation. This experience seems to support the thesis that in a world of largely integrated capital markets, the exchange rate can only play its role as a hinge of cyclical demand balancing to a limited extent. Overall, one may follow the forecast of a period of weakness of rather short duration for the USA. But one must remain aware of the latent risks of a possibly suddenly occurring less favorable course. In Asia, too, the outlook has darkened, also  but not only  as a result of the slowdown in the USA. This is especially true in Japan, where the essential structural renewals are progressing only slowly. Against the backdrop of severely deficit public budgets and significant risks in the financial system, the decline in demand in recent months has once again disappointed hopes for a recovery. To what extent and how quickly the measures taken by the Bank of Japan will take effect remains to be seen. Despite all the well-founded concerns about further developments in Asia, it is important to 11 I would like to draw attention to the structural progress made following the financial crisis of 97/98. Two aspects are in the foreground. On the one hand, most countries register unproblematic developments in their current account balances. This largely excludes refinancing crises such as those that shook the entire region and the international financial markets in 97/98. On the other hand, the majority of countries no longer apply fixed but flexible exchange rate regimes, which significantly increases adjustment flexibility. That justifies confidence. Nevertheless, it is clear that global economic activity is subject to slowing influences not only from the US, but also from Asia. What does this mean for Europe? Overall, the European economic development is encouraging. Forecasts are favorable on average and the chances are high that our continent will be the global growth leader for some time. With moderate inflation, the eurozone achieved growth of 3.4% last year. That is certainly significantly less than the 5% that the US achieved. Based on consensus forecasts, GDP in Europe will grow by only 2.8% in the current year, but ahead of the USA, whose growth forecast is only 2%. And you don't need to be a particular optimist to see important progress in the structural area  especially in the labour markets and in the tax area. They have played their part in reducing unemployment from 11.5 to 8.8 percent since 1997 and also increasing the activity rate. Growth has once again created jobs in Europe  an important step forward. After all, serious imbalances, such as those that have built up in the United States in terms of saving and household debt or in the current account, are not to be found on our continent. Despite all the justified confidence, however, it would be wrong to underestimate the influence of global development on the economy of the European currency area. Simple milkmaid bills should be warned. The fact that the euro area's exports to the USA amount to less than three percent of Europe's gross domestic product does not make Europe a quasi-closed, self-sufficient economy. The networks with the world are diverse. They create complex interactions and dependencies beyond mere trade relationships. Undoubtedly, also about soft determinants of economic activity, the willingness to take risks, the general mood, the confidence in the future. More specifically about the financial markets, which  for example on the stock exchanges  have considerable global parallels. Finally, through direct investment, which transfers regional economic movements within groups of companies to other economic areas more strongly than in the past. With such indications, I do not want to distance myself from the confident European economic consensus, but I do want to point out risks that need to be considered. All the more so as we are in a phase in which expectations are being revised in the same direction, namely downwards, almost everywhere in the world. In this constellation, it can easily happen that the cumulative overall effect of the changes is underestimated. Risk-conscious confidence is also important with regard to the prospects for Switzerland. The current growth rate has declined from four percent in the first quarter of last year to just under two percent in the second half of the year, i.e. to a level roughly in line with the estimated long-term growth potential. This consolidation, which is welcome in itself, is mainly the result of slowdowns in consumption and construction investment, i.e. domestic demand. By contrast, investment in equipment and exports are growing steadily. Despite full employment, yes in 12 In various areas of the labour market, inflation is developing favourably. It reached 1.6 percent in the fourth quarter of last year and shows a downward trend with 1.3 percent in January and 0.8 percent in February, mainly due to oil prices. We completed our quarterly analysis last week and decided to lower the target range for the three-month interest rate by 1/4 percent to 2 3/4 to 3 3/4 percent. We have done this for two reasons. On the one hand, because the medium-term prospects for inflation are favourable. The expected economic development and the course of the monetary aggregates do not point to any increased inflation risks for the next three years. On the other hand, with this moderate interest rate cut, we wanted to respond to the fact that global economic risks have increased in recent months. Critics may object that we acted prematurely and, in the interest of tangible facts, had better waited a little longer in order to possibly make a major interest rate hike. Alone, because of the considerable delays with which monetary policy measures affect the economy, it seemed more expedient to us to make a moderate interest rate hike last week. Whether it will be enough, the future must show. In any case, the continuing favourable economic development and the confident expectations of consumers and companies do not currently signal any need for further action. For the current and next year, we expect growth of just under 2 percent, i.e. in the order of magnitude of the growth potential of our economy. Alone, monetary policy is and remains to a large extent a craft characterized by uncertainty. Consensus in favour of a scenario that is likely to be favourable must never distract from the existence of problematic risk scenarios. They affect the USA, the Far East, but also the European and not least the German economy, which has lost quite a lot of momentum in recent months. Uncertainties and potential for surprises also characterise the development of the stock market and  particularly important for Switzerland  the development of exchange rates against the USD and the euro. Such a decision-making situation, to which entrepreneurs as well as monetary policymakers are exposed, requires critical openness and the willingness to act quickly and decisively if necessary.

Risikobewusste Zuversicht ist auch in Bezug auf die Aussichten fr die Schweiz am Platze. Die laufende Wachstumsrate hat sich von vier Prozent im ersten Quartal des letzten Jahres auf knapp zwei Prozent in der zweiten Jahreshlfte zurckgebildet, d.h. auf ein Niveau, das in etwa dem geschtzten langfristigen Wachstumspotential entspricht. Diese an sich willkommene Konsolidierung ist vor allem das Ergebnis von Verlangsamungen im Konsum und in den Bauinvestitionen, d.h. der inlndischen Nachfrage. Dagegen erreichen die Ausrstungsinvestitionen und die Exporte anhaltende Zuwchse. Trotz Vollbeschftigung, ja in 12 verschiedenen Bereichen des Arbeitsmarktes offensichtlicher Verknappungstendenzen, nimmt die Teuerungsentwicklung einen gnstigen Verlauf. Sie erreichte im vierten Quartal des letzen Jahres 1.6 Prozent und zeigt mit 1.3. Prozent im Januar und 0.8 Prozent im Februar vor allem lpreisbedingt eine rcklufige Tendenz. Wir haben letzte Woche unsere Quartalsanalyse abgeschlossen und entschieden, das Zielband fr den Dreimonatszinssatz um  Prozent auf 2  bis 3  Prozent zu senken. Wir haben dies aus zwei Grnden getan. Zum einen, weil die mittelfristigen Perspektiven fr die Teuerung gnstig sind. Die erwartete konjunkturelle Entwicklung und der Verlauf der monetren Aggregate deuten fr die kommenden drei Jahre auf keine erhhten Teuerungsgefahren hin. Zum andern wollten wir mit dieser massvollen Zinssenkung auf den Umstand reagieren, dass sich in den letzten Monaten die globalen Konjunkturrisiken erhht haben. Kritiker mgen einwenden, wir htten vorschnell gehandelt und im Interesse einer handfesten Faktenlage besser noch etwas zugewartet, um dann mglicherweise einen grsseren Zinsschritt vorzunehmen. Allein, wegen den erheblichen Verzgerungen, mit denen sich geldpolitische Massnahmen auf die Volkswirtschaft auswirken, schien es uns zweckmssiger, schon letzte Woche einen massvollen Zinsschritt vorzunehmen. Ob er ausreichen wird, muss die Zukunft weisen. Jedenfalls signalisieren die anhaltend gnstige konjunkturelle Entwicklung und die bei Konsumenten und Unternehmen zuversichtlichen Erwartungen gegenwrtig keinen weiteren Handlungsbedarf. Wir rechnen fr das laufende und das nchste Jahr mit einem Wachstum von knapp 2 Prozent, d.h. in der Grssenordnung des Wachstumspotentials unserer Volkswirtschaft. Allein, Geldpolitik ist und bleibt in hohem Masse ein durch Unsicherheit geprgtes Handwerk. Der Konsens zu Gunsten eines mit einiger Wahrscheinlichkeit gnstigen Szenarios darf nie und nimmer ablenken von der Existenz problematischer Risikoszenarien. Sie betreffen die USA, den Fernen Osten, aber auch die europische und nicht zuletzt die deutsche Konjunktur, die in den vergangenen Monaten recht viel Schwung eingebsst hat. Unwgbarkeiten und berraschungspotentiale kennzeichnen auch die Brsenentwicklung und  fr die Schweiz besonders wichtig  den Verlauf der Wechselkurse zum USD und zum Euro. Eine so geartete Entscheidungssituation, der Unternehmer ebenso ausgesetzt sind wie Geldpolitiker, verlangt kritische Offenheit und die Bereitschaft, ntigenfalls rasch und entschlossen zu handeln.

Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the President of the Bank Council
text: Opening address by Mr Eduard Belser, Chairman of the Bank Council, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 20 April 2001 Strong impact of gold on accounts for 2000 The Swiss National Bank is in a good financial and operational position. Routine operations proceeded normally. However, the annual report and the annual accounts show exceptional developments. In my presentation, I would first like to comment on these particularities. Valuation of gold at the market price Last year, the sum of the SNB's balance sheet increased sharply, and the overall result reached an exceptional amount. The change in the principle applied to the valuation of the gold stock is the reason for this. Since 1 May 2000, the date of entry into force of the Federal Act on the Monetary Unit and Means of Payment, the issuing institution is no longer required to cover part of the banknotes in circulation with gold. In addition, for decades he had to value gold at the price of fr. 4595.74 per kilogram. Since May 1, gold has been on the balance sheet at its market price. This move to a new valuation method has led to an increase of around CHF 28 billion in the sum of the balance sheet. As a result, all marketable assets held by the SNB are now valued at market prices. Such a method better responds to an accurate and faithful evaluation. The Bank's financial situation can be judged more simply and with greater reliability. Gold sales begin The new legal bases have given the SNB more room for manoeuvre. Of the 2590 tons of gold held by the issuing institution, about half, it is estimated, is no longer needed for monetary purposes. As a result, this share has no longer been managed according to monetary criteria, but taking into account the interests of current and future beneficiaries. That is why the SNB started selling gold little by little at the beginning of May. Until the end of 2000, it sold 171 tonnes at an average price of just over 15,000 francs per kilogram. Sales were made - with deliberate regularity - at the rate of about one tonne per day. In its sales, the Bank complied with the quotas set out in the gold agreement signed by fifteen European central banks in Washington on 26 September 1999. 2 Building a portfolio of free assets If, as I have already pointed out, 1300 tonnes of gold are no longer needed for monetary purposes, the proceeds of these gold sales can also, of course, be used for other purposes. Revenue from sales up to the end of 2000 amounted to CHF 2.6 billion. This amount was invested, and the possibilities provided for in the National Bank Act had to be taken into account in the investments. These funds were therefore invested in bonds of first-class Swiss and foreign debtors. The beneficiary or beneficiaries of the free assets will no doubt be interested in holding first and foremost investments in Swiss francs, which are both safe and offer a good return; these free assets are thus distinguished from monetary reserves which, by definition, consist of foreign currency and gold, but not securities in Swiss francs, and which, moreover, must be the subject of liquid investments. At the end of 2000, free assets, valued at market prices, amounted to approximately CHF 19 billion; of this amount, about 16 billion francs were held in the form of gold - the amount still to be sold - and nearly 3 billion were bonds in foreign currencies and francs. As this portfolio of free assets does not constitute, in the legal sense, a special patrimony, it does not appear separately on the balance sheet. Establishment of a provision for the disposal of free assets The valuation of gold at market prices and the inclusion of the planned disposal of 1300 tonnes of gold - which is gradually being converted into financial assets - have also led to the creation of two substantial liabilities items on the Bank's balance sheet. The item "Provision for the disposal of free assets" is the larger of the two. Prudent bookkeeping requires that a provision be made if an extraordinary expense is expected. The establishment of the provision for the disposal of free assets therefore takes into account the high probability that the SNB will sell 1300 tonnes of gold, or the proceeds of the sale of this quantity, for other public purposes. The provision for the disposal of free assets therefore amounted to almost CHF 19 billion at the end of 2000. Establishment of a provision for price risk on gold The second provision that has been made concerns monetary gold, i.e. gold to remain in the assets of the SNB. It takes into account market and liquidity risks on this part of the gold stock. As monetary gold will remain intangible, this provision is not included in the calculation of the profit to be distributed. An amount of CHF 6.6 billion has been allocated to this provision. 3 Day-to-day operations After recalling the structural changes made to the accounts for the financial year 2000, I would like to briefly review some key figures in our income statement. On the product side Foreign currency investments - around CHF 50 billion on average per year - generated revenue of CHF 3.4 billion, excluding losses due to exchange rate developments, which amounted to a total of CHF 1.1 billion. Compared to the previous year, this revenue increased by no less than 800% due to the evolution of interest rates on the world markets. Indeed, capital gains were recorded in 2000 as a result of interest rate reductions, while capital losses had been incurred the previous year as a result of interest rate increases. In the area of monetary reserves, positions are deliberately not hedged against foreign exchange risk; it is therefore to be expected, on this side too, to sharp fluctuations in the product. The proceeds of Swiss franc claims arising from repurchase agreements - repurchase agreements became the SNB's main monetary policy instrument - amounted to CHF 513 million, exceeding the amount of the previous year by almost 250%. This strong increase was the result of the slight increase in the average volume of these claims, but also, and above all, of significantly higher interest rates than in 1999. On the load side The SNB's operating expenses are well under control. In 2000, the Bank's expenses amounted to CHF 565 million. Compared with the previous year, they increased by CHF 100 million, which corresponds quite exactly to the additional expenses that the increase in short-term remuneration has entailed on commitments to the Confederation. Their increase was offset by additional revenue on assets. Personnel costs decreased slightly. The reorganization of cash movements is still having an effect. However, changes in the remuneration paid in the rest of the banking sector make it more difficult to recruit staff. Banknote charges have become normalised, following the high costs resulting from the transition from the old to the new series of banknotes. Excluding the extraordinary impact of the new gold valuation, the overall result for the year was CHF 2.7 billion. The profit on the balance sheet is 1508 million francs, the same amount as in 1999. It will be distributed in accordance with legal requirements, as before. 4 An amount of CHF 1.2 billion was thus allocated to the general provision for market, credit and liquidity risks. Final remarks As a result of the valuation of gold at market prices, the SNB's balance sheet and profit and loss account will be subject to greater fluctuations in the future than in the past. The price risk on gold, which is considerable, cannot be managed because of the Washington agreement that I have already mentioned. The SNB, I would like to stress once again, would be happy to be able to transfer the assets it no longer needs for monetary purposes in the near future future so that their future beneficiaries can manage them. It would be desirable for it to concentrate, also in future, on its monetary policy tasks.
