Title: Summary of a speech given by the Chairman of the Governing Board
text: Presentation by Mr. Jean-Pierre Roth, Chairman of the Executive Board, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 20 April 2001 The economic situation Last year, the Swiss economy gained considerable momentum. After growth of 1.5% in 1999, real gross domestic product grew by 3.4% in 2000, according to initial estimates. Such a performance had not been observed since 1989. Thanks to the strength of the economic situation during the first part of the year, the underutilization of productive capacity, which we had experienced since 1992, was eliminated in the middle of the year. In the second half of the year, the pace of expansion gradually slowed, and the economy moved on its long-term growth path. The main support for economic activity came from exports of goods and services, which grew twice as fast as the previous year. This success can be attributed primarily to the good economic situation in the United States and Europe, but it is also the result of the competitiveness regained by our companies after several years of industrial restructuring and wage moderation. Domestic demand has also developed favourably. Consumer sentiment has warmed markedly; investment has accelerated due to the gradual depletion of productive resources and the good financial situation of enterprises. The most pleasing aspect of the cyclical recovery has been the development of the labour market. Employment has increased, and the unemployment rate has fallen sharply. The creation of new jobs has been particularly strong in the service and construction sectors. For the first time since the early nineties, industry recorded an increase in the number of persons employed. The unemployment rate has thus risen from 2.3% at the end of 1999 to 1.8% at present. Unable to find the qualified people they are looking for in Switzerland, companies turn to foreign markets. It is to be hoped that the lessons of the past have been understood: it is indeed in the interests of the long-term development of our economy to rely mainly on skilled foreign labour. The economic recovery has been accompanied by a moderate trend in inflation. Inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, was 1.6% in 2000, a level that we consider compatible with price stability. The dominant factor was the evolution of the price of oil, which contributed to the increase in prices by 1 percentage point. The rise in the prices of Swiss goods, which, fortunately, was 2 remained weak until then, has resumed a slightly upward path since last fall. This is particularly the case for rents and prices for certain services. In sectors subject to strong competitive pressure, great moderation and even price reductions have been observed. Monetary policy At the beginning of last year, we changed the way we conduct our monetary policy. Three new elements have taken place: 95 First - and in order to ensure greater transparency of our action - we have clarified what we understand by price stability. In our view, price stability is ensured if the rise in the consumer price index is less than 2% per year. In defining price stability in this way, we have taken two factors into account. On the one hand, not every price increase is necessarily inflationary. On the other hand, a small economy like ours often sees the evolution of its prices subject to strong external influences. 95 Then we make our monetary policy decisions on the basis of a medium-term inflation forecast. As the effects of monetary policy on prices are only unfolding with a significant delay, our forecast horizon is set at three years. 95 Finally, we conduct our monetary policy by orienting ourselves in relation to the interest rate on the money market. We set a fluctuation band for the three-month interest rate - the Libor - the position of this band reflecting the course of our policy. We indirectly influence Libor through short-term repo. At the beginning of 2000, we noticed that the Swiss economy was gaining momentum rapidly. In addition, the drying up of the labour market was becoming increasingly evident. At the same time, the continued strength of the dollar was effectively leading to an undesirable easing of monetary conditions in our country. To neutralize the resulting inflationary risks, we tightened monetary policy firmer and faster than we had previously imagined in December 1999. Until the middle of the year, we raised the Libor fluctuation band three times. It increased by 1.75 percentage points to 3%-4%. During the second half of 2000, the degree of restraint on our policy seemed to us to be adequate to avoid a situation of overheating and to ensure price stability in the medium term. Many indicators showed us that the economic recovery was well assured and that it was unfolding in an orderly manner. In particular, signs of a slowdown in the U.S. economy and a slowdown in the pace of growth in Europe suggested a slowdown in the dynamism of our exports. At the same time, the franc appreciated against the euro, leading to a slight tightening of monetary conditions. Moreover, price stability in the medium term did not seem to us to be threatened, as the M3 money supply even tended to decline. Similar signs came to us from bank loans that grew only slightly. 3 The evolution of the franc against the euro has clearly supported our monetary policy action. The stability of the franc until the beginning of 2000 contributed to the recovery of our economy. But when it came time to tighten monetary conditions, the franc reacted quickly and gained ground against the European currency. As a result, we have been able to make more limited interest rate increases than would have been necessary if the Swiss franc had remained stable. The consistent behaviour of the franc on the market shows that our currency has not lost its identity and that it is judged by traders for its own qualities. It is this autonomy that ensures a favourable interest rate differential. A relatively low cost of capital has advantages for Switzerland. The low level of interest rates corresponds to high capital formation, which is favourable to the development of productivity and wages. Our first experiences with the new way of conducting monetary policy are positive. The need for regular inflation forecasting requires us to carefully and systematically analyse all the factors determining the future development of inflation. The result within the SNB is a deepening of the exchange of views on the interactions between monetary policy, price developments and the economic situation. We also feel that the new mode of conduct has been well received by communities that follow our policy. These circles can better interpret our decisions to the extent that our policy has become more transparent. It is probably for this reason that the fluctuation band and Libor quickly became key elements of monetary policy discussions and have not left the spotlight since then. Transparency allows the public to better understand our decisions; it therefore contributes to market stability. I would like to conclude this section on our monetary policy by taking stock of the current economic situation. The economic outlook for the current year is positive, although several new risks have emerged. We expect the Swiss economy to grow at a pace close to its long-term potential. Domestic demand is expected to remain one of the strong points of growth, while exports will slow. The international environment is undoubtedly a significant source of risk to our economy: in recent months, US growth has weakened much more sharply than we expected last December. Japan is experiencing new difficulties that could spill over to the entire Asian continent, and the European Union has revised its growth forecasts downwards several times. The slowdown in our foreign trade could therefore be stronger than expected. In addition, there are significant uncertainties in financial markets. It is because of the multiplication of sources of risk that we decided, on March 22, to lower the libor fluctuation band by a quarter of a point. This relaxation of our policy does not jeopardise price stability in the medium term. My overview would be incomplete if I did not mention an important event that is taking place before our eyes and that, in a few months' time, will profoundly change the environment in which our economy operates. From 1 January next, the currencies of twelve European countries will disappear in favour of the euro, the common currency of the European Union. The euro has already been introduced as a scriptural currency for more than two years. From 2002, euro banknotes and coins will replace the old ones 4 national currencies. For the first time in its history, our country will be surrounded by a uniform monetary zone. This will not be without consequences for our economy. Our exporters must expect an increase in the use of the euro as an international means of settlement, and many tourists will want to use euros on Swiss territory. The increased use of the euro should not give rise to any particular difficulties, as our exporters and the tourist community already have experience of operating in foreign currencies. There is no doubt that the monetary unification of our neighbours will simplify our external transactions, but let us be vigilant because it will not lower our exchange rate risks. Indeed, I fear that the low volatility observed between the franc and the euro over the last two years will lead those who use the euro to think that the exchange rate risk on the European currency has now disappeared. This is not the case. The exchange rate relationship between the franc and the euro is set freely by the market. Although there is a broad convergence between the economic situation in the European Union and that prevailing in Switzerland, this relationship can still fluctuate. Companies operating in euros must therefore protect themselves against currency risk on the euro, as they do with the dollar or the pound sterling. Traditional precautionary measures are therefore still required. For its part, the SNB is aware of the importance that the euro represents for the Swiss economy. It shall be careful, in the conduct of its policy, to preserve as far as possible the smooth functioning of the markets; however, it cannot guarantee this. The Bank's mandate As our past action shows, our monetary policy aims to preserve price stability by taking into account the cyclical environment. This is how we understand the mandate entrusted to us by art. 99 of the Federal Constitution, namely "to conduct a monetary policy serving the general interests of the country". In order to avoid conflicts of interpretation, it would be desirable for this general mandate to now be defined more closely in the law. This is provided for in the draft revision of the National Bank Act, which is currently under consultation and will be the subject of parliamentary debate next year. It gives the Bank the task of ensuring price stability while taking into account economic developments. This provision is new. The law currently in force, which was drafted in 1953 when exchange rates were still fixed, merely takes over the constitutional mandate, i.e. mentions that the SNB must pursue a policy that serves the general interests of the country. The lack of specification of the Bank's mandate in the 1953 Act is not surprising. Indeed, under a fixed exchange rate regime, the objective of our monetary policy did not need to be defined more precisely. We carried out the necessary operations to ensure that the exchange rate of the Franc stabilized at the level defined by the official parity. Thus, in the sixties and seventies, when our country was fighting against cyclical overheating, it could not rely on monetary policy, but had to resort to exceptional instruments, such as the control of credits and issues, or even 5 the imposition of negative interest. Since the transition to floating exchange rates, monetary policy is no longer aimed at defending the parity of the franc; it can now be engaged for domestic stabilization purposes. The bill specifies the conditions for this commitment. The reference to price stability in the Bank's mandate therefore gives a general meaning to our action. From an economic point of view, the benefits of price stability are obvious, and it is clear that monetary policy is the most appropriate instrument to preserve it. No one doubts that money creation by the central bank is the factor that determines the evolution of prices in the medium term. On the other hand, the hope of sustainably improving growth and employment through monetary inflation has generally led to disillusionment. Experience shows that solid growth is only possible on sound monetary foundations. Speaking of sound monetary foundations, I of course rule out any situation of inflation and deflation, both of which are the source of considerable economic costs. But it is also clear that monetary policy has repercussions, at least in the short term, on the real economy. Already today, the SNB takes into account the economic situation in its assessments of the situation. The fact that the draft law indicates that the objective of price stability must be pursued in the light of cyclical developments clearly places the SNB's action in its general economic context. The draft law also specifies the conditions under which the SNB should carry out its mandate. Here two aspects are important to us: the Independence of action of the Bank and its accountability. The principle that the conduct of monetary policy should be entrusted to an independent central bank is already enshrined in the new Constitution. The bill gives concrete form to its implementation. Above all, the aim is to give the SNB's Governing Board the decision-making autonomy it needs to implement a policy that ensures the fulfilment of the price stability mandate. Autonomy goes no further than the freedom necessary for the execution of the mandate. Autonomy and mandate are two closely linked aspects. Autonomy without a specific mandate would certainly be a source of problems. As a counterweight to autonomy, the draft law provides for a formal obligation for the SNB to be accountable for the performance of its mandate. Through this obligation, its autonomy receives democratic legitimacy, and the transparency of its action is ensured. Accountability and the definition of a mandate are also linked: the Bank must have a clear mandate to fulfil if it is held accountable to the authorities for its implementation and if it wants its action to be understood by the public. By adding price stability to the definition of the Bank's mandate, our country would be in line with current international practice. It would have a monetary order comparable to that adopted for the European Central Bank, which has been taken up by many other countries and which is recommended as a standard of good behaviour by the International Monetary Fund. Finally, it should be stressed that the introduction of the objective of price stability - tempered by taking account of cyclical developments - would correspond to sentiment. 6 Widely spread in Switzerland that monetary policy must ensure the defence of the purchasing power of the currency in the medium term, which leaves the Issuing Institute the possibility of taking into account the economic situation. Failure to specify the Bank's mandate in this sense would give the impression that our country wants to distance itself from a rule of sound management. That would be very unfortunate. The obligation to hold sufficient monetary reserves The second area in which the draft SNB Act gives concrete form to the provisions recently introduced in the Constitution is that of monetary reserves. Indeed, art. 99 of the Federal Constitution requires, in its 3rd paragraph, that the SNB establish, with the help of its income, sufficient monetary reserves. The draft revision of the SNB Act creates a solid legal basis not only for the distribution of the Bank's profits - as the current law already does - but also for the way in which they are to be established. The proposed rules are not new. In principle, they correspond to the provisions contained in the Agreement on the Distribution of Profits, drawn up in 1991 by the Confederation and the National Bank. The profit distribution agreement is sometimes criticised for allowing the SNB to build up unnecessarily high monetary reserves. The SNB would thus deprive the Confederation and the cantons of profits that could be used more judiciously than in the form of additional monetary reserves. What to make of this criticism? Remember that our monetary reserves include foreign exchange reserves and gold reserves. When we concluded the first profit distribution agreement, our foreign exchange reserves had reached a level that corresponded to that of comparable small European countries. We had measured ourselves against other small countries because the desirable level of a country's monetary reserves depends heavily on its degree of integration into the world economy. At the time, therefore, we considered that our foreign exchange reserves were at an appropriate level. In addition, we started from the idea that our future needs for reserves would depend on the expansion of the Swiss economy. For this reason, the agreement with the Confederation gives the SNB the possibility of replenishing provisions - and thus accumulating foreign exchange reserves - at a rate commensurate with the growth of gross national product. In 1991, gold reserves could only be easily integrated into our assessment of the desirable level of monetary reserves. Under the legal framework of the time, our metal reserves were valued at their official value, thus de facto immobilized and unfit for monetary use, at least under normal circumstances. Since the abolition of the gold parity of the Swiss franc, the SNB can, in principle, freely dispose of its gold stock. Compared to the small European countries I just mentioned, our metal cash holdings are very high. The question then arose as to whether the Bank needs such a large stock to carry out its tasks. An expert report showed that half of our 7 gold stock can be allocated for non-monetary purposes. The legislator will decide, in due course, on the use of the proceeds of the sales of this first half of our gold cash. With the other half of the gold stock, we are now well endowed with monetary reserves. This relatively comfortable situation seems justified to us in view of Switzerland's particular economic and political position. Indeed, let us not forget that Switzerland is in a different situation from other small European countries in two respects: 95 First of all, Switzerland is home to a financial centre with an international dimension. The result is financial integration that makes us more sensitive than others to possible financial or exchange rate crises. Well endowed with reserves, we can intervene in the markets in the event of a crisis and thus try to protect our country from external disturbances. In addition, a good endowment of reserves by the SNB strengthens market confidence in the financial stability of our country and protects us from speculative attacks. 95 Secondly, our country does not belong to the European Union or the euro area. In the event of a crisis, we must therefore be able to operate independently without having to rely on our neighbours. Some refute these arguments. In particular, they believe that we do not need large monetary reserves since we rarely intervene in the foreign exchange market. Those who reason in this way misunderstand the role of crisis prevention measures. Preventive measures are not there to deal with a normal situation, it is the extreme case that must be considered. If it were otherwise, they would not make sense. Of course, we all hope that such extreme cases will not occur and that we will never have to use all of our reserves. I recognise that defining the necessary level of monetary reserves is also a matter of assessment. We have conducted this review without complacency towards us, in full awareness of our responsibilities. Conclusion Since 1994, our country has been in a situation of price stability. More than three years ago, the economy began to recover. Output and employment have risen sharply. In the middle of last year, we returned to full employment, without any significant risks of inflationary slippage. Our mission now is to ensure the monetary conditions that will allow our country to maintain this achievement. We have an excellent year 2000 behind us, and 2001 should show sufficient growth to maintain full employment in our country. We owe this good situation to all those who have committed themselves in recent years to making our country more economically efficient. Many sacrifices 8 were granted during this period of restructuring. We are now seeing the fruits of it. Let us know how to preserve them by not relaxing our adaptation efforts. I would like to associate the Bank's authorities and the employees of the National Bank with the positive outcome of 2000. Everyone is fully committed to ensuring that the SNB can fulfil its mandate. I would also like to thank you, ladies and gentlemen, for your interest in our activities.

Title: Competitiveness and growth prospects of the Swiss economy on the threshold of the 21st century
text: Competitiveness and growth prospects of the Swiss economy on the threshold of the 21st century Presentation by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank 55th Annual General Meeting of the Association of Swiss Companies in Germany Wednesday, May 9, 2001 2 Dear Sir or Madam, I look forward to the opportunity to speak to you today. Its association counts the leading Swiss companies among its members. They are anchored in our country, very familiar with at least one foreign location - with Germany - and have always been exposed to competition. Your circle therefore seemed to me to be particularly suitable for discussing the competitiveness and growth prospects of the Swiss economy. Today, the Swiss economy is in good and balanced shape. From 1997 to 2000, real gross domestic product grew by an average of 2.2%, last year by 3.4%. The rapid decline in unemployment was particularly encouraging. There is full employment again today. In recent months, the international environment has deteriorated. Thanks to robust domestic demand, however, we can continue to expect considerable economic growth for the current year. Few would have thought this turnaround in the economy and the labour market possible just a few years ago. The recession and stagnation of the nineties had discouraged many and undermined confidence in the performance of our economy. What are the reasons for the change in mood? The recovery of the global economy and the calming of the exchange rate situation have undoubtedly contributed to this. Equally important, however, is what was done in the nineties to give new impetus to the economy. These include the far-reaching restructuring of many companies, the deregulation and liberalisation of markets and the development of new economic policy solutions. In the following, I will first briefly look back on the nineties. The second part deals with the question of whether the Swiss economy as a whole has become more competitive. I would like to conclude my presentation with a few concluding remarks. 3 I Nineties - Stagnation and rapid change I do not want to say much about the concept of competitiveness. For companies, it means the ability to compete with other companies, to sell products and services at home and abroad and, if possible, to gain market share. The entrepreneurial services and the business costs are in the foreground. A company has to keep up with its competitors in order to assert itself in the market. If he does not succeed in this, sooner or later it disappears from the scene. The economic view of competitiveness brings an additional dimension. It is about the ability of an economy as a whole to create sustainable prosperity and jobs. Unlike a company, a country does not go bankrupt even with poor economic policies; however, the standard of living of the population can fall almost arbitrarily. The rough measure of a country's competitiveness is the income per capita of the population. Today I am concentrating on the economic view. Of course, from this perspective, companies are also of central importance. Without vital and innovative companies, there is neither prosperity nor employment. In the nineties, a lot of things got going in Switzerland. At the same time, this period was marked by stagnation and high unemployment over a long period of time. I would like to comment briefly on both aspects. I'll start with change. The employment structure continued to shift towards the service sector. Today, this sector employs almost 70% of the workforce, while the share of industry has shrunk to just over a quarter. New industries such as computer science quickly gained in importance. At the end of the eighties, 6% of the workforce was employed in IT and business services, ten years later it was 9%. This does not include all those specialists who ensure that the computer systems are running in the companies and in the administration. Second, labor productivity increased. Total economic value added per person in employment rose by 1% per year after stagnating in the eighties. The productivity improvements in the industry were impressive. They fell modestly there- 4 against in the service sector. Considering that productivity in this sector had fallen significantly in the eighties, even minimal growth must be regarded as a success. The dismantling of obsolete regulations and increased competition from abroad also gave this sector, which has so far been largely isolated, more dynamism. A third aspect of the change is the increasing international division of labour: an increasing proportion of Swiss production is going abroad; at the same time, domestic demand is increasingly being met by imports. Interdependence increased more strongly in the case of industrial goods than in the case of services, most of which are linked to the location. However, an important service sector - the financial sector - is now globally active. The growing international interdependence is particularly evident in direct investment. There are numerous reasons why companies get involved abroad. This includes market development and the exploitation of more favourable production conditions. The new means of communication have strengthened the trend towards globalisation. Between 1990 and 1999, the capital stock of Swiss companies abroad grew from CHF 85 billion to more than CHF 300 billion. Direct investment by service companies developed particularly dynamically. Their share of the total capital stock rose from 41% to 66%. Direct investment by foreign companies in Switzerland developed somewhat less dynamically, but also considerably. Foreign engagements of companies have always been important vehicles for technology transfer. They promote the spread of technological progress and thus contribute to increasing growth opportunities worldwide. A final point concerns changes in economic policy, to which I attach particular importance. I am thinking of the Internal Market Act and the total revision of the Antitrust Act, the introduction of an active labour market policy, the reorientation of agriculture, the reform of the education system and the liberalisation and deregulation of public services, particularly in the telecommunications sector. The economic difficulties had sharpened the view of necessary changes. However, an important impetus also came from the emerging common European market. He made it clear that the highly cartelised and regulated domestic economy 5 had become a mortgage for the export sector, which reduced its chances on the European market. For many, however, the nineties are not remembered for the innovations, but for the high unemployment and the economic problems in key areas of the Swiss economy. The nineties brought Switzerland to the end of the growth parade of the industrialized countries. First of all, it was the inevitable correction of the economic overheating and the excesses, especially in the real estate sector, which had characterized the end of the eighties. The restrictive monetary policy needed to combat inflation burst the speculative bubble in the real estate sector. This was followed by painful structural adjustments at the banks and in the construction industry. Efforts to keep public finances unbalanced despite falling revenues were also not conducive to a rapid overcoming of the recession. An additional burden was the exchange rate turbulence. In two bursts in the summers of 1992 and 1993, the European Monetary System collapsed. In addition, there was the dollar crisis at the beginning of 1995. The Swiss franc served as a refuge currency, not least because there was great uncertainty about the planned introduction of the European common currency. In real and export-weighted terms, the Swiss franc was on average 15% higher in 1995 than in 1992. The currency turbulence - especially the massive devaluation of the lira and the pound - did not leave Germany and France untouched. The German and French economies grew by just under 1% per year from 1993 to 1996 and unemployment rose significantly. The pronounced weak growth of the two important trading partners, to which a third of our exports go, has not been without consequences for the Swiss economy. It is undisputed that the competitiveness of Swiss companies suffered from the exchange-rate-related cost increase. It is more difficult to answer the question of what could have been done about it. The SNB loosened monetary policy sharply from mid-1992 to 1994 and then again in 1995. By the end of 1995, short-term interest rates had fallen by eight percentage points to 1.5%; as a result, the decline in interest rates was considerably stronger than in Germany. If the economy is doing badly, the focus is on 6 Regularly refers to the central banks. This is also the case in Switzerland. Some claim that an even more aggressive interest rate cut would have noticeably alleviated the difficult situation of the Swiss economy. Others believe that inflation would have given way even with a less restrictive monetary policy, and still others see the SNB's main mistake in the overly expansionary monetary policy of the later eighties. An analysis of past monetary policy provides important insights. In all retrospective studies, however, the fundamental difficulty is to adequately reconstruct the previous decision-making situations: what information was available, what were the uncertainties and the risks. Only in this way can it be fairly assessed whether alternative courses of action existed in reality at all. From today's perspective, the former central bank management must be attested that its clear goal of restoring price stability has sustainably strengthened the credibility of monetary policy. This benefits the Swiss economy today, among other things, in the form of a low level of interest rates. What we would do differently after the experience of that time certainly concerns the communication of monetary policy. We would stress that the SNB takes exchange rate developments into account in its monetary policy decisions, as it had effectively done. In a country like Switzerland, which is strongly intertwined with foreign countries, this is a matter of course, regardless of whether we conducted a monetary policy oriented towards the money supply as we did then or pursue a broader-based concept of stability as we do today. Admittedly, more transparent and simpler communication would not have eliminated the economic difficulties. However, certain misunderstandings and often fruitless, ideologically tinged debates about monetary policy could probably have been avoided. Let me close the review of the nineties and take a look into the future. 7 II Consequences for the competitiveness and growth prospects of the Swiss economy Is the Swiss economy competitive? If we stick to the European Commission's definition, there is no doubt about it: an economy is considered competitive if it sustainably generates a high and growing standard of living for the local population and enables a high level of employment. Switzerland has the fourth highest gross domestic product per capita in the world. It has the highest level of employment of all OECD countries and enjoys a comparatively very good environmental quality. Prosperity results from the interplay of various factors. These include stable macroeconomic conditions such as low inflation, low interest rates, reasonable taxes and legal certainty. A moderate density of regulation, the integration of the economy into the global economy and an efficient financial system are also beneficial. And it is impossible to imagine life without a high-quality and open education system, a flexible labour market and a well-functioning infrastructure. All of these factors mean that the workforce is well educated, abundant physical and human capital is formed, and advances can be made in technology. Technical progress and the innovative capacity of companies play a key role. They are the basis for increasing productivity and thus the basis for the rising standard of living of the population. Since 1975, economic growth in Switzerland has been lower than in most other industrialised countries, and the prosperity advantage over foreign countries has narrowed. This is likely to be the case even if one takes into account the difficult measurement problems and takes into account the fact that Switzerland has had a high standard of living for a long time. An important reason for Switzerland's poor performance is the incrustations in the domestic economy. The already mentioned decline in productivity of the service sector in the eighties, but also the excessive domestic price level, points in this direction. With the Internal Market Act and the revision of the Antitrust Act, such growth-inhibiting undesirable developments were clearly in sight. 8 For a few years now, there have been signs that the growth opportunities of the Swiss economy have improved. Considering the far-reaching structural adjustments, the deregulation and liberalisation measures and the technological progress of recent years, this is plausible. In fact, calculations show that the higher trend growth does not come because there is only more work. It can be partly explained by an increased use of capital, but above all by the increase in the so-called total factor productivity. This mysterious residuum captures all those contributions to economic growth that cannot be explained by an increased use of labor and capital. This reflects technical progress, for example in the field of communications and INFORMATION technology, as well as the positive effects of deregulation and liberalisation. How can this promising trend be strengthened? There are no patent remedies that have to be applied to all factors. As mentioned above, the labour supply has not provided any significant growth impetus in recent years. The working-age population is barely growing any more. Meanwhile, the employment rate also stagnated, which had risen continuously until the nineties. A decline in the activity rate would not be in the economic interest, if only not with regard to the financing of old-age provision. One possible field of action are changes in the tax system, which create increased incentives to work. In any case, our labour market policy, which contains a reasonable level of worker protection and flexibility, must be preserved, thus making a significant contribution to the rapid reduction of unemployment. The need for increased immigration is also sometimes pointed out. However, it should be borne in mind that broad growth does not automatically raise the average standard of living of the population. The use of capital plays an important role in Switzerland's economic growth in view of the scarcity of labour resources. The comparatively high investment ratio and capital base are favoured by the low nominal and real interest rates. These, in turn, are an expression of the high level of saving activity in Switzerland, the long tradition of stability and the low risk of inflation. These advantages must continue to be preserved. 9 Finally, it is clear that the structural reforms that have been undertaken must be continued. For example, the tightening of the Antitrust Act, which the federal government recently proposed, can further strengthen competitive forces. The education system must be adapted to new requirements at all levels. Other measures such as the liberalisation of agriculture, deregulation in the energy sector and the promotion of competition within Switzerland are important in order to reduce the still excessive domestic price level. Finally, fiscal and monetary policy is also addressed. The importance of sound public finances and moderate taxation for economic growth has long been known. High deficits increase uncertainty and limit the flexibility of the state. A high tax burden has a negative impact on work performance. As far as monetary policy is concerned, there is a broad consensus that stable monetary conditions promote economic growth. The SNB will therefore continue to strive to ensure a high degree of price stability. In Switzerland, the strong economic upswing with low inflation has given a serious boost to the myth that low inflation would inhibit growth. At the same time, there has been a growing recognition that a monetary policy geared to price stability is compatible with a balanced economic cycle and a high level of employment. This pleasing development is not least due to the new monetary policy concept that we introduced a year and a half ago. Its three elements are the clear definition of price stability, the publication of an inflation forecast and the communication of monetary policy on the change of the target range for the three-month Libor. The new monetary policy approach has been well received. It seems to be more understandable than the previous monetary policy, which was based on an intermediate target for a money supply. In particular, today's concept makes it easier to explain the importance of the exchange rate for monetary policy. The SNB cannot ignore the exchange rate if it wants to fulfil its stability mandate. Its influence is first shown in the definition of the Libor target band. By focusing on a three-month interest rate and setting a target range, the SNB has gained a certain amount of leeway, 10 to counteract temporary disruptions in the money and foreign exchange markets. The definition of price stability - inflation below 2% - is also chosen in such a way that monetary policy can react flexibly to external disturbances. The influence of the exchange rate on the monetary policy decisions of the Executive Board, which are published quarterly, is mainly determined by the inflation forecast. The inflation forecast is based on a broad collection and analysis of all important data on the economic situation in Switzerland and abroad. Among these variables is also the exchange rate. It influences projected inflation primarily through two channels. On the one hand, a real appreciation of the Swiss franc leads to a decline in aggregate demand and thus to a decline in production and employment. Such a decline has a dampening effect on the prices of goods with a certain delay. On the other hand, the exchange rate influences inflation through the prices of imported goods. A higher valuation of the Swiss franc reduces import prices expressed in Swiss francs and thus dampens inflation as measured by the consumer price index. As part of the inflation forecast, we try to quantify the effects of the exchange rate on output and inflation. To put it simply, the SNB takes the exchange rate into account to the extent that it influences the inflation forecast. With the new monetary policy concept, the SNB adheres to the principle of an autonomous monetary policy. As an alternative, the peg of the Swiss franc to the euro is sometimes proposed. Since Switzerland is not a member of the EU, such a policy would essentially consist of defending a fixed nominal franc exchange rate of the euro with unlimited foreign exchange purchases and sales. This would be associated with two disadvantages in particular. Firstly, the SNB would no longer be in a position to take account of the economic situation in its own country with its monetary policy. Monetary policy would de facto be delegated to the ECB, over whose decisions Switzerland has no influence. Second, Swiss interest rates would rise. Since the exchange rate risk disappears with a credible peg of the Swiss franc to the euro, the domestic interest rate level would have to approach the higher European level. Switzerland has so far come to the conclusion that the benefits of an autonomous monetary policy outweigh the disadvantages. This need not mean that the SNB steers a course that is different from that of the ECB. Since the economic situation in Switzerland and the 11 The SNB's monetary policy is often very similar to that of the ECB. However, the SNB always has the option of steering a different course if the economic situation so requires. She also made use of it in the past. In view of the unfavourable economic situation in Switzerland, the SNB conducted a more expansionary monetary policy in the second half of the nineties than the Deutsche Bundesbank and later the ECB. When the Swiss economy picked up rapidly at the end of 1999 and the risk of inflation increased again, the SNB tightened monetary policy more strongly. Recently, we decided to loosen the monetary policy stance slightly autonomously in view of the increased global economic risks and the reduced risk of inflation. I conclude with these comments on monetary policy. III Schlussbemerkungen You have noticed that I am optimistic about the growth prospects of the Swiss economy. My confidence is essentially based on the fact that the revitalisation of the economy over the last decade and the reorientation of economic policy towards more market has given the Swiss economy new impetus and improved its competitiveness. The recent economic uncertainty cannot dampen this fundamentally positive assessment. Of course, it requires a prudent monetary policy. The long-term preservation of the competitiveness of the Swiss economy must be a primary objective for economic policy actors. Only in this way can we ensure that prosperity increases, that the level of employment remains high and that the environment is used sparingly. An increase in living standards cannot be achieved simply by redistributing income. Rather, all factors that promote sustainable economic growth must be promoted. A prosperous economic development presupposes stable monetary conditions. In recent years, the SNB has been fortunate enough to support the movements in the exchange rate in its efforts to ensure price stability and balanced economic development. However, we must reckon with this. 12 This favourable constellation will not always be the case in the future and that monetary policy will once again be faced with delicate decisions. Rapid technological progress and growing international integration opened up new opportunities for the Swiss economy. Naturally, however, innovations are also associated with considerable risks. New things must first be tested on the market. A lot of things prevail, some fail. If the economy is to prosper, risks must be taken. Success and failure are therefore often close to each other. The turbulence on the financial markets, but also the recent corporate crises in Switzerland, have clearly demonstrated this. This makes it all the more important to maintain moderation and reason in times of rapid change. If this is also taken into account, the chances of the Swiss economy on the threshold of the 21st century are good.
