Title: Introductory Remarks, Half-yearly Media News Conference
text: Berne, 14 June 2001 Introductory remarks by Jean-Pierre Roth The National Bank has decided to continue its current monetary policy. It is leaving the target range for the three-month Libor rate unchanged at 2.75% to 3.75%. For the time being, the three-month Libor rate is to be kept in the middle of the target range. Monetary policy was last adjusted on 22 March 2001, when the target range was lowered by 0.25 percentage points. Since then, economic prospects in Switzerland have scarcely changed. The National Bank thus sees no reason at present for a further relaxation of its monetary policy. The National Bank is expecting GDP to grow by 2.0% in 2001 and by 2.1% in 2002. In the next three years, inflation should amount to between 1.3% and 1.6%. The dotted curve in the figure shows our inflation forecast of December 2000. Then we expected inflation in 2001 to temporarily increase to more than 2%, i.e. the upper end of the range which the National Bank equates with price stability. This forecast was made against the background of the strong economic upswing in 2000, and particularly based on the substantially higher oil prices at that time. In December 2000, we assumed that oil prices would only decline gradually in the course of 2001 and would not stabilise until near the end of 2003. Already in our assessment of the economic situation of 22 March we changed our views on the course of inflation, inducing us to lower the Libor rate by a quarter percentage point. Oil prices declined within a very short time, and the US economy weakened more markedly than had still been anticipated at the end of 2000. This has reduced the risk of a temporary rise in inflation in excess of the 2% level in the current year. This assessment is confirmed by the development of the national consumer price index so far this year. Inflation has dropped, compared with the previous year, from 1.6% in the fourth quarter 2000 to 1.0% in the first quarter 2001. Clearance sale prices for clothing were taken into consideration for the first time; since these were particularly low due to the mild winter, however, this had the effect of putting an additional temporary damper on inflation. This effect diminished somewhat in April and May of this year, resulting in a renewed slight increase in measured inflation. The dashed curve in the figure shows our latest inflation forecast. The table contains the average annual inflation rate according to the new forecast. Based on an unchanged three-month Libor rate of 3.25% during the next three years, inflation should reach 1.4% in 2001, move up slightly to 1.6% in 2002 and fall back to 1.3% in 2003. At the beginning of 2004 we are expecting 1.2% inflation. Inflation is thus likely to remain within the limits which we have defined as price stability during the entire forecasting horizon. The slight increase in the forecast inflation for 2002 is due to the anticipated Jean-Pierre Roth SNB Berne, 14 June 2001 2 tighter situation on the real estate market, which will probably lead to higher housing rents, and to the slowdown in the price decline in the field of telecommunications. In making our forecasts we assumed that the expansion of the US economy will again accelerate somewhat by the end of this year. In Europe, too, we are confident that economic activity will pick up speed next year. We are expecting the US dollar to remain at its current level and are putting the price of oil at around 25 per barrel. The price development in the first half of 2001 was strongly influenced by the decline in price increases for imported goods. If solely domestic goods and services are taken into account it becomes clear that in this field inflation has moved up compared with December 2000. This is in particular due to the favourable course of economic activity in Switzerland since mid-1999, which impacts on the development of prices for domestic goods with a time lag. The slowdown in growth in the last three quarters, however, shows that currently no long-term inflationary pressure should emanate from economic activity. The expected development of wages and salaries likewise does not give cause for great concern. The money supply M3, which plays an important role in the long-term course of inflation, has been expanding again since the beginning of 2001. However, the development of the money stock M3 is still in line with the goal of price stability as well. Overall, therefore, at the moment no inflationary threats are discernible for the next three years. The Swiss economy expanded by 2.5% year-on-year in the first quarter. If annualised growth rates are compared with the previous quarter it becomes evident that real GDP has been growing at a practically unchanged rate of approximately 1.8% since mid-2000. Economic development has thus been near the long-term potential growth level in the past six months. The growth of private consumption again improved somewhat and more or less corresponds to the long-term average. By contrast, the growth of investment, notably expenditure on machinery and equipment, has declined substantially. Exports continue to record very robust growth. The Swiss economy is set to follow this growth path and to enjoy full employment in the next few quarters. Nevertheless, the level of orders on hand and the development of incoming orders point to a weakening of export growth. Economic activity should, however, be supported by domestic demand. Consumer sentiment continues to be optimistic, and real wage increases are likely to have a positive effect on consumer expenditure of private households. The outlook for the Swiss economy has scarcely changed since March. According to our assessment, the lowering of the target range for the Libor rate by 0.25 percentage points at that time is adequate for keeping the economy on a path of balanced growth. Inflation prospects, however, clearly show that currently a further relaxation of monetary conditions is not indicated. Such a relaxation increases the risk of an excessive demand for resources and in turn affect inflation. The present position of the target range is adequate in the given economic situation. Jean-Pierre Roth SNB Berne, 14 June 2001 3 Like every long-term outlook, our forecast, too, is fraught with some uncertainties. One such uncertain factor is the oil price, which has been exceedingly volatile in the recent past and has again risen slightly. Should the oil price - contrary to our expectations increase further in the coming months our inflation forecast would be too optimistic. More significant, however, are the risks emanating from the development of US economic activity. If the US economy cools more markedly than expected or if the dollar depreciates excessively, then the National Bank would have to reconsider its monetary policy course. Title: Introductory Remarks, Half-yearly Media News Conference
text: Berne, 14 June 2001 Introductory remarks by Niklaus Blattner Centre of Competence for System Stability With effect from the year 2001, the Swiss National Bank has set up a Centre of Competence for System Stability. In doing so, it is putting into practice a lesson learned from long experience  namely, that a stable and competitive financial system is an essential prerequisite for successful monetary policy. A central bank can influence price stability only in an indirect way, i.e. by changing the supply of money  which means through the money and capital markets. It is thus particularly interested in maintaining a solid financial system, as only such a system will respond reliably to changes in monetary policy. The stability of the financial system is of interest not merely to the National Bank but also to the Federal Banking Commission as well as to other federal authorities and private institutions that have self-regulatory responsibilities. The Banking Commission is the National Bank's principal partner, and is also involved in the work of the Centre of Competence. Other authorities and institutions are called upon to assist in specific areas. In addition to the stability of the financial system in general, the Centre is also concerned with the stability of the payment systems, which also includes securities clearing. Efficient and reliable financial market infrastructure is conducive to the profitability, smooth functioning, solvency and stability of its users and customers. By contrast, poorly constructed or badly managed infrastructure is a source of systemic instability. Financial market infrastructure not only offers advantages in terms of size and product range but also provides networks  and users of networks depend on the stability of the entire structure. Consequently, financial market infrastructure has two distinct aspects: under favourable circumstances it contributes to the stability of financial systems, whereas under unfavourable circumstances it jeopardises them. This ambivalence shapes the attitude of the supervisory authorities and the central bank towards financial market infrastructure. From the regulators' point of view, the operation of important financial market infrastructure requires both initial authorisation and continuous supervision  however much trust may exist. The National Bank's supervisory function in Swiss Interbank Clearing (SIC) is set out in contractual form. The draft revision of the National Bank Law (NBL), which is currently at the consultation stage, explicitly states that the National Bank will be empowered to supervise the operation of cashless payment systems if these are likely to pose a threat to the stability of the financial system. It also provides for sanctions to be imposed under Niklaus Blattner SNB Berne, 14 June 2001 2 administrative law should the parties operating the payment system fail to meet the minimum requirements. A system could, for example, be denied access to the sight deposit account at the National Bank. The National Bank could also issue a public warning against the use of a defective system. Any further sanctions, however, would have to be imposed by the Swiss or foreign authorities responsible for supervising the system's operator and users rather than by the National Bank. The proposals contained in the draft legislation would create a clear legal basis for the National Bank's traditional efforts to contribute to the stability of the payments infrastructure. The National Bank is by no means interested in becoming a regulatory activist. It is purely concerned with monetary policy. The fact that its security requirements for payment systems enhance Switzerland's appeal as an international centre of finance is merely a welcome side effect. Switzerland's attractiveness as a business location is one of the main factors in the competitiveness of financial service providers. And competitive financial service providers are themselves essential to stable financial systems. Sustainable success can only be achieved if the operating conditions are right. That is why the Centre of Competence for System Stability also addresses the general background, i.e. the regulatory and supervisory framework of the financial markets, including aspects of tax law and money laundering. To avoid misunderstanding, we should mention that the competitiveness of the financial sector is by no means the primary goal of the financial market supervisory authorities or of the central bank. The chief concern of the financial market supervisory authorities  i.e. the Banking Commission  is to protect creditors and investors. For its part, the National Bank focuses on conducting monetary policy serving the interests of the country as a whole. Specifically, it aims to safeguard price stability while taking due account of the cyclical development of the Swiss economy. For the supervisory authorities and for the National Bank, the competitiveness of the financial sector is a secondary goal which is important only insofar as it affects the primary objectives. Competitive financial service providers are also profitable ones. If profitability is lacking, solvency will be at risk in the long run. Service providers whose profitability is doubtful will therefore ultimately jeopardise the security of creditors and investors. And sooner or later they will also cease to be partners to the National Bank's monetary policies. What makes matters worse is the fact that the weakness of banks and defective payment systems is contagious: problems can spread, undermining the solvency of the financial system as a whole. The Centre of Competence for System Stability is headed by the Head of the National Bank's Department II. The Governing Board of the National Bank is advised regularly on these matters and takes the major decisions. By setting up the Centre of Competence for System Stability, the National Bank is concentrating the resources it already has in this area, thus enhancing its contribution to the security and soundness of Switzerland as an international financial centre. This does not, of course, call into question the existing allocation of powers in the field of financial market regulation and supervision.

Title: Switzerland  a business location facing profound changes
text: Switzerland - a business location in upheaval Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Presentation on the occasion of the 200th anniversary of the Chamber of Commerce and Employers' Association Winterthur Winterthur, 22 June 2001 2 I am pleased and thank you for allowing me to speak to you on this anniversary event, organized in an original and impressive way. The jubilant Winterthur Chamber of Commerce and Employers' Association deserves today's reference to a great extent. For a long time as a commercial company, it has experienced Winterthur and Swiss economic history in its 200 years of work and helped to shape it in phases of rapid industrial development, but also in periods of bitter setbacks. In doing so, it has served the people living and working in this economic area. For this, the numerous generations of officials and members deserve thanks and recognition. Thematically, I would like to stay close to the objectives of the Chamber of Commerce in the next 20 minutes and make some reflections on the perspectives of Switzerland as a business location. I will begin with a brief look back at the 90s - admittedly only the last 5 percent of the Chamber's work considered today. But at least the last decade has been as turbulent as it is instructive, and with all the effect-busting talk of something completely new, unprecedented, it is still the case that the present and the future arise from the past. Under the fashionable keywords of globalization and the new economy, I would then like to think about trends that also challenge those who are also, especially those who are doing business in Switzerland, in order to finally draw some conclusions. The 90s - Stagnation and Reform The 90s were a difficult time for Switzerland and the economic region of Winterthur, in which what had been achieved fell apart and validity had always been called into question. A country that had become accustomed to the state of full employment in the post-war period was unexpectedly confronted with the economically and socially serious problem of unemployment, which peaked at 5.7% at the beginning of 1997. This undesirable development and countless other burdens were based on a stubbornly frustrating weak growth. Thus, the average growth in the 90s was no more than 3/4 percent. This is not only significantly less than the 2 percent achieved in the two decades before, but also ranks Switzerland at the very bottom of the growth ranking of industrialized countries, namely in third last place ahead of Hungary and the Czech Republic. Moreover, Switzerland was the only industrialised country whose real per capita income even fell during this period. With this sobering finding, the question of the causes must be of broad interest. There is no simple answer. The most plausible thesis seems to be that 3 a combination of cyclical and structural factors, which have reinforced each other, have led to this development. The following should be mentioned: - the legacy of the economic overheating of the late 80s, particularly serious in the construction and real estate sector; - justifies the restrictive monetary policy aimed at combating inflation at the beginning of the period, later the measures to restructure public finances and, in parallel, a marked appreciation of the SFR; - the competitive environment, which has become significantly more competitive, which ruthlessly exposed the structural weaknesses in the once protected domestic sector of our economy; - and probably also the mental circumstance that it took some time and some suffering until the situation was correctly assessed and restructuring efforts were initiated. However, the turnaround that came about three years ago shows that action has been taken in the phase of lethargy and many disappointments. Under the pressure of stagnation, a painful adjustment process began in countless companies, but also at the economic policy level. The Swiss capital stock has been fundamentally modernised in many sectors and adapted to the requirements of the times. The internationally oriented industry has impressively increased its competitiveness, even under the pressure of the Swiss franc, which is expensive at times, and the inevitable structural change towards a strengthened service sector in industrialised countries such as Switzerland has made further progress. Economic policy also initiated necessary changes. The public budget situation, which was alarmingly skewed 8 years ago, has been brought into balance and various regulatory framework conditions have been improved. First of all, the liberalisation of infrastructure services - above all telecommunications - and agriculture. There were also innovations in the form of the new Internal Market Act and stricter competition law, which represent important steps towards a more efficient internal market. These measures at federal level were joined by cantonal flexibilisation measures, such as deregulation in the hospitality industry and shop opening hours. 4 Switzerland and the world in transition Some things have been visibly achieved, much has been set in motion. We have learned to grow again, a good 2% on average over the last three years, even 3.4% last year, and fortunately full employment is back. To what extent we owe this progress only to the cyclical momentum of the economy and to what extent it has been achieved as a result of structural efforts is a difficult question. Despite all the self-critical restraint, there is much to suggest that structural improvements have made a significant contribution. In stark contrast to the late 80s, the revival in demand was not exuberant. Growth is to a large extent productivity-driven, and inflation prospects are favourable. Alone, after the still present experiences of the 90s with their immense economic costs of a self-sufficient economic and enterprise policy, it must be clear that shorter would be a short-sighted, in the long run disastrous recipe. The change continues: facing its challenges decisively is not a freestyle, but a duty for an open country that wants to maintain and strengthen its achievements of prosperity, full employment and social balance. Two buzzwords denote vague and suggestively foreseeable and not yet foreseeable challenges: globalization and the new economy. Globalization Globalization is certainly a dazzling, emotionally dense term. Often abused to surrender to the relentless clout of the market, feared by many as etiquette for a process in which our Western European civilization brutalizes into a society of hyenas. Globalisation is nothing entirely new, but this process goes far beyond the mere continuation of trade liberalisation. Globalisation is not the result of a political programme, even if it is true that it creates political decision-making constraints. Rather, globalization is the result of technical progress, first and foremost in the functions of information, communication and transport. In particular, these developments have three novel effects in their scope: - Firstly, larger, in extreme cases global markets are emerging for a growing number of products as well as for debt and equity. That means more competition, 5 especially since the field of competitors has become much more heterogeneous. Increasingly, the chances of hiding in this world are dwindling. - Secondly, the new technologies allow a rigorous optimization and control of production with high cost transparency, which leads in particular to vertical specialization at different locations. The location-based exporter is supplemented and replaced by the transnational company. - Thirdly, progress in communication is enabling productivity gains in the service sector as never before in history. This results in considerable efficiency potential. Services that previously could only be provided in physical customer contact can now be provided almost independently of distance. Certainly, there are three insights. Firstly, that globalisation is an irreversible process as long as we do not abolish the premise of the peaceful coexistence of peoples. Secondly, that globalisation opens up a potential for prosperity for the world as a whole that would otherwise remain unattainable. Globalization offers countless people an unprecedented opportunity for prosperity, security and development. Thirdly, however, this opportunity is countered by the risk that fundamental qualities of human interaction will be damaged in the legally little, not at all or incorrectly regulated area of cross-border competition. Globalization therefore requires a normative consensus that can be achieved and enforced in effective cooperation between states and actors involved. New Economy In recent years, a second buzzword has entered into a competition with globalization: the new economy. Hardly less fuzzy and therefore richly filled with emotions, the new economy must also be about separating facts from legends. Admittedly, this is easier said than convincingly done. After all, it can be stated as a fact that in the 90s there were increased differences in the trend growth of the industrialized countries, which was independent of economic fluctuations. A prominent leader in this process is the USA, where the augurs understandably argue whether the trend growth rate has increased to four or only three percent. Such uncertainties and the fact that the US is currently struggling with a significant economic setback must not lead to the comfortable conclusion behind the label of the new economy. 6 To dismiss suspected as inconsequential fantasy. Even small differences in trend growth lead to considerable differences in prosperity over time. A forward-looking economic and corporate policy cannot afford to ignore this potential for prosperity, even if much seems vague and intangible. Indeed, there is evidence in the U.S. and elsewhere that the growth pattern has experienced shifts in emphasis in the recent past. In the mirror of numerous studies, four features of this growth pattern crystallize: Firstly, the massive use of new capital, which is used in conspicuous concentration for investments in the information and communication sector. Secondly, a marked increase in labour productivity and employment. One registers the stark opposite of what many feared: the more intensive use of capital does not lead to a decline, but to an increase in labour demand. Thirdly, recent growth experiences in many areas show increased demands on the qualification of the workforce, both in terms of initial and continuing training. And fourthly, there is a significant increase in the so-called total factor productivity, i.e. the performance contribution that must not be attributed to the productivity of individual factors, but to the effectiveness of their combination. This label makes it clear that in the renewed growth pattern, information and communication technologies are central, but not only decisive for success. Equally important are the development of human skills for their sustainable meaningful use and the creation of optimal operational and organizational structures. In other words, what is needed is the ability to implement technical progress in a holistically balanced way into the reality of companies and markets. Conclusion Globalization and the new economy - even if these terms are not taken to full headline value, they denote a bundle of requirements that our 7 The economy must be sufficient for it to successfully maintain its position. What this means in detail is primarily and decisively to be explored and put into practice in the countless companies. In general, two entrepreneurial qualities are likely to be particularly challenged. On the one hand, the ability to deal with risks in a skilful, controlled manner. Not everything that seems new and attractive will turn out to be sustainable and in many ways only a few can achieve commercial success. On the other hand, in a time of accelerated change, movement and responsiveness is becoming increasingly important. The accent shifts from thinking in multi-year detailed plans to a state of mind in which the sense of timely realizable alternatives and scope for movement moves to the center of the leadership process. At the political level, ensuring excellent location quality is and remains a priority. With regard to its locational qualities, our country regularly performs very well to well in periodically undertaken comparisons. No wonder for a country where, relative to its size, more international companies have their headquarters than elsewhere. On its own, securing relative attractiveness advantages is a permanent task in which what has been achieved remains constantly at risk. Anyone who, like Switzerland, is and wants to remain at the forefront of prosperity cannot afford to slip into mediocrity in terms of location factors. Three fields of action are in the foreground: continuing to increase the efficiency of the domestic economy, the labour market and training, and ensuring stable monetary conditions. Allow me to conclude with a few remarks: Increasing the efficiency of the domestic economy The efforts initiated in the stagnation of the 90s to revitalize and strengthen the domestically oriented area of our economy must be resolutely continued. Our growth potential is likely to have increased in recent years, but it is certainly below the benchmark for EU countries. There may be several reasons for this. One is undoubtedly that the revitalisation of our domestic economy, which has been shielded from competition for decades, has begun, but has not yet achieved the goals it has set. This is not surprising, however, because the restructuring associated with this process, despite all the seriousness of the effort, takes time. In a certain sense, it is revenge that in this country the understanding of competition in the post-war period was very ambivalent. A rich expression experienced with us the 8 Economic freedom as the right to free private economic activity, which even included the option of collective renunciation of competition. A much less important role - compared to Anglo-Saxon countries, for example - has traditionally been played by competition as a guarantor of the lowest possible prices for the benefit of consumers: the obligation to compete as a correlate to the right to free commercial activity. This peculiarity of our economic cultural history may explain why we have lived for so long with prosperity-reducing competitive deficits, have not eliminated them out of our own conviction and now have to act quickly on many fronts under the pressure of international competition for locations - and justified by this. Labour market and training This brings me to the area of the labour market and training, the most important part of the state-dominated framework conditions for the long-term chances of success of our economy. Important not only because it is about - technocratically speaking - the supply of the economy with the decisive factors of production, but rather because the design of these two areas has essentially to do with the chances of people for professional fulfillment and personal realization. Certainly, the starting conditions in our country are pleasingly good. The basic structure of our education and training system has proven itself to a great extent - also and especially in international comparison. And with the establishment of universities of applied sciences, significant modernisations at universities, the revision of the Vocational Training Act and several renewal steps in the secondary and primary school sector, a powerful reform process has been set in motion. It is recognised that our labour market is an excellent element of institutional strength that must be preserved and defended against ill-considered, short-sighted demands. Thanks to the clever balance between the objectives of social protection and the indispensable flexibility, our labour market has passed its test in recent years. It has made a significant contribution to the rapid reduction of our unemployment at a very high employment rate to remarkably low levels internationally, for the benefit of workers and employers. However, the salvo of such compliments, also given by international organisations, must not distract from significant future challenges and constraints for action. In view of the technologically and structurally predetermined trends 9 it is foreseeable that the supply of highly knowledge- and learning-intensive jobs will increase significantly and that it will increasingly depend on the ability of the workforce to reorient themselves professionally in the company or on the labour market. Those for whom the measures for educational reform go too far should be reminded that in this area, far-reaching reconstruction and expansion projects worldwide are the rule and by no means the exception. It is not only in the course of the economic recovery that we have weaknesses in the technical and scientific fields, not so much in terms of quality as in terms of the number of trainees. In the longer term, as the working population begins to shrink, such skills shortages will have a somewhat acute adverse effect. Finally, references to the consistent and equal inclusion of women in the world of work and the design of an appropriate immigration policy also show that the area of the labour market and training must remain a priority from an economic point of view. Monetary framework conditions Thirdly, I come to the role of monetary policy. Admittedly, it cannot solve structural problems and it cannot make a direct contribution when it comes to exploiting the innovation potential of new technologies or changed global economic trends in prosperity. Rather, the role of monetary policy refers to the monetary framework in which the real adjustment processes take place: it should be as stable, predictable and therefore calculable as possible. Monetary policy makes the most positive contribution to the prosperous development of the real sector if it strives for and achieves persistently low inflation rates, i.e. a high degree of purchasing power stability. If this does not succeed, investment decisions are distorted by variable and therefore highly uncertain inflation expectations. This increases the likelihood of costly wrong decisions and thus paralyzes the entrepreneurial adaptation process. This statement is not only intuitively insightful. Rather, it is clear from experience gained worldwide: the real growth trend of an economy weakens when a stable monetary regime is replaced by a scenario of high and variable inflation rates. 10 We therefore believe that under the title "Swiss economy in transition" we will make the most useful contribution if we manage to achieve low inflation rates in the long term and credibly predictably. This does not mean that we do not want to worry about anything other than inflation. It is undoubtedly also our task to contribute to smoothing out any cyclical fluctuations in demand in the handling of our instruments. But this attempt must find its limit where the use of cyclical policy resources, which is naturally geared towards shorter periods of impact, would jeopardise the longer-term objective of price stability. If there is one thing that central banks have learned from bitter experiences, it is this: a policy that allows itself to be carried away by short-term manoeuvres at the expense of price stability leads in the long run to uncontrolled, major damage to the real sector. Moreover, the consistent focus on price stability is worthwhile because it leads to low interest rates. Even taking into account the differences in inflation between currencies, interest rates in Switzerland are significantly lower than elsewhere. This makes the use of capital relatively cheap in this country. This advantage should not be underestimated in view of the inevitable adjustment constraints in the industrial and service sectors. Low and relatively low-volatility interest rates - like buying power stability - are an important component of stable monetary conditions. Our policy, which is thus geared towards internal stability, accepts that the exchange rate of the Swiss franc moves freely on the market. The fact that we do not actively control the exchange rate does not mean that we are indifferent to price movements. On the contrary, the value of the Swiss franc is an important part of our monetary policy assessment. As an important component of monetary conditions, it is incorporated into current interest rate decisions. Nevertheless, it is clear that players in Switzerland have to live with a certain exchange rate risk. It is the counterpart to the advantage of low interest rates and the opportunity to contribute to economic success in our country with an independent monetary policy. End I will conclude with that. The Swiss economy is well prepared for the manifold challenges. This statement is important. But less important than the insight that the persistent, creative and constructive commitment of entrepreneurs, employees and state authorities is needed to maintain and further strengthen the position achieved in the future. 11 I wish the Winterthur Chamber of Commerce energy, commitment and good luck for the next 200 years.
