Title: Regions and monetary policy
text: Regions and monetary policy Presentation by Mr. Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Inaugural conference of the academic year 2001/2002 at the Faculty of Law and Economics University of Neuche2tel Monday, October 22, 2001 1. Introduction It is a great honour - and a real pleasure - to be here tonight. I thank the University authorities for inviting me to address you on the occasion of the opening of the academic year 2001-2002. I would like to discuss with you an unusual subject, that of the regions and monetary policy. This subject seems to me particularly appropriate in this canton, which has passed through painful adjustments to its industrial structure over the past two decades, and in this university, which is home to a renowned university institute dedicated to research in the field of regional economy. With the ever more relative significance of political boundaries, the concept of regions has taken off. Basel collaborates intensively with France and Germany, Geneva is in close contact with the Savoyard hinterland. What is true for transnational realities is also true for intercantonal realities: we like to talk about the Jura Arc or the Espace mittelland to highlight areas sharing common economic realities. My purpose this evening is not to dwell on the particularities of these regions - particularities that you all know much better than I do - but to discuss with you the possible conflicts between monetary policy - which is essentially national in nature - and regional economic policy. I admit that this issue is often neglected by central banks. The reason for this lack of interest lies in the nature of the sometimes conflictual relationship between regions and monetary policy. This does not mean, however, that the monetary authorities are not concerned with the realities on the ground. In our case, we listen to the different regions of the country through our network of branches and through our many direct contacts with the cantonal authorities. In the first part of my presentation, I will try to identify the sources of "tensions" between monetary policy and regional economies. In the second part, I will show that there is no easy way to eliminate them. Nevertheless, and this will be the subject of the last part, I will explain how the SNB's policy endeavours to take into account all interests, including regional interests, as far as possible. 2. Tension between regions and monetary policy As I have just mentioned, the relationship between regions and monetary policy is essentially characterised by tension. This tension already appears symbolically in the choice of words: it refers to the regions and the central bank. Talking about regions is therefore necessarily talking about differences, elements that make it possible to distinguish them from each other and policies to promote them. To talk about the central bank, on the other hand, is to talk about monetary policy and its consequences, the interest rate conditions that are created in the market, the situation of the foreign exchange market that is imposed on everyone at the same time. At the origin of the tension between the regions and monetary policy is thus the disparity of regional conditions while monetary conditions are the same throughout the country. Let me elaborate on those two aspects. 2.1 The diversity of regional realities The degree of development of the regions is varied. It is explained by the distribution of natural resources, geography, history or politics, or the general evolution of demand. All these regions form the national economic fabric. As economic activity is distributed in a non-uniform way, the result is a diversity of production structures and therefore a diversity of regions. The reality of Saint-Gall is thus different from that of Neuche2tel or Geneva. Let us mention in passing that while geography and the regional economy have long accepted to consider the economy as a very contrasting mosaic, political economy, with the hindsight imposed by the macroeconomic vision of things, necessarily attaches less importance to differences in tone. This is particularly the case in the monetary field since monetary and financial conditions are the same throughout the country. Monetary and financial conditions refer to the situation of interest rates and exchange rates. The characteristic of an integrated monetary area, as is our country, is to show identical interest rates for debtors with equal goodness. As for the rate of the franc, it is determined by a global market and is imposed in an undifferentiated way on all companies regardless of their location. Faced with variations in financial parameters, companies - and, beyond that, regions - do not react uniformly. For example, Construction are more sensitive than others to a rise in interest rates. Both the industrial and tourism sectors will be more affected by exchange rate fluctuations than the financial sector. And this impact will be different depending on the branch if the turbulence concerns one currency rather than another. Much therefore depends on the structure of companies, their markets, their products and the location of their competition. However, a distinction can be made between the situation of enterprises operating mainly on the domestic market and those which are export-oriented. The former are rather sensitive to changes in interest rates while the latter are particularly affected by exchange rate fluctuations. Moreover, it is a reality that the production units interested in the domestic market are distributed relatively evenly throughout the national territory, since they generally have local activities, while export-oriented enterprises are established very unevenly, in density as well as in specialty. This leads to a very simple observation: while changes in interest rates affect the economic fabric in a way that is not geographically differentiated, exchange rate variations can have a significant regional impact. This is certainly where the strongest source of tension between monetary conditions and local realities lies. 2.2 Monetary conditions What is the link between monetary conditions and the SNB's actions? In fact, the Swiss National Bank has only partial control over monetary conditions. Our policy is to control an interest rate from the range of existing interest rates. All other rates are determined by the market. The interest rate we have chosen as our target serves as a kind of guide to market conditions. Exchange rates, on the other hand, are beyond our direct control. They are the result of many factors, among which the development of economic fundamental factors in Switzerland and abroad plays an important role. The interest rate therefore depends essentially on the specific conditions of the Swiss economy, the exchange rate is an "interface" between Swiss and foreign realities. The interest rate that serves as a benchmark for our monetary policy is the three-month Libor rate. This is the rate at which banks lend themselves liquidity for this period. We are looking to stabilize the Libor at three months in the middle of a fluctuation band with an amplitude of 100 basis points. Since September 24, this band is between 1.75% and 2.75%. In order to maintain the interest rate at the desired level, we operate in a particular market, that of catches and repurchase agreements. The conditions - interest rates, duration and volume - under which these operations are carried out are set by us. I do not want to dwell further on this very technical description. The bottom line is that we only act in this particular repo market and, above all, that we have only one interest rate in our sights: the three-month rate. To meet the different needs of the regions, some imagine that it would be possible, for example, for us to offer funds at a preferential rate to banks located in areas suffering from economic difficulties. Is this realistic? The answer is clearly no. Indeed, what would happen in such a case? Funds obtained at a preferential interest rate would be immediately transferred by the market to areas where rates are higher. These investments would continue until interest rates equalize. This phenomenon is due to the fact that, within a monetary zone, the financial markets function as communicating vessels. Therefore, at equal goodness, the arbitration mechanisms ensure equal interest rates throughout the territory. Thus, the interest rate at which commercial banks can finance and refinance themselves with the SNB can only be the same for all banks, regardless of their location. A modulation of monetary policy according to the particular, and perhaps divergent, needs of the various branches and regions is not an option. This, of course, means that monetary policy may not be appropriate for all regions of the country at all times. Sources of conflict are therefore inevitable. 3. Lack of solution Are there monetary strategies to mitigate these conflicts? As we have seen, the unequal territorial distribution of export-oriented enterprises makes the exchange rate the main source of tension between regions and monetary policy. Therefore, it seems natural, if we want to limit conflicts, to question whether other exchange rate strategies could be envisaged that would allow the regions to be protected from the disturbances of the common monetary policy. Let us allow ourselves to be carried away by an exercise in theoretical reflection as we are entitled to do in a university environment. Four strategies can be envisaged to mitigate the effects of the foreign exchange market on regional realities: 95 the creation of a regional currency, 95 the use, on a regional basis, of a foreign currency - e.g. the euro, 95 the adoption of multiple exchange rates, 95 The introduction of a fixed exchange rate relationship between the franc and the euro. Let's look at the respective advantages and disadvantages of these strategies: Scenario 1: Creation of a regional currency The creation of a regional currency would be the most obvious theoretical option. Such a solution would make it possible to maintain exchange rate relations at the level desired by the region. It would avoid a priori the negative consequences of fluctuations in the national currency on the profit margins of local companies. The regional economy would thus be protected from disturbances caused by the national currency. If this regional logic were the right one, the trend should be towards the fragmentation of the monetary landscape, each region, each valley would seek to improve its chances by conducting its own monetary policy. Obviously - and history shows it - the movement is the opposite. In the 19th century, a first wave of monetary unification occurred on the occasion of the constitution of the European states; a multitude of local currencies have disappeared. At the beginning of the 21st century we are living a second phase of integration through the establishment of the euro, which will become the common currency of 12 European states. Why this headlong rush when the theoretical ideal seems to argue for a regional currency? This is due first of all, and I readily admit, to the fact that monetary integration is generally an act linked to political unification. This was clearly the case in the 19th century. Switzerland was an example of this. Today, the process of monetary unification in Europe, if it is not part of a state-building plan, is in any case an instrument of political integration. But it is also because the theoretical ideal of a regional currency is based on inadequate economic premises. Proponents of a regional currency have a mercantilist vision of monetary policy. They believe that the monetary authorities are always able to manipulate the external value of the currency in order to preserve the competitiveness of the national economy. This view is simplistic for two reasons: The first reason is that exchange rate policy cannot be dissociated from monetary policy, and therefore from domestic price stability. As many experiences have shown, countries that have sought to maintain or improve their competitiveness through an active exchange rate policy have all faced a problem of rising prices. The advantages gained on the exchange rate front were gradually erased by rising domestic costs, prompting them to make their exchange rate policy even more accommodative. The second reason is the reality of the markets. In order to ensure favourable monetary conditions for the development of their economies, monetary authorities must have a good credibility capital without which monetary conditions can become highly volatile. This credibility is of course acquired over the years and the results, but it is also due to the economic realities of the monetary zone and its central bank. The area must be sufficiently diversified so that its currency does not become a reflection of the difficulties encountered by the dominant economic activity. Its central bank must be sufficiently endowed with foreign exchange reserves to be a strong interlocutor on the markets. In this particular light, the movement towards European monetary unification has its logic. Some countries, which were not in a position to implement sustainable stability policies and regularly resorted to parity adjustments, recognized the futility of weak currency strategies. They considered that by joining the euro they had the best chance of breaking with their past. Others, who could hardly take autonomous action because of the weakness of their national economies, sought to gain credibility by integrating into a more powerful whole. Although the idea of competition between regional currency areas is tempting, it thus appears that the political constraints and economic realities of our time argue more in favour of monetary consolidation than fragmentation. Clearly, a region of our country would be too small to be monetarily viable. So what about Switzerland as a whole? Do we have sufficient critical mass against the euro and the dollar? I am convinced of that. This is not just a feeling but an observation. In the two years that the Swiss franc has rubbed shoulders with the euro, we have not lost our ability to influence the interest rate according to the needs of the Swiss economy and our currency has not become more volatile in the foreign exchange market. The SNB therefore still has the means to conduct an independent monetary policy in the new environment created by European monetary integration. Scenario 2: Use of the euro on a regional basis Let us continue this theoretical exercise and consider a second scenario. This time it is not a question of creating a new regional currency but of considering the substitution, in the region, of the national currency by a foreign currency. Admittedly, that region should choose the currency of a country with which it has close trade links. In Switzerland, it is clear that only the common European currency could be taken into consideration given our geographical proximity to Euroland. If our regions had the choice between the franc and the euro, why should they not choose the European currency? In order to judge the advantages of different currency areas, a region must question its degree of integration because it has every interest in linking itself to the monetary area with which it has developed the closest links, particularly in terms of labour mobility. Why is the factor of mobility of toy work a central role here? Because if the policy of the monetary zone does not meet the needs of the region, it is necessary, in the event of over-employment or regional underemployment, that a balance can be found with the rest of the monetary zone. Obviously, the greater the mobility of work, the easier integration will be. The mobility of work leads to the agglomeration of activities in specific places of the territory. This phenomenon of agglomeration is perfectly normal. It must be carefully distinguished from the phenomenon of polarization. The agglomeration process leads to a redistribution of jobs throughout the economic territory in areas of relatively strong economic growth. While some regions are experiencing a decline in employment, other regions are experiencing rapid job creation. The phenomenon of polarization is different. It is the creation of pockets of prosperity alongside pockets of unemployment, without these areas participating in a common dynamic. Insufficient labour mobility is the reason for this. A region that losing jobs due to the attractiveness of the neighboring region is probably located in the right monetary area, the one that becomes an isolated pole of unemployment has a fundamental problem. One consequence of this distinction between agglomeration and polarization is that the decline in jobs is not a sufficient criterion for judging the adequacy of a region's participation in a monetary area. The phenomenon of agglomeration also involves costs. The decline in population in a region, even if it is not accompanied by an increase in the unemployment rate, is a source of problems since the financing of existing infrastructure may no longer be assured. In addition, the loss of jobs may affect the degree of diversification of the region's industrial fabric. Concentration in specific branches can be a source of fragility. Industrial monoculture, like a poorly diversified portfolio, has a riskier profile. Before concluding with this scenario, let me recall that an important factor in choosing a currency area must be the comparison of performance in the area of monetary stability over time. Low inflation is part of the economic benefits specific to a currency area; in addition to the good price performance, there is a good performance in terms of interest rates. Here too, we understand the logic of the monetary integration movement in Europe. Some countries had poor performance in monetary stability. By joining the euro area, they hope to have better framework conditions, and therefore also better financing conditions. Southern Europe has thus benefited greatly from the integration process. By the way, it should be noted that Switzerland's integration into the euro zone does not have any advantage in this respect. Our stability performance is comparable to that of the most stable countries in the area and our interest rates are currently 1.5 percentage points lower than those appearing on the European market. We would therefore have nothing to gain in this area. This privileged situation of low interest rates also benefits all regions of our country. I will conclude this second scenario by noting that economic factors clearly indicate that a region such as the Jura Arc is better placed in the franc area than in the euro area. What for? Because the nearest poles of development are on this side of the border, often even they are at a distance that can be covered daily. In addition, conditions of monetary stability and low interest rates offer better prospects for financing equipment. The balance is therefore clearly in favour of the franc. Scenario 3: The adoption of multiple exchange rates Having examined the creation of a regional currency and the adoption, in a region, of an already existing foreign currency, I come to a third theoretical solution. This is the application of a multi-exchange rate regime. By this we mean an exchange rate regime in which not all transactions involving a foreign currency are carried out at the same rate. In the minds of a few, multiple exchange rates can only belong to the policy mix of developing countries. It is to forget that we have also had our experiences in this area. In the seventies, in order to help the watch, textile and clothing industries facing the rise of the franc, the SNB set up a "foreign exchange purchase rights" (DAD) regime that allowed exporters to sell their currency to the SNB at a preferential rate in the event of an appreciation of the franc. Today, it cannot be ruled out that voices will be raised for us to study the possible introduction of a dual exchange rate regime - a so-called "commercial" exchange rate for trade in goods and services and a "financial" exchange rate for capital transactions - if significant turbulence were to occur on the foreign exchange market. Such institutional arrangements would pose three types of difficulties: The first, and most important, is that these preferential systems pose virtually insurmountable administrative problems. It is indeed very difficult, if not impossible, to ensure that the provisions only benefit the rights holders. With the integration of financial markets, significant arbitrage operations are to be expected. To prevent abuse, a very cumbersome administrative apparatus would be required and control methods would be ineffective. Our experience in the seventies showed us that even in the relatively unglobal environment of the time, some companies had resorted to DADs to an extent that cast doubt on the strictly commercial justification for their operations. The second problem is that of international law. A preferential exchange rate or dual market regime would put us in breach of the Articles of Agreement of the International Monetary Fund, which we accepted when we joined that institution. Indeed, these statutes of the Fund explicitly provide that member countries renounce the practice of multiple exchange rates. Finally, let us also not overlook the fact that a system of preferential exchange rates in favour of a sector of the economy or enterprises in a particular region would be equivalent to the distribution of subsidies from the profits of the National Bank. And this without the legislator ruling on it. The SNB would thus exceed its mandate to serve the general interests of the country and not certain special interests. Scenario 4: The introduction of a fixed exchange rate relationship between the franc and the euro I arrive at a plausible solution, but one that I do not find desirable. This solution would consist in fixing the exchange rate of the franc against the euro and thus making the rate of the franc more dependent on the exchange rate desired by a region particularly sensitive to this parameter. The possibility of the franc clinging to the euro has sometimes been raised since the appearance of the single currency. Some believe that in the face of the new European reality, Switzerland has an interest in aligning itself monetarily rather than risking the franc becoming an object of speculation. For all regions that trade closely with the surrounding Europe, a pegging of the franc to the euro would then be good news. There is no doubt that Switzerland will join the Monetary Union on the day it joins the European Union. As long as this decision is not taken, it is in our interest to follow an autonomous monetary line. Indeed, I doubt that a unilateral attachment of Switzerland to the European monetary train will bring us the benefits that some hope for. My doubts lie on two levels: Firstly, we must understand that linking the franc to the euro by parity is not the same as adopting the euro as a national currency as the Twelve are currently doing. It would not be a definitive marriage but a unilateral declaration of alliance which could be the subject of a subsequent revision. At the time of setting the parity, the exchange rate may seem adequate, yet it is not said that the markets will be continually convinced. If economic developments between Switzerland and Euroland are not to converge closely, due to the existence of an inflation differential or a growth differential, a parity adjustment will be perceived as inevitable. The central bank will realize this, but so will the markets. Expectations of adjustment will emerge, leading to speculation at the correction, stimulating capital movements and forcing the central bank to intervene increasingly until it agrees to give in to pressure. It is may then be forced to make a much greater parity adjustment than justified by the fundamentals of the economy. Such adjustment crises have hit many countries that have decided to fix the external value of their currencies. Let me recall the abandonment of the Bretton Woods system, the successive crises of the monetary systems of the Common Market and, more recently, the various crises in the emerging countries. In our uncertain world, given the place of Switzerland and its currency on the international financial scene, I do not believe that the attachment of the franc to the euro can permanently protect us from external disturbances. On the contrary, I fear that this kind of arrangement, which may be useful in the short term, will quickly become a burden and a source of further disruption. Secondly, it must be remembered that linking the franc to the euro means giving up our monetary sovereignty. Under such a regime, the SNB would no longer be able to pursue a policy that corresponds to the needs of the Swiss economy but would have to align itself with the decisions of the European Central Bank (ECB). Our 'Swiss region' would then be only one element of the vast European monetary area. The advantage of the loss of monetary autonomy is that it eliminates exchange rate risk, as well as the disadvantage of no longer allowing the SNB to pursue an independent interest rate policy. These would certainly tend to rise at the European level. As you know, interest rates in Switzerland are lower than the rates in the euro area. This difference amounts to about 1.5 percentage points and applies to the entire maturity spectrum. If the franc rate were to be fixed, it is very likely that this difference would diminish sharply. The decrease will be all the greater as parity is perceived as sustainable by the markets. This would lose one of our competitive advantages. 4. Flexible exchange rate regime and regions However, renouncing the fixing of the exchange rate does not mean that the SNB remains insensitive to its evolution. On the contrary, we are well aware of the importance of the exchange rate for the evolution of the economic situation and prices in Switzerland. This is not new. Currency considerations have never been absent from our analyses. Quite often, I admit, we have had difficulty communicating it through the because our action was oriented with the help of a compass - monetary aggregates - which was not directly under the influence of the foreign exchange market. That has changed. We are now basing our policy on a forecast of the development of inflation over the medium term, based on an analysis of all the factors influencing future price increases. Monetary aggregates have their place, as do exchange rates. The impact of the Swiss franc on our inflation forecasts is both direct and indirect. The exchange rate has a direct impact on the price level through the price of imported products. As we can see, in the event of an appreciation of the franc, competition on the markets leads to a fall in import prices. This has the effect of rapidly reducing the rate of inflation. If domestic prices are stable, the price level may even fall. The exchange rate also has an indirect impact on the price level through its effect on economic activity. If the Franc strengthens, the economy's competitiveness weakens, slowing down exports and stimulating imports. Growth is slowing and the cyclical slowdown is easing pressure on prices. Through this roundabout path, the rise in the exchange rate also helps to curb inflation. Our behaviour during the recent events of September is indicative of the role of the exchange rate in the assessment of the monetary situation. What happened and what did we do? On Monday, September 17, the day the New York Stock Exchange reopened after the tragic events of September 11, the Federal Reserve Bank - the central bank of the United States - cut interest rates by half a percentage point. On the same day, the ECB did the same. We joined this movement in anticipation of a downward decision that was to fall three days later. We wanted to react immediately because we wanted to avoid at all costs that the markets, and in particular the foreign exchange market, unnecessarily question the price of our future share. We felt that the market balance was fragile and we feared that a security reflex would cause an overreaction of the franc rate. In such an environment, leaving doubts about our policy would have been a mistake. Despite this, on the Friday of the same week, 21 September, the euro fell to 1.44 francs, the lowest point since 1 January 1999, the day of its creation. Between these two dates, the franc had appreciated against the currency of our main trading partner by some 10% in nominal terms. However, it was less this development as such - which partly reflects the different price and economic developments in Switzerland and the euro area - than the extent and speed with which the Swiss franc appreciated during the month of September that preoccupied the SNB. Half of that assessment occurred between 11 and 21 September. This latest increase was triggered by increased political uncertainty. The Swiss franc once again played a safe haven role, which had not been the case for a very long time. Faced with this situation, on Monday, September 24, we decided to lower the band of changes in the interest rate a second time to three months. Have we, however, abandoned our monetary mode of conduct, which - as I indicated earlier - is based on an inflation forecast, and moved to a policy of stabilizing the exchange rate? Not at all. The appreciation of some 5% of the franc during the week in question had introduced a new deflationary element into the Swiss economy, which had to be corrected by the only instrument at our disposal: a reduction in interest rates. This second rate cut was therefore the logical response to the new situation created by the foreign exchange market. Taken together, these two actions have now created more expansive monetary conditions in our country. This direction is well suited because of the prospects for a cyclical slowdown, the high degree of uncertainty in which we are all currently operating and the price stability environment that we can anticipate for the coming years. And regional considerations, what happens to them in all this? They are at first sight absent. Indeed, while the creation of broadly expansive monetary conditions is adequate from the point of view of the general interest, this does not mean that the change in the structure of monetary conditions remains without sectoral or regional consequences. Our previous analysis showed us that exporting regions suffer more from the rise in the franc than they benefit from interest rate cuts. However, a closer look at the recent behaviour of the SNB allows us to draw a slightly more nuanced conclusion. By taking into account exchange rate developments in determining its monetary policy, the SNB has contributed to the extent that the means at its disposal are at its disposal to mitigate the negative impact of exchange rate developments on certain regions. In hindsight, we must even recognize that uncertainties have affected our currency less than feared. The rapid appreciation of the Swiss franc in mid-September has been half corrected. Compared to the situation prevailing at the time of the events of 11 September, the franc appreciated by 3% against the euro, which means that the security reflex that has been much talked about has finally been limited. This is good news for the Swiss economy. Obviously, the second rate cut, by its surprise effect, may have helped to calm some speculative ardor. The turbulence of recent weeks has therefore partly faded. This does not mean, however, that the horizon is serene. We have always lived, and we live, in an environment marked by uncertainty and instability. This is the reality of companies such as that of the National Bank. Everyone, in their field of action, must take this into account. For our part, we are responding to this uncertainty by applying a strategy focused on the stability of the medium-term monetary framework. We have put this strategy into practice by setting an inflation target and we regularly publish our forecasts for price increases. Within this framework, we strive to operate in a consistent and transparent manner. In doing so, we provide market insights and contribute to their stability. But we cannot ensure the stability of financial markets - especially the foreign exchange market - in an unstable world. Through our policy, we seek to mitigate the negative effects of this instability on the Swiss economy. We cannot completely protect it. Regardless of the monetary regime in place, our economy has always suffered from external monetary turbulence. We know that some regions are more affected than others in such circumstances. I believe that the regions and businesses are well aware of the limits of our possibilities. They must draw the necessary conclusions. At regional level, the aim is to promote the establishment of an economic fabric sufficiently diversified to avoid excessive concentration of risks in the face of the foreign exchange market or in the face of a particular sector of activity. Sometimes it's difficult, I know. However, it is only by systematically making efforts in this direction that the fragility of structures can be corrected in the long term. Companies also must arm themselves as much as possible against the imponderables of the foreign exchange market. Here, too, diversification is a response to external turbulence. In addition, there is close management of exchange rate risks and the search for production niches that ensure sufficient added value to absorb margin fluctuations. 5. Conclusion Over the years, the evolution of technology, demand and organization of the world economy has placed our country under a continuous adaptation constraint. Entire branches have been put under the pressure of international competition, have had to reorganize or reorient their production. Often the exchange rate has been perceived as having been the cause of the problems when it has only been the revealer. In this light, the apparent conflict between regions and monetary policy must be put into perspective. The tension between monetary policy and the regions exists. There is no point in denying it. However, the division of tasks between the central bank and the regions helps to mitigate the consequences. In this sense, the SNB has a responsibility to create the monetary framework conditions that allow our economy to develop optimally over time. It applies itself resolutely, within its means and in the international environment that is binding on all. Regions and businesses have a responsibility to fit better into this framework by making use of their comparative advantages. They have a difficult strategic reflection to carry out because each one is a little prisoner of its history and its geographical position. I believe that your canton and your businesses have understood this situation. Considerable efforts, both private and public, have been made to ensure that the Jura Arc can best integrate into world markets. This required imagination and courage on the part of both the authorities and the population. Great successes have been achieved, setbacks have also been recorded. The work must be continuously put back on the job. With the globalization of markets and the development of trade, new opportunities have emerged for the export industry, but the functioning of the international system has become uncompromising. The SNB is aware of the harshness of competition and the sensitivity of certain regions to the exchange rate of the Swiss franc. It applies a policy aimed at preserving the stability of the monetary framework. The situation on the foreign exchange market is one of its elements of appreciation. In doing so, it cannot prevent the Swiss economy from suffering the effects of external shocks. His approach however, consistent and transparent limits volatility on the foreign exchange front. This is how it acts not only in the general interest of the country, but also in that of our exporting regions.

Malgr cela, le vendredi de la mme semaine, le 21 septembre, leuro tombait  1,44 francs, le point le plus bas depuis le 1er janvier 1999, jour de sa cration. Et les considrations rgionales, que deviennent-elles dans tout cela ? Elles sont  premire vue absentes. Par rapport  la situation qui prvalait au moment des vnements du 11 septembre, le franc s'est apprci de 3 % face  l'euro, ce qui signifie que le rflexe scuritaire dont on a beaucoup parl a finalement t limit. Ceci est une bonne nouvelle pour l'conomie suisse. Evidemment, la seconde baisse des taux, par son effet de surprise, a pu contribuer  calmer quelques ardeurs spculatives. Conclusion Au fil des annes, l'volution de la technologie, de la demande et de l'organisation de l'conomie mondiale a plac notre pays sous une contrainte d'adaptation continue. Title: Continuity and change in Swiss monetary policy
text: Consistency and change in Swiss monetary policy Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank at the Swiss-German Business Club, Frankfurt, 30 October 2001 I am very pleased and grateful to you that I can be a guest of the Swiss German Business Club today. I would like to use this right of hospitality to present you with some reflections on three aspects of monetary policy under the rather broad title "Continuity and Change". I would like to start with the general, with references to changes that have prevailed in the monetary policy of most developed countries over the past three or four decades. I would like to add to you remarks on the concept of monetary policy in Switzerland and on the experiences we have had with it and are currently making with it. My third and final part will be dedicated to the not easily comprehensible current developments and a brief outlook. Three change trends A look at post-war monetary policy practice reveals at least three general trends in change, despite all the differences between member states. They have their reason on the one hand in the increasing integration, even dissolution of boundaries of the financial markets and on the other hand in good and less good experiences that the central banks have made with different concepts. Firstly, it is striking that market processes today play a much more powerful and comprehensive role than in the past. The global integration of financial markets is now a reality that must be given priority in everything central banks do or not do. Monetary policy impulses  such as the lowering of the money market interest rate  trigger reactions in a very complex adjustment process of interest rates and financial market prices, through which such measures can only become effective. In the integrated interaction of the financial markets, instruments have become obsolete that were regularly used under the once prevailing conditions of relatively isolated national financial markets and limited convertibility: dirigiste interventions such as credit limits, emission controls, maximum interest rate rules and capital controls of all kinds. These instruments have disappeared in most countries. In an integrated financial world, they are no longer enforceable, easy to handle and inevitably associated with distorting, costly side effects. The central banks therefore no longer use sovereign administrative measures, but operate with their possibilities as monopolistic providers of central bank money on the open market for foreign exchange and investments. So it is logical that in the current Revision of the Swiss National Bank Act, the sovereign instruments are to be largely disposed of. A second major difference between once and now concerns the assessment of the possibilities and limits of monetary policy. In many countries, it is only in the last decade that monetary policy has been unambiguously geared towards maintaining price stability. Previously, it often had to meet a variety of sometimes contradictory demands. Until the end of the sixties  and in some countries far beyond  the prevailing view was that an expansionary monetary policy could lead to a permanent reduction in unemployment. Monetary policy  so the expectation  should therefore be used at the price of slightly higher inflation to keep employment high and unemployment at a low level. This view was shipwrecked in the seventies, just as some economists had predicted years earlier. The expansionary monetary policy led to an acceleration of inflation without succeeding in securing the hoped-for employment successes in the long term. The word that made the rounds at the time and described the situation very aptly was "stagflation". A third trend of change concerns the relationship between the government and the central bank. Until the late eighties, many central banks were subordinate to the government. The government  usually the finance minister  often not only set the objectives, but also determined the use of instruments, for example by determining the timing and extent of an adjustment of the key interest rates. Over the past decade, various central banks  including the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan as the most prominent examples  have been granted independence. As a rule, this step was linked to the explicit mandate to focus monetary policy primarily on maintaining price stability. Instructed by bad experiences, a central bank that was primarily committed to price stability and operated independently had a better chance of success than an authority exposed to the waves and waves of day-to-day political calculations. These three general trends of change  moving away from dirigiste instruments, prioritising price stability and securing independence  have affected different countries to varying degrees. Some countries made a real U-turn, and the way they conduct their monetary policy today changed fundamentally. The most impressive example is the Bank of England, which has become the model case of "inflation targeting". Elsewhere, the necessary Changes of less or they took place very early. In addition to Germany, this second group certainly also includes Switzerland. Our two countries have long had central banks that have been given a high degree of independence by lawmakers. Both quickly and explicitly focused their monetary policy on maintaining price stability, having been given the opportunity to do so with the collapse of the Bretton Woods system. Both hardly embarked on the illusory undertaking of buying more real growth and employment with slightly greater inflation tolerance. And both said goodbye to dirigiste measures quite early. In Switzerland, this was in fact already the case in 1980. A changing concept Despite the rather pronounced continuity in the broad lines, however, there have also been some remarkable changes in Switzerland in recent years, which I would like to turn to in the second part of the presentation. They relate to our mandate, the strategy of decision-making and the implementation of policy on the market. In doing so, I would like to make some cross-references to other central banks, in particular to the European Central Bank (ECB). Mandate I will start with the mandate that outlines the tasks and objectives of the central bank in the law. In Switzerland, the monetary policy mandate was and is very vaguely defined. The Federal Constitution stipulates that the SNB shall conduct a monetary policy that serves the overall interest of the country. The National Bank Act, which specifies this task, is not clearer with regard to the mandate, but is currently being revised. The expert group that presented a draft law proposes a more precise wording. Accordingly, the SNB must ensure price stability. In doing so, it should take into account economic developments. In our opinion on the draft, we welcomed this mandate formulation in the conviction that the focus on price stability must be at the heart of monetary policy and must therefore be prescribed by law. The addition of taking account of economic developments in this endeavour must also be part of the mandate. In monetary policy practice, there are certainly situations in which one has to weigh up price stability and growth, especially during periods of adjustment. For example, when deciding how quickly to correct an inflationary development that has once occurred through restrictive measures, or when it comes to reacting optimally to a supply shock such as a wave of inflation caused by energy prices. Due to these relationships, the proposed mandate is formulated in a dual-hierarchical manner. It contains price stability as a primary objective with the proviso that the respective economic situation be taken into account. In substance, this solution is broadly in line with the ECB's mandate, even if the Maastricht Treaty formulates the primacy of price stability more sharply than the draft of our experts. According to Article 105, the ECB is to support the general economic policy of the Community only if this is possible without compromising price stability. On the other hand, the Federal Reserve's mandate is also dual, but  with its policy focus on price stability and growth to the same extent  it is not hierarchical. Especially with regard to accountability, it is important to enshrine a modern and realistic mandate formulation in law. But we do not want to forget that the vagueness of the valid mandate to pursue a policy in the overall interest of the country did not prevent the SNB from operating comparatively successfully in the post-war period. More important than the wording of the order for the results of the policy are probably two conditions that have long been clearly fulfilled in Germany and Switzerland: the independent position of the central bank and  more importantly  the broad social consensus on the high value of price stability. Strategy and implementation More obvious than the mandate, our monetary policy strategy and the way in which it is implemented have undergone changes in the recent past. Like the Deutsche Bundesbank, the SNB had mostly pursued a money supply strategy in the period after the transition to floating in 1973, first with annual growth targets, later  in the 90s  with a five-year target path for the central bank money supply. In practice, however, there have always been considerable and persistent deviations from the target in the money supply. Their primary reason was the need to react flexibly and pragmatically to specific constellations. For good reason, the target path was not stubbornly targeted, but only used as a rough guideline. This flexibility became even more important in the late 90s because the underlying approach The stability of demand for central bank money increasingly eroded. Thus, the relationship between the monetary aggregate as an intermediate objective and the ultimate objective of price stability was less and less reliable. In this situation, it was clear by 1997 at the latest that the conditions for a reasonable definition of the trajectory were no longer met. The decision for a conceptual renewal was imperative. We put the new concept into force at the beginning of last year. It consists of three elements: 1. An explicit definition of price stability. Accordingly, price stability is achieved when inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, is below 2% over the medium term; 2. A three-year inflation forecast published in December and June; 3. The use of a 100 basis point target range for the three-month LIBOR as an operational implementation target, which applies "until further notice". In a cross-comparison with the ECB's strategy, three comments in particular are appropriate. First, both solutions share the definition of price stability: inflation rates of no more than 2%, as measured by consumer goods prices. In contrast to a point target, such as that set by the Bank of England with an inflation rate of 2.5%, our definition of price stability  inflation below 2%  takes into account the fact that even with optimal monetary policy, inflation will fluctuate slightly over the course of the economy. We have also omitted the explicit mention of 0% as the lower limit in our definition of price stability. This is to make it clear that, like most central banks, we do not think it makes sense to aim for an inflation rate of 0%. There are two reasons for this. On the one hand, price indices tend to slightly overestimate inflation because they cannot capture quality improvements and innovations or cannot record them in a timely manner. On the other hand, the solution taken reflects an aversion even to small deflation rates. Due to numerous downward price rigidities, especially in the administrative sector and in wages, negative inflation rates are likely to lead to relevant but difficult to estimate adjustment costs. With the ambitious goal of zero inflation monetary policy would be entering unfamiliar territory. With the exception of Japan (since 1992), there is no industrialized country in modern economic history whose inflation rate has been less than one percent for five or more consecutive years. Economic policy must not allow itself to accept uncertainties of this kind, especially since the example of Japan seems anything but worthy of imitation. The second comment on the comparison with the ECB relates to a difference. In our concept, a broad-based inflation forecast is the central instrument of communication and the decisive basis for interest rate decisions. The ECB, on the other hand, follows a two-pillar concept. In addition to assessing the inflation outlook, the ECB uses a reference path for M3 money supply growth compatible with long-term price stability. We have dispensed with the second pillar in the opinion that communication with two reference or target variables would rather hinder the comprehensibility of our decisions. This does not mean, however, that the development of monetary aggregates is irrelevant in our considerations. M3 is also an important indicator of inflation prospects in Switzerland. Together with other indicators, it is an important component in the inflation forecast. The most striking differences  thirdly  are in the operational implementation of the policy. It is true that both institutions use the same instrument to create liquidity, namely repo transactions. But the ECB does this at fixed repo rates with weekly tender auctions. Our procedure is a bit more complicated, but it gives us more flexibility. On the basis of our assessment of the situation, we are not announcing a fixed repo rate, but a 100 basis point target range for the three-month interest rate, the three-month LIBOR. In our daily repo operations, we set the short-term repo interest and the auctioned liquidity amounts in such a way that the target interest rate is set within the announced band, usually in the middle range. Within the target range, we can let the LIBOR fluctuate up and down by up to 50 basis points. In this way, we can take into account temporary problems on the money or foreign exchange market without having to signal a change in monetary policy. This flexibility seems essential to us in a small, open economy. Experience The experience we have gained with the new concept over the past two years has been positive overall. In public, it has already after a short time Time found a good acceptance. This applies in particular to the inflation forecast, which is at the heart of our approach. In fact, it makes perfect sense for an institution that is primarily intended to ensure price stability to make its goal-oriented assessment of the situation known to the markets and the public. This transparency can and should make politics predictable and stabilize expectations, which improves the efficiency and impact of the measures taken. Certainly, it should be borne in mind that inflation forecasts over three years must be constantly revised and updated. Like all other economic players, we operate under uncertainty. New information and surprising developments force adjustments to the forecasted development and, if necessary, to politics. Inflation forecasts are valid until further notice and are always "work in progress". The implementation on the money market  the (indirect) management of the three-month LIBOR with very short-term, daily repo auctions  did not cause any particular problems after a short probationary period, although we had to make a rather significant price correction soon after the concept change. In the first half of 2000, for example, we increased the interest rate band in three steps from 11/4  21/4% to 3  4% in order to limit the risks of a surprisingly strong economic acceleration at the time. This was followed  from the summer of 2000  by a sideways development of around nine months. In response to the looming economic slowdown, we made a slight interest rate cut last June. The rapid deterioration of the economic environment then prompted us in September to significantly correct the monetary policy stance within just one week with two interest rate band cuts of 50 basis points each. This manoeuvre was certainly extraordinary. Allow me to make a few further comments on this. The first of these two rate cuts was the result of our regular quarterly assessment. On the basis of the broadly weaker economic outlook and reduced inflation risks, we considered it appropriate to reduce the interest rate band by half a percentage point to 21/4 to 31/4 %. We merely brought forward the timing of this correction by three days to 17 September, because on that Monday there was a coordinated rate cut in response to the very turbulent market conditions, in which the Federal Reserve and the ECB also participated. The fact that just one week later  on 24 September  we lowered the interest rate band by another 50 basis points was due to the development of the SFR exchange rate. In the course of the general risk aversion, the SFR against the USD and  more economically important  against the euro quickly and considerably more expensive. In a few days, the euro fell from over Chf 1.51 to below CHF 1.45. This, together with an even greater weakening of the dollar, led to an undesirable tightening of monetary conditions. We wanted and had to react to this in order to signal to the markets that we would decisively oppose such an exchange rate shock caused by extraordinary factors. In the meantime, the exchange rate development has stabilized again to some extent at around SFR 1.48 per euro. Whether this is primarily the result of our measure or more the result of a general normalization of the financial markets is difficult to determine. Exchange rate fluctuations are and remain extremely complex phenomena for their intended purpose. View This brings me to the outlook for economic trends. Finally, I would like to add a few comments on the introduction of the euro cash. Boom The global economic situation has deteriorated markedly in recent months. The brusque downward revision of expected investment income after an illusory high has brought sharp stock market corrections not only in the USA, but worldwide. A considerable part of the capital stock, which was hopefully accumulated, especially in the later 90s, became economically obsolete. No wonder that this correction has severely affected investment activity and trade flows  which are structurally capital goods-heavy. The consequences of the slump have been exacerbated by the tragic shock of September 11 and the associated additional uncertainties. From two points of view, the current global economic situation differs from the cyclical experiences of the post-war period. On the one hand, we are not dealing with the regression of a demand boom, but with the effects of a prolonged period of excessive capital accumulation, i.e. instability not on the demand side but on the supply side of macroeconomic activity. Comparable phases of our historical experience date back a long way, namely in the period before and after the First World War. On the other hand, the pronounced synchronicity of the slowdown in the various global economic regions is striking. Large parts of Asia are in a  sometimes quite deep  recession. The US economy is also likely to have entered a phase of negative growth. Finally, there is also an unexpectedly significant slowdown in growth for the EU, even if there is clearly no need to speak of a recession for our continent. In the past, the global economic landscape was more heterogeneous, characterized by the interaction of regions with opposing cyclical trends. Is it a characteristic of a globalized economy that such balancing and compensation effects disappear? For the OECD countries  they embody the industrialized world  the OECD expected growth of 2% for the current year even last May. This rate has now been halved to 1% and for 2002 the estimate is 1.2%. If this assessment is correct, OECD countries as a whole are in one of the more pronounced periods of weakness of the post-war period. In any case, under such conditions, the global economic outlook is characterized by high uncertainties and considerable forecast differences. How deep will the slowdown be in the individual regions, how long will the weakness last? These are the obvious but difficult questions. Several factors weigh on the outlook: the marked parallelism of cyclical movements, the unresolved structural damage associated with the correction of the technology boom, Japan's continued lethargy, the internal and external imbalances affecting the US economy, and the political and military risks associated with the events of September 11. However, such burdens are countered by several positive aspects. Inflation risks are very low worldwide, which clearly expands the scope for monetary policy and, in many places, also for fiscal policy. These opportunities to stimulate aggregate demand, in particular, have been consistently exploited by the US authorities, prompting many analysts to predict a significant economic recovery as early as the first half of next year. A second factor supporting the level of activity is the favourable development of energy and raw material prices for consumer countries. Certainly, there are risks in this regard, but the chances are intact that this advantage will last on the one hand because of the decline in demand and on the other hand on the basis of an agreement comprising the most important suppliers. This point of view illustrated a fundamental tendency towards change. The shock of 11 September has had an impact on the Military and diplomatic measures have also strengthened their willingness to take multilateral action. We registered joint action not only in monetary policy, but also in the supply of oil to the world and possibly also in trade policy, where the chances of a successful round of liberalisation of the WTO in mid-November have improved significantly. This is  at least in the medium and longer term  an essential element of strength. Forecasts for the Swiss economy have also been revised downwards over the past few months. The published growth expectations for the coming year are currently between one and two percent. The current indicators signal a trend towards a slowdown, but in detail they are still at a relatively good level for the most part. Our country benefits above all from two factors. On the one hand, the slump in the technology and communications sector in our country has had less of an impact for structural reasons. On the other hand, the persistently favourable situation on the labour market is proving to be an important pillar of consumer spending and consumer confidence. But experience has shown that the international economic trend plays a powerful role in economic activity. The foreign trade figures for August and even more so for September signal a significant slowdown in momentum. For our economically most important neighbour  Germany  the leading research institutes are forecasting growth rates of 0.7% for the current year and 1.3% for next year, which are far below potential growth. Against this background, it can be assumed that our growth in the coming year will be in the order of one and hardly two percent. In addition, as always in periods of heightened uncertainty, the course of the exchange rate will be of particular importance. It can have a noticeable positive or negative impact on monetary conditions. In any case, we will pay the necessary attention to the development of the Swiss franc exchange rate in our analysis and in the design of policy. Coexistence with the euro My outlook would be incomplete if it excluded the imminent introduction of euro cash. For many players in Switzerland, this step also involves considerable changes and efforts. Based on careful own observations and in the mirror of the opinions of banks, trade and tourism providers, we do not expect any fundamental changes in the modalities of our coexistence with the euro. From an economic point of view, the euro has been in operation since almost three years there. Its presence has not significantly influenced our ability to conduct an independent monetary policy geared to the stability of our economy. Exchange rate volatility has become smaller than before in relation to the DM. And taking into account the inflation differential, a significant part of the nominal depreciation of the euro from Fr. 1.60 to the current level is fundamentally justified. With around 1.6% in the ten-year range, the interest rate bonus is proving to be a fairly robust phenomenon. It is certainly not a target, but it is a welcome by-product of our own political course, and therefore a not insignificant economic location factor. What will the imminent availability of euro cash achieve? Realistically, it is to be expected that there will be more payments against euros in our country than there were previously transactions against the predecessor currencies. As a result, additional players  positive and negative  are likely to be affected by exchange rate movements. But this effect will remain within narrow limits and limited to selected sectors. If anything further, it will not reach the extent that could constitute a substantial hindrance to monetary governance. Will the franc survive in the long run or will it one day be replaced by the euro? This is and remains a question of carefully weighing the advantages and disadvantages of the two regimes. With the availability of euro cash, money users in our country will be able to choose more concretely and tangibly whether they want to use the SFR or the euro as a medium of payment, investment and as a measure of value. Your individual preference will provide an important indication of whether or not something will change in the balance of advantages and disadvantages, which has so far been assessed fairly uniformly.
