Title: Reflections on Swiss monetary policy
text: Reflections on Swiss monetary policy Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Vice-President of the Governing Board Of the Swiss National Bank Guest Lecture at the University of St. Gallen, 9 January 2002 As in most areas of life, there are no eternal truths in monetary policy. Concepts and implementation practices are subject to change. Novel economic explanations, technological and institutional innovations and changed economic structures repeatedly force monetary policymakers to question what has become habitual, to examine alternatives and to implement improvements. Monetary policy concepts are "work in progress"  this is also what the experience gained in Switzerland stands for. However, with the remarkable caveat that in this country the change has largely been limited to the how of the monetary order. With regard to the objective, on the other hand, there has been a consensus that has been unbroken for generations and has never been seriously jeopardised, that monetary policy should primarily serve to safeguard price stability. Such a consensus came about in various countries much later and was institutionally anchored. In the case of Switzerland, the change has little to do with the objectives, but much to do with the means of achieving monetary policy objectives. My presentation has five thematic parts. It begins with a summary review of the conceptual steps taken by the Swiss National Bank over the past three decades. I would then like to comment on three changes that can easily be seen in the development of monetary policy concepts in many countries: the functional loss of importance of monetary aggregates, the massively increased requirements for transparency and the increasing spread of inflation forecasts. In the final part, some reflections on current macroeconomic trends and our current monetary policy stance follow. The SNB concept in transition In Switzerland, the monetary "modern era" began in 1973 with the collapse of the Bretton Woods system, when the dollar standard transitioned into a regime of floating exchange rates. With the disappearance of price parity as a nominal anchor, a phase of monetary policy autonomy began almost thirty years. Soon after the start of floating, the SNB decided to use a monetary aggregate as an intermediate objective of monetary policy. At the time, this was a progressive and courageous step, facilitated by the broad political consensus that the SNB's primary task should be to safeguard price stability. The role of the From 1975 to 1978 the intermediate target fell to the money supply M1, from 1980 to the (seasonally adjusted) central bank money supply. Until 1990, annual monetary growth targets were set. This approach was justified by the fact that a management geared to the intermediate target of monetary growth would lead to the safeguarding of price stability. Although the performance measured by inflation rates was good, the credibility of the approach suffered from the fact that the annual targets were missed several times and to a significant extent. The SNB responded with a modified variant of money supply control. From 1990 onwards, the growth target for the central bank money supply was no longer set for one year, but as a trend target for a period of five years. Conceptually, this created a scope for flexibility for responding to shocks. Such reactions  mainly to distortions in the real exchange rate  were the main reason for the target deviations accepted in the past. The medium-term target path has expanded the political scope for flexibility, but  if the interim target concept had been consistently implemented  it would also have created the compulsion to compensate for past deviations from the target path in current policy. Conceptually, the step towards the multi-year target path amounted to a shift in emphasis: the envisaged aggregate growth was no longer an intermediate target, but the main indicator of monetary policy. For good reason, the given path was not stubbornly targeted, but used as a rather rough guideline. The need to react flexibly and pragmatically to specific constellations resulted in considerable and lasting deviations from the envisaged trend. This flexibility became even more important in the late '90s as the approach's underlying stability of the money demand function increasingly eroded. In this situation, it was clear by 1997 at the latest that the conditions for a reasonable definition of the trajectory were no longer met and that a conceptual renewal was indicated. Our concept, which has been implemented since the beginning of 2000, is based on three pillars:  An explicit definition of price stability. Accordingly, price stability is achieved when inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, is below 2% over the medium term;  A three-year inflation forecast to be published in December and June;  The use of a 100 basis point target range for the three-month LIBOR as an operational implementation target, which applies "until further notice" when announced. We have provided detailed information on this approach on numerous occasions. In the following, I would like to focus my remarks on conceptual questions that arise in a general way for the practice of monetary policy. If necessary, I will refer to our concept and our experience. If you study the history of monetary policy since the end of Bretton Woods in different countries, you will notice a variety of changes. Some are specific to individual countries, others have a more general meaning. I would like to turn to three trends of change that shape the monetary policy scene in general, place them in a broader context and try to assess their consequences. In detail, I will deal with  with the departure from money supply control  with the obvious and far-reaching efforts of central banks for transparency  and with the widespread practice of publishing inflation forecasts. Moving away from money supply control If you look at the development of monetary policy concepts over the past 30 years, it quickly becomes apparent that money supply management  still an innovative strategy when I was a student  has largely become obsolete in the OECD area and beyond. The idea, once hopefully propagated and implemented in many places, of reducing the monetary control process to the control of a monetary aggregate as an intermediate goal in order to achieve the last goals of politics, has been replaced by other concepts. In most countries, the control process today is based directly on the inflation rate, often additionally on the deviations of the current output from the potential path. And operational management is carried out via short-term money market rates. This conceptual development requires some qualifications and additions. Five comments on this. First, this shift in opinion does not mean that monetary aggregates have become irrelevant to monetary policy. Although they have their once prominent function lost as intermediate targets, but as indicators and explanatory variables in the inflation forecasting process, they continue to play an important role, including in Switzerland. Persistent and substantial deviations from the objective of price stability continue to be a predominantly monetary phenomenon for which central banks are responsible, provided that there is sufficient room for manoeuvre. This insight is effectively and bindingly expressed in the practice of inflation targets. Secondly, the fact that most countries have largely achieved the objective of price stability to a large extent for a long time undoubtedly plays a role in the move away from money supply control. This was not the case in the heyday of money supply control. If, in a country with galloping monetary devaluation, the aim is to regain a reasonable degree of price stability, there is still no alternative to a controlled, pre-announced reduction in monetary growth. Thirdly, the argument against money supply control was the fact that in various countries the demand for money proved to be increasingly unstable. There were and still are various reasons for this: technological changes in payment transactions, institutional developments such as the merger of two major banks or hardly anticipateable changes in the desired demand for banknotes. In contrast to money supply management, inflation-forecast-oriented interest rate management proves to be relatively immune to such uncertainties because it automatically compensates for these shifts in demand. Fourth, the move away from money supply control takes into account the fact that while most central banks focus their policies primarily on the objective of price stability, they also react to cyclical changes. To be sure, central banks have always done so, even if they had embraced a money supply control regime. In this regard, there has always been a gap between theory and practice. The leading monetarists were classical macroeconomists with a dominant interest in long-term economic contexts and the greatest skepticism about any attempt to influence short-term macroeconomic dynamics. Monetary growth targets have therefore always been geared towards long-term development, and were also intended as a disciplining requirement to protect central banks from pressures in favour of short-term manoeuvres. In practice, however, there have been and continue to be situations in which monetary policy also reacts to short-term changes. This is not about fine-tuning everything and everything, but about the intention to respond to persistent macroeconomic shocks that are undesirable in their consequences. Examples include strong movements in energy prices, real exchange rate distortions or cyclical shifts in expectations, as we have recently seen in the technology sector. In the interim target concept, such reactions regularly led to deviations from the targeted monetary growth, especially in Switzerland. This has called into question the credibility of money supply management and accelerated conceptual renewal. Finally, fifthly, the rejection of money supply control is also of some importance from a political and communicative point of view, even if this aspect must be relativized insofar as most money control concepts have not been implemented rigorously, but with a high tolerance for deviation. Conceptually, money supply control is an elegant and simple regime. It is easy to communicate, makes the behavior of the central bank predictable and protects the monetary authority from pressures to leave the virtue path of price stability in the stress of the moment. Deviations from the targeted money growth quickly create a compulsion to justify and justify. On the other hand, in a concept aimed directly at price stability, a central bank can go astray for a very long time due to the delays in its effects until misconduct becomes apparent in the relentless TARGET/ACTUAL comparison. The institutionalised control typical of the intermediate target approach must be ensured in alternative approaches by means of special arrangements. The focus is on precautions for optimized transparency and the publication of inflation forecasts. I turn to these efforts in the following two sections. Transparency as a condition of legitimation and efficiency Central banks must be transparent. This demand is undisputed today. That wasn't always the case. Certainly, in the gold standard and also in the Bretton Woods system, there were few compelling motives for the call for openness: central banks were programmed for predetermined automatisms. Apart from incidents, they had no significant discretionary leeway. The appearance of central banks was generally characterized by communicative restraint. To justify this only with the tendency of bureaucrats to secrecy in order to maximize power and influence, however, falls short. There were quite solid reasons. In the case of fixed exchange rates, as revaluations or devaluations usually the end of a lost There was no alternative to secrecy about intentions. And little openness was to be expected from central banks pulled out by their governments to finance deficits. After all, in the case of a strategy aimed at permanent employment maximization, the preference for lack of transparency was based on the belief of many economists that only unexpected, surprising policy impulses can be expected to have real effects. The demand for transparency  ex ante and ex post  was conspicuously accompanied by the decision of legislators to give their central banks a mandate related to price stability and to grant them an independent position at least in terms of the use of instruments. This is illustrated, for example, by the Bank of England, which was only granted independence in 1998. This step was associated with far-reaching transparency requirements as an effective means of legitimizing an institution that could not yet present its own stability policy success story when it was reconstituted four years ago. In this optics, transparency was in many places also a substitute for trust that had not yet been acquired to an adequate extent. The experience gained in England since then makes it clear that systematically practiced openness effectively contributes to gaining credibility in a relatively short time. Undoubtedly, it corresponds to a contemporary understanding of the state that the independent exercise of the money monopoly includes the duty of extensive transparency and institutionalized accountability. The demand for transparency, however, has to do not only with political legitimacy, but also with effective aspects of monetary policy measures. If we have learned a lot in macroeconomics in the last 30 years, it is certainly this: expectations are key variables in the process of micro- and macroeconomic adjustment. Whether and how quickly a monetary impulse achieves the intended effects depends crucially on the efficiency of the expectation formation. Thus, the return to price stability envisaged by a restrictive monetary policy correction should succeed more quickly and with less loss of growth if economic agents understand the policy change and can rely on the central bank to deliver what it promises. Transparency plays a central role in this process. Actually, monetary policy is a rather poor craft: we can only move the very short-term interest rates directly, in our concept the repo rates, which at best some foreign exchange and money market traders are interested in, but not the large and significant majority of economic actors. In fact, monetary policy only becomes a powerful macroeconomic means of control when announced interest rate impulses change expectations and thus transfer them to the entire spectrum of financial assets. A central bank that credibly communicates its goals, intentions and mindset accelerates and facilitates the rapid and successful adjustment of expectations to new circumstances. This makes monetary policy more effective, minimizes the frequency of false expectations and thus of wrong decisions by actors who set prices and quantities under uncertainty. Against this background, it is not surprising that monetary policy has become a very transparent area of state action in almost all countries. This change is probably irreversible, because its two important justifications  the legitimacy of state policy and the efficiency of measures  will also apply tomorrow and the day after tomorrow. Since its foundation almost 100 years ago, the SNB's position has been characterised by extensive independence by international standards. However, the competence to change the gold content of the Swiss franc, for a long time the most serious monetary policy competence, lay with the Federal Council. However, it has become virtually obsolete with the transition to floating in 1973. The SNB effectively stepped up its efforts to achieve transparency as early as the 70s. And we were aware a good two years ago that the move away from money supply targets had to be accompanied by special communication efforts. For this reason, we have quantitatively clarified what we mean by price stability and have begun to disclose our assessment of inflation prospects with an inflation forecast. It also seemed sensible to us to put the economic models used for discussion. We wanted and want to create as much clarity as possible about our goals, our conceptual regime and the way in which we analyse macroeconomic developments and include them in the political decision-making process. Are we transparent enough with what we have achieved? Certainly, optimising the content and means of communication with markets and the public is and will remain a permanent task. As part of a project on our website and in brochure form, we intend to provide a wider audience with improved and more user-friendly means of information about our activities. And, of course, we strive to make additions and improvements to the ongoing communication activities whenever this seems necessary. That said, must: it also remains clear that transparency must be optimized and not maximized. It must serve to fulfil the monetary policy mandate and must not hinder it. This should be remembered, for example, by those who, with reference to practices abroad, reproachfully complain that we do not publish the minutes of meetings of the Executive Board. It should be replied that we decide in accordance with the law as a three-member collegial authority. In contrast to the "Monetary Policy Committee" of the Bank of England, a nine-member body composed of five internal and four external members, which does not work according to the rules of the collegial authority, but follows an individualistic approach. In order to be optimally capable of acting, a small collegial authority needs an area of activity shielded from the public in which critical objections can be raised and withdrawn without political considerations. Such a body is designed to fight for the right decision. This includes the possibility for each member to change his mind in this process, to be convinced by the better argument, without having to justify himself on all sides. Maximized transparency can easily come at the expense of decision-making quality. It would not be in the interest of the matter. Inflation forecast and interest rate management This brings me to the issue of inflation forecasting and interest rate management. Indeed, the inflation forecast is at the heart of our monetary policy approach. If price stability over the medium term is the primary objective, the projected inflation trend defines the room for manoeuvre in monetary policy at all times. We publish the forecast in June and December. It covers a period of three years. This long forecast horizon takes into account the fact that in Switzerland the transfer of monetary impulses to the price level is only completed after about three years. This is a conditional forecast that describes the presumed course of inflation under the assumption that the three-month interest rate remains unchanged throughout the forecast horizon: namely in the middle of the target range for LIBOR valid at the time of the forecast. This interest rate conditionality of our forecast is an important difference to the forecasts of banks and scientific institutions, which regularly make assumptions about presumed future interest rate changes. It would be counterproductive for a central bank to explicitly impute later interest rate hikes to its published forecast. This could change expectations, trigger price movements and in the As a consequence, the political room for manoeuvre  e.g. the ability to react to a shock  is fatally restricted. The interest rate path must be set in such a way that the expected inflation rates tend to be within the range of less than two percent specified by our definition of stability. The rule is simple, its application is not. The crux of the implementation lies in the ubiquity of uncertainty. The determinants relevant to the inflation trend and economic development are subject to ongoing, often surprising changes. When implemented, monetary policy is a search process in which the interest rate path must be continuously optimized in such a way that the specified goal is achieved. This has nothing to do with economic fine-tuning, as it shaped the stability policy discussion in the 60s and early 70s and  in retrospect we know this  repeatedly misled it. It is not a question of making a choice, as always, between the objectives of real growth and price stability. Rather, it corresponds to a broad consensus that monetary measures cannot generate real growth in the long run. But monetary policy can and must take account of economic developments when determining the interest rate path. Most changes in interest rates are reactions to emerging or occurring deviations in real output from the long-term trend. They make sense not only because fluctuations in production are associated with social costs, but also because persistent positive or negative trend deviations endanger the objective of price stability. A monetary policy geared to price stability can only be successful if it takes account of economic dynamics in current interest rate decisions. On the other hand, the recent past offers impressive visual instruction. About a year ago, a phase of highly expansionary policy began  first in the US, later in most other countries  in response to the surprisingly strong economic slowdown. The chains of interest rate cuts were and are economic management with monetary means, which the central banks have implemented not at cost, but in the interest of price stability. The once actively debated question of whether monetary policy should be rule-bound or discretionary seems rather outdated. Realistically, it requires both components: the binding of rules with regard to its long-term anchoring and the design of its decision-making methodology, the discretionary willingness to react with regard to the ongoing optimization of the interest rate path in the service of achieving goals. Our policy, which has been pursued with the new concept since the beginning of 2000, expresses this interaction. In June and again in December 2000, we expected inflationary accelerations to temporarily more than 2 percent, with a three-month LIBOR of 3 1/2 percent. As a result, we felt compelled to significantly revise our assessment of the situation. In the changed current environment, we expect significantly lower inflation rates with the money market interest rate halved to 1 3/4 percent, namely 0.9% for 2002, 1.3% for 2003 and 1.5% for 2004. This illustrates that inflation forecasts need to be constantly updated and revised. This has less to do with the structure of the models used than with the assumptions to be made when using the models, for example about the course of the oil price, the international economic development or individual exchange rates. We have to live with such uncertainties. This makes it all the more important to analyse ongoing developments openly and critically and to make interest rate decisions when conditions have changed. This willingness to react is both cyclical and essential in the interests of price stability. Over the past few years, several central banks have begun to publish inflation forecasts on a regular basis. And all monetary authorities that conduct an independent monetary policy are guided by a price stability or inflation target. In this general sense, all central banks, including the National Bank, pursue a policy of inflation targeting. However, this uniform rhetoric masks not insignificant differences between the current regimes. They have primarily to do with the extent of the target autonomy granted to various central banks. For example, the Bank of England, which is considered a model case of inflation targeting, has little target autonomy. It is the Chancellor of the Exchequer who gives the bank the inflation target and the relevant index. It is up to him to review, confirm or change this requirement in the annual budget process. In this order of competences, it would be conceivable for the government to modify the inflation target with a view to cyclical considerations, for example by raising it in a recessive environment. In comparison, the SNB's target autonomy goes considerably further. The constitution and the law give us the vague mandate to pursue a policy in the overall interest of the country. The specification primarily on price stability and quantitative clarification two years ago was not made by the legislator, but by the Bank. Just as the formation of opinion can currently be estimated, the revision of the National Bank Act initiated will lead to a mandate according to which the SNB should ensure price stability while taking into account economic developments. We welcomed such a solution in our consultation. It is dual and hierarchical: primarily price stability, in addition  but in second priority  economic stabilization. This legal clarification is sensible and necessary. It defines our mission in principle, i.e. beyond the cyclical. The SNB remains objectively autonomous in key respects, especially in cyclically difficult decision-making situations characterised by a trade-off between price stability and growth. For example, with regard to the questions of how quickly an inflationary aberration should be corrected or how to react to a sharp increase in the oil price, which simultaneously increases inflation and slows down production. Such decisions, which are rather relevant in the short term, should not be made by an institution exposed to day-to-day political constraints. In this area, it seems advisable to leave target autonomy with the central bank. Macroeconomic outlook and current policies After these considerations, which are more conceptually related, I come to topicality in the final part of my presentation. I will begin with a few remarks on macroeconomic developments and then turn to current monetary policy. OECD Economic Cycle: Diagnosis With regard to global economic activity, we have had an eventful phase: an unexpected slowdown in the OECD economy in terms of extent and intensity. After an unusually long period of growth, the US  according to official confirmation in March of last year  entered a recession. Japan's persistent lethargy began much earlier, and Europe has also lost economic momentum in recent quarters. Above all, the German economy, which stagnated in the second quarter of last year and recorded a negative growth rate in the third quarter. The economic areas of Southeast Asia  badly hit by the collapse of high-tech exports to the USA  and Latin America  with Argentina as a tragic source of crisis  are also suffering from pronounced economic weakness. On the overall gloomy map, only Russia and China stand out as economically positive areas. Although market economy systems are repeatedly characterized by economic fluctuations, these do not take place in mechanistic regularity. Rather, they are the aggregated result of shocks to which economic actors are exposed and to which they respond. Therefore, it is analytically expedient to understand and examine the current slowdown as a unique episode like any economic change. Looking at the latest experience, two things stand out. On the one hand, the extensive synchronicity with which the slowdown has gripped the economies is striking. The last time we experienced a similar synchronisation was in 1973. At that time, however, in contrast to today, in a highly inflationary environment. This synchronicity makes the OECD economic area an appropriate framework for analysing what is going on and what is likely to be in store for us. For the OECD and thus the main part of global economic activity, the finding is clear: While the real growth of OECDBIP in the 80s and 90s averaged around 3% p.a., we register a slowdown to around 1% for the past and the current year for everything we already know and can estimate for the near future. This is a strong slump by historical standards. On the other hand, what is striking about the current downturn is that its origin is not the correction of a previous monetary demand boom, but on the supply side of macroeconomic activity. The process pattern experienced several times in post-war history  large monetary and fiscal policy  Demand boom with acceleration of growth  Inflationsanstieg  Fighting inflation  Recession, if not stagflation does not apply to the topicality. Instead, the current slowdown has its origin in the rising earnings expectations after 1995, which will continue to be excessive. Overly optimistic ideas about the commercial value of new technologies led to a spectacular rise in stock prices and an unprecedented investment boom. What built up gradually gave way to an abrupt disillusionment in the first half of 2000: sharp corrections in equity valuations, especially in the technology sector, a sharp decline in investment activity and, as a result, a rapid slowdown in cross-border trade activity, which is structurally heavy on capital goods. In the course of this supply shock, the industrial sector was particularly hard hit, while consumer activity proved to be remarkably robust in most countries, including Switzerland. In the meantime, it has also lost momentum, exacerbated by the loss of confidence associated with the shock of 11 September. The latter is likely to remain a temporary burden. In any case, various consumer sentiment indices justify this restriction. This process pattern has experienced its most striking expression in the USA. But to conclude from this that the US economy  similar to a locomotive  has dragged the world into recession and that global potential growth can only be expected again in the wake of an upswing in the USA is probably not the whole reality. As economists, we should also and more systematically engage in the analysis of shocks that hit national economies together and simultaneously. In fact, we have seen several of these common shocks in recent years: the fluctuations in the price of oil, which stood at USD 10 per barrel at the end of 1998, escalated to over USD 35 by mid-2000 and currently stands at USD 20, the expansive accompanying measures of the Millennium Change and their subsequent compensation, and the consequences of the formation and bursting of the technology bubble, that have affected all economies, albeit with varying degrees of intensity. I believe that the concept of common shocks has a considerable macroeconomic explanatory value, which is generally given too little attention in the economic analyses, which are mainly focused on national economies. OECD Economy: Outlook As always, the economic outlook for the OECD region is fraught with uncertainty. How long will the trend towards slowing down continue and how quickly will activity recover to potential growth?  these are the crucial questions. Allow me to make three comments on this. Firstly, investment is likely to remain weakened for some time to come, although destocking is indeed very advanced in most countries. But the capital overhang accumulated in the course of excessive investment activity can only be absorbed by the enterprise sector and must be absorbed by it, and that requires Time. In this painful correction process, demand-driven adjustment aids such as monetary stimulus cannot do much. Certainly, the stock markets have recovered quickly and markedly from their lows reached on September 21. They reflect widespread optimism. Whether this rapid return of confidence is justified, the near future will show. Secondly, the further course of consumer activity is of central importance. A somewhat slowdown is to be expected in the foreseeable future, because unemployment is on the rise in most countries. But there is much to be said for the consensus opinion of economists that the foreseeable correction will not be sharp, but will continue well into the current year. Thirdly, this relative confidence is based on two positive framework conditions of the global economy. On the one hand, in the very moderate development of energy and commodity prices, which have a positive effect on costs and real incomes everywhere. On the other hand, in the powerful monetary stimulus that began in most countries about a year ago. Led by the Federal Reserve, all central banks have cut interest rates since the beginning of last year: the European Central Bank and the SNB four, the Bank of England 7 and the Federal Reserve even 11 in number. Even though the rate cut has been much smaller for medium and longer rates, this monetary correction should gradually support demand. The monetary policy U-turn has been widely welcomed, but this is the norm for interest rate cuts. But there have also been critical voices who have diagnosed blind activism and increased inflation risks for the future. I do not think the objection of blind activism is valid. Of course, series of rate cuts are an unusual monetary policy pattern. But they are the result of the effort to optimize the interest rate path at all times: optimally and in a timely manner with regard to an economic assessment that had to be revised downwards several times over the last year. Or as one commentator put it: Blind people have not become sighted in a unique enlightenment, but only in several stages and have updated their visor at each stage. On the other hand, it is clear that the high willingness to react in the downward trend must be matched by the will to correct interest rates upwards if the indications of a global economic trend reversal credibly intensify. Otherwise, the prospects for Sustained price stability and a sustainable safeguarding of potential growth will soon be in danger. Outlook for Switzerland The swiss economic development follows in the basic features of the course described for the OECD. Compared to the previous year, our real growth gradually declined from 3.4% in the first quarter of 2000 to 2% in the second quarter and to only 0.8% in the third quarter of last year. The slowdown was marked by severe setbacks in equipment investment and exports. These two components still recorded double-digit growth in the second quarter of 2000. In the third quarter of last year, they declined: year-on-year, investment in equipment fell by 3.4% and exports by 3.7%. Consumption in Switzerland has also impressively passed the endurance test so far. In the first three quarters of last year, it has risen undeterred by 2.4% each. The leading indicators, in particular the KOF Economic Barometer, signal a period of weakness that will continue into the middle of the current year. Over the course of the year, consumption growth is also likely to weaken somewhat. But these setbacks should remain moderate. Certainly, consumer sentiment has also weakened in Germany, but the retail trade reports a pleasing course of the Christmas business. And the development of household incomes shows a fairly favorable course into the current year. More important than these aspects, however, are the prospects for the labour market. They have also deteriorated somewhat in individual sectors, but the correction as a whole should remain within relatively narrow limits if the majority opinion of economists is correct that the international economy will accelerate again in the course of the second half of the year. In terms of monetary policy, we already reacted to the intensifying signs of weakening last March and reduced the interest rate band by 25 basis points. This correction was followed by two more rate cuts of 50 basis points each in Quick Succession in September. And on December 7, we lowered the interest rate band again to the current level of 11/4 to 21/4 percent. There are two main comments on this interest rate path. Firstly, we were and still are convinced that the inflation risks for the Swiss economy are low. Conversely, we also assess the risks of deflationary developments as very small. Certainly, it cannot be ruled out that the price index, which has become much more volatile with the last revision, will temporarily show us negative inflation rates. This has mainly to do with the base effect. Especially in the spring months, it will contribute to reduced annual control rates. However, we rule out a deflationary phase in the sense of a downward trend in the price level. We have endeavoured and will continue to do so to respond to the increasingly difficult economic situation as part of our stability mandate. This also includes concerns about exchange rate developments. For this reason, we responded in September with a second interest rate cut to the undesirable appreciation trend of the Swiss franc, as it has adjusted as a direct consequence of increased risk aversion, but has since corrected somewhat. Exchange rate considerations also played a role in the further interest rate cut towards the end of the year. We are aware that exchange rate developments represent a very important risk factor for the Swiss economy. Our inflation forecast presented on 7 December has not changed in the meantime. Assuming the current interest rate level for LIBOR, we expect inflation to rise by around one percent for the year that has just begun and inflation to rise slightly to around 1.5% in the following two years. Our real growth, which is currently expected to be close to zero, should move back towards the potential of around 2% in the second half of the year. This would result in GDP growth of around one percent for the current year. However, we are aware of the uncertainties inherent in this forecast. It can get better, but also worse. Whether a next interest rate step upwards or downwards again will be necessary will depend on further economic developments and their presumed consequences for price stability. Finally, A comment on the introduction of euro cash. Macroeconomically, this event is a non-event. The euro has been there since 1.1.99; we know him and have learned to live with him. In a long time quiet coexistence, which was only interrupted by the wave of risk aversion triggered by the shock of September 11. This shock, however, had nothing to do with the existence of the euro; in all experience, it would not have been absent even in the juxtaposition with the DM. On the other hand, the availability of euro cash in daily payment transactions will also leave its mark within our borders. It will be foreseeable give more transactions against euros than before against the previous currencies. As a result, additional players  positive and negative  are likely to be affected by exchange rate movements. But this effect will remain within narrow limits and limited to individual sectors. It will be far from reaching the level that could be a substantial hindrance to monetary governance.

Als konomen sollten wir uns auch und systematischer mit der Analyse von Schocks befassen, welche die nationalen Volkswirtschaften gemeinsam und gleichzeitig treffen. Tatschlich haben wir in den vergangenen Jahren mehrere dieser gemeinsamen Schocks erlebt: Die Ausschlge des lpreises, der Ende 1998 bei 10 USD pro Fass lag, bis Mitte 2000 auf ber 35 USD eskalierte und gegenwrtig bei 20 USD liegt, die expansiven Begleitmassnahmen des Milleniumwechsels und deren anschliessende Kompensation und die Konsequenzen der Bildung und des Platzens der Technologie-Bubble, die alle Volkswirtschaften beeinflusst haben, wenn auch mit unterschiedlicher Intensitt. Ich glaube, dass dem Konzept gemeinsamer Schocks ein erheblicher makrokonomischer Erklrungswert zukommt, der in den vorwiegend auf nationale Volkswirtschaften fokussierten Konjunkturanalysen im allgemeinen zu wenig Beachtung findet. Konjunktur OECD: Ausblick Der konjunkturelle Ausblick fr den OECD-Raum ist wie immer mit Unsicherheiten behaftet. Wie lange wird der Trend zur Verlangsamung noch nachhalten und wie rasch wird die Erholung der Aktivitt in den Bereich des Potentialwachstums erfolgen?  das sind die entscheidenden Fragen. Erlauben Sie mir dazu drei Bemerkungen. Erstens drfte die Investitionsttigkeit noch fr etwelche Zeit geschwcht bleiben, auch wenn in der Tat der Lagerabbau in den meisten Lndern stark fortgeschritten ist. Aber der im Zuge der exzessiven Investitionsttigkeit akkumulierte Kapitalberhang kann nur durch den Unternehmungssektor und muss durch diesen absorbiert werden, und das erfordert Zeit. In diesem schmerzlichen Korrekturprozess knnen nachfrageorientierte Anpassungshilfen wie monetre Stimulierung nicht viel bewirken. Gewiss, die Aktienbrsen haben sich von ihren am 21. September erreichten Tiefstwerten schnell und markant erholt. Sie spiegeln verbreiteten Optimismus. Ob diese rasche Rckkehr der Zuversicht gerechtfertigt ist, wird die nchste Zukunft zeigen. Zweitens kommt dem weiteren Verlauf der Konsumttigkeit zentrale Bedeutung zu. Da ist absehbar noch mit etwas Verlangsamung zu rechnen, weil in den meisten Lndern die Arbeitslosigkeit ansteigende Tendenz aufweist. Aber es spricht Vieles fr die Konsensmeinung der konomen, dass die absehbare Korrektur nicht scharf ausfallen, aber bis deutlich ins laufende Jahr hinein andauern wird. Diese relative Zuversicht grndet  drittens  in zwei Rahmenbedingungen der globalen Konjunktur, die positiv sind. Einerseits in der sehr moderaten Entwicklung der Energieund Rohstoffpreise, die sich berall gnstig auf Kosten und Realeinkommen auswirken. Anderseits in der in den meisten Lndern vor rund einem Jahr begonnenen, kraftvollen monetren Stimulierung. Angefhrt durch das Federal Reserve haben seit anfangs letzten Jahres alle Zentralbanken Zinssenkungen vorgenommen: die Europische Zentralbank und die SNB vier, die Bank of England 7 und das Federal Reserve gar 11 an der Zahl. Auch wenn die Zinssenkung bei den mittleren und lngeren Stzen viel geringer ausgefallen ist, sollte sich diese monetre Korrektur sukzessive nachfrageuntersttzend auswirken. Die geldpolitische Kehrtwende ist weitherum begrsst worden, was indessen bei Zinssenkungen den Normalfall darstellt. Aber es hat auch kritische Stimmen gegeben, die blinden Aktivismus und fr die Zukunft erhhte Inflationsrisiken diagnostiziert haben. Ich halte den Einwand des blinden Aktivismus fr wenig stichhaltig. Natrlich sind reihenweise Zinssenkungen ein ungewhnliches geldpolitisches Muster. Aber sie sind das Ergebnis des Bestrebens, den Zinspfad zu jedem Zeitpunkt optimal zu gestalten: Optimal und zeitgerecht in Bezug auf eine Konjunkturbeurteilung, die im Verlauf des letzten Jahres mehrfach nach unten zu revidieren war. Oder wie es ein Kommentator formuliert hat: Da sind Blinde nicht in einer einmaligen Erleuchtung, sondern erst in mehreren Etappen sehend geworden und haben bei jedem Etappenpunkt ihr Visier aktualisiert. Dagegen ist klar, dass der hohen Reaktionsbereitschaft im Abwrtsgang der Wille entsprechen muss, die Zinsstze nach oben zu korrigieren, wenn sich die Indikationen einer globalen konjunkturellen Tendenzwende glaubhaft verdichten. Andernfalls wren die Aussichten fr anhaltende Preisstabilitt und eine nachhaltige Sicherung des Potentialwachstums bald in Gefahr. Ausblick fr die Schweiz Die schweizerische Konjunkturentwicklung folgt in den grundlegenden Zgen dem fr die OECD beschriebenen Verlauf. Im Vorjahresvergleich hat sich unser reales Wachstum von 3.4% im ersten Quartal 2000 sukzessive auf 2% im zweiten und auf nur noch 0.8% im dritten Quartal des letzten Jahres zurckgebildet. Die Verlangsamung war geprgt durch empfindliche Rckschlge bei den Ausrstungsinvestitionen und den Exporten. Diese beiden Komponenten verzeichneten im zweiten Quartal des Jahres 2000 noch zweistellige Zuwchse. Im dritten Quartal des letzten Jahres waren sie rcklufig: im Vorjahresvergleich fielen die Ausrstungsinvestitionen um 3.4 und die Exporte um 3.7%. Der Konsum hat auch in der Schweiz den Hrtetest bislang eindrcklich bestanden. Er hat in den ersten drei Quartalen des vergangenen Jahres unbeirrt um jeweils 2.4% zugenommen. Die vorlaufenden Indikatoren, insbesondere auch das Konjunkturbarometer der KOF, signalisieren eine noch bis in die Mitte des laufenden Jahres anhaltende Schwchephase. In ihrem Verlauf drfte sich auch das Wachstum des Konsums etwas abschwchen. Aber diese Rckschlge sollten moderat bleiben. Gewiss, auch hierzulande hat sich die Konsumentenstimmung abgeschwcht, aber der Detailhandel berichtet ber einen erfreulichen Verlauf des Weihnachtsgeschfts. Und die Entwicklung der Haushaltseinkommen zeigt ins laufende Jahr hinein einen recht gnstigen Verlauf. Wichtiger als diese Aspekte sind indessen die Perspektiven fr den Arbeitsmarkt. Sie haben sich in einzelnen Sektoren auch etwas eingetrbt, aber die Korrektur sollte insgesamt in verhltnismssig engen Grenzen bleiben, wenn die Mehrheitsmeinung der konomen zutrifft, dass sich die internationale Konjunktur im Verlauf der zweiten Jahreshlfte wieder beschleunigen wird. Geldpolitisch haben wir schon letzten Mrz auf die sich verdichtenden Zeichen der Abschwchung reagiert und das Zinsband um 25 Basispunkte zurckgenommen. Dieser Korrektur folgten im September kurz nacheinander zwei weitere Zinssenkungen um jeweils 50 Basispunkte. Und am 7. Dezember senkten wir das Zinsband nochmals auf das aktuelle Niveau von 1 bis 2 Prozent. Zu diesem Zinspfad sind vor allem zwei Bemerkungen am Platz. Erstens waren und sind wir der berzeugung, dass die Inflationsrisiken fr die Schweizer Wirtschaft gering sind. Umgekehrt schtzen wir die Risiken einer deflationren Entwicklung ebenfalls als sehr klein ein. Gewiss ist nicht auszuschliessen, dass uns der mit der letzten Revision deutlich volatiler gewordene Preisindex vorbergehend negative Teuerungsraten anzeigen wird. Das hat vor allem mit dem Basiseffekt zu tun. Insbesondere in den Frhlingsmonaten wird er zu reduzierten Jahresteuerungsraten beitragen. Eine deflatorische Phase im Sinne eines Abwrtstrends des Preisniveaus schliessen wir indessen aus. Wir waren bestrebt und werden dies weiterhin sein, im Rahmen unseres Stabilittsauftrags auf die schwieriger gewordenen Konjunkturverhltnisse zu reagieren. Dazu gehrt auch die Sorge um die Wechselkursentwicklung. Aus diesem Grund haben wir im September mit einer zweiten Zinssenkung auf den unerwnschten Aufwertungstrend des Frankens reagiert, wie er sich als unmittelbare Folge erhhter Risikoaversion eingestellt, mittlerweile aber wieder etwas korrigiert hat. Und auch fr die gegen Jahresende vorgenommene weitere Zinssenkung spielten Wechselkurserwgungen mit eine Rolle. Wir sind uns bewusst, dass die Wechselkursentwicklung fr die schweizerische Konjunktur einen sehr wichtigen Risikofaktor darstellt. An unserer am 7. Dezember prsentierten Inflationsprognose hat sich zwischenzeitlich nichts gendert. Wir erwarten unter der Annahme des aktuellen Zinsniveaus fr den LIBOR eine Teuerung fr das begonnene Jahr von etwa einem Prozent und einen leichten Teuerungsanstieg auf etwa 1.5% in den beiden folgenden Jahren. Unser reales Wachstum, das gegenwrtig nahe beim Nullpunkt liegen drfte, sollte sich in der zweiten Jahreshlfte wieder in die Richtung des Potentials von rund 2% bewegen. Das ergbe fr das laufende Jahr ein BIP-Wachstum von rund einem Prozent. Wir sind uns indessen der Unsicherheiten bewusst, welche dieser Prognose anhaften. Es kann besser, aber auch schlechter kommen. Ob ein nchster Zinsschritt nach oben oder nochmals nach unten erforderlich sein wird, wird von der weiteren konjunkturellen Entwicklung und ihren mutmasslichen Folgen fr die Preisstabilitt abhngig sein. Zum Schluss noch eine Bemerkung zur Einfhrung des Euro-Bargelds. Makrokonomisch ist dieses Ereignis ein Non-event. Der Euro ist seit dem 1.1.99 da; wir kennen ihn und haben mit ihm zu leben gelernt. In einem lange Zeit ruhigen Nebeneinander, das erst in der durch den Schock von 11. September ausgelsten Welle von Risikoaversion unterbrochen wurde. Diese Erschtterung hatte indessen mit der Existenz des Euro nichts zu tun; sie wre aller Erfahrung nach auch im Nebeneinander mit der DM nicht ausgeblieben. Dagegen wird die Verfgbarkeit von Euro-Bargeld im tglichen Zahlungsverkehr auch innerhalb unserer Grenzen Spuren hinterlassen. Es wird absehbar mehr Transaktionen gegen Euros geben als vorher gegen die Vorgngerwhrungen. Damit drften zustzliche Akteure  positiv und negativ  von Wechselkursbewegungen betroffen sein. Aber dieser Effekt wird in engen Grenzen und beschrnkt auf einzelne Sektoren bleiben. Er wird bei weitem nicht jenes Ausmass erreichen, das fr die geldpolitische Steuerung eine substanzielle Behinderung darstellen knnte.

Title: The euro's impact on Switzerland and on the monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank
text: The euro: impact on Switzerland and on the monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank Prof. Dr. Niklaus Blattner Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Swiss Bankers' Club Bern, 11 February 2002 1. Benefits and Costs of a Monetary Union: Foundations The introduction of a common currency promises benefits and costs. Since the benefits are mainly due to structural improvements and the costs are mainly due to the complication of inflation and economic management, and since the benefits and costs are distributed in a complex way over time, it is difficult to calculate the advantages and disadvantages of a monetary union. Above all, it cannot be done on the "first day". Whether a monetary union provides benefits or costs on balance depends on many things, but not least on the characteristics of the common currency area. Theoretically, it is undisputed that in order to form a so-called optimal currency area, its member countries must have similar structures and a high degree of flexibility. The benefits of a monetary union consist of reducing the transaction costs of exchanging money, eliminating internal exchange rate uncertainty, intensifying competition thanks to simplified price comparisons, increasing intra-regional trade, preventing competitive devaluations, preventing speculative currency attacks and increasing the liquidity of financial markets. In particular, those advantages associated with increasing competition and expanding trade in goods and services take time to unfold. Most of the costs of a monetary union manifest themselves from the outset, even if some of them are only temporary in nature. First of all, the one-off expenses for the cash introduction are to be mentioned as costs. In the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), these are estimated at around 0.5  0.6% of gross domestic product (GDP). In addition, from the point of view of the member states, there is the redistribution of the so-called seignorage towards the community. Seignorage results from the income that accrues to a central bank as a result of the fact that it does not incur any interest costs from the liability item notes in circulation on its balance sheet, but the corresponding assets do indeed trigger income. The redistribution of seignorage is permanent in nature. Their importance depends on the total seignorage generated by the new common currency and the distribution key used. The potentially greatest costs of a monetary union result from the loss of independent monetary policy at the level of the member states. These costs weigh heavily, especially at the beginning, i.e. they can decrease over the years. What is the problem? The more asymmetric shocks occur, the more drastic the task of monetary autonomy becomes. Asymmetric shocks are disturbances that affect the economic structure, the economy and inflation of the member states differently and thus cannot be combated with a uniform economic policy. The recession of 199092 is a vivid example of the potential consequences of a single currency in divergent regional economic situations. At that time, Great Britain and Italy withdrew from the exchange rate mechanism (European Monetary System) and devalued their currencies. This measure allowed them to recover relatively quickly from their recessions, while accepting higher inflation. Conversely, and at the same time, the Federal Republic of Germany found itself confronted with the price-driving consequences of reunification. The Deutsche Bundesbank raised interest rates for the sake of price stability. What would have happened if the monetary union had already existed at that time and italy, Great Britain and Germany had been members of the monetary union? Italy and Great Britain would have been denied the devaluation option. The only instrument would have been monetary policy. The European Central Bank (ECB), had it already existed at that time, might not have raised interest rates at all out of consideration for Great Britain and Italy, or at least would not have let them rise to the same extent as the Bundesbank deemed necessary. Neither Germany nor Italy and Great Britain would have been able to serve with it. Now it can be argued that monetary policy is not the only economic policy instrument. Fiscal policy measures such as a tax cut or an increase in public spending are also available to boost aggregate demand. However, the Stability and Growth Pact, which serves to ensure budgetary discipline in Euroland, imposes restrictions on the fiscal policy of the individual members. On the other hand, fiscal policy interventions at EMU level would in principle not contradict the Stability and Growth Pact. However, the Union budget is likely to be too modest for a long time to come to produce the desired effects by means of a stability-compliant fiscal policy at Union level. Fiscal policy is therefore not a realistic option for the time being. Apart from this historical case study, the faster economic adjustments are made, the lower the costs of losing monetary independence. The better the markets function, the lower the need for economic policy action. The speed at which the economy recovers depends to a large extent on the flexibility of the labour market and the mobility of jobs. If wages adapt to the regional economy and there is potential for direct investment, then regionally different shocks can be absorbed more easily despite a single monetary policy. Labour mobility can also help. If workers are mobile, they will partly leave a country plagued by a crisis and settle where employment opportunities are greater. On the other hand, it should be noted that a monetary union naturally promotes the division of labour between the participating countries. Instead of being levelled, differences between countries can become more acute. The fact is that regional specialization in the US is more pronounced than it is today in Euroland. Large industries have come together in national clusters  the car manufacturers in Detroit, the software producers in Silicon Valley, the filmmakers in Hollywood. As a result of regional specialization, the recession of 199091, which was mainly triggered by cuts in military spending, had particularly affected the regions with a high proportion of military bases and weapons manufacturers, especially California. In California, the unemployment rate rose much faster than in the rest of the country. As a result, the federal tax and transfer system not only supported the unemployed, but also subsidized the conversion of military installations into civilian facilities. In addition, from 1993 to 94 there was a net emigration of over 250,000 workers from California, after 200,000 net people had been attracted by this region in the last boom year before. While the adjustment processes have been painful for many, considerable labor market flexibility and large federal budget deficits have dampened the costs of recession and regional specialization in the U.S. The US is a state with a large budget of its own, its own fiscal power and a flexible labour market. The European Union (EU) is still a long way from that today. The only thing that makes it directly comparable to the US today is a single monetary policy for twelve of the fifteen member states. Therefore, it cannot be ruled out that income redistribution between the member countries will have to be used in Euroland for a longer period of time to come. Transfers are always suitable for levelling the regional differences in the impact of asymmetric shocks when markets are not sufficiently flexible and all other means of economic policy are insufficient. Finally, despite all reservations, it should not be overlooked that a monetary union creates facts. The elimination of transaction costs and exchange rate uncertainty contribute to a reduction in interest rates, stimulate trade and facilitate direct investment within the monetary union. The European internal market project, which has been promoted since 1992 and which also serves to promote labour mobility, will thus receive further valuable impetus. In addition, the Stability and Growth Pact contributes to the harmonisation of economic policies. The probability of asymmetric shocks should be reduced accordingly over time. And it is precisely this type of shock that puts the most strain on the functioning of a monetary union. 2. Impact of the introduction of the euro on Switzerland 2.1. Impact on the Swiss economy and on the use of the Swiss franc as a means of payment Like companies in the euro area, Swiss companies benefit from the increased price transparency when purchasing goods from Euroland thanks to the euro. In addition, this increases domestic competition, which increases economic prosperity. Another positive effect for Switzerland is the reduction in the number of European currencies. Foreign currency management is easier. The risk of extreme exchange rate fluctuations, such as the 70% real depreciation of the lira between 1992 and 1995, has drastically decreased with the disappearance of the most volatile European currencies. Nevertheless, in a system of flexible exchange rates, exchange rate fluctuations are always to be expected. A hedging strategy for the Swiss entrepreneur would be to use the euros collected to settle supplier invoices or even wages in Switzerland. Wage payments in euros were already discussed in the run-up to the launch of the euro book money. On the one hand, passing on the exchange rate risk to the workforce could have a stabilising effect on employment. On the other hand, however, the assumption of the exchange rate risk by wage earners is likely to meet with resistance. More obvious is the so-called natural hedging. In this case, the Swiss exporter uses the euro income to pay for the intermediate consumption or Suppliers from Euroland. There are indications that this form of hedging plays a growing role in the Swiss economy, which is strongly intertwined with the EU. Euro cash also brings with it a welcome simplification. The introduction of cash will primarily affect the hospitality and retail sectors. But a new world will not emerge. For many shops and hotels, especially in the border area and in the holiday resorts, the acceptance of foreign currencies is proven practice. Hotels and businesses in Switzerland will continue to try to protect themselves against exchange rate risks by means of a margin. Of course, the euro will not leave the Swiss financial centre untouched. The integration of European financial markets driven by the single currency will trigger a surge in innovation and, above all, consolidation. The financial centre is likely to face increasingly strong competition. As the virt-x stock exchange in London demonstrates, financial markets are not location-based. An increase in international competition between locations is tantamount to a major challenge that is desirable in Switzerland's economic interest. On the other hand, the declining importance of the Swiss franc, which was previously weighted disproportionately as an investment currency for several years, has nothing primarily to do with the creation of the single currency. This trend was observed long before 1999. Certainly, the introduction of the euro has not increased the attractiveness of Swiss franc bonds, especially because the market liquidity of euro bonds has grown strongly since 1999. 2.2. Impact on the exchange rate Basically, the more the single currency establishes itself as a stable and strong currency, the greater its advantages will also be for Switzerland. With the introduction of the euro, the standard deviation of the trade-weighted exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the currencies of the European trading partners has fallen significantly. This reduction in exchange rate volatility, which is beneficial for Switzerland, can be attributed to the fact that, as already mentioned, the euro has partly replaced weak and extremely volatile currencies. Measured against its introductory exchange rate against the US dollar, yen and Swiss franc, the euro lost a relatively large amount of ground. However, there are a number of factors that speak in favour of a future increase in international demand for the euro. This includes the growth of the EuroFinanzmarkt and its liquidity. In addition, with an increasing importance of the Euro as the reference currency, especially in Eastern Europe. It is also to be expected that the single currency will be increasingly recognised as an international currency in the medium to long term, not least because of the world's largest share of euro area trade, and as such will find its way into international foreign exchange portfolios. A stronger euro is also supported by the fact that macroeconomic fundamentals in EMU as a whole performed better than originally expected. Inflation rates have been low overall since 1999 and debt and unemployment have fallen. The gap between the US growth rate and that of the Euroland has become significantly smaller, albeit recently for economic and thus undesirable reasons. Finally, the returns on financial assets have converged. The most decisive, positive factors for the future course of the single currency are, on the one hand, a convincing elimination of the structural and institutional weaknesses in many member states and the EU institutions. The willingness to continue and implement reforms will decisively determine the growth path of EMU. On the other hand, the euro exchange rate is determined by confidence in the ECB's monetary policy. Despite initial uncertainties in communication, no one should seriously doubt their determination to achieve price stability. Finally, there is the potential danger that Switzerland derives from the traditional idea that the franc has the character of a "safe haven". It should be noted that even a glance at the map of Europe, but certainly a look at the relative orders of magnitude on the one hand and at the interdependence of the Swiss and euroland economy on the other, should be enough to convince every investor that the Swiss franc is an unsuitable rescue platform in the event of a European stability crisis. The Swiss franc could not escape a major crisis in the euro area. 2.3. Impact on interest rates in Switzerland Both nominal and more important real interest rates for growth have remained relatively low in Switzerland since World War 1. On average over the past 20 years, the interest rate spread on money market rates compared to Germany was between 1 and 1.5 percentage points, while the difference between capital market rates was around 2.5 percentage points. This difference in interest rates represents an advantage for the Swiss economy that should not be underestimated. The reasons for the "interest island" are manifold. First of all, a lower real interest rate could only be seen as a reflection of the Swiss franc that appreciates over time. According to this interpretation, lower interest rates do not represent a real advantage for the Swiss economy. However, the prerequisite would be that Switzerland's real interest rate advantage would be fully compensated by a corresponding real appreciation of the Swiss franc. This condition has not been met in recent decades. Rather, the real interest rate advantage here in Germany went on average beyond the trendy real appreciation. Thus, the appreciation trend of the Swiss franc can only justify part of the interest rate island. A more convincing explanation is the high savings rate in Switzerland. Other reasons for the interest rate bonus in Switzerland are political stability, the performance of the financial sector and overall investor-friendly legal framework conditions. However, monetary arguments are likely to be in the foreground. From an international perspective, Switzerland has very low inflation rates and correspondingly low inflation fluctuations over a very long period of time. In addition, their above-average gold and foreign exchange reserves have a confidence-building effect. The relatively low Swiss franc interest rates can therefore be seen as a kind of insurance premium that investors pay to protect their portfolio against crises. The three years of more or less quiet coexistence with the euro have not noticeably reduced the interest rate differential in favour of the Swiss franc. As long as the Swiss National Bank (SNB) can pursue an autonomous monetary policy, the Swiss franc will remain a crisis-resistant investment currency and the interest rate bonus will continue. 3. Impact of the euro on the SNB's monetary policy 3.1. Impact of the euro on money demand In the run-up to the introduction of euro cash, there was a sharp increase in demand for Swiss banknotes. This is due to the fact that a significant proportion of the cash in circulation of the currencies in the euro, mainly the DM, is held abroad. Some of the holders of this cash probably did not wait for the new banknote issue for risk reasons, but exchanged it into other currencies, especially into US dollars, pounds sterling and, to a lesser extent, Swiss francs. However, since the physical presence of the euro, it is also foreseeable that transactions will be made in euro cash instead of In Swiss banknotes, which in turn will have a negative impact on the demand for Swiss francs. Certainly, however, the large majority of payments between residents will still be processed in Swiss francs. Overall, the decrease in seignorage, i.e. the aforementioned profit that the SNB makes on cash in circulation, is likely to be kept within narrow limits. 3.2. Impact on the monetary policy approach 3.2.1. The monetary policy approach Even if the creation of the EMU were to lead to a significant change in Swiss franc demand for money, which, as justified, cannot be assumed, this would not detract from the suitability of the SNB's monetary policy concept. A possible shift in demand for money complicates monetary policy decisions, especially when a central bank is aiming for money supply targets. The management of the money supply as a monetary policy concept has now become obsolete in many countries. A prominent exception is the ECB. Their monetary policy strategy is based on three elements: a quantitative definition of price level stability as an end objective, a broadly based assessment of inflation prospects and risks to price stability, and finally the setting of a reference value for the growth of the money supply M3. Two years ago, the SNB abandoned money supply management. The new concept is based on an inflation forecast and an operational implementation target for the three-month Swiss franc LIBOR. The main objective is and remains price stability, whereby the SNB already today, as stated in the draft of the Central Bank Act to be revised, never ignores economic developments. Price stability is achieved when inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, is below 2% in the medium term. While some central banks, such as the English and New Zealand, have to adopt the inflation target set by the government, the SNB enjoys the autonomy to define what it means by price stability and also to decide under what circumstances it tolerates short-term deviations from price stability. It shares this responsibility with the ECB, the Fed and the Bank of Japan. As a result of the change in strategy from money supply to inflation-forecast-oriented interest rate management, shifts in money demand have become less problematic as they are automatically compensated. Even if it no longer has an intermediate target function, the development of the money supply continues to play an important role in the preparation of the inflation forecast  among other indicators. The centuries-old observation that permanent changes in price levels are linked to changes in the money supply has not changed. 3.2.2. The importance of the exchange rate An important variable in the process of determining the medium-term inflation forecast is the exchange rate. The importance of the Swiss franc exchange rate of the most important currencies results from the smallness and openness of the Swiss economy. The export share of gross national product (GNP) is around 42%. The corresponding figures for Germany and the USA are 29% and 12% respectively. Switzerland's most important trading partners are the EU countries, which account for 59% of its exports. The interdependence on the import side is even greater, as 75% of Swiss imports come from the EU. The exchange rate influences total demand via foreign trade and, of course, consumer prices in Switzerland. All in all, the development of the Swiss franc exchange rate of the euro was quite stable until recently. In the wake of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, investors' risk aversion has increased. This has strengthened the franc. The interest rate cuts in rapid succession, which the SNB has announced since that date, were also the result of concerns about a threat to the economy posed by the exchange rate. This significant easing of monetary policy was possible because there was no threat to price stability. 3.2.3. Control of the exchange rate? Despite the fact that, as described, the SNB takes exchange rates into account when setting its monetary policy, it is occasionally asked to do even more. It should, it is said, even pay attention  at least temporarily  exclusively to the exchange rate. The idea is that the SNB could not only set a certain, lower Swiss franc exchange rate, but also that export activity would subsequently revive to the desired extent. Theoretically, it is possible to bring about a nominal weakening of the Swiss franc through a strongly expansionary monetary policy. Whether interest rate cuts are helpful, however, in view of the empirically strongly relativized importance of interest rates as a determinant of exchange rates, it must be doubted. The US interest rate cuts have repeatedly led not to a weakening, but to a strengthening of the US dollar exchange rate. Ultimately, the supply of Swiss francs would probably have to be increased until the desired weakening of the swiss franc exchange rate would be achieved. However, this would mean that the money supply would have to be significantly expanded, which would not be possible without a massive increase in inflation risks. As a result, the SNB would no longer be able to fulfil its mandate to safeguard price stability. As experience has shown, however, not only would high costs have to be borne later in the form of rising inflation, but also in the short term problems would be raised. The first, immediate consequence would be an erosion of the interest island. This erosion would be all the more pronounced the clearer the change in strategy from a price stability-oriented to an exchange-rate-oriented monetary policy. The demise of the interest island would trigger considerable redistributive effects from debtors to creditors. In addition, a significant reduction in the earnings values of real capital (e.g. real estate) would have to be expected, which would increase counterparty risks in addition to interest rate risks. The financial system would come under pressure. Economic losses were inevitable. In addition, the hope for increased export opportunities thanks to a falling Swiss franc exchange rate is understandable, but at the same time deceptive. The exchange rate is only one of the determinants of export success. Exports depend not only on price elasticity, but also on their income elasticity or on the economic development abroad. There is no question that we are confronted with an uncertain global economy today. However, setting an exchange rate target will not improve the global economy. It is advantageous for Swiss monetary policy that there is now a large economic bloc in Europe that pursues similar monetary policy objectives to Switzerland. The Swiss-Euro exchange rate is likely to be more stable than the DM exchange rate used to be. However, exchange rate fluctuations are still to be expected, as the events following the terrorist attacks in the USA revealed. But the euro will not become a parallel currency. Most employment and credit agreements in Switzerland will continue to be concluded in Swiss francs. The same applies to domestic payments. The SNB's monetary policy concept remains unchanged. This means that the SNB is continuing its independent monetary policy geared to the needs of the Swiss economy and oriented towards price stability. The lower level of interest rates is likely to remain with Switzerland. Exchange rate targets are incompatible with the SNB's mandate. However, the exchange rate is still an important element in determining inflation forecasts. The SNB will therefore continue to attach great importance to the exchange rate when setting its monetary policy.

Diese deutliche Lockerung der Geldpolitik war mglich, da keine Gefahr fr die Preisstabilitt bestand. 3.2.3. Steuerung des Wechselkurses? Trotz der Tatsache, dass die SNB wie beschrieben die Wechselkurse anlsslich der Festlegung ihrer Geldpolitik bercksichtigt, wird sie hin und wieder aufgefordert, noch mehr zu tun. Sie sollte, so heisst es, ihre Aufmerksamkeit  zumindest vorbergehend  sogar ausschliesslich dem Wechselkurs schenken.
