Mrz 2002 Einleitung Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren Gibt es an den Devisenmrkten Turbulenzen und neigt der Schweizer Franken zur Strke, taucht regelmssig die Frage auf, ob die Schweiz nicht besser den Wechsel-kurs fixieren sollte. Oft wird sterreich als Beispiel herangezogen. Nach dem Zusammenbruch des Fixkurssystems von Bretton-Woods im Jahre 1973 fixierte sterreich den Kurs des Schillings zuerst an einen Korb von europischen Wh-rungen. Dann, von 1981 bis 1999, band die sterreichische Nationalbank den Wech-selkurs des Schillings strikt an die DMark, d.h. an die Whrung des wichtigsten Handelspartners des Landes. Der Schillingkurs war so stabil, dass sterreich Anfang 1999 ohne Wenn und Aber der Europischen Whrungsunion beitreten konnte. Ein solches Whrungsumfeld mag Schweizer Exporteuren paradiesisch vorkommen. Bis heute mssen sie mit Wechselkursschwankungen leben, die recht stark ausfallen knnen. So bereitete beispielsweise der Aufwertungsschub des Frankens gegenber dem Euro im letzten September nicht nur der Exportindustrie, sondern auch der Nationalbank einige Sorgen. Bekanntlich reagierten wir damals mit einer weiteren Lockerung der Geldpolitik. Warum also hat sich die Schweiz die Brde flexibler Wechselkurse aufgeladen, wenn es doch - wie das Beispiel sterreichs zeigt - auch einen anderen, erfolgreichen Weg zu geben scheint? Es versteht sich, dass die Natur des Wechselkursregimes fr die Geldpolitik erheb-liehe Konsequenzen hat. Ein Land, das seinen Wechselkurs gegenber einer anderen Whrung fixiert, verzichtet auf eine eigenstndige Geldpolitik. Die Hauptaufgabe der Zentralbank besteht dann darin, dafr zu sorgen, dass sich der Wechselkurs in der vorbestimmten Bandbreite bewegt. Weicht er davon ab, muss die Zentralbank syste-matisch die eigene Whrung kaufen oder verkaufen, bis sich der angestrebte Kurs wieder einstellt. Das Land bernimmt mit anderen Worten die Geldpolitik desjenigen Landes, an das es seine Whrung gebunden hat. Im Falle von sterreich war dies Deutschland. Umgekehrt ermglichen flexible Wechselkurse einem Land, eine unabhngige Geld-politik zu fhren. Die Zentralbank kann die kurzfristigen Zinsstze autonom vern-dern und damit die Geldpolitik auf die spezifischen Bedrfnisse des Landes abstim-men. Auf welchem Niveau der Wechselkurs liegt, bestimmen die Marktkrfte. Dies ist in der Schweiz seit 1973 der Fall. Warum also gingen zwei Lnder wie sterreich und die Schweiz, die vieles gemein haben und beide der wirtschaftlichen Stabilitt hohe Bedeutung beimessen, auf dem Gebiet der Geldpolitik verschiedene Wege? Diese Frage mchte ich in der folgenden halben Stunde diskutieren. Sie ist fr die Schweiz seit Bestehen der Europischen Whrungsunion, die nun Anfang 2002 mit der Einfhrung des Euro-Bargeldes vollen-det wurde, besonders wichtig. 1. Warum wurde der Franken nicht angebunden? Ein Exportunternehmen braucht wohl nicht lange, um die Nachteile flexibler Wechselkurse zu nennen: Wechselkursschwankungen erschweren die Kalkulation. Das Absichern des Whrungsrisikos ist mit Kosten und Aufwand verbunden. Wertet sich die eigene Whrung whrend einer lngeren Zeit gar auf, so droht das Unternehmen seine auslndischen Kunden zu verlieren oder es muss Preiskonzessionen machen, die seine Marge verringern. All diese Nachteile fallen bei einem festen Wechselkurs - wie er in sterreich bis 1999 bestand - weg. Trotz unbestrittener Vorteile sind fixe Wechselkurse aber kein Patentrezept. Es ms-sen nmlich eine Reihe von Bedingungen erfllt sein, damit es fr ein Land von Vor-teil ist, seinen Wechselkurs eng an eine andere Whrung zu binden und auf eine eigenstndige Geldpolitik zu verzichten. Eine Fixierung des Wechselkurses ist in erster Linie sinnvoll, wenn ein Land mit einem bestimmten Handelspartner enge wirtschaftliche Beziehungen unterhlt. In diesem Fall fllt ein grosser Teil des Aussenhandels im Verkehr mit diesem Land an und die Mobilitt der Arbeitskrfte zwischen den beiden Lndern ist hoch. Auch die Wirtschaftsstruktur der beiden Lnder sollte hnlich sein. Nur dann besteht die Aus-sieht, dass sich die Konjunktur in den beiden Lndern im Gleichschritt entwickelt und das feste Kursverhltnis nicht unter Druck kommt. Und schliesslich bindet ein Land seine Whrung mit Vorteil an ein Land, das selbst der Preisstabilitt einen hohen Stellenwert beimisst und diese ber den festen Wechselkurs auf das andere Land bertrgt. Natrlich sind dies grobe Anhaltspunkte. Sie machen jedoch verstndlich, weshalb die Schweiz - anders als sterreich - nach 1973 eine feste Bindung des Frankens gegenber der D-Mark nie wirklich ins Auge fasste. Ein erster Unterschied zeigt sich bereits beim Aussenhandel. Zwar ist Deutschland auch fr die Schweiz der wichtigste einzelne Handelspartner. Mit einem Export- und Importanteil von heute 22% bzw. 35% ist die Bindung aber doch weniger stark als im Falle von sterreich, das mehr als einen Drittel seiner Gter nach Deutschland exportiert und ber 40% von dort einfhrt. Eine Fixierung des Wechselkurses gegen-ber der D-Mark htte damit fr die Schweiz weniger gebracht als fr sterreich. Ein weiterer Unterschied betrifft die Finanzpolitik. Die Schweiz hat ein dezentrales Finanzsystem mit den drei ungefhr gleich starken Ebenen Gemeinden, Kantone und Bund. Diese Gewaltenteilung auf dem Gebiet der Finanzpolitik verringert die Wahrscheinlichkeit eines potenziell immer mglichen Konflikts zwischen der Geld- und Finanzpolitik. Es war damit fr die Schweizerische Nationalbank von Anfang an ein-facher als fr andere Zentralbanken, eine auf Preisstabilitt ausgerichtete Geld-politik zu fhren. Dementsprechend geringer war der Anreiz oder Vorteil, ber die Fixierung des Wechselkurses Preisstabilitt zu importieren. Drittens unterscheidet sich die schweizerische Wirtschaftsstruktur von der Struktur des wichtigsten Handelspartners deutlich. So spielt insbesondere der Finanzsektor in der Schweiz eine ungleich grssere Rolle als in Deutschland. Sein Anteil an der gesamten Wertschpfung ist mehr als doppelt so hoch. Gemessen am Bruttoinland-produkt ist die Bilanzsumme der Banken um ein Vielfaches grsser als in unserem nrdlichen Nachbarland. Vor allem aber war der Franken - wie die D-Mark - eine internationale Anlage-whrung. Frankenanlagen werden besonders zur Diversifizierung von Portefeuilles verwendet. Damit war unsere Whrung oft Schocks ausgesetzt, die mit der wirt-schaftlichen Situation in unserem Land nichts zu tun hatten. Wre der Wechselkurs fixiert gewesen, so htten die Finanzmrkte wohl die Standfestigkeit der National-bank immer wieder zu testen versucht. Dies umso mehr, als spekulative Attacken unter solchen Voraussetzungen fr die Marktteilnehmer risikolos sind. Der National-bank wren nur zwei Mglichkeiten geblieben: Entweder sie htte die feste Paritt dezidiert verteidigt und damit eine inflationre Aufblhung der Geldversorgung in Kauf genommen, oder sie htte die Paritt anpassen mssen. Beide Alternativen sind wenig attraktiv und sprachen gegen eine Fixierung des Wechselkurses gegen-ber der D-Mark. Sie sehen damit, dass der Entscheid fr flexible Wechselkurse und eine unabhngige Geldpolitik nicht einfach Ausdruck von Starrsinn war. Vielmehr ergab er sich aus den speziellen wirtschaftlichen Bedingungen unseres Landes. Dies erklrt auch, weshalb in der Schweiz keine breite Strmung zugunsten einer Fixierung des Wechselkurses entstand. Unzufriedenheit mit dem Wechselkursregime kam nur dann auf, wenn Aufwertungsschbe den Exportbranchen Probleme bereiteten. 2. Erfahrungen mit flexiblen Wechselkursen Die Schweiz hat in den letzten 30 Jahren gelernt, mit flexiblen Wechselkursen zu leben. Insgesamt wurden die Exportbranchen mit den kurzfristigen Schwankungen des Wechselkurses gut fertig. Damit besttigten sich die Ergebnisse vieler empiri-scher Studien. Diese zeigen, dass die kurzfristige Volatilitt der Wechselkurse keinen nennenswerten Einfluss auf das Wachstum der Exporte hat, da sich Gewinne und Verluste rasch ausgleichen. Auch knnen die Exporteure das Wechselkursrisiko effi-zient absichern, sei es mit Devisentermingeschften oder durch ein natrliches Hedging. Heikler wurde die Lage jeweils, wenn sich der Franken whrend mehrerer Monate nominell und real stark aufwertete. Die Nationalbank musste mehrmals gegen solche Entwicklungen vorgehen. Zum ersten Mal war dies im Jahre 1978 der Fall, als wir vorbergehend sogar eine Untergrenze fr den Franken-D-Mark-Kurs bekanntgaben und diese mit einer massiven Lockerung der Geldpolitik auch durchsetzten. Ein jngeres, etwas anders gelagertes Beispiel ist die Aufwertung des Frankens im Zusammenhang mit den Terroranschlgen vom 11. September. Wie bereits eingangs erwhnt, senkte die Nationalbank die kurzfristigen Zinsstze im zweiten Halbjahr 2001 deutlich. Dies geschah zum Teil auch explizit vor dem Hintergrund dieser Fran-kenaufwertung. Damit verhinderten wir, dass sich die monetren Rahmenbedingun-gen in einer konjunkturell heiklen Phase gefhrlich verschrften. Schliesslich zeigt ein Blick auf die achtziger und neunziger Jahre, dass sich der Franken real, also bereinigt um die Inflationsdifferenzen, tendenziell aufwertete. Von 1981 bis 1999 gewann er gegenber der D-Mark real um insgesamt 10% an Wert. Interessant ist, dass in jenen knapp zwanzig Jahren auch der Schillingkurs gegenber der D-Mark real stieg, und zwar um rund 6%. Dies zeigt, dass mit einer Fixierung des Wechselkurses zwar nominelle Schwankungen ausgeschaltet werden knnen, sich der reale Kurs aber dennoch ber unterschiedliche Preisentwicklungen verndern kann. Die konomie hlt fr lang anhaltende Bewegungen des realen Wechselkurses vor allem zwei Erklrungen bereit. Eine erste Erklrung setzt bei den relativen Produktivittsunterschieden zwischen dem Sektor der handelbaren und der nicht handel-baren Gter an. Im Falle der Schweiz kann beispielsweise gezeigt werden, dass die Produktivittsentwicklung zwischen diesen beiden Sektoren viel strker auseinander klafft als in Deutschland. Schutzmassnahmen zugunsten des Binnenmarktes drften massgeblich dazu beigetragen haben. Als Folge davon ist das Preisniveau fr inln-dische Produkte in der Schweiz heute deutlich hher als in unserem nrdlichen Nachbarland. Dies drfte ein Grund dafr sein, weshalb sich der Franken gegenber der Whrung Deutschlands in den letzten zwanzig Jahren real verteuert hat. Die zweite Erklrung setzt bei der Entwicklung der Ertragsbilanz an. Ein Land, das wie die Schweiz anhaltend hohe Ertragsbilanzberschsse aufweist, baut ber die Zeit ein betrchtliches Auslandvermgen auf. In der Schweiz sind dies heute rund 500 Mrd. Franken; pro Kopf der Bevlkerung entspricht dies weltweit dem hchsten Wert. Aus verschiedenen Grnden drften die inlndischen Anleger eine gewisse Prferenz fr Schweizer-Franken-Anlagen haben. Die hohen Ertragsbilanzberschsse tragen damit dazu bei, dass Anlagen in Schweizer Franken stark nachgefragt werden und der Franken am Devisenmarkt real hher bewertet wird. Es sind solche realwirtschaftliche Grnde, die zur Erklrung von langfristigen oder dauerhaften Wechselkursbewegungen herangezogen werden mssen. Eine Zentral-bank kann mit geldpolitischen Massnahmen letztlich nichts dagegen unternehmen. Im Falle der Schweiz htte eine Anbindung des Wechselkurses beispielsweise an die D-Mark zu einer hheren Teuerung gefhrt und der reale Aussenwert des Frankens wre auf diesem Weg gestiegen. Die Schweizer Exportindustrie hat sich trotz der langfristigen realen Hherbewertung des Frankens im internationalen Wettbewerb sehr gut behauptet. Dies ist daraus ersichtlich, dass sich der Anteil der Exporte am Bruttoinlandprodukt in den letzten dreissig Jahren fast verdoppelte und sich damit hnlich entwickelte wie in anderen Lndern. Gleichzeitig zeigte der reale Wertgewinn des Frankens, dass die Schweiz die eigenen Produkte im Verhltnis zu den importierten Gtern teurer verkaufen konnte. Dies bedeutete einen Wohlstandsgewinn. Damit mchte ich auf zwei Argumente zu sprechen kommen, die meines Erachtens in der Schweiz nach wie vor zugunsten flexibler Wechselkurse sprechen. Es geht - erstens - um den relativen Zinsvorteil der Schweiz gegenber dem Ausland und - zweitens - um die Autonomie der Geldpolitik. Dass die schweizerische Geldpolitik mit flexiblen Wechselkursen bis heute breite Untersttzung findet, liegt vermutlich zum grssten Teil hier begrndet. In der Schweiz sind die langfristigen Zinsstze traditionellerweise tiefer als die entsprechenden Zinsstze in Europa oder den USA. Nehmen wir an, der Schweiz wre es wie sterreich gelungen, den nominellen Wechselkurs gegenber der D-Mark glaubwrdig zu fixieren. In diesem Fall htten die Investoren Anlagen in Schweizer Fran-ken als perfekte Alternativen zu vergleichbaren D-Mark-Anlagen betrachtet und die schweizerischen Zinsstze htten sich den deutschen Stzen angeglichen. Nun werden Sie vermutlich einwenden, dass fr die Wirtschaft nicht die Nominal-zinsen, sondern die Realzinsen entscheidend sind, also die Zinskosten nach Abzug der Inflationsrate. Da die Teuerung in der Schweiz bei einer Fixierung des Wechsel-kurses tendenziell etwas hher ausgefallen wre als im Ausland, wre die Schweiz dementsprechend weiterhin in den Genuss tieferer realer Zinskosten gekommen. Dies trifft grundstzlich zu. Der Zinsabstand zum Ausland htte sich aber mit grosser Wahrscheinlichkeit verkleinert. Bis heute fllt nmlich auf Frankenanlagen eine posi-tive Risikoprmie an, welche das reale Zinsniveau vergleichsweise tief hlt. Darin widerspiegelt sich unter anderem die hohe Glaubwrdigkeit der schweizerischen Stabilittspolitik. Bei einer Fixierung des Wechselkurses und dem damit verbundenen Verzicht auf eine unabhngige Geldpolitik wrde dieser Bonus wegfallen. Die Schweiz wrde mit anderen Worten einen wichtigen internationalen Wettbewerbs-vorteil verlieren. Kommen wir damit zur Frage der geldpolitischen Autonomie. Die Deutsche Bundes-bank und die Nationalbank trafen oft gleiche Entscheidungen. Konnte sich also die Nationalbank trotz flexibler Wechselkurse nicht von der Bundesbank abgrenzen? Die Erfahrung zeigt, dass der Handlungsspielraum der Nationalbank zwar nicht unbe-grenzt, aber doch beachtlich war. Sie nutzte ihn mehrere Male, um die Geldpolitik auf die spezifischen Bedrfnisse der Schweiz auszurichten. So lockerte sie beispiels-weise im Sommer 1992 und erneut im Sommer 1993 die Geldpolitik rascher als die Bundesbank. In Deutschland hatte die Einigung zu einer Beschleunigung der lnfla-tion gefhrt, welche der Bundesbank die Hnde band. Der Zinsunterschied zwischen der Schweiz und Deutschland erreichte damals fast 3 Prozentpunkte. Auch im letzten Jahr senkten wir die Zinsstze rascher und strker als die Europische Zentralbank, da uns die sehr gnstige Teuerungsentwicklung mehr Spielraum liess. Natrlich sind dem Handlungsspielraum der Nationalbank von ihrem Auftrag her Grenzen gesetzt. Wir verfolgen letztlich die gleichen Ziele wie damals die Deutsche Bundesbank und heute die Europische Zentralbank, nmlich die Sicherung der Geldwertstabilitt sowie einer ausgewogenen wirtschaftlichen Entwicklung. So lange diese bereinstimmung da ist, werden auch die geldpolitischen Massnahmen hnlich sein. Zwischen einem begrenzten und gar keinem Handlungsspielraum besteht den-noch ein betrchtlicher Unterschied. 3. Was bringt die Zukunft? Versuchen wir rckblickend, die Vor- und Nachteile der schweizerischen Lsung abzuwgen, so fllt die Bilanz aus unserer Sicht positiv aus. Der eingeschlagene Weg mit flexiblen Wechselkursen und einer unabhngigen Geldpolitik wurde unseres Erachtens den Bedrfnissen der Schweiz am besten gerecht. Wir sind auch berzeugt, dass nur dieser Weg glaubwrdig und damit fr uns gangbar war. Die Zeiten ndern sich. Im Zuge der Globalisierung, aber auch infolge politischer Entscheide wie dem Abschluss der bilateralen Vertrge mit der EU, wird die wirtschaftliche Verflechtung zwischen der Schweiz und Europa weiter zunehmen. Kon-junktur und Inflation drften sich noch synchroner entwickeln und damit der Vorteil einer autonomen Geldpolitik kleiner werden. In dem Masse, wie sich der Euro international als wertstabile Whrung etabliert, knnte zudem auch die Zinsdifferenz zwischen der Schweiz und Europa abnehmen. Damit wrden Faktoren, die bis heute fr einen eigenstndigen Weg sprachen, allmhlich an Bedeutung verlieren. Noch deutet aber nichts auf eine solche Entwicklung. Eine unabhngige Geldpolitik mit flexiblen Wechselkursen scheint weiterhin die beste Strategie fr die Schweiz zu sein. Sollte die Schweiz eines Tages einen Strategiewechsel ins Auge fassen, so mssten die Kosten und der Nutzen vorurteilslos einander gegenbergestellt werden. Fest steht, dass ein ein-faches Anbinden des Frankens an den Euro - entsprechend dem frheren Beispiel sterreichs und der D-Mark - nach wie vor keine glaubwrdige Lsung wre. Nur ein Beitritt zur Europischen Whrungsunion und damit letztlich auch zur EU knnte die Finanz-mrkte von der Dauerhaftigkeit der Bindung zwischen dem Franken und dem Euro berzeugen. Bis heute war die Schweiz zu diesem Schritt nicht bereit.

Title: Will the Euro Make the Swiss Franc Obsolete?
text: Will the Euro Make the Swiss Franc Obsolete? Ulrich Kohli Chief Economist Swiss National Bank Paper prepared for the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce New York, NY Thursday, March 7, 2002 I am deeply honored to have been invited to address such a distinguished audience, and it is with great pleasure that I will share with you some thoughts about the euro and what it might mean for Switzerland. Will the euro make the Swiss franc obsolete? I originally thought of a different title for my talk: Heidi in Euroland, but then I thought that perhaps this would sound somewhat frivolous coming from a central banker. There is no question, though, that the Swiss monetary environment has changed drastically with the introduction of the euro, and that most Swiss residents will feel the change. The Swiss monetary zone, which includes Liechtenstein, is totally surrounded by the euro-zone. It is often described as an island amidst the euro-ocean. In fact, Switzerland might well qualify for the Guinness Book of Records as the only land-locked island in the world! 1. Birth of the euro After a long pregnancy, the euro has finally seen the light of day. In truth, the euro is already a toddler. It was born over three years ago, on January 1, 1999. It has been widely used as a means of payment and a store of value ever since, and we have long learnt how to live with it. What happened just over two months ago, on January 1, 2002, however, was the most spectacular phase of the entire operation, the introduction of the physical euro: euro coins and euro notes. To the public at large, the euro has finally become a reality. People throughout Europe can now see it, they can touch it, they can own it, and they can spend it. The creation of a monetary union between a dozen independent nations was a bold and unprecedented move. Twelve countries willingly giving up monetary sovereignty is an achievement of historical proportions. It was all the more daring as it precedes political unity and fiscal integration. 2. Monetary union: pros and cons Monetary integration brings many benefits to its members. Transaction costs are sharply reduced. Exchange-rate volatility and uncertainty vanish within the union. Price comparisons are facilitated and transparency more generally is enhanced. Trade and capital flows between the participating states are invigorated, and this in turn should fuel economic growth. Monetary integration under the Maastricht Treaty also promises price stability to those countries that, in the past, had seemed incapable of achieving it on their own. Furthermore, the common currency is becoming a powerful political and social force stimulating further integration. Naturally, monetary integration has its costs too. The most important one is the loss of monetary sovereignty. That is, member countries are no longer able to pursue a monetary policy of their own. There is now just one monetary policy for the entire euro-zone. If you turn it upside down, you will see the stamp made in Frankfurt. And, in smaller print, one size fits all. This could lead to severe problems in case of asymmetrical shocks; that is, if one country, or one group of countries, is affected by specific external events. Given the large diversity of the European economy that ranges from Portugal and Greece to Germany and Finland, asymmetries cannot be ruled out. The situation could even become trickier with enlargement and the arrival of new members. Under monetary union, adjustments that would otherwise occur through changes in the exchange rate and domestic interest-rate conditions must imperatively take place through changes in prices and wages, and through adjustments in quantities, all of which can be very painful. True, the situation is somewhat similar in the United States. There is only one monetary policy for all 50 states. It is made in Washington. Given the diversity of the land, it is obviously challenging to come up with the right policy for the entire country. West Virginia might be in a recession, whereas Arizona is booming. California might be particularly affected by a downturn in the high tech industry, while Michigan is more dependent on the good fortune of the car industry. One important difference compared to Europe, however, is that the adjustment here is facilitated by the more flexible goods and labor markets. Labor mobility in the United States has traditionally been high and it is made easier by cultural similarities, and the fact that most people in this country speak more or less the same language. Moreover, fiscal integration means that public transfers can take place between regions and that powerful automatic stabilizers are at work. Monetary integration has been costly in terms of resources as well. It has necessitated numerous high-level government meetings, working groups, conferences and seminars, not to forget the fancy and expensive dinners, banquets, and parties. For the private sector too, preparing for the changeover has been an expensive proposition and it proved to be a distraction. Businesses had to adapt their accounting practices, update their computer hardware and software, and transform or replace numerous machines, from cash registers and coke machines to public phones and ATMs, from ticket dispensers and toll machines to gas pumps and taximeters. The cost to the European economy has been in the tens of billions of euros. But these preparations are now behind us. The phase-in of the new currency over the past two months has worked remarkably well, with hardly a glitch. It was an extremely well prepared operation, and our European neighbors ought to be congratulated on this achievement. 3. Monetary union: a Swiss perspective There is no question that Switzerland, too, will greatly benefit from European monetary integration. It will make life much easier for all the Swiss who travel and do business in Europe. In the past, every Swiss returning from a journey abroad came back with a pocketful of small change from the countries he or she visited. Marks, shillings, guilders, liras, pesetas, escudos, or drachmas, all of which had to be carefully saved for the next trip, in the knowledge that they would often have lost much of their value in the meantime. Now all that is needed for a trip through much of Europe is a fistful of euros. This is a great convenience, and we will save a lot in foreign exchange fees, transaction costs, and other worries. Business, too, will find it easier to deal in merely three or four currencies, rather than fifteen. Prices will become more transparent for everyone, and this should foster competition in Switzerland as well. At the same time, the costs for Switzerland have been relatively small. True, many businesses had to make some adjustments. In the border areas, some ATMs had to be reprogrammed to spit out euros instead of liras, shillings or marks. Some cash registers have been modified to show both Swiss franc and euro prices, and some menus and wine lists had to be reprinted to show the prices in both currencies. 4. Will the euro displace the Swiss franc? Many observers have expressed the view -the hope or the fear, as the case may be that the euro will become a parallel currency in Switzerland. Will the euro circulate in Switzerland? The answer is, undoubtedly, yes. Will it threaten to displace the Swiss franc, thus leading to the de facto integration of Switzerland into the euro-zone? Hardly. The euro will circulate -in fact it already does -in Switzerland, particularly in the border areas and in the tourist regions. This is nothing new. French francs and German marks have long been accepted in shops in Geneva or in Basie. So are U.S. dollars on the Bahnhofstrasse in Zurich, for that matter. But the reverse is also true, your Swiss francs will gladly be accepted on the other side of the border, in Como or in Megeve. This is no joke, the Swiss franc circulates in the euro-zone, but rest assured, we do not believe that it will displace the euro! In many shops, restaurants and hotels euros will, and already are, accepted as a form of payment. But let us not kid ourselves. This practice will remain very limited. First of all, in nearly all cases the change is given back in Swiss francs. Second, the exchange rate is generally unattractive. These businesses provide a foreign-exchange service to their customers as a convenience, but this is obviously not where their comparative advantage lies, and the visitors will therefore almost always be better off converting their money at a bank or using their credit cards. It may well be that the use of euros in Switzerland will somewhat exceed the sum of the French francs, Italian liras, German marks and Austrian shillings used within our borders in the past, but we expect the total figure to remain fairly trivial. Indeed, the overwhelming majority of internal payments will continue to be denominated in Swiss francs. Wages, rents, insurance premia, and taxes will go on being paid in francs. Payments in euros at the bank or the post office will still be more cumbersome and more expensive than payments in the local currency. Whereas it is perfectly possible in Switzerland to have a bank account denominated in foreign currencies, I know of no bank that offers the possibility to make foreign cash withdrawals at no extra cost. While the option of using a foreign currency when one is short of local money is convenient, there is generally no need for a country to have more than one currency as a means of payment. As long as the existing currency is widely accepted, as long as the public trusts it, and as long as it is expected to keep its value, there is no need to replace it. Parallel currencies would only make life more complicated for the ordinary citizen. Historically, spontaneous dollarization has only taken place in those countries that no longer had a sound currency of their own. Euro-ization, if I may call it this, will not take place in Switzerland in the foreseeable future. Admittedly, the Swiss franc has lost some of its importance on international capital markets in recent years. The use of our currency in international debt issues has steadily declined over the past two decades. This trend, which clearly predates the creation of the euro, is probably indicative of a return to a more normal situation, in check with Switzerland's economic size, after a long period during which the Swiss franc was one of the world's few fully convertible currencies. At the same time, the Swiss franc also seems to lose some of its safe-haven attractiveness, which is not something that we at the SNB will complain about, since this characteristic of our currency has always made our life a little bit more difficult. Although the Swiss franc weighs much less compared with its young sibling than it did compared with either the German mark or the French franc, it has gained in stature simply because it is a member of the dwindling family of international currencies. For this reason, we would expect it to remain attractive as an instrument of portfolio diversification, for lenders as well as for borrowers. 5. Exchange-rate policy But short of encouraging the domestic use of the euro, shouldn't the Swiss National Bank at least aim at fixing the exchange rate between the franc and the euro? Many calls, coming from industry and the unions, demand no less than that. Our critics argue that the appreciation of the franc against the euro is undermining the Swiss export industry and, if left unchecked, it will generate mass unemployment. By targeting the exchange rate, they say, the SNB could eliminate an important source of uncertainty and safeguard the international competitiveness of our export industry. One must remember that about twothirds of Switzerland's foreign trade is with countries from the euro-zone. One should put things in perspective, though. Over the past three years, the Swiss franc has appreciated by about 8% against the euro. In real terms, the appreciation is only about half as large. A 4% or 5% real appreciation over a three-year period is not extraordinary by historical standards. Furthermore, it must be said that over the same period the Swiss franc has depreciated against the dollar and against the yen. It is therefore far from obvious that the Swiss franc is overvalued. It is rather the euro that is undervalued. In any case, fixing the nominal exchange rate against the euro, even if it were possible for a while, would not solve many problems, and it would create a number of new ones. For a start, only the exchange rate against euro-area countries would be fixed, but the policy would do nothing to stabilize the exchange rate against the U.S. dollar, the Japanese yen or the British pound. More importantly, it is well known that in the long run monetary policy has no hold on real variables. The real exchange rate, which is the only one that matters for production decisions and trade flows, cannot be manipulated by monetary policy for any length of time. A more expansionary monetary policy, aimed at depreciating the Swiss franc, would eventually lead to more inflation without any real benefits, quite the contrary. The long-run real appreciation of the Swiss franc against most other currencies would persist, but it would take the form of a rate of inflation that would be higher in Switzerland than in the rest of Europe. This is to say that fixing the value of the Swiss franc against the euro is not compatible with the SNB's objective of price stability. Moreover, nominal interest rates would necessarily increase to the same level as in the rest of Europe, which would mean that Switzerland would lose its interest-rate advantage. One can only begin to imagine what this would do to the Swiss financial center, to the building industry, or to Swiss asset prices. The very risk of higher inflation in Switzerland would stretch the credibility of a policy aimed at targeting the nominal exchange rate. Given the well-known Swiss preference for price stability, the determination of the SNB to maintain a fixed parity would rapidly be tested by the markets. Large speculative inflows betting that the monetary policy would have to change course would make the situation untenable. The problem with fixed exchange rates is that they only remain fixed until they change! Fixed exchange-rate regimes have a habit of collapsing at the worst possible time in an environment of crises and confusion. Economic theory and empirical evidence suggest that the only exchangerate regimes that are plausible in the long run are the ones at the extreme ends of the spectrum, flexible exchange rates, or monetary union leading to a single currency. Monetary union does not solve all the problems, though. The example of the Netherlands is a case in point. The Netherlands -perhaps the country within Europe that is the most similar to Switzerland -is a part of Euroland. It shares its currency-the euro -with France and Germany, among others. There cannot therefore be any nominal exchangerate adjustments between these countries. Yet, over the course of last year, Dutch prices have increased by about 4.4%, whereas inflation was only 1.3% in France and 1.7% in Germany. This is to say that, over the past year, the Dutch currency has appreciated by about 3% in real terms relative to its two large euro-partners. Dutch exporters have suffered an even larger loss of competitiveness than Swiss firms, without even being able to enjoy the benefits of price stability and low interest rates. To be sure, if Switzerland joins the European Union one day, it will almost certainly have to adopt the euro as part of the package. However, this will be a political decision, not an economic one. Until then, it is not in Switzerland's interest to tie the franc to the euro. I argued earlier on that the Swiss franc remains a significant vehicle for portfolio diversification, but this is only true if Switzerland conducts an independent monetary policy; that is, for as long as the franc is not perfectly correlated with the euro. The Swiss franc is an important asset for the Swiss financial center. It is a very successful product, and we have exclusive rights to it: so why throw it away? While a strong currency is often viewed as a source of many problems, one should always keep in mind that fundamentally it is a very positive factor for the country as a whole. A strong currency is synonymous with high purchasing power. It is a source of economic welfare, and ultimately it is a mark of success. According to a recent study, Swiss wages are the second highest in Europe, after Denmark. True, this can be viewed as a burden for business. But of course, we should also look at the bright side. High wages mean a high standard of living, and they reflect the high productivity of Swiss workers. The overwhelming majority of firms are obviously able to pay such high wages, otherwise we would not record them. Naturally, there might be firms engaged in activities where Switzerland no longer has a comparative advantage, and these find it more and more difficult to survive given this high cost structure. This is an unavoidable part of the economic development process, however, and it would happen even in a closed economy. Marginal firms drop out and profitable ones prosper. Having said this, I must add, though, that the Swiss National Bank is fully aware of the pain that sudden moves in the exchange rate can inflict. Exchange-rate movements are closely monitored, and they play an important indirect role in the formulation of our policy. Our action is aimed at price stability, which we define as a rate of inflation between zero and two percent. Our policy is based on an inflation projection over a three-year horizon. An appreciation of the Swiss franc will affect our inflation forecast through several channels, through its impact on import prices and through its influence on activity, in particular. A sudden appreciation of the Swiss franc is thus equivalent to a tightening in monetary conditions, which might need to be offset by a loosening of policy, that is, by a lowering of interest rates. 6. Concluding comments We love the euro in Switzerland. But we like the Swiss franc even better. In many ways, we got the best of both worlds. We enjoy most of the advantages of the euro, without the loss of an important degree of freedom. We benefit from the simplicity, the transparency and the more stable European monetary environment promised by the euro, but we keep the trump card of an independent monetary policy. Will the euro make the Swiss franc obsolete? The only thing that seems to have become redundant in this affair is the word Swiss. With the demise of the French franc and of the Belgian franc earlier this year, the Swissie is the only international currency left named a franc. It is therefore no longer necessary to refer to it as the Swiss franc. We do not call it the European euro, after all. I rephrase the question. Will the euro make the franc obsolete? The short answer is no! Thank you for your attention.

Title: Are any surprises to be expected from a central bank?
text: Is a central bank good for surprises? Presentation by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Statistical-Economic Society Basel Monday, March 25, 2002 Introduction Dear Sir or Madam, I am very pleased to be able to speak about a monetary policy issue here in Basel today. After all, Basel is the capital of the central banks, where the central bank governors of many countries meet regularly in all discretion. The question of discretion is also addressed in my presentation: Should central banks operate in secret at all, surprise the market with unexpected measures? In other words, are central banks good for surprises? More specifically, is the Swiss National Bank good for surprises? I would like to explain to you this evening why surprises in monetary policy are not necessarily a positive thing. I will advocate that a central bank should make its monetary policy as transparent as possible. Transparency means that the public and the financial markets largely anticipate the central bank's measures and surprises are therefore rare. However, I must immediately emphasise what this does not mean: surprises should not be avoided by the central bank slavishly bowing to market expectations. On the contrary, a central bank ideally influences the markets in such a way that the resulting market expectations are as consistent as possible with its own monetary policy intentions. My commitment to transparency may surprise them a little. In the past, central banks often surrounded themselves with a mysterious aura. Transparency was a foreign word in some places. The prevailing opinion was that monetary policy had to act unnoticed and unexpectedly in order to be efficient. A well-known popular science book from the 80s on American monetary policy, for example, was entitled "Secrets of the Temple". Very often important decisions were prepared over the weekend behind closed doors and came on Sunday evening like a thunderclap. This attitude has changed a lot in the past twenty years. Central banks may still seem like temples to many, but they maintain an active communication strategy. The trend towards transparency has become irreversible. Before I explain to you why we have gone in this direction, however, I would like to define the concept of "transparency" in more detail. What does "transparency" mean in relation to a central bank and its policies? With regard to which aspects should or can Monetary authorities act transparently at all? And what are the limits of transparency? A central bank should provide information about its strategy in two areas in particular. These are, firstly, the long-term objective of monetary policy and, secondly, the methods by which this objective is to be achieved. Transparency means clearly communicating goals and methods. By methods, I mean the monetary policy concept and its implementation in practice. What are the reasons for transparency and thus against deliberate surprises in monetary policy? I will first explore this question before discussing our experience with the implementation of the principle of transparency in the Swiss National Bank's monetary policy. Finally, I want to show that complete transparency can sometimes be counterproductive, however desirable it may be to inform the public as widely as possible in general. Transparency reaches its limits where it can no longer promote the efficiency of monetary policy. First of all, there are two reasons for transparency and thus against surprises in monetary policy: transparency enhances the effect of monetary policy, and transparency protects the independence of the central bank. First reason: Transparency enhances the impact of monetary policy Why does a transparent monetary policy strategy enhance the impact of monetary policy? In today's environment of broad and competitive financial markets, a central bank has only limited influence on the economy. In fact, it is only able to directly influence very short-term interest rates. From a technical point of view, this is done in Switzerland by the SNB concluding repo transactions with the banks. For the maturities of these repo transactions, which are usually less than one month, the National Bank can directly determine the interest rate itself. However, the effect of monetary policy on economic activity is only to a limited extent via short-term interest rates. The main effect of monetary policy is through long-term interest rates and the pricing and wage-setting behaviour of individuals. These two factors, in turn, depend on inflation expectations. Monetary policy therefore works mainly through the inflation expectations of market participants. Short-term interest rates, in particular changes in short-term interest rates by the central bank, provide economic actors with important indications of the future Monetary policy orientation and therefore have a high influence on inflation expectations. This is the link between monetary policy and economic events. It is therefore of central importance that the changes in short-term interest rates are correctly interpreted by market participants. This is only possible if sufficient information is available from the central bank - if, in other words, there is transparency. How exactly does a transparent strategy increase the impact of monetary policy?  First, transparency accelerates the impact of monetary policy. It allows the central bank to influence market participants' expectations more quickly and accurately. Transparency improves market participants' knowledge of the central bank's objectives and methods, thus facilitating the classification of monetary policy action. As a result, monetary policy gains predictability and market participants can align their own expectations more quickly and accurately with the central bank's expectations and intentions. Transparency even leads to the fact that the financial markets of the central bank do a large part of the work. If the monetary authorities only indicate that they have concerns about price stability and could therefore raise interest rates in the future, these expectations alone will immediately increase long-term interest rates. This makes the monetary environment more restrictive, mind you, without changing short-term interest rates, in line with the central bank. Transparency enables the central bank to work with and not against the markets. This cooperation makes life easier for both sides. Transparency thus automatically leads to the fact that the assessments of the market and the central bank largely coincide. This avoids most surprises. Once again, I would like to emphasize that surprises are avoided, not because the central bank sees the expectations of the market as a guide, but because the markets understand the actions of the central bank correctly and position themselves accordingly.  Secondly, transparency leads not only to a faster and more precise transmission of monetary policy impulses, but also to greater stability and less volatility in the economy and financial markets. If the goals and methods of a central bank are open and understandable, misunderstandings are avoided and uncertainties are reduced. This is important because the economy and financial markets are always exposed to smaller and larger shocks. Transparency allows markets to monitor the central bank's responses to such shocks. anticipate. Surprises and the associated volatility can thus be minimized. Transparency allows markets not to lose the compass.  The third advantage I see is the flexibility that a central bank gains through transparent and credible policies. It consists in the fact that a central bank can deviate from the expectations of the markets in the short term if there are special reasons without immediately triggering major market turbulence. Markets know that such a deviation is only temporary, and that it does not call into question the long-term objectives of monetary policy. However, it must be stressed that the degree of freedom of the monetary authorities should not be overestimated in this regard. Deviations from the longer-term strategy always contain a certain risk potential. All surprises, which is a matter of course, can of course not be avoided even with the greatest transparency. The market's expectations about future developments may vary. Smaller surprises are therefore always possible for a part of the market. Ultimately, however, it is important that with a transparent monetary policy, the very big surprises - the misjudgements - can be largely avoided. For example, it should not normally happen that in the run-up to an interest rate decision, market expectations differ by half or a whole percentage point from the actual decision. Second reason: Transparency protects the independence of the central bank The second reason for transparency is political. Many central banks around the world have been released into independence by the government in recent years. Independence in a democratic system obliges us to be accountable to society. This is to avoid arbitrariness. Accountability has thus become the counterpart to independence. Accountability can only be credibly presented by a central bank if the matter on which information must be provided is sufficiently transparent. Until a few years ago, the independence of the central bank was the exception rather than the rule. Monetary policy in most states was either conducted directly by the government or dictated to the central bank by the government. So the government has always stood between the central bank and the public. This made it unnecessary also the central bank's duty of accountability and transparency. However, a central bank's dependence on the government and thus on day-to-day political events has not proved successful. The reason for this is that the target horizon of day-to-day policy is much shorter than the target horizon of a monetary policy based on price stability. Short-term political influence is not compatible with the long-term objective of price stability. In addition, in the 70s and 80s, it became clear that inflationary monetary policy could not reduce unemployment in the long term and increase economic growth in the long term. On the contrary, high inflation rates cause many economic costs and should therefore be avoided. These theoretical and empirical insights have led to the fact that many central banks worldwide have been granted independence over the past ten to twenty years. Independence increases the credibility of a central bank and leads to a better achievement of the objective of price stability. In Switzerland, the independence of the SNB is enshrined in the Federal Constitution (Article 99(2) of the Federal Constitution). This means that it must be observed as a constitutional principle of legislation and government. Being accountable means explaining one's own approach and taking responsibility for it. An important element in this is the provision of the necessary information. Without insight into the strategy and implementation of monetary policy, the actions of the central bank are incomprehensible to the public. As a result, accountability cannot be effectively accounted for. If no accountability is made, the central bank endangers its credibility and independence. Transparency therefore also serves as a means of maintaining independence. The Swiss National Bank has always been accountable to the public in the form of an annual report and was one of the first central banks to regularly inform about its monetary policy intentions at media conferences. Accountability to the Confederation takes place in discussions with the Federal Council and in presentations to parliamentary commissions. In the new National Bank Act, periodic hearings with the competent committees of the Federal Assembly are to be explicitly anchored. What does transparency involve? To which areas should transparency in monetary policy extend in concrete terms? I said at the beginning that transparency should cover two areas: the objective of monetary policy and the methods by which this objective is to be achieved. What are the objectives and methods of the National Bank, and how do we try to make these goals and methods transparent? Transparency regarding the objectives According to Article 99 of the Federal Constitution, the SNB is to conduct a monetary policy that serves the overall interest of the country. The draft for a new National Bank Act contains an explicit objective for monetary policy: "It (the SNB) ensures price stability. In doing so, it takes into account economic developments." The SNB's long-term objective is therefore price stability. Provided that this objective is not jeopardised, the SNB takes the economy into account. There is no fundamental contradiction between these two elements, the long-term objective of price stability and the consideration of the economy. On the contrary, monetary policy measures to safeguard price stability have a dampening effect on economic movements in the medium term. If, for example, the economy is in recession, this leads to a decrease in inflationary pressures, which allows a more expansionary monetary policy with lower interest rates and promotes economic activity. A certain problem, however, is that monetary policy only has a delayed effect on the economy. In addition, monetary policy has a faster effect on economic growth than on inflation. It affects economic growth after just a few months or a few quarters, but only affects inflation after several quarters or even years. This delay in impact makes it difficult to dampen economic fluctuations, as even a central bank does not have perfect foresight of future economic development. Monetary policy fine-tuning, i.e. the attempt to completely smooth out the economy, therefore always runs the risk of misjudging the situation and, in the end, of increasing economic fluctuations instead of smoothing them out. The global monetary policy experience with such fine-tuning urges us to be cautious and humble. The SNB can only make large and longer-term deviations from the Taking balance into account, short-term fine-tuning by means of monetary policy activism does not make sense. "Price stability" is a relatively broad term. Quantification goes a long way towards increasing transparency. That is why we have explicitly stated in our concept what we mean by price stability: an inflation rate, measured by the national consumer price index, of less than 2% per year. Incidentally, this description also coincides with the European Central Bank's definition of price stability. The quantification of price stability is not a matter of course: the US central banking system, the Federal Reserve System, has no quantitative definition of price stability. However, it is also discussed from time to time in the USA whether such a clarification would not be beneficial. In my opinion, clarifying the concept of price stability makes a major contribution to transparency. In the long term, this quantification reduces a great deal of uncertainty, namely the uncertainty about the real, i.e. purchasing power-adjusted value of nominal amounts of money in the future. This makes it possible to enter into long-term contracts without bearing the risk that the sums to which the contracts are denominated will have a completely different real value in the future than was envisaged when the contract was concluded. This argument may sound a bit far-fetched, but I can assure you that it is very important in reality. Let me explain this by means of a savings insurance or a pension insurance. Such insurances are basically contracts for nominal values (i.e. apart from surplus shares). They pay premiums and receive a fixed sum much later at their retirement date or as a pension. If one can now assume that inflation will always be in the range of O to 2 percent by then, this already severely limits the possible range of the real purchasing power-adjusted value of the payout. You can therefore be relatively sure that the payment of the insurance still has a certain value at the time of retirement. Taking out a mortgage is a similar case. Again, you enter into a long-term contract with the bank for the repayment of a nominal amount. The certainty about the future price development promotes in the context of the mentioned examples, but also in general, the long-term propensity to save. As a result, more can be invested, which in turn promotes economic growth in the long term. A quantitative definition of price stability is very important from this long-term perspective. The SNB's objective is therefore price stability. In addition to the influence on prices, monetary policy also has an influence on other variables in the short term, in particular, of course, the exchange rate. We are often confronted with the demand to give greater weight to the exchange rate and, so to speak, to include it as a second variable in the catalogue of objectives alongside price stability. This overlooks the fact that monetary policy, with the one instrument it has at its disposal, namely interest rate management, cannot pursue different objectives, but only precisely one goal. The exchange rate (in the long term one would have to speak of the real exchange rate) is an endogenously determined quantity, which cannot be permanently influenced by a central bank, in contrast to the price level. The ultimate goal of a central bank cannot therefore be the real exchange rate - or competitiveness. Such an objective would not be credible. However, this does not mean that the exchange rate is not included in the SNB's assessment. The exchange rate exerts a strong influence on the inflation rate, firstly through the prices of imported goods, which directly influence the inflation rate, and secondly through the development of exports, which influence the inflation rate through domestic economic activity. If, for example, the value of the Swiss franc rises, this leads to a reduction in the price of imported goods. In addition, exports are weakening, leading to reduced domestic economic activity and thus also to lower price pressure. These two inflation-dampening effects allow the SNB to make its policy more expansionary after a strengthening of the Swiss franc, which will lead to a calming of the situation and to less restrictive framework conditions. The trend towards the appreciation of the Swiss franc creates adjustment problems for our export industry. However, it is not primarily the long-term appreciation of the Swiss franc that is causing problems for the export industry, but the temporarily high volatility of the exchange rate, i.e. the appreciation surges within a short period of time, as we experienced in the mid-90s or to a somewhat lesser extent last autumn. We view such rapid movements of the Swiss franc with great concern and are also prepared to respond with the necessary interest rate decisions. I would like to remind you that, following the events of 11 September last year, the SNB lowered its target range for the three-month interest rate by a whole percentage point within a few days and by another half a percentage point in December. This response was not a departure from our objective of maintaining price stability. It was particularly appropriate because the appreciation of the Swiss franc would have led to the expected inflation pressure had weakened sharply. Any other behaviour would have been incompatible with our announced strategy. It would have raised doubts about our motives and worried the markets. Transparency forces coherence, which has a stabilizing effect. Transparency regarding the methods In addition to the objectives of monetary policy, the concept and methods for implementation, as I mentioned, should also be made as transparent as possible. The monetary policy concept is nothing more than a plan or a program to achieve the objectives of monetary policy. Which monetary policy concepts are even possible? A very simple concept would be, for example, the pegging of the exchange rate to a reserve currency. Another similar concept is a currency board, i.e. a peg to an anchor currency and the one hundred percent coverage of the circulating money supply by assets denominated in the anchor currency. These two concepts are simple and transparent. In a system of flexible exchange rates, monetary policy concepts become more complicated and transparency is no longer automatically ensured. One concept that has been implemented under these circumstances is money supply control. It was applied by the National Bank from 1974 to 1999. The SNB took advantage of the fact that for a long time money supply and price developments were closely correlated. A growth target for the central bank money supply was used to stabilise price developments. In the course of the 90s, however, the correlation between the money supply and the development of prices declined. Difficulties in achieving monetary growth targets undermined the credibility of this concept and, ultimately, its transparency. A correction became necessary. Today, the SNB's monetary policy concept is based on three elements. Every element contributes to the transparency of our actions:  The first element is the above-mentioned definition of price stability.  The second element is to base monetary policy decisions, i.e. interest rate decisions, on a medium-term inflation forecast. This opens up a wide field of transparency. The SNB uses a variety of models and indicators to map the Swiss economy and forecast future economic events. Information about the models used is advantageous because it allows the markets to evaluate the possible actions and To better anticipate the SNB's reactions. In the area of the methods used, the SNB strives for maximum transparency. It currently publishes in its quarterly bulletins a whole series of articles on the models used to forecast inflation. The inflation forecast not only serves to support interest rate decisions, but is also published semi-annually and serves as a concentrated summary of the SNB's assessment of the current situation. It is supplemented by a quarterly report explaining monetary policy decisions. Another important source through which the SNB can convey its view of things to the markets is public appearances and interviews in the media.  The third element of the monetary policy approach is the target range for the chosen reference rate, the three-month Libor (London interbank offered rate). This target range is one percentage point wide. At last week's monetary policy assessment, it was decided to leave the target range unchanged. It has thus been at 1.25% - 2.25% since December. Shifts in this target range each express a change in monetary policy. The SNB controls the three-month interest rate through repo transactions, which it concludes with the banks. It can lower the three-month interest rate by providing banks with more liquidity through repo transactions, or it can cause interest rates to rise through a shortage of liquidity or an increase in repo rates. Thanks to the introduction of repo business, the implementation of our policy has become much more transparent for the markets. Are there limits to transparency? Now, as announced, some critical considerations on the subject of transparency. One of the SNB's tasks is to implement its monetary policy as efficiently as possible. As we have seen, transparency can greatly help with this. The goal, however, is and remains the effective implementation of monetary policy and not transparency per se. There are now also areas where transparency is not necessary or even disadvantageous. This includes, for example, the details of the decision-making process for interest rate adjustments. Normally, we decide on possible interest rate adjustments four times a year on our assessments of the situation. The last assessment of the situation took place a few days ago, on 21 March. As is customary in these assessments, the first summarized the current economic situation. The monetary policy alternatives were then discussed. Subsequently, the Board of Directors, consisting of three persons, decided whether an interest rate adjustment was necessary or not. The decision was subsequently published and justified in a press release. However, we refrained from publishing detailed minutes of the meeting. The public is thus deprived of which members of the Board of Directors have supported which policies with which arguments. A first reason for this approach is that it is very difficult to correctly reproduce the various opinions and various arguments by means of a protocol. A protocol cannot claim to be exhaustive. The danger would be great that this would generate more misunderstandings and uncertainties than would be avoided. "Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler." This sentence by Albert Einstein aptly summarizes my argument. Better not to communicate something at all than to simplify it too much through the constraints of communication and therefore to falsify it. A second and, in my opinion, more important reason for not publishing detailed minutes of meetings and votes is the danger that public pressure could negatively affect today's very open and honest opinion-forming process. Interest rate decisions are usually made by consensus. However, this does not mean that dissenting opinions are not expressed at the beginning of the discussions, which are usually abandoned during the discussion in favor of the consensus decision. A publication of verbatim protocols could distort this opinion-forming process in various ways. Due to the knowledge of latent surveillance of the public, unpleasant or dissenting points of view could not be expressed in the first place. The person who wants to express such an opinion would have to fear coming under pressure from outside. On the other hand, permanent public surveillance could encourage populism and provide an incentive to adopt pleasing attitudes. This would have fatal consequences for monetary policy. The art of monetary policy also lies in recognizing turning points in the development of inflation and the economy at an early stage and reacting accordingly. However, such turning points are often difficult or delayed for the general public to perceive. It is precisely in such phases that the unhindered and open exchange of views within the Executive Board is important. Only it ultimately enables monetary policy decisions of high Quality. Permanent monitoring on the basis of the publication of minutes of meetings and votes would not be conducive to this open exchange of views. End Because central banks exert a strong influence on the financial markets, they have increasingly come into the public eye. That is why the call for more transparency has become loud in recent years. Another reason for more transparency is the increasing recognition that transparency strongly promotes the effect of monetary policy and is therefore also desirable from a monetary policy point of view. Finally, independence is also indispensably linked to a duty of accountability towards society. This calculation storage also requires transparency. Many points therefore speak in favour of an open attitude. For all these reasons, it was also important to us to further improve transparency when our new monetary policy approach was introduced two years ago. The influence of central banks on interest rates and thus on the prices of fixed assets is very large today. Even seemingly meaningless remarks by central bank representatives can create, destroy or redistribute value between debtors and creditors within seconds. As a result, central banks are increasingly exposed to the crossfire of criticism from various stakeholder groups. However, silence is not an alternative. A central bank functioning according to the principle of a "black box" would very soon fall into an explanatory emergency and thus lose its democratic legitimacy and credibility. Attack is the best defense, or in other words, an independent central bank can only legitimize itself today by going public, creating transparency and fulfilling its accountability. Transparency is the best protection against attacks on the independence of a central bank.

Andererseits knnte eine permanente berwachung durch die ffentlichkeit zum Populismus ermuntern und den Anreiz geben, wohlgefllige Haltungen zu vertreten. Dies htte fatale Folgen fr die Geldpolitik. Die Kunst der Geldpolitik liegt nmlich auch darin, Wendepunkte in der Entwicklung der Inflation und der Konjunktur frhzeitig zu erkennen und entsprechend zu reagieren. Oft sind solche Wendepunkte fr die breite ffentlichkeit jedoch nur schwer oder mit Versptung wahrzunehmen. Gerade in solchen Phasen ist der ungehinderte und offene Meinungsaustausch innerhalb des Direktoriums wichtig. Nur er ermglicht letztlich geldpolitische Entscheidungen von hoher Qualitt. Eine permanente berwachung aufgrund einer Publikation von Sitzungs- und Abstimmungsprotokollen wre diesem offenen Meinungsaustausch nicht zutrglich. Schluss Weil die Notenbanken einen starken Einfluss auf die Finanzmrkte ausben, sind sie immer mehr in den Blickpunkt der ffentlichkeit gerckt. Deshalb ist in den letzten Jahren der Ruf nach mehr Transparenz laut geworden. Ein weiterer Grund fr mehr Transparenz ist die zunehmende Einsicht, dass Transparenz die Wirkung der Geldpolitik stark frdert und deshalb auch aus geldpolitischer Sicht erstrebenswert ist. Schliesslich ist Unabhngigkeit auch unabdingbar mit einer Rechenschaflspflicht gegenber der Gesellschaft verbunden. Diese Rechenschaflsablage erfordert ebenfalls Transparenz. Viele Punkte sprechen also fr eine offene Haltung. Aus all diesen Grnden war es uns auch ein Anliegen, bei der Einfhrung unseres neuen geldpolitischen Konzepts vor zwei Jahren die Transparenz weiter zu verbessern. Der Einfluss der Notenbanken auf die Zinsen und damit die Preise von Anlagegtern ist heute sehr gross. Bereits scheinbar nichtssagende Bemerkungen von Notenbankvertretern knnen innerhalb von Sekunden Werte schaffen, vernichten oder zwischen Schuldnern und Glubigern umverteilen. Dadurch sind die Notenbanken auch immer strker dem Kreuzfeuer der Kritik verschiedener Anspruchsgruppen ausgesetzt. Schweigen ist jedoch keine Alternative. Eine nach dem Prinzip einer black box funktionierende Notenbank wrde schon sehr bald in Erklrungsnotstand geraten und dadurch ihre demokratische Legitimation und Glaubwrdigkeit verlieren. Angriff ist die beste Verteidigung, oder in anderen Worten: eine unabhngige Notenbank kann sich heutzutage nur noch legitimieren, indem sie an die ffentlichkeit tritt, Transparenz schafft und ihrer Rechenschaftspflicht nachkommt. Transparenz ist der beste Schutz vor Angriffen gegen die Unabhngigkeit einer Notenbank.

Title: What can the National Bank do for the economy?
text: What can the Swiss National Bank do for the economy? Presentation by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Zurcher Volkswirtschaftliche Gesellschaft Zurich Wednesday, April 10, 2002 Introduction Dear Sir or Madam, I am very pleased to be able to address the Zurich Economic Society today. I would like to take this opportunity to discuss various aspects of Swiss monetary policy under the title "What can the Swiss National Bank do for the economy?". The question of what a central bank can do for the economy is not new. It is certainly not answered equally by all people. Differences in personal interests play just as much a role as different ideas about economic contexts. In addition, we see again and again how public opinion can change over the years. In times of high inflation, a central bank usually has broad support for the task of restoring price stability. However, if inflation is low and no acute risk of inflation can be identified, many quickly ask themselves whether central banks can do more for the economy than simply maintain price stability. The question of what the SNB can do for the economy thus largely resembles the question of the possibilities and limits of monetary policy. I would like to start with some basic insights about monetary policy, on which there is broad agreement. I will then go into why the SNB has always avoided giving priority to the exchange rate over the last thirty years- with the exception of a short period of time in 1978/79. Finally, I would like to explain our monetary policy concept and the role that the exchange rate plays in it, and make a few comments on the current economic situation. 1. Why do central banks prioritise price stability? Inflation and deflation are monetary phenomena  this is a principle that is hardly controversial. Inflation and deflation can thus in principle be prevented if the central banks conduct an appropriate monetary policy. The empirical evidence for this principle is overwhelming, regardless of whether we are looking at different countries or different eras. In Switzerland, we have not had any significant inflation in recent years. But the period with high inflation rates is not so far back. From the beginning of the seventies to the beginning of the nineties we experienced three inflation cycles. A massive increase in money supply growth was followed by a significant increase in inflation in each of these cycles. Although the monetary expansion took place for different reasons, the effects on prices, which can be observed after two to three years, remained similar. At the peak of the first cycle in December 1973, the annual inflation rate was almost 12 percent, at the peak of the second in September 1981 7 1/2 percent and at the peak of the third in June 1991 a good 6 1/2 percent. Inflation declined in all three cases after monetary expansion had been slowed down. But each time, the economic structures distorted by inflation had to be cleaned up with high social costs. There is also a great deal of agreement - and this brings me to the second fundamental insight - that no lasting gains in production or employment can be achieved with an expansionary monetary policy. That inflation is a welcome lubricant for the economy and thus enables higher long-term economic growth is now clearly refuted. While an expansionary monetary policy will usually initially stimulate output and employment, these effects are fleeting. What remains in the long term is only inflation and its negative impact on the economy. These negative effects have often been described. However, they are sometimes difficult to quantify. In recent years, however, studies for various countries have shown that even moderate inflation rates cause considerable economic costs due to the lack of indexation of tax systems. The consideration that inflation is costly and that monetary policy can only influence price developments in the long term, but not economic growth, gives rise to the priority of the objective of price stability. If a central bank succeeds in maintaining price stability, it has already achieved a great deal for the economy. A stable monetary framework allows firms and households to make their decisions on a more reliable basis, to anchor their inflation expectations. It is then up to them to make the most of it. However, price stability as a priority objective does not mean that economic developments do not play a role. As a rule, the economy precedes price developments. In addition, monetary impulses have a significant impact on production and employment - even if this is only temporary. Central banks are therefore paying close attention to economic developments, and they are also reacting to them. Does the Inflation, for example, from the target value, they often refrain from bringing it back into the realm of price stability immediately and at any economic price. The wording of the central bank mandate proposed in the context of the total revision of the National Bank Act reflects this view well. "The SNB guarantees price stability," says the first sentence. And immediately afterwards: "In doing so, it takes into account the economic development". A word on the definition of price stability. With the general decline in inflation rates, a relatively precise definition of price stability has become more urgent for many central banks. We, too, have met this need. Today, we define price stability as inflation of less than 2% as measured by the national consumer price index. With this definition, which corresponds to that of the ECB, we want to express two things:  First, we do not aim at a specific path of price level. High inflation rates do not have to be compensated for in the following years. What is over is over. It is enough that the annual inflation rate is returned to the range of 0-2%. I acknowledge that this is a weaker form of price stability compared to a definition based on the path of the price level. The reason for our choice is essentially that we believe that it will result in lower fluctuations in production and employment.  Second, we do not equate price stability with zero inflation. The positive increase in the target can be explained above all by the fact that the consumer price index slightly overestimates the true inflation due to quality improvements in the products of the shopping basket. 2. Can the SNB do more for the economy? Can the central bank really do no more for the economy than provide it with a stable monetary framework? We will, you can imagine, be confronted with this question again and again. Because price stability prevails today, there is hope that there will be room for further goals. In our country, the exchange rate is always at the centre of discussion in this context. Exchange rate fluctuations, but also the long-term appreciation of the Swiss franc, are contributing to this. Moreover, since Swiss economic policy has hardly any instruments that can be used quickly and effectively in periods of weak economic activity. Exchange rate manipulation is repeatedly advocated by some commentators as a quick fix for the problems of the Swiss economy. I will go into more detail later on the role of the exchange rate in the SNB's concept. In order to avoid misunderstandings, however, I would like to emphasise here that we attach great importance to the exchange rate in our monetary policy assessment and thus also react to the exchange rate. At this point, therefore, the only question is why the SNB is not doing everything in its power to weaken the Swiss franc in the event of an economic downturn. The SNB's position becomes understandable when we consider what the exchange rate is: the exchange rate is a market price that reflects expectations about the future actions of central banks. With regard to the Swiss franc exchange rate of the euro, for example, there are expectations about the monetary policy stance of the SNB and the ECB. We cannot influence what the market expects with regard to monetary policy in the euro area. If we want to have a lasting impact on the nominal exchange rate, we must therefore start with the market's expectations about our own monetary policy stance. However, this is a risky undertaking, as these expectations about the SNB's future monetary policy stance will be strongly influenced by our goal of keeping consumer inflation below 2%. So if we want to lower the Swiss franc exchange rate, we must ultimately abandon our priority objective of maintaining price stability. In other words, we need to move to an expansionary monetary policy that raises inflation expectations. The stakes are high. And it should therefore come as no surprise that since the collapse of the Bretton Woods fixed rate system in 1973, we have resorted to the means of an uncompromising exchange rate policy only once, under extraordinary conditions in the autumn of 1978. The close relationship between the monetary policy stance, the corresponding market expectations and the exchange rate makes it clear that a purely verbal downplaying of the exchange rate, which many business circles repeatedly expect from us, can rarely achieve success even in the short term. And a sustained influence on the nominal exchange rate requires a credible change of monetary policy. After all, the markets don't want facts! Part of the discussion about the exchange rate is less about the level of the Swiss franc exchange rate than about its fluctuations. Therefore, the next question is whether it would make sense to fix the exchange rate permanently. This is a well-known issue and the arguments have been exchanged many times. Therefore, here only briefly. The main advantage of a fixed nominal exchange rate is often seen in the fact that it can also reduce the volatility of the real exchange rate, i.e. adjusted for the different inflation rate between countries. This connection is empirically well confirmed, but of course not true in every case. The fact that the differences can be relatively small is shown, for example, by a comparison between Switzerland and the Netherlands since the beginning of 1999, the date of the introduction of the euro. From January 1999 to January 2002, the Swiss franc rose by 5% in real terms against the euro. Over the same period, consumer prices in the Netherlands rose by 4.5% more than in the euro area as a whole. The situation of Swiss and Dutch exporters vis-a-vis their competitors in the euro area has therefore developed quite similarly since the beginning of 1999, although Switzerland has a flexible nominal exchange rate, while the Netherlands is integrated into the euro area. Fixed exchange rates and stable competitiveness do not necessarily go hand in hand! Another point to consider in the context of fixed exchange rates is the problem of speculative attacks. Through the experience of the nineties, exchange rates that are fixed in principle but can be adjusted by discretionary parity changes have been widely discredited. As a result, the choice has essentially been reduced to two options: either flexible exchange rates or a fixed peg as can be achieved by a currency board or even better by a monetary union. These conclusions are based on the experience of countries, some of which differ significantly from Switzerland. However, they are of particular importance to us, as the Swiss franc is an international currency. If one can still be divided on the risk of speculative attacks, this is hardly true of the effects of fixed exchange rates on interest rates. If the SNB were to stabilise the nominal exchange rate, the Swiss interest rate level would have to align with that of the foreign exchange rate. Monetary policy would no longer be conducted in Zurich, but in Frankfurt. The SNB would no longer be able to set interest rates in the way that is appropriate in view of the economic and inflation developments in Switzerland. An alignment of the Swiss interest rate level with that of the foreign one would result from the fact that the exchange rate risk is smaller under fixed exchange rates and, in extreme cases, a completely credible exchange rate peg is completely eliminated. Any remaining interest rate differentials mainly reflect debtor risk or political risks. As the alignment of the yields of the government bonds of the euro countries impressively demonstrates, this factor is not very important. The interest rate differential would disappear with a credible fixation over the entire maturity spectrum. This would have consequences for Switzerland, especially with regard to long-term interest rates. For years, Switzerland's long-term interest rates have practically always been significantly lower than foreign ones.
