Certes, un taux de change fixe nous garantirait la stabilite, en termes nominaux, de la valeur exterieure du franc mais ii ne renforcerait pas pour autant la competitivite de nos exportations. Pour s'en convaincre, comparons !'evolution, ces dernieres annees, de notre competitivite avec celle des Pays-Bas, un pays semblable au notre qui est integre dans la zone euro depuis sa creation, le 1er janvier 1999. Depuis cette date, l'indice neerlandais des prix a augmente de 11,5%, une progression qui depasse de 4,4 points !'inflation moyenne dans la zone euro. Les exportateurs neerlandais ant ainsi vu leur competitivite face a leurs concurrents europeens s'effriter dans une mesure comparable a ce qu'ont connu nos propres exportateurs. Cela nous montre que la fixite de la valeur exterieure d'une monnaie n'est pas la veritable reponse aux problemes de competitivite. Deux pays aux structures economiques proches, aux progres paralleles en matiere de productivite voient leur taux de change reel -done leur degre de competitivite -evoluer en parallele, quel que soit leur regime de change. Un taux de change fixe ne garantit pas la competitivite sur la duree. N'oublions pas non plus qu'un accrochage du franc a l'euro -du fait de la disparition du risque de change -entrainerait egalement une hausse generale des taux d'interet dans notre pays. En arrimant le franc a l'euro, nous perdrions notre double avantage de prix stables et de taux d'interet bas, sans cependant beaucoup gagner en contrepartie. Tout bien pese, je suis convaincu que la voie delicate de cohabitation que nous suivons comporte finalement pour l'economie suisse plus d'avantages que d'inconvenients. Cela dit, la Banque nationale reste tres preoccupee par !'evolution du franc, en particulier par les mouvements de la relation entre le franc et l'euro etant donne l'etroitesse de nos relations commerciales avec la zone euro. Nous integrons le cours du franc dans nos appreciations periodiques de la situation et savons reagir lorsqu'un developpement defavorable sur le marche des changes vient fausser le degre de rigueur de notre politique monetaire. L'apparition des billets et pieces en euros Je ne puis quitter le chapitre de l'euro sans evoquer la recente mise en circulation des billets et pieces en euros. Bien que l'euro soit une realite avec laquelle nous vivons depuis plus de trois ans, son introduction fiduciaire a marque l'etape la plus spectaculaire du long processus d'integration monetaire europeenne. Nous avons ete heureux de constater que cette phase a connu un franc succes, sans le moindre incident notable. II n'empeche que, pour notre pays, la donne est desormais nouvelle. La Suisse et la Principaute de Liechtenstein sont totalement entourees par les pays de l'Union monetaire, telle une ile dans l'euro-ocean. La monnaie unique apportera des avantages indeniables a nos concitoyens et a nos entreprises. lls beneficieront des memes retombees positives que leurs voisins dans leurs transactions avec les residents de la zone euro, a savoir une simplicite et une transparence accrues, une reduction des frais de change et une incertitude mains forte. En meme temps, ils continueront a profiter des atouts du franc suisse et des avantages d'une politique monetaire independante: la stabilite des prix, des taux d'interet tres bas en comparaison internationale et une politique monetaire taillee sur mesure et adaptee aux besoins specifiques de la Suisse. L'euro est-ii en passe de devenir une monnaie parallele en Suisse? L'euro va-t-il circuler en Suisse? La reponse acette derniere question doit etre prudente. II est vrai que l'euro a ete accepte des le premier jour, en particulier dans les regions frontalieres et touristiques, tout comme le franc franc;ais ou le mark allemand l'etaient l'annee derniere encore, et tout comme le dollar americain continue al'etre. Mais ii ne taut pas se faire d'illusions. Nos commerc;ants rendent la monnaie en francs suisses et le taux de conversion qu'ils appliquent est generalement plus defavorable que le taux bancaire. A chacun son metier, on ne s'improvise pas cambiste. Le visiteur etranger continuera done a avoir tout interet a utiliser sa carte de credit ou a se procurer des francs suisses aupres d'une banque ou d'un bureau de change. La masse des euros circulant en Suisse pourrait fort bien finir par depasser la somme des francs franc;ais, marks et autres lires qui etaient utilises dans notre pays, mais cela restera un phenomene marginal aussi longtemps que nos impots, nos salaires, nos layers ou nos cotisations d'assurance seront factures ou payes en francs suisses. L'attrait d'une monnaie en tant que moyen de paiement tient au fait qu'elle est acceptee par chacun. Une seconde monnaie n'apporte rien de plus, si ce n'est une complication inutile. L'histoire demontre que seules les monnaies dent le pouvoir d'achat etait en perdition ant ete detronees par des concurrents etrangers. Nous ne craignons rien sur ce plan, nos performances en matiere de stabilite sent aussi bonnes -voire meilleures -que celles des pays voisins. A man avis, ceux qui prevoient que l'euro supplantera prochainement le franc comme moyen de paiement sur notre territoire se trompent lourdement. La reforme de la loi sur la Banque nationale En janvier dernier, le Conseil federal a adopte les grandes lignes de la revision de la lei sur la Banque nationale. Ces prochains mois, ii sera saisi d'un projet de lei et de message. Ces textes seront soumis aux Chambres federales probablement en automne. Dans son etat actuel, le projet correspond a ce que je vous avais presente l'an dernier. II precise le mandat de la Banque et definit son obligation de rendre compte. Le cercle de nos operations est elargi, ainsi que notre responsabilite dans la surveillance des systemes de paiement et de reglement. Une collaboration etroite avec la Commission federale des banques sera instituee dans ce domaine. La reforme de nos organes conduira a un redimensionnement du Conseil de banque, qui ne comptera plus que 11 membres. La Direction generale restera chargee de la conduite de la politique monetaire, alors que le Conseil de banque assurera la surveillance generale et arretera en particulier la politique en matiere de constitution de provisions. Le projet de lei comporte egalement une mise ajour des dispositions relevant du droit de la societe anonyme. II est prevu que la BNS garde son statut de societe anonyme cotee en bourse. La forme juridique de la societe anonyme contribue a notre autonomie financiere et cree les meilleures bases institutionnelles pour la conduite d'une politique monetaire independante. Le capital-actions de la Banque, qui est actuellement de 50 millions de francs et dent la moitie est liberee, sera ramene a 25 millions de francs selon le projet de lei. Les actionnaires n'auront ainsi plus !'obligation de liberer le non-verse en cas de necessite. Un capital de 25 millions peut paraitre modeste en regard de la somme de notre bilan. Le desequilibre n'est toutefois qu'apparent car notre capital ne constitue en aucune maniere une garantie couvrant nos engagements. La reduction du capital sera realisee par un abaissement a 250 francs de la valeur nominale des actions. Le dividende maximal restera fixe a 6%. Entin, je puis rassurer ceux d'entre vous qui craignent une limitation du cercle des actionnaires. A l'avenir egalement, les actions de la Banque nationale pourront etre detenues par des collectivites publiques, ainsi que par des personnes morales et physiques. Seule la Confederation demeurera exclue de notre capital. II ne fait pas de doute que la presence des actionnaires prives est un gage supplementaire de notre autonomie institutionnelle. Si le Parlement approuve les grandes lignes du projet, ce que j'espere, la Banque nationale disposera d'une lei moderne, adaptee aux realites du moment, qui lui permettra de remplir sa mission dans les meilleures conditions. La distribution des benefices de la Banque Permettez-moi, avant de conclure, de revenir brievement sur un sujet qui a fait couler beaucoup d'encre et que le President du Conseil a deja aborde dans son expose: je veux parler dela distribution de nos benefices. La Banque nationale est-elle devenue un moyen commode d'accroitre les ressources financieres des collectivites publiques? Je vous rappelle que la distribution de nos benefices est clairement reglee par la lei. Apres !'attribution au fonds de reserve, le paiement du dividende et le versement de l'indemnite par tete en faveur des cantons, le surplus de benefices est distribue a raison d'un tiers a la Confederation et de deux tiers aux cantons. La lei actuelle ne definit pas les conditions dans lesquelles le benefice est determine. La Constitution federale precise cependant a son article 99 que la BNS doit constituer, a partir de ses revenus, des reserves monetaires suffisantes. Depuis plusieurs annees, nous appliquons ce principe sur la base d'une convention passee avec la Confederation. La convention actuelle arrivera ason terme le 31 decembre prochain. Une nouvelle convention, vous le savez, prevoit que le surplus verse a la Confederation et aux cantons passera a2,5 milliards de francs pendant 11 ans. Nombreux sont ceux qui ant pense que la Banque nationale avait cede a des pressions politiques et qu'elle avait ainsi perdu une partie de son autonomie. lls se trompent. Le chiffre de 2,5 milliards de francs n'est pas le resultat d'un marchandage entre la Banque nationale et !'Administration federale, mais un montant calcule en partant de la profitabilite attendue de notre institut et de la distribution graduelle des 13 milliards de francs de provisions excedentaires qui figurent actuellement dans notre bilan. Cette distribution accrue est exceptionnelle, et chacun doit en etre bien conscient. II appartient a la Confederation et aux cantons d'en faire un usage prudent, afin de ne pas etre confrontes a des difficultes de tresorerie lorsque la normalisation interviendra. En bonne logique financiere, des allocations temporaires ne devraient pas conduire a une augmentation des charges permanentes de l'Etat. Sur le plan monetaire, je puis vous assurer que la distribution accrue de benefices ne pose pas de probleme particulier: nous resterons en mesure de gerer les liquidites du marche et de controler les taux d'interet acourt terme. II n'y aura pas d'interference negative entre la politique monetaire et la distribution des benefices. Conclusion L'annee 2001 a ete riche en evenements. L'action de la Banque nationale a vise a defendre les interets generaux du pays, aassurer la stabilite des prix en tenant compte de la conjoncture economique. L'economie suisse a vu sa croissance flechir, les attentats de septembre dernier ant cree beaucoup d'inquietudes et d'incertitudes. En abaissant quatre fois les taux d'interet, nous avons fortement assoupli notre politique monetaire. L'horizon semble se degager maintenant: les perspectives sont au rechauffement progressif de l'activite economique, a l'etranger comme chez nous. Sauf turbulences imprevues du cote des changes, nous pouvons esperer que la croissance retrouvera en fin d'annee un rythme proche de son potentiel. Les conditions monetaires sont favorables acet egard, et la stabilite des prix est assuree. Pour remplir son mandat, la Banque nationale a pu compter sur !'engagement des autorites de Banque, sur le devouement de son personnel et sur votre soutien attentif. Que chacun en soit ici remercie.

Title: Swiss capital market: current topics
text: SWISS CAPITAL MARKET: CURRENT TOPICS Prof. Dr. Niklaus Blattner Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank 71st Annual General Meeting of Pfandbriefbank St. Gallen, 15 May 2002 2 1. Swiss capital market: facts in a snapshot Viewed in a snapshot, there is hardly anything to complain about in the International Financial Centre Switzerland and its capital market. The banks, i.e. the most important service providers for the international mediation between saving and investing, present themselves in an excellent international state. Their competitiveness is largely intact and the banking system as a whole has the necessary resources to address the structural challenges ahead. Although the Swiss capital market has lost some of its luster over the years, it remains attractive. This is not least due to the fact that an above-average proportion (around 30%) of global assets held abroad are managed in Switzerland. The banks in Switzerland thus have a unique customer base. However, Switzerland's attractiveness is by no means only on the investor side, but also on the side of the debtors. In addition to the professionalism of investment banking, the traditionally low CHF interest rates, i.e. the interest bonus, also play a role for the debtors. The total outstanding CHF bonds exceeds the gross domestic product (GDP). The public sector claims less than a fifth of this. The remainder is divided between banks, financial companies and Pfandbrief institutions (around 40%) on the one hand and foreign debtors, i.e. foreign banks and companies (around 45%) on the other. The replacement of foreign exchange swaps by repos as the SNB's central monetary policy instrument has not only increased the effectiveness of monetary policy, but has also made a significant contribution to the fact that the formerly rather modest Swiss money market has developed significantly. The Swiss stock exchange SWX ranks 10th in the ranking of share turnover. The market capitalization of the Swiss Performance Index (SPI) is more than double the GDP. SWX is highly internationalized. virt-x, a joint venture between SWX and Tradepoint, based in London, is 3 one of the most modern and secure securities trading systems, is based on a platform developed by SWX and handles, among other things, the trading of all Swiss blue-chip stocks. A respectable market for warrants, i.e. for non-standardised, securitised options, is also settled via a SWX platform. In addition, all standardized derivatives are traded via Eurex. The latter emerged from a merger of the Swiss SOFFEX with the Deutsche Terminborse DTB. Finally, the Swiss foreign exchange market should be mentioned. The foreign exchange volumes traded in Switzerland rank 6th in the world and are practically the same as those in Germany. Daily trading volume is around 30% of GDP, with the EUR being the second most important currency traded after the USO. It is obvious that such services are inconceivable without excellent financial market infrastructures. SWX's trading systems have already been mentioned. Swiss international bank clearing (SIC) is also decisive for the security and efficiency of payment transactions. Its architecture was developed in Switzerland with the substantial participation of the SNB and continues to meet the highest international standards. This electronic real-time grass settlement system (RTGS) is used to make an average of around 180 billion euros in payments per day. CHF. About half of this is directly or indirectly linked to the global activity of the Swiss International Financial Centre. The SIC is an essential component of the so-called straight-through processing (STP)1, which characterizes the so-called Swiss Value Chain and enables the above-average security and efficiency of clearing and settlement of securities trading via the SWX platforms in conjunction with SIC and SIS SegalnterSettle (SIS). 1 The STP refers to the electronic linking of information on holistic processes from trading to the settlement of financial transactions without manual intervention. With a single mouse click, trading (SWX), title (SIS) and monetary (SIC) settlement can be ensured without any manual intervention. 4 2. Swiss capital market: a view with a more critical lens The Swiss capital market can also be viewed with a more critical lens. The view becomes more critical, especially when it focuses on developments over longer periods of time. First of all, it is obvious to deal with the issues of bonds and shares. Looking at the development of the last ten years, i.e. from March 1992 to March 2002, little spectacular can be seen. The issues of bonds issued by domestic debtors amount to an average of around 2 billion per month. CHF to around 2.5 billion CHF. They thus followed the relatively leisurely pace of economic growth in Switzerland. By contrast, the issuance of bonds issued by foreign debtors has risen more rapidly, namely by around 1 billion. CHF to around 3.5 billion CHF per month. Equity issuance has even increased sharply over the last ten years, but remains at a comparatively modest level, despite the fact that equity capital is becoming increasingly important worldwide in financing growth and structural change under the prevailing conditions of globalization. From practically zero ten years ago, however, the share issues are still just under 1 billion. CHF per month. The longer-term comparison allows further findings: Over the period 1991-2001, bond issues denominated in CHF grew by an average of 6.7% per year. Compared to the longer period from 1960 to 1998, during which the annual average growth rate was still 14%, this is a significant slowdown. However, even over this long period of time, CHF bonds grew less strongly than the total of all bond issues worldwide, which increased by 20% per annum. Although THE CHF bonds issued by foreign debtors have grown in recent years and have thus contributed to stabilising bond issues in Switzerland, they have by no means been able to halt the international decline in the CHF share of global bond issues. After a maximum value of 20 % anno 5 In 1980, the SHARE of the CHF denomination in the total number of new issues of international bonds worldwide fell to 1% by 2001. In addition to the issues (primary market), the volumes of traded holdings of shares and bonds (secondary market) are of interest. The monthly figures for June 1993-December 2001 show the following picture. While the monthly trading volume of Swiss equities is more than 20 billion. CHF to four times, i.e. to around 80 billion. CHF, the volumes of bonds of Swiss debtors traded in Switzerland moved only slightly upwards overall, namely from around 7 billion. CHF to less than 10 billion CHF. It is interesting to note that until 1998 the volume of shares and bonds rose at a similar rate. But then the bonds lost their attractiveness, which is undoubtedly due to the particularly good economy and the boom in the stock market, which came to a temporary end in March 2001. Similarly, the trading volumes of Swiss derivatives initially followed those of Swiss equities, only to significantly and permanently detach themselves from the development of equities in late summer 1998. This process is due, among other things, to the collapse of the US hedge fund "Lang Term Capital Management" (LTCM), which not only stopped the partial upswing in derivatives in Switzerland and, as is well known, also had other consequences at the level of Swiss banks. In addition to the volumes of issues and trading, of course, the price development and yields are also of interest. The fact that the nominal yields of CHF bonds have been lowest in international comparison since 1960 to 1993 and were only then undercut by those of YEN bonds only confirms the "stylised fact" of low interest rates in Switzerland. This fact was not called into question by the introduction of the euro in January 1999. Over the past twelve months, the yield differential between the 10-year benchmark bonds in Switzerland and Germany has remained virtually unchanged at around 1.5 percentage points. This nominal interest bonus would disappear in real terms if the inflation rate in Germany had been more than 1.5 percentage points higher than in Switzerland in the same period of the previous year. This was not the case. 6 The price performance of the shares, measured by index series, shows a pronounced international correlation, although Japan is dancing out of line. Its above-average price growth came to a brutal halt after 1990 and even turned into the opposite. Overall, prices on the relevant stock exchanges, including Switzerland, have risen by 7-9% per year since 1953. This includes ten-year periods with price growth rates of 1015%. However, in August 2000 the picture changed. The stock exchanges worldwide recorded considerable losses. The events of September 11, 2001 additionally underlined the end of the recent high-altitude flight, but without a crash actually occurring. After September 11, 2001, the stock markets recovered surprisingly quickly. However, indecisiveness still prevails everywhere today, which is certainly due to the increasing political uncertainties, but also to disappointments in the so-called New Economy segment, to the delays in the economic recovery in the USA and Europe, to the persistent economic crisis in Japan, and, as a special factor, to the loss of investor confidence following the events surrounding Enron in autumn 2001. The Swiss stock exchange is also affected by all these things. During the last twelve months, however, it has proven to be comparatively resilient despite all the disappointment. Against the background of the historically enormous pace of price increases on the stock exchanges over the past decades, the question of its sustainability arises. An interesting indicator is the price-earnings ratio (P-E ratio). It measures the ratio of share price and profits and thus indirectly the rate of profit. A P-E ratio of 20 corresponds to a reciprocal rate of profit of 5%, a P-E ratio of 40 corresponds to a rate of profit of 2.5%. Given the pronounced volatility of stock market prices and the volatility of reported corporate profits, which is by no means always aligned, it is not surprising that the P-E ratio fluctuates strongly with the stock market. The indicator is therefore mainly 7 interesting on a long-term average. 2 When P-E ratios of 60 (Standard & Poors 500, Nikkei), 45 (DAX) and 30 (SPI) are measured for March 2002, the question arises as to whether or not they can last. A long-term comparison shows for Standard & Poors 500 that between 1997 and today the P-E ratio rarely exceeded the 20 threshold until the nineties, but then swung beyond that and easily rose above the 40 mark. This is tantamount to a reduction in nominal profit rates, which is accompanied by real profit rates that are below the economic growth rate. However, the growth rate of economic output potential is an interesting benchmark for assessing the real returns of all types of investments. Real returns, which - apart from risk-related deviations - are permanently much lower than the long-term economic growth rate are just as difficult to imagine as those that are significantly higher in the long term. In the case of very high P-E ratios, therefore, sooner or later there must be either a reduction in stock market valuations or an increase in corporate profits to a level that would justify the high stock market valuations. In the second half of the 90s, the P-E ratio of the SPI also began to overcome the 20 mark over long distances, also showed short-term outliers upwards, i.e. to over 70, and then fell back to below 20 in the second half of 2001. The P-E ratio of the SPI is significantly more volatile than that of the Standard & Poors 500 or the DAX. Although the stock exchanges are able to attract investors by means of rising or high prices or with high P-E ratios, they also offer them little security against valuation corrections. 2 Or the indicator is estimated based on the discounted expected profits. Only then does the actual stock market development lose influence, and the profit estimates or the assumed growth rate of profits and the discount factor dominate. 8 The problem described is accentuated by the fact that investors are currently unsettled anyway. After the bursting of the Enron bubble in the USA, which could not have arisen without the participation of the auditing company, more and more investors are asking themselves who they can still trust. Of course, after every major scandal, there is a danger of inadmissible generalization. However, investors' sensitivity to the quality of accounting, corporate governance and financial analysis has been increasing for some time. The Enron case has raised awareness of these issues. 3. Priority topics: A selection After these two perspectives, a first from a distance, which showed a favorable picture of the Swiss capital market, and a second, more critical one, which made it clear that the capital market Switzerland was already more attractive and, how could it be otherwise, is subject to the large, currently unfavorable global trends and topics in a similar way to foreign capital markets, In the following, I will deal with a number of questions in more detail. I do not claim to be complete. The Strengths Weakness Analysis of the Swiss Capital Market is not to be provided in the context of a lecture. First of all, I would like to address the issues of corporate governance, accounting and financial analysis, knowing full well that these issues do not only or primarily affect the Swiss capital market. The choice of this topic is justified by its fundamental importance for the functioning of the capital market. Next, my attention is focused on the Swiss Value Chain, whose contribution to the performance of the Swiss capital market I have already pointed out, but whose enforcement on the market is not self-evident. I then turn to the aforementioned erosion of the CHF's position as the debt currency of foreign bondholders. Then I will address the question of the refinancing of banks, which is of particular interest in this circle. Finally, I allow myself a trip to the 9 Macroeconomics, i.e. we visit the "interest island of Switzerland" together, before I finally recall the motivations that explain the SNB's commitment to the Swiss International Financial Centre. 4. Corporate governance, accounting and financial analysis in transition Observers have been criticizing for some time that the "checks and balances" of the Swiss public companies work only inadequately. The dominant presence of Swiss nationals on the boards of directors of local globally active companies is noted. From the reference to the small-scale nature of Swiss society and its tendency to the friendly Compromise, an insufficient control of the management is derived. By far, the disclosure requirements of Swiss companies would not comply with international standards. In addition to the low level of transparency, restrictions on voting rights and other barriers would also limit the influence of shareholders. In recent weeks, listed companies have published a number of aggregated management and board fees. Even the SNB has decided to do so. The fact that everyone has been discussed in the media shows how far we are still away from Anglo-Saxon self-evident things here. The large companies and those with significant foreign participations have modernized the corporate governance structures more strongly. The influence of active foreign investors as well as international competitive pressure via the capital markets are the forces driving forward the modernisation of corporate control in Switzerland as well. Efforts to increase transparency in Switzerland have recently increased significantly. Investors are demonstrably willing to pay higher prices for shares of companies with better corporate governance. Because the Swiss financial market has not been in a particularly good position in terms of corporate control so far, SWX on 17 April 2002, after approval, 10 issued by the Federal Banking Commission (SFBC) a guideline on transparency, a central prerequisite for functioning corporate governance. In particular, the SWX Directive now makes the summary disclosure of all remuneration of the Executive Board and the Board of Directors of listed companies mandatory. In addition to salary and bonus payments, options and share allocations, pension fund entitlements and board loans are also to be attributed to the remuneration. According to the will of a nationally criminal motion, it is even required by law for listed companies as well as special statutory stock corporations and federal institutions that the remuneration of the management and the compensation of the boards of directors are to be disclosed individually and not palely summarily, as in the Anglo-Saxon countries. Finally, the Federal Council has also promised a comprehensive report in which stock corporation law is to be examined under the principles of corporate governance. Here, too, the focus will be on strengthening the separation of powers within the company, on the separation of operational and strategic leadership, on the composition and independence of the Board of Directors as well as on transparency of the remuneration of the Board of Directors and management. The SWX guideline supplements and specifies the so-called "Swiss Code of Best Practice" adopted by economiesuisse at the beginning of April. economiesuisse also relies on self-regulation. The Code defines corporate governance and formulates 30 recommendations and guiding principles. The definition already makes it clear that governance is geared towards the interests of shareholders, that consequently decision-making capacity and efficiency must not be impaired, and that it concerns the principles of management, control and transparency. The fact that it is not easy to find the right balance can be seen, for example, in the independence of the boards of directors. With regard to the independence of the Board of Directors, its audit and compensation committees, as well as with regard to board memberships "across the cross", nuanced regulations are proposed, always with the aim of not throwing the baby out with the bathwater. The Code undoubtedly provides valuable guidance. For the 11 Implementation is the responsibility of the companies, i.e. the management, the boards of directors and the shareholders. Now to the topic of accounting: In the European Union (EU) from 2005 onwards, accounting according to the international ! AS standards for listed companies become mandatory. Swiss companies see themselves challenged. If they adhere to national standards, which are difficult to compare and less transparent internationally, they will become less attractive on the capital market. Not least in the banking sector, apart from a handful of the largest institutions, there is a need to catch up with regard to IAS. The conversion is time-consuming. On the one hand, IT, process adaptation and training costs are incurred. The treatment of financial instruments in accordance with IAS is complex. The method of valuation of credit risks may change and the freedom to design profits over reserves for general banking risks is restricted. The reported results are becoming more volatile. It is true that IAS will bring greater transparency and truthfulness. However, accounting is not getting any easier, which mainly raises the question of how far they want to go, especially in medium-sized banks. It should be remembered that an entity that wishes to file its invoice under IAS must do so from the outset for at least three years. The accounting system must therefore be changed as early as 2003 if the 2005 accounts are to be presented in accordance with IAS. Probably the most "palatable" topic of this section is the quality of financial analysis and the independence of analysts. For some time now, the news has referred to the investigations that Attorney General Spitzer is conducting against several of the largest investment banks in New York to determine whether their analysts have violated the interests of customers in a criminally relevant manner. Class action lawsuits, how could it be otherwise, are also pending in the USA. The background is the failure of analysts and banks, e.g. in the case of Enron, but also quite simply disappointments of investors as a result of stock market losses. The accusation is that the banks have deceived investors with embellished analyses. Special provisions and value adjustments of the banks are foreseeable. However, the effects could go further. Once again, the pros and cons of the summary 12 various services under one roof on the topic. Conflicts of interest between financial engineering, issuing and credit departments, value step trading and financial analysis do not mean the end of horizontally integrated banks, but the spin-offs, e.g. of financial analysis into separate organizational units or even into independent companies, could alleviate the problem in the future. The Swiss Bankers Association (SBA) is also currently developing recommendations to increase the independence of financial analysis. The work is still ongoing. What has become known about the content so far is within the scope of the usual. Work on these recommendations was started by the SBA at an early stage, i.e. before the current and intensified discussion. Undoubtedly, this will influence the recommendations. I await with interest the result of this additional self-regulation of the banks. 5. Swiss Value Chain under pressure The Swiss financial market infrastructure, i.e. the organisational arrangements and the Swiss systems, which are mainly information technology, are at least on a par with those of the other leading financial centres. The so-called Swiss Value Chain may probably even claim an absolute top position. The Swiss Value Chain is a prime example of constructive Swiss cooperation. The SNB or the SIC takes care of the money transactions, the stock exchange or the SWX and virt-x the value step trading and the SIS the transaction processing and the custody of value steps. The system covers all steps from order entry to trading, clearing, settlement and custody to reporting. The processes are fully automated and designed from A to Z on the so-called "straight-through processing", which minimizes the risks, the error rate is lower than elsewhere and the links to foreign infrastructures are unsurpassed in terms of speed and reliability. What SIC, SWX, virt-x, Eurex and SIS are doing for the financial centre deserves high recognition. But the sky is not cloudless. Value step trading and - 13 settlement are volume transactions. In the case of virt-x, success is not yet assured. Superficially, this is probably due to the still limited liquidity. It cannot be ruled out that the advantages of virt-x in terms of efficiency and security will not be fully exploited due to inadequate internal incentive structures in the banks. From time to time, traders seem to pay attention only to the spread rather than the total cost of the transaction (including the cost of settlement and correction of settlement errors). If these shortcomings were remedied, liquidity would also grow and spreads would fall to the required level. The problem highlighted by the virt-x example can also be seen elsewhere in the infrastructure - to varying degrees and in a modified form: SIS knows it, and the banks themselves know it in the back office area. The volumes are too low, the unit costs too high due to the investments. What to do if state-of-the-art technologies enable cost reductions and quality improvements, but the volume required for this is constantly increasing and the individual bank or even a financial centre as a whole becomes too small to keep up? The Swiss financial centre is currently in the midst of dealing with this issue. The financial market infrastructures, e.g. the companies of the Telekurs Group, no longer offer banks everywhere shelter under a common and correspondingly low cost ceiling. The big banks offer themselves to the banks partly as alternatives to the joint efforts. A forward-looking project, the Securities Transaction Bank, which was developed in the bosom of SIS and which could have offered considerable advantages to most banks, did not come about because it did not meet the interests of the big banks. However, the game is not only played according to the pattern "David against Goliath". Within the various banking groups and across several banking groups, the question of cooperation is more pastoral than ever. Individual larger institutions continue to afford to go it alone well below the big bank threshold, e.g. in computer science or in important groups. 14 different IT solutions are run in parallel. I will come back to the related problem of refinancing. Competitive pressure is increasing. The appeal to the Competition Commission and the invocation of the "Third Force" are not sufficient. Concrete action is needed. It is obvious that the risks of going it alone or playing group or subgroup games are growing. The Swiss financial centre has not undergone structural change, but rather, despite all its achievements in the past since the nineties, is still ahead of it. Against this background, the recent news of 7 May 2002, according to which a group of cantonal banks together with the Swiss Raiffeisen banks has still succeeded in designing a promising project for a securities transaction bank, is of course gratifying. The "Davide" emancipate themselves. 6. International CHF bonds: where are we headed? The CHF played a very prominent role as a denomination currency of international bonds, especially in the eighties, but also in the nineties. The high volumes could only be partly attributed to genuine CHF requirements of foreign issuers. More important were portfolio optimizations or arbitrage. In recent years, however, the issue currency CHF has calmed down. After a maximum value of 20% around 1980, the share of the world market fell continuously. This amounted to 1% of new issues in the first half of 2001. Of course, the global market share of the CHF in the total outstanding bonds also declined sharply. Over the past five years, this has halved from 1.6% (1996) to 0.8% (2001). The CHF, which has slipped from 3rd to 5th place (today) in the issuance statistics of international bonds since 1988, is not only facing competition from the main currencies, but recently also from East Asian currencies. The possible reasons for the declining importance of the CHF as an international investment and issuing currency are manifold. These include: 15  The comparative advantages of the Swiss emissions market are dwindling as a result of foreign competition catching up.  Reduced market liquidity or significant increase in liquidity in the Euro Segment.  Reduced diversification value of the CHF due to the reduced number of currencies and the similarity of CHF and euro exchange rates.  Discussion about bank client secrecy and expected introduction of a paying agent tax on interest income.  Anchoring principle as the cause of a missed development of a CHFEurobond market. So much for the anchoring principle: It states that the lead institution of a CHF issue must be based in Switzerland. It dates back to 1993 and was introduced by the SNB for monetary policy reasons, after the syndication obligation ceased to exist for competition policy reasons. The aim was to secure information about what is happening in the area of CHF issues, on the basis of the reporting obligation of the lead banks. Whether this justification is still equally valid today, however, must be examined. After all, it cannot be ruled out that the effects on the Swiss financial centre were not only positive. Admittedly, this may have been accompanied by a certain promotion of the issuing activities of the banks in Switzerland, which brought additional added value to the financial centre. On the other hand, this may have made it more difficult to issue so-called Eurobonds denominated in CHF in London, which may have contributed to the fact that the CHF has lost so much importance as a denomination of bonds issued by foreign debtors. a Also the discussion about bank client secrecy la Suisse, which is now for many years, and in particular the expectation that sooner or later Switzerland will grant the European Union a concession in the form of a paying agent tax on the interest income of holders of bonds with 16 Tax domicile in the European Union does not contribute to the attractiveness of CHF bonds. Overall, however, neither the anchoring principle nor the paying agent tax should be overestimated as explanations for the decreasing importance of the CHF as a denomination for bonds of foreign debtors. Rather, the development of recent years primarily reflects the normalization of market conditions after the Second World War. Unlike in the past, the issuing business in Switzerland is no longer unique. Other issuing centres, notably London, have become more attractive in terms of regulation and economy. And the introduction of a large euro market has reduced the market liquidity of CHF bonds. Nevertheless, the SNB is currently asking itself whether it should abolish the anchoring principle. Its monetary policy importance has probably diminished compared with 1993. If it turns out that the anchoring principle has become superfluous in monetary policy and that it has a disruptive effect on competition policy and even counterproductive in terms of industrial policy, its abolition should be envisaged. However, miracles should not be expected from it. The London financial centre has now become a kind of "self-runner" in the issuing business, and the euro is and remains attractive. This means that the issuing business will hardly be able to be brought back to Switzerland on a large scale. In addition, an increased weight of the CHF as an international investment and debt currency must not only bring advantages in terms of monetary policy. The CHF could become even more of a pawn in international speculation than before. However, this should be countered by the fact that with the expansion of the market for CHF bonds, its liquidity and depth would also increase, which in turn could reduce the vulnerability of the CHF. Finally, it should not be forgotten that the international significance of the CHF as an investment and debt currency will not converge towards zero one way or another. Regardless of the anchoring principle and paying agent tax, the CHF is unlikely to have played out. Much speaks for him in the future as well. This includes the 17 Stability-oriented, autonomous monetary policy of the SNB and the disappearance of many currencies caused by the introduction of the euro. The more alternative currencies are eliminated, the more important the function of the CHF as a diversification instrument is. 7. Refinancing banks facing new challenges 3 While the volume of mortgages in the Swiss economy continues to grow, traditional savings have been declining for years. At the beginning of the nineties, over 100% of loans could be covered by traditional passive funds. For the time being, the Raiffeisen banks, but the cantonal banks and even more so the regional banks are confronted with growing difficulties in refinancing. While the regional banks (cantonal banks) were still able to cover more than 100% (105%) of their mortgage loans with customer custody accounts in 1996, this ratio declined to around 85% (90%) at the end of 2000. There are several reasons for this funding gap. Savers and investors are better informed than before and can compare offers and change investment instruments with little effort. The attitude of investors has changed especially in the years of the stock market boom. The securities markets and the investment funds rightly pushed by the banks deprived the banks of their assets. In order to adapt to this trend, the individual bank can obtain more funds from other banks in the short term. Depending on the yield curve, credit ratios and local competition, this can be a way out. However, it is certainly not a permanent solution for an entire industry. Going to a foreign bank, e.g. a German Landesbank, which occurs among cantonal banks, can also lead to disappointment. One has to ask oneself why a 3 Although, of course, the large banks also have to deal with refinancing, the refinancing of the banks is dealt with in the following exclusively with regard to the other banks active in the retail business in Switzerland. 18 foreign bank is willing to lend money to a Swiss bank on Swiss terms, i.e. at low international interest rates. Certainly, with all due respect to the creditworthiness of the cantonal banks, there is also the hope, perhaps even the speculation of the creditor on an appreciation of the CHF behind it. Appreciations that follow the productivity differences of the currency areas are of course always to be expected and desired. These generally take place relatively slowly and do not exceed a certain extent. From the SNB's point of view, the CHF is not suitable as a pawn in movements beyond this. Should this view prevail in the market, as desired by the SNB, it cannot be ruled out that the conditions of international bank loans will deteriorate noticeably. Of course, banks also have the opportunity to go to the capital market. The focus is on Pfandbrief and bond bonds. However, the direct route to the bond market is only open to the larger institutions with a rating. In addition, important debtors, i.e. the cantonal banks, predominantly benefit from the state guarantee, which puts the other banks at a competitive disadvantage. This is also significant if the banks take the path of issuing Pfandbriefe or indebtedness via an issuing vehicle created specifically for this purpose in the sense of the KMB Bank, as is currently being promoted by the RBA Group, or approach the capital market via the Central Bank of the Raiffeisen Banks. Pfandbrief loans require compliance with strict regulations that give Pfandbrief bonds an exceptionally high credit rating. The wide range of participants and the opportunity to participate even with small amounts favours the liquidity of the Pfandbriefe. The high demands of the Pfandbrief institutions on the documentation of the Pfander force the participants to discipline and act as an additional monitoring. The instrument is indispensable, especially for the smaller institutes. However, the growth potential is limited. The low loan-to-value limit, the de facto restriction to first-class pawns, i.e. residential buildings, and, this applies in particular to the regional banks, whose sub-representation in the economically dynamic agglomeration 19 At best, these and regions allow for a step in step with GDP growth. Finally, as far as the alternatives to Pfandbriefe, the so-called mortgage-backed sectors, are concerned, Swiss issues remained the exception for the time being. So far, in addition to the big banks, only zurcher Kantonalbank has issued such an instrument, and it has done so on its own. The access of mortgage institutions to the capital market is and remains arduous. This is still particularly evident in the case of regional banks, but their competitors face fundamentally similar problems. We assume that the share of mortgage loans financed by Pfandbriefe will continue to be around 20% for the regional banks, while the corresponding shares for the cantonal and large banks will be 30-35%. What can a regional bank do in this situation? Further optimisation of Asset and Liabilities Management (ALM) is likely to hold potential. It is striking that the regional banks face the largest financing gap, but at the same time do not have the smallest liquidity ceiling. Is this merely an expression of justified caution or does too high an operational demand for liquidity play into it? Can the liquidity cushions be reduced somewhat against the background of the financing problems? The observer of the banking behavior around the repo business notices that the possibilities of capital optimization are generally by no means exhausted and the collateral management in some places hardly deserves this name. It almost seems as if equity is available without restrictions. In any case, it is not easy to understand why the blank business still dominates so strongly compared to the repo. However, the ALM raises even more fundamental questions. Are interest rate risks so under control that even shock-like developments did not lead to embarrassment? Have the necessary precautions been taken for the perhaps massed decays in the future? Just as, for example, the confederation must prepare for the expiry of jumbo bonds by building up counter-positions in good time, so even the small mortgage bank cannot prepare for automatic refinancing. 20 leave favorable conditions. Even if today's low interest rate phase has been going on for a long time, no one should forget that other times will come. At the end of this chapter, allow me to make a comment on the RBA Holding SME project: in view of the problems of refinancing the mortgage business in Switzerland described above and the major trends that are going against the small institutions and groups, it seems to me highly desirable that the SME project makes progress. Let me remind you of what it is all about. In order to improve access to the capital market, especially for smaller regional banks, they are to join a contractual group with banking status, which will be capital marketable thanks to a rating and its size. While the participants would remain legally and operationally independent, the Group - similar to the Raiffeisen headquarters - would also be given control and instruction powers to protect the community of solidarity. Without a restriction of the autonomy of the participating banks, the contracting group is not available. However, participation would still be worthwhile for the banks, especially if the SME Group became sufficiently well-funded to cover the acute refinancing needs of the participating banks temporarily and on the basis of its own funds or to adapt the sequence of its issues to market conditions. The quality of the RBA Group would therefore be further strengthened by the implementation of the SME project. The RBA member banks would become more equal to each other because they are regrouped and thus better positioned in the capital market. The RBA banks would thus take another, and in my view essential, step towards maintaining their viability. 8. The interest island is retained The SNB pursues an autonomous monetary policy. This means that it aligns its interest rate decisions with the needs of Switzerland. An important consequence of monetary policy autonomy is the world's lowest interest rate level, with the exception of Japan. On average over the past 20 years, short-term 21 Interest rates 1 to 1.5 percentage points lower than in Germany, the country with the historically lowest interest rates in Europe after Switzerland. For longer maturities, the difference was even 2.2 percentage points. From an international perspective, Switzerland has had low inflation rates for a very long time. This promotes trust in the CHF. The greater the trust, the less interest the buyers of investments in CHF demand. Low interest rates are an advantage for an economy that should not be underestimated. In addition to the successful autonomous monetary policy, there are other reasons for the interest rate island. One explanation is the high savings rate in Switzerland. Political stability, the performance of the financial sector and the overall investor-friendly legal framework are also important. Accordingly, investors are prepared to pay an insurance premium in the sense of lost interest income when buying CHF investments in order to secure their portfolio against crises. The interest rate advantage in Switzerland would be largely eliminated at the latest if Switzerland were to renounce its monetary policy autonomy. This would happen if we joined the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). However, an increase in Swiss nominal interest rates to the European level would already be possible if the SNB no longer allowed the CHF to fluctuate freely, but would link it to the euro. With a euro peg, the SNB undertook to keep the exchange rate of the CHF against the euro at a certain rate. Since the exchange rate risk would disappear and euro and CHF investments would hardly be distinguishable from each other, the interest bonus would also disappear. The consequences of a permanent interest rate hike would be complex and mostly undesirable. First, any rise in interest rates would also mean a real rate hike. Real interest rate hikes tend to have a negative impact on Swiss GDP. The reason lies in the reduced willingness to invest as a result of the increased interest rate level. There would also be a redistribution between debtors and creditors. While the creditors of a higher return 22 , the debtors would face a higher interest burden. On the debtor side, the state, companies, private mortgage debtors and, indirectly, the many tenants would be most affected. The winners included nominal value savers and pension funds. During the adjustment period from a low to a higher level of interest rates, wages would come under pressure as a result of the decline in production. Experience has shown that wage reductions are difficult to enforce. The adjustment process would therefore be accompanied by a recession in which employment would decline and unemployment would rise. The exact duration of this adjustment process cannot be predicted. It depends on the flexibility of the economy. If interest rates rise, the earned value of existing capital goods also decreases. The value of an investment, be it a government bond, real capital or a single-family house, corresponds to the current value of the expected future returns that this investment yields. If the interest rate rises, the discounted values of the assets decrease. A lower valuation of asset assets can impair the willingness of those affected to consume for a while and intensify the recession in the transitional period. The pension funds, which achieved a higher return on their investments in the long term, would also have to accept losses in the short term. Finally, the stability of the financial system could also suffer. A revaluation of assets would also affect in particular those companies that use their real estate as collateral for bank loans. The lower the property values, the lower the degree of credit coverage. The outstanding loans become riskier for the banks. Furthermore, a rise in interest rates could cause certain debtors to financial difficulties and increase the volume of bad loans. The banks would have to set up appropriate provisions and review their credit policy. In the long term, however, the most important thing would probably be the consequences for price stability in Switzerland. Linking the CHF exchange rate to the euro exchange rate would remove the SNB's autonomy in monetary policy. Switzerland's inflation rate would 23 adapt to those in the euro area. Although this would reduce the rise in real interest rates expected in the initial period after the regime change of monetary policy, the special stability of the CHF would be eliminated and the mandate of the SNB, which has to ensure price stability, would probably be interpreted differently than before. A link between the CHF exchange rate and the euro exchange rate is therefore not justifiable for this fundamental reason. 9. The SNB is committed to the Swiss capital market The SNB is not only part of the Swiss money and capital market and plays a key role in shaping payment transactions, but is also committed to the Swiss International Financial Centre and its capital market. The SNB conducts the country's monetary policy. It ensures price stability and smoothly functioning payment transactions. Thus, it bears responsibility for the stability of the financial system, which is further underlined by its function as a so-called "lender of last resort". The SNB has an obvious and strong interest in the soundness, flexibility and performance of the Swiss financial system, including efficient and robust securities and payment systems. Most important for the SNB is the role of the financial system as a platform for conducting a successful monetary policy. The SNB relies on commercial banks domiciled in Switzerland to conduct its monetary policy operations, not just repos. The SNB can use the repo interest rate, i.e. the interest that the banks have to pay to the SNB for the provision of liquidity, to make the money cheaper or more expensive for the banks. An efficient monetary policy requires flexible pricing on the money and capital markets as well as the reliability and stability of the SNB's counterparties. This is the only way to implement and transfer an interest rate change triggered by the SNB to the financial markets, the price level and the real sector in the desired way. If a financial centre has the desired characteristics, the financial indicators, and in particular interest rates, reflect the economic reality more accurately and the monetary policy impulses are rapidly and predictably translated into the 24 Economy brought in. And the Lender of Last Resort is also less stressed. For these reasons, the SNB has always been involved in shaping the financial system. Your contribution to the SIC is the most striking. The SNB will continue along this path. In 2001, it created a competence centre for system stability. The task of the Competence Center is to help detect and prevent undesirable developments in the financial system. The means for this are good framework conditions, i.e. good regulation and supervision, but also the construction of pre-emptive indicators in order to identify systemically important developments at an early stage. Abroad, these are often used to write so-called "Financial Stability Reports", some of which are published regularly. Switzerland cannot afford the failure of the Swiss International Financial Centre, including its capital market. Too much is at stake. However, this is not about preserving old or comfortable structures, but about promoting the competitiveness of an important part of the Swiss economy. Many have to participate in this task. The SNB's contribution primarily concerns safeguarding monetary stability. Monetary stability is a central component of the framework conditions that must be met in order for an appropriate further development of prosperity in Switzerland to be possible. In addition, the SNB bears part of the responsibility for the stability of the financial system and contributes to its appropriate development.

Die Zinsinsel bleibt erhalten Die SNB betreibt eine autonome Geldpolitik. Das heisst, dass sie ihre Zinsentscheide an den Bedrfnissen der Schweiz ausrichtet. Die Banken mssten entsprechende Rckstellungen bilden und ihre Kreditpolitik berprfen. langfristig am wichtigsten wren aber wohl die Folgen fr die Preisstabilitt in der Schweiz. Eine Anbindung des CHF- an den Eurowechselkurs wrde die geldpolitische Autonomie der SNB beseitigen. Die Inflationsrate der Schweiz wrde 23 sich jener im Euroraum anpassen. Dadurch wrde der in der ersten Zeit nach dem Regimewechsel der Geldpolitik erwartete Anstieg der Realzinsen zwar wieder vermindert, doch die besondere Stabilitt des CHF wre eliminiert und der Auftrag der SNB, welche die Preisstabilitt zu sichern hat, wre wohl anders als bisher zu interpretieren. Die SNB engagiert sich fr den Kapitalmarkt Schweiz Die SNB ist nicht nur Teil des Geld- und Kapitalmarkts Schweiz und gestaltet den Zahlungsverkehr massgebend mit, sondern sie engagiert sich auch fr das Internationale Finanzzentrum Schweiz und fr dessen Kapitalmarkt. Die SNB fhrt die Geld- und Whrungspolitik des Landes. Sie sorgt fr Preisstabilitt und reibungslos funktionierenden Zahlungsverkehr. Die SNB hat ein offensichtliches und hohes Interesse an der Soliditt, Flexibilitt und Leistungfhigkeit des schweizerischen Finanzsystems einschliesslich effizienter und robuster Wertschriften- und Zahlungssysteme. Am wichtigsten ist fr die SNB die Rolle des Finanzsystems als Plattform zur Fhrung einer erfolgreichen Geldpolitik. Zur Durchfhrung ihrer geldpolitischen Geschfte, nicht nur der Repos, ist die SNB auf Geschftsbanken mit Domizil in der Schweiz angewiesen. ber den Repozins, d.h. den Zins, den die Banken der SNB fr die Zurverfgungstellung von Liquiditt zu bezahlen haben, kann die SNB das Geld fr die Banken verbilligen oder verteuern. Nur so kann eine von der SNB ausgelste Zinsnderung in der gewnschten Weise auf die Finanzmrkte, das Preisniveau und den realen Sektor umgesetzt und bertragen werden. Und auch der Lender of Last Resort wird weniger beansprucht. Die SNB hat aus diesen Grnden schon immer an der Gestaltung des Finanzsystems mitgewirkt. Ihr Beitrag zum SIC ist der augenflligste.
