Aufgabe des Kompetenzzentrums ist es dazu beizutragen, Fehlentwicklungen im Finanzsystem zu entdecken und zu verhindern. Mittel dazu sind gute Rahmenbedingungen, also gute Regulierung und Aufsicht, aber auch die Konstruktion vorauseilender Indikatoren, um systemrelevante Entwicklungen frhzeitig zu identifizieren. Im Ausland werden diese hufig dazu eingesetzt, sog. Financial Stability Reports zu verfassen, die zum Teil regelmssig verffentlicht werden. Die Schweiz kann sich ein Scheitern des Internationalen Finanzzentrums Schweiz einschliesslich dessen Kapitalmarkts nicht leisten. Zu viel steht auf dem Spiel. Dabei geht es allerdings nicht um die Erhaltung von alten bzw. bequemen Strukturen, sondern um die Frderung der Wettbewerbsfhigkeit eines wichtigen Teils der schweizerischen Volkswirtschaft. An dieser Aufgabe mssen sich viele beteiligen. Der Beitrag der SNB betrifft primr die Sicherung der Geldwertstabilitt. Geldwertstabilitt ist ein zentraler Bestandteil der Rahmenbedingungen, welche erfllt sein mssen, damit eine angemessene Fortentwicklung des Wohlstands in der Schweiz mglich ist. Darber hinaus trgt die SNB einen Teil der Verantwortung fr die Stabilitt des Finanzsystems, und sie trgt zu dessen angemessener Fortentwicklung bei.

Title: Does the National Bank devote sufficient attention to the Swiss franc exchange rate?
text: Is the Swiss National Bank concerned about the exchange rate of the Swiss franc? Presentation by Jean-Pierre Roth, Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank In the framework of the Annual General Assembly of the Delegates of the Federation of Employers' Unions, Geneva Thursday, 16 May 2002 I'm happy to I have the opportunity today to speak here in Geneva on a subject which is not new but which is currently of great concern to economic circles. This is the role that the SNB attaches to the exchange rate of the Swiss franc in the definition of its monetary policy . In view of the reactions to our recent decision to lower the fluctuation band of our interest rates by half a point, the title of man exposed could very well be reformulated in two ways: is the SNB not concerned about the Swiss franc? On the contrary, is the SNB sufficiently concerned about the Swiss franc? Each of these variants is indicative of the concerns arising from the current situation: is there not a risk that a central bank will be guided by exchange rate considerations, whereas it should aim to preserve the country's internal monetary stability while, conversely, is there a risk that the SNB will underestimate the negative effects of the development of the franc on our economy and, in particular, for our export industry? My purpose will be to show you what the real place that the franc occupies in the conduct of our policy, what answers we give to those who would like us to do more and how we reassure those who fear that we are currently trapping it. 1. The Swiss franc: an essential factor for the development of our economy Switzerland is very aware of importance of monetary factors for the development of its economy and the well-being of its population. We are a country of liberal tradition, open to trade with the world. In the 19th century, we were among the less developed countries in Europe, forgotten by Providence as far as natural resources and access to the sea were concerned. 150 years later, we are among the leading industrialized countries, with one of the highest per capita incomes in the world. Our economy operates at the forefront of research and has an indisputable quality label. The prosperity of our country owes much to courage, has imagination, the genius of generations of entrepreneurs. It is also the result of a realist policy of openness to the world and acceptance of the rules of libre echange. In the monetary and financial field, we have wisely followed a prudent policy avoiding excessive public debt and ensuring good domestic monetary health. Today, Switzerland is a financially sound country: savings are abundant, public debt - even if it may be lower - remains within acceptable standards in international comparison, interest rates are the lowest in Europe and ! Inflation inferior ace which is observed among our citizens. The Swiss franc summarises this success story in an exemplary way: it has established itself internationally as a benchmark for stability and solidity, and it occupies the 5th place in the concert of convertible currencies. With an economy that is largely open to the world and a currency that plays an international role, Switzerland is inevitably sensitive to the turbulence of the financial markets. Let us remember the disorders which accompanied the collapse of the fixed exchange rate regime at the beginning of the seventies and, closer to us in the nineties, the difficulties caused by the successive crises of the European monetary system. Today -with Emergence of the euro - The European monetary landscape is profoundly different, but the challenges of thecoexistence of the franc with the currency of our neighbours are still very present. 2. The euro: a challenge At the end of its first three years of existence, the euro is good news for our country, but also a source of concern. The good news comes first of all from the fact that around us a monetary regime has been set up and the stability objectives correspond exactly to those we have been pursuing for years. Price stability, taking account of economic developments, guides the action of the European Central Bank like ours. It is also positive that a single currency is circulating in 12 countries of the European Union, which ensures greater transparency in prices and simplifies transactions. The source of concern comes from the fact that Switzerland is now completely surrounded by a monetarily unified group of more than 300 million inhabitants, which alone absorbs half of our exports and is the source of more than 70% of our imports. Monetary unification makes our country even smaller than before on the European map. This means that we must expect the euro to become increasingly the currency of regulation for our external trade, but it also means that the exchange rate risk we bear against the euro will be greater than that which we accumulated against the currencies which have now disappeared. Let us not, however, paint the diable on the wall. In the heart of Euroland, the franc has not become unstable and volatile. On the contrary, our experience of these three years of cohabitation with the euro zone has shown us that European monetary unification hasa stabilizing effect. Indeed, it is clear that the disappearance of the monetary mosaic that we knew in the past has eliminated the risk of an exchange rate crisis in Europe and, consequently, protected the franc from the tensions which frequently arosebetween European currencies. The crises of the Italian lira still feel very present in our minds. But the relationship between the franc and the euro is not fixed. Even if, over time Experience shows us thatChang's classes reflect fairly accurately Evolution of the fundamental elements of the economies involved (by fundamental elements I mean the differential inflation and the deviations in the progress of productivity), we know that floating exchange rates can involve periods of undervaluation or overvaluation of one currency against another. These situations are painful for economies, because they lead to distortions of competitiveness in the short term, distortions which feelall the more serious that the currency in question is the currency in which a large part of external trade is settled. How do we take that into account in our policy formulation? 3. The integration of the Swiss franc into themonetary policy strategy In order to answer this question, it is first necessary to remember what the objective of the SNB's action is. The Federal Constitution requires us to conduct a monetary policy aimed at the general interests ofthe country. The mandate is vague. In practice, we aim to preserve the monetary stability of the country, i.e. to protect it from situations of inflation or deflation, while taking into account the current economic situation. These two elements complement each other: by moderating a cyclical boom which is likely to degenerate into overheating, we simultaneously slow down the pace of price increases, and by pursuing an expansive policy at a time when aggregate demand is weak, we are supporting the economy withoutthreatening price stability in the medium term. The difficulty of our task lies in the fact that monetary impulses spread their effects on economic activity relatively quickly, while the impact on prices only becomes apparent after aperiod of 2 to 3 years. Thus, an overly generous monetary policy may have a positive effect on the economy in the short period, but create an inflationary problem on the duration, a situation that will require a subsequent brake. To avoidsuch stop-and-go actions, we constantly ask ourselves about the long-term consequences of our action. We do this by regularly forecasting inflation over a three-year horizon. If, in periods ofeconomic heap, we find that Future price developments allow us to pursue a more expansive monetary policy without taking the risk of an unacceptable rise in prices Inflation In the medium term, we are using the room for manoeuvre available to support economic activity as well as possible. A Conversely, if we expect overheating, a brake stroke, which will necessarily affect the current economic situation, will be necessary. To ensure the transparency of our action, we have estimated the tolerable level of price increases at a maximum of 2%. Below this bar, we consider that there is a situation of price stability. We are not aiming for a zero number. Because not all price changes necessarily smell inflationary , they can also come from Improvement of product quality. On the other hand, it must also be recognized that the measurement of price increases is an unclear exercise, so that a certain tolerance is required. The room for manoeuvre we have in the short term depends on the long-term consequences of our action. It is a constraint that we constantly keep in mind. How does the exchange rate of the Swiss franc concretely enter into our assessment of the situation? First of all, let us say that it cannot be the objective of our action, since it aims to avoid excessive price increases or falls over the long term. It enters it indirectly, through its impact on future price developments. If the Swiss franc strengthens, for example, we can expect prices to rise slowly, due to the drag on our export growth and the fall in the costs of imported goods. This correction of inflation forecasts makes it possible to face an immediate easing of monetary policy, leading to a reduction in interest rates. By lowering interest rates, we are thus relaxing the monetary constraints artificially tightened by the autonomous rise of the franc. The reduction in interest rates is not then simply a measure aimed at trying to influence the exchange rate market or to defend a level of exchange rates - as some often interpret it - but it is a more global decision with a view to maintaining balanced monetary conditions in the economy. Obviously, a decrease in our interest rates also contributes to weakening the attractiveness of investments in Swiss francs. However, the impact of such a measure on the exchange rate of the franc is difficult to predict in the short term, as the markets are subject to irrational factors. To those who accuse us of ignoring the conditions of the exchange rate market in our assessments of the situation, we reply that we give the franc its rightful place, not that of an objective in itself, but that of an important element for the development of the economic situation and prices. In recent years, our action has always been defined according to this strategy. We publish an inflation forecast every six months, and we justify each of our monetary policy decisions by referring not only to the economic development prospects of the moment, but also to the economic development prospects of the moment. A medium term price developments. 4. Could we do more? Having said that, I know that many economic circles believe that our consideration of the exchange rate market situation is insufficient. They call for more decisive action to limit the movements of the franc against the euro. The European currency has lost almost 10% of its value since its creation in January 1999, a downward trend that has been particularly evident over the last 18 months. Believe me, the SNB has followed this development closely. Of With the emergence of the euro, we were sensitive to the risks that a lack of confidence in the new currency could pose to the Swiss economy. Until the spring of 2000, despite the weakness of the euro against the dollar, the franc/euro relationship had changed very little. It was a happy surprise, but this situation could not last. Indeed, it was to be expected that the markets would react to the fact that the Swiss economy was more stable and flexible than its European counterpart. For our part, we did not miss any opportunity to remind those who operated on external markets that caution was required: the relative stability of the initial period of our cohabitation with the euro could not be perceived as indication of a lasting situation. The correction that has taken place since then is significant. When measured in real terms, i.e. taking into account the inflation differential between Switzerland and the euro area, the appreciation of the Swiss franc is much smaller. Since January 1999, prices have been feeling more slowly in Switzerland than in our neighbours. On The whole period this difference now stands at 3.4%. Currently, the real revaluation of the franc is 6.6% over a little more than 3 years, or about 2% per year. Compare a As the franc has moved against the currencies that now make up the euro zone, the real appreciation of the franc is higher than the previous trend, which was of the order of 1% per year. But if the euro is an important currency for the Swiss economy, we must not forget that part of our foreign trade goes to the dollar area or is influenced by the dollar rate. A balanced picture of the situation on the exchange rate front makes it look into it All the currencies of our partners by weighting them by the intensity of our commercial relations. Seen in this light, the situation over the last three years gives a more reassuring picture. From January 1999 to January 2002, the real exchange rate index of the franc against our trading partners remained stable, with the weakness of the euro being offset by the strength of the dollar. This comfortable situation has deteriorated this year with the decline of the US currency. The franc exchange rate index is now 0.7% above its level at the beginning of 1999. When we look at the situation, we try to step back and look at the whole change rate landscape as we look at the full spectrum of interest rates and all information relating to the economic situation in Switzerland and abroad. It is at the end of this broad appreciation of things that we take our monetary policy decisions. The exchange rate of the franc is not exclusive. However, some would like us to change our shoulder and focus our policy primarily on the franc/euro relationship. Their position is simple: given the intensity of trade relations between Switzerland and the Euroland, would it not be preferable to simply link the franc and the euro in order to eliminate any exchange rate uncertainty? It is clear that if our country were to join the European Union, it would also become part of the Monetary Union. As you know, the prospect of accession is still a long way off and there is no specific political agenda. Nor is membership retained as a possibility by the financial markets. Proof of this is the fact that they do not anticipate for it Instant a disappearance of the Swiss franc, even at a distant time. At present, on the futures market, it can be seen that over an 8-year horizon, operators expect interest rates on the franc to be 1.5 percentage points higher than European rates, as is the case today. The lack of convergence of interest rates means that the markets still assume a franc independent of the euro. Since monetary integration of Switzerland is not on the cards, it would be practically impossible to pursue a credible policy aimed at defending a fixed parity between the franc and the euro. Which parity to choose? Would parity still be defendable in the coming years? Would this bet be that of future membership? Such uncertainties smell like beni bread for speculation. Experience has shown us that a monetary decision is credible, done stabilising, only if it is irrevocable. As soon as the market hangsover grey areas, it is constantly testing their reality. Let us remember that the speculation between the European currencies did not disappear until the irretrievable lock-in of parites on 1 January 1999. The situation is the same for our country: only integration into the euro zone would definitively eliminate the problems of monetary cohabitation with our neighbours. But Monetary integration would certainly pose other problems for us. Economists like to point out that nothing is free lunch. An integration of the Swiss franc into the euro area, while it has advantages from the point of view of exchange rate stability, would also entail costs. We would lose our monetary autonomy, which means that we would no longer be able to set interest rates according to the needs of the Swiss economy. Monetary policy would no longer be the business of the SNB but of the European Central Bank, and Swiss interest rates would be at the level of European rates, 1.5 to 2 percentage pointshigher than today. Compared to a traditional situation of low interest rates, this would mean a brake on investment, a rise in the mortgage financing coot, a reality that would weigh on the development of the Swiss economy. Finally, let us not forget that fixing the external value of the Swiss franc is not necessarily a panacea that will solve the problems of competitiveness. Our competitiveness does not depend only on the exchange rate, it also depends on the progress ofproductivity and the mastery of our internal costs. The image of Switzerland, an expensive country, is not simply a monetary phenomenon but covers a reality of protection of whole sections of our internal market. Let us not make the franc the emissary of our difficulties of competitiveness, let us have the courage to slow down the rise in our prices by accepting more vigorous competition, let us fight effectively to centre cartel behaviour, let us seek the moderation of administered prices. Theresult will be a greater attraction for our production location. 5. Are we overdoing it? In the introduction I told you that the title of exposed men could be reformulated in two ways. For some, the SNB is not sufficiently concernedabout the situation of the franc, for others it should be cashed out. I have tried to show you that our policy is one of the middle ground. Exchange rate factors are among the elements of appreciation that we take into account when making our monetary policy decisions. Our approach is necessarily global, it cannot privilege one economic relationship over another. Our recent decision to lower the fluctuation band of the three-month interest rate by 50 basis points illustrates our approach. How did we get there? The Swiss economy entered a phase of stagnation last year, as happened in the United States and Europe. At the beginning of this year, the scenario we have adopted is that of a gradual recovery of activity or economic growth would return to a pace close to its potential of 2% by the end of the year. At the end of the first quarter of this year, we had no tangible evidence that the Swiss economy was not developing according to our initial assumptions. We noted, however, that economic growth remained weak and that the situation was particularly fragile, as the recovery seemed to be more inline than in practice. It is in this precarious environment that we have observed with concern a new trend towards the strengthening of the franc against the euro, then against the dollar. To offset the negative impact of the exchange rate, we preceded a slight rate cut in the week leading up to Easter. As the movement continued at the beginning of May, we lowered rates a second time by adjusting the fluctuation band which symbolizes our monetary policy somewhat more dramatically. These successive reactions are aimed at easing pressure on the Swiss franc and rebalancing monetary conditions, while in the background, the economic recovery is not yet assured. In spite of this correction, our estimates of Future price trends tell us that the probability of a resurgence of inflation is limited. In doing so, even if our action is fully in line with the strategy of mastery of Price developments which is ours, we are quite aware of taking risks. The current level of interest rates is not the one that will allow us to preserve monetary stability when economic growth has regained its cruising speed. This risk-taking seeks to alleviate the difficulties currently encountered by those who feel particularly affected by the strengthening of the franc. It seems justified to us given it uncertainty of the business environment. It will be a question of correcting things when the situation becomes clearer. Those who are worried that monetary policy is taking an expansive turn beyond what is bearable in terms of sustainability can be reassured. We remain vigilant and do not take our eyes off our eyes Medium-term price trends 6. Conclusion In an economy as integrated as ours in international markets, monetary policy cannot ignore Evolution of foreign exchange markets. Between monetary complacency and Indifference, we have chosen a rational and balanced strategy which gives exchange rates their rightful place. They are part of our assessments of the situation to the extent that they affect future price developments. A strengthening of the franc thus creates additional room for manoeuvre for a reduction in interest rates, whereas a weak franc would limit our freedom of action. Our strategy is to make full use of the degrees of monetary freedom at our disposal in order to enable the Swiss economy to develop as well as possible in the wake of the world economy. However, we only have partial control of things because the Swiss economy is very dependent on the course of international events. If, with the help of monetary instruments, we try to create the most favourable framework for its development, we cannot fully protect it from external disturbances. Especially if they come from the exchange market. It is clear that our economic climate is strongly influenced by what happens outside our borders. Some cannot be satisfied with this observation and want us to do more. They misunderstand the scope of our means. If we followed their advice, there would be a great risk that we would jeopardize the financial stability of the country and the low interest rates and low inflation rates that we currently have. And this without being guaranteed to benefit from a better economic situation than that of our trading partners.
text_original: La Banque nationale suisse se preoccupe-t-elle du cours du franc suisse? Expose de Jean-Pierre Roth President de la Direction generale de la Banque nationale suisse Dans le cadre de l'Assemblee generale annuelle des delegues de la Federation des Syndicats Patronaux, Geneve Jeudi 16 mai 2002 Je suis heureux de !'occasion qui m'est donnee aujourd'hui de m'exprimer ici aGeneve sur un theme qui n'est pas nouveau mais qui preoccupe actuellement beaucoup les milieux economiques. II s'agit de la place que la Banque nationale donne au cours du franc dans la definition de sa politique monetaire. Au vu des reactions qui ant suivi notre recente decision d'abaisser d'un demi-point la bande de fluctuation de nos taux d'interet, le titre de man expose pourrait tres bien etre reformule de deux manieres: la Banque nationale ne se preoccupe-t-elle pas trap du franc suisse? au, au contraire, la Banque nationale se preoccupe-t-elle suffisamment du franc? Chacune de ces variantes est revelatrice des inquietudes qui naissent de la situation actuelle: n'est-il pas risque de voir une banque centrale se laisser guider par des considerations de change, alors qu'elle devrait viser a preserver la stabilite monetaire interieure du pays au, inversement, taut-ii craindre que la Banque nationale sous-estime les effets negatifs de l'evolution du franc pour notre economie et, en particulier, pour notre industrie d'exportation? Mon propos visera avous montrer quelle est la veritable place que le franc occupe dans la conduite de notre politique, quelles sont les reponses que nous donnons a ceux qui souhaiteraient que nous en fassions plus et comment nous rassurons ceux qui craignent que nous en fassions actuellement trap. 1. Le franc: un facteur essentiel pour le developpement de notre economie La Suisse est tres consciente de !'importance des facteurs monetaires pour le developpement de son economie et le bien-etre de sa population. Nous sommes un pays de tradition liberale, ouvert au commerce avec le monde. Au 19eme siecle, nous figurions parmi les pays peu developpes d'Europe, oublies de la Providence pour ce qui concernait les ressources naturelles et l'acces ala mer. 150 ans plus tard, nous nous situons dans le peloton de tete des pays industrialises, avec un revenu par tete parmi les plus eleves au monde. Notre economie opere ala pointe de la recherche et dispose d'un label inconteste de qualite. La prosperite de notre pays doit beaucoup au courage, a !'imagination, au genie de generations d'entrepreneurs. Elle est aussi le fruit d'une politique realiste d'ouverture au monde et d'acceptation des regles du libre echange. Dans le domaine monetaire et financier, nous avons suivi avec sagesse une politique prudente evitant l'endettement public excessif et veillant a la bonne sante monetaire interieure. Aujourd'hui, la Suisse est un pays financierement sain: l'epargne y est abondante, l'endettement public -meme si on peut le souhaiter plus faible -reste dans des normes acceptables en comparaison internationale, les taux d'interet y sent les plus bas d'Europe et !'inflation inferieure ace qui est observe chez nos voisins. Le franc suisse resume de maniere exemplaire cette success story: ii s'est impose sur le plan international comme reference de stabilite et de solidite, et ii occupe la 5eme place dans le concert des monnaies convertibles. Avec une economie largement ouverte sur le monde et une monnaie jouant un role international, la Suisse est forcement sensible aux turbulences des marches financiers. Rappelons-nous les desordres qui accompagnerent l'effondrement du regime des changes fixes au debut des annees septante et, plus pres de nous dans les annees nonante, les difficultes entra1nees par les crises successives du systeme monetaire europeen. Aujourd'hui -avec !'apparition de l'euro -le paysage monetaire europeen est profondement different, mais les defis de la cohabitation du franc avec la monnaie de nos voisins sent toujours bien presents. 2. L'euro: un defi Au terme de ses trois premieres annees d'existence, l'euro est, pour notre pays, une bonne nouvelle, mais egalement une source d'inquietudes. La bonne nouvelle vient d'abord du fait qu'autour de nous s'est mis en place un regime monetaire dent les objectifs de stabilite correspondent exactement a ceux que nous poursuivons depuis des annees. La stabilite des prix, en tenant compte des developpements de la conjoncture guide l'action de la Banque centrale europeenne comme la notre. Positif est egalement le fait qu'une seule monnaie circule dans 12 pays de l'Union europeenne, ce qui assure pour taus un gain de transparence dans les prix et une simplification des transactions. La source d'inquietude vient du fait que la Suisse se trouve maintenant totalement entouree par un ensemble monetairement unifie de plus de 300 millions d'habitants, ensemble qui absorbe a lui seul la moitie de nos exportations et qui est a l'origine de plus de 70% de nos importations. L'unification monetaire rend notre pays encore plus petit qu'auparavant sur la carte europeenne. Cela signifie que nous devons nous attendre a ce que l'euro s'impose de maniere croissante comme monnaie de reglement pour notre commerce exterieur, mais cela signifie aussi que le risque de change que nous supportons face a l'euro sera plus important que celui que nous cumulions face aux monnaies qui ant maintenant disparu. Ne peignons toutefois pas le diable sur la muraille. lsole au coeur de l'Euroland, le franc n'en est pas pour autant devenu instable et volatil. Au contraire, notre experience de ces trois annees de cohabitation avec la zone euro nous a montre que !'unification monetaire europeenne exerce un effet stabilisateur. En effet, ii est clair que la disparition de la mosa"ique monetaire que nous connaissions par le passe a elimine les risques de crise de change en Europe et, partant, mis le franc a l'abri de tensions qui se manifestaient frequemment entre les devises europeennes. Les crises de la lire italienne sent encore bien presentees a nos esprits. Mais la relation entre le franc et l'euro n'en est pas pour autant fixe. Meme si, sur la duree, !'experience nous montre que les cours de changes refletent assez fidelement !'evolution des elements fondamentaux des economies en presence (par elements fondamentaux j'entends le differentiel d'inflation et les ecarts dans les progres de la productivite), nous savons que des changes flottants peuvent comporter des periodes de sous-evaluation ou de surevaluation d'une monnaie par rapport a une autre. Ces situations sent douloureuses pour les economies, car elles conduisent a des distorsions de competitivite sur le court terme, distorsions qui sent d'autant plus graves que la monnaie en question est celle dans laquelle se regle une partie importante du commerce exterieur. Comment tenons-nous compte de ce genre de situation dans la definition de notre politique? 3. L'integration du franc dans la strategie de politique monetaire Pour repondre a cette question, ii convient tout d'abord de se rappeler quel est l'objectif de l'action de la Banque nationale. La Constitution federale nous demande de mener une politique monetaire visant les interets generaux du pays. Le mandat est vague. Dans la pratique, nous visons a preserver la stabilite monetaire du pays, c'est-a-dire a le proteger de situations d'inflation ou de deflation, tout en tenant compte de la conjoncture du moment. Ces deux elements se completent: en moderant un essor conjoncturel qui risque de degenerer en surchauffe, nous freinons simultanement le rythme de la hausse des prix, et en menant une politique expansive alors que la demande globale est faible, nous soutenons la conjoncture sans pour autant menacer la stabilite des prix a moyen terme. La difficulte de notre tache tient au fait que les impulsions monetaires deploient leurs effets sur l'activite economique relativement rapidement, tandis que l'impact sur les prix ne se manifeste qu'apres une periode de 2 a 3 ans. Ainsi, une politique monetaire trop genereuse peut avoir un effet positif sur la conjoncture dans la courte periode, mais creer un probleme inflationniste sur la duree, situation qui reclamera un coup de frein ulterieur. Pour eviter de telles actions de stop and go, nous nous interrogeons constamment sur les consequences a long terme de notre action. Nous le faisons en procedant regulierement a des previsions d'inflation a un horizon allant jusqu'a trois ans. Si, en periode de tassement economique, nous constatons que !'evolution future des prix nous permet de mener une politique monetaire plus expansive sans prendre le risque d'une montee inacceptable de !'inflation a moyen terme, nous utilisons la marge de manreuvre a disposition pour soutenir au mieux l'activite economique. A !'inverse, si nous nous attendons a une surchauffe, un coup de frein, qui affectera forcement la conjoncture du moment, sera necessaire. Pour assurer la transparence de notre action, nous avons chiffre a 2% au maximum le niveau tolerable du rythme de la hausse des prix. Au-dessous de cette barre, nous considerons que regne une situation de stabilite des prix. Nous ne visons pas un chiffre zero. Car tous les changements de prix ne sent pas forcement de nature inflationniste, ils peuvent aussi provenir de !'amelioration de la qualite des produits. Par ailleurs, ii taut aussi reconnaltre que la mesure de la hausse des prix est un exercice peu precis, si bien qu'une certaine tolerance s'impose. La marge de manreuvre dent nous disposons dans le court terme depend done des consequences a long terme de notre action. C'est une contrainte que nous gardens constamment a l'esprit. Comment le cours du franc entre-t-il concretement dans nos appreciations de situation? Soulignons d'abord qu'il ne saurait etre l'objectif de notre action, puisque celle-ci vise a eviter sur la duree des hausses ou des baisses excessives des prix. II y entre de maniere indirecte, au travers de son impact sur !'evolution future des prix. En cas de renforcement du franc, par exemple, nous pouvons nous attendre a une hausse ralentie des prix, en raison du frein apporte a l'essor de nos exportations et de la baisse des coots des biens importes. Cette correction des previsions d'inflation permet d'envisager un assouplissement immediat de la politique monetaire, done une baisse des taux d'interet. En baissant les taux, nous relachons ainsi les contraintes monetaires artificiellement resserrees par la montee autonome du franc. La baisse des taux n'est pas alors simplement une mesure visant a essayer d'influencer le marche des changes ou a defendre un niveau de cours -comme certains l'interpretent souvent -, mais elle est une decision de portee plus globale en vue de maintenir dans l'economie des conditions monetaires equilibrees. Evidemment, une baisse de nos taux d'interet contribue aussi a affaiblir l'attrait des placements en francs suisses. L'impact d'une telle mesure sur le cours du franc est toutefois difficilement previsible dans le court terme lorsque les marches sont sous l'empire de facteurs peu rationnels. A ceux qui nous reprochent d'ignorer les conditions du marche des changes dans nos appreciations de situation, nous repondons done que nous donnons au franc sa juste place, non pas celle d'un objectif en soi, mais celle d'un element important pour le developpement de la conjoncture et des prix. Ces dernieres annees, notre action a toujours ete definie en fonction de cette strategie. Nous publions chaque semestre une prevision d'inflation, et nous justifions chacune de nos decisions de politique monetaire en nous referant non seulement aux perspectives de developpements economiques du moment, mais aussi a!'evolution des prix amoyen terme. 4. Pourrions-nous en faire plus? Cela dit, je sais que de nombreux milieux economiques estiment que notre prise en compte de la situation du marche des changes est insuffisante. lls appellent de leurs vreux une action plus decidee visant alimiter les mouvements du franc face al'euro. La monnaie europeenne a en effet perdu pres de 10% de sa valeur depuis sa creation en janvier 1999, un mouvement de baisse qui s'est particulierement manifeste durant les 18 derniers mois. Croyez bien que la Banque nationale a suivi de pres cette evolution. Des !'apparition de l'euro, nous etions sensibles aux risques qu'un manque de confiance dans la nouvelle monnaie pouvait faire courir a l'economie suisse. Jusqu'au printemps 2000, en depit des acces de faiblesse de l'euro face au dollar, la relation franc/euro n'avait que tres peu varie. C'etait une heureuse surprise, mais cette situation ne pouvait durer. En effet, ii fallait s'attendre ace que les marches reagissent au fait que l'economie suisse etait plus stable et plus flexible que sa consreur europeenne. Pour notre part, nous ne manquions aucune occasion de rappeler a taus ceux qui operaient sur les marches exterieurs que la prudence s'imposait: la relative stabilite de la periode initiale de notre cohabitation avec l'euro ne pouvait etre perc;ue comme !'indication d'une situation durable. La correction intervenue depuis lors est importante. Lorsqu'on la mesure en termes reels, c'est-a-dire en tenant compte du differentiel d'inflation entre la Suisse et la zone euro, la revalorisation du franc est heureusement de moindre ampleur. Depuis janvier 1999, les prix sent mantes plus lentement en Suisse que chez nos voisins. Sur !'ensemble de la periode ce differentiel se chiffre maintenant a 3,4%. Actuellement, la revalorisation reelle du franc est done de 6,6% sur un peu plus de 3 ans, soit environ 2% par annee. Compare a !'evolution passee du franc face aux monnaies qui constituent aujourd'hui la zone euro, la revalorisation reelle du franc est superieure a la tendance anterieure, celle-ci etait de l'ordre de 1 % par an. Mais si l'euro est une monnaie importante pour l'economie suisse, nous ne devons pas oublier qu'une partie de notre commerce exterieur se dirige vers la zone dollar ou est influencee par le cours du dollar. Une image equilibree de la situation sur le front des changes demande done que l'on considere !'ensemble des monnaies de nos partenaires en les ponderant par l'intensite de nos relations commerciales. Vue sous cet angle, la situation de ces trois dernieres annees donne une image plus rassurante. De janvier 1999 a janvier 2002, l'indice du cours reel du franc face a nos partenaires commerciaux est reste stable, la faiblesse de l'euro etant compensee par la force du dollar. Cette situation confortable s'est deterioree cette annee avec la baisse de la devise americaine. L'indice du cours du franc se situe maintenant 0,7% au dessus de son niveau de debut 1999. Lorsque nous procedons a un examen de situation, nous nous efforc;ons de prendre du recul et de considerer tout le paysage des taux de change comme nous analysons le spectre complet des taux d'interet et !'ensemble des informations relatives a la conjoncture en Suisse et a l'etranger. C'est a l'issue de cette large appreciation des choses que nous prenons nos decisions de politique monetaire. Le cours du franc n'y a pas de place exclusive. Certains aimeraient toutefois que nous changions de fusil d'epaule et que nous axions notre politique prioritairement sur la relation franc/euro. Leur position est simple: etant donne l'intensite des relations commerciales entre la Suisse et l'Euro-land, ne serait-il pas preferable de lier simplement le franc et l'euro afin d'eliminer toute incertitude de change? II est evident que si notre pays adherait a l'Union europeenne, ii deviendrait egalement membre de l'Union monetaire. Comme vous le savez, la perspective d'adhesion est encore lointaine et aucun echeancier politique precis n'existe. Une adhesion n'est pas non plus retenue comme eventualite par les marches financiers. On en veut pour preuve le fait qu'ils n'anticipent pas pour !'instant une disparition du franc suisse, meme a une echeance lointaine. Actuellement, sur le marche des futures, on note qu'a un horizon de 8 ans, les operateurs s'attendent a ce que les taux d'interet sur le franc soient inferieurs de 1,5 points de pourcentage aux taux europeens comme c'est le cas aujourd'hui. L'absence de convergence des taux signifie que les marches retiennent toujours l'hypothese d'un franc independant de l'euro. Comme une integration monetaire de la Suisse n'est pas dans les cartes, ii serait pratiquement impossible de mener une politique credible visant a defendre une parite fixe entre le franc et l'euro. Quelle parite choisir? La parite serait-elle encore defendable dans les annees a venir? Cette parite serait-elle celle d'une adhesion future? De telles incertitudes sent du pain beni pour la speculation. L'experience passee nous l'a montre: une decision monetaire n'est credible, done stabilisatrice, que si elle est irrevocable. Des que le marche pen;oit des zones grises, ii ne cesse d'en tester la realite. Rappelons-nous que la speculation entre les monnaies europeennes n'a disparu qu'au moment du verrouillage irremediable des parites au 1er janvier 1999. La situation est la meme pour notre pays: seule une integration dans la zone euro eliminerait definitivement les problemes de cohabitation monetaire avec nos voisins. Mais !'integration monetaire ne manquerait pas de nous poser d'autres problemes. Les economistes rappellent volontiers que rien n'est gratuit. Une integration du franc dans la zone euro, si elle presente des avantages du point de vue de la stabilite du change, comporterait aussi des coots. Nous perdrions notre autonomie monetaire, ce qui signifie que nous ne serions plus en mesure de fixer les taux d'interet en fonction des besoins de l'economie suisse. La politique monetaire ne serait plus l'affaire de la BNS mais de la Banque centrale europeenne, et les taux d'interet suisses se situeraient au niveau des taux europeens, soit 1,5 a 2 points de pourcentage plus haut qu'aujourd'hui. Par rapport a une situation traditionnelle de taux d'interet bas, cela signifierait un frein a l'investissement, un relevement du coot du financement hypothecaire, une realite qui peserait sur le developpement de l'economie suisse. N'oublions pas, enfin, que la fixation de la valeur exterieure du franc suisse n'est pas forcement une panacee qui reglera taus les problemes de competitivite. Notre competitivite ne depend pas que du change, elle depend aussi des progres de la productivite et de la maitrise de nos coots interieurs. L'image de la Suisse, pays cher, n'est pas simplement un phenomene monetaire mais recouvre une realite de protection de pans entiers de notre marche interieur. Ne faisons pas du franc le bouc emissaire de nos difficultes de competitivite, ayons le courage de ralentir la progression de nos prix en acceptant une concurrence plus vive, luttons efficacement centre les comportements cartellaires, recherchons la moderation des prix administres. II en resultera un plus grand attrait pour notre place de production. 5. En faisons-nous trop? En introduction je vous disais que le titre de men expose pouvait etre reformule de deux manieres. Pour certains, la Banque nationale ne se preoccupe pas suffisamment de la situation du franc, pour d'autres elle devrait mains s'en saucier. J'ai essaye de vous montrer que notre politique est celle du juste milieu. Les facteurs de change ant leur place parmi les elements d'appreciation que nous retenons au moment de prendre nos decisions de politique monetaire. Notre approche est forcement globale, elle ne peut privilegier une relation economique plutot qu'une autre. Notre recente decision de baisser la bande de fluctuation du taux d'interet atrois mois de 50 points de base illustre bien notre approche. Comment y sommes-nous arrives? L'economie suisse est entree l'an dernier dans une phase de stagnation, a l'image de ce qui s'etait produit aux Etats-Unis et en Europe. Au debut de cette annee, le scenario que nous avons retenu est celui d'une reprise progressive de l'activite ou la croissance economique retrouverait un rythme proche de son potentiel de 2% en fin d'annee. A la fin du premier trimestre de cette annee, nous ne possedions pas d'elements tangibles nous indiquant que l'economie suisse ne se developpait pas selon nos hypotheses initiales. Nous constations toutefois que la croissance economique demeurait faible et que la situation etait particulierement fragile, car la reprise semblait etre plus dans les esprits que dans les faits. C'est dans cet environnement precaire que nous avons observe avec inquietude une nouvelle tendance au renforcement du franc face a l'euro, puis face au dollar. Pour contrebalancer l'impact negatif du change, nous avons precede a une legere baisse de taux dans la semaine qui precedait Paques. Comme le mouvement se poursuivait debut mai, nous avons abaisse les taux une seconde fois en ajustant de maniere un peu plus spectaculaire la bande de fluctuation qui symbolise notre politique monetaire. Ces reactions successives ant vise a alleger la pression sur le franc et a reequilibrer les conditions monetaires, alors qu'en arriere-plan, la reprise conjoncturelle n'est pas encore assuree. En depit de cette correction, nos estimations de !'evolution future des prix nous indiquent que la probabilite d'une resurgence de !'inflation est limitee. Ce faisant, meme si notre action s'inscrit pleinement dans la strategie de maitrise de !'evolution des prix qui est la notre, nous sommes tout a fait conscients de prendre des risques. Le niveau actuel des taux d'interet n'est pas celui qui nous permettra de preserver la stabilite monetaire lorsque la croissance economique aura retrouve sa vitesse de croisiere. Cette prise de risques cherche a attenuer les difficultes rencontrees actuellement par ceux qui sent particulierement touches par le renforcement du franc. Elle nous parait justifiee etant donne !'incertitude de l'environnement conjoncturel. II s'agira de corriger les choses lorsque la situation se sera eclaircie. Ceux qui s'inquietent de voir la politique monetaire prendre un tour expansif allant au-dela de ce qui est supportable en duree peuvent done etre rassures. Nous restons vigilants et ne quittons pas des yeux !'evolution des prix a moyen terme. 6. Conclusion Dans une economie aussi integree que la notre dans les marches internationaux, la politique monetaire ne peut ignorer !'evolution des marches des changes. Entre la complaisance monetaire et !'indifference, nous avons choisi une strategie rationnelle et equilibree qui donne aux cours de change leur juste place. lls entrent dans nos appreciations de situation dans la mesure ou ils affectent !'evolution future des prix. Un renforcement du franc cree ainsi une marge de manoeuvre supplementaire pour une baisse des taux, alors qu'un franc faible limiterait notre liberte d'action. Title: Bank and financial market regulation in Switzerland: a permanent construction site
text: BANKING AND FINANCIAL MARKET REGULATION : CONSTRUCTION SITE SWITZERLAND Prof. Dr. Niklaus Blattner Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Annual General Meeting of the Swiss Association of Independent Securities Dealers Berne, 29 May 2002 1. Introduction My presentation on "Banking and financial market regulation: Swiss construction site" is divided into five parts. I will start with the question of why banking and financial market regulation is necessary and what problems are associated with its implementation. Due to the global nature of the financial markets, it is not possible to work on the Swiss construction site in isolation from international events. That is why, in the second part, I give an overview of the most important international bodies that deal with current issues and adopt standards. These form the actual building standards that we have to consider when designing our construction plan in Switzerland. In the third and fourth parts, I come to the situation in Switzerland. First, I take a look at the existing financial market supervision and point out the need for regulation identified by two expert groups, the actual blueprint. Afterwards I invite you to a tour of the construction site of the reforms. The fifth part contains a concluding remark on the role of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) in the field of banking and financial market regulation. 2. Conceptual and practical requirements for regulation The economic literature provides various explanations for the fact that the financial sector in general and banks in particular are subject to special regulatory treatment. The first approach emphasizes the danger of so-called systemic risks. Banks are basically potentially illiquid. The reason for this lies in their special balance sheet structure. Banks finance illiquid bank assets, i.e. loans, through short-term liquid deposits. If liquidity problems arise, the transition to insolvency is fluid. Banks are closely linked via international loans and the payment system. The difficulties of a single institution can therefore be transferred to entire groups of banks or even to the entire banking system. A second justification for regulation is based on the argument of information asymmetry. For example, a bank's customers are less well informed about its creditworthiness or the quality of the financial products it offers than the bank itself. Both at the time of conclusion of the contract and afterwards, they are hardly or only with great effort in a position to obtain the necessary information. In this case, regulation serves as a substitute for competition, i.e. for the monitoring of markets or suppliers and products by customers. The third reason for the strict regulation of the financial sector compared to other sectors is of a politico-economic nature: financial and banking crises severely damage large parts of the population. Accordingly, the pressure of those affected on the state to compensate them for the losses may be great. In order to reduce this implicit insurance obligation, the state resorts to prevention, i.e. to the means of regulation and monitoring. However, regulation and monitoring are not free. Expenses arise on the part of the authorities or the other bodies responsible for regulation and monitoring, but then also on the part of the customers. In the sense of an optimization rule, the market should only be intervened as long as the so-called "net regulatory burden" is negative or as long as the benefits of the additional regulation exceed its costs. To illustrate, a drastic example. The risk of insolvency could be excluded with a hundred percent own funds requirement. The consequence, however, would be a significant increase in the price of financial intermediation or the credit function of the banking system, which made neither business nor economic sense. The regulatory optimum is not easy to determine in practice. The determination of the so-called "net regulatory burden", i.e. the difference between the added benefits and costs of regulation both before and after the introduction of a measure, is conceptually and empirically difficult. Despite this difficulty, the British Financial Service Authority (FSA), for example, basically reviews the costs and benefits of each new regulatory measure before pursuing it further. - In Switzerland, too, every legislative proposal includes an assessment of the regulatory consequences. All carriers of regulatory and monitoring functions are constantly in a field of tension between "regulatory arbitrage" on the one hand and "regulatory overkill" on the other. The former is an outflow of the natural defensive behavior of the regulated and manifests itself in the shift of activities from regulated spaces or segments to less or not at all regulated areas. A particularly recent example is the trading of credit risks, which are transferred from regulated carriers to those that are less subject to supervision. Countermeasures regularly provoke the accusation of "regulatory overkill". The international networking of markets, the growing complexity of the law and the Financial products, which are increasingly confusing, partly in response to existing regulations, are constantly awakening new regulatory needs. More comprehensive rules increase the costs of regulation and supervision, i.e. the net regulatory burden, and can also reduce the caution of stakeholders, thereby contributing to the threat to the financial system and proving counterproductive. Between regulators and monitored ones, a continuous race between hare and hedgehog takes place, as it were, with the participants constantly alternating in the role of the hare and the hedgehog. Such a race is likely to hinder the functioning of markets. After all, it would be naive to believe that regulation and monitoring can be carried out without regard to the competitiveness of the actors. Although "regulatory dumping" vis-a-vis other financial centres must of course be avoided, the question of the consequences of the measures on the attractiveness of the Swiss International Financial Centre must always be included in the evaluation. The concrete design of regulation and supervision is, in fact, in fact one of the essential determinants of the attractiveness of every financial centre. Clear regulatory requirements are important to ensure the integrity of the Swiss International Financial Centre both for the protection of savers, investors and policyholders and by rejecting funds of criminal origin. They are also needed to ensure the functioning, efficiency and stability of the financial system in the long term and to maintain and strengthen international competitiveness. Regulators must therefore consistently adhere to these objectives and, despite the associated difficulties, systematically review all potential measures with regard to costs and benefits. 3. Trends of the Challenges International Discussion and current Kurt Tucholsky wrote as early as the twenties: "As far as the world economy is concerned, it is intertwined." This is especially true today - not least for the world financial markets. Regional crises can become national crises, national crises can become international ones. All the more It is more understandable that the discussion of banking and financial market regulation has become internationalized. Purely nationally oriented regulations cannot protect the globalised financial markets from crises. Successful regulation and supervision can only be ensured if it takes into account the interconnectedness of banks and financial markets. In recent years, financial market supervision has therefore continued to internationalise. Where in the past there were great differences in setting priorities, the standards converged. International bodies develop standards that are implemented nationally. The goal remains the same: the stability and integrity of the financial markets should remain high. At the same time, however, the thought of competition always plays a role. Minimum standards are intended to limit international regulatory arbitrage, i.e. the legendary "race to the bottom" of regulation and supervision, downwards. The most influential "standard setting bodies" are groupings of state supervisory authorities. (See slide: International bodies for financial market regulation and see Annex). Committees primarily concerned with the stability of financial institutions, including securities dealers, are the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the International Organization of Securities Trading and Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS) and the Joint Forum on Financial Conglomerates. The Basel Committee aims to improve cooperation between banking supervisory authorities and to enable effective, cross-border banking supervision. To this end, the Committee adopted the so-called Basel Concordat in 1983, which regulates the competence of the supervisory authorities in the case of cross-border banking activities. In addition, the Committee laid down minimum requirements for the supervision of international banking groups and their foreign branches. In 1997, the Basel Committee also worked closely with the supervisory authorities in emerging economies to develop "core principles for effective banking supervision". The Basel Committee also systematically advocates universally applicable supervisory guidelines and standards for the banking business, in particular with regard to solvency. Its best-known standards are in the Equity agreement from 1988. Ten years later, in 1998, the Basel Committee decided to revise it comprehensively. A definitive regulation is not yet available. However, there is agreement on the main features: Basel II, as the revised agreement is called, is intended to adapt the supervisory capital requirements to the actual risks of the banks and to establish more effective banking supervision and more far-reaching disclosure requirements. This is reflected in the three pillars of the new agreement, minimum capital requirements, supervisory review procedures and effective use of market discipline. The reform aims to increase the incentives for the use of advanced risk management methodologies and for increased transparency regarding the risks taken. The more risk-sensitive design of capital requirements is reflected in two respects: On the one hand, banks can now choose between three approaches to credit risks, a standard approach and two approaches based on internal bank ratings, the latter explicitly recognising elements of credit risk (e.g. the creditworthiness of the debtor) for calculating the supervisory capital requirements. Thus, the lower the risk can be classified, the lower the required capital requirements. Of course, the internal models have to meet minimum requirements. On the other hand, in addition to market and credit risks, operational risks must now also be underpinned with own funds, whereby banks also have different approaches at their disposal here. The implementation of the rules, originally planned for 2004, has having regard to the consultation on the second consultation paper of January 2001, and Due to the complex work to estimate the quantitative consequences (so-called "quantitative consequences"). Quantitative Impact Study). I expect an implementation by the end 2006. The question of definition and evaluation has emerged as controversial issues. operational risks and, especially abroad, the impact of the agreement on small and medium-sized enterprises. It is also criticized that the Statutory total own funds for institutions which are mainly invested in the Asset management, will increase under Basel II: These institutions benefit little from the reduction in credit and market risks, but must also reserve capital for operational risks. Of these, too the Independents Effektenhandler shocked. Macroeconomically relevant is the so-called "procyclicality". It is feared that the new capital adequacy rules will encourage banks to adopt a lending practice that prolongs the boom and recession phases: in phases of economic recovery, risks decrease and lending expands. Conversely, this is reduced in phases of economic decline, in which the risks increase. However, the Basel Committee has largely taken these concerns into account in its revised drafts. An attempt is currently being made to measure the impact of the new rules in quantitative terms before the Committee launches its third and probably final consultation paper for consultation. The International Organization of Securities Trading and Securities Commissions (IOSCO) groups the supervisory authorities in securities trading. It was founded in 1974 and has been open to members from all over the world since 1985. The objectives are to protect investors, ensure fair and transparent markets and reduce systemic risks. Specifically, this madrid-based organisation develops market surveillance standards and promotes international cooperation between the authorities. Fundamental are the "Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation", which were published in 1998. The International Association of Insurance Supervisory Authorities (IAIS) deals with the insurance sector. The IAIS was founded in 1994 by over a hundred different state insurance regulators. The headquarters of the committee is also located at the BIS in Basel. The association aims to develop supervisory standards in the insurance sector and to strengthen cooperation and the exchange of information between insurance supervisors. The most important publications are the IAIS "Core Principles" and the "lnsurance Concordate". - The Joint Forum on Financial Conglomerates was established in 1996 in response to increasing cross-industry interdependence in the financial sector. This is made up of the Basel Committee, IOSCO and the IAIS. The Joint Forum seeks to coordinate the regulation and supervision of cross-sectoral financial conglomerates internationally. The main objective of the forum is to develop globally recognised principles for shaping cross-sector supervision and improving cooperation between banking, stock exchange and insurance supervisory authorities. In 1999, recommendations on the "Supervision of Financial Conglomerates". These Guidelines are carried out in Switzerland during the total revision of the Insurance Supervision Act (VAG) implemented. The Swiss Building project "Insurance Supervision Act" we will be on the construction site tour again and then take a closer look at it. Next, let's take a look at the regulatory standards in the area of financial market infrastructure: In recent years, payment flows in electronic payments and securities trading have increased sharply. This has also increased the importance of stable payment and securities settlement systems. The two most important bodies working to strengthen the financial market infrastructure and the associated reduction of systemic risk are the BIS's Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS) and the IOSCO, which has already been discussed, which deals not only palely with securities dealers, but also with trading and settlement systems. The Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS) deals with the efficiency and stability of national and international payment and settlement systems. At the beginning of last year, the CPSS published the "Basic Principles for Payment Systems, Which Are Important for the Stability of the Financial System". The Basic Principles provide guidance for central banks and payment system operators. At the end of 2001, the International Securities Trading and Securities Commissions (IOSCO), together with the CPSS, issued 19 recommendations on the minimum requirements for securities settlement systems. As the explanations show, many doctors bend over the "patient". Since each of these doctors specializes in specific ailments, the individual lacks the necessary information and capacity to fully evaluate the patient's state of health and possible risks. To remedy this problem, the So-called Group of Seven (G7) convened the Financial Stability Forum in 1999. This is intended to coordinate all international bodies and the standards they adopt and to identify new needs for action. Various other organizations are committed to preventing abuses in the financial business and promoting correct business practices. The most important bodies in this context are the Financial Action Task Force on Money Laundering (FATF) and the OECD. The FATF was founded by the G7 in 1989 and published forty anti-money laundering recommendations a year later. In 1996, these were adapted to the current circumstances. The FATF currently has 31 countries. In the area of banking and financial market supervision, the OECD is endeavouring to harmonise the various national supervisory practices in general. In addition, it publishes "Corporate Governance Standards". With the exception of the Financial Stability Forum, Switzerland is a member of all listed bodies. It participates in the creation of international rules and implements them in an exemplary manner. In order to assess the financial sector of a country and to judge whether and to what extent a country applies the described, internationally recognized standards, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has introduced the so-called "Financial Seetor Assessment Program" together with the World Bank. At the invitation of the relevant country, the national financial services market is thoroughly reviewed by a team of experts. Last year, Switzerland was one of the first leading industrial nations to undergo this test. On 3 June 2002, a media conference on this topic will be held in Bern, which will provide information on the results and their evaluation by the federal authorities. 4. State of affairs in Switzerland A country's financial market supervision is not only influenced by international standards. National developments and findings are also incorporated into the regulations. The dynamics of the markets make an ongoing review of supervisory law indispensable: banking and financial market regulation has also become a permanent construction site in Switzerland. In recent years, the existing financial market supervision in Switzerland has been subjected to a comprehensive assessment twice: On the one hand, a group of experts appointed by the Federal Department of Finance and chaired by Professor Jean-Baptiste Zufferey examined the strengths and weaknesses of the Swiss regulatory and supervisory system. On the other hand, as mentioned, Switzerland participated in the Financial Seetor Assessment Program (FSAP) of the IMF and the World Bank. In its final report of November 2000, the Zufferey Expert Group assessed the current regulation and supervision as generally positive, but identified a need for action in some areas. The most important of these 42 proposals, divided into six thematic areas, are listed below. I will only address the three most important questions and recommendations from the SNB's point of view: (1) the supervision and regulation of general finance and financial conglomerates, (2) the simplification and differentiation of banking and financial market regulation, and (3) the extension of the supervisory function to other financial service providers. In its final report, the Expert Group points out that the regulation and supervision of financial conglomerates raises the particular question of whether systemic risk is increased or reduced through diversification. It therefore proposes to develop an individual supervisory approach for each individual financial conglomerate instead of a general regulation and to determine whether the assessment of risks must be carried out by means of aggregation or consolidation. In this way, experience is to be gained for a later appropriate regulation. The first results have already been incorporated into the total revision of the. I will come back to that. Conglomerate supervision is one of the main arguments for the creation of an integrated supervisory authority. Subject area Main recommendation General: Simplification and differentiation of banking and financial market regulation. Banks: Special organisational structure required for the supervision of the two major banks Uedoch: no separate supervisory authority) (already implemented at the level of the Federal Banking Commission (SFBC)). Insurances: Transition from supervision with a strong focus on product control to solvency supervision.
