Non-regulated Fi- Independent asset managers, "lntroducing brokers" Nancial services and foreign exchange traders are to be subject to prudential supervision provider: be assumed. Organization of the creation of an integrated financial market supervisory authority, Complete supervision: which define the supervisory functions sfbc and the Federal Office for private insurance (FOPI). The SNB welcomes increased cooperation between supervisory authorities. The integration of the Federal Banking Commission (SFBC) and the Federal Office of Private Insurance (FOPI) into a single financial market supervisory authority can also bring advantages, provided that this project is approached appropriately and not formalistically. The SNB also supports the recommendation to differentiate and simplify financial market and banking regulation, particularly in the area of capital adequacy requirements. In view of the heterogeneity of financial intermediaries, such a measure also seems unavoidable to us, with a change in the capital adequacy rules to be made within the framework of the new capital adequacy agreement of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel II). However, increased differentiation does not necessarily simplify the rules. For smaller institutions, the search for a simplified regime is therefore recommended. Although the SNB welcomes regulation that takes into account the specificities of the various financial service providers, it also expresses concerns. A multiplication of supervisory regimes, as already laid out in the proposals for Basel II, entails the risk of so-called adverse selection. The institutions are de facto invited to opt for the regime that is most cost-effective for them, but not necessarily optimal overall. This phenomenon is feared, for example, in the case of the new capital adequacy rules: banks with high credit risks are more likely to opt for the standard approach, while those with relatively safe loans are more likely to opt for the risk-differentiated approach. On the other hand, differentiation also entails the risk of distortion of competition if actors operating on the same market are subject to different supervisory systems and thus also different requirements. Closely linked to the aspect of differentiation is also the recommendation of the Zufferey expert group to subject the "lntroducing brokers", the foreign exchange traders and the independent asset managers to separate regulation and supervision. The Expert Group justifies its proposal in particular with the Customer and investment protection, with the neutrality of competition and with the reputation protection of the International Financial Centre Switzerland. However, these reasons have not yet been able to convince the SNB. The argument of investor protection is inadequate for three reasons: First, in the case of independent asset managers, the risks are low as long as the assets under management are deposited with banks on behalf of the clients. Secondly, the clients of foreign exchange traders are mainly composed of institutional investors, which is why the need for protection is also limited here. Finally, it should be noted that customers can also conduct their business through a financial intermediary subject to prudential supervision, such as a bank. Customers are therefore free to choose a regulated or non-regulated provider. Even the argument of competitive neutrality is not convincing, as the market share of non-regulated financial service providers is at most 15 percent. Finally, with regard to reputation protection, we would like to point out that the integrity of the financial centre is in the very best interest of these non-regulated categories: they are the first to suffer from possible reputation problems. However, the regulation of additional financial service providers does not seem to us to be urgent for other reasons. On the one hand, in view of the heterogeneity of the financial service providers concerned, we fear a variety of practical problems in monitoring. On the other hand, there is a risk of overloading the supervisory authorities. This could prove counterproductive in the sense that previous tasks are neglected and/or the implementation of new, in our opinion more important concerns (conglomerate supervision, Basel II) are impaired. The functioning of supervision must in any case be preserved. I am aware that your association does not share this attitude of the SNB. Let me say the following: your dissatisfaction with the current regulation of securities dealers is not incomprehensible. In your opinion, the current situation does not fully do justice to the principle of differentiation. However, it seems to me that the real problem is not solved by regulating independent asset managers, but requires a different approach. A mountaineer only reaches the summit faster if he reduces the weight of his own luggage, but not if he puts stones in the backpack of the other climbers. In this sense, the demands of your association are aimed at regulating securities dealers, especially in the Comparison to the banks to facilitate, in the right direction. However, this concern can be pursued separately from the question of whether independent asset managers are to be subject to supervision. The most important recommendations of Zufferey's final report after the evaluation of the statements are now being drafted by the new expert group set up by the Federal Council under the leadership of Professor Ulrich Zimmerli. The focus is on the organisational integration of banking and insurance supervision as well as the extension of prudential supervision to previously unregulated financial service providers. 5. Construction site Switzerland: a travelogue Before we enter the construction site of the ongoing regulatory reforms in Switzerland, I would like to take a look at the construction plan (see slide Swiss construction site: ongoing reform projects in the appendix). Some of the listed reform projects are already a response to the results of the final report of the Zufferey Expert Group. However, many reforms have been initiated before and are awaiting completion. Some of the reforms are regulatory new buildings. An example of this is the creation of statutory conglomerate supervision. Often, however, only conversions or increases are carried out, as in the case of the revision of the National Bank Act (NBA), and sometimes minor repairs are sufficient to repair the damage. This is the case with the improvement of auditing. As you can see on the blueprint, the ongoing reform projects in the area of banking and financial market regulation are numerous. To report on all of them would go beyond the time frame of my presentation. Allow me therefore to single out a few particularly interesting construction projects. a) Integrated supervision: One of the recommendations of the Zufferey report is the creation of integrated financial market supervision. In concrete terms, this means an organisational merger of the SFBC with FOPI. Increased cooperation between supervisory authorities takes account of market developments. The boundaries between insurance companies and banks are becoming increasingly permeable. The mixed banking and insurance groups, the financial conglomerates, present the supervisory authorities with new challenges. The question arises as to who should assume the role of lead regulator in such groups and which sector-specific requirements must be met. Although the tasks and instruments of banks and insurance companies and thus also the risks in certain areas (e.g. in asset investment or credit insurance) are becoming more and more converging, a materially standardized supervision of financial conglomerates does not make sense. The monitoring of systemic risks and compliance with a certain level of liquidity are much more important in banking supervision than in the supervision of insurance companies. To this end, the supervisory authority's focus in insurance is on solvency, which is no less important for banks, and on the specific technical provisions and their investment. Nevertheless, the basic idea of "same business, same risk, same rules" is valuable and can serve as an approach for the regulatory treatment of risks. b) Conglomerate supervision: The creation of a legal basis for the group supervision of financial conglomerates is currently particularly urgent. Today, insurance supervision does not have an explicit legal basis for consolidated supervision either for financial conglomerates or for pure insurance groups. Today's supervision of the conglomerates existing in Switzerland is based on individual solutions. The supervisory concept for an institution is drawn up by the SFBC, FOPI and the conglomerate concerned and placed in the form of a ruling. The first injunction was issued by the SFBC in 1998 and has been applicable to Credit Suisse Group ever since. The second injunction was issued by FOPI in 2001 and concerns the Zurich Financial Services Group (ZFS). Conglomerate supervision has thus been given a concrete face. With the total revision of the and a partial revision of the Banking and Stock Exchange Act, Group supervision can be anchored for both insurance-dominated and bank-dominated conglomerates. In the proposed law, the individual solution is formally enshrined, as already applied today and proposed in the Zufferey report. The lead regulator of an insurance-dominated financial conglomerate is FOPI, the one for a bank-dominated financial conglomerate is the SFBC. As far as the various subgroups of the conglomerate are concerned, FOPI reviews the insurance part in accordance with insurance standards and the SFBC in accordance with banking standards. The proposal to introduce consolidated supervision for pure insurance groups is important. To date, FOPI only has individual supervision of insurance companies domiciled in Switzerland. To date, domestic or foreign insurance subsidiaries belonging to the Group have not been included in a consolidated risk assessment. The draft law and the dispatch should go to the Federal Council as soon as possible. c) Bank restructuring, liquidation and sweep protection: Based on the experience gained with the closure and subsequent liquidation of Spar- und Leihkasse Thun at the beginning of the nineties, the head of the Federal Department of Finance commissioned a group of experts chaired by Dr. Barbara Schaerer, Federal Finance Administration (FFA), in March 1999 to develop proposals for bank restructuring, bank liquidation and depositor protection. The aim was to remedy the weaknesses of the current bank liquidation law and to adapt the procedure to today's circumstances, to adopt provisions for the restructuring of a bank and to improve depositor protection. In its final report of February 2001, the Schaerer Expert Group proposes a completely revised and harmonised procedure for the reorganisation and winding-up of banks, the latter being closely linked to ordinary bankruptcy proceedings, with the exception of a number of special provisions. To simplify the liquidation, small stone deposits of up to CHF 5,000 are to be paid out immediately. Also new is the better protection of banking secrecy: In order to gain insight into the list of liabilities, a legitimate interest must be demonstrated. Probably the most important innovation of the design, however, is the remediation procedure. This can be compulsorily initiated by the SFBC and is based on the recognition that the liquidation of a bank destroys substance that could often be preserved by creditors. In the consultation process, it was not so much the law of reorganisation and liquidation that gave rise to discussions as the protection of depositors. There is agreement on the proposal to extend the increased bankruptcy privilege of CHF 30,000 per person to other types of accounts and to make deposit insurance mandatory for all banks, while at the same time a solution on self-regulation within the framework of the Swiss Bankers Association (SBA) should remain possible. On the other hand, the amount of the upper limit of deposit insurance, which so far amounts to CHF 1 billion and is necessary for reasons of system protection, is controversial. d) Banking audit: Audit firms are the SFBC's extended arm in auditing and supervising banks and securities dealers. The SFBC must check whether the auditors meet the strict requirements for recognition and whether they fulfil their task with independence, expertise and care. The events at the Geneva and Vaud Cantonal Banks, and not least the bankruptcy of Enron, have shown that poorly functioning auditors can burden the financial system. The SFBC intends to appoint the statutory audit firms working for it in the future systematic supervision. On the other hand, the banks are to be controlled even more intensively. For example, every financial institution should be subject to regular auditing by a second audit firm. These two innovations can be implemented immediately and largely within the framework of the existing legal bases. In the middle of this year, the interim report of the Auditing Working Group, which succeeded a group of experts chaired by Prof. Peter Nobel, is expected. One can hope that the report will lead to proposals for stricter rules on auditing at the legislative, regulatory and circular levels. e) NBG: Many provisions of the current National Bank Act (NBG) of 1953 are no longer up to date. A total audit was therefore undertaken. As far as financial market regulation is concerned, the new NBA contains an important innovation in particular: the SNB's monitoring function over payment and securities settlement systems will be anchored more explicitly than before at the legislative level. Switzerland is thus following an international trend towards formal legal anchoring of system monitoring. This trend reflects the increasing importance of monitoring payment and securities settlement systems in ensuring the stability of the financial system. The new NBG creates a basis for the SNB to impose requirements on those payment and securities settlement systems that pose risks to the stability of the financial system. The purpose of the rules is to help ensure that such technical equipment does not become a systemic risk. If an operator of a system does not comply with the requirements, he can be sanctioned administratively according to the draft law. The SNB coordinates its monitoring activities with the SFBC via the securities settlement systems. The complementary model is to be applied to the division of labour, with the Banking Commission supervising system operators and the SNB supervising the systems. The new NBG is expected to enter into force in 2004. 6. Schlussbemerkungen Changing framework conditions on the global financial markets have clearly shown that adjustments in global banking and financial market regulation are urgently needed. Various international bodies adopt universal regulatory standards to increase the stability and integrity of financial markets and to promote a level playing field among financial centres. Switzerland has A number of global players share responsibility for global financial market stability. Adjustments due to the implementation of international standards as well as current national challenges have made banking and financial market regulation a major construction site in Switzerland as well. Where does the SNB stand in this context? What role does it play in banking and financial market supervision? The SNB's task is to conduct monetary policy taking into account the overall interest of the country. In order to fulfil this task, it depends on a stable financial system and, in particular, on efficient and secure securities and payment systems. For this reason, the SNB takes care of the supervision of these systems. In this way, the SNB contributes to the soundness and performance of Switzerland's international financial centre. It does so without diminishing the responsibility of the other institutions. However, the SNB is always available as a competent partner, whether in the Basel Committee as part of the Swiss delegation together with the SFBC or in the expert groups that have become numerous over the last few years, which operate the construction site of banking and financial market regulation in Switzerland together with the various offices. Konzeptionelle und praktische Anforderungen an die Regulierung Die konomische Literatur liefert verschiedene Erklrungsanstze dafr, dass der Finanzsektor allgemein und die Banken im Speziellen einer besonderen regulatorischen Behandlung unterliegen. Der erste Ansatz betont die Gefahr der sogenannten systemischen Risiken. Banken sind grundstzlich potenziell illiquid. Der Grund dafr liegt in ihrer besonderen Bilanzstruktur. Banken finanzieren illiquide Bankaktiva, d.h. Kredite, durch kurzfristige liquide Depositeneinlagen. Treten Liquidittsprobleme auf, ist der bergang zur Insolvenz fliessend. Banken sind ber lnterbankenkredite und das Zahlungssystem eng miteinander verknpft. Die Schwierigkeiten eines einzelnen Institutes knnen sich daher auf ganze Gruppen von Banken oder gar auf das gesamte Bankensystem bertragen. Eine zweite Begrndung fr Regulierungen sttzt sich auf das Argument der Informationsasymmetrie. So sind z.B. die Kunden einer Bank ber deren Bonitt bzw. ber die Qualitt der von ihr angebotenen Finanzprodukte schlechter informiert als die Bank selbst. Sowohl zum Zeitpunkt des Vertragsabschlusses als auch danach sind sie kaum oder nur mit grossem Aufwand in der Lage, sich die ntigen Informationen zu verschaffen. Regulierung dient in diesem Fall als Ersatz fr den Wettbewerb, d.h. fr die berwachung der Mrkte bzw. der Anbieter und Produkte durch die Kunden. Die dritte Begrndung fr die im Vergleich zu anderen Sektoren strenge Regulierung des Finanzsektors ist politkonomischer Natur: Finanz- und Bankenkrisen schdigen weite Teile der Bevlkerung empfindlich. Um diese implizite Versicherungspflicht zu reduzieren, greift der Staat zur Prvention, d.h. zu den Mitteln von Regulierung und berwachung. Regulierung und berwachung sind jedoch nicht gratis. Aufwendungen entstehen auf Seiten der Behrden bzw. der brigen Trger der Regulierung und berwachung, dann aber auch auf Seiten der Kunden. Im Sinne einer Optimierungsregel sollte nur solange in den Markt eingegriffen werden, als der sogenannte net regulatory burden negativ ist bzw. solange der Nutzen der zustzlichen Regulierung deren Kosten bersteigt. Die Folge wre allerdings eine wesentliche Verteuerung der Finanzintermediation bzw. der Kreditfunktion des Bankensystems, was weder betriebs- noch volkswirtschaftlich Sinn machte. Das Regulierungsoptimum lsst sich in der Praxis nicht leicht bestimmen. Die Bestimmung des sog. net regulatory burden, d.h. der Differenz von Zusatznutzen und -kosten der Regulierung sowohl vor als auch nach Einfhrung einer Massnahme ist konzeptionell und empirisch schwierig. Alle Trger von Regulierungs- und berwachungsfunktionen bewegen sich stndig in einem Spannungsfeld von regulatory arbitrage einerseits und regulatory overkill andererseits. Segmenten in weniger oder berhaupt nicht regulierte Bereiche. Ein besonders aktuelles Beispiel ist der Handel mit Kreditrisiken, welche von regulierten Trgern auf solche bertragen werden, die der Aufsicht weniger unterworfen sind. Gegenmassnahmen provozieren regelmssig den Vorwurf des regulatory overkill. Die internationale Vernetzung der Mrkte, die wachsende Komplexitt des Rechts und die zum Teil als Antwort auf bestehende Regulierungen entwickelten, immer unbersichtlicheren Finanzprodukte wecken immer wieder neue Regulierungsbedrfnisse. Umfassendere Regeln erhhen die Kosten der Regulierung und Aufsicht, d.h. den net regulatory burden, und knnen zudem die Vorsicht der Akteure schmlern, wodurch sie zur Gefhrdung des Finanzsystems beitragen und sich als kontraproduktiv erweisen. Zwischen Regulatoren und berwachten findet gleichsam ein andauerndes Rennen zwischen Hase und Igel statt, wobei sich die Beteiligten in der Rolle des Hasen und des Igels stndig abwechseln. Ein solcher Wettlauf ist geeignet, die Funktionsfhigkeit der Mrkte zu behindern. Schliesslich wre es naiv zu glauben, Regulierung und berwachung knnten ohne Rcksicht auf die Konkurrenzfhigkeit der Akteure betrieben werden. Die konkrete Ausgestaltung der Regulierung und berwachung ist in Tat und Wahrheit sogar einer der wesentlichen Bestimmungsfaktoren der Attraktivitt jedes Finanzplatzes. Klare aufsichtsrechtliche Vorgaben sind wichtig, um die Integritt des Internationalen Finanzzentrums Schweiz sowohl zum Schutz der Sparer, Anleger und Versicherungsnehmer, als durch die Abweisung von Geldern krimineller Herkunft zu gewhrleisten. Es braucht sie zudem, um die Funktionsfhigkeit, Effizienz und Stabilitt des Finanzsystems auch langfristig sicherzustellen und um die internationale Wettbewerbsfhigkeit zu erhalten und zu strken. Die Regulatoren haben sich deshalb durchwegs an diese Ziele zu halten und trotz der damit verbundenen Schwierigkeiten alle potentiellen Massnahmen einer systematischen berprfung bezglich Kosten und Nutzen zu unterziehen. 3. Trends der Herausforderungen internationalen Diskussion und aktuelle Kurt Tucholsky schrieb schon in den zwanziger Jahren: Was die Weltwirtschaft angeht, so ist sie verflochten. Das gilt gerade auch heute noch - nicht zuletzt fr die Weltfinanzmrkte. Aus regionalen knnen nationale, aus nationalen knnen internationale Krisen werden. Umso verstndlicher ist es, dass sich die Diskussion der Banken- und Finanzmarktregulierung internationalisiert hat. Rein national ausgerichtete Regulierungen vermgen die globalisierten Finanzmrkte nicht vor Krisen zu schtzen. Eine erfolgreiche Regulierung und Aufsicht kann nur gewhrleistet werden, wenn sie der Verflechtung der Banken und Finanzmrkte Rechnung trgt. In den letzten Jahren hat sich die Finanzmarktaufsicht daher weiter internationalsiert. Wo frher die nationalen Unterschiede in der Priorittensetzung gross waren, glichen sich die Normen einander an. Durch Mindeststandards soll die internationale regulatorische Arbitrage, d.h. das legendre race to the bottom von Regulierung und Aufsicht, nach unten begrenzt werden. Als die einflussreichsten standard setting bodies wirken Gruppierungen staatlicher Aufsichtsbehrden. (Siehe Folie: Internationale Gremien fr Finanzmarktregulierung und aufsieht im Anhang). Der Basler Ausschuss hat das Ziel, die Kooperation zwischen den Bankenaufsichtsbehrden zu verbessern und eine wirksame, lnderbergreifende Bankenaufsicht zu ermglichen. Zu diesem Zweck beschloss der Ausschuss 1983 das sogenannte Basler Konkordat, welches die Zustndigkeit der Aufsichtsbehrden im Falle grenzberschreitender Bankaktivitten regelt. Zustzlich legte der Ausschuss Mindestanforderungen an die Aufsicht ber internationale Bankkonzerne und deren Auslandsniederlassungen fest. Der Basler Ausschuss setzt sich zudem systematisch fr allgemeingltige Aufsichtsrichtlinien und -standards des Bankgeschfts ein, insbesondere bezglich der Solvenz. Seine bekanntesten Standards sind in der Eigenkapitalvereinbarung aus dem Jahre 1988 enthalten. Zehn Jahre spter, 1998, hat der Basler Ausschuss beschlossen, diese umfassend zu revidieren. Die Institute werden de facto eingeladen, sich fr das fr sie kostengnstigste, gesamthaft jedoch nicht zwingend optimale Regime zu entscheiden. Dieses Phnomen wird beispielsweise bei den neuen Eigenmittelvorschriften befrchtet: Banken mit hohen Kreditrisiken werden sich eher fr den Standardansatz, jene mit verhltnismssig sicheren Krediten eher fr den nach Risikoart differenzierten Ansatz entscheiden. Zum anderen birgt Differenzierung auch die Gefahr von Wettbewerbsverzerrung in sich, wenn auf dem gleichen Markt ttige Akteure verschiedenen Aufsichtssystemen und somit auch verschiedenen Anforderungen unterliegen. Eng mit dem Aspekt der Differenzierung verbunden ist auch die Empfehlung der Expertengruppe Zufferey, die lntroducing Brokers, die Devisenhndler sowie die Unabhngigen Vermgensverwalter einer gesonderten Regulierung und Aufsicht zu unterstellen. Die Expertengruppe begrndet ihren Vorschlag insbesondere mit dem Kunden- resp. lnvestorenschutz, mit der Wettbewerbsneutralitt sowie mit dem Rufschutz des Internationalen Finanzzentrums Schweiz. Diese Begrndungen vermochten die SNB bisher jedoch noch nicht zu berzeugen. Das Argument des lnvestorenschutzes ist aus drei Grnden unzulnglich: Erstens sind die Risiken im Falle der Unabhngigen Vermgensverwalter solange gering, als die verwalteten Guthaben bei Banken im Namen der Kunden deponiert sind. Zweitens setzen sich die Kunden von Devisenhndlern zur Hauptsache aus institutionellen Investoren zusammen, weshalb das Schutzbedrfnis auch hier begrenzt ist. Schliesslich ist darauf hinzuweisen, dass Kunden ihre Geschfte auch ber einen der prudentiellen Aufsicht unterstellten Finanzintermedir - beispielsweise eine Bank - ttigen knnen. Den Kunden steht es somit frei, sich fr einen regulierten oder nicht-regulierten Anbieter zu entscheiden. Auch das Argument der Wettbewerbsneutralitt vermag nicht zu berzeugen, betrgt der Marktanteil der nicht-regulierten Finanzdienstleistungsanbieter doch hchstens 15 Prozent. Zu bedenken geben mchten wir hinsichtlich des Rufschutzes schliesslich, dass die Integritt des Finanzplatzes im ureigensten Interesse auch dieser nichtregulierten Kategorien steht: Sie haben als erste unter mglichen Reputationsproblemen zu leiden. Eine Regulierung zustzlicher Finanzdienstleister erscheint uns jedoch auch noch aus weiteren Grnden nicht vordringlich. Zum einen befrchten wir angesichts der Heterogenitt der betroffenen Finanzdienstleister vielfltige praktische Probleme in der berwachung. Zum anderen besteht die Gefahr einer berlastung der Aufsichtsbehrden. Diese knnte sich als kontraproduktiv in dem Sinne erweisen, als bisherige Aufgaben vernachlssigt und/oder die Umsetzung neuer, unseres Erachtens wichtigerer Anliegen (Konglomeratsaufsicht, Basel II) beeintrchtigt werden. Die Funktionsfhigkeit der Aufsicht muss in jedem Fall gewahrt bleiben. Mir ist bewusst, dass Ihr Verband diese Haltung der SNB nicht teilt. Lassen Sie mich dazu folgendes sagen: Ihre Unzufriedenheit mit der geltenden Regulierung der Effektenhndler ist nicht unverstndlich. Die aktuelle Situation wird dem Prinzip der Differenzierung Ihrer Meinung nach nicht vollstndig gerecht. Jedoch scheint mir, dass das eigentliche Problem nicht mittels einer Regulierung der Unabhngigen Vermgensverwalter gelst wird, sondern einen anderen Ansatz erfordert. Ein Bergsteiger erreicht den Gipfel auch nur dann schneller, wenn er das Gewicht des eigenen Gepcks reduziert, nicht jedoch, wenn er den anderen Bergsteigern Steine in den Rucksack legt. In diesem Sinne zielen die Forderungen Ihres Verbandes, die Regulierung der Effektenhndler insbesondere im Vergleich zu den Banken zu erleichtern, in die richtige Richtung. Dieses Anliegen kann aber losgelst von der Frage verfolgt werden, ob Unabhngige Vermgensverwalter einer Aufsicht zu unterstellen sind. Die nach der Auswertung der Stellungnahmen wichtigsten Empfehlungen des Schlussberichtes von Zufferey werden nun von der vom Bundesrat neu eingesetzten Expertengruppe unter der Leitung von Professor Ulrich Zimmerli zu einem Gesetzesentwurf ausgearbeitet. Dabei stehen die organisatorische Integration von Banken- und Versicherungsaufsicht sowie die Ausweitung der prudentiellen Aufsicht auf bisher nicht-regulierte Finanzdienstleistungsanbieter im Vordergrund. 5. Baustelle Schweiz: ein Reisebericht Bevor wir die Baustelle der laufenden regulatorischen Reformen in der Schweiz betreten, mchte ich einen Blick auf den Bauplan werfen (siehe Folie Baustelle Schweiz: laufende Reformvorhaben im Anhang). Die aufgelisteten Reformprojekte sind zum Teil bereits eine Antwort auf die Ergebnisse aus dem Schlussbericht der Expertengruppe Zufferey. Viele Reformen wurden jedoch schon vorher initiiert und warten auf ihre Vollendung. Zum Teil handelt es sich bei den Reformen um regulatorische Neubauten. Ein Beispiel dafr ist die Schaffung einer gesetzlichen Konglomeratsaufsicht. Oft wird aber nur umgebaut oder aufgestockt wie bei der Revision des Nationalbankgesetzes (NBG), und manchmal reichen kleinere Reparaturen, um die Schden zu beheben. Dies ist bei der Verbesserung des Revisionswesens der Fall. Wie Sie auf dem Bauplan sehen, sind die laufenden Reformvorhaben im Bereich Bankenund Finanzmarktregulierung zahlreich. ber alle zu berichten, wrde den Zeitrahmen meines Vortrags sprengen. Erlauben sie mir deshalb, ein paar besonders interessante Bauprojekte herauszugreifen. a) Integrierte Aufsicht: Eine der Empfehlungen aus dem Zufferey-Bericht ist die Schaffung einer integrierten Finanzmarktaufsicht. Konkret bedeutet dies eine organisatorische Zusammenfhrung der EBK mit dem BPV. Eine verstrkte Kooperation zwischen den Aufsichtsbehrden trgt der Marktentwicklung Rechnung. Die Grenzen zwischen Versicherungen und Banken werden immer durchlssiger. Die gemischten Bank- und Versicherungskonzerne, die Finanzkonglomerate, stellen die Aufsichtsbehrden vor neue Herausforderungen. Es stellt sich die Frage, wer bei solchen Konzernen die Rolle des Lead Regulators bernehmen soll und welche sektorspezifischen Anforderungen erfllt werden mssen. Obwohl sich die Aufgaben und Instrumente von Banken und Versicherungen und damit auch die Risiken in gewissen Bereichen (z.B. in der Vermgensanlage oder in der Kreditversicherung) immer mehr annhern, ist eine materiell durchgngig vereinheitlichte Aufsicht ber Finanzkonglomerate nicht sinnvoll. Die berwachung von Systemrisiken und die Einhaltung eines gewissen Liquidittsniveaus sind bei der Bankenaufsicht ungleich wichtiger als bei der Aufsicht ber Versicherungen. Dafr liegt bei den Versicherungen das Augenmerk der Aufsicht auf der auch bei den Banken nicht minder wichtigen Solvenz und den spezifischen versicherungstechnischen Rckstellungen sowie deren Anlage. Trotzdem ist der Grundgedanke des same business, same risk, same rules wertvoll und kann als Ansatz fr die regulatorische Behandlung von Risiken dienen. b) Konglomeratsaufsicht: Besonders dringend ist zur Zeit die Schaffung einer gesetzlichen Grundlage fr die Konzernaufsicht von Finanzkonglomeraten. Die Versicherungsaufsicht kennt heute nmlich weder fr Finanzkonglomerate noch fr reine Versicherungskonzerne eine explizite Rechtsgrundlage fr eine konsolidierte berwachung. Die heutige Aufsicht ber die in der Schweiz existierenden Konglomerate sttzt sich auf Einzellsungen. Das Aufsichtskonzept fr ein Institut wird jeweils von der EBK, dem BPV und dem betroffenen Konglomerat ausgearbeitet und in die Form einer Verfgung gebracht. Die erste Verfgung wurde 1998 von der EBK erlassen und gilt seither fr die Credit Suisse Group. Die zweite Verfgung erging 2001 vom BPV und betrifft die Zurich Financial Services Group (ZFS). Damit hat die Konglomeratsaufsicht ein konkretes Gesicht erhalten. Mit der Totalrevision des VAG und einer Teilrevision des Banken- und des Brsengesetzes kann die Konzernaufsicht sowohl fr versicherungsdominierte als auch fr bankdominierte Konglomerate verankert werden. Im vorgeschlagenen Gesetz wird die Einzellsung, wie bereits heute gehandhabt und im Zufferey-Bericht vorgeschlagen, formell verankert. Der Lead Regulator eines versicherungsdominierten Finanzkonglomerates wird das BPV, derjenige fr ein bankdominiertes Finanzkonglomerat die EBK. Was die verschiedenen Untergruppen des Konglomerats betrifft, so berprft das BPV den Versicherungsteil gemss Versicherungs- und die EBK den Bankenteil gemss Bankennormen. Von Bedeutung ist der Vorschlag, fr reine Versicherungskonzerne eine konsolidierte Aufsicht einzufhren. Bis heute hat das BPV nur die Einzelaufsicht ber in der Schweiz ansssige Versicherungen. Zum Konzern gehrende in- oder auslndische Versicherungstchter konnten bisher nicht in eine konsolidierte Risikobeurteilung einbezogen werden. Der Gesetzesentwurf und die Botschaft sollen so rasch als mglich an den Bundesrat gehen. c) Bankensanierung, -liquidation und Einfegerschutz: Aufgrund der Erfahrungen mit der Schliessung und nachfolgenden Liquidation der Spar- und Leihkasse Thun zu Beginn der Neunzigerjahre beauftragte der Vorsteher des Eidgenssischen Finanzdepartements im Mrz 1999 eine Expertengruppe unter dem Vorsitz von Frau Dr. Barbara Schaerer, Eidgenssische Finanzverwaltung (EFV), mit der Entwicklung von Vorschlgen zu Bankensanierung, Bankenliquidation und Einlegerschutz. Das Ziel bestand darin, die Schwchen des geltenden Bankenliquidationsrechts zu beheben und das Verfahren den heutigen Gegebenheiten anzupassen, Bestimmungen zur Sanierung einer Bank zu erlassen sowie den Einlegerschutz zu verbessern. Die Expertengruppe Schaerer schlgt in ihrem Schlussbericht vom Februar 2001 ein vollstndig berarbeitetes und vereinheitlichtes Verfahren zur Sanierung und Liquidation von Banken vor, wobei sich letzteres mit Ausnahme einiger besonderer Regelungen eng an das ordentliche Konkursverfahren anlehnt. Zur Vereinfachung der Liquidation sollen neu Kleinsteinlagen bis 5'000 Fr. sofort ausbezahlt werden. Neu ist auch der bessere Schutz des Bankgeheimnisses: Um Einblick ins Passivenverzeichnis zu erhalten, muss ein berechtigtes Interesse nachgewiesen werden. Die wohl wichtigste Neuerung des Entwurfs ist jedoch das Sanierungsverfahren. Dieses kann von der EBK zwangsweise eingeleitet werden und beruht auf der Erkenntnis, dass die Liquidation einer Bank Substanz vernichtet, die den Glubigern oft erhalten werden knnte. In der Vernehmlassung gab denn auch weniger das Sanierungs- und Liquidationsrecht als vielmehr der Einlegerschutz zu Diskussionen Anlass. Einigkeit besteht bezglich des Vorschlages, das erhhte Konkursprivileg von 30'000 Fr. pro Person auf weitere Kontenarten auszuweiten sowie die Einlagensicherung fr alle Banken obligatorisch zu erklren, wobei gleichzeitig eine Lsung ber Selbstregulierung im Rahmen der Schweizerischen Bankiervereinigung (SBVg) weiterhin mglich bleiben soll. Umstritten ist hingegen die Hhe der Obergrenze der Einlagensicherung, die bisher 1 Mrd. CHF betrgt und aus Grnden des Systemschutzes ntig ist. d) Bankenrevision: Revisionsgesellschaften sind der verlngerte Arm der EBK bei der Prfung und berwachung von Banken und Effektenhndlern. Die EBK hat zu berprfen, ob die Revisionsstellen den strengen Anerkennungsvoraussetzungen gengen und ob sie ihre Aufgabe mit Unabhngigkeit, Sachkunde und Sorgfalt erfllen. Die Ereignisse bei der Genfer und Waadtlnder Kantonalbank und nicht zuletzt der Konkursfall von Enron haben gezeigt, dass schlecht arbeitende Revisionsstellen das Finanzsystem belasten knnen. Die EBK will die fr sie ttigen gesetzlichen Revisionsgesellschaften in Zukunft systematisch beaufsichtigen. Andererseits sollen auch die Banken noch intensiver kontrolliert werden. So soll sich jedes Finanzinstitut regelmssig einer Prfung durch eine zweite Revisionsgesellschaft unterziehen lassen. Diese beiden Neuerungen lassen sich sofort und weitgehend im Rahmen der bestehenden Gesetzesgrundlagen umsetzen. Mitte dieses Jahres wird der Zwischenbericht der Arbeitsgruppe Revisionswesen erwartet, die einer Expertengruppe unter dem Vorsitz von Prof. Peter Nobel nachfolgte. Vom Bericht darf man sich Vorschlge zu strafferen Vorschriften zum Revisionswesen auf Gesetzes-, Verordnungs- und Rundschreibenstufe erhoffen. e) NBG: Viele Bestimmungen des geltenden Nationalbankgesetzes (NBG) aus dem Jahr 1953 sind nicht mehr zeitgemss. Eine Totalrevison wurde darum in Angriff genommen. Das neue NBG enthlt, was die Finanzmarktregulierung anbelangt, insbesondere eine wichtige Neuerung: Die berwachungsfunktion der SNB ber Zahlungs- und Effektenabwicklungssysteme wird expliziter als bisher auf Gesetzesstufe verankert. Damit folgt die Schweiz einem internationalen Trend zur formellen gesetzlichen Verankerung der Systemberwachung. Dieser Trend spiegelt die zunehmende Bedeutung der berwachung von Zahlungs- und Effektenabwicklungssystemen bei der Sicherung der Stabilitt des Finanzsystems. Das neue NBG schafft eine Grundlage fr die SNB, Anforderungen an jene Zahlungs- und Effektenabwicklungssysteme zu stellen, von denen Risiken fr die Stabilitt des Finanzsystems ausgehen. Durch die Vorschriften soll dazu beigetragen werden, dass solche technischen Einrichtungen nicht zu einem Systemrisiko werden. Hlt sich ein Betreiber eines Systems nicht an die Auflagen, kann er gemss Gesetzesentwurf verwaltungsrechtlich sanktioniert werden. Die SNB koordiniert ihre berwachungsttigkeit ber die Effektenabwicklungssysteme mit der EBK. Bei der Arbeitsteilung soll das Komplementrmodell zur Anwendung kommen, wobei die Bankenkommission die Institutsaufsicht ber Systembetreiber und die SNB die Aufsicht ber die Systeme bernimmt. Das neue NBG wird voraussichtlich 2004 in Kraft treten. 6. Schlussbemerkungen Vernderte Rahmenbedingungen auf den globalen Finanzmrkten haben deutlich vor Augen gefhrt, dass Anpassungen in der weltweiten Banken- und Finanzmarktregulierung dringend notwendig sind. Verschiedene internationale Gremien erlassen allgemeingltige Regulierungsstandards, um die Stabilitt und Integritt der Finanzmrkte zu erhhen und um die Wettbewerbsgleichheit unter den Finanzzentren zu frdern. Die Schweiz hat als Sitzstaat einiger Global Players eine Mitverantwortung fr die weltweite Finanzmarktstabilitt. Anpassungen aufgrund der Umsetzung internationaler Standards sowie aktuelle, nationale Herausforderungen liessen die Banken- und Finanzmarktregulierung auch in der Schweiz zu einer Grossbaustelle werden. Wo steht die SNB in diesem Geschehen? Welche Rolle spielt sie in der Banken- und Finanzmarktaufsicht? Die SNB hat die Aufgabe, die Geld- und Whrungspolitik unter Bercksichtigung des Gesamtinteresses des Landes zu fhren. Um diese Aufgabe erfllen zu knnen, ist sie auf ein stabiles Finanzsystem und insbesondere auf effiziente und sichere Wertschriften- und Zahlungssysteme angewiesen. Aus diesem Grund kmmert sich die SNB um die Aufsicht ber diese Systeme. Die SNB trgt auf diese Weise zur Soliditt und Leistungsfhigkeit des Internationalen Finanzzentrums Schweiz bei. Sie tut dies, ohne dabei die Verantwortung der brigen Trger zu schmlern. Immer steht die SNB aber auch als kompetente Partnerin zur Verfgung, sei es im Basler Ausschuss als Teil der schweizerischen Delegation gemeinsam mit der EBK oder sei es in den ber die letzten Jahre hinweg zahlreich gewordenen Expertengruppen, welche die Baustelle der Banken- und Finanzmarktregulierung in der Schweiz gemeinsam mit den verschiedenen Amtsstellen betreiben. Title: An upswing with risks  Some reflections on the current economic development
text: An upswing with risks - Reflections on the current economic development Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Annual General Meeting of the Association of Swiss Industrial Holding Companies (Industrie-Holding) on 18 June 2002 at the Hotel Bellevue Palace, Bern The Swiss economy, and industry in particular, can look back on a difficult year. Admittedly, there is much to suggest that the change for the better has now occurred. However, the recovery process could be slower than we had hoped for six months ago. Despite some bright spots, skepticism and uncertainty still prevail in many industries. I would like to take this opportunity today to discuss the economic situation, the outlook and the risks. In doing so, I would also like to show you the SNB's options for action. Finally, we want to address a number of structural aspects of economic development that are valid beyond the course of the economy and that we must not lose sight of. 1. Global economic development Especially with regard to Switzerland, the global economic environment is of crucial importance. The economic development in our country is not nearly as dependent on any single influencing factor as on economic activity abroad. Acceleration In 2000, the global economy was doing better than it has been for a long time. Driven by the boom in information technology, but also by impressive progress in other industries, growth in OECD countries reached an annual average of almost 4%. Developing and emerging countries recorded growth of almost 6%. The volume of world trade expanded twice as much. In the OECD region, productivity growth, falling unit labour costs and remarkably low inflation were observed. At the top was the American economy, which expanded very strongly. However, many other countries also showed high growth rates. This coincidence of technological impulses on the supply side, massive investment and the hope of an almost insatiable demand for the new products was unique in the post-war period and is reminiscent of distant developments such as the railway boom in the 19th century. However, such comparisons also aroused some unease. Many central banks were worried about when and how the The investment boom would end and the speculative bubble on the stock markets would burst and did not lack warnings. Slowdown In the course of 2000, when OECD growth was strong at 3.7%, the first signs of slowing down became apparent. In the following year, the real gross domestic product of the OECD countries grew by only 1%. The turnaround in investment was particularly marked. After rising by a good 5% annually from 1996 to 2000, real gross capital formation fell by 1% in 2001. what was surprising was not only the rapid economic turnaround, but also the fact that almost all countries were similarly affected. In retrospect, the cause of the synchronous turnaround is obvious. On the one hand, the primary factor was the built up investment and capital overhang. However, a number of negative events are also partly to blame, which affected the majority of the countries together: In 1999, the price of crude oil tripled. Shortly thereafter, central banks tightened their monetary policy to prevent inflationary overheating. A good two years ago, the stock market boom ended. Finally, with the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001 came another shock, the long-term political, economic and possibly also military consequences of which can hardly be estimated. At the end of the nineties, the whole world had hoped for a "soft landing" of the American economy, whereby it was more intuitive than logically clear what exactly was meant by a soft-landing economy. The landing we finally experienced was perhaps not quite as gentle as hoped. In view of the considerable turbulence that has shaken the global economy in the last two years, however, it has been somewhat successful. While the OECD's market economies have generated an important shock themselves with the technology boom and its subsequent bursting, they have weathered these and additional exogenous shocks with remarkable flexibility and robustness. One could not assume in advance that there would not be a real recession last year. In retrospect, it was helpful that the monetary policy of the later 90s remained disciplined towards price stability. The central banks raised their key interest rates after the millennium transition in view of the threat of overheating tendencies, but they did not have to initiate painful braking manoeuvres anywhere. Inflation remained moderate and inflation expectations low. In order that the prerequisites were met to ease monetary policy again soon and thus to support the economy substantially. It is precisely this latest economic experience that should dispel existing doubts: price stability aimed at with priority and sustainably achieved pays off. Not only with regard to the social and economic damage of inflationary undesirable developments. In addition, price stability and low inflation expectations create the conditions for monetary policy to react to cyclically-relevant shocks with some chances of success and thus make a useful contribution to economic stabilization. Risks The global economy probably overcame the doldrums at the beginning of this year. The American economy grew strongly in the first quarter, while most other industrialized countries at least found their way back to a flat growth path. However, the recovery we expect this year is not broadly based. It is still on weak feet and is exposed to a variety of old and new dangers. One of the old dangers is the high external imbalance between the US and the rest of the world. The US current account deficit grew rapidly at the end of the nineties and is likely to be too high in the long run with the achieved size of over 4% of the gross domestic product. Its correction requires a weakening of the dollar, which has begun, but the end of which is difficult to estimate. It makes American goods more competitive with European and Japanese products, stimulates growth in the US and helps reduce the trade deficit. The main question - and increasingly the main concern - is how quickly and sharply the dollar will continue to weaken. A gentle decline in the dollar over the next few months would have more positive than detrimental consequences for the global economy. European exports, for example, would probably become more expensive. At the same time, however, inflationary pressures would also ease somewhat, which in turn would increase the ECB's room for manoeuvre. A sharp fall in the dollar, on the other hand, would bring a rude awakening, especially for Europe, which has been accustomed to the expensive dollar in recent years. The export sector would receive a severe dampener - Europe would lose its most important pillar of growth. Finally, for Switzerland, there would also be a risk of excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro. We will have to come back to that. Certainly, there are always risks. The only question is how likely they are to occur. To this day, the general consensus again expects a "soft landing", this time with regard to the American dollar. We all love this scenario. But we must also keep an eye on the other, inconvenient case. An additional aspect of risk is that the American economy may take longer to return to its old form than is commonly assumed. The end of the technology and investment boom has hit many companies hard. The pleasingly robust consumer activity of private households in most countries stands in marked contrast to the financial and earnings situation of many companies that have been hit hard by the consequences of the setbacks. In addition, serious deficiencies in corporate governance, such as those revealed by the Enron scandal, shook confidence in the transparency of the capital markets and unsettled investors in the long term. In addition, the consequences of September 11 are difficult to assess. Both factors dampen the willingness to invest and consumer confidence. They could prevent the US from playing the role of a powerful economic engine. Europe would have to bury the hope of being able to jump on the American economic train again. This makes it all the more important for our continent to make its own efforts to overcome the economic downturn and to tackle the delicate structural reforms without which Europe cannot achieve its own growth power in the longer term. This brings me to Switzerland. 2. Development in Switzerland Against the backdrop of the weak global economy, the Swiss economy was also unable to exploit its potential growth of an estimated 2%. From the second quarter of 2001, it stagnated and unemployment rose again. The decline in business investment was massive. However, declining exports of capital goods and intermediate products had a greater impact on domestic production. Last year, real gross domestic product rose by 1.3%. Growth was thus slightly lower than the average for EU countries. Thanks to the strong However, growing private consumption and the resilient construction industry were significantly higher than, for example, in Germany, our most important trading partner. The Swiss industrial sector, with its high share of capital goods, felt the economic slump much more strongly than the economy as a whole. Significant parts of the industry were marginalized or even plunged into recession. The machinery industry and its suppliers were severely affected. However, companies active in the field of new technologies also had to accept sometimes dramatic losses in sales. Other parts of the industry - such as the chemical industry and the consumer-related sectors - developed and continue to develop satisfactorily to well. Hardly anyone denies that the problems were largely due to the global economic slowdown and the slump in investment activity. An additional complication, however, was the higher valuation of the Swiss franc. It adversely affected price competitiveness, especially in industry, and largely demanded high margin sacrifices. Exchange rate and monetary policy Today, the Swiss franc is around 5% higher against the euro in real terms than it was two years ago. Using the export-weighted real exchange rate, industry had to cope with an appreciation of almost 7%. Even if the extent cannot be compared with that of the mid-nineties, the appreciation surge came at a very bad time and triggered the greatest fears in industrial circles. The SNB was unequivocally called upon to declare war on the franc bull market. We are well aware of the problems of the export industry, given the importance of this sector. Nevertheless, it was and still is important to keep an eye on the overall economic view. What have we done? In March a year ago, we lowered the target range for the three-month Libor by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.75-3.75%, thus reacting - notabenely earlier than other central banks - to the impending economic slowdown. After the terrorist attacks of 11 September, the situation on the foreign exchange markets deteriorated and the Swiss franc came under strong appreciation pressure. Within a week, we reduced the three-month Libor by another percentage point. In December and again at the beginning of May of this year, we lowered the key interest rate again by half a percentage point each to finally 1.25%. With our interest rate hikes - but also on many other occasions - we made no secret of the fact that we were concerned about the upward pressure on the Swiss franc. With our monetary policy, we have tried to respond to this change. To illustrate this, it is worth recalling the three elements of our monetary policy concept: The first element obliges us to conduct a stability-oriented monetary policy, specifically to keep inflation below 2%. The second element, the medium-term inflation forecast, is the guardrail on which we orient ourselves and assess the need for monetary policy action. The third element consists of the target band for the three-month Libor, with which we communicate our monetary policy decisions. You may be wondering where there is room for the exchange rate? In fact, it does not occur explicitly, not because no central bank can pursue the objective of price stability and that of a stable exchange rate at the same time. However, this does not change the importance of the exchange rate for monetary policy. Especially since in a small, open economy, a real appreciation of the currency dampens the economy and thus tends to have a deflationary effect. Conversely, a lower valuation is expected to have stimulating effects and thus price-rising effects. This correlation is clearly expressed in the forecast of the economy and the development of inflation and thus influences our monetary policy. The discussion of the exchange rate situation and the playing through of different exchange rate scenarios is therefore an important element of any monetary policy assessment. Not least with regard to the exchange rate, we do not set a point target for our key interest rate, but a target range of one percentage point. This band gives us the opportunity to react to disruptions in the money and foreign exchange markets in the short term. We made use of this possibility shortly before Easter, when we let the three-month Libor slide into the lower range of the target range in view of the renewed strong appreciation tendency. Experience has shown that changes in key interest rates cannot control an exchange rate with viable reliability because the relationship between the interest rate differential and the exchange rate is very vague. Rather, our intention was to react to the restrictive upward pressure with a stimulating interest rate stimulus in order to compensate for the economy. We decided to cut interest rates in the belief that there was room for manoeuvre in terms of maintaining price stability. On the use of interventions on the foreign exchange market we refrain from doing so, not for reasons of principle, but in the opinion that this instrument, which experience has shown to be associated with high uncertainties, should only be used in rare exceptional cases. This makes intact structural prerequisites for entrepreneurial ability to act all the more important. Structural aspects The economy - the Swiss export sector - has proven for many years that it can hold its own on the world market despite occasional problems with exchange rates. There were probably relocations of production abroad, and Swiss direct investment by industry abroad increased sharply in the nineties. However, this was generally not due to exchange rate developments. For example, the high costs for wages and domestic intermediate consumption in international comparison were more significant. Direct investments abroad also often served to consolidate the market position and open up new sales markets. This is often a necessary addition to Switzerland as a business location and an indispensable effort to concentrate production in our country on value-added-intensive activities. Certainly, our export economy benefits from significant locational advantages, especially with regard to the labour market, fiscal conditions, infrastructure and, last but not least, the low cost of capital. These advantages have made it easier for it to increase its productivity - even in a European comparison - and to be at the forefront of technology in many areas. This is the inevitable result of state restrictions on the one hand, but above all of numerous private restrictions of competition. It may be that the comparatively weakly developed will to compete can be explained by special historical and economic-cultural conditions. The fact is that we have to pay a substantial price for this in the form of considerable sacrifices of prosperity. In Switzerland, domestic goods are not only much more expensive in individual areas, but on average. For the export industry, this is undoubtedly the most important competitive disadvantage. This is particularly true of tourism, which receives almost all intermediate consumption domestically. The higher inflation not only at the moment, but in the long-term trend, is also likely to be one of the reasons why the Swiss franc has tended to appreciate in real terms, in the 80s and 90s by an average of 0.6% per year against the Deutschmark. Everything indicates that this trend against the euro will continue. It is helpful that the problem of the lack of competition at home has recently been addressed several times. The International Monetary Fund has been pointing this out in its annual monitoring of the Swiss economy and economic policy for years. The growth report recently published by the FDEA argues in the same direction. And recently, the OECD has also placed some emphasis on this in its report on the Swiss economy. It seems highly necessary to achieve the revitalisation of the internal market, which began in the nineties, with increased commitment. After this detour into the area of structural framework conditions, I come - in the final part - to some considerations on the economic outlook. 3. Outlook In the OECD, the economic downturn was probably overcome at the beginning of this year, but the recovery is not yet broadly based. A significant part of the turnaround was due to the end of destocking, thus to a naturally eroding impulse. This created an important prerequisite for the start of industrial activity. However, there was still little sign of a recovery in investment activity. After the strong start in the first quarter, we have to expect the American economy to grow more leisurely in the further course of the year. In Europe, the economy was still on a weak footing. The economic stimulus in the first quarter came from exports, while domestic demand stagnated. Growth in Switzerland was also still weak in the 1st quarter. The continued very robust private consumption and stable construction activity were encouraging. As expected or feared, the development of investment in equipment and exports was characterised by weakness. This is unlikely to have changed much in the current quarter. It was and is still too early for an improvement in the labour market. In recent months, positive signals have increased. In the industrial sector, business stabilized at a low level. Demand also seems to have been consolidating for two months. Both the domestic and export industries reported an increase in orders in March and April. At the same time, business expectations regarding demand and production have improved once again. As in December last year, we expect the Swiss economy to grow by an annual average of around 1%. This is only little at first glance. To achieve such a result, the upswing would have to gain momentum in the second half of the year and the economy would have to grow around 2% at the end of the year. Only then is the demand for labour likely to pick up again and unemployment to slowly decline. Against the background of this economic assessment and on the basis of a non-problematic inflation forecast, we decided last Friday to leave the key interest rate unchanged at 1'X percent. But we are and remain aware of the risks mentioned in the introduction to the OECD. For the Swiss economy, much depends on how quickly and how strongly the European economic environment will consolidate in the coming months. With increased attention - and to this day not without concern - we follow the economy in Germany. The biggest risk factor is undoubtedly the exchange rate in an environment that is not immune to new waves of risk aversion. But the economic development can also surprise us in a positive way, as we are experiencing in the months after the millennium change. have. We remain ready to act in the service of our mandate to ensure price stability and to make our contribution to stabilising the economy within the scope of the room for manoeuvre thus provided.
