Ausblick In der OECD konnte die konjunkturelle Flaute vermutlich zu Beginn dieses Jahres berwunden werden, aber die Erholung ist noch nicht breit abgesttzt. Ein bedeutender Teil der Wende war auf das Ende des Lagerabbaus zurckzufhren, somit auf einen naturgemss erodierenden Impuls. Damit wurde zwar eine wichtige Voraussetzung fr das Anspringen der Industriekonjunktur geschaffen. Von einer Erholung der Investitionsttigkeit war aber noch kaum etwas zu spren. Nach dem krftigen Auftakt im ersten Quartal mssen wir damit rechnen, dass die amerikanische Wirtschaft im weiteren Verlauf des Jahres gemchlicher wachsen wird. In Europa stand die Konjunktur noch auf schwachen Beinen. Die konjunkturellen Impulse gingen im ersten Quartal von den Exporten aus, whrend die Binnennachfrage stagnierte. Auch in der Schweiz fiel das Wachstum im 1. Quartal noch schwach aus. Erfreulich waren der weiterhin sehr robuste private Konsum und die stabile Bauttigkeit. Wie erwartet bzw. befrchtet war die Entwicklung bei den Ausrstungsinvestitionen und bei den Exporten durch Schwche geprgt. Daran drfte sich auch im laufenden Quartal wenig gendert haben. Auch fr eine Besserung am Arbeitsmarkt war und ist es absehbar noch zu frh. In den letzten Monaten mehrten sich positive Signale. Im Industriesektor stabilisierte sich der Geschftsgang auf einem tiefen Niveau. Gemss den Umfragen der Konjunkturforschungsstelle an der ETH vermochte die Industrie ihren Auftragsbestand zu halten und der Abbau der Fertigfabrikatelager kam zum Stillstand. Seit zwei Monaten scheint sich auch die Nachfrage zu festigen. Sowohl die Binnen- als auch die Exportindustrie meldeten im Mrz und April einen Anstieg der Bestellungen. Gleichzeitig haben sich die Unternehmererwartungen bezglich der Nachfrage und der Produktion nochmals verbessert. Wir gehen -wie schon im Dezember letzten Jahres - davon aus, dass die schweizerische Wirtschaft im Jahresdurchschnitt um etwa 1% wachsen wird. Dies ist nur auf den ersten Blick wenig. Um ein solches Ergebnis zu erreichen, msste der Aufschwung im zweiten Halbjahr an Kraft gewinnen und die Wirtschaft am Ende des Jahres gegen 2% wachsen. Erst dann drfte auch die Nachfrage nach Arbeitskrften wieder anziehen und die Arbeitslosigkeit langsam zurckgehen. Wir haben auf dem Hintergrund dieser konjunkturellen Lagebeurteilung und auf der Basis einer nicht problematischen Inflationsprognose letzten Freitag beschlossen, den Leitzins bei 1'X Prozent unverndert zu belassen. Aber wir sind und bleiben uns der einleitend fr die OECD erwhnten Risiken bewusst. Fr die schweizerische Wirtschaft hngt besonders viel davon ab, wie rasch und wie stark sich das europische Konjunkturumfeld in den kommenden Monaten festigen wird. Mit erhhter Aufmerksamkeit - und bis heute nicht ohne Sorge - verfolgen wird die Konjunktur in Deutschland. Den grssten Risikofaktor bildet ohne Zweifel der Wechselkurs in einem Umfeld, das vor neuen Wellen der Risikoaversion nicht gefeit ist. Aber die wirtschaftliche Entwicklung kann uns auch im Positiven berraschen, wie wir das in den Monaten nach dem Milleniumswechsel erlebt haben. Wir bleiben handlungsbereit im Dienste unseres Auftrags, Preisstabilitt zu sichern und im Rahmen des damit vorgegebenen Handlungsspielraums unseren Beitrag zur Stabilisierung der Konjunktur zu leisten.

Title: Six months of living with the euro
text: Six months of living together with the euro Presentation by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Tuttlingen Economic Forum 25 June 2002 Introduction Dear Sir or Madam, I am very pleased to discuss with you this evening the issue of the euro from the point of view of a neighbour who, as an outsider, is affected in many ways by the European internal market and in particular by the introduction of the euro. Ten years ago, you invited the Swiss National Bank as a guest. The then President of the National Bank, Dr. Markus Lusser, spoke on the subject of "The Monetary Integration of Europe - Some Considerations from a Swiss Perspective." At that time, the EU was still called the EC. The common European currency was only on paper, in the Union Treaties of Maastricht. Switzerland was about to vote on accession to the European Economic Area, the EEA. Accession would have allowed Switzerland to participate in the European single market, which became a reality at the beginning of 1993. At the time, Markus Lusser put forward a resounding yes to this first step towards Switzerland's integration. As a central bank politician, he judged him primarily from the point of view of monetary policy. He attached great importance to the fact that the independence of Swiss monetary policy would not be affected by accession to the EEA. At that time, he was critical of Switzerland's full accession to the EC. In his view, he would have assumed either participation in the European Monetary System and the exchange rate mechanism of the EMS or later in the European Monetary Union. With regard to the planned monetary union, he doubted whether the member states would actually grant the central monetary authority the independent status that is essential for a stability-oriented monetary policy and thus for the prosperity of a monetary union. Ten years later, the European currency landscape is undergoing fundamental change. The European Central Bank enjoys a high reputation as an independent central bank and, together with the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan, is one of the three leading central banks in the world. Within a very short time, the euro has gained great importance as an investment currency and is still on the rise. For half a year, it has also been the physical means of payment in 12 EU countries. Ten years ago, Switzerland rejected accession to the European Economic Area. However, contacts with the EU have not diminished as a result. At the beginning of June this year, the seven bilateral agreements with the EU will enter into force after difficult and long negotiations. trodden. This treaty links Switzerland more closely than ever with the European Union. The introduction of the euro as a common means of payment affects our country in many ways. I believe that the euro will also be of benefit to us. Let me elaborate on this. I'll start with the benefits of the euro for the euro countries and look at what the European single currency can mean for Switzerland. In the third part, I would like to briefly address the exchange rate problem, a topic that is always controversial in Switzerland. I shall conclude my remarks with a brief assessment. 1. Benefits of the euro for euro area countries The advantages of a common currency are obvious - I would not really have to calculate them for you. Exchange rate risk has fallen sharply since the introduction of the euro. Today, only about 10% of the gross domestic product of the euro countries is accounted for by exports outside the European currency area. The costs for exchanging currencies and for hedging exchange rate risks were thus massively reduced. In one fell swoop, the European price landscape has also become much more transparent. The changeover to the euro was associated with great costs. Also, probably not everyone has become accustomed to the new prices and is still quietly converting euro amounts into Deutschmarks. Trouble - perhaps also fears - has apparently also caused here and there the price increases made when the euro cash was introduced. This bad memory is likely to fade quickly. Because these are certainly one-off price adjustments and not the prelude to a new round of inflation. Thanks to the stability-oriented monetary policy of the monetary authorities in Frankfurt, the euro is and will remain a stable currency in value! What has fundamentally changed with the creation of a common currency is the way the economy adapts to changes - to disruptions. European companies have indeed gotten rid of a significant part of the exchange rate risk. However, they increasingly have to deal with the price risk. As had to be expected, the economy in the various countries and regions of the large and diverse euro area is not developing synchronously. Companies are therefore exposed to different cost developments. Since the If exchange rates can no longer be adjusted, the adjustment must necessarily take place via a change in margins. This requires a significant degree of adaptability from companies. Those who are unable to do so lose competitiveness vis-a-vis providers from other European countries. But this is not just a side effect of the euro. The promotion of the movement of goods, services and capital within the EU is one of the main benefits hoped for from the introduction of a common currency. The euro is intended to complete the European single market, increase the performance of the European economy and ultimately act as a catalyst for The political integration of Europe. The positive impulses that the euro is supposed to generate will come from increased price transparency on the European market, a trend that is further supported by modern information technologies. However, it can also be expected that European small and medium-sized enterprises will increasingly operate across countries and that larger companies will re-optimize their structures. The bottom line is that this should make the European economy more innovative, efficient and productive. However, such a transformation does not happen overnight. The introduction of the euro has created a favourable monetary environment. In order for competitive forces to develop and, last but not least, to achieve the hoped-for employment gains, more is needed. The many government and private regulations must also be critically reviewed with regard to their suitability for growth. For example, it is an illusion to believe that the reason for the high performance of the American economy lies in the dollar. Their roots lie in the rules of economic policy, which leave much more room for market forces than is the case here in Europe - including Switzerland. We Europeans like to refer to the disadvantages of the American system, such as the large income differences or the less developed state social security net compared to Europe. These may be disadvantages that we in Europe do not want to accept. On the other hand, the costs of social security on our continent have become so high that financing is difficult in the long term. There is therefore no way around an increase in productivity, an increase in economic dynamism. As I said, this applies to both the euro area and Switzerland. 2. The euro from Switzerland's point of view Let me move on to the euro from a Swiss point of view. I would like to anticipate a result of my deliberations. If there is one thing I hope for from the euro for Switzerland, it is this: it should also become a catalyst for growth- and innovation-friendly economic policy in our country. What can Switzerland expect from the euro? In the summer of a year ago, we commissioned our regional economic observers to explore the mood in the Swiss economy before the introduction of the EuroBargeld. We were particularly interested in whether the companies had prepared sufficiently for the changeover, whether their IT, accounting and calculation systems were suitable for euros. We were reasonably reassured afterwards. In fact, the introduction of euro cash also went smoothly for Switzerland. What struck us in our exploratory talks was the generally positive attitude of Swiss companies towards the euro. Why is this? Some reasons for this are obvious. In some respects, the euro has also simplified the lives of Swiss companies. It is true that there is additional effort, for example in the form of double accounting in Swiss francs and in euros, which has become necessary in many companies. Nor does the Swiss entrepreneur benefit from the elimination of exchange rate risk, as the Swiss franc can fluctuate against the euro. With the replacement of 11 foreign currencies by a single one, however, foreign currency management and thus also the management of currency risks was noticeably simplified. And finally, the incalculable risks of the former European Monetary System, which were a major source of disruption for Switzerland in the nineties, have also disappeared. On the other hand, companies assume that the Swiss franc will continue to lose importance as a billing currency in Swiss-European business. This is a disadvantage in that a larger proportion of the proceeds will be generated in foreign currency and must therefore be hedged by Swiss exporters. However, this fact is of secondary importance for price competitiveness. In the event of an appreciation of the Swiss franc, an exporter who invoices in Swiss francs has comparable problems. He is quickly forced to lower the swiss franc price if he does not want to lose his customers. The exchange rate thus remains unchanged for Swiss Companies have a potential source of interference, regardless of whether invoices are made in Swiss francs or in euros. 2. 1 Does the euro displace the Swiss franc as a means of payment? One of the first questions that arose in Switzerland in connection with the introduction of the euro was whether the large euro would not automatically displace the small franc as a means of payment. There is no question that the euro will circulate in Switzerland as a means of payment. He is already doing so. In the run-up to the introduction of euro cash, many companies, including the major retailers, have announced that they would also accept euro cash. What had long been common in tourism centers and border regions - paying with foreign currencies - thus expanded to other areas. Price addresses in Francs and Euros are already a familiar sight. Initial experience shows that the euro is hardly used more frequently as a means of payment than the D-Mark, the franc, the schilling or the lira used to be. The main reason is certainly the usually very unfavorable exchange rate, which is charged in each case. Over time, the euro may become more important than the previous European currencies. However, this is unlikely to cause any problems, not even for Swiss monetary policy. With reassurance, we have also noticed that the Swiss franc is still easily accepted as a means of payment in foreign countries close to the border - but also at a less attractive exchange rate! Another question is whether the euro will displace the franc as a means of payment in Switzerland. From our point of view, there is no reason for this. The Swiss franc enjoys a high level of trust in Germany. It has always had a high value stability - so why use a different currency? Sometimes one hears that in view of the high Swiss franc exchange rate, export companies are thinking of paying wages in euros, in other words passing on the exchange rate risk to the employees. This is unrealistic. The social partners would rightly not accept this. Currency risk - against the euro or against the dollar and other currencies - is one of the corporate risks. Quite apart from this, many Swiss companies benefit from the strong Franc in the form of low interest rates and cheap imports. This does not change the fact that the exchange rate can cause concern for companies and that the SNB has to consider how best to respond to the exchange rate problems. 2.2 Does the euro endanger the Swiss franc as an international investment currency? In connection with the euro, the question also arises as to the future of the Swiss franc as an international investment and issuing currency. The Swiss franc has lost some of its importance on the international capital markets in recent years. For example, the use of the Swiss franc in the issuance of debt securities has been declining for some time. We basically interpret this as normalization at a time when other fully convertible currencies have established themselves in addition to the Swiss franc and the international monetary system has generally become safer. However, the explosive emergence of a broad and highly liquid euro bond market may have further weakened the position of the Swiss franc. Even today, however, the Swiss franc is still one of the 5 main currencies for international bond issues, after the US dollar, the euro, the yen and the British pound. We expect it to continue to play an important role as a diversification currency in international portfolios because it still has some attractive attributes. There is no question, however, that the Swiss franc is far behind the euro. The euro is the second most important investment and reserve currency after the American dollar. For example, the Swiss National Bank now holds most of its foreign exchange reserves, 46%, in the form of euro investments. The euro is also of great importance in foreign exchange transactions. In addition, many countries have started to peg their currencies to the euro. The euro will undoubtedly also intensify competition in the European financial system. It is to be expected that there will be further bank mergers and consolidations in Europe. For the Swiss financial centre, this also means increased competition and increased pressure to increase its own performance. Let me move on to the impact of the euro on the Swiss internal market. 2.3 The euro as a catalyst for a more dynamic Swiss internal market? Switzerland has a highly productive export sector with many leading international companies. Despite the high productivity of our export companies, however, the Swiss economy has grown much more slowly than the Average of OECD countries. It is probably possible that the growth gap will be reported as too large for a number of reasons. However, this does not change the fact that the domestic price level is much higher than, for example, in our neighbouring countries - including Germany. Numerous calculations show that this is the case, but above all the fact that in Switzerland there is lively shopping tourism across the border. One of the main reasons for the high cost of living in Switzerland is likely to be the lack of competition in the domestic economy. Over the decades, a dense network of state and private barriers to competition has emerged. It paralyzes the willingness of the domestic sector to innovate. As a result, the productivity of this sector is low compared to the export sector. Today, the high prices for domestic intermediate consumption represent an important weakness in intra-European location competition and represent a considerable burden for export-oriented industries. It is true that in the nineties some promising measures were taken to renew the internal market in a market economy. These include the creation of the Internal Market Act, the revision of the Antitrust Act, the liberalisation of the telecommunications market and the reorientation of agricultural policy. However, the momentum seems to have diminished in the meantime. It also shows that both the Internal Market act and the Antitrust Act need to be made more effective. The deregulation of markets involves sacrifices. In some sectors, for example, agriculture - there have already been losers. On the other hand, the economy must be understood as a dynamic entity. If we maintain the status qua, this protects the acquis of today's actors. However, those who are new to the labour market do not have much of it. They would be able and willing to find their way in a new environment. Certainly, one must not forget the victims of structural change. Unlike many European countries, Switzerland has a flexible and efficient labour market. The balance between the important concern of worker protection and the needs of a dynamic market environment is quite reasonable in our country. Thanks to this flexibility, it should be easier in Switzerland than in other countries to change structures and quickly reintegrate the losers of structural change into the labour market. But what does all this have to do with the euro? An important impulse to put the revitalisation of the internal market on the political agenda in the nineties was the creation of the European internal market. In order to ensure the competitiveness of Swiss companies against this newly emerging huge market, we had to go over the books in Switzerland. The euro will raise awareness of the need for structural changes in the Swiss internal market. Swiss companies will also feel the effects of better price transparency and increased competitive pressure in the euro area. If the internal market does not adapt, some sectors will fall behind their European competitors. This brings me to the last part, to the risks associated with the euro for Switzerland. First and foremost is the exchange rate. 3. The euro and exchange rate risk As mentioned, our survey on the euro last summer revealed an open, confident attitude of Swiss companies towards the euro. Above all, the advantages of the new currency were emphasized, there were hardly any negative voices. In part, this positive mood undoubtedly reflected the hitherto rather calm development of the Swiss franc against the euro. The fears expressed at the beginning of the monetary union that the euro could lose substantial value against the Swiss franc did not seem to come true. As you may have noticed, the Swiss franc has appreciated against the euro in recent months. Today, in real terms, i.e. adjusted for the inflation differential, it is around 4% higher than a year ago. The extent of the appreciation cannot be compared with the currency turbulence and the appreciation spurts in the first half of the nineties. After the global economic slump last year, however, the rise in the price of the Swiss franc for the Swiss export industry came at a very bad moment. In addition, the euro has a greater weight compared to the previous European currencies, and since the mid-nineties the interdependence of the Swiss economy with the European economic area is likely to have increased further. The Swiss National Bank reacted to the economic slowdown and the appreciation tendencies of the Swiss franc by sharply easing monetary policy. Within a year, we lowered our key interest rate, the three-month Libor, by 2.25 percentage points to 1.25%. In this way, we counteracted the undesirable tightening of the monetary framework conditions caused by the appreciation of the Swiss franc. This was also linked to the hope that the reduction in the interest rate would also stop the appreciation trend of the Swiss franc. In recent weeks, the franc-euro relationship has eased somewhat. This may have something to do with the fact that the general situation of the global economy seems to be consolidating noticeably and that positive economic signals have also increased in Europe recently. The appreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro took place in a phase of rapidly declining dollar quotations, a development that is quite familiar to us. The franc thus seemed to have maintained its status as a safe haven in turbulent times. This role, whose roots probably go back far into history, is associated with considerable exchange rate risks and repeatedly poses problems for the Swiss export industry. No one would therefore be unhappy if the franc lost some of this nimbus. Ultimately, I am optimistic that this will happen in the next few years. My hope is that the euro will be a currency stable in value and will give impetus to the European economy. Surrounded by a dynamic European internal market, Switzerland is likely to lose importance as a haven of refuge. However, as I said at the beginning of my presentation, the positive effects of the euro on the European market do not occur overnight or automatically. They must be accompanied by appropriate economic policy measures. Among them are also some cracking nuts. I will conclude with that. 4. Schlussbemerkungen In the ten years since the last visit of a National Bank representative to you, fundamental changes have changed. The euro has become a reality, even physically hands-on. Its introduction went smoothly - a logistical masterpiece. Presumably, even the biggest supporters of the euro did not expect such a development. And the skeptics? I believe that we must continue to take seriously the objections and fears they had about the creation of a common currency in Europe. A common currency means more than the pale circulation of uniform notes and coins. Countries are giving up their monetary sovereignty in favor of a common solution. Whereas in the past different developments in the individual European countries could be compensated for periodically by means of exchange rate adjustments, today the adjustment is made through the price competitiveness of companies in an increasingly competitive market. This is a profound change in the process of economic adjustment. The creation of an independent central bank has created an important prerequisite for a transparent, stability-oriented monetary policy. However, the European Central Bank can ensure stable monetary conditions, i.e. low inflation, low inflation, low inflation expectations and low nominal interest rates, no more and no less than in its sphere of influence. It cannot influence how quickly and sustainably the European economy grows in the long term and how productive it is. The long-term growth path results from the interaction of the innovative capacity of the economy with the economic policy and institutional framework conditions. One could go even further. Monetary policy is even dependent on the other elements of economic policy - I am thinking in particular of fiscal policy - to fit into the stability-oriented environment. If this is not the case, or if there is a constant struggle, the credibility of monetary policy is jeopardised. But then the confidence of international investors in the currency is also damaged. Switzerland has a vital interest in a dynamic European economy and a strong euro. But this is not enough. Switzerland, too, must be prepared to rethink its structures. The aim is to create framework conditions in which the innovative forces of the economy can develop optimally.

Vorteile des Euro fr die Euro-Lnder Die Vorteile einer gemeinsamen Whrung liegen auf der Hand - ich msste Sie Ihnen eigentlich nicht vorrechnen. Ihre Wurzeln liegen in den wirtschaftspolitischen Spielregeln, die den Marktkrften viel mehr Raum lassen, als dies bei uns in Europa - auch in der Schweiz - der Fall ist. Wir Europer verweisen jeweils gerne auf die Nachteile des amerikanischen Systems, etwa die grossen Einkommensunterschiede oder das im Vergleich zu Europa weniger stark ausgebaute staatliche Sozialnetz. Dies mgen Nachteile sein, die wir in Europa nicht hinnehmen wollen. Auf der anderen Seite sind gerade die Kosten der sozialen Sicherung auf unserem Kontinent inzwischen so hoch geworden, dass die Finanzierung langfristig schwierig ist. Es fhrt deshalb kein Weg an einer Steigerung der Produktivitt, einer Erhhung der wirtschaftlichen Dynamik vorbei. Dies gilt - wie gesagt - sowohl fr den Euro-Raum wie auch fr die Schweiz. 2. Der Euro aus Sicht der Schweiz Lassen Sie mich damit zum Euro aus Schweizer Sicht bergehen. Ich mchte ein Ergebnis meiner berlegungen gleich vorwegnehmen. Wenn ich mir vom Euro fr die Schweiz eines erhoffe, dann dies: Er soll auch bei uns zu einem Katalysator fr eine wachstums- und innovationsfreundliche Wirtschaftspolitik werden. Was kann die Schweiz vom Euro erwarten? Im Sommer vor einem Jahr haben wir unsere regionalen Wirtschaftsbeobachter beauftragt, die Stimmung in der Schweizer Wirtschaft vor der Einfhrung des EuroBargeldes zu erkunden. Uns interessierte vor allem, ob sich die Unternehmen auf die Umstellung gengend vorbereitet hatten, ob ihre Informatik-, Buchhaltungs- und Kalkulationssysteme eurotauglich waren. Wir waren danach einigermassen beruhigt. In der Tat verlief die Einfhrung des Euro-Bargeldes auch fr die Schweiz reibungslos. Was uns bei unseren Sondierungen auffiel, war die generell positive Haltung der Schweizer Unternehmen gegenber dem Euro. Warum dies? Einige Grnde dafr liegen auf der Hand. Der Euro hat in mancher Hinsicht auch das Leben der Schweizer Unternehmen vereinfacht. Zwar gibt es Mehraufwand, beispielsweise in Form der doppelten Rechnungslegung in Franken und in Euro, die in vielen Unternehmen notwendig geworden ist. Auch profitiert der Schweizer Unternehmer nicht vom Wegfall des Wechselkursrisikos, da der Franken gegenber dem Euro schwanken kann. Mit dem Ersatz von 11 Fremdwhrungen durch eine einzige vereinfachte sich indessen das Fremdwhrungsmanagement und damit auch die Bewirtschaftung der Whrungsrisiken sprbar. Und schliesslich sind auch die unkalkulierbaren Risiken des frheren Europischen Whrungssystems weggefallen, die in den neunziger Jahren fr die Schweiz eine grosse Strquelle waren. Auf der anderen Seite gehen die Unternehmen davon aus, dass der Franken als Fakturawhrung im schweizerisch-europischen Geschft weiter an Bedeutung einbssen wird. Das ist insofern ein Nachteil, als ein grsserer Anteil der Erlse in fremder Whrung anfallen wird und daher durch die schweizerischen Exporteure abgesichert werden muss. Fr die preisliche Wettbewerbsfhigkeit ist dieser Umstand jedoch von sekundrer Bedeutung. Bei einer Frankenaufwertung hat ein Exporteur, der in Franken Rechnung stellt, vergleichbare Probleme. Rasch ist er gezwungen, den Frankenpreis zu senken, wenn er seine Kunden nicht verlieren will. Der Wechselkurs bleibt damit fr Schweizer Unternehmen eine potenzielle Strquelle, unabhngig davon, ob in Franken oder in Euro fakturiert wird. 2. 1 Verdrngt der Euro den Franken als Zahlungsmittel? Eine der ersten Fragen, die in der Schweiz im Zusammenhang mit der Einfhrung des Euro aufkam, war, ob der grosse Euro den kleinen Franken nicht automatisch als Zahlungsmittel verdrngen werde. Keine Frage ist, dass der Euro in der Schweiz als Zahlungsmittel zirkulieren wird. Er tut dies bereits. Im Vorfeld der Einfhrung des EuroBargeldes haben viele Unternehmen, darunter die grossen Detailhndler, bekannt gegeben, sie wrden auch Euro-Bargeld akzeptieren. Was in den Tourismuszentren und Grenzregionen schon lange blich war - das Bezahlen mit Fremdwhrungen - weitete sich damit auf andere Bereiche aus. Preisanschriften in Franken und Euro sind bereits ein gewohnter Anblick. Die ersten Erfahrungen zeigen, dass der Euro kaum hufiger als Zahlungsmittel verwendet wird als frher die D-Mark, der Franc, der Schilling oder die Lira. Der Hauptgrund ist sicher der meist sehr ungnstige Wechselkurs, der jeweils in Rechnung gestellt wird. Mglicherweise wird der Euro mit der Zeit grssere Bedeutung erlangen als die frheren europischen Whrungen. Probleme drfte dies jedoch keine bereiten, auch nicht fr die schweizerische Geldpolitik. Mit Beruhigung haben wir zudem festgestellt, dass auch der Franken im grenznahen Ausland nach wie vor problemlos als Zahlungsmittel akzeptiert wird - auch da allerdings zu einem wenig attraktiven Wechselkurs! Eine andere Frage ist, ob der Euro den Franken als Zahlungsmittel in der Schweiz verdrngen wird. Dafr gibt es aus unserer Sicht keinen Grund. Der Franken geniesst im Inland hohes Vertrauen. Er weist seit je eine hohe Wertstabilitt auf - weshalb also eine andere Whrung verwenden? Mitunter hrt man, dass Exportunternehmen angesichts des hohen Frankenkurses daran dchten, die Lhne in Euro auszubezahlen, mit anderen Worten das Wechselkursrisiko auf die Arbeitnehmer abzuwlzen. Dies ist unrealistisch. Zu Recht wrden dies die Sozialpartner nicht akzeptieren. Das Whrungsrisiko - gegenber dem Euro oder gegenber dem Dollar und anderen Whrungen - gehrt zu den Unternehmensrisiken. Ganz abgesehen davon profitieren viele Schweizer Unternehmen vom starken Franken in Form tiefer Zinsstze und gnstiger Importe. Dies ndert nichts daran, dass der Wechselkurs den Unternehmen Sorgen bereiten kann und sich die Nationalbank berlegen muss, wie sie am besten auf die Wechselkursprobleme reagieren soll. 2.2 Gefhrdet der Euro den Franken als internationale Anlagewhrung? Im Zusammenhang mit dem Euro stellt sich auch die Frage nach der Zukunft des Frankens als internationale Anlage- und Emissionswhrung. Der Franken hat in den letzten Jahren auf den internationalen Kapitalmrkten etwas an Bedeutung verloren. So nimmt die Bentzung des Frankens bei der Emission von Schuldtiteln schon seit einiger Zeit ab. Wir interpretieren dies grundstzlich als Normalisierung in einer Zeit, wo sich neben dem Franken auch andere, voll konvertible Whrungen etabliert haben und das internationale Whrungssystem allgemein sicherer geworden ist. Das explosionsartige Entstehen eines breiten und hoch liquiden Euro-Obligationenmarktes hat die Position des Frankens mglicherweise aber zustzlich geschwcht. Auch heute gehrt der Franken bei internationalen Anleihen-Emissionen aber noch zu den 5 Hauptwhrungen, nach dem US-Dollar, dem Euro, dem Yen und dem britischen Pfund. Wir gehen davon aus, dass er in den internationalen Portefeuilles weiterhin eine wichtige Rolle als Diversifikationswhrung spielen wird, weil er nach wie vor ber einige attraktive Attribute verfgt. Keine Frage ist aber, dass der Franken hinter dem Euro weit zurckliegt. Der Euro ist nach dem amerikanischen Dollar die zweitwichtigste Anlage- und Reservewhrung. So hlt beispielsweise die Schweizerische Nationalbank heute den grssten Teil ihrer Devisenreserven, nmlich 46%, in Form von Euro-Anlagen. Grosse Bedeutung hat der Euro auch bei Devisentransaktionen. Dazu kommt, dass viele Lnder dazu bergegangen sind, ihre Whrungen an den Euro zu binden. Der Euro wird zweifellos auch den Wettbewerb im europischen Finanzsystem verschrfen. Es ist zu erwarten, dass es in Europa zu weiteren Bankenzusammenschlssen und Konsolidierungen kommen wird. Dies bedeutet auch fr den Finanzplatz Schweiz eine verstrkte Konkurrenz und einen erhhten Druck, die eigenen Leistungen zu steigern. Lassen Sie mich damit zu den Auswirkungen des Euro auf den schweizerischen Binnenmarkt bergehen. 2.3 Der Euro als Katalysator fr einen dynamischeren Schweizer Binnenmarkt? Die Schweiz verfgt ber einen hoch produktiven Exportsektor mit vielen international fhrenden Unternehmen. Trotz der hohen Produktivitt unserer Exportunternehmen wuchs die Schweizer Wirtschaft in den letzten 20 Jahren aber deutlich langsamer als der Durchschnitt der OECD-Lnder. Wohl ist es mglich, dass der Wachstumsabstand aus einer Reihe von Grnden als zu gross ausgewiesen wird. Dies ndert jedoch nichts daran, dass das inlndische Preisniveau um einiges hher ist als etwa in unseren Nachbarlndern - auch in Deutschland. Dass dem so ist, zeigen zahlreiche Berechnungen, vor allem aber die Tatsache, dass in der Schweiz ein lebhafter Einkaufstourismus ber die Grenze stattfindet. Ein Hauptgrund fr die hohen Lebenshaltungskosten in der Schweiz drfte der mangelnde Wettbewerb in der Binnenwirtschaft sein. ber Jahrzehnte hinweg ist ein dichtes Netz von staatlichen, aber auch von privaten Wettbewerbshemmnissen entstanden. Es lhmt die Innovationsbereitschaft des Binnensektors. Als Folge davon ist die Produktivitt dieses Sektors im Vergleich zum Exportsektor gering. Die hohen Preise fr inlndische Vorleistungen stellen heute eine wichtige Schwche im innereuropischen Standortwettbewerb dar und bedeuten fr die exportorientierten Wirtschaftszweige eine erhebliche Belastung. Zwar wurden in den neunziger Jahren einige vielversprechende Massnahmen zur marktwirtschaftlichen Erneuerung des Binnenmarktes ergriffen. Dazu gehren die Schaffung des Binnenmarktgesetzes, die Revision des Kartellgesetzes, die Liberalisierung des Telekommunikationsmarktes sowie die Neuausrichtung der Agrarpolitik. Der Elan scheint aber mittlerweile nachgelassen zu haben. Auch zeigt sich, dass sowohl das Binnenmarkt- wie auch das Kartellgesetz griffiger ausgestaltet werden mssen. Die Deregulierung von Mrkten ist mit Opfern verbunden. In einigen Sektoren beispielsweise der Landwirtschaft - hat es bereits Verlierer gegeben. Auf der anderen Seite muss die Wirtschaft als dynamisches Gebilde verstanden werden. Halten wir am Status qua fest, so schtzt dies zwar den Besitzstand der heutigen Akteure. Diejenigen, die neu ins Erwerbsleben eintreten, haben davon aber nicht viel. Sie wren in der Lage und auch bereit, sich in einem neuen Umfeld zurechtzufinden. Sicher darf man dabei die Opfer des Strukturwandels nicht vergessen. Die Schweiz verfgt im Unterschied zu vielen europischen Lndern ber einen flexiblen und leistungsfhigen Arbeitsmarkt. Das Gleichgewicht zwischen dem wichtigen Anliegen des Arbeitnehmerschutzes und den Bedrfnissen eines dynamischen Marktumfeldes ist in unserem Land recht vernnftig. Dank dieser Flexibilitt sollte es in der Schweiz leichter sein als in anderen Lndern, die Strukturen zu ndern und die Verlierer des Strukturwandels rasch wieder in den Arbeitsmarkt zu integrieren. Was aber hat dies alles mit dem Euro zu tun? Ein wichtiger Anstoss, in den neunziger Jahren die Revitalisierung des Binnenmarktes berhaupt auf die politische Traktandenliste zu setzen, war die Schaffung des europischen Binnenmarktes. Um die Konkurrenzfhigkeit der Schweizer Unternehmen gegenber diesem neu entstehenden riesigen Markt zu sichern, mussten wir in der Schweiz ber die Bcher gehen. Der Euro wird die Notwendigkeit fr Strukturvernderungen auf dem schweizerischen Binnenmarkt wieder verstrkt ins Bewusstsein bringen. Denn auch die Schweizer Unternehmen werden die bessere Preistransparenz, den erhhten Wettbewerbsdruck im Euro-Raum zu spren bekommen. Passt sich der Binnenmarkt nicht an, werden einige Bereiche gegenber den europischen Konkurrenten ins Hintertreffen geraten. Damit komme ich zum letzten Teil, zu den Risiken, die mit dem Euro fr die Schweiz verbunden sind. An erster Stelle steht der Wechselkurs. 3. Der Euro und das Wechselkursrisiko Wie erwhnt brachte unsere Umfrage zum Euro vom letzten Sommer eine offene, zuversichtliche Haltung der Schweizer Unternehmen gegenber dem Euro zu Tage. Hervorgehoben wurden vor allem die Vorteile der neuen Whrung, negative Stimmen gab es kaum. Zum Teil widerspiegelte dieses positive Stimmungsbild zweifellos auch die bis dahin recht ruhige Entwicklung des Frankens gegenber dem Euro. Die zu Beginn der Whrungsunion geusserten Befrchtungen, der Euro knnte gegenber dem Franken substanziell an Wert verlieren, schienen sich nicht zu bewahrheiten. Wie Sie vielleicht mitverfolgt haben, hat sich der Franken in den letzten Monaten gegenber dem Euro aufgewertet. Er liegt heute real, d.h. um die Inflationsdifferenz bereinigt, rund 4% hher als vor einem Jahr. Das Ausmass der Aufwertung lsst sich zwar nicht mit den Whrungsturbulenzen und den Aufwertungsschben in der ersten Hlfte der neunziger Jahre vergleichen. Nach dem weltweiten Konjunktureinbruch im letzten Jahr kam indessen die Verteuerung des Frankens fr die Schweizer Exportindustrie in einem denkbar schlechten Moment. Zudem hat der Euro im Vergleich zu den frheren europischen Whrungen ein grsseres Gewicht, und seit Mitte der neunziger Jahre drfte auch die Verflechtung der Schweizer Wirtschaft mit dem europischen Wirtschaftsraum weiter zugenommen haben. Die Schweizerische Nationalbank reagierte auf die konjunkturelle Abschwchung und die Aufwertungstendenzen des Frankens mit einer starken Lockerung der Geldpolitik. Innerhalb eines Jahres senkten wir unseren Leitzins, den Dreimonate-Libor, um 2,25 Prozentpunkte auf 1,25%. Damit wirkten wir der unerwnschten Verschrfung der monetren Rahmenbedingungen durch die Frankenaufwertung entgegen. Damit verbunden war zudem die Hoffnung, die Senkung des Zinssatzes wrde auch den Aufwertungstrend des Frankens stoppen. In den letzten Wochen hat sich die Franken-Euro-Relation etwas entspannt. Dies hat mglicherweise damit zu tun, dass sich die allgemeine Lage der Weltwirtschaft zusehends zu festigen scheint und sich auch in Europa in letzter Zeit die positiven konjunkturellen Signale mehrten. Die Aufwertung der Frankens gegenber dem Euro erfolgte in einer Phase rasch sinkender Dollarnotierungen, eine fr uns recht vertraute Entwicklung. Der Franken schien damit seinen Status als sicherer Hafen in turbulenten Zeiten beibehalten zu haben. Diese Rolle, deren Wurzeln vermutlich weit in die Geschichte zurckreichen, ist mit erheblichen Wechselkursrisiken verbunden und stellt die schweizerische Exportwirtschaft immer wieder vor Probleme. Niemand wre deshalb unglcklich, wenn der Franken etwas von diesem Nimbus verlieren wrde. Letztlich bin ich optimistisch, dass es in den nchsten Jahren dazu kommen wird. Meine Hoffnung basiert darauf, dass der Euro eine wertstabile Whrung ist und der europischen Wirtschaft Impulse verleihen wird. Umgeben von einem dynamischen europischen Binnenmarkt drfte die Schweiz als Zufluchtshafen an Bedeutung verlieren. Wie ich allerdings schon zu Beginn meines Referates angetnt habe, stellen sich die positiven Effekte des Euro auf dem europischen Markt weder ber Nacht, noch automatisch ein. Sie mssen von entsprechenden wirtschaftspolitischen Massnahmen begleitet sein. Darunter sind auch einige Knacknsse. Ich komme damit zum Schluss. 4. Schlussbemerkungen In den zehn Jahren seit dem letzten Besuch eines Nationalbankvertreters bei Ihnen hat sich Grundlegendes verndert. Der Euro ist Wirklichkeit geworden, auch physisch zum Anfassen. Seine Einfhrung erfolgte reibungslos - eine logistische Meisterleistung. Vermutlich haben selbst die grssten Befrworter des Euro mit einer solchen Entwicklung nicht gerechnet. Und die Skeptiker? Ich glaube, dass wir ihre Einwnde und Befrchtungen, die sie gegenber der Schaffung einer gemeinsamen Whrung in Europa hatten, nach wie vor ernst nehmen mssen. Eine gemeinsame Whrung bedeutet mehr als das blasse Zirkulieren von einheitlichen Noten und Mnzen. Die Lnder geben ihre monetre Souvernitt zugunsten einer gemeinsamen Lsung auf. Liessen sich frher unterschiedliche Entwicklungen in den einzelnen europischen Lndern periodisch ber Wechselkursanpassungen ausgleichen, erfolgt die Anpassung heute ber die preisliche Wettbewerbsfhigkeit der Unternehmen in einem kompetitiver werdenden Markt. Dies ist eine tiefgreifende nderung des wirtschaftlichen Anpassungsprozesses. Mit der Schaffung einer unabhngigen Zentralbank wurde eine wichtige Voraussetzung fr eine transparente, stabilittsorientierte Geldpolitik geschaffen. Die Europische Zentralbank kann aber nicht mehr und nicht weniger, als in ihrem Einflussbereich fr stabile monetre Rahmenbedingungen, d.h. eine geringe Teuerung, tiefe Inflationserwartungen und niedrige nominelle Zinsstze sorgen. Wie rasch und nachhaltig die europische Wirtschaft langfristig wchst und wie produktiv sie ist, kann sie nicht beeinflussen. Der langfristige Wachstumspfad ergibt sich aus dem Zusammenspiel der Innovationsfhigkeit der Wirtschaft mit den wirtschaftspolitischen und institutionellen Rahmenbedingungen. Man knnte noch weiter gehen. Die Geldpolitik ist sogar darauf angewiesen, dass sich auch die anderen Elemente der Wirtschaftspolitik - ich denke vor allem an die Finanzpolitik - in das stabilittsorientierte Umfeld einordnen. Ist dies nicht der Fall oder muss darum stndig gerungen werden, so gert die Glaubwrdigkeit der Geldpolitik in Gefahr. Dann aber nimmt auch das Vertrauen der internationalen Anleger in die Whrung Schaden. Die Schweiz hat ein vitales Interesse an einer dynamischen europischen Wirtschaft und an einem starken Euro. Dies gengt aber nicht. Auch die Schweiz muss bereit sein, ihre Strukturen zu berdenken. Ziel ist es, Rahmenbedingungen zu schaffen, in denen sich die innovativen Krfte der Wirtschaft optimal entfalten knnen.

Title: In what shape is the Swiss financial centre?
text: WHAT IS THE STATE OF THE SWISS FINANCIAL CENTRE? Prof. Dr. Niklaus Blattner Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank 3rd IIR Annual Conference Clearing and Settlement for Securities The Swiss capital market in upheaval Zurich, 23 July 2002 1. The importance of the financial centre With only 3 to 4% of the workforce, the banking sector contributes around 12% to Switzerland's economic value added. Labour productivity and wages are above average and are otherwise only achieved in the pharmaceutical industry. The tax revenue from the banking sector corresponds to its share of value added, i.e. it is well above 10%. A specialty of banks in Switzerland is asset management. According to the statistics of the Swiss National Bank (SNB), the value incremental holdings in customer custody accounts at domestic bank offices amounted to CHF 3.4 trillion at the end of 2001. If customer funds were added to bank balance sheets and those in escrow accounts, the value of assets under management would increase again by around a quarter to a third. These figures reflect the position of the Swiss International Financial Centre in offshore wealth management. Around 30% of the global cross-border assets under management are exported by Switzerland. Of the aforementioned CHF 3.4 trillion in assets under management, three-fifths are accounted for by foreign clients and half of these, i.e. about 30% of the total, by private individuals. However, the financial centre is not only strong in asset management. He is also impressive in the rest of the bank and in the insurance business. The performance of the financial centre contributes to Switzerland's attractiveness as a location for the production of non-financial products and services. Financial intermediation in Switzerland takes place at low interest rates and narrow margins. The overall picture is as follows: The Swiss International Financial Centre is efficient in all sectors. His special competence is asset management. Its special feature is solidity. This is reflected in the fact that the banks in Switzerland have coped better with the technological and economic changes since the nineties than their competitors elsewhere. 2. Success factors of the Swiss financial centre The success of the Swiss International Financial Centre is not the result of a deliberate state strategy or even an industrial policy that coddles the financial centre. Rather, it resulted from the interaction of several factors. A first success factor is stability. Stability creates predictability and this in turn creates trust, without which the financial business is made much more difficult. Switzerland is a direct democracy. As a liberal democracy, it affirms self-responsibility on the one hand and solidarity on the other. In the political sphere, it cultivates constructive compromise. Social partnership is based on mutual respect. From a financial centre perspective, the stability contributions of monetary policy, financial policy and banking and financial market legislation are particularly important. Stability is based on foresight. Financial centre policy must be long-term and prudent. Timely adjustment to new developments avoids costly and trust-damaging adjustments at the wrong time and under pressure. At the same time, legal certainty and property rights must be preserved, as must financial privacy. A second success factor is openness. It is rooted in the fact that Switzerland forms an interface of three European languages in the middle of the European cultural area. Emigration and immigration, exports and imports as well as direct investment have been a decisive experience of this country for centuries. The international competition is affirmed. Access to the market from abroad is generally free. The latter also applies to the financial sector. There is little comparable to the number of around 150 foreign-controlled banks and branches of foreign banks in other financial centres. The option of encapsulation does not exist for Switzerland. The image of Switzerland as an island in the middle of continental Europe is a fiction. Switzerland, whether it is part of the European Union (EU) or not, has a much stronger international network than most other countries. Moving in a globalized space requires mentally open, constructive participation. Authorities, companies and associations must be active with all direct and indirect stakeholders, from Germany and abroad. communicate - about the positive achievements of the country as well as about the conflict-prone one. The progress made in this area in recent years is remarkable. Of course, communication is not only possible in good weather. Cold air zones, such as those in the field of EU taxation of savings, are unavoidable. However, they are rooted less in a conflict over fundamental values than in the facts of system competition. System competition is productive. The demands on the parties to the conflict are correspondingly high. A third success factor is competence. The Swiss financial industry has a large pool of well-trained, multilingual professionals at all levels who are familiar with international finance. Specialist and management training enjoys a good reputation. A constant willingness to renew is a prerequisite for this. Internationally recognized training courses and universities that not only focus on teaching, but also give research its place, are essential components of success. The quality of the range of services determines the attractiveness of Switzerland's International Financial Centre. This in turn depends on the people who operate the financial centre, namely at the front, in the back office, in the financial market infrastructure, but also where the framework conditions are defined and implemented, i.e. in politics and authorities. After all, a whole bundle of components determines the attractiveness of a financial center. And it is always people with their professional and social competence who determine its profile. The fourth success factor is integrity. Deregulation and globalization brought new room for manoeuvre, but also confusion. Responsibility and reputational risk increased. The financial business is particularly vulnerable in such situations. Vabanque and sophistication produce successes that dazzle, even if they are consistently short-lived. The investor, relying entirely on trust, now distinguishes more and more according to criteria of integrity. At present, the crisis of confidence triggered by Enron and WorldCom and dissatisfaction with the state of corporate governance are having a full impact on share prices. It is obvious that transparent accounting and corporate governance that meets the interests of shareholders have become a question of the company's existence. The described development, which took its starting point in the USA, also contaminates the Swiss markets. In this respect, integrity as the fourth success factor is still capable of development in Switzerland, even if the conditions in Switzerland, not least because of other accounting standards, undoubtedly differ in a good sense from those in the USA. It is also convenient that in the field of crime, whether money laundering, terror or fraud, the measures taken in Switzerland now receive high international recognition. 3. Pending financial market regulation Regulation and supervision are among the success factors of a financial centre. The financial sector is regulated more strongly than other sectors because confidence is critical and the loss potential is high. But regulation also costs money. Consequently, the regulatory optimum must be sought. Various cliffs have to be circumnavigated. One can regulate too large, too rigorously, too much or too little adapted to foreign countries, i.e. regulatory dumping, regulatory overkill or regulatory arbitrage. Clumsy navigation can be momentous. Regulatory measures should therefore be systematically subjected to an economic cost-benefit analysis. The fact that the path taken in Switzerland is fundamentally correct is shown by the attractiveness of its financial centre that has lasted for decades. This verdict was recently confirmed by the International Monetary Fund, whose Financial Seetor Assessment Program could hardly have been more favorable for Switzerland. Switzerland has recently become a major regulatory construction site. Some ongoing reform projects are briefly recalled:  Integrated supervision: Based on the example of the British Financial Services Authority, financial market supervision is also to be further integrated in Switzerland. The Federal Banking Commission (SFBC) is already working in an integrated manner. It is not only responsible for banking supervision, but also supervises stock exchanges and securities dealers, investment funds and Pfandbrief institutions. An additional integration of the supervision of private insurance, a supervision of independent asset managers and possibly the money laundering control body to be defined specifically in a Federal Financial Market Supervisory Authority, which would also include the SFBC, is currently being carried out by a commission of experts on behalf of of the Swiss Federal Council. First results are expected by the end of the year.  Conglomerate supervision The creation of a legal basis for the consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates is urgent. It is true that the future of all-finance models is not set in stone. But they also exist in Switzerland, and today's supervision, which is pragmatically based solely on Federal Council rulings, requires increased legal protection in the Insurance Supervision Act, which is currently being revised.  Bank restructuring, liquidation and depositor protection: The Schaerer Expert Group proposes a fundamentally revised procedure for managing the banking crisis. Among other things, the aim is to promote bank restructuring in the interest of preserving the substance by allowing it to be forcibly initiated by the SFBC from now on. Depositor protection is to be promoted. It is to become mandatory for all banks that are active in the deposit business. The increase in the bankruptcy privilege to 30,000 francs per person and bank and the immediate payment of the small stone deposits (up to 5,000 francs) are established. As a result, the counterparty risks of depositor protection can be virtually completely eliminated. At the same time, the obligations of deposit protection are to be provided with a sustainable upper limit for reasons of system protection.  Banking audit: The SFBC is responsible for determining the scope of the external statutory bank audit. It must also check whether the revisions are really independent, knowledgeable and careful. With this in mind, it intends to systematically supervise the statutory audit companies in the future and to check even more whether they meet the strict requirements. The banks themselves are to be monitored more intensively and must undergo regular audits by a second audit firm. Proposals for stricter audit regulations are to be expected from the forthcoming interim report of a SFBC Working Group on Auditing. 4. Bilateral II On 1 June 2002, ten years after the Swiss sovereign rejected the Treaty on the European Economic Area (EEA), seven sectoral agreements between Switzerland and the EU entered into force (Bilateral Agreements 1). The agreements facilitate access to the European internal market, without the actual integration path of legal unification having to be taken. Negotiations on the so-called Bilateral Agreements II are now underway. Bilateralism, the cooperation among independents, is to be pursued, since accession to the EU is not politically feasible for Switzerland. Ten dossiers have been defined. From the point of view of the financial centre, two are particularly relevant. They are both closely linked to Swiss bank client secrecy. This ensures financial privacy without at the same time being an obstacle to the fight against crime, including tax fraud.  There is agreement in the anti-fraud dossier on the objective of making the fight against customs fraud even more efficient. The EU wants a comprehensive administrative and mutual legal assistance agreement that covers all illegal financial activities and provides for a reporting obligation in case of suspicion of such violations. Switzerland will have to insist on a precise definition of the facts in order to prevent undesirable repercussions on bank client secrecy in the direct tax sector.  In the Savings Taxation dossier, the EU requires the automatic reporting of all savings income of natural persons to the tax authorities. It requires third countries to adopt an "equivalent solution", but only seems to want to accept the exchange of information as equivalent. However, this would be diametrically opposed to the core of Swiss bank client secrecy. Let me elaborate on this. - The Federal Council has long taken a position: bank client secrecy is non-negotiable. Any concession would be contrary to the will of the people or the Swiss appreciation of financial privacy. The Federal Council is not prepared to adopt the EU reporting system. On the other hand, he also does not want to prevent the EU from realizing its ideas on savings taxation on its own territory. In order to avoid a diversion of EU taxpayers to Switzerland, the Federal Council therefore wants to offer the EU a modification of the withholding tax, which has been successful in this country for decades. A paying agent tax is envisaged on the interest income of natural persons with an EU domicile accruing in Switzerland, which would be levied by the banks in Switzerland, and whose income would be transferred to the EU. Does the Federal Council's offer bring equivalence? The answer is yes. The tax as the sole purpose of the measure may well be levied in this way become. An expert opinion has proven the feasibility. The equivalence of the withholding tax system had never been disputed in the EU until Feira. Maria Monti's coexistence model was explicitly recognized in 1998. Rhetorical power games, as they have occurred sporadically in recent times, show a certain doggedness in the fight for the exchange of information and against the withholding tax. However, they have not shown any factual arguments against a withholding tax. 5. The Swiss National Bank and the financial centre The Swiss National Bank (SNB) has a natural interest in the soundness and performance of the Swiss financial system. This applies in general, but especially with regard to the financial market infrastructure, i.e. to the payment and settlement systems. This interest is due to the SNB's monetary policy mandate. The SNB must maintain price stability, facilitate payment transactions and contribute to system stability. The financial system is the platform of monetary policy. The transactions are carried out through the banks. Pricing on the money and capital markets must therefore be efficient. The SNB's business partners must be solvent. Monetary policy can only be transferred to financial markets, the economy and price levels in the desired way through functioning, solvent financial intermediaries. The infrastructures of cashless payment transactions have a critical function. Large cash flows flow between the banks. Resolution problems could therefore cause far-reaching disruptions to the financial system and the economy as a whole. Security is therefore indispensable. Central bank surveillance is aimed at ensuring the smooth functioning of systems and protecting against domino effects. At the same time, however, monitoring should also contribute to efficiency. Swiss lnterbank Clearing (SIC) is currently the only Swiss payment system of systemic relevance. The banks use it for large-value and retail payment transactions. The large amounts come from foreign exchange or money and capital market transactions, but also from large payments from the non-banking sector. Among other things, SIC also processes payments from transactions in SWX, virt-x, EUREX and soon also CLS (Continuous Linked Settlement System as an instrument for reducing settlement risks in foreign exchange trading). Payments in the SIC are made via the banks' current accounts with the SNB. SIC is a RealTime Grass Settlement System (RTGS), i.e. payment orders are executed individually and irrevocably in real time. The SNB does not operate the SIC itself, but has commissioned SIC AG to do so. This is a joint effort of the Swiss banks. In addition to ongoing operations, it also takes care of technical development. All payment systems should meet certain minimum standards. Payment systems that are important for the stability of the financial system should in particular comply with the ten basic principles of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). Central requirements of security are both trouble-free technology and precautions against the transfer of the insolvency of one participant to others. In addition to the security of the systems, the SNB is also concerned about their efficiency. An infrastructure can be considered efficient if functionality and security are ensured with minimal economic use of resources. A central bank can contribute to security and efficiency by providing payment services itself. However, the SNB's strategy leaves operations to the private sector. The SNB would only have to act directly as an operator if the private sector did not have adequate infrastructure in place. Today, the SNB limits itself to making central bank money available via current accounts for the processing of payment transactions between banks and to monitoring payment systems. The provision of central bank money directly promotes stability. Central bank money as a means of payment offers the recipient bank the advantage of having receivables without credit and liquidity risks. Due to its monopoly on the creation of central bank money, the SNB can fully meet its obligations at any time. Today, all retail payments of banks are processed via SIC. Focusing on a single payment system allows banks to pool their liquidity and thus reduce the costs of liquidity management. The SNB's second task in cashless payment transactions is to monitor payment systems. Under surveillance, the SNB subsumes all its efforts to optimise the economic design of the payment infrastructure. She pays particular attention to systemically important payment systems in which negative externalities are particularly large. In the case of the The SNB conducts its monitoring activities are strongly guided by international standards such as the basic principles of the BIS. In addition, monitoring is always directed only at systems and their operators and never at the individual system participants, who are usually under the supervision of the SFBC or a foreign supervisory authority. Institutional supervision and payment system supervision are therefore complementary tasks, both of which contribute to the stability of the financial system. 6. A look into the future of surveillance The mandate laid down in the National Bank Act (NBA) to facilitate payment transactions forms the legal basis for the monitoring of payment systems. In order to monitor SICs, the SNB has also concluded contracts under private law with the system operator, SIC AG, and the system participants. This arrangement has proven its worth. However, there are reasons why the revision of the NBA provides for an explicit regulation at the legislative level for the monitoring of payment systems in the future. The monitoring of the SIC has so far been facilitated by the fact that settlement in the SIC is carried out with central bank money. Due to the current legal situation, it would be difficult for the SNB to monitor other systems well. Added to this is the generally increased importance of payment and securities settlement systems from a stability point of view. Corresponding legal bases have also been created in other countries in recent years, such as Australia, Canada and the EU. The new NBG, which is expected to enter into force in 2004 or 2005, follows this trend. The SNB is to be empowered to monitor cashless payment systems, regardless of whether their settlement takes place in central bank money or not. A three-stage control model is envisaged. At a first stage, operators of payment systems are subject to a statistical obligation to provide information. This provides the SNB with a comprehensive information base. Second, payment systems where systemic risk cannot be ruled out are subject to an extended disclosure requirement. This enables the SNB to answer the question of whether a systemically important payment system exists with sufficient certainty. Finally, the SNB may set minimum requirements for systemically important payment systems. These can concern the organization, the operational security precautions and the disposition in the event of a failure of system participants. The SNB may also check the terms and conditions, the means of payment used and the admission of participants. In the event of non-compliance with the minimum requirements: administrative penalties are foreseen. The SNB may refuse to hold a current account and publicly warn against the use of a defective system. The new NBG also regulates the monitoring of securities settlement systems. From now on, such systems will be jointly supervised by the SFBC and the SNB. From today's perspective, this applies above all to the securities settlement system SECOM. The now announced central counterparty x-clear will also fall into this category. The SNB will only act in securities settlement where it has a comparative advantage: in the assessment of settlement risks. Stock exchange supervision and institution supervision are not among its core competencies. Federal authorities such as the SFBC, but also private organisations such as the stock exchanges themselves, are working more effectively here. In Switzerland, as in other countries, the monitoring of payment and processing systems is in full development. While the SNB has a wealth of experience and a good track record in the area of payment systems thanks to SIC, it is breaking new ground in the settlement of securities. Although it knows the settlement risks, it knows less about the system operators. Cooperation with the SFBC, which continues to exercise institutional supervision, is therefore essential. 7. The Swiss National Bank as a committed partner The SNB is committed to the financial centre within the framework of its functions, i.e. primarily monetary policy and system monitoring. At the same time, however, it is also committed to increasing the attractiveness of Switzerland's international financial centre. This is preferably done on a practical level. The SNB is guided by the objective of system stability, but is also consistently committed to maintaining internationally competitive framework conditions. In 1998, SIC was also opened to securities dealers due to the new securities dealer status. In the same year, due to the internationality of the financial centre, those supervised foreign institutions that are involved in EUREX or SWX were granted access. In 1999, lntraday repos were offered for the first time with regard to CLS and have been continuously expanded ever since. By converting its monetary policy instruments from foreign exchange swaps to repos, the SNB has significantly increased the number of its counterparties and thus also Creation of a modern Swiss money market. Repos reduce the lnterbank credit risk and thus the contagion and systemic risk. As an advisor to the Federal Council, the SNB contributes to many expert commissions. In 2001, the SNB created a competence centre for system stability to analyse and prepare the basis for decision-making. In the same year, the SNB and the SFBC jointly formed a System Stability Steering Committee. Conceptual and practical questions of system stability are dealt with on an ongoing basis. The SNB has also always been part of the Swiss delegation to the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, where, together with the SFBC, contributes to the further development of what is probably the most important international supervisory standards. The SNB fulfils the same tasks within the Committee on Payment and Securities Settlement Systems of the Group of Ten at the BIS. The SNB is thus pursuing the promotion of Switzerland's international financial centre in a comprehensive manner and out of responsibility for the whole. It is therefore neither about industrial policy nor about protectionism, but about promoting the competitiveness and stability of the Swiss financial system. Many have to participate in this task. The SNB's primary contribution is to ensure monetary stability. In addition, it shares responsibility for the stability and further development of the financial system. She does this as a supervisor of payment and securities settlement systems, in the function of lender of last resort and as an advisor to the Federal Council on questions of financial centre policy. 8. Conclusion The question in the title of my presentation is: What is the state of the Swiss financial centre? - My answer will not surprise you: Good! The Swiss financial centre is economically sound. The providers of financial services are efficient. The financial market infrastructures, regulation and supervision, the legal, economic, financial and monetary policy as well as the social framework conditions are good. It is true that the technological, economic and political challenges are numerous. However, the Swiss financial centre is well equipped to successfully adopt them.
