Zahlungen im SIC erfolgen ber die Girokonten der Banken bei der SNB. SIC ist ein RealTime Grass Settlement System (RTGS), d.h., Zahlungsauftrge werden in Echtzeit individuell und unwiderruflich ausgefhrt. Die SNB betreibt das SIC nicht selbst, sondern hat damit die SIC AG beauftragt. Diese gehrt als Gemeinschaftswerk den Schweizer Banken. Sie besorgt nebst dem laufenden Betrieb auch die technische Weiterentwicklung. Alle Zahlungssysteme sollten gewisse Minimalstandards erfllen. Zahlungssysteme, die fr die Stabilitt des Finanzsystems bedeutsam sind, sollten insbesondere die zehn Grundprinzipien der Bank fr Internationalen Zahlungsausgleich (BIZ) erfllen. Zentrale Forderungen der Sicherheit sind sowohl eine strungsfreie Technik als auch Vorkehren gegen die bertragung der Zahlungsunfhigkeit eines Teilnehmers auf andere. Nebst der Sicherheit der Systeme ist der SNB auch deren Effizienz ein Anliegen. Eine Infrastruktur kann als effizient betrachtet werden, wenn Funktionalitt und Sicherheit bei minimalem volkswirtschaftlichem Ressourceneinsatz gewhrleistet sind. Eine Zentralbank kann zu Sicherheit und Effizienz beitragen, indem sie Zahlungsverkehrsdienstleistungen selbst anbietet. Die von der SNB verfolgte Strategie berlsst den Betrieb jedoch dem Privatsektor. Die SNB wrde nur dann direkt als Betreiberin auftreten mssen, wenn der Privatsektor keine adquate Infrastruktur bereit hielte. Heute beschrnkt sich die SNB auf das Zurverfgungstellen von Zentralbankgeld ber Girokonten fr die Abwicklung des Zahlungsverkehrs zwischen den Banken und auf die berwachung der Zahlungssysteme. Die Zurverfgungstellung von Zentralbankgeld frdert die Stabilitt direkt. Zentralbankgeld als Zahlungsmittel bietet der Empfngerbank den Vorteil, ber Forderungen ohne Kredit- und Liquidittsrisiken zu verfgen. Die SNB kann aufgrund ihres Monopols zur Schaffung von Zentralbankgeld ihren Verpflichtungen jederzeit uneingeschrnkt nachkommen. Heute werden alle Massenzahlungen der Banken ber SIC abgewickelt. Die Konzentration auf ein einziges Zahlungssystem ermglicht es den Banken, ihre Liquiditt zu poolen und so die Kosten des Liquidittsmanagements zu senken. Die zweite Aufgabe der SNB im bargeldlosen Zahlungsverkehr besteht in der berwachung von Zahlungssystemen. Unter berwachung subsummiert die SNB alle ihre Bestrebungen, die Zahlungsverkehrsinfrastruktur volkswirtschaftlich optimal zu gestalten. Besonderes Augenmerk richtet sie dabei auf systemisch bedeutsame Zahlungssysteme, bei denen negative Externalitten besonders gross sind. Bei der Ausbung ihrer berwachungsttigkeit orientiert sich die SNB stark an internationalen Standards wie den Grundprinzipien der BIZ. Die berwachung richtet sich zudem immer nur auf Systeme und deren Betreiber und nie auf die einzelnen Systemteilnehmer, die in der Regel unter der Aufsicht der EBK oder einer auslndischen Aufsichtsbehrde stehen. Die Institutsaufsicht und die Zahlungssystemberwachung sind somit komplementre Aufgaben, die beide zur Stabilitt des Finanzsystems beitragen. 6. Ein Blick in die Zukunft der berwachung Der im Nationalbankgesetz (NBG) festgehaltene Auftrag, den Zahlungsverkehr zu erleichtern, bildet die rechtliche Basis fr die berwachung von Zahlungssystemen. Zur berwachung von SIC hat die SNB zudem mit der Systembetreiberin, der SIC AG, und den Systemteilnehmern privatrechtliche Vertrge abgeschlossen. Dieses Arrangement hat sich bewhrt. Doch gibt es Grnde, weshalb die Revision des NBG fr die berwachung von Zahlungssystemen in Zukunft eine explizite Regelung auf Gesetzesstufe vorsieht. Die berwachung des SIC wurde bisher dadurch erleichtert, dass die Abwicklung im SIC mit Zentralbankgeld erfolgt. Aufgrund der heutigen Gesetzeslage wre es fr die SNB schwierig, auch andere Systeme gut zu berwachen. Hinzu kommt die unter Stabilittsaspekten allgemein gestiegene Bedeutung der Zahlungs- und Effektenabwicklungssysteme. Auch in anderen Lndern wurden in den letzten Jahren entsprechende gesetzliche Grundlagen geschaffen, so in Australien, Kanada und der EU. Das neue NBG, das 2004 oder 2005 in Kraft treten drfte, folgt diesem Trend. Die SNB soll ermchtigt werden, bargeldlose Zahlungssysteme zu berwachen, unabhngig davon, ob deren Abwicklung in Zentralbankgeld stattfindet oder nicht. Vorgesehen ist ein dreistufiges Regelungsmodell. Auf einer ersten Stufe werden Betreiber von Zahlungssystemen einer statistischen Auskunftspflicht unterstellt. Die SNB erhlt dadurch eine umfassende Informationsbasis. Zweitens unterstehen Zahlungssysteme, bei denen ein Systemrisiko nicht ausgeschlossen werden kann, einer erweiterten Offenlegungspflicht. Damit kann die SNB die Frage, ob ein systemisch bedeutsames Zahlungssystem vorliegt, mit hinreichender Gewissheit beantworten. Schliesslich kann die SNB fr die systemisch relevanten Zahlungssysteme Mindestanforderungen aufstellen. Diese knnen die Organisation, die Vorkehren zur operationellen Sicherheit und das Dispositiv beim Ausfall von Systemteilnehmern betreffen. Ferner kann die SNB die Geschftsbedingungen, das verwendete Zahlungsmittel sowie die Zulassung von Teilnehmern prfen. Fr den Fall der Nichterfllung der Mindestanforderungen sind verwaltungsrechtliche Sanktionen vorgesehen. Die SNB kann die Fhrung eines Girokontos verweigern und ffentlich vor der Benutzung eines mangelhaften Systems warnen. Im neuen NBG wird auch die berwachung von Effektenabwicklungssystemen geregelt. Solche Systeme sollen fortan gemeinsam von der EBK und der SNB beaufsichtigt werden. Aus heutiger Sicht betrifft dies vor allem das Wertschriftenabwicklungssystem SECOM. Auch die inzwischen angekndigte zentrale Gegenpartei x-clear wird in diese Kategorie fallen. Die SNB wird in der Wertschriftenabwicklung nur dort ttig werden, wo sie einen komparativen Vorteil hat: bei der Beurteilung der Abwicklungsrisiken. Brsenaufsicht und Institutsaufsicht gehren nicht zu ihren Kernkompetenzen. Bundesbehrden wie die EBK, aber auch private Organisationen wie die Brsen selbst, wirken hier effektiver. In der Schweiz wie auch in anderen Lndern ist die berwachung von Zahlungs- und Abwicklungssystemen in voller Entwicklung. Whrend die SNB im Bereich der Zahlungssysteme dank SIC ber reiche Erfahrung und ber einen guten Leistungsausweis verfgt, betritt sie in der Abwicklung von Effekten Neuland. Sie kennt zwar die Abwicklungsrisiken, weniger aber die Systembetreiber. Die Kooperation mit der EBK, welche die Institutsaufsicht weiterhin ausbt, ist deshalb unerlsslich. 7. Die Schweizerische Nationalbank als engagierte Partnerin Die SNB engagiert sich fr den Finanzplatz im Rahmen ihrer Funktionen, also primr der Geldpolitik und der Systemberwachung. Gleichzeitig setzt sie sich jedoch auch fr die Steigerung der Attraktivitt des Internationalen Finanzzentrums Schweiz ein. Dies geschieht vorzugsweise auf der praktischen Ebene. Die SNB orientiert sich am Ziel der Systemstabilitt, setzt sich aber auch konsequent fr die Erhaltung international konkurrenzfhiger Rahmenbedingungen ein. 1998 wurde aufgrund des neuen Effektenhndlerstatus SIC auch fr Effektenhndler geffnet. Im selben Jahr bekamen - der Internationalitt des Finanzplatzes wegen - jene berwachten auslndischen Institute Zugang, die sich in EUREX oder SWX engagieren. 1999 wurden im Hinblick auf CLS erstmals lntraday-Repos angeboten und seither laufend ausgebaut. Mit der Umstellung des geldpolitischen Instrumentariums von Devisenswaps auf Repos hat die SNB die Zahl ihrer Gegenparteien wesentlich erhht und damit auch zur Entstehung eines modernen Schweizer Geldmarktes beigetragen. Repos reduzieren das lnterbank-Kreditrisiko und damit das Ansteckungs- und Systemrisiko. Als Beraterin des Bundesrates leistet die SNB zu vielen Expertenkommissionen Beitrge. 2001 hat die SNB zur Analyse und Aufbereitung von Entscheidungsgrundlagen ein Kompetenzzentrum fr Systemstabilitt geschaffen. Im gleichen Jahr bildeten SNB und EBK gemeinsam einen Steuerungsauschuss Systemstabilitt. Darin werden fortlaufend konzeptionelle und praktische Fragen der Systemstabilitt behandelt. Seit jeher ist die SNB zudem Teil der schweizerischen Delegation im Basler Ausschuss fr Bankenaufsicht und trgt dort gemeinsam mit der EBK zur Fortentwicklung der wohl wichtigsten internationalen Aufsichtsstandards bei. Gleiche Aufgaben erfllt die SNB innerhalb des Ausschusses fr die Zahlungs- und Effektenabwicklungssysteme der Zehnergruppe bei der BIZ. Der SNB betreibt somit die Frderung des Internationalen Finanzzentrums Schweiz in umfassender Weise und aus Verantwortung fr das Ganze heraus. Es geht also weder um Industriepolitik noch um Protektionismus, sondern um Frderung der Wettbewerbsfhigkeit und der Stabilitt des schweizerischen Finanzsystems. An dieser Aufgabe mssen sich viele beteiligen. Der primre Beitrag der SNB ist die Sicherung der Geldwertstabilitt. Darber hinaus trgt sie Mitverantwortung fr die Stabilitt und die Fortentwicklung des Finanzsystems. Dies tut sie als berwacherin von Zahlungs- und Wertpapierabwicklungssystemen, in der Funktion als Lender of last resort und als Beraterin des Bundesrates in Fragen der Finanzplatzpolitik. 8. Schlussbemerkung Die Frage im Titel meines Referats lautet: Wie ist es um den Finanzplatz Schweiz bestellt? - Meine Antwort wird Sie nicht berraschen: Gut! Der Finanzplatz Schweiz ist wirtschaftlich solid. Die Anbieter der Finanzdienstleistungen sind leistungsfhig. Die Finanzmarktinfrastrukturen, die Regulierung und Aufsicht, die gesetzlichen, wirtschafts-, finanz- und whrungspolitischen ebenso wie die gesellschaftlichen Rahmenbedingungen sind gut. Zwar sind die technologischen, wirtschaftlichen und politischen Herausforderungen zahlreich. Der Finanzplatz Schweiz ist aber bestens gerstet, um sie erfolgreich anzunehmen.

Title: The Swiss National Bank in the Service of the Economy
text: The National Bank at the service of the economy Presentation by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Regional Economic Development Lucerne Central Swiss Chamber of Commerce Tuesday, September 10, 2002 Introduction Rural Switzerland is not only a Switzerland in Switzerland in name. It is also economically typical for our country in many ways. The export industry and tourism play an important role for both. For both, however, the advantages of good diversification also come into play, as both high-tech and mature industries contribute to economic performance. Monetary policy can make a difference in this environment. Today I will discuss the possibilities of monetary policy, but also the limits within which the SNB can use its monetary policy instruments in the service of the economy. 1. What can the central bank do? Benefits of price stability The greatest service a central bank can do to the economy is to keep the purchasing power of money stable. Keeping inflation at a stable, persistently low level has many economic and social benefits. Inflation - as well as deflation - disrupts the functioning of markets and affects economic development. Thus, the prices of individual goods lose their significance, the formation of price expectations is made more difficult, cash holding and the redistribution of wealth become more expensive, and finally income and wealth redistribution create social injustice. Price stability is very popular. Fighting inflation is less important. Once inflation has reached a certain dynamic, only painful monetary corrections often lead back to equilibrium. The effects of fighting inflation may even be a temporary recession and unemployment. They are difficult to quantify. Nevertheless, no one today doubts that these are significant economic costs. For a central bank, monetary stability is crucial because its instruments can have the greatest impact here. If monetary stability is not given, the cause is usually miscalculations by the central banks. That is why a central bank has the task in advance of not committing any serious mistakes in this area. Monetary policy can be compared to steering a boat: the boat often does not react immediately to turns on the rudder, a "stop and go" policy is not appropriate and only causes confusion on deck. When it comes to monetary policy measures, a policy of a steady hand is recommended. The stabilisation of monetary policy is of great importance. The service that the SNB can provide to the economy and society is therefore primarily to keep inflation low in the long term. Fortunately, there has been a broad political consensus on this in Switzerland, a strongly export-oriented country, for generations. And the real economy? The primacy of monetary stability does not mean that the SNB loses sight of the real economy. It is true that the long-term growth path depends primarily on the competitiveness and structure of an economy. The ups and downs on the road to prosperity are not only linked to the global economy, but also to monetary policy. In the short term, the link between the economy and central bank policy may seem problematic. The long-term goal of price stability contrasts with the short-term claim not to throw sand into the gears of the economy through excessively high interest rates. This fact is taken into account in the revision of the National Bank Act. "The National Bank at the service of the economy", this maxim is implemented in the text of the law with the following words: "The NATIONAL Bank guarantees price stability. In doing so, it takes into account economic developments." Above all, this formulation clarifies one thing: the SNB's main objective, namely to ensure price stability, must not lead to extreme real costs being accepted for rapid gains on the inflation front. For a central bank, however, "service to the economy" does not mean that it strives "a tout prix" for an immediate improvement in the economic climate, with the risk of creating a long-term inflationary development. One must have no illusions about the possibilities for action of a central bank. Part of the nature of the economy is that it changes - and usually more quickly than monetary policy can work. Their determinants are often complex and beyond the control of the authorities. Attempts to stimulate the economy with monetary policy measures are therefore usually doomed to failure. And the effect of monetary policy measures on inflation only occurs with a delay of two to three years. If a central bank were to react immediately to the respective economic situation, it would run the risk of losing sight of the goal of price stability. It would ultimately be a disservice to the economy. prove. "Observing economic developments" does not therefore mean cyclical activism, but means that the SNB must take into account the consequences of the real economy when determining its monetary policy and must exploit its room for manoeuvre in interest rate policy to the extent permitted by the foreseeable development of prices. The SNB's room for manoeuvre is also limited by the fact that we live in a small open economy. The course of the global economy thus sets certain guardrails that we cannot escape. Standing up to international trends is associated with great risks and rarely leads to success. Monetary policy is not fully comprehensive insurance against the vicissitudes of the economy. However, it takes into account the economic environment and exploits existing room for manoeuvre. And the exchange rate? In addition to the global economic development, the exchange rate is of great importance to Switzerland. Not only for companies suffering from price-related sales problems abroad, but also for the SNB, which is aware of their concerns and takes them seriously. The exchange rate enters the monetary policy decision-making process through the two channels already mentioned. On the one hand, directly by paying attention to the economic development. And on the other hand, indirectly via import prices, which are included in the consumer price index and thus affect the goal of price stability. The conflict of objectives between economic development and price stability, which occasionally exists in the short term, is exacerbated between exchange rate stability and price stability. If the SNB wanted to bring the Swiss franc exchange rate down at all costs, it would ultimately have to abandon the priority objective of price stability - with the consequences discussed at the beginning and without any guarantee that the reduction of the nominal franc exchange rate would bring about a lasting improvement in competitiveness. As you can see, the SNB must take a whole range of aspects into account in its monetary policy decisions in order to ensure price stability in the medium term and to enable the economy to achieve balanced growth. How does it proceed in practice? 2. How is monetary policy implemented between price stability and the economy? Our monetary policy approach, which we have been pursuing since 2000, is based on these three elements: definition of price stability, inflation forecast and target range for the 3-month Swiss franc Libor rate. We equate price stability with an increase in inflation of less than 2% per year. Of course, we also want to avoid any deflation and are therefore anxious to keep inflation between 0% and 2% in the medium term. Due to the long delay in the effect of monetary policy on prices, the SNB is forced to adopt a forward-looking stance and to orient itself on a forecast. The second element of our approach is therefore the use of an inflation forecast as the main indicator for monetary policy decisions. The inflation forecast ultimately summarizes how we assess price and economic developments. The forecast horizon is about as long as the delay in the impact of monetary policy, i.e. around 3 years. To put our policy into practice, we use a target range for the short-term interest rate, the three-month Swiss franc rate on the London international banking market, the 3-month Libor. With our liquidity policy, we influence interest rates on the money market. We work with this concept. However, we cannot do justice to our tasks if we apply it mechanically. Monetary policy decisions are therefore always made on the basis of a broad discussion of all available information. 3. "Where do we stand today?" Let me look back briefly to answer this question. If, shortly after the millennium celebrations - at the beginning of 2000 - the general economic situation and the mood on the financial markets had to be put into a headline, then the title "boom without end" would probably have offered itself for the USA and some industries. After a decade of strong growth with comparatively low inflation in the USA, Europe and even Japan, with its past economic problems, had again achieved impressive growth rates. Nevertheless, at the end of 2000, many economic reports had a big question mark. From mid-2000 onwards, economic growth lost significant momentum. Above all, investment activity began to falter. Although there was still an increase initially, the period of double-digit growth rates in equipment investment, such as in the USA, was coming to an end. It was remarkable how synchronously different economies were affected, even though they were in different economic stages. This can be explained above all by some special factors. Three of them have helped shape economic development in Switzerland, albeit to varying degrees. Synchronous shocks A first such factor was the significant increase in oil prices in 1999 and 2000. The high demand due to the economic situation itself had contributed to this. Now, however, the higher oil price made production, which was already running at full speed, even more expensive, with which the fever curve of prices began to rise. As a second factor, monetary policy also set dampening accents. At the end of the 90s, the central banks of many countries gradually raised their interest rates to counter the risk of overheating. There were good reasons for this at that time. The third factor was hardly predictable: the correction of the previous exaggerations in the financial markets; in particular, the bursting of the techno bubble. The setback was almost as impetuous as the development showed upwards for a long time. This also shattered the dream of endless inflation-free growth. On the stock exchanges, there were extensive revaluations of the shares. Not only technology stocks, but also financial stocks came under pressure. The profit and growth prospects had to be reconsidered in many places. Anyone who invested 100 francs in an index two years ago still has 80 francs in the case of the DJI, 70 francs with the SPI and only 50 francs for the EuroSTOXX.50. Reaction of monetary policy, investors and consumers The year 2001 thus became a stress test for the global economy. It was marked by declining industrial production and the decline in investment activity. It was no longer the word "boom" that dominated the headlines, but the term "recession". The low inflation rates and the previous monetary policy discipline allowed monetary policy to intervene decisively in what was happening. The slowdown in momentum was responded to with a rapid and pronounced easing of monetary conditions. In the midst of monetary and fiscal policy efforts, the attacks of September 11, 2001 fell. They were not the cause of the downturn, but accelerated development, increased uncertainty and further slowed down momentum. Monetary policy once again exploited its room for manoeuvre with a concerted interest rate cut. The reaction of consumers and investors varied: consumption remained the pillar of the economy; especially in the USA European consumption - especially German consumption - is reacting noticeably more cautiously. For investors, on the other hand, uncertainties have so far weighed more heavily than the favorable interest rate environment. They acted extremely cautiously. For the second half of 2002, business activities were expected to strengthen in many places and thus a revival of the economy. At first, this seemed to be true. Especially in the USA, the economy developed better again in the first quarter of 2002. This also applies if it is taken into account that half of the effect there was due to the fact that the warehouses were largely empty and the increasing demand immediately had an impact on production. Crisis Since the beginning of this year, however, the economic uncertainty that still prevails has been increasingly accompanied by uncertainty about the correctness of balance sheet information: the economic crisis was joined by the crisis of confidence. The information society has thus been hit at a sore spot. The prevailing measuring instruments for assessing the creditworthiness of companies are only suitable if the balance sheet information is correct. In response to this crisis of confidence, stricter rules of the game for listed companies have already been introduced or are in preparation. However, restoring trust remains a major challenge. The past summer months were marked by the slump on the international stock exchanges, which took place under the impression of this uncertainty. At the same time, the risk premium for corporate bonds rose to a level hardly ever reached. This shows that investor mistrust remains pronounced. Although a certain restraint is understandable, there is still no reason to paint a black picture. With the return of trust, the desire to invest will also return. However, the upswing expected by most forecasters to be in the middle of the year needs even more time before it gains in breadth and strength. The economic momentum has been postponed, not cancelled! ... and in Switzerland? When the US coughs, there is a risk of a cold on all sides. This is especially true for a small open economy like Switzerland, especially when Germany, our most important trading partner, is also struggling. The ups and downs of the Swiss economy depend largely on the economic downturn abroad. In addition to the interdependence of product markets, increasing capital and financial transactions are increasingly interdependence. Switzerland could not escape international developments. Export-oriented industries were particularly hard hit. To make matters worse, the Swiss franc gained strength at the same time. This was felt above all by the machinery industry in its order books. The tourism sector also recorded marked declines. This can be illustrated by the Lucerne hotel industry: Compared to the peak year 2000, a tenth fewer overnight stays were registered here in Lucerne last year and in the first half of 2002 overnight stays still fell by 7.5%. Above all, the declining desire to travel of tourists from the USA was noticeable. During this time, the SNB has repeatedly demonstrated that it is aware of these economic difficulties and the increased burden of the exchange rate. We have significantly loosened our monetary policy: for the first time at the beginning of 2001, when economic weakness began to emerge; then after 11 September and finally against the background of the persistently difficult economic environment and the upward pressure on the Swiss franc. Just over a month ago, we lowered our target range by 0.5 percentage points to 0.25 to 1.25%. Let us not forget one thing: these supportive actions of the National Bank were only possible because the current situation and the prospects for inflation left us room for it. In Switzerland, but also elsewhere, we have hardly seen any inflationary pressure for some time now due to the economic situation. The appreciation of the Swiss franc shows a positive side here for once. Declining import prices are a major contributor to the low Inflation rates. There is already talk of deflation here and there, but this assessment is wrong. The slightly negative Swiss price development of 0.1% in July is due to special factors that will disappear towards the end of the year. Without them, the price increase would have been 0.5%. If the inflation calculation is made without the cheaper oil prices and food (core inflation), a price increase of around 1% can be seen. The same applies to core inflation in the euro area and the USA, at around 2.5%. 4. What's next? Earlier this year, the majority of forecasters expected the economy to pick up and move towards a sustainable growth path for the second half of the year  that is, now. Since the middle of the year, the signals have intensified that the recovery is getting off to a slower and more moderate pace than we had all hoped. We now expect the economic picture to brighten only slowly but steadily. Economic development will remain flat this year and GDP will grow by significantly less than 1%. Unemployment will increase towards the end of the year, but should recede in 2003. However, these assumptions can only come true if the us and European economies pick up again from the end of the year and return to a sustainable growth path. Exports and equipment in particular would benefit from this. Consumption growth, on the other hand, is likely to weaken in line with developments on the labour market and real disposable incomes in the current year, and will only benefit from economic developments with a certain delay in 2003. The impulses from the construction sector are divided into two parts: While there is an excess demand for apartments, many office and commercial spaces are empty. Overall, therefore, despite low construction costs, only weak momentum is likely to result. This is the most likely scenario for economic development. However, as various leading indicators show, it is characterized by particular uncertainty. Uncertainty about the global economy The economic locomotive USA is currently making a stopover, but it is not a derailment. Although entrepreneurs are still showing a great deal of caution, there are signs of a recovery in investment in equipment. Although consumption is likely to weaken, it will continue to contribute to growth. Nevertheless, we must: keep an eye on the risk of a further slowdown - especially if it affects Europe - even if it does not seem likely today. The risk of "exchange rate" Further uncertainty arises on the exchange rate front. The higher prices of Swiss products abroad are of great concern to the export industry, even though the euro stabilised this year. The imbalance in the US current account increasingly manifested itself in a marked depreciation of the dollar. A decline in the dollar makes imports of consumer goods and raw materials, especially oil, cheaper. But much depends on the pace of devaluation. If the imbalances on both sides of the Atlantic slowly subside, then the benefits in the form of cheaper imports will outweigh europe. However, if the devaluation takes place within a short period of time, the shock of the failing American demand is likely to weigh heavily on the European and thus also on the Swiss economy. The risk of "political conflicts" Against the background of 11 September, political uncertainty is also painfully recalled. The consequences of the terrorist attacks have been coped with - at least this can be claimed for the economy. The economic community has proved to be vulnerable, but not destructible by terrorist activities. In the political field, the consequences of 11 September are not yet over. Political unrest creates uncertainty. For the economy in general, despite the lower interest rates, this means a difficult investment climate, for Switzerland the risk of an appreciation through the inflow of funds seeking protection. Political unrest also repeatedly brings oil price turbulence, another possible burden on the global economy. Seizing the opportunities despite risks But we have good reasons to appreciate the opportunities in addition to the risks. exaggerated pessimism and skepticism are just as out of place today as the exaggerated optimism and exuberance of yesterday. Switzerland is prepared for an upswing. It has learned the lessons of times of weak growth. The incentives are largely set correctly. The production apparatus is in good condition. A lot has been invested in promising markets, it has been redimensioned, where necessary. Progress has also been made in liberalisation. The field is cultivated to a large extent, we can trust that we will harvest the fruits. 5. Schlussbemerkungen The SNB puts itself at the service of the economy by primarily pursuing price stability, but not losing sight of the economy. The primacy of price stability applies for good reason, but room for manoeuvre should be exhausted. The recent past has shown that the SNB does not remain passive. We reacted first to the slowdown in growth, then to the strong and rapid rise in the Swiss franc exchange rate and finally to the fact that the recovery will be delayed. However, we were only able to do this because we had managed to maintain price discipline in times of strong economic growth. Only then did we have the necessary room for manoeuvre. This shows that price stability, as the primary objective of monetary policy, ultimately provides a very direct service to the economy. But always bear in mind that the SNB's possibilities are not unlimited: a swallow does not yet make a summer and low interest rates are not yet a guarantee of prosperity. The SNB can pave the way for recovery, but you as investors and consumers must follow this path yourself.
