Bei unseren Zinsschritten - sowie bei zahlreichen anderen Gelegenheiten - verliehen wir unserer Sorge um die Aufwertung des Frankens Ausdruck. In einer Zeit nachlassenden Wirtschaftswachstums kam eine solche Hherbewertung unserer Whrung einer unerwnschten Verschrfung der monetren Rahmenbedingungen in der Schweiz gleich. Dieser entschieden entgegenzutreten war uns ein wichtiges Anliegen. Zweifellos kam uns zugute, dass keine Anzeichen fr eine Gefhrdung der Preisstabilitt in der nahen und mittleren Zukunft bestanden. Daher hatten wir einen recht grossen Handlungsspielraum, um auf die unerwnschte Frankenstrke zu reagieren. Dabei war und ist uns klar, dass man - zumal in Phasen erhhter Unsicherheit - den Wechselkurs mit Manipulationen der Zinsdifferenz zu auslndischen Whrungen nicht verlsslich steuern kann. Aber man kann auf Wechselkursvernderungen mit Zinsanpassungen reagieren, um einen konjunkturell restriktiv wirkenden Aufwertungseffekt mit einem entgegengesetzten Zinsschritt wenigstens teilweise zu kompensieren. Das haben wir in den vergangenen 18 Monaten wiederholt getan. Zwar bewegt sich der EuroWechselkurs seit dem Schock vom 11. September im Bereich von etwa 1,45 bis 1,48 CHF pro Euro, dafr hat sich am Geldmarkt die Zinsdifferenz zum Euro von einem Prozentpunkt auf 2% Prozentpunkte ausgeweitet. Die letzte, am 26. Juli vorgenommene Zinssenkung um 50 Basispunkte war entscheidend durch eine weniger gnstige Konjunktureinschtzung motiviert, an der sich zwischenzeitlich nichts gendert hat. Das am 26. Juli bei % bis 1% Prozent festgelegte Zinsband scheint uns nach wie vor angemessen. Wir haben daher an der letzte Woche vorgenommenen vierteljhrlichen Lagebeurteilung entschieden, den Geldmarktzins unverndert bei rund % Prozent zu belassen. Aber wir werden auf der Hut sein mssen und auf Vernderungen des Umfeldes ntigenfalls rasch reagieren. Ausblick Die Perspektiven fr die Konjunktur in der Schweiz versprechen keine rasche Erholung. 2002 war und ist ein Jahr der Stagnation, und fr das kommende Jahr zeichnet sich im Schlepptau der internationalen Entwicklung eine eher langsame Beschleunigung ab. Bei diesem Ausblick ist trotz sehr tiefer Zinsen auf absehbare Zeit keine Teuerungsgefahr zu erkennen. Selbst wenn uns die Konjunkturerholung im Verlauf der nchsten Monate und Quartale positiv berraschen sollte, bleibt fr notwendige Zinsanpassungen gengend Zeit. Die konjunkturelle Risikobalance hat sich in den letzten Monaten auf die Seite wirtschaftlicher Schwche verschoben, sowohl in den USA als auch - und dies ausgeprgter - in Europa. Obwohl die Teuerungsraten in der Schweiz tief sind, halten wir eine deflatorische Entwicklung fr recht unwahrscheinlich. Unsere Kernteuerung betrgt seit lngerer Zeit rund ein Prozent, und die lnlandpreise weisen steigende Tendenz auf. Unser Bankensystem ist stabil, und damit droht keine pltzliche Kreditverknappung, wie man dies im Falle erhhter finanzieller Systemrisiken befrchten msste. Die Hauptsorge zahlreicher Akteure - insbesondere der Exporteure und ihrer Zulieferer gilt naheliegenderweise der Wechselkursentwicklung des Frankens, vorab gegenber dem Euro. Es entspricht der Erfahrung und es ist berdies konomisch leicht nachvollziehbar, dass in Zeiten erhhter Unsicherheit die Whrung eines internationalen Glubigerlandes zur Strke tendiert. Leider ist nicht auszuschliessen, dass politisch-militrische Ereignisse zustzliche ngste auslsen und den Aufwertungsdruck auf den Franken weiter verstrken. Aber es ist auch mglich, dass sich die Entwicklung normalisiert. Wir werden, wenn ausserordentliche Schocks unsere Stabilitt ernsthaften Gefahren aussetzen, entschlossen reagieren, ntigenfalls auch mit ausserordentlichen Massnahmen. Lassen Sie mich schliessen mit einer zwar unoriginellen, aber gerade in der aktuellen Situation wichtigen berlegung. Sie setzt an bei der hufig und mit Besorgnis gestellten Frage: Woher soll denn der Aufschwung kommen? Diese Frage suggeriert ein irrefhrendes Bild der konjunkturellen Wende. Eine Konjunkturerholung kommt realistischerweise nicht dadurch zustande, dass da pltzlich eine kraftvolle Energiequelle zu sprudeln beginnt. Vielmehr stellt sich die Wende in der wenig spektakulren Weise ein, dass zahllose Akteure sich in einem bestimmten Moment ein bisschen anders verhalten; dass sie ein wenig mehr ausgeben, dass sie einen zurckgestellten Ersatzbedarf an Ausrstungsgtern nicht mehr weiter hinausschieben, oder dass sie tief gehaltene Lagebestnde wieder leicht anheben. Vieles spricht dafr, dass die Voraussetzungen fr solche graduellen Korrekturen, deren Multiplikation den Aufschwung generieren kann, durchaus gegeben sind und eine solide Dosis an Zuversicht rechtfertigen. Wir sind berzeugt, dass die Schweizer Wirtschaft strukturell und in Bezug auf den monetren Rahmen gut positioniert ist, um von einer Beschleunigung der Nachfrage schnell und nachhaltig zu profitieren.

Title: Real estate prices and monetary policy
text: Real estate prices and monetary policy Presentation by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Presidents' Conference Homeowners' Association Switzerland Saturday, November 30, 2002 Introduction The global economy has cooled further in the course of this year. However, it has not collapsed, even though the speculative bubble of the "New Economy" burst two years ago and the titles of the "Old Economy" subsequently suffered massive setbacks. Strong consumer demand played a supporting role, especially in the USA. This is partly supported by additional mortgage debt, which was made possible thanks to sharply rising real estate prices and falling interest rates. It is sometimes feared that a real estate bubble will develop. Indeed, the question of what impact excessive prices of assets or goods can have is not without significance for the assessment of the future economy and inflation. In market circles, at the academic level and at the central banks, this is currently being intensively discussed. Should central banks take into account large fluctuations in asset prices in their decisions? The debate has not yet produced a generally accepted consensus. There are two ways for a central bank to respond to bloated asset prices. It can wait until the boom collapses and then act according to the respective effects. The other strategy is to intervene proactively. In this case, the monetary authority tries not to let a boom arise in the first place. This is intended to contain the consequences of a later possible price slump. Pronounced speculative bubbles are nothing new in economic history. A famous bubble is the Dutch "tulip mania" in the 17th century. From 1634 onwards, legions of private investors from home and abroad drove the prices of tulip bulbs higher and higher until they fell by around 90 percent three years later. The bursting of this speculative bubble hit the Dutch economy hard. The 20th century experienced several bubbles that were predestined to burst. The two most significant were the American stock boom at the end of the 20s and the stock and real estate boom in Japan in the late 80s and early 90s. In both cases, the valuation corrections led to severe recessions. In Switzerland, among other things, the end of the real estate price boom in the 80s has throttled the economy for several years. As a result, the local banking landscape experienced significant upheavals. The most recent speculative bubble emerged on the international stock markets. It ended in the spring of 2000, when prices began to fall massively after years of double-digit growth rates. This correction did not come as a complete surprise. Since the second half of the 90s, the question of whether stock valuations were not too high has become increasingly urgent. Recently, sharply rising property prices have caused a stir in the USA, Canada, Great Britain, Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands and Australia. Are such asset price fluctuations a problem for central banks? 1. What does price stability mean? Today, there is a global consensus that the main task of a central bank is to ensure stable prices in the medium term. For example, the draft of the new National Bank Act requires the SNB to ensure price stability. In doing so, it should take into account economic developments. Opinions differ as to what is meant by price stability. For the SNB, price stability prevails when the annual rate measured by the national consumer price index (KPI) is below 2% in the medium term. Other central banks, however, do not orient themselves on the consumer price index, but on a core inflation that excludes particularly volatile index components. No central bank explicitly integrates asset prices into its definition of inflation. However, the events of the 90s have shown that speculative bubbles can also occur with price stability. They are then above all a consequence of exaggerated expectations about future earnings and growth prospects. Since such bubbles are doomed to burst sooner or later and can cause greater damage, it is sometimes expected that central banks should take into account not only consumer prices but also asset prices. The price of future consumption - for which wealth is usually formed - is just as important as the price of goods and services that are consumed today. Therefore, it is sometimes claimed that a sharp price increase in the real estate sector or on the stock market is just as much a danger as price increases on the goods market. 2. Possible effects of excessive asset prices Indeed, asset price inflation, like consumer price inflation, can affect economic growth primarily by distorting price signals. A sharp rise in share prices can lead companies to: too much to invest. In recent years, there have been overinvestments, especially in the telecommunications sector and in Internet companies. Furthermore, rising land and stock prices can encourage investors to speculate on a continuation of the boom. This can lead them to go into excessive debt. Furthermore, exaggerated asset prices risk being reflected in higher consumer price inflation. If individuals feel wealthier from higher-valued stocks or land, they will spend more. If the economy produces close to the capacity limit, the prices of goods and services will also rise over time. An additional consequence of higher valuations of wealth is increasing revenues for the state. Such tax revenues often lead to higher expenditures or tax reductions that cannot be sustained in the long term. Real estate price fluctuations can also have a noticeable impact on the economic cycle. In some countries, house prices are now rising at double-digit growth rates. The relationship between house prices and disposable income has in some places almost risen to the peak reached at the end of the 80s or is above the long-term average. This indicates an overvaluation. Experience shows that sooner or later market prices tend towards their equilibrium values. This can occur when demand - with inelastic supply - unexpectedly recedes. An abrupt decline in demand for real estate can be triggered by a rise in interest rates or an economic slump. A study of asset prices in OECD countries over the past 30 years has revealed interesting results. Of 24 stock boom phases, only 3 led to major bankruptcies. On the other hand, a real estate boom caused significant valuation corrections in 10 out of a total of 19 cases. Drastic corrections to inflated assets were often accompanied by financial problems, banking crises and a credit crunch. The economy cooled down. Sometimes there was a decline in growth, the real costs became noticeable. 3. The importance of asset prices for monetary policy Collective speculation is a true drug. Everyone benefits; no one wants to see the negative sides. Although this danger is recognized by central banks, monetary authorities only include asset prices in their considerations when there is a risk that they will affect consumer prices. Why this Restraint? The reason is simple: central banks and market participants find it difficult to reliably distinguish a speculative bubble from a justified higher valuation. Rising asset prices are safe to reflect changing economic fundamentals. If, for example, rising stock prices are based on a leap in productivity and better profit prospects, the central bank does not need to worry about this. But even if there are signs that a bubble is emerging, it is unclear whether the central bank should intervene. It finds itself in a predicament: if it fails to end the boom, it risks that the bubble will burst at some point. The consequences can be devastating. However, if it intervenes preventively, e.g. by raising interest rates sharply, it can cause a price slump on the financial and real estate markets. In times of low inflation, it would be extremely difficult to make this policy understandable to the public. Most people reject inflation. However, only a few are likely to approve monetary policy measures that reduce the value of their assets as a precaution! The prices of different assets often move in the opposite direction. In the US and the UK, share prices have fallen this year. This would suggest a rate cut. At the same time, real estate prices in these countries have risen quite sharply, which has sometimes raised fears of a real estate bubble. Against this background, interest rates would have to be raised. The dilemma is obvious. However, monetary policy tightening would hardly be appropriate at present because the real estate market supports private consumption and thus the weak economy. 4. The real estate boom of the 80s and its consequences In the 80s, the marked economic growth in Switzerland was reflected particularly clearly in the price development on the real estate markets. The average price increase for condominiums and single-family homes was 7% annually. Gradually, price increases led to further price increases. Fewer and fewer realistic return expectations determined prices. Rather, they increasingly oriented themselves towards exaggerated prospects. How did this come about? Many banks pursued a poorly thought-out credit policy in the 80s. Domestic mortgage investments expanded from CHF 150 billion to CHF 380 billion between 1981 and 1991. Since the mortgage business was considered a safe banking business, the lenders did not regard the generous financing of real estate a priori as careless. Total lending activity expanded from 1983 to 1990 with annual growth rates of 4% to 15%. Although real estate prices had virtually doubled, falling prices at the height of the boom were considered completely unthinkable by many. It turned out differently. In 1991, property prices began to fall. Several factors led to this. Initially, the SNB reduced its money supply from 1989 onwards in order to combat rising inflation. Interest rates rose. At the same time, economic growth in OECD countries slowed. At the end of 1990, the significant decline in construction investment heralded the economic slowdown in Switzerland. Housing construction was the first to be affected. Higher mortgage rates and rising unemployment increasingly restricted the scope for financing. The demand for single-family homes weakened. The slowdown in construction investment in 1991 also extended to commercial construction. Slowly, the signs of weakening became noticeable on a broad front. Since the banks had a lively share in the real estate boom, they had to accept large losses on their domestic loans, with the exception of the Raiffeisen Group. Between 1991 and 1996, these losses accounted for almost 6% of the total volume of loans for the cantonal banks. In the case of the big banks, they amounted to over 12%. The losses on the real estate market to be borne by the banking sector amount to more than CHF 40 billion. The real estate crisis triggered a drastic restructuring of the banking system in Switzerland. The number of banks visibly shrank. Regional banks accounted for most of the decline. However, there were also significant structural changes within the cantonal banking group. Ultimately, the takeover of Schweizerische Volksbank by Schweizerische Kreditanstalt at the time was also the result of the real estate crisis. In retrospect, both households and companies in Switzerland took on excessively high interest rate risks in the 80s. As a result, the tightening of the monetary policy stance, which the SNB felt compelled to adopt in the face of high inflation, had far-reaching and painful effects on the economy. In addition to monetary policy, other factors also influence the development of real estate prices. Studies on the real estate crises that occurred in the 80s and 90s in Sweden, Japan, Thailand and the USA show certain similarities. Some of them also apply to Switzerland.  One thing they had in common was that investors often overestimated the value of an object. They sensed a chance for big wins. This prompted them to invest corresponding sums. everywhere was built. The relationship between price and quality receded into the background. After the bubble burst, a significant part of the invested funds were destroyed.  Another commonality was false incentives. Market participants benefited from activities that caused prices to rise inexorably. Real estate was largely financed by debt. On the one hand, the willingness to take risks was increased. Many real estate investors assumed that in the event of failure, the lenders would have to bear the losses to a large extent. On the other hand, bank employees often had an incentive to give the highest possible loans. The quality hardly played a role, the volume achieved was decisive for their salary. The banks, for their part, reacted only hesitantly to a worsening of the situation. Instead of realizing bad credit, they hoped for a market recovery. In the absence of such a rule, they would rely in part on their governments.  A third factor has been investigated in the context of behavioural economics, a field of research that deals with the behaviour of economic agents. Economic agents, it turned out, consider an event to be all the more likely the easier they can imagine. The imagination is influenced by their experiences. Because a long time had passed since the last real estate bubble, it was difficult for investors to imagine a repeat. 5. The development of real estate prices in recent years Stock prices have been declining for almost three years. Industrial production and investment have shrunk. Corporate profits declined significantly. At the same time, real estate prices have risen. This applies mainly to the USA, but also to Switzerland. The economic downturn could do little to change this. This is a significant difference from previous downturns. This is how we started of the 80s and also the 90s, real estate prices fell in line with the economic deterioration. Several explanations lend themselves to the current real estate bull market. The improved economy in the second half of the 90s certainly stimulated the demand for residential and commercial space significantly. Because the supply of real estate is more or less fixed in the short term, prices are mainly determined by demand. As the economy cooled, central banks lowered interest rates, supporting demand for home ownership. The SNB, for example, has lowered the target range for its key interest rate by a total of 275 basis points since March 2001. These interest rate cuts were made possible by low inflation rates. Especially in the US and the UK, the low cost of capital encouraged homeowners to top up mortgages. Property purchases also increased. On several occasions, investors have shifted money from equity investments to real estate, which is considered relatively safe. While stock prices fell, property prices continued to rise. Until recently, it looked as if the positive prosperity effect of rising real estate prices was dominating. For many people, an apartment or house is still the largest component of wealth. Even in the U.S., where stock ownership is most common, the average household owns four times more wealth in the form of real estate than in the form of stocks. That's why many more people feel when property prices change than when their shares are revalued. This is one explanation for the robustness of private consumption in an otherwise weak economy. 6. The real estate market in Switzerland Real estate prices in Switzerland show clear parallels with economic development. At the beginning of the ? In the years, prices rose sharply. This phase was followed by a decline from 1974/75, replaced by a resurgence until 1981/82. In the second half of the 80s, prices rose again massively. The past decade, on the other hand, has been largely marked by lower valuations. For some years now, Switzerland has also been recording rising prices for residential property. The low mortgage interest rates and the good income situation of many households stimulated the demand for residential property. In addition, the demand for living space per capita continues to increase. Last but not least, the accelerated population growth is also having an effect. The supply lags behind. The number of newly built apartments has tended to increase since 1995 declining. The stock of vacant rental and condominium apartments as well as single-family houses has been declining for four years. In the third quarter of this year, the number of condominiums offered in print and online advertisements fell by 8% compared to the previous year. The supply of single-family homes decreased by 9%. In the case of rental apartments, the decline is even just under 15%. The excess demand is reflected in rising prices. In the third quarter of this year, single-family homes cost 4% more than a year ago. Condominiums were almost 8% more expensive. There are considerable regional differences. Prices for single-family homes rose most strongly in the geneva (9%) and Zurich (8%) regions, while condominiums in the Zurich region cost a good 13%, and on Lake Geneva more than 8% more than in the previous year. Whether this development will continue in view of the economic uncertainties remains to be seen. Tenants have also felt the imbalances in the real estate market. In the third quarter of 2002, prices for rental apartments were a good 4% higher than in the same period of the previous year. The largest price increase was recorded in Switzerland with 10%. At over 6%, prices on Lake Geneva, southern Switzerland and Zurich have also risen. Only in eastern Switzerland did rental apartment prices decline slightly. The development of real estate prices in Switzerland does not justify any monetary policy measures. Firstly, a significant increase in prices can be observed mainly in urban areas. It is not a sign of a generally inflationary development. It is basically a change in relative prices. Second, the price development in the real estate markets does not indicate a risk of overheating for the rest of the economy, as banks are pursuing a much more cautious credit policy than in the 80s. Thirdly, the current economic stagnation is likely to dampen price developments. Clear signs of this can be found in the market for office space. In the third quarter of this year, vacancy rates throughout Switzerland rose sharply by 0.5 percentage points to over 8%. In addition, there is a clear trend towards declining office rents. 7. Should the SNB take greater account of real estate prices today? Even if real estate prices in Switzerland do not seem to indicate an overvaluation, they are high by international standards. There are several reasons for this. Our country is densely populated and the supply of land is scarce. Furthermore, the quality standards and the demands are high. A comparatively high price level is offset by relatively low mortgage interest rates. Short- and long-term interest rates in Switzerland are much lower than comparable euro or dollar rates. Low and stable interest rates, readily available mortgage loans, comparatively high job security, and the ability to deduct passive interest from taxable income encourage homeowners to take on high debts. Over 70% of personal loans are covered by land or real estate. This proportion of land collateral is higher than in other industrialized countries. It means that the high level of private sector debt is mainly due to land and real estate acquisitions. With 70% of the population in rent, mortgage loans granted by banks to households are highly concentrated. For the lenders, this means a not negligible cluster risk. This gives an idea of how important the comparatively low level of interest rates and thus an autonomous monetary policy are for Switzerland. As in other countries, real estate investments in Switzerland are more important than equities. It is true that Switzerland has the highest equity market capitalisation in relation to GDP. However, a significant part of the shares are in foreign hands. At the same time, the Swiss hold large quantities of foreign shares. Public and private pension funds also have a high level of equity holdings. However, individuals can hardly estimate how fluctuations in the stock market will affect their future retirement. What is important for monetary policy is that the wealth effect of equities and other assets is likely to be smaller than the effect of real estate prices. It is also more difficult to detect. Should the SNB now take asset prices into account in its monetary policy decisions? We believe that we should only pay attention to asset prices to the extent that they affect future inflation. Initial studies show that greater attention to bond rates, goods, share and real estate prices cannot be justified. Real estate prices only provide additional information for inflation forecasts. They therefore only offer themselves as an additional indicator that allows further Provides information on the assessment of the monetary policy stance. They must not be an objective of monetary policy. The SNB has a very direct interest - and I am referring to a different but related subject - in the efforts to improve the current tenancy law. We are particularly interested in a solution that affects monetary policy less than the existing regulation. The current link between rents and mortgage interest rates has undesirable monetary policy effects in the short term. If the SNB tightens the monetary policy reins, for example to counter looming inflation, there will be a disproportionate increase in rents and thus first of all a surge in inflation. The SNB will then have to put on the brakes for longer in order to reduce inflation than would be necessary without linking rents to mortgage interest rates. The Federal Council's dispatch on the relevant law has been available since September 1999. In line with the message, the Federal Parliament would no longer like to link rent adjustments to the development of mortgage interest rates, but to inflation. Linking rents to inflation is preferable to today's de facto peg to mortgage rates. Although a central bank cannot enjoy price indexation per se, we consider the outlined solution to be the second-best option behind a pure market solution. 8. Summary and conclusions The decline in stock market prices has so far had only limited consequences for the global economy. However, it cannot be ruled out that a sustained bear market in the USA will have an impact on the global economy. Much depends on whether consumers and companies assess the price losses as permanent and adjust their behavior accordingly. The real estate market has so far acted as an economic pillar. Real estate enjoys great popularity, not least because equity investments currently appear to many investors to be unattractive. The escape into the material assets of brick and mortar, which are classified as safe, is underway. Whether the real estate sector will be able to cushion recessive tendencies in the future remains to be seen. The risk of a bubble seems to exist mainly in some major foreign cities. The continuing sluggish economic trend is likely to counteract excesses and lead to a soft landing of the Real estate prices contribute. The biggest danger for the real estate market - a sharp rise in interest rates - is currently nowhere to be seen. In Switzerland, there are no signs of exaggerated price developments in the real estate sector. After years of falling valuations, the local market began to improve in 1999 thanks to the strong economic slowdown. In line with this, prices have risen since then. However, in terms of household income, homes are still around a third cheaper than before the real estate crisis of the 90s. Due to the significant increase in housing permits, residential construction activity is expected to increase. The mismatch between supply and demand in the housing market should be corrected in the coming years. The current situation differs in essential points from that at the end of the 80s. At that time, a multi-year economic upswing phase came to an end in Switzerland. In addition to rapidly rising real estate prices, a marked increase in the money supply was observed. In addition, there were double-digit loan growth rates. The franc tended to weaken. Inflation was in the suit. We are a long way from that at the moment. The global economy continues to hope for a recovery. Inflation is kept in check. The management of credit risks by banks has improved significantly in recent years. In addition, stricter loan-to-value conditions are applied. Nor does the weak growth of domestic loans point to any immediate danger. Should a central bank prevent alleged exaggerations in the financial and real estate markets at an early stage? For some, just looking at consumer prices is no longer enough. They want central banks to proactively burst speculative bubbles, even if consumer goods prices are stable. There are three reasons against this: First, central banks cannot recognize over- or undervaluations better than the market. Second, a boom is a complex phenomenon. It is hardly possible for monetary policy to successfully carry out surgical interventions against speculative bubbles. The risks of collateral damage would be enormous. Third, changes in key interest rates targeting asset prices may run counter to the economy in the short term without any guarantee of improving the outlook for price stability.
