La Hollande qui, comme la priphrie, a connu une forte croissance et une forte inflation est un cas particulier, j'y reviendrai ultrieurement. Peut-tre faut-il affiner encore ce modle centre/priphrie et distinguer la priphrie du Nord de celle du Sud. Les pays priphriques du Nord ont souvent une balance commerciale excdentaire, c'est a dire que leurs exportations dpassent leurs importations. La croissance de ces pays sexplique alors en partie par une forte demande externe. Faut-il rappeler que certaines entreprises finlandaises et irlandaises exportent dans tout l'Euroland des produits technologiques innovateurs? En revanche les pays de la peripherie du Sud, comme le Portugal ou I'Espagne, ont souvent une balance commerciale dficitaire. On peut donc supposer que la demande intrieure y explique en partie la forte croissance. Quels sont donc les principaux carts entre les attentes a long terme lies a |'Euroland et les rsultats de l'histoire recente? Il y en a deux: e Premirement, on remarque que les taux dinflation, qui s'taient pourtant fortement uniformiss au moment de la mise en place du systeme monetaire europen dans les annes nonante, ont a nouveau tendance a diverger depuis la cration de leuro. e Deuximement, seule une partie de IlEuroland bnficie pour linstant d'un accroissement significatif d'activit. Les divergences de croissance sont apparues des la mise en place du march unique. Alors quon aurait pu sattendre a ce que les pays possdant dja un march intrieur important bnficient en premier du grand marche europen, parce que leurs entreprises se sont spcialises dans des activites ou les rendements d'chelles sont importants, c'est l'inverse qui a t le cas. Ce sont les pays de la priphrie qui sortent gagnants jusquici. 4. Les forces d'ajustement Comment expliquer ces evolutions? Quelles sont les forces qui ont modele la nouvelle carte conomique europenne? Lexplication principale est a chercher dans la dynamique qui a rsult des carts trs importants qui existaient dans lEuroland entre les cotuts nationaux du travail et du capital au moment de I'intgration. Ces diffrences ont dclench des mcanismes d'ajustement extremement puissants lorsque les barriere nationales sont tombes. Concentrons-nous dabord sur les cotts du travail. Ils taient  et sont toujours  nettement plus bas dans tous les pays que nous avons classs dans la peripherie dynamique. Par exemple les couts horaires du travail, prestations sociales inclues, taient infrieurs de quinze pour cent aux Pays-Bas compar a I'Allemagne en 1995, ce qui justifie que nous ayons class ce pays dans la priphrie de |'Euroland. En Finlande les cotts d'une heure de travail taient les trois-quarts, et en Irlande la moiti de ceux de l'Allemagne toujours en 1995. Au Portugal ils n'en reprsentaient mme pas le quart! Si nous avons choisi l'anne 1995, c'est parce que les statistiques y taient completes mais le tableau n'a pas fondamentalement chang depuis. Mme si les comparaisons internationales des coUts salariaux restent problematiques, les differences sont telles qu'il est facile de comprendre que les pays de la pripherie aient eu des atouts a jouer lorsque le march unique sest cr, ceci d'autant plus que d'importantes incitations a l'investissement avaient t mises en place par la Commission de Bruxelles. Comme les cotts salariaux reprsentent une part majeure des codts de production, les entreprises situes dans les pays priphriques ont t, d'entre, des lieux de production tres attrayants a main d'ceuvre abondante et a bon marche. Inversement, les entreprises des pays du centre ont vu leur position relative se dtriorer, et elles ont dU se battre pour maintenir leurs parts de marche et ont souvent procd a des dlocalisation de production. Un processus d'galisation des couts salariaux est ainsi en cours. Dans la pripherie, la forte croissance provoque une augmentation des salaires plus rapide que dans le centre. Etant donne limportance des carts de remuneration, cette disparite durera encore longtemps, ceci d'autant plus que le mouvement vers |lgalisation est entrav par la relative immobilit du facteur travail. (Mme si les salaires sont infrieurs dans la peripherie, les perspectives d'emploi et de croissance y soit meilleures, ce qui n'incite pas a l'emigration). De toute fagcon la main-d'ceuvre peu qualifige de la priphrie ne peut guere esperer trouver un emploi dans le centre ou les rigidites du marche du travail l'exclueraient du processus de production. Venons-en maintenant aux couts du capital. Limitons notre discussion aux taux dintert si importants pour le financement externe des entreprises et des collectivits publiques. Les taux d'intrt se sont mis a converger dans I|'Europe des douze a partir de 1995 dja. En 1999, ils taient dja quasiment galiss. Aujourd'hui, une obligation avec un horizon de 10 ans offre un rendement pratiquement identique indpendamment du pays de lEuroland qui met. Comme le loyer de largent tait en gnral lev dans les pays de la periphrie avant 1999, lgalisation des taux a amlior leurs conditions de financement. Cette baisse a eu deux consequences bnfiques immdiates. Premirement, la charge des dettes privees et publiques sest vue rduite. Deuxiemement, les taux plus bas favorisent un niveau de consommation et dinvestissement plus leve. Les entreprises de la priphrie qui disposaient dja de l'avantage de faibles coUts du travail, se sont mise a gagner sur les deux tableaux en profitant en plus d'une baisse des coUts du capital. Elles ont bnefici d'un vritable coup de fouet montaire. Les taux dintert en termes nominaux ont donc baiss pour les pays de la periphrie mais ils n'ont pas ncessairement augment dans les pays du centre. Cependant l'galisation en elle-mme reprsente tout de mme un grave handicap pour les entreprises des pays qui, jusque-la, disposaient de l'avantage de taux d'intrt infrieurs aux autres. Elle prive ces entreprises d'un avantage comparatif important et diminue ainsi leur comptitivit relative. De plus, en termes rels les taux d'intrt du centre sont maintenant suprieurs a ceux de la priphrie car l'inflation y est plus faible. Avec la croissance affaiblie de l'investissement gui en rsulte, et la baisse concomitante de la demande du travail, les salaires rels des pays du centre devraient croitre moins vite ou voire mme baisser. Mais vu la rigidit des salaires nominaux a la baisse, un chmage leve persiste au coeur de l'Euroland. Quelles conclusions tirer de cette analyse a grands traits du paysage europen au cours des dernires annes? e ba premire conclusion est que les rigidits du march du travail europen, renforce par la faible mobilit de la main-d'ceuvre, favorisent l'expansion de l'activite des zones priphriques  a salaires bas  au dtriment du centre a marche contrdle et cout lev. La croissance de la priphrie va rester forte, celle du centre faible. C'est la consquence logique des forces dajustement mises en ceuvre par le processus d'intgration dclench par la cration du grand march europen. e ba deuxime conclusion est d'ordre montaire. Si la monnaie unique n'existait pas, l'acclration de la croissance dans la priphrie entrainerait une appreciation des monnaies de la zone par rapport aux monnaies du centre. Ainsi, par la voie du taux de change, se corrigerait l'cart de comptitivite entre les pays a salaire rel bas et les pays a salaire rel leve. Ce mcanisme de rquilibrage par le taux de change ne peut plus fonctionner puisque l'euro a maintenant remplac les monnaies nationales. Un autre facteur doit s'ajuster: le taux d'inflation. La dynamique d'intgration va donc faire apparaitre des taux d'inflation plus levs dans les pays de la priphrie et plus bas dans le centre, ce qui rodera peu a peu la comptitivit de la zone priphrique. L'Union monetaire, dans le contexte du grand march, provoque ainsi un largissement des diffrentiels d'inflation. Ceci nous montre que I'introduction de la monnaie unique  qui correspond en fait a une soudure irrmdiable des anciennes parits nominales  ne bloque pas pour autant les ajustements en termes rels: si la comptitivit des pays de la zone priphrique ne se corrige plus par une apprciation de leur monnaie par rapport a celles du centre, elle s'rode par une hausse accelre des salaires et des prix. La problematique est la mme, seuls les canaux d'ajustement sont diffrents. C'est aussi ainsi que l'on comprend le cas un peu paradoxal des Pays-Bas, un pays du centre qui a connu une croissance et un taux d'inflation proches de ceux de la priphrie. Cette situation particulire vient du fait que, durant la seconde moiti des annes 1990, ce pays a entrepris d'importantes rformes structurelles: libralisation du march intrieur, flexibilisation du march du travail, autant de mesures qui ont accru sa comptitivit par rapport a lAllemagne. Paralllement le florin tait fixe par rapport au DM. Au moment de l'Union montaire, la monnaie hollandaise tait ainsi certainement sous-value. Une fois l'euro introduit, les ajustements se sont effectus par la voie des prix. La comptitivit des Pays-Bas s'est dtriore ces quatre dernires annes par un taux d'inflation annuel moyen qui a dpass de 1,5% celui de I'Allemagne. Une fois encore, le blocage des parites ne peut interrompre les ajustements ncessaires. 5. Et si la Suisse faisait partie de I'Euroland? Tout dabord je rappelle que la question dune participation de la Suisse a lEuroland est une rflexion purement thorique. Il n'y a pas de discussions allant dans ce sens actuellement. De toute facon une adhsion a leuro prsupposerait une adhsion a l'Union Europenne. Nous en sommes encore loin. Mais si la Suisse en tait, oll se situerait-elle dans cette nouvelle gographie conomique europenne? Peut-on la classer parmi les pays priphriques, auxquels elle ressemble par sa petite taille, ou bien appartient-elle aux pays du centre, comme le laisse supposer sa position gographique? En termes de structure de son appareil de production, de son intensit en travail et du niveau de salaires rels, c'est incontestablement a la seconde catgorie qu'elle doit tre assimile. Il y a en effet beaucoup de similitudes entre les caractristiques de la Suisse et celles de I'Allemagne dans ces domaines. Mais mme si notre Economie ressent, comme Allemagne, la comptitivite accrue des pays de la priphrie, sa position est diffrente a deux gards: Premierement, nos entreprises n'ont pas perdu l'avantage comparatif que reprsentent des taux d'intrt bas. Nos taux sont en effet plus bas de deux points de pourcentage environ en termes nominaux comme en termes rels que ceux du march allemand. Cette difference est appellee a persister tant que la Suisse n'est pas intgre dans |'union monetaire; elle pourrait mme s'accroitre si la Banque centrale europenne devait tolrer une inflation moyenne plus leve en raison des difficults rencontres par les pays de la zone priphrique. En cas d'intgration toutefois, nos taux d'intrt monteraient au niveau europen, ce qui entrainerait non seulement un choc dflationniste pour l'conomie suisse mais accroitrait durablement ses couts de production par rapport a ses concurrents europens. Nous serions donc dans une position relativement inconfortable car nos conditions de financement se dtrioreraient non seulement en termes relatifs mais aussi en termes absolus. Une exprience douloureuse que le@conomie allemande n'a pas vcue. En second lieu, nous avons l'exprience d'une monnaie forte qui, ces 30 dernires annes, s'est tendanciellement renforce face au mark, d'abord, a l'euro ensuite. Et cette apprciation est alle au-dela de la simple compensation du diffrentiel d'inflation entre la Suisse et l'Allemagne, entre la Suisse et la Zone euro depuis 1999. Pour une bonne part, l'apprciation relle du franc est le reflet d'une @conomie helvtique plus flexible que l'6conomie europenne, une Economie ou les progres de competitivite sont, en moyenne, plus assurs que sur le front europen, en Allemagne en particulier. Ma constatation peut paraitre surprenante car les Suisses ont souvent une image ngative de leur propre situation. Mais si l'on jette un regard sur ce qui s'est passe chez nous ces 10 dernieres annes, on se convainc rapidement que nos structures ont t plus flexibles que celles de nos voisins: une rforme profonde du secteur bancaire, une libralisation du march du travail, une ouverture au echanges, des ajustements importants dans les structures de production qui ont souvent mis nos entreprises sous le feux des projecteurs. Depuis 1990 la population trangere a augmente de 25% et le nombre de personnes actives a progress de pres de 9%, des chiffres peu en accord avec l'image de stagnation economique que nous avons souvent a l'esprit. En termes relatifs l'economie suisse s'est revele plus dynamique que l'conomie allemande, un pays qui devait aussi digrer sa reunification, si bien que l'apprciation relative du franc n'est pas une surprise. Quelles seraient les consquences de ce relatif dynamisme si nous tions membre de l'Union montaire? Ici c'est l'exprience des Pays-Bas qui est instructive: nous verrions vraisemblablement le taux d'inflation suisse se situer en dessus du rythme de la hausse des prix de la zone euro, et particuligrement en dessus de celui des pays les moins dynamiques. Les forces d'ajustement, aujourd'hui a l'ceuvre par le biais du taux de change, se manifesteraient au travers de l'volution du niveau gnral des prix. Ceux qui considerent que le cours du franc est une menace pour la comptitivit seraient alors inquiets de voir l'inflation helvtique tre suprieure a celle de nos partenaires sans que nous ayons les moyens de la contrdler. 6. Conclusions Permettez-moi de conclure ce survol en tirant quelques enseignements du processus d'integration monetaire dans lequel s'est engage l'Europe. Je vous ai rappele les promesses et espoirs lis a lEuroland dans le long terme. Nous avons constate que sur le chemin qui mne a ces bienfaits, il y a des gagnants et des perdants et qu'une nouvelle gographie conomique sest mise en place. Les pays du centre de l'Europe souffrent actuellement d'un dficit de croissance et d'un chmage leve alors que les pays situs en periphrie progressent rapidement. Ce n'est que trs lentement, au travers d'une evolution differencie des prix que leur comptitivite se rtablit. Ce mouvement prendra dautant plus de temps que les marchs du travail des pays concerns sont peu flexibles et que la mobilit du travail sur le plan europen reste limite. Des differences entre les taux d'inflation vont perdurer au sein de la zone euro et la hausse des prix dans les pays priphriques rendra la dfense de la stabilit des prix au niveau de l'ensemble de la zone particulirement difficile. Quelles conclusions tirer pour notre pays? e A l'vidence, la Suisse n'a aucun intrt pour l'instant a vouloir s'intgrer dans cette gographique monetaire europenne. Un ajustement de nos taux d'intert au niveau europen  plus lev que le notre  affaiblirait la position concurrentielle de nos entreprises. e Nous devons nous attendre a ce que les taux d'inflation des pays de la priphrie europenne demeurent relativement lev, si bien que I'inflation europenne moyenne sera suprieure a celle de la Suisse. e En cas d'adhsion a |'Union montaire, nous ne devons surtout pas esprer tre dynamiss de l'extrieur, c'est-a-dire par le reste de I'Euroland. Lalignement des taux d'intert suisses sur les taux europens, donnerait des atouts concurrentiels a nos partenaires, a l'image des avantages quont retir I'Irlande et la Finlande par rapport a Allemagne. Dans Il'union montaire, comme aujourd'hui, le dynamisme de notre economie dpendra de ses propres forces, de sa capacit a innover, des progrs de sa productivit et de son exploitation des niches d'exportations les plus productives. e Si notre conomie demeure plus flexible que celle des pays voisins, une adhsion a l'Union monetaire ne rglerait pas tous nos problemes. Certes, nous ne serions plus confronts a une apprciation tendancielle de notre monnaie par rapport a l'euro, comme jusquiici, mais la pression sur nos ressources productives conduirait a une hausse des prix plus rapide chez nous que dans les pays du centre europen. Chassez les problemes de change par la porte, ils reviennent sous la forme d'inflation par la fentre, comme on le dit d'un importun. L'exprience des Pays-Bas est exemplaire a ce sujet. Le titre de notre expos: la Suisse au coeur de |'Euroland acquiert ainsi une toute autre dimension. Nous sommes effectivement un petit pays au coeur de l'Europe. Avec nos voisins nous entretenons traditionnellement des relations commerciales et financires etroites et fortes. Nous bnficions de la dynamique du march europen et nous souffrons lorsque sa croissance se ralentit. A la difference de nos voisins nous disposons encore de I'avantage d'une politique monetaire indpendante: a savoir des taux d'intrt bas et un taux de change flexible. La flexibilit du cours de change est souvent considre comme un handicap pour notre conomie. C'est une vision trop rductrice. Si la Suisse a son dynamisme propre, elle sera toujours confronte a des problemes monetaires, quils viennent du change ou qu'ils viennent de la hausse des prix, et ceci quelle fasse partie ou non de PUnion monetaire. Aucun rgime de change n'est en mesure de garantir la comptitivite de nos entreprises. La cration de la monnaie unique a profondment modifi le paysage europen et les conditions de fonctionnement de lEuroland. Au cours des dernires annes, le procession dintgration semble avoir fait des gagnants et des perdants. Les perdants sont ceux dont l'appareil de production est relativement rigide aux changements, ils souffrent dune faible croissance et dun chmage leve. Notre pays nadhrera pas a |'Union europenne et a lEuroland dans les annes a venir. Ce qui se passe autour de nous est toutefois riche en enseignements. Si nous ne voulons ne tre places un jour dans la mme situation que nos voisins du centre, nous devons veiller a nous adapter continuellement aux ralits dun march international en constante evolution, nous efforcer de crer des conditions-cadres favorables au dveloppement d'activits porteuses, encourageant productivit et valeur ajoute, et prserver la flexibilit de notre march du travail. Ce sont-la les paramtres essentiels a notre prosprit future. Ce sont ceux qui doivent retenir toute notre attention et tous nos efforts.

Title: A challenge for monetary policy  considerations on the concept and the current development
text: Required monetary policy Reflections on the concept and current development Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board Of the Swiss National Bank Guest Lecture at the University of St. Gallen, 24 January 2003 The time to reflect on conceptual aspects of monetary policy is well chosen. At the beginning of 2003, the global economic development was characterized by areas of tension and situational peculiarities, which gave rise to concerned questions in large circles. How can the global economy regain its growth potential when the room for manoeuvre in two of the three major regions has been completely or almost exhausted? How can the spirit of economic initiative be restored if there is a lack of basic trust on several levels: in geopolitical stability, in job security, in the commercial opportunities of products, in the honesty of managers? Is there a cyclically acceptable, steady correction of the foreign imbalances that have built up, or is there a threat of another adjustment shock on this front? There are many questions. In the following, I would like to emphasise monetary policy, let myself be inspired by the topicality, but nevertheless put the conceptual aspects in the foreground. My presentation is divided into six sections. I would like to start with a somewhat stylized history, reminding you that the theory and practice of monetary policy action have undergone various developmental steps and will go through them in the future (1). Then I would like to deal with the gratifying fact that price stability has been achieved in all major countries and ask how this should continue with the central banks (2). In the third part, I deal with the monetary policy mandate, in particular with the objective ratio of price and economic stability (3). The fourth section refers to the asset price bubbles and the importance that this phenomenon should play in monetary policy decisions (4). This is followed by some reflections on the risk of deflationary development (5). In the last part, I will give you some thoughts on the current economic outlook (6). 1. Monetary policy - a stylized review Let me start with some monetary history by pointing out - rather woodcut-like - important facts that are important for assessing the topicality. A topicality that is characterized by the fact that most countries have managed to achieve price stability. This is certainly good news, but we must not overestimate its historical significance. Inflation is and has never been a quasi-natural law inevitability. Although we have all grown up in an inflationary environment and therefore perceive some inflation as normal, persistent, widespread inflation is a very recent phenomenon. Inflationary periods were the exception before the twentieth century, not the rule. Never before have stubbornly high inflation rates been as widespread in all currencies of the world as they were in the 20th century. Worldwide, the rise in prices in the second half of the 20th century dwarfs all other inflationary episodes in human history. The advantages of a paper currency over a gold currency had to be bought at a really high price. For reasons of data availability, this finding, which is anything but flattering for politicians, is illustrated by the example of the USA; the key message, however, applies to almost all countries. Supplement 1: Commodity prices USA 1665 - 2001 Purchasing power, as measured by the consumer goods price index, tended to remain stable well into the 20th century. Inflation occurred mostly and only when gold backing was suspended, typically for reasons of war financing. In the case of the USA, for example, the gold standard was temporarily abolished during the Civil War (1861 - 1865): a significant inflationary acceleration was the result. It is interesting, however, that - before the 20th century - the price level usually fell back to the original level after periods of inflation; inflation was followed by compensatory deflation. After World War 2, this pattern changed. A return to the original price level did not materialize and was rightly never sought. In contrast to the post-war generations, people used to have some practice in dealing with deflationary phases. 70s. The abandonment of the dollar's gold peg and the collapse of the Bretton Woods monetary system led to blatant inflationary excesses from the seventies to the eighties. Growing public deficits had to be financed. A generous interpretation of the Phillips curve fostered the misconception that slightly higher inflation rates could permanently reduce unemployment. Finally, the oil price shocks also favored a rise in prices. Double-digit inflation rates were the norm in most developed countries. However, the hoped-for positive effects on unemployment were increasingly absent. The term stagflation was coined, i.e. stagnation coupled with inflation. 80s. At the beginning of the eighties, the famous Volcker disinflation gave the starting signal for a worldwide fall in inflation rates. This was followed by a decade of falling inflation rates. High inflation rates were generally recognised as harmful. "Monetary neutrality" and "rational expectations" also theoretically explained why inflationary demand stimulation cannot have any positive effects in the long run. nineties. The 90s were the decade of sustainably low inflation rates. Inflation expectations and interest rates fell to lows worldwide. Central banks gained independence from the political process. In almost all countries, they were given the mandate to ensure purchasing power stability as a matter of priority. A lot has been achieved. Societies have learned to take advantage of the obvious benefits of material-valueless monetary systems while securing the even more obvious benefits of purchasing power stability, at least during a few years of our recent past. 2. Achieved price stability-what now? This brings me to my second section and at the same time to looking ahead. Price stability has been achieved, and most central banks are quite independent. Their control concepts converge in an obvious way in some form of lnflation targeting. Is this - to use a term by Francis Fukuyama - "the end of history" in monetary policy? Will monetary policy only be about securing what has been achieved? My short answer is: No! Central banks have by no means reached a state close to nirvana. They will have to continue to perfect themselves and be challenged by new developments and twists. I am thinking, for example, of their tasks in the area of system protection, which are rightly much more prominent today than they were in the past. In this area, a variety of undesirable developments, including regulatory ones, are possible because it is closely linked to crises, fears and problems of moral hazard. But even in the narrower field of monetary stability, there is no reason for unambitious complacency. Restrictions begin with the concept of price stability. Central banks have been successful in stabilising consumer prices. At least that's how most people understand their mandate. There are good reasons for this, but it may make the task a little too easy. In the literature, inflation is generally understood to mean an increase in the general price level. There is hardly any talk of restricting it to consumer goods prices only. Certainly, instabilities of the Consumer price levels are a bad thing because they lead to the misallocation of scarce resources and unfounded redistributive effects. However, this argument could also be applied to prices outside the consumer sector, e.g. to means of production, prefabrications and financial assets. The chapter of assured price stability is far from closed or somehow ticked off. It still requires the efforts of critical economists and self-critical monetary policymakers to achieve the best for their economies. In this view, in the following three sections, I would like to discuss topics that relate to the core task of central banks and which - especially with low inflation rates - have a considerable current interest. I will begin by reflecting on the monetary policy mandate, on the supposed trade-off between price and economic stability. Then I turn to the phenomenon of "asset price bubbles", which is particularly difficult for monetary policymakers, followed by the question of the current risk of a deflation scenario. 3. Price and economic stabilisation in the monetary policy mandate The fact that securing the purchasing power stability of money belongs at the heart of the central bank's mandate is seriously disputed by no one. Indeed, there is a solid and broad consensus among economists that a persistent inflation or deflation trend is essentially a monetary phenomenon. Permanent deviations from price stability are always due to the behaviour of monetary policy. It is therefore not surprising that the safeguarding of price stability appears prominent in the mandate formulations of all independently operating central banks. On the other hand, the answers to the question of the extent to which central banks should take care of the economy and growth are quite different. In this fascinating macroeconomic debate, extreme positions have also caused a sensation. Until the 70s, the idea was widespread that one could, indeed must, systematically stimulate employment and real growth with monetary and fiscal fine-tuning of aggregate demand. In practical economic policy, this activist view has not proven itself: it contributed decisively to the inflationary aberration of the 70s, which caused serious upheavals in most countries. This disillusionment gave rise to growing scepticism about a monetary policy objective that contained more than ensuring price stability. The radical dogmatic position arose in and with the theory of rational expectations, which - in its hardest form - denies monetary policy any chance of achieving real effects in a systematic way. In this view, monetary policy has only nominal consequences: it should only take care of the trend of the price level. The monetary policy reality played and continues to play between the extreme positions. This - but also remarkable nuances - can be seen in some valid formulations of central bank orders. In most cases, and without exception in recent laws, price stability is a priority; other objectives, essentially economic stabilisation, are subordinate to price stability. Article 105 of the EC Treaty states: "The primary objective of the ESCB is to ensure price stability. To the extent possible without prejudice to the objective of price stability, the ESCB shall support general economic policies in the Community'. And in the draft of Switzerland's new Central Bank Act, the wording in Article 5 reads: "The National Bank ..... ensures price stability. In doing so, it takes into account economic developments." These two formulations basically amount to a dual target system: price stability and economic stabilization are relevant requirements. Alone, there should be a hierarchical relationship between these two goals. Priority should be given to price stability. A policy that generates short-term economic effects at the price of a deviation from the objective of price stability would therefore be contrary to the mandate. This dual, hierarchical goal formulation is a meaningful, well-justifiable concept. The primary position of price stability has its convincing justification in the fact that in the long term - i.e. after the expiry of all adjustment processes - monetary policy impulses only affect the price level, while the effects on employment and growth are temporary. Experience has shown that the attempt to achieve sustainable growth effects with sustained monetary stimulus will fail - it will end in an inflationary aberration. To avoid such a fiasco, price stability must take precedence. This limits the scope in which monetary policy can be used to steer the economy. The decisive tool that defines the field of possible courses of action at any time is the inflation forecast. In concrete decision-making situations, price and economic stability are often compatible goals, and they even depend on each other. Inflationary pressures arising during the boom endanger price stability, which prompts the central bank to make monetary policy more restrictive and to slow down the economy. In a recession, these inflationary pressures disappear and deflationary tendencies can even arise, forcing the central bank to pursue an expansionary policy so as not to miss the inflation target downwards. There is thus a significant area of harmony between the two goals. Empirically, for almost all countries, we find that there is a clearly positive relationship between the level of the inflation rate and the volatility of the real growth rate of GDP. Supplement 2: Inflation rate and growth volatility This connection is also clearly expressed for Switzerland. The trend towards more price stability, which has been in place since the 70s, was accompanied by decreasing fluctuations in GDP. But even in situations where one cannot speak of target harmony, monetary policy in many cases has significant room for manoeuvre to react to shocks without endangering price stability. The reason lies in the long "time-lags" between monetary policy measures (setting the key interest rate) and the resulting effects on the price level. This lag is variable, but very long. On average, it is just over three years in Switzerland. Price stability does not depend on where the money market interest rate is today and tomorrow, the entire interest rate path over several quarters is decisive. In other words, there is not only one interest rate path that ensures price stability. Not all, but many concrete interest rate paths lead to this goal. A central bank may well react expansionarily to a shock in the short term, for example in concern for financial market stability. The only condition is that the expansive phase is followed by a restrictive compensation. From this becomes clear once again - the high importance of the inflation forecast. It forms the decisive anchor that limits the short-term possibilities for action and thus helps to secure the course of price stability. Responding to shocks in this context  a massive increase in oil prices, a stock market crash or a surge in appreciation  is anything but a precise undertaking. With more than one impact contribution in the desired direction, one may do not calculate. Here, too, what makes economic "finetuning" so unsuccessful applies: the correlations are uncertain, the information fragmentary and the delays variable. In the event of major supply shocks, real effects will be unavoidable. Therefore, when reacting to shocks, the monetary policymaker should exercise restraint and not overestimate himself. However, these justified restrictions must not distract from the fact that the Monetary policy's willingness to respond to shocks has been growing strongly in recent years Has gained importance. There are three main reasons for this. The The first and most important is that a high level of price stability is achieved worldwide has been. Economic stabilization with monetary means can only be achieved at low Inflation rates and low inflation expectations can be successful. Second, a Role that in the course of the last few years the frequency and extent Macroeconomic shocks have visibly increased. And thirdly, expected Central banks have shown an increased willingness to react because in most countries the short-term room for manoeuvre of fiscal policy has tended to diminish, and oneself especially with regard to demographically conditioned public Financing constraints - will be further narrowed in the foreseeable future. 4. Asset Price Bubbles - a difficult challenge I would like to turn to the topic of asset price bubbles. Not from the perspective of a frustrated equity investor, but from the perspective of the macroeconomist and monetary policymaker, who has no less good reasons to ask himself self-critical questions after what he has experienced in recent years. How could it happen that, precisely at a time of globally successful disinflation and record-low output variability, important asset markets have not become more stable, but - on the contrary - the main source of macroeconomic instability? Has the thesis of the inherent stability of unregulated financial markets become obsolete? How could the cumulative expertise of countless economists, analysts and speculators be so blatantly wrong: by massively underestimating both the stock market boom after 1996 and the bear market that began in the first half of 2000? To be honest, we economists will have to admit that such questions embarrass us because we cannot yet properly classify and understand many things. The monetary policymaker cannot dispense with this issue. The experience of recent years shows that such asset price shocks have significant macroeconomic effects: on financing conditions on corporate investment activity, on balance sheets and the prospects of old-age provision on household consumption, or on changes in risk appetite and their exchange rate effects on the external contribution to aggregate demand. I would like to reflect on three questions below in order to draw some conclusions.  Is the macroeconomic stability achieved itself a relevant cause of financial market instability?  Are central banks even able to identify bubbles in the pricing of assets such as stocks or real estate? And third, when bubbles are diagnosed, can central banks take effective corrective action? The thesis that successful macroeconomic stabilization is the cause of financial market instability has a prominent author in Alan Greenspan. I quote from the minutes of the Federal Reserve's Federal Reserve Open Market Committee of September 24, 1996: I recognize that there is a stock market bubble problem at this point. We have very great difficulty in monetary policy when we confront stock market bubbles. That is because, to the extent that we are successful in keeping product price inflation down, history tells us that price-earnings ratios under those conditions go through the roof. What is really needed to keep stock market bubbles from occurring is a lot of product price inflation, which historically has tended to undercut stock markets almest everywhere. There is a clear tradeoff. lf monetary policy succeeds in one, it fails in the other. This provocative thesis, if it were empirically really relevant, would have serious consequences for the concept and practice of monetary policy. One would be faced with an interesting trade-off between macro and financial stability: central bankers might have to curb their macro ambitions in order to limit the tendency of financial markets to instability. However, there are doubts as to the validity of this thesis. Certainly, risk premia declined sharply in the late 90s and thus contributed to the boom. But did this have much to do with achieved disinflation and low inflation expectations? I don't think so. Rather, the excessive euphoria was the result of a serious overestimation of the commercial potential associated with new technologies and the consequence of herd effects that have generalized and intensified such miscalculations on the market. Therefore, the vulnerability of financial markets to destabilising runs with less macro stability cannot be overcome. Rather, what is needed is that market participants learn from their failures that they maintain respect for proportions in the formation of their expectations and do not fall into childlike naivety of the sweet illusion that the restrictions of history are out of force. Realistically, one has to prepare for the fact that asset price bubbles will continue to occur in the future. At first glance, it may seem desirable to assign the central bank the task of counteracting such distortions at an early stage. Anyone who demands this, however, presupposes two things. On the one hand, that monetary authorities can value stocks or real estate more competently than the market and, secondly, that they might be able to use their instruments to burst an emerging bubble in the early stages. Both conditions are not met. Central banks are no better able to value equities correctly than all market participants. In such efforts, they would always be wrong and lose their credibility. And the process of capital allocation on the stock exchanges would be impaired if it were to be expected again and again that a sovereign authority would intervene in this process. The rational process of valuation in the market would be superimposed, if not substituted, by rumors and speculation about the central bank's intentions. moreover, central banks do not normally have the tools necessary to correct a valuation bubble. You can change the interest rate, not much more. The interest rate instrument is characterized by its extremely broad spectrum of effects, while a mispricing is most likely to build up in a selective area, e.g. in high-tech stocks. The sledgehammer is hardly suitable as an instrument for brain surgery. Central banks and asset price bubbles - my reflections on the room for manoeuvre are quite sobering. Ex ante is realistically not much to do. Perhaps learning processes among market participants will lead to these distortions will tend to be more moderate. But even that is not certain. Central banks have little more to offer than what they have tried to do in recent bubble episodes: to take the best possible account of the macroeconomic consequences of such distortions and to limit the economic damage of the shocks as much as possible. If asset bubbles could actually be detected in good time - with whatever diagnostic means - they might have to be attacked with other instruments, e.g. with measures of fiscal policy or banking supervision. 5. Monetary policy and deflation This brings me to the problem of deflation, a term that until recently was avoided as far as possible outside the special case of Japan. In the combination of low, even largely negligible inflation rates worldwide and a series of cyclically depressing events, deflation has become a widely discussed topic. I would like to start with some conceptual considerations and then draw some conclusions for monetary policy. Deflation refers to a persistent decline in the price level, a development in which the majority of prices fall and wages fall. A fall in the price of only individual products or in a selected sector does not qualify as deflation. Because with little general inflation, the relative price mechanism constantly leads to price declines - this is unproblematic. Our national index of consumer goods prices records over 200 index positions, some of which are constantly declining. For example, in January 2002, when the inflation rate was % percent, exactly one third of the items recorded price declines. That is not what we mean when we talk about deflation. Deflation in the sense of a general, broad price decline has historically occurred again and again, especially under the regime of the gold standard. In Switzerland, for example, from 1871 to the turn of the century, the price level in 17 out of 30 years was recorded compared to the previous year's level. Overall, the price level fell by 28% during this period. In the same period, real GDP grew by a respectable 85% (Source: Historische Statistik der Schweiz, edited by H. Ritzmann, Zurich 1996). In this phase, prices fell with average positive growth, decisively driven by the significant productivity gains of industrialization. The experience of the thirties is different, when - from 1929 to 1936 - a declining Aggregate demand led to a simultaneous regression of price levels and real GDP. This experience of the crisis has made deflation a concept of pathology in economic policy, a state of affairs which, according to unanimous opinion, must be prevented by almost all means. I believe that there are essentially three arguments that justify a marked aversion to the risks of deflation. First, the effect of (unexpected) deflation on debts, which play a much greater role today than they did in the past. Deflation increases the real value of existing debt. As a result, the balance sheets of companies and households deteriorate, which can trigger bankruptcies, a credit crunch and shocks to the banking system, in short: a vicious circle with depressive signs. Unexpected deflation, i.e. not taken into account in credit conditions, can easily lead to an intensifying chain of severe shocks. In the case of inflation, which also triggers undesirable redistributive effects, this shock potential is much lower. Second, in a deflationary environment, destabilizing effects on demand can occur. The scenario of weak consumption is in the foreground as a consequence of increased job risks or the worthwhile postponement of consumer spending when prices fall. Thirdly, the explosiveness of a deflationary development lies in the fact that the central bank cannot set the nominal key interest rate below zero. In the event of low or even negative inflation rates, this restriction can become binding and prevent the monetary authority from stimulating the economy with its traditional interest rate instrument. It will then be impossible to lower the real interest rate below the expectation of deflation. It is even conceivable that intensifying deflation expectations will raise the real interest rate, thus exacerbating the slowdown for at least a while. Under such conditions, the central bank would have to act directly on deflation expectations with unconventional measures. These brief hints justify the conclusion that it is highly worthwhile to avoid the economic minefield of deflation. In terms of monetary policy, two conclusions emerge: Firstly, the inflation target must not be set too low. For good reason, no central bank is aiming for zero inflation. Reduced with a slightly positive inflation rate the risk that an unexpected demand shock will lead to a slide into deflation. Second, central banks must act preventively in the event of low inflation if there is a threat of a further deterioration in the economic situation. Being late is particularly disastrous under such conditions. In other words, the fault tolerance downwards ("too restrictive") is obviously much smaller in this constellation than upwards ("too expansive"). After these rather general considerations, it is appropriate to make some comments on the deflation risk with which the Swiss economy is currently confronted. There is no doubt that this risk exists, but we currently consider it to be very small. What we are experiencing is a persistent weakness in demand, strongly influenced by declining investments in equipment and construction, but by no means an erosion of demand, as would be characteristic of a deflationary process. The development of inflation has been in the range of just under one percent for some time. If, when assessing this level of inflation, one also considers that several important prices tend to fall for productivity reasons (telecommunications) or due to regulatory changes (liberalisation in the agricultural sector), the risk picture is considerably defused. The reference to the different development of domestic and foreign prices also contributes to this finding. Over the past two years, import prices have tended to fall, while domestic prices (which are of particular importance to us) have risen much faster than the overall index. Finally, in the current environment, there are no discernible reasons to fear a massive correction in asset prices that could trigger a deflationary shock. This is especially important for the real estate market, which plays a key role in a country with record mortgage debt. Supplement 3: Real estate prices Switzerland In all three real estate categories, there were huge excesses in the late 80s and then profound corrections. We are currently confronted with a rather moderate price development. It does not rule out price surprises, but overall there is nothing to suggest a threatening risk of price collapse. For these reasons, it is reasonable to conclude that the risk of deflationary development in Switzerland is small. I now come to the outlook for the Swiss economy in the last section of my presentation. 6. Current outlook Our policy over the past two years has been shaped by the gradual recognition that the global economic upswing - contrary to expectations - will only be very hesitant and weak. With risks to price stability still considered to be low, we were able and wanted to exploit the scope for stabilising the economy in good time and credibly. Earlier than most central banks - as early as March 2001 - we made the first reduction in the interest rate band in anticipation of increasing economic weaknesses. After the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001 in the USA, the situation on the foreign exchange markets deteriorated and the Swiss franc came under strong appreciation pressure. In order to counter the uncertainty on the financial markets, we reduced the three-month Libor by another percentage point in two steps within eight days. Overall, we loosened the monetary policy reins by 2.75 percentage points between March 2001 and today. In these interest rate hikes - as well as on numerous other occasions - we expressed our concern about the appreciation of the Swiss franc. At a time of declining economic growth, such an appreciation of our currency amounted to an undesirable tightening of the monetary environment in Switzerland. It was important to us to oppose this decisively. It was and is clear to us that - especially in phases of increased uncertainty - the exchange rate cannot be reliably controlled by manipulating the interest rate differential to foreign currencies. But one can react to exchange rate changes with interest rate adjustments in order to at least partially compensate for an economically restrictive appreciation effect with an opposite interest rate step. We have done this repeatedly over the past two years. Although the euro exchange rate has been in the range of around CHF 1.45 to CHF 1.48 per euro since the shock of 11 September, the interest rate differential against the euro on the money market has widened from one percentage point to over 2 percentage points. Medium- and longer-term interest rates have also declined significantly during this time, bringing significant relief to countless debtors. However, there is no denying that increased credit risk premiums have compensated for part of this effect. We are aware that exchange rate conditions are difficult for many areas of our economy. The franc has become expensive, both against the euro and against the USO. Even though our economy has had to cope with much greater appreciation shocks in past episodes, the current burdens on the exchange rate front are unfavorably significant, especially in a long-unsatisfactory economic environment. Supplement 4: Real Swiss franc - Exchange rate index On a trade-weighted basis, the real Swiss franc exchange rate has appreciated by an average of around 0.6 percent p.a. over the past twenty years. Whether and to what extent there will continue to be an appreciation trend of the Swiss franc in the future is a difficult open question. In any case, however, it will be possible to state that our economy has coped well with the appreciation trend of the Swiss franc. On the other hand, the sometimes massive appreciation spurts over several quarters were problematic. At present, the Swiss franc is under the influence of a risk appetite that has been battered worldwide for known reasons. It leads to additional net demand for Swiss franc assets, especially from domestic investors who want to reduce their currency risks. The economic development abroad, which is more important for our economic development than all other factors, promises - at least for the coming quarters - at best moderate impulses. It is a disadvantage that our most important partner Germany has to contend with particularly pronounced weaknesses. Against this backdrop, economic conditions in Switzerland will remain tense. The at first glance favourable development of quarterly growth to 1.3% in the third quarter of 2002 should not obscure this. It mainly reflects well-maintained exports with significantly weaker imports. Experience has shown that the latter are not a sign of a recovery that is about to begin. In terms of investments, we are still waiting for convincing signs of the turnaround, even though the slowdown has now lasted seven quarters. Despite our long-standing stimulus policy, we expect real growth of little more than one percent for the current year and low inflation rates of between half and one percent for this year and next. A return to the long-term achievable trend growth of an estimated one and a half to two percent will therefore take a few more quarters. This is due to the viscosity of recovery, especially in our European Environment. But in contrast to the early 90s, the chances are good today that the Swiss economy will be able to benefit quickly and to a significant extent from an economic acceleration abroad. What are the main risks of this scenario? They lie primarily in geopolitical and military shocks, which could cause considerable damage to the global economy, especially if the phase of extreme uncertainty lasts for a long time. Experience has shown that the greatest uncertainties for Switzerland lie in the area of the exchange rate, i.e. in the risk of an appreciation that seriously endangers economic stability. The SNB would firmly oppose such a distortion. Although the interest rate margin for money market rates below % percent is no longer large, it has not yet been fully exhausted. moreover, if necessary, we would intervene in the foreign exchange market to correct the price distortion and provide additional liquidity to the economy. On the other hand, it is also possible that economic forecasters are now too pessimistic about the world after two years of being mistaken with overly optimistic predictions. The epicenter of such a positive surprise would most likely be in the US, where the current indicators indeed allow for contradictory economic conclusions. This note is intended to remind us once again that things often turn out quite differently than we think. More important than perfecting forecasts is the ability to react quickly when things take a different course and then take the right measures. Geldpolitik - ein stilisierter Rckblick Lassen Sie mich mit etwas monetrer Geschichte beginnen, indem ich - eher holzschnittartig - auf wichtige Fakten hinweise, die fr die Einschtzung der Aktualitt von Bedeutung sind. Erreichte Preisstabilitt-was nun? Damit komme ich zu meinem zweiten Abschnitt und zugleich zum Blick nach vorn. Preisstabilitt ist erreicht, die meisten Zentralbanken sind recht unabhngig. Ihre Steuerungskonzepte konvergieren in augenflliger Weise bei irgendwelchen Formen des lnflation-Targeting. Ist das - um einen Terminus von Francis Fukuyama zu benutzen - in der Geldpolitik das Ende der Geschichte? Wird es in der Geldpolitik nur noch um die Sicherung des Erreichten gehen? Meine kurze Antwort ist: Nein! Die Zentralbanken haben keinesfalls einen Zustand nahe des Nirwana erreicht. Sie werden sich weiter perfektionieren mssen und durch neue Entwicklungen und Wendungen gefordert sein. Ich denke etwa an ihre Aufgaben im Bereich des Systemschutzes, denen heute zurecht ein viel prominenterer Stellenwert zukommt als frher. In diesem Bereich sind vielfltige, auch regulatorische Fehlentwicklungen mglich, weil er aufs engste mit Krisen, ngsten und Problemen des moral hazard verbunden ist. Aber auch im engeren Feld der monetren Stabilitt besteht kein Grund zu ambitionsloser Selbstgeflligkeit. Einschrnkungen beginnen schon beim Begriff der Preisstabilitt. Erfolgreich sind die Zentralbanken bei der Stabilisierung von Konsumentenpreisen. So jedenfalls verstehen die meisten ihr Mandat. Dafr gibt es gute Grnde, aber mglicherweise macht man sich damit die Aufgabe etwas zu leicht. In der Literatur meint man mit Inflation gemeinhin einen Anstieg des allgemeinen Preisniveaus. Von einer Beschrnkung nur auf Konsumgterpreise ist so gut wie nirgendwo die Rede. Gewiss sind Instabilitten des Konsumentenpreisniveaus etwas Schlechtes, weil sie zur Fehlallokation knapper Ressourcen und zu unbegrndeten Umverteilungswirkungen fhren. Allein, dieses Argument knnte doch auch auf Preise ausserhalb des Konsumbereichs bezogen werden, z.B. auf Produktionsmittel, Vorfabrikate und Finanzaktiva. Das Kapitel gesicherter Preisstabilitt ist lngst nicht abgeschlossen oder irgendwie abgehakt. Es bedarf weiterhin des Bemhens kritischer konomen und selbstkritischer Geldpolitiker mit dem Ziel, fr ihre Volkswirtschaften das Beste zu erreichen. In dieser Optik mchte ich in den drei folgenden Abschnitten Themen zur Diskussion stellen, die sich auf die Kernaufgabe von Zentralbanken beziehen und denen - zumal bei tiefen Inflationsraten - ein erhebliches aktuelles Interesse zukommt. Ich beginne mit berlegungen zum geldpolitischen Mandat, zum vermeintlichen Trade-off zwischen Preisund Konjunkturstabilitt. Dann wende ich mich dem fr Geldpolitiker besonders schwierigen Phnomen der Asset Price Bubbles zu, anschliessend der Frage nach dem aktuellen Risiko eines Deflationsszenarios. 3. Preis- und Konjunkturstabilisierung im geldpolitischen Mandat Dass die Sicherung der Kaufkraftstabilitt des Geldes ins Zentrum des Notenbankmandates gehrt, wird ernsthafterweise durch niemanden bestritten. Es gibt unter konomen in der Tat einen soliden und breiten Konsens darber, dass ein andauernder Inflations- oder Deflationstrend im Wesentlichen ein monetres Phnomen darstellt. Dauerhafte Abweichungen von der Preisstabilitt sind immer bedingt durch das Verhalten der Geldpolitik. Daher kann nicht berraschen, dass die Sicherung der Preisstabilitt in den Mandatsformulierungen aller unabhngig operierenden Zentralbanken prominent erscheint. Title: Monetary policy in difficult times
text: The Swiss National Bank's policy in difficult times Presentation by Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Business Club of Geneva Tuesday, 11 February 2003 1. 2002: A disappointing year From an economic point of view, 2002 was a disappointing year. A year ago, just a few months after the attacks of 11 September, the international economic situation seemed to be stabilizing and gave us cautious optimism. The first quarter of '02 was looking relatively good and the global economy seemed to be on the verge of gradually returning to growth. Our forecast, which at the time was described as timid, envisaged an average GDP growth of around 1% for the whole year, with a clear acceleration in activity from the end of the first half of the year. We quickly had to become disillusioned. Contradictory signals began to multiply as early as April. On top of that, the franc strengthened against the euro. This appreciation of our currency, which meant a tightening of monetary conditions in our country, came at the worst possible time. We then reacted by lowering the three-month Libor fluctuation interval by 50 basis points. This has not only stopped the upward movement of our currency in its tracks, but it has also provided a breath of fresh air to our economy. By the summer, it was becoming clear that the long-awaited recovery was slow to come. The U.S. economy was increasingly hesitant, with positive signals systematically counterbalanced by negative ones. On the European front, starting with ' In Germany, the sky was becoming more and more threatening. This delay in the recovery was all the more unfortunate as the franc was once again approaching record highs against the European currency. We acted quickly, once again lowering the Libor fluctuation band by 50 basis points, which has since been centred at a rate of 0.75%, almost an all-time high. How can we explain this succession of disappointments? In fact, some of the causes of the global economy's weakness had already been identified a year ago. The bursting of the speculative bubble at the end of the 1990s, the excesses in investment  particularly in the field of information technology  and the surplus of capital, all these factors were known to us, but their destabilizing potential has obviously been underestimated by all economists. Similarly, a year ago, we already knew about the Enron bankruptcy, but we all thought it was an isolated case. The even more serious case of Worldcom, on the other hand, had not yet been revealed, and no one could have imagined just 12 months ago that fraudulent accounting practices were so widespread. These events have shaken investor confidence in ways that are as unfortunate as they are unpredictable. The risk premiums demanded by the market have been increased. The stock market, which had already fallen for two years in a row, fell even more heavily. The soundness of insurance companies and pension funds was suddenly called into question, which made many households more secure. Companies' financing costs have risen and their confidence has evaporated, and investment has collapsed far more than expected. Switzerland has been particularly affected by these developments. Like most of its neighbours, it has been hit hard by the fall in investment and has felt the slowdown in the global economy. However, our country has been hit particularly hard because our exports are intensive in capital goods and our neighbour to the north is precisely our main customer. Moreover, let us not forget that the financial sector accounts for a significant share of gross domestic product in our country, estimated at nearly 15%. The deterioration in the stock market and the ensuing declines in financial income have been an additional burden on our growth. On top of that, geopolitical considerations were added. Of course, we were all familiar with the decade-long situation in Iraq, but few could have anticipated a year ago the escalation of tensions in the Middle East and the prospects of a new armed conflict, so soon after the cessation of operations in Afghanistan. New attacks in Bali and Pakistan, foiled plots in Europe, renewed tensions with North Korea, so many events that have undermined the morale of all economic actors, consumers and entrepreneurs alike. It will be a long time before the final figures of the national accounts for the past year are known, but we believe that growth last year was essentially nil. This stagnation @conomique has resulted in an increase in unemployment for the first time in five years. While the franc appreciated against the euro on an annual average, this was mainly due to the jump recorded in September 2001, in the aftermath of the attacks on New York and Washington. In fact, the exchange rate between the euro and the franc remained remarkably stable throughout 2002, fluctuating mainly in a very narrow band between Fr. 1.45 and Fr. 1.48. As far as price trends are concerned, the results are very satisfactory. Our objective of price stability has been achieved once again. As a result, the purchasing power of our currency remained intact throughout the year. 2. Back to the Future In many ways, then, 2002 was a year for nothing. We now find ourselves in a situation similar to that of a year ago. As we did 12 months ago, we now expect a gradual recovery in the global economy. While we are comforted by a number of positive developments, we must exercise great restraint  and humility  in the face of the prevailing uncertainty and our dashed hopes from last year. Nevertheless, the surplus capital stock is being absorbed, in part through the mechanism of economic and technological obsolescence. Monetary and fiscal policies remain expansive. In fact, the monetary impulse in the pipeline, as they say, is considerable. Interest rates are extremely low in most countries without any threat to price stability. With the exception of Japan, banking institutions are in relatively good health and are able to fulfil their role. In general, as a result of the numerous restructurings that took place during the 1990s, the Swiss economy is well positioned and ready to benefit from a global economic awakening. If our assumptions about the international environment are correct, growth in the 6th Swiss economy should be able to reach 1% this year and continue to strengthen. That said, the risks remain considerable, and they are all pointing downwards. We are not immune to a new financial scandal or a new terrorist attack, and the prospect of war in the Middle East, with uncertain consequences, is likely to shake the confidence of the most inveterate optimists. On a strictly economic level, too, there is still a great deal of uncertainty. A sharp rise in the price of oil, even if it were to be short-lived, could cut off the momentum of the global economy. The U.S. recovery, although it seems to be confirmed, remains hesitant. It is true that the recession was shallow, so that the slope to climb is less steep. Closer to home, Germany seems to be struggling to extricate itself from the economic slump in which it has been plunged for several years. Let us not delude ourselves, we will find it very difficult to restart if the German economy fails us. The current risks for our country are twofold. On the one hand, we can fear that the world economy will not restart according to the pattern adopted for 2003; On the other hand, our currency could come under pressure in the event of great geopolitical instability. In the first case, we can expect a new reaction from the monetary authorities on both sides of the Atlantic. In our country, the Monetary policy is already markedly expansive, but there is still some room for manoeuvre. In the second case, we would be faced with a problem specific to our country. Our franc is already heavy and we know that an unreasonable market reaction could push it to new highs. We would then risk that our economy would be excluded from the recovery when it takes shape internationally and that price developments in Switzerland would be closer to the danger zone of negative figures. We want to avoid that. Therefore, in the event of a shock of this nature, we will use all necessary means of defence  without excluding interventions. 3. The D-word What about the risk of deflation? The British weekly The Economist regularly counts in the international press the frequency of use of certain key words, such as those that begin with R  for recession  or D  for deflation. The use of the D-word, in particular, is said to be on the rise. Is this a harbinger of a new threat? Central banks cannot remain indifferent to the danger posed by a sustained fall in the price level. The pursuit of price stability means the fight against inflation as well as deflation. Deflation has just as perverse effects as inflation. By distorting the function of price signals, it leads to a misallocation of resources, induces economic agents to make code-making errors and provokes a completely arbitrary redistribution of income between debtors and creditors. Deflation has a particularly sinister reputation because it is often associated with the Depression  another D-word  of the 1930s. However, we need to be discerning in this area, because the example of China, which is experiencing fabulous economic growth while seeing its price level fall, is there to remind us that deflation is not synonymous with recession, any more than inflation is synonymous with economic boom. The fact remains  as I said earlier when I mentioned the possible consequences of speculation on the franc  that the danger of deflation must be averted with determination and even pre-emption. This is because things do not appear to be perfectly symmetrical in the area of price dynamics. It is well known that nominal interest rates tend to increase with the But because of the very existence of money, the movement in the opposite direction is limited by the impossibility of nominal interest rates falling below zero. Once this threshold is reached, any worsening of deflation means a perverse rise in real interest rates against which monetary policy can do nothing. This does not mean, however, that the SNB is helpless in the face of deflation. Deflation, like inflation, is still a monetary phenomenon after all. However, in the event of deflation, the SNB would be deprived of its preferred instrument, the short-term interest rate, precisely because of the zero lower bound on interest rates. But there are still other channels through which it can influence the economy and price formation, including those of the exchange rate and the long-term interest rate. It is no less true that a central bank will not be happy to see itself amputated from its main instrument in this way. In this area, as in so many others, prevention is better than cure. That said, we do not see deflation as a significant threat to our country today. While our inflation rate is low, this is largely due to lower prices for imported goods. The price of domestically sourced goods and services is rising at a rate slightly above 1%. Core inflation, which excludes certain goods with highly volatile prices such as food and petroleum products, is also stable at nearly 1%. If, on the other hand, we consider the magnitude of the monetary stimulus applied for almost two years and the extremely low level of our interest rates, we must admit that the risk of deflation is indeed minimal. Our inflation forecast, which we will now publish every three months, confirms this analysis. This does not mean that it is impossible that the 12-month inflation rate may occasionally fall below zero due to particular factors, such as a decline in the price of oil, for example. But it would take a totally unforeseen shock of rare violence for deflation to truly become a topical issue in our country. 4. The Challenge of Foreign Exchange For Switzerland, it is obvious that such a shock could come from the foreign exchange market. What has been our experience in this area over the past few years? Since its introduction on 1 January 1999, the euro has lost almost 9% of its value against the franc. However, due to the inflation differential, the real depreciation of the euro is only half. A 5% movement in the real exchange rate over a period of Four years is not unusual, although it can be painful for some sectors of our economy. We have had much more difficult times in the past. But could we set our policy the objective of changing the real exchange rate according to the needs of the economy? It's a tempting option at first glance, but it's not realistic. Indeed, experience  as well as economic theory  shows us that in the long run monetary policy has no hold on the real variables of the economy, including the real exchange rate. Any attempt to weaken the franc in the long term would eventually lead to higher inflation and thus higher nominal interest rates. This would result in no lasting gain in competitiveness, while price and cost stability would be lost. Fixing the exchange rate between the franc and the euro is also not an attractive option. Even if such a measure could be credibly enforced, it would create more problems than it solved. On the one hand, only the nominal exchange rate between the franc and the euro would thus be stabilised, but the real exchange rate  the only one that matters for foreign trade and production decisions  would continue to evolve in line with economic circumstances and inflation differentials. In reality, any adjustment that normally takes place through the exchange rate would have to be made through changes in prices, wages and activity, a process that is much more painful. Some Member States of I' Euroland is now experiencing this. Let us take the example of Germany, where part of the present difficulties probably stems from the fact that it can no longer pursue an autonomous monetary policy. If it could still do so, the Bundesbank would certainly have lowered interest rates faster and more sharply than the European Central Bank did, and the weakening of the mark against the franc would probably have been greater than what we have experienced with the euro. A peg of the franc to the euro would also lead to a massive rise in our interest rates. The user cost of capital would increase substantially, but the cost of labour would not fall. This would seriously undermine the competitiveness of our companies. Worse still, the price of Swiss assets, especially real estate, would fall, which would discourage investment in our country. The recessionary effects of such a policy would be far worse than the disadvantages associated with nominal exchange rate fluctuations. If we add to this the fact that Switzerland would lose any possibility of conducting an independent monetary policy, i.e. one tailored to its needs, we see that it would be expensive to pay for this illusion of a fixed exchange rate guaranteeing our competitiveness. In recent months, the dollar has become fashionable again. Its reduction, so long announced and so often postponed, has finally come. From January 2002 to the present, the U.S. currency has lost one-fifth of its value against the euro. In itself, this correction should be welcomed, if it can help to reduce international financial imbalances. However, it must be carried out in an orderly manner and not exaggerated. An undershooting phenomenon would be completely unwelcome. It is perhaps worth remembering, however, that the dollar is still well above the lows it reached against the franc in 1995, especially in real terms. The SNB can only take note of this development. Needless to say, it is unable to change the parity between the dollar and the euro. It is well aware, however, that this correction in the US currency comes at the worst possible time, when the economic situation in our export markets is already difficult and the franc  even if it was stable in 2002  has appreciated against the euro since the introduction of the euro in 1999. Of course, we are factoring this new negative factor into our assessments. 5. Our seaworthiness remains intact We are thus in a difficult period due to the international economic situation, which has been slow to wake up, and because of contrary developments on the foreign exchange market. And everything seems to indicate that the coming weeks will be even more delicate. Nevertheless, we can remain confident. Our economy is very adaptable, and we are well positioned to take advantage of the global recovery when it finally happens. The relationship between the franc and the euro has not been destabilised by the recent fall in the dollar and the rise in geopolitical risks. The traditional role of our currency as a safe haven is now much less pronounced than in the past. Even if the Swiss economy were to be shaken by violent explosions again in the near future, we are comforted to know that much has been done to enable our companies to cope with market uncertainties and to get through a difficult phase. Our boat is holding the sea and we can hope that after the storm and its tumultuous waves, we will find calmer waters and milder skies. On the eve of the America's Cup final, while Geneva is brilliantly defending the colours of Switzerland in the Antipodes, I do not need to remind you that we have a lot to offer in our summer. Our vessel incorporates state-of-the-art technology and reflects our country's know-how; Our crew is well prepared, gifted and hyper-motivated; Our skipper and tactician know the waters they are sailing in inside out. Against all odds, we have everything we need to succeed. Let us stay the course, the winds will soon be favourable to us.

De mme, il y a un an, nous avions dja connaissance de la faillite d'Enron, mais nous pensions tous qu'il s'agissait d'un cas isol. Ces vnements ont branl la confiance des investisseurs d'une maniere aussi malencontreuse qu'imprvisible. Les primes de risque rclames par le marche se sont trouves augmentes.
