La Suisse a t particuligrement affecte par ces dveloppements. Comme la plupart de ses voisins, elle a t frappe de plein fouet par la chute de l'investissement et elle a ressenti le ralentissement de la conjoncture mondiale. Toutefois, notre pays a ete touche de maniere particuligrement violente du fait que nos exportations sont intensives en biens d'quipement et que notre voisin du nord constitue prcisment notre client principal . De plus, n'oublions pas que le secteur financier reprsente dans notre pays une part importante  estime a pres de 15%  du produit intrieur brut. La dgradation boursire et les baisses de revenus financiers qui s'ensuivirent ont constitue un _ boulet supplementaire pour notre croissance. La-dessus sont venues se greffer les considrations gopolitiques. Bien entendu, nous connaissions tous la situation irakienne qui dure depuis dix ans, mais rares sont ceux qui auraient pu, il y a une anne, anticiper l'escalade des tensions au Moyen-Orient et les perspectives d'un nouveau conflit arm, si peu de temps apres la cessation des operations en Afghanistan. De nouveaux attentats a Bali et au Pakistan, des complots djoues en Europe, un regain de tension avec la Core du Nord, tant d'vnements qui ont sap le moral de tous les acteurs conomiques, consommateurs et entrepreneurs confondus. Il faudra longtemps encore avant que les chiffres dfinitifs de la comptabilite nationale pour l'anne coule soient connus, mais nous pensons que la croissance I'an dernier fut essentiellement nulle. Cette stagnation @conomique s'est traduite par une hausse du chmage, et ce pour la premire fois depuis cing annes. Si le franc s'est apprcie par rapport a l'euro en moyenne annuelle, ceci est essentiellement dd au saut quill a enregistr en septembre 2001, au lendemain des attaques sur New York et Washington. En ralit, le taux de change entre l'euro et le franc est rest remarquablement stable pendant toute l'anne 2002, oscillant pour l'essentiel dans une bande tres troite situee entre Fr. 1.45 et Fr. 1.48. En ce qui concerne l'volution des prix, le constat est des plus satisfaisants. Notre objectif de stabilit des prix a t atteint une fois de plus. Le pouvoir d'achat de notre monnaie est ainsi reste intact tout au long de l'anne. 2. Retour vers le futur A bien des gards donc, 2002 fut une anne pour rien. Nous nous retrouvons ds lors dans une situation similaire a celle d'il y a un an. Comme il y a 12 mois, nous tablons aujourd'hui sur une reprise progressive de la conjoncture mondiale. Mme si nous sommes rconforts par un certain nombre d'lements positifs, nous devons faire preuve d'une grande retenue  et d'humilite  au vu de l'incertitude regnante et de nos espoirs dcus de l'an dernier. Il n'en demeure pas moins que le stock de capital excdentaire est en train de se resorber, en partie par le mcanisme de l'obsolescence conomique et technologique. Les politiques montaire et budgtaire restent expansives. En fait, 'impulsion montaire dans le pipeline, comme on dit, est considrable. Les taux d'intrt sont extremement bas dans la plupart des pays sans que la stabilite des prix ne soit menace pour autant. Hormis au Japon, les institutions bancaires sont relativement en bonne sant et elles sont aptes a remplir leur rle. D'une manire gnrale, suite aux nombreuses restructurations qui ont eu lieu pendant les annes nonante, l'economie suisse est bien positionne et prte a profiter d'un rveil de la conjoncture mondiale. Si nos hypotheses concernant l'environnement international se vrifient, la croissance de l'6conomie suisse devrait pouvoir atteindre 1% cette anne et aller en se renforcant. Ceci dit, les risques restent considrables et ils pointent tous vers le bas. Nous ne sommes a l'abri, ni d'un nouveau scandale financier, ni d'une nouvelle attaque terroriste, et les perspectives d'une guerre au Moyen-Orient, aux consquences incertaines, sont en mesure d'branler la confiance des optimistes les plus invtrs. Sur le plan strictement economique galement, l'incertitude demeure grande. Une monte en flche du prix du petrole, mme si elle ne devait tre que de courte dure, pourrait couper I'lan de la conjoncture mondiale. La reprise amricaine, bien qu'elle semble se confirmer, reste hsitante. Il est vrai que la recession fut peu profonde de telle sorte que la pente a grimper est moins raide. Plus pres de nous, Il'Allemagne semble avoir beaucoup de peine a s'extirper du marasme conomique dans lequel elle se trouve plonge depuis plusieurs annes. Il ne faut pas se faire dillusions, nous aurons beaucoup de peine a redmarrer si l'conomie allemande nous fait faux bond. Pour notre pays, les risques actuels sont de deux ordres. D'une part, nous pouvons craindre que l'conomie mondiale ne redmarre pas selon le schema retenu pour cette anne 2003; d'autre part, notre monnaie pourrait tre mise sous pression en cas de grande instabilite gopolitique. Dans le premier cas, nous pouvons nous attendre a une nouvelle raction des autorits monetaires de part et d'autre de I'Atlantique. Chez nous, la politique monetaire est dja nettement expansive, mais une certaine marge de manceuvre existe encore. Dans le second cas, nous serions confronts a un probleme spcifique a notre pays. Notre franc est dja lourd et nous savons qu'une raction draisonne des marches pourrait le pousser vers de nouveaux sommets. Nous risquerions alors de voir notre economie tre exclue de la reprise lorsqu'elle se dessinera sur le plan international et l'volution des prix en Suisse se rapprocherait de la zone dangereuse des chiffres ngatifs. Nous voulons viter une telle situation. Aussi, en cas de choc de cette nature, nous engagerons tous les moyens de dfense ncessaires  sans exclure des interventions. 3. Le D-word Que penser du risque de dflation ? L'hebdomadaire britannique The Economist s'amuse rgulirement a compter dans la presse internationale la frquence d'utilisation de certains mots cls, comme ceux qui commencent par R  pour rcession  ou par D  pour deflation. L'utilisation du D-word, en particulier, serait en nette augmentation. Est-ce le signe prcurseur d'une nouvelle menace qui nous guette? Dans ce domaine, comme dans tant d'autres, il vaut mieux prvenir que guerir. Ceci dit, nous ne considrons pas aujourd'hui la dflation comme une menace significative pour notre pays. Certes, notre taux d'inflation est bas, mais ce rsultat est atteint en grande partie grace au repli du prix des produits imports. Title: Monetary policy assessment
text: Monetary policy assessment Presentation by Dr Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Economic Society of the Canton of Bern Monday, 17 March 2003 Bern 1. Introduction "No Change" is clearly visible on a metal plate at the main entrance door of the National Bank in Bern. I can assure you that this applies neither to the institution of the National Bank in general nor to Swiss monetary policy in particular. Rather, the SNB has recently made several significant changes. This includes a new monetary policy concept. At the moment, we are also experiencing anything but "no change" in monetary policy practice. Both aspects will be the focus of my current assessment. The SNB conducts a monetary policy independent of the political authorities of our country. This independence is an important, indeed a decisive prerequisite for a successful monetary policy in accordance with the constitutional mandate. This independence means not only that the SNB can set interest rates, but also that it can choose its own monetary policy strategy. The SNB introduced a new monetary policy concept at the beginning of 2000. An event of the Economic Society of the Canton of Bern is certainly a suitable opportunity to discuss the experiences with this concept in front of a knowledgeable audience. I will also devote myself to the process of monetary policy decision-making and opinion-forming within the SNB, which is rarely discussed in public. After that, I will turn to the monetary policy challenges we are facing at the moment. 2. Monetary policy approach The SNB was one of the first central banks to introduce a money supply target strategy after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system. It has aligned its monetary policy with the guardrails of this principle for around 25 years. It took a pragmatic approach and was quite successful in international comparison despite a number of problems. During these 25 years, the SNB has applied various versions of the money supply target strategy, most recently the concept of a medium-term target path for the central bank money supply. From 1997 onwards, the demand for central bank money in Switzerland began to destabilise more and more and the deviation from the medium-term target path could no longer be used as a monetary policy indicator. When it became apparent that there was no prospect of a stabilization of money demand in the near future, the Board instructed an internal working group to Developing a new approach to monetary policy. The concept was then developed in the course of 1999 and adopted by the Management Committee towards the end of 1999. This concept represents a strategy for maintaining price stability. Price stability is essential for the smooth functioning of an economy. Price stability means avoiding inflation and deflation. The aim is to maintain or achieve price stability over the medium term. Focusing on the medium term is important for two reasons. On the one hand, we cannot fine-tune inflation, i.e. unforeseen fluctuations in inflation cannot be compensated for in the short term. On the other hand, we can also temporarily deliberately allow deviations from price stability in order to prevent excessive economic costs that would be associated with an excessively radical fight against inflation in certain situations. In this context, it is also important to see that a monetary policy geared to medium-term price stability helps to dampen economic fluctuations. Because of the different inflationary pressures, monetary policy tends to be tightened during a boom, while it is loosened during a period of economic downturn. This leitmotif for the implementation of monetary policy corresponds exactly to the idea of the mandate for the National Bank in the draft of the new National Bank Act. The introduction of this concept was the most important step for the SNB since the transition to a flexible Swiss franc exchange rate in 1973. Compared to the previous money supply target strategy, this entailed significant changes in both monetary policy decision-making and the implementation of monetary policy. On the other hand, the fundamental orientation of monetary policy towards maintaining price stability in the medium term remained unchanged. The concept consists of three elements. The first element is an explicit definition of price stability. The SNB defines price stability as a situation in which the annual rate measured by the national consumer price index is below 2%. Inflation of 2% is therefore the upper limit at which we can still speak of price stability. Why have we chosen an upper limit that deviates from 0% inflation? The reason is that the consumer price index systematically overstates actual inflation by about 0.5 to 1.0 percentage points. This is because the consumer price index captures the effects of quality improvements, the introduction of new products and the substitution between goods only incompletely or distorted. This systematic Measurement errors must therefore be taken into account when defining price stability. In addition, we have taken into account a margin of 1 percentage point in order to accept a slightly higher inflation rate depending on the course of the economy. This takes into account the fact that inflation cannot be fine-tuned and that a slightly positive inflation rate of this magnitude is not harmful to the economy. As already mentioned, price stability excludes deflation. However, we have refrained from including a lower limit in the definition of price stability for the following reasons: On the one hand, an explicit lower limit would give the impression that the SNB intends in principle to always target exactly the middle of the range of price stability. Instead, we can accept slightly different inflation rates depending on the economic situation. On the other hand, the systematic measurement error in the consumer price index can change over time. The absence of an explicit lower limit allows us to take into account changes in the systematic measurement error without having to adjust the definition of price stability. By defining price stability, the SNB defines the basic direction of its monetary policy and allows market participants to form corresponding expectations. The definition of price stability should remain valid over a longer period of time and should not be subject to annual changes. Defining price stability is also important for accountability to the public and federal agencies. We are ultimately measured by whether we can keep inflation in the realm of price stability over the medium term. The second element of the new monetary policy approach involves the use of an inflation forecast over the following three years as the main indicator, or in other words as a compass for monetary policy decisions. This is a consensus forecast based in an undogmatic way on various models and indicators. It helps us to assess the consequences of monetary policy decisions with a view to maintaining price stability over the medium term. However, we do not react mechanically to the inflation forecast. Rather, we use them as a basis in a complex decision-making environment. The inflation forecast also plays an important role in communication, in explaining our monetary policy decisions. Starting this year, the SNB will publish its inflation forecast on a quarterly basis, namely in March, June, September and December together with the "Monetary Policy Assessment" report. We have Recently described in detail in our quarterly bulletin how the inflation forecast must be interpreted and on which models it is based. By using an inflation forecast, we can conduct a forward-looking monetary policy. This is important because monetary policy measures only have a long delay in affecting inflation. Studies on the transmission mechanism show that a change in monetary policy has its greatest impact on production around 4-8 quarters later. The greatest effect on prices only occurs after around 6 - 12 quarters. Monetary policy hardly has much influence on inflation in the short term. It therefore makes no sense to react to a temporary rise in inflation. On the other hand, we are committed to preventing a persistent breach of price stability. Favourable prospects for inflation thus increase the SNB's scope to take economic aspects into account. However, monetary policy is not in a position to fine-tune the economy. The third element in our concept is a target band for the three-month Libor with a width of usually 100 basis points or 1 percentage point. The target range has been 0% - 0.75% since our last rate cut on March 6. Because of the natural lower limit of 0% for nominal interest rates, the interest rate band is currently only 75 basis points. With this target band, the Governing Board sets the guidelines for the operational implementation of monetary policy. By announcing the target band, our intentions on the money market become transparent to the audience. In each case, we also indicate in which area of the target band we would like to keep the Libor. Unlike most other central banks, we have chosen a slightly longer-term interest rate and a broad target range for the operating target. This gives us greater flexibility to respond to the frequent disruptions in the exchange rate and liquidity supply without having to announce an actual change in monetary policy. It is often not understood why we use a London-based interest rate as our operating goal with Libor. We chose libor because it is the most important interest rate in the money market for Swiss franc investments and is considered a key factor for the refinancing of first-class banks and companies. It cannot be influenced by random actions of a single bank. The Libor is set in a transparent manner by the main banks in London on a daily basis. Although libor is fixed in London, it is ultimately determined by our refinancing conditions. The Swiss franc money market is an international market. The conditions on this Market depends on the amount and price of the liquidity we provide. We control this and thus indirectly also the three-month Libor via our repo auctions, which we carry out on a daily basis. 3. Monetary policy decision-making process The introduction of the New Approach was also accompanied by significant changes in monetary policy decision-making. I would now like to take a closer look at this aspect. We decide on monetary policy on the basis of our quarterly assessments. The dates of these assessments are known to the public and market participants in advance. In addition, we can also change our monetary policy at any time due to special events on the financial markets. In the quarterly assessments of the situation, we proceed according to a precise schedule, which clearly structures the provision and evaluation of the relevant information. The process begins about five to six weeks before the assessment of the situation with the assessment of the global economic development. Typically, a baseline scenario and some alternative scenarios are defined. In our view, the baseline scenario represents the most likely development of the global economy and forms the framework for our forecasts. The alternative scenarios are mainly used for sensitivity and risk analysis. The Board evaluates the scenarios proposed by the responsible economists and thus gives the starting signal for the calculation of the forecasts and simulations with the various econometric models. About three to four weeks before the assessment of the situation, the forecasts of the individual models and the interpretation of other indicators - including the development of money supply and exchange rates - are available. Subsequently, a broad-based consensus forecast for the inflation rate over the following 12 quarters is prepared in an intensive process. It does not arise from a fixed weighting of the individual model forecasts and indicators. Rather, the various pieces of information are critically assessed against the current background and used for consensus forecasting according to their plausibility. Together with the inflation forecast, the models and indicators also give an expectation about the future course of the economy. After the consensus forecast has been calculated, the reports for the assessment of the situation are written. They are sent to the Executive Board approximately one to two weeks before the meeting. The Board receives very detailed information on forecasts and indicators and an in-depth analysis of monetary policy alternatives. My department is making a proposal on the direction in which monetary policy should lead and how this course should be pursued. The Board of Directors then decides on the basis of the extensive information. Switzerland's openness and its dependence on what is happening on the international financial markets sometimes require us to react quickly and flexibly without waiting for a quarterly assessment of the situation. Especially recent times have clearly shown this necessity. In particular, we carry out extraordinary assessments of the situation in the event of strong changes in the exchange rate or events such as September 11, 2001. Only a reduced set of information is available for the extraordinary assessments of the situation. In particular, an updated inflation forecast is missing. Instead, we assess the impact of the changed situation on future inflation. We have developed various tools for the period between the regular assessments of the situation in order to be able to review the monetary policy indicators on an ongoing basis. Discussions are also taking place on an ongoing basis between the members of the Governing Board and the senior economists on the current situation. The SNB has the great advantage that its decision-making body comprises only three people. This allows a very efficient process of the situation assessment and usually a quick decision-making. With the involvement of senior economists, open factual questions can be clarified directly. The last two years in particular have shown that we are able to act quickly. 4. Challenges The SNB is currently facing various challenges. As you know, about two weeks ago we again significantly lowered the target for the key interest rate. The three-month Libor is now just over 0%. In this context, various questions arise: Does this interest rate cut bring anything, or is it just a drop in the ocean? Have we fired our powder too early in view of the uncertain situation and the existing risks? Has the SNB gone too far and is inflation already building up? What monetary policy instruments can we use in If we had to pursue an even more expansionary monetary policy? What consequences would this have on our monetary policy concept? I would like to answer these questions one by one. Why did we make this rate cut? We are currently assuming a gradual recovery of the Swiss economy. However, in view of the global economic and political uncertainty, the recovery expected for this year in Switzerland could still be somewhat delayed. The financial markets are also particularly nervous at the moment. At the same time, the inflation outlook over the medium term is favourable, which gives us room for manoeuvre in monetary policy. We have used this room for manoeuvre with our recent interest rate cut so that our economy has the most favourable monetary conditions for a future upswing at this critical stage. It is argued that interest rate cuts have no noticeable effects because of the high level of uncertainty. I would strongly disagree with that. Indeed, we have lowered interest rates in an environment of greatest uncertainty. We know that in such situations the risk premiums and thus the refinancing costs for companies increase significantly. A reduction in interest rates by the SNB means that refinancing costs for companies will at least increase less or possibly even fall. In addition, the interest rate cut leads to a reduction in the attractiveness of Swiss franc investments, which dampens the upward pressure on the franc. We therefore assume that with our interest rate cut we can achieve the desired effect and support the upswing of the economy. Have we, and this brings me to the second question, shot the powder too early with our last interest rate cut? Should we have kept it in reserve for emergencies? Our interest rate hike was made after careful consideration, preventively and after an in-depth analysis of the inflation forecast. With this step, we sent a clear signal to the markets and expressed our concern about exchange rate developments. We took this step at the same time as the European Central Bank, but went further in scope. In this way, we prevented speculation about our possible intentions from the outset. We have thus used our interest ammunition at a time when it can still produce a certain effect. It is a fallacy to think that saving a small margin of interest rates would have helped us in a possible crisis. In a crisis, significantly more and also a different kind of ammunition would be necessary. It is also dangerous to keep the existing ammunition unused for too long. The Market participants could otherwise assume that the central bank would not go below a certain interest rate level even in the event of a crisis. Such an expectation formation would have negative consequences for the economic upswing. Have we, and this brings me to the next question, already gone too far with our expansive policy? As mentioned, we have to decide under the greatest uncertainty. Of course, this is not possible without taking certain monetary policy risks. It is undisputed that our expansionary monetary policy has greatly increased liquidity. This is also desirable in view of the sluggish economic situation. That is why we cannot speak of a dangerous monetary overhang or a threat to medium-term price stability at this stage. However, we are following developments very closely and will have enough time to make the necessary corrections. Despite our cautiously optimistic assessment of the economic outlook, we must also keep an eye on economic risks. They are still downwards at present. This brings me to the question of what means we still have at our disposal to bring about a further easing of monetary policy if necessary in the event of a significant deterioration in the economic situation or strong exchange rate turbulence. It is clear that monetary policy cannot shield Switzerland from all foreign influences. Nevertheless, we still have various options to combat a continuing deterioration in the economic situation in Switzerland if necessary. We can further increase liquidity in the system even at an interest rate of 0%. The SNB could directly try to bring down longer-term interest rates even further by purchasing bonds in general. Lower long-term interest rates have a positive effect on investment and construction activity. A large expansion of liquidity would also have an impact on the foreign exchange market through a weakening of the Swiss franc and would help the export industry. The most powerful weapon in a crisis situation is to directly influence the exchange rate. With foreign exchange market interventions, we can decisively counter an excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc. The use of these instruments would partly mean new territory for us and is associated with risks. Should we use these instruments, we will therefore estimate very precisely when and to what extent. This will depend heavily on the inflation forecast and economic development. Finally, what consequences would the use of unconventional instruments have for our monetary policy concept? The concept is directly aligned with the ultimate goal of maintaining price stability. Regardless of the level of interest rates, the SNB pursues the objective of price stability and uses an inflation forecast as a compass for its decisions. So we can continue with our concept even in difficult times. However, we need to complement the operational implementation of monetary policy if we can no longer provide expansionary stimulus through interest rates. 5. Conclusions Let me conclude my remarks. The monetary policy approach introduced around three years ago has so far proved its worth; the experience has been consistently positive. With this concept, the SNB has demonstrated a great capacity to act and has been able to pursue a flexible monetary policy. This applies both to the period in which we had to tighten monetary policy and to today's period of loose monetary policy. Our concept has been well received by the Swiss public. The most important international organisations have also given it good marks. Both the OECD and the IMF, which regularly assess Swiss economic policy, came to the conclusion that the SNB's monetary policy concept was convincing and up to today's challenges. At the moment, we expect the Swiss economy to recover moderately this year. The risks are still great. They exist on the one hand in the geopolitical situation and on the other hand in the economic development in the USA and Europe. We see less of a risk of deflation and depression than of a renewed delay in the upswing. We have therefore used our monetary policy space. With money market rates close to 0%, we have created a favourable environment for the recovery without jeopardising price stability.

Mrz 2003 Bern 1. Einleitung No Change steht bestens sichtbar auf einer Metallplatte an der Haupteingangstre der Nationalbank in Bern. Ich kann Ihnen versichern, dass dies weder auf die Institution der Nationalbank im Allgemeinen noch auf die schweizerische Geldpolitik im Speziellen zutrifft. Vielmehr hat die Nationalbank in letzter Zeit verschiedene bedeutende Vernderungen vorgenommen. Dazu gehrt auch ein neues geldpolitisches Konzept. Alles andere als No Change erleben wir im Moment auch in der geldpolitischen Praxis. Beide Aspekte werden das Schwergewicht meiner heutigen Standortbestimmung sein. Die Nationalbank fhrt eine von den politischen Behrden unseres Landes unabhngige Geldpolitik. Diese Unabhngigkeit ist eine wichtige, ja sogar eine entscheidende Voraussetzung fr eine erfolgreiche Geldpolitik im Einklang mit dem verfassungsmssigen Auftrag. Zu dieser Unabhngigkeit gehrt nicht nur, dass die Nationalbank die Zinsstze festlegen kann, sondern auch dass sie ihre geldpolitische Strategie selber whlen kann. Die Nationalbank hat Anfang 2000 ein neues geldpolitisches Konzept eingefhrt. Eine Veranstaltung der Volkswirtschaftlichen Gesellschaft des Kantons Bern ist sicher eine passende Gelegenheit, um die Erfahrungen mit diesem Konzept vor einem sachkundigen Publikum zu diskutieren. Ich werde mich dabei auch dem Prozess der geldpolitischen Entscheidungsfindung und Meinungsbildung innerhalb der Nationalbank widmen, ber den in der ffentlichkeit selten gesprochen wird. Danach werde ich mich den geldpolitischen Herausforderungen zuwenden, welchen wir im Moment gegenberstehen. 2. Geldpolitisches Konzept Die Nationalbank hat als eine der ersten Notenbanken nach dem Zusammenbruch des Bretton Woods Systems eine Geldmengenziel-Strategie eingefhrt. Sie hat ihre Geldpolitik rund 25 Jahre nach den Leitplanken dieses Prinzips ausgerichtet. Sie ging dabei pragmatisch vor und war im internationalen Vergleich trotz einer Reihe von Problemen recht erfolgreich. Whrend diesen 25 Jahren hat die Nationalbank verschiedene Versionen der Geldmengenziel-Strategie angewendet, zuletzt das Konzept mit einem mittelfristigen Zielpfad fr die Notenbankgeldmenge. Ab 1997 begann sich die Nachfrage nach Notenbankgeld in der Schweiz mehr und mehr zu destabilisieren und die Abweichung vom mittelfristigen Zielpfad konnte nicht mehr als geldpolitischer Indikator verwendet werden. Als sich abzeichnete, dass keine Aussicht auf eine baldige Stabilisierung der Geldnachfrage bestand, beauftragte das Direktorium eine interne Arbeitsgruppe mit der Ausarbeitung eines neuen geldpolitischen Konzepts. Das Konzept wurde dann im Verlaufe von 1999 erarbeitet und vom Direktorium gegen Ende 1999 verabschiedet. Dieses Konzept stellt eine Strategie zur Erhaltung der Preisstabilitt dar. Preisstabilitt ist fr das reibungslose Funktionieren einer Wirtschaft unentbehrlich. Preisstabilitt bedeutet die Vermeidung von Inflation und Deflation. Dabei soll Preisstabilitt auf mittlere Frist erhalten bzw. erreicht werden. Die Ausrichtung auf die mittlere Frist ist aus zwei Grnden wichtig. Einerseits knnen wir die Inflation nicht feinsteuern, d.h. unvorhergesehene Schwankungen bei der Teuerung knnen in der kurzen Frist nicht ausgeglichen werden. Andererseits knnen wir vorbergehend auch bewusst Abweichungen von der Preisstabilitt zulassen, um bermssige volkswirtschaftliche Kosten zu verhindern, die mit einer zu radikalen Bekmpfung der Teuerung in bestimmten Situationen verbunden wren. In diesem Zusammenhang ist es auch wichtig zu sehen, dass eine auf mittelfristige Preisstabilitt ausgerichtete Geldpolitik hilft, Konjunkturschwankungen zu dmpfen. Wegen des unterschiedlichen Inflationsdrucks wird die Geldpolitik whrend eines Booms tendenziell gestrafft, whrend sie in einer Phase des wirtschaftlichen Abschwunges gelockert wird. Dieses Leitmotiv fr die Durchfhrung der Geldpolitik entspricht genau der Idee des Auftrages fr die Nationalbank im Entwurf zum neuen Nationalbankgesetz. Die Einfhrung dieses Konzepts brachte fr die Nationalbank die wichtigste Weichenstellung seit dem bergang zu einem flexiblen Frankenkurs im Jahre 1973. Es waren damit im Vergleich zur frheren Geldmengenziel-Strategie sowohl bei der geldpolitischen Entscheidungsfindung als auch bei der Implementierung der Geldpolitik wesentliche nderungen verbunden. Unverndert blieb hingegen die grundlegende Ausrichtung der Geldpolitik auf die mittelfristige Erhaltung der Preisstabilitt. Das Konzept besteht aus drei Elementen. Das erste Element ist eine explizite Definition der Preisstabilitt. Die Nationalbank definiert Preisstabilitt als eine Situation, in der die am Landesindex der Konsumentenpreise gemessene Jahresteuerung unter 2% liegt. Eine Inflation von 2% stellt also die Obergrenze dar, bei der noch von Preisstabilitt gesprochen werden kann. Weshalb haben wir eine Obergrenze gewhlt, welche von einer 0%-Teuerung abweicht? Der Grund ist, dass der Konsumentenpreisindex die tatschliche Teuerung systematisch um ca. 0,5 1,0 Prozentpunkte berzeichnet. Dies liegt daran, dass der Konsumentenpreisindex die Auswirkungen von Qualittsverbesserungen, der Einfhrung neuer Produkte und der Substitution zwischen Gtern nur unvollstndig bzw. verzerrt erfasst. Dieser systematische Messfehler muss daher bei einer Definition der Preisstabilitt mitbercksichtigt werden. Zudem haben wir noch eine Marge von 1 Prozentpunkt bercksichtigt, um je nach Konjunkturverlauf eine leicht hhere Inflationsrate zu akzeptieren. Dies trgt dem Umstand Rechnung, dass die Inflation nicht feingesteuert werden kann und dass eine leicht positive Inflationsrate in dieser Grssenordnung volkswirtschaftlich nicht schdlich ist. Preisstabilitt schliesst wie bereits erwhnt Deflation aus. Wir haben aber auf den Einschluss einer Untergrenze bei der Definition der Preisstabilitt aus folgenden Grnden verzichtet: Zum einen wrde eine explizite Untergrenze zu stark den Eindruck erwecken, die Nationalbank beabsichtige im Grundsatz immer genau die Mitte des Bereichs der Preisstabilitt anzusteuern. Stattdessen knnen wir je nach Wirtschaftslage leicht unterschiedliche Inflationsraten akzeptieren. Zum anderen kann sich der systematische Messfehler beim Konsumentenpreisindex ber die Zeit verndern. Der Verzicht auf eine explizite Untergrenze erlaubt es uns, nderungen im systematischen Messfehler zu bercksichtigen, ohne die Definition der Preisstabilitt anpassen zu mssen. Mit der Definition der Preisstabilitt legt die Nationalbank die grundlegende Ausrichtung ihrer Geldpolitik fest und erlaubt den Marktteilnehmern, entsprechende Erwartungen zu bilden. Die Definition der Preisstabilitt soll ber lngere Zeit gltig bleiben und nicht jhrlichen nderungen unterworfen sein. Die Preisstabilitt zu definieren ist auch wichtig fr die Rechenschaftsablage gegenber der ffentlichkeit und den Bundesbehrden. Wir werden letztlich daran gemessen, ob wir die Inflation ber die mittlere Frist im Bereich der Preisstabilitt halten knnen. Das zweite Element des neuen geldpolitischen Konzepts beinhaltet die Verwendung einer Inflationsprognose ber die nachfolgenden drei Jahre als Hauptindikator, oder anders ausgedrckt als Kompass fr die geldpolitischen Entscheidungen. Dabei handelt es sich um eine Konsensprognose, die sich in einer undogmatischen Art auf verschiedene Modelle und Indikatoren sttzt. Sie hilft uns, die Konsequenzen der geldpolitischen Entscheidungen im Hinblick auf die mittelfristige Erhaltung der Preisstabilitt abzuschtzen. Wir reagieren indes nicht mechanisch auf die Inflationsprognose. Vielmehr verwenden wir sie als Grundlage in einem komplexen Entscheidungsumfeld. Die Inflationsprognose spielt auch eine wichtige Rolle in der Kommunikation, bei der Erluterung unserer geldpolitischen Entscheide. Die Nationalbank publiziert die Inflationsprognose ab diesem Jahr vierteljhrlich, nmlich im Mrz, Juni, September und im Dezember zusammen mit dem Bericht Geldpolitische Lagebeurteilung. Wir haben krzlich in unserem Quartalsheft ausfhrlich beschrieben, wie die Inflationsprognose interpretiert werden muss und auf welche Modelle sie sich sttzt. Mit der Verwendung einer Inflationsprognose knnen wir eine vorausschauende Geldpolitik fhren. Dies ist wichtig, weil geldpolitische Massnahmen nur mit grosser Verzgerung auf die Inflation wirken. Studien ber den Transmissionsmechanismus zeigen, dass eine Vernderung der Geldpolitik ihre grsste Wirkung auf die Produktion rund 4 - 8 Quartale spter hat. Der grsste Effekt auf die Preise erfolgt sogar erst nach rund 6 - 12 Quartalen. Auf die Inflation in der kurzen Frist hat die Geldpolitik kaum einen grossen Einfluss. Es macht daher keinen Sinn, auf einen vorbergehenden Anstieg der Inflation zu reagieren. Hingegen sind wir bestrebt, eine anhaltende Verletzung der Preisstabilitt zu verhindern. Gnstige Aussichten bei der Teuerung erhhen dabei den Spielraum der Nationalbank, konjunkturelle Aspekte zu bercksichtigen. Allerdings ist die Geldpolitik nicht in der Lage, eine konjunkturelle Feinsteuerung vorzunehmen. Das dritte Element in unserem Konzept ist ein Zielband fr den Dreimonats-Libor mit einer Breite von blicherweise 100 Basispunkten bzw. 1 Prozentpunkt. Das Zielband liegt seit unserer letzten Zinssenkung vom 6. Mrz bei 0% - 0,75%. Wegen der natrlichen Untergrenze von 0% fr nominelle Zinsstze betrgt das Zinsband im Moment somit nur 75 Basispunkte. Mit dem Zielband setzt das Direktorium die Leitplanken fr die operative Umsetzung der Geldpolitik. Durch die Bekanntgabe des Zielbandes werden unsere Absichten auf dem Geldmarkt fr das Publikum transparent. Wir geben jeweils noch zustzlich an, in welchem Bereich des Zielbandes wir den Libor halten mchten. Im Gegensatz zu den meisten anderen Zentralbanken haben wir fr das operative Ziel einen etwas lngerfristigen Zinssatz sowie ein breites Zielband gewhlt. Wir haben dadurch eine grssere Flexibilitt, um auf die hufig auftretenden Strungen beim Wechselkurs und bei der Liquidittsversorgung zu reagieren, ohne eine eigentliche nderung der Geldpolitik ankndigen zu mssen. Oft wird nicht verstanden, weshalb wir mit dem Libor einen in London fixierten Zinssatz als unser operatives Ziel benutzen. Wir haben den Libor gewhlt, weil er der bedeutendste Zinssatz im Geldmarkt fr Frankenanlagen ist und als zentrale Grsse fr die Refinanzierung von erstklassigen Banken und Unternehmen gilt. Er kann nicht durch Zufallsaktionen einer einzelnen Bank beeinflusst werden. Der Libor wird durch die wichtigsten Banken in London tglich in transparenter Weise festgelegt. Obwohl der Libor in London fixiert wird, wird er letztlich durch unsere Refinanzierungsbedingungen bestimmt. Der Frankengeldmarkt ist ein internationaler Markt. Die Konditionen auf diesem Markt hngen von Menge und Preis der von uns zur Verfgung gestellten Liquiditt ab. Diese und damit indirekt auch den Dreimonats-Libor steuern wir ber unsere RepoAuktionen, die wir tglich durchfhren. 3. Ablauf der geldpolitischen Entscheidungsfindung Die Einfhrung des neuen Konzepts war auch mit wesentlichen nderungen in der geldpolitischen Entscheidungsfindung verbunden. Ich mchte nun diesen Aspekt etwas genauer beleuchten. Wir entscheiden jeweils an unseren vierteljhrlichen Lagebeurteilungen ber die Geldpolitik. Die Termine dieser Lagebeurteilungen sind der ffentlichkeit und den Marktteilnehmern im Voraus bekannt. Daneben knnen wir unsere Geldpolitik aber auch jederzeit aufgrund von speziellen Ereignissen auf den Finanzmrkten ndern. An den vierteljhrlichen Lagebeurteilungen gehen wir nach einem genauen Ablaufplan vor, welcher die Bereitstellung und Auswertung der relevanten Informationen klar strukturiert. Der Prozess beginnt rund fnf bis sechs Wochen vor der Lagebeurteilung mit der Einschtzung der weltwirtschaftlichen Entwicklung. blicherweise werden ein Basisszenario und einige Alternativszenarien festgelegt. Das Basisszenario stellt die aus unserer Sicht wahrscheinlichste Entwicklung der Weltwirtschaft dar und bildet den Rahmen fr unsere Prognosen. Die Alternativszenarien dienen vor allem der Sensitivittsund Risikoanalyse. Das Direktorium evaluiert die von den verantwortlichen konomen vorgeschlagenen Szenarien und gibt damit den Startschuss fr die Berechnung der Prognosen und Simulationen mit den verschiedenen konometrischen Modellen. Rund drei bis vier Wochen vor der Lagebeurteilung stehen die Prognosen der einzelnen Modelle und die Interpretation von weiteren Indikatoren - u.a. der Geldmengen- und Wechselkursentwicklung - bereit. Anschliessend wird in einem intensiven Prozess eine breit abgesttzte Konsensprognose fr die Inflationsrate ber die nachfolgenden 12 Quartale erstellt. Sie entsteht nicht durch eine feste Gewichtung der einzelnen Modellprognosen und Indikatoren. Vielmehr werden die verschiedenen Informationen jeweils vor dem aktuellen Hintergrund kritisch beurteilt und entsprechend ihrer Plausibilitt fr die Konsensprognose verwendet. Zusammen mit der Inflationsprognose ergibt sich aus den Modellen und Indikatoren auch eine Erwartung ber den zuknftigen Konjunkturverlauf. Nach der Berechnung der Konsensprognose werden die Berichte fr die Lagebeurteilung verfasst. Sie werden dem Direktorium rund ein bis zwei Wochen vor der Sitzung zugestellt. Das Direktorium erhlt sehr detaillierte Angaben zu den Prognosen und Indikatoren und eine eingehende Analyse der geldpolitischen Alternativen. Mein Departement unterbreitet einen Vorschlag darber, in welche Richtung der Kurs der Geldpolitik fhren soll und wie dieser Kurs zu verfolgen sei. Das Direktorium entscheidet dann aufgrund der umfangreichen Informationen. Die Offenheit der Schweiz und ihre Abhngigkeit von den Geschehnissen auf den internationalen Finanzmrkten erfordern manchmal, dass wir rasch und flexibel reagieren, ohne eine vierteljhrliche Lagebeurteilung abzuwarten. Gerade die letzte Zeit hat diese Notwendigkeit deutlich gezeigt. Insbesondere bei starken Vernderungen des Wechselkurses oder bei Ereignissen wie dem 11. September 2001 fhren wir ausserordentliche Lagebeurteilungen durch. An den ausserordentlichen Lagebeurteilungen steht nur ein reduziertes Set von Informationen zur Verfgung. Insbesondere fehlt eine aktualisierte Inflationsprognose. Stattdessen schtzen wir die Auswirkungen der vernderten Lage auf die zuknftige Inflation ein. Wir haben fr die Zeit zwischen den ordentlichen Lagebeurteilungen verschiedene Tools entwickelt, um die geldpolitischen Indikatoren laufend berprfen zu knnen. laufend finden auch Gesprche zwischen den Mitgliedern des Direktoriums und den leitenden konomen ber die aktuelle Lage statt. Die Nationalbank hat den grossen Vorteil, dass ihr Entscheidungsgremium nur drei Personen umfasst. Dies erlaubt einen sehr effizienten Ablauf der Lagebeurteilung und blicherweise eine rasche Entscheidungsfindung. Mit dem Beizug von leitenden konomen knnen offene Sachfragen direkt geklrt werden. Gerade die letzten zwei Jahre haben gezeigt, dass wir rasch handlungsfhig sind. 4. Herausforderungen Die Nationalbank steht im Moment verschiedenen Herausforderungen gegenber. Wie Sie wissen, haben wir vor etwa zwei Wochen das Ziel fr den Leitzins erneut markant gesenkt. Der Dreimonats-Libor ist heute nur noch wenig ber 0%. In diesem Zusammenhang stellen sich verschiedene Fragen: Bringt diese Zinssenkung etwas, oder ist sie nur ein Tropfen auf den heissen Stein? Haben wir unser Pulver in Anbetracht der unsicheren Lage und der vorhandenen Risiken zu frh verschossen? Ist die Nationalbank zu weit gegangen und baut sich bereits Inflation auf? Welche geldpolitischen Instrumente knnen wir in Zukunft noch einsetzen, falls wir eine noch expansivere Geldpolitik fahren mssten? Welche Konsequenzen htte dies auf unser geldpolitisches Konzept? Diese Fragen mchte ich nacheinander beantworten. Weshalb haben wir diese Zinssenkung vorgenommen? Wir gehen zurzeit von einer graduellen Erholung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft aus. Allerdings knnte sich angesichts der weltweiten wirtschaftlichen und politischen Unsicherheit die fr dieses Jahr erwartete Erholung in der Schweiz noch etwas verzgern. Auch sind die Finanzmrkte im Moment besonders nervs. Gleichzeitig sind die Inflationsaussichten ber die mittlere Frist gnstig, was uns einen geldpolitischen Spielraum einrumt. Wir haben diesen Spielraum mit unserer jngsten Zinssenkung genutzt, damit unsere Wirtschaft in dieser kritischen Phase ber mglichst gnstige monetre Rahmenbedingungen fr einen knftigen Aufschwung verfgt. Verschiedentlich wird argumentiert, dass Zinssenkungen wegen der hohen Unsicherheit keine sprbaren Wirkungen haben. Ich mchte dem entschieden widersprechen. Wir haben in der Tat die Zinsen in einem Umfeld grsster Unsicherheit gesenkt. Wir wissen, dass in solchen Lagen die Risikoprmien und somit die Refinanzierungskosten fr die Unternehmen deutlich zunehmen. Eine Zinssenkung der Nationalbank bewirkt, dass die Refinanzierungskosten fr die Unternehmen zumindest weniger ansteigen oder mglicherweise sogar sinken. Zudem fhrt die Zinssenkung zu einer Verminderung der Attraktivitt von Frankenanlagen, was den Aufwertungsdruck auf den Franken dmpft. Wir gehen daher davon aus, dass wir mit unserer Zinssenkung durchaus die gewnschte Wirkung erzielen und den Aufschwung der Wirtschaft untersttzen knnen. Haben wir, und damit komme ich zur zweiten Frage, mit unserer letzten Zinssenkung das Pulver zu frh verschossen? Htten wir es fr den Notfall in Reserve halten sollen? Unser Zinsschritt erfolgte nach reiflicher berlegung, prventiv und nach eingehender Analyse der Inflationsprognose. Mit diesem Schritt sandten wir ein klares Signal an die Mrkte und brachten unsere Besorgnis ber die Wechselkursentwicklung zum Ausdruck. Wir nahmen diesen Schritt gleichzeitig mit der Europischen Zentralbank vor, gingen im Ausmass aber weiter. So verhinderten wir von vorneherein Spekulationen ber unsere mglichen Absichten. Wir haben damit unsere Zinsmunition in einem Zeitpunkt verwendet, in dem sie noch eine bestimmte Wirkung erzeugen kann. Es ist ein Trugschluss zu glauben, das Aufsparen eines kleinen Zinsspielraums htte uns in einer mglichen Krise geholfen. In einer Krise wre deutlich mehr und auch eine andere Art von Munition ntig. Auch ist es gefhrlich, die vorhandene Munition allzu lange ungebraucht aufzubewahren. Die Marktteilnehmer knnten sonst davon ausgehen, dass die Notenbank auch im Krisenfall nicht unter ein bestimmtes Zinsniveau gehen wrde. Eine solche Erwartungsbildung htte negative Folgen fr den wirtschaftlichen Aufschwung. Sind wir, und damit komme ich zur nchsten Frage, mit unserer expansiven Politik bereits zu weit gegangen? Wie erwhnt, mssen wir unter grsster Unsicherheit entscheiden. Dies geht natrlich nicht, ohne bestimmte geldpolitische Risiken einzugehen. Es ist unbestritten, dass unsere expansive Geldpolitik die Liquiditt stark erhht hat. Dies ist angesichts des schleppenden Wirtschaftsganges auch erwnscht. Deshalb kann man im jetzigen Zeitpunkt auch noch nicht von einem gefhrlichen monetren berhang oder einer Gefhrdung der mittelfristigen Preisstabilitt sprechen. Wir verfolgen die Entwicklung aber sehr genau und werden gengend Zeit haben, um die ntigen Korrekturen vorzunehmen. Trotz unserer vorsichtig optimistischen Einschtzung der wirtschaftlichen Aussichten mssen wir auch die Konjunkturrisiken im Auge behalten. Sie sind gegenwrtig immer noch nach unten gerichtet. Dies bringt mich zur Frage, welche Mittel wir noch zur Verfgung haben, um im Falle einer deutlichen Verschlechterung der Wirtschaftslage oder von starken Wechselkursturbulenzen ntigenfalls eine weitere Lockerung der Geldpolitik herbeizufhren. Es steht fest, dass die Geldpolitik die Schweiz nicht gegen alle Auslandeinflsse abschirmen kann. Trotzdem haben wir noch verschiedene Mglichkeiten, um bei Bedarf eine anhaltende Verschlechterung der Wirtschaftslage in der Schweiz zu bekmpfen. Wir knnen die Liquiditt im System auch bei einem Zins von 0% weiter erhhen. Die Nationalbank knnte direkt versuchen, ber den Ankauf von Obligationen generell die lngerfristigen Zinsen noch weiter nach unten zu bringen. Tiefere Langfristzinsen haben einen positiven Effekt auf die Investitions- und Bauttigkeit. Eine grosse Ausdehnung der Liquiditt wrde sich auch auf dem Devisenmarkt ber eine Abschwchung des Frankens auswirken und der Exportwirtschaft helfen. Die strkste Waffe in einer Krisensituation besteht in der direkten Einflussnahme auf den Wechselkurs. Mit DevisenmarktInterventionen knnen wir einer bermssigen Aufwertung des Frankens entschieden entgegentreten. Die Verwendung dieser Instrumente wrde zum Teil Neuland fr uns bedeuten und ist mit Risiken verbunden. Sollten wir diese Instrumente einsetzen, werden wir daher sehr genau abschtzen, wann und in welchem Ausmass. Dies wird stark von der Inflationsprognose und der Wirtschaftsentwicklung abhngen. Welche Konsequenzen htte schliesslich der Einsatz von unkonventionellen Instrumenten fr unser geldpolitisches Konzept? Das Konzept ist direkt auf das Endziel, die Aufrechterhaltung der Preisstabilitt, ausgerichtet. Unabhngig von der Hhe der Zinsstze verfolgt die Nationalbank das Ziel der Preisstabilitt und verwendet eine Inflationsprognose als Kompass fr ihre Entscheidungen. Wir knnen also auch in schwierigen Zeiten mit unserem Konzept weiterfahren. Allerdings mssen wir die operative Umsetzung der Geldpolitik ergnzen, wenn wir ber die Zinsstze keine expansiven Impulse mehr geben knnen. 5. Schlussfolgerungen Lassen Sie mich zum Schluss meiner Ausfhrungen kommen. Das vor rund drei Jahren eingefhrte geldpolitische Konzept hat sich bisher bewhrt; die Erfahrungen sind durchwegs positiv. Die Nationalbank hat mit diesem Konzept eine grosse Handlungsfhigkeit bewiesen und eine flexible Geldpolitik verfolgen knnen. Dies gilt sowohl fr die Phase, in der wir die Geldpolitik straffen mussten, als auch fr die heutige Periode der lockeren Geldpolitik. Unser Konzept ist in der schweizerischen ffentlichkeit gut angekommen. Auch die wichtigsten internationalen Organisationen haben ihm gute Noten erteilt. Sowohl die OECD als auch der IWF, welche die schweizerische Wirtschaftspolitik regelmssig beurteilen, kamen zum Schluss, dass das geldpolitische Konzept der Nationalbank berzeugend und den heutigen Herausforderungen gewachsen sei. Wir gehen im Moment davon aus, dass sich die schweizerische Wirtschaft in diesem Jahr moderat erholen wird. Die Risiken sind immer noch gross. Sie bestehen einerseits in der geopolitischen Lage und andererseits in der Wirtschaftsentwicklung in den USA und Europa. Wir sehen dabei weniger eine Deflations- und Depressionsgefahr als vielmehr das Risiko einer erneuten Verzgerung des Aufschwunges. Wir haben daher unseren geldpolitischen Spielraum ausgentzt. Mit Geldmarktstzen in der Nhe von 0% haben wir gnstige Rahmenbedingungen fr den Aufschwung geschaffen, ohne die Preisstabilitt zu gefhrden.

Title: In the midst of Europe, but not part of the EU  experience and perspectives of Swiss monetary policy
text: In the middle of it, but not with experiences and perspectives of Swiss monetary policy Prof. Dr. Bruno Gehrig Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Presentation to the German-Swiss Society in Hamburg I am very pleased and grateful to you for the fact that I can enjoy hospitality in your circle today and speak to you. Your invitation opens up two valuable opportunities for me- apart from maintaining personal contacts. On the one hand, in a friendly neighbouring country and for the first time in Hamburg, I am allowed to explain our policy and explain why we have embarked on this path and would like to continue it. And on the other hand, with this visit I would like to express my highest appreciation for the German-Swiss Society of Hamburg, for your successful commitment to maintaining economic, political and cultural relations between your city and my country. Thank you very much for that. "In the middle of it, but not there" - under this heading I would like to offer you a four-part lecture. I'll start with the "right in the middle of it", with some references to the networking of the Swiss economy with that of the European Union (EU) and in particular with that of Germany. This has consequences for monetary policy. In the second part, in the sense of an interim assessment, I turn to the experiences we have had so far in living together with the euro. I will then examine the monetary policy implications of Switzerland's possible accession to the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). Finally, I would like to look at current economic trends and prospects. 1. Switzerland is more "European" than many EU countries Ten years ago, the Swiss sovereign rejected accession to the European Economic Area (EEA). This has not changed the fact that the Swiss economy is intimately linked to its European environment in many respects and is therefore obviously also dependent on the prosperity of this Europe. This striking exposure is particularly evident in the importance of Swiss foreign trade with the EU. EU countries are our main trading partners. Around 60% of Swiss exports go into these, while more than 70% of our imports come from these countries. moreover, exports of goods to the EU have been rising sharply since 1996. In 1999, they amounted to more than 18% of Switzerland's gross domestic product (GDP) in terms of value. Interestingly, the comparative value is lower in the average of the EU member states for their exports to the other member states. With regard to exports of goods, the The Swiss economy is more EU-oriented than most of the economies of the EU member states. Two conclusions emerge from this close interdependence. On the one hand, economic activity in Switzerland largely moves with the economic development in the EU. Switzerland has a vital interest in an economically strong and functioning EU. On the other hand, the exchange rate ratio between the Swiss franc and the euro is of central importance for large parts of economic activity in Switzerland. A special proximity to Germany The close economic relationship applies above all with Germany. On the one hand, it is explained by similarities in the structure of the productive apparatus, the intensity of labour and the real wage level. Germany and Switzerland are also known for their sustained success in the fight against inflation. Its inflation rates have been among the lowest in the world over the past three decades. German and Swiss companies work together excellently in many areas. One example among many is Eurex, the world's largest derivatives exchange, which is equally owned by the German and Swiss stock exchanges. On the other hand, Switzerland maintains very close foreign economic relations with Germany, its most important trading partner. Exports to Germany account for 23% of total Swiss exports, while imports from Germany account for as much as 33%. It is therefore not surprising that economic growth in the two countries has been quite similar for some time. On the other hand, there was a decoupling at the beginning of the 90s. While Germany went through a brief boom as a result of reunification, the Swiss economy slipped into six long years of stagnation, even though interest rates were around 2 percentage points lower than DM rates. Between 1991 and 1997, Germany recorded significantly higher overall economic growth than Switzerland. It was not until 1997 that the Swiss economy began to revive, supported by aggressive interest rate cuts. According to the study, growth rates in Switzerland were in some cases even higher than in Germany. The slump in growth over the past two years was almost synchronous. Similar to Germany, we can look back on an unsatisfactory decade in terms of growth. The growth rate in the EU averaged 2%, in the USA even 3.2%. Together with Italy (1.5%) and Germany (1.4%), Switzerland is one of the countries with the lowest growth rates in Europe, with an average growth rate of 1% since 1992. The increase in labour productivity in Germany and Switzerland was lower than the EU average. Despite the obvious cyclical parallelism, there are marked structural and institutional differences between our two countries. I am thinking of the different fiscal relations between central government and local authorities or of the structure of old-age provision. The conditions on the labour markets differ particularly strikingly. Although Switzerland is no longer an island of full employment, unemployment has reached an average of 3.5% over the past ten years, less than half of the level registered in Germany. Also in terms of the employment rate - the share of employees in the workforce - Switzerland achieves a significantly higher value of almost 80% than Germany, where this share is just under 70%. This big difference undoubtedly has a number of reasons. Some are of an institutional regulatory nature and are currently the subject of important reform efforts in this country. Switzerland's small and very open economy has always been structurally dependent on a high degree of labour market flexibility. In an environment of rapid economic change, this need is proving to be an advantage from many points of view today. If Switzerland's cyclical dependence on its main European neighbours was evident in the past, it will - to a greater extent - also shape the future. Switzerland's links with the EU are clearly increasing, so that economic dependencies tend to become more pronounced. The euro has reinforced this process. But there will also be phases of different developments in which targeted monetary policy impulses will be necessary on their own. 2. In contrast, the hard franc puts the export sector and its suppliers under particular competitive and adjustment pressure. The Trend is that the Swiss economy has coped well with this pressure. The adjustment flexibility imposed by the exchange rate may even increase the international competitiveness of the economy. A first indication of this is that Swiss exports of goods and services have risen from 33% to over 40% of GDP since 1990. From the point of view of competitiveness, however, it is not exports alone that are relevant, but the balance of exports minus imports. It has increased from 3% to over 6% of GDP since 1990. The fact that our export industry has learned to deal with the appreciation trend of the Swiss franc is positive. However, we must not close our eyes to the fact that massive short- and medium-term fluctuations in the real Swiss franc exchange rate make the adjustment problems more difficult and in some cases unsolvable. We have already experienced several phases in which the Swiss franc appreciated by double-digit percentages in real terms within a short period of time. Striking examples of this are the late seventies and the first half of the nineties. These phases destabilized our economy and led to serious adjustment burdens. With the introduction of the euro, the shape of the exchange rate risk to which our companies are exposed changed. On the one hand, we also benefit from the fact that the euro has also replaced the devaluation-prone predecessor currencies. At the same time, the euro-franc exchange rate represents a cluster risk for our economy and economy, which is further accentuated with the increasing "Europeanization" of the Swiss economy. In the run-up to monetary union, it was unclear what fluctuation range of the euro - as a weighted average of the predecessor currencies - against the Swiss franc was to be expected. The fears here and there that fluctuations would increase have not been confirmed. Since its introduction, the euro has not fluctuated more against the Swiss franc than the D-Mark used to. However, the appreciation trend of the Swiss franc was accentuated. Compared to Germany, Switzerland's most important trading partner, the real exchange rate has risen by more than 7% since 1999. This deterioration in competitiveness is causing problems for our export economy. Real exchange rateSwitzerland/Germany 110 105 100 95 90 85 80 Introduction of the Euro 75 Let me briefly recapitulate our experience with the euro since its introduction in 1999. In a first phase, lasting 14 months, the Swiss franc-euro exchange rate was practically stable at a level of 1.60. The reason for this was an obvious monetary and cyclical parallelism between Switzerland and the euro area. Our announcement that we would not accept the threat of an appreciation of the Swiss franc may also have contributed to this. From spring 2000 onwards - in view of the economic upturn at that time - we tightened our monetary policy stance more than the European Central Bank. This resulted in an appreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro to around 1.53 in a short period of time. On our part, the appreciation of the Swiss franc was not intended. However, it supported our intention to tighten monetary conditions and ultimately helped keep interest rate hikes moderate. The Swiss franc experienced a second appreciation boost after the shock of 11 September. Within a few days, the Swiss franc rose by a further 5% against the euro. This appreciation boost was solely due to a change in the markets' perception of risk and was very inconvenient in view of the economic downturn. At To counter a tightening of monetary conditions, we responded with two interest rate cuts in quick succession. Since then, the euro-franc exchange rate has stubbornly held between 1.45 and 1.48. In other words, the premium paid on the Swiss franc since 11 September continues to exist. The Swiss franc remained in high demand despite a growing interest rate disadvantage. This also shows that the exchange rate can be influenced with interest rate measures, but cannot be reliably controlled. Nevertheless, whenever the exchange rate situation becomes difficult, the interest rate differential with the euro is an essential element of monetary policy governance for us. We also underlined this with the latest interest rate hike at the beginning of March. It ultimately helped to relieve appreciation pressure from the Swiss franc and stabilise the euro-franc exchange rate. Overall, the euro has lost a good 9% in nominal terms against the Swiss franc since its introduction. Part of this is due to the inflation differential between the two currency areas. Adjusted for this inflation differential, there is still a real appreciation of the Swiss franc of 5.5%. Even more pronounced is the real appreciation compared to our most important trading partner Germany. As a result, the prices of our exporters' products increased considerably compared to those of their German competitors. What conclusions do we draw from what has been said for the central bank's operational monetary policy "in the middle of it, but not in it"?  The exchange rate is of central importance. Monetary policy impulses often work faster through the exchange rate channel than through the interest rate channel. Conversely, the exchange rate is exposed to much greater disturbances and is therefore less controllable than the interest rate.  Nevertheless, the overall monetary conditions, i.e. the mix of interest rates and exchange rates, are decisive for the management of monetary policy. If the Swiss franc appreciates and monetary conditions worsen, this effect can be at least partially compensated for by interest rate cuts.  The renewal of the monetary policy concept in 2000, which included a move away from money supply control towards interest rate management, made it easier for us to take greater account of the euro-franc exchange rate. Precise exchange rate control is neither possible nor desirable. It is crucial that monetary policy is able to cushion shocks emanating from the exchange rate. Only in exceptional cases - such as the extreme strength of the Swiss franc in 1978 - can a temporary exchange rate target make sense.  An "independent" monetary policy in this sense is also possible and effective in an economy closely intertwined with foreign countries.  In the current environment of weak economic activity, with money market rates close to zero and a highly valued Swiss franc, we are operationally challenged. We need to resort to other instruments where necessary. First and foremost, interventions in the foreign exchange market come into question. The use of such extraordinary instruments must be decided wisely. Because in an emergency, determination and perseverance are required. 3. One EU accession - at most one long-term option Economically, Switzerland is closely intertwined with the EU. Institutionally, integration was relatively timid. There are 30 years between the free trade agreement of 1972 - at that time still with the EC - and the sectoral docking to the EU internal market in mid-2002. Politically, the Swiss population has traditionally had a hard time with the EU question. The time for accession to the EU is not yet ripe. As recently as March 2002, 77% of voters said no to a request aimed at rapid EU accession. The application for membership submitted prophylactically by the Swiss government in 1992 is now on "glacier-thick" ice. Original Swiss independence and independence thinking coupled with scepticism about big throws accompanies Switzerland on its unspectacular path of small steps. But there are also monetary policy concerns about EU accession. In the event of EU accession, we would have to replace the franc with the euro and abandon our independent monetary policy. Inflation and economic management would be made more difficult. Above all, however, costs would arise in the form of higher nominal and real interest rates. Swiss money and capital market interest rates would inevitably align with the higher euro interest rate level. This is after they have been structurally 1.5 to 3 percentage points below German rates for decades, despite inflation at about the same level over this period. One of the reasons why the interest rate advantage is valuable for the Swiss economy is that it goes well beyond the trendy appreciation of the Swiss franc. In international competition for locations, the interest bonus is of considerable importance. Comparatively low capital costs increase the Capital intensity, increase productivity and ultimately generate additional income and employment. The long-term effects of a permanently higher real interest rate would be profound and harmful. Basically, Germany has joined the monetary union with similar conditions. Your country also had lower nominal interest rates and lower inflation compared to the other participating countries. By entering the monetary union, the interest rate advantage disappeared completely, but the inflation difference only partially disappeared. For this reason, Germany has long been confronted - compared to the other countries of the monetary union - with higher real interest rates and the resulting adjustment burdens. It also had lower real interest rates than the other participating countries and is therefore now confronted with adjustment burdens - also in foreign countries. For the Swiss population, the interest rate advantage is the outstanding economic argument against joining the EU and monetary union. And this interest bonus may well last. The core prerequisite for this is a successful stability policy. Almost as important, however, is that the international competitiveness of our economy is maintained despite exchange rate shocks. Monetary policy must also make its contribution to this. An independent monetary policy is particularly advantageous when economic developments diverge, e.g. because economic disturbances affect the individual countries inconsistently. Let's take an exaggerated example. Suppose that Switzerland opts for the euro tomorrow and is located the day after tomorrow in the probably inevitable interest rate adjustment crisis; at the same time, contrary to all expectations, the European economy is recovering rapidly and vigorously. In such a situation, would the ECB, with regard to Switzerland, refrain from a forced interest rate hike at the price of an EU-wide inflation risk? I think this remains a rhetorical question! In addition, the structural strength of the Swiss franc would not simply vanish into thin air. In the long term, central banks can only influence the nominal exchange rate, but not the real exchange ratios. The trending real appreciation of the Swiss franc is due either to a nominal appreciation under price stability or - at fixed exchange rates - to higher inflation than abroad. A Swiss exporter would face a nominally fixed exchange rate after the introduction of the euro. In the event of a higher inflation trend in Switzerland, however, it would still have to struggle with a real appreciation. Even such a development would not be ruled out for Switzerland in the event of EU accession, as a look at the Netherlands, probably the most similar EU country to Switzerland, shows. Germany is the most important trading partner for both Switzerland and the Netherlands. In contrast to Switzerland, the Netherlands has the same currency as Germany and thus no nominal exchange rate risk. Nevertheless, Dutch firms can lose competitiveness vis-a-vis their German competitors if inflation is higher in the Netherlands. This has been the case for the last four years. While inflation in Germany averaged 1.4%, it was 3.4% in the Netherlands. This means a real appreciation of 2% per year. In other words, Dutch companies were under even greater appreciation pressure than their Swiss competitors during this period. On the other hand, Holland benefited from significantly lower real interest rates than Germany. Similar to Switzerland outside the monetary union, it has thus had a real appreciation in recent years, but lower real interest rates on the other. A monetary union therefore guarantees neither stable real exchange rates nor uniform real interest rates. 4. Current trends and perspectives Finally, I come to the topicality, to the attempt to assess the situation and development prospects, first for the international economy, then for Switzerland. This cannot be more than an attempt: the forecast performance of economists over the past three years has been extremely unsatisfactory. This is not a very surprising finding for two reasons in particular. On the one hand, we had and still have it - for the first time since the World War II - not with a bout of weakness driven by demand, but by supply, capital formation. The lack of experience with this type of economic downturn has significantly affected forecasting work. On the other hand, the significantly increased geopolitical risks since 11 September 2001 at the latest are very difficult to assess: What is "increased risk aversion" really and what does this expectation lead to in the short, medium and long term? Such reservations are not arguments against forecasts or at least an effort to think about the future course of events, on the contrary. But they are an appeal to the willingness to self-criticism and the unbroken will to constantly cast doubt on one's own assessment and to modify it in the light of changed circumstances. Global economic environment Regardless of regional and country-specific peculiarities, several factors can be identified that shape the global economic situation and influence its further development. Geopolitical risks are rightly at the forefront of most of the comments and considerations of economic actors. economically, they lead to increased risk premiums, depressed goodwill and economic lethargy, especially with regard to the willingness to invest. But it would be wrong to link the existing problems exclusively to geopolitical factors. Rather, it must be noted that these geopolitical risks meet a global economy that is highly fragile. At the end of this first quarter of 2003, the global economy is in much weaker shape than expected six or twelve months ago. Anyone who takes the trouble to compare the growth forecasts issued and periodically adjusted since the beginning of 2001 for this current year 2003 quickly comes to a sobering conclusion: In all relevant regions, growth expectations had to be successively revised downwards. This causes disappointment and leads to the anxious question of how far this slowdown dynamic will go. At the level of global economic contexts, three aspects in particular are likely to be important. First, it is far from clear to what extent the excesses of the late 90s have been dismantled and overcome. Everyone agrees on the starting position created in the 90s: In the corporate sectors of all OECD countries, it is too large Capital formation excesses and - as an inevitable consequence of disillusionment - painful losses of wealth have come. It is difficult to estimate how far the absorption of these shocks has progressed. The answer to this question decisively determines the chances for a normalization of investment in the course of the coming quarters. This leads to the second set of questions. Consumer activity, which has been remarkably robust in the recent past, threatens to flatten out in the US and Europe. How justified is the hope that the revival of private investment will begin in time and prevent a fall in aggregate demand? A third problem relates to the persistently large US current account deficit, which is joined by rapidly rising budget deficits. An external deficit of currently around 5% of gross domestic product can hardly be financed in the long term. Two developments can lead to the correction of this state of imbalance. On the one hand, a noticeable growth lead outside the USA; this would mean higher exports and lower imports for the US, thus a decreasing trade deficit. Unfortunately, this perspective cannot be discerned. In 2003 and 2004, there are signs of an increase in the growth differential in favour of the USA. The disappointing finding that Europe contributes almost nothing to global economic growth and is waiting for US stimulus in a free-riding position does not seem to change in the near future. Thus, for the time being, the adjustment of external imbalances seems to take place only via the exchange rate of the USO. After all, the USO has lost around 20% against the euro and the Swiss franc since the beginning of last year. To what extent the correction - which has now been somewhat reduced - can correct existing imbalances and how far it will continue is an open question. In the current global economic environment, risk aspects dominate. There is hardly any talk of opportunities at the moment. Nevertheless, and precisely for this reason, in the interest of a realistic assessment of the situation, it is necessary to point out clearly positive factors. Three factors are highlighted. Firstly, we have been registering a very expansionary course of monetary and fiscal policy worldwide for several quarters. Interest rates are low and inflation risks seem so low that this stimulating course can continue for a while. This is an important element of strength. Secondly, the disappointing valuations of companies on the stock exchanges must not obscure the fact that restructuring processes are already well advanced in many places. These Efforts cost a lot of strength and initially contributed to lethargy. At the same time, however, this is the focus on the future success of the company, the creation of new jobs and higher incomes. Finally, the difficult economic conditions in some countries have obviously increased the political chances of structural reforms being implemented. Of course, the economy will not benefit quickly from such efforts, but in the long run they will make a decisive contribution to sustainable economic success. Prospects for Switzerland In Switzerland, too, economic development has been disappointing in recent quarters. The "acceleration in the second half of the year" envisaged by almost all augurs did not materialise for the second time in 2002. Instead, the snb's assessment of the situation had to be gradually revised downwards. Convinced that the risks to price stability are minimal, we have exploited our room for manoeuvre in interest rate policy without much waiting. Since miltte 2001, we have lowered our key interest rate - the 3 months of LIBOR - by three percentage points to percent.
