This means that our traditional monetary policy instrument has been exhausted. This is certainly an uncomfortable finding that must give rise to some questions. Wouldn't we have waited a little longer with the last step? Of course, we have also thought about this intensively. We have firmly answered the question in the negative and acted swiftly, i.e. on the same day as the ECB. Precisely because we assessed the economic downside risks as still significant, we wanted to exploit the remaining room for manoeuvre in good time and preventively. If you are late, life punishes you. This word coined by Gorbachev also applies to monetary policymakers, and the closer one has come to zero interest rate policy, the more relentless. Do such low key interest rates really benefit the real sector? This question also needs to be seriously examined. We think it should be affirmed. After all, there are credit agreements to a not inconsiderable extent that are - more or less directly - tied to money market interest rates. And long-term interest rates  on 10-year bund bonds, for example  have fallen by over 100 basis points over the past 12 months, not only but probably also because of our rate cuts. Admittedly, this effect has largely bypassed the real sector, because lenders have massively increased risk premia in the face of high uncertainties. Once again, not only in Switzerland, we have to note that the mechanism of credit supply tends to have pro-cyclical effects. But this finding does not alter the finding that financing conditions for the real sector would have been less favourable without our contribution. The prospects for economic development in Switzerland are characterised by a wide range of uncertainties. However, one thing is clear: there can only be a significant upswing in our country if the global economy is able to recover in the coming quarters. Hopes to the contrary are unrealistic given the smallness and openness of our economy. In detail, it seems plausible to distinguish between three rather burdensome and three rather favorable aspects for Switzerland's economic prospects. The important position of the financial industry could prove to be a burdensome factor. With a value added share of well over 10%, it is very significant. If it is true that capacities have to be permanently released in this area after the boom of the late 90s, this has a negative macroeconomic impact. Especially in your circles, I do not want to conceal the fact that we are particularly concerned about the unsatisfactory economic development in Germany. If the forecasters are right and Germany does not achieve more than a black zero in terms of growth in the current year, this will have an unfavorable effect on development in Switzerland. Finally, I would like to mention the exchange rate as the third risk factor. No one can rule out the possibility that the Swiss franc will once again come under upward pressure in an environment of increased risk aversion. From an economic point of view, one would instead wish for a moderate weakening against both the USO and the euro. Since we no longer have any significant room for manoeuvre in terms of interest rate policy, we will intervene in the foreign exchange market if necessary to counter an undesirable appreciation. We are aware that such a maneuver would not be free of unwanted side effects. But under difficult economic conditions - just as in medicine - there are constellations in which one reasonably has to accept some side effects. But there are also positive aspects that should have a positive effect on Swiss development. Our inflation rates and inflation expectations are at record lows. This will allow the SNB to maintain its expansionary stance for some time to come. Secondly, the Swiss economy has a good chance of benefiting above average from a normalisation of global investment activity, which will hopefully begin soon. And thirdly, the comparatively high flexibility of the labour and capital markets should make it easier for our economy to react quickly to the expected acceleration of demand. Overall, the prospects give a mixed picture. From an economic point of view, the downward risks continue to prevail. For the current year, hardly any significant acceleration in growth is to be expected; a return to the magnitude of the long-term growth potential of around 1.5 percent will not be possible until 2004 at the earliest. Despite these depressed prospects, we consider the risks of a deflationary development to be extremely low. In the trend of the next six to eight quarters, we expect inflation rates of between half and one percent.

Nachdem wir zinspolitisch ber keinen nennenswerten Spielraum mehr verfgen, werden wir ntigenfalls am Devisenmarkt intervenieren, um einer unerwnschten Aufwertung entgegenzutreten. Wir sind uns bewusst, das ein solches Manver nicht frei von unerwnschten Nebenwirkungen wre. Aber es gibt unter erschwerten wirtschaftlichen Bedingungen - genauso wie in der Medizin Konstellationen, in denen man vernnftigerweise einige Nebenwirkungen in Kauf zu nehmen hat. Aber es gibt auch positive Aspekte, die sich fr die schweizerische Entwicklung gnstig auswirken sollten. Unsere Teuerungsraten und die Inflationserwartungen sind rekordtief. Dies wird es der SNB erlauben, den expansiven Kurs noch fr einige Zeit beizubehalten. Zweitens hat die Schweizer Wirtschaft gute Chancen, von einer hoffentlich bald einsetzenden Normalisierung der weltweiten Investitionsttigkeit berdurchschnittlich profitieren. Und drittens sollte die vergleichsweise hohe Flexibilitt des Arbeits- und des Kapitalmarktes es unserer Wirtschaft erleichtern auf die zu erwartende Beschleunigung der Nachfrage rasch zu reagieren. Die Perspektiven ergeben insgesamt ein gemischtes Bild. Konjunkturell berwiegen die Risiken nach unten weiterhin. Fr das laufende Jahr ist kaum mit einer nennenswerten Wachstumsbeschleunigung zu rechnen; eine Rckkehr in die Grssenordnung des langfristigen Wachstumspotentials von rund 1.5 Prozent wird frhestens 2004 mglich sein. Trotz dieser gedrckten Perspektiven halten wir die Risiken einer deflationren Entwicklung fr usserst gering. Im Trend der kommenden sechs bis acht Quartale erwarten wir Inflationsraten zwischen einem halben und einem Prozent.

Title: Interest rates and exchange rates: topics of Swiss monetary policy
text: INTEREST RATES AND EXCHANGE RATES AS TOPICS OF SWISS MONETARY POLICY Prof. Dr. Niklaus Blattner Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Opening Symposium Finanz-Institut Thurgau FITg Euregio-lnstitut fur monetare okonomik und Financial Management at the University of Konstanz Kreuzlingen, 31 March 2003 Introduction There would be quieter moments to deal with interest rates and exchange rates as topics of Swiss monetary policy than today. Right now, the economy and financial markets are exposed to major stress tests. The same applies, of course, to monetary policy. But there could hardly have been a better time for the opening symposium of the Finanz-Institut Thurgau FITg, i.e. the Euregio Institute for Monetary Economics and Financial Management at the University of Konstanz. No one will now be able to claim that he is taking part in an event of glass bead players. This sets the right accent. The new institute stands for practical relevance. Directly relevant questions are dealt with. The answers should not be given pale out of the moment, but based on the essential theoretical contexts and on economic experience. My remarks must also meet these requirements. Why are we interested in interest rates and exchange rates? Both affect output, employment and prices, and both can respond quickly to monetary stimulus. That is why the Swiss National Bank (SNB) is repeatedly called upon to influence the interest rate or exchange rate front. Such demands accumulate when the economy slows down and a lower interest rate level or a weaker franc promises relief. I deal with interest rates and exchange rates from a medium to long-term perspective. With this I do not want to flee from the topicality. Rather, it is the essence of monetary policy to make decisions in the light of their medium- to long-term effects. On a current occasion, I will also deal with monetary policy at very low interest rates. I will also turn to the possibilities of combating deflation. Exchange rates The Swiss franc exchange rate has been a cause for concern in recent months. The reason for this was, on the one hand, the significant appreciation of the Swiss franc against the dollar and, on the other hand, the fact that the Franc has been at a level against the euro for over a year that makes life difficult for many exporters. However, there is some contrast between these current concerns and what the longer-term comparison shows. Between January 1999, the date of the introduction of the euro, and December 2002, the trade-weighted nominal external value of the Swiss franc increased by 7%. In real terms, i.e. adjusted for the inflation differential with foreign countries, the appreciation of the Swiss franc was a paltry 2.5%. This corresponds to an appreciation that is roughly in line with the long-term average (0.6% per year since 1980). However, the real appreciation was accentuated in January, but the Swiss franc is still below previous highs in real terms. On the positive side, the trade-weighted real Swiss franc exchange rate has fluctuated much less since the introduction of the euro than in previous periods. Now, of course, one can object that the past is not a yardstick and that the level and volatility of the Swiss franc was already too high at that time. What is to be made of this? 30 years ago, Bretton Woods' fixed-rate system collapsed. At that time, in January 1973, Switzerland was one of the first countries to abandon its exchange rate peg and switch to flexible exchange rates. The reason for this was a massive overheating of the economy and an increase in the inflation rate, which was soon to reach double digits. As long as the SNB had to defend fixed exchange rates, it had no way of defending itself against overheating and inflation. It only gained this opportunity with the transition to a flexible exchange rate, which allowed it to conduct an independent monetary policy. In the meantime, various countries - some temporarily, others permanently - have returned to an exchange rate peg. In addition, the euro was introduced. The question of whether Switzerland should peg its currency to the euro is repeatedly raised in view of the strong interdependence of our economy with the euro area. What would be gained? What is certain is that exporters could calculate with a fixed euro exchange rate in this case. Exchange rate stability would increase. Stable exchange rates are beneficial for exporters. However, too little attention is often paid to the difference between nominal and real stability. In the long run, the real exchange rate is more important than the nominal one. The lower the inflation in Switzerland, the lower the appreciation in real terms. If inflation is lower in Switzerland than abroad, the exporter can benefit from a lower cost base. A nominal appreciation of the exchange rate - which of course, initially causes costs - he can successfully counter the lower labour, capital and material costs in Switzerland. What would be the consequences of a fixed nominal exchange rate for the real trade-weighted exchange rate? Two aspects are of interest here, firstly volatility and secondly the level of the real exchange rate. As a result of a nominal peg of the Swiss franc to the euro, the volatility of the real franc exchange rate would decrease. This would probably be the only advantage of such a step. In a system of flexible exchange rates, the volatility of the real exchange rate is higher than in a system of fixed exchange rates. The reason is that nominal exchange rates are more volatile than the much sluggish prices of goods and services that determine real exchange rates. A fixed nominal exchange rate thus reduces the fluctuations of the real exchange rate. Nevertheless, the real exchange rate can and will continue to change. However, the peg of the Swiss franc to the euro would have no influence on the trend of the real exchange rate. In the long term, the real exchange rate is determined not by monetary factors, but by real factors. This includes, in particular, Switzerland's current account surplus, which amounted to around 12% of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2002, for example. The current account surplus pushes the exchange rate of the Swiss franc upwards. The associated considerable and growing foreign assets of Switzerland are the cause of a constant additional demand for Swiss francs. It results as a result of the normal repatriation of at least part of the yields. In times of increasing uncertainty, experience has shown that the movement in the Swiss franc is accentuated, as it is then a matter of hedging an additional part of the foreign assets against growing exchange rate risks. Behind the traditionally high current account surplus is a long history of successful Swiss exports and investments abroad. For both, a high propensity to save, a high employment rate and a constant willingness to increase productivity are the prerequisites. The continued rise in the real swiss franc exchange rate that we have observed over the last 30 years reflects the strength of the Swiss economy, i.e. it is the result of an above-average will to perform. The real appreciation is therefore a hallmark of success and not a damage to the economy. It is an indicator of our above-average prosperity. We all benefit as consumers as well as producers by having to give less of our own goods and services in exchange for foreign goods than we did 10, 20 or 30 years ago. If we are aware of this willingness to perform and would be "spared" real revaluations. No exporter who looks beyond a few quarters and who thinks both economically and economically can wish for this. I summarize and add. The benefits of pegging to the euro may seem tempting to some at first glance, but they are an illusion: the nominal exchange rate would be fixed and the volatility of the real exchange rate would decrease. Nevertheless, no exporter could sit back and settle for what has been achieved if he wants to survive permanently. In addition, there would be the disadvantages of not pursuing an independent monetary policy. The SNB would no longer be in a position to set interest rates in the way that corresponds to the local economic and inflation outlook. Just how heavy the abandonment of an independent monetary policy can be in Germany today. Germany depends on the monetary policy of the European Central Bank (ECB). This must be geared to the risk of inflation throughout the euro area. The ECB can only respond to the specific needs of the German economy, which currently has no inflation, to a very limited extent. Finally, it should be added that for Switzerland, a peg of the Swiss franc to the euro would be a completely unilateral act that would not entail any rights of participation in the ECB. The famous "autonomous follow-up" is also not a recipe for success for monetary policy. I will come back specifically to the negative consequences of such a policy on interest rates in Switzerland. Interest The SNB controls the supply of liquidity via short-term interest rates. The focus is on repo interest rates and the three-month Libor for Swiss francs, an international bank interest rate for Swiss franc investments in London. With our money market operations, we steer this interest rate to a level that is intended to ensure price stability over the medium term, i.e. over two to three years. With our policies, we want to ensure that neither inflation nor deflation occurs. Focusing on price stability does not mean disregarding the development of output and employment. The SNB is aware that it is production output that is behind our country's prosperity. Moreover, we cannot determine our expectations about inflation and deflation without assumptions about the development of output and employment. We know: Would we increase the interest rate , we would trigger a recession and risk deflation. If we were to set the interest rate too low and flood the economy with liquidity, we would be threatened with economic overheating and inflation in the medium term. Nevertheless, we never direct monetary policy towards employment and production. The reason is that a "fine-tuning" of monetary policy according to production or employment targets would hopelessly overwhelm it in the long run. Experience shows that the instrument of monetary policy is indeed suitable for ensuring price stability. On the other hand, it is not suitable for achieving high-flying employment and growth targets. Nevertheless, monetary policy makes an indispensable contribution to the good framework conditions of the Swiss economy. Price stability, i.e. the absence of inflation as well as deflation, is an essential prerequisite for full employment and growth. In addition, it contributes to distributive justice. If, on the other hand, growth is low because productivity develops only slowly, because there is a lack of competition, for example, if there is unemployment because the labour market is failing, or if there is a lack of demand simply because the global economy is deteriorating, then nothing can be done about it even with the best monetary policy. Despite its limitations, however, monetary policy embodies many valuable opportunities. They follow from the interdependencies between interest rates, exchange rates, employment and production and from the resulting consequences for price stability, which ultimately determine the SNB's room for manoeuvre. In 2000, we raised interest rates a little slower than the US Federal Reserve (Fed), but faster than the ECB. When we had to take countermeasures in 2001, we did so much faster and more strongly than the ECB, which had to struggle with stubborn inflation in its currency area. Our decision to reduce the interest rate band by another 0.5 percentage points on 6 March 2003 coincided with that of the ECB, but was again more generous. Short-term Swiss franc interest rates (3 months, euro market) are currently around 0.25%. This is a good 2 percentage points less than the corresponding euro interest rates. Even with the long maturities, the Swiss franc interest rates are well below the corresponding euro interest rates. While spot interest rates on 10-year government bonds in the euro area are well above 4%, in Switzerland they amount to just over 2.5%. That's still a massive difference. This statement provides an opportunity to return to the disadvantages of pegging the Swiss franc to the euro. The so-called interest bonus, i.e. the lower money and capital market rates in Switzerland, would largely disappear as a result of the peg, because the previous difference between the currencies Swiss franc and euro would fall away. The consequences would be far-reaching. The first thing to do would be to cope with the increase in Swiss interest rates to the euro level. The yield values of the plants would fall drastically. The creditworthiness of many companies and institutions would be tested hard. Credit risks would increase. After the change, those companies and institutions that have made the transition would also have to live with the permanently higher interest costs. - So much for the subsequent digression on the disadvantages of pegging the Swiss franc to the euro. Short-term interest rates are now only slightly above zero. Does this mean that the SNB has now reached the end of its monetary policy Latin? My answer is clear: No! Monetary policy does not influence the economy only through a single short-term interest rate. In addition, purchases of foreign currency are open to them. The SNB can thus aim for a decline in the exchange rate, even though the short-term interest rate is already zero. Through interventions in the foreign exchange market and, in extreme cases, through open market operations on the securities markets, the liquidity supply of the Swiss economy can continue to be managed according to needs. Admittedly, in such circumstances we would have to move into a new, operationally more difficult monetary policy area. Conceptually, however, nothing fundamental would change. The objective of price stability would remain decisive, and monetary policy would continue to be conducted transparently and consistently. Monetary policy would remain credible and therefore effective. Deflation Finally, I turn to the topic of "deflation". Deflation is just as undesirable as inflation. Deflation makes economic development more difficult. Their effects on production and employment can be described as follows. First of all, deflation expectations lead to rising real interest rates. With rising deflation expectations, real interest rates rise continuously above zero despite nominal interest rates of zero. To the extent of effective deflation, the later the repayment of nominally constant debt weighs more heavily. In purely mathematical terms, deflation favors creditors, just as inflation relieves debtors. Part of the debtors will therefore run into payment difficulties, and the banks, which are increasingly suffering from bad loans, can get into a tight spot. Investments are collapsing even further in the face of rising real interest rates. Last but not least, deflation leads to rising real wages due to often rigid nominal wages. These reduce the demand for labour. Unemployment continues to rise. Given these effects of deflation, we rightly speak of the danger of a "deflation trap". But how great is the danger of deflation in the current reality? First of all, I would like to emphasise that we do not see any signs of deflation in Switzerland today. What we are observing is a decline in the prices of individual product groups of the Consumer Price Index (KPI). What we have sometimes noticed in recent years has been a decrease in the KPI in individual months compared to the previous period. However, this is not yet deflation, but rather a natural side effect of price stability. Price stability implies that part of prices must fall as long as another part of prices rises. Deflation is a trend decline in the price level. The last deflation that Switzerland experienced was a long time ago. It was so massive that it still has an effect on the memory today. It is the deflation that accompanied the great world economic crisis in the 30s. At that time, consumer prices fell by 20% in a few years, wholesale prices by as much as 40%. This was due to persistent weaknesses in demand and overcapacity, which were exacerbated by a failed monetary and economic policy. However, there are a number of factors that clearly distinguish the situation at that time from today's. I limit myself to those that have to do with monetary policy. The most important is the role of the gold standard. The gold standard, in the words of Barry Eichengreen, seemed like a deflation machine. On the one hand, the fixed exchange rates of the gold standard led to the international transfer of deflation to the whole world. On the other hand, the gold standard led to an initially hardly unusual recession becoming the Great Depression. The uncertainty about the future of the gold parities of the currencies that determined the exchange rates at that time led to private individuals as well as central banks exchanging their foreign exchange reserves for gold. The central banks that lost gold were forced to raise their interest rates to defend their gold parity. The central banks that received gold inflows increased the gold backing of their banknotes in circulation and thus also had a restrictive effect. One country after another has been Currency crises shaken. In addition, there were banking crises that went hand in hand with the currency crises. Companies and households withdrew their bank deposits and instead held their liquidity in the form of notes. The banks, in turn, increased their liquidity reserves in order to be prepared against the withdrawal of deposits. As a result, the money supply regressed worldwide. Deflation was the consequence. No country managed to initiate an economic recovery until it had moved away from the gold standard, i.e. either devalued its currency or introduced capital controls. This also applies to Switzerland. In Switzerland, too, the recovery only began after the franc had depreciated by 30% in 1936. Unlike then, today we have no gold standard and no fixed exchange rates. Central banks therefore basically have their hands free to fight deflation. All the more astonishing, therefore, is the current situation in Japan, where, despite all the progress, it has not yet been possible to definitively scare away the specter of deflation. Apparently, the abolition of the gold standard and fixed exchange rates alone is no guarantee of the prevention of deflation. It is true that a modern monetary policy counteracts deflation. But in practice, the option of foreign exchange market intervention is limited, especially in a large exporting country such as Japan. A systematic devaluation of the yen would soon be opposed by competitors as a "beggar-thy-neighbour" policy, i.e. as a kind of "dumping". The possibilities of open market policy or the acquisition of assets of all kinds in order to increase liquidity and eliminate deflationary expectations remain. But this increases the risk of loss for the central bank and the taxpayer. Above all, however, the backlog of reforms in the Japanese economy, especially in the banking sector, is likely to counteract a rapid economic recovery. Without reform, i.e. with the means of monetary policy alone, deflation in this case can hardly be tamed. Schlussbemerkungen But now back to Switzerland. What does the SNB expect if it is not afraid of deflation, you will ask? Due to the disputes over Iraq, there is currently a great deal of uncertainty. The scenario, which we consider to be the most likely, shows real GDP growth of just under 1% for the current year. This implies a slight pick-up in the economy in the second half of the year. Provided that the price of oil and the exchange rate do not thwart our calculations, the Inflation continues to cause no problems. We also expect average consumer inflation of just under 1% for the current year. In the event that the exchange rate would unexpectedly challenge us, we do not rule out foreign exchange market interventions, as has often been emphasized.
text_original: ZINSEN UND WECHSELKURSE ALS THEMEN DER SCHWEIZERISCHEN GELDPOLITIK Prof. Dr. Niklaus Blattner Mitglied des Direktoriums der Schweizerischen Nationalbank Erffnungssymposium Finanz-Institut Thurgau FITg Euregio-lnstitut fr monetre konomik und Finanzmanagement an der Universitt Konstanz Kreuzlingen, 31. Mrz 2003 Einleitung Es gbe ruhigere Momente, sich mit den Zinsen und Wechselkursen als Themen der schweizerischen Geldpolitik auseinanderzusetzen als heute. Gerade jetzt sind Wirtschaft und Finanzmrkte grossen Belastungsproben ausgesetzt. Dasselbe gilt natrlich auch fr die Geldpolitik. Doch htte es wohl kaum einen besseren Zeitpunkt fr das Erffnungssymposium des Finanz-Instituts Thurgau FITg, d.h. des Euregio-lnstituts fr monetre konomik und Finanzmanagement an der Universitt Konstanz, geben knnen. Niemand wird jetzt nmlich behaupten knnen, er nhme an einer Veranstaltung von Glasperlenspielern teil. Damit wird der richtige Akzent gesetzt. Das neue Institut steht fr den Praxisbezug. Bearbeitet werden unmittelbar relevante Fragen. Die Antworten sollen nicht blass aus dem Augenblick heraus gegeben werden, sondern gesttzt auf die wesentlichen theoretischen zusammenhnge und auf die wirtschaftliche Erfahrung. Meine Ausfhrungen haben diesen Ansprchen ebenfalls zu gengen. Weshalb interessieren wir uns fr Zinsen und Wechselkurse? Beide wirken auf die Produktion, die Beschftigung und die Preise, und beide knnen rasch auf geldpolitische Impulse reagieren. Deshalb wird die Schweizerische Nationalbank (SNB) immer wieder aufgefordert, auf die Zins- oder Wechselkursfront einzuwirken. Solche Forderungen hufen sich, wenn die Konjunktur nachlsst und ein tieferes Zinsniveau oder ein schwcherer Franken eine Entlastung verspricht. Ich befasse mich mit Zinsen und Wechselkursen aus einer mittel- bis langfristigen Perspektive. Damit will ich nicht vor der Aktualitt fliehen. Vielmehr ist es geradezu das Wesen der Geldpolitik, Entscheide im Licht ihrer mittel- bis langfristigen Auswirkungen zu fllen. Aus aktuellem Anlass werde ich mich ausserdem mit der Geldpolitik bei sehr tiefen Zinsstzen befassen. Ebenso werde ich mich den Mglichkeiten der Deflationsbekmpfung zuwenden. Wechselkurse Der Schweizer Frankenwechselkurs bereitete in den letzten Monaten Sorge. Grund war einerseits die deutliche Hherbewertung des Frankens gegenber dem Dollar und andererseits die Tatsache, dass sich der Franken gegenber dem Euro seit ber einem Jahr auf einem Niveau bewegt, das vielen Exporteuren das Leben schwer macht. Zwischen diesen aktuellen Sorgen und dem, was der lngerfristige Vergleich zeigt, besteht allerdings ein gewisser Kontrast. Zwischen Januar 1999, dem Zeitpunkt der Einfhrung des Euro, und Dezember 2002 ist der handelsgewichtete nominelle Aussenwert des Frankens zwar um 7% gestiegen. Real, d.h. bereinigt um die Inflationsdifferenz zum Ausland, betrug die Aufwertung des Frankens indessen blass 2,5%. Dies entspricht einer Aufwertung, die ungefhr im langfristigen Durchschnitt liegt (0,6% pro Jahr seit 1980). Allerdings hat sich im Januar die reale Aufwertung akzentuiert, doch liegt der Franken real nach wie vor unter frheren Hchststnden. Positiv ist im brigen, dass der handelsgewichtete reale Frankenkurs seit der Einfhrung des Euro deutlich weniger stark schwankt als in frheren Perioden. Nun kann man natrlich einwenden, die Vergangenheit sei kein Massstab und das Niveau und die Volatilitt des Frankens seien eben schon damals zu hoch gewesen. Was ist davon zu halten? Vor 30 Jahren brach das Festkurssystem von Bretton Woods zusammen. Die Schweiz gehrte damals, im Januar 1973, zu den ersten Lndern, die ihre Wechselkursbindung aufgaben und zu flexiblen Wechselkursen bergingen. Der Anlass waren eine massive berhitzung der Konjunktur und ein Anstieg der Inflationsrate, die bald zweistellig werden sollte. Solange die SNB die festen Wechselkurse verteidigen musste, hatte sie keine Mglichkeit, sich gegen berhitzung und Inflation zu wehren. Diese Mglichkeit gewann sie erst mit dem bergang zu einem flexiblen Wechselkurs, der es ihr erlaubte, eine eigenstndige Geldpolitik zu fhren. In der Zwischenzeit sind verschiedene Lnder - einige vorbergehend, andere dauerhaft zu einer Wechselkursbindung zurckgekehrt. Ausserdem wurde der Euro eingefhrt. Die Frage, ob die Schweiz ihre Whrung an den Euro binden solle, wird angesichts der starken Verflechtung unserer Wirtschaft mit dem Euro-Raum immer wieder gestellt. Was wre damit gewonnen? Sicher ist, dass die Exporteure in diesem Fall mit einem festen Eurokurs kalkulieren knnten. Die Wechselkursstabilitt wrde zunehmen. Stabile Wechselkurse sind fr die Exporteure vorteilhaft. Allerdings wird dabei oft zu wenig auf den Unterschied zwischen nomineller und realer Stabilitt geachtet. Auf die Dauer wichtiger als der nominelle ist der reale Wechselkurs. Je geringer die Inflation in der Schweiz ist, desto geringer ist real die Aufwertung. Wenn die Inflation in der Schweiz geringer ist als im Ausland, kann der Exporteur von einer tieferen Kostenbasis profitieren. Einer nominellen Aufwertung des Wechselkurses - die ihm selbstverstndlich zunchst Kosten verursacht - kann er die tieferen Arbeits-, Kapital- und Materialkosten in der Schweiz erfolgreich entgegensetzen. Welche Folgen htte ein fixer nomineller Wechselkurs fr den realen handelsgewichteten Wechselkurs? Hier interessieren zwei Aspekte, erstens die Volatilitt und zweitens das Niveau des realen Wechselkurses. Als Folge einer nominellen Anbindung des Frankens an den Euro wrde die Volatilitt des realen Frankenkurses sinken. Dies wre wohl der einzige Vorteil eines solchen Schritts. In einem System flexibler Wechselkurse ist die Volatilitt des realen Wechselkurses hher als in einem System fester Wechselkurse. Der Grund liegt darin, dass nominelle Wechselkurse volatiler sind als die sehr viel trgeren Gter- und Dienstleistungspreise, welche die realen Wechselkurse bestimmen. Ein fester nomineller Wechselkurs vermindert also die Schwankungen des realen Wechselkurses. Trotzdem kann und wird sich der reale Wechselkurs weiter verndern. Auf den Trend des realen Wechselkurses htte die Bindung des Frankens an den Euro demgegenber jedoch keinen Einfluss. Der reale Wechselkurs wird langfristig nicht durch monetre, sondern durch reale Faktoren bestimmt. Dazu zhlt insbesondere der Ertragsbilanzberschuss der Schweiz, der beispielsweise im Jahr 2002 rund 12% des Bruttoinlandsprodukts (BIP) betrug. Der Ertragsbilanzberschuss drckt den Wechselkurs des Frankens nach oben. Das damit verbundene, beachtliche und wachsende Auslandsvermgen der Schweiz ist Ursache einer stndigen Zusatznachfrage nach Schweizer Franken. Sie ergibt sich als Folge der normalen Repatriierung mindestens eines Teils der Ertrge. In Zeiten zunehmender Unsicherheit wird die Bewegung in den Franken erfahrungsgemss akzentuiert, da es dann darum geht, einen zustzlichen Teil des Auslandsvermgens gegen wachsende Wechselkursrisiken abzusichern. Hinter dem traditionell hohen Ertragsbilanzberschuss steht eine lange Geschichte erfolgreichen schweizerischen Exportierens und lnvestierens im Ausland. Fr beides sind eine hohe Sparneigung, eine hohe Erwerbsquote und eine stndige Bereitschaft, die Produktivitt zu steigern die Voraussetzung. Der anhaltende Anstieg des realen Frankenkurses, den wir in den letzten 30 Jahren beobachtet haben, widerspiegelt die Strke der Schweizer Wirtschaft, d.h., sie ist Ausfluss eines berdurchschnittlichen Willens zur Leistung. Die reale Aufwertung ist also ein Kennzeichen des Erfolgs und kein Schaden fr die Volkswirtschaft. Sie ist ein Indikator unseres berdurchschnittlichen Wohlstands. Wir alle profitieren als Konsumenten wie als Produzenten davon, indem wir im Tausch fr auslndische Gter weniger eigene Gter und Dienstleistungen hingeben mssen als noch vor 10, 20 oder 30 Jahren. Wenn wir uns von dieser Leistungsbereitschaft und -fhigkeit verabschieden wrden, blieben uns reale Aufwertungen zwar erspart. Kein Exporteur, der ber ein paar Quartale hinausblickt und der sowohl betriebswirtschaftlich als auch volkswirtschaftlich denkt, kann sich dies wnschen. Ich fasse zusammen und ergnze. Die Vorteile einer Anbindung an den Euro mgen Manchen auf den ersten Blick als verfhrerisch erscheinen, sie sind aber eine Illusion: Zwar wrde der nominelle Wechselkurs fixiert, und die Volatilitt des realen Wechselkurses nhme ab. Trotzdem knnte sich kein Exporteur zurcklehnen und sich mit dem Erreichten zufrieden geben, wenn er dauerhaft berleben mchte. Hinzu kmen die Nachteile des Verzichts auf eine eigenstndige Geldpolitik. Die SNB wre nicht mehr in der Lage, die Zinsstze so zu setzen, wie dies den hiesigen Konjunktur- und Inflationsaussichten entspricht. Wie schwer die Preisgabe einer eigenstndigen Geldpolitik wiegen kann, zeigt sich gerade heute in Deutschland. Deutschland hngt von der Geldpolitik der Europischen Zentralbank (EZB) ab. Diese muss sich nach der Inflationsgefahr im ganzen Euroraum ausrichten. Auf die konkreten Bedrfnisse der deutschen Volkswirtschaft, die zur Zeit keine Inflation kennt, kann die EZB nur hchst begrenzt eingehen. Schliesslich ist beizufgen, dass fr die Schweiz eine Anbindung des Frankens an den Euro ein gnzlich einseitiger Akt wre, der keinerlei Mitwirkungsrechte in der EZB mit sich brchte. Der berhmte autonome Nachvollzug ist auch fr die Geldpolitik kein Erfolgsrezept. ber die negativen Folgen einer solchen Politik auf die Zinsen in der Schweiz komme ich noch speziell zurck. Zinsen Die SNB steuert die Liquidittsversorgung ber die kurzfristigen Zinsstze. Im Vordergrund stehen die Repozinsstze und der Dreimonats-Libor fr Schweizer Franken ein lnterbankenzinssatz fr Frankenanlagen in London. Mit unseren Geldmarktoperationen steuern wir diesen Zinssatz auf ein Niveau, das die Preisstabilitt auf mittlere Sicht, also ber zwei bis drei Jahre, gewhrleisten soll. Wir wollen mit unserer Politik erreichen, dass weder Inflation noch Deflation auftreten. Die Ausrichtung auf die Preisstabilitt bedeutet keine Missachtung der Produktions- und Beschftigungsentwicklung. Die SNB ist sich bewusst, dass es die Produktionsleistung ist, die hinter dem Wohlstand unseres Landes steht. Ausserdem knnen wir unsere Erwartungen ber Inflation und Deflation ohne Annahmen ber die Produktions- und Beschftigungsentwicklung gar nicht bestimmen. Wir wissen: Wrden wir den Zinssatz zu hoch ansetzen, so wrden wir eine Rezession auslsen und eine Deflation riskieren. Wrden wir den Zinssatz zu tief ansetzen und die Wirtschaft mit Liquiditt berfluten, so wrde uns mittelfristig eine konjunkturelle berhitzung und eine Inflation drohen. Trotzdem richten wir die Geldpolitik niemals direkt auf die Beschftigung und die Produktion aus. Der Grund liegt darin, dass ein fine-tuning der Geldpolitik gemss Produktions- oder Beschftigungszielen diese auf die Dauer hoffnungslos berfordern wrde. Die Erfahrung zeigt, dass das Instrument der Geldpolitik zwar dafr geeignet ist, die Preisstabilitt zu gewhrleisten. Zur Erreichung hochfliegender Beschftigungs- und Wachstumsziele ist es dagegen nicht tauglich. Trotzdem leistet die Geldpolitik einen unverzichtbaren Beitrag zu den guten Rahmenbedingungen des schweizerischen Wirtschaftens. Preisstabilitt, d.h. die Absenz von Inflation ebenso wie Deflation, ist eine wesentliche Voraussetzung fr Vollbeschftigung und Wachstum. Hinzu kommt, dass sie zur Verteilungsgerechtigkeit beitrgt. Liegt hingegen das Wachstum tief, weil sich die Produktivitt nur schleppend entwickelt, weil es z.B. an Wettbewerb mangelt, besteht Arbeitslosigkeit, weil der Arbeitsmarkt versagt, oder fehlt es an der Nachfrage, weil ganz einfach die Weltkonjunktur darbt, dann ist dagegen auch mit der besten Geldpolitik nichts auszurichten. Trotz ihrer Grenzen verkrpert die Geldpolitik aber viele wertvolle Mglichkeiten. Sie folgen aus dem Wirkungszusammenhang von Zinsen, Wechselkursen, Beschftigung und Produktion und aus den sich daraus ergebenden Folgen fr die Preisstabilitt, welche den Handlungsspielraum der SNB letztlich bestimmen. Im Jahre 2000 haben wir die Zinsstze etwas langsamer als die US-amerikanische Zentralbank (Fed), aber schneller als die EZB erhht. Als wir im Jahre 2001 Gegensteuer geben mussten, haben wir dies wiederum deutlich schneller und auch strker getan als die EZB, die in ihrem Whrungsgebiet mit einer hartnckigen Teuerung kmpfen musste. Unsere Entscheidung, am 6. Mrz 2003 das Zinsband nochmals um 0,5%-Punkte zu senken, fiel zwar gleichzeitig mit jener der EZB, war aber wiederum grosszgiger. Die kurzfristigen Frankenzinsen (3 Monate, Euromarkt) bewegen sich derzeit um rund 0,25%. Dies sind gut 2 Prozentpunkte weniger als die entsprechenden Eurozinsen. Auch bei den langen Laufzeiten liegen die Frankenzinsen deutlich unter den entsprechenden Eurozinsen. Whrend sich die Kassazinsstze auf 10-jhrigen Staatsobligationen im Euroraum deutlich ber 4% bewegen, belaufen sie sich in der Schweiz auf etwas mehr als 2,5%. Das ist immer noch ein massiver Unterschied. Diese Feststellung bietet Anlass, nochmals auf die Nachteile der Anbindung des Schweizer Frankens an den Euro zurckzukommen. Der sog. Zinsbonus, d.h. die tieferen Geld- und Kapitalmarktstze in der Schweiz, wrde in der Folge der Anbindung weitgehend verschwinden, weil der bisherige Unterschied zwischen den Whrungen Franken und Euro dahinfallen wrde. Die Folgen wren weit reichend. Als erstes glte es, die Erhhung der schweizerischen Zinsen auf das Euroniveau zu verkraften. Die Ertragswerte der Anlagen wrden drastisch sinken. Die Bonitt vieler Firmen und Institutionen wrde hart getestet. Die Kreditrisiken wrden zunehmen. Nach dem Wechsel mssten zudem jene Unternehmen und Institutionen, welchen den bergang geschafft htten, mit den dauerhaft hheren Zinskosten leben. - Soviel zum nachzulieferndem Exkurs zu den Nachteilen einer Anbindung des Schweizer Frankens an den Euro. Die kurzfristigen Zinsstze liegen heute nur noch wenig ber null. Heisst das, dass die SNB nun am Ende ihres geldpolitischen Lateins angekommen ist? Meine Antwort lautet klar: Nein! Die Geldpolitik beeinflusst die Wirtschaft keineswegs nur ber einen einzigen kurzfristigen Zinssatz. Zustzlich stehen ihr Kufe von Devisen offen. Die SNB kann somit einen Rckgang des Wechselkurses anstreben, obwohl der kurzfristige Zinssatz bereits bei null liegt. Durch Interventionen auf dem Devisenmarkt und, im Extremfall, durch Offenmarktoperationen auf den Wertschriftenmrkten kann die Liquidittsversorgung der schweizerischen Volkswirtschaft weiterhin bedrfnisgerecht gesteuert werden. Zugegeben, wir mssten uns unter solchen Umstnden in ein neues, operationell schwierigeres geldpolitisches Gelnde begeben. Konzeptionell wrde sich dagegen nichts Grundlegendes ndern. Es bliebe dabei: Das Ziel der Preisstabilitt bliebe massgebend, und die Geldpolitik wrde weiterhin transparent und konsistent gefhrt. Die Geldpolitik bliebe weiterhin glaubwrdig und deshalb wirksam. Deflation Zum Schluss wende ich mich noch dem Thema Deflation zu. Deflation ist ebenso unerwnscht wie Inflation. Deflation erschwert die wirtschaftliche Entwicklung. Ihre Wirkungen auf die Produktion und die Beschftigung lassen sich wie folgt beschreiben. Zunchst einmal fhren Deflationserwartungen zu steigenden Realzinsen. Bei steigenden Deflationserwartungen erhhen sich die Realzinsen trotz Nominalzinsen von null fortlaufend ber null hinaus. Im Ausmass der effektiven Deflation wiegt die Rckzahlung nominell konstanter Schulden je spter desto schwerer. Rein rechnerisch begnstigt Deflation die Glubiger, so wie Inflation die Schuldner entlastet. Ein Teil der Schuldner wird deshalb aber in Zahlungsschwierigkeiten kommen, und die Banken, die zunehmend unter faulen Krediten leiden, knnen in die Klemme geraten. Die Investitionen brechen angesichts steigender Realzinsen noch weiter ein. Nicht zuletzt fhrt Deflation aufgrund von oft rigiden Nominallhnen zu steigenden Reallhnen. Diese vermindern die Nachfrage nach Arbeitskrften. Die Arbeitslosigkeit nimmt weiter zu. Angesichts dieser Auswirkungen der Deflation sprechen wir zu Recht von der Gefahr einer Deflationsfalle. Wie gross ist aber nun die Gefahr einer Deflation in der aktuellen Realitt? Zunchst mchte ich unterstreichen, dass wir heute in der Schweiz keinerlei Anzeichen einer Deflation feststellen mssen. Was wir beobachten, ist ein Rckgang der Preise einzelner Warengruppen des Konsumentenpreisindex (KPI). Was wir in den letzten Jahren manchmal feststellten, war ein Rckgang des KPI in einzelnen Monaten gegenber der Vorperiode. Das ist aber noch keine Deflation, sondern vielmehr eine ganz natrliche Begleiterscheinung von Preisstabilitt. Preisstabilitt impliziert, dass ein Teil der Preise fallen muss, solange ein anderer Teil der Preise steigt. Deflation ist ein trendmssiger Rckgang des Preisniveaus. Die letzte Deflation, welche die Schweiz erlebte, liegt schon lange zurck. Sie war so massiv, dass sie in der Erinnerung bis heute nachwirkt. Es ist die Deflation, welche die grosse Weltwirtschaftskrise in den 30er Jahren begleitete. Damals fielen die Konsumentenpreise in wenigen Jahren um 20%, die Grosshandelspreise gar um 40%. Ursache waren dauerhafte Nachfrageschwchen und berkapazitten, die durch eine verfehlte Geld- und Wirtschaftspolitik noch verschrft wurden. Es gibt aber eine Reihe von Faktoren, welche die damalige Situation von der heutigen deutlich unterscheiden. Ich beschrnke mich auf jene, die mit Geldpolitik zu tun haben. Die wichtigste ist die Rolle des Goldstandards. Der Goldstandard wirkte, in den Worten von Barry Eichengreen, wie eine Deflationsmaschine. Auf der einen Seite fhrten die fixen Wechselkurse des Goldstandards zur internationalen bertragung der Deflation auf die ganze Welt. Zum anderen fhrte der Goldstandard dazu, dass eine zunchst kaum aussergewhnliche Rezession zur Grossen Depression wurde. Die Ungewissheit ber die Zukunft der Goldparitten der Whrungen, welche damals die Wechselkurse bestimmten, fhrte dazu, dass Private ebenso wie Zentralbanken ihre Devisenreserven in Gold umtauschten. Die Zentralbanken, die Gold verloren, waren gezwungen, ihre Zinsstze zu erhhen, um ihre Goldparitt zu verteidigen. Die Zentralbanken, die Goldzuflsse erhielten, erhhten die Golddeckung ihres Notenumlaufs und wirkten damit ebenfalls restriktiv. Ein Land nach dem anderen wurde von Whrungskrisen erschttert. Dazu kamen Bankenkrisen, die mit den Whrungskrisen Hand in Hand gingen. Firmen und Haushalte zogen ihre Bankeinlagen ab und hielten ihre Liquiditt stattdessen in Form von Noten. Die Banken wiederum erhhten ihre Liquidittsreserven, um gegen den Abzug von Einlagen gewappnet zu sein. Als Folge davon bildete sich die Geldmenge weltweit zurck. Deflation war die Konsequenz. Keinem Land gelang es damals, eine wirtschaftliche Erholung einzuleiten, bevor es vom Goldstandard abgerckt war, d.h. entweder seine Whrung abgewertet oder Kapitalverkehrskontrollen eingefhrt hatte. Dies gilt auch fr die Schweiz. Auch in der Schweiz setzte die Erholung erst ein, nachdem der Franken im Jahre 1936 um 30% abgewertet worden war. Im Unterschied zu damals haben wir heute keinen Goldstandard und keine festen Wechselkurse. Die Notenbanken haben also grundstzlich die Hnde frei, die Deflation zu bekmpfen. Umso erstaunlicher ist daher die aktuelle Situation in Japan, wo es trotz aller Fortschritte bisher noch nicht gelungen ist, das Gespenst der Deflation definitiv zu verscheuchen. Offenbar ist der Wegfall des Goldstandards und der festen Wechselkurse allein noch keine Garantie fr die Verhinderung von Deflation. Zwar wirkt eine moderne Geldpolitik der Deflation entgegen. Doch in der Praxis ist die Option der Devisenmarktintervention vor allem in einem grossen Exportland wie Japan beschrnkt. Eine systematische Abwertung des Yen wrde von den Konkurrenten schon bald einmal als beggar-thy-neighbour-Politik, d.h. als eine Art von dumping bekmpft. Es bleiben die Mglichkeiten der Offenmarktpolitik bzw. des Erwerbs von Aktiven aller Art zwecks Steigerung der Liquiditt und der Beseitigung der deflatorischen Erwartungen. Doch damit wachsen die Verlustrisiken der Zentralbank bzw. des Steuerzahlers. Vor allem aber wirkt wohl der Reformstau in der japanischen Wirtschaft, insbesondere im Bankwesen, einer raschen konjunkturellen Erholung entgegen. Ohne Reform, d.h. mit den Mitteln der Geldpolitik allein, ist die Deflation in diesem Fall kaum zu zhmen. Schlussbemerkungen Doch nun zurck in die Schweiz. Womit, werden Sie fragen, rechnet die SNB, wenn sie sich schon nicht vor einer Deflation frchtet? Aufgrund der Auseinandersetzungen um den Irak ist die Unsicherheit derzeit gross. Das Szenario, das wir als das wahrscheinlichste ansehen, zeigt fr das laufende Jahr ein Wachstum des realen BIP von knapp 1%. Dies impliziert ein leichtes Anziehen der Konjunktur in der zweiten Jahreshlfte. Sofern uns der lpreis und der Wechselkurs keinen Strich durch die Rechnung machen, drfte die Teuerung weiterhin keine Probleme bereiten. Wir rechnen fr das laufende Jahr mit einer durchschnittlichen Konsumententeuerung von ebenfalls knapp 1%. Fr den Fall, dass uns der Wechselkurs unerwartet herausfordern wrde, schliessen wir, wie schon fters unterstrichen, Devisenmarktinterventionen nicht aus.

Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the Chairman of the Governing Board to the Annual General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank
text: Presentation by Mr. Jean-Pierre Roth, Chairman of the Executive Board, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 25 April 2003 2002: Une anne9e de9cevante 2002 was a very disappointing year for the Swiss economy. A little over a year ago, after the shock of events in September 2001, the international situation seemed to be on the way to normalization and inspired us with cautious optimism. The first quarter of 2002 went relatively well; the world economy was on the verge of gradually returning to the path of growth. At the time, we expected average GDP growth of around 1% for the year as a whole, with a sharp acceleration in activity in the second half of the year; a forecast that many observers described as too pessimistic. We had to quickly become disillusioned. Conflicting signals began to multiply as early as the second quarter of 2002. In addition, the franc strengthened against the euro. This appreciation of our currency came at the worst time because it led to a tightening of monetary conditions in our country. We responded by lowering the three-month Libor fluctuation band by 50 basis points in May. This has not only brought the swiss franc up a net halt, but also breathed new life into our economy. As early as the summer, it became clear that the long-awaited recovery was slow to manifest itself. The U.S. economy was increasingly fragile, with positive signals regularly being supplanted by negative ones. On the European front, starting with Germany, the horizon was inexorably darkening. This delay in the recovery was all the more unfortunate as the franc was once again approaching highs against the European currency. At the end of July, we again lowered the Libor fluctuation band by 50 basis points. A few weeks ago, due to an increasingly hesitant recovery and a particularly nervous foreign exchange market, we took a further step and reduced the three-month rate to 0.25%. Not all of these difficulties have their origin in Switzerland; the world economy is going through a painful phase of readjustment. We have behind us the bursting of the stock market bubble and the excesses committed on the investment side, particularly in the field of information technology. These events have shaken investor confidence, and the risk premiums demanded by the market have increased. The cost of financing small and medium-sized enterprises has often increased, despite the relaxation of monetary policies. Investment plans have been revised downwards. The financial sector has been forced to undertake structural reforms in depth in order to digest the consequences of the stock market correction. On top of this, geopolitical considerations have been added that have reinforced the insecurity and wait-and-see attitude of all economic actors, consumers and entrepreneurs alike. Switzerland - which is traditionally said to earn one franc out of two on the export front - could not escape these negative developments. Like most of its neighbours, it has been hit very hard by the fall in investment and the slowdown in the global economy. Our country has been hit hard by the fact that its exports are largely in capital goods. In addition, let us not forget that the financial sector represents in our country a significant share estimated at more than 10% - of the gross domestic product. The stock market deterioration and the ensuing declines in financial income were an additional drag on our growth. Thus, 2002 was a year of stagnation. This economic stagnation has resulted in a fall in corporate profitability, a significant rise in unemployment and a rapid deterioration in public finances. On the exchange rate front, the franc remained relatively stable against the euro, with the single currency essentially hovering within a range of fr. 1.45 to fr. 1.48. On the other hand, like all European countries, we have had to face a sharp correction in the dollar, a correction that was long overdue but which came at the worst time from the point of view of the economic situation. Over the year as a whole, the US currency lost almost one-fifth of its value, falling to its 1998 level. As far as price developments are concerned, the findings are most satisfactory. Our objective of price stability has been achieved once again. The purchasing power of our currency thus remained intact throughout the year. Outlook for 2003 In many ways, therefore, 2002 was a useless year. Today, we find ourselves in a situation just as uncertain as last year. We are once again placed in the expectation of an early recovery of the global economy, a determining factor for our growth. Compared to last year, however, the situation has become more difficult for our companies, more socially tense and tighter in the management of public budgets. And this situation is expected to continue in the coming months. But there are sources of hope: monetary and fiscal policies. are expansionary; interest rates are extremely low in most countries; banking institutions are relatively healthy and able to fulfil their role. After the many restructurings of recent years, the Swiss economy is now well positioned and ready to benefit from a revival of the global economy. If our assumptions about the international environment hold true, we should see activity in Switzerland strengthen over the course of the year. Consumption and exports are expected to hold steady and, after a multi-year eclipse, investment in capital goods will return to contributing to growth. However, the latter will remain behind our expectations last December. Our economy is emerging more slowly than expected from the stagnation it entered in the second half of 2001. On the monetary side, low interest rates and ample liquidity in the market will facilitate the recovery. However, price stability is not threatened. According to our forecasts, the average inflation rate will be around 0.7% this year, around 1% in 2004 and close to 2% in 2005. The gradual trend towards accelerating price increases over the next few years shows us that the current course of monetary policy will have to be corrected once the economy normalizes. That said, the risks of a further deterioration of the situation are still present and substantial, both in Switzerland and abroad. Industrialized countries were not immune to terrorist attacks, and developments in the Middle East remained highly uncertain. On the strictly economic level too, there are many questions. The expansion of international trade is highly dependent on the economic recovery in the United States. This seems to be confirmed, but it remains hesitant. Closer to home, Germany is struggling to get out of the economic slump in which it has been plunged for several years. In concrete terms, we are particularly concerned about two scenarios. On the one hand, we can fear a further delay in the recovery of the world economy; on the other hand, our currency could be put under pressure on the foreign exchange market. In the first case, we would observe a further deterioration of the framework conditions in which we operate, with little possibility of reaction on our part. In the second case, we would be faced with a problem specific to our country. In the event of turbulence in the franc, we always have the instrument for intervention; one a risky instrument, as it can lead to a strong expansion of domestic liquidity, but a necessary instrument if markets move irrationally. As you can see, although the franc remained relatively stable in 2002, it remains a constant source of concern. We know from experience that excessive movements cannot be ruled out in the foreign exchange markets and that their correction is most often slow and costly for our economy. Faced with the potential for shocks from financial markets, we strive to integrate currency considerations as widely as possible into our strategy. Those who criticise us for not doing enough in this respect do not do justice to the very active interest rate policy we have followed over the last two years or to the constant concern we have shown for developments in the financial markets. In the end, we have four years of cohabitation with a European currency that experienced its initial difficulties and four years of dramatic adjustments in the dollar's exchange rate, all sources of disruption that have not destabilized the franc as markedly as one might have feared. Since 1999, when the euro was introduced, our currency has appreciated in real terms by just over 1% per year against the single currency. This rate is certainly higher than the trend appreciation noted in the past against the German mark, but this is not surprising because the euro is not the mark, just as Euroland is not the former Federal Republic of Germany. So things went better than feared. The challenge of growth In 2002, the growth of our economy was once again lower than that of the industrialized countries, and this situation is likely to be repeated again this year. We are now almost used to this because, in most international comparisons of industrialized countries, Switzerland ranks last in terms of real GDP growth. Often, the franc is seen as the main obstacle to more sustained growth. I disagree with this allegation. Over the past twenty years, despite a strong trend of the franc, the share of foreign trade in our domestic product has increased markedly. Today, our export industry sees its competitiveness threatened more by the weight of its domestic costs than by an overvaluation of the Franc. Nevertheless, our situation of low growth must concern us even if it must be put into perspective somewhat. Indeed, it is paradoxical to note that Switzerland is the red lantern of growth while it is systematically in the leading pack in terms of real income per capita. Its very high standard of living gives it, today as in the past, a very enviable situation. This image of a Switzerland that moves slower than the others but which is always ahead, is due in particular to the fact that real GDP, as it is usually calculated, tends to underestimate the value added in our country because it neglects the positive effects caused by the continuous improvement of our terms of trade. Moreover, we must not forget that our economy invests considerable amounts abroad every year and that the fruit of these investments is also not included in the calculation of domestic product. Thus, our nominal per capita income - which includes internal and external incomes - grew at an average rate of 2.4% from 1992 to 2000, while GDP per capita grew during the same period by only 1.7% per year. Nevertheless, Switzerland's economic performance has been disappointing over the past decade. This situation is worrying because the ageing of our population, due to the low birth rate in Switzerland and the increase in life expectancy for everyone, raises very important challenges. At the heart of the problem is the preservation of social security achievements. From a financial point of view, it is clear that the proper functioning of the AHV and the health of our second pillar - in view of very low interest rates - will require a special effort. Increases in resources - in the form of taxes or contributions - are likely to be necessary to preserve pensions over time. These additional transfers will be all the easier to absorb as growth is sustained. In terms of production, it is necessary to ensure that the volume of goods and services produced in our country covers the growing needs of the entire population, active and inactive alike. Whatever the approach chosen, the sustainability of our social insurance and general well-being therefore depend on the development of productive activities. We must therefore do everything we can to support the work effort, innovation and investment: 95 encouraging everyone's participation in the productive process and, here, the question of raising the retirement age in the long term is unavoidable; 95 promote mobility and ensure that no obstacles to work effort are created; 95 to continuously improve the quality of our education system by promoting scientific research and transmitting new knowledge, factors that fuel technological progress. Productivity gains are a key factor in an environment of full employment; 95 make the most of our comparative advantages in high value-added activities in order to reap the full benefits promised by international trade; 95 constantly adapt, modernize and strengthen our country's productive capital, as investment remains the main driver of growth. Finally, let us not forget that good framework conditions are essential to the success of any economic enterprise: an efficient public infrastructure, a favourable social climate, an efficient and reliable judicial system, economic policies that give free rein to sustainable growth. Great efforts must also be made in the area of the internal market, where excessive regulation, lack of competition and low productivity are holding back the enthusiasm of entrepreneurs and are sources of excessive costs that penalise consumers. While our industries exposed to global competition are generally extremely successful, those that operate mainly in the domestic market often lag behind. Cartel cartels, distortions of competition, as well as administrative and other obstacles to the proper functioning of markets, are all obstacles to growth. What can monetary policy do? The SNB is aware of the importance of sustainable economic growth. Its constitutional mandate requires it to conduct a monetary policy in the general interest of the country, a formulation in which long-term growth considerations naturally have their place. In the draft new law on the National Bank, which is currently under discussion in Parliament, the constitutional mandate is supplemented by the task of ensuring price stability and, in so doing, taking account of the economic situation (art. 5). By mentioning price stability, the bill emphasizes an important contribution of monetary policy to growth. Indeed, a monetary policy that does not create conditions for stability has negative consequences for the the functioning of the economy, just like a poorly tuned engine coughs and only idles. It is true that the preservation of monetary stability has unspectacular effects, but they are of paramount importance. Price stability allows the economy to reach its growth potential by avoiding unnecessary costs, it encourages investment by generating low interest rates and avoids misallocation of resources. However, it should not be expected to push back the frontier of the possible, that is, to boost the economy and increase its capacity to produce. Similarly, a mechanic, no matter how skilled, should not be expected to defy the laws of physics and bring a machine to develop a power that is not commensurate with its potential. Any attempt in this direction would lead to overheating and would be likely to result in breakage. Revision of the National Bank Act Last year, I guided you on the main aspects of the draft new law on the National Bank. Where are we today? The revision of the National Bank Act is currently under discussion in Parliament. This new law will complete the modernization of monetary provisions that was made possible by the entry into force in 2000 of the new constitutional article on monetary policy. The new law makes the SNB an independent central bank, responsible for carrying out a clearly defined mandate and accountable for the performance of its tasks. It does not change the legal structure of the Bank but simplifies its governance bodies. In particular, the staff of the Bank Council is reduced from 40 to 11 members, 5 of whom are appointed by the General Meeting of Shareholders. The other powers of the General Assembly shall not be altered. The draft law, which has already passed the stage of the Council of States, is currently under discussion in the Committee on the Economy and Royalties of the National Council. So far, it has been well received. An important point, however, is the rule governing the appointment of members of the Directorate-General and their alternates. The draft law has taken up the current rule which entrusts the Bank Council with the task of drawing up proposals for the appointment of the members of the Executive Board and their alternates for the Federal Council. The Council of States wishes to amend the draft and give the Federal Council the power to make these appointments after simply consulting the Bank Council. Such a rule is quite conceivable. It is also in line with the practice in many countries. But the provisions of the bill - which are the ones we have always known about - offer undeniable advantages that we should not ignore. They provide for the Bank Council to select the candidates and then make a proposal to the Federal Council, which takes the decision. This solution is balanced. Indeed, the Bank Council is familiar with the functioning of the SNB and will be called upon, under the new law, to know it even better. Thus, it fulfils the technical requirements necessary for the selection of candidates and the formulation of an objective proposal. For its part, the Federal Council has the legal competence and moral authority to oppose any proposal that it considers contrary to the interests of the country. I therefore hope that Parliament, at the time of the final decision, will appreciate the merits of the procedure contained in the bill. This procedure has proven its worth and allows for the most serene selection of candidates. If the legislative programme is kept, the new SNB law could already be under the roof this autumn and enter into force next spring at the end of the referendum deadline. It will then be up to the 2004 General Assembly to begin to establish the Bank's new authorities. Conclusion We are in a difficult economic period and everything seems to indicate that the coming months will remain delicate. Our companies are doing their best to defend their position in a particularly depressed global market. Restructuring is needed. They are all the more painful as the horizon is still uncertain. The SNB strives to implement a monetary policy that serves the general interests of the country. It is not able to fully insulate our economy from external disturbances or to compensate for its structural weaknesses. Tomorrow, as today, it can only have the ambition to create the best monetary framework conditions allowing the private sector to adapt to the existing environment. It ensures monetary stability; in this way, it gives the economy every opportunity to grow at its potential pace. Ladies and gentlemen shareholders, distinguished guests, thank you for being here and for your interest in the SNB and its activities.
