Jean-Pierre Roth, prsident de la Direction gnrale,  l'Assemble gnrale des actionnaires de la Banque nationale suisse du 25 avril 2003 2002: Une anne dcevante L'anne 2002 a t trs dcevante pour l'conomie suisse. Il y a un peu plus d'un an, aprs le choc des vnements de septembre 2001, la situation internationale semblait pourtant en voie de normalisation et nous inspirait un optimisme prudent. Le premier trimestre 2002 s'est relativement bien droul; l'conomie mondiale tait sur le point de regagner progressivement le chemin de la croissance. A l'poque, nous nous attendions  une croissance moyenne du PIB de l'ordre de 1% pour l'ensemble de l'anne, avec une nette acclration de l'activit au second semestre; une prvision que de nombreux observateurs qualifiaient de trop pessimiste. Il nous a fallu rapidement dchanter. Les signaux contradictoires ont commenc  se multiplier ds le deuxime trimestre de 2002. De plus, le franc s'est raffermi face  l'euro. Cette apprciation de notre monnaie survenait au plus mauvais moment car elle entranait un resserrement des conditions montaires dans notre pays. Nous avons ragi en abaissant de 50 points de base, en mai, la marge de fluctuation du Libor  trois mois. Cela a permis non seulement de stopper net le mouvement de hausse du franc, mais aussi de donner une bouffe d'oxygne  notre conomie. Ds l't, il est devenu vident que la reprise tant attendue tardait  se manifester. L'conomie amricaine se montrait de plus en plus fragile, les signaux positifs tant rgulirement supplants par d'autres, ngatifs. Sur le front europen,  commencer par l'Allemagne, l'horizon s'assombrissait inexorablement. Ce retard de la reprise tait d'autant plus fcheux que le franc frisait de nouveau des sommets face  la monnaie europenne. A fin juillet, nous avons abaiss une nouvelle fois de 50 points de base la marge de fluctuation du Libor. Il y a quelques semaines, en raison d'une reprise toujours plus hsitante et d'un march des changes particulirement nerveux, nous avons fait un pas supplmentaire et ramen le taux  trois mois  0,25%. Ces difficults n'ont pas toutes leur origine en Suisse; l'conomie mondiale traverse une phase douloureuse de rajustement. Nous avons derrire nous l'clatement de la bulle boursire et les excs commis du ct des investissements, en particulier dans le domaine de la technologie d'information. Ces vnements ont branl la confiance des investisseurs, et les primes de risque demandes par le march ont augment. Le cot de financement des petites et moyennes entreprises a souvent renchri, en dpit du relchement des politiques montaires. Les plans d'investissement ont t revus  la baisse. Le secteur financier a t contraint d'entreprendre des rformes structurelles en profondeur afin de digrer les consquences de la correction boursire. L-dessus sont venues se greffer des considrations gopolitiques qui ont renforc l'inscurit et l'attentisme de tous les acteurs conomiques, consommateurs et entrepreneurs confondus. La Suisse - dont on dit traditionnellement qu'elle gagne un franc sur deux sur le front des exportations - ne pouvait chapper  ces dveloppements ngatifs. Comme la plupart de ses voisins, elle a t affecte trs durement par la chute des investissements et le ralentissement de la conjoncture mondiale. Notre pays a t touch de plein fouet du fait que ses exportations portent dans une forte proportion sur des biens d'quipement. De plus, n'oublions pas que le secteur financier reprsente chez nous une part importante estime  plus de 10% - du produit intrieur brut. La dgradation boursire et les baisses de revenus financiers qui s'ensuivirent ont constitu un boulet supplmentaire pour notre croissance. Ainsi, l'anne 2002 a t une anne de stagnation. Cette stagnation conomique s'est traduite par une chute de la rentabilit des entreprises, par une hausse sensible du chmage et une dgradation rapide des finances publiques. Sur le front des changes, le franc est rest relativement stable par rapport  l'euro, la monnaie unique oscillant pour l'essentiel  l'intrieur d'une fourchette comprise entre fr. 1,45 et fr. 1,48. En revanche, comme tous les pays europens, nous avons d faire face  une forte correction du dollar, une correction qui tait certes attendue depuis longtemps mais qui est survenue au plus mauvais moment sous l'angle de la conjoncture. Sur l'ensemble de l'anne, la devise amricaine a ainsi perdu prs d'un cinquime de sa valeur, tombant  son niveau de 1998. En ce qui concerne l'volution des prix, le constat est des plus satisfaisants. Notre objectif de stabilit des prix a t atteint une fois de plus. Le pouvoir d'achat de notre monnaie est ainsi rest intact tout au long de l'anne. Perspectives pour 2003 A bien des gards donc, 2002 a t une anne inutile. Aujourd'hui, nous nous retrouvons dans une situation tout aussi incertaine que celle de l'an dernier. Nous sommes une nouvelle fois placs dans l'attente d'une reprise prochaine de l'conomie mondiale, un facteur dterminant pour notre croissance. Par rapport  l'an dernier, la situation est toutefois devenue plus difficile pour nos entreprises, plus tendue sur le plan social et plus serre dans la gestion des budgets publics. Et cette situation devrait encore durer ces prochains mois. Mais des sources d'espoir existent: les politiques montaire et budgtaire sont expansionnistes; les taux d'intrt sont extrmement bas dans la plupart des pays; les tablissements bancaires sont relativement en bonne sant et aptes  remplir leur rle. Aprs les nombreuses restructurations de ces dernires annes, l'conomie suisse est maintenant bien positionne et prte  profiter d'un rveil de la conjoncture mondiale. Si nos hypothses concernant l'environnement international se vrifient, nous devrions voir l'activit en Suisse aller en se renforant au cours de l'anne. La consommation et les exportations devraient se maintenir et, aprs une clipse de plusieurs annes, les investissements en biens d'quipement se remettre  contribuer  la croissance. Cette dernire restera nanmoins en retrait par rapport  nos attentes de dcembre dernier. Notre conomie sort plus lentement que prvu de la situation de stagnation dans laquelle elle est entre durant le second semestre de 2001. Du ct montaire, le bas niveau des taux d'intrt et l'ampleur des liquidits dans le march faciliteront le mouvement de reprise. La stabilit des prix n'est pas menace pour autant. Selon nos prvisions, le taux moyen d'inflation sera de l'ordre de 0,7% cette anne, d'environ 1% en 2004 et proche de 2% en 2005. La tendance progressive  l'acclration de la hausse des prix au cours des prochaines annes nous montre que le cours actuel de la politique montaire devra tre corrig une fois que la conjoncture se normalisera. Cela dit, les risques d'une nouvelle dgradation de la situation sont toujours bien prsents et substantiels, en Suisse comme  l'tranger. Les pays industrialiss ne sont pas  l'abri d'attaques terroristes et l'volution de la situation au Moyen-Orient demeure trs incertaine. Sur le plan strictement conomique aussi, les interrogations sont nombreuses. L'expansion du commerce international est fort dpendante de la reprise conomique aux Etats-Unis. Celle-ci semble se confirmer, mais elle reste hsitante. Plus prs de nous, l'Allemagne a beaucoup de peine  sortir du marasme conomique dans lequel elle se trouve plonge depuis plusieurs annes. Concrtement, deux scnarios nous proccupent tout particulirement. D'une part, nous pouvons craindre un nouveau retard de la reprise de l'conomie mondiale; d'autre part, notre monnaie pourrait tre mise sous pression sur le march des changes. Dans le premier cas, nous observerions une nouvelle dtrioration des conditions-cadres dans lesquelles nous oprons et cela avec peu de possibilit de raction de notre part. Dans le second cas, nous serions confronts  un problme spcifique  notre pays. En cas de turbulences du franc, nous disposons toujours de l'instrument des interventions; un instrument risqu, car il peut conduire  une forte dilatation de la liquidit intrieure, mais un instrument ncessaire si les marchs voluent de manire irrationnelle. Comme vous le constatez, bien que le franc soit demeur relativement stable en 2002, il reste une source constante de proccupations. Nous savons par exprience que des mouvements excessifs ne peuvent tre exclus sur les marchs des changes et que leur correction est le plus souvent lente et coteuse pour notre conomie. Confronts  un potentiel de chocs en provenance des marchs financiers, nous nous appliquons  intgrer aussi largement que possible les considrations de change dans notre stratgie. Ceux qui nous reprochent de ne pas en faire suffisamment sur ce plan ne rendent pas justice  la politique trs active de taux d'intrt que nous avons suivie ces deux dernires annes ni au souci constant que nous avons manifest par rapport aux dveloppements des marchs financiers. En fin de compte, nous avons derrire nous quatre ans de cohabitation avec une monnaie europenne qui a connu ses difficults initiales et quatre annes d'ajustements spectaculaires du cours du dollar, autant de sources de perturbations qui n'ont pas dstabilis le franc de manire aussi marque qu'on aurait pu le craindre. Depuis 1999, anne de l'apparition de l'euro, notre monnaie s'est apprcie en termes rels d'un peu plus de 1% par an par rapport  la monnaie unique. Ce taux est certes suprieur  l'apprciation tendancielle note par le pass face au mark allemand, mais cela n'a rien de surprenant car l'euro n'est pas le mark, comme l'Euroland n'est pas l'ancienne Rpublique fdrale d'Allemagne. Les choses se sont donc mieux droules que ce que l'on pouvait craindre. Le dfi de la croissance En 2002, la croissance de notre conomie a, une nouvelle fois, t infrieure  celle des pays industrialiss, et cette situation se rptera vraisemblablement cette anne encore. Nous en avons maintenant presque l'habitude car, dans la plupart des comparaisons internationales portant sur les pays industrialiss, la Suisse occupe le dernier rang en termes de progression du PIB rel. Souvent, on voit dans le cours du franc l'obstacle essentiel  une croissance plus soutenue. Je m'inscris en faux contre cette allgation. Au cours des vingt dernires annes, en dpit d'un franc tendanciellement fort, la part du commerce extrieur a nettement augment dans notre produit intrieur. Aujourd'hui, notre industrie d'exportation voit sa comptitivit menace davantage par le poids de ses charges intrieures que par une survaluation du franc. Nanmoins, notre situation de faible croissance doit nous proccuper mme s'il faut la relativiser quelque peu. En effet, il est paradoxal de constater que la Suisse est la lanterne rouge de la croissance alors qu'elle se situe systmatiquement dans le peloton de tte en matire de revenu rel par habitant. Son niveau de vie trs lev lui confre, aujourd'hui comme hier, une situation fort enviable. Cette image d'une Suisse qui va moins vite que les autres mais qui reste toujours devant, tient notamment au fait que le PIB rel, tel qu'il est habituellement calcul, tend  sous-estimer la valeur ajoute dans notre pays car il nglige les effets positifs entrans par l'amlioration continue de nos termes de l'change. Par ailleurs, il ne faut pas oublier que notre conomie investit chaque anne des montants considrables  l'tranger et que le fruit de ces investissements n'entre pas non plus dans le calcul du produit intrieur. Ainsi, notre revenu nominal par tte - qui intgre les revenus internes et externes - a augment au rythme moyen de 2,4% de 1992  2000, alors que le PIB par tte ne progressait durant la mme priode que de 1,7% par an. Il n'en demeure pas moins que la performance conomique de la Suisse a t dcevante ces dix dernires annes. Cette situation est proccupante car le vieillissement de notre population, d  la faible natalit que connat la Suisse et  l'augmentation de l'esprance de vie de chacun, soulve des dfis trs importants. Au cur du problme se trouve la prservation des acquis en matire de scurit sociale. Sur le plan financier, il est clair que le bon fonctionnement de l'AVS et la sant de notre second pilier - au vu de taux d'intrt fort bas - vont demander un effort particulier. Des augmentations de ressources - sous forme fiscale ou de cotisations - seront vraisemblablement ncessaires pour prserver les rentes dans la dure. Ces transferts supplmentaires seront d'autant plus faciles  absorber que la croissance sera soutenue. En termes de production, il faut veiller  ce que le volume de biens et services produits dans notre pays couvre les besoins croissants de l'ensemble de la population, actifs et inactifs confondus. Quelle que soit l'approche retenue, la prennit de nos assurances sociales et le bien-tre gnral dpendent donc du dveloppement des activits productives. Nous devons ainsi tout entreprendre pour soutenir l'effort de travail, l'innovation et l'investissement:  encourager la participation de chacun au processus productif et, ici, la question d'un relvement  terme de l'ge de la retraite est incontournable;  promouvoir la mobilit et veiller  ne pas crer d'entraves  l'effort de travail;  rehausser sans relche la qualit de notre systme ducatif par la promotion de la recherche scientifique et la transmission des nouvelles connaissances, facteurs qui alimentent le progrs technologique. Les progrs de la productivit sont un facteur cl dans un environnement de plein-emploi;  exploiter le plus possible nos avantages comparatifs qui rsident dans les activits  forte valeur ajoute afin de rcolter pleinement les gains promis par le commerce international;  adapter, moderniser et renforcer sans cesse le capital productif de notre pays car l'investissement reste le premier moteur de la croissance. Enfin, n'oublions pas que de bonnes conditions-cadres sont essentielles au succs de toute entreprise conomique: une infrastructure publique performante, un climat social favorable, un systme judiciaire efficace et fiable, des politiques conomiques qui donnent libre cours  une croissance durable. De gros efforts sont  entreprendre galement dans le domaine du march intrieur o des rglementations excessives, un manque de comptition et une productivit en retrait freinent les ardeurs des entrepreneurs et sont sources de cots excessifs qui pnalisent les consommateurs. Alors que nos industries exposes  la comptition globale sont gnralement extrmement performantes, celles qui oprent essentiellement sur le march intrieur sont souvent  la trane. Les ententes cartellaires, les entorses  la concurrence ainsi que les entraves administratives et autres obstacles au bon fonctionnement des marchs sont autant de freins  la croissance. Que peut faire la politique montaire? La Banque nationale est consciente de l'importance d'une croissance conomique durable. Son mandat constitutionnel lui demande de mener une politique montaire dans l'intrt gnral du pays, formulation dans laquelle les considrations de croissance  long terme ont tout naturellement leur place. Dans le projet de nouvelle loi sur la Banque nationale qui est actuellement en discussion au Parlement, le mandat constitutionnel est complt par la mission d'assurer la stabilit des prix et, ce faisant, de tenir compte de la conjoncture (art. 5). En mentionnant la stabilit des prix, le projet de loi met l'accent sur une contribution importante de la politique montaire en faveur de la croissance. En effet, une politique montaire qui ne cre pas des conditions de stabilit a des consquences ngatives sur le fonctionnement de l'conomie, tout comme un moteur mal rgl tousse et ne tourne qu'au ralenti. Il est vrai que la prservation de la stabilit montaire a des effets peu spectaculaires, mais ils sont pourtant de premire importance. La stabilit des prix permet  l'conomie d'atteindre son potentiel de croissance en lui vitant des cots inutiles, elle incite  l'investissement en gnrant des taux d'intrt bas et vite de mauvaises allocations des ressources. Cependant, il ne faut pas attendre d'elle qu'elle puisse repousser la frontire du possible, c'est--dire doper l'conomie et augmenter sa capacit  produire. De mme, il ne faut pas attendre d'un mcanicien, si habile soit-il, qu'il puisse dfier les lois de la physique et amener un engin  dvelopper une puissance qui ne soit pas en rapport avec son potentiel. Toute tentative allant dans ce sens mnerait  la surchauffe et risquerait fort de se solder par de la casse. La rvision de la loi sur la Banque nationale L'an dernier, je vous ai orient sur les principaux aspects du projet de nouvelle loi sur la Banque nationale. O en sommes-nous aujourd'hui? La rvision de la loi sur la Banque nationale est actuellement en discussion au Parlement. Cette nouvelle loi achvera la modernisation des dispositions montaires qui a t rendue possible par l'entre en vigueur, en 2000, du nouvel article constitutionnel relatif  la politique montaire. La nouvelle loi fait de la BNS une banque centrale indpendante, en charge d'excuter un mandat clairement dfini et tenue de rendre compte de l'accomplissement de sa mission. Elle ne modifie pas la structure juridique de la Banque mais simplifie ses organes de conduite. En particulier, l'effectif du Conseil de banque est rduit de 40  11 membres, dont 5 sont dsigns par l'Assemble gnrale des actionnaires. Les autres comptences de l'Assemble gnrale ne sont pas modifies. Le projet de loi, qui a dj pass le cap du Conseil des Etats, est actuellement en discussion dans la Commission de l'conomie et des redevances du Conseil national. Jusqu'ici, il a t bien accueilli. Un point important fait toutefois l'objet de dbats: il s'agit de la rgle rgissant la nomination des membres de la Direction gnrale et de leurs supplants. Le projet de loi a repris la rgle actuelle qui confie au Conseil de banque le soin d'tablir -  l'intention du Conseil fdral - les propositions en vue de la nomination des membres de la Direction gnrale et de leurs supplants. Le Conseil des Etats souhaite modifier le projet et donner au Conseil fdral la comptence de procder  ces nominations aprs avoir simplement consult le Conseil de banque. Une telle rgle est tout  fait envisageable. Elle correspond aussi  la pratique en vigueur dans de nombreux pays. Mais les dispositions du projet de loi - qui sont celles que nous connaissons depuis toujours - offrent des avantages incontestables que nous ne devrions pas ignorer. Elles prvoient que le Conseil de banque slectionne les candidats et fait ensuite une proposition au Conseil fdral qui prend la dcision. Cette solution est quilibre. En effet, le Conseil de banque connat bien le fonctionnement de la BNS et sera appel, sous la nouvelle loi,  le connatre encore mieux. Ainsi, il remplit les exigences techniques ncessaires  la slection des candidats et  la formulation d'une proposition objective. De son ct, le Conseil fdral a la comptence juridique et l'autorit morale lui permettant de s'opposer  toute proposition qui lui semblerait contraire aux intrts du pays. Je souhaite donc que le Parlement, au moment de la dcision finale, apprcie  leur juste valeur les avantages de la procdure qui figure dans le projet de loi. Cette procdure a fait ses preuves et permet une slection aussi sereine que possible des candidats. Si le programme lgislatif est tenu, la nouvelle loi sur la BNS pourrait tre sous toit cet automne dj et entrer en vigueur au printemps prochain  l'issue du dlai rfrendaire. Il incombera alors  l'Assemble gnrale 2004 de commencer  mettre en place les nouvelles autorits de la Banque. Conclusion Nous sommes dans une priode conomique difficile et tout semble indiquer que les mois  venir resteront dlicats. Nos entreprises s'efforcent au mieux de dfendre leur position dans un march mondial particulirement dprim. Des restructurations sont ncessaires. Elles sont d'autant plus douloureuses que l'horizon reste encore bien incertain. La Banque nationale s'efforce de mettre en uvre une politique montaire servant les intrts gnraux du pays. Elle n'est pas en mesure de mettre notre conomie pleinement  l'abri des perturbations extrieures ou de compenser ses faiblesses structurelles. Demain, comme aujourd'hui, elle ne peut avoir que l'ambition de crer les meilleures conditions-cadres montaires permettant au secteur priv de s'adapter  l'environnement existant. Elle veille  la stabilit montaire; c'est ainsi qu'elle donne  l'conomie toutes ses chances de crotre  son rythme potentiel. Mesdames et Messieurs les actionnaires, Mesdames et Messieurs les invits, Je vous remercie de votre prsence, ainsi que de l'intrt que vous manifestez  l'gard de la Banque nationale et de ses activits.

Title: Summary of a speech delivered by the President of the Bank Council to the Annual General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank
text: Opening address by Mr Hansueli Raggenbass, Chairman of the Bank Council, at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 25 April 2003 In my opening address to this General Assembly, I would like to comment on three themes, namely the annual accounts for 2002, free assets and, thirdly, corporate governance and the revision of the National Bank Act. 1. Annual accounts for 2002 For the SNB, the past financial year was characterised by conflicting developments which led to an overall satisfactory result. Significant decline in gross income The SNB generated a gross profit of CHF 2.6 billion in 2002, compared with CHF 4.5 billion the previous year. The decrease was mainly due to heavy exchange losses resulting from the conversion of items denominated in foreign currencies, including items in United States dollars, into Swiss francs. On a year-over-year basis, gold's profit rose by CHF 0.2 billion to CHF 1.5 billion. Half of this can be explained by a capital gain recorded thanks to the rise in the price of gold and by the income from interest on gold loans, and the other half by the forward transactions which were concluded in order to hedge against exchange rate risk the proceeds, in dollars, of future sales of gold. For its part, the result of foreign currency investments amounted to 0.5 billion francs in 2002, compared with 2.4 billion the previous year. Interest receipts and capital gains alone amounted to CHF 4.7 billion. However, the Bank suffered exchange losses amounting to CHF 4.2 billion, with the rate of the UNITED States dollar rising from FR 1.68 to FR 1.39, and that of the euro from FR 1.48 to FR 1.45. In addition, a loss of CHF 0.3 billion was recorded on all other foreign currency assets, namely the reserve position at the IMF, international means of payment and monetary aid credits. Financial assets in Swiss francs generated a profit of CHF 0.8 billion, about the same amount as in 2001. While the income from repo against Swiss francs - the most important monetary policy instrument - fell sharply as a result of lower short-term interest rates, the result of securities in Swiss francs increased significantly. The decline in interest rates also led to high capital gains on the bond portfolio. Decrease in ordinary expenses Ordinary expenses decreased from CHF 425 million in 2001 to CHF 320 million in 2002. Their decrease is mainly due to lower interest expenses on Federal funds. These expenses, which amounted to CHF 204 million in 2001, amounted to CHF 75 million in 2002. Other items of ordinary expenses increased by a total of 10.5% to CHF 245 million. The increase in banknotes in circulation and the replacement of more used banknotes led to a 20% increase in banknote charges. As for personnel costs, they increased by about 6%. This development is mainly due to the increase in the number of staff in organizational units such as economic affairs, international affairs, systemic stability and supervision, risk management and information technology, but also by salary adjustments (compensation for price increases, individual increases). Overall result The overall result was CHF 2.3 billion in 2002, just over half of the CHF 4.1 billion recorded the previous year. It was initially used to increase the provision for the disposal of free assets by CHF 1.1 billion to CHF 20.3 billion. When it was constituted, this provision represented the equivalent of the 1300 tons of gold that were no longer needed for monetary purposes. The amount of the provision is calculated today in such a way that it corresponds to the market value of the share of gold that has not yet been sold, the proceeds of sales already made and the result of foreign exchange hedging operations on the proceeds, in United States dollars, of gold sales. In addition, a share of CHF 0.4 billion of the comprehensive result was allocated to the provision for market and liquidity risks on monetary gold. The strengthening of this provision seems sensible given the fluctuations in the price of gold on the market. After these allocations, an amount of CHF 0.8 billion remained available. The new agreement on the distribution of the issuing institution's profits provides for an increase in annual payments to the Confederation and the cantons for the 2002 financial year to CHF 2.5 billion. In order to pay more than CHF 2.5 billion to the Confederation, the cantons and shareholders, CHF 1.7 billion had to be taken from the provision for market, credit and liquidity risks. Benefits of the SNB: distribution and medium-term potential The accounts for the financial year 2002 clearly show the considerable risks to which the SNB is exposed as a result of developments in the price of gold, exchange rates and interest rates. The SNB must hold sufficient monetary reserves, and these reserves can only really fulfil their role if they are not hedged against risks by forward operations. Because of the risks it incurs, the Bank does not fully distribute its surplus income. It devotes part of it to increasing its provisions. According to the agreement with the Federal Department of Finance on the distribution of the issuing institution's profits, provisions must increase in line with the average growth of nominal gross domestic product. Over the years, the provisions have been increased well beyond the target amount, with revenues significantly exceeding the forecasts made in 1998 when the penultimate agreement was concluded. The last agreement, signed in 2002, takes this fact into account and provides for an annual distribution of CHF 2.5 billion until 2012. Two thirds of this amount goes to the cantons, and one third is paid to the Confederation. The distribution of CHF 2.5 billion per year is higher than the Bank's potential profitability in the medium to long term and therefore implies a gradual reduction in the share of provisions that exceeds the target amount. This reduction has already begun with the 2002 financial year. Once the surplus has been fully absorbed, the SNB will distribute a significantly smaller annual amount. It is currently estimated that the distribution potential from 2013 onwards is around CHF 0.9 billion per year. As a result, the Confederation and the cantons will only be able to count on a lower distribution of profits after 2013. 2. Free assets Since May 2000, the SNB has been gradually selling the 1300 tonnes of gold that it no longer needs for monetary purposes. These are the "free assets". The proceeds of sales are invested in various financial assets. These investments are managed separately, but are not shown separately in the Bank's accounts. The popular vote of 22 September 2002, as you know, did not settle the question of the final allocation of these funds. As a result, the free assets remain on the SNB's balance sheet for the time being and the SNB continues to manage them. At the end of 2002, free assets amounted to CHF 21 billion, taking into account investment income. Most of them consisted of financial investments; the remaining gold for sale, 627 tons, represented only 46% of free assets. If the Bank had not sold any gold, the total value of free assets would have been CHF 1.1 billion lower than at the end of 2002. Thus, the decision to sell the surplus gold will benefit the future beneficiaries of the free assets. In 2002, the SNB sold 282 tonnes of gold at an average price of CHF 15,500 per kilogram. The price of gold in dollars rose by 23%, but this increase was almost entirely offset by the fall in the price of the US currency. However, the SNB systematically hedged against exchange rate risk a 35% share of the proceeds, in dollars, of gold sales. In this way, it was able to mitigate the negative impact of the dollar's decline. Since the beginning of gold sales, the hedging of the dollars receivable has generated a gain of no less than 500 million francs. The proceeds of gold sales are invested according to a strategy that aims above all to maintain the substance of the portfolio. At the end of 2002, the portfolio consisted of 68% of receivables denominated in francs or foreign currencies hedged against exchange rate risk, 21% in euros, 4% in dollars and 8% in other currencies. The average remaining duration of investments was three years. Investment returns reached 5.2% in 2002, compared to 4.4% the previous year. This encouraging result can be explained by the rise in bond prices, following the decline in interest rates, and by the low exposure of the portfolio to currency risks. The conservative investment strategy we have been pursuing for almost three years can be described as sound. The restrictions imposed on investments by the SNB Act have not had any negative effects. Thus, the ban on acquiring shares has been profitable, given the unfavorable stock market climate of the last three years. Similarly, the concentration on first-class debtor bonds has worked in our favour. However, the performance achieved is not always a good indicator of the future. The risk profile resulting from the investment strategy should prevent us from large capital losses, but such a strategy cannot guarantee us, in the medium or long term, returns as high as those of the last two years. If we consider all free assets, the risk that dominates always comes from fluctuations in the price of gold. However, this risk decreases as gold sales progress. 3. Corporate governance and revision of the National Bank Act Since our last General Assembly, economic developments have not lived up to expectations. Uncertainties and disappointments dominated. In addition to geopolitical crises, scandals that have shaken companies - and our country has not been spared by such events - have contributed a lot to this. Although these are isolated cases, these cases, which are partly spectacular, have caused great concern. We have witnessed not only the destruction of a considerable mass of material and immaterial values, but also something more fundamental, namely a collapse of trust. In a complex world, trust is a fundamental, irreplaceable value. This is true both at the level of organizations and personal relationships and at the level of economic and social systems as a whole. As the future is always uncertain and does not depend solely on our own decisions, we must be able to count on trust. Anyone who flies on vacation or attends a conference must be able to rely on the planned flight plan. Whoever decides, in view of the figures on a company's balance sheet, to acquire shares must be able to rely on the veracity of these figures. If this trust is lacking, fundamental mechanisms of our society and economy are being called into question. A loss of confidence can have such broad repercussions that consumption and investment, and thus the growth of an economy, will be permanently affected. If confidence in the fundamental mechanisms of the economy is disappointed, mistrust sets in and becomes widespread. There is then a risk of resorting to regulatory measures of defence and safeguard and, thus, of restricting too much the room for manoeuvre of economic agents. Trust must therefore be rebuilt on a new basis. At the corporate level, efforts in this direction have led to principles of corporate governance. Basically, they are rules and systems for the conduct and supervision of companies, which take into account the various aspects from the point of view of all interested parties. Each party has its own interests, but ultimately all parties have a joint interest in the company conducting a cautious policy and acting effectively and sustainably with the resources invested. If this common interest is systematically flouted, negative consequences will result not only for the undertaking concerned and its staff, but perhaps for an entire branch, a region or even the economic system as a whole. One view that prevailed in the stock market euphoria phase was that the increase in the value of a company ("shareholder value") and a management remunerated according to the share price automatically lead to a positive evolution for all parties concerned. Since then, we have seen things differently. We now know that it is precisely such mechanisms that have paved the way for various scandals. Therefore, the emphasis is now on conduct and control structures that must ensure that companies pursue a policy that takes into account not only the interests of shareholders but also those of all other parties concerned. In this respect, the Management Board is called upon to play a key role; its members must meet professional requirements. In addition, a transparent information policy is also considered important. It must enable shareholders and investors to make their decisions on as objective a basis as possible. The rules of corporate governance and responsible business conduct alone cannot guarantee the success of an economic activity. However, they help to ensure that wrong developments are detected early enough and can be corrected. Thus, it is possible to regain the lost trust. As companies compete globally today, a strong culture of corporate governance is also a factor that is becoming increasingly important in choosing a location. Although Switzerland became aware of corporate governance issues rather late, the regulations it has adopted in this area, particularly for financial institutions, show that, in substance, we do not have to fear international comparisons. Trust in money is undoubtedly of great importance for society as a whole. This is one of the reasons why it is planned to strengthen corporate governance at the issuing institution through the revision of the National Bank Act. The new organization, as reflected in the bill, aims for more effective and professional oversight, with a good balance between the various bodies. The Bank Committee will be abolished, but the Bank Council will emerge strengthened from the review. This body will increase from forty to eleven members, which will give more weight and responsibility to each of them. The powers of the Bank Council will be extended. These will include the establishment of organizational structures, the approval of the Bank's terms and conditions, senior management in the area of personnel, the determination of the appropriate level of provisions, as well as the supervision of asset investment and risk management. In the new act, the Corporate governance at the SNB will be adapted to the current conditions also in the field of revision. The current Supervisory Board will be replaced by an audit body, composed of independent chartered accountants. At the spring session, the Council of States, the first of the two chambers to examine the draft, approved the main lines of the revision, as provided for in the Federal Council's dispatch. Ladies and gentlemen, with the revised law, the SNB will, I am sure, have corporate governance structures that meet modern requirements. These structures will help us to continue to place the necessary trust in our issuing institution. But, in addition to the legal bases and organisational structures, trust will depend very much, also in the future, on the people who decide the bank's fate. These people will always need our trust, as they have to make important central bank policy decisions usually at times when uncertainties are particularly high. I cannot conclude my presentation without expressing my warm thanks to the members of the Executive Board and to all the staff of the SNB for the work they have done over the past year.

Mesdames et Messieurs, avec la loi rvise, la Banque nationale sera dote, j'en suis persuad, de structures de gouvernement d'entreprise qui rpondent aux exigences modernes. Mais, en plus des bases lgales et des structures organisationnelles, la confiance dpendra beaucoup,  l'avenir galement, des personnes qui dcident du destin de la Banque. Ces personnes auront toujours besoin de notre confiance, car elles doivent prendre les dcisions importantes de politique de banque centrale gnralement  des moments o les incertitudes sont particulirement grandes. Title: Banks and economic activity
text: The banking sector and the economic situation Presentation by Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Seminaire Banks and Conjuncture Centre of Banking Studies Villa Negroni, Vezia Tuesday, 6 May 2003 The Swiss economy has a decade of turbulence behind it. Since 2001, the hope that a solid economic recovery will put it back on its long-term growth path on a sustainable basis has not yet been realized. The boom of 2000 was followed by a phase of recession and stagnation that has continued until today, with its share of restructuring and a further rise in unemployment. At the origin of the sudden economic cooling is the fall of the stock markets. Although a significant number of indicators and signs made it clear that the rise in prices in previous years could not be sustained, it was difficult to estimate the magnitude of the upcoming correction and its consequences for the economy. In retrospect, it turns out that we have underestimated the measure of adjustment, and therefore its effects. The bursting of the speculative bubble has created difficulties for many sectors: for savers and pension funds, which have seen part of their assets melt away; for start-ups which have no longer been able to refinance themselves on terms as advantageous as before; for the financial sector, which has seen its investments depreciate and its sources of income decline sharply. I am thinking, of course, of insurance but also, and this is the subject that interests us today, of banks. Despite these shocks, the stability of the Swiss financial system has never been jeopardised. Nevertheless, the decline in profits and turnover of banking institutions, which generate nearly 10% of the added value of the entire economy, has inevitably led to a significant loss of wealth creation. The financial sector - banks and insurance combined - which until recently was characterized by continuous job creation, is now cutting jobs and is being forced to undertake radical consolidation measures. The banks have not only made headlines because of their own setbacks; their role as providers of funds is also under fire. Some criticize them for protecting themselves at the expense of their debtors by applying credit conditions that are too restrictive. Others blame them for inhibiting the stimulating effects of expansive monetary policy. In other words, their behaviour would be poorly adapted to the current economic situation. Have banks become a burden on our economy? To answer this question, I would like to focus on the following two aspects: on the one hand, on the evolution of the banking sector during the current economic cycle and, on the other hand, on its role in the transmission of monetary policy through the credit market. To do this, I will draw on recent examples and start with a brief retrospective of the development of the banking sector over the past four years. 1. Glory and misery of the banking sector In 1997, Switzerland emerged from a long period of stagnation that had taken it to the bottom of international comparisons of economic growth. After a final dip following the Asian crisis of 1998, economic growth accelerated significantly until 2000, when the capacity of the Swiss economy was again operating at full capacity and the labour market was already showing some signs of labour shortages. This rapid recovery, and especially the robust growth in exports of goods and services, was greeted with relief and satisfaction. They demonstrated that our economy remained competitive and that its performance could be aligned with that of the countries of the European Union. During this phase, the banking sector was particularly dynamic. It should be remembered that at the beginning of the nineties, this same sector was forced to make drastic adjustments and digest losses of more than 40 billion francs following the real estate crisis. Many banks have disappeared. The bankruptcy of the Thun Savings and Loans Bank remains a painful memory. This period has also left its mark on the banking statistics we report to the SNB. In 1995, there were only 382 establishments, compared with 457 in 1990. This decline is almost entirely attributable to savings banks and regional banks particularly affected by the real estate crisis, from 204 to 157. Many troubled banks have been taken over by other institutions, others have merged. Even if the structural adjustment process proceeded quickly and to a large extent without state support, it still created a significant burden on the economy for several years. The weakness of Swiss economic growth in the nineties is undoubtedly partly attributable to the real estate crisis and its consequences for the banking system. In 1995, the Swiss banking sector began an impressive recovery. According to estimates by the Basel Institute for Short-term Economic Analysis BAK, the value added of banks increased by an average of 5% per year over the next five years, which is twice as large as the growth of the product. real gross domestic during the same period. In 2000, the share of banks with national value added was almost 12%. In parallel with this domestic expansion, banks have also expanded their presence abroad in the context of strategies that have become global. This can be seen in the strong increase in direct investment by the banking sector abroad. In 2000, the capital stock accumulated abroad by banks amounted to 54 billion francs, representing 14% of the total amount of capital accumulated abroad. The expansion of banking activities benefited greatly from the rise in stock prices. It thus recalls, at first glance, the developments observed at the end of the 80s when banks, following the rise in real estate prices, massively expanded their credit activities. However, it remains an important nuance. Unlike the role played at the time by real estate stocks, the rise in stock prices did not form the basis of an excessive credit policy. Above all, it has led to a strong expansion of activities related to wealth management and investment banking. For the year 2000, almost a third of total economic growth is attributable to the banking sector. The cyclical recovery at the end of the last decade was thus less balanced than it seemed at first glance. It is therefore not surprising that the collapse of stock market values that began in Switzerland in September 2000 hit the banking sector hard and had a strong impact on the growth of our economy. However, not all banks have been affected in the same way by the phenomenon. Institutions with a strong focus on wealth management and investment activities were the most affected. Many of them are now left with excessive capacity, both in Switzerland and abroad, and are forced to reduce their activities in these areas. Unlike banks active in wealth management and investment banking, institutions focused on traditional credit activities have, for the most part, performed well over the past two years. Nevertheless, they are feeling the effects of the bad economic situation and are facing higher credit risks, resulting in a tended more selective crediting policy. Certain sectors, such as tourism and the hotel industry, which have a significant proportion of small and medium-sized enterprises in their ranks, are particularly affected by this situation. Between 2001 and 2002, the value added generated by banks fell by 6%. Measured as a percentage of gross domestic product, this corresponds to a national growth loss of 0.5%. For this year, the banking sector is expected to recover slightly. However, we cannot count on a rapid expansion of wealth management and investment banking activities, which means that the economic recovery expected for the second half of the year will have to take place without the support of the banking sector. This observation undoubtedly represents an additional handicap for the normalization of economic activity in our country. As we can see now, the growth of the Swiss economy has largely benefited from the stock market boom of the late 1990s. The fall in the value added of the financial sector over the past two years has significantly slowed growth. But, unlike the situation we experienced about ten years ago, during the deflation of the real estate bubble, the rise in prices did not lead to an unhealthy expansion of bank loans. The financial situation of banks and households - although affected by the fall in stock prices - has not deteriorated as much as it did then. Nevertheless, banks are once again at the heart of the adjustment and there is no doubt that the fall in securities has weighed on the economy, not only because it has led to wealth losses but also because it has hampered the ability of the banking sector to meet the financing needs of our economy. 2. Banks and the monetary policy transmission mechanism I now come to the second part of my presentation: the role of banks in the current phase of the economic situation. As you know, the central banks of the industrialized countries reacted quickly to cyclical weakness and eased their monetary policy from the beginning of 2001. The US Federal Reserve lowered its benchmark short-term interest rate by 4.75 percentage points to 1.25% today, the European Central Bank by 2.25 points to 2.5% and the Swiss National Bank by 3.75 points to 0.25%. Currently, the monetary policy of most central banks can be described as expansive. This is especially true when it comes to our institute. Despite the generous provision of liquidity, the Swiss economy remained sluggish. Total activity stagnated during 2001 and, despite a modest increase in growth in the second half of 2002, the trend in recent months has been marked by renewed weakness. Some are eagerly wondering why monetary policy is not moving faster, as long as it is still acting. A few others believe they have identified those responsible for the current stagnation, in this case the banks that pursue a very restrictive credit policy and keep commercial interest rates high. Before returning to this point, I would like to briefly recall the three main channels through which monetary policy affects the economic situation. An expansive monetary policy stimulates aggregate demand primarily by lowering the level of interest rates. Central banks are lowering the terms of the loans they grant to banks, a move that affects the cost of refinancing banks and the overall structure of interest rates. Competition between banks then leads to a reduction in the rates applied to loans. Investment projects that previously remained unprofitable then become profitable, as does the financing of durable goods. Demand for credit is increasing and banks are expanding their lending. In an open economy, the interest rate channel is added to the exchange rate channel. And to the extent that the interest rate abroad is not simultaneously reduced by the same proportion, a decline in the domestic interest rate leads to a depreciation of the exchange rate. In comparison with foreign goods and services, indigenous goods and services become cheaper and companies become more competitive, both abroad and at home. Finally, there is a third channel, technically called the credit channel, but which I will rather call the collateral guarantee channel of credits. In recent years, this channel has been a privileged subject of study in the economic literature and is of central importance to my analysis today. Everyone knows the development of the technique of collateralized credits by assets in recent years. In fact, this is the modern form of mortgages that are so familiar in Switzerland. The presence of collateral guarantees aims to lower the cost of credit while creditors, having a partial view of the situation of their customers and their projects, want to limit their risks. Ultimately, the more debtors are able to provide significant collateral collateral collateral and good quality, the closer their financing conditions will be to those enjoyed by the best addresses. In the 1980s, the most widespread collateral in Switzerland was the real estate asset that served as collateral not only for housing financing but also for industrial projects. Donors often paid little attention to the industrial viability of the projects they financed because they had the land pledge to cover their risks. The crisis of the 1990s led banks to revise the way they allocate credit and adopt a more selective attitude. Since then, they have been analysing more precisely the chances of success of the investment projects submitted to them and often require additional guarantees, where possible, in the form of financial collateral. What are the links between monetary policy and the operation of collateralized asset-backed credit? It is clear that if lower interest rates lead to higher prices for stocks, bonds or real estate, they lead to an improvement in the balance sheets of companies and the portfolios of individuals. Lenders are then more willing to provide them with funds on favourable terms. In other words, an easing of monetary policy can lead, through the capital gain of collateral and the net present value of cash flow, to a downward trend in spreads and a dilation in the supply of credit. This stimulating effect for the economy can be further amplified if we consider that, beyond its effects on the net worth of companies and households, the fall in interest rates also improves the balance sheets of banking institutions, which will then be encouraged to grant credit on more advantageous terms. As credit is the only means of foreign financing for many households and businesses, an additional positive boost is thus given to the economy. Monetary policy, confidence in the future and asset price developments are therefore essential ingredients for financing the economy, which can support or neutralize each other depending on the business cycle. Obviously this interaction is not without risk because the artificial swelling of securities or real estate, if it facilitates the financing conditions of the moment, contains the germ of future difficulties. Caution is therefore required. Let us now return to the situation we are concerned about and ask ourselves about the effects of the expansive monetary policy pursued by the SNB over the past two years. First of all, we must note the significant fall in the level of interest rates. The yield on the Confederation's 10-year bonds has fallen below 3% and mortgage rates for first mortgages are at their lowest level since the fifties. The exchange rate once again proved to be a cause for concern. One of the reasons remains the role of the Swiss franc as a safe haven currency in times of global political and economic insecurity. Although the difference between European and Swiss interest rates has clearly increased due to our particularly expansive monetary policy, the Swiss franc has remained at a high level against the Euro throughout 2002 and has only recently fallen sharply. Still, strong movements of appreciation could be avoided. What about the credit guarantee channel? The destruction of assets caused by the stock market correction is certainly one of the important reasons for the increase in the price of bank credit, even though the remuneration of the confederation's loans has fallen sharply. Some time will still be needed for the balance sheets of households, businesses and banks to be cleaned up. As for investor mistrust, it is still relevant following the cascade of financial scandals. Financing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) is thus particularly difficult. The latter, which represent the most important source of jobs in our country, do not have access to the capital market and remain largely dependent on bank loans. The economic recovery of the late nineties had led to a marked improvement in their financial situation, so that the accusations they generally make about the banks' credit policy had then evaporated. In recent years, problems have resurfaced and criticism has resurfaced with the deterioration of the economic situation. And the banks are once again in the spotlight. However, the problems of financing SMEs are not new, since they have already been of great concern to us throughout the nineties. Many of them, active in particular in the field of construction, had found themselves in a precarious financial situation. Others, who financed their development projects with mortgage-backed loans, found themselves in difficulty as a result of the turnaround in the real estate market. Since then, banks have changed their credit policy and systematically apply active management of their credit portfolio, using the rating of corporate customers and differentiating the conditions in depending on the risks involved. This new approach has generated a wave of criticism and concern among many companies. In 1998, the then Federal Office for Economic Affairs and Labour drew up a report ordered by Parliament on the financing of SMEs. A survey of about 5,000 companies revealed that a large proportion of them were in serious financial difficulties. The new orientation of the banks' credit policy contributed in part to this. The major source of difficulty, however, lay in the hedging of capital, a coverage that had become very thin, if not completely non-existent following the economic difficulties of the nineties. The study also addressed the problem of the difference in the level of information between debtors and creditors about the financial situation of a company and the probabilities of success of its investment projects, a theme we mentioned earlier. A small business that has few guarantees, usually does not have the easy task when it comes to taking out credit. With this in mind, the study highlighted the importance of collecting and presenting as broad and substantial information as possible about the company's activities and financial health. Finally, the report states to the State the need to take measures to reduce administrative procedures in favour of SMEs and thus contribute to improving their profitability. Some relief in this direction has been implemented since then. 3. Lessons from monetary policy What monetary policy lessons can be drawn from the analysis of the effectiveness of transmission channels? The discussion showed that the transmission of monetary policy takes place through complex mechanisms. It takes place by the interest rate, the exchange rate and by the evolution of the values that can be pledged. The complexity of the transmission mechanism means, first of all, that it is not enough to focus on short-term interest rates alone. In order to assess the degree of restriction of its monetary policy, the SNB must analyse all sources of financing for the economy. Indicators such as the evolution of interest rate spreads thus acquire great importance, as well as the qualitative information on the financing conditions of companies that it obtains through its regular discussions with banks and companies. Next, we must also take into account the indicators of stock and real estate prices. As I have just mentioned, the evolution of the value of assets and that of cash flow play a crucial role in the context of the credit guarantee channel. But unhealthy developments are also possible. The explosion in the price of real estate, which allowed a massive expansion of credit activities during the eighties, illustrates this observation. Remember, from 1982 to 1990, the amount of loans pledged by mortgage had almost doubled, a development clearly incompatible with real investment needs and which led to the difficulties of the 1990s. By way of comparison, during the recent period of boom in the economy, between 1997 and 2000, the volume of domestic credit increased by only 1% per year. Nothing comparable then. Why have we not seen a dangerous expansion of credit to the economy in parallel with the rise of stock markets? This is likely due to the fact that SMEs have limited access to financial collateral. If excesses have been committed, it is rather in the sector of large companies with direct access to the capital market and with a significant financial profile. Nevertheless, it is indisputable that, as a result of the evolution of the value of guarantees, banks' credit policy tends to have a pro-cyclical effect on cyclical developments. This is due to changes in the financial situation of companies and banks themselves. This finding is perfectly rational and reflects the assessment of the situation, prospects and risks. Ultimately, the interest earned on loans must cover the costs of financing and make it possible to make sufficient provisions to be able to counter increased risks of default. A credit policy aligned with the risks involved is thus an essential element of the stability of the banking system. There is no alternative. The experience of the 1990s has shown us this. It is essential for the SNB to adapt to the situation. Urging banks to lower interest rates more quickly or to be more generous in the allocation of credit would be useless at best and even counterproductive if the banking system were to weaken. The SNB must live with the current situation and endeavour to interpret credit statistics, spreads and asset prices appropriately in order to properly balance the course of its policy. When the collateral environment is unfavourable, monetary policy should become a little more expansive than in otherwise. The task here is delicate. But the difficulty of the exercise can in no way justify inaction. 4. Summary and conclusions Banks played a leading role in the dynamics of the business cycle of the late 1990s. A significant part of our economic boom during this period is due to them. In retrospect, we note that in the wake of the stock market euphoria many sectors, including banks, have experienced a development that could not be sustained. Since then, the activities related to wealth management and investment banking have undergone a radical resizing. The economic recovery expected in the second half of the year should offer an oxygen balloon to these industries, even if a new boom in this sector is not in sight and is probably not desirable in the long term. Growth prospects for this year remain subdued. After having to postpone the economic recovery for the first time by a year, both forecasting institutes and central banks have become cautious. For 2003, we expect real economic growth of less than 1% while stressing the importance of downside risks. With the improvement in the economic outlook, margins and spreads applied to credit conditions will also gradually correct. Moreover, the present stabilisation of the stock market situation does not, at the very least, lead to any further deterioration in financial guarantees. Ultimately, we can see that while the stock market downturn posed many problems for the financial sector, it did not have the same negative impact on the economy as the housing crisis of the early 1990s. Contrary to what we observed at the time, the banks' credit policy did not get excited with the soaring price of financial assets. On the contrary, the SME sector has seen its access to credit made more difficult by the application of the new banking strategies adopted for the allocation of funds. "To something misfortune is good" it is often said. This is the case in recent developments in the bank credit market. The use of collateral collateral guarantees did not lead to the credit expansion that might have been feared. Unlike in the early nineties, banks are therefore not facing major problems in the domestic credit market. The good results posted by the regional banks bear witness to this. This relatively advantageous situation, coupled with low interest rates, creates good conditions for financing the economic recovery. We can thus hope that, when the economic horizon clears in the industrialized countries, our economy will return to the path of growth with the support of bank credit. A long phase of stagnation, such as the one we experienced in the early 1990s following the real estate crisis, is not to be feared.
