Toujours est-il que de forts mouvements d'apprciation ont pu tre vits. Qu'en est-il finalement du canal des garanties de crdit ? Les destructions de patrimoine engendres par la correction boursire sont certainement l'une des raisons importantes du renchrissement du crdit bancaire alors mme que la rmunration des emprunts de la confdration a nettement baiss. Un peu de temps sera encore ncessaire pour que les bilans des mnages, des entreprises et des banques soient assainis. Quant  la mfiance des investisseurs, elle reste toujours de mise suite  la cascade de scandales financiers. Le financement des petites et moyennes entreprises (PME) s'avre ainsi spcialement difficile. Ces dernires, qui reprsentent la source la plus importante de places de travail dans notre pays, n'ont pas accs au march des capitaux et demeurent largement dpendantes des crdits bancaires. La reprise conjoncturelle de la fin des annes nonante avait entran une nette amlioration de leur situation financire, si bien que les accusations qu'elles portent gnralement sur la politique de crdit des banques s'taient alors vapores. Ces dernires annes, les problmes ont ressurgi et les critiques sont rapparues avec la dgradation de la situation conjoncturelle. Et les banques sont  nouveau portes sur les devants de la scne. Les problmes de financement des PME ne sont pourtant pas nouveaux puisqu'ils nous ont dj fortement proccup tout au long des annes nonante. Beaucoup d'entre elles, actives notamment dans le domaine de la construction, s'taient retrouves dans une situation financire prcaire. D'autres, qui finanaient leurs projets de dveloppement par des crdits gages par hypothque se sont trouves en difficult du fait du retournement de la situation dans le march de l'immobilier. Depuis lors, les banques ont modifi leur politique de crdit et appliquent systmatiquement une gestion active de leur portefeuille de crdit, recourant au rating de la clientle d'entreprise et diffrenciant les conditions en fonction des risques encourus. Cette nouvelle approche a engendr une vague de critiques et d'inquitude auprs de nombreuses entreprises. En 1998, l'Office fdral de l'conomie et du travail de l'poque rdigea un rapport ordonn par le Parlement sur le financement des PME. Un sondage auprs d'environ 5'000 entreprises rvla qu'une grande partie d'entre elles taient en proie  d'importantes difficults financires. La nouvelle orientation de la politique de crdit des banques y contribuait partiellement. La source majeure de difficult rsidait pourtant dans la couverture de capital, une couverture devenue trs mince, voire compltement inexistante suite aux difficults conomiques des annes nonante. L'tude aborda galement le problme de la diffrence du niveau d'information entre dbiteurs et cranciers  propos de la situation financire d'une entreprise et des probabilits de succs de ses projets d'investissement, thme que nous avons voqu auparavant. Une petite entreprise qui dispose de peu de garanties, n'a gnralement pas la tche facile au moment de contracter un crdit. Dans cette perspective, l'tude souligna l'importance que revt la collecte et la prsentation d'informations aussi larges et substantielles que possible sur les activits et la sant financire de l'entreprise. Finalement, le rapport formula,  l'adresse de l'tat, la ncessit de prendre des mesures pour rduire les procdures administratives en faveur des PME et contribuer ainsi  l'amlioration de leur rentabilit. Quelques allgements allant dans ce sens ont t mis en uvre depuis lors. 3. Enseignements de politique montaire Quels enseignements de politique montaire peut-on tirer de l'analyse de l'efficacit des canaux de transmission ? La discussion a montr que la transmission de la politique montaire intervient au travers de mcanismes complexes. Elle s'opre par le taux d'intrt, le cours de change et par l'volution des valeurs pouvant tre mises en nantissement. La complexit du mcanisme de transmission signifie tout d'abord qu'il ne suffit pas de focaliser son attention sur les seuls taux d'intrt  court terme. Afin de juger du degr de restriction de sa politique montaire, la Banque nationale doit analyser l'ensemble des sources de financement de l'conomie. Des indicateurs tels que l'volution des spreads de taux d'intrt acquirent ainsi une grande importance, tout comme les informations d'ordre qualitatif sur les conditions de financement des entreprises qu'elle obtient par ses entretiens rguliers avec les banques et les entreprises. Ensuite, nous devons galement prendre en compte les indicateurs des prix des actions et des biens immobiliers. Comme je viens de l'voquer, l'volution de la valeur des actifs et celle du cash-flow jouent un rle capital dans le cadre du canal des garanties de crdit. Mais des volutions malsaines sont aussi possibles. L'explosion du prix de l'immobilier qui a permis une expansion massive des activits de crdit durant les annes quatre-vingts illustre bien ce constat. Rappelez-vous, de 1982  1990, le montant des crdits gags par hypothque avait quasiment doubl, une volution clairement incompatible avec les besoins rels d'investissement et qui conduisit aux difficults des annes 1990. A titre de comparaison, durant la rcente priode de haute conjoncture, entre 1997 et 2000, le volume des crdits domestiques n'a augment que de 1% par an. Rien de comparable donc. Pourquoi n'avons-nous pas observ de dilatation dangereuse du crdit  l'conomie en parallle avec l'envol des bourses ? Cela tient vraisemblablement au fait que les PME ne disposent que d'un accs limit aux collatraux financiers. Si des excs ont t commis, c'est plutt dans le secteur des grandes entreprises ayant accs direct au march des capitaux et prsentant un profil financier important. Il est nanmoins incontestable qu'en raison de l'volution de la valeur des garanties, la politique de crdit des banques exerce tendanciellement un effet pro-cyclique sur l'volution conjoncturelle. Cela s'explique par l'volution de la situation financire des entreprises et des banques elles-mmes. Cette constatation est parfaitement rationnelle et reflte l'apprciation de la situation, des perspectives et des risques. Il faut en dfinitive que les intrts perus sur les crdits couvrent les cots de financement et permettent de constituer des provisions suffisantes pour pouvoir parer  des risques accrus de dfaut. Une politique de crdit aligne sur les risques encourus est ainsi un lment essentiel de la stabilit du systme bancaire. Il n'y a pas d'alternative. L'exprience des annes 1990 nous l'a montr. Il est primordial pour la Banque nationale de s'adapter  la situation. Enjoindre aux banques d'abaisser plus rapidement leurs taux d'intrt ou de faire preuve d'une plus grande gnrosit dans l'attribution des crdits serait inutile dans le meilleur cas et mme contre-productif si le systme bancaire devait s'affaiblir. La Banque nationale doit s'accommoder de la situation telle qu'elle se prsente et s'efforcer d'interprter de manire adquate les statistiques de crdits, les spreads ainsi que le prix des actifs afin de doser judicieusement le cours de sa politique. Lorsque l'environnement est dfavorable en matire de garanties, la politique montaire doit devenir un peu plus expansive que dans le cas contraire. La tche est ici dlicate. Mais la difficult de l'exercice ne peut en aucun cas justifier l'inaction. 4. Rsum et conclusions Les banques ont jou un rle prpondrant dans la dynamique du cycle conjoncturel de la fin des annes 1990. Une part importante de notre essor conomique durant cette priode leur est d. Rtrospectivement, nous constatons que dans le sillage de l'euphorie boursire beaucoup de secteurs, parmi lesquels celui des banques, ont connu un dveloppement qui ne pouvait s'inscrire dans la dure. Depuis, les activits lies  la gestion de fortune et  la banque d'affaires ont subi un redimensionnement radical. La reprise conjoncturelle attendue pour la deuxime partie de l'anne devrait offrir un ballon d'oxygne  ces branches d'activit, mme si un nouveau boom dans ce secteur n'est pas en vue et n'est probablement pas souhaitable  terme. Les perspectives de croissance pour cette anne restent modres. Aprs avoir d repousser une premire fois la reprise conjoncturelle d'une anne, tant les instituts de prvisions que les banques centrales sont devenues prudentes. Pour 2003, nous tablons sur une croissance conomique relle infrieure  1% tout en soulignant l'importance des risques  la baisse. Avec l'amlioration des perspectives conjoncturelles se corrigeront aussi progressivement les marges et les spreads appliques aux conditions de crdit. Par ailleurs la stabilisation prsente de la situation boursire n'entrane, pour le moins, plus de dgradation des garanties financires. En fin de compte, nous pouvons constater que si le retournement boursier a pos de nombreux problmes au secteur financier, il n'a pas eu le mme impact ngatif sur l'ensemble de l'conomie que la crise immobilire du dbut des annes 1990. Contrairement  ce que nous avions observ  l'poque, la politique de crdit des banques ne s'est pas emballe avec l'envol du prix des actifs financiers. Au contraire, le secteur des PME a vu son accs au crdit tre rendu plus difficile en raison de l'application des nouvelles stratgies bancaires adoptes pour l'attribution de fonds. A quelque chose malheur est bon dit-on souvent. C'est le cas dans l'volution rcente du march du crdit bancaire. L'utilisation des garanties collatrales n'a pas conduit  la dilatation du crdit que l'on aurait pu craindre. Contrairement au dbut des annes nonante, les banques ne sont donc pas confrontes  des problmes majeurs sur le march intrieur du crdit. Les bons rsultats affichs par les banques rgionales en tmoignent. Cette situation relativement avantageuse, couple avec des taux d'intrt bas, cre de bonnes conditions pour le financement de la reprise conomique. Nous pouvons ainsi esprer que, lorsque l'horizon conjoncturel s'claircira dans les pays industrialiss, notre conomie retrouvera le chemin de la croissance avec l'appui du crdit bancaire. Une longue phase de stagnation, comme celle que nous avons connue au dbut des annes 1990  la suite de la crise immobilire, n'est pas  craindre.

Title: Swiss Monetary Policy: Current Challenges and Future Prospects
text: Swiss Monetary Policy: Current Challenges and Future Prospects Ulrich Kohli Chief Economist Swiss National Bank Text prepared for the 4th Annual Swiss Equities Conference May 21, 2003 -BOrgenstock, Lucerne 1. The New Millennium: A letdown so far The New Millennium was announced with bells and whistles, but so far it has been a major letdown. As any purist will tell you, it begun on January 1st, 2001. Its first quarter coincides almost exactly with the beginning of the long period of economic stagnation to which we seem to be confined ever since. The start of the youngest U.S. recession has been dated March '01, and its end has not yet been officially announced. From a macroeconomic perspective, the last couple of years have been very disappointing. Expectations of an imminent recovery have been repeatedly deceived. And the prospects, for the time being, remain highly uncertain. This raises many challenges for policymakers. At the Swiss National Bank (SNB) too we were surprised by this lack of conviction, and we have had to keep revising our projections downwards. Just over one year ago we were still expecting a gradual recovery to take place in '02, mostly during the second semester, to produce an average growth rate of about 1 %. By early summer it became increasingly clear that this was not going to happen. Indeed, economic growth, last year, was essentially nil. What went wrong? There are several causes that can explain this lackluster performance. First, the worldwide recovery has been repeatedly delayed. The U.S. economy has been very hesitant and, even though U.S. growth has remained positive, it has been less than potential. Positive signals kept alternating with bad news. The stock market performed dismally. Corporate scandals have fed mistrust. The capital overhang kept investment at depressed levels. The U.S. budget deficit has been rapidly increasing. Geopolitical uncertainties have been rising throughout last year. The only bright spot was personal consumption, although consumers are now exhausted and confidence has declined. Europe too has suffered. Hopes that it would remain little affected by a U.S. economic slowdown were ill founded. Investment and consumption have been weak. Inflation has remained stubbornly above the 2% upper limit set by the European Central Bank (ECB). This has made it difficult for the ECB to lower rates. In the past, Europe and its neighbors have come to rely on the "German locomotive" to pull them out of weak spots. Unfortunately, this time around, the German engine is stalled. Germany has become a drag on European growth. Domestic demand is weak. Unemployment is rising. To make things worse, Germany is facing a growing budget deficit. It is in violation of the Maastricht Growth and Stability Pact. Consequently, tax reductions have been delayed, and new taxes might be on the horizon. Against this backdrop, the Swiss economy has been hard pressed to take off. We had always said that a Swiss upturn was unlikely until a decisive U.S. and European economic recovery was under way. In a sense, Switzerland has been hit by a double, or even a triple, whammy. Like elsewhere, investment in equipment has collapsed. Furthermore, because its exports contain a large proportion of capital goods, net exports fell significantly. This was made even worse by the fact that Switzerland's main trading partner is Germany. Nonetheless, the '01-'02 recession was weak. Unemployment, although too high and rising, remains low by international standards. On a brighter note, inflation remains very low. The SN B's objective of price stability has been achieved for the fifth year in a row and our currency has thus kept its purchasing power intact. 2. '03: A recovery waiting to happen In many ways, '02 was a wasted year, and we are now standing where we were 12 months ago. Our current forecast looks almost like a Xerox copy of last year's. We expect Swiss growth to remain subdued until the middle of the year, and then to pick up steam during the second semester. In view of the huge remaining uncertainties and of our deceived expectations of last year, we must, however, remain very cautious. Nonetheless, we believe that the U.S. recovery is on its way, and that it will strengthen throughout '03. Once that the U.S. recovery will be firmly established, we expect Europe to follow suit. The worldwide capital overhang is being progressively absorbed, in parts through economic and technological obsolescence. Monetary and fiscal policies remain very expansionary. In fact, the amount of monetary stimulus in the pipeline is considerable. Interest rates are very low, and yet price stability is not being threatened. With the exception of Japan, banks are in reasonably good shape and are in a position to fulfill their role. Everything in Switzerland is in place to take advantage of a worldwide -and particularly a European -recovery. A lot of restructuring has taken place in the 1990s and it has left us with a more flexible and efficient economy. The fiscal position remains satisfactory. Inflation and interest rates are extremely low. Monetary policy remains decisively expansionary, and the Swiss franc has weakened considerably against the euro. If our scenario for a U.S. and a European upswing proves correct, we should see a gradual revival of the Swiss economy as the year progresses, led by rising exports and investment. Inflation should remain low, at somewhat less than 1 % on average, but, unfortunately, unemployment will keep increasing for a while yet. 3. Risks and uncertainties Risks, however, remain considerable, and many of them point to the downside. Although one cannot exclude that the U.S. recovery will be stronger than expected, the danger is rather that it will be delayed once again. A double-dip recession in the United States seems increasingly unlikely, but it cannot be excluded entirely. It may also be that Europe will go through a period of stagnation. Germany is particularly worrisome. A further drop in the stock market and additional accounting scandals remain possible. In spite of the rapid resolution of the war in Iraq, geopolitical uncertainties remain large. Fortunately, oil prices have receded in recent weeks, and consumer confidence might again be rising. And as if this were not enough, new risks can pop up almost any day: SARS is an acronym that was unheard of only three months ago. Although the Swiss economy today is much more flexible than ten years ago, much remains to be done. It is important, in particular, that efforts directed at liberalizing the internal market do not subside. Like many other European nations, Switzerland is suffering from excessive rigidities and over-regulation. More competition in domestic markets would undoubtedly contribute to increase the efficiency of the Swiss economy and to improve its growth prospects. 4. Real growth: A digression Allow me a short digression on the topic of growth. Switzerland has the reputation of being a laggard when it comes to real growth. In almost every international GDP comparison, Switzerland is found to have a growth rate that is significantly lower than that of other industrialized nations. Nonetheless, when one looks at average living standards, Switzerland always ranks among the top nations. How can Switzerland go slower than everybody else, and yet stay ahead? One could of course argue that this has to do with convergence. If Switzerland has a relatively high living standard initially, it is perfectly possible that it grow less rapidly than its neighbors, and nevertheless that it maintain its leading position for a while yet. Sooner or later, though, it will be caught up. It turns out, however, that the Swiss growth paradox is not new. On the basis of an international comparison expanding from 1880 to 1995, one finds that Switzerland occupies the second-last position. Knowing that in the 19th century Switzerland was a poor country in European comparison, and that apparently growth there was lower than elsewhere, how can one explain that today it is one of the countries where real income is highest? There might be many partial answers to this puzzle, but my own work leads me to believe that real GDP underestimates the growth of real value added in Switzerland by about half a percentage point per year. The reason is that the Swiss terms of trade have improved steadily over the past few decades. An improvement in the terms of trade is similar to a technological progress, in that it allows you to get more for less. But unlike technological progress, the terms of trade effect it is not captured by real GDP data. Instead, it is viewed by the national accounts as a price effect. A drop in the price of imports, which must unambiguously increase welfare, will lead to an increase in the GDP price deflater (because imports enter the calculation with a negative weight), whereas it has clearly no inflationary impact, quite the contrary. This also shows that the GDP price deflater is a poor indicator of a country's general price level. Yet, many international comparisons are based precisely on this index. A second reason why real GDP growth underestimates the increase in the Swiss purchasing power is that Switzerland traditionally is a capital exporter. It thus invests much of its savings abroad. The income earned on these investments is captured by GNP, but it is left out from GDP. It is interesting to note that in recent years, Swiss GNP has grown much more rapidly than GDP. Over the past decade, the difference has averaged about 0.7% annually. Yet another factor that might hold measured economic growth back in Switzerland is the tendency that we have to invest in projects that yield very intangible, if not dubious, returns. The systematic building of bomb shelters, for instance, or perhaps more importantly at the moment, the construction of major new alpine railway tunnels mobilize considerable resources at a very high cost, without increasing the Swiss production potential in any visible way. 5. What monetary policy can do Nonetheless, the Swiss growth performance is far from stellar, and this raises the question as to what monetary policy can do. Most economists today would agree that in the long run, monetary policy has little hold on real variables. Or perhaps, I should rephrase this, for there is an asymmetry in what monetary policy can do or not do. Indeed, a poorly-run monetary policy can have devastating effects on the economy, whereas a well-run policy is quite unspectacular. In particular, it cannot increase the long-run growth potential of the economy. In our view, the most important contribution monetary policy can make to economic welfare is price stability. Price stability enables the economy to reach its full potential. Inflation has many perverse effects on the economy. It distorts signals and leads to a misallocation of resources. It tends to hurt most the economically weakest members of society. Even an apparently harmless inflation rate of 3% will lead to a doubling in the price level in less than 24 years. A worker retiring on a fixed pension at age 60 would see his/her purchasing power reduced by half before having reached the age of 84. Over the course of a century, a 3% rate of inflation would result in the price level being multiplied by a factor of 19. In other words, in terms of purchasing power, a franc would be worth little more than 5 centimes, a dollar little more than a nickel. This cannot be defined as price stability by any stretch of the imagination. The fight against inflation, however, must not be dogmatic, and the central bank must take into account the short-run effects of its policy when setting its course. In particular, it should use its available degree of freedom to support activity whenever possible. At the SNB, we define price stability as an inflation rate of less than 2%. Our operating target is the 3-month Libor interest rate. Since this is an interest rate that we do not control directly, we aim at maintaining the Libor within a range 100 basis points wide. The position of the range itself is set on the basis of a 3-year inflation projection. Given the current economic situation, and given that price stability is not threatened, we have used our leeway in full, and we have lowered interest rates aggressively. Since March '01, we have taken the range down a full 325 basis points, moving its mid-point from 3.5% to 0.25%. This low level is unsustainable in the long run. Interest rates will sooner or later to have been raised. The challenge for monetary policy will be to do so at the right time, neither too early -for this might choke off the recovery -, nor too late -for it would fuel future inflation. 6. The asset-price challenge Many economists argue that central banks define price stability too narrowly. Instead of focusing on the consumer price index alone, they should also include asset prices in their definition of price stability. I see many difficulties with this argument. Asset prices are very complex animals. They are essentially equal to the present value of an expected future income stream. Many factors can affect asset prices, some of which are real and some of which are nominal. A drop in the discount rate or a positive productivity shock, for instance, will tend to lead to an increase in asset prices, and yet such shocks can hardly be viewed as inflationary. Stable asset prices are neither necessary nor sufficient for price stability. In my view, it therefore would be pointless, and even counter-productive, to use monetary policy to try to regulate asset prices. Stabilizing the price level, period after period, on the other hand, would go a long way in enhancing the stability of the financial system and reducing the risk of asset price bubbles developing. A further obvious difficulty with asset price targeting concerns the choice of the relevant assets. Should one look at money, at bonds, at equities, at foreign exchange, at real estate, at commodities, at human capital? Very often the prices of these assets move in opposite directions, which makes it impossible to target them all at the same time. Money is the only asset that central banks control. If they are to target asset prices, it would therefore make sense to focus on money; that is, to target the real price of money, which is simply equal to the inverse of the cost of living. One is thus led back full circle at aiming at stabilizing consumer prices. Let us not forget also that assets are a way to transfer purchasing power through time, and that the purpose of income is ultimately to finance consumption, which is what yields utility. This too argues in favor of safeguarding the purchasing power of money in terms of consumption. Nonetheless, asset prices do convey much information, and therefore they must be watched carefully. A rapid change in asset prices may or may not have any direct implications for price stability, but it almost always has an indirect impact that can materialize through many different channels. Central banks are well aware of this, and they therefore follow asset market developments with great attention. 7. The D-challenge As you know, Switzerland has a very low rate of inflation. Interest rates are very low as well. The D-word has recently become more prevalent in the public discussion. Is deflation another threat that we have to deal with? The pursuit of price stability means the fight against inflation as well as deflation. Deflation has a particularly sinister reputation, for it reminds us of the great Depression -another O-word -of the thirties. One must be careful, however, the example of China, that currently experiences astronomical growth and a falling price level, is here to remind us that deflation is not synonymous with depression, just like inflation does not rime with economic boom. Nonetheless, a steady decrease in the price level leads to many of the same problems as inflation does. It must be fought off decisively and pre-emptively. Indeed, things are not quite symmetrical when it comes to price and interest-rate dynamics. As we all know, nominal interest rates tend to increase with inflation, but the reverse is true only up to a point. This is because nominal interest rates cannot fall below zero. Once the zero lower bound has been reached, any increase in the rate of deflation implies an increase in the real rate of interest that cannot be countered by monetary policy. That is, one of the main channels of monetary policy, the one that works through short-run interest rates, becomes out of order. This is not to say that monetary policy becomes incapable of influencing prices and activity. Deflation, like inflation, is a monetary phenomenon after all, and monetary policy can do something about it. There are other channels remaining, including those that operate through long-run interest rates, the exchange rate and expectations, as well as quantitative measures. Nonetheless, the central bank should do it utmost not to find itself deprived of its main instrument. All in all, however, we do not view deflation as a serious menace for Switzerland at the moment. Monetary policy remains very expansionary, and our inflation projection points decisively upwards towards the end of our forecasting horizon. This does not mean that we could not occasionally observe a monthly drop in the price level, or that the prices of certain goods might not decline, but, short of a brutal external shock, the likelihood of a sustained fall in the price level is very remote. In any case, we monitor the situation very closely and would not hesitate to take resolute countermeasures if needed. 8. The -challenge Over the past four years, the Swiss monetary environment has been transformed. The Swiss monetary zone, which includes Liechtenstein, is now surrounded by the euro-area. It is like an island in the euro-ocean. Monetary integration brings many benefits to its members. Transaction costs are sharply reduced. Exchange-rate volatility and uncertainty vanish within the union. Price comparisons are facilitated and transparency more generally is enhanced. Monetary integration under the Maastricht Treaty also promises price stability to those countries that, in the past, had been incapable of achieving it on their own. Naturally, monetary integration has its costs too. The most important one is the loss of monetary sovereignty. That is, member countries are no longer able to pursue a monetary policy of their own. There is now just one monetary policy for the entire euro-zone. The motto is "one size fits all". This could lead to severe problems in case of asymmetrical shocks; that is, if one country, or one group of countries, is affected by specific external events. Thus, today, one could argue that Germany needs lower interest rates, whereas Ireland, for instance, requires higher ones. Under monetary union, adjustments that would otherwise occur through changes in the exchange rate and domestic interest rate conditions must imperatively take place through changes in prices and wages, and through adjustments in quantities, all of which can be very painful. 9. What course for the Swiss franc? The Swiss franc has shown a tendency to appreciate against the euro. This has led to calls for the Swiss National Bank to fix the exchange rate between the franc and the euro. Our critics argue that the appreciation of the franc against the euro is undermining the Swiss export industry. By targeting the exchange rate, they say, the SNB could eliminate an important source of uncertainty and safeguard the international competitiveness of our export industry. One must remember that about two thirds of Switzerland's foreign trade is with countries from the euro-zone. One should put things in perspective, though. Over the course of the past four years, the appreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro has not exceeded 5% in real terms. In fact, using today's exchange rate, the figure is closer to 2 or 3%, which, over a four-year period, is not extraordinary by historical standards. In any case, fixing the nominal exchange rate against the euro, even if it were possible for a while, would not solve many problems, and it would create a number of new ones. For a start, only the exchange rate against euro-area countries would be fixed, but the policy would do nothing to stabilize the exchange rate against the U.S. dollar, the Japanese yen or the British pound. More importantly, as I argued earlier, monetary policy has no lasting impact on real variables. The real exchange rate, which is the only one that matters for production decisions and trade flows, cannot be manipulated by monetary policy over the long run. Pegging the franc against the euro would bring no lasting relief to our export industry. The long-run real appreciation of the Swiss franc against most other currencies would continue, but it would take the form of a rate of inflation that would be higher in Switzerland than in the rest of Europe. This in itself would stretch the credibility of such a policy. Even more seriously, nominal interest rates would necessarily increase to the same level as in the rest of Europe, which would mean that Switzerland would lose its interest-rate advantage. The user cost of capital would increase even though labor costs would remain unchanged. This would put additional pressure on the competitiveness of our industry. This rise in interest rates would also have serious repercussions for the Swiss financial center and it would lead to a drop in Swiss asset prices. Real investment would most likely collapse, depressing aggregate demand, possibly for many years. Given that we would have lost our ability to charter our own course, there is nothing the SNB could do about it. We firmly believe that we are best off pursuing an independent monetary course. Unavoidably, this occasionally means undesired developments on the foreign exchange market, but this is a small price to pay to be able to continue to offer Switzerland a monetary policy that is custom-made, so to speak. In this regard, it was gratifying to see that the war in Iraq has not led to a sudden surge in the franc. On the contrary, our currency has weakened significantly against the euro over the past two months. The franc seems to have lost some of its safe-haven luster, which will not lead us to shed any tears. Similarly, the fall in the value of the dollar, which had been long announced, yet repeatedly delayed, has been orderly, and it has not led to severe turbulence of foreign exchange markets. In conclusion, I would like to make it clear that the SNB is fully aware of the pain that sudden moves in the exchange rate can inflict. Exchange-rate movements are closely monitored, and they play an important indirect role in the formulation of our policy. A sudden appreciation of the Swiss franc is equivalent to a tightening in monetary conditions. In the current economic situation, any such tightening is clearly undesirable. The Swiss National Bank has demonstrated several times in recent months that it does not hesitate to take decisive policy measures in such a case. It is true that our interest rates are extremely low at the moment, but, even if there is little scope for further cuts, there are other instruments at our disposals that we can use if necessary.

Title: Switzerland's financial center in the European context
text: The Swiss financial centre in the European context Presentation by Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Committee of International Conferences of the French Banking Federation and French Banking Federation, Paris Thursday, May 22, 2003 The recently decided enlargement of the European Union is once again changing the map of our Continent. The highly contrasting mosaic inherited from the 19th century is gradually followed by a more uniform area. Thus continues an integration movement born from the ruins of the Second World War and which today finds its justification in the global challenges that we all have to face. Switzerland seems to escape this trend even though it is a European country par excellence. Is it not the first State to have succeeded in achieving harmonious cohabitation between linguistic, religious and cultural communities that have so often clashed in the past? With its long tradition of economic openness and free trade, does it not run at the pace of the surrounding Europe? Is it not at the crossroads between North and South Europe, a buffer state between the three continental powers? This exceptional geopolitical position, this willingness to trade with neighbouring countries, all mixed with the prudence and tenacity characteristic of mountain peoples, explains to a large extent the economic development of my country, both in its industry and, more recently, in its financial centre. My presentation is devoted to the Swiss financial centre. First of all, I would like to present the importance of the Swiss economy and on the international scene. I will then discuss the main challenges that our banks - like their European competitors, for that matter - are facing today, as well as the responses they are trying to provide. Finally, I would like to conclude by mentioning the consequences for the Swiss economy and its financial system of the fundamental change in the environment that was the creation of the euro on 1 January 1999. The importance of the financial centre in the Swiss economy Seen from the outside, Switzerland often gives the feeling of being a special case. There are many cliches and preconceived ideas circulating about him: Switzerland, the land of watches, cows and chocolate, the land of banks and their numbered accounts! As is often the case, the cliches reflect an outdated reality but still present in popular imagery. Indeed, even if Switzerland remains a champion in the watchmaking sector, it also occupies a leading position in micro-technology and electronics. To its performance in the food industry, we must oppose its leading position in the chemical and pharmaceutical fields. As for the banks, they do occupy a prominent place in the Swiss economy, but anonymous accounts have long been a thing of the past and our financial centre is at the forefront of the fight against money laundering. Two figures illustrate the place that the financial sector occupies today in our economy. Banks alone generate just over 10% of the country's added value, twice as much as in France. The financial centre, including insurance, employs nearly 9% of active people compared to 4.5% in your country. A similar comparison could be made between Switzerland and Germany. But the Swiss financial centre also has its particularities at the international level. Thus, according to unofficial estimates, Swiss banks manage about a third of the world's wealth placed abroad (off-shore wealth). Wealth management, one of the characteristics of our financial centre, tends to make us forget that our banks are also important players in other sectors. The country's two largest banks, UBS and Credit Suisse Group, are among the ten largest banks in the world. They are widely present in all financial centers, creating more jobs outside than on our national territory. In addition to the major international banks, Switzerland has a very dense network of cantonal and regional banks, a hundred in all, whose activities are mainly oriented towards the domestic market. The factors behind the success of the Swiss financial centre The traditionally strong position of the Swiss financial centre is no coincidence. It is due to several factors that can be classified into two categories: factors specific to our financial sector such as, for example, the quality of its services and infrastructure, and factors derived from the relatively favourable framework conditions of the Swiss economy and from which the banking industry also benefits. In terms of factors specific to the Swiss banking sector, the know-how and professional qualities of employees in the banking business are frequently cited as examples. In Switzerland, banks do have access to a highly qualified, multilingual population with extensive experience in service activities. The country's long banking tradition (the oldest private banks date back to the 17th century) has familiarized generations of bankers with client advice and wealth management techniques. In addition to this pool of qualified employees, our banks also have efficient and modern financial infrastructures that allow them to develop or maintain their comparative advantages over abroad. For example, the Swiss financial centre was the first to set up a fully automated interbank payments system. Nor have we experienced the development of payment by cheque, as in France, preferring payments by postal or bank transfer that are much cheaper. For its part, the Swiss Stock Exchange has developed a fully integrated trading, clearing and settlement platform for securities, unique in its kind. She is behind the creation of Virt-x, the pan-European blue chip exchange, an exchange based on an innovative electronic system that allows all stages of a cross-border transaction to be carried out at a reduced cost. Finally, it should be noted that the Swiss franc was the only "small" currency to participate in the new CLS settlement system during the first phase of its implementation. The attractiveness of Swiss financial services lies not only in a traditional taste for precision and quality of execution but also in a reputation for integrity and respect for privacy, a very essential factor because the proper functioning of a banking system depends largely on the trust it inspires. The Swiss authorities and financial institutions are well aware that a good reputation and a high degree of trust are essential assets for the long-term development of a financial centre. This is why various institutions have been set up to guarantee the soundness and integrity of our banks and the confidentiality of their operations. The Federal Banking Commission, an independent supervisory authority, ensures the good health of institutions. A modern legislative framework ensures the integrity of the system, including in the fight against money laundering. Finally, banking secrecy guarantees the confidentiality of transactions. Banking secrecy was introduced into Swiss law in 1934, at a time when the need to protect privacy was evident. It is one of the comparative advantages of our financial centre but has fuelled a number of myths questioning the integrity of Swiss banks. I will come back to this point in a few moments. It is undeniable that banking secrecy, combined with moderate Swiss taxation, makes the investment of foreign capital in Switzerland attractive. In this regard, I would like to point out that, unlike other financial centres, Switzerland does not grant special privileges to non-resident capital. Our financial centre is not an offshore centre: foreign funds are treated like those of residents. And Switzerland does not want to become the privileged place for tax evasion in Europe. That is why we have negotiated an agreement with the European Union to introduce a withholding tax on funds from the Union, the bulk of the proceeds of which will be transferred to Brussels. This mechanism will make it possible to prevent our financial centre from being the easy way to circumvent the European provisions on the taxation of savings which should soon enter into force. Apart from the factors specific to the banking industry that I have just mentioned, the success of the Swiss financial centre also owes much to the general operating conditions of the Swiss economy. These include the opening up of the Swiss economy to the world and to Europe in particular. As proof, exports represented 41% of Swiss GDP in 2001 compared to 27% for the France. Even the banking sector is highly internationalized: Swiss banks are present abroad with nearly 230 subsidiaries and counters, and about 140 foreign banks operate on our territory. For its part, the Swiss Stock Exchange cooperates with its German counterpart in the financial derivatives trading platform Eurex, the European leader in this market, which operates from Frankfurt. As you can see, the Swiss financial centre has a long experience of being open to international operations; it is accustomed to foreign competition as well as cross-border collaboration. Finally, the success of the Swiss financial centre is also the result of the political and monetary stability prevailing in our country. The continuity of the Swiss political system ensures a stable legal environment that respects the rights of savers, which is essential for the trust they place in banks. The stable monetary environment, synonymous with low inflation and a strong Swiss franc, even though it no longer plays the same role as it did during the currency turbulence of the 1980s and 1990s, contributes to the country's reputation for financial soundness. This reputation is also based on the reality of strong national savings reflected in a large surplus in our current account balance. In 2002, Switzerland's external surplus amounted to the equivalent of 34 billion, while during the same period the euro area generated a surplus of 62 billion. Monetary stability and the external surplus are all macroeconomic factors that inspire confidence in the soundness of financial institutions. Challenges for the Swiss financial centre But it is clear that the traditional advantages of the Swiss financial centre are now increasingly shared by other financial centres. Fortunately, we live in a much more stable monetary environment than we did 20 years ago; free trade and the free movement of capital are now widely accepted principles. The Swiss financial centre can therefore no longer be satisfied with the comparative advantages inherited from the past. The international financial environment is constantly evolving and subjects it, like other European markets, to strong competitive pressures. In order to maintain their privileged position and attractiveness, Swiss institutions must therefore adapt to market changes and anticipate future developments. Currently, the banking sector, whether Swiss or French, faces four particularly important challenges for its future: increased globalization, and its consequences on banking competition; the fall in bank revenues following the implosion of the stock market bubble; loss of confidence in companies' financial statements and the fight against financial crime. Globalization and increased competition The trend towards the globalization of financial markets and increased competition between banking institutions is not recent. It has taken root in the liberalization of financial markets and the development of technology. Over the past decade, there has been rapid deregulation of financial markets and increasing exposure of domestic banking sectors to foreign competition. The European Commission's desire to create an integrated European financial market is the best example of this. In parallel with the liberalization of the markets, the IT and financial tools made available to banks have developed considerably. Transactions have been automated, risk management techniques have become more complex, banking activity has diversified, and advances in communication technologies have broken down traditional boundaries between markets, both in terms of demand and supply. These developments have profoundly changed the mode of production and the cost structure of financial institutions. Fixed costs, those of setting up infrastructure, have increased considerably, thus favouring large establishments. at the expense of the little ones. The trend is not new and I do not teach you anything by mentioning the wave of bank consolidations that we have observed in recent years. However, I think it is important not to consider it as a thing of the past: it will continue to shape the Swiss, French and international banking landscape in the near future. The globalization of markets does not affect all banks in the same way. It affects traditional banks less strongly than investment banks for which concentration trends are evident and could even accelerate further. But other banks, such as retail banks, are not immune to this movement because they too must adapt to the constraints imposed by technological development, particularly in terms of IT and risk management. Small banks are therefore seeing a continuous increase in their fixed costs and are looking for economies of scale. Fall in revenues from financial market transactions The second challenge facing banks today is the fall in their current revenues. The stock market correction has profoundly changed the operating conditions of many of them, particularly the large investment banks. The latter have obviously suffered significant losses on the value of their own securities, but they have also noted a decline in the commissions collected on their transactions. Added to this is the sharp decline in mergers and acquisitions and IPOs, two types of transactions that were important sources of income during the second half of the nineties. Wealth management, which has traditionally been a stable source of bank income, has also suffered from the stock market correction. The value of capital under management was negatively influenced by prices and the end of the stock market euphoria led to a significant decline in customer orders. The range of services and infrastructure previously put in place has proved to be unsuited to new market conditions. As a result, many institutions have been forced to restrict their scope of activity and correct previous developments that were no longer in line with the new commercial realities. Loss of confidence in companies' financial statements The two challenges I have just described mainly concern the banking industry, its cost structure and its revenue structure. The point I will address now is different: it refers to questions about the reality of companies' financial situations and the integrity of financial institutions in general. This phenomenon took on its full scope during the revelation of balance sheet manipulation in the United States, cases that sowed doubt among analysts and the public about the veracity of the accounts published by companies and therefore their real financial health. These various cases, to which others have been added, have of course had direct consequences for the banks involved. A number of them are now subject to collective complaints; the sanctions they may bear will obviously be reflected in their results and will tarnish their reputation with the public. But we must not forget that these scandals indirectly affect the entire financial sector through their depressing negative impact on stock markets, and even on public confidence in the soundness of the banking system itself. However, as I said earlier, customer confidence in banks is one of the essential conditions for banks to play their full role in financing the economy. Possible increase in financial crimes The last challenge I would like to mention is a natural consequence of the political and economic developments of the last 20 years: I am talking about the increased risk of financial crime. Clearly, financial centres at the heart of international payments and investment flows must fear that their services will be used for illegal or criminal purposes. This poses a significant threat to their reputation. The fight against money laundering and the flow of criminal funds is thus one of the major challenges facing banks, together with supervisory institutions. The swiss financial centre's responses The Swiss financial centre has taken many initiatives to meet the challenges I have just outlined. Its efforts are aimed at controlling costs, transparency of procedures and the fight against funds of dubious origin. Cost control In the face of increasing international competition and declining revenues from stock exchange activities, Swiss banks have embarked on major cost-cutting programmes over the past two years. To achieve this, they followed essentially three strategies: mergers, internal reorganizations and finally, cooperation agreements. The strategy of mergers between institutions is not new in Switzerland and it has already significantly changed our banking landscape over the past decade. During the nineties, the number of our banks decreased by 40%, and that of their branches by 30%. This consolidation took place mainly through the consolidation of regional banks and the absorption of smaller banks by larger institutions. But we have also seen the merger of two of the three largest banks in the country. This wave of restructuring was facilitated by the liberalisation of the labour market in Switzerland during the same period and the consequent increase in flexibility. More recently, and particularly in the face of the fall in the stock markets, the consolidation movement has continued, also affecting banks focused on wealth management activities. New mergers have taken place between Swiss institutions, but also between Swiss and foreign partners. Without going through mergers, many Swiss banks, especially the two largest ones, have now implemented significant internal cost-cutting programs. These plans are generally aimed at better exploiting existing synergies, redefining activities and products, and promoting productivity. They are therefore seeking to correct mistakes often made during the period of stock market euphoria of the late nineties and to adapt supply to new financial market conditions. Finally, many small institutions, in particular regional banks, have joined forces to set up common infrastructures allowing them to achieve economies of scale while maintaining their independence. These collaborations mainly concern the development of common IT platforms, an area where fixed costs are particularly important, but also the establishment of collective structures for access to the capital market or liquidity management. Restoring confidence in financial statements and corporate governance Let me now briefly dwell on the measures taken by the Swiss financial centre to restore public confidence in financial statements and corporate governance. This is only a set of measures taken at national level. I am convinced that the solution to this problem will have to be achieved through the adoption at international level of common and secure accounting standards and the definition of codes of conduct on corporate governance. To move in this direction, the Swiss Stock Exchange issued a directive last year based on currently recognized international standards. Swiss law also obliges stock exchange operators to comply with internationally accepted rules on investor information. Finally, I would point out that one of the major Swiss banks has reacted to criticism of the lack of transparency surrounding the relationship between financial analysis and business services by announcing its intention to divest itself of its analysis department to become an independent consulting firm. Fight against money laundering and terrorism But of all the current challenges, the fight against money laundering and funds of criminal origin is a priority for the attention of the Swiss financial centre and the Swiss authorities. This is all the more so since banking secrecy can give the feeling of being an easy way to escape justice. It is important here to clarify a few points about Switzerland's policy in these areas. First of all, it should be remembered that banking secrecy was originally introduced with the aim of ensuring respect for the private sphere and increasing depositors' confidence in their bank. Banking secrecy is not intended to protect funds of dubious origin. The Swiss authorities are well aware that they must take all necessary measures in this regard to avoid any slippage. They have therefore attached extremely strict clauses to banking secrecy concerning money laundering and the financing of criminal activity. For several years, Switzerland has become one of the leaders in the fight against money laundering. Our system is based on four pillars:  First, banks have an obligation to know the exact identity and nature of the of their clients' activities. Contrary to a widely held opinion to abroad, it is therefore impossible to open an account in Switzerland anonymously.  Second, a bank that has doubts about the nature of the funds it receives. are entrusted with the obligation to notify the supervisory authorities so that they be able to carry out the necessary investigations.  Third, the Swiss anti-money laundering law applies to a circle very wide range of financial intermediaries: it obviously concerns banks, but also insurance, fund managers, lawyers and trustees.  Finally, if criminal proceedings against a customer of a Swiss bank are Banking secrecy is immediately lifted, whether the crime was committed in Switzerland or abroad. Thanks to these provisions, the Swiss anti-money laundering system complies with the highest international standards and is recognised as such by the various international institutions. With regard to the fight against terrorism, the Federal Administration had recently issued a new ordinance extending the Money Laundering Act to all financial transactions related to terrorist activities. This order follows the recommendations of the FATF, the Financial Action Task Force on Money Laundering, in the fight against the financing of terrorism. In recent years, the Swiss financial centre has sometimes made headlines following the identification and blocking of funds of dubious origin. These cases show that the system put in place has some effectiveness. We also hope that it will act as a deterrent to those who would like to try to abuse the rules of confidentiality. I am not impressed by the fact that other financial centres with an international dimension seem to be protected from scandal. In my opinion, the absence of proven fault is not a proof of holiness. The monetary challenge of the euro The list of challenges facing the Swiss financial centre would not be complete if I did not mention the introduction of the euro here. Over the past three years, the Swiss economy has had time to experiment with and adapt to the European currency. To convince you of the importance of the euro for Switzerland and its financial centre, I would like to point out that the European Union is the most important economic partner. Swiss companies. Half of our exports go to the euro area from where we derive more than 60% of our imports. France and Germany are our main trading partners and Switzerland is completely surrounded by the euro area. What experiences do we draw from these years spent alongside the single currency? First, even though the euro is readily accepted as a means of payment in Switzerland, the use of the Swiss franc to settle transactions has not decreased. The share of the euro in our domestic payments corresponds approximately to that of the currencies it replaced. The euro obviously circulates more visibly in the border areas than in the centre of the country. The second observation we have made concerns the relationship between the franc and the euro. Many observers feared that the euro would cause a destabilization of the Swiss franc, exacerbating its role as a safe haven currency. This has not been the case at all. Of course, the franc has appreciated against the euro since the latter's introduction, but its price has not been as volatile as one might have feared. Since 1999, the franc has gained 7% in nominal terms against the European currency, some 3% if we take into account the inflation differential, i.e. in real terms. The fundamental tendency of the franc to appreciate, which was noted in the past against the German mark, has thus been maintained against the euro. In my opinion, the euro has played an important stabilizing role on the international scene by neutralizing the tensions that arose during rapid adjustments of the dollar. This effect is evident on the European front as the single currency has now replaced currencies that were often destabilized by the movements of the greenback. But this is also the case for the Swiss franc. The recent fall of the dollar is proof of this: while in the past the Swiss franc would have been under pressure, it has remained on the sidelines. In my opinion, the creation of the euro has profoundly changed the conditions under which the foreign exchange market operates. The euro and the dollar are now two currencies that serve each other as safe havens. The franc - given the relative narrowness of its market - no longer plays this role, a role that was its when Europe was not yet unified in monetary terms. Our currency is now evolving more in line with the fundamentals of the Swiss economy than with the tensions in the international monetary system. The emergence of the euro has therefore helped to stabilise the Franc market, which is excellent news for our exporters. However, the introduction of the euro poses a considerable challenge to the Swiss economy. Indeed, now that most of our trade with Europe is in a single currency, Swiss companies are faced with a concentration of their exchange rate risks. To protect themselves in this respect, they can use traditional financial instruments but they also practice natural "hedging", i.e. aiming to balance buying and selling transactions denominated in euros. Despite these exchange rate risk management techniques, it is undeniable that the degree of competitiveness of the Swiss economy, at least in the short term, remains largely dependent on the relationship between the Swiss franc and the euro on the market. Given this reality, the question of a possible peg of the franc to the euro is often raised. This strategic option is not current at National Bank for several reasons:  First, as we have seen, the cohabitation between the Swiss franc and the euro has so far been rather harmonious.  Secondly, the strength of the franc in recent years is for a largely a reflection of the fundamental factors of the Swiss and European economies. The real appreciation of the Swiss franc can be associated with greater flexibility in the economy Switzerland compared to that of the euro area. This finding may seem surprising. because Switzerland often projects the image of a country that is slow to react to changes environment. It's a mistake. Over the past ten years, there have been profound changes in the framework conditions of our economy: restructuring deep banking system, labour market liberalisation and adjustments consequent in the structure of industrial production. Admittedly, much remains to be done. we are also in the field of structural policy. Nevertheless, the economy Switzerland has probably proved to be more flexible than that of some of its neighbours this is reflected in the appreciation of the Franc. In case of anchoring of the latter to the euro, the forces of adjustment, today at work through the exchange rate, would be expressed through price developments. Swiss inflation would be in this case probably higher than that of its trading partners, without us having the means of controlling it.  Finally, the pegging of the Swiss franc to the euro would have consequences for the level of interest rates in Switzerland. The latter are currently the lowest in Europe, which is an important advantage for local businesses. If a credible anchor of the franc to the euro was to intervene, this difference would quickly fade by an increase Swiss rates of around two percentage points, which would seriously penalise our economy. In the end, therefore, it is not certain that the benefits of pegging the Swiss franc to the euro would offset the costs I have just mentioned. This conclusion prompted the Swiss National Bank to pursue an independent monetary policy based on the pursuit of price stability rather than on aligning the franc with the new European currency. That said, the franc-euro relationship remains essential for our economic development and has a great deal of weight in our monetary appreciations. Conclusion To conclude, I would like to stress that even if the Swiss financial centre faces new challenges, it can continue to rely on favourable conditions that have made it successful in the past: a stable political and monetary environment, tradition and know-how, and a reputation for discretion and efficiency. These conditions still give it a certain comparative advantage over its European competitors, particularly in the field of wealth management. However, this situation is changing rapidly. I have outlined four trends that I believe are currently critical to the future: increased global competition, declining revenues from financial transactions, loss of public confidence in financial statements and corporate governance, and rising risks of financial crime. These challenges concern both the Swiss financial centre and its French and European competitors. To thrive, financial centres have no choice but to be flexible and innovative. The globalization of markets and the intensification of competition impose on them the painful path of structural adjustments. In addition, the general liberalization of capital movements and the intensification of financial flows require them to effectively combat money-laundering and white-collar crime. Switzerland is aware of this. There is no doubt that the future position of its financial centre will depend directly on the responses it provides to these challenges.
