Im Mrz 2001 haben wir damit begonnen, die Zinsen massiv zu reduzieren, wodurch das angestrebte Niveau des Dreimonats-Libors von damals 3.50% auf heute 0.25% gesunken ist. Die Tatsache, dass die Geldpolitik keine dauerhafte Wirkung auf die realen Variablen hat, gilt selbstverstndlich auch fr den realen Wechselkurs. Natrlich kann man immer einen niedrigeren Wechselkurs wnschen, doch die Geldpolitik ist nicht in der Lage, einen solcher Wunsch zu erfllen. Der reale Wechselkurs ist  wie aus der Bezeichnung hervorgeht  von realen Faktoren wie den Produktivittsunterschieden zwischen den Lndern, der Entwicklung der Rahmenbedingungen und der Vernderung der Prferenzen abhngig. Es handelt sich um eine endogene Variable  um den Fachbegriff der konomen zu verwenden -, welche die Geldpolitik nicht dauerhaft kontrollieren kann. Jede dahingehende Bestrebung wre nicht nur nutzlos, sondern knnte auch usserst destabilisierend wirken. In den meisten internationalen Vergleichen unter den Industrielndern bildet die Schweiz das Schlusslicht, wenn es um das Wachstum des realen Bruttoinlandprodukts geht. Diese Lage ist Besorgnis erregend, auch wenn man sie etwas relativieren sollte. In der Tat hlt sich die Schweiz beim realen Pro-Kopf-Einkommen hartnckig in der Spitzengruppe. Heute wie gestern ist die Situation unseres Landes dank seines sehr hohen Lebensstandards beneidenswert. Das Paradox einer Volkswirtschaft, die langsamer fortschreitet als die anderen Volkswirtschaften und trotzdem immer vorn dabei ist, entsteht dadurch, dass das reale Bruttoinlandprodukt  so wie es blicherweise unter Vernachlssigung des aus der Verbesserung unserer Terms of Trade hervorgehenden Erfolgs berechnet wird  dazu neigt, die Wertschpfung in unserem Land zu unterschtzen. Gemss meinen eigenen Berechnungen, welche die letzten zwanzig Jahre umfassen, wird das Wachstum in der Schweiz jhrlich um durchschnittlich ungefhr 0.5% unterschtzt. Auch muss erwhnt werden, dass die Schweiz beachtliche Summen ins Ausland investiert und dass die Ertrge dieser Investitionen zwar in die Berechnung des Bruttosozialprodukts, nicht aber in jene des Bruttoinlandprodukts einfliessen. Interessanterweise berstieg im Verlauf des letzten Jahrzehnts die Wachstumsrate des Bruttosozialprodukts jene des Bruttoinlandprodukts jhrlich um ungefhr 0.6%. Schliesslich ist noch einzurumen, dass die offiziellen Statistiken dem helvetischen Perfektionismus nicht immer gerecht werden. Die Qualitt unserer Leistungen, unserer Infrastruktur und unserer Umgebung  also unsere Lebensqualitt  wird in den internationalen Vergleichen nicht immer zu ihrem richtigen Wert eingeschtzt. Zugegebenermassen kann dieser Perfektionismus allerdings sehr weit gehen. Es scheint, als besitze die Schweiz die Gabe, sich in Projekte zu strzen, deren Ertrge entweder kaum je greifbar oder aber hchst zweifelhaft sind. Wir investieren zum Beispiel betrchtliche Summen in die NEAT, obwohl es keinesfalls sicher ist, dass dieses Projekt unser Bruttoinlandprodukt jemals sichtbar oder messbar erhhen wird. Wie dem auch sei, die Schweiz hat in den letzten zwei Jahrzehnten in Sachen Wachstum eine enttuschende Leistung erbracht. Was kann dagegen unternommen werden? Da die Produktionskapazitt eines Landes in der Regel durch dessen Ausstattung mit Produktionsfaktoren, dessen Technologie, dessen Zugang zu den internationalen Mrkten und dessen Rahmenbedingungen definiert wird, muss auf diese Faktoren eingewirkt werden. Beginnen wir mit dem wichtigsten Faktor, der Arbeit. Alle Mittel mssen eingesetzt werden, um so viel Arbeitsleistung bereitzustellen wie mglich. Die Schlsselparameter sind die Beteiligungsquote, die Arbeitslosenquote, die wchentliche Arbeitszeit und das Rentenalter, sowie natrlich die steuerliche Belastung und die Lohnabzge. Es ist bedauerlich festzustellen, dass in den letzten Jahrzehnten nicht die Anreize zu arbeiten vermehrt worden sind, sondern diejenigen, unttig zu bleiben. Im brigen fllt auf, dass in den meisten europischen Lndern, darunter der Schweiz, der Beitrag des Faktors Arbeit zum Wirtschaftswachstum sehr bescheiden war. In einigen unserer Nachbarlnder war er sogar negativ. Glcklicherweise ist die Schweiz reich an Humankapital. Das muss zwingend so bleiben. Das Schulwesen und die Bildung sind wichtige Elemente in der Schaffung und Entwicklung dieses Kapitals. Es sei auch ohne Zgern auf die Immigration hingewiesen. Lngerfristig drfte die Aufnahme hoch qualifizierter Arbeitnehmer aus dem Ausland ebenfalls dazu beitragen, das Wachstumspotential in einem Land mit einer immer lter werdenden Bevlkerung zu erhalten. Ein anderer Produktionsfaktor, an dem kein Weg vorbeifhrt, ist das physische Kapital, das durch die Investitionen geufnet wird. In zahlreichen Lndern ist das physische Kapital der Hauptantrieb des Wirtschaftswachstums. Daher muss darauf geachtet werden, dass dieser Mechanismus nicht beeintrchtigt wird, sei es durch administrative Hindernisse oder andere Hrden. Unser Produktionswerkzeug muss stndig angepasst, modernisiert und verstrkt werden. Ein immer kapitalintensiverer Produktionsprozess darf nicht als Bedrohung fr die Arbeiter angesehen werden. Diese Entwicklung steigert im Gegenteil ihre Produktivitt und demnach auch ihr Einkommen. Auch sollte nicht davor zurckgeschreckt werden, jenseits unserer Grenzen zu investieren, und zwar in Lndern, die uns gegenber ein strkeres Wachstumspotential aufweisen, sei es wegen einer jngeren Bevlkerung, eines geringeren Kapitalbestands oder wegen grsserer natrlicher Ressourcen. Der Ertrag aus diesen Investitionen wird immer mehr an Bedeutung gewinnen, auch wenn er nicht in die Berechnung des Bruttoinlandprodukts einfliesst. Auf der oben erwhnten Grundlage beruht der technologische Fortschritt, der die Produktivittsgewinne erhht. Die Einfhrung neuer Technologien muss weder gefrchtet noch hinausgeschoben werden. Sie muss entschlossen vorangetrieben werden, denn sie bt auf die Wertschpfung eine Hebelwirkung aus. Die wissenschaftliche Forschung und die Aneignung neuer Kenntnisse leisten einen beachtlichen Beitrag zu dieser Dynamik. Darber hinaus darf die Bedeutung der Institutionen und der Rahmenbedingungen nicht unterschtzt werden. Sie spielen fr alle wirtschaftlichen Unterfangen eine grundlegende Rolle. Eine leistungsfhige Infrastruktur, gesunde Staatsfinanzen, ein wirksames und zuverlssiges Rechtssystem sowie eine dem nachhaltigen Wachstum frderliche Wirtschaftspolitik sind allesamt Faktoren, denen wir unsere volle Aufmerksamkeit schenken mssen. Grosse Anstrengungen mssen noch im Bereich des Binnenmarkts unternommen werden, wo bermssige Regulierungen, ein Mangel an Wettbewerb und eine rcklufige Produktivitt die Initiative der Unternehmer bremsen und die Konsumenten belasten. Diese werden durch eine beschrnkte Auswahl und durch im internationalen Vergleich hohe Preise gleich doppelt benachteiligt. Unsere dem globalen Wettbewerb ausgesetzten Industrien sind im Allgemeinen sehr leistungsfhig, whrend die fast ausschliesslich auf den Binnenmarkt ausgerichteten Unternehmen oft im Rckstand liegen. Die Kartellabsprachen und die Wettbewerbsverzerrungen mssen energisch und entschlossen bekmpft werden. Die administrativen Hindernisse und andere Hrden, die das Funktionieren der Mrkte einschrnken, mssen identifiziert und gnadenlos beseitigt werden. Als letzten Faktor mchte ich den Beitrag des internationalen Handels erwhnen, der uns erlaubt, unsere Uhren in l und unsere Schokolade in Computer umzuwandeln. Die Vorteile des Austausches sind ein wichtiger Punkt fr unseren wirtschaftlichen Wohlstand. Jede Initiative, die es uns erlaubt, unsere komparativen Vorteile  die in den Aktivitten mit hoher Wertschpfung liegen  bestmglich auszuspielen und unsere Terms of Trade ausbauen zu knnen, untersttzt direkt unser Einkommenswachstum. Selbst wenn das Wirtschaftswachstum der Allgemeinheit zu Gute kommt, kann es unbestreitbar fr einige Mitglieder unserer Gesellschaft schmerzliche Vernderungen verursachen. Strukturelle Anpassungen sind nie einfach, und Spannungen kommen oft vor. Es ist wichtig, dass sich die Allgemeinheit dieser Schwierigkeiten bewusst ist und dass sie bereit ist, Massnahmen zur Erleichterung des bergangs zu ergreifen und den betroffenen Personen zu helfen. Wenn dies nicht der Fall ist, steigt der Widerstand gegen nderungen, unabdingbare Reformen werden auf spter verschoben. Die Anpassungskosten sind unausweichlich und sie mssen in voller Kenntnis der Sachlage getragen werden. Je eher man die Anpassungen an die Hand nimmt, desto frher erntet man die Frchte des Wachstums. Zusammenfassend kann festgehalten werden, dass das Wirtschaftswachstum vorwiegend auf realen Faktoren beruht. Auf sie muss zuerst eingewirkt werden. Die Geldpolitik kann das Wachstumspotential nicht erhhen, aber sie kann wesentlich zu einem guten Verlauf des Wachstums beitragen, indem sie fr die Stabilitt der Preise und des Finanzsystems sorgt.

Title: Introductory Remarks, Half-yearly Media News Conference
text: Berne, 13 June 2003 Introductory remarks by Niklaus Blattner 1. Publication of a report on the stability of the financial system In future, the National Bank will publish a report annually on the stability of the Swiss financial system (Stability Report). The first such report will be included in the June issue of the National Bank's Quarterly Bulletin. From today, the report is available in electronic form on the National Bank's website. The publication forms part of the financial stability reporting by central banks which has become increasingly common in the past few years. This form of reporting reflects the growing significance of system stability. Confidence in the stability of the financial system is a decisive factor for economic development. It enables decision-makers in the business world to adopt a rational approach to consumption and savings. Furthermore, a stable financial system is a precondition for properly functioning financial markets. It thus creates the environment needed for implementing monetary policy. The National Bank's Stability Report gives the public an insight into the state of the financial system. It conveys the National Bank's evaluation of the stability of the system and provides indicators that may be used for an in-depth analysis. The report helps to identify potential areas of friction or imbalances that could jeopardise the stability of the system. The National Bank contributes to the stability of the financial system. This includes periodically informing the public on its assessment of the situation. The key characteristic of a stable financial system is that its components fulfil their function and prove resistant to shocks. The current report concentrates on two main components of the financial system: the banking sector and the financial market infrastructure. Individual banks are only considered if this is relevant for the overall picture. The report is designed as a supplement to the publications of the Federal Banking Commission (FBC). While one of the latter's responsibilities consists in monitoring individual banks (supervision of institutions), the National Bank has the task of overseeing the banking system, including its infrastructure (system supervision). The first section of the analysis of the banking sector is concerned with risk factors relevant to the system. It contains a description of the macro-economic and stock market environments. The consequences of these risks are then evaluated. Finally, the resilience of the banking sector is assessed. The second section of the report covers the main characteristics and developments of the financial market infrastructure and assesses their effects on system stability. Niklaus Blattner SNB Berne, 13 June 2003 2 The situation of the financial system The Swiss banking sector has proved resistant to the deterioration in the economy and to the collapse of the stock markets in 2002. On the one hand, the banking sector again showed positive results in the past year: despite a marked decline in profits compared with the previous year, earning power is close to the average for the last decade. On the other hand, the sector has maintained its capacity to absorb shocks. The capital ratios of the banking sector at the end of 2002 can be regarded as favourable both in an international and an historical comparison. It must be noted that institutions with considerable losses have introduced significant measures to strengthen their capital adequacy. Finally, no major imbalance was identified as the source of a potential crisis. The Swiss banking system is thus considered to be stable. The relatively robust results of the banking sector point to the significance of credit business as a source of income. The price collapse on the stock markets has led to a considerable reduction in income from asset management and investment banking and to losses in the banks' own trading portfolios. By contrast, the results from lending business are fairly satisfactory despite the economic slowdown. The growing risks connected with economic stagnation have therefore not impacted perceptibly on the banks' books. A deterioration in the quality of the banks' credit portfolio has so far not been observed. Nevertheless, two sources of potential tension in the banking system must be emphasised. First, should the economy remain weak, creditors' financial standing is likely to go from bad to worse, and this would make it necessary for banks to increase their provisions. A massive increase in reserve requirements, however, seems unlikely in view of the cautious credit policy pursued by the banks in recent years. It must also be borne in mind that the easing of monetary policy by the SNB helps to limit the extent and duration of the economic downturn in Switzerland. Second, the banks do not have unlimited possibilities to improve their income. They have introduced measures to increase their efficiency and to re-position themselves. These measures are designed to arrest the slide in income from trading and asset management business. However, the desired consolidation of income from off-balance-sheet business, which is of such great importance to the banks in Switzerland, would be called into question should the financial market slump persist or become even worse. The financial market infrastructure relating to the clearing and settlement of payments and of transactions with securities and other financial instruments presents a favourable picture. In this field, the Swiss financial centre operates with the Swiss Interbank Clearing (SIC) payment system and the SECOM securities settlement system, both of which have stood the test over the years and which contribute, by dint of their architecture, to minimising settlement risks. The launching of the international multi-currency payment system Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS) in September 2002 and of the central counterparty SIS x-clear in May 2003 makes it possible to further reduce the risks arising from the settlement of foreign exchange and securities transactions. In addition, Niklaus Blattner SNB Berne, 13 June 2003 3 organisational and technical measures are constantly taken to enhance the operational reliability of the systems. Overall, the Swiss financial centre has a well-functioning infrastructure, which also compares very favourably as regards security and efficiency with those of other countries. 2. Further improvement in banknote security Small denominations now also have perforated number Between October 1995 and October 1998, the Swiss National Bank put the different denominations of the current series of banknotes into circulation. They were phased in one at a time, beginning with the three smaller denominations and finishing with the three large ones. The banknotes in circulation have a large number of security features permitting holders to check whether the notes are genuine. Today we may say that the security system of this banknote series has stood the test. The number of counterfeits is low in an international comparison. Nevertheless, we should not rest on our laurels. The breakneck speed at which copying technology is developing offers counterfeiters increasingly better and cheaper technological possibilities to reproduce banknotes that look deceptively genuine. We therefore consider it our duty to introduce preventive measures with a view to constantly improving the security of our banknotes. As a further step towards improving this security system, we have upgraded the three smaller denominations with the perforated number. Only the larger denominations were equipped with this security feature up to now, because at the time the three small denominations were first issued the necessary technology was not yet available. The change relates to the 10-franc, 20-franc and 50-franc notes; the serial numbers of these banknotes start with 00. Thus all banknotes of the current series now bear the same security features. The perforated number is made up of laser-perforated figures. They can be applied thanks to a technology developed by Orell Fussli Security Printing Ltd, our banknote printers. When held up to the light, the denomination number of the note is seen as a perforated surface. A leaflet on this security feature, which also contains information on five other security features, can be obtained at all National Bank counters and will also be available at most commercial banks and post offices within the next few days. Banknotes with a small face value bearing a perforated number have already been put into circulation. Concurrently, banknotes without a perforated number are still in circulation. They will stay in circulation until they are worn out and replaced. Niklaus Blattner SNB Berne, 13 June 2003 4 3. Normalisation of banknote circulation following completion of the euro launch From the beginning of 2001 until the end of 2002, the change in the circulation of Swiss franc banknotes, expressed as percentages vis-a-vis the corresponding year-back values, was determined wholly by the introduction of euro cash on 1 January 2002. Based on a growth rate in the value of banknote circulation of approximately 2% at the beginning of 2001, note circulation rose steadily, reaching a peak of close to 12% at the end of January 2002. Subsequently, growth rates declined continuously. The current growth figure for banknote circulation  approximately 2%  again conforms to former rates. During the launch of the euro, circulation of the US dollar and the pound sterling largely corresponded to Swiss franc circulation. Annexe Selected passages from the Stability Report General operating conditions Both financial market conditions and the general operating environment for the banking sector deteriorated in 2002. For the first time since the mid-seventies, a downturn on the stock markets, accompanied by high volatility, coincided with a period of economic stagnation. The downtrend on the stock market, which started in mid-2000, continued in 2002 and volatility increased strongly, reaching a relatively high level by the end of 2002. This was accompanied by a rise in yield spreads on the bond market and an increase in the number of bankruptcies. In view of the weakness of the economy, this indicates a general reduction in the credit standing of borrowers. Profitability The Swiss banking sector was profitable overall in 2002. However, profits were far lower than in 2001. Moreover, there were major differences in level of profits and profit trends within the sector. Banks whose business is heavily dependent on stock market trends did far worse than those that focus on lending. Should economic stagnation last, the need for risk provisioning will increase, leading to lower profitability at banks that specialise in lending. Risk factors To assess the risk factors affecting banks, the SNB uses indicators for three types of risk: credit risk, interest rate risk and market risk. In terms of the proportion of non-performing loans and the level of write-downs and provisions, there was a further decline in credit risk of Swiss banks compared with 2001, bringing this indicator to a low level. Interest rate risk remains low and market risk declined slightly in 2002 compared with 2001. In Niklaus Blattner SNB Berne, 13 June 2003 5 short, the risk factors in the banking sector therefore declined slightly last year. However, credit risk is expected to rise this year as a result of the poor economic conditions. Capital adequacy At year-end 2002 the banks as a whole had a lower equity base than at the end of the previous year. The level of capitalisation is nevertheless adequate overall, and only a few banks have a low level of capital adequacy. Historically and by international standards, Swiss banks can be regarded as well-capitalised. Market assessment Market sentiment on the soundness of a bank is reflected in credit ratings, yield spreads and share prices. Although these indicators suggest that the Swiss banking sector is in relatively good shape, its position has deteriorated considerably over the past few years. This trend is mainly due to difficulties at individual banks.

Title: Review of economic situation
text: Economic overview Presentation by Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank General Assembly of the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry Thursday, 26 June 2003 Fribourg 2 1. Introduction For a small open economy like Switzerland - and I will not learn this from the members of your Federation - global economic development plays a central role. I will therefore begin my presentation with a presentation of the international environment and an analysis of the current economic cycle. Then I will take stock of the prospects for recovery in the major industrialized regions and emerging countries. I will then turn to the economic situation of our country and conclude with monetary policy considerations. 2. The international environment The first signs of a slowdown in the U.S. economy date back to mid-2000  exactly three years ago  when the bursting of the new technology bubble precipitated the correction of the stock markets. The ensuing crushing of demand for capital goods caused manufacturing output to fall. Private consumption subsequently weakened, but to a lesser extent. Watch exports across the Atlantic confirm this pattern: after experiencing high growth rates in 2000, they fell at the beginning of 2001. The countries of the European Monetary Union quickly followed America's lead. The contraction in external demand caused the euro area's exports of goods and services to stagnate in the 1st quarter of 2001, while they had still grown strongly in the previous months. The sluggishness of the external sector then spread to the domestic economy: Private consumption virtually stopped growing from the 3rd quarter of 2001. Here too, your figures reflect the cyclical evolution: there was a decline in watch sales in Europe from 2001, the countries of the East being less affected because of their need to catch up. 3 The attacks of 11 September and their devastating effects on confidence plunged the world economy further into recession. After a recovery began in the 1st half of 2002, activity in the main industrialized countries weakened again, against a backdrop of revelations of large-scale financial embezzlement, geopolitical tensions and sharp rise in energy prices. 2.1. Implications of the investment crisis for the international economy If I wanted to remind you of the main stages of the global economic cycle since the turn of the century, it is because they offer us important keys to identify the likely trends of the future economic evolution. Before reviewing the short-term growth prospects of industrialized regions and some emerging countries, I would like to develop two points of a more general nature. The first point concerns the macroeconomic consequences of what is generally referred to as the bursting of the information technology bubble. The essential characteristic of the late nineties was the overinvestment of companies, particularly in the United States, in high-tech capital goods, particularly computers. While it is still too early to offer a reliable analysis of the precise reasons for this excessive investment, we can nevertheless note the dynamics of outbidding that prevailed at the time. Many companies seemed eager not to miss the turning point of the IT revolution, even if the benefits of their investments seemed very unclear. Encouraged by the rapid fall in the prices of computer products and by the anxieties of the transition to the year 2000, the investment frenzy took on crazy proportions between 1996 and 2000. It has been intimately associated with soaring stock prices and the dollar as well as the rapid widening of the US current account deficit. Global savings, particularly in Europe, have not only made it possible to finance the investment of companies located on the other side of the Atlantic, but have also supported a boom in American private consumption. In other words, at the end of the nineties there was a phenomenon of transfer of 4 purchasing power to the United States. The Swiss watch industry has also benefited from this situation: according to your Federation's figures, watch exports to the US market recorded excellent results in the second half of the nineties. It is important to stress that this macroeconomic mechanism was perfectly understandable. From the point of view of the European, Japanese or Saudi investor, it was rational to take advantage of the new investment prospects across the Atlantic. On the side of American households, it was quite normal to consume more, even if it meant going into debt, to the extent that purchasing power grew, following the rise in real wages and the strengthening of the dollar. But obviously this evolution was unbalanced. What happens if the prospects for a high return on investment do not materialize? Well, it is the opposite movement that is underway: The flow of global savings to the United States is drying up and the dollar is falling, which leads to a slowdown in the American economy and a gradual rebalancing of the external deficit. We can thus see how the expansion of the late nineties was based on fragile and highly speculative foundations. I now come to my second general point, which relates to the current state of monetary policy. In the face of the slowdown in activity, central banks in developed countries have reduced their benchmark interest rates to a level rarely reached in the last fifty years. Calculated in real terms, i.e. adjusted for inflation, most of the remuneration paid on short-term papers flirts with zero and bond prices are at their zenith. Monetary conditions are therefore severely loosened and ultimately incompatible with price stability. When demand revives, significant monetary tightening will be inevitable. Some factors favorable today to consumption and real estate will no longer be present. 5 These considerations lead me to three thoughts.  First, the continued surge in U.S. domestic demand seen in the late nineties is not expected to be repeated as indebted U.S. consumers will have little room to grow spending faster than their income.  Secondly, the decline of the dollar below the peak reached at the beginning of 2002 is an integral part of the adjustment mechanism for the gradual reduction of the United States' external deficit. For many observers, its level in recent years was artificially supported by exceptional capital flows. Its current level therefore better corresponds to the fundamental realities of the US economy and should contribute to the rebalancing of its external accounts.  Finally, the global economic recovery will only be likely to be balanced - and therefore sustainable - if Europe is able to offer attractive investment opportunities for its savings. 2.2. Short-term outlook for the world economy Let us now turn to the short-term economic outlook for the major industrialized and emerging economies. In the United States, the marked slowdown in the dynamics of private consumption is at the origin of the slowdown in GDP growth observed during the 4th quarter of 2002 and the first quarter of this year. Rarely, consumption of durable goods fell two quarters in a row, contracting by nearly 3%. While the exact timing of the recovery is particularly difficult to identify, recent developments point to an early acceleration in growth. 6  First of all, a massive fiscal policy impulse is now in place. President Bush has just signed his second plan for tax relief and increased public spending, which for the next four quarters amounts to 1.5% of GDP. The sharp rise in household disposable income expected in the 3rd quarter should give a boost to private consumption.  Second, the Federal Reserve, the Fed, has announced that it wants to vigorously combat any danger of deflation. This determination has helped to ease financial conditions significantly: Yields on ten-year federal government bonds have risen from nearly 4% to 3.3% in less than two months, risk premia in the bond market have stabilized at a low level, stock prices are rising and the dollar has accelerated its decline against major currencies.  The third positive element is the rather encouraging signals of economic activity indicators recorded after the end of hostilities in Iraq. In particular, there is a trend stabilization of employment and a normalization of activity in the manufacturing sector. The significant increase in new orders recorded in May, if confirmed, gives hope for an acceleration of production in the near future, especially since the level of stocks is particularly low.  Finally, on the investment side, over the past year and a half, there has been a strong recovery in demand for IT products, which testifies to the increased need for renewal in an area marked by rapid obsolescence. In the field of industrial and transport equipment, net capital accumulation (i.e. taking depreciation into account) was very low or even negative. This implies that an increase in final demand will quickly translate into the need to expand production capacity. This extension will be encouraged by a very low financing cost. 7 In summary, highly expansive economic policy conditions coupled with a growing need to catch up in the area of investment and private consumption will be the drivers of the acceleration of growth in the short term. On a more distant horizon, the inevitable rise in interest rates combined with the necessary rebalancing of global demand should keep US growth below its performance in the second half of the nineties. The short-term outlook for the Eurozone economy is less encouraging than that of the United States:  Firstly, the less expansive nature of economic policy, particularly in the area of taxation, must be stressed. As the necessary budgetary reforms in the area of expenditure have been neglected during the boom years, the sharp slowdown in activity and therefore in revenue has dangerously brought the deficits of the three largest economies in the euro area closer to the limit imposed by the European Stability and Growth Pact, namely 3% of GDP. The France and Germany are expected to exceed this limit in 2002 and 2003. While a temporary overrun of the 3% may be economically justified in the event of a downturn in the economy in order to allow automatic stabilisers to operate, the current situation excludes more radical structural measures such as the reduction of the tax burden or the discretionary increase in state expenditure. At the dawn of the challenge posed by the financing of pensions and health costs as well as the integration of new members into the union, it would be disastrous to let deficits and public debt slip away. On monetary policy, the ECB did not consider it desirable to intervene as quickly and massively as the Fed did. Between May 2001 and June 2003, the ECB lowered its benchmark interest rate by 275 basis points. The reduction is half that of the Fed. The main difficulty encountered by the European issuing institution was the high inertia of inflation to meet the formal criterion of price stability, i.e. to be between 0 and 2%. 8  The second unfavourable element relates to the continued and strong appreciation of the euro, in particular against the dollar. As we all know very well here, the appreciation of the currency reduces the competitiveness of domestic industry vis-a-vis its foreign competitors. The strength of the euro is therefore likely to slow down the transmission of cyclical impulses from the United States to Europe.  The third element is the total sluggishness of European domestic demand. This weakness, peculiar to the economies of continental Europe, has multiple and complex causes that are still insufficiently understood. One of the reasons is certainly the lack of flexibility and competition in the field of the labour market in particular. In particular, the rigidity of contractual forms does not make it possible to adapt production structures quickly in the event of a shock and restricts the willingness of companies to invest and create new places of work. The IMF recently estimated that a reform of the labour, goods and services markets in order to achieve the level of competition observed in the United States would ultimately boost European GDP by 10%. Not to mention the very large material gain, this would contribute positively to the readjustment of global spending that I mentioned earlier. In summary, growth in the Eurozone is expected to remain more modest than in the other part of the Eurozone and to restart only in its wake. The export sector will undoubtedly be the driving force behind the recovery but will suffer from the high level of the European currency. Given the lack of dynamism in domestic demand, particularly in Germany, there is little hope of an autonomous recovery of activity within the zone. The short-term economic outlook for the Japanese economy remains subordinate to developments in the external environment, particularly in the United States and Asia. The engine of domestic demand is completely gripped by a financial sector on the verge of bankruptcy and by the continuous fall in prices. Unless there is a complete consolidation of the banking sector and public finances, it is very unlikely that growth will eventually and sustainably exceed 1%. The own positive element 9 Japan lies in its increased interdependence with one of the world's most dynamic economies: China. After having been a competitor and forcing Japanese industry to many relocations, the Chinese economy now represents a very important outlet for Japanese exports. Sales of Japanese products to China account for about 10% of the total value of exports. In 2002, their growth exceeded 30% compared to 6.4% for total exports. Once the effects of atypical pneumonia have subsided in China and the recovery emerges across the Atlantic, it is reasonable to expect a significant contribution of foreign trade to Japanese growth even if, as I mentioned before, the overall performance of the Japanese economy should remain very modest. In emerging economies, cyclical situations are generally very different. However, most of them are linked to one factor: international trade. After the latter recovered strongly in the first three quarters of 2002, causing a sharp acceleration in growth in emerging countries, particularly in Asia, it is a safe bet that it has weakened again since then. The development of Asian exports remains closely linked to the evolution of activity in industrialized countries, even if the emergence of demand from China has caused a slight decoupling. Economies in the region are also suffering from the after-effects of atypical pneumonia. In Hong Kong, where the epidemic has already infected nearly 2,000 people and killed nearly 300, retail, hotels and more generally tourism have been strongly affected. Morgan Stanley estimates the decline in retail and leisure consumer spending at 20% year-on-year during the month of April. Even though the infectious peak seems to have passed and although the WHO has recently lifted its recommendation to avoid Hong Kong, the return to normal activity levels will take time. As the emerging economies of Asia are specialized in the production of electronic equipment, it is reasonable to expect that the necessary renewal of equipment in industrialized countries will support their export activity in the short and medium term. 10 For oil-dependent economies such as the Gulf countries or Russia, the recent drop in oil prices is expected to slow activity. In particular, Russian private consumption is unlikely to maintain the tremendous momentum observed during 2002. Middle Eastern countries, for their part, are expected to suffer from a prolonged slowdown in tourism and investment following the military intervention in Iraq. For the major economies of South America, with the notable exception of Venezuela, the situation has recently improved significantly. It is true that the region suffered in 2001-02 the worst reversal of fortune in 20 years. Whether in Brazil or Argentina, activity recovered in the second half of 2002 thanks in part to the sharp devaluation of the Real and peso, which boosted the net contribution of foreign trade. Even though confidence among international investors  particularly in the case of Brazil  and consumers appears to be returning, domestic demand remains hesitant. The expected recovery in industrialized countries, particularly the United States, should help gradually put the region's economies back on a safer track. Given the size and structure of their external debt, however, they remain particularly exposed to fluctuations in international foreign exchange and capital markets. 3. The Swiss economy 3.1. Switzerland in the face of the global investment crisis In Switzerland, economic developments have closely followed those of the world economy. As in the United States, growth peaked in the fourth quarter of 1999. Our economy was then in a situation of full utilization of its production capacity, the overcapacity inherited from the previous period of stagnation having been absorbed. A slowdown in growth was therefore desirable to the extent that excessive demand should not lead to overheating. Constraints 11 which limited the growth of production became particularly visible with regard to the labour force, particularly in the search for qualified personnel. As inflationary pressures soon emerged in such circumstances, the SNB considered it necessary to pursue a more restrictive monetary policy. Thus, starting in February 2000, we tightened monetary conditions. In the course of 2000, the Swiss economy seemed to be converging towards gross domestic product growth closer to its long-term potential, i.e. 1.5% to 2% per year. This could have made it possible to maintain the situation of full capacity utilisation while limiting the risks of price pressure. Unfortunately, this soft landing of the economy did not take place. From the first quarter of 2001 onwards, the Swiss economy entered a phase of sudden stagnation when domestic and international demand for capital goods fell sharply. The international investment crisis and the collapse of the stock markets have hit us particularly hard. The decline in activity was more marked here than in the United States or the Eurozone. The reason lies in the fact that our economy is specialized in two sectors that have been most affected by the decline in demand: I am thinking of course of the capital goods industry, but also the financial sector. Let us first address the aspect of demand for capital goods. In the second half of the nineties, we experienced a period in Switzerland during which the growth of investment in equipment was stronger and more resilient than in past business cycles. The tendency towards over-investment manifested itself in us too. The correction that followed was, therefore, particularly abrupt. In the second quarter of 2000, investment in equipment was still up by 9%. Three quarters later, they fell by 8%. At present, investment has been declining for nine consecutive quarters. 12 It is interesting to note that the phase of strong expansion did not affect all categories of capital goods in the same way. While the growth in investment in machinery and apparatus has been only modest, investment in precision instruments has evolved more markedly. However, the investment boom has been fuelled mainly by spending on information technology. For example, investment in computers increased by about 300% between 1993 and 2000. When the correction took place, from the beginning of 2001, it was indeed in this sector of new technologies that it was the strongest. In addition, another sector in which the decline in investment has been particularly massive is that of air transport. This is related to the specific problems that the sector is going through, problems painfully felt these days. One of the factors that characterizes the fall in investment during this cycle is the perfect simultaneity with which it has taken place at the international level. As a result, Swiss producers of capital goods have been confronted not only with the decline in domestic demand but also with the collapse of international demand. However, one third of our merchandise exports are capital goods. The fact that Switzerland has been more affected than other countries by the crisis in global demand for capital goods is confirmed by the evolution of manufacturing activity: the decline in manufacturing production has been significantly more marked here than in the United States or Euroland. For its part, the correction in the financial markets has hit the banking and insurance sector hard. The fall in asset prices has led to a sharp decrease in the volume of transactions and therefore in revenues for banks and asset managers. As a result, many institutes have suffered losses. This sector, which had hitherto been one of the engines of growth in value added and employment, contracted in 2001 and 2002. Given the importance of banks and insurance companies for the Swiss economy  almost 13% of total value added  the decline in activity in these branches weighed heavily on growth. The industry quickly responded to these 13 difficulties through a restructuring and consolidation effort. In the short term, this has resulted in new strategic orientations, reorganizations of productive structures, mergers  especially in the field of wealth management  as well as job reductions. This effort  which is also still ongoing  is however necessary to ensure the strength and competitiveness of the sector in the medium term. 3.2. The current situation remains gloomy So what is the current economic situation? Productive activity remained very weak at the beginning of this year. Real gross domestic product fell by 1% in the first quarter. Second-quarter indicators have so far failed to provide the signs of recovery in activity that might have been expected after the end of the conflict in Iraq. Despite the decline in oil prices and the stabilization of financial markets, the economies of our main partner countries are struggling to recover. In Switzerland, domestic demand experienced several quarters of decline, before returning to slight growth in the first quarter of this year. However, throughout this period - and contrary to what has generally been observed during past cycles - private consumption has never stopped growing. At this level, however, an important distinction must be made. The components of private consumption that have continued to grow are primarily consumption of health services and expenditure on housing, the changes of which are determined rather by medium- and long-term structural factors, such as demographic factors or changes in preferences. Consumption of goods of a more cyclical nature, on the other hand, shows signs of weakness. Two categories of products are particularly affected: durable goods and luxury goods. Thus, new car registrations have been in constant decline since the end of 2000. In February and March, the 'Personal effects' component of the Swiss retail turnover index - of which watch sales are a key component - fell sharply in real terms compared to the same months of the previous year. Uncertainty is now pushing Swiss consumers to be cautious and therefore to delay 14 expenditure on goods not immediately necessary. This uncertainty arises from several factors. Among these is undoubtedly the deterioration of conditions on the labour market. Unemployment has been on the rise since the spring of 2001. In addition, job cuts are also affecting sectors  particularly banking and insurance  that are important for the demand for non-essential or luxury goods. A second factor is related to the increased influence of financial market performance on consumer behaviour as the number of households investing part of their savings in equities has risen sharply since the early nineties. There is no doubt that the evolution of stock market indices is probably considered by households, much more than in the past, as an indicator of the state of health of the economy and therefore of their financial prospects. Finally, the problems faced by pension funds encourage households to be cautious. As a result, the difficulties experienced by the financial markets in 2001 and 2002 certainly had a negative impact on consumer demand. For its part, public consumption has so far helped to support demand. Despite the economic slowdown, it has indeed continued to grow, even in periods markedly. However, public finances are now in a difficult situation. The cause of the negative evolution of the public accounts lies in the decrease in tax receipts (direct tax, withholding tax, VAT and stamp duty) caused by the poor macroeconomic performance, while expenditure continued to grow at a steady pace. The Federal Council has responded by adopting a package of expenditure reduction measures. Most of their effect will not be perceived until 2005. In the short term, therefore, public consumption should continue to grow, but the momentum is destined to slow down. Investments in equipment are currently providing tentative signs of improvement. Since the beginning of the crisis in 2001, they have fallen by almost 20%. It can thus be assumed that the excesses in this area have largely been corrected. In the first quarter of this year, investments were still declining. However, the decline was significantly smaller than in previous quarters. By 15 elsewhere, new orders recorded by Swiss producers of capital goods have stopped falling for three quarters. However, investments depend on two factors: their cost and their return. Monetary policy is acting on the first: the reduction of interest rates helps to create favourable conditions for the recovery of investments by reducing the cost of financing them. But this is not enough. A real return to investment growth depends crucially on improving companies' sales prospects. Only an improvement in expectations regarding the evolution of demand and the degree of utilization of production capacity can push firms to renew or even increase their capital stock. Switzerland's economic recovery therefore depends on the recovery in demand for our export goods. In 1980, 30% of gross domestic product was made up of exports of goods and services. This figure has grown steadily over time. Currently, the share of foreign trade in Swiss GDP is 45%. This means that foreign demand plays a central role for the Swiss economy. A revival of exports is expected to increase the degree of use of the productive apparatus in industry. Given the long period of investment restraint, the improvement in production prospects should, in turn, trigger a recovery in capital formation fairly quickly. This, in turn, will ensure further job creation, a reduction in unemployment and an improvement in consumer sentiment. Of course, this mechanism will not be able to be triggered until the recovery takes hold in the United States and Europe. The current weakness in activity in these two regions means that Swiss exports were still declining in April. The SURVEYS OF COMPANIES conducted in May by the KOF Institute did not yet send signals of improvement. New orders remained down overall and manufacturing output declined, so that firms continue to cope with weak demand through a cost-cutting effort in the form of a squeeze on their 16 stocks as well as a decrease in staff. In the second quarter, we are unlikely to see GDP growth. 3.3. Framework conditions are favourable for recovery As we have just seen, signs of a recovery in activity are slow to appear. Experience shows, however, that cyclical downturns usually occur suddenly and quickly. So what are the hopes for a return to growth based on?  One element is undoubtedly the correction of overcapacity that has taken place. But there are other arguments. Economic policies have been oriented to create an enabling environment for recovery. In particular, monetary policies at the international level have been eased to facilitate a recovery in activity, even though, as I described above, the US Federal Reserve has reacted more quickly and aggressively than the European Central Bank. In Switzerland too  and I will come to this in a moment  the effort to ease monetary conditions has been very important.  Financial markets seem to want to bet cautiously on an economic upturn. The rapid end of the conflict in Iraq has eliminated a number of uncertainties in the global economy. The price of oil fell and as soon as the positive outcome of the conflict became clear, the stock markets stopped their downward movement. Since then, equity price indices have returned to an upward trend. Thus, compared to the lowest point reached in mid-March, the Dow Jones rose by more than 20% while the Swiss Stock Exchange (SPI) rose by nearly 35%. The losses that had been recorded in the first three months of the year were thus more than compensated.  Price developments remain under control, both in Switzerland and abroad. Our recent inflation forecast indicates that inflation is expected to remain very low in 2003 and 17 2004. Through its effects on production costs, a monetary policy oriented towards price stability contributes to maintaining the competitive capacity of Swiss industry. For its part, the decentralized structure of the wage bargaining system ensures that wage dynamics align with productivity gains. Since the mid-nineties, these two factors have ensured a moderate evolution of labour costs. In addition, it should also be noted that the flexibility of our labour market allows Swiss companies to quickly adjust their production structure to new needs.  Overall, exchange rate developments are satisfactory. Since the beginning of this year, the Swiss franc has depreciated by almost 6% against the euro. The European currency has lost about 5% of its value since its introduction. In real terms, however, the depreciation is minimal (0.4%). Meanwhile, the dollar exchange rate has fallen to around CHF 1.30/. In June last year it was still above 1.50 CHF/. This drop in the price of the Us currency penalizes companies that export to the dollar zone, especially watch exports. As I indicated earlier, however, this decline in the dollar is a correction that reflects a rebalancing of international capital flows. In this sense, more than an appreciation of the Swiss franc, this is a problem specific to the US currency. 4. Swiss monetary policy Let me now turn to monetary policy considerations. Over the past two years, the SNB has reacted vigorously to the economic slowdown and the pressures that may have arisen on the foreign exchange market. The environment of price stability has allowed us to reduce the libor fluctuation band by 325 basis points since March 2001. The most recent action was on March 6 of this year. On this occasion, we have reduced the fluctuation band of the libor of 18 50 basis points at 0-0.75% specifying that we intend to keep the rate in the lower part of the band, around 0.25%. Just recently, we decided to leave the degree of monetary policy restraint unchanged. In a context of still uncertain global economic recovery, we intend to apply an expansive monetary policy and maintain unattractive yields on the Swiss franc. However, price stability is not threatened. Assuming that the libor remains constant at 0.25%, annual inflation is expected to be around 0.6% in 2003 and to decline slightly in 2004 before gradually increasing to 1.2% in 2005. It should be noted that the slowdown expected at the beginning of 2004 is the direct consequence of a base effect due to the evolution of the price of oil. Despite our desire to maintain expansive monetary conditions, the economic upturn is not guaranteed and some are concerned that low inflation will turn into deflation. We consider the risk of a generalized and sustained decline in the price level to be very low. It is quite possible that prices will fall during a specific month, for example as a result of a decrease in the price of imported goods. Nevertheless, deflation combined with a significant and persistent contraction in demand and output seems unlikely to us, provided that the Swiss franc does not appreciate strongly. In this case, we would take all necessary measures to restore appropriate monetary conditions, including intervening directly in the foreign exchange market. It will certainly not have escaped some of you that monetary aggregates  which measure the amount of money present in the economy  have been growing at a very steady pace for several quarters. The speed of their progression even equals that observed during the eighties. The question therefore arises of the possible inflationary impact of such a development. I would like to point out three things. First of all, this situation simply reflects the fact that we are currently and deliberately offering a generous supply of bank liquidity. Secondly, the public, scalded by 19 stock market setbacks, and uncertain economic developments, tend to hold more liquidity than usual, which translates into an increase in monetary aggregates. This additional liquidity is retained as a precautionary measure and is not used to increase spending. The quite normal development of bank credit confirms this. Finally, our economy has enough unused capacity, especially in the area of labour, to cope with an increase in demand without an immediate inflationary threat. We are therefore confident that we have sufficient time to tighten monetary controls when the recovery is confirmed without risking reviving inflationary pressures that could threaten price stability. Some are calling for the dollar factor to enter more weight into our monetary policy decisions. They greatly underestimate everything that has already been done to create the best possible conditions in the foreign exchange market and greatly overestimate our real ability to adjust the economic situation. The SNB is well aware of the problems posed to our economy by the recent correction of the dollar. We take into account developments in the foreign exchange market in our assessments of the economic situation and price developments. Those who argue for a more active foreign exchange policy generally have the secret hope that the SNB, through a deliberate policy of depreciation of the franc, can boost exports. Such a strategy  reminiscent of the competitive devaluations of the past  is based on the illusion that the Central Bank can manipulate exchange rate relations in a sustainable way to its liking without compromising monetary stability. Experience has shown us that this cannot be the case. Today, it must be recognized that the franc is not overvalued. The relationship that has been established between the franc and the euro shows this. Of course the relationship between the franc and the dollar is more volatile and more difficult to judge. It depends directly on the rate between the dollar and the euro. If we knew that the dollar was overvalued when it was worth 1.80 francs, it is certainly closer today to an equilibrium rate than it was at the time. Wanting to artificially create new exchange rate relations would only be possible through massive interventions - the success of which would only be successful. 20 not even insured but whose risks would be certain - while our economy already has ample liquidity. Conclusion What conclusions can be drawn from this analysis?  First, we must maintain confidence: the recovery of the world economy is underway, past mistakes will soon be corrected, but cyclical warming is more gradual than expected last year. In the United States, growth will no longer benefit from the extremely favourable conditions of the late nineties. The lack of savings will not stimulate the revival of domestic demand. In Europe, slow progress in the process of structural adjustments of economies will remain a burden on growth. It is highly desirable for our Continent to emancipate itself at the economic level. For the moment it remains directly dependent on the American engine.  Switzerland is able to capture any shudder in global demand. Our production apparatus is cost competitive and technologically level. It was able to restructure during the phase of low growth that we are still experiencing.  The recovery of our economy will therefore depend directly on the evolution of the world economy. In this respect, it is desirable that we make the most of opportunities outside Europe. Asia and South America are poles of growth; the U.S. market will be the first to recover. In this regard, the well-balanced distribution of watch exports is an example to follow.  In Switzerland, growth will recover moderately as it will initially be driven only by exports. Then investments, then consumption will take 21 the relay. It is probably that this recovery pattern will also be that of our European neighbours.  Monetary policy is currently expansive in our country, and it will remain so as long as price stability is not threatened. The recent correction of the franc against the euro has led to a further  and welcome  easing of monetary conditions. The course of our policy is well suited to the circumstances of the moment.  Finally, the economic recovery will only be sustainable at the international level if it is more balanced than in the previous cycle. Europe and Switzerland must do everything possible to make investment more attractive in their markets. The flight of savings to the United States was at the root of the distortions we experienced in the late nineties. It would not have happened if a more courageous policy of liberalising European markets had been applied. It is in this direction that our efforts must now go so that we can achieve stronger European growth - necessary for full employment and the defence of our social achievements - and ensure a more balanced functioning of the international financial markets.

Cette baisse du cours de la devise amricaine pnalise des entreprises qui exportent dans la zone dollar, notamment les exportations horlogres. Comme je lai indiqu auparavant toutefois, ce repli du dollar est une correction qui reflte un rquilibrage des mouvements internationaux de capitaux. En ce sens, plus que dune apprciation du franc suisse il sagit dun problme propre  la devise amricaine. 4. La politique montaire suisse Jen viens maintenant aux considrations de politique montaire. Au cours des deux dernires annes, la banque nationale a nergiquement ragi face au ralentissement conjoncturel et aux pressions qui ont pu se manifester sur le march des changes. Lenvironnement de stabilit des prix nous a permis de rduire la marge de fluctuation du libor de 325 points de base depuis mars 2001. Laction la plus rcente remonte au 6 mars de cette anne. A cette occasion, nous avons ramen la marge de fluctuation du libor de 18 50 points de base  0-0,75% en spcifiant que nous entendions maintenir le taux dans la partie infrieure de la bande, aux alentours de 0,25%. Tout rcemment, nous avons dcid de laisser inchang le degr de restriction de la politique montaire. Dans un contexte de reprise conomique mondiale encore incertain, nous entendons ainsi appliquer une politique montaire expansive et conserver des rendements peu attractifs sur le franc suisse. La stabilit des prix nest cependant pas menace. Si lon part de lhypothse que le libor reste constant  0,25%, linflation annuelle devrait avoisiner 0,6% en 2003 pour flchir lgrement en 2004 avant daugmenter progressivement et atteindre 1,2% en 2005. Il faut noter que le ralentissement prvu au dbut de 2004 est la consquence directe dun effet de base d  lvolution du prix du ptrole. Malgr notre volont de conserver des conditions montaires expansives, lembellie conjoncturelle nest pas garantie et certains sinquitent que le bas niveau de linflation ne se mue en dflation. Nous estimons le risque dun recul gnralis et durable du niveau des prix comme trs faible. Il est tout  fait possible que les prix baissent durant un mois prcis, suite par exemple  une diminution du prix des biens imports. Nanmoins, une dflation associe  une contraction importante et tenace de la demande et de la production nous semble improbable, pour autant que le franc suisse ne sapprcie fortement. Dans ce cas de figure, nous prendrions toutes les mesures ncessaires au rtablissement de conditions montaires appropries, y compris intervenir directement sur le march des changes. Il naura certainement pas chapp  certains dentre vous que les agrgats montaires  qui mesurent la quantit de monnaie prsente dans lconomie  croissent  un rythme trs soutenu depuis plusieurs trimestres. La vitesse de leur progression gale mme celle observe au cours des annes quatre-vingt. Il se pose donc la question de lventuel impact inflationniste dune telle volution. Je ferai remarquer trois choses. Tout dabord, cette situation reflte simplement le fait que nous offrons actuellement et de manire dlibre un apport gnreux de liquidit bancaire. Deuximement, le public, chaud par 19 les revers boursiers, et incertain de lvolution conjoncturelle, tend  dtenir plus de liquidit que dhabitude, ce qui se traduit par une augmentation des agrgats montaires. Cette liquidit supplmentaire est conserve  titre de prcaution et ne sert pas  augmenter les dpenses. Le dveloppement tout  fait normal du crdit bancaire nous le confirme. Finalement, notre conomie dispose de suffisamment de capacit inemploye, en particulier dans le domaine de la main duvre, pour faire face  une augmentation de la demande sans menace inflationniste immdiate. Nous sommes, par consquent, convaincus que nous disposons de suffisamment de temps pour resserrer les rnes montaires lorsque que la reprise se confirmera sans risquer de ranimer des tensions inflationnistes susceptibles de menacer la stabilit des prix. Certains demandent que le facteur dollar entre avec plus de poids dans nos dcisions de politique montaire. Ils sous-estiment largement tout ce qui a dj t entrepris pour crer les meilleures conditions possibles sur le march des changes et surestiment grandement nos capacits relles de rglage de la conjoncture. La Banque nationale est bien consciente des problmes que pose  notre conomie la rcente correction du dollar. Nous tenons compte des dveloppements du march des changes dans nos apprciations de la conjoncture et de l'volution des prix. Ceux qui plaident pour une politique plus active dans le domaine des changes ont gnralement le secret espoir que la BNS, par une politique dlibre de dprciation du franc, puisse doper les exportations. Une telle stratgie - qui rappelle les dvaluations comptitives du pass - repose sur l'illusion que la Banque centrale puisse manipuler  son got les relations de change de manire durable sans compromettre la stabilit montaire. L'exprience nous a montr que cela ne peut tre le cas. Aujourd'hui force est de reconnatre que le franc n'est pas survalu. La relation qui s'est tablie entre le franc et l'euro le montre. Bien sr la relation entre le franc et le dollar est plus volatile et plus difficile  juger. Elle dpend directement du cours qui s'tablit entre le dollar et l'euro. Si nous savions que le dollar tait survalu lorsqu'il valait 1.80 francs, il est certainement plus proche aujourd'hui d'un cours d'quilibre qu'il ne l'tait  l'poque. Vouloir crer artificiellement de nouvelles relations de change ne serait possible que par des interventions massives - dont le succs ne serait 20 mme pas assur mais dont les risques seraient certains - alors que notre conomie dispose dj d'amples liquidits. Conclusion Quelles conclusions tirer de cette analyse ?  En premier lieu, nous devons garder confiance : le redressement de l'conomie mondiale est en cours, les erreurs passes seront bientt corriges, mais le rchauffement conjoncturel est plus progressif que ce que l'on attendait l'an dernier. Aux Etats-Unis la croissance ne bnficiera plus des conditions extrmement favorables de la fin des annes nonante. Le manque d'pargne ne permettra pas de stimuler la relance de la demande interne. En Europe, la lenteur des progrs du processus des ajustements structurels des conomies restera une charge pour la croissance. Il est hautement souhaitable que notre Continent s'mancipe sur le plan conjoncturel. Pour l'instant il reste directement dpendant du moteur amricain.  La Suisse est apte  saisir tout frmissement de la demande mondiale. Notre appareil de production est comptitif au plan des cots et il est  niveau au plan technologique. Il a su se restructurer durant la phase de faible croissance que nous connaissons encore.  Le redmarrage de notre conomie va donc dpendre directement de l'volution de l'conomie mondiale. A cet gard il est souhaitable que nous exploitions autant que faire se peut les opportunits extra-europennes. L'Asie et l'Amrique du Sud sont des ples de croissance; le march amricain sera le premier  se redresser. A ce propos, la distribution bien quilibre des exportations horlogres est un exemple  suivre.  En Suisse, la croissance va se redresser modrment car elle ne sera tout d'abord tire que par les exportations. Ensuite les investissements, puis la consommation prendront 21 le relais. Il est probablement que ce schma de reprise sera aussi celui de nos voisins europens.  La politique montaire est actuellement expansive dans notre pays, et elle le restera tant que la stabilit des prix ne sera pas menace. La rcente correction du franc face  l'euro a provoqu un relchement supplmentaire - et bienvenu - des conditions montaires. Le cours de notre politique est bien adapt aux circonstances du moment.  Enfin la reprise conomique ne sera durable au plan international que si elle est plus quilibre que lors du cycle prcdent. L'Europe et la Suisse doivent tout entreprendre pour rendre l'investissement plus attrayant dans leur march. La fuite de l'pargne vers les Etats-Unis a t  l'origine des distorsions que nous avons connues  la fin des annes nonante. Elle ne se serait pas produite si une politique plus courageuse de libralisation des marchs europens avait t applique. C'est dans ce sens que doivent aller maintenant nos efforts afin que nous puissions enregistrer une plus forte croissance europenne - ncessaire au plein-emploi et  la dfense de nos acquis sociaux - et assurer un fonctionnement plus quilibr des marchs financiers internationaux.

Title: Monetary policy: current situation and development
text: MONETARY POLICY: SITUATION AND DEVELOPMENT Prof. Dr. Niklaus Blattner Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank economiesuisse Directors and Managing Directors Conference Zurich, August 19, 2003 Dear Sir or Madam, I look forward to joining your circle today. My task is to comment on the current economic situation and recent market movements from the point of view of the Swiss National Bank. Above all, however, I would like to deal with the topic of "monetary policy and the exchange rate". This topic is regularly critically monitored, especially from your circle, sometimes with the request that the National Bank should have a direct influence on one or the other currency pair. Economic situation and market movements There can be no doubt that a sustainable upswing in Switzerland presupposes a prior recovery abroad. The prospects for this have recently improved somewhat, at least with regard to the USA. However, caution is still warranted, as the indicators are by no means clear yet. After all, they show a more balanced picture than just a few months ago. The strong monetary and fiscal stimulus contributed significantly to the brightening of the picture in the USA. Some leading indicators improved. For the first time in a long time, investments in the USA also rose again in the 2nd quarter. The situation in Europe is different. The expectation expressed here and there of an imminent recovery, also in Europe, is still largely based on sentiment indicators and less on effectively improved data. In Switzerland, we still have little evidence of an improved situation. A further decline in economic activity is likely to have taken place in the 2nd quarter. We expect a stabilization in the current quarter and a slight recovery in the 4th quarter at the earliest, but probably not until spring 2004. The prerequisite for this is that the expected recovery in the USA is lasting and also gives impetus to European countries. The international financial markets are signalling confidence. The recovery of the stock markets began in March. Yields on the capital markets have also been rising since June. The US Federal Reserve also contributed to this: at the end of June, it lowered key interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, albeit accompanied by a mixed statement. Low key interest rates, deflation risks and upswing expectations formed a strange combination. This was apparently difficult for the markets to interpret. Finally, long-term interest rates rose very significantly. The bottom line was that the effective monetary Conditions, i.e. the sum of interest rates and the rate of change in exchange rates after the key interest rate cut are more restrictive than before the decision. This episode illustrates two things: firstly, the risk taken with the attempt at fine "expectation management" on the part of central banks; secondly, the well-known fact that monetary policy with its traditional instruments can only directly influence short-term interest rates. Incidentally, Swiss franc interest rates were also unable to escape the global rise in interest rates. While we continued to generously provide the money market with liquidity, returns on the capital market also rose in Germany. However, the increase was relatively moderate. Historically, nominal capital market interest rates are still low. They reflect the moderate inflation outlook. Monetary policy and exchange rates On the exchange rate side, we have noted with some satisfaction the recovery of the euro against the Swiss franc in recent months. Our low interest rate policy undoubtedly contributed to this. In addition, the markets understood very well that, in view of the depressed economic situation, we would not allow the Swiss franc to appreciate, which would lead to an undesirable tightening of monetary conditions. A tightening of monetary conditions, i.e. an increase in the sum of interest rates and the rate of appreciation, is particularly undesirable as long as there are no signs of inflation, as is the case today. The euro-franc exchange rate has thus returned to normal after the long-lasting distortion following the terrorist attacks of September 2001. This is illustrated particularly well by the real exchange rate, i.e. adjusted for the different inflation rates. This is now back at the level it was when the euro was introduced at the beginning of 1999. From what we have experienced in the meantime, this is a remarkable statement. In addition to the euro, the decline in the value of the US dollar was, and still is, a cause for concern. Sometimes the SNB is asked to do something about it. We understand, of course, the problems that arise from the decline in the dollar. Conversely, during the previous dollar bull market, we have repeatedly argued that such a strong dollar in the face of the massive imbalances in the US economy in the longer term, it is not tenable. In this sense, the dollar correction was, at least in part, a desirable normalization. We live in a system of flexible exchange rates and stick to it. This may seem to one or the other as a contradiction, since I have just made very precise statements on the euro-franc exchange rate. However, I would ask you not to overlook, as I have argued. I said that the SNB had to ensure that monetary conditions remained reasonable. The exchange rate changes also determine the monetary conditions. The SNB therefore pays very close attention to them. But it does not set exchange rate targets and does not peg the franc to either the euro or the US dollar. No one denies that the foreign exchange markets are always prone to exaggerations. Price movements are often stronger than would be fundamentally justified. This is especially a problem when the price trend is in a direction that is not desirable in monetary policy. An example of this is the appreciation of the Swiss franc following the terrorist attacks in September 2001. In such situations, monetary policy must take countermeasures. We did this by lowering interest rates several times and significantly. I have already talked about this. Such a consideration of exchange rate developments in monetary policy is not only unproblematic, but downright mandatory. However, if one were to argue that it is particularly true for the internationally strongly intertwined Swiss economy that monetary policy impulses often act faster via the exchange rate channel than via the interest rate channel and that therefore an explicit control of the exchange rate by the central bank would be the better medicine than interest rate policy, one would go far too far. Experience has shown that exchange rate movements are unpredictable. A monetary policy that engages in exchange rate management carries the risk of strong and undesirable side effects. It is worth recalling once again the fundamental problems of exchange rate control:  When the Swiss franc is pegged, Switzerland automatically adopts the monetary policy of the central bank of the reserve currency. Of course, this does not take into account the requirements of Switzerland. How delicate it is when a country renounces its own monetary policy is currently evident in the euro area.  A credible fixation of an exchange rate results in an alignment of the interest rate level with that of the reserve currency. Compared to the euro area (e.g. Germany), this would lead to an increase in the interest rate level in Switzerland of about two percentage points.  If the markets judge the fixed exchange rate level as no longer sustainable, massive speculative attacks must be expected. In the event of house speculation, the SNB has only two options: either to buy up large quantities of foreign currency, thereby massively expanding the Swiss franc money supply and jeopardising the objective of price stability, or to adjust or abandon the exchange rate target altogether. The SNB made similar experiences in the years after 1978.  Only the nominal exchange rate can be fixed. The real exchange rate, i.e. inflation-adjusted, which is relevant for long-term economic development, results from the change in relative price levels. It is by no means constant, even with a stable nominal exchange rate. Regardless of a nominal peg of the Swiss franc to another currency, any fundamental upward pressure in favour of the Swiss franc always prevails in such a way that the price level and thus also the cost level in Switzerland rises more strongly than in other countries that are less attractive to investors. Or, in other words, a fixed exchange rate does not eliminate differences in international competitiveness.  Finally, the exchange rate can only be kept stable against one currency at a time. Thus, the fluctuations of this reserve currency against other currencies are taken over one-to-one. In the hypothetical case, in which, for example, in 1999 the Swiss franc would have been fixed against the US dollar at the then level of Fr. 1.37, we would have had to accept euro exchange rates of up to Fr. 1.15 against the euro until the beginning of 2003. Concluding remark Against this background, the SNB does not have a realistic alternative to the pragmatic approach taken so far. We walk it in the knowledge that stability-oriented management of monetary conditions is a balancing act. That The aim must be to ensure price stability while taking into account the needs of the economy as a whole. It is necessary to react appropriately to external disturbances, the long-term optics can never be lost sight of. This is about the risks and side effects of our policy. Monetary policy decisions are always taken under uncertainty. It is not self-evident that our decisions, however carefully they have always been prepared and considered in detail, will prove themselves in retrospect.

In der Schweiz haben wir noch wenig Anhaltspunkte fr eine verbesserte Situation. Im 2. Quartal drfte ein weiterer Rckgang der wirtschaftlichen Aktivitt stattgefunden haben.
