Die Voraussetzung dafr ist, dass die erwartete Erholung in den USA dauerhaft ist und auch den europischen Lndern Impulse verleiht. Die internationalen Finanzmrkte signalisieren Zuversicht. Die Erholung der Aktienmrkte setzte schon im Mrz ein. Seit Juni steigen auch die Renditen an den Kapitalmrkten. Dazu trug auch die amerikanische Notenbank bei: Ende Juni senkte sie die Leitzinsen um 0,25 Prozentpunkte, allerdings begleitet von einer gemischten Stellungnahme. Tiefe Leitzinsen, Deflationsgefahren und Aufschwungserwartungen bildeten ein merkwrdiges Gespann. Dies war offenbar fr die Mrkte schwierig zu interpretieren. Schliesslich stiegen die Langfristzinsen sehr deutlich an. Unter dem Strich waren die effektiven monetren Bedingungen, d.h. die Summe von Zinsen und Vernderungsrate der Wechselkurse nach der Leitzinssenkung restriktiver als vor dem Entscheid. Diese Episode illustriert zweierlei: Erstens das Risiko, das mit dem Versuch eines feinen Erwartungsmanagement seitens der Notenbanken eingegangen wird, zweitens die bekannte Tatsache, dass die Geldpolitik mit ihrem traditionellen Instrumentarium nur die kurzfristigen Zinsstze direkt beeinflussen kann. Auch die Frankenzinsen konnten sich dem globalen Zinsanstieg im brigen nicht entziehen. Whrend wir den Geldmarkt weiterhin grosszgig mit Liquiditt versorgten, stiegen die Renditen am Kapitalmarkt auch hierzulande an. Allerdings war der Anstieg relativ moderat. Historisch sind die nominellen Kapitalmarktzinsen immer noch tief. Sie reflektieren die moderaten Teuerungsaussichten. Geldpolitik und Wechselkurse Wechselkursseitig nahmen wir in den letzten Monaten mit einer gewissen Genugtuung die Erholung des Euro gegenber dem Franken zur Kenntnis. Dazu trug zweifellos auch unsere Tiefzinspolitik bei. Darber hinaus wurde von den Mrkten sehr wohl verstanden, dass wir angesichts der gedrckten Wirtschaftslage keine Aufwertungen des Frankens zulassen wrden, welche zu einer unerwnschten Verschrfung der monetren Bedingungen fhren wrden. Eine Verschrfung der monetren Bedingungen, d.h. eine Erhhung der Summe von Zinsstzen und Aufwertungsrate ist insbesondere solange unerwnscht, als sich, wie heute, keine Inflationsgefahren abzeichnen. Der Euro-Frankenkurs hat sich also, nach der lange anhaltenden Verzerrung im Anschluss an die Terroranschlge vom September 2001, wieder normalisiert. Besonders gut illustriert dies der reale, also um die unterschiedlichen Inflationsraten bereinigte Wechselkurs. Dieser befindet sich nun wieder auf jenem Niveau, wo er bei der Einfhrung des Euro Anfang 1999 war. Nach allem, was wir zwischenzeitlich erlebt haben, ist dies eine bemerkenswerte Feststellung. Neben dem Euro bereitete, und bereitet noch, der Wertverlust des US-Dollar Sorgen. Bisweilen wird die Nationalbank aufgefordert, auch dagegen etwas zu unternehmen. Wir verstehen natrlich die Probleme, die sich aus dem Dollarrckgang ergeben. Umgekehrt haben wir whrend der frheren Dollarhausse mehrfach die Meinung vertreten, dass ein so starker Dollar angesichts der massiven Ungleichgewichte der US-Wirtschaft lngerfristig nicht haltbar sei. In diesem Sinn war die Dollarkorrektur mindestens zum Teil eine durchaus erwnschte Normalisierung. Wir leben in einem System der flexiblen Wechselkurse und halten daran fest. Dies mag dem Einen oder Andern als Widerspruch erscheinen, nachdem ich doch eben ganz przise Aussagen zum Euro-Franken-Wechselkurs gemacht habe. Ich bitte Sie aber nicht zu bersehen, wie ich argumentiert habe. Ich sagte, dass die Nationalbank darauf achten msse, dass die monetren Bedingungen angemessen bleiben wrden. Die Wechselkursvernderungen bestimmen die monetren Bedingungen mit. Die Nationalbank beachtet sie daher sehr genau. Aber sie fixiert keine Wechselkursziele und bindet den Franken weder an den Euro noch an den US-Dollar an. Niemand bestreitet, dass die Devisenmrkte immer wieder zu bertreibungen neigen. Kursbewegungen fallen oft strker aus, als fundamental gerechtfertigt wre. Dies ist vor allem dann ein Problem, wenn die Kursentwicklung in eine Richtung luft, die geldpolitisch nicht erwnscht ist. Ein Beispiel dafr ist die Aufwertung des Frankens im Anschluss an die Terroranschlge im September 2001. In solchen Situationen muss die Geldpolitik Gegensteuer geben. Wir taten das, indem wir die Zinsstze mehrfach und deutlich zurcknahmen. Ich habe darber bereits gesprochen. Ein solches Bercksichtigen der Wechselkursentwicklung in der Geldpolitik ist nicht nur unproblematisch, sondern geradezu Pflicht. Wenn man jedoch argumentieren wrde, dass speziell fr die international stark verflochtene Schweizer Wirtschaft gelte, dass geldpolitische Impulse oft schneller ber den Wechselkurs- als ber den Zinskanal wirken wrden und dass daher eine explizite Steuerung des Wechselkurses durch die Notenbank die bessere Medizin als die Zinspolitik wre, ginge man viel zu weit. Wechselkursbewegungen sind erfahrungsgemss unberechenbar. Eine Geldpolitik, welche sich auf die Wechselkurssteuerung einlsst, birgt das Risiko starker und unerwnschter Nebenwirkungen. Es lohnt sich, dass wir uns wieder einmal die grundstzliche Probleme einer Wechselkurssteuerung in Erinnerung zu rufen:  Bei einer Anbindung des Frankens bernimmt die Schweiz automatisch die Geldpolitik der Zentralbank der Leitwhrung. Diese nimmt selbstverstndlich keine Rcksicht auf die Erfordernisse der Schweiz. Wie heikel es ist, wenn ein Land auf eine eigene Geldpolitik verzichtet, zeigt sich momentan im Euroraum.  Eine glaubwrdige Fixierung eines Wechselkurses hat eine Angleichung des Zinsniveaus an jenes der Leitwhrung zur Folge. Gegenber dem Euroraum (z.B. Deutschland) wrde dies eine Erhhung des Zinsniveaus in der Schweiz um etwa zwei Prozentpunkte nach sich ziehen.  Wenn von den Mrkten das fixierte Wechselkursniveau als nicht mehr nachhaltig beurteilt wird, muss mit massiven spekulativen Attacken gerechnet werden. Im Falle einer Haussespekulation hat die Nationalbank nur zwei Mglichkeiten: Entweder grosse Mengen Fremdwhrung aufzukaufen, dadurch die Frankengeldmenge massiv auszuweiten und das Ziel der Preisstabilitt zu gefhrden, oder das Wechselkursziel anzupassen oder ganz aufzugeben. Entsprechende Erfahrungen machte die Nationalbank in den Jahren nach 1978.  Fixiert werden kann nur der nominelle Wechselkurs. Der fr die langfristige Wirtschaftsentwicklung relevante reale, d.h. inflationsbereinigte Wechselkurs ergibt sich aus der Vernderung der relativen Preisniveaus. Er ist auch bei stabilem nominellen Wechselkurs keineswegs konstant. Ein allenfalls vorhandener, fundamentaler Aufwertungsdruck zugunsten des Frankens setzt sich unabhngig von einer nominellen Anbindung des Frankens an eine andere Whrung immer durch und zwar so, dass das Preis- und damit auch das Kostenniveau in der Schweiz eben strker steigt als im fr die Anleger weniger attraktiven Ausland. Oder, anders ausgedrckt: Ein fixer Wechselkurs eliminiert die Unterschiede in der internationalen Wettbewerbsfhigkeit nicht.  Schliesslich: Der Wechselkurs kann immer nur gegenber einer Whrung stabil gehalten werden. Damit werden die Schwankungen dieser Leitwhrung gegenber anderen Whrungen eins zu eins bernommen. Im hypothetischen Fall, in welchem z.B. 1999 der Franken gegenber dem US-Dollar auf dem damaligen Niveau von Fr. 1.37 fixiert worden wre, htten wir ber die ganze Zeit der ausgeprgten Dollarstrke gegenber dem Euro bis Anfang 2003 Eurokurse von bis zu Fr. 1.15 in Kauf nehmen mssen. Schlussbemerkung Vor diesem Hintergrund bleibt der Nationalbank keine realistische Alternative zum bisherigen pragmatischen Weg. Wir beschreiten ihn im Wissen darum, dass die stabilittsorientierte Steuerung der monetren Bedingungen eine Gratwanderung ist. Das Ziel muss sein, die Preisstabilitt sicherzustellen und dabei Rcksicht auf die Bedrfnisse der gesamten Wirtschaft zu nehmen. Auf externe Strungen ist angemessen zu reagieren, die langfristige Optik ist nie aus den Augen zu verlieren. Hier geht es um die Risiken und Nebenwirkungen unserer Politik. Geldpolitische Beschlsse werden immer unter Unsicherheit gefllt. Es ist nicht selbstverstndlich, dass unsere Entscheide, so sorgfltig sie im einzelnen immer auch vorbereitet und erwogen worden sind, sich im Nachhinein bewhren.

Title: Importance of the Swiss Financial Centre
text: Importance of the Swiss financial centre Presentation by Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank 81st Congress of the Swiss Abroad Saturday, 30 August 2003 Crans-Montana As the Swiss Abroad are well aware, the image of our country abroad is most often made up of cliches: Switzerland is the country of milk and cheese, Switzerland is the country of watches and chocolate, Switzerland is the country of banks and numbered accounts! These cliches stick to our skin, they often give a very nice image, although rather romantic and outdated of the Swiss reality, with the exception of the allusions to our financial center. When it comes to the financial center, the cliche is neither romantic nor sympathetic. Are you not struck by the fact that in any cinematographic scenario the proceeds of a hold up or ransom must necessarily go to Zurich or Geneva but never to London or Frankfurt? This cliche associates the Swiss financial centre with banking secrecy in the service of criminal activities. The organizers of our meeting today have clearly perceived this problem since they have planned a round table on the theme "Financial centre: mortgage for the image of Switzerland abroad?" Is this image justified? Is the development of the Swiss financial centre primarily the result of banking secrecy? Has Switzerland developed activities in the financial sector that are contrary to its long-term interests? My presentation will try to show you the opposite:  The production of financial services corresponds to a long Swiss tradition;  our country has comparative advantages in the production of financial services; the tradition of protecting privacy, in other words banking secrecy, is one of this comparative advantage;  the expansion of our financial centre is a logical evolution of our economic structure and the result of the globalisation of the financial markets. For these reasons, the Swiss financial centre has become an important sector of the country's economic activity, both in terms of added value and in terms of jobs and tax resources. I will show it to you with a few numbers. But like any economic activity, the production of financial services is subject to the harsh rules of competition. I will therefore conclude with the challenges facing our financial centre today. 1. A Swiss tradition It was not in Switzerland but in Italy that the banking profession appeared in Europe in the 12th century. At the time, it was above all a question of ensuring the exchange of currencies and the transfer of funds. Financial activities were linked to those of trade fairs. It was not until the 16th century that credit developed. In Switzerland, the rise of cities and especially the accumulation of income from foreign service are at the origin of the first loan funds. Then, in the 18th century, private banking appeared in Geneva, Basel and Zurich. This is the real beginning of the tradition of international activities of Swiss banks. A century later, the industrial revolution and the gradual increase in welfare led to the creation of cantonal and regional banks and the development of the credit market. During the second half of the 19th century, the industrialization of the country was accompanied by the creation of the first investment banks from which our current major banks originated - and the establishment of large insurance companies. On this momentum, the 20th century was, for the Swiss financial center, only a century of consolidation and openness to the world. Two key features have contributed to the development of our financial sector: First of all, the abundance of national savings. It was indeed thanks to the revenues derived from foreign service - the only services that we were able to export at the time - that the first lending capacity of our economy was built. And it was thanks to the collection of savings from the middle class that the banking fabric of the 19th century was formed and that regional and cantonal banks developed. Secondly, our history shows us that the Swiss banking sector has always had to - and has been able to - develop in an international market. The tradition of private bankers is exemplary in this regard. The fact that our country is the only European country that has never experienced restrictions on capital exports shows that we are not afraid of competition from other financial centres. The liberalism of our external relations testifies to the strength of our national funding base. By constantly exposing our banking sector to international competition, we have also forced it to remain competitive. 2. The ingredients needed for an international financial centre The high savings capacity is therefore the first essential element in the constitution of a solid financial centre. Certainly, today, some offshore centers claim to be financial centers. They are often artificial constructions whose success depends directly on the attractiveness they represent for external funds. Switzerland, on the other hand, has a natural role to play in financing the global economy because its saving capacity far exceeds its domestic financing needs. This gap, which is visible in the traditional surplus of our current external payments, ensures a low cost of capital. The abundance of savings and price stability make Switzerland the European country with the lowest interest rates. A strong financing capacity is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the sustainable development of a financial centre. To this must be added a number of favourable framework conditions:  a stable political environment, guaranteeing legal continuity;  appropriate legislation ensuring the soundness and integrity of the financial system;  a population open to the world and to multicultural dialogue;  an educated workforce capable of adapting to an ever-changing environment;  a financial sector able to provide itself with the necessary management tools. All these elements are, to varying degrees, assets of the Swiss financial centre and explain its growth. They are not static but have evolved over the years:  With the increase in per capita income, national savings are growing faster than the country's financial needs. Our external financing capacity is growing, fluctuating around 2% of national income 30 years ago and currently stands at more than 8%.  Switzerland is no longer the only country to ensure a stable political environment. However, it remains one of those who pay the most attention to the protection of the private sphere of individuals. It remains fiercely opposed to centralizing tendencies and the tutelage of individuals by the state.  Our financial legislation is constantly changing in order to best adapt to the challenges of constantly changing markets. In the fight against money laundering and the financing of terrorism, our country plays a pioneering role. The supervision of our financial markets is now moving towards consolidated supervision of banks and insurance.  The Swiss financial centre has been able to equip itself with high-tech payment and settlement systems that ensure the efficient and rapid execution of financial transactions.  Finally, constant efforts are being made in the field of training - whether continuing or academic - to promote knowledge in finance and management. Many factors, both historical and economic, are therefore at the origin of the development of the Swiss financial centre. Its growth is explained by the abundance of our savings as well as by favorable structural elements. To think that it is only the product of banking secrecy is abusive, especially since the anonymity of accounts no longer exists and banking secrecy is lifted in the event of criminal activity. Bank secrecy, as an integral part of the legislative framework, is only one success factor among others. 3. The place of the financial sector in the Swiss economy It is fair to say that the financial sector has become one of the pillars of the Swiss economy. Everyone knows that the machinery industry or the chemical industry are important parts of our production apparatus. It is generally unknown that the financial sector - with almost 13% of GDP - now far exceeds them. 10 years ago his position was still very different. During the 1990s, the activities of the financial centre developed much faster than those of other branches of our economy. In international comparison we also occupy a special place: in Germany or the United Kingdom - countries that also have important financial centres the share of the financial sector in national income is less than half of what we know in Switzerland. We must also realize that the geographical distribution of financial activities is very uneven across the country. In Geneva, the financial sector accounts for 25% of cantonal value added. In Zurich this proportion is somewhat lower. In Ticino it is of the order of 20%. Such a degree of concentration of activity is found only in New York. In London and Frankfurt, the financial centre accounts for only 10% of regional value added. Our financial centre is therefore not only relatively important in terms of all the country's activities, it is also decisive for the development of certain regions. In terms of employment, the image given by the financial centre is a little different. Its relative stability is at 6 - 6.5% of overall employment. With relatively stable employment and strong output growth, the financial sector has made the most productivity gains over the past two decades. We still had 625 banks and 120,000 bank employees in 1990, today there are only 356 establishments employing 104,500 employees. Everyone remembers the many restructurings that took place in the nineties. It should be noted in this regard that, in recent years, our financial institutions have followed expansion strategies leading them to create more jobs abroad than at home. The trend is towards the development of onshore activities, which requires significant external investment. In 2001, outward investment by banks and insurance companies accounted for more than a third of foreign investment in the Swiss economy. Currently, with 190,000 employees, the number of employees in the banking and insurance sector working outside our borders is only slightly lower than the number of employees in Switzerland itself. As a key sector in terms of value added and employment, the financial centre has also become an important source of revenue for public coffers. Last year, taxes levied on banks' profits amounted to CHF 2 billion, or about 4% of the Confederation's revenues. Stamp duty on financial transactions and withholding tax accounted for more than 10% of federal revenues. In addition to all this, it would be appropriate to add - at all levels of the State - the proceeds of direct taxes levied on wage income paid by banks, which can represent significant amounts in cantons where the banking sector is highly developed. In the year 2000, taxes levied directly or indirectly on banking activity constituted more than 10% of the total amount - at federal, cantonal and communal level - of our country's tax revenues. But not all financial professions have developed with the same success in our territory. Wealth management operations have experienced the most spectacular growth. Heirs to the tradition of private bankers, the wealth management professions represent today the most important source of added value in the financial sector. It is estimated that more than a quarter of the global cross-border wealth management market is in Swiss hands, placing our country well ahead of Luxembourg or the United Kingdom. The rise of the Swiss financial centre is therefore not in the in the field of credit or investment banking - activities in which New York and London play a leading role - but in a very particular niche, better suited to our traditional assets and expertise. Wealth management activities also have the advantage of being less sensitive to economic fluctuations than credit activities, but they are also subject to fierce competition at the international level. These few figures show you that the financial centre is indeed one of the pillars of our economy. It contributes significantly to national income and is one of the main sources of employment. On the external front, no sector of our economy has as much presence in terms of investment and jobs. However, this presence is highly concentrated in the major financial centres. 4. The challenges of the financial centre The tremendous growth of the Swiss financial centre during the nineties is due to the fact that it was able to seize the opportunities brought about by the globalization of the financial markets. During this period, no market benefited as much from advances in communications technology and the rise of liberalism as the financial market. It has thus built up a global capital market, highly integrated and competitive. Funds move on a simple phone call. The rivalry between financial centres has also become much more intense, especially since financial know-how can be easily transferred from one place to another and trust, an important factor in success in finance, is an asset that can be quickly questioned. In my opinion, increasing the know-how of our financial centre and strengthening the confidence it inspires are the two challenges of the day. Increasing know-how means aiming to improve the quality of financial services, which are now much more complex than in the past. To meet this challenge, our institutions must invest in training and rationalization, increase productivity and adapt their products to the specific needs of their customers. We must also accept that financial institutions are restructuring and reorienting their activities. A flexible response to customer needs is, in finance as in any other economic activity, the key to success. Building trust is just as necessary because no lasting financial relationship can be established without customer trust. Here integrity plays an essential role. And I do Return to the cliches set out at the beginning of my presentation: we must fight vigorously against the image of a Swiss financial centre interested in hosting funds in search of a new virginity. If she were willing to do so, she would have little sense of her own interests. The market for honest funds is large enough that it is worth doing everything possible to protect oneself from funds of dubious origin. The fight against money-laundering must therefore be carried out without complacency. Let us not be afraid to learn that accounts have been blocked in Swiss institutions. This obviously indicates that mistakes may have been made, but above all it shows that the control mechanisms put in place are working properly. Unless we assume that total probity reigns abroad, the fact that the financial centres competing with ours catch only a few fish in their net should not be taken as proof of holiness. Switzerland now occupies a leading position in the fight against money laundering. This effort must continue to ensure that the old cliches disappear. This is in the very interest of our country, which, in the financial field, has a weight that far exceeds its political weight. 5. Conclusion The development of the activities of the Swiss financial centre is in line with the development of the Swiss economy. Essentially an agricultural country under the old regime, it industrialized in the 19th century before evolving towards the production of services. In this area, several factors predisposed Switzerland to produce financial services by giving it comparative advantages: a tradition of political and monetary stability, a tradition of respect for privacy and discretion, as well as a tradition of quality. As it developed, the banking and insurance sector has become one of the main sources of income in our country. In banking, wealth management ranks first. In the production of financial services as in the production of other goods, Switzerland is exposed to strong international competition. It fully accepts it and nothing can guarantee it to preserve the relatively advantageous position it has been able to create for itself. It will only be able to do so by taking care of its framework conditions, by continuously increasing its know-how and by strengthening confidence in the solidity and probity of its financial centre. It is a task that calls for everyone's effort: a resolute will financial institutions to continually adapt their services to market realities, and a determined policy of the authorities to closely ensure the soundness and probity of the financial centre in a world dominated by the free movement of capital.

C'est une tche qui appelle l'effort de chacun: une volont rsolue des tablissements financiers d'adapter continuellement leurs services aux ralits du march, et une politique dtermine des autorits de veiller troitement  la solidit et  la probit de la place financire dans un monde domin par la libre circulation des capitaux.

Title: The SNB's role in financial market regulation
text: THE SNB'S ROLE IN FINANCIAL MARKET REGULATION Prof. Dr. Niklaus Blattner Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Management Forum 2003 of the Cantonal Banks Furigen, 9 September 2003 1. Introduction In addition to all the good and beautiful things we can say about the financial sector, this also applies: financial centres all over the world are regularly hit by economic downturns, financial market instabilities and even banking crises. Supervisory authorities strive to prevent crises with appropriate measures and regulations. The regulatory framework is under continuous pressure to adapt, because the dynamics of the markets repeatedly produce changes that entail opportunities, but also risks. In order for regulation to remain effective, it must address these risks. Efforts to achieve an efficient and secure financial sector require the participation of all stakeholders. With their internal risk management, the supervised entities, i.e. the individual financial institutions, lay the foundation for a healthy and stable company. These control mechanisms are aimed at the stability and security of one's own institution. Since private interests may differ from the public interest, conflicts of interest are possible. Banking supervisors pursue the public interest. They issue generally applicable rules at the micro level and ensure that banks comply with them, for example. These requirements are intended to prevent banks from exposing themselves to risks that create unreasonable problems for themselves and thus also for their depositors or customers. For a long time, less importance was attached to regulation at the macro level. This aims at the stability of the entire financial system. A stable financial system is characterized by its ability to absorb shocks in such a way as to maintain the essential functions of the system. In recent years, maintaining systemic stability has become an important concern for central banks. The Swiss National Bank (SNB) is also committed to system stability. It focuses mainly on the banking system as well as on payment and settlement systems. This focus follows from its monetary policy mandate. On the one hand, the SNB relies on a secure and efficient financial market infrastructure for the day-to-day implementation of monetary policy. On the other hand, a stable banking system makes it easier to achieve monetary policy targets. At the same time, however, monetary policy decisions influence the stability of the banking sector. A second reason why the SNB's efforts to achieve system stability focus primarily on banks and less on other actors such as insurance companies or stock exchanges. is due to the special balance sheet structure of the banks. Banks finance loans to a large extent through short-term deposits. This maturity transformation means that once a bank is confronted with liquidity problems, the transition to insolvency is fluid, as it may have to sell illiquid assets at high cost. Liquidity and solvency problems of an institution can also be quickly transferred to an entire group of banks or even to the entire banking system through intermediary bank loans and payment systems due to the close link between the banks. As lender of last resort, the SNB can now give the illiquid but solvent bank a covered loan. A third reason why the SNB, like the other authorities, is committed to strict regulation of the banking sector compared to other sectors is of a politico-economic nature: financial and banking crises severely damage large parts of the population. In order to prevent possible crises, the SNB is resorting to prevention, i.e. to the means of regulation and monitoring. The growing importance of system stability from the point of view of central banks has led in recent years to the fact that this task has been enshrined in law in more and more countries. Switzerland's new National Bank Act also stipulates that the SNB must contribute to system stability. The SNB bases its efforts to achieve system stability on three pillars: information, financial market regulation and active crisis management. These three pillars form the structure of my presentation. 2. Information as a contribution to system stability The SNB's aim is to identify threats to system stability and imbalances at an early stage in order to be able to eliminate them in good time. Financial crises are usually associated with high costs. These must be avoided. To this end, the SNB obtains information on the economic environment and the situation on the financial markets as well as on profitability, credit, interest rate and market risks as well as the banks' capital base. With the in-depth analysis and assessment of this information, it makes a first contribution to system stability. On the one hand, it tries to identify systematic risk factors for the banking sector: if banks operate in similar business areas and pursue similar strategies, they are exposed to similar risks. When a shock occurs, a significant part of the System at the same time. On the other hand, the SNB investigates how the problems of individual banks can be transferred to other - generally healthy - banks and how large such systemic risks are. The SNB bases its assessment of stability on financial market and individual bank data as well as on qualitative 1nformations. Its assessment of the current situation in the financial system and possible trends should not only serve as a basis for decision-making by the SNB itself. For this reason, the SNB has recently published an annual stability report. It contains an assessment of the stability of the Swiss banking system and its infrastructure. The focus is on the banking system as a whole. Individual banks are only considered if this is relevant to the overall assessment. Incidentally, this is a difference between our approach and that of the Federal Banking Commission (SFBC). While we pursue a system-wide approach, the SFBC has an institute-oriented perspective. The tasks of the two institutions are complementary. The aim of our report is to inform the public, not only with assessments of the National Bank, but also with indicators and data that allow market participants to make their own judgements. The stability report is intended to make it easier for banks to react and take measures at the first signs of imbalances. The best possible information about the state of the financial system, its institutions and infrastructure is a prerequisite for maintaining stability. This finding explains the growing importance of financial stability reporting for central banks. 3. Financial market regulation as a contribution to system stability However, analyses and the publication of information alone are not sufficient to create and maintain system stability. However, they are a valuable complement to financial market regulation - the mainstay of promoting system stability. A stable financial system is based on healthy financial institutions and a secure and efficient financial market infrastructure. Both are sought through effective financial market regulation. The SNB plays two roles: on the one hand, it is a co-designer and advisor on financial market reforms, and on the other hand, it is the supervisor of payment and settlement systems. In the following, I would like to briefly discuss both roles. 3. 1 The SNB's formative/advisory role in financial market regulation It is in the SNB's own interest to identify sources of stability in the financial system and to develop concepts that strengthen stability. However, the SNB is also involved in numerous regulatory projects of other authorities and international organisations. Together with the Federal Government and the SFBC, we work in working groups to determine the need for reform, help to revise existing laws and enact new ones. At international level, the SNB participates in various working groups of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). I would like to illustrate our contribution with five current reform projects: These are (1) the partial revision of the Banking Act, (2) the revision of the Basel Capital Accord, (3) the creation of an integrated financial market supervisory authority, (4) the drafting of a Securities Custody Act and (5) the development of the Core Principles for systemically important payment systems and the launch of the clS (Continuous Linked Settlement) foreign exchange settlement system. (1) Partial revision of the Banking Act: Bank restructuring, liquidation and depositor protection The partial revision of the Banking Act aims at far-reaching improvements in the three areas of bank restructuring, bank liquidation and depositor protection. The SNB has been particularly committed to ensuring that the revised Banking Act now explicitly provides for a restructuring procedure for banks with solvency problems. This can be initiated by the SFBC - with a justified prospect of success and in the interest of the creditors. Behind this is the realization that liquidation often unnecessarily destroys substance that could have been preserved by the creditors through a restructuring. moreover, an inefficient liquidation of a systemically important bank can massively weaken other banks and have significant real economic consequences. The revised Banking Act offers restructuring instruments that can help solve crises without state aid. If an efficient restructuring is hopeless, only liquidation remains. The revision of the Banking Act also brings improvements in this respect: in particular, a new jurisdiction regulation is intended to optimize the liquidation procedure. In contrast to the third area - the protection of depositors - the revision of bank restructuring and liquidation law was hardly controversial in the consultation. Depositor protection consists of the two components bankruptcy privilege and deposit insurance. While the bankruptcy privilege secures the substance of the deposits, the deposit insurance ensures their rapid disbursement. The bankruptcy privilege will now apply to all deposits up to a maximum of CHF 30,000 per person cover. A system-wide upper limit for deposit insurance will be maintained, up to which the banks must bear the depositor protection themselves. On the one hand, this is to be increased from chf 1 billion to CHF 4 billion. On the other hand, the banks are to hold additional liquid funds for half of their obligations, which they would have to pay in the event of insolvency. The deposit guarantee should also be made compulsory; a solution through self-regulation within the framework of the Swiss Bankers Association will continue to be possible. Depositor protection, and in particular deposit insurance, make an important contribution to the stability of the banking system. By guaranteeing the preservation of substance and the rapid availability of privileged deposits, creditors are prevented from withdrawing their money in a panic in crisis situations or simply in response to rumours. Since a storm could exacerbate the liquidity problems of the bank concerned or cause them in the first place, depositor protection strengthens system stability. You may now think that the cantonal banks cannot have a Sehaltersturm anyway due to the state guarantee. But the state guarantee guarantees the deposits only in their substance; it does not guarantee their rapid availability. I therefore think it makes sense for the cantonal banks to also have to participate in deposit insurance. This is the logical consequence of the extensive equality of the cantonal banks with the other banks, which began with the revision of the Banking Act of 1999. After all, banking regulation not only serves to protect creditors, but also to protect taxpayers and system stability. (2) Participation in the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision: Revision of the Capital Adequacy Agreement The SNB's role is not limited to its involvement in Swiss financial market regulation. As a member of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision of the BIS, the SNB is significantly involved in the revision of the Basel Capital Adequacy Agreement. Making its know-how available and taking an active role in the reorganisation of capital adequacy rules is not an altruistic act on the part of the SNB: even a central bank that does not exercise banking supervision has an interest in ensuring that banks are provided with sufficient capital. Firstly, this is due to the fact that the capital adequacy requirements can have a substantial impact on the stability of the banking system, on which the SNB relies for the implementation of monetary policy. Secondly, as a possible lender of last resort, the SNB has an interest in adequate capitalisation of banks, as weakly capitalised banks are more likely to have liquidity difficulties. Thirdly, capital adequacy rules can influence bank lending. This, in turn, has an impact on the real economy and on the effect of monetary policy. The SNB's main concern was and is to design the capital requirements in such a way that the capital adequacy is in line with the risks - in particular credit and interest rate risks - of the banks. The current 1988 capital adequacy agreement cannot guarantee this satisfactorily. At the time, the Basel Committee based it on two objectives: firstly, it should strengthen the stability of the international banking system and, secondly, it should standardise the minimum capital requirements internationally. The focus was clearly on credit risk. However, financial markets, banking and, last but not least, risk management practices are subject to constant change. As early as 1996, this prompted the Basel Committee to explicitly consider a second category of risks - market risks. In 1999, he decided to fundamentally revise the capital agreement. The new capital agreement is intended to become more flexible and risk-oriented and consist of three pillars: firstly, minimum capital requirements, secondly, review by supervisory authorities and thirdly, the effective use of market discipline. The current definition of equity and the minimum equity ratio of 8% of risk-weighted assets will be retained. Banks have two approaches to risk assessment - a standard approach and an approach based on internal ratings. In both cases, the risk determination will be more differentiated and sophisticated than under the applicable capital adequacy agreement. From the SNB's point of view, Basel I primarily has the following shortcomings: On the one hand, the risk weighting of loans only insufficiently reflects their quality. On the other hand, neither the risk concentration nor the interest rate risks are taken into account in the banking book. Does Basel II bring an improvement in these criticisms? As far as the first point concerns the risk weighting of loans - it can be said in principle that the new capital adequacy rules better reflect the quality of the credit portfolio - but not perfectly. The standard approach now provides for a more differentiated risk weighting, which largely relates to external ratings. This is to be welcomed in principle, but can also lead to distortions and overall to a lower equity base. Because the incentive to be "guessed" is different for the companies: Successful, creditworthy companies obtain a rating and thus reduce their financing costs, while worse companies deliberately waive a rating in order not to increase their financing costs. In the case of the approach based on internal ratings, on the other hand, I do not see the incentive problem in the companies, but in the weakly capitalized banks. The reason for this is that the banks determine the amount of capital required by their own assessment of the quality of their credit portfolio. Of course, these assessments are not tacitly accepted by banking supervision as the ultimate truth, but are checked and objectified. However, this second approach, based on internal ratings, requires both experience and time for banks and banking supervision. In order to ensure that the equity cushion does not shrink massively, I therefore consider the additional minimum requirements applicable for the first two years after implementation to be absolutely necessary. We also support the SFBC's intention to equip Basel II with a so-called Swiss finish when it is transposed into Swiss law - as basel 1 already did. We regret that the other two points - risk concentration and interest rate risks - are not explicitly taken into account in the capital adequacy requirement, even under the new rules, but only indirectly through the second pillar - the review by the supervisory authorities. A frequent criticism is that the new capital requirements are pro-cyclical. would work. This means that in recessive phases, the ratings of the Debtor. This, in turn, increases with the same loan volume that Capital requirements of lending banks. In order to meet own funds requirements, Banks must either reduce lending, parts of the Securitize credit portfolios or increase own funds. Reduce the Lending, so this can further slow down the economy and the recession amplify. A fear that a central bank must undoubtedly be concerned about. However, a cyclical restriction on lending is not an inevitable consequence of the new capital adequacy rules. On the one hand, the banks themselves are aware of this mechanism and will hold a capital cushion that protects them from an unwanted credit crunch and facilitates long-term customer relationships. On the other hand, the cyclical nature of the risks is also known to banking supervision, which is already at the first signs in the stress test Results can demand more own funds from the banks. The pro-cyclical effect is therefore by no means mandatory for the new rules. The Basel Committee intends to finalise the new Capital Adequacy Agreement by the end of 2003 so that it can be implemented in each country by December 2006. However, Basel II is now under heavy fire again shortly before it is signed. Since Basel II is too complicated for the majority of banks, the US intends to apply the new rules only to a few large banks. This jeopardises the hard-won compromise. The future of Basel II has thus become more uncertain. However, I hope that the new equity agreement will nevertheless prevail, because merely maintaining Basel 1 is not desirable. Improvements are imperative in order to achieve an appropriate risk-based capital adequacy. (3) Establishment of integrated financial market supervision When we talk about the SNB's role in financial market regulation, one should certainly not fail to mention a reform project: the creation of a new Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA). Let's take a look back: At the end of 1998, the Federal Council set up an expert group chaired by Prof. JeanBaptiste Zufferey with the task of evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of Swiss financial market regulation and attention. Another group headed by Prof. Ulrich Zimmerli has been working on the legislative follow-up to the final report of this expert group for a good one and a half years. In its first interim report, which was recently published, it sets out proposals for FINMA's organisation and its interdisciplinary supervisory instruments. An integrated financial market supervisory authority is to be created to take over the tasks currently carried out by the SFBC and the Federal Office of Private Insurance (FOPI). The integration of other authorities such as the Anti-Money Laundering Control Authority and the Federal Gaming Commission is not planned for the time being. However, it will be discussed in depth together with the question of whether independent asset managers, lntroducing brokers and foreign exchange traders such as banks and insurance companies should be subject to supervision. At present, however, the Zimmerli Commission is primarily concerned with the differentiation of the catalogue of sanctions and with the possibilities of making administrative law more effective. The SNB's main concern is to create a functioning authority. The cart FINMA must not be overloaded. In concrete terms, this means that further authorities cannot be integrated at the present time, and we do not consider the subordination of further financial market participants to be urgent. The current effectiveness of banking supervision must not be jeopardised by a new structure. Even without a trend towards all-finance, the challenges facing banking and insurance supervision are currently and will be great enough for the foreseeable future. Incidentally, the intended integration steps are by no means based solely on the reality of financial conglomerates. More important arguments are, on the one hand, professional competence, which is fundamentally similar in different supervisory fields and whose bundled use promises efficiency gains. On the other hand, there are also materially similar problems. The market and credit risks of insurance companies and banks, for example, are very similar. This, too, speaks for the superiority of integrated financial market supervision. (4) Drafting of a Securities Custody Act Another project I would like to mention is the drafting of a securities custody law. Swiss securities law dates back to 1936 and still assumes a close link between law and paper. A security cannot be transferred without also transferring ownership of the deed. And without this document, the right from the paper can not be asserted. However, in today's markets, the reality is different. The security itself does not play a role in the transfer or assertion of rights. Securities are often held in collective custody at central bodies and are no longer held directly by the authorised person. Often they are also replaced by non-notarised rights with the same function as securities so-called stock rights. In Switzerland, as in most other financial centres, there is no legal basis for the collective custody of securities and the transfer of stock rights. In cross-border situations, the centuries-old rule that the laws of the place where a thing is located cannot be applied. The consequence of this is that today we have great difficulty in answering the question of which law is applicable when a Frenchman sells to a German American shares that are held in England. A new Securities Custody Act is intended to close the existing gaps: For this purpose, the Federal Department of Finance has set up a project group to process a draft law. The project group, led by the SNB, is tasked with revising the draft securities custody act by the end of the year. The SNB has a twofold concern in closing this legal loophole: firstly, it averts potential threats to the stability of the financial system and, secondly, it contributes to the competitiveness of the financial centre. It is undisputed that the stability of the financial system would be threatened if one day, for example as a result of the insolvency or liquidation of a medium-sized bank, it became apparent that certain transactions in securities were legally problematic or unenforceable. The competitiveness of the financial centre is affected by the fact that a broad international consensus has emerged that in the 21st century securities transactions should not be carried out on the basis of a law whose spirit stems from the 19th century. The new law creates legal certainty, which can mean an important locational advantage for an international financial centre such as Switzerland. (5) Development of the Core Principles for systemically relevant Payment systems and launch of the CLS system The SNB's further involvement in financial market regulation concerns its representation in various working groups of the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems affiliated to the BIS. The aim of the Committee is to promote the efficiency and stability of domestic as well as cross-border payment transactions. Two projects in particular in which the SNB has worked intensively should be highlighted. On the one hand, these are the basic principles for systemically important payment systems published in 2000. With these principles, internationally applied standards have been created. On the other hand, there are the efforts of the central banking community to reduce settlement risks in foreign exchange transactions. The efforts resulted in the launch of the global foreign exchange settlement system Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS), which went into operation last September. 3.2 The SNB's supervisory role in financial market regulation In addition to its role as a consultant and co-designer in the creation of new regulatory requirements, the SNB also has a role to play in their implementation: the SNB acts as a supervisory authority for payment and securities settlement systems. Transactions carried out on national and global financial markets are mainly processed via payment and securities settlement systems. Such systems increase the efficiency of processes and contribute to a strong reduction of risks. The CLS system, for example, was created to eliminate the settlement risk that was unavoidable in the usual settlement of foreign currency transactions. Conversely, payment and securities processing systems can also become a source of instability if their operation is not reliable or if the architecture of the system has weaknesses. Thus, the failure of a system can be associated with disruptions to the entire financial system. Moreover, as all participants in a financial system are directly or indirectly connected through settlement systems, such systems can also be a channel for transferring credit or liquidity problems to other system participants. This means that payment and securities settlement systems also entail systemic risks. In recent years, a broad international consensus has emerged that central banks have a share of responsibility in mitigating systemic risks. This co-responsibility is also to be formally anchored in Switzerland. The new National Bank Act, which is currently being discussed in Parliament, not only states that the SNB must contribute to the stability of the financial system, but also grants the SNB formal powers to supervise payment and securities settlement systems. The SNB includes all its measures to influence the rules and architecture of a payment or securities settlement system. The SNB will pay particular attention to systemically important payment and securities settlement systems. Systemically relevant are those systems that can be both the cause and the channel for the spread of a systemic crisis. Various criteria are used to define the systemically important systems. For example, the total value or amount of individual transactions processed via the system, the type of transactions or the networking of the system with other systems. For the SNB, it is also relevant whether a system is used to clear or settle transactions that are related to the implementation of monetary policy. The draft law provides for a three-stage monitoring approach. In a first stage, the operators of payment systems are subject to a statistical obligation to provide information. This information makes it possible to exclude smaller payment systems from closer monitoring in advance. The second stage consists of an extended disclosure obligation for securities settlement systems as well as those payment systems in which a systemic risk cannot be excluded a priori due to the total value of the transactions processed. Comprehensive information on such systems is necessary in order for the SNB to assess whether a resolution system that is important for the stability of the financial system exists. Finally, the SNB will impose minimum quality requirements on systems that may pose risks to the stability of the financial system. These are regulated in a regulation and are closely based on internationally recognized standards. The new National Bank Act is expected to enter into force in May 2004. 4. Active crisis management as a contribution to system stability The third pillar with which the SNB contributes to the stability of the financial system is active crisis management. While a targeted information policy and efficient financial market regulation are ex ante measures aimed at preventing a financial crisis, the SNB also contributes ex post to damage reduction. If, due to market inefficiencies, illiquid but solvent banks are no longer able to obtain their required liquidity on the market or through the SNB's permanent liquidity facilities, the SNB can provide them with Lender of Last Resort Loans. As a rule, central banks have a policy of so-called constructive ambiguity in this regard, which basically means that they leave the banks in the dark about their Lender of Last Resort policy. We believe that this is not a sensible approach and have opted for a more transparent system. In concrete terms, this means that we inform potential borrowers in advance about the applicable rules of the game. However, increased transparency does not change the old principle: the SNB only grants liquidity against collateral. The SNB therefore requires that a Lender of Last Resort loan is always backed by collateral. Before granting a Lender of Last Resort loan to a bank, the SNB assures the SFBC that the solvency and licensing requirements of the institution are met. The amount of cover required depends on the quality of the collateral deposited, i.e. on its creditworthiness, liquidity and volatility. The amount of the Lender of Last Resort loan is limited solely by the presence of collateral. The SNB refrains from providing a Lender of Last Resort loan with a penalty interest rate, as this would further exacerbate the problems of the institution concerned. By announcing the rules of the game that apply to the granting of Lender of Last Resort loans, the SNB is creating transparency with regard to the modalities of liquidity assistance if it is granted to a bank. In this way, it enables banks to adapt their liquidity and crisis management to these conditions. However, the SNB will have to decide on a case-by-case basis whether liquidity support will be granted on the basis of the available information. 5. Conclusion The SNB makes a significant contribution to system stability at various levels: it carries out prevention work by identifying imbalances in the financial system and making its analyses and assessments available to the public. On the other hand, it contributes to reforms in financial market regulation and monitors payment and settlement systems. If a crisis nevertheless arises, it has the opportunity to provide liquidity assistance. In "uncertain times", the topic to which this conference is dedicated, a stable financial system, i.e. a financial system that can absorb shocks intact, is of particular importance. If financial market regulation proves adaptable to the changed market environment, new challenges can be overcome. However, financial market reforms not only serve system stability, but also strengthen the competitiveness of the Swiss financial centre by creating favourable framework conditions. In its conclusion on the Financial Seetor Assessment, which it carried out with Switzerland in autumn 2001, the International Monetary Fund praised regulation and supervision, in particular for its reform efforts, but also for the sound and effective risk management of financial institutions. However, as long as the financial system is constantly confronted with new challenges and financial market supervision has to take these changes into account on an ongoing basis, we must never be satisfied with what has been achieved.

Liquiditts- und Solvenzprobleme eines Instituts knnen sich zudem durch die enge Verknpfung der Banken untereinander ber lnterbankenkredite und Zahlungssysteme rasch auf eine ganze Gruppe von Banken oder gar auf das gesamte Bankensystem bertragen. Die SNB kann nun als Lender of Last Resort der illiquiden, aber solventen Bank einen gedeckten Kredit geben. Um mgliche Krisen zu verhindern, greift die SNB zur Prvention, das heisst zu den Mitteln von Regulierung und berwachung. Die wachsende Bedeutung der Systemstabilitt aus Sicht der Zentralbanken hat in den letzten Jahren dazu gefhrt, dass in immer mehr Lndern diese Aufgabe gesetzlich verankert wurde. Auch im neuen Nationalbankgesetz der Schweiz soll festgehalten werden, dass die SNB zur Systemstabilitt beizutragen hat. Die SNB sttzt sich bei ihren Bemhungen um Systemstabilitt auf drei Pfeiler: Information, Finanzmarktregulierung und aktive Krisenbewltigung. Diese drei Pfeiler bilden die Struktur meines Referats. 2. Information als Beitrag zur Systemstabilitt Ziel der SNB ist es, Gefahren fr die Systemstabilitt und Ungleichgewichte frhzeitig zu identifizieren, um diese rechtzeitig beseitigen zu knnen.
