Title: How does Switzerlands monetary policy influence Swiss franc loans in Austria?
text: How does Swiss monetary policy affect Swiss franc loans in Austria? Prof. Dr. Thomas J. Jordan Deputy Member of the Board of Directors Head of Financial Market Operations Swiss National Bank Event Foreign Currency Loans, Monforthaus Feldkirch, Austria 23 September 2004 Dear Sir or Madam, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to you here in Feldkirch this evening. The Austrian and Swiss National Banks have long maintained friendly contact with regular exchanges of ideas in various areas. I was therefore very happy to come to Feldkirch and would like to thank Mr. Director Mag. Armin Schneider from the OeNB for the excellent organisation of this event. Before I begin my remarks, let me suggest the following currency speculation in my mind: I offer you to exchange Swiss francs for euros today and to exchange the two currencies back in three months' time. [See Figure 1] Today's Euro franc exchange rate is 1.54. I give you 154 francs and you give me  according to today's rate  100 euros. After three months we meet again. I will then give you back the 100 euros and you will give me the corresponding sum of francs at the then valid exchange rate. Would you accept the speculation? I will come back to the proposal at the end of my speech. I will structure my presentation as follows: First, I will place the topic of foreign currency loans in a somewhat larger macroeconomic framework, then I will discuss the situation with foreign currency loans in Switzerland and finally I will explain the importance of Swiss monetary policy for Swiss franc loans in Austria. I will also talk about the exchange rate between the Swiss franc and the euro and the interest rate differential between Swiss franc and euro investments. 1. Foreign currency loans in a macroeconomic context Reasons for foreign currency loans Let me now begin with a few more fundamental remarks. Lending and borrowing across national borders has always been an "everyday" phenomenon in open economies. If, for example, the domestic savings volume is smaller than the domestic investment, the difference is forced to be borrowed abroad. This represents an import of capital for the domestic market and an export of capital for foreign countries. If the two countries concerned do not share the same currency, the result is automatically for one of the two parties. a foreign currency loan. While this classic type of foreign currency loan is always associated with a capital import or capital export, this does not necessarily have to be the case with foreign currency mortgages in Austria. In principle, the Swiss franc can serve as a pure unit of account and all transactions between the borrower and lender in Austria could be settled in euros. Foreign currency loans as part of financial optimization or speculation What is the possibility of borrowing in foreign currency to be seen from the point of view of borrowers? With the possibility of obtaining a loan in a foreign currency, the financing options of borrowers are expanded. From the point of view of the borrowers, this increase in financing options is generally to be evaluated positively. Due to their risk appetite, they can realize a possibly better structure of their debt, i.e. a debt with a lower expected interest rate. While when investing balances, the choice of currency and the search for higher returns through currency diversification are a matter of course, in most countries, especially among private households, debt in domestic currency is common. This may be due to legal reasons, risk considerations or habits. With its high share of foreign currency loans, Austria is an exception throughout Europe. Austrian foreign currency borrowers are trying to take advantage of the lower Swiss franc or yen interest rates against the euro. Economics clearly shows that a higher expected profit, here in the form of lower interest costs, is usually associated with a higher risk. Specifically, for an Austrian foreign currency borrower calculating in euros, there is a risk that the repayment of the loan and the interest payments will be higher than assumed at the time of conclusion of the loan due to an appreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro. The crucial question is therefore whether borrowers actually use the greater choices offered by foreign currency loans in the sense of optimization or whether they are not sufficiently aware of the risk associated with foreign currency loans. It is extremely important to have the speculative element inherent in every foreign currency loan clearly in mind. My guess is that many borrowers pay too little attention to the speculative element of foreign currency loans. Importance of foreign currency loans for monetary policy How are foreign currency loans to be evaluated from the point of view of monetary policy? Monetary policy unfolds an important part of its effect on the economy through interest rates. If more and more investments are financed by loans or bonds in foreign currency, the domestic interest rate level tends to lose importance for the domestic economy. There is therefore a risk that the effectiveness of national monetary policy will be restricted. However, it depends on the share of foreign currency loans in the total loan volume. In Switzerland, but also in the euro area, the share of foreign currency loans in the total loan volume is so small that the monetary policy of the SNB and the ECB has so far hardly been affected. In this context, one can also ask whether Swiss franc loans in Austria play a role in the monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank. The volume of Swiss franc loans in Austria is insignificantly small compared to the entire Swiss franc credit market. It can also be assumed that currency shifts in these loans do not take place in a concentrated manner in a short period of time and can therefore have little impact on exchange rates. Swiss franc loans in Austria do not affect Swiss monetary policy. Another relevant point for monetary policy is the stability of the financial system. The granting of foreign currency loans must not jeopardise the stability of the financial system. This primarily addresses the risk management of credit institutions. Just like borrowers, they must be aware of the various risks involved in granting foreign currency loans and take appropriate measures. 2. Foreign currency loans and Switzerland Foreign currency loans in Switzerland In the following, I will discuss the situation with regard to foreign currency loans in Switzerland. In Switzerland, banks' domestic loans are divided into mortgage claims and non-mortgage-backed loans, so-called claims on customers. Non-mortgaged domestic loans amounted to 134.5 billion at the middle of this year (end of June). Swiss franc. This corresponds to around 88 billion at the then valid exchange rate (CHF/EUR1,528). Euro. Of these, 15% were denominated in a currency other than the Swiss franc. This proportion may seem high. A look at the distribution of these loans by currency makes it clear that these loans do not exist for reasons of an interest rate advantage of the foreign currency against the Franc. By far the largest share is denominated in US dollars (9%) and euros (4%)  the two most important currencies in Switzerland's foreign trade. The remaining currencies (including the yen) together accounted for only 2% of all non-mortgage-backed loans. [See Figure 2] These foreign currency loans are therefore almost entirely related to the borrower's cross-border business. Most of them are sourced from companies. Domestic mortgage receivables amounted to 556 billion in the middle of the year. Franconia (363 billion) Euro). They are therefore around four times larger than the receivables from customers. Of the mortgage claims, only a negligible proportion of 0.016% is denominated in a foreign currency. Mortgages in euros amounted to only EUR 29 million, while those in Japanese yen amounted to only EUR 3 million. [See Figure 3] Foreign currency loans are therefore a marginal phenomenon in Switzerland. An obvious explanation is certainly the low interest rate level in Switzerland: In most cases, it is simply more expensive to borrow in a currency other than the Swiss franc. In addition, the interest rate advantage of a yen loan compared to a Swiss franc loan is comparatively small. In addition, the yen franc exchange rate fluctuates much more than the euro franc exchange rate. However, representatives of Swiss banks also stress that this product is deliberately not actively promoted by them. In addition, when customers ask for loans in yen, the banks specifically point out the high exchange rate risk. They usually advise against such mortgages. Pricing of foreign currency loans in Switzerland What about interest rates and risk premiums, so-called pricing, for foreign currency loans in Switzerland? If a private individual in Switzerland wants to take out a mortgage in a foreign currency, he normally does not have to accept a higher premium on the respective reference interest rate than would be the case with a mortgage in Swiss francs. However, he has to bring in more collateral, because in addition to the risk of a price decline on the real estate market, there is also the risk of the appreciation of the foreign currency. In particular, the loan-to-value limit for foreign currency mortgages is set lower than for Swiss franc loans. In the case of unsecured foreign currency loans, which go almost exclusively to larger companies, according to bank representatives, the Foreign currency risk is considered as one of many determinants of individual pricing. In summary, it can be said that foreign currency loans in Switzerland are only a marginal phenomenon and go primarily to internationally active companies. Mortgage loans in Germany are rarely obtained in a currency other than the Swiss franc. Swiss banks and Swiss franc mortgages abroad In the border area  especially in the Basel and Ticino area  Swiss banks issue franc mortgages to cross-border commuters from abroad. This makes sense, since cross-border commuters receive their income in francs and interest must also be paid in francs. If the Swiss franc appreciates, the interest burden  calculated in euros  will be higher, but income will also increase. In the Austrian mortgage business, Swiss banks are only present with insignificant amounts. At the end of 2003, the mortgage receivables in Austria of the reportable Swiss banks amounted to only CHF 12 million, which corresponds to around EUR 8 million. The receivables of Swiss banks from customers in Austria stood at CHF 635 million. This is also a small amount compared to the total volume of loans in the two countries. Swiss capital market and Swiss franc loans in Austria The Swiss financial market and The Swiss banks have a certain role to play in the refinancing of Austrian lenders. On the one hand, Austrian debtors issue bonds in Swiss francs on the Swiss capital market. On the Swiss stock exchange SWX are bonds of Austrian debtors with an issue value of over 22 billion. Swiss francs (approx. 14 billion) Euro) outstanding. Of this, just over 5 billion are accounted for. Franconia (approx. 3.2 billion) Euro) to the Austrian State. The proportion of the remaining bonds spent on the refinancing of Swiss franc loans cannot be clearly assigned. On the other hand, Swiss banks grant interbank loans to Austrian credit institutions and conclude currency swaps. There are also some Austrian banks participating in the Monetary Policy Revisions of the Swiss National Bank. Austrian banks in Switzerland It is also interesting to know that about three years ago, Austrian banks tried to penetrate the Swiss mortgage market and issue yen mortgages in Switzerland. However, the offers could not establish themselves at that time due to falling interest rates in Switzerland and appreciation tendencies of the yen. 3. Swiss franc loans in Austria and the SNB's monetary policy In the following, I will now go into more detail about the importance of Swiss monetary policy for Swiss franc loans in Austria. I assume that this is of particular interest to you, as a representative of a commercial bank or as a foreign currency borrower. Whether a franc loan against a euro loan is worthwhile for an Austrian borrower depends above all on two factors: the exchange rate of the franc to the euro and the interest rate difference between the two currencies. The Swiss National Bank's monetary policy has an influence on both. It is therefore important to understand how the Swiss National Bank sets its monetary policy stance. Monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank The main task of the Swiss National Bank is to conduct a monetary policy that serves the overall interest of the country. It ensures price stability while taking into account the economic situation. We equate price stability with an increase in the national consumer price index of less than 2% per year. This is a definition similar to that of the European Central Bank. The Swiss National Bank uses various indicators to ensure that the current monetary policy stance is appropriate to the objective of price stability. It regularly publishes a forecast for the development of inflation over the next three years. Three years roughly corresponds to the period required for the transfer of monetary impulses to the price level. If the projected inflation deviates from the defined price stability, a review of monetary policy is imperative. If inflation threatens to rise above 2% in the medium term, the SNB will tend to tighten its monetary policy. The SNB therefore sets its key interest rates with the aim of maintaining price stability in the medium term. It does not pursue an exchange rate target, neither against the euro nor against the US dollar. There However, the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the euro and the economic development in the eurozone have a major influence on the development of the Swiss economy and on prices in Switzerland, they are carefully monitored by the SNB and represent important elements in determining the monetary policy rate. The implementation of these monetary policy intentions takes place by influencing the level of interest rates on the Swiss franc money market. The SNB sets a target range for the three-month Libor. This is the economically most important money market rate for Swiss francs. Let me briefly explain the monetary policy concept described on the basis of the Swiss National Bank's latest interest rate hike. As expected, the Swiss economy developed robustly in the first half of the current year and we expect solid growth for next year as well. The inflation forecast indicates that if the key interest rate remained unchanged, consumer prices would show an annual growth rate of over 2% until the end of the forecast horizon. [See Figure 4] A tightening of the monetary policy stance was therefore indicated. The SNB's monetary policy remains expansionary despite raising the target range for the three-month Libor by 25 basis points. [See Figure 5] Exchange rate of the Swiss franc to the euro (or schilling) Now to the exchange rate development. Over the past three decades, the Swiss franc has had a clear trend towards appreciating against the Austrian schilling. [See Figure 6] At the beginning of the 70s, more than 17 francs had to be paid for 100 shillings, but at the time of the introduction of the euro they were available for less than 12 francs. The upward trend has weakened since the introduction of the euro in 1999. Between the beginning of 1999 and today, the Swiss franc has appreciated nominally by around 4.5%. Today, one euro costs about 1.54 francs. In the meantime, however, the euro stood at a high of 1.62 and a low of 1.45. This corresponds to a maximum appreciation of the Swiss franc of over 10% or a maximum depreciation of only 0.4% compared to the exchange rate at the introduction of the euro. [See Figure 7] This long-term appreciation trend of the Swiss franc against the euro and previously the schilling is working against the Swiss franc borrowers abroad, because with the appreciation the debt calculated in euros grows. The fluctuations in the euro franc exchange rate are significantly smaller than at other exchange rates of the Swiss franc (measured by the standard deviation as a percentage of the average value over 90 days). [See Figure 8] Nevertheless, in the last five years, appreciations and devaluations of up to 5% within three months have occurred on several occasions. For the success or failure of a Swiss franc mortgage, the time of entry is therefore crucial. The volatility of the Euro franc exchange rate also shows that the "right" entry point is difficult to meet. [See Figure 9] It is important to understand that volatility and the appreciation trend can change over time. Trends cannot simply be continued into the future. As has been shown on several occasions, exchange rates can hardly be predicted in the short term and only unreliably in the long term. Interest rate differential between Swiss franc and euro investments What about the interest rate differential between Swiss franc and euro investments? The so-called "interest bonus" of the Swiss franc against the euro has averaged around 1.5 percentage points over the past five and a half years, measured by the difference in the interest rate on unsecured three-month loans to first-class banks. Debtors of Swiss franc mortgages in the euro area therefore benefit from a lower interest rate. The interest bonus has been quite stable in recent years, fluctuating between 1 and 2.5 percentage points. [See Figure 10] The fluctuations in the interest rate differential are therefore significantly smaller than those in the exchange rate. A foreign currency loan therefore involves speculation that the Swiss franc will appreciate less than the interest rate differential between the euro and the franc. Of course, the additional costs associated with a Swiss franc loan compared to a euro loan must also be taken into account. Current monetary policy and foreign currency loans in Austria The impact of the SNB's monetary policy on Swiss franc loans in Austria can also be nicely illustrated by the SNB's current interest rate decisions. The reference interest rate for Swiss franc mortgages in Austria is usually the three-month Libor. The mortgage costs of Swiss franc mortgages in Austria thus depend directly on monetary policy decisions by the SNB. As already mentioned, on 16 September the Swiss National Bank again raised its target range for the Swiss franc three-month Libor by 25 basis points. The The European Central Bank is still waiting for a change in its key interest rates. This means that the interest rate advantage over the three-month Euribor has shrunk from over 1.8 to less than 1.4 percentage points within just over three months. The interest rate advantage of loans in Swiss francs has therefore melted down somewhat  at least temporarily. For the loan in Swiss francs, therefore, higher interest rates have to be paid. At the same time, the Swiss franc has also appreciated somewhat against the euro since the beginning of the year. As a result, the debt in euros has risen. The current development shows that there are no guarantees that a Swiss franc mortgage is worthwhile. There is no certainty that the Swiss franc will not appreciate more strongly against the euro again, nor that the interest rate differential will remain at its current level. In particular, short-term movements in interest rates and exchange rates can result in an unfavorable situation for a borrower. 4. Fremdwhrungskredite im gesamtwirtschaftlichen Rahmen Grnde fr Fremdwhrungskredite Lassen Sie mich nun mit einigen mehr grundstzlichen Bemerkungen beginnen. Die Kreditgewhrung und die Kreditaufnahme ber die Landesgrenzen hinweg sind bei offenen Volkswirtschaften seit jeher ein alltgliches Phnomen. Ist z.B. das inlndische Sparvolumen kleiner als die inlndischen Investitionen, wird die Differenz gezwungenermassen im Ausland als Kredit aufgenommen. Bedeutung der Fremdwhrungskredite fr die Geldpolitik Wie sind nun Fremdwhrungskredite aus der Sicht der Geldpolitik zu werten? Die Geldpolitik entfaltet einen wichtigen Teil ihrer Wirkung auf die Wirtschaft ber die Zinsen. Wenn mehr und mehr Investitionen durch Kredite oder Anleihen in fremder Whrung finanziert werden, verliert das inlndische Zinsniveau tendenziell an Bedeutung fr die heimische Wirtschaft. Es besteht somit ein Risiko, dass die Wirksamkeit der nationalen Geldpolitik eingeschrnkt wird. Allerdings kommt es auf den Anteil der Fremdwhrungskredite am gesamten Kreditvolumen an. Fremdwhrungskredite und die Schweiz Fremdwhrungskredite in der Schweiz Ich werde im Folgenden auf die Situation bei den Fremdwhrungskrediten in der Schweiz eingehen. Frankenkredite in sterreich und die Geldpolitik der SNB Im Folgenden werde ich nun nher auf die Bedeutung der schweizerischen Geldpolitik fr die Frankenkredite in sterreich eingehen. Ich nehme an, dass das fr Sie, als Vertreter einer Geschftsbank oder als Fremdwhrungskreditnehmer, von besonderem Interesse ist. Ob sich fr einen sterreichischen Kreditnehmer ein Frankenkredit gegenber einem Eurokredit lohnt, hngt vor allem von zwei Faktoren ab: dem Wechselkurs des Frankens zum Euro und der Zinsdifferenz zwischen beiden Whrungen. Auf beide hat die Geldpolitik der Schweizerischen Nationalbank einen Einfluss. Es ist deshalb wichtig zu verstehen, wie die Schweizerische Nationalbank ihren geldpolitischen Kurs festlegt. Die Geldpolitik der Schweizerischen Nationalbank Die Hauptaufgabe der Schweizerischen Nationalbank besteht darin, eine Geld- und Whrungspolitik zu fhren, die dem Gesamtinteresse des Landes dient. Sie sorgt fr Preisstabilitt und beachtet dabei die Konjunkturlage. Wir setzen Preisstabilitt mit einem Anstieg des Landesindexes der Konsumentenpreise von unter 2% pro Jahr gleich. Dies ist eine hnliche Definition wie diejenige der Europischen Zentralbank. Die Schweizerische Nationalbank verwendet verschiedene Indikatoren um sicherzustellen, dass der aktuelle geldpolitische Kurs im Hinblick auf das Ziel der Preisstabilitt angemessen ist. Sie gibt in regelmssigen Abstnden eine Prognose fr die Entwicklung der Inflation in den nchsten drei Jahren bekannt. Drei Jahre entsprechen in etwa dem Zeitraum, den die bertragung monetrer Impulse auf das Preisniveau bentigt. Weicht die prognostizierte Inflation von der definierten Preisstabilitt ab, drngt sich eine berprfung der Geldpolitik auf. Droht die Teuerung mittelfristig ber 2% zu steigen, wird die Nationalbank ihre Geldpolitik tendenziell straffen. Die SNB setzt ihre Leitzinsen also mit dem Ziel fest, mittelfristig die Preisstabilitt aufrecht zu erhalten. Sie verfolgt kein Wechselkursziel, weder zum Euro noch zum US-Dollar. Da der Wechselkurs des Schweizer Frankens zum Euro und die wirtschaftliche Entwicklung in der Eurozone aber einen grossen Einfluss auf die Entwicklung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft und auf die Preise in der Schweiz haben, werden sie von der SNB sorgfltig beobachtet und stellen wichtige Elemente bei der Festlegung des geldpolitischen Kurses dar. Die Umsetzung dieser geldpolitischen Absichten geschieht ber die Beeinflussung des Zinsniveaus auf dem Geldmarkt fr Schweizer Franken. Die Nationalbank legt ein Zielband fr den Dreimonats-Libor fest. Dieser ist der wirtschaftlich bedeutendste Geldmarktsatz fr Schweizer Franken. Lassen Sie mich das geschilderte geldpolitische Konzept anhand des letzten Zinsschrittes der Schweizerischen Nationalbank kurz erlutern. Die Konjunktur in der Schweiz entwickelte sich in der ersten Hlfte des laufenden Jahres erwartungsgemss robust und auch fr das nchste Jahr gehen wir von einem soliden Wachstum aus. Die Inflationsprognose zeigt an, dass die Konsumentenpreise bei unverndertem Leitzinssatz bis zum Ende des Prognosehorizonts eine Jahreswachstumsrate von ber 2% ausweisen wrden. [Siehe Grafik 4] Eine Straffung des geldpolitischen Kurses war also angezeigt. Die Geldpolitik der SNB bleibt trotz Anhebung des Zielbandes fr den Dreimonats-Libor um 25 Basispunkte weiterhin expansiv. [Siehe Grafik 5] Wechselkurs des Frankens zum Euro (bzw. Schilling) Nun zur Wechselkursentwicklung. Der Schweizer Franken hatte in den vergangenen drei Jahrzehnten einen deutlichen Trend, sich gegenber dem sterreichischen Schilling aufzuwerten. [Siehe Grafik 6] Mussten zu Beginn der 70er Jahre noch ber 17 Franken fr 100 Schilling bezahlt werden, waren diese zum Zeitpunkt der Einfhrung des Euro fr weniger als 12 Franken erhltlich. Der Aufwertungstrend hat sich seit der Einfhrung des Euro 1999 abgeschwcht. Zwischen Anfangs 1999 und heute hat sich der Franken um rund 4.5% nominell aufgewertet. Heute kostet ein Euro ca. 1.54 Franken. Zwischenzeitlich stand der Euro aber bei einem Hchststand von 1.62 und einem Tiefststand von 1.45. Dies entspricht einer maximalen Aufwertung des Frankens von ber 10% beziehungsweise einer maximalen Abwertung von lediglich 0.4% gegenber dem Kurs bei der Einfhrung des Euro. [Siehe Grafik 7] Diese langjhrige Aufwertungstendenz des Schweizer Frankens gegenber dem Euro und zuvor dem Schilling arbeitet gegen die Frankenkreditnehmer im Ausland, denn mit der Aufwertung wchst die in Euro gerechnete Schuld. Die Schwankungen beim Eurofrankenkurs sind deutlich kleiner als bei anderen Wechselkursen des Frankens (gemessen an der Standardabweichung in Prozent des Mittelwertes ber 90 Tage). [Siehe Grafik 8] Trotzdem sind in den letzten fnf Jahren Aufund Abwertungen von bis zu 5% innerhalb von drei Monaten verschiedentlich vorgekommen. Fr den Erfolg oder Misserfolg einer Frankenhypothek ist daher der Einstiegszeitpunkt entscheidend. Die Volatilitt des Eurofrankenkurses zeigt auch, dass der richtige Einstiegszeitpunkt schwierig zu treffen ist. [Siehe Grafik 9] Es ist wichtig zu verstehen, dass sich die Volatilitt und der Aufwertungstrend ber die Zeit verndern knnen. Trends lassen sich nicht einfach in die Zukunft fortschreiben. Wie verschiedentlich gezeigt wurde, lassen sich nmlich Wechselkurse in der kurzen Frist kaum und in der langen Frist nur unzuverlssig prognostizieren. Zinsdifferenz zwischen Franken- und Euroanlagen Wie sieht es nun mit der Zinsdifferenz zwischen Franken- und Euroanlagen aus? Der so genannte Zinsbonus des Schweizer Frankens gegenber dem Euro betrug in den letzten fnfeinhalb Jahren durchschnittlich rund 1.5 Prozentpunkte, gemessen an der Differenz im Zinssatz fr ungesicherte dreimonatige Kredite an erstklassige Banken. Schuldner von Frankenhypotheken im Euroraum profitieren daher von einem tieferen Zinssatz. Der Zinsbonus war in den letzten Jahren recht stabil und schwankte zwischen 1 und 2.5 Prozentpunkten. [Siehe Grafik 10] Die Schwankungen bei der Zinsdifferenz sind daher deutlich kleiner als diejenigen beim Wechselkurs. Ein Fremdwhrungskredit beinhaltet also eine Spekulation, dass der Schweizer Franken sich weniger als die Zinsdifferenz zwischen Euro und Franken aufwertet. Dabei sind selbstverstndlich auch die zustzlichen Kosten zu bercksichtigen, mit denen ein Frankenkredit gegenber einem Eurokredit verbunden ist. Aktuelle Geldpolitik und Fremdwhrungskredite in sterreich Die Auswirkungen der Geldpolitik der SNB auf die Frankenkredite in sterreich lassen sich auch schn anhand der aktuellen Zinsentscheidungen der SNB illustrieren. Als Referenzzinssatz fr Frankenhypotheken in sterreich wird blicherweise der Dreimonats-Libor verwendet. Die Hypothekarkosten von Frankenhypotheken in sterreich hngen damit unmittelbar von geldpolitischen Entscheidungen der SNB ab. Wie bereits erwhnt, hat die Schweizerische Nationalbank am 16. September ihr Zielband fr den Schweizer Franken Dreimonats-Libor erneut um 25 Basispunkte angehoben. Die Europische Zentralbank wartet mit einer Vernderung ihrer Leitzinsen weiterhin zu. Damit ist der Zinsvorteil gegenber dem Dreimonats-Euribor innerhalb von etwas mehr als drei Monaten von ber 1.8 auf unter 1.4 Prozentpunkte geschrumpft. Der Zinsvorteil von Krediten in Schweizer Franken ist demnach  zumindest vorbergehend  etwas zusammengeschmolzen. Fr den Kredit in Schweizer Franken sind also hhere Zinsen zu bezahlen. Gleichzeitig hat sich der Franken gegenber dem Euro seit anfangs Jahr auch wieder etwas aufgewertet. Damit ist die Schuld in Euro gerechnet gestiegen. Die aktuelle Entwicklung zeigt, dass es keine Garantien gibt, dass sich eine Frankenhypothek lohnt. Es gibt weder eine Sicherheit, dass sich der Franken nicht wieder strker gegenber dem Euro aufwertet, noch dass die Zinsdifferenz im heutigen Ausmass bestehen bleibt. Insbesondere knnen kurzfristige Bewegungen bei den Zinsstzen und den Wechselkursen fr einen Kreditnehmer eine ungnstige Situation ergeben. 4. Schlussbemerkungen Ich komme nun auf die zu Beginn meiner Ausfhrungen unterbreitete Whrungsspekulation zurck. Ich hoffe, dass Sie zu einer Entscheidung kommen konnten. [Siehe Grafik 1] Ich habe Ihnen angeboten, zum heutigen Kurs Franken gegen Euro zu tauschen und in drei Monaten zum dann gltigen Kurs zurckzutauschen. Dieses Gedankenexperiment soll zeigen, dass die Entscheidung, sich in einer fremden Whrung zu verschulden, mit einer klaren Vorstellung ber die knftige Entwicklung dieser Whrung verbunden sein sollte. Falls Sie das Geschft eingehen wollen, sollten sie auch fr die nchsten drei Monate keinen Frankenkredit aufnehmen. Sie glauben, dass sich das Halten von Franken lohnt  eine Verschuldung in Franken kann sich also nicht lohnen. Die Aufwertung des Frankens ist Ihrer Meinung nach grsser als die Zinsdifferenz zum Euro. Sollten Sie unschlssig sein, ob Sie das Angebot annehmen sollen, haben Sie keine klare Vorstellung ber die Wechselkursentwicklung, eine Verschuldung in Schweizer Franken ist daher fr Sie eher fragwrdig. Nur falls Sie das vorgeschlagene Geschft entschieden ablehnen, sollte fr Sie im Moment ein Frankenkredit in Frage kommen. Sie sind dann offensichtlich der Meinung, dass die knftige Wechselkurs- und Zinsdifferenzentwicklung eine Verschuldung in Schweizer Franken attraktiv macht. Lassen Sie mich nun zum Abschluss meiner Ausfhrungen kommen. Bei den vorhandenen Chancen eines Fremdwhrungskredits mssen dessen erheblichen Risiken klar betont werden. Der geldpolitische Kurs der Schweizerischen Nationalbank bt ber den Zinssatz und den Wechselkurs einen erheblichen Einfluss auf die Kosten eines sterreichischen Frankenkredits aus. Ein gutes Verstndnis der schweizerischen Geldpolitik ist daher fr Kreditnehmer und Kreditgeber von Frankenkrediten in sterreich sehr wichtig. Ich danke Ihnen fr Ihre Aufmerksamkeit. Title: Monetary policy situation and economic prospects
text: Economic outlook and monetary policy Philipp M. Hildebrand Member of the Executive Board Swiss National Bank Centre for Banking Studies, Villa Negroni, Vezia Lugano 1. Introduction Crossing the Alps towards the South is always a pleasure, but today my visit has a special resonance, as it is my first in Ticino since my arrival at the Swiss National Bank (SNB). This morning I had the privilege of having a meeting with local representatives for an in-depth discussion of the evolution of the Ticino economy. I would like to thank Mr Picchi, the Manager of our Lugano branch, for this opportunity. A few days ago, the SNB carried out its quarterly assessment of the economic situation. On this occasion, we raised the fluctuation band of the Libor by 0.25% to three months. Today, I would like to discuss in a few details the economic and monetary outlook as it stands following our latest monetary decision. As a preamble, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to make some general reflections on monetary policy and briefly recall the monetary concept of the SNB. 2. Uncertainty - a sine qua non for monetary policy Uncertainty is the daily bread of a central banker. Basically, it derives from the fact that the vast complexity of the global economy does not allow - and probably will never allow - to know precisely its dynamics. First, our primary instruments of measurement - economic statistics - reflect economic reality in a very partial way. As you know, their quality is far from uniform, they are available only late and are often subject to major revisions. Second, in our efforts to assess the state of the economy, we will make greater use of unobservable concepts, such as the "output gap" or "excess liquidity". These concepts depend not only on the quality of the statistical series from which they are constructed, but also on the model behind their construction. These concepts are therefore subject to more uncertainty than directly observable economic statistics. A third source of uncertainty is related to the multiple shocks that affect the real economy and cause it to deviate from the expected trajectory. Identification of different shocks is already a difficult challenge for any central bank. But even in the most favorable case where these shocks are correctly identified, their consequences often remain extremely difficult to assess. Beyond this issue of uncertainty, monetary policy is characterized by an additional "timing" difficulty, because the action of a central bank has little or no instantaneous effect on economic activity and price levels. On the contrary, it must be long-term. Mechanical rules of monetary policy do not address the challenges posed by the fundamental uncertainty of the economic environment. This does not mean, however, that monetary policy can operate in a vacuum. The existence of a monetary concept with a clear objective and a transparent line of action is essential to anchor inflation expectations in the long term. Such a concept allows economic agents to develop a reliable representation of the reaction function of their central bank. Consumers, producers or investors can thus make informed decisions. 3. The SNB's monetary concept According to the constitution and the law, the SNB must serve the general interests of the country. In its policy of price stability, the SNB takes account of the economic situation. By price stability, we mean a trend increase in the Swiss consumer price index of less than 2% per year. We use different indicators to ensure that current monetary policy is consistent with our objective of price stability. Our assessment of inflationary risks is presented to the general public in the form of a quarterly inflation forecast. In order to account for the time between monetary impulses and their effects on prices, we make an inflation forecast for three consecutive years. This forecast indicates what the future price development should be if the economy were to develop in line with our expectations and if monetary conditions were to remain unchanged. In the event that the forecast deviates from price stability, this means that an adjustment of monetary policy must be considered. Inflation forecasting, however, is not an automatic rule because, as I pointed out before, the uncertain environment underlying its construction does not allow mechanical use. The judgment of the SNB's Executive Board therefore remains an important element in the monetary decision-making process. The objective of the SNB's monetary policy is to maintain price stability over the medium term. It has no exchange rate target. Nevertheless, as the rate of the euro against the franc and the European economic situation have a preponderant influence on the economic situation and price developments in Switzerland, these two parameters are important elements in our assessment of the situation. The implementation of our monetary policy is usually done through action on short-term interest rates. In concrete terms, we define a fluctuation band for the three-month Libor rate and aim to stabilise it by modulating the banks' liquidity endowment. Reverse repurchase agreements (repos) are our instrument of choice. So these are the most important elements of our monetary concept. Let me now present its implementation to you, referring to the current economic and monetary situation. 4. The international economic environment For a small open economy like Switzerland, it goes without saying that any economic analysis must begin with an overview of the international environment. From the point of view of the world economy, 2004 should prove to be one of the best vintages of the last 30 years. Global growth is expected to approach 5%. In industrialized countries, the economic recovery has gained momentum, although growth momentum has weakened somewhat in recent months. After holding above 4% in the previous four quarters, U.S. growth slowed in Q2 of this year. Economic activity rose by 2.8%, a respectable figure but below economic potential. This decline is mainly due to the weakness of private consumption, which in the second quarter grew at its slowest pace (1.6%) since the 2nd quarter of 2001. Several factors can explain this sluggishness: First, the lack of new impetus from monetary and fiscal policies has had a moderating effect on private consumption. The increase in interest rates in Q2 had the effect of reducing refinancing activities in the U.S. households. Similarly, the tax breaks decided by the Bush administration saw their stimulating effect decrease during the year. Second, it is undeniable that the rise in the price of oil has absorbed some of the purchasing power of households. In two and a half years, the price of a barrel of crude has more than doubled and is now approaching USD 50, a level never reached in the past. Still, in real terms, the current price of black gold is close to the level of the 1st Gulf War and represents only half of that reached during the 2nd oil shock of 1979. Third, the U.S. economic recovery remains characterized by below-average employment growth. Admittedly, observers no longer speak of "jobless recovery", but the fact remains that job creation remains below expectations. However, in the absence of external stimulus, maintaining a high level of household consumption requires increased confidence in employment prospects. Most observers agree that the slowdown in private consumption in the United States is temporary in nature and that the economy will regain more strength in the coming months. Thus, the OECD's recent forecasts predict a return to average growth of 3.5% for the second part of 2004. The latest economic indicators seem to confirm the scenario of a temporary "air hole". Financial conditions have improved since July thanks to lower long-term interest rates and a slight recovery in the equity market. The assumption of US growth returning to its potential also corresponds to the SNB's baseline scenario. In Europe, the economic recovery has been later and more moderate than in the United States. Initially mainly driven by exports, it has gained in depth in recent months. However, not all euro area countries are showing the same dynamism: among our neighbours, France is experiencing significant growth (3.4%) stimulated by strong domestic demand; Germany's growth is rather in the average (1.9%), thanks in particular to a very dynamic external demand. Private consumption, on the other hand, has not given a significant boost to growth since the 4th quarter of 2000. Italy, for its part, continues to underperform the rest of Europe, with a very moderate growth rate (1.2%). Finally, a few words on the Asian continent, which should have an exceptional year in 2004, thanks in particular to the good performance of the two heavyweights of the region. In Japan, the economic outlook has been continuously revised upwards. Despite a slowdown in the second quarter, market participants now expect economic growth to exceed 4%. Another piece of good news from the East is that the Chinese authorities seem poised to successfully land their economy. Growth is still expected to be above 7% compared to 9.1% in 2003. This short-term picture would not be complete without a few words on price developments. In this regard, despite rising oil prices and the highly expansive monetary policies followed by most central banks since the turn of the century, the risk of inflation slippage seems limited. In both the United States and Europe, core inflation remains below or around 2%, while it is slightly negative in Japan. More importantly, long-term inflation expectations remain well contained in all developed countries. In a context where the world's major economies are expected to grow at a rate close to or even slightly above potential, and inflation to remain subdued, it is not surprising that markets are anticipating a rather moderate tightening of monetary policies, which generally remain accommodative. 5. Economic developments in Switzerland For more than a year, the Swiss economy has been evolving at a pace close to or even above its potential. In the 2nd quarter, growth compared to the previous quarter edged down to 1.6%. Domestic demand remained strong but exports declined. Private consumption, supported by catch-up effects of certain types of consumer durables, grew at a pace slightly above its long-term average. Investment grew at a moderate pace. In this respect, it is interesting to note that the revised national accounts figures no longer show a massive fall in investment in equipment for 2002, which significantly mitigates the presumed need for catching up. Striking is the strong growth in housing investment that we have been experiencing for almost a year. Commercial constructions, on the other hand, have not experienced the same dynamic. Since the beginning of the year, foreign trade has certainly suffered from the anemia of European demand - particularly in Germany - but the negative growth in exports in the 2nd quarter can be explained. also for more technical reasons. The monthly statistics of exports of goods of the customs administration allow to be optimistic for the 3rd quarter of this year. While the leading short-term indicators (KOF, PMI, OECD) have declined, they still indicate a positive direction in economic activity. The revival of activity has so far not been enough to get the labour market out of its torpor. Labour demand indicators continue to provide no signal of recovery. While the recovery in activity has been more moderate than in the past, this is not enough to explain the lack of reaction from the labour market. One reason could be that companies cut relatively few jobs during the recession. This led to a negative evolution of labour productivity during this phase. We are currently experiencing the opposite situation: companies are not yet hiring, despite the revival of activity, which allows them to make up for the accumulated delays in labour productivity growth. It will probably be necessary to wait until 2005 to see a significant fall in unemployment. While spare capacity remains substantial on the labour market side, the degree of technical capacity utilisation in industry has increased, which tends to support the hypothesis of an increase in productivity. In the coming months, growth momentum is expected to remain above the economy's potential. Excess capacity is therefore expected to gradually decrease. In Switzerland too, price dynamics remain very moderate. On an annual basis, the price increase reached 1% last August. Inflation has seen a slight upward correction since the beginning of the year, mainly due to higher oil prices and higher rents. Core inflation is also rising slightly but remains below 1%. 6. Implications for monetary policy To summarize our assessment of the economic environment, we believe that the economic environment remains buoyant. Today, the three-month Libor has returned to its pre-March 2003 decline, which occurred in exceptional circumstances. The SNB's monetary policy remains expansive and continues to strongly support the economic recovery. Moreover, the inflation forecast drawn up in mid-September (see the graph in the annex) tells us that in the event of a further recovery in Switzerland and abroad, the current level of short rates would not be sufficient to stabilize inflation at less than 2% by mid-2006. Rate hikes of interest are not, however, programmed in advance. They will depend crucially on the future development of the economy. I am convinced that we would be wrong to almost mechanically raise our policy rates to a supposedly neutral level. Moreover, ex ante, we cannot know precisely where this "neutral" rate is located. A cautious attitude in the rate normalization phase is therefore justified for the following reasons: First, the Swiss economy still has spare capacity. As a result, it can withstand a few quarters of above-potential growth without immediate price pressure. But as our inflation forecast indicates, this does not mean that we can maintain the degree of expansion of current monetary policy indefinitely. Second, while our scenario of sustained global economic growth remains the most likely, it remains subject to risks. Among the developments to be followed closely, there is first of all the dynamics of the labor market in the United States and its potential effect on private consumption and growth. Then there is the difficult geopolitical situation and the risks of a further increase in the price of oil. Finally, among the longer-term dangers to the global economy is the persistence of current account imbalances in the United States. Third, the monetary policy of a small country such as Switzerland must also take into account the exchange rate, as the latter is an important component of general monetary conditions. To avoid a pronounced appreciation of the franc, our monetary tightening policy must be conducted with skill, especially if this tightening is carried out autonomously vis-e0-vis the European Central Bank. A sharp revaluation of the Swiss franc following an unforeseen event would require an appropriate response from the SNB. Finally, from a structural point of view, the general economic environment should remain favourable to maintaining price stability over the next few years, thus facilitating the task of monetary policy. Thus, the continuation of the globalization process, with the integration of economies as important as China or India, should maintain strong competitive pressure on companies and limit their opportunities to raise prices. In Switzerland, the announcement of the upcoming arrival of more aggressive "discounter" chains (Aldi, Lidl) is already shaking up the retail sector. Increased competition is expected to have a favourable effect on prices, without the need for the government to take drastic measures such as lowering prices imposed on major French or Italian distributors. In the long term, a third moderating effect could result from the entry into force of the 2nd phase of the agreement on the free movement of persons between Switzerland and the European Union. A more flexible labour offer limits the risk of triggering a price-wage spiral. 7. Conclusions The SNB's analytical framework seeks to reconcile the need for long-term monetary action with the uncertainty surrounding the changing economic environment. Monetary policy is not aimed at a fine-tuning of economic activity but remains oriented towards maintaining price stability over the medium term. However, it is modulated according to the differences between the supposed productive potential of the economy and the actual use of the country's resources. This is why the assessment of inflationary potential requires an estimate of the future evolution of the economic situation. However, this estimate is subject to revision because shocks can cause the economy to deviate from the expected trajectory, and because our knowledge of the mechanisms of operation of the economy is imperfect. Today, we believe that the economic recovery remains robust, both in Switzerland and abroad. For our country, we expect real GDP growth of almost 2% in 2004 and continued sustainable economic growth over the next two years. Thus, the rate of capacity utilisation will tend to increase, while unemployment will fall slowly. The increase in the rate of capacity utilisation will lead to a strengthening of inflationary pressures in the medium term. However, this scenario could be revised in the light of new elements. That is why we will continue to carefully analyse economic developments in order to draw the necessary monetary conclusions. ANNEX

Title: Minimizing risk and securing liquidity through the use of repo transactions
text: Risk minimization and liquidity protection through the use of repo transactions Prof. Dr. Thomas J. Jordan Deputy Member of the Board of Directors Swiss National Bank Conference: "Liquidity"  a challenge for banks 11 January 2005 Dear Sir or Madam, The subject of my remarks is the repo business, in particular the reduction of risks and the safeguarding of liquidity through the use of repo transactions instead of traditional money market instruments. The presentation builds on the problems in the unsecured money market pointed out by Philipp Hildebrand. I will structure my remarks as follows: First, I will briefly discuss the emergence and development of the repo business in Switzerland. After that, I would like to present the risks that exist in the traditional money market business and show how these can be reduced by using repos. Finally, I will discuss the possibility of securing liquidity through the use of repo transactions and the role of the SNB in the secured Swiss franc money market. The aim of my remarks is to convince you that your bank should primarily carry out repo transactions for liquidity management. 1. Origin and development of the repo business in Franconia In Switzerland, the repo market emerged only a few years ago, although repo stores have existed internationally for a long time. Until the end of 1996, these transactions in our country were subject to stamp duty because they were legally regarded as purchases or sales of securities. This duty to pay prevented the emergence of a repo market in Switzerland. At the suggestion of the SNB and the banks, the Federal Tax Administration reinterpreted the Federal Act on Stamp Duties on 1 January 1997. From then on, it regarded repos as financing transactions, which eliminated stamp duty. In addition, during the revision of the National Bank Act of November 1997, repo operations were included in the SNB's monetary policy instruments. This created the necessary conditions for the establishment of a repo market in Switzerland. The starting signal for Swiss franc repo trading was finally given on 20 April 1998. The late introduction of the repo business in Switzerland had the advantage that  in line with international practice  a repo system that was completely new and world-leading in terms of infrastructure and processes could be set up. Our repo system differs significantly from the usual triparty systems and over-the-counter repo transactions in terms of standardization and integration of the settlement processes. The Swiss franc repo system is based on an integration of the Eurex Repo trading platform, the securities settlement system SECOM and the real-time payment system SIC. This infrastructure is commonly referred to as the Swiss Value Chain. As a triparty service provider, SIS SegaInterSettle AG plays an important role in minimizing risks and increasing efficiency with processing and risk management. This system was set up in close cooperation between the National Bank, commercial banks and service providers. The repo business is traditionally used by many central banks as an instrument for implementing their monetary policy. The SNB, on the other hand, mainly used foreign exchange swaps to manage liquidity over a long period of time. With the introduction of the repo business, we now have a versatile and efficient monetary policy instrument that has proven itself for interest rate and liquidity management even in exceptional situations due to its flexible handling. The Swiss franc repo market has grown steadily in recent years. The outstanding repo volume has fluctuated between 60 and 70 billion Swiss francs in recent months. Since, following the introduction of the repo business, the SNB provided liquidity to the banking system practically exclusively via this instrument, the volume of SNB repos rose to a level of CHF 20 to 25 billion in a relatively short period of time. Since then, the volume of outstanding repos has increased only slightly to around CHF 30 billion today. With the introduction of the electronic trading platform Eurex Repo in mid-1999, the basis for the emergence of the interbank market was laid. The repo trade between the banks has developed steadily since then. The outstanding repo volume of the interbank market has fluctuated between CHF 30 billion and CHF 40 billion in recent months (see Figure 1). 2. Risks in traditional money market business I now come to the risks in the traditional money market business, which is mainly known as the foreign exchange swap US dollar against Swiss francs and the unsecured money market business, the so-called custody business. The interbank foreign exchange swaps US dollars against francs with a maturity of up to seven days are expected to reach an outstanding volume of several 100 billion francs. The market volume of custodian transactions is somewhat lower, but still considerable. We estimate the outstanding stock at around CHF 100 billion. Both the foreign exchange swap business and the custody business currently have a significantly larger volume than the repo business. In foreign exchange swapping, two currencies are exchanged for a certain period of time. This instrument is particularly suitable for the direct balancing of two opposing currency positions. This is basically a secured transaction. Nevertheless, the foreign exchange swap is fraught with risks. The focus is on market risk during the term of the swap, because due to exchange rate fluctuations, the amount of the claim no longer has to be fully covered and losses can therefore arise. In practice, this risk is limited by credit limits. However, the counterparties are also exposed to a settlement risk in the case of foreign exchange swaps, unless the settlement is carried out according to the principle of "payment against payment" via Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS). In the case of unsecured money market business, credit risks in particular are assumed. The lender incurs the credit risk due to a possible default of the counterparty. It is important to understand that counterparty limits do not eliminate credit risk, but merely limit the potential loss. Unsecured money market business is based exclusively on confidence in the good creditworthiness of the counterparty, which experience has shown can prove problematic, especially in exceptional situations. 3. Reduction of risks from repo transactions in Swiss francs The risks associated with traditional money market instruments can be significantly reduced by using repo transactions and their settlement via the Swiss Value Chain. Let me explain this briefly. In the case of a repo, the borrower sells securities to the lender with the simultaneous agreement to buy back securities of the same class and quantity from the lender at a later date. For the duration of the transaction, interest is paid by the borrower. The repo business is basically comparable to a covered loan. A significant difference, however, is that in the repo business, the fluctuations in the value of the securities during the term and thus the coverage are regularly compensated by margin balancing. In principle, there are also certain risks in the repo business during settlement and during the term. However, these are significantly reduced in our Swiss franc repo system through the use of the Swiss Value Chain and special services of SIS. The repo transaction is concluded via the electronic trading platform Eurex Repo. By means of straight-through processing, all according to the transactions resulting from the transaction are automatically triggered by SIS. The condition for automatic settlement is that the borrower has corresponding securities and the lender has sufficient credit. As soon as these requirements are met, the transaction is processed according to the principle of "delivery against payment". The securities are transferred to the lender's SIS securities custody account and the money is credited to the borrower's SNB current account at the same time (see Figure 2). When the transaction matures, the reversal is triggered by SIS in the same way by including the repo interest. With the standardized Swiss franc repo, the amount of money must always be 100 percent covered by securities. Therefore, between two counterparties, all open repo transactions are evaluated daily by the SIS on the money and title page. In the case of securities in foreign currencies, fluctuations in value due to exchange rate movements are also taken into account. If an imbalance occurs that exceeds the unilaterally set tolerance limit, a corresponding value compensation is automatically generated. This compensation takes place through the delivery of securities. If no securities are available, SIS will initiate a debiting of the SNB current account of the obligated counterparty. This SIS triparty service limits credit and market risks to fluctuations in the value of securities from one day to the next (see Figure 3). Automated processing also virtually eliminates operational risks and fulfillment risk. Over the past six months, out of more than 60,000 transactions, only five commitments have not been fulfilled on time or with a delay of one day. This illustrates how efficiently and safely the Franken repo system works. SIS's repo services and transactions have been specifically designed to meet the needs of small and medium-sized banks. The externally executed processes only have to be recorded by the business partners in their books. As a result of the convincing infrastructure, Swiss franc repo transactions are almost exclusively handled via the Swiss Value Chain. 4. Compensation for risk in unsecured money market transactions Although the risks of unsecured money market operations are much greater than those of repo operations, the interest rate differential between the two instruments is relatively small. From In our view, the risk in the custody business is still insufficiently compensated. I would like to explain this briefly. If a bank lends money to another bank in the form of an unsecured loan, it takes on counterparty risk. This transaction causes the lender own funds costs. These reflect the risk taken and the targeted return on equity and amount to between 10 and 30 basis points of the loan amount granted. Own funds costs must not be neglected even if sufficient own funds are available, because these costs reflect the credit risk incurred. Various banks have therefore begun to offset the capital costs internally to the polluter. In contrast to custodian transactions, repo transactions in Swiss francs do not have to be backed by own funds, because our repo system balances value on a daily basis and thus no credit risk is assumed. Currently, the custody account rate is only 5 to 10 basis points higher than the repo rate. This reduced income in the repo business represents an extremely favorable "insurance premium" to eliminate credit risk. No external insurance company would be willing to insure the credit risk on such terms. Experience has shown that the credit rating of a counterparty often reacts belatedly to the actual circumstances. Neither the risk taken nor the targeted return on equity are adequately taken into account in the custody interest rate. These considerations show that the risk-based interest rate in the custody account business would have to be significantly higher compared to the repo rate. It seems to us to be an important task of the bank management to provide the right incentives internally for money trading by offsetting the costs of own funds. 5. Securing liquidity through repo transactions So far, I have mainly spoken of the reduction of credit, market and settlement risks through repo transactions. However, the repo business also makes an important contribution to securing liquidity. This applies both in everyday life and in extraordinary situations. In his presentation, Philipp Hildebrand impressively demonstrated the importance of having reliable sources of liquidity for extraordinary situations. Unsecured money market business is based solely on confidence in the good creditworthiness of a counterparty. Even borrowers with a good rating can participate in extraordinary Situations get into trouble. In such cases, the credit limits are usually immediately reduced or completely deleted. Dependence on credit limits is dangerous from the point of view of the borrower. Credit limits do not provide sufficient security for liquidity in difficult times. A functioning repo market allows refinancing on the interbank market regardless of credit limits. In addition, access to the National Bank is only possible via repo transactions. The repo market therefore makes a significant contribution to securing liquidity, even in exceptional situations. One must be aware that a quick change from the unsecured to the secured money market at the time of a crisis is an illusion. A lack of know-how, the time required to set up the technical infrastructure and an insufficient volume of SNB-repo-capable effects can prove to be stumbling blocks. Even in normal times, the repo business helps to secure the liquidity of the banking sector. The reason for this is that the lender can freely dispose of the securities received until the maturity of the transaction. If necessary, the lender can convert these securities back into money on the market at any time and thus increase his liquidity. As a result of an efficient repo market, effects are increasingly developing into a valuable asset with multiple applications. They can also be used to obtain intraday liquidity or to use the congestion financing facility at the National Bank. In addition to securing liquidity, securities often also have to be deposited as collateral for other purposes. For example, as initial margin to cover open positions in foreign exchange and derivatives trading or as margin to operators of trading systems with a central counterparty. 6. The SNB's contribution to securing liquidity in the Swiss franc money market In the following, I will make a few remarks about the role of the National Bank in the secured money market. Since the beginning of the "Repo Project" in 1997, we have taken an active role both in the development of the repo trade and in its further development. In addition, the SNB's decision to make the repo business its main monetary policy instrument was an important prerequisite for the development of a liquid repo market in Switzerland. The SNB's motivation to promote the Swiss franc repo business is twofold. On the one hand, for the reasons already explained, we want to further promote the secured interbank market for Swiss francs. By reducing risks in the money market, the stability of the financial system tends to increase. On the other hand, we want a modern, efficient set of instruments for the implementation of our monetary policy. The repo business can cover all of the SNB's monetary policy needs. For the implementation of monetary policy, the repo business has the following advantages over the previously used foreign exchange swap. First, the risks have been reduced. Secondly, the circle of potential business partners could be increased from a few to around 100 banks. This broad access to central bank money increases efficiency in the Swiss franc money market. Since the Swiss franc has traditionally been of great international importance, banks abroad are also important partners in the Swiss franc money market. We therefore liberalised access to our facilities. Today, internationally active banks domiciled abroad can also make use of the SNB's various facilities. We have recently published our monetary policy instruments and related procedures under a directive. All of the SNB's ordinary monetary policy instruments are now based on repo business. Only the Lombard loan is an exception. However, it will be replaced by the repo business at the special rate by the end of 2005. In the following, I would like to briefly discuss the most important instruments. The SNB's main financing operations serve to provide the banking system with liquidity on a regular basis. We conclude main financing transactions with the banks on a daily basis. The terms of these transactions usually vary between one day and several weeks. The transaction is concluded via an auction procedure in the form of a volume tender. This means that the banks ask for a certain amount of liquidity for a fixed repo rate. If the total demand exceeds the auction volume we are aiming for, we reduce the bids received proportionately. A few minutes after the end of the auction, the banks receive information about their allocation amount. Our process is at the forefront of efficiency compared to other central banks. The repo rate, the auction volume and the duration of the individual main financing operations are based on the SNB's monetary policy requirements. Our daily presence in the market allows us to exert a targeted influence on money market interest rates. Fine-tuning transactions serve to compensate for undesirable effects of exogenous influences on liquidity supply as well as strong fluctuations in short-term money market interest rates. Fine-tuning is carried out via bilateral repo transactions, the terms of which may differ from the main financing transactions. During the day, the SNB provides counterparties with interest-free intraday liquidity via repo transactions in order to facilitate the processing of payment transactions in Swiss Interbank Clearing (SIC) and foreign exchange transactions in Continuous Linked Settlement (CLS). The amount of money withdrawn must be repaid at the latest at the end of the same bank working day. Therefore, this liquidity is not counted towards compliance with the minimum reserve requirements and the liquidity requirements of banking law. The congestion financing facility serves banks to bridge unexpected liquidity bottlenecks in the short term. The interest rate on the receipt of liquidity under this facility is two percentage points above the level of the overnight lending rate. This interest premium is intended to discourage banks from using the Facility as a permanent source of funding. From the beginning of 2006, the congestion financing facility can only be used via a repo transaction at a special rate. A prerequisite for the conclusion of a repo transaction at the special rate is the granting of a limit by the SNB and the permanent coverage of this limit with securities eligible for SNB repo. The limit determines the maximum possible withdrawal of liquidity by a bank. The limit is claimed in the form of an overnight repo transaction. The securities are stored in a "SNB" cover account denominated in the counterparty at SIS. Certain classes of securities are required to conclude repo transactions with the SNB. We currently accept securities denominated in Swiss francs and euros that meet certain requirements relating to the issuer's creditworthiness and market liquidity. The euro-denominated securities are also increasingly accepted by domestic banks in the interbank business. Because the volume of securities on the domestic capital market is limited, we consider two developments in particular to be crucial for the Swiss franc repo market to grow in line with its potential. On the one hand, the range of accepted securities in foreign currencies must be broadened and, on the other hand, SIS must establish and expand secure and efficient links with national and international securities depositaries. Individual steps in these directions have already been taken. There are already efficient links between SIS and Euroclear Brussels and Clearstream Luxembourg. In addition, in spring 2005 the SNB intends to include bonds issued by other European countries in its securities baskets. In addition, we are considering accepting securities in US dollars and pounds sterling as cover for repo transactions in the future. Overall, we strive to create the most favorable conditions possible for the further development of the repo market in order to make a significant contribution to securing liquidity in the Swiss money market. 7. Conclusion I hope that I was able to convince you of the positive qualities of the repo business and would like to conclude by briefly highlighting the key messages of my presentation. In the Swiss franc money market, the repo business has clear advantages in terms of risk reduction compared to the foreign exchange swap and the custodian business. In the repo business, credit risks are minimized because the cash receivable is fully covered with securities at all times. Operational risks and fulfillment risk are also virtually eliminated in repo business through the use of the Swiss Value Chain and SIS risk management. Unsecured money market business, on the other hand, is based solely on confidence in the counterparty's willingness to pay. In the case of foreign exchange swaps, exchange rate fluctuations can also result in losses on the receivable amount. Therefore, even if sufficient own funds are available, the cost of own funds should be adequately taken into account in the internal performance calculation. The corresponding incentives should be set by the bank management. In terms of securing liquidity, the repo business also has clear advantages over the foreign exchange swap and the custody business. A functioning repo market contributes significantly to securing liquidity in the banking sector. SNB-repo-eligible securities can be converted into money on the interbank market at any time, even if they are already come from a repo business. Liquidity risks can therefore be significantly limited by the use of repo transactions. Dependence on credit limits, on the other hand, is risky because this liquidity potential can disappear in a very short time. In addition, from 2006 onwards, access to all of the SNB's facilities will only be possible via repo transactions. In order to be able to ensure liquidity at all times, every independent domestic bank should therefore join the Franken RepoSystem. Thank you for your attention. Figure 1: Franconian Repo Market Mio.
