Conclusion Il est vident, que la position de choix occupe actuellement par la place financire suisse au niveau international est le rsultat d'une longue tradition helvtique dans les mtiers de 10 la banque. Le dveloppement de l'industrie bancaire s'est appuy sur la stabilit politique et montaire du pays, sur une volont de respect de la sphre prive et de discrtion, ainsi que sur une recherche continue de qualit. Comme le reste de notre conomie, le secteur bancaire suisse s'est galement toujours caractris par une grande ouverture vers l'extrieur. Cette ouverture permet  nos banques d'tendre leur march mais elle les expose aussi  une forte concurrence internationale. La place financire suisse accepte pleinement cette situation, consciente de la force de ses avantages comparatifs hrits du pass, mais aussi de la ncessit de sadapter  un march en continuelle transformation. L'augmentation de la concurrence globale observe ces dernires annes a eu pour consquence de modifier profondment le paysage bancaire helvtique. Nos banques ont ainsi d passer par le chemin parfois douloureux des restructurations et des consolidations. Elles l'ont fait avec la volont affiche de prserver leur position dans un march maintenant globalis. Mais cette situation doit tre consolide en permanence. Notre place financire ne pourra conserver sa position internationale qu'en augmentant continuellement son savoir-faire et en renforant sa rputation de solidit et de probit. C'est une tche qui appelle l'effort de chacun. Nos tablissements financiers font preuve dune volont rsolue d'adapter leurs services aux ralits du march. De leur ct, les autorits se sont fix pour objectif de promouvoir une lgislation conforme aux normes internationales les plus exigeantes, sans compromis contre les abus, garantissant la solidit des tablissements bancaires et facilitant les adaptations ncessaires  leur prennit. Notre place financire ne cherche donc pas  cultiver le mythe de la forteresse alpine. Elle a fait le pari de la concurrence, de louverture et de la prservation de ses avantages compars. Cette stratgie lui demande de dvelopper une forte capacit dadaptation sans renoncer pour autant  ce qui a fait sa tradition. Title: Monetary policy in the grip of the euro?
text: Monetary policy under the spell of the euro? Prof. Dr. Thomas J. Jordan Deputy Member of the Board of Directors Head of Financial Market Operations Swiss National Bank "Federal Conference of Economics Professors at Universities of Applied Sciences and Universities of Applied Sciences from Germany, Austria and Switzerland" ZHW Winterthur, 19 May 2005 Dear Sir or Madam, I was happy to accept the invitation of the Zurich University of Applied Sciences Winterthur and am pleased to be able to participate in the conference of economics professors. The topic of your conference is "Economic Structural Problems in Germany, Austria and Switzerland". Professor Armin Jans asked me to speak on monetary policy and the euro. Whether he sees the euro as a structural problem for the three countries, I do not know exactly. The fact is that the euro has become an integral part of the process of economic and political integration of Europe. Even for Switzerland  although not a member of the European Monetary Union  the euro has changed the monetary policy situation considerably. In the next 40 minutes, I will try to explain to what extent Switzerland and the monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) are influenced or even cast a spell over by the euro. In my presentation, I will first make a few general remarks on European Monetary Union. I then analyse how the euro affects Switzerland and the Swiss franc in various areas. In particular, I will address the question of whether the SNB can continue to conduct an autonomous monetary policy. I conclude my presentation with an economic and monetary policy outlook as well as some conclusions. European Monetary Union A common currency area brings advantages and disadvantages to the participating countries. An important economic advantage is that transaction costs are reduced overall and efficient factor allocation is promoted. There is no need to hedge exchange rate risks and simplify the comparison of prices and the processing of payments across national borders. A single currency also leads to integrated and liquid capital markets. All this increases transparency and competition, thus leading to more efficient flows of goods and capital between member countries and should therefore have a positive impact on economic growth throughout the currency area. However, a single currency also has economic disadvantages. In a monetary union, there is only one monetary policy. Necessary adjustments to influences that the 2 In a monetary union, countries can no longer be achieved by changing nominal exchange rates and setting interest rates differently. Rather, the adjustments must be made through changes in the prices of goods and wages or through the migration of workers. Such adjustments are often associated with cyclical fluctuations as long as the flexibility of labour and product markets is limited. For a common European currency to be economically worthwhile, the advantages of a monetary union must outweigh the disadvantages as a whole. The extent to which this applies to the European Monetary Union is an open debate. Today, the eurozone is still a rather heterogeneous community. A future accession of the new EU members to the European Monetary Union is likely to increase the heterogeneity within the eurozone, at least temporarily. However, the increasing integration of markets in Europe should improve the conditions for a well-functioning currency area over time. For Europe, however, monetary union also has a political dimension: the single currency is a strong force in the direction of further integration and therefore also has a great symbolic character for the European Union (EU). Overall, the economic development of the eurozone has so far been rather disappointing. Real GDP growth in the eurozone was just under 2.0% between 1999 and 2004, while it was around 3% in the US. Unemployment has hardly decreased since the introduction of the euro, averaging over 8%. However, unsatisfactory growth and high unemployment throughout the eurozone are largely not due to a wrong monetary policy of the European Central Bank (ECB) or to the lack of opportunity to adjust nominal exchange rates between countries. Rather, it is the backlog of structural reforms in Europe compared to other economic areas that is primarily responsible for this. Looking at the member states individually, it is striking that the economic differences within the European Monetary Union have been considerable in recent years. Since the introduction of the euro, for example, in Ireland the average 3 Real GDP growth was 7% and the average inflation rate was around 4%. Germany, on the other hand, recorded real GDP growth of around 1% and an average inflation rate of 1.4%. (Figure 1). However, differences in inflation and growth rates between member countries are not necessarily a sign of a poorly functioning currency area in Europe. On the one hand, we have a convergence process in which the economically weaker countries catch up over time. Growth and inflation are higher than average during this period. This convergence process has been particularly strong for some peripheral countries such as Ireland and Greece. Differences in growth and inflation rates due to catch-up effects of individual countries do not pose a major problem for monetary policy. On the other hand, temporary differences in growth and inflation are also necessary between member states with similar levels of development in order to be able to compensate for imbalances within the monetary union - for example due to different production structures. Monetary policy is problematic if these adjustment processes are not sufficiently rapid due to insufficient flexibility of the product and labour markets and the boom and recession phases in individual member states are prolonged due to a lack of monetary policy instruments. In this case, long-lasting differences in growth and inflation would be a sign of a poorly functioning monetary union. However, the persistent differences in growth within the eurozone are not only due to convergence and slow adjustment processes. In various Member States, necessary structural reforms are being carried out only hesitantly, so that growth in these countries remains low compared to the more reform-minded ones. Differences in growth within the eurozone, which are due to this, have nothing to do with the single monetary policy. Nevertheless, the ECB sees itself increasingly under pressure to use its monetary policy to solve the various structural problems, which is not without danger for the future of the euro. 4 Eurozone and Switzerland What does the European Monetary Union mean for Switzerland? As a very open economy, Switzerland is strongly intertwined with foreign countries. Well over 40% of Switzerland's economic output is exported. The eurozone is by far Switzerland's most important trading partner. In 2004, more than half of Switzerland's exports went to the eurozone and Switzerland obtained over 70% of its imports from these countries (Figure 2). It is therefore not surprising that Switzerland's economic cycle is strongly correlated with that of the eurozone. If one compares Switzerland with the various countries of the eurozone, the following is striking: In terms of real GDP growth, Switzerland joins the low-growth countries of the European Monetary Union. In addition, it has almost always performed slightly worse in recent years compared to the eurozone as a whole (Chart 3). In Switzerland, it is the still partially protected domestic sector that is mainly responsible for the low growth. However, Switzerland has very low inflation. Inflation in Switzerland is usually even lower than in the country with the lowest inflation in the European Monetary Union (Figure 4). Due to a monetary policy that has been credible for a long time, the SNB has acquired a high reputation on the markets, which is very important for maintaining price stability. As a young institution, the ECB has yet to build up this reputation. Switzerland is also doing well in terms of the labour market compared to the eurozone. Over the past six years, unemployment has consistently been at the lower end of the corresponding rates in the euro area (Figure 5). This is mainly a consequence of the much more flexible labour market in Switzerland. The impact of the euro on Switzerland and the Swiss franc was assessed differently in the run-up to the introduction of the euro. While some market observers predicted the demise of Switzerland's monetary autonomy, others warned of a massive appreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro and the associated problems for the Swiss export industry. However, developments to date have shown that these fears were not justified. The introduction of the euro has had a positive effect on Switzerland and has not jeopardised the independence of the franc. Let me now explain this in more detail. 5 More stable currency conditions While the first half of the nineties was marked by abrupt and massive exchange rate adjustments of some European currencies against the Swiss franc, the introduction of the euro brought Swiss exporters much more stable currency conditions (Chart 6). With the euro, there is now a currency in a large part of Europe whose quality corresponds to the old DM. It is therefore not surprising that in the last six years there has been no clear upward or downward trend of the Swiss franc against the euro. In the event of temporary fluctuations, the Swiss franc appreciated by around 3.8% in nominal terms between January 1999 and April 2005. In real terms, a depreciation of around 1.5% can be recorded (Figure 7). The volatility of the export-weighted exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the countries of the European Monetary Union has also decreased significantly since the introduction of the euro (Figure 8). The euro-franc exchange rate is generally one of the exchange rates with the lowest volatility ever. The volatility of the euro-franc exchange rate is significantly lower than that of the euro-pound exchange rate or the euro-krone exchange rate, although both England and Sweden are members of the EU (Chart 9). Looking at the cumulative deviation of a member country's inflation rate from inflation throughout the European Monetary Union, it can be seen that real exchange rate conditions within the eurozone change quite significantly over time. The most extreme examples are Ireland and Germany: since the introduction of the euro, Ireland has recorded a real appreciation of more than 10% compared to the eurozone, while Germany has depreciated by around 4%. The real exchange rate index of the Swiss franc against the eurozone has been much more stable over this period (Chart 10). Swiss foreign trade is thus exposed to relatively moderate real exchange rate fluctuations in an international comparison, even compared to individual countries in the eurozone. Use of the euro as a means of payment in Switzerland A much-discussed question is whether the euro can displace the franc as a means of payment in Switzerland over time, or whether the euro has the potential to become a parallel currency in Switzerland. Experience so far shows that neither is the case. Although the euro is used in many shops and in practically all hotels in Switzerland as 6 Means of payment accepted. However, the use of the swiss franc in Switzerland both as a means of payment and as a store of value has not decreased as a result of the introduction of the euro. In the case of cash payments, the euro's share appears to be roughly equivalent to that of the european currencies replaced. The use of the euro focuses mainly on border regions and tourism. Even in cashless payment transactions, we cannot see a trend towards an increased processing of payments within Switzerland in euros. In the case of deposits by customers at domestic branches of Swiss banks, the euro has not yet been able to increase at the expense of the Swiss franc and the franc's share of financial assets at Swiss banks has also not declined. In order for the euro to become a parallel currency, important contracts such as employment contracts, loan agreements or rental agreements would have to be concluded in euros in Switzerland and the euro would have to be used to a greater extent for domestic transactions. To date, such contracts are concluded almost exclusively in Swiss francs and relatively few domestic transactions are carried out in euros. There are few signs that this situation will change anytime soon. On the contrary, the Swiss franc is used as a currency in the eurozone when taking out mortgage loans. However, this phenomenon is mainly limited to Austria. Euro and Swiss franc on the financial markets I explained earlier that the euro has not yet been able to displace the franc in Switzerland. What is the situation on the international financial markets? Could there be a displacement of the Franc by the euro? Let me first note that the Swiss franc plays a far more important role in the international financial markets than one would expect given Switzerland's economic size. The Swiss franc is one of the most important currencies in the world, which not only has a positive effect on liquidity in the Swiss franc financial markets, but also contributes significantly to the importance of the Swiss financial centre. For Switzerland, however, the international role of the franc also has a downside. In times of crisis, there can be large fluctuations 7 the exchange rate of the Swiss franc, which can lead to serious problems for our foreign trade. I will come back to this "safe haven" problem later. As already mentioned, the Swiss franc is attractive for raising capital due to the low level of interest rates. This can be seen as an example of the Swiss franc bonds listed on the Swiss stock exchange SWX: Almost half of the bonds traded come from foreign issuers, of which around 60% are accounted for by the eurozone (Chart 11). Swiss franc bonds have not been able to benefit from the strong growth of the bond markets in recent years and have gained only slightly in terms of amount. The euro, on the other hand, has become increasingly important in recent years in international comparison on the bond markets. Since the first quarter of 2004, there have been even more bonds in euros than in dollars (in US dollars). On the foreign exchange markets, the Swiss franc is one of the top five currencies traded after the US dollar, the euro, the Japanese yen and the British pound. A survey by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) shows that in 2004 the Swiss franc accounted for over 6% of the total turnover volume of the reporting foreign exchange markets. The share of the euro was about 37%. This makes the euro the second most frequently traded currency after the US dollar. However, the US dollar remains the dominant currency in the foreign exchange markets: it was involved in almost 90% of foreign exchange transactions in 2004. Both the euro and the Swiss franc have lost some market share in the foreign exchange markets since the last survey in 2001 (Chart 12). We can therefore see that the euro has been able to establish itself as a leading currency on the international financial markets, but the Swiss franc has not been displaced by this. For international investors, the Swiss franc has long played a role as a safe haven in crises. This was associated with rapid and massive appreciation of the Swiss franc. For Switzerland, as a small and very open economy, these abrupt revaluations have always been a major problem. Overnight, they could severely affect the competitiveness of certain export sectors. Several times 8 the fear was expressed that this problem could be exacerbated with the introduction of the euro. In recent years, however, it has become clear that the role of the Swiss franc as a safe haven tends to be less important. One possible explanation is that, as outlined above, the euro has gained in importance and credibility in international financial markets. During crises, for example, there are now more and more adjustments between the dollar and the euro, and less financial capital flows into the Franc. This is a positive development for Switzerland, because it strengthens the possibilities of an autonomous monetary policy of the SNB  to which I will come to in a moment. Autonomous monetary policy of the SNB The SNB sets the band for the three-month Libor with the aim of maintaining price stability in Switzerland in the medium term; it does not pursue an exchange rate objective. The experience of the last six years makes it clear that the SNB can pursue an independent policy towards the ECB and continue to exploit its room for manoeuvre: during this time, it has made an overall more determined change in key interest rates than the ECB. In 2000, for example, the SNB raised interest rates earlier and more decisively, and in the period 2001 to 2003 we lowered interest rates earlier and more. While the ECB has left its key interest rate unchanged since June 2003, the SNB made two interest rate hikes of 25 basis points each in 2004 (Chart 13). In this comparison, it should be noted that inflation in the eurozone during this period was mostly outside the realm of price stability, which limited the ECB's flexibility. The SNB will continue to conduct an autonomous monetary policy in the future. However, this does not mean that the SNB is ignoring the euro. The euro-franc exchange rate and economic developments in the eurozone have a strong influence on the development of the Swiss economy and on prices in Switzerland. They therefore represent important elements in determining the SNB's monetary policy stance. 9 Let me briefly explain in detail the influence of the euro on our monetary policy decisions (Chart 14). The euro-franc exchange rate was close to 1.60 throughout 1999. Contrary to expectations, the introduction of the euro did not lead to any turbulence. The economy then picked up significantly at the beginning of 2000. At the same time, the Swiss franc depreciated against the dollar. This led to an undesirable easing of the monetary environment. The SNB responded by gradually increasing the target range for the three-month Libor. In contrast, the euro appreciated against the Swiss franc from 1.60 to 1.52 by mid-2000. This appreciation of the Swiss franc was justifiable from the point of view of monetary policy in view of the economic situation at the time. After signs of a slowdown in economic growth and an increase in economic risks at the beginning of 2001, the SNB lowered the target range for the three-month Libor by 25 basis points in March 2001. After the events of 11 September, the Swiss franc appreciated rapidly and strongly against the euro. The abrupt rise of the Swiss franc against the euro, combined with a slowdown in economic growth, forced the SNB to act quickly. In September 2001, it therefore lowered the target range for the three-month Libor by a total of 100 basis points within one week. The key interest rate cuts in December 2001, May 2002 and July 2002 were also largely due to the appreciation risks of the Swiss franc against the euro, which was now between 1.45 and 1.48. Due to the weak economy, a further appreciation against the euro would have been highly problematic at the time. The SNB made it clear to the markets that it would react at any time to a renewed appreciation of the Swiss franc due to the great uncertainties and possible deflation risks. It did so in March 2003 with a surprising reduction of the target range by 0.5 percentage points. Short-term interest rates were thus at an all-time low. In retrospect, this interest rate hike, which was tactically probably optimally chosen, was not without effect. The exchange rate situation eased significantly and the euro depreciated from 1.46 in March 2003 to over 1.58 in March 2004. In view of the uncertain economic outlook and low inflationary pressure, the very expansionary monetary policy was able to continue until June 2004. 10 As the economic recovery had strengthened in the course of 2004 and the risk of deflation had diminished, monetary policy was slightly tightened in June and September 2004. Since then, however, the share price has remained very expansionary with a target range of 0.25% - 1.25%. The SNB proceeded very cautiously with these interest rate hikes and the euro-franc exchange rate remained virtually unchanged. Reasons for an autonomous monetary policy There are always voices that vote for a peg of the Swiss franc to the euro. From the SNB's point of view, what are the reasons against such a connection? Thanks to its autonomy, the SNB can pursue a monetary policy tailored to Switzerland. It can react by appropriate means to influences that affect Switzerland differently from the eurozone. This would no longer be possible if the Swiss franc were linked to the euro. There is an interest rate differential of around 1.5 percentage points between Swiss franc and euro investments (Figure 15). A peg to the Swiss franc would quickly make this interest rate advantage disappear. This would place a heavy burden on Swiss companies and households and inhibit investment activity in Switzerland for a long time. A disappearance of the interest bonus would also have a clear negative impact on property, share and bond prices in Switzerland. The persistence of the interest rate bonus after the introduction of the euro is clear evidence that the markets do not assume that the Swiss franc will be linked to the euro. In recent decades, the Swiss franc has had a tendency to appreciate slightly in real terms against eurozone currencies. However, this appreciation has also taken place against other major currencies. It has nothing to do with monetary policy and is above all a consequence of the strong productivity progress of the Swiss export industry (Chart 16). A peg of the Swiss franc to the euro cannot prevent this appreciation based on real factors. In the event of a peg, the long-term real appreciation of the Swiss franc would simply manifest itself in the form of a correspondingly higher inflation rate in Switzerland. 11 Conclusion and outlook I shall conclude my remarks. In addition to a conclusion on the influence of the euro on Switzerland, I would like to give you a brief economic and monetary policy outlook. After six years of experience with the euro, Switzerland can draw a very positive balance. The Swiss franc continues to play a more important role in the international financial and foreign exchange markets. There was also no displacement of the franc by the euro as a means of payment in Switzerland. On the other hand, we have much more stable currency conditions in Europe today than before the introduction of the euro, and the development between the euro and the Swiss franc has so far been quite calm. The exchange rate risk for the Swiss foreign trade sector has been significantly reduced by the introduction of the euro. At the same time, Switzerland continues to enjoy the opportunity to conduct an independent monetary policy that can respond to Switzerland's economic circumstances. The euro has thus cast a spell over neither Switzerland nor Swiss monetary policy. However, we always keep a close eye on the euro and developments in the euro area and, if necessary, react with the instruments at our disposal. However, a peg of the Swiss franc to the euro is out of the question for the SNB under today's circumstances, as it would entail considerable risks and disadvantages for Switzerland. What is the economic and monetary policy outlook? In the last year, the economic recovery has strengthened somewhat and the risks of deflation have decreased significantly. This allowed us to slightly raise the target range for the three-month Libor and say goodbye to the zero interest rate policy. However, monetary policy is still extremely expansionary with negative real short-term interest rates. At the same time, however, the momentum of the upswing has weakened somewhat. This loss of momentum in the last two quarters is mainly due to a modest development of exports and investment in equipment, which in turn was a consequence of the slight slowdown in global economic growth in connection with higher oil prices. The SNB has therefore paused the normalisation of its monetary policy since last December. We have this leeway because the 12 Inflation risks at the moment are still moderate despite already long-lasting expansionary monetary policy and higher oil prices in Switzerland. The generally disappointing economic indicators so far this year point to lower GDP growth in Switzerland in 2005 compared to 2004. However, growth is likely to pick up again somewhat from the second or third quarter onwards and the upswing should then continue more clearly. The decisive factor for this scenario is that the global economy does not continue to lose momentum and that Swiss exports grow more strongly again. At the moment, the risks are rather directed downwards. The SNB therefore continues to support the economic recovery and will proceed cautiously in the further normalisation of monetary policy. Sooner or later, however, expansionary monetary policy must be corrected in order not to jeopardise price stability and to avoid distortions in asset prices. The SNB is therefore monitoring developments in the economy and on the financial markets very closely and will do everything in its power to follow the right timing in the normalisation process. Ich werde in meinem Referat zuerst einige generelle Bemerkungen zur Europischen Whrungsunion machen. Es mssen keine Wechselkursrisiken abgesichert werden und der Vergleich von Preisen sowie die Abwicklung von Zahlungen ber die Landesgrenzen hinweg werden vereinfacht. Eine einheitliche Whrung fhrt zudem zu integrierten und liquiden Kapitalmrkten. Dies alles erhht die Transparenz und den Wettbewerb, fhrt somit zu effizienteren Gter- und Kapitalflssen zwischen den Mitgliedslndern und sollte demnach das Wirtschaftswachstum im gesamten Whrungsraum positiv beeinflussen. Eine Einheitswhrung hat aber auch wirtschaftliche Nachteile. In einer Whrungsunion gibt es nur noch eine einzige Geldpolitik. Erforderliche Anpassungen an Einflsse, die die 2 Lnder unterschiedlich treffen, knnen in einer Whrungsunion nicht mehr durch eine Vernderung der nominellen Wechselkurse und eine unterschiedliche Festsetzung der Zinsstze erfolgen. Vielmehr mssen die Anpassungen ber Vernderungen der Gterpreise und der Lhne oder ber die Migration von Arbeitskrften geschehen. Solche Anpassungen sind oft mit konjunkturellen Schwankungen verbunden, solange die Flexibilitt der Arbeits- und Gtermrkte eingeschrnkt ist. Damit sich eine gemeinsame europische Whrung wirtschaftlich lohnt, mssen die Vorteile einer Whrungsunion die Nachteile insgesamt berwiegen. Inwieweit dies auf die Europische Whrungsunion zutrifft ist eine offene Debatte. Heute ist die Eurozone noch immer eine recht heterogene Gemeinschaft. Ein knftiger Beitritt der neuen EU-Mitglieder zur Europischen Whrungsunion drfte die Heterogenitt innerhalb der Eurozone zumindest vorbergehend noch vergrssern. Fr Europa hat die Whrungsunion aber auch noch eine politische Dimension: Die einheitliche Whrung ist eine starke Kraft in Richtung weiterer Integration und hat deshalb fr die Europische Union (EU) auch grossen symbolischen Charakter. Vielmehr ist es der Rckstand bei den strukturellen Reformen in Europa gegenber anderen Wirtschaftsrumen, der dafr vor allem verantwortlich ist. Title: The Swiss franc and the globalization marathon
text: The Franc in the Globalization Marathon Philipp M. Hildebrand Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Business Club Zurich September 22, 2005 2 Introduction I am pleased about the opportunity to outline some thoughts on the topic of The Franconia in the Globalization Marathon in front of your Business Club. I am particularly pleased to be a guest of entrepreneurs who know globalized competition from their own experience and who themselves contribute a lot to Switzerland's competitiveness. Less than a week ago, the SNB's Governing Board decided to leave interest rates unchanged for the time being. In our subsequent press release, we also briefly commented on the exchange rate situation, as usual. Today I will take up the topic of the exchange rate a little more broadly and put it in the real context. I would like my thoughts on our currency to be understood as a hopefully convincing plea for Switzerland's openness as the only correct answer to the opportunities and challenges of globalisation. This is because I believe that our experience with the Swiss franc since the transition to floating in 1973 shows that the Swiss economy is quite capable of reacting to changing challenges and prospering under changing conditions. Historical development of the Swiss franc When we think about the Swiss franc, today we mainly have its relationship to the dollar and the euro in mind. I would like to begin my remarks with the dollar, which as a world currency and anchor of many national currencies unfolds significance far beyond the USA. Ratio of Swiss franc to US dollar The relationship between the Swiss franc and the dollar has been characterized by more or less high volatility since the end of the Bretton Woods system with its fixed exchange rates. As you can see in Figure 1, 3 This volatility has tended to decrease somewhat since the mid-nineties, especially if you look at the extreme points. Nevertheless, the dollar-Swiss franc ratio remains characterised by comparatively high volatility. This results in advantages and disadvantages. Those of you who exported to the US or China in the last two years have been under permanent pressure on margins because of the dollar weakening that occurred during that time. However, the last few months should have already brought some relief with the slight countermovement in the dollar development. Others of you have undoubtedly benefited from the general weakness of the dollar over the last two years, because it has relieved our economy on the import side. Especially at a time of sharply rising oil and commodity prices, the weak dollar has brought relief to those of you who are heavily dependent on energy and raw materials, but also to end consumers. You see this relative currency-related relief in Chart 2 as the difference between the red and blue lines. While the Asian region has so far been mostly classified as a US dollar risk, the recent two percent appreciation of the Chinese currency against the US dollar is tantamount to the slow emergence of a third currency bloc in the global currency structure. Even though the US dollar will remain an important reference point for Asian currencies and the Asian monetary authorities will be watching each other closely due to strong export competition, more volatility is to be expected in the longer term. For the SNB, movements in the dollar-franc exchange rate, like all exchange rate movements, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, a stronger Swiss franc leads to lower import prices, which in turn can have a positive effect on price stability. On the other hand, a falling dollar disadvantages our exports to the US and the rest of the dollar area, which tends to have a negative impact on our GDP. Now 4 Ladies and gentlemen, in our case, it is important to integrate the dollar movements into an overall economic picture and, based on this, to formulate and implement an appropriate monetary policy in order ultimately to preserve the price stability that is so central to you as entrepreneurs and investors. However, stabilising the dollar-franc exchange rate is neither possible nor sensible in terms of monetary policy. In your case as an entrepreneur, it is therefore important to react as flexibly as possible to changes in the value of the US dollar. There are many possibilities: you can try to diversify your risks by conquering new, non-dollar-based markets. They can try to be active in specialized markets that are less price sensitive and where they can more easily pass on their costs to prices. You can become more productive and thus compensate for a reduction in your profit margins. You can implement various hedging strategies or you can temporarily accept yield losses in order to preserve your market share. Although in reality the implementation of these strategies is not always easy, most of you will probably act on all these fronts at the same time. This flexible attitude on the part of entrepreneurs to respond to changing framework conditions with appropriate strategies is a good sign for Switzerland's competitiveness. Swiss franc-euro ratio I now come to the relationship between our franc and the euro. Overall, this ratio is enormously important, as around 60% of our exports go to the euro area. Even though the Swiss economy has repeatedly succeeded in generating higher annual growth rates than Germany or later the eurozone over the past 25 years, Switzerland's economic cycle ultimately remains relatively strongly correlated with that of the eurozone. Accordingly, it should come as no surprise that the euro-Swiss franc currency pair also occupies a special position in the SNB's monetary policy assessment. 5 How did the introduction of the euro around 6 years ago affect Switzerland? While the first half of the nineties was marked by abrupt and massive exchange rate adjustments of some European currencies against the Swiss franc, the introduction of the euro brought Swiss exporters much more stable currency conditions. You can see this stability impressively from Figure 3. With the euro, there is now a currency in a large part of Europe whose quality corresponds to the old DM. It is therefore not surprising that in the last six years there has been no clear upward or downward trend of the Swiss franc against the euro. With temporary fluctuations, the Swiss franc appreciated nominally by almost 3.9% between January 1999 and September 2005. In real terms, a depreciation of 2.5% can be recorded. The volatility of the export-weighted exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the countries of the European Economic and Monetary Union has also decreased significantly since the introduction of the euro, as you can see from Chart 4. The EuroFranken exchange rate is generally one of the exchange rates with the lowest volatility ever. The volatility of the euro-franc exchange rate is significantly lower than that of the euro-pound exchange rate or the euro-krona exchange rate, even though both England and Sweden are members of the EU. As you can see in Chart 5, despite a single currency, real exchange rate conditions within the eurozone can change quite significantly over time because inflation rates do not develop the same everywhere. The most extreme examples are Ireland and Germany: since the introduction of the euro, Ireland has recorded a real appreciation of around 10% compared to the eurozone, while Germany has depreciated by around 4%. The real exchange rate index of the Swiss franc against the eurozone has been more stable over this period. Swiss foreign trade is thus exposed to relatively moderate real exchange rate fluctuations in an international comparison and even compared to individual countries in the eurozone. 6 The introduction of the euro has therefore had a very positive effect on Switzerland overall. We have much more stable currency conditions in Europe today than before the introduction of the euro, and the development between the euro and the Swiss franc has so far been quite calm. The exchange rate risk for the Swiss foreign trade sector has been significantly reduced by the introduction of the euro. At the same time, Switzerland continues to enjoy the opportunity to conduct an independent monetary policy that can respond to Switzerland's economic circumstances. In addition, the Swiss franc continues to play an important role in the international financial and foreign exchange markets and we can continue to benefit from an interest rate bonus. But the euro is also a success for the countries of the European Monetary Union. Thoughts of a possible return to the old national currencies are absurd. The ECB has so far done a convincing job in a difficult environment. The problems of growth and unemployment in various European countries are not due to the euro or the ECB's policies, but to the backlog of structural reforms. Globalisation and opening-up Let me now move on to the necessary opening up of Switzerland with a view to surviving in global competition, as mentioned at the beginning. We were originally a poor country. Until the 19th century, Switzerland was still regarded as the "poorhouse of Europe". Without having a natural wealth, it took special efforts to achieve today's prosperity. Openness, freedom and self-responsibility were the values with which Switzerland has been successful for a long time. There is no doubt that we have also been favoured by the political and historical developments in Europe. However, it is essential that access to world markets has always been important. Without the achievements and successes of our export industry, Switzerland would never have been able to achieve today's prosperity. 7 With increasing globalization, the conditions on the world markets are also changing. New and efficient suppliers compete and compete with existing producers. Switzerland's response to this increased competition must lie in further opening up and not in isolation. Only by opening up existing protected sectors of the economy will we be able to withstand competitive pressure and preserve our prosperity in the long term. On the one hand, the internal market provides inputs for the export sector, which must also be competitive. On the other hand, a protected internal market leads to massive distortions in cross-sectoral markets such as the labour market. The imperative therefore lies in the opening up and permanent adaptability to new situations. The underlying values that originally brought Switzerland forward  openness, freedom and self-responsibility  will continue to be decisive in the future. The longer-term appreciation of the Swiss franc is precisely a testimony to the fact that the Swiss export industry has repeatedly made considerable progress in productivity and has been able to survive in global competition. It has also coped well with exchange rate volatility and has adapted flexibly to new currency conditions. The export industry must continue to do so in the future. But the rest of the economy must also be made fit for increased competition. It will also be interesting to see how Switzerland's greater opening will affect the exchange rate of the Swiss franc. As you can see in Chart 6, the Swiss franc has appreciated trend-wise over the past decades as measured by the real trade-weighted exchange rate index. The average appreciation was around 0.5% per year. There are different theories to explain this upward trend. One of them is the so-called BalassaSamuelson effect. According to this explanatory approach, the appreciation trend of a currency depends on how much the productivity growth gap between the export and domestic economies at home differs from that abroad. Countries where the increase in productivity in the export economy compared to 8 that is comparatively large in the domestic economy, is experiencing a trend-based appreciation. This was the case for Switzerland for a long time. The efforts to open up the domestic economy will hopefully lead to a reduction in the gap between the domestic economy and the export economy in terms of productivity growth in Switzerland. However, this would also mean that the longer-term appreciation trend of the Swiss franc would have to weaken or even disappear altogether. Certainly, there are other factors that influence the long-term real exchange rate. But it seems quite possible to me that we will experience such an inverse Balassa-Samuelson effect over the next few years. Inferences Finally, allow me to think about the following: Imagine you are training for a marathon. You know that you have to endure several hours and a good 42 kilometers to reach your destination. You will prepare accordingly with consistent training. Whether you will ultimately run the Zurich Marathon or the Boston Marathon is only of limited relevance. The focus is on the performance required for a marathon. For Switzerland, the marathon is globalization. A difference to your possible personal marathon goals is that we as a country and economy ultimately do not have the choice not to run the marathon. A second difference to your personal marathon is that we do not know the difficulty level of the globalization marathon and that its distance tends to be endless. We know, however, that he will demand a great deal from us. But we also know that the prize money is extraordinarily high, which in turn should spur us on to make our preparation as optimal as possible. Today I would like to plead with you that we get to work with innovative training methods, hard work and a commitment to performance in order to be fit for the coming economic challenges. 9 to stay or just get fit. The decisive factor will not be whether our fate lies in the European Union or elsewhere. The decisive factor will be whether we are able to face the challenges of a global economy and seize its opportunities. I have no doubt that the Swiss economy has this ability and will continue to have it in the future. In the area of constantly changing exchange rate conditions, you as an entrepreneur have proven your adaptability again and again. It is you who ultimately generate growth and thus prosperity in our country with your entrepreneurial activities. Of course, our state will continue to play an important role in the future. We must recognise that there are also short-term losers in the globalisation process. It is important for these fellow citizens to open up new perspectives and new opportunities through retraining and, in extreme cases, to support them directly. Especially in times of global change, it is important to strengthen our education system and to prevent it from slipping into mediocrity at all costs. Globalization does not make the state superfluous in any way. But in the end, the state only has the funds that are generated by you and handed over to it in the interest of the overall interest of our society. The SNB also has its clearly defined role. As part of our legal mandate, we make every effort to provide them with optimal monetary conditions. Ultimately, however, only you can generate growth. I admire you for this and wish you a lot of courage, endurance and above all confidence during further marathon training. text_original: Der Franken im Globalisierungsmarathon Philipp M. Hildebrand Mitglied des Direktoriums Schweizerische Nationalbank Business Club Zrich 22. September 2005 2 Einfhrung Ich freue mich ber die Gelegenheit, vor ihrem Business Club einige Gedanken zum Thema Der Franken im Globalisierungsmarathon skizzieren zu knnen. Besonders freut es mich, bei Unternehmern zu Gast zu sein, die den globalisierten Wettbewerb aus eigener Erfahrung kennen und selber viel zur Wettbewerbsfhigkeit der Schweiz beitragen. Vor knapp einer Woche hat das Direktorium der Nationalbank entschieden, die Zinsen vorlufig unverndert zu lassen. In unserem darauf folgenden Pressecommuniqu haben wir uns wie blich auch kurz zur Wechselkurssituation geussert. Ich werde heute das Thema Wechselkurs etwas breiter aufgreifen und in den realen Kontext stellen. Ich mchte meine Gedanken zu unserer Whrung als hoffentlich berzeugendes Pldoyer zur Offenheit der Schweiz als einzig richtige Antwort auf die Chancen und Herausforderungen der Globalisierung verstanden wissen. Dies deshalb, weil ich der Meinung bin, dass unsere Erfahrungen mit dem Schweizer Franken seit dem bergang zum Floating im Jahre 1973 zeigen, dass die schweizerische Wirtschaft durchaus in der Lage ist, immer wieder auf wechselnde Herausforderungen zu reagieren und unter sich wandelnden Rahmenbedingungen zu prosperieren. Historische Entwicklung des Schweizer Frankens Wenn wir uns ber den Schweizer Franken Gedanken machen, dann haben wir heute vor allem sein Verhltnis zum Dollar und zum Euro im Kopf. Ich mchte in meinen Ausfhrungen beim Dollar beginnen, der als Weltwhrung und Anker vieler nationaler Whrungen Bedeutung weit ber die USA hinaus entfaltet. Verhltnis Franken  US-Dollar Das Verhltnis zwischen dem Schweizer Franken und dem Dollar ist seit dem Ende des Bretton Woods Systems mit seinen fixen Wechselkursen von mehr oder weniger hoher Volatilitt geprgt. Wie Sie Grafik 1 entnehmen knnen, 3 hat diese Volatilitt zwar seit Mitte der neunziger Jahre tendenziell etwas abgenommen, insbesondere wenn man die Extrempunkte betrachtet. Nichtsdestotrotz bleibt das Verhltnis Dollar  Schweizer Franken von vergleichsweise hoher Volatilitt geprgt. Daraus ergeben sich Vorteile und Nachteile. Diejenigen von Ihnen, die in den letzten zwei Jahren in die USA oder nach China exportierten, standen wegen der in dieser Zeit eingetretenen Dollarabschwchung unter permanentem Margendruck. Allerdings sollten die letzten Monate mit der leichten Gegenbewegung bei der Dollarentwicklung bereits einiges an Erleichterung gebracht haben. Andere von Ihnen haben zweifelsohne von der allgemeinen Dollarschwche in den letzten beiden Jahren profitiert, denn sie hat unsere Wirtschaft auf der Importseite entlastet. Insbesondere in einer Zeit stark steigender Erdl- und Rohstoffpreise hat der schwache Dollar denen unter Ihnen, die stark von Energie und Rohstoffen abhngig sind, aber auch den Endkonsumenten, eine Entlastung gebracht. Sie sehen diese relative whrungsbedingte Entlastung in Grafik 2 als Differenz zwischen der roten und der blauen Linie. Whrenddem der asiatische Raum bis anhin mehrheitlich als US-Dollar-Risiko eingestuft werden konnte, kommt die vor kurzem erfolgte zweiprozentige Aufwertung der chinesischen Whrung gegenber dem US-Dollar dem langsamen Entstehen eines dritten Whrungsblocks im globalen Whrungsgefge gleich. Auch wenn der US-Dollar ein wichtiger Referenzpunkt der asiatischen Whrungen bleiben wird und sich die asiatischen Whrungshter aufgrund der starken Exportkonkurrenz gegenseitig stark beugen werden, ist hier lngerfristig doch mehr Volatilitt zu erwarten. Fr die Nationalbank sind Bewegungen des DollarFranken-Kurses wie alle Wechselkursbewegungen ein zweischneidiges Schwert. Auf der einen Seite fhrt ein strkerer Franken zu tieferen Importpreisen, was sich wiederum positiv auf die Preisstabilitt auswirken kann. Auf der anderen Seite benachteiligt ein fallender Dollar unsere Exporte in die USA und in den brigen Dollarraum, was sich tendenziell negativ auf unser BIP auswirkt. Nun, 4 meine Damen und Herren, in unserem Fall gilt es, die Dollarbewegungen in ein gesamtwirtschaftliches Bild zu integrieren und darauf basierend eine angemessene Geldpolitik zu formulieren und umzusetzen, um letztlich die Preisstabilitt, die fr Sie als Unternehmer und Investoren so zentral ist, zu bewahren. Eine Stabilisierung des Dollar-Franken-Kurses ist aber weder geldpolitisch mglich noch sinnvoll. In Ihrem Fall als Unternehmer geht es daher darum, mglichst flexibel auf Wertvernderungen des US-Dollar zu reagieren. Mglichkeiten gibt es deren viele: Sie knnen versuchen, Ihre Risiken zu diversifizieren, indem Sie neue, nicht Dollar-basierte Mrkte erobern. Sie knnen versuchen, in spezialisierten Mrkten aktiv zu sein, die weniger preissensitiv sind und wo sie ihre Kosten einfacher auf die Preise berwlzen knnen. Sie knnen produktiver werden und so eine Reduktion Ihrer Gewinnmargen kompensieren. Sie knnen verschiedene Hedging-Strategien umsetzen oder Sie knnen vorbergehend Ertragsverluste akzeptieren um damit Ihre Marktanteile zu bewahren. Obwohl in der Realitt die Umsetzung dieser Strategien nicht immer einfach ist, werden die meisten von Ihnen wohl an all diesen Fronten gleichzeitig agieren. Diese flexible Haltung der Unternehmer, auf vernderte Rahmenbedingungen mit entsprechenden Strategien zu reagieren, ist ein gutes Zeichen fr die Wettbewerbsfhigkeit der Schweiz. Verhltnis Franken - Euro Ich komme nun zum Verhltnis zwischen unserem Franken und dem Euro. Gesamtwirtschaftlich ist dieses Verhltnis enorm wichtig, da rund 60% unserer Exporte in den Euroraum fliessen. Auch wenn es der Schweizer Wirtschaft in den vergangenen 25 Jahren immer wieder gelungen ist, hhere Jahreswachstumsraten zu generieren als Deutschland oder spter die Eurozone, so bleibt der Konjunkturzyklus der Schweiz letztendlich relativ stark mit demjenigen der Eurozone korreliert. Dementsprechend sollte es nicht verwundern, dass das Whrungspaar Euro-Schweizer Franken auch in der geldpolitischen Lagebeurteilung der Nationalbank eine besondere Stellung einnimmt. 5 Wie hat sich nun die Einfhrung des Euro vor rund 6 Jahren auf die Schweiz ausgewirkt? Whrend die erste Hlfte der Neunzigerjahre durch abrupte und massive Kursanpassungen einiger europischer Whrungen gegenber dem Franken gekennzeichnet war, brachte die Einfhrung des Euro den schweizerischen Exporteuren deutlich stabilere Whrungsverhltnisse. Sie knnen diese Stabilitt eindrcklich aus Grafik 3 ablesen. Mit dem Euro existiert heute in einem Grossteil Europas eine Whrung, deren Qualitt der alten DM entspricht. Es erstaunt deshalb nicht, dass in den letzten sechs Jahren keine klare Auf- oder Abwertungstendenz des Frankens gegenber dem Euro zu beobachten war. Bei temporren Schwankungen wertete sich der Franken zwischen Januar 1999 und September 2005 nominal um knapp 3.9% auf. Real ist eine Abwertung von 2.5% zu verzeichnen. Auch die Volatilitt des exportgewichteten Wechselkurses des Frankens gegenber den Lndern der Europischen Wirtschafts- und Whrungsunion hat seit der Einfhrung des Euro deutlich abgenommen, was Sie aus Grafik 4 ersehen knnen. Der EuroFranken-Kurs gehrt generell zu den Wechselkursen mit der tiefsten Volatilitt berhaupt. Die Volatilitt des Euro-Franken-Kurses ist deutlich tiefer als diejenige des Euro-Pfund-Kurses oder des Euro-Krone-Kurses, obwohl sowohl England als auch Schweden Mitglied der EU sind. Wie sie in Grafik 5 feststellen, knnen sich die realen Wechselkursverhltnisse innerhalb der Eurozone trotz einer einheitlichen Whrung ber die Zeit recht deutlich verndern, weil sich die Inflationsraten nicht berall gleich entwickeln. Die extremsten Beispiele sind Irland und Deutschland: Seit der Einfhrung des Euro verzeichnete Irland eine reale Aufwertung von rund 10% gegenber der Eurozone, Deutschland hingegen eine Abwertung von rund 4%. Der reale Wechselkursindex des Frankens gegenber der Eurozone ist ber diesen Zeitraum stabiler verlaufen. Der schweizerische Aussenhandel ist somit im internationalen Vergleich und sogar im Vergleich zu einzelnen Lndern der Eurozone relativ moderaten realen Wechselkursschwankungen ausgesetzt. 6 Die Einfhrung des Euro hat sich auf die Schweiz also insgesamt sehr positiv ausgewirkt. Wir haben heute in Europa deutlich stabilere Whrungsverhltnisse als vor der Einfhrung des Euro, und die Entwicklung zwischen Euro und Franken ist bisher recht ruhig verlaufen. Das Wechselkursrisiko hat sich fr den Schweizer Aussenhandelssektor durch die Einfhrung des Euro erheblich vermindert. Gleichzeitig geniesst die Schweiz weiterhin die Mglichkeit, eine eigenstndige Geldpolitik zu fhren, die auf die wirtschaftlichen Begebenheiten der Schweiz eingehen kann. Zudem spielt der Franken auf den internationalen Finanz- und Devisenmrkten nach wie vor eine wichtige Rolle und wir knnen weiterhin von einem Zinsbonus profitieren. Der Euro ist aber auch ein Erfolg fr die Lnder der Europischen Whrungsunion. Gedanken an eine eventuelle Rckkehr zu den alten nationalen Whrungen sind absurd. Die EZB hat bisher eine berzeugende Arbeit in einem schwierigen Umfeld geleistet. Die Wachstums- und Arbeitslosigkeitsprobleme in verschiedenen europischen Lndern sind weder auf den Euro noch auf die Politik der EZB sondern auf die Rckstnde bei den Strukturreformen zurckzufhren. Globalisierung und ffnung Lassen Sie mich nun bergehen zur eingangs erwhnten ntigen ffnung der Schweiz im Hinblick auf ein Bestehen im globalen Wettbewerb. Wir waren ursprnglich ein armes Land. Die Schweiz galt noch bis ins 19. Jahrhundert als das Armenhaus Europas. Ohne ber einen natrlichen Reichtum zu verfgen, brauchte es besondere Anstrengungen, um den heutigen Wohlstand zu erreichen. Offenheit, Freiheit und Selbstverantwortung waren die Werte, mit denen die Schweiz lange Zeit erfolgreich war. Wir waren zweifelsohne auch durch die politische und historische Entwicklung in Europa begnstigt. Wesentlich ist aber, dass seit jeher der Zugang zu den Weltmrkten wichtig war. Ohne die Leistungen und Erfolge unsere Exportindustrie htte die Schweiz nie den heutigen Wohlstand erreichen knnen. 7 Mit der zunehmenden Globalisierung ndern sich auch die Verhltnisse auf den Weltmrkten. Neue und effiziente Anbieter treten an und konkurrenzieren bisherige Produzenten. Die Antwort der Schweiz auf diesen erhhten Wettbewerb muss in der weiteren ffnung und nicht in der Abschottung liegen. Nur mit der ffnung bisheriger geschtzter Wirtschaftsbereiche werden wir langfristig in der Lage sein, dem Wettbewerbsdruck standzuhalten und unseren Wohlstand zu bewahren. Der Binnenmarkt liefert einerseits Inputs fr den Exportsektor, die ebenfalls kompetitiv sein mssen. Andererseits fhrt ein geschtzter Binnenmarkt zu massiven Verzerrungen auf sektorbergreifenden Mrkten wie dem Arbeitsmarkt. Der Imperativ liegt also in der ffnung und der permanenten Anpassungsfhigkeit an neue Situationen. Die Basiswerte, die die Schweiz ursprnglich nach vorne brachten - Offenheit, Freiheit und Selbstverantwortung  werden auch in Zukunft entscheidend sein. Die lngerfristige tendenzielle Aufwertung des Frankens ist gerade ein Zeugnis davon, dass die schweizerische Exportindustrie immer wieder beachtliche Produktivittsfortschritte erzielen und im weltweiten Wettbewerb bestehen konnte. Sie ist auch mit der Wechselkursvolatilitt gut zurechtgekommen und hat sich flexibel auf neue Whrungsverhltnisse eingestellt. Die Exportindustrie muss dies auch in Zukunft tun. Aber auch der Rest der Wirtschaft muss fr den vermehrten Wettbewerb fit gemacht werden. Interessant wird auch sein, wie sich die strkere ffnung der Schweiz auf den Wechselkurs des Frankens auswirken wird. Wie Sie in Grafik 6 sehen, hat sich der Franken gemessen am realen handelsgewichteten Wechselkursindex ber die letzten Jahrzehnte trendmssig aufgewertet. Die Aufwertung betrug im Durchschnitt rund 0,5% pro Jahr. Es gibt unterschiedliche Theorien um diesen Aufwrtstrend zu erklren. Eine davon ist der so genannte BalassaSamuelson Effekt. Gemss diesem Erklrungsansatz hngt der Aufwertungstrend einer Whrung davon ab, wie stark sich das Produktivittswachstumsgeflle zwischen der Export- und der Binnenwirtschaft im Inland von demjenigen im Ausland unterscheidet. Lnder in denen die Zunahme der Produktivitt in der Exportwirtschaft gegenber 8 derjenigen in der Binnenwirtschaft vergleichsweise gross ist, erfahren eine trendmssige Aufwertung. Dies war lange Zeit fr die Schweiz der Fall. Die Anstrengungen zur ffnung der Binnenwirtschaft werden hoffentlich dazu fhren, dass der Rckstand der Binnenwirtschaft gegenber der Exportwirtschaft beim Produktivittswachstum in der Schweiz geringer wird. Dies wrde aber auch bedeuten, dass der lngerfristige Aufwertungstrend des Frankens sich abschwchen oder sogar ganz wegfallen msste. Sicher gibt es noch andere Faktoren, die den langfristigen realen Wechselkurs beeinflussen. Mir scheint es aber durchaus mglich zu sein, dass wir ber die nchsten Jahre einen solchen inversen Balassa-Samuelson Effekt erleben werden. Schlussfolgerungen Erlauben Sie mir zum Schluss folgendes Gedankenspiel: Stellen Sie sich vor, Sie trainieren fr einen Marathonlauf. Sie wissen, dass Sie mehrere Stunden und gut 42 Kilometer durchhalten mssen um Ihr Ziel zu erreichen. Sie werden sich dementsprechend mit konsequentem Training vorbereiten. Ob Sie letztlich den Zrich Marathon oder den Boston Marathon laufen werden, ist nur bedingt relevant. Im Vordergrund steht die fr einen Marathon notwendige Leistungsfhigkeit. Fr die Schweiz ist der Marathon die Globalisierung. Ein Unterschied zu Ihren allflligen persnlichen Marathonzielen ist, dass wir als Land und Wirtschaft die Wahl, den Marathon nicht zu laufen, letztlich nicht haben. Title: The Swiss National Banks monetary policy and Swiss franc loans in Austria
text: The monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank and Swiss franc loans in Austria Prof. Dr. Thomas J. Jordan Deputy Member of the Board of Directors Head of Financial Market Operations Swiss National Bank Event "Foreign Currency Loans", Congress Innsbruck 3 October 2005 Dear Sir or Madam, I have the privilege of attending an event on foreign currency loans in Austria for the second time. About a year ago, I spoke in Feldkirch and was impressed by the enormous public interest in this topic. That's why I was very happy to come to Innsbruck today. The Austrian and Swiss National Banks maintain intensive contact at various levels and I am very friendly to Director Christl and Director Schneider. During my visit to Feldkirch, I suggested a deal to the audience  currency speculation. Although the deal was intended to be purely hypothetical, a number of spectators contacted me at the end of the event who would have liked to respond to the speculation. The fairly stable exchange rate development between the euro and the swiss franc allows me to propose the same currency speculation to you on practically the same terms: I offer you to exchange Swiss francs for euros today and to exchange the two currencies back in three months' time. [See Figure 1] Today's Eurofranken exchange rate is 1.55. I give you 155 francs and you give me  according to today's rate  100 euros. After three months we meet again. I will then give you back the 100 euros and you will give me the corresponding sum of francs at the then valid exchange rate. Please consider whether you would accept this business. I will come back to the proposal at the end of my speech  in about 20 minutes. However, I would like to emphasise that, unfortunately, I can only offer you one business in my mind. As a substitute member of the GOVERNING Board of the SNB, I am not allowed to conclude any currency speculation transactions. I would like to build up my presentation as follows: First, I will look at the issue of foreign currency loans from the point of view of the financial optimisation of borrowers, then I will focus on the situation with regard to foreign currency loans in Switzerland and the costs of Swiss franc mortgages in Switzerland. 2 Finally, I shall explain the importance of Swiss monetary policy for Swiss franc loans in Austria. In this context, I will also emphasise the exchange rate between the Swiss franc and the euro and the interest rate differential between Swiss franc and euro investments. 1. Foreign currency loans as part of financial optimization Let me start with a few remarks on financial optimisation or speculation in foreign currency loans. When investing balances, achieving a higher return through a clever choice of currencies is now a matter of course. Private investors also usually hold stocks and bonds denominated in foreign currencies, such as US dollars. On the other hand, in most countries, especially among private households, debt in domestic currency is common. This may be due to legal reasons, risk considerations or habits. With its high share of foreign currency loans, Austria is an exception throughout Europe  if not worldwide. With the possibility of obtaining a loan in a foreign currency, the financing possibilities of the borrower are expanded. This increase in financing options is generally positive from the point of view of the borrower. Due to his risk appetite, a borrower can achieve a possibly better structure of debt for him, i.e. debt with lower expected costs. A foreign currency borrower in Austria tries to take advantage of the lower Swiss franc or yen interest rates against the euro. However, economics clearly shows that a higher expected profit, here in the form of lower interest costs, is usually associated with a higher risk. Specifically, for an Austrian foreign currency borrower calculating in euros, there is a risk that the repayment of the loan and the interest payments will be higher than when the loan was concluded due to an appreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro. 3 adopted. The crucial question is therefore whether borrowers actually use the greater choices offered by foreign currency loans in the sense of optimization or whether they are not sufficiently aware of the risk associated with foreign currency loans. 2. Foreign currency loans in Switzerland In the following, I would like to briefly discuss the situation with regard to foreign currency loans in Switzerland. In Switzerland, banks' domestic loans are divided into mortgage claims and non-mortgage-backed loans, so-called claims on customers. Non-mortgaged domestic loans amounted to 134.1 billion at the middle of this year (July 2005). Swiss francs or around 30% of the year gross domestic product of Switzerland (GDP nom: 435.93 billion). CHF). This corresponds to around 86 billion at the then valid exchange rate (CHF/EUR1.5525). Euro. Of these, 18% were denominated in a currency other than the Swiss franc. This proportion may seem high. However, a look at the distribution of these loans by currency makes it clear that these loans do not exist for reasons of an interest rate advantage of the foreign currency against the Swiss franc. By far the largest share is denominated in US dollars (11%) and euros (5%)  the two most important currencies in Switzerland's foreign trade. The remaining currencies (including the yen) together accounted for only 2% of all non-mortgage-backed loans. [See Figure 2] These foreign currency loans are therefore almost entirely related to the borrower's cross-border business. Most of them are sourced from companies. Domestic mortgage receivables amounted to over 586 billion in mid-2005. Franconia (378 billion) Euro). They are therefore around four times larger than the receivables from customers. Of the mortgage claims, only a negligible proportion of 0.028% is denominated in a foreign currency. Mortgages in euros amounted to only EUR 64 million, while those in Japanese yen amounted to only EUR 1 million. [See Figure 3] 4 These figures do not include loans from banks based abroad that grant loans to Swiss companies and households across the border. However, such loans are likely to have only an extremely marginal significance. We know that a few years ago, Austrian banks tried to penetrate the Swiss mortgage market with yen mortgages. However, the offers could not establish themselves due to falling interest rates in Switzerland and the exchange rate risk. In summary, it can be said that foreign currency loans in Switzerland are only a marginal phenomenon and go primarily to internationally active companies. Mortgage loans in Germany are rarely obtained in a currency other than the Swiss franc. An obvious explanation for this is certainly the low interest rate level in Switzerland: In most cases, it is simply more expensive to borrow in a currency other than the Swiss franc. In addition, the interest rate advantage of a yen loan against a franc loan is comparatively small and the yen franc exchange rate fluctuates much more than the euro franc exchange rate. However, representatives of Swiss banks also stress that this product is deliberately not actively promoted by them. In addition, when customers ask for loans in yen, the banks specifically point out the high exchange rate risk. They usually advise against such mortgages. 3. Interest on Swiss franc mortgages in Switzerland If you are a Swiss franc borrower, you are probably interested in finding out how much a Swiss franc mortgage loan currently costs in Switzerland. The published benchmark interest rates for a fixed first mortgage of CHF 500,000 with a term of five years are currently between 2.5 and 3 percent. Variable mortgages of the same amount cost about three percent at most banks. This corresponds to a premium on the three-month Libor of 1.75 to 2.25 percent. For Libor mortgages, a lower premium is required: Usually, this is 1 to 1.5 percent on the three- or six-month Libor. [Figure 4] 5 If you compare these figures with the interest rates for Swiss franc Libor mortgages in Austria, you can see that the premium in Switzerland is similar. Fees and commissions  for example for currency exchange  are therefore not yet taken into account. Taking into account all costs, a Swiss franc loan in Switzerland should therefore be cheaper than in Austria. 4. Swiss franc loans in Austria and the SNB's monetary policy Whether a Swiss franc loan against a euro loan is worthwhile for an Austrian borrower depends above all on two factors: the exchange rate of the franc to the euro and the interest rate difference between the two currencies. The Swiss National Bank's monetary policy has a considerable influence on both. For you as a representative of a commercial bank or as a foreign currency borrower, it is therefore important to understand how the Swiss National Bank determines its monetary policy stance. I shall therefore discuss this in more detail below. The main task of the Swiss National Bank is to conduct a monetary policy that serves the overall interest of Switzerland. It ensures price stability while taking into account the economic situation. We equate price stability with an increase in the national consumer price index of less than 2% per year. This is a definition similar to that of the European Central Bank. The Swiss National Bank regularly publishes a forecast for the development of inflation over the next three years. If the projected inflation deviates from the defined price stability, a review of monetary policy is imperative. If inflation threatens to rise above 2% in the medium term, the SNB will tend to tighten its monetary policy. [Figure 5] The SNB therefore sets its key interest rates with the aim of maintaining price stability in the medium term. It does not pursue an exchange rate objective, neither against the euro nor with the 6 US dollar. However, since the exchange rate of the Swiss franc to the euro and the economic development in the eurozone have a major influence on the development of the Swiss economy and on prices in Switzerland, they are carefully monitored by the SNB and represent important elements in determining the monetary policy stance. The implementation of these monetary policy intentions takes place by influencing the level of interest rates on the Swiss franc money market. To this end, the SNB sets a target range for the three-month Libor. This is the economically most important money market rate for Swiss francs. [Figure 6] Now to the exchange rate development. Over the past three decades, the Swiss franc has had a clear trend towards appreciating against the Austrian schilling. [Figure 7] At the beginning of the 70s, more than 17 francs had to be paid for 100 shillings, but at the time of the introduction of the euro they were available for less than 12 francs. The upward trend has weakened since the introduction of the euro in 1999. Between the beginning of 1999 and today, the Swiss franc has appreciated nominally by around 4.5%. Today, one euro costs about 1.55 francs. In the meantime, however, the euro stood at a high of 1.62 and a low of 1.45. This corresponds to a maximum appreciation of the Swiss franc of over 10% or a maximum depreciation of only 0.4% compared to the exchange rate at the introduction of the euro. [Figure 8] This long-term appreciation trend of the Swiss franc against the euro and previously the schilling is working against the Swiss franc borrowers abroad, because with the appreciation the debt calculated in euros grows. The fluctuations in the euro franc exchange rate are significantly smaller than at other exchange rates of the Swiss franc. Looking at the exchange rates against the euro, it can be seen that among the major currencies, the Swiss franc has the lowest fluctuations against the euro after the Danish kroner. (Standard deviation of the percentage daily exchange rate changes from Jan. 1999 to Sept. 2005). [Figure 9] Nevertheless, in the last five years, revaluations and devaluations of up to 5% within three months have occurred on several occasions. 7 For the success or failure of a Swiss franc mortgage, the time of entry is therefore crucial. The volatility of the Euro franc exchange rate also shows that the "right" entry point is difficult to hit. [See Figure 10] It is important to understand that volatility and the appreciation trend can change over time. Trends cannot simply be continued into the future. As has been shown on several occasions, exchange rates can hardly be predicted in the short term and only unreliably in the long term. What about the interest rate differential between Swiss franc and euro investments? The so-called "interest bonus" of the Swiss franc against the euro has averaged around 1.5 percentage points over the past five and a half years, measured by the difference in the interest rate on unsecured three-month loans to first-class banks. Borrowers of Swiss franc mortgages in the euro area therefore benefit from a lower interest rate than if they had borrowed in euros. The interest bonus has been quite stable in recent years, fluctuating between 1 and 2.5 percentage points. [Figure 11] The fluctuations in the interest rate differential are therefore significantly smaller than those in the exchange rate. A foreign currency loan therefore involves speculation that the Swiss franc will appreciate less than the interest rate differential between the euro and the franc. Of course, the additional costs associated with a Swiss franc loan compared to a euro loan must also be taken into account. Let me briefly explain the SNB's monetary policy concept described above in the light of our last monetary policy assessment of 15 September. As you surely know, the Swiss National Bank has left the target range for the three-month Libor unchanged at 0.25  1.25%. We raised the target range twice last year by 25 basis points each, after a period of virtually zero interest rate policy. 8 We expect the economic recovery in Switzerland to continue. However, the impact of the recent rise in oil prices on the economy and inflation is difficult to assess. Due to the oil price, we expect inflation to rise slightly higher this year than expected in June. Against this background, the SNB remains waiting for the time being. If the economic recovery is confirmed or even accelerates, however, we will have to correct the long-expansionary monetary policy stance and adjust the target range for the three-month Libor upwards. What impact will our future monetary policy decisions have on the question of whether a Swiss franc loan in Austria is worthwhile? The reference interest rate for Swiss franc mortgages in Austria is usually the three-month Libor. The cost of a Swiss franc mortgage compared to a Euro mortgage in Austria thus depends directly on the SNB's monetary policy decisions. Of course, it also depends on how the ECB adjusts its monetary policy. Let's assume hypothetically that the economic situation in Switzerland will improve significantly in the coming months, while the euro area will stagnate. In this case, the SNB would probably raise the target range for the three-month Libor soon, and the ECB would leave interest rates unchanged or even lower them. This would increase the interest costs for a loan in Swiss francs and fall for the loan in euros. In addition, the Swiss franc could appreciate at least temporarily due to the interest rate hikes in Switzerland. This would also increase the debt of a Swiss franc mortgage calculated in euros. In such a scenario, the Swiss franc borrower would therefore be left with a reduced interest rate advantage and a larger debt. Of course, we could also look at the opposite case, where the SNB lowers interest rates and the ECB raises interest rates. However, the example impressively shows that there are no guarantees that a Swiss franc mortgage will pay off in euros. 9 Household in Austria is worthwhile. There is no certainty that the Swiss franc will not appreciate more strongly against the euro again, nor that the interest rate differential will remain at its current level. In particular, short-term movements in interest rates and exchange rates can result in an unfavorable situation for a borrower. To be fair, however, it must also be emphasized that the economic cycles in Switzerland and the euro area are normally positively correlated. For example, the historical interest rate differential was quite stable and the volatility of the euro franc exchange rate is comparatively low. 5. Schlussbemerkungen I now come back to the currency speculation put forward at the beginning of my speech. I hope that you were able to come to a decision. [Figure 1] I have offered you to exchange francs for euros at today's rate and to exchange them back in three months at the then valid rate. This thought experiment is intended to show that the decision to borrow in a foreign currency should be accompanied by a clear idea of the future development of that currency. If you want to enter into the business, you should not take out a Swiss franc loan for the next three months. They believe that holding francs is worthwhile  so debt in francs cannot be worthwhile. In your opinion, the appreciation of the Swiss franc is greater than the interest rate differential against the euro. If you are undecided whether you should accept the offer, you do not have a clear idea about the exchange rate development, a debt in Swiss francs is therefore rather questionable for you. Only if you decisively reject the proposed transaction, a Swiss franc loan should be an option for you at the moment. They are then obviously of the opinion that the future development of exchange rates and interest rate differentials makes debt in Swiss francs attractive. As already mentioned, I already offered the same shop to the public in Feldkirch on September 23, 2004. In retrospect, it is now possible to determine whether 10 the business would have been worth it. From 23 September 2004 (EURCHF 1.5464) to 16 December (EURCHF 1,533) (60 working days later), the Swiss franc appreciated by 0.9% against the euro. The interest rate differential in favour of the euro at that time was 1.457% per year (measured by the three-month Libor). This corresponds to 0.36% for three months. A foreign currency borrower would have gained 0.36% through the interest rate advantage at that time but lost 0.9% due to the appreciation of the Swiss franc. The foreign currency loan would therefore not have been worthwhile. With a debt in francs you would have made losses  with an investment in francs profits. Let me now conclude my remarks. Given the existing opportunities of a foreign currency loan, its considerable risks must be clearly emphasized. The Swiss National Bank's monetary policy stance exerts a considerable influence on the costs of an Austrian franc loan via the interest rate and the exchange rate. A good understanding of Swiss monetary policy is therefore very important for borrowers and lenders of Swiss franc loans in Austria. The great interest of the audience in Austria, which I have now experienced at two events, indicates that the Austrian borrowers seem to be dealing with the problem in detail. In any case, I recommend that you soberly weigh up all the advantages and disadvantages before concluding a foreign currency mortgage.
