Aus den Erhebungen ber die Direktinvestitionen knnen immerhin Hinweise auf die Finanzierung gewonnen werden. Darauf gesttzt, wage ich die Hypothese, dass die Unternehmen ihre Direktinvestitionen grsstenteils selbst finanzieren. Die Direktinvestitionsstatistik gibt Auskunft ber die von den Investoren im auslndischen Unternehmen reinvestierten und die zum Investor transferierten Ertrge. Zusammengenommen ergibt sich fr die letzten sieben Jahre eine volle Deckung der Kapitalexporte durch die Ertrge. Dies ist das erste Indiz fr eine Selbstfinanzierung. Fr einen hohen Selbstfinanzierungsgrad spricht ferner die Entwicklung auf dem Kapitalmarkt. Sie zeigt eine Tendenz zur Entschuldung der Industrie. Dies lsst sich aus den rcklufigen Emissionsvolumina von Anleihen und den hheren Rckzahlungen an den Markt ableiten. Auch die Eigenfinanzierung durch Emission von Aktien scheint eher kein Thema in diesem Zusammenhang zu sein. Hier ist die gleiche Entwicklung wie bei den Anleihen zu konstatieren. Mitverantwortlich fr die rcklufige Kapitalmarktbeanspruchung drften auch regulatorische Faktoren sein. Diese scheinen die Kapitalmarktfhigkeit von Unternehmen einzuschrnken, oder, anders ausgedrckt, die Attraktivitt des Kapitalmarkts als Finanzquelle zu schmlern. Die Industrie-Holding weist in ihrem Geschftsbericht 2003/2004 auf die hohen Kosten der Kapitalmarktfhigkeit hin. Die Kosten betreffen insbesondere die zeitli- che Beanspruchung des Managements fr Compliance- und Kommunikationsaufgaben. Der Bericht bringt die ersten Dekotierungen von der Schweizer Brse damit in Verbindung. Haben die Investoren einen Anreiz, die Ertrge aus Direktinvestitionen wieder zu investieren? Ein Blick auf die erzielten Renditen liefert dafr Indizien. Die Ertrge der Direktinvestitionen betrugen im Durchschnitt der letzten sieben Jahre beachtliche 10 % des investierten und zu Buchwerten gerechneten Kapitals. Natrlich erreichten nicht alle Branchen gleich gute Ergebnisse. Interessant ist aber festzuhalten, dass nach dieser Berechnung die Direktinvestitionen der Industrie in den letzten Jahren berdurchschnittliche Ertrge erzielten. Unterdurchschnittlich waren dagegen die Ertrge im Dienstleistungsbereich. Dieses Resultat war nicht zuletzt auf grosse Verluste einzelner Banken, Versicherungen und Unternehmen aus dem Transport- und Kommunikationsbereich in den Jahren 2001 und 2002 zurckzufhren. 5. Interpretationen Die aus der auslndischen Investitionsttigkeit resultierenden Kapitaleinkommen erklren einen wesentlichen Teil des traditionellen Ertragsbilanzberschusses der Schweiz. (Letztmals wies die Schweiz 1980 einen geringen negativen Ertragsbilanzsaldo aus.) 2004 erreichte der Ertragsbilanzberschuss 65 Mrd. Franken oder 15 % des Bruttoinlandprodukts. Zur Hlfte stammte der berschuss aus den Einkommen von Direktinvestitionen. Diese Einkommen sind in den letzten Jahren viel strker gestiegen als die Kapitalertrge auf Wertpapieranlagen im Ausland. Letztere litten unter den tiefen Zinsstzen. Die Bedeutung der Kapitalertrge auf Wertpapieranlagen hat sich dadurch eindeutig verringert. Nicht wenig trgt aber auch die Handelsbilanz zum Ertragsbilanzberschuss bei. Die Entwicklung der Exporte ist bemerkenswert. Trotz Konjunkturflaute in den wichtigen Abnehmerlndern schweizerischer Produkte erzielte die Schweiz Exportberschsse. Vieles spricht dafr, dass die Entwicklung der Warenexporte und jene der Direktinvestitionen zusammenhngen, d.h., dass Direktinvestitionen auch Exporte generieren und umgekehrt. Dazu passt auch die Feststellung, dass der Welthandel von den Multinationalen Unternehmen dominiert wird. Die UNCTAD (World Investment Report 2002) schtzt, dass der Welthandel zu einem Drittel innerhalb der Multinationalen Unternehmen stattfindet, also einem Handel zwischen Muttergesellschaft und Tchtern gleichkommt. Auch eine Untersuchung der KOF aus dem Jahre 2001 besttigt, dass schweizerische Direktinvestitionen im Ausland den Aussenhandel, insbesondere die Exporte frdern. Direktinvestitionen im Ausland steigern die Attraktivitt des Produktionsstandorts Schweiz. Die OECD berechnete bereits 1997 fr vierzehn OECD-Lnder folgenden Effekt: Pro Franken Direktinvestitionen im Ausland wurden von 1984-1997 Exporte in der Hhe von 2 Franken und ein Handelsberschuss in der Hhe von 1,7 Franken ausgelst.2 Allerdings erzwingen Direktinvestitionen Strukturanpassungen im Inland. Die Entwicklung zeigt eine Verlagerung von wertschpfungsschwachen Arbeitspltzen ins Ausland, whrend hochwertige Arbeitspltze etwa in der Forschung, Entwicklung, Planung und Logistik in der Schweiz verbleiben oder entstehen. Schliesslich bringen Direktinvestitionen im Ausland der Schweiz auch Steuereinnahmen. Ertrge aus Dividenden mssen in der Schweiz von den Unternehmen als Einkommen versteuert werden. Im Jahre 2003 wurden nach Abzug der Quellensteuer im Ausland knapp 26 Mrd. Franken an Dividenden an schweizerische Unternehmen ausbezahlt. Die Kantone Zrich, Genf, Basel-Stadt, Waadt, Zug und Neuenburg profitieren von den Dividendenausschttungen in ausgeprgtem Masse. Neun Zehntel der Dividenden aus dem Ausland flossen in diese sechs Kantone. Abschliessend lsst sich sagen, dass die Schweiz von den Direktinvestitionen im Ausland in mancherlei Hinsicht profitiert. Ihre Auswirkungen auf das Arbeits- und Kapitaleinkommen sind positiv. Sie generieren Steuereinnahmen. Nicht zuletzt bewirken sie eine willkommene Risikodiversifikation. Die Schweiz ist nicht nur auf die im Inland generierten Einkommen angewiesen, sondern sie kann sich auch auf die Kapitaleinkommen aus dem Ausland absttzen. Angesichts der Mhe, welche unser Land mit dem Binnenwachstum bekundet, sind die Einkommensstrme aus dem Ausland besonders willkommen. Alles in Allem sind die Direktinvestitionen eine Quelle des Wohlstands und des Wachstums, zu welcher in einem kleinen und ressourcenarmen Land wie die Schweiz spezielle Sorge getragen werden muss. 2 Die OECD untersuchte den Zusammenhang von Direktinvestitionen und Exporten anhand eines Samples von vierzehn Lndern im Zeitraum 1984-93. Die Lnder werden nicht einzeln aufgefhrt. Die Studie stammt von Lionel Fontagn und wurde 1997 und 1999 in Arbeitspapieren des OECD Directorate for Science, Technology and Industry verffentlicht.

Title: Securing liquidity with repo transactions
text: Repurchase agreements, an instrument for the supply of liquidity Thomas J. Jordan Substitute Member of the Executive Directorate of the Swiss National Bank Money market 17 November 2005 Ladies and Gentlemen, The primary objective of a bank is to achieve in the long term as high a return as possible on the capital invested. The potential level of this profitability is directly related to the risks that the bank is prepared to run. The bank taking higher risks can increase its average profitability. Higher risks, however, imply an increase in the potential for losses. Therefore, a bank should only take risks that, in total, cannot endanger its survival. The survival of a bank, however, depends not only on its solvency, but also on its liquidity. For a bank, it is indeed essential to be able to meet, at any time and on time, its payment commitments. Banks short of cash can quickly become insolvent. The bank that aims for high profitability in the long term must therefore not forget that it also has secondary objectives to achieve in terms of risk and liquidity. Today I would like to focus on the liquidity side. Normally, a solvent bank should be able to obtain, without too much difficulty, the liquidity it needs. It may, to cover its liquidity needs, draw on the credit limits it has with other banking institutions or use its own liquid assets. By liquid assets I mean means of payment and assets that can either be easily sold or temporarily converted into cash on the market or with the SNB. In exceptional situations, however, the bank that needs to obtain liquidity may face serious difficulties. Liquidity needs can increase massively, while recourse to the usual sources of liquidity is suddenly no longer possible. That is why it is important that each bank takes the necessary steps early enough to have reliable sources of liquidity, also in exceptional situations. Each bank is itself responsible for its liquidity, both in normal times and in difficult phases. It is true that the SNB can grant exceptional aid in the form of liquidity, but only systemically important banks are involved, and the conditions under which such aid is provided are very restrictive. In my brief presentation, I would first like to draw your attention to various situations that can lead to liquidity problems. I will then show you why the repo market is a source of liquidity, even in the event of a crisis. Finally In a few words, I will talk about the SNB's contribution to maintaining a sufficient level of liquidity on the Swiss franc money market. Liquidity problems and their origin Liquidity crises can be generalized to the whole or a large part of the system. In such a case, many banks face a more or less severe shortage of liquidity at the same time. But liquidity problems can also affect only one bank. This is called an isolated liquidity crisis. Let me first look at the case of an isolated crisis. Sometimes all it takes is a few negative pieces of information for a bank to quickly become a topic of discussion in the market. For example, news about a large credit loss, embezzlement, mismanagement or operational difficulties can lead to uncertainty. The rumours that then begin to run about the magnitude of the difficulties and the possible repercussions know little limit, because all the facts, at that time, are generally not yet established. This uncertainty undermines confidence, and the bank concerned may face difficulties if it has to refinance itself, through blank operations, on the money market. It is not excluded that, at a later stage, the customers of this bank will withdraw their deposits en masse. Therefore, a bank must make the necessary arrangements in calm weather and take into account, in its liquidity management, storms that may arise if it wants its probability of falling into an isolated liquidity crisis to remain low. Generalized seizures can have various origins. Financial market turbulence, natural disasters, terrorist attacks, poorly designed software or human error can cause or even paralyze vital payment and securities settlement systems. The terrorist attacks that struck New York on 11 September 2001 caused major problems to vital infrastructure in the financial system and greatly increased the need for liquidity. Many companies have had to relocate some of their staff. Various infrastructures were no longer able to function or were only partially functioning. Financial market participants no longer knew where their liquidity situation stood and could no longer issue payment orders. A few banks then accumulated liquidity, while others faced a shortage. Today, local crises can spread much faster to other markets. This is due to the developments we have seen in financial markets in recent years, in particular the increasing globalisation and interdependence of markets and the many groupings of financial institutions. Banks, in their liquidity management, must be prepared for widespread crises. They must be ready to implement, at any time, the measures required by a crisis situation. The importance of central bank-eligible securities for liquidity supply Liquidity management is therefore part of a bank's key tasks. On a day-to-day basis, it is essentially a question of balancing the cash flows occurring in a period of time that leaves little room for unpleasant surprises. The task is therefore relatively easy. The real challenge for every liquidity manager is to estimate the liquidity needs to maintain the bank's ability to pay even in the event of a crisis. These needs depend on the structure of assets and liabilities. However, the maturity structure of liabilities and receivables and the degree of liquidity of assets vary greatly from one bank to another. The legal provisions governing liquidity require that a bank's short-term liabilities be covered, to a certain extent, by liquid assets. In the event of a crisis, the sale of such assets must enable the bank to obtain the necessary means of payment. However, the short-term sale of assets is often synonymous with selling at a loss. In exceptional situations, these losses are likely to be heavy, because markets can lose their liquidity due to a lack of interested buyers. Securities that can be mobilised from the SNB or another central bank are also included in liquid assets. These securities, instead of being sold, can be repurchased and thus temporarily converted into cash. The repo market is therefore an important source of liquidity. Securities eligible for the SNB make it possible, even in difficult times, to obtain liquidity on the market or at the central bank. This is why banks can only be recommended to hold their liquid assets in the form of securities that can be mobilized from the central bank and to connect to the repo system. Genesis and development of the Swiss franc repo market In Switzerland, it was not until the end of the nineties that a repo market was created. This is mainly due to the tax burden on these transactions and the fact that repurchase agreements were not included in the monetary policy instruments available to the SNB. But the late introduction of repo trading in Switzerland has also had an advantage: it has indeed been possible to set up a fundamentally new system, at the forefront of global progress, in terms of infrastructure and workflow. The Swiss franc repo market has grown steadily in recent years. On average in 2005, outstanding repurchase agreements amounted to CHF 64 billion. About one-third of this amount comes from our monetary policy operations and the other two-thirds comes from transactions in the interbank market. Open market operations between the SNB and the banks stabilised at around CHF 20 billion. On the other hand, transactions on the interbank market have increased significantly in recent years. Their outstanding amount exceeds 40 billion francs. Repo trading is concluded using the Eurex Repo electronic trading platform. The transactions then take place on a "delivery against payment" basis via SIS SegaInterSettle AG and the transfer accounts at the SNB. This integrated infrastructure is called the "Swiss Value Chain". Thanks to the management provided by SIS, credit and market risks during the term of a repo are limited to the fluctuations in securities prices from one day to the next, and these fluctuations are offset every day by margin calls. Thanks to workflow automation, operational risks and settlement risks are almost completely non-existent. This year, more than 100,000 transactions have already been concluded, but only seven commitments have not been fulfilled or have been fulfilled with a delay of one day. This clearly shows how efficient and safe the Swiss repo system is. The services provided by SIS in relation to repo and the procedures applied to the conduct of operations have been designed specifically to take into account the needs of small and medium-sized banks. Repo payments, an instrument ensuring access to liquidity As I have already pointed out, it is extremely important for a bank to be able to have a reliable source of liquidity at all times. Repo provides an important contribution in this regard, in both ordinary and extraordinary situations. On the side of the bank that lends funds, repo is particularly attractive for two reasons. Indeed, the bank holds monetary claims that are constantly hedged by securities and, in addition, it can strengthen its degree of liquidity. This reinforcement stems from the fact that it has freely disposed of the securities it has repurchased until the maturity of the operation. If necessary, it may convert these securities at any time for liquidity with the central bank or on the market. Banks that borrow liquidity should also make greater use of collateralized operations to cover their money market needs. Even banks with a high rating may run into difficulties at some point. If such a case occurs, the credit limits available to them are likely to be immediately reduced or even eliminated altogether. Reliance on credit limits is dangerous. A liquid repo market allows for rapid refinancing in the interbank market, regardless of credit limits, and thus provides an important contribution to the stability of the financial system. Banks that do not actively operate in this market are deluding themselves if they think they can, in the event of a crisis, change their system quickly, in other words from unsecured to collateralized operations overnight. They will face obstacles such as a lack of know-how, the time required to install the technical infrastructure and a portfolio that is too poorly stocked with securities that can be mobilized in pensions. With the development of the repo market, the securities that the SNB accepts in its operations are increasingly becoming valuable assets with multiple possibilities of use. Thus, they make it possible, always from the SNB, to obtain intraday liquidity and to use the liquidity tightening facility. But these securities can also be used as collateral in other transactions. They may be used, inter alia, as an 'initial margin' to hedge open positions in currency and derivatives transactions or as a 'margin' at operators of CCP trading systems. The SNB's contribution to maintaining a sufficient level of liquidity on the Swiss franc money market The introduction of repurchase agreements has also brought serious benefits to the SNB. Today, we have an effective and very flexible instrument. Repo payments, through their flexibility, allow us to manage interest rates and liquidity well, even in exceptional situations. That is why all our ordinary monetary policy instruments are implemented through repurchase agreements. I think it would be useful to briefly describe our main monetary policy instruments. Through its main financing operations, the SNB regularly supplies the banking sector with liquidity. Every day, we spend main financing operations with banks. Our daily presence in the market allows us to act in a very targeted way on short-term interest rates. We also have an intraday facility. Banks use it a lot today. They can thus obtain liquidity, without interest, but only during the day. This intraday facility contributes to the smooth running of payment transactions. The Liquidity Tightening Facility is designed to enable banks to cope with temporary and unexpected liquidity shortages. It is especially important for banks that do not receive payments they expected and for banks that cannot obtain timely liquidity in the market. The liquidity tightening facility is only occasionally used by banks, but the role it can play in maintaining a bank's ability to pay should not be underestimated. That is why I believe that it is up to the management of a bank to set the desired limit under this facility. From the beginning of 2006, banks will only be able to use the liquidity tightening facility through repo at the special rate. This new instrument will thus take over from the traditional Lombard loans. The majority of banks have either already switched to the new system or are in the process of migrating. The limits we have opened up to banks already amount to CHF 10.6 billion. This amount exceeds by about 20% the old limits for Lombard credits. This week, we sent a circular to the banks informing them of a simplification that we will bring, on 1 December 2005, to the use of the facility for liquidity tightening. From 1 December, we will invite banks to announce to us, usually between 16:00 and 16:15 approximately, their liquidity needs under this facility on the Eurex Repo platform. In order to conclude repurchase agreements with the SNB, it is necessary to have value papers belonging to certain categories, i.e. securities eligible for the SNB. Currently, we accept securities denominated in Swiss francs or euros and meeting certain conditions with regard to the quality of their issuer and their liquidity. In interbank transactions, Swiss banks are increasingly accepting repurchase agreements denominated in euros. Given the important role that the Swiss franc traditionally plays internationally, we felt that banks abroad should also have access to our facilities. We have more than 100 banks, in Switzerland and abroad, which are potential counterparties for us. This broad access to the central bank - to the central currency - increases the efficiency of the Swiss franc money market. A large number of participants also contributes to making the repo market a reliable source of swiss franc liquidity, even in the event of a crisis. Conclusion Let me conclude by recalling a few points that I think are important. A bank must be able to meet its payment commitments at any time and on time. Traditional sources of liquidity may close in exceptional situations. Therefore, in order to deal with possible crises, any bank should hold a sufficient amount of assets eligible for the central bank to be able to obtain liquidity at all times on the market or from the central bank. Liquidity management is part of a bank's key tasks. Given the importance it can take on in the event of a crisis, this task should be the direct responsibility of the management of each bank. Compared to traditional money market transactions, repo offers undeniable advantages from a security perspective. In repurchase agreements, the credit risk is minimal, since monetary claims are fully and permanently covered by securities. Another advantage of repo transactions is that they provide much better access to Cash. A well-functioning repo market thus goes a long way towards maintaining each bank's access to liquidity. Securities accepted by the SNB in its repo can be converted into cash at any time on the interbank market, even if they already come from repurchase agreements. Relying on credit limits with other banks is risky because these sources of liquidity can close quickly. In addition, the use of all SNB facilities will be made exclusively through repurchase agreements from the beginning of 2006. In Switzerland, every autonomous bank would have to join the system of repo against swiss francs if it wants to have a liquidity management that is modern and safe. Thank you for your attention.
