Jordan Membre supplant de la Direction gnrale de la Banque nationale suisse March montaire 17 novembre 2005 Mesdames, Messieurs, L'objectif premier d'une banque est d'atteindre  long terme une rentabilit aussi leve que possible sur les fonds propres investis. Le niveau potentiel de cette rentabilit est en rapport direct avec les risques que la banque est prte  courir. La banque prenant des risques plus levs peut accrotre sa rentabilit moyenne. Des risques plus levs impliquent cependant une augmentation du potentiel de pertes. Par consquent, une banque ne devrait prendre que les risques qui, au total, ne peuvent mettre en danger sa survie. La survie d'une banque dpend toutefois non seulement de sa solvabilit, mais aussi de ses liquidits. Pour une banque, il est en effet indispensable de pouvoir faire face,  tout moment et dans les dlais,  ses engagements de paiement. Les banques  court de liquidits peuvent rapidement devenir insolvables. La banque qui vise une rentabilit leve  long terme ne doit donc pas oublier qu'elle a aussi des objectifs secondaires  atteindre en matire de risques et de liquidits. Je voudrais aujourd'hui axer mes propos sur le volet liquidits. En temps normal, une banque solvable devrait pouvoir se procurer, sans trop de difficults, les liquidits qui lui sont ncessaires. Elle peut, pour couvrir ses besoins de liquidits, tirer sur les limites de crdit qu'elle a auprs d'autres tablissements bancaires ou recourir  ses propres actifs liquides. Par actifs liquides j'entends les moyens de paiement et les actifs qui peuvent tre soit facilement vendus, soit convertis temporairement en liquidits sur le march ou auprs de la Banque nationale. Dans des situations exceptionnelles, la banque qui doit se procurer des liquidits peut toutefois se heurter  de srieuses difficults. Les besoins en liquidits peuvent augmenter massivement, alors qu'un recours aux sources de liquidits habituelles n'est tout  coup plus possible. C'est pourquoi il est important que chaque banque prenne suffisamment tt les mesures ncessaires pour disposer, dans des situations exceptionnelles galement, de sources fiables de liquidits. Chaque banque est elle-mme responsable de ses liquidits, en temps normal comme dans les phases difficiles. La Banque nationale peut, il est vrai, accorder une aide exceptionnelle sous forme de liquidits, mais seules des banques revtant une importance systmique entrent en ligne de compte, et les conditions auxquelles une telle aide est fournie sont trs restrictives. Dans mon bref expos, je voudrais d'abord attirer votre attention sur diverses situations qui peuvent engendrer des problmes de liquidits. Je vous montrerai ensuite pourquoi le march des pensions de titres est une source de liquidits, mme en cas de crise. Enfin, j'aborderai en quelques mots la contribution de la Banque nationale au maintien d'un niveau suffisant de liquidits sur le march montaire en francs. Les problmes de liquidits et leur origine Les crises de liquidits peuvent tre gnralises  l'ensemble ou  une grande partie du systme. Dans un tel cas, de nombreuses banques se heurtent en mme temps  une pnurie plus ou moins forte de liquidits. Mais les problmes de liquidits peuvent aussi ne toucher qu'un seul tablissement bancaire. On parle alors d'une crise isole de liquidits. Permettez-moi d'examiner d'abord le cas d'une crise isole. Il suffit parfois de quelques informations ngatives pour qu'une banque devienne rapidement un sujet de discussion sur le march. Ainsi, des nouvelles au sujet d'une grosse perte subie sur un crdit, de malversations, d'une mauvaise gestion ou de difficults oprationnelles peuvent engendrer de l'incertitude. Les rumeurs qui se mettent alors  courir sur l'ampleur des difficults et sur les rpercussions possibles ne connaissent gure de limites, parce que tous les faits,  ce moment-l, ne sont gnralement pas encore tablis. Cette incertitude branle la confiance, et la banque concerne peut se heurter  des difficults si elle doit se refinancer, par des oprations en blanc, sur le march montaire. Il n'est pas exclu que, dans une tape ultrieure, les clients de cette banque retirent en masse leurs dpts. Par consquent, une banque doit prendre les dispositions ncessaires par temps calme et tenir compte, dans sa gestion des liquidits, des temptes pouvant surgir si elle veut que sa probabilit de tomber dans une crise isole de liquidits reste faible. Les crises gnralises peuvent avoir diverses origines. Des turbulences sur les marchs financiers, des catastrophes naturelles, des attentats terroristes, des logiciels mal conus ou des erreurs humaines peuvent engendrer des problmes de fonctionnement dans les systmes vitaux de paiement et de rglement des oprations sur titres, voire paralyser de tels systmes. Les attentats terroristes qui ont frapp New York le 11 septembre 2001 ont caus de gros problmes  des infrastructures vitales du systme financier et fortement accru les besoins en liquidits. De nombreuses entreprises ont d dlocaliser une partie de leur personnel. Diverses infrastructures n'taient plus en mesure de fonctionner ou ne fonctionnaient plus que partiellement. Des oprateurs sur les marchs financiers ne savaient plus o en tait leur situation en matire de liquidits et ne pouvaient plus donner d'ordres de paiement. Quelques banques ont alors accumul des liquidits, tandis que d'autres taient confrontes  une pnurie. Aujourd'hui, les crises locales peuvent s'tendre beaucoup plus rapidement  d'autres marchs. Cela est d aux volutions que nous avons observes ces dernires annes sur les marchs financiers, en particulier  la mondialisation et  l'interdpendance toujours plus pousses des marchs et aux nombreux regroupements d'tablissements financiers. Les banques, dans leur gestion des liquidits, doivent se prparer  faire face  des crises gnralises. Elles doivent tre prtes  mettre en uvre,  tout moment, les mesures qu'exige une situation de crise. L'importance des titres ligibles  la banque centrale pour l'approvisionnement en liquidits La gestion des liquidits entre donc dans les tches cls d'une banque. Au quotidien, il s'agit essentiellement d'quilibrer les flux de liquidits intervenant dans un laps de temps qui ne laisse gure de place  de mauvaises surprises. La tche est donc relativement aise. Le vrai dfi que chaque gestionnaire de liquidits doit relever est d'estimer les besoins en liquidits permettant de maintenir la capacit de paiement de la banque mme en cas de crise. Ces besoins dpendent de la structure des actifs et passifs. La structure des chances des engagements et des crances et le degr de liquidit des actifs varient toutefois fortement d'une banque  l'autre. Les dispositions lgales qui rgissent les liquidits exigent que les engagements  court terme d'une banque soient couverts, dans une certaine proportion, par des actifs liquides. En cas de crise, la vente de tels actifs doit permettre  la banque de se procurer les moyens de paiement ncessaires. Or la cession  court terme d'actifs est souvent synonyme de vente  perte. Dans des situations exceptionnelles, ces pertes risquent d'tre lourdes, parce que les marchs peuvent perdre leur liquidit par manque d'acheteurs intresss. Les titres mobilisables auprs de la Banque nationale ou d'une autre banque centrale entrent eux aussi dans les actifs liquides. Ces titres, au lieu d'tre vendus, peuvent tre mis en pensions et, ainsi, convertis temporairement en liquidits. Le march des pensions de titres est donc une source importante de liquidits. Les titres ligibles  la Banque nationale permettent, mme dans les moments difficiles, d'obtenir des liquidits sur le march ou  la banque centrale. C'est pourquoi on ne peut que recommander aux banques de dtenir leurs actifs liquides sous forme de titres mobilisables auprs de la banque centrale et de se raccorder au systme des pensions de titres. Gense et dveloppement du march en francs des pensions de titres En Suisse, il a fallu attendre la fin des annes nonante pour qu'un march des pensions de titres voie le jour. Cela est d essentiellement  la charge fiscale qui grevait ces oprations et au fait que les pensions de titres n'entraient pas dans les instruments de politique montaire  la disposition de la Banque nationale. Mais l'introduction tardive des pensions de titres en Suisse a eu aussi un avantage: il a t en effet possible de mettre en place un systme fondamentalement nouveau,  la pointe du progrs sur le plan mondial, pour ce qui a trait  l'infrastructure et au droulement des oprations. Le march en francs des pensions de titres a connu une progression continue ces dernires annes. En moyenne de l'anne 2005, l'encours des pensions de titres atteint 64 milliards de francs. Un tiers environ de ce montant dcoule de nos oprations de politique montaire et les deux autres tiers proviennent des oprations passes sur le march interbancaire. Les oprations d'open market entre la Banque nationale et les banques se sont stabilises autour de 20 milliards de francs. En revanche, les oprations passes sur le march interbancaire ont nettement augment ces dernires annes. Leur encours dpasse 40 milliards de francs. Les pensions de titres sont conclues  l'aide de la plate-forme de ngoce lectronique Eurex Repo. Les oprations se droulent ensuite selon le principe livraison contre paiement, via la SIS SegaInterSettle AG et les comptes de virement  la BNS. Cette infrastructure intgre est appele la Swiss Value Chain. Grce  la gestion assure par la SIS, les risques de crdit et de march pendant la dure d'une pension de titres sont limits aux fluctuations que les cours des titres enregistrent d'un jour  l'autre, et ces fluctuations sont compenses chaque jour par des appels de marge. Grce  l'automatisation du droulement des oprations, les risques oprationnels et le risque de rglement sont presque totalement inexistants. Cette anne, plus de 100'000 oprations ont dj t conclues, mais seuls sept engagements n'ont pas t tenus ou l'ont t avec un retard d'un jour. Cela montre clairement combien le systme suisse des pensions de titres est efficace et sr. Les prestations fournies par la SIS en rapport avec les pensions de titres et les procdures appliques au droulement des oprations ont t conues tout spcialement pour tenir compte des besoins des petites et moyennes banques. Les pensions de titres, un instrument assurant l'accs  des liquidits Comme je l'ai dj soulign, il est extrmement important pour une banque de pouvoir disposer en tout temps d'une source fiable de liquidits. Les pensions de titres fournissent une importante contribution sur ce plan, dans les situations ordinaires aussi bien que dans les situations extraordinaires. Du ct de la banque qui prte des fonds, les pensions de titres sont particulirement attrayantes pour deux raisons. En effet, la banque dtient des crances montaires qui sont constamment couvertes par des titres et, de surcrot, elle peut renforcer son degr de liquidit. Ce renforcement dcoule du fait qu'elle dispose librement, jusqu' l'chance de l'opration, des titres qu'elle a pris en pension. Au besoin, elle peut convertir en tout temps ces titres contre des liquidits auprs de la banque centrale ou sur le march. Les banques qui empruntent des liquidits devraient elles aussi recourir davantage  des oprations assorties de garanties pour couvrir, sur le march montaire, leurs besoins. Mme des banques ayant une notation leve peuvent se heurter un jour ou l'autre  des difficults. Si un tel cas se produit, les limites de crdit dont elles disposent risquent fort d'tre immdiatement rduites, voire purement supprimes. La dpendance de limites de crdit est dangereuse. Un march liquide des pensions de titres permet de se refinancer rapidement sur le march interbancaire, indpendamment de limites de crdit, et fournit ainsi une importante contribution  la stabilit du systme financier. Les banques qui n'oprent pas activement sur ce march se font une illusion si elles pensent pouvoir, en cas de crise, changer rapidement leur systme, en d'autres termes passer du jour au lendemain des oprations non assorties de garanties  des oprations assorties de garanties. Elles se heurteront  des obstacles tels qu'un manque de savoir-faire, le temps ncessaire  l'installation de l'infrastructure technique et un portefeuille trop peu garni en titres mobilisables dans des pensions. Avec le dveloppement du march des pensions, les titres que la Banque nationale accepte dans ses oprations deviennent de plus en plus des biens prcieux, aux multiples possibilits d'utilisation. Ainsi, ils permettent, toujours auprs de la Banque nationale, d'obtenir des liquidits intrajournalires et de recourir  la facilit pour resserrements de liquidits. Mais ces titres peuvent aussi servir de garanties dans d'autres oprations. Il est possible de les utiliser notamment comme initial margin pour couvrir des positions ouvertes dans les oprations sur devises et sur produits drivs ou comme margin chez des exploitants de systmes de ngoce  contreparties centrales. La contribution de la Banque nationale au maintien d'un niveau suffisant de liquidits sur le march montaire en francs L'introduction des pensions de titres a apport aussi de srieux avantages  la Banque nationale. Aujourd'hui, nous disposons d'un instrument efficace et trs souple. Les pensions de titres, par leur souplesse, nous permettent de bien grer les taux d'intrt et les liquidits, mme dans des situations exceptionnelles. C'est la raison pour laquelle tous nos instruments ordinaires de politique montaire sont mis en uvre par des pensions de titres. Il me parat utile de vous dcrire brivement nos principaux instruments de politique montaire. Par ses oprations principales de financement, la Banque nationale approvisionne rgulirement le secteur bancaire en liquidits. Chaque jour, nous passons des oprations principales de financement avec des banques. Notre prsence quotidienne sur le march nous permet d'agir de manire trs cible sur les taux d'intrt  court terme. Nous avons galement une facilit intrajournalire. Les banques y recourent beaucoup aujourd'hui. Elles peuvent ainsi se procurer des liquidits, sans intrt, mais uniquement pendant la journe. Cette facilit intrajournalire contribue au bon droulement du trafic des paiements. La facilit pour resserrements de liquidits est prvue pour permettre  des tablissements bancaires de faire face  des manques passagers et inattendus de liquidits. Elle est importante surtout pour les banques qui ne reoivent pas des paiements qu'elles attendaient et pour les banques qui ne peuvent se procurer  temps des liquidits sur le march. La facilit pour resserrements de liquidits n'est utilise qu'occasionnellement par les banques, mais le rle qu'elle peut jouer dans le maintien de la capacit de paiement d'une banque ne doit pas tre sous-estim. C'est pourquoi j'estime qu'il appartient  la direction d'une banque de fixer la limite souhaite au titre de cette facilit. A partir du dbut de 2006, les banques ne pourront recourir  la facilit pour resserrements de liquidits que par des pensions de titres au taux spcial. Ce nouvel instrument prendra ainsi le relais des crdits lombard traditionnels. En majorit, les banques sont soit dj passes au nouveau systme, soit en train de migrer. Les limites que nous avons ouvertes aux banques portent dj sur 10,6 milliards de francs. Ce montant dpasse d'environ 20% les anciennes limites pour crdits lombard. Cette semaine, nous avons adress une circulaire aux banques pour les informer d'une simplification que nous apporterons, au 1er dcembre 2005, au recours  la facilit pour resserrements de liquidits. A partir du 1er dcembre, nous inviterons chaque jour les banques  nous annoncer, gnralement entre 16h00 et 16h15 environ, leurs besoins en liquidits, au titre de cette facilit, sur la plate-forme Eurex Repo. Pour conclure des pensions de titres avec la Banque nationale, il faut disposer de papiersvaleurs appartenant  certaines catgories, soit de titres ligibles  la BNS. Actuellement, nous acceptons des titres libells en francs ou en euros et remplissant certaines conditions pour ce qui a trait  la qualit de leur metteur et  leur liquidit. Dans les oprations interbancaires, les banques suisses acceptent de plus en plus de prendre en pension des titres libells en euros. Etant donn le rle important que le franc joue traditionnellement sur le plan international, nous avons estim que des banques  l'tranger doivent elles aussi avoir accs  nos facilits. Nous avons ainsi plus de 100 banques, en Suisse et  l'tranger, qui sont pour nous des contreparties potentielles. Ce large accs  la banque centrale   la monnaie centrale  renforce l'efficacit du march montaire en francs. Un nombre lev de participants contribue aussi  faire du march des pensions de titres une source fiable de liquidits en francs, mme en cas de crise. Conclusion Permettez-moi, en guise de conclusion, de rappeler quelques points qui me paraissent importants. Une banque doit pouvoir faire face,  tout moment et dans les dlais,  ses engagements de paiement. Des sources traditionnelles de liquidits peuvent se fermer dans des situations exceptionnelles. C'est pourquoi, en vue de faire face  de possibles crises, toute banque devrait dtenir une quantit suffisante d'actifs ligibles  la banque centrale pour tre en mesure de se procurer en tout temps des liquidits sur le march ou  la banque centrale. La gestion des liquidits entre dans les tches cls d'une banque. Etant donn l'importance qu'elle peut prendre en cas de crise, cette tche devrait tre sous la responsabilit directe de la direction de chaque banque. Compares aux oprations traditionnelles qui sont passes sur le march montaire, les pensions de titres prsentent d'incontestables avantages sous l'angle de la scurit. Dans les pensions de titres, le risque de crdit est minime, puisque les crances montaires sont couvertes intgralement et en permanence par des titres. Un autre avantage des pensions de titres dcoule du fait qu'elles assurent beaucoup mieux un accs  des liquidits. Un march des pensions de titres qui fonctionne bien contribue ainsi grandement  maintenir l'accs de chaque banque  des liquidits. Les titres accepts par la BNS dans ses pensions peuvent tre convertis en liquidits en tout temps sur le march interbancaire, mme s'ils proviennent dj de pensions de titres. Tabler sur des limites de crdit ouvertes auprs d'autres banques est risqu parce que ces sources de liquidits peuvent se fermer rapidement. De plus, le recours  toutes les facilits de la Banque nationale passera exclusivement par des pensions de titres ds le dbut de l'anne 2006. En Suisse, chaque banque autonome devrait se raccorder au systme des pensions de titres contre francs si elle veut avoir une gestion des liquidits qui soit moderne et sre. Je vous remercie de votre attention.

Title: Results of design competition for new banknote series: Introductory remarks
text: Berne, 23 November 2005 Introductory remarks Niklaus Blattner, Vice-Chairman of the Governing Board Allow me to begin by welcoming you all to todays . After reporting on the new banknote series earlier this year, on 2 February, we are pleased to announce that the preparatory work for a new banknote series is going ahead as planned. Although our current banknotes are still adequately protected against counterfeiting, we must nevertheless strive to remain one step ahead of technological developments. At the moment, we are focusing on the design of the new banknotes. At todays conference we will present the results of the competition for the artistic design of the banknotes. The jury made their selection from the eleven designs exhibited here. Unfortunately, one of the participants had to withdraw from the competition. Although the Swiss National Bank still aims to bring the new banknotes into circulation from 2010, a great deal remains to be done between the design stage and the end product. I would now like to give the floor to Mr Ammann, who, as chairman of the jury, will report on the different designs and the results of the competition, which are of course the focal point of todays conference.

Title: Results of design competition for new banknote series: Remarks on further procedure
text: Berne, 23 November 2005 Remarks on further procedure Roland Tornare, Director, Head of Cash After acknowledging the jurys decision as to the result of the competition, the Governing Board of the National Bank will decide on the next steps by spring 2006. It is quite possible that more than one designer will be asked to further develop one of the banknotes. After evaluating their submissions, a decision will then be made as to which designer will be chosen to develop the entire series. The SNB is not bound by the jurys assessment. For its decision, the Governing Board will take into consideration several criteria, including the technical requirements and the possibilities the designs allow for incorporating the new security technology. In the coming years, we will therefore devote considerable time to the design of the new banknotes. The projects concerning the new security features are going ahead on schedule. The new security technology allows us to ensure that the public can at any time easily verify the authenticity of our banknotes without any aids. Since we are dealing with new technologies, these projects will still require a few years of work. No decision has been made with regard to the symbols for the vision-impaired, and activities are progressing in this area as well. We are currently assessing the technical implementation of different solutions and will contact the appropriate associations in due time. According to our planning, the first banknotes should be ready for production in 2008 so that they can be put into circulation in 2010. I would like to mention the public exhibition of the designs at the National Banks Kaiserhaus Conference Centre, Amthausgasse 22 in Berne, 3rd floor. It is open to the public from 24 November to 2 December 2005 between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. On Saturdays and Sundays, the exhibit closes at 4 p.m.

Title: Switzerland's Growth Challenge
text: Switzerlands Growth Challenge Ulrich Kohli Chief Economist Alternate Member of the Governing Board Swiss National Bank Paper prepared for presentation at the Osec Business Network Switzerland Podium Zurich, December 7, 2005 1. Switzerland's growth deficit For the past quarter of a century, Switzerland's growth rate has been exceedingly low. Switzerland regularly shows up at the bottom of international rankings. In fact, according to the OECD, it has now been passed by Ireland in terms of real income per capita.1 It has been said that if current trends continue, Switzerland will eventually become one of the poorest countries of Western Europe.2 According to a recent report, Switzerland is less competitive than Hong Kong and Singapore.3 For some analysts, Switzerland has been in a great depression for the past thirty years.4 Its productivity is said to be falling.5 Switzerland has the reputation of being a high-price island, so that its apparently high income level might be just an illusion.6 These assessments are worrisome, to say the least, for growth is essential to satisfy the expanding needs and aspirations of the population. Even in Switzerland, there are pockets of poverty, with many households struggling to make ends meet, and growth is the best way to bring about an improvement in everyones living standards. Moreover, we must bear in mind the ageing of the population. Irrespective of how future pension benefits will be financed, it is vital that the consumption needs of coming generations, whether working or retired, be met as fully as possible.7 This requires that the size of the national economic pie be maximised. While the situation is alarming and needs to be urgently corrected, it is essential to remain credible if one expects one's recommendations to be taken seriously. Yet some of the more sensational declarations that have been made are hardly tenable, at least not without serious qualifications. So let us have a brief look at the evidence. 1 OECD Bulletin (2005). 2 J.-D. Gerber in NZZ am Sonntag, January 30, 2005. 3 IMD World Competitiveness Yearbook 2005. 4 T.J. Kehoe and E.C. Prescott Great Depressions of the 20th Century, Review of Economic Dynamics 5 (2002) 1-18; T.J. Kehoe and K.J. Ruhl Recent Great Depressions: Aggregate Growth in New Zealand and Switzerland, New Zealand Economic Papers 37 (2003) 5-40; T.J. Kehoe and K.J. Ruhl Is Switzerland in a Great Depression?, Review of Economic Dynamics 8 (2005) 759-775. 5 Departement federal de l'economie (2002) "Le rapport sur la croissance", Grundlagen der Wirtschaftspolitik Nr. 3F, p. 21. 6 See "Tagung Hochpreisinsel Schweiz", seco, July 1, 2003. 7 U. Kohli "Le cout reel de la securite sociale" paper presented at the Schweizerische Gesellschaft fur Konjunkturforschung, May 15, 1997. 2. Switzerland's growth paradox Switzerland seems to be going slower than anybody else, and yet in terms of standards of living it stays in the lead pack. How can that be? In my opinion, part of the answer to this paradox has largely to do with measurement issues. I have argued elsewhere that when it comes to Switzerland, real gross domestic product (GDP) growth is a poor measure of economic performance, and this for a number of reasons.8 First, real GDP figures do not take into account terms-of-trade improvements. An improvement in the terms of trade is like a technological advance: one gets more for less, and it unquestionably raises a country's real income. Of all the countries in the OECD, Switzerland has experienced the largest improvement in its terms of trade  about 25%  over the past quarter of a century. Yet this is unaccounted for by real GDP. Second, GDP does not take into account the net income from abroad. Here, too, is Switzerland an outlier, with its gross national income (GNI) growing significantly more rapidly than its GDP thanks to its huge investments abroad. In 2004, GNI exceeded GDP by 8.3%; ten years ago, the difference was merely 3.3%. Another issue has to do with the fact that GDP figures do not fully take into account the services produced by public and club goods. Switzerland invests unusually large amounts in its public infrastructure and in the protection of the environment. Such investments mobilise considerable quantities of resources that could be used elsewhere. They presumably raise Switzerland's economic welfare, but they have little impact on its measured output potential. I should also mention that there are some technical issues regarding the choice of a functional form for index numbers that come into play.9 These and other reasons lead me to conclude that Switzerland's real income growth broadly defined is being significantly underestimated by real GDP.10 After all, Swiss cities regularly end up at or near the top of the Mercer quality of city life reports. For whatever such international rankings might be worth, it suggests that Switzerland is doing something right after all. 8 U. Kohli Real GDP, Real Domestic Income, and Terms-of-Trade Changes, Journal of International Economics 62 (2004), 83-106; U. Kohli Wachstumsschwache der Schweiz: Moglichkeiten und Grenzen der Geldpolitik, paper presented at the Verband akademischer Volks- und Betriebswirtschafter, Zurich, January 20, 2004; U. Kohli "Switzerland's Growth Deficit: A Real Problem, But Only Half as Bad as it Seems" in L. Steinmann and H. Rentsch (eds.) Diagnose: Wachstumsschwache (Verlag Neue Zurcher Zeitung: Zurich) 2005. 9 U. Kohli An Implicit Tornqvist Index of Real GDP, Journal of Productivity Analysis 21 (2004) 337-353; U. Kohli Inexact Index Numbers and Economic Monotonicity Violations: The GDP Price Deflator prepared for the SSHRC International Conference on Index Number Theory and the Measurement of Prices and Productivity, Vancouver, B.C., June 30July 3, 2004. 10 It is sometimes thought that while Switzerland's income is falling behind, the Swiss people do not notice it because their wealth remains extremely high. This explanation is not convincing, for the return from wealth must also be incorporated in any comprehensive definition of income. 3. Low competitivity? Is Switzerland really less competitive than Singapore and Hong Kong? Quite frankly, I do not find competitiveness a very meaningful concept when applied to nations. A firm or an industry needs to remain competitive, otherwise they would decline in size and eventually die out. Nations do not die out, at least not of economic causes. As elementary trade theory teaches us, every country has at least one comparative advantage. All countries survive trading in world markets at world prices. In that sense, they all are competitive. Of course, some countries are more successful than others, be it because of their factor endowments, their access to technology, or their institutions. Such countries have a higher income. It turns out that Switzerland's GDP per capita at market exchange rates exceeds that of Singapore's by 92% and that of Hong Kong's by 102%. Even at PPP exchange rates, the differences are not trivial (16% relative to Singapore, and 6% relative to Hong Kong). By this yardstick, Switzerland is clearly more successful than Singapore and Hong Kong. Admittedly, one can always do better, and there are many areas where there is room for improvement. I will get back to this in what follows. 4. Low productivity? Swiss growth fell quite dramatically in the 1990s. In spite of my earlier reservations, let me use real GDP as a yardstick to measure Switzerland's performance, since the data are readily available and widely used. As shown by Table 1, real GDP growth averaged 1.6% between 1981 and 2000. For the first part of this period, from 1981 to 1990, growth averaged 2.2%. For the second sub-period, from 1991 to 2000, it fell to 1.0%, barely keeping up with population growth. The 1990s can thus be viewed as a lost decade in terms of growth. Real GDP Labour Capital TFP Table 1 Decomposition of real GDP growth, 1981-2000 1981-2000 1.6% 0.1% 1.0% 0.5% 1981-1990 2.2% 0.5% 1.2% 0.4% 1991-2000 1.0% -0.2% 0.8% 0.5% What are the reasons for this dismal performance? It is sometimes argued that the answer lies in the decline of Swiss productivity. Productivity is difficult to measure, both over time and over space. Nonetheless, let us look at the best concept available. The most encompassing measure of productivity changes is what economists call total factor productivity (TFP). TFP captures the effects of technological and institutional changes. An improved technology, a better educated and healthier labour force, more competition, a better infrastructure, better institutions, and fewer administrative impediments are all conducive to higher TFP.11 As shown in Table 1, there is no evidence that TFP fell in the 1990s. On the contrary, it increased slightly to contribute about 0.5% to the annual growth of real GDP. Table 1 also shows the growth contributions of the accumulation of capital and labour. It is striking that the contributions of both factors fell dramatically in the 1990s, from 1.2% to 0.8% as far as capital is concerned, and from 0.5% to -0.2% for labour.12 Thus, it appears that the Swiss economic slowdown is mostly due to a fall in private domestic investment and a decline in work effort. While TFP is the productivity measure favoured by economists, the popular debate generally focuses on labour productivity. Here one must distinguish between average and marginal labour productivity. Headline figures typically refer to the former, whereas from an analytical viewpoint, it is the latter that is the more relevant. In equilibrium, the marginal product of labour must equal the real wage. Thus, considering the high level of Swiss real wages, one must conclude that the marginal product of labour in Switzerland is indeed very high, and rising. This is not surprising considering that most Swiss labour is skilled and that capital intensity is high. What about the average productivity of labour? I must admit, I do not view average labour productivity as a very useful concept, given that it essentially relates output to just one input, namely labour, overlooking the contributions of technological change (i.e. TFP) and of capital.13 Nonetheless, if we look at the figures shown in Table 2, we see that average labour productivity, far from declining, has actually increased, from a yearly average of 1.2% to 1.4%.14 Thus, there is no evidence that average labour productivity has fallen dramatically, at least not over the past two decades. 11 At the same time, it must be remembered that TFP is measured as a residual. Better data and smaller measurement errors are likely to reduce TFP. 12 These figures are based on K.J. Fox and M. Zurlinden "On Understanding Sources of Growth and Output Gaps for Switzerland" (2005), unpublished, and U. Kohli Labour Productivity vs. Total Factor Productivity, Irving Fisher Committee Bulletin (2005). All estimates are computed as Tornqvist indices. 13 Explaining output growth by compounding the increase in employment and the rate of change in average labour productivity, as it is often done, is almost tautological. This procedure is all the more questionable because an increase in employment would, ceteris paribus, reduce the average productivity of labour. Note also that one could equally well "explain" output growth by considering the rate of growth of the capital stock and the average productivity of capital, or do the same for any other input, for that matter. 14 This may appear quite modest compared to headline data reported for the United States, for instance. However, it must be remembered that, even though the recent US performance has been nothing short of stellar, US headline figures typically relate to the non-farm, private business sector. That is, household production and government, where productivity gains are either low or ruled out by construction, are left out. In fact, even the decomposition of average labour productivity has remained little changed during the past quarter of a century, with about two-thirds due to capital deepening and one-third to TFP. Table 2 Decomposition of average labour productivity growth, 1981-2000 Av. labour productivity Capital deepening TFP 1981-2000 1.3% 0.9% 0.5% 1981-1990 1.2% 0.8% 0.4% 1991-2000 1.4% 1.0% 0.5% 5. High-price island? Switzerland has the reputation of being a high-price country. To some extent, the high prices we pay for the goods and services we consume reflect a lack of competition, rigidities, administrative hurdles, and inefficiencies that afflict our domestic market. I will return to this issue shortly. By and large, however, the high prices that we face reflect the high wages that we enjoy. Our country is well endowed with capital and scarce in labour and land. Consequently, returns to capital are relatively low and real wages are high by international standards. Land is relatively expensive, too. As mentioned earlier, the high level of wages in Switzerland reflects the high value of the marginal product of its workers. To be sure, there are some activities where productivity is no higher than in the rest of the world. These are typically highly labour intensive, non-traded services, such as haircuts. Given our high wages, this translates into relatively high prices for these products. There is no way around it, though, at least not as long as we expect these services to continue to be offered in Switzerland. Given current technology, it would be most inconvenient and prohibitively expensive to travel to Portugal or Indonesia every time one needed a haircut. Nonetheless, the traded component of what we consume  except for agricultural products  is hardly more expensive than in the rest of the world.15 Our high wages therefore still imply a comparatively high purchasing power. This is for real, it is not an illusion. Deregulation, more competition, globalisation and technological progress will lead to adjustments in relative prices, and to a more efficient utilisation and allocation of resources. Our purchasing power will increase further, together with our real income. What impact this evolution might have on the price level is unclear, however, and indeed quite 15 A recent study by PricewaterhouseCoopers looking at the prices of new cars in a sample of 19 European countries finds that they are lowest in Switzerland. irrelevant. The price level per se is a quite meaningless concept: it cannot be assessed in abstracto, i.e. independently of wages, the exchange rate and monetary conditions in general. Ultimately, it is the course of monetary policy that will shape the path of the price level. Some voices have been heard calling for a drop in all prices, including wages, in Switzerland. Even if such a drop could somehow be engineered (what happened to yesterdays fears about deflation?), it would have little real impact, since the price of foreign exchange would most likely fall in the same proportions, leaving the real exchange rate  the only one that matters  unchanged, and still leaving us under the impression that Switzerland is a high-price country. As a first approximation, such a development would have no real impact. A closer look, though, would reveal a potentially damageable side effect, namely an arbitrary redistribution of wealth from debtors to creditors. 6. What went wrong? While the sky is not falling just yet, there is no denying that our growth deficit is real and needs to be rectified. What went wrong over the past couple of decades? Most economists would argue that our problems are structural, rather than cyclical. Admittedly, demand factors do matter as well, particularly in the short run. The 1990s have witnessed a number of shocks that have had a negative impact on activity and on capital formation in Switzerland. Without going into the details, one can mention here the restrictive monetary policy of the early 1990s that was made necessary by the rise in inflation in the late 1980s; the bursting of the housing bubble that had a adverse impact on household consumption, on construction and on financial intermediation; the unrelenting increase in health insurance premiums, which has severely amputated disposable income and penalised consumption; the burden of German reunification and the restrictive European fiscal policies in a struggle to satisfy the Maastricht criteria that impacted negatively on Swiss exports. While every period brings its share of positive and negative shocks, it seems that the 1990s were characterised by an unusual string of bad luck. There is little doubt, though, that in the longer run, it is the amounts of resources mobilised and the available technology that shape the growth path of an economy. As Table 1 indicates, the 1990s were characterised by low contributions of capital and labour. Private domestic investment was low, and the number of hours worked actually fell. How can that be? In my view, the main reason why employment growth stagnated during the 1990s is that a great deal was done to discourage work and encourage inactivity. Payroll taxes, such as unemployment and disability insurance levies, which have been raised repeatedly over the past several decades, act as a burden on work effort. Increased benefits, on the other hand, tend to subsidise inactivity. Proposals aired during the 1990s aimed at reducing the length of the working week or lowering the retirement age also contributed to conveying the fallacious notion that working less would actually be wealth generating. As for the reduced level of domestic investment in the 1990s, I see two possible  although not mutually exclusive  causes. First, the investment climate did deteriorate, with little impetus coming from the employment front, and with Switzerland probably gradually falling behind in the global race towards more competition and less regulation. This too is worrisome. Second, and this is not necessarily bad, European integration and globalisation have most likely led to a reduction in the home bias. Swiss investors have therefore become more comfortable investing abroad. Given the relative abundance of capital in Switzerland, which translates into modest returns to capital and low real interest rates, capital has flown out of Switzerland as testified by our huge current account surplus. I would argue that it makes perfect sense for Swiss firms and households to invest in countries where capital is relatively scarce and labour relatively abundant (and relatively young). The return to investments would be higher there than in Switzerland, and this would make a positive net contribution to Swiss national income. True, investments abroad to do not create any jobs in Switzerland, nor do they raise Swiss labour productivity. Given that we are close to full employment, though, the job argument carries little weight. According to some estimates, Swiss firms employ 1.8 million people abroad. Needless to say, it would be unfeasible to fill that many extra positions domestically. As for labour productivity, this discussion demonstrates once more that what is important is income, rather than output. One might also object that social security taxes are typically levied on labour income, and thus investments abroad creating jobs in foreign countries do not contribute to the Swiss social safety net. While few additional jobs would be created domestically, it is true that forcing investments to be made in Switzerland rather than abroad would raise the marginal product of labour, real wages and social security contributions, just as it would also depress the return to capital. Higher wages would call for higher pension benefits, however, so that the net effect on the social security system would essentially be nil; while investing capital where it is less productive would lower national income and this would be counter-productive. 7. What is to be done? The solutions to our problems are simple: one must mobilise all possible factors of growth and use them efficiently. The main growth engines are labour and capital, technological progress and international trade.16 To make the best possible use of these, the key is to avoid distortions, artificial hurdles and disincentives. As far as labour is concerned, one must encourage activity and discourage inactivity, rather than the reverse. Regulations that prevent workers from working as much as they please, for as long as they want or whenever they wish ought to be revoked. Distortions that inhibit the hiring of older workers must be eliminated. More day schools would encourage labour force participation. Labour mobility, which is an essential element for the efficient allocation of resources, must be promoted. This might require a wide range of measures, such as harmonising the inter-cantonal school system or reducing real estate transaction fees. Labour mobility could also be enhanced by a reform in our pension system. The free selection of a pension fund would allow workers to switch jobs without changing pension schemes, and vice-versa, thus giving them more freedom and flexibility. Indeed, there is no reason why the choice of employment should be linked to the choice of the provider of a financial service. Elementary portfolio theory teaches us that it is unwise to invest ones two largest assets (human capital and pension capital) in more or less the same institution. Furthermore, a system of widespread, transparent, individual pension accounts might do much to incite workers to increase their work effort.17 The tendency to tax work effort and subsidise inactivity is reflected by the very substantial increase in the size of the public sector that has taken place since the late 1970s. The sum of government purchases and transfers has grown enormously.18 In fact, of all the OECD countries, it is Switzerland that has experienced the largest increase in the public sector share over the past couple of decades. In view of the negative correlation that exists between real growth per capita and the increase in the size of the public sector, our poor 16 While this proposition might seem perfectly obvious to most economists, it is not always well understood by the population at large, where fallacious notions (such as that older workers must make room for younger ones, that investment and technological progress cause unemployment, and that international trade exports jobs to the rest of the world) often prevail. Such thinking reveals a serious and worrisome deficiency in economic literacy. 17 U. Kohli L'impact economique de la securite sociale, in Funf Expertenberichte zur Dreisaulenkonzeption der Schweizerischen Alters-, Hinterlassenen- und Invalidenvorsorge (Berne: Departement federal de l'interieur) 1991. 18 Public expenditure is a better gauge of the ascendancy of the public sector than current taxes would be, since it is the spending that means that resources are being absorbed or diverted, and since expenditure must necessarily be fully financed, either by taxes now, or by taxes later. performance should probably not come as a surprise.19 Within Europe, Switzerland has long been an outlier when it comes to the size of its public sector. This is no longer true. If one adds up the spending on all levels of government, the social insurances (including health insurance and compulsory pension schemes), and the public enterprises (the utilities, the railways, the post office, etc.), one is not far off 50% of GDP.20 In fact, if one refers to nominal net domestic product, which is a better measure of domestic net output, the 50% mark is probably already breached. Thus, just about every second franc that is spent in Switzerland transits through, is diverted by, or is regulated in some way by the public sector. When the allocation of resources no longer responds to economic forces it tends to become inefficient. Some might object that it is misleading to include the railways, the post office or public television in the sphere of government, since in some countries these are part of the private sector. This is precisely the point, though: in Switzerland, they are not. Besides inducing an inefficient allocation of resources and thus holding back productivity, the rapid growth in the public sector has also had a direct, negative impact on the measurement of TFP and average labour productivity. Indeed, since output is conventionally measured by input when it comes to the government sector, productivity gains are ruled out by construction, which weighs negatively on the average productivity performance of the economy as a whole. The lack of competition in many sectors of the Swiss economy is often cited as one of the main causes for Switzerlands lacklustre growth performance. Sheltered industries are not inclined to increase their productivity. Too many regulations, restrictions and domestic barriers to internal trade take their toll. Administrative hurdles use up valuable resources and create distortions. There seems to be no end to Swiss creativity when it comes to devising exotic taxes and duties. Some new levies are probably on the drawing board as we speak. More competition and less red tape would not only contribute to increasing TFP, but it would also make Switzerland as a business location more attractive to investors and stimulate domestic capital formation, thereby yielding a double dividend. Finally, international trade provides a formidable lever, thanks to which a country can transform the products for which it has a comparative advantage into those for which it does not. I have already mentioned the improvement in the terms of trade that Switzerland 19 U. Kohli Le veritable impot, University of Geneva, 1999. 20 U. Kohli La montee des depenses publiques en Suisse, University of Geneva, 1998. has enjoyed over the years. This did not just happen by accident: it is a mark of the success of the Swiss export industry. As all the Osec members in this audience well know, relentless efforts go into the search for new markets and into the development of new products. These efforts must continue. Globalisation and the increased fragmentation of production made possible by technological progress offers new opportunities. Switzerland must resolutely embrace free trade. In international trade rounds, negotiators often demand concessions from the other parties. This ignores the fact that, for a small open economy, free trade  even unilateral free trade  is first best. In this sense, adopting the cassis de Dijon principle would do much to stimulate our economy and raise our real income. It is also essential that the Doha round of trade talks be conducted to a successful conclusion. The federal government recently launched a 17-point programme devised to revitalise the Swiss economy. It is very broad in scope, including measures in the areas of education, health, the domestic market, competition, public finance, agriculture and immigration. This initiative is to be applauded and needs to be supported. Some of its measures have already been implemented. If all of them are eventually put in place, it will do much to increase the efficiency of the Swiss economy and to raise TFP. For the programme to be effective, however, it is important that it be viewed as a whole package that must not be unbundled, rather than as a menu from which a few individual items can be picked according to ones taste. 8. Will Switzerland win? Switzerland is facing many economic challenges. The march towards a single European market, European Union (EU) enlargement, and globalisation, with the economic integration of many additional countries, have given rise to many new opportunities and have led to profound changes in relative prices. These price changes require quantity adjustments. Comparative advantages may shift, some industries may decline, and others will prosper. These changes create both opportunities and risks for Switzerland: opportunities to further exploit our comparative advantages and to reap the benefits from the fragmentation of production and expanded international trade. Many of the required adjustments will be difficult and painful, though. The benefits will only be felt over time, but the pain is immediate. The risk therefore arises that these adjustments will be resisted. If the necessary changes in relative prices and wages are not allowed to take place, and if the reallocation of resources is hindered, some new equilibrium will emerge nonetheless, but it will be an unattractive one for us: one with more distortions, less income and fewer prospects. Will Switzerland win? It is up to all of us to answer this question and to decide whether we want a 21st-century income, or whether we are content with an income level from the past. As far as I am concerned, I am very bullish about Switzerland!

Title: Monetary policy from 2000 to 2005: What lessons have we learned?
text: Monetary Policy 2000-2005: What have we learned? Presentation by Jean-Pierre Roth Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank University of St. Gallen on 18 January 2006 1. Introduction Just over five years ago, at the beginning of 2000, the SNB opted for a new monetary policy concept. It was abandoning the control of monetary aggregates that it had practiced for 25 years, a technique that had produced good results in the fight against inflation, but which was becoming less reliable because of the novelties that had taken place on the financial markets. Like the previous strategy, the strategy put in place in 2000 aims to preserve price stability over the medium term. The objective of monetary action therefore remains unchanged, but the ways and means to achieve it have been adapted to the circumstances. My presentation tonight will begin by presenting the logic of our new concept. I will then highlight the changes in the environment in which our monetary policy is conducted, in particular the consequences of European monetary unification and globalisation. Finally, I will draw from this analysis conclusions that are useful for the implementation of our policy. 2. Elements of the concept put in place in 2000 The concept introduced in 2000 is more sophisticated than the one adopted by the SNB when the franc floated in 1973. From the control of monetary aggregates, it has moved to a strategy based on three elements: 95 an inflation forecast to guide monetary action, 95 a clear definition of price stability, 95 the use of the three-month Libor rate as an instrument of conduct. Inflation forecasting The great novelty of our current concept is the quarterly establishment of an inflation forecast. Using various econometric models that incorporate all relevant information at the moment, the SNB estimates the evolution of inflation over the next three years, assuming that monetary policy remains unchanged. This forecast - commonly referred to as a conditional forecast - does not claim to indicate to the public what the actual evolution of prices will be, as is often believed, but how the rise in prices would develop if the level of interest rates - and therefore the course of monetary policy - were to no longer vary in the future. An unrealistic hypothesis, but which makes it possible to highlight the medium-term consequences of the monetary policy of the moment. It should be remembered here that today's monetary decisions only affect the reality of prices after a relatively long and variable adjustment period, in Switzerland on average. Compared to the concept of the 1980s and 1990s, the new approach is more sophisticated in the sense that, in the past, only monetary aggregates were used as indicators of future price development, whereas now a whole host of indicators are part of our assessments. There are obviously monetary indicators, but also the development of the international economy and that of the Swiss economy. Our estimation methods use both conventional and advanced econometric techniques. So we do not have a "black box", but a real "portfolio" of models. It is on this basis that we establish the forecast that will finally be published. The key role of inflation forecasting is to give the SNB a medium-term compass, with the Bank's mission to preserve price stability over time and not from month to month. Inflation forecasting thus allows us to have enough hindsight to be able to define a preventive action in favour of price stability. In monetary matters, it is less painful to prevent than to cure! The definition of price stability The second element of our new concept is the definition of what can be considered price stability. The measurement of price stability raises many statistical and definitional problems: should we talk about producer prices, consumer prices, core inflation or actual price developments? How to take into account price changes due to technological innovations, how to deal with indirect tax increases? We have aligned ourselves with international practice that emphasizes consumer prices and tolerates a certain increase to take into account changes in product quality. We therefore associate price stability with an increase in the consumer price index of between 0% and 2%. We are not aiming for 2%, but simply believe that our mission is fulfilled if the pace of increase is below 2%. That said, it is also important to stress that our objective of price stability must not be achieved from month to month, but over the medium term. It is therefore important to see inflation trending in the range of 0% to 2%, temporary exceedances remain possible. In any case, monetary instruments have little influence on the immediate development of prices. Our approach to price stability therefore leaves us a wide margin of appreciation. We do not want our action to be guided by short-term considerations, but by medium-term developments. Our inflation forecast allows us to do that. The use of the three-month Libor rate as an operating variable The practical implementation of monetary policy always involves the management of market liquidity, which must be tightened if policy becomes more restrictive and relaxed if, on the contrary, policy becomes more expansive. To do this, each central bank gives itself an operational variable indicating the degree of liquidity of the market. We chose the three-month Libor rate, which we believe is the most representative of the state of the Swiss money market. Our monetary policy decisions result in the definition of a fluctuation band in which we control the three-month rate by acting daily on the Swiss franc market using rest operations. In fact, our rest credit operations are at shorter maturity (usually one week). The three-month rate is freely determined by the interbank market according to its actual state of liquidity and expectations. What is the logic of our concept? Our concept is oriented towards medium-term price developments. The factors triggering price increases can be real (evolution of the output gap) or monetary (excessive liquidity in relation to demand) and fuelled by bullish expectations. Since the general equilibrium models used to establish our inflation forecast always presuppose a gradual return to a situation of full utilization of the means of production, inflation forecasting typically takes an upward form in times of recovery and a downward form in times of monetary restraint. This profile is not surprising, it tells us that an expansive monetary policy will have to be corrected if the economic situation normalizes, to avoid a price slippage. Conversely, a restrictive policy will have to be relaxed when the economy slows down, if deflation is to be avoided. One of the advantages of publishing a conditional inflation forecast, such as that of the SNB, is that it presents these situations in a completely transparent manner. 3. Our experiences since 2000 In terms of results, our experiences with the new concept have been positive: price stability has been preserved and there is no indication that it will be threatened in the near future. In terms of communication, our monetary policy decisions have generally been well understood and markets are very confident in our ability to control future price developments. Over the years, however, our way of thinking within the framework of the new concept has evolved, due to two major international developments: monetary integration in Europe and the globalization of economic flows. European monetary integration At the end of the 1990s, we expected the arrival of the euro to significantly change the market environment for the Swiss franc. We feared at the time that the franc, deprived of the support of the German Mark, would be at the forefront of speculative attacks, especially in the event of a dollar crisis. In reality, our experience was very different from our expectations. Indeed, the arrival of the euro has profoundly changed the functioning of the foreign exchange market, with the European currency acting as a counterweight to the American currency. When in doubt about the value of the dollar, the euro appreciates, and vice versa. The "small" currencies are then largely forgotten by speculation. Thus, over the past five years, we have seen that the volatility between the franc and the euro has been lower than that observed between the franc and the German mark. The arrival of the euro has also changed the European landscape. In the first place, and this is obvious, the fragile currencies of the past have disappeared; Europe is no longer experiencing monetary crises as was still the case in the nineties, crises that were often very painful for the Swiss economy, especially for its export sector. But the disappearance of national currencies does not only have positive effects. While monetary discipline now reigns on the continent, there is a growing difficulty in complying with the rules of fiscal discipline. National governments, which knew in the past that financial markets could harshly sanction a slippage in their macroeconomic policy, now feel free from this constraint and have less scruples about the budget deficit. The good resolutions that surrounded the conclusion of the Stability and Growth Pact seem largely forgotten. These five years have also shown us that the euro area is more heterogeneous than we imagined. Catching-up phenomena have led to an inflation rate around the upper limit of the European Central Bank's (ECB) definition of price stability (0%-2% as in Switzerland). Despite the common currency, inflation rates and national economic conditions have diverged sharply. This makes the ECB's decisions all the more difficult to take and trigger strong negative reactions from political circles. The globalization of economic flows At the global level, the most striking event of recent years has been the take-off of emerging Asian countries and the arrival of China in the circle of economic powers of global dimension. Europe is not left behind with the sustained development of the economies of Eastern Europe. The globalization of markets, driven by the development of transport and communications, is a reality for consumers and producers alike. The latter do not hesitate to relocate part of their production in order to lower their costs. Switzerland, a country traditionally well established on foreign markets, has benefited from this development: today there are 1.8 million people working in Swiss companies located abroad, while our country has only 4 million jobs on its territory. For its part, the opening of markets to foreign products fuels domestic competition and allows consumers to benefit from the lowest prices. In Switzerland, for example, the price index for imported goods (excluding energy products) has fallen by 2.7% over the last five years (2000 100.12; 2005 97.41). Competitive pressure has also been exerted on domestic products, whose inflation has been steadily declining since 2001. Here, the only sub-indices showing some price increase are those of markets where there is little competition (administered prices; housing). In the end, it seems that the measures taken in recent years to make our economy more flexible by opening it up to more competition are now beginning to bear fruit and that the image of Switzerland as an island of high prices is gradually being corrected. The other side of the coin of this dynamic global economy, especially energy-hungry countries, is rising commodity prices. The latter has been the main cause of the increase in consumer prices in our country over the past two years. Without the surge in oil prices, our inflation would have been between 0% and 0.5%, all other things being equal, of course. Another indicator of increased competition is the moderation of wage pressures. In many countries, the unemployment rate remains relatively high. Despite increased labour market flexibility, firms are prioritising productivity gains over new hires. Cost increases remain moderate, and if they occur, as in the case of oil, they are absorbed by productivity gains rather than shifts to consumers. With globalization, we are therefore seeing a change in pricing mechanisms. Competition from products from emerging countries leads to lower import prices, the rapid growth of the world economy is causing higher commodity prices, and increased competitive pressure limits the ability of companies to pass on their cost increases to consumers. These structural changes have transformed the framework for monetary policy. 4. Lessons for monetary policy To what extent do changes in the international environment affect the application of our monetary policy concept? I draw six main lessons: (a) Firstly, the emergence of the euro has contributed to reducing the volatility of the franc. The latter reacts less to speculative movements than in the past. This is good news for the Swiss economy, it is also good news for the SNB, which is less concerned that its monetary policy decisions will provoke unrational reactions from the Swiss franc. As the Swiss franc "sticks" better to its fundamentals, the SNB can now apply its concept of monetary policy with greater conviction. b) Secondly, we note that monetary decision-making in the euro area is part of a more complex and heterogeneous framework than in Switzerland. On the one hand, national economic situations can diverge sharply; on the other hand, the decision-making mechanisms of the 18 members of the ECB Council are heavier than those of the three members of our Directorate-General. In addition, interactions with the Politics are more complex, between the ECB and the Euro-Group, than between the SNB and the authorities of our country. In such an environment, it is not surprising that the ECB only takes its decisions on the basis of proven facts, rather than with a view to future developments. The SNB's policy, on the other hand, can take a more preventive turn - based on an inflation forecast - than that of the ECB. Thus, over the past five years, the SNB has lowered interest rates faster and more sharply than the ECB. As a result, it was also the first to start raising rates in 2004. Waiting for the ECB to act would be a mistake for us; we can - and must - implement our policy according to the needs of the Swiss economy. Moreover, the fact that these different temporal profiles of monetary policies have not led to movements in the exchange rate of the franc against the euro shows that the markets understand very well that the ECB and the SNB act in somewhat different environments. (c) Developments in the European environment also show us that significant potential risks are still present: inflation in the euro area has been higher than ours for many years; some countries are even experiencing relatively high rates accompanied by a possible housing bubble. In addition, fiscal discipline is struggling to prevail, which is particularly worrying at a time when all industrialized countries will face financial difficulties due to the ageing of their populations. All these factors tell us that sources of tension exist that could disrupt the European financial market in the coming years and jeopardize the remarkable stability of the franc's exchange rate against the euro. These five years of stability should not make our companies forget that currency risk exists and that appropriate hedging strategies must be applied even in calm weather. d) We also note that globalization has changed the dynamics of price adjustments. Our price index today reflects more relative price changes, driven by structural adjustments, than a fundamental upward trend in all prices. The term "inflation" should therefore be used with caution. The inflation we see today is the statistical result of prices going up or down, sometimes somewhat randomly. Thus our "inflation" in 2005 was largely of oil origin: without the increases in oil prices, the consumer price index would have almost stagnated. Once the oil effect disappears in 2006, we expect a new slower pace of index increase. This situation makes current inflation a very different phenomenon from the inflation of the 1980s and 1990s. The fact that the expansive policy applied since 2001 has had no visible impact on price increases is a demonstration of this. These reflections prompt us to interpret the results of our inflation forecasts with great caution. The parameters of these forecasts are necessarily estimated using observations of past inflationary realities. If the latter are no longer transposable to our current environment, our models would tend to overestimate future inflationary pressures. It may also be that inflationary phenomena have not disappeared today, but are simply temporarily masked by the relative price adjustments mentioned above. Excess liquidity would no longer systematically trigger a consumer price reaction through the effects of increased competition in goods and labour markets, but would provoke a reaction from other prices. This is why a close look must be paid to the evolution of financial assets and real estate, markets that largely escape the structural adjustments observed in the goods market. e) The uncertainties surrounding the nature of current inflation show us that our definition of price stability - a price index increase of less than 2% - is particularly appropriate. Setting a one-off target (e.g. 2%), as some central banks do, would be a mistake; to want to neutralize the consequences on the price index of renewed competition in the goods markets would be contraindicated. Thanks to globalization, it may be that our inflation rate remains permanently below 2% without any weakness in demand being observed. The relatively low inflation rates that we have now seen for several years are not a reflection of an overly restrictive past policy and therefore do not particularly worry us. (f) The globalization of goods markets has led to a slowdown in price increases. The general decline in inflation has strengthened the credibility of central banks and firmly anchored expectations. Markets today expect less inflation and less volatile inflation than in the past. This development suggests that the equilibrium level of nominal interest rates may now be lower than it was in the past decade. It is also not excluded that we have entered a phase of lower real interest rates. This however, the last question remains very hypothetical. Nevertheless, we must remain very critical of any estimate of the "normal" level of interest rates because historical experience can hardly guide us in this area. 5. Conclusion These reflections tell me that the monetary policy concept adopted by the SNB in 2000 remains fully adapted to the current environment. The use of an inflation forecast ensures a high degree of transparency in our policy and obliges us to act preventively by measuring our action against future price developments. The framework created at the time is flexible enough to be used in changing environments. Indeed, the experience of the last five years, to which are also added the structural transformations brought about by European monetary unification and the globalisation of the markets, encourage us to operate in a slightly different way from that which we envisaged at the end of the 1990s. European monetary unification has given the franc a less pronounced financial profile, without making it lose its identity, thus increasing the SNB's room for manoeuvre. Globalization has intensified competition and moderated the pace of price increases. The low inflation rates we have been experiencing for many years are certainly lower than those we imagined to be "normal" in past decades. As our inflation is lower than in neighbouring countries and the Swiss franc has remained relatively stable, the price differentials between Switzerland and abroad have partly narrowed. The low level of inflation we are experiencing today is not the result of weak aggregate demand. We are in a period where inflation well below 2% is not a cause for concern. Some of the ideas that were ours in the late 1990s therefore need to be revised. But these changes do not require a change in our current concept of monetary policy. In particular, its focus on medium-term price developments remains key to our strategy. However, the new international environment and structural changes are now weighing risks and uncertainties differently. Once again, it has been demonstrated that monetary policy is as much an art as it is a science!
