Title: How successful has the SNB's monetary policy approach been in practice?
text: How has the SNB's monetary policy concept worked*? Thomas J. Jordan Alternate Member of the Board of Directors Swiss National Bank Vereinigung Berner Wirtschaftswissenschaftlerer, VBW 27 February 2007, Bern * The speaker would like to thank Dr. Caesar Lack and Dr. Marlene Amstad from the Financial Market Analysis Organizational Unit of the Swiss National Bank, Zurich, for their valuable support in the preparation of this lecture. The paper is based in part on a contribution by T. J. Jordan and M. Peytrignet, "Der Weg zur Zinssteuerung und zur Inflationsprognose", to the commemorative publication for the centenary of the SNB in 2007. 1. Introduction I am extremely pleased to be able to speak today before the Association of Bernese Economists, the alumni organisation of business students at the University of Bern. Your association fulfils a very important task, namely to maintain contact between alumni and the university and to bring practice-relevant views and experiences to the university. As I can see, 2007 is not only an anniversary year for the SNB. Their association celebrates its 30th anniversary this year. This age seems to me to be proof enough of the importance of this association. I hope that you will be able to celebrate many more anniversaries in the future. Over the past 35 years, economists at the University of Bern have repeatedly provided important impetus to Swiss monetary policy. First of all, I would like to mention Karl Brunner, who, together with Milton Friedman, is considered a co-founder of monetarism. At the beginning of the seventies, Brunner brought monetarist ideas from the USA to Europe, especially to Germany and Switzerland. The SNB was one of the first central banks to introduce the money supply control propagated by Brunner in 1975 after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system. Later, Jurg Niehans and Ernst Baltensperger, both also outstanding monetary theorists, played a decisive role in shaping the SNB's monetary policy as advisors. As you probably know, the SNB abandoned its money supply concept a few years ago. Since the beginning of 2000, the SNB has had a new monetary policy concept that focuses on an inflation forecast. In my presentation today, I would first like to explain this concept and then report on the experiences with it. A basic concern of Karl Brunner, namely the binding of monetary policy, is still a very topical topic in the monetary policy discussion today. In the following, I will therefore focus in particular on the balance between rules and discretion in the new concept. 2. The new monetary policy approach Until the end of 1999, the SNB pursued a money supply concept. The central bank money supply served as its monetary target. A prerequisite for the successful implementation of money supply control is a stable demand for money, or in other words, a stable relationship between the development of the money supply on the one hand. and economic and price developments, on the other hand. However, the central bank money supply fulfilled this requirement less and less in the second half of the nineties. This made monetary policy considerably more difficult. On the one hand, the information content of the money supply increasingly dwindled, and on the other hand, there was an increased need for explanation for the increasingly frequent and larger deviations from targets. An alternative would have been to use a broader money supply, such as M3, as a monetary target. However, such a broad monetary aggregate would have been much more difficult to control than the central bank money supply, which can be directly influenced by a central bank. The SNB therefore decided not to renew the money supply concept and to adopt a completely new approach. Intents Before I come to the description of the new monetary policy concept, I would first like to say a few words about the intentions of the SNB in 1999 with the introduction of the new concept. These were: continuity, clear rules, broad-based decision-making as well as improved transparency and communication. First, the new approach was intended to ensure a certain continuity in order to maintain the credibility that the SNB had acquired over many decades in the fight against inflation. An important element in maintaining credibility was that the primary objective of monetary policy  namely to maintain price stability  remained unchanged in the New Approach. Today, it is largely undisputed that the essential contribution of a central bank to long-term economic development lies in safeguarding price stability. The new concept thus only describes a new way to achieve the objective, while the objective of monetary policy itself remained unchanged. An important factor in creating and maintaining credibility in monetary policy is a rule binding. Second, the new approach should therefore continue to be based on clear rules in order to make monetary policy credible and predictable and to anchor inflation expectations in the long term. However, it should also provide some leeway to respond appropriately to shocks in the short term  but only if it does not jeopardise the overarching objective of price stability. In the short term, with a high level of credibility of monetary policy and strongly anchored inflation expectations, there is certainly the possibility of helping to cushion disruptions without jeopardising price stability in the longer term. Such a free space is of great importance, especially for a small open economy like Switzerland. Thirdly, they wanted to support monetary policy decisions more broadly. In the New Approach, all relevant information on future economic and price developments should be taken into account without dogmatically excluding certain indicators or forecasting models. Finally, the introduction of a new approach should also be accompanied by an increase in transparency and an improvement in communication. Thanks to transparency and good communication, markets better understand the central bank's intentions. This increases credibility and facilitates the implementation of monetary policy. In the nineties, the SNB experienced that monetary policy was very difficult to explain on the basis of monetary interim targets, which were also often missed. The public can follow monetary policy much more easily if the central bank communicates its decisions in the form of operational interest rate targets. One consequence of the quest for more transparency was therefore the introduction of an operating interest rate target. Elements of the new concept The new concept was developed in the course of 1999 and adopted in December of the same year. It is essentially based on the following elements: an explicit definition of price stability as the anchor of monetary policy, an inflation forecast as the main indicator of monetary policy, and a target range for the three-month libor as an operational objective for the implementation of monetary policy. Furthermore, communication is another important part of the concept. Explicit definition of price stability In order to give the public an indication of the medium- and long-term orientation of its monetary policy, the SNB decided to define quantitatively its objective of price stability. According to our definition, price stability is achieved when the national consumer price index (LIK) rises by less than 2% per year. As we have repeatedly explained, a persistently falling price level, i.e. deflation, is also incompatible with this definition. As a yardstick for defining price stability, the LIK was imposed because the public is well acquainted with it. Choosing a lesser-known mass of inflation, such as for example, a core increase would have made communication unnecessarily difficult. However, the LIK is not a perfect measure of actual inflation, as it is fraught with measurement errors. At the time, the SNB estimated that the LIK was overstating actual inflation by around 0.5%1%. Moreover, fluctuations in the LIK of /- 1% around the inflation trend are not unusual and do not require a monetary policy response. On the basis of these considerations, the SNB came to the conclusion that LIK inflation of up to 2% was compatible with effective price stability. The SNB decided against setting a lower limit for price stability. A definition of 0%2% might have been misunderstood by the audience as a point target of 1% with a tolerance of /- 1%. However, the SNB did not want to give the appearance of aiming for exactly 1% inflation, because any positive inflation rate below 2% is fundamentally compatible with price stability for it. We do not want to and cannot fine-tune inflation in this area. Inflation forecast as the main indicator As a replacement for the monetary target, the SNB needed a new guide for its monetary policy decisions. Because of the long delay between a monetary stimulus and its effect on the economy and prices, the use of an inflation forecast was obvious. In contrast to the so-called inflation targeting, a popular monetary policy concept pursued by the Bank of England, among others, the inflation forecast in the SNB's concept plays the role of a main indicator and not that of an intermediate target. The difference is that the SNB may be able to make decisions that are not or not exclusively based on the inflation forecast. In addition, our concept does not specify the period in which inflation should return to the desired range after a possible breach of price stability. With inflation targeting, on the other hand, the central bank must constantly align its monetary policy with the fact that its intermediate target  the inflation forecast  corresponds exactly to the inflation target for the specified horizon. The SNB prepares its inflation forecast on the basis of various econometric models and a number of indicators. The results of the models and the signals of the indicators are condensed into a consensus forecast in the sense of a synthesis. In recent years, the SNB has built up a great deal of know-how in modelling the Swiss economy and forecasting inflation. At Taking into account new findings and specific circumstances, it happens that the models and indicators as well as their weighting change over time. Models and indicators can therefore be described as "permanent work in progress". The intellectual openness in the preparation of the inflation forecast is intended to guarantee that all relevant information is incorporated into the decision-making process via the inflation forecast. The SNB's concept is characterised by monetary policy freedom within clear rules. The guiding principle of the concept is that the SNB reacts to inflation risks that emerge from the inflation forecast. If the inflation forecast indicates a permanent deviation from price stability under the assumption of a constant interest rate, a monetary policy adjustment must be expected sooner or later. The scope of the concept is that the SNB does not react mechanically to a deviation, as would be the case with strict inflation targeting. Rather, it depends on the economic environment how quickly the SNB adjusts interest rates to ensure the return of the inflation forecast to the realm of price stability. The SNB can also react to distortions whose effects on inflation are only expected beyond the horizon of the inflation forecast. The inflation forecast also plays an important role in communication and thus contributes significantly to the transparency of monetary policy. The forecast is published quarterly on the occasion of the monetary policy assessment. Target range for the three-month Libor as an operational target The third element of the new monetary policy concept is a target range for the three-month Libor as the operational objective of monetary policy (Libor: London Interbank Offered Rate). The target range comprises one percentage point, with the SNB usually aiming for the middle of the target range. The target range is reviewed on the occasion of the quarterly assessment of the situation and adjusted if necessary. However, the SNB reserves the right to make adjustments outside the official dates. The SNB's operational objective is unusual in three respects. First, the reference rate has a maturity of three months and not, as with most other central banks, of one day or a week. Secondly, the SNB sets a target range and not a point target. And third, the operating target refers to an interest rate set outside the home market. The setting of a target range for the three-month interest rate allows the SNB to temporarily vary the liquidity supply and thus react flexibly to disruptions on the financial markets without having to immediately adjust the operating target. However, a broad interest rate band is also necessary because, in contrast to the overnight rate, the three-month rate is influenced by interest rate expectations and thus cannot be fully controlled by the SNB. The Libor was chosen as the reference interest rate because the Swiss franc money market is considered very liquid and cannot be manipulated in London trading. Communication As part of the new concept, communication has also been strengthened. The SNB devotes great efforts to explaining its concept and current policies to the public. Communication platforms are the quarterly assessments of the situation, on which the SNB publishes detailed press releases with the current target range for the three-month libor and the associated new inflation forecast, the quarterly bulletin, as well as presentations and interviews with members of the Governing Board. 3. Experiences with the new concept since 2000 The new concept has proven itself well over the past seven years in an eventful environment. I would now like to briefly review monetary policy since 2000 and then compare it with a hypothetical monetary policy as it might have been conducted on the basis of a monetarist concept. Since the introduction of the new concept, inflation has always been in the realm of price stability. The SNB has achieved the objective of price stability under the new approach. It is therefore particularly important to assess how the SNB reacted to the various shocks and how it used its freedom. Since the introduction of the New Approach, monetary policy can be divided into three phases: a tightening of monetary policy until mid-2001, a monetary policy expansion by mid-2004 and a third phase of gradual normalisation, which we are still in today. Phase 1: Tightening The new concept was put to the test right from the start. At the beginning of 2000, it became apparent that the economic recovery in Switzerland would be much stronger than expected shortly before. Within a few months, the SNB sets its interest rate target in several steps from 1.75% to 3.5%. Inflation forecasts showed a significant upward trend during this period, in some cases exceeding the 2% mark. The rapid increase in the three-month libor turned out to be a wise decision, as the growth spurt of 2000 proved to be even stronger and broader than had been assumed at the time. The rapid response of monetary policy prevented the inflation rate from rising above the 2% mark in 2001. This early test also gave the SNB the opportunity to convince the markets shortly after the introduction of the new concept that it was willing to pursue an autonomous monetary policy vis-a-vis the ECB. Phase 2: Easing and low interest rate policy In the course of 2001, economic risks increased significantly. The rapid and sharp slowdown in the American economy and the worldwide decline in share prices threatened to slow down export development in Switzerland. This and the decline in the price of oil prompted the SNB to revise its inflation forecast downwards. As early as March 2001, the SNB therefore decided to lower the target range for Libor for the first time. Following the terrorist attacks of 11 September, the SNB lowered the target range by a total of 150 basis points in three steps by the end of 2001. In doing so, it wanted to counter the changed economic outlook and the appreciation of the Swiss franc. In the following year 2002, the SNB lowered its interest rate target two more times by 50 basis points each to 0.75%. This interest rate was clearly too low in the long term. This was reflected in inflation forecasts, which rose above the 2.0% mark towards the end of the forecast horizon. In this situation, strict inflation targeting would have required that the SNB should not have lowered its interest rate target further, but should have raised it again as soon as possible. At the beginning of 2003, however, the economic outlook deteriorated again. In addition, fears of deflation arose worldwide. There was also a latent risk of an appreciation of the Swiss franc. Against this background, the SNB decided at an extraordinary assessment of the situation on 6 March 2003 to reduce the target interest rate by another half a percentage point to 0.25%. Markets were surprised by the scale and timing of this decision. In retrospect, this measure proved to be tactically optimal: the SNB's signal was so strong that the Swiss franc weakened continuously over the following months. During this critical phase, the SNB succeeded in making its monetary policy much more expansionary, even though the interest rate was practically at zero. At the time, the SNB estimated that it would have sufficient time to correct its expansionary stance and ensure price stability in the medium term. Phase 3: Gradual normalization When the first signs of an improvement in the economy became apparent in 2004, the SNB began a gradual increase in the Libor target range, initially in two steps of 25 basis points each. However, after the upswing slowed down again in the course of 2004 and the Swiss franc regained some strength, the SNB interrupted the monetary policy normalisation process for a year at the level of 0.75%. As the economy regained strength in 2005, the SNB continued to normalise monetary policy. The favourable inflation outlook allowed for a gradual adjustment with steps of 25 basis points each. We are still in this phase of normalization today. Even the most recent inflation forecast from December 2006 still shows a tendency for projected inflation to rise during the forecast horizon. The neutral interest rate level has therefore not yet been reached. Comparison with a strictly monetarist monetary policy What would a monetarist monetary policy have looked like in this period? To estimate this, I rely on the growth rate of M3. I choose M3 because the central bank money supply after 1999 would hardly have been considered as a monetary target due to its unstable demand; a possible continuation of the monetary policy would therefore probably have been based on M3 as an interim target. A strictly monetarist monetary policy, which would have been based exclusively on the development of the money supply, would probably have been significantly different from the policy effectively pursued by the SNB under the new concept. The divergence begins as early as 2000, when the money supply was declining. At that time, the development of the money supply was not in line with the economy in full swing and gave no indication that monetary policy should be made more restrictive. On the contrary, it might have allowed for an even more expansionary monetary policy. A strictly monetarist monetary policy would therefore probably have been wrong at this stage. She would have been very likely to lead to an overheating of the economy and a breach of price stability in 2001. The marked interest rate cuts to just 0.25% led to a sharp increase in monetary aggregates: M3 growth reached almost 10% in 2003, M2 grew by 20% at times and M1 by over 25%. Such growth rates would not have been acceptable in a monetarist concept and would have resulted in an immediate tightening of monetary policy. In particular, the last expansion step in March 2003 would have been impossible under a strict monetarist concept. In retrospect, however, it can be stated that the aggressive expansion of monetary policy and in particular the last interest rate cut to almost 0% were justified by the existing risks. A more restrictive monetary policy in 2002 and 2003 might have led to a slide into deflation in the critical year of 2003. Almost certainly, however, a more restrictive monetary policy would have slowed down the economic recovery. With the beginning of interest rate normalization in 2004, a decline in money supply growth rates was observed. Currently, these are very moderate; M3 grew by only 2.5% in 2006; M1 and M2 even declined slightly. A purely monetarist monetary policy would probably have seen no reason for further normalization of interest rates from mid-2006 onwards. However, it is obvious that the economy is currently extremely strong and that the current normalisation of interest rates is necessary to ensure price stability over the long term. A monetarist view would thus lead to wrong conclusions even in the current situation. Overall, it can be said that a monetarist concept based solely on the money supply would probably have been wrong several times in the past seven years. However, this statement must not be interpreted as meaning that the SNB should ignore the money supply; the development of the money supply is also an important source of information in the New Concept. However, the one-sided focus on the money supply has been replaced by the consideration of a broad set of models and indicators. I therefore dare to say that the SNB's new monetary policy concept is clearly superior to a strictly monetarist monetary policy. Rules vs. Discretion I would now like to return to the new approach and make some reflections on the balance between rules-based and discretionary monetary policy in the new concept. The rule-bound nature of monetary policy was a fundamental concern of the monetarists and still gives much cause for discussion today. A first reason why monetarists advocated a strictly rule-based monetary policy is that there is always a risk of abuse in the case of non-rule-bound, i.e. discretionary monetary policy. I would argue that this risk is limited today. It is true that the SNB has made generous use of its freedom due to the long period of low interest rates and the gradual normalisation. However, this did not jeopardise the objective of price stability. The current very low inflation rate and the favourable inflation outlook prove this without a doubt. Karl Brunner's warning against abuse and his advocacy of strict rules were quite justified in the seventies. At that time, central banks were often the extended arm of the Ministry of Finance. Today, however, most central banks are institutionally independent of their governments and thus immune to the demands of politics. Independence replaces part of the strict rule binding demanded by the monetarists and opens up a certain freedom for discretion. The greater the independence of a central bank from politics and thus its credibility, the greater its freedom for short-term stabilization policy. However, there is a second reason that still speaks against an overly discretionary monetary policy even with independent central banks, namely uncertainty. Monetary policy is constantly facing a great deal of uncertainty, which particularly affects the current state of the economy and the transmission mechanism. Great efforts have been made over the past thirty years to reduce this uncertainty. Today, we have significantly more indicators describing the state of an economy. We also have a better knowledge of the transmission mechanism and better techniques for modelling economies. Despite this progress, uncertainty in monetary policy is still very high as economies have become more complex and open. Dealing with this uncertainty is now seen as one of the biggest challenges for monetary policy. The uncertainty about the The current economic situation and the transmission mechanism of monetary policy make it impossible, even prohibits the attempt at an ambitious fine-tuning of the economy. The SNB's monetary policy can and will therefore never be geared under the new concept to iron out every small economic downturn. Rather, monetary policy is about responding to larger and persistent deviations from equilibrium. 4. Conclusion and outlook Let me now draw a conclusion. Over the past seven years, the new approach has allowed the SNB to react decisively to a series of positive and negative shocks and to exploit the room for manoeuvre in monetary policy. In particular, in a delicate situation for the Swiss economy, the SNB succeeded in halting the appreciation trend of the Swiss franc and paving the way for today's upswing without jeopardising price stability in the long term. The new concept has therefore undoubtedly proved its worth. The question now arises as to whether the new approach is necessarily a guarantee of continued successful monetary policy. Of course, the new concept is not such a guarantee. No concept can rule out monetary policy mistakes. However, the new concept provides a suitable framework for monetary policy that is significantly more flexible and broadly based than that of the previous money supply concept. With it, the SNB is well prepared for all possible developments. Monetary policy, however, remains a very demanding task. The SNB must therefore not rest on its laurels acquired in recent years, but must continue to conduct its monetary policy with the utmost care and vigilance. On the one hand, this requires highly qualified economists who use scientific methods to provide model-based foundations for monetary policy decisions. On the other hand, decision-makers are also needed who supplement the model-based results with their "judgment" and wealth of experience in order to draw the right conclusions. Incidentally, it was this combination of model-based analysis and "judgment" that Jurg Niehans meant when he said that monetary policy was ultimately also an art. Finally, I would like to make a few observations on the current monetary policy situation. In my remarks on the concept, I pointed out that the SNB's monetary policy is primarily based on medium- and long-term inflation developments. aligned. Occasionally expressed assumptions that the SNB has no further need for action due to the currently low inflation rate are therefore not appropriate. At the moment, despite a current annual rate of practically 0%, the SNB sees no reason to move away from its policy of gradual normalisation. There are several reasons for this. On the one hand, the very low inflation is above all an expression of the decline in the price of oil. The core inflation rates calculated by the SNB are currently around 1%. On the other hand, inflationary pressures are still increasing over the relevant horizon of three years, assuming unchanged monetary policy. The reason for this is the continued strong economic growth in Switzerland. Although potential growth is very likely to have increased somewhat in recent years due to various liberalisation steps, current economic growth is likely to be above potential growth and thus exert upward pressure on inflation in the medium term. Furthermore, the Swiss franc, which is prone to weakness, also has an inflationary effect over time. The slowdown is making our imports more expensive and has an expansionary effect on the export economy. Other indicators that reinforce our view are the economic recovery in Germany, the main consumer of our exports, as well as robust domestic credit growth. A reasonable normalization of the interest rate level in Switzerland over the near future prevents interest rates from having to be raised much more sharply later. With these statements, it should be noted that they are always made from today's point of view. It is in the nature of monetary policy that shocks often occur that require an adjustment of previous assessments. I hope that my remarks will convince you of the advantages of the SNB's monetary policy concept. I also hope to have found the right balance between the length of my talk and the opportunity cost of your time. Thank you for your attention!

Das neue Konzept gibt aber einen geeigneten Rahmen fr die Geldpolitik vor, der bedeutend flexibler und breiter abgesttzt ist als derjenige des frheren Geldmengenkonzeptes. Mit ihm ist die SNB gut fr alle mglichen Entwicklungen gerstet. Geldpolitik bleibt aber eine sehr anspruchsvolle Aufgabe. Die SNB darf sich daher nicht auf den in den vergangenen Jahren erworbenen Lorbeeren ausruhen, sondern muss ihre Geldpolitik weiterhin mit hchster Sorgfalt und Wachsamkeit fhren. Dazu braucht die SNB einerseits hochqualifizierte konomen, welche nach wissenschaftlichen Methoden modellbasierte Grundlagen fr die geldpolitischen Entscheide bereitstellen. Andererseits braucht es auch die Entscheidungstrger, welche die modellbasierten Resultate mit ihrem "judgment" und Erfahrungsschatz ergnzen, um daraus die richtigen Schlsse zu ziehen. Diese Kombination von modellbasierter Analyse und "judgment" war es brigens, welche Jrg Niehans meinte, als er von der Geldpolitik sagte, sie sei letztlich auch eine Kunst. Zum Schluss mchte ich noch einige berlegungen zur aktuellen geldpolitischen Lage anstellen. In meinen Ausfhrungen zum Konzept habe ich darauf hingewiesen, dass die SNB ihre Geldpolitik in erster Linie an der mittel- und langfristigen Inflationsentwicklung ausrichtet. Hin und wieder geusserte Mutmassungen, dass die SNB wegen der momentan tiefen Inflationsrate keinen weiteren Handlungsbedarf mehr hat, sind daher nicht angebracht. Die SNB sieht im Moment, trotz einer aktuellen Jahresteuerung von praktisch 0%, keinen Anlass, von ihrer Politik der graduellen Normalisierung abzurcken. Dafr gibt es mehrere Grnde. Zum einen ist die sehr tiefe Inflation vor allem Ausdruck des Rckgangs des lpreises. Die von der SNB berechneten Kernteuerungsraten liegen im Moment bei rund 1%. Zum anderen nimmt der Inflationsdruck beim relevanten Horizont von drei Jahren unter der Annahme einer unvernderten Geldpolitik immer noch zu. Grund dafr ist das anhaltend starke Wirtschaftswachstum in der Schweiz. Obwohl sich das Potentialwachstum aufgrund verschiedener Liberalisierungsschritte in den vergangenen Jahren sehr wahrscheinlich etwas erhht hat, drfte das aktuelle Wirtschaftswachstum ber dem Potentialwachstum liegen und somit mittelfristig Aufwrtsdruck auf die Inflation ausben. Ferner wirkt auch der zur Schwche neigende Franken ber die Zeit inflationr. Die Abschwchung verteuert unsere Importe und wirkt in der Exportwirtschaft expansiv. Weitere Indikatoren, die uns in unserer Ansicht bestrken, sind die Wirtschaftsbelebung in Deutschland, dem Hauptabnehmer unserer Exporte, sowie das robuste Kreditwachstum im Inland. Eine vernnftige Normalisierung des Zinsniveaus in der Schweiz ber die nchste Zeit verhindert, dass spter allenfalls die Zinsen viel strker angehoben werden mssten. Bei diesen Aussagen ist zu beachten, dass sie immer aus heutiger Sicht gemacht werden. Es liegt in der Natur der Geldpolitik, dass hufig Schocks auftreten, die eine Anpassung der bisherigen Einschtzungen verlangen. Ich hoffe, dass ich Sie mit meinen Ausfhrungen von den Vorteilen des geldpolitischen Konzepts der SNB berzeugen konnte. Zudem hoffe ich auch, die richtige Balance zwischen der Lnge meines Vortrages und den Opportunittskosten Ihrer Zeit gefunden zu haben. Vielen Dank fr Ihre Aufmerksamkeit!

Title: Current challenges for the Swiss National Bank in the area of monetary policy
text: Current monetary policy challenges for the Swiss National Bank* Thomas J. Jordan Alternate Member of the Board of Directors Swiss National Bank Summary Of the Money Market Aperitif Unit 22 March 2007 * The speaker would like to thank Rita Kobel Rohr and Dr. Marlene Amstad from the Financial Market Analysis Unit of the Swiss National Bank, Zurich, for their support in the preparation of this lecture. 1. Economic situation and inflation outlook On 15 March 2007, the Swiss National Bank raised the target range for the three-month Libor by 0.25 percentage points to 1.75%-2.75%. This decision was made against the background of an economic development in Germany and abroad, which is still to be assessed favourably, as well as a slight increase in inflation forecast over time. The SNB continues to expect a "soft landing" for the American economy. Despite a slowdown in the housing market, growth in the US is likely to rise against potential again over the course of this year. In Europe, the economy will continue to develop positively. After a hitherto strongly export-driven upswing, the signs of increasingly self-sustaining economic growth are increasing. Economic development in Asia is particularly dynamic. Overall, global economic growth in 2007 is likely to be only slightly lower than in the previous year. Recent events on the financial markets illustrate that the assessment of future international economic developments is always fraught with uncertainty. For example, there is a risk of abrupt changes in exchange rates and a renewed rise in oil prices. The global economic outlook would also be adversely affected by increasing protectionism. Finally, the risk of a "hard landing" in the USA in the event of a significantly negative development in the housing and mortgage market should be mentioned. The Swiss economy is currently in strong shape. Thanks to its competitiveness and industry mix, it was able to participate fully in the global economic upswing in 2006. The SNB expects balanced and broad-based growth in the current year as well. However, at around 2%, the growth in gross domestic product in 2007 is likely to be slightly lower than in the previous year. However, the Swiss economy is still growing beyond its potential. The high pace of expansion of the Swiss economy in recent quarters has had an impact on the utilization of technical and personnel capacities. At the end of 2006, technical capacity utilization in industry was well above its long-term average. At the same time, employment increased sharply. Despite the high growth momentum and strong capacity utilization, inflation as measured by the National Consumer Price Index (LIK) is low. In the current year, base effects in energy prices are dampening the increase in the LIK. But also under Excluding energy prices, the SNB expects low inflation in the short term. However, the SNB must act with foresight in order to be able to guarantee price stability in the medium term. Monetary policy measures only work with a delay. The SNB therefore uses a medium- to long-term inflation forecast as the main indicator for monetary policy. If the economic trend goes as expected and interest rates are left at today's level, the SNB expects inflation to rise to 1.75% by the end of 2009. This current forecast already takes into account the interest rate decision of 15 March. 2. Current monetary policy challenges Structural changes are currently making it difficult to determine key equilibrium values in the Swiss economy. Uncertainty about these equilibriums poses a monetary policy challenge for the SNB. Knowledge of these equilibriums is very important for assessing the neutral interest rate, i.e. the level of interest rates at which monetary policy neither stimulates nor slows down economic activity and keeps inflation in check. Three aspects are specifically addressed here: The opening of the labour market makes it difficult to determine the degree of utilisation at which wage pressure arises in Switzerland. Reforms and the opening up of the Swiss economy make it difficult to assess the level of potential growth. It is therefore tricky to estimate when the output gap becomes positive and overheating is imminent. However, structural changes can also lead to the real exchange rate of the Swiss franc following a new trend. This makes it difficult to assess the risk of inflation as a result of the weakening of the Swiss franc against the euro. 2.1. Determining the equilibrium of the labour market Fortunately, the favourable economic development has not left its mark on the labour market. The labour market situation is better than it has been for years. Employment increased from 2005; in 2006 it increased very strongly. What is striking is the strong growth in the number of people in employment who have immigrated from abroad in parallel with the accelerated economic growth since the end of 2005. However, the immigration of foreign workers was already relatively high in 2003 and 2004, when Swiss economic growth was still moderate. In comparable phases, a declining immigration of foreign workers was observed in the past. Overall, the labour supply seems to have become more elastic. This is likely to be largely due to the opening of the Swiss labour market in June 2002 in the context of the free movement of persons with the EU-15. To date, despite the continuing pleasing economic situation, no generally increased wage pressure has been observed. The opening up of the Swiss labour market is likely to be a structural change that will lead to a new equilibrium. Wage pressures could occur in the future with higher employment and economic growth than in the past. However, the opening up of the labour market will hardly lead to no bottlenecks at all and wage pressure would no longer be an issue in Switzerland at all. It will be crucial to find out where the critical threshold lies in the new environment  when, in other words, wage pressure arises. As the guardian of price stability, the SNB must therefore closely monitor whether the labour supply reacts flexibly to an additional demand for labour. If this is not the case, there is a risk of excessive wage developments. Especially in fast-growing sectors and with the demand for highly qualified workers, tensions could soon arise. It should be noted that a wage increase is unproblematic as long as it is based on an increase in productivity. 2.2. Determination of potential growth Determining potential growth is very important for monetary policy. In order to be able to assess whether there are overheating risks in an economy, the economic growth actually achieved is related to the maximum possible growth in this economy, to the potential growth. With the help of potential growth, the output gap is also estimated. Potential growth is determined by labour supply, productivity and capital investment. The opening up of the Swiss labour market increases the supply of labour. This may contribute to an increase in the potential growth of the Swiss economy not only directly through the increased number of available employees, but also indirectly through an increased qualification of the employees. The attractive conditions in Switzerland lead to an immigration of well-qualified people from the EU area. This should also have an impact on productivity. Productivity is also boosted by the increased investments of local companies in new and efficient technologies. Finally, the strong utilization of technical capacities suggests a strong increase in investment activity and thus in the use of capital in the near future. Structural changes also mean that national resource restrictions have tended to lose importance as a limiting factor for domestic production due to the increased mobility of the factors. Thus, the national output gap has lost importance compared to the global output gap. In the current age of globalization, characterized by an intensive international division of labor and the exchange of goods within companies but also between third-party companies, a strong capacity utilization in Germany does not automatically or later lead to higher inflation than had previously been the case. All three determinants of production potential are therefore changing. For the SNB, it is important to correctly estimate potential growth and its significance for inflation dynamics in this changing environment. 2.3. Determining the trend for the real exchange rate For a long time, the Swiss franc followed an appreciation trend against the main currencies. In recent years, however, it has lost value against the euro. This depreciation occurred despite strong economic growth in Switzerland, an increased current account surplus and a more favourable inflation trend compared to the euro zone. Against the US dollar and the yen, however, the Swiss franc continued to appreciate. However, due to the great importance of the euro countries as Switzerland's trading partner, the export-weighted real exchange rate of the Swiss franc is depreciating overall. For monetary policy, it is important to assess whether structural changes in the economy may have broken the long-term appreciation trend of the Swiss franc, especially against the euro. Many of the determinants of a currency's appreciation or depreciation trend are long-term in nature. Accordingly, recognizing a change in the trend in the exchange rate is complex and fraught with great uncertainty. In the event that a change in fundamental factors is not responsible for the depreciation of the Swiss franc against the euro, the recent development of the swiss franc carries some risks. Thus, the inflation outlook is influenced by the exchange rate directly through the prices of imported goods and indirectly through the stimulation of the economy. So far, however, hardly any significant effect on inflation can be observed. However, this does not guarantee that the weakening of the Swiss franc will not have an impact on inflation later. In addition to the risk of exchange rate-induced inflation potential, a weak Swiss franc could also cause the following problems: Firstly, abrupt and strong appreciation of the Swiss franc cannot be ruled out in line with fundamentals. Second, there could be misallocation of resources. For example, if restructuring is not carried out and/or investments are made in production facilities that would no longer be profitable with a stronger franc in reliance on a supposedly persistently low Swiss franc exchange rate. 3. Conclusion The Swiss economy is expected to continue to grow faster than its potential in 2007. Inflation forecast by the SNB will continue to rise in a trend-like manner over time assuming unchanged monetary policy. This indicates that the current interest rate level in Switzerland is not yet neutral. From today's perspective, the normalisation of the SNB's monetary policy has not yet been completed. However, the flattening of the new inflation forecast compared to previous forecasts suggests that the need for monetary policy action has diminished. The assessment of this need for action is currently fraught with greater uncertainties. In addition to the uncertainties about the international economy, there are uncertainties as a result of structural changes in the Swiss economy. The level of the neutral interest rate is variable over time and can hardly ever be determined exactly. In an environment with structural changes, however, the assessment of the neutral interest rate is particularly difficult. The high level of uncertainty about the inflation outlook and the structural changes in the Swiss economy call for increased vigilance and flexibility on the part of the SNB. The aim is neither to stifle growth opportunities nor to take inflation risks. This situation suggests a gradual approach to monetary policy. The favourable economic situation and low inflation in Switzerland allow the SNB to approach the neutral interest rate. Thomas J. Jordan Stellvertretendes Mitglied des Direktoriums Schweizerische Nationalbank Kurzfassung Referat Geldmarkt-Apro 22. Mrz 2007 * Der Referent dankt Rita Kobel Rohr und Dr. Marlene Amstad von der Organisationseinheit Finanzmarktanalyse der Schweizerischen Nationalbank, Zrich, fr ihre Untersttzung bei der Vorbereitung dieses Vortrages. 1. Konjunkturlage und Inflationsaussichten Die Schweizerische Nationalbank hat am 15. Mrz 2007 das Zielband fr den DreimonatsLibor um 0,25 Prozentpunkte auf 1,75%-2,75% angehoben. Dieser Entscheid erfolgte vor dem Hintergrund einer nach wie vor gnstig einzuschtzenden Konjunkturentwicklung im In- und Ausland sowie einer ber die Zeit leicht ansteigenden Inflationsprognose. Fr die amerikanische Wirtschaft erwartet die Nationalbank weiterhin ein "soft landing". Trotz einer Abschwchung im Husermarkt drfte das Wachstum in den USA im Verlauf dieses Jahres wieder gegen das Potenzial ansteigen. In Europa wird sich die Konjunktur weiter positiv entwickeln. Nach einem bis anhin stark exportgetriebenen Aufschwung mehren sich die Anzeichen eines sich zunehmend selbst tragenden Wirtschaftswachstums. Besonders dynamisch verluft die Wirtschaftsentwicklung in Asien. Insgesamt drfte 2007 das Wachstum der Weltwirtschaft nur leicht tiefer als im Vorjahr ausfallen. Die jngsten Ereignisse an den Finanzmrkten veranschaulichen, dass die Einschtzung ber die zuknftige internationale Konjunkturentwicklung immer mit Unsicherheiten behaftet ist. So besteht etwa das Risiko von abrupten Vernderungen bei den Wechselkursen sowie eines erneuten Anstiegs der Erdlpreise. Beeintrchtigt wrden die weltwirtschaftlichen Perspektiven auch durch einen zunehmenden Protektionismus. Schliesslich ist das Risiko eines "hard landing" in den USA im Falle einer deutlich negativen Entwicklung im Huser- und Hypothekarmarkt zu nennen. Die Schweizer Wirtschaft ist zurzeit in einer starken Verfassung. Dank ihrer Wettbewerbsfhigkeit und ihres Branchenmix konnte sie am Weltwirtschaftsaufschwung 2006 voll partizipieren. Die Nationalbank rechnet auch im laufenden Jahr mit einem ausgewogenen und breit abgesttzten Wachstum. Allerdings drfte der Zuwachs des Bruttoinlandprodukts 2007 mit rund 2% etwas tiefer ausfallen als im Vorjahr. Die Schweizer Wirtschaft wchst aber immer noch ber ihrem Potenzial. Das hohe Expansionstempo der Schweizer Wirtschaft in den vergangenen Quartalen hat sich auf die Auslastung der technischen und personellen Kapazitten ausgewirkt. So lag die technische Auslastung in der Industrie Ende 2006 deutlich ber ihrem langjhrigen Durchschnittswert. Gleichzeitig nahm die Beschftigung stark zu. Trotz der hohen Wachstumsdynamik und starken Auslastung der Kapazitten ist die am Landesindex der Konsumentenpreise (LIK) gemessene Teuerung niedrig. Im laufenden Jahr dmpfen Basiseffekte bei den Energiepreisen den Anstieg des LIK. Aber auch unter Ausklammerung der Energiepreise erwartet die Nationalbank in der kurzen Frist eine tiefe Teuerung. Die Nationalbank muss jedoch vorausschauend handeln, um die Preisstabilitt auch mittelfristig gewhrleisten zu knnen. Geldpolitische Massnahmen wirken nmlich nur mit einer Verzgerung. Als Hauptindikator fr die Geldpolitik verwendet die Nationalbank daher eine mittel- bis langfristige Inflationsprognose. Verluft die Konjunkturentwicklung wie erwartet und wrden die Zinsen auf dem heutigen Niveau belassen, rechnet die Nationalbank mit einem Anstieg der Inflation auf 1,75% fr Ende 2009. Bei dieser aktuellen Prognose ist der Zinsentscheid vom 15. Mrz bereits bercksichtigt. 2. Aktuelle geldpolitische Herausforderungen Strukturelle nderungen erschweren im Moment die Bestimmung von zentralen Gleichgewichtswerten in der schweizerischen Wirtschaft. Die Unsicherheit ber diese Gleichgewichte stellt eine geldpolitische Herausforderung fr die Nationalbank dar. Kenntnisse ber diese Gleichgewichte sind fr die Einschtzung des neutralen Zinssatzes, d.h. das Zinsniveau, bei dem die Geldpolitik die Wirtschaftsaktivitt weder stimuliert noch bremst und die Inflation im Zaun hlt, sehr wichtig. Auf drei Aspekte wird hier speziell eingegangen: Die ffnung des Arbeitsmarkts macht es schwierig zu bestimmen, ab welchem Auslastungsgrad Lohndruck in der Schweiz entsteht. Reformen und ffnung der schweizerischen Wirtschaft erschweren die Einschtzung der Hhe des Potenzialwachstums. Es ist daher heikel abzuschtzen, ab wann die Outputlcke positiv wird und sich eine berhitzung anbahnt. Strukturelle Vernderungen knnen aber auch dazu fhren, dass der reale Wechselkurs des Frankens einem neuen Trend folgt. Dies erschwert die Einschtzung der Inflationsgefahr als Folge der Abschwchung des Frankens gegenber dem Euro. 2.1. Bestimmung des Gleichgewichts am Arbeitsmarkt Die gnstige Konjunkturentwicklung ist erfreulicherweise nicht spurlos am Arbeitsmarkt vorbei gegangen. Die Arbeitsmarktlage ist so gut wie seit Jahren nicht mehr. Die Beschftigung stieg ab 2005 an; im Jahr 2006 nahm sie sehr stark zu. Auffllig dabei ist der krftige Zuwachs der aus dem Ausland zugewanderten Erwerbsttigen parallel zum beschleunigten Wirtschaftswachstum seit Ende 2005. Die Zuwanderung von auslndischen Erwerbsttigen war aber bereits 2003 und 2004 relativ hoch, als das Schweizer Wirtschaftswachstum noch moderat war. In vergleichbaren Phasen war frher jeweils eine sinkende Zuwanderung von auslndischen Erwerbsttigen zu beobachten. Insgesamt scheint das Arbeitsangebot elastischer geworden zu sein. Dies drfte zu einem grossen Teil auf die ffnung des Schweizer Arbeitsmarkts im Juni 2002 im Rahmen der Personenfreizgigkeit mit der EU-15 zurckzufhren sein. Bis heute war denn auch trotz anhaltend erfreulicher Konjunkturlage kein allgemein erhhter Lohndruck zu beobachten. Bei der ffnung des schweizerischen Arbeitsmarkts drfte es sich um eine strukturelle Vernderung handeln, die zu einem neuen Gleichgewicht fhrt. Lohndruck knnte in Zukunft bei einem hheren Beschftigungs- und Wirtschaftswachstum auftreten als in der Vergangenheit. Die ffnung des Arbeitsmarkts wird aber kaum dazu fhren, dass gar keine Engpsse mehr entstehen knnen und Lohndruck in der Schweiz berhaupt kein Thema mehr wre. Entscheidend wird sein herauszufinden, wo die kritische Schwelle im neuen Umfeld liegt  ab wann, mit anderen Worten, Lohndruck entsteht. Als Hterin der Preisstabilitt muss die Nationalbank daher genau beobachten, ob das Arbeitsangebot ausreichend flexibel auf eine zustzliche Nachfrage nach Arbeitskrften reagiert. Ist dies nicht der Fall, besteht die Gefahr einer bermssigen Lohnentwicklung. Gerade in stark wachsenden Sektoren und bei der Nachfrage nach hoch qualifizierten Arbeitskrften knnten Anspannungen schon bald auftreten. Dabei ist zu beachten, dass ein Lohnanstieg solange unproblematisch ist, als er auf einem Produktivittszuwachs begrndet ist. 2.2. Bestimmung des Potenzialwachstums Die Bestimmung des Potenzialwachstums ist fr die Geldpolitik sehr wichtig. Um einschtzen zu knnen, ob in einer Volkswirtschaft berhitzungsrisiken bestehen, wird das tatschlich erzielte Wirtschaftswachstum in Beziehung gesetzt mit dem maximal mglichen Wachstum in dieser Volkswirtschaft, mit dem Potenzialwachstum. Mit Hilfe des Potenzialwachstums wird auch die Produktionslcke geschtzt. Das Potenzialwachstum wird durch das Arbeitsangebot, die Produktivitt sowie den Kapitaleinsatz bestimmt. Die ffnung des Schweizer Arbeitsmarkts erhht das Arbeitsangebot. Dies trgt mglicherweise nicht nur direkt ber die erhhte Anzahl verfgbarer Arbeitnehmer, sondern auch indirekt ber eine erhhte Qualifikation der Arbeitnehmer zu einem Anstieg des Potenzialwachstums der Schweizer Wirtschaft bei. Die attraktiven Verhltnisse in der Schweiz fhren zu einer Zuwanderung von gut qualifizierten Personen aus dem EU-Raum. Dies sollte sich auch auf die Produktivitt auswirken. Produktivittssteigernd wirken zudem die vermehrten Investitionen der hiesigen Unternehmen in neue und effiziente Technologien. Schliesslich lsst die starke Auslastung der technischen Kapazitten einen krftigen Anstieg der Investitionsttigkeit und somit des Kapitaleinsatzes in nchster Zukunft erwarten. Strukturelle nderungen fhren auch dazu, dass nationale Ressourcenrestriktionen wegen der erhhten Mobilitt der Faktoren als limitierende Grsse fr die inlndische Produktion tendenziell an Bedeutung verloren haben. So hat die nationale Produktionslcke gegenber der globalen Produktionslcke an Bedeutung verloren. Im gegenwrtigen Zeitalter der Globalisierung, geprgt durch eine intensive internationale Arbeitsteilung und den Gteraustausch innerhalb von Unternehmen aber auch zwischen Drittunternehmen, fhrt eine starke Kapazittsauslastung im Inland nicht automatisch oder spter zu einer hheren Teuerung, als dies frher der Fall gewesen war. Alle drei Bestimmungsfaktoren des Produktionspotenzials sind somit im Wandel. Fr die Nationalbank gilt es, das Potenzialwachstum und dessen Bedeutung fr die Inflationsdynamik in diesem sich verndernden Umfeld richtig zu schtzen. 2.3. Bestimmung des Trends fr den realen Wechselkurs Der Franken folgte lange Zeit einem Aufwertungstrend gegenber den Hauptwhrungen. In den letzten Jahren verliert er jedoch gegenber dem Euro an Wert. Dieser Wertverlust erfolgte trotz eines krftigen Wirtschaftswachstums in der Schweiz, eines gestiegenen Ertragsbilanzberschusses sowie einer im Vergleich zur Euro-Zone gnstigeren Inflationsentwicklung. Gegenber dem US-Dollar und dem Yen wertete sich der Franken jedoch weiterhin tendenziell auf. Aufgrund der grossen Bedeutung der Euro-Lnder als Handelspartner der Schweiz wertet sich der exportgewichtete reale Wechselkurs des Frankens aber insgesamt ab. Fr die Geldpolitik gilt es abzuschtzen, ob mglicherweise strukturelle Vernderungen in der Wirtschaft den langfristigen Aufwertungstrend des Frankens insbesondere gegenber dem Euro gebrochen haben. Viele der Bestimmungsfaktoren eines Aufwertungs- bzw. Abwertungstrends einer Whrung sind langfristiger Natur. Dementsprechend ist das Erkennen einer Trendnderung beim Wechselkurs komplex und mit grosser Unsicherheit behaftet. Fr den Fall, dass nicht eine Vernderung fundamentaler Faktoren fr den Wertverlust des Frankens gegenber dem Euro verantwortlich sein sollte, birgt die jngere Entwicklung des Frankens einige Risiken. So werden die Inflationsaussichten durch den Wechselkurs direkt ber die Preise importierter Gter und indirekt ber die Stimulierung der Konjunktur beeinflusst. Bislang ist aber kaum eine nennenswerte Auswirkung auf die Teuerung feststellbar. Dies stellt aber noch keine Garantie dar, dass die Abschwchung des Frankens sich nicht spter auf die Inflation auswirkt. Nebst der Gefahr eines Wechselkurs-induzierten Inflationspotenzials knnte ein schwacher Franken auch noch folgende Probleme verursachen: Sollte die Wechselkurs- Entwicklung nicht den Fundamentaldaten entsprechen, sind erstens abrupte und krftige Aufwertungen des Frankens nicht auszuschliessen. Zweitens knnte es zu Fehlallokationen von Ressourcen kommen. So etwa, wenn im Vertrauen auf einen vermeintlich anhaltend tiefen Frankenkurs Restrukturierungen nicht durchgefhrt und/oder Investitionen in Produktionsanlagen gettigt werden, die bei einem strkeren Franken nicht mehr rentabel wren. 3. Fazit Die Schweizer Wirtschaft drfte auch 2007 strker wachsen als ihr Potenzial. Die von der Nationalbank prognostizierte Inflation steigt unter der Annahme einer unvernderten Geldpolitik ber die Zeit weiterhin trendartig an. Dies deutet darauf hin, dass das gegenwrtige Zinsniveau in der Schweiz noch nicht neutral ist. Aus heutiger Sicht ist die Normalisierung der Geldpolitik der Nationalbank noch nicht abgeschlossen. Die Abflachung der neuen Inflationsprognose im Vergleich zu frheren Prognosen lsst aber vermuten, dass der geldpolitische Handlungsbedarf kleiner geworden ist. Die Einschtzung dieses Handlungsbedarfs ist zurzeit mit grsseren Unsicherheiten behaftet. Neben den Unsicherheiten ber die internationale Konjunktur gibt es Unsicherheiten als Folge von strukturellen nderungen in der schweizerischen Wirtschaft. Das Niveau des neutralen Zinses ist ber die Zeit variabel und kann kaum je exakt bestimmt werden. In einem Umfeld mit strukturellen nderungen ist aber die Einschtzung des neutralen Zinses besonders schwierig. Die hohe Unsicherheiten ber die Inflationsaussichten und die strukturellen nderungen in der Schweizer Wirtschaft verlangen eine erhhte Wachsamkeit und Flexibilitt der Nationalbank. Dabei geht es darum, weder Wachstumschancen abzuwrgen noch Inflationsrisiken einzugehen. Diese Situation spricht fr ein graduelles Vorgehen in der Geldpolitik. Die gnstige Konjunkturlage und die niedrige Teuerung in der Schweiz erlauben es der Nationalbank, sich an den neutralen Zins heranzutasten. Thomas J. Jordan 22.
