Title: Some thoughts on the Swiss franc exchange rate
text: Embargo period: April 24, 2007, 18:15 Considerations on the Swiss franc exchange rate1 Philipp M. Hildebrand Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Center for Comparative and International Studies (CIS) of the University, ETH and KOF Zurich ETH Zurich Main Building, 24.4.2007 1 The speaker would like to thank Dr. Marlene Amstad and Dr. Caesar Lack from the Financial Market Analysis Organizational Unit of the Swiss National Bank for their valuable support in the preparation of this lecture. In addition, the speaker thanks Prof. Dr. Ulrich Kohli and Prof. Dr. Thomas Jordan for valuable comments. 1/16 1. Introduction A prominent former central banker claimed a few years ago that exchange rate developments were no more predictable than coin tosses. Investment advisors and asset managers may find this statement difficult. Nevertheless, it is suitable for pointing out the difficulties of exchange rate forecasts, especially in the short term. Theoretically, in the longer term, the uncovered interest rate parity or the deviations from the purchasing power parity should give indications of the longer-term trend. In practice, however, their predictive ability is often modest. Despite the difficulties of forecasting, exchange rate movements can be explained at least in part ex post. My following reflections on the exchange rate are not to be understood as a forecast in this sense. Rather, they are intended to be an attempt to make some fundamental considerations about the determinants of the external value of the Swiss franc since the transition to flexible exchange rates in 1973. The Swiss franc is currently increasingly finding its way back into the financial press and the investment recommendations of analysts. Unlike in the last 35 years, however, the reason this time is not an appreciation of the Swiss franc, although Swiss economic data are currently very strong. Figure 1 shows the development of the Swiss franc since 1973 on the basis of the real exchange rate - i.e. adjusted for inflation - on the one hand to the euro (or to an index from its predecessor currencies) and on the other hand to the currencies of our main trading partners. Figure 1. External value of the Swiss franc effective in real terms (export-weighted, 24 countries) real against Europe (euro or predecessor currencies) 160 155 150 145 140 135 130 125 120 115 110 105 100 1973 1978 1983 1988 1993 1998 2003 2/16 Overall, there is a trend towards a slight appreciation of the Swiss franc, but this was not linear. In recent decades, there has been repeated increased volatility in the short to medium term. Nevertheless, the price correction since 2003, which has also accelerated in recent months, disturbs the overall impression of a sustained, long-term appreciation trend. The decline of the Swiss franc against the euro in the recent past has been particularly pronounced. Nominally, the euro currently costs only marginally more than in 1999, when the European single currency was introduced. However, taking into account that inflation in Switzerland has been significantly lower in the meantime than in the European monetary union, the euro has appreciated significantly against the Swiss franc since 1999, by around 10%. A large part of the decline in the real effective Swiss franc exchange rate is thus linked to a period of euro strength. You can see this very nicely from the next picture. Ultimately, the value of a currency is determined in particular on the basis of its "trading power", i.e. how it holds its own against the currencies of the most important trading partners. Figure 2 shows the CHF, the USD, the euro and the yen, each trading-weighted since 1988. The following overall picture is clear: the Swiss franc and the dollar are now trade-weighted at a comparable level to twenty years ago. The yen is at a level that is about 30% lower than at the end of the eighties. The euro is also at a level comparable to that of twenty years ago (measured by an index of its predecessor currencies). In between, however, there is on the one hand a significant depreciation phase in the years before the introduction of the euro and on the other hand a pronounced appreciation phase of the euro since the introduction of the single currency. 3/16 Figure 2. Real effective exchange rates USD (27 countries) EUR (27 countries) JPY (27 countries) CHF (24 countries) 130 120 110 100 90 80 70 60 1987 1992 1997 2002 2007 Since around 60% of our exports go to the eurozone and over 70% of our imports come from these countries, the total real trade-weighted Swiss franc exchange rate is of course strongly influenced by the ratio to the euro. In the following, I would like to make some fundamental observations on various possible reasons for determining the Swiss franc and in particular to the current development. Let me first state the general importance of the exchange rate for the SNB. The SNB's legal mandate is clear: we are obliged by the legislator to ensure price stability while taking economic developments into account. As a result, the exchange rate plays a role in the SNB's monetary policy to the extent that it influences price stability. In Switzerland, as a small and very open economy, the exchange rate is an important transmission channel through which the SNB's monetary policy in turn affects economic events and long-term price levels. The SNB must therefore inevitably deal with the exchange rate. However, it has no exchange rate target, but is committed to price stability. 4/16 2. Reasons for determining the exchange rate I would like to discuss three groups of possible reasons for determining the exchange rate of the Swiss franc exchange rate. First, structural factors that can provide a long-term explanation of real exchange rate developments. By this I mean, for example, the development of the current account and the so-called Balassa-Samuelson effect2, which in the past was often used as an explanation for the real appreciation trend of the Swiss franc since 1973. A second reason for determining the franc is likely to be the attractiveness of the franc in the eyes of foreign investors as a diversification instrument and as a so-called "safe haven". Finally, as a third determinant, which has a more short- and medium-term effect, I would like to mention monetary policy itself. This is primarily about the nominal - or only in the short term - the real exchange rate. 2.1 Structural factors An important possible determinant of the exchange rate is the current account.3 A negative current account may indicate unsustainable development and an imminent course correction. Exactly this argument has been used again and again in recent years in connection with the price development of the U.S. dollar. In fact, the real trade-weighted dollar has weakened by around 15% since mid-2002. A positive current account, on the other hand, can be a sign of a strong economy and an undervalued currency. Since 1973, the Swiss current account has only been negative for a single year, namely 1980. In recent years, the current account surplus has risen again significantly, from less than 8% in 2001 to almost 19% in the first three quarters of last year. This is one of the highest values in the world. The high surplus indicates a too current 2 Balassa (1964), "The Purchasing Power Parity Doctrine: A Reappraisal", in: Journal of Political Economy, S. 584-596. Samuelson (1964), "Theoretical Notes on Trade Problems", in: Review of Economics and Statistics, S. 145-154. 3 The current account is often referred to as the current account. The current account includes trade in goods and services, labour and capital income, and current transfers. 5/16 Exchange rates are extremely competitive export industry and, from a fundamental point of view, rather speak for an appreciation of the Swiss franc, also and especially in recent years. In the following, I would like to talk in more detail about another structural factor, the so-called Balassa-Samuelson effect. This is often used as an explanatory approach for the long trend-based real appreciation phase. The following figure graphically shows the Balassa-Samuelson effect. Put simply, the Balassa-Samuelson effect explains the real exchange rate between two countries, based on the respective productivity differences between the export and domestic sectors. According to this theory, the currency of a country with the larger productivity gap tends to appreciate in real terms. Why? Let me try to describe this with a simple example. The productivity gap changes the relative prices between goods of the export sector and goods of the domestic sector. Let us now assume that a situation with 0% inflation prevails overall. This means that the goods of the export sector will become cheaper in Swiss francs and those of the domestic sector more expensive. Since the goods of the export sector in the world market still cost the same amount in foreign currency, the Swiss franc must nominally appreciate. With inflation of 0%, this nominal appreciation also corresponds to a real appreciation. 6/16 A total of four productivity growth rates thus determine the development of the real exchange rate in the Balassa and Samuelson model: namely, the relationship between the productivity growth of the export sector and the productivity growth of the domestic sector domestically, as well as the corresponding ratio for foreign countries. As a result, there are four starting points within the framework of the model to explain a long-term real appreciation or depreciation. Specifically, the main reason given for the trendy real appreciation of the Swiss franc since 1973 was the large difference in the productivity development of the competitive Swiss export sector and the protected internal market.4 The productivity gap was significantly greater in Switzerland than abroad. If the Balassa-Samuelson effect is blamed for the real appreciation of the franc, at least until the nineties, then of course the question immediately arises as to whether the development of the franc in recent years can be explained by the Balassa-Samuelson effect. According to the model, a reduction in the productivity gap in Switzerland compared to other countries would lead to a reduction in the trend towards real appreciation. There are two plausible starting points for this: firstly, it is conceivable that productivity growth in the Swiss domestic market has accelerated ceteris paribus, and on the other hand, it is possible that productivity growth in the export sector abroad has accelerated, again ceteris paribus. An acceleration in the productivity growth of our domestic sector may have been caused by increased competitive pressure and a series of deregulation steps in recent years. An acceleration in productivity growth in the export sector abroad could be related to the fall of the Iron Curtain, China's entry into world trade and possibly also to the productivity gains of the German export industry. With this hypothesis, however, one would ultimately have to assume that our most important trading partners have been more affected by globalisation and liberalisation than we have been. This seems rather questionable to me. 4 See also Aebersold and Brunetti (1998), "The Long-Term Real Appreciation of the Swiss Franc against the D-Mark  Non-Tradable Goods and the Balassa-Samuelson Effect", Foreign Trade, Issue III, pp. 365-386; and Baltensperger, Fischer and Jordan (1999), "Soll die Schweizerische Nationalbank den Franken an den Euro binden?", in: Aussenwirtschaft, Vol. 54, Issue 1. 7/16 Research on these developments is very important to the SNB. Preliminary research from our economists suggests that in the previous research in the available data, there is no clear evidence of a reversal of the Balassa-Samuelson argument. If, however, changes have actually occurred or are still occurring in the four productivity growth rates mentioned, these effects should only become visible over a longer-term horizon. It could therefore simply be too early to make definitive statements on this topic. As I have tried to illustrate in my brief remarks, the situation is empirically extraordinarily complex. Further research in this area is required at the National Bank. 2.2 Swiss francs as an investment currency As the second possible reason for determining the external value of the franc, I see the demand of foreign investors for the franc as an investment currency. In addition to its function as a means of payment in Germany, the Swiss franc fulfils another function as an internationally sought-after denomination of asset classes such as shares, bonds and bank balances. One of the main reasons for the relatively wide international spread of the Swiss franc as an investment currency is likely to be the stability of the franc in the broadest sense: it is ultimately about investor confidence in the Swiss financial centre and the general social, political and institutional stability of our country. As a result of this stability, the Swiss franc has built up a reputation as a "safe haven" currency over the years. As you know, in the past this has often manifested itself in the form of strong upward pressure in times of political or economic crisis. In addition to this "safe haven" function in times of crisis, the Swiss franc can also be an interesting addition to an internationally diversified currency portfolio in quieter times, as it can improve the risk/return profile of a currency portfolio through its independence. In absolute terms, investments in Swiss francs continued to rise. The relative importance of the Swiss franc as an investment currency, on the other hand, tends to decline, albeit for ten to twenty years. 8/16 Figure 4. Share of central bank foreign exchange reserves denominated in Swiss francs 0.4% 0.3% 0.2% 0.1% 0.0% 1995 1996 1997 1998 1999 2000 2001 2002 2003 2004 2005 2006 As you can see from Figure 4, the Swiss franc's share of the foreign exchange reserves of the world's central banks is trending downwards, with the figures being relatively volatile from year to year, not least characterized by valuation effects depending on exchange rate developments. According to a survey by the IMF, between 1995 and 2005 central banks increased their total foreign exchange reserves from 4% to 10% of global GDP. Over the same period of time, the share of Swiss francs in total currency reserves has decreased. While in 1995 the share of the Swiss franc was still over 33 per thousand, from 2004 the share was below 20 per thousand. The decline in the role of the Swiss franc as an investment currency described above must not be forgotten that this is a relative decline, i.e. a decline compared to the market as a whole. In absolute terms, not only the currency reserves denominated in Swiss francs, but also the Swiss franc turnover on the foreign exchange markets and the outstanding Franc bonds have all grown significantly in recent years. However, the growth was less strong than the respective overall market, which led to the aforementioned percentage decline. The main reason for the relative loss of importance of the Swiss franc is primarily the positive development of foreign financial markets and currencies. Here, too, the focus is on the euro. The successful introduction of a European currency has contributed significantly to this. 9/16 That a dynamic and very liquid capital market has been able to develop in the immediate vicinity of Switzerland. The integration of the European capital market is not yet complete. Nevertheless, the development of the last eight years is impressive. The government bond market in Europe today is on a par with the market for outstanding U.S. government bonds. In addition, of course, there is globalization in the broadest sense. Other non-European financial markets have also developed exceptionally well in recent years. This tends to lead to an expansion of the global investment universe. Ladies and gentlemen, let me put these figures into perspective. I am convinced that it would be wrong for us in Switzerland to fall into a kind of melancholy in the face of these developments and mourn the old times. As a small open economy with an extremely competitive financial sector, Switzerland benefits greatly from the dynamic development of the global economy and the associated deepening of the global capital market. After all, black painting is not the order of the day because, compared to the size of the Swiss economy, the franc still plays a disproportionate role internationally. I now come back to the question of whether the dwindling role of the Swiss franc as an international investment currency is possibly a determinant of the exchange rate. It would be wrong to conclude from the relative decline in the importance of the Swiss franc to a decline in international demand and thus possibly to explain a weakening of the appreciation trend of the Swiss franc. An exchange rate always arises from the interplay of demand and supply. For example, the development shown in Figure 4 may have both demand-side and supply-side reasons. In order to justify an effect on the exchange rate, we would have to identify concrete developments on the demand or supply side. I would therefore like to focus a little more specifically on some demand-side developments. One explanation for a possible decline in demand for the Swiss franc could be that the Swiss franc has lost its diversification power and therefore its attractiveness for international investors, as Switzerland is increasingly closely linked to the EU economically with the advance of globalisation and the integration of Europe and is therefore increasingly subject to similar fundamental factors. Figure 5 shows that the exchange rate volatility of the Swiss franc against the euro (or, before 1999, the German mark) is indeed at a very low level. Dar- 10/16 It is also likely that the Swiss franc is indeed exercising a less diversification function at the moment than in previous years. However, Figure 5 also shows that volatility itself has always been relatively volatile. Cyclical lows, such as those we saw last year, repeatedly replaced with more volatile phases. Figure 5. Historical CHF exchange rate volatility DEMCHF EURCHF Standard deviation of daily changes over 260 trading days 0.8% 0.7% 0.6% 0.5% 0.4% 0.3% 0.2% 0.1% 0.0% 1975 1980 1985 1990 1995 2000 2005 Another argument against the thesis of lower demand for diversification reasons is that with the introduction of the euro, many European currencies have disappeared and the remaining European currencies should therefore have become more attractive as diversification instruments. One reason why the Swiss franc may have lost its attractiveness as a diversification currency, especially against the euro, is the increase in liquidity and efficiency of european financial markets since the introduction of the euro. The "safe haven" phenomenon, i.e. the appreciation tendency of the Swiss franc in international crisis situations, can be regarded as a special case of the diversification function of the franc. The Swiss franc thus plays a kind of insurance role in a portfolio. While the "safe haven" function of the Swiss franc was considered undisputed until the nineties, it has often been questioned in recent years. 11/16 Since the terrorist attacks of September 2001, there has been no event that has clearly and sustainably confirmed the "safe haven" role of the Swiss franc. This indeed indicates a possible weakening of the "safe haven" function. However, it may be premature to judge this conclusively. On the one hand, a safe haven is by definition only sought after in storms and - compared to real shipping ports - perhaps only then recognizable. On the other hand, it should be borne in mind that both risk perception and risk aversion of investors are very low in the current positive global economic environment, which should reduce the demand for portfolio insurance in the form of a "safe haven" currency. Ladies and gentlemen, only after the next real storm will we be able to say with certainty to what extent the franc has actually lost its historic "safe haven" function. 2.3 Monetary policy As a third possible determinant of the exchange rate, I would now like to discuss monetary policy. The interest rate differential between the Swiss franc and other currencies is generally an important determining factor for the Swiss franc. By controlling interest rates with its monetary policy, the SNB implicitly influences the exchange rate in principle.5 Following the global economic slowdown that began in 2001, the SNB loosened its monetary policy very quickly in order to prevent deflation risks and support the economy. It has lowered the key interest rate much faster and to a lower level than the ECB. In the subsequent normalization phase, in which we are still today, it again raised the key interest rate only slowly and cautiously within the framework of a favorable price environment. It is therefore not entirely surprising that the long period of an expansionary monetary policy compared to foreign countries is reflected in a declining Swiss franc. At the same time, inflation in Switzerland, in contrast to the eurozone, has remained permanently below 2% and thus in the area of price stability. 5 Siehe Hildebrand (2006), "Monetary Policy and Financial Markets", in: Financial Markets and Portfolio Management,Vol. 20, No. 1, pp. 7-18. 12/16 At this point I would like to express some thoughts on the keyword "carry trades". As you all know, there has been a lot of speculation lately that "carry trades" could be responsible for the weakening of the Swiss franc. First of all, when considering this assumption, it must be borne in mind that "carry trades" are basically nothing out of the ordinary. Various forms of "carry trades" have always existed in the market and will always exist. In the "carry trade", market participants enter into a classic arbitrage trade. They hope to generate a profit over a certain period of time. In its simplest form, when building a "carry trade" position, a short position in a debt currency and a long position in an investment currency are taken at the same time. An increase in carry trades thus weakens the debt currency and strengthens the investment currency. Such "carry trades" are speculative insofar as they assume that any exchange rate movements will not be large enough to erode the positive and thus profitable interest margins. In other words, market participants speculate when entering their carry trades that they will be able to close them and dry up profits before major exchange rate shifts occur. Specifically, it is argued that the comparatively low Swiss franc interest rates of recent years could have led to the swiss franc increasingly being used as a debt currency in "carry trades" and thus being devalued. Unfortunately, there is no reliable information on the extent to which the Swiss franc is used as a debt currency in carry trades, so we have little concrete evidence for this hypothesis. According to the theory of uncovered interest rate parity, "carry trades", as already indicated, should not generate excess returns. Sooner or later, the income from the interest rate differential will be offset by a corresponding counter-movement in the exchange rates. In recent years, this compensating counter-movement of exchange rates has been delayed, making "carry trades" very profitable. From this, the conclusion cannot and should not be prematurely drawn that the theoretical connections no longer apply at all. The Swiss franc has always been a low-interest currency, without it having been mentioned in previous years in connection with "carry trades". For example, the interest rate spread between the Swiss franc and the euro was in the 2002/2003 phase, when the swiss franc 13/16 was in a strong appreciation phase at basically the same level (around 150 basis points) as today. The current interest rate spread between European and Swiss money market interest rates is almost exactly in line with the average of the past eight years since the introduction of the euro. The argument of the interest rate spread alone is therefore not convincing. However, there are other factors that could explain why the Swiss franc may actually have been affected by the phenomenon of "carry trades" in recent quarters. One factor is undoubtedly the low volatility and risk premia worldwide and the associated high risk appetite of many market participants. In addition, there is probably also the fact that modern financial market instruments now also allow small investors to participate in "carry trades" at low transaction costs. In this context, I would like to refer in particular to the high popularity of Swiss franc loans in Austria and various Eastern European countries, which have meanwhile taken on significant proportions. According to data from the BIS and various national central banks, the net positions in Swiss francs of the banking sector in the non-banking sector outside Switzerland amount to around 237 billion and have grown by around 30 billion since 2002. Some of the developments that may have favoured "carry trades" in the Swiss franc are in the process of weakening. Not only in Switzerland, but worldwide, monetary policy has become more restrictive in recent quarters, which should gradually reduce global liquidity. It is also to be expected that the record-low volatilities and risk premia will not last forever. This should gradually deprive the "carry trade" in the Swiss franc of its livelihood. "Carry trades" are therefore cyclical phenomena that cannot last. There is no reason for monetary policy to react directly to the phenomenon of carry trades. However, what the SNB can react to within the framework of its concept are possible consequences of "carry trades" for the exchange rate. The fact is that, among other things, the recent development of the Swiss franc exchange rate has meant that the monetary framework conditions remain favourable overall despite progressive monetary policy normalisation. This is particularly true against the background of a very robust economic development and an increasingly strong utilisation of capacities in the Swiss economy. If the SNB comes to the conclusion that the development of the Swiss franc exchange rate is directly linked to the 14/16 Import prices or indirectly through their cyclical effects pose a threat to price stability, it must and will react accordingly in monetary policy terms. 3. Conclusion I would now like to conclude. In my lecture, I made various reflections on the long-term determinants of the Swiss franc exchange rate from 1973 to the present day. As I tried to explain at the very beginning, the topic is very complex. Even an ex post analysis is fraught with great uncertainty. In a nutshell, I would summarize that the trend towards the real appreciation of the Swiss franc up to a maximum of 2003 can be explained relatively plausibly with the BalassaSamuelson model. With the development that has been ongoing since 2003, the explanatory patterns are more difficult to identify, not least because we simply lack the necessary temporal distance to this period. From today's perspective, the success of the European single currency to date, the global decline in market volatility and the compression of risk premia seem to me to be the most valid medium-term explanations. In the current market environment, it is plausible that a variety of forms of "carry trades" have played a role in the development of the Swiss franc in recent months. Ultimately, however, the global financial market environment, which is characterized by extraordinarily low volatility, cannot be guaranteed forever. There are many factors that could be potential triggers for re-pricing risk. Central banks will continue to be attentive observers of the economic situation and financial markets. If the global inflation outlook deteriorates, monetary policy will  globally  make further interest rate hikes. When it comes to a "re-pricing" of risk in the global financial markets, currency pairs that are characterized by "carry trades" can react very abruptly. I am thinking, for example, of the autumn of 1998, when the yen rose by 30% against the dollar within ten weeks, and by almost 15% within four days alone. By then at the latest, it will become clear that the old rule of economics is valid after us: "There is no free lunch." This also applies to the interest rate spread between two currency pairs. The SNB considers it its duty to make financial market participants and actors aware of the risk of such a development by exposing the exchange rate and not to project the apparent risk-free environment on the exchange rate front infinitely into the future. 15/16 For its part, the SNB will do everything in its power to ensure price stability in the future. 16/16

Bestimmungsgrnde des Wechselkurses Ich mchte auf drei Gruppen von mglichen Bestimmungsgrnden des FrankenWechselkurses eingehen. Samuelson (1964), "Theoretical Notes on Trade Problems", in: Review of Economics and Statistics, S. 145-154. 3 Die Ertragsbilanz wird oft auch als Leistungsbilanz bezeichnet. Dies scheint mir eher fragwrdig. 4 Siehe dazu auch Aebersold und Brunetti (1998), "Die langfristige reale Aufwertung des Schweizer Frankens gegenber der D-Mark  Nichthandelbare Gter und der Balassa-Samuelson-Effekt", Aussenwirtschaft, Heft III, S. 365-386; sowie Baltensperger, Fischer und Jordan (1999), "Soll die Schweizerische Nationalbank den Franken an den Euro binden?", in: Aussenwirtschaft, Bd. 54, Heft 1. 7/16 Forschungsarbeiten zu diesen Entwicklungen sind fr die Nationalbank sehr wichtig. Neben der Funktion als Zahlungsmittel im Inland erfllt der Franken eine weitere Funktion als international nachgefragte Denomination von Anlageklassen wie Aktien, Anleihen und Bankguthaben. Ein Hauptgrund fr die relativ weite internationale Verbreitung des Frankens als Anlagewhrung drfte die Stabilitt des Frankens im weitesten Sinne sein: Es geht letztlich um das Vertrauen von Anlegern in den Schweizer Finanzplatz sowie die allgemeine soziale, politische und institutionelle Stabilitt unseres Landes. Als Folge dieser Stabilitt hat sich der Franken ber die Jahre den Ruf einer "safe haven"-Whrung geschaffen. Die relative Bedeutung des Frankens als Anlagewhrung ist dagegen tendenziell abnehmend, allerdings schon seit zehn bis zwanzig Jahren. 8/16 Abbildung 4. Meine Damen und Herren, lassen Sie mich dieses Zahlenmaterial in Perspektive setzten. Ich bin berzeugt, dass es verfehlt wre, wenn wir in der Schweiz angesichts dieser Entwicklungen in eine Art Melancholie verfallen und den alten Zeiten nachtrauern wrden. Die Schweiz als kleine offene Volkswirtschaft mit einem usserst kompetitiven Finanzsektor profitiert in hohem Masse von der dynamischen Entwicklung der Weltwirtschaft und der damit verbundenen Vertiefung des globalen Kapitalmarktes. Es wre falsch, vom relativen Bedeutungsrckgang des Frankens auf einen Rckgang der internationalen Nachfrage zu schliessen und somit womglich eine Abschwchung des Aufwertungstrends des Frankens erklren zu wollen. Ein Wechselkurs entsteht immer aus dem Zusammenspiel von Nachfrage und Angebot. So kann etwa die in Abbildung 4 dargestellte Entwicklung sowohl nachfrageseitige wie angebotsseitige Grnde haben. Daher mchte ich etwas konkreter auf einige nachfrageseitige Entwicklungen eingehen. Eine Erklrung fr einen mglichen Nachfragerckgang nach dem Franken knnte sein, dass der Franken an Diversifikationskraft und daher an Attraktivitt fr internationale Anleger verloren hat, da die Schweiz mit dem Fortschreiten der Globalisierung und mit der Integration Europas wirtschaftlich immer enger mit der EU verknpft ist und daher immer strker hnlichen fundamentalen Einflussfaktoren unterliegt. Das "safe haven"-Phnomen, also die Aufwertungstendenz des Frankens in internationalen Krisensituationen, kann als ein Spezialfall der Diversifikationsfunktion des Frankens betrachtet werden. Der Franken spielt somit in einem Portfolio eine Art Versicherungsrolle. Whrend die "safe haven"-Funktion des Frankens bis in die Neunzigerjahre als unbestritten galt, wurde diese in den vergangenen Jahren des fteren in Frage gestellt. 11/16 Seit den Terroranschlgen vom September 2001 gab es kein Ereignis mehr, welches die "safe haven"-Rolle des Frankens eindeutig und nachhaltig besttigt htte. Dies deutet in der Tat auf eine mgliche Abschwchung der "safe haven"-Funktion hin. Allerdings drfte es verfrht sein, darber abschliessend zu urteilen. Meine Damen und Herren, wir werden erst nach dem nchsten richtigen Sturm mit Sicherheit sagen knnen, inwieweit der Franken seine historische "safe haven"-Funktion tatschlich verloren hat. 2.3 Geldpolitik Als dritten mglichen Bestimmungsgrund des Wechselkurses mchte ich nun auf die Geldpolitik eingehen. Die Zinsdifferenz zwischen dem Franken und andern Whrungen ist grundstzlich ein wichtiger Bestimmungsfaktor des Frankens. Indem die SNB mit ihrer Geldpolitik die Zinsen steuert, beeinflusst sie implizit also grundstzlich auch den Wechselkurs.5 Auf die im Jahr 2001 einsetzende weltweite Wirtschaftsabkhlung hat die SNB ihre Geldpolitik sehr rasch gelockert, um Deflationsrisiken vorzubeugen und die Konjunktur zu sttzen. In der darauffolgenden Normalisierungsphase, in welcher wir uns heute noch befinden, hat sie den Leitzins wiederum im Rahmen eines gnstigen Preisumfeldes nur langsam und vorsichtig erhht. Es ist daher nicht durchwegs erstaunlich, dass sich die lange Phase einer im Vergleich zum Ausland expansiven Geldpolitik in einem rcklufigen Franken widerspiegelt. Gleichzeitig ist die Inflation in der Schweiz im Gegensatz zur Eurozone permanent unter 2% geblieben und somit im Bereich der Preisstabilitt. 5 Siehe Hildebrand (2006), "Monetary Policy and Financial Markets", in: Financial Markets and Portfolio Management,Vol. 20, No. 1, pp. 7-18. 12/16 An dieser Stelle mchte ich noch einige Gedanken zum Stichwort "carry trades" ussern. Wie Sie alle wissen, wird in letzter Zeit oft die Vermutung geussert, dass "carry trades" fr die Abschwchung des Frankens verantwortlich sein knnten. Zuerst gilt es bei Betrachtung dieser Vermutung zu bedenken, dass "carry trades" grundstzlich nichts Aussergewhnliches sind. Diverse Formen von "carry trades" hat es im Markt schon immer gegeben und wird es immer geben. Beim "carry trade" gehen Marktteilnehmer einen klassischen Arbitrage Handel ein. Sie erhoffen sich dabei ber eine gewisse Zeit einen Gewinn zu erwirtschaften. In seiner einfachsten Form wird beim Aufbau einer "carry trade"-Position gleichzeitig eine Short-Position in einer Verschuldungswhrung und eine Long-Position in einer Anlagewhrung eingegangen. Eine Zunahme von "carry trades" schwcht somit die Verschuldungswhrung und strkt die Anlagewhrung. Solche "Carry trades" sind insofern spekulativ als sie davon ausgehen, dass allfllige Wechselkursbewegungen nicht gengend gross sein werden, um die positiven und somit gewinnbringenden Zinsmargen zu erodieren. Anders ausgedrckt kann man auch sagen, die Markteilnehmer spekulieren beim Eingehen ihrer carry trades darauf, dass sie in der Lage sein werden, sie zu schliessen und die Gewinne ins Trockene zu bringen bevor es zu grsseren Wechselkursverschiebungen kommt. Konkret wird argumentiert, dass die vergleichsweise tiefen Frankenzinsen der letzten Jahre dazu gefhrt haben knnten, dass der Franken vermehrt als Verschuldungswhrung in "carry trades" Verwendung fand und dadurch abgewertet wurde. Leider gibt es keine gesicherten Angaben ber das Ausmass der Verwendung des Frankens als Verschuldungswhrung in "carry trades", so dass wir nur wenig konkrete Anhaltspunkte fr diese Hypothese haben. Gemss der Theorie der ungedeckten Zinsparitt drften "carry trades", wie bereits angedeutet, keine berrenditen erwirtschaften. Der Ertrag aus der Zinsdifferenz wird ber kurz oder lang durch eine entsprechende Gegenbewegung in den Wechselkursen wettgemacht. In den letzten Jahren liess diese kompensierende Gegenbewegung der Wechselkurse auf sich warten, wodurch "carry trades" sehr profitabel wurden. Daraus kann und sollte nicht voreilig der Schluss gezogen werden, dass die theoretischen Zusammenhnge berhaupt nicht mehr gelten. Der Franken war schon immer eine niedrig verzinste Whrung, ohne dass er in frheren Jahren deswegen im Zusammenhang mit "carry trades" genannt worden wre. Beispielsweise war der Zinsspread zwischen dem Franken und dem Euro in der Phase 2002/2003, als der Franken 13/16 sich in einer starken Aufwertungsphase befand auf grundstzlich gleichem Niveau (rund 150 Basispunkte) wie heute. Der aktuelle Zinsspread zwischen den europischen und schweizerischen Geldmarktzinsen liegt ziemlich genau im Durchschnitt der vergangenen acht Jahre seit der Einfhrung des Euro. Das Argument des Zinsspreads alleine berzeugt also nicht. Es gibt jedoch andere Faktoren, welche erklren knnten, warum der Franken in den vergangenen Quartalen tatschlich vom Phnomen der "carry trades" erfasst worden sein knnte. Ein Faktor sind zweifelsohne die weltweit tiefen Volatilitten und Risikoprmien und der damit verbundene hohe Risikoappetit vieler Marktteilnehmer. Dazu kommt wohl auch die Tatsache, dass moderne Finanzmarktinstrumente mittlerweile auch Kleinanlegern erlauben, sich zu geringen Transaktionskosten an "carry trades" zu beteiligen. Ich mchte in diesem Zusammenhang insbesondere auf die hohe Popularitt von Franken-Krediten in sterreich und verschiedenen osteuropischen Lndern verweisen, welche mittlerweile bedeutende Ausmasse angenommen haben. Gemss Daten der BIZ und verschiedenen nationalen Notenbanken betragen die Nettopositionen in Franken des Bankensektors in den Nichtbankensektor ausserhalb der Schweiz rund 237 Mrd. und sind seit 2002 um rund 30 Mrd. gewachsen. Einige der Entwicklungen, welche mglicherweise "carry trades" im Franken begnstigten, sind im Begriff, sich abzuschwchen. Nicht nur in der Schweiz, sondern weltweit wurde die Geldpolitik in den vergangenen Quartalen restriktiver, was die globale Liquiditt allmhlich verringern drfte. Es ist zudem zu erwarten, dass die rekordtiefen Volatilitten und Risikoprmien nicht auf ewig anhalten. Damit drfte dem "carry trade" im Franken allmhlich die Existenzgrundlage entzogen werden. "Carry trades" sind somit zyklische Phnomene, welche nicht von Dauer sein knnen. Es gibt keinen Anlass fr die Geldpolitik, direkt auf das Phnomen der "carry trades" zu reagieren. Worauf jedoch die SNB im Rahmen ihres Konzeptes reagieren kann, sind mgliche Folgen von "carry trades" fr den Wechselkurs. Tatsache ist, dass unter anderem die Entwicklung des Franken Wechselkurses in letzter Zeit dazu gefhrt hat, dass die monetren Rahmenbedingungen trotz fortschreitender geldpolitischer Normalisierung insgesamt weiterhin gnstig sind. Dies gilt insbesondere vor dem Hintergrund einer sehr robusten konjunkturellen Entwicklung und einer zusehends starken Auslastung der Kapazitten der schweizerischen Wirtschaft. Wenn die SNB zum Schluss kommt, dass die Entwicklung des Franken Wechselkurses direkt ber die 14/16 Importpreise oder indirekt ber ihre konjunkturelle Wirkung eine Gefhrdung des Preisstabilitt darstellt, muss und wird sie geldpolitisch entsprechend darauf reagieren. 3. Fazit Ich mchte nun zum Schluss kommen. In meinem Vortrag habe ich verschiedene berlegungen ber die langfristigen Determinanten des Frankenkurses von 1973 bis heute angestellt. Wie ich ganz am Anfang darzulegen versuchte, ist die Thematik sehr komplex. Selbst eine ex post Analyse ist mit grossen Unsicherheiten behaftet. Stark verkrzt wrde ich zusammenfassen, dass der Trend zur realen Aufwertung des Frankens bis maximal 2003 relativ plausibel mit dem Modell von BalassaSamuelson erklrt werden kann. Bei der seit 2003 anhaltenden Entwicklung sind die Erklrungsmuster schwieriger zu identifizieren, nicht zuletzt weil uns schlichtweg die notwendige zeitliche Distanz zu dieser Periode fehlt. Aus heutiger Sicht erscheinen mir der bisherige Erfolg der europischen Einheitswhrung, der weltweite Rckgang der Marktvolatilitten sowie die Komprimierung von Risikoprmien als die wohl stichhaltigsten mittelfristigen Erklrungsanstze. Im Rahmen des aktuellen Marktumfeldes ist es plausibel, dass eine Vielfalt von Formen von "carry trades" bei der Entwicklung des Frankens in den letzten Monaten eine Rolle gespielt haben. Letztlich kann aber das von ausserordentlich tiefer Volatilitt geprgte globale Finanzmarktumfeld nicht auf ewig gewhrt sein. Es gibt viele Faktoren, die potentielle Auslser eines re-pricing von Risiko sein knnten. Notenbanken werden weiterhin aufmerksame Beobachter der Wirtschaftslage und Finanzmrkte bleiben. Falls sich die weltweiten Inflationsaussichten verschlechtern sollten, wird die Geldpolitik  global gesehen  weitere Zinserhhungen vornehmen. Wenn es zu einem re-pricing von Risiko in den globalen Finanzmrkten kommt, knnen Whrungspaare welche von "carry trades" geprgt sind sehr abrupt reagieren. Ich denke hier zum Beispiel an den Herbst 1998, als der Yen gegenber dem Dollar innerhalb von zehn Wochen um 30% stieg, alleine innert vier Tagen um beinahe 15%. Sptestens dann wird ersichtlich werden, dass die alte Regel der konomie eben nach wir vor Gltigkeit hat: There is no free lunch. Dies gilt auch fr den Zinsspread zwischen zwei Whrungspaaren. Die Nationalbank erachtet es als ihre Pflicht, den Finanzmarktteilnehmern und Akteuren mit einer Wechselkursexponierung das Risiko einer solchen Entwicklung ins Bewusstsein zu rufen und nicht das scheinbare risikolose Umfeld an der Wechselkursfront unendlich in die Zukunft zu projizie- 15/16 ren. Ihrerseits wird die Nationalbank alles tun, um auch in Zukunft die Preisstabilitt zu gewhrleisten. 16/16

Title: The SNB facilitates and secures payment transactions
text: Embargo: 25 April 2007, 10:00 a.m. The SNB facilitates and ensures payment transactions* Thomas J. Jordan Alternate Member of the Executive Board Swiss National Bank Swiss Banking Operations Forum 25 avril 2007, Zurich * The author thanks Robert Fluri and Marlene Amstad, from the Banking and Financial Market Analysis Organizational Units of the Swiss National Bank, Zurich, for their support in preparing this paper. 1/6 1. Introduction It is with great pleasure that I address you today at the seminar organised by the Swiss Banking Operations Forum on "Payment transactions - Switzerland is preparing for the Single Payments Area in Europe". 2007 is a special year for payment transactions in Switzerland; we are celebrating the hundredth anniversary of the SNB, but also the twenty years of the Swiss Interbank Clearing (SIC). The SIC is currently the main pillar of payment transactions in our country and is of great importance to the SNB. These two anniversaries give me the opportunity to recall the main stages in the development of our payment system. I will highlight the role played by the SNB in this area. At the end of my presentation, I will comment on the ongoing efforts to create a single payments area in Europe. In this last part, I will highlight the importance of SEPA (Single Euro Payments Area) for Switzerland. Many challenges had to be overcome before achieving a single payments area in Switzerland. Before the opening of the SNB's counters, our country had neither a national monetary policy nor a single payments area. At that time, payment systems were mainly focused on a region or canton. The fact that it was not possible to make payments in cash in a simple way throughout Switzerland significantly hampered the country's economic development. That is why, a century ago, the legislator entrusted the National Bank with the task of conducting a monetary and credit policy that serves the general interests of the country, but also that of facilitating payment transactions. 2. Steps towards CIS: moving from a net settlement system to a gross settlement system Let me briefly recall the main stages in the development of payment transactions in Switzerland. In the first half of the twentieth century, the circulation of cashless payments was based on two main pillars in our country: the transfer system of the National Bank and the postal cheque system of the PTT. Free access to transfer accounts at the SNB was then a matter of course. The establishment, in the fifties, of a bank clearing at the national level has changed the situation. The banks have thus opened a new phase in payment transactions in Switzerland. The new bank clearing included eight central offices, one of which was managed by the National Bank itself. The banks entrusted their payments, for reciprocal compensation, to these centrals. The resulting balances were then either increased on the transfer accounts at the SNB or settled by deductions from these accounts. As a result, the SNB still held a key position within the Swiss system. But its transfer system was gradually losing its importance, as a system of general scope, if the number of transactions is taken into account. At that time, most payments were made through the postal cheque system and the new bank clearing. For the most part, the participants in the SNB's credit transfer system were banks, the Confederation and some large industrial or commercial companies. 2/6 At the beginning of the eighties, banks carried out transactions totalling some 15,000 billion francs per year (about 60 to 70 billion francs per day) via bank clearing. The share of manual labour was still high. The system was therefore cumbersome and not very transparent. It could take up to four days for a payment to be executed. Under these conditions, effective liquidity management was not possible. The banks participating in the system therefore had to hold high liquidity. In addition, the risks inherent in the system were considerable. Those risks were, moreover, borne by the SNB, since it tolerated, in the interests of the proper functioning of the system, overdrafts during the day on the banks' transfer accounts. Taking these risks, however, led the SNB to play a role that was hardly in line with the legislator's intention. The obvious flaws in the system prompted the banks and the SNB to reflect. Thus, a project study, the "Spiezer-Papier", was drawn up. The first ideas on the fundamental principles of a new system for interbank payments were formulated. This system, the "Swiss Interbank Clearing", entered into operation in 1987. The "Spiezer-Papier" defined various requirements that the system had to meet. According to the main one, all transactions had to be executed directly, i.e. without going through the clearing stage, on the transfer accounts that the participants held at the National Bank, which meant settlement with central bank money. In current terminology, the payment systems that apply immediate and final accounting for each transaction are real-time gross settlement systems. In a way, they are the model that is opposed to net settlement systems, of which the former bank clearing was a part. Unlike net settlement systems, gross settlement systems eliminate systemic risks as they do not provide participants with the opportunity to dispose of amounts from payments that are not yet definitively and irrevocably executed. In gross settlement systems, all payments are executed directly to the transfer accounts at the central bank. They thus have a quality equivalent to that of cash payments. The special feature of the CIS is that it is used for the settlement of payments of large amounts and mass payments. Mass payments - these are amounts not exceeding 5000 francs - represent about 90% of the number of payments made by the SIC, but only 5% of the sum of payments. The use of a real-time gross settlement system for mass payment transactions is not the rule at the international level. Experience shows that the CIS does not, however, encounter any serious technical problems because it is also used for the settlement of small payments. There are undeniable advantages to having all interbank payments through a single system: it reduces costs and increases the efficiency of the banking system. In addition, the settlement of mass payments by central bank money contributes to strengthening systemic stability. 3. Outsourcing and control of the CIS Let me now turn to two important aspects of the relationship between the SIC and the SNB, namely the outsourcing of the operation of the system and the possibilities for the SNB to exercise control and influence over the SIC. Basically, a central bank can contribute in two ways to a secure and efficient infrastructure for payment transactions. It may either operate the payment system itself or entrust the technical operation of the system to the financial sector and confine itself to 3/6 provide liquidity for the settlement of payments and ensure the management of the system. When designing the CIS, the SNB chose the second solution, as it had already done at the time in the case of bank clearing. One company, Swiss Interbank Clearing AG (Telekurs AG until 1996), is responsible for the technical operation of the SIC, while the SNB is responsible for liquidity management and system management. Entrusting the services of a data centre to a third-party company meant splitting the transfer account of each participant into two accounts, namely an SIC clearing account, for the accounting of transactions by the data centre, and a basic account, for the accounting of transactions between the participant and the SNB. Thus, cash withdrawals and payments are recorded not in the SIC clearing account but directly in the basic account at the SNB. The split of the transfer accounts was not unanimously accepted within the SNB. The reluctance was mainly concerned with the transfer of assets from the basic accounts at the SNB to the SIC clearing accounts opened at the data centre. The SNB, it was feared, would give up some of its most legitimate competence if it allowed payments to be made outside the issuing institution with assets in transfer accounts and if the banks transmitted their payment orders to a third party. This objection now seems a bit far-fetched. Indeed, the splitting of transfer accounts has so far caused little trouble. The proper functioning of the system is explained in particular by the fact that SIC SA has always fulfilled its mandate with a strong sense of responsibility and great care. It must be admitted, however, that the terms 'Swiss Interbank Clearing' and 'SIC clearing account' are confusing. Rather, they are reminiscent of a net settlement system. I would therefore like to point out, for the avoidance of doubt, that payments in the SIC are not cleared against each other, in a first phase, on the SIC clearing accounts. Each payment order is executed individually in the CIS, according to the 'first in first out' principle, with assets in transfer accounts, in other words with commitments from the SNB. Legally, the SIC clearing account in the SIC system and the basic account at the SNB form a single unit, the transfer account. In this sense, the SIC is an "inhouse" payment system of the SNB. However, its operation has been outsourced. Today, CIS is at the heart of a very complex technical and organizational constellation. It is used not only for interbank payment transactions, but also, since 2001, for payment transactions between PostFinance and banks. Since 2002, the CLS ("Continuous Linked Settlement") system has been connected to the SIC. For a longer time, since 1995, the SIC, SECOM, i.e. the SIS system for the real-time settlement of securities transactions, and various trading platforms of SWX and Eurex have been part of the so-called "Swiss Value Chain", the integrated infrastructure of the Swiss financial market. The proper functioning of the SIC is absolutely crucial for the Swiss financial centre and for the implementation of monetary policy. Therefore, in addition to the responsibility of each participant and SIC AG, the possibility for the SNB to exercise control and influence over the system plays an important role. The SNB can act in this respect from two angles: Since the introduction of the SIC, the rights and obligations of the SNB and the operator of the data centre, now SIC AG, have been specified in a contract. SIC SA is 4/6 thus responsible for the operation of the SIC system and the development of technical extensions. The contractual provisions grant the SNB extensive rights to approve changes and extensions to the technical part of the system. In addition, the SNB decides on the circle of participants insofar as it lays down the conditions for opening, blocking and closing transfer accounts. It can also influence the pricing policy of the system. The contract also regulates the SNB's obligations in keeping the accounts and assigns the SNB the task of managing crises that may arise in the system. Legal jurisdiction allows the SNB to exert influence from another angle. Since the entry into force of the revised law governing it, the SNB has been empowered to impose minimum requirements for the operation of payment systems or securities settlement systems that may pose risks to the stability of the financial system. The CIS is part of such systems. The SNB's supervisory responsibilities help to prevent instabilities and risks in the financial system. Such disturbances could significantly impede the implementation of monetary policy and thus have a negative impact on economic developments. 4. The SNB's principles on payment transactions As I pointed out at the beginning of my presentation, the SNB's task is to ensure and facilitate the proper functioning of payment transactions. I would also like to recall the philosophy behind the SNB in its decisions on payment transactions. This philosophy is based on at least two principles. The SNB - the first principle - prefers market-oriented solutions as much as possible rather than direct interventions. Essentially, it is limited to establishing reliable framework conditions. The SNB - the second principle - is open to new needs in the market. It has demonstrated this time and time again in the past. Thus, the "Swiss Value Chain" was made possible because the SNB authorised transactions involving entries not only on credit, but also on the debit of its transfer accounts. In 1998, it also enabled joint ventures of banks abroad, foreign clearing organisations and foreign banks participating in such joint ventures or clearing organisations to open transfer accounts with it. The Swiss financial market thus had access to CLS, the system for the settlement of foreign exchange transactions, and to Eurex. In addition, since 1999 the SNB has been granting interest-free intraday loans to avoid liquidity shortages in the CIS. Such appropriations considerably facilitate the processing of payments in the SIC system. With this policy, the SNB integrates the financial sector, in particular the banks' joint ventures, into the responsibilities and leaves the door wide open to innovations in both products and processes. Thanks to this, the SIC is today a system that, in international comparison, is extremely inexpensive and works with speed and reliability. This policy has also led to a broad functional integration of swiss financial market infrastructures. Our financial centre has thus become more efficient, which contributes to its high reputation. 5/6 5. SEPA as seen by the SNB In the last part of my presentation, I would like to comment briefly on SEPA. The creation of a single payments area in Europe will lead to considerable productivity gains, hence the great importance of this project. In Europe, the systems for cashless customer payments are still strongly focused on the various national states, which does not contribute to European economic integration. Thanks to SEPA, the situation is expected to improve significantly, as cross-border payments made by credit transfers, direct collections and payment cards will be regulated by well-defined framework conditions and binding standards. For industry, commerce and consumers, the implementation of SEPA will abolish any difference between domestic and cross-border payments in euro. This will result in substantial savings. SEPA is a logical follow-up to the introduction of the euro. In the absence of a single area for cashless payments in euros, the creation of the single European currency would remain an unfinished business, and the benefits of this single currency would not be able to have their full effect. In addition, a single payments area will facilitate the implementation of euro area monetary policy. Currently, SEPA includes euro area countries, other EU countries and EFTA countries, totalling 31 countries. Its importance therefore extends far beyond the euro area. Since the beginning of 2006, banks in Switzerland have been able to participate. In our country, more than 300 banks with around 3500 counters will be able, thanks to SEPA, to take advantage of the European payments area. For them and for the Swiss economy as a whole, SEPA is of the utmost importance: the EU has around 460 million inhabitants and 310 million of them live in the euro area. Switzerland has forged very close economic ties with the EU: in 2006, 82% of our imports came from the EU and 62% of our exports went to the countries of this zone. SEPA, it should not be forgotten, concerns only payments in euros. For the Swiss financial centre, payments in other foreign currencies, mainly in dollars, are also important. SEPA is therefore a significant, but not the last, step on the road to as wide and efficient a payments space as possible. The EU's legislative bodies and the European Central Bank (ECB) deliberately leave a large margin for market self-regulatory processes. The SNB is very pleased with this approach and - as I mentioned earlier - is in line with our principles for payment transactions. In the implementation of SEPA, the European Payments Council (EPC) plays a key role. The SNB supports measures that help strengthen the position of the Swiss financial industry on the international financial markets. In Switzerland, work on the implementation of SEPA has already started and some have made good progress. They place high demands on the employees of the banks and specialised bodies concerned. Seminars such as the one you are holding today help banks in their preparatory work. I can only support these efforts and urge the representatives of the banks to make extensive use of the many possibilities that are available. I wish you every success in today's seminar and thank you for your attention. 6/6
text_original: Embargo: 25 avril 2007, 10h00 La Banque nationale facilite et assure le trafic des paiements* Thomas J. Jordan membre supplant de la Direction gnrale Banque nationale suisse Swiss Banking Operations Forum 25 avril 2007, Zurich * L'auteur remercie Robert Fluri et Marlene Amstad, des units d'organisation Oprations bancaires et Analyse des marchs financiers de la Banque nationale suisse, sige de Zurich, du soutien qu'ils lui ont apport dans la prparation du prsent expos. 1/6 1. Introduction C'est avec un trs grand plaisir que je m'adresse  vous aujourd'hui,  l'occasion du sminaire organis par le Swiss Banking Operations Forum sur le thme Trafic des paiements  La Suisse se prpare en vue de l'espace unique de paiements en Europe. L'anne 2007 est particulire pour ce qui a trait au trafic des paiements en Suisse; nous ftons en effet le centime anniversaire de la Banque nationale, mais aussi les vingt ans du Swiss Interbank Clearing (SIC). Le SIC est actuellement le principal pilier du trafic des paiements dans notre pays et revt une grande importance pour la Banque nationale. Ces deux anniversaires me donnent l'occasion de rappeler les principales tapes du dveloppement de notre systme de paiement. Je mettrai en lumire le rle jou par la Banque nationale dans ce domaine. A la fin de mon expos, je commenterai les efforts entrepris actuellement pour crer en Europe un espace unique de paiements. Dans cette dernire partie, je soulignerai l'importance du SEPA (Single Euro Payments Area) pour la Suisse. Il a fallu relever de nombreux dfis avant de parvenir  un espace unique de paiements en Suisse. Avant l'ouverture des guichets de la Banque nationale, notre pays n'avait ni une politique montaire nationale ni un espace unique de paiements. Les systmes de paiement taient alors axs essentiellement sur une rgion ou un canton. Le fait de ne pas pouvoir effectuer des paiements en monnaie scripturale, d'une manire simple, dans l'ensemble de la Suisse entravait considrablement le dveloppement conomique du pays. C'est pourquoi le lgislateur a confi  la Banque nationale, il y a un sicle, la tche de conduire une politique montaire et une politique de crdit servant les intrts gnraux du pays, mais aussi celle de faciliter les oprations de paiement. 2. Les tapes vers le SIC: passage d'un systme  rglement net  un systme  rglement brut Permettez-moi de rappeler brivement les grandes tapes du dveloppement du trafic des paiements en Suisse. Dans la premire moiti du XXe sicle, le trafic des paiements sans numraire reposait sur deux piliers principaux dans notre pays: le systme de virement de la Banque nationale et le systme des chques postaux des PTT. Le libre accs aux comptes de virement  la BNS allait alors de soi. La mise sur pied, dans les annes cinquante, d'un clearing bancaire sur le plan national a modifi la donne. Les banques ont ainsi ouvert une nouvelle phase dans le trafic des paiements en Suisse. Le nouveau clearing bancaire comprenait huit centrales, dont une tait gre par la Banque nationale elle-mme. Les banques confiaient leurs paiements, pour compensation rciproque,  ces centrales. Les soldes qui en rsultaient taient alors soit bonifis sur les comptes de virement  la Banque nationale, soit rgls par des prlvements sur ces comptes. Par consquent, la Banque nationale occupait toujours une position cl au sein du systme suisse. Mais son systme de virement perdait peu  peu de son importance, en tant que systme de porte gnrale, si l'on tient compte du nombre de transactions. A cette poque, la plupart des paiements taient effectus par le systme des chques postaux et par le nouveau clearing bancaire. Pour l'essentiel, les participants au systme de virement de la Banque nationale taient des banques, la Confdration et quelques grandes entreprises industrielles ou commerciales. 2/6 Au dbut des annes quatre-vingt, les banques excutaient, via le clearing bancaire, des transactions totalisant quelque 15'000 milliards de francs par an (environ 60  70 milliards de francs par jour). La part de travail manuel tait encore leve. Le systme tait par consquent lourd et peu transparent. L'excution d'un paiement pouvait prendre jusqu' quatre jours. Dans ces conditions, une gestion efficace des liquidits n'tait pas possible. Les banques participant au systme devaient par consquent dtenir des liquidits leves. En outre, les risques inhrents au systme taient considrables. Ces risques taient au demeurant supports par la Banque nationale, tant donn que celle-ci tolrait, dans l'intrt du bon fonctionnement du systme, des dcouverts en cours de journe sur les comptes de virement des banques. La prise de ces risques amenait toutefois la Banque nationale  jouer un rle qui n'allait gure dans le sens voulu par le lgislateur. Les dfauts vidents du systme ont incit les banques et la Banque nationale  une rflexion. C'est ainsi qu'une tude de projet, le Spiezer-Papier, a t labore. Les premires ides sur les principes fondamentaux d'un nouveau systme pour les paiements interbancaires y taient formules. Ce systme, le Swiss Interbank Clearing, est entr en service en 1987. Le Spiezer-Papier dfinissait diverses exigences auxquelles le systme devait satisfaire. Selon la principale d'entre elles, toutes les transactions devaient tre excutes directement, donc sans passer par l'tape de la compensation, sur les comptes de virement que les participants dtenaient  la Banque nationale, ce qui signifiait un rglement avec de la monnaie de banque centrale. Dans la terminologie actuelle, les systmes de paiement qui appliquent la comptabilisation immdiate et dfinitive de chaque opration sont des systmes  rglement brut en temps rel. Ils constituent en quelque sorte le modle qu'on oppose aux systmes  rglement net, dont l'ancien clearing bancaire faisait partie. Contrairement aux systmes  rglement net, les systmes  rglement brut liminent les risques systmiques puisqu'ils n'offrent pas aux participants la possibilit de disposer de montants provenant de paiements qui ne sont pas encore excuts de manire dfinitive et irrvocable. Dans les systmes  rglement brut, tous les paiements sont excuts directement sur les comptes de virement  la banque centrale. Ils ont ainsi une qualit quivalente  celle des paiements en numraire. Le SIC a pour particularit de servir au rglement des paiements portant sur des montants levs et des paiements de masse. Les paiements de masse  il s'agit des montants n'excdant pas 5000 francs  reprsentent environ 90% du nombre des paiements excuts par le SIC, mais seulement 5% de la somme des paiements. Recourir  un systme  rglement brut en temps rel pour le trafic des paiements de masse n'est pas la rgle sur le plan international. Le SIC, l'exprience le montre, ne se heurte cependant  aucun problme technique srieux du fait qu'il sert aussi au rglement de petits paiements. Faire passer tous les paiements interbancaires par un seul systme prsente d'incontestables avantages: cela rduit les cots et accrot l'efficacit du systme bancaire. En outre, le rglement des paiements de masse par de la monnaie de banque centrale contribue au renforcement de la stabilit systmique. 3. L'externalisation et le contrle du SIC Permettez-moi d'aborder maintenant deux aspects importants des relations entre le SIC et la Banque nationale,  savoir l'externalisation de l'exploitation du systme et les possibilits, pour la Banque nationale, d'exercer un contrle et une influence sur le SIC. Fondamentalement, une banque centrale peut contribuer de deux manires  une infrastructure sre et efficace du trafic des paiements. Elle peut soit exploiter elle-mme le systme de paiement, soit confier l'exploitation technique du systme au secteur financier et se borner  3/6 mettre  disposition des liquidits pour le rglement des paiements et  assurer le pilotage du systme. Lors de la conception du SIC, la Banque nationale a choisi la seconde solution, comme elle l'avait dj fait,  l'poque, dans le cas du clearing bancaire. Une socit, la Swiss Interbank Clearing SA (Telekurs SA jusqu'en 1996), est charge de l'exploitation technique du SIC, la Banque nationale assurant pour sa part la gestion des liquidits et le pilotage du systme. Confier les services d'un centre de calcul  une socit tierce signifiait scinder le compte de virement de chaque participant en deux comptes,  savoir un compte de compensation SIC, pour la comptabilisation des oprations par le centre de calcul, et un compte de base, pour la comptabilisation des oprations passes entre le participant et la Banque nationale. Ainsi, les retraits et versements de numraire sont comptabiliss non pas sur le compte de compensation SIC, mais directement sur le compte de base  la Banque nationale. La scission des comptes de virement ne faisait pas l'unanimit au sein de la Banque nationale. Les rticences portaient principalement sur le transfert d'avoirs des comptes de base  la Banque nationale aux comptes de compensation SIC ouverts au centre de calcul. La Banque nationale, craignait-on, abandonnerait une parcelle de sa comptence la plus lgitime si elle tolrait que des paiements soient faits, hors de l'institut d'mission, avec des avoirs en comptes de virement et si les banques transmettaient leurs ordres de paiement  un tiers. Cette objection semble aujourd'hui un peu tire par les cheveux. En effet, la scission des comptes de virement n'a jusqu'ici gure occasionn de problmes. Le bon fonctionnement du systme s'explique notamment par le fait que SIC SA a toujours rempli son mandat avec un sens aigu des responsabilits et un grand soin. Il faut toutefois bien admettre que les expressions Swiss Interbank Clearing et compte de compensation SIC prtent  confusion. Elles font plutt penser  un systme  rglement net. Je tiens par consquent  rappeler, pour viter tout malentendu, que les paiements dans le SIC ne sont pas compenss entre eux, dans une premire phase, sur les comptes de compensation SIC. En effet, chaque ordre de paiement est excut individuellement dans le SIC, selon le principe first in first out, avec des avoirs en comptes de virement, en d'autres termes avec des engagements de la Banque nationale. Juridiquement, le compte de compensation SIC, dans le systme SIC, et le compte de base,  la Banque nationale, ne forment qu'une seule et mme unit, le compte de virement. Le SIC est en ce sens un systme de paiement inhouse de la Banque nationale. Son exploitation a toutefois t externalise. Aujourd'hui, le SIC est au cur d'une constellation technique et organisationnelle fort complexe. Il sert non seulement au trafic des paiements interbancaires, mais aussi, depuis 2001, au trafic des paiements entre PostFinance et les banques. Depuis 2002, le systme CLS (Continuous Linked Settlement) est raccord au SIC. Depuis plus longtemps, soit depuis 1995, le SIC, le SECOM, c'est--dire le systme de la SIS pour le rglement en temps rel des oprations sur titres, et diverses plates-formes de ngoce de la SWX et d'Eurex entrent dans ce qu'on appelle la Swiss Value Chain, l'infrastructure intgre du march financier suisse. Le bon fonctionnement du SIC est absolument dterminant pour la place financire suisse comme pour la mise en uvre de la politique montaire. C'est pourquoi, en plus de la responsabilit incombant  chaque participant et  SIC SA, la possibilit pour la Banque nationale d'exercer un contrle et une influence sur le systme joue un rle important. En la matire, la Banque nationale peut agir sous deux angles: Depuis l'introduction du SIC, les droits et les obligations de la Banque nationale et de l'exploitant du centre de calcul, aujourd'hui SIC SA, sont prciss dans un contrat. SIC SA est 4/6 ainsi charge de l'exploitation du systme SIC et du dveloppement des extensions techniques. Les dispositions contractuelles accordent  la Banque nationale des droits tendus en ce qui concerne l'approbation de modifications et d'extensions  apporter  la partie technique du systme. En outre, la Banque nationale dcide du cercle des participants dans la mesure o elle fixe les conditions d'ouverture, de blocage et de fermeture des comptes de virement. Elle peut aussi exercer une influence sur la politique tarifaire du systme. Le contrat rgle galement les obligations de la Banque nationale dans la tenue des comptes et attribue  la Banque nationale la tche de grer les crises qui pourraient surgir dans le systme. Une comptence lgale permet  la Banque nationale d'exercer une influence sous un autre angle. Depuis l'entre en vigueur de la loi rvise qui la rgit, la Banque nationale est habilite  imposer des exigences minimales pour lexploitation de systmes de paiement ou de systmes de rglement des oprations sur titres pouvant engendrer des risques pour la stabilit du systme financier. Le SIC fait partie de tels systmes. Les attributions de la Banque nationale en matire de surveillance contribuent  prvenir des instabilits et des risques au sein du systme financier. De telles perturbations pourraient entraver sensiblement la mise en uvre de la politique montaire et, ainsi, avoir des rpercussions ngatives sur l'volution de l'conomie. 4. Les principes de la BNS en matire de trafic des paiements La Banque nationale, je l'ai soulign au dbut de mon expos, a pour tche d'assurer et de faciliter le bon fonctionnement du trafic des paiements. Je voudrais encore rappeler la philosophie dont s'inspire la Banque nationale dans ses dcisions en matire de trafic des paiements. Cette philosophie repose sur au moins deux principes. La Banque nationale  premier principe  prfre autant que possible recourir  des solutions axes sur le march plutt qu' des interventions directes. Pour l'essentiel, elle se borne  tablir des conditionscadres fiables. La Banque nationale  deuxime principe  est ouverte aux besoins nouveaux qui se font sentir sur le march. Elle l'a dmontr  maintes reprises dans le pass. Ainsi, la Swiss Value Chain a pu tre ralise parce que la Banque nationale a autoris des transactions impliquant des critures non seulement au crdit, mais aussi au dbit de ses comptes de virement. Elle a galement permis, en 1998,  des entreprises communes de banques  l'tranger,  des organisations trangres de clearing et  des banques trangres participant  de telles entreprises communes ou  de telles organisations de clearing d'ouvrir des comptes de virement auprs d'elle. Le march financier suisse a eu ainsi accs  CLS, le systme pour le rglement des oprations de change, et  Eurex. De plus, la Banque nationale accorde, depuis 1999, des crdits intrajournaliers, sans intrt, pour viter des pnuries de liquidits dans le SIC. De tels crdits facilitent considrablement le droulement des paiements dans le systme SIC. Par cette politique, la Banque nationale intgre le secteur financier, en particulier les entreprises communes des banques, dans les responsabilits et laisse la porte largement ouverte aux innovations dans le domaine des produits comme dans celui des processus. Grce  cela, le SIC est aujourd'hui un systme qui, en comparaison internationale, est extrmement peu coteux et fonctionne avec rapidit et fiabilit. Cette politique a galement conduit  une large intgration fonctionnelle des infrastructures du march financier suisse. Notre place financire a ainsi gagn en efficacit, ce qui contribue  sa haute rputation. 5/6 5. Le SEPA vu par la BNS Dans la dernire partie de mon expos, je voudrais commenter brivement le SEPA. La cration d'un espace unique de paiements en Europe permettra d'obtenir des gains de productivit considrables, d'o la grande importance que revt ce projet. En Europe, les systmes pour les paiements sans numraire de la clientle sont encore fortement axs sur les divers Etats nationaux, ce qui ne contribue pas  l'intgration conomique europenne. Grce au SEPA, la situation devrait s'amliorer sensiblement, tant donn que les paiements transfrontires effectus par des virements, recouvrements directs et cartes de paiement seront rglements par des conditions-cadres bien dfinies et des normes contraignantes. Pour l'industrie, le commerce et les consommateurs, la mise en uvre du SEPA abolira toute diffrence entre paiements nationaux et paiements transfrontires en euros. Il en rsultera de substantielles conomies. Le SEPA est une suite logique  l'introduction de l'euro. En l'absence d'un espace unique pour les paiements sans numraire en euros, la cration de la monnaie unique europenne resterait une uvre inacheve, et les avantages de cette monnaie unique ne pourraient dployer tous leurs effets. En outre, un espace unique de paiements facilitera la mise en uvre de la politique montaire de la zone euro. Actuellement, le SEPA comprend les pays de la zone euro, les autres pays de l'UE et les pays de l'AELE, soit au total 31 pays. Son importance s'tend donc bien au-del de la zone euro. Depuis le dbut de 2006, les banques en Suisse peuvent y participer. Dans notre pays, plus de 300 banques disposant d'environ 3500 comptoirs pourront, grce au SEPA, profiter de l'espace europen de paiements. Pour elles comme pour l'ensemble de l'conomie suisse, le SEPA est de la plus haute importance: l'UE compte environ 460 millions d'habitants et 310 millions d'entre eux vivent dans la zone euro. La Suisse a tiss des liens conomiques trs troits avec l'UE: en 2006, 82% de nos importations provenaient de l'UE et 62% de nos exportations taient destines aux pays de cette zone. Le SEPA, il convient de ne pas l'oublier, concerne uniquement les paiements en euros. Pour la place financire suisse, les paiements dans d'autres monnaies trangres, en dollars principalement, sont eux aussi importants. Le SEPA est donc une tape significative, mais non la dernire, sur la voie vers un espace de paiements aussi large et efficace que possible. Les organes lgislatifs de l'UE et la Banque centrale europenne (BCE) laissent dlibrment une grande marge aux processus d'autorgulation du march. Cette approche plat beaucoup  la Banque nationale et correspond  comme je l'ai mentionn prcdemment   nos principes en matire de trafic des paiements. Dans la ralisation du SEPA, le Conseil europen des paiements (CEP) joue un rle cl. La Banque nationale soutient les mesures contribuant  renforcer la position de l'industrie financire suisse sur les marchs financiers internationaux. En Suisse, les travaux de mise en uvre du SEPA ont dj dmarr et certains ont bien progress. Ils posent des exigences leves aux collaboratrices et aux collaborateurs des banques et des organes spcialiss qui sont concerns. Des sminaires tels que celui que vous tenez aujourd'hui aident les banques dans leurs travaux prparatoires. Je ne puis que soutenir ces efforts et inciter les reprsentants des banques  faire un large usage des nombreuses possibilits qui sont offertes. Je vous souhaite plein succs pour le sminaire de ce jour et vous remercie de votre attention. 6/6

Title: Address at the General Meeting of Shareholders
text: Embargo: Friday, 27 April 2007, 10.00 a.m. Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, President of the Bank Council at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 27 April 2007 Dear Shareholders Ladies and Gentlemen Dear Guests I would like to start by welcoming you to our 99th General Meeting of Shareholders  undeniably one of the highlights of our centenary year. And yes, you did hear me correctly! This is indeed only the 99th General Meeting, and not the 100th. And its not because our archivist made a mistake in counting. It is in fact because the Federal Council decided back in 1907, at the request of the Bank Council, not to hold the first ordinary general meeting in 1908, as one would expect, but to wait until 1909. Thus, the first business period lasted roughly one and a half years. Be that as it may, todays General Meeting marks the 100-year anniversary of our institution. It is therefore not only an ordinary General Meeting, but also a somewhat extraordinary one. I am delighted to be able to celebrate this special day with you, the shareholders of the Swiss National Bank. My speech today is dedicated to you and will address the significance of the SNBs shareholders and how the ownership structure has evolved over the years. A joint-stock company The National Banks relationship with its shareholders has always been a particularly special one. Not least because it is rather unusual for a central bank to have shareholders in the first place. A glance at central banks around the world shows that those structured as shareholding banks are more the exception than the rule these days. Most are stateowned institutions. It is therefore even more unusual for a central bank to allow private individuals to own its shares. Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council at the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank on 27 April 2007 2 I will thus start by explaining why the SNB is set up as a joint-stock company. I will then look briefly at how the ownership structure has evolved, before taking a closer look at the SNB share itself.
