Title: Address to the General Meeting of Shareholders
text: Embargo: Friday, 17 April 2009, 10.00 Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 17 April 2009 Dear Shareholders Ladies and Gentlemen Dear Guests Last year, the SNB centenary was the focus of the meeting. At the time, I drew attention to the fact that the SNB had been faced with particular challenges, not only in the year it was founded, but also in its major anniversary years. As the particular challenge faced in the centenary year, I mentioned the financial market turmoil that began in August 2007. This turmoil has now mushroomed into the deepest and most complex financial crisis the world has seen since the Great Depression. Furthermore, the financial crisis has widened into a global economic crisis, which has taken full hold of the Swiss economy, too. Financial crisis deepens and measures taken to reinforce Swiss financial system In 2008, the financial crisis was a major concern for the SNB. At an early stage, it became clear that Switzerland, with its important financial sector and especially with its two international big banks, is particularly vulnerable. Hardly any other country has a banking system in which individual banks are of such tremendous importance to the economy as the two big banks are for Switzerland. Their sheer size alone assures UBS and CS a key role in the stability of the entire financial system. Consequently, if one of the big banks is at risk, the Swiss financial system as a whole is put at risk. Article 5 of the National Bank Act stipulates that the SNB shall contribute to the stability of the financial system. Conscious of its shared responsibility for the stability of the financial system, the SNB began drawing up measures for a possible emergency at an early stage  always hoping that such an emergency would not eventuate. In doing so, it was in permanent contact with the Federal Department of Finance and the Swiss Federal Banking Commission (now FINMA). When the financial market crisis deepened further following the collapse of the Lehman Brothers investment bank last September, it became increasingly Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 17 April 2009 2 likely that such an emergency could occur in the Swiss financial system. Consequently, on 16 October, the Federal Council, the SNB and the SFBC announced a package of measures aimed at strengthening the Swiss financial system. This package combined a reinforcement of depositor protection, thorough revision of the deposit guarantee scheme and targeted measures to strengthen the balance sheet of Switzerlands largest bank, UBS. UBS would transfer illiquid assets amounting to a maximum of USD 60 billion from its balance sheet to a special purpose vehicle (SPV) established by the SNB, and would contribute capital equivalent to 10% of the amount to be transferred to the SPV. At the same time, the Swiss Confederation would strengthen the UBS equity base by underwriting mandatory convertible notes (MCN) for CHF 6 billion. The SNB, for its part, would grant the SPV a long-term loan amounting to a maximum USD 54 billion. The SNB loan would be secured by the assets held by the stabilisation fund. When the package of measures was announced last October, it was assumed that the assets to be transferred would amount to no more than USD 60 billion. Following a detailed examination of the portfolio and the resulting negotiations between UBS and the SNB, a portfolio now amounting to USD 38.7 billion was taken over by the stabilisation fund. Accordingly, the SNB loan to the stabilisation fund was reduced from a maximum of USD 54 billion to USD 34.8 billion. The size of the UBS participation in the SPV fell from USD 6 billion to USD 3.9 billion. Statutory mandate and powers of the SNB The SNBs powers to establish and finance the SPV arise out of its constitutional mandate to pursue a monetary policy that is in the interests of the country as a whole. Within this framework, it also has a mandate to contribute to the stability of the financial system. Under article 46 of the NBA, the Governing Board has sole responsibility for the conduct of monetary policy. Thus the decision to establish and finance the SPV fell within the Governing Boards exclusive powers and responsibilities. The NBA specifies that the Governing Board shall render account to the Federal Assembly on the fulfilment of its tasks. These requirements also apply with regard to the SPV. Thus, in its accountability report to the Federal Assembly which constitutes the first part of the Annual Report, the SNB provided detailed accounts of the establishment of the SPV, the transfer of the Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 17 April 2009 3 illiquid assets and the granting of the loan. The Chairman of the Governing Board has also informed the relevant Federal Assembly commissions about the SPV at a number of discussion meetings. The SNB Bank Council has no monetary policy powers, serving rather as the National Banks supreme supervisory and monitoring body. However, these supervisory and monitoring powers relate not to monetary policy but to the business management of the SNB. This organisation of powers is based on the SNBs special corporate governance model which differentiates clearly between the conduct of monetary policy, on the one hand, and business management matters, on the other. The Governing Board has sole and exclusive responsibility for the conduct of monetary policy. In business management matters, however, the NBA (like the Banking Act), works on the principle that supervisory and executive functions should be separated. Thus, the Governing Board is the supreme management and executive body, while the Bank Council supervises and monitors the management. The individual powers of the Bank Council are listed in the Organisation Regulations. In particular, the Bank Council sets out the basic principles according to which the SNB should be organised, regulates the basic structure of its accounting, financial monitoring and financial planning systems, monitors and assesses risk management and the investment process, and reviews its resource strategies. In addition, the Bank Council approves the business and financial report for submission to the Federal Council and the General Meeting of Shareholders, and prepares the General Meeting. Bank Council tasks in connection with special purpose vehicle What are the consequences of the division of powers between the Governing Board and the Bank Council with regard to the SPV? First, the actual decision to establish and finance the SPV was taken by the Governing Board alone. The Bank Council had no say in the matter. Second, the Bank Council was not obliged to retrospectively review the decision  which was, after all, a decision of a monetary policy nature. Nevertheless, important tasks fall to the Bank Council in connection with the SPV  as part of its supervisory and monitoring functions. These tasks are derived from the Bank Councils responsibility first, for supervising and monitoring the accounts and, second, for monitoring and assessing risk management and the investment process. Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 17 April 2009 4 In order to fulfil its supervisory and monitoring responsibilities optimally, the Bank Council established an Audit Committee and a Risk Committee back in 2004. Each of the committees consists of three Bank Council members with special knowledge and experience in the specific field. The Audit Committee oversees accounting and financial reporting, while the Risk Committee assesses the suitability and effectiveness of the investment process and oversees risk management. The committees fulfil a preparation and support function with respect to Bank Council decisions. However, the actual supervisory powers lie with the Bank Council itself. The two committees face particular challenges in connection with the establishment of the SPV and the transfer of the illiquid assets. The Audit Committee is dealing with complex accounting issues, in particular relating to reporting, valuation, entry and presentation in the Annual Report. It is working closely with the heads of internal and external audit. The Risk Committee is dealing with questions relating to financial risks and management of the acquired assets. It is monitoring the risk control process and ensuring that it obtains regular risk evaluations. The Risk Committee therefore stays in close contact with the head of SNB risk management. Both committees also ensure that the SNBs resources, expertise and organisation are appropriate for mastering these new tasks. The Audit Committee and the Risk Committee both receive comprehensive quarterly reports on developments in the stabilisation fund. Illiquid assets  accounting and management As you will gather from reading the Annual Report, the transfer of the illiquid assets and the long-term investment strategy being pursued in this connection have had a fundamental impact on the current financial report. For the first time, we are presenting you with consolidated financial statements in which both the financial accounts of the SNB, as the parent company, and the interim results of the SPV, as the subsidiary company, are presented in consolidated form. All of these financial statements are audited by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), our external auditors. Financial statements for the stabilisation fund are drawn up in accordance with the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). In view of the long time horizon, the illiquid assets are valued not at market price, but rather (where this is permissible under Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 17 April 2009 5 the accounting standard), at amortised cost. Due to the illiquidity of the assets, market prices are almost non-existent at present and, where they do exist, have little meaning. In other words, fair value has lost a great deal of its significance and is not useful for valuations of the assets in question. Impairment tests are being conducted periodically, however, to determine the recoverable value of the assets. This ensures that, in the medium term, the assets are not stated in the balance sheet at a value higher than the amount they will reach, while, at the same time, due consideration is given to unrecoverable losses in value. An initial impairment test was conducted as per end-2008 and, where necessary, value adjustments were made. Losses on assets in the stabilisation fund will initially be absorbed by the capital contributed by UBS, which corresponds to 10% of the assets that have been transferred. Should there be further losses, secondary loss protection is foreseen. The SNB has a warrant for 100 million UBS shares in the event of a loss on its loan when the assets are liquidated. The SNB does not value the assets itself. It has outsourced this task to third parties, whose work it monitors and checks carefully. This approach was already adopted at the time that the purchase price was established. The calculation of the purchase price was based on the book value of the assets as stated in the UBS interim balance sheet as at 30 September 2008. In addition, the SNB asked independent experts to provide a valuation of the assets as at the same date. The valuations were carried out by specialised companies with different valuation approaches. This gave rise to two different figures: the book value calculated by UBS and the valuation provided by the SNBs independent experts. The assets were acquired at the lower of these two figures. The assets are being managed by third parties on the basis of investment guidelines drawn up by the SNB. The SNB is participating in this outsourced work and monitoring it actively. It intends to hold the transferred assets until maturity  or at least until the markets in question have recovered. Should the assets be sold later, the sales strategy will be crucial, since the stabilisation fund is competing with other market participants to realise assets, all of which are similar in nature. Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 17 April 2009 6 Concluding remarks The SNB is conscious of its shared responsibility for the stability of the Swiss financial system and the entire Swiss economy. In establishing and financing the SPV, it has not shied away from resorting to exceptional measures. In doing so, it has taken a considerable risk. However, the alternative was to risk a destabilisation of the financial system. The SNB judged the risk to the financial system to be greater than the risk of the UBS operation. It therefore decided in favour of the latter. Now that this decision has been taken, the principle of separating supervision and management functions applies to the SPV as it does for all business matters at the SNB. In connection with the SPV, the Bank Council takes its function as supervisory and monitoring body very seriously. It bears responsibility for supervising and checking accounting procedures and for overseeing and assessing risk management and the investment process. In order to fulfil its task, the Bank Council receives regular and comprehensive information on developments in the stabilisation fund, and remains in permanent contact with the relevant SNB managers via its two committees. Within the limits of its constitutional mandate and practical possibilities, the SNB will continue to make its contribution to fighting the crisis and smoothing the way to recovery. I would like to thank you, as shareholders, for supporting and trusting in your National Bank in these difficult times.

Title: Financial markets and the global economy
text: Embargo period: 14 May 2009, 9:00 Financial markets and the global economy Thomas J. Jordan Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank* Swiss Economic Forum Thun, 14 May 2009 * The speaker would like to thank Dr. Caesar Lack and Dr. Marlene Amstad for their valuable support in the preparation of this presentation. 1 Introduction The current financial market crisis is often called a debt crisis. This is not without reason  not only in the USA (Figure 2), but worldwide debt has increased rapidly in recent years. Part of the increase in debt can be explained by structural factors. 1 However, the accelerated increase in debt since the nineties in particular may also have been an expression to a certain extent of an increasing appetite for risk. This was already expressed in the IT stock bubble of the late nineties and finally culminated in the global real estate bubble of recent years. In the US, for example, real property prices have doubled over the course of the recent housing boom (Figure 3); in some other countries, price increases were even more pronounced. However, due to the specific structure of real estate financing in the U.S. and the sheer size of the U.S. housing market, the collapse of the U.S. real estate market is considered the real trigger of today's crisis. Brief outline of the financial crisis The crisis was already apparent at the beginning of 2007, when the first losses appeared on securities based on bundled subprime mortgages (Figure 4). In August 2007, liquidity on the interbank money market dried up practically overnight, bringing the crisis to the attention of the general public for the first time. The crisis then gradually spread to other financial market segments. In autumn 2008, the crisis escalated completely with the bankruptcy of the investment bank Lehman Brothers. Virtually all investments traded on the financial markets then fell massively in value and reached new lows in December; most equity markets in March 2009 even fell below their December 2008 levels. In the past two months, the financial markets have recovered somewhat. The financial dimension of the current crisis is only comparable to the stock market crash of 1929. Although the comparison of share price developments at the present time is slightly in favour of the current crisis (Figure 5), the wealth losses are likely to be significantly greater today than they were then. 1 Such as an increasing capital stock, falling inflation and interest rates, lower risks of all kinds, technological progress, demographic ageing in the West and the high propensity to save in Asia. 2 Capitalization in terms of GDP is greater than it was then, and secondly, there are now significantly more assets on which huge losses have also been incurred (such as corporate bonds, structured products, commodities, etc.). From the financial market crisis to the economic crisis The real economy, which until the summer of 2008 was not very impressed by the creeping deterioration of the situation on the financial markets, was finally brought down by the escalation last autumn  the financial market crisis was followed by a global economic crisis. Like the financial market crisis, the economic crisis is proceeding in historically almost unprecedented dimensions. Very impressive  and worrying  is, for example, the dramatic slump in world trade (Figure 6): while world trade has increased almost continuously over the past 18 years (since data collection began), the volume of trade fell by 18% within three months (from November 2008 to January 2009) after the escalation of the crisis. Other indicators and, increasingly, data on economic growth also show massive setbacks. Nevertheless, the current economic crisis is likely to be much less severe than the Great Depression (Figure 7). The following three factors in particular are decisive for this. First, massive monetary and fiscal support measures have been and are being implemented today. An important difference from then is in particular that monetary policy is no longer tied to the gold standard  this made an expansionary monetary policy impossible at the beginning of the thirties. Second, in the current crisis, comprehensive measures have been taken to support the banking system, resulting in few bank failures. This is in contrast to the thirties, when thousands of banks went bankrupt in the US alone. In this context, deposit insurance in particular plays a major role, which did not yet exist at the beginning of the Great Depression. Thirdly, automatic stabilisers are much more important today than they were then; this means that a larger state sector and better developed social systems stabilize the economy more strongly today than was the case then. Although a repeat of the Great Depression is therefore not to be feared, a severe recession and a subsequent phase with relatively low economic 3 growth is inevitable. History teaches that after a major real estate and financial market crisis, an economy only returns to a sustainable growth path after the bad loans have been written off and the banking system has been recapitalized. This may take some time. The capital misinvested in real estate will not be available for economic growth in the coming years. In addition, servicing the massive increase in public debt is also detrimental to economic growth. Challenges The financial market crisis presented governments and central banks with enormous challenges. The most urgent measures concerned securing system stability  a global banking panic was averted last autumn. Now it is time to remove the bad loans from the banking system and recapitalize the banks. An expansionary monetary and fiscal policy should also dampen the economic downturn, prevent a credit crunch and avert the risk of a deflationary spiral. In the longer term, a key challenge is to make the financial system more robust. It would be presumptuous to believe that financial market cycles can be avoided in the future. There will again be shocks on the financial markets in the future. The aim must therefore be to limit the impact of these shocks on the stability of the financial system and the real economy and to make it impossible for the costs of undesirable developments to be passed on to the general public. This does not necessarily require more regulation, but better regulation. The following elements are pillars of more robust financial market regulation: First, regulation must become more comprehensive, i.e. all systemically relevant financial market participants must be subordinate to it. Sufficient capital and liquidity buffers are another central element of a robust financial market order. In addition, problematic incentive structures and corporate governance in financial institutions need to be reconsidered. A final important point concerns institutions that are "too big to fail". Solving the "too big to fail" problem is a major task of financial market regulation in the future, especially for small Switzerland with its large financial sector. Solving this problem also requires an appropriate legal framework for the orderly liquidation of systemically relevant financial market institutions. 4 In addition to designing robust financial market regulation, another long-term challenge for the international community is to avoid a refuge in protectionism. Protectionism is extremely detrimental to prosperity and growth. Finally, central banks and governments must critically weigh the benefits and costs of their expansionary monetary and fiscal policies; in particular, central banks must normalise their expansionary monetary policy at the right time to prevent inflation from overshooting. Even if the normalisation of monetary policy will be highly unpopular, central banks must not shy away from it. 5 Thomas Jordan, Swiss Economic Forum, 14 5 2009 Financial markets and the global economy Thomas Jordan Member of the Governing Board Of the Swiss National Bank Swiss Economic Forum, 14.5.2009 From a historically unique debt expansion... 2 1 Thomas Jordan, Swiss Economic Forum, 14 5 2009 ... to a historically unprecedented real estate bubble... Mai 2009 * Der Referent dankt Dr. Caesar Lack und Dr. Marlene Amstad fr die wertvolle Untersttzung bei der Vorbereitung dieses Referats. 1 Einleitung Die aktuelle Finanzmarktkrise wird oft auch eine Schuldenkrise genannt. Dies nicht ohne Grund  nicht nur in den USA (Abbildung 2), sondern weltweit hat die Verschuldung in den vergangenen Jahren rasch zugenommen. Ein Teil des Anstiegs der Verschuldung ist durch strukturelle Faktoren erklrbar. 1 Doch insbesondere der beschleunigte Anstieg der Verschuldung seit den Neunzigerjahren drfte in einem gewissen Ausmass auch Ausdruck einer zunehmenden Risikofreude gewesen sein. Diese usserte sich bereits in der IT-Aktienblase der spten Neunzigerjahre und kulminierte schliesslich in der globalen Immobilienblase der letzten Jahre. In den USA zum Beispiel war im Laufe des jngsten Immobilienbooms eine Verdoppelung der realen Immobilienpreise zu beobachten (Abbildung 3); in einigen andern Lndern waren die Preisanstiege sogar noch ausgeprgter. Aufgrund der spezifischen Struktur der Immobilienfinanzierung in den USA und der schieren Grsse des amerikanischen Husermarktes gilt jedoch der Kollaps des US-Immobilienmarktes als der eigentliche Auslser der heutigen Krise. Kurzer Abriss der Finanzkrise Die Krise zeichnete sich schon zu Beginn des Jahres 2007 ab, als erste Verluste auf Wertpapieren auftraten, die auf gebndelten Subprime-Hypotheken basierten (Abbildung 4). Im August 2007 trocknete dann praktisch ber Nacht die Liquiditt auf dem InterbankenGeldmarkt aus, was die Krise erstmals in das Bewusstsein der breiten ffentlichkeit rckte. Die Krise breitete sich anschliessend sukzessive auf weitere Finanzmarktsegmente aus. Im Herbst 2008 eskalierte die Krise mit dem Konkurs der Investmentbank Lehman Brothers dann vollumfnglich. Praktisch alle an den Finanzmrkten gehandelten Anlagen verloren danach massiv an Wert und erreichten im Dezember neue Tiefstwerte; die meisten Aktienmrkte sanken im Mrz 2009 sogar noch unter ihren Stand vom Dezember 2008. In den vergangenen zwei Monaten haben sich die Finanzmrkte wieder etwas erholt. Die finanzielle Dimension der aktuellen Krise ist einzig mit dem Brsencrash von 1929 vergleichbar. Zwar fllt der Vergleich der Aktienkursentwicklung zum aktuellen Zeitpunkt leicht zugunsten der aktuellen Krise aus (Abbildung 5), trotzdem drften die Vermgensverluste heute bedeutend grsser sein als damals: Erstens ist heute die globale Aktienmarkt- 1 Wie zum Beispiel einen zunehmenden Kapitalstock, fallende Inflation und Zinsen, geringere Risiken aller Art, technologischen Fortschritt, die demographische Alterung im Westen und die hohe Sparneigung in Asien. 2 kapitalisierung gemessen am BIP grsser als damals, und zweitens existieren heute deutlich mehr Vermgenswerte, auf welche ebenfalls riesige Verluste angefallen sind (wie Corporate Bonds, strukturierte Produkte, Rohstoffe etc.). Von der Finanzmarktkrise zur Wirtschaftskrise Die reale Wirtschaft, welche sich bis zum Sommer 2008 von der schleichenden Verschlechterung der Lage an den Finanzmrkten wenig beeindruckt zeigte, wurde schliesslich von der Eskalation im letzten Herbst regelrecht zum Einsturz gebracht  auf die Finanzmarktkrise folgte eine globale Wirtschaftskrise. Wie die Finanzmarktkrise verluft auch die Wirtschaftskrise in historisch fast przedenzlosen Dimensionen. Sehr beeindruckend  und beunruhigend  ist beispielsweise der dramatische Einbruch des Welthandels (Abbildung 6): Whrend der Welthandel in den vergangenen 18 Jahren (seit Beginn der Datenerfassung) praktisch ununterbrochen anstieg, ging das Handelsvolumen nach der Eskalation der Krise innert dreier Monate (von November 2008 bis Januar 2009) um 18% zurck. Andere Indikatoren und zunehmend auch Daten zum Wirtschaftswachstum zeigen teilweise ebenfalls massive Rckschlge. Trotzdem drfte die aktuelle Wirtschaftskrise deutlich weniger heftig ausfallen als die Grosse Depression (Abbildung 7). Massgeblich hierfr sind insbesondere folgende drei Faktoren. Erstens wurden und werden heute massive geld- und fiskalpolitische Sttzungsmassnahmen implementiert. Ein wichtiger Unterschied zu damals liegt insbesondere darin, dass die Geldund Whrungspolitik heute nicht mehr an den Goldstandard gebunden ist  dieser verunmglichte zu Beginn der Dreissigerjahre eine expansive Geldpolitik. Zweitens wurden in der gegenwrtigen Krise umfassende Massnahmen zur Sttzung des Bankensystems ergriffen, so dass nur wenige Bankenzusammenbrche erfolgten. Dies im Gegensatz zu den Dreissigerjahren, als alleine in den USA Tausende von Banken Konkurs gingen. In diesem Zusammenhang spielt insbesondere auch die Einlagenversicherung eine grosse Rolle, welche zu Beginn der Grossen Depression noch nicht existierte. Drittens sind die automatischen Stabilisatoren heutzutage bedeutend wichtiger als damals; darunter versteht man, dass ein grsserer Staatssektor und besser ausgebaute Sozialsysteme die Wirtschaft heute strker stabilisieren, als dies damals der Fall war. Obwohl eine Wiederholung der Grossen Depression somit nicht zu befrchten ist, drfte eine schwere Rezession und eine anschliessende Phase mit relativ niedrigem Wirtschafts- 3 wachstum unvermeidlich sein. Die Geschichte lehrt, dass eine Volkswirtschaft nach einer grossen Immobilien- und Finanzmarktkrise erst wieder auf einen nachhaltigen Wachstumspfad zurckfindet, nachdem die faulen Kredite abgeschrieben wurden und das Bankensystem rekapitalisiert wurde. Dies kann einige Zeit dauern. Das in Immobilien fehlinvestierte Kapital wird in den kommenden Jahren fr das Wirtschaftswachstum nicht zur Verfgung stehen. Zudem ist die Bedienung der massiv ansteigenden Staatsschulden dem Wirtschaftswachstum ebenfalls abtrglich. Herausforderungen Die Finanzmarktkrise stellte Regierungen und Notenbanken vor gewaltige Herausforderungen. Die dringendsten Massnahmen betrafen die Sicherung der Systemstabilitt  eine globale Bankenpanik konnte im letzten Herbst abgewendet werden. Nun gilt es, die faulen Kredite aus dem Bankensystem zu entfernen und die Banken zu rekapitalisieren. Eine expansive Geld- und Fiskalpolitik soll zudem den Konjunkturabschwung dmpfen, eine Kreditklemme verhindern und die Gefahr einer deflationren Spirale bannen. Lngerfristig besteht eine zentrale Herausforderung darin, das Finanzsystem robuster zu gestalten. Es wre vermessen zu glauben, dass Finanzmarktzyklen in Zukunft vermieden werden knnen. Es wird auch in Zukunft wieder zu Schocks auf den Finanzmrkten kommen. Es muss somit darum gehen, die Auswirkungen dieser Schocks auf die Stabilitt des Finanzsystems und die Realwirtschaft zu begrenzen und zu verunmglichen, dass die Kosten von Fehlentwicklungen auf die Allgemeinheit abgewlzt werden. Dazu ist nicht unbedingt mehr Regulierung notwendig, sondern bessere Regulierung. Folgende Elemente sind Sulen einer robusteren Finanzmarktregulierung: Zunchst muss die Regulierung umfassender werden, d.h. alle systemisch relevanten Finanzmarktteilnehmer mssen ihr unterstellt sein. Ausreichende Kapital- und Liquidittspuffer sind ein weiteres zentrales Element einer robusten Finanzmarktordnung. Ferner mssen problematische Anreizstrukturen und die Corporate Governance in Finanzinstitutionen berdacht werden. Ein letzter wichtiger Punkt betrifft Institutionen, welche "too big to fail" sind. Die Lsung des "too big to fail"-Problems stellt insbesondere fr die kleine Schweiz mit ihrem grossen Finanzsektor eine knftige Hauptaufgabe der Finanzmarktregulierung dar. Zur Lsung dieses Problems gehrt auch ein zweckmssiger gesetzlicher Rahmen zur geordneten Liquidation systemisch relevanter Finanzmarktinstitutionen. 4 Neben der Ausgestaltung einer robusten Finanzmarktregulierung besteht eine weitere langfristige Herausforderung an die Staatengemeinschaft darin, eine Zuflucht zum Protektionismus zu vermeiden. Protektionismus ist dem Wohlstand und dem Wachstum usserst abtrglich. Und schliesslich mssen Notenbanken und Regierungen Nutzen und Kosten ihrer expansiven Geld- und Fiskalpolitik kritisch abwgen; insbesondere mssen die Notenbanken ihre expansive Geldpolitik zum richtigen Zeitpunkt normalisieren, um ein berschiessen der Inflation zu verhindern. Title: The Swiss franc repo market  a successful first decade
text: Embargo: Thursday, July 2, 2009, 08:30 10 years of the Swiss franc repo market - a success story Thomas J. Jordan* Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank Repo Conference of the Swiss National Bank Hotel Schweizerhof Lucerne 2 July 2009 * The speaker would like to thank Dr. Caesar Lack, Dr. Marlene Amstad and Karl Hug for their valuable support in the preparation of this presentation. 1 The Swiss franc repo market is celebrating its tenth anniversary this year - in June 1999, repo transactions were carried out via the Swiss Value Chain for the first time. 1 The development of the Swiss franc repo market is a success story. Initially received with scepticism by the banks and intended from the point of view of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) only as a supplement to the instruments of the time, the repo market has developed within a few years into the central hub for secured Swiss franc liquidity and repo business has become the main instrument of the SNB's monetary policy. At this point, the emergence and development of the Swiss franc repo market and its baptism of fire in the financial market crisis are looked back on, and possible further developments are discussed, which are not least based on the lessons of the financial crisis. Interbank business in Switzerland took place predominantly on an unsecured basis before the creation of the repo market. The snb's main instrument of monetary policy was foreign exchange swapping. Complementary instruments were the re-placement of federal funds, swaps with money market book receivables and the Lombard business. These instruments had several disadvantages. In addition, the wide range of instruments made it difficult to apply orderly procedures and equal treatment of business partners. Foreign exchange swaps, for example, could only be concluded with the big banks, as only they had sufficient foreign exchange holdings. The fine distribution of liquidity in the Swiss financial system therefore had to be carried out by a few private banks. A lack of competition and insufficient efficiency sometimes led to undesirable fluctuations in interest rates and liquidity on the Swiss franc money market. Foreign exchange swaps were concluded by telephone, and foreign currency settlement took place abroad. In addition to market and credit risks, foreign exchange swaps therefore also included significant operational risks. In the mid-1990s, the SNB came to the conclusion that a repo market in Switzerland would bring significant advantages. At that time, repo business had already successfully established itself as the main monetary policy instrument in many countries. In Switzerland, on the other hand, regulatory hurdles prevented the emergence of a repo market for a long time. These hurdles had to be overcome first. A central hurdle was the stamp 1 Repo trading had already begun in April 1998, but still on the basis of telephone trading. 2 duty. At the suggestion of the SNB and the commercial banks, the Federal Tax Administration reinterpreted the Federal Act on Stamp Duty in 1997, which exempted repo business from stamp duty. In the same year, the National Bank Act was also amended and repo transactions were permitted as an instrument. The fact that repo transactions are hedged investments also prompted the Federal Banking Commission (SFBC) to set favourable conditions for repo transactions with regard to capital adequacy and liquidity provisions compared to unsecured money market transactions. With the introduction of the Swiss franc repo market, the SNB pursued several objectives. It hoped that this would be the first to benefit monetary policy. In particular, the implementation of monetary policy through repo business should lead to a reduction in credit, market and operational risks, greater efficiency of the money market and greater transparency in monetary policy.2 Secondly, considerations related to financial stability played a role. A liquid secured money market is a cornerstone of financial stability, as it is indispensable for the refinancing of banks in times of crisis. The events of the past two years have shown how important this aspect is. The uncovered money market practically dried up in the financial market crisis or became prohibitively expensive, and commercial banks had to refinance themselves by other means, not least through the covered money market. And thirdly, with the introduction of the repo market, the SNB also wanted to create an efficient and flexible platform for trading and processing money market transactions. The relatively late emergence of a repo market in Switzerland by international standards also had advantages. A modern system could be introduced without having to take into account the existing system. The result was a system that is still considered a world leader. Success factors were the principles of standardization, automation, integration and openness, on which the Franken repo market is based. The transactions are standardized with regard to collateral basket, contract type and other specifications, are automatically concluded on the electronic trading platform Eurex Repo and then fully integrated via the securities settlement system. 2 The fixing of the repo rate is more transparent than an implicit interest rate for foreign exchange swaps, which must be derived from the exchange rate and the interest rate difference. 3 SECOM of SIX SIS and the real-time payment system SIC of SIX SIC. This unique integration of trading and settlement is known as the Swiss Value Chain. The Swiss franc repo market is open to participants abroad and allows collateral in foreign currencies. Great importance was also attached to comprehensive risk reduction: The settlement of transactions is based on the principle of "delivery against payment", i.e. the securities and the money are finally transferred at the same time. In addition, the risk management of the repo business, i.e. the value adjustment, is carried out automatically during its term: compensation deliveries are made twice a day. Since the collateral is freely available to the lender during the term of the repo, its liquidity is maintained. In an international comparison, it is also unusual for the interbank repo market and the repo transactions to implement monetary policy to use the same platform and are subject to the same collateral requirements defined by the SNB. This requires close cooperation between the SNB and the private sector (banks, Eurex, SIX SIS, SIX SIC) in setting up, operating and further developing the system. The creation of the new market took place very quickly. In 1996, the SNB decided to introduce the repo business as a regular instrument. In 1997, the development of the repo system was started. The first repo transactions took place in 1998. Since 1999, the SNB has largely made its basic and fine-tuning liquidity available through repo auctions and individual repo transactions. In the same year, the Intraday Facility was introduced to facilitate payments. The repos, which were initially intended only as a supplement to the existing instruments, very quickly replaced all previous ordinary monetary policy instruments (Figure 1). Finally, in 2005, the Lombard business was abolished and replaced by the Congestion Financing Facility. For both facilities, liquidity is obtained through the conclusion of repo transactions. In the first years of its existence, the Swiss franc repo market was mainly characterised by the turnover generated by the SNB, which remained relatively constant over the years. Turnover traded between commercial banks, on the other hand, experienced rapid growth. They rose from an average of CHF 1 billion per day in 1999 to over CHF 10 billion per day last year (Figures 2 and 3). The number of 4 Participants have risen significantly from around 30 at the beginning of 1999 to around 150 at present, with growth experiencing two spurts: A first boost took place in 1999 as a result of feared liquidity bottlenecks due to the year 2000 problem. A second boost came in the recent financial market crisis, which made the benefits of the secured business particularly apparent (Figure 4). In an international comparison, the internationality of the Swiss franc repo market is probably unique. Banks abroad account for a significant proportion of participants and turnover. In the financial market crisis, their importance increased again (Figure 5). The targets set by the SNB when it introduced the Swiss franc repo market 10 years ago were largely achieved. Due to its advantages in normal times, the repo instrument has replaced all other instruments within a very short time. The SNB's monetary policy concept, which is based on the management of the 3M Libor and implemented via repo transactions, has proven to be very flexible and useful. Thanks to the repo business, the SNB was able to manage the 3M Libor well even in the crisis (Figure 6), even if it sometimes took a long time to achieve the desired target due to high risk premiums. The expectation that the repo business could contribute to system stability was also met. The Swiss franc repo market has also functioned well in the last two difficult years, allowing banks that had sufficient high-quality collateral to refinance without any problems. The platform could also be used to introduce other instruments such as the SNB Bills. These serve to siphon off liquidity and thus increase the flexibility of monetary policy. The SNB Bills will play an important role in the transition from the current zero interest rate policy to regular interest rate management. However, the crisis has also revealed some limits. Despite the security provided by securities, certain lenders have expressed doubts about the quality of the counterparty and/or collateral. And despite the openness and internationality of the platform, it became necessary last autumn to use the instrument of foreign exchange swaps again in order to meet the liquidity demand of banks abroad that were not connected to the Swiss franc repo market or did not have sufficient eligible collateral. 5 (Figure 7). In addition, the liquidity of the Swiss franc repo market was not always optimal. In order to counter the identified limits, the SNB is examining several ideas. These include the introduction of cash collateral, which in fact amounts to a foreign exchange swap in the form of a repo transaction, and the expansion of the group of participants, possibly also to non-banks. It also examines whether the introduction of a CCP could increase confidence in the system. The ultimate goal is to increase the liquidity of the repo market and thus ensure that the success story of the Swiss franc repo market will continue over the next 10 years. 6 Figure 1 Figure 2 7 Figure 3 Figure 4 8 Figure 5 Figure 6 9 Figure 7 10
text_original: Embargo: Donnerstag, 2. Juli 2009, 08:30 10 Jahre Franken-Repomarkt  eine Erfolgsgeschichte Thomas J. Jordan Mitglied des Direktoriums Schweizerische Nationalbank Repo-Tagung der Schweizerischen Nationalbank Hotel Schweizerhof Luzern 2. Juli 2009  Der Referent dankt Dr. Caesar Lack, Dr. Marlene Amstad und Karl Hug fr die wertvolle Untersttzung bei der Vorbereitung dieses Referats. 1 Der Franken-Repomarkt feiert dieses Jahr sein zehnjhriges Bestehen  im Juni 1999 wurden erstmals Repo-Geschfte ber die Swiss Value Chain abgewickelt. 1 Die Entwicklung des Franken-Repomarkts ist eine Erfolgsgeschichte. Von den Banken anfnglich mit Skepsis aufgenommen und aus Sicht der Schweizerischen Nationalbank (SNB) nur als Ergnzung zum damaligen Instrumentarium gedacht, haben sich der Repomarkt innert weniger Jahre zum zentralen Umschlagplatz fr gesicherte Frankenliquiditt und das Repogeschft zum Hauptinstrument der Geldpolitik der SNB entwickelt. An dieser Stelle wird auf die Entstehung und Entwicklung des Franken-Repomarkts sowie auf dessen Feuertaufe in der Finanzmarktkrise zurckgeblickt, und es wird auf mgliche Weiterentwicklungen eingegangen, die nicht zuletzt auf den Lehren aus der Finanzkrise beruhen. Das Interbankengeschft in der Schweiz fand vor der Schaffung des Repomarktes berwiegend auf ungesicherter Basis statt. Das Hauptinstrument der Geldpolitik der SNB war der Devisenswap. Ergnzende Instrumente waren die Weiterplatzierung von Bundesgeldern, Swaps mit Geldmarktbuchforderungen und das Lombardgeschft. Diese Instrumente wiesen verschiedene Nachteile auf. Zudem erschwerte das breite Spektrum an Instrumenten die Anwendung geordneter Verfahren und die Gleichbehandlung der Geschftspartner. Devisenswaps konnten zum Beispiel nur mit den grossen Banken abgeschlossen werden, da nur sie ber ausreichende Devisenbestnde verfgten. Die Feinverteilung der Liquiditt im schweizerischen Finanzsystem musste somit von wenigen privaten Banken vorgenommen werden. Dabei fhrte mangelnder Wettbewerb und ungengende Effizienz mitunter zu unerwnschten Zins- und Liquidittsschwankungen am Franken-Geldmarkt. Devisenswaps wurden telefonisch abgeschlossen, und die Fremdwhrungsabwicklung erfolgte im Ausland. Neben den Marktund Kreditrisiken beinhalteten Devisenswaps somit auch betrchtliche operationelle Risiken. Mitte der 1990er Jahre kam die SNB zum Schluss, dass ein Repomarkt in der Schweiz wesentliche Vorteile bringen wrde. Damals hatte sich das Repogeschft bereits in vielen Lndern als geldpolitisches Hauptinstrument erfolgreich durchgesetzt. In der Schweiz hingegen verhinderten regulatorische Hrden lange Zeit die Entstehung eines Repomarktes. Diese Hrden mussten zuerst genommen werden. Eine zentrale Hrde war die Stempel- 1 Der Repohandel hatte schon im April 1998 begonnen, allerdings noch auf Basis des Telefonhandels. 2 pflicht. Auf Anregung der SNB und der Geschftsbanken nahm die Eidgenssische Steuerverwaltung 1997 eine Neuinterpretation des Bundesgesetzes ber die Stempelabgabe vor, wodurch das Repogeschft von der Stempelsteuer befreit wurde. Im selben Jahr wurde auch das Nationalbankgesetz angepasst, und Repogeschfte wurden als Instrument zugelassen. Die Tatsache, dass es sich bei Repogeschften um gesicherte Anlagen handelt, veranlasste zudem die Eidgenssische Bankenkommission (EBK) dazu, bei Repo-Geschften in Bezug auf die Eigenmittel- und Liquidittsbestimmungen im Vergleich zu ungesicherten Geldmarktgeschften gnstige Rahmenbedingungen zu setzen. Mit der Einfhrung des Franken-Repomarktes verfolgte die SNB mehrere Ziele. Sie versprach sich davon als erstes Vorteile fr die Geldpolitik. Die Implementierung der Geldpolitik ber das Repogeschft sollte insbesondere eine Verringerung der Kredit-, Markt- und operativen Risiken, eine hhere Effizienz des Geldmarktes und eine hhere Transparenz bei der Geldpolitik bewirken.2 Zweitens spielten berlegungen im Zusammenhang mit der Finanzmarktstabilitt eine Rolle. Ein liquider gesicherter Geldmarkt ist ein Grundpfeiler der Finanzmarktstabilitt, da er fr die Refinanzierung der Banken in Krisenzeiten unabdingbar ist. Die Ereignisse der vergangenen zwei Jahre haben aufgezeigt, wie wichtig dieser Aspekt ist. Der ungedeckte Geldmarkt ist in der Finanzmarktkrise praktisch versiegt oder wurde prohibitiv teuer, und die Geschftsbanken mussten sich ber andere Wege, nicht zuletzt ber den gedeckten Geldmarkt, refinanzieren. Und drittens wollte die SNB mit der Einfhrung des Repomarktes auch eine effiziente und flexible Plattform fr Handel und Abwicklung von Geldmarktgeschften schaffen. Das im internationalen Vergleich relativ spte Entstehen eines Repomarktes in der Schweiz hatte auch Vorteile. Es konnte ein zeitgemsses System eingefhrt werden, ohne dass auf Bestehendes Rcksicht genommen werden musste. Das Ergebnis war denn auch ein System, das immer noch als weltweit fhrend gilt. Erfolgsfaktoren waren die Prinzipien Standardisierung, Automatisierung, Integration und Offenheit, auf denen der Franken-Repomarkt basiert. Die Transaktionen sind bezglich Collateral-Korb, Kontrakttyp und andern Spezifikationen standardisiert, werden automatisiert auf der elektronischen Handelsplattform Eurex Repo abgeschlossen und danach voll integriert ber das Wertschriftenabwicklungssystem 2 Die Fixierung des Reposatzes ist transparenter als ein impliziter Zinssatz bei Devisenswaps, der aus dem Wechselkurs und der Zinsdifferenz hergeleitet werden muss. 3 SECOM der SIX SIS und das Echtzeit-Zahlungssystem SIC der SIX SIC abgewickelt. Diese einzigartige Integration von Handel und Abwicklung wird als Swiss Value Chain bezeichnet. Der Franken-Repomarkt steht Teilnehmern im Ausland offen und erlaubt Collateral in fremden Whrungen. Es wurde zudem auch grossen Wert auf eine umfassende Risikoreduktion gelegt: Die Abwicklung der Geschfte beruht auf dem Prinzip "Lieferung gegen Bezahlung", d.h. die Wertschriften und das Geld werden zeitgleich endgltig bertragen. Ausserdem wird das Risikomanagement des Repo-Geschftes, d.h. der Wertausgleich, whrend dessen Laufzeit automatisch durchgefhrt: Zweimal tglich werden Ausgleichslieferungen vorgenommen. Da dem Geldgeber das Collateral whrend der Laufzeit des Repos zur freien Verfgung steht, bleibt seine Liquiditt erhalten. Im internationalen Vergleich unblich ist zudem, dass der Interbanken-Repomarkt und die Repogeschfte zur Implementierung der Geldpolitik dieselbe Plattform benutzen und denselben Collateralanforderungen unterliegen, die von der SNB definiert werden. Dies bedingt eine enge Zusammenarbeit zwischen der SNB und dem Privatsektor (Banken, Eurex, SIX SIS, SIX SIC) bei Aufbau, Betrieb und Weiterentwicklung des Systems. Die Schaffung des neuen Marktes ging sehr zgig vonstatten. 1996 beschloss die SNB, das Repo-Geschft als ordentliches Instrument einzufhren. 1997 wurde die Entwicklung des Reposystems in Angriff genommen. Erste Repo-Transaktionen fanden 1998 statt. Seit 1999 stellt die SNB ihre Basis- und Feinsteuerungsliquiditt weitgehend ber Repo-Auktionen und Repo-Einzelgeschfte zur Verfgung. Im gleichen Jahr wurde die Innertagsfazilitt zur Erleichterung des Zahlungsverkehrs eingefhrt. Die zunchst nur als Ergnzung zum bestehenden Instrumentarium vorgesehenen Repos ersetzten schon sehr rasch alle bisherigen ordentlichen geldpolitischen Instrumente (Abbildung 1). Im Jahr 2005 wurde schliesslich das Lombard-Geschft aufgehoben und durch die Engpassfinanzierungsfazilitt ersetzt. Bei beiden Fazilitten erfolgt der Bezug von Liquiditt ber den Abschluss von RepoGeschften. In den ersten Jahren seines Bestehens war der Franken-Repomarkt vor allem durch die von der SNB gettigten Umstze geprgt, die ber die Jahre relativ konstant blieben. Die zwischen den Geschftsbanken gehandelten Umstze hingegen erlebten ein rasantes Wachstum. Sie stiegen von durchschnittlich 1 Mrd. Franken pro Tag im Jahre 1999 auf ber 10 Mrd. Franken pro Tag im vergangenen Jahr (Abbildungen 2 und 3). Auch die Zahl der 4 Teilnehmer ist deutlich von ca. 30 anfangs 1999 auf aktuell rund 150 gestiegen, wobei das Wachstum zwei Schbe erlebte: Ein erster Schub erfolgte 1999 als Folge befrchteter Liquidittsengpsse aufgrund des Jahr-2000-Problems. Ein zweiter Schub erfolgte in der jngsten Finanzmarktkrise, die den Nutzen des gesicherten Geschftes besonders augenfllig werden liess (Abbildung 4). Im internationalen Vergleich wohl einmalig ist die Internationalitt des Franken-Repomarktes. Banken im Ausland machen einen bedeutenden Teil der Teilnehmer und des Umsatzes aus. In der Finanzmarktkrise stieg deren Bedeutung nochmals an (Abbildung 5). Die Ziele, die sich die SNB bei der Einfhrung des Franken-Repomarktes vor 10 Jahren gesteckt hatte, konnten weitestgehend erreicht werden. Das Repo-Instrument hat aufgrund seiner Vorteile in normalen Zeiten innert krzester Zeit smtliche anderen Instrumente ersetzt. Das geldpolitische Konzept der SNB, das auf der Steuerung des 3M-Libors basiert und ber Repo-Geschfte implementiert wird, hat sich als sehr flexibel und ntzlich erwiesen. Dank dem Repo-Geschft konnte die SNB den 3M-Libor auch in der Krise gut steuern (Abbildung 6), auch wenn das Erreichen der gewnschten Zielgrsse aufgrund hoher Risikoprmien manchmal lngere Zeit in Anspruch nahm. Die Erwartung, dass mit dem Repogeschft ein Beitrag zur Systemstabilitt geleistet werden knne, wurde ebenfalls erfllt. Der Franken-Repomarkt hat auch in den letzten zwei schwierigen Jahren gut funktioniert und den Banken, die ber gengend hochwertiges Collateral verfgten, eine problemlose Refinanzierung ermglicht. Die Plattform konnte zudem verwendet werden, um weitere Instrumente wie die SNB Bills einzufhren. Diese dienen der Abschpfung von Liquiditt und erhhen somit die Flexibilitt der Geldpolitik. Den SNB Bills wird beim bergang von der aktuellen Nullzinspolitik zu einer regulren Zinssteuerung eine wichtige Rolle zukommen. Die Krise hat aber auch einige Grenzen offengelegt. Trotz der Sicherung durch Wertschriften haben bestimmte Geldgeber Zweifel an der Qualitt der Gegenpartei und/oder des Collaterals erkennen lassen. Und trotz der Offenheit und Internationalitt der Plattform wurde es letzten Herbst notwendig, wieder auf das Instrument des Devisenswaps zurckzugreifen, um die Liquidittsnachfrage von Banken im Ausland, die nicht an den Franken-Repomarkt angeschlossen waren oder nicht ber gengend notenbankfhiges Collateral verfgten, zu 5 befriedigen (Abbildung 7). Die Liquiditt des Franken-Repomarktes war zudem nicht jederzeit optimal. Um den erkannten Grenzen zu begegnen, prft die SNB mehrere Ideen. Dazu gehren die Einfhrung von Cash Collateral, was faktisch einem Devisenswap in Form eines Repogeschftes gleichkommt, und die Ausweitung des Teilnehmerkreises, mglicherweise auch auf Nichtbanken. Ferner wird auch geprft, ob die Einfhrung einer zentralen Gegenpartei das Vertrauen in das System erhhen knnte. Ziel ist es letztlich, die Liquiditt des Repomarktes zu steigern und somit dafr zu sorgen, dass die Erfolgsgeschichte Franken-Repomarkt in den kommenden 10 Jahren eine Fortsetzung finden wird. 6 Abbildung 1 Abbildung 2 7 Abbildung 3 Abbildung 4 8 Abbildung 5 Abbildung 6 9 Abbildung 7 10

Title: Saron - An innovation for the financial markets
text: Embargo: 11.30 a.m., 25 August 2009 SARON  An innovation for the financial markets Thomas J. Jordan Member of the Governing Board Swiss National Bank* Launch event for Swiss Reference Rates Hotel Widder, Zurich 25 August 2009 , Zurich/Berne 2009 1 Introduction For monetary policy and the financial markets alike, informative and reliable reference rates are extremely important. Since January 2000, the Swiss National Bank (SNB) has used the steering of the interest rate level in the Swiss franc money market as a tool to implement its monetary policy decisions. Both the secured and unsecured money market play an important role in this. The SNB uses the three-month Swiss franc Libor as the reference rate for monetary policy, and sets a target range for the Libor. The level of the target range is determined by the need for monetary policy action, which itself is mainly dictated by the inflation forecast. The SNB steers the three-month Libor by concluding repo transactions with its counterparties. For market participants, reference rates are the basis for fair pricing of loans and derivatives. Lack of reference rates for the secured Swiss franc money market Since 1989, the Libor has been fixed daily in London by the British Bankers Association (BBA) on the basis of reports from 12 international banks. The Libor reflects conditions on the unsecured money market, and contains a credit risk and liquidity premium. The SNB chose the three-month Libor as its monetary policy reference rate because, in economic terms, it is the most important Swiss franc money market rate and thus plays a key role in the monetary policy transmission mechanism. In the light of the growing doubts expressed about the Libor during the financial crisis, the SNB decided to re-examine its relevance and usefulness as an indicator. The examination showed that there was no evidence of a systematic distortion in the Swiss franc Libor and that the Libor continues to have very high economic relevance in Switzerland. For example, the three-month Libor is an important reference variable in loan pricing (cf. chart 1), and plays a key role in the pricing of financial contracts and derivatives, whereas other reference variables such as the TOIS curve are hardly used at all. The Libor is even used in cases where the characteristics of unsecured money market business  which contains a credit risk and liquidity premium  play little or no role in price determination. The SNB can only operate in the secured money market, as it can only lend money to banks on a collateralised basis. Thus, to implement its monetary policy, the SNB needs an efficient secured money market whose impulses are passed through effectively to interest rates in the unsecured market. To this end, it set up the repo market ten years ago, and uses repo transactions as the most important instrument for steering the three-month Libor. And it has stood up well during the financial crisis. But for the SNB, the repo market is not just important for steering the Libor: it is also absolutely central to ensuring system stability. For reasons of systemic stability, the majority of interbank business should be conducted via the secured money market. A well-functioning repo market is vital for ensuring the flow of liquidity during a crisis. Over these past two turbulent years, the Swiss franc repo market has functioned well and has proved to be a valuable source of refinancing for banks with sufficient high-quality collateral. What has so far been missing for the secured Swiss franc money market, or the Swiss franc repo market, is a system of reference rates. Introduction of the Swiss Reference Rates To take account of both the growing importance of the repo market and the market demand for reference rates for secured business, the Swiss Reference Rates were developed jointly by the SNB and the Swiss stock exchange. What is the intended role of the Swiss Reference 2 Rates? First, the introduction of these rates gives a further boost to the Swiss franc repo market. The rates will make it easier for market participants to use repos as a short-term refinancing and investment instrument for liquidity management purposes. The Swiss Reference Rates provide participants with clear cost/benefit benchmarks for their liquidity management. This increases the attractiveness of the Swiss franc repo market even further. Second, the rates will provide a stable benchmark for financial instruments which are not priced on the basis of a variable credit risk and liquidity premium. Third, for the SNB, the Swiss Reference Rates represent a kind of barometer with which it can gauge conditions on the Swiss franc money market in real time. This allows it to better monitor developments on the money market and, consequently, to optimise the timing of interest rate steering operations. The new reference rates differ from the Libor in a few significant ways. First, the Swiss Reference Rates are based on data from the secured money market, whereas the Libor reflects conditions on the unsecured market. Second, the calculation of the Swiss Reference Rates takes into account concluded repo transactions and trade quotes posted on the Eurex Zurich trading platform. This covers transactions and quotes from all repo participants (currently around 150 banks). The Libor, on the other hand, is fixed on the basis of nonbinding prices reported by a panel of 12 banks. And while the Libor contains a credit risk and liquidity premium, with the Swiss Reference Rates, counterparty and liquidity risks are negligible. The Swiss Reference Rates thus show little reaction to changes in bank confidence levels. A glance beyond Switzerlands borders shows that the Swiss Reference Rates are also innovative in international terms. This is not only due to the calculation method, which takes both concluded transactions and quotes into account, but also because the entire maturity spectrum of the secured money market is covered, rather than only the call rate. A reference rate must provide a representative picture of market events, in order for it to be accepted by the market and regularly used for transactions. If we compare the volume of business underlying SARON with the corresponding volume for EONIA, we can see that SARON is supported by very healthy volumes (cf. chart 2). Indeed, this even increased during the crisis, reaching around CHF 14 billion on average. The decline during the later stages of the crisis was the result of the massive liquidity injections by the SNB, which rendered part of interbank business superfluous. Importance of the Swiss Reference Rates for the SNB Using the Swiss Reference Rates, the SNB can better monitor developments on the money market, enabling it to optimise interest rate steering operations. The SNB sees the overnight rate, SARON, as particularly important, since up to now there has not been an overnight rate with high relevance for the financial markets, either for secured or for unsecured transactions. For this reason, the Swiss franc interest rate curve calculation will in future be based on SARON, since this rate reacts most strongly to conditions on the repo market and serves as a general indicator of changes in short-term rates. SARON replaces the Repo Overnight Index (SNB), which was previously used by the SNB as the basis for calculating the special rate for the liquidity-shortage financing facility and the penalty rate for non-compliance with the minimum reserve requirements. This function will now be performed by SARON. 3 In many countries, overnight rates act as reference rates for monetary policy  either explicitly, as with the federal funds rate of the US Federal Reserve, or implicitly, such as EONIA for the European Central Bank. SARON will also play a key role for the SNB and the financial markets, but its introduction does not signal a change to the SNBs monetary policy stance. The use of the three-month Libor as a monetary policy reference rate, and its indirect steering via repo transactions, have proved their worth over many years, including during the crisis. So long as the Libor retains its economic significance, there is no reason to switch to another reference rate. Importance of the Swiss Reference Rates for the market The introduction of the Swiss Reference Rates completes the range of reference rates for the Swiss franc money market, since it represents an important complement to the Swiss franc Libor and the TOIS fixing. The Swiss Reference Rates can be used as a benchmark for secured loans, as well as for a host of different financial market instruments. As regards derivatives, they are suitable for use in interest rate swaps, overnight indexed swaps, futures and forwards. They can also be used for traditional money market investments, such as setting interest rates on money market accounts, or for structured products and exchange traded funds. Concretely, we might see the creation of, say, a SARON swap. This would be comparable to the existing TOIS, with the SARON fixing being used as the variable interest rate instead of the TOIS fixing. A comparison of the movements in the SARON and TOIS fixings over the past year shows that SARONs volatility was considerably lower (cf. chart 3). The volatility of the TOIS fixing was six times higher on average, especially during the most turbulent phase of the crisis, following the collapse of Lehman Brothers. In calmer times, the TOIS fixings volatility only diverges from that of SARON at month-end, as a result of the change in month. In October 2008, the collapse of Lehman Brothers led to severe tension on the unsecured Swiss franc money market, as a number of foreign banks were confronted with tighter refinancing conditions. The excess demand for Swiss franc liquidity caused a rise in the liquidity component of the risk premium, which in turn led to a marked increase in the TOIS fixing. By contrast, the turbulence on the money market during that period had no effect on SARON. Swap sellers (fixed rate receivers) using the TOIS suffered heavy losses. Depending on the reason for concluding a swap (hedging interest rate risk, speculating on changes in interest rates or taking advantage of opportunities for arbitrage), SARON can offer advantages over other reference rates. Conclusion The introduction of the Swiss Reference Rates creates a risk-neutral Swiss franc interest rate curve which complements the Swiss franc Libor and the TOIS fixing and is calculated in Switzerland. The SNB attaches particular importance to SARON. It will be a key reference variable for the repo business which lies at the heart of our monetary policy. But the Swiss Reference Rates offer new possibilities for all innovative market participants. The SNB is keen to see the Swiss Reference Rates establishing themselves in the market. It has thus been heavily involved in the development of these rates, and will continue to promote them in the future. 4 Chart 1 Reference rates for loan pricing Government bonds TOIS Repo rates SNB rates Internal curve Libor based 0% 20% 40% 60% 80% 100% Source: SNB 3 Launch event for Swiss Reference Rates Thomas J.
