Title: President's address to the General Meeting of Shareholders
text: Embargo: Friday, 30 April 2010, 10.00 Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 30 April 2010 Adjusting the policy on provisions Dear Shareholders Ladies and Gentlemen Dear Guests In December 2009, the SNB announced that over the next few years it would be increasing the allocation to its provisions. By adjusting its policy on provisions, the National Bank aims to strengthen its equity capital. I would like to use todays occasion to explain to you the background and the significance of this decision. Swiss National Bank equity capital The provisions constitute the most important part of the SNBs equity capital. They are accrued from retained profits and have essentially two functions. First, they serve to finance the currency reserves. According to the National Bank Act, the SNB is required to accrue provisions that allow it to maintain its currency reserves at a level that is adequate for its monetary policy. Second, the provisions have the traditional function of equity capital: they must be large enough to absorb even exceptional losses. Equity capital also consists  along with the provisions  of the distribution reserve. While the level of the provisions reflects the targeted equity capital, the distribution reserve is of a temporary nature, in that it is used to smooth the annual SNB profit distribution payments to the Confederation and cantons. The SNB tempers the effects of large fluctuations in the annual results by allocating a portion of the distributable profits in good years to the distribution reserve. These funds are available for distribution at a later date. In this way, in leaner years the SNB can resort to the distribution reserve and thereby continue to carry out the agreed profit distribution. Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 30 April 2010 2 Increase in assets Why was it necessary to adjust the policy on provisions? As you know, since the onset of the financial and economic crisis the SNBs balance sheet has almost doubled. Higher currency reserves account for a major part of this. In 2009 alone, these reserves increased by more than CHF 50 billion, due largely to the SNBs purchase of foreign exchange to counter the threat of deflation. In the same year, the value of gold climbed by more than CHF 7 billion. Furthermore, the loan to the stabilisation fund set up by the SNB to take over illiquid assets from UBS lengthened the SNB balance sheet by a further CHF 20 billion. While the stabilisation fund will be gradually phased out, the additional currency reserves are set to remain on the balance sheet for some while to come. In the past, the SNBs currency reserves have tended to be relatively low, owing to the fact that over the years the level of reserves had not kept pace with the extensive and steadily growing integration of the Swiss economy and financial centre into the global economic system. Although it was not necessary to tap into the currency reserves during the recent crisis, their presence nevertheless contributed to the SNBs credibility and ability to act. The crisis demonstrated the importance of being equipped to deal with the unexpected. Sufficient currency reserves are essential if the National Bank is to be able to act rapidly and autonomously. Provisions unchanged The additional foreign exchange reserves, the valuation gains on gold, and the stabilisation fund together constitute a significant increase in risky assets on the balance sheet. Because there has been no corresponding increase in the provisions to offset this, the provisions to risky assets ratio has deteriorated significantly. This applies also more generally to the total equity capital. Taking into account the distribution reserve, the SNBs equity capital at the end of 2009 amounted to approximately CHF 63 billion. Almost a third of this was made up of the distribution reserve. The reserve, as part of the equity capital, also serves to absorb losses. However, once the existing distribution reserve has Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 30 April 2010 3 been depleted, the equity capital will consist almost solely of the provisions. In the absence of other measures, the SNB would then be confronted with a provisions to risky assets ratio which would, again, have deteriorated. Its ability to absorb even substantial losses using its equity capital would therefore be less assured. Adjusting the rule for allocation to the provisions To avoid this predictable scenario, the SNB has decided to gradually increase its provisions. In the past, the SNB has increased these provisions year-on-year at a rate equivalent to average nominal GDP growth for the preceding five years. This transparent approach has proved its worth, and we will continue to adhere to the principle of allocating the provisions according to a fixed rule and taking account of nominal GDP growth. What is new, however, is that henceforth, the provisions will increase at double this growth rate. Thus the allocation for 2009, instead of being CHF 1.5 billion as per the original rule, now amounts to CHF 3 billion. The adjustment to the allocation rule  seen from the current perspective  applies to the financial years 2009 to 2013. Influence on profit distribution This measure affects future distributions in two opposing ways. In the short term, the additional provisions will not be available for distribution. The measure therefore reduces the potential for distribution. In the long term, however, the increase in assets will contribute to a rise in earnings potential. Moreover, as the higher level of assets will be financed in the future by more equity capital, there will also be less interest on borrowed capital, and this, too, will increase the potential for distribution. The current agreement on profit distribution between the Swiss National Bank and the Federal Department of Finance still applies. It envisages until 2017 an annual distribution to the Confederation and cantons of CHF 2.5 billion, and from the current perspective, it appears likely that this distribution will be met. I must, however, explicitly stress the qualification from the current perspective. As we have always made clear, the SNB earnings can fluctuate substantially from one year to the next. They are particularly susceptible to movements in exchange rates and the gold price, and major losses can Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 30 April 2010 4 never be completely ruled out. In the event of serious losses, profit distribution could be affected. The agreement caters for this scenario with different measures, which, depending on the level of the distribution reserve, range from a review of the agreement to a reduction or suspension of the distribution. Irrespective of this, the agreement is due to undergo a routine review in 2013. Concluding remarks The SNB balance sheet remained largely robust even during the financial and economic crisis. On the one hand, this is due to the foresight and long-term thinking underpinning the profit distribution agreement. When the agreement was revised in the early nineties, it was determined that each year a portion of the annual profits would be allocated to the provisions. This has ensured a consistent increase in the SNBs equity capital despite the rise over the years in the distributions. The decision taken at that time to couple the accrual of equity capital with the distribution of profit has since proved its worth. On the other hand, the SNB has also benefited from the exceptional rise in recent years in the price of gold. That we have, at CHF 19 billion, a very solid distribution reserve at our disposal is due almost solely to this surge in the gold price. Therefore I want to point out that favourable market conditions as well as responsible management have contributed towards the healthy state of our balance sheet. However, as has been amply demonstrated, we cannot afford to rely on favourable market conditions. The SNB balance sheet is in its current state by virtue of events which, in the time leading up to their occurrence, seemed very unlikely indeed. Nobody can predict what surprises the next few years have in store for us. It is our duty, therefore, to equip ourselves against the possibility of serious shocks. The fact is the current resilience of our balance sheet depends to a large extent on the size of the distribution reserve. Once the existing reserve has been depleted, should major shocks subsequently occur, those shocks would have to be absorbed by the provisions alone. Presidents address by Hansueli Raggenbass, SNB President of the Bank Council, to the General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank, 30 April 2010 5 Against this backdrop, the Bank Council and the Governing Board have decided to adopt a forward-looking approach and begin taking the necessary steps to ensure the long-term strength of the balance sheet. Increasing the allocations to the provisions will help to ensure that the SNB balance sheet continues to meet the high demands on its robustness even after the distribution reserve has been depleted. It means that the SNB will continue to have at its disposal the currency reserves necessary for the fulfilment of its responsibilities, and it will ensure that in future crises, it still has the leeway it needs to carry out its monetary policy. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Monetary policy challenges and the Swiss real estate market
text: Embargo: 28 October 2010, at 16:30 THE CHALLENGES OF MONETARY POLICY AND THE REAL ESTATE MARKET PHILIPP M. HILDEBRAND* PRESIDENT OF THE EXECUTIVE BOARD OF THE SWISS NATIONAL BANK Ticino Economy Day Lugano, 28 October 2010 * The speaker thanked Gregor Be4urle, Robert Bichsel, Rita Kobel Rohr and Attilio Zanetti for their valuable contributions to the writing of this paper. (c) Swiss National Bank, Zurich 2010 Introduction Ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to be here with you today in Ticino and thank you for your friendly welcome. The SNB fulfils its legal mandate in the general interest of the country. That is why it is very important for me and for my colleagues in the Branch to periodically visit all regions of our country. Even in normal times, monetary policy is a very varied task. In exceptional times, such as the one we are currently experiencing, it faces significant challenges. Importance of the real estate market In my presentation today, I will discuss developments in the real estate market. This market occupies a central position, in the true sense of the word. It is central because it brings together various actors in economic life: on the one hand, construction companies, in the broad sense, and on the other, tenants and owners of buildings1. As you know, both households and businesses give their buildings as collateral when taking credit. Banks are also important players as mortgage lenders. The real estate market also plays a central role in economic developments. Its influence on the entire economy is manifested in particular during real estate crises. History shows it eloquently: recessions that result from both a financial and real estate crisis last longer and are more severe than others2. The evolution we are currently witnessing is further proof of this. Countries that have weathered the financial crisis without experiencing disruptions in the housing market are recovering relatively quickly from a recession. On the other hand, the economies hit 1 In Switzerland, about half of private wealth is invested in real estate, i.e. 42.6% of gross wealth and 54% of net worth ( gross wealth minus debts); status at the end of 2008, source: BNS. 2 See also Carmen M. Reinhart and Kenneth S. Rogoff, This time is different, Eight Centuries of Financial Folly, 2009. 2 simultaneously by a financial crisis and by a real estate crisis recover only very slowly. The United States is now the most telling example of this. But the United Kingdom, Ireland and Spain, countries where the recovery is very slow, have also suffered the effects of the bursting of a housing bubble in recent years; you can see it on this graph. During the financial crisis, Switzerland did not suffer a real estate crisis. Our country experienced "its" real estate crisis in the nineties. Construction has not been the only branch affected by the serious consequences of this crisis. Until 1995, the Swiss economy had not grown much. Households and businesses suffered significant wealth losses, while unemployment jumped and then remained high for several years. In such a context, it is not surprising that consumption has increased slightly for about five years. In addition, banks have had to deal with a huge volume of bad debts. And consolidation and consolidation measures have taken years. I am convinced that if Switzerland has not yet experienced a new real estate crisis, it owes it in part to the dramatic experiences of the early nineties. 3 The central importance of the real estate market for an economy is widely recognized. On the other hand, there is somewhat less unanimity with regard to the factors that could ultimately be at the origin of a real estate crisis3. There is some evidence to suggest that monetary aspects play a certain role. The role of monetary policy Let me make a small digression here. As you know, the main monetary policy instrument for managing the economy is a nominal interest rate. For this purpose, the SNB uses the three-month Libor as the reference rate. With each monetary policy decision, the following question arises: what nominal interest rate affects the incentives of the actors of an economy in such a way that price stability is ensured in the medium and long term? By price stability, the SNB means an increase in prices of less than 2% and the prevention of deflation. Since the end of 2008, the SNB has been pursuing an expansionary monetary policy with a view to ensuring price stability in our economy. Interest rates are close to zero. From March 2009, the SNB also took so-called unconventional measures - mainly in the form of foreign currency purchases - in order to bring about a clear easing of monetary conditions. At its last review of the economic and monetary situation in mid-September, the SNB decided - as you know - to continue its expansionary monetary policy. The SNB's conditional inflation forecast, which is our main indicator for assessing monetary policy, shows that this policy is currently appropriate. However, it cannot be ruled out that, in the event of a long phase of very low interest rates, imbalances may result in our economy. In the real estate market specifically, there is a risk of imbalances forming if interest rates remain at a very low level for a long time. This could lead to a 3 Cf. par exemple Jane Dokko, Brian Doyle, Michael T. Kiley, Jinill Kim, Shane Sherlund, Jae Sim et Skander Van den Heuvel, Monetary Policy and the Housing Bubble, Finance and Economics Discussion Series 2009-49. Washington: Conseil des gouverneurs du Syste8me de Re9serve fe9de9rale, de9cembre; ou John B. Taylor, Housing and Monetary Policy, NBER Working Paper Series 13682, Cambridge, Mass.: National Bureau of Economic Research, de9cembre 2007. 4 classic boom-bust cycle. And the dramatic consequences of such a cycle are all well known to us. In other words, even if the expansionary nature of monetary policy is appropriate for the economy as a whole, it may prove to be unoptimistic for some industries. Ladies and gentlemen, the question now arises as to whether imbalances are forming in the real estate market. Activity is now very strong in construction, especially in housing construction. More and more companies in this sector are announcing that they are reaching the limits of their capacities. If the currently very low interest rates contribute to the strong activity in construction, imbalances could occur in the real estate market. Regional disparities in price developments This is why I would now like to present some thoughts and assessments on the issue of sustainable developments in the real estate market. Let me start with the real aspects. I will therefore analyse the interactions between housing supply and demand and price developments. Housing prices have risen steadily in Switzerland since the turn of the century. On the graph, you can see the evolution of the prices of owner-occupied apartments per floor and detached houses4. 4 These are hedonistic indices of Wfcest & Partner's transaction prices. In addition to Wfcest & Partner, CIF AG and Fahrle4nder Partner AG also use hedonistic real estate price indices. In the short term, there are some divergent developments due to the use of various methods and, in part, different data sources. However, over longer periods, there is no noticeable difference. 5 The prices of owner-occupied apartments per floor have risen steadily since the turn of the century. However, an analysis of the Swiss real estate market must take into account the fact that this market is very heterogeneous. The demand for housing is characterized by large regional disparities. This is, of course, due to the geographical location; proximity to major centres, in particular, plays an important role. The possibility of expanding the offer is also very uneven depending on the location. This interaction between supply and demand can lead to divergent price developments at regional level. The histogram shows, for various regions and from 2001 to 2009, the relative frequency of price increases - on an annual average - of owner-occupied apartments per floor. In other words, it illustrates the share of the regions, in percentage, which corresponds to a given price increase. These regions, defined by the Federal Statistical Office, number 1065. 5 Spatial mobility region or MS region. This is a division of Switzerland into 106 regions which are characterised by a certain spatial homogeneity and follow the principles of small employment areas with a functional orientation towards regional centres (source: Federal Statistical Office, FSO). As for the prices indicated, these are hedonistic indices of Wfcest & Partner's transaction prices. 6 Let me draw your attention to two points. First, price increases range from 1% to 4% per year in most regions. They are thus rather moderate overall. However, there are - and this is the second point - some very marked increases, but these are exceptions. The regions with the largest increases were, as expected, Zurich and Geneva as well as the surrounding municipalities. These regions are characterised by very low supply and very high demand for housing. The following graph also illustrates this situation. 7 On the horizontal axis, you can see the vacancy rate, on average from 2001 to 2009, which is the ratio of vacant dwellings to the housing stock6. This rate is an indicator of the narrowness of supply in relation to existing demand. As for the vertical axis, it represents the annual average price increase, the same as in the previous graph. A more pronounced increase can be expected when supply is low relative to demand. This link is also visible on the graph. Indeed, prices have recorded the largest increases where supply is lowest relative to demand, i.e. where the vacancy rate is very low. To the extent that the rise in prices is related to the narrowness of the market, it can be deduced that this development is not explained by exaggerated expectations. On the other hand, if prices were to rise despite a large number of vacant homes, it would be a sign that weak supply is not the only factor pushing prices up. 6 Vacant dwellings are those offered for permanent rental or sale. According to the FSO's definition, detached houses are treated as dwellings. 8 This analysis shows that price developments in recent years appear to be broadly consistent with fundamental factors. However, it does not make it possible to make a definitive decision on the sustainable evolution of each segment of the market. But what are these fundamental factors that determine supply and demand? Income is the first important factor that determines demand. On the following graph, you can see the per capita income (red line) and the housing stock, in volume, also per capita (blue line)7. Per capita income rose sharply in the late eighties. The housing stock, on the other hand, has evolved in a much less dynamic way. The rather weak growth of the housing stock compared to the increase in income led, in the first phase, to a sharp rise in prices. An extension of the offer resulted, but with some delay. However, income growth has not been sustainable.8 Incomes fell significantly, while the supply of housing continued to rise. Prices then fell sharply in the early nineties, which eventually led to the real estate crisis in Switzerland. This experience shows that exaggerated fluctuations in income can cause unhealthy dynamics in the real estate sector. 7 The housing stock, in volume, is based on the FSO statistics on investment in housing construction. The figures for 2010 are based on an FSO forecast for investment in housing construction and on the FSO's demographic development scenario. Per capita income is gross domestic product per capita in real terms; the figures for 2010 are based on forecasts by the SNB and the FSO. 8 The strong income growth in the late eighties was partly the result of an overheating of the economy. Inflation reached 6.6% in mid-1991 and could only be combated by a resolute tightening of monetary policy. At the same time, the European economic environment deteriorated due to the rise in interest rates that followed the reunification of Germany. The combination of these two factors has led to a recession in the Swiss economy. 9 The demographic factor In the previous graph, income and housing stock are represented per capita. Population growth is not included; this growth also affects the "gap" between housing supply and demand. The supply of housing can generally only be adapted slowly, while the population is changing dynamically due to migratory flows. Some imbalances can therefore hardly be avoided temporarily. This can lead, for example, to supply-side bottlenecks and, as a result, to price increases. Several studies confirm that short-term price developments are closely correlated with demographic developments. Fundamental factors such as income and demographics therefore play an important role in the real estate market. Analyses by the SNB show that income increases and strong population growth, which has been observed in recent years, have led to a sharp surge in demand9. Between 2000 and 2009, the permanent resident population grew by almost 10% to 7.8 million people, mainly as a result of a net inflow of foreigners. The market 9 Different approaches to modelling the real estate market in Switzerland are published in the Swiss National Bank's Working Papers series: Christian Hott, Explaining House Prices Fluctuations, 2009 or Elisabeth Steiner, Estimating a stock-flow model for the Swiss housing market, 2010. 10 of housing has become ever narrower, and home ownership prices and rents have risen. In recent years, however, the very sustained activity in housing construction has made it possible to increase supply gradually. As a result, the ratio of supply to demand has become increasingly normalized, leading to a slight slowdown in price increases in some segments. Overall, the evolution of real estate prices seems to be explained by fundamental factors. Risks But why has the SNB been warning for some time about worrying developments in the real estate market? The SNB has a legal mandate to contribute to financial stability. Early identification of possible risks is one of the tasks of this mandate. Although the evolution of real estate prices seems to be based on fundamental factors and the SNB expects moderate growth in the housing market over the next twelve months - based on its baseline scenario- there is indeed reason to be concerned about risks. As I just mentioned, the real estate market is affected not only by income and demographics, but also by monetary factors. The costs of owning a home depend on the level of interest rates. This is why the expansionary monetary policy pursued since October 2008 has undoubtedly stimulated demand for home ownership. The longer expansionary monetary policy continues, the greater the danger of undesirable developments. Already today, there are some warning signs here and there. In some regions, very sharp increases in home ownership prices bear witness to this. In addition, it has been found that symptoms of speculative bubbles frequently follow large price increases due to fundamental factors. This situation has presented itself in the U.S. real estate market. According to estimates by 11 Until about 2004, with a few exceptions, the price increases were due to fundamental factors10. This development, which was healthy in itself, was however quickly enough packed up to lead to excessive momentum. As you know, the SNB has made it clear on several occasions in recent months that caution is required when granting mortgages. The current environment offers particularly favourable conditions for risk-taking: mortgage rates are low and competition in this market is fierce. Last spring, the SNB launched an extensive survey of the most important mortgage banks in Switzerland. The purpose of this survey was to examine the criteria by which mortgages are granted in practice. In recent months, the SNB has also held an intensive dialogue with bank managers. The results of the survey and discussions show that risks are multiplying in the mortgage market. The SNB has not found any systematic relaxation of the lending criteria. Some banks, however, stand out for their unceremonious application of these criteria. They take advantage of the room for manoeuvre allowed and even grant a significant proportion of credits that do not meet the criteria they have set. Another indication that there are current problems with the granting of credit is that some banks do not seem to be able to provide information on the effective application of the criteria for granting credit. This could mean that these banks have difficulty systematically assessing the risks of their debtors. In close cooperation with FINMA, the SNB will further strengthen monitoring in this area. The aim will be to be able to assess more reliably the risk appetite at the level of the individual bank, but also at the aggregate level. 10 Cf. par exemple Karl E. Case et Robert J. Shiller, Is There a Bubble in the Housing Market? Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Economic Studies Program, The Brookings Institution, vol. 34 (2003-2), pages 299-362, septembre 2003, ou Christian Hott et Pierre Monnin, Fundamental Real Estate Prices: An Empirical Estimation with International Data, The Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics, Springer, vol. 36 (4), pages 427450, mai 2008. 12 A more reliable risk assessment is particularly important for the development and implementation of targeted remedies. Banks themselves must be able, through responsible risk management, to contribute to the sustainability of the real estate market. The Swiss Bankers Association can also make an important contribution in this regard. In particular, when assessing the sustainability of debt servicing, it should not be forgotten that interest rates are now at a historically very low level. Borrowers, for their part, must be able to bear an increased interest burden if interest rates were to rise. Their situation would become particularly delicate in the event that, at the same time, real estate prices fell. The value of real estate would then decrease, while the volume of outstanding loans would remain constant. As a result, responsible risk management should also take into account the consequences of price reductions. But prices can also fall in the absence of significant imbalances in the real estate market. Underestimating risk when granting credit can ultimately amplify the effects of market fluctuations. If the share of debtors with repayment difficulties were to increase, banks would face a serious and growing challenge. Conclusion Ladies and gentlemen, I now come to the conclusion. As far as the Swiss real estate market is concerned, there is no reason to panic today. But there is also no need to give the signal of the end of the alert. As you may have inferred from what I have said, the rise in prices seems to be explained in recent years, with a few exceptions, by demographic and income developments. These exceptions are, however, warning signs. The risks to which we have been drawing attention for some time stem, in the first place, from the granting of mortgages. We must be well aware of the fact that interest rates are now at a historically very low level. On the other hand, the 13 competition is fierce in the mortgage market. That is why all parties should pay the utmost attention to signs of laxity in the granting of credit. Current experiences in the United States and our own experience in the early nineties have eloquently shown what serious consequences an unhealthy development can have on the real estate market. The SNB will therefore continue to closely monitor future developments in this market, in close cooperation with FINMA and the banks. If necessary, the authorities will not hesitate to take targeted corrective measures. The SNB will also examine the possibility of adopting macroprudential measures in addition to monetary policy. But don't get me wrong: banks and borrowers are not relieved of their responsibility to thoroughly monitor risks and assess the risks they can bear. We all have a common responsibility. Switzerland has weathered the most serious post-war global economic and financial crisis better than many countries. Gross domestic product has returned to its pre-crisis level. And, despite the difficulties endured, the current situation is looking good. It would therefore be regrettable to jeopardise these conditions conducive to employment and prosperity through irresponsible actions in the mortgage market. The SNB will continue to fulfil its mandate to make a contribution to financial stability and to make its expertise in this area fully available. To this end, it will have to resort, if necessary, to new instruments. Conventional monetary policy instruments cannot - and should not - solve all problems. Monetary policy remains focused on maintaining price stability in our country. This is the supreme objective of the SNB. Thank you for your attention. 14

Title: Monetary policy in turbulent times
text: Embargo until 4 November 2010, 18:00 Monetary policy in bad weather Jean-Pierre Danthine Member of the Executive Board of Swiss National Bank Aperitif Money Market Geneva, 4 November 2010 ___________________________ , Zurich, 2010 Introduction Ladies and gentlemen, let me welcome you to this money market aperitif, an event that the Swiss National Bank (SNB) has been organising every six months for almost four years now. As you all know, the last four years have been characterised by radical changes in the economic and financial landscape, both globally and in Switzerland. I would like to take this opportunity to present to you, firstly, our vision of the situation in which the Swiss economy finds itself as a result of these transformations, and secondly to describe the measures that the SNB has introduced into its policy to deal with this new situation. These measures consist of the use of so-called non-conventional monetary policy tools, an adaptation of monetary policy instruments and proposals for a regulatory framework aimed at reducing the problem posed by so-called "too big to fail" banks. Current economic situation I would therefore like to begin by outlining the current economic situation in Switzerland. For this, a return to the global situation is necessary. It is clear, ladies and gentlemen, that three years after the first signs of the crisis and two years after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, a new global economy is emerging. On the surface, however, little seems to have changed! Indeed, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts 4.8% global growth for 2010 and 4.2% for 2011, the same rate on average as that observed during the five years preceding the crisis. However, the comparison stops there for two reasons: firstly, because these forecasts are unusually uncertain and, above all, secondly, because there is an incredible heterogeneity of situations behind these simple figures. 2 For most, if not all, emerging markets, the crisis has passed and GDP levels are currently higher than before the crisis. This is not the case for Western economies or for Japan. In the United States, for example, there are still questions about the possibility of a "double-dip" or the emergence of deflation. Moreover, the crisis has left deep wounds in Western economies: high public and private debt, high unemployment rates, vulnerabilities in banking sectors and depressed real estate markets. Do these handicaps doom growth? We do not think so. Indeed, we still expect moderate growth in the global economy. These expectations correspond to the main scenario of the SNB and the IMF. However, this scenario is fragile and fraught with dangers, which leads to a sense of vulnerability and, consequently, significant market volatility. Thus, since our assessment of the economic and monetary situation in June, economic activity in the United States and Asia has rather slowed down. Although this slowdown was partially offset by the dynamism of the European economy (Germany in particular), we have revised our growth forecasts slightly downwards. In this context, we can say that the Swiss economy stands out positively. Even though the latest SECO statistics show that the crisis has been deeper than we initially estimated, growth since then has been more dynamic than the first figures at our disposal showed us. Between the third quarter of 2009 and the second quarter of 2010, real economic activity approached its potential. The recovery was particularly significant in industry, a sector hit hard by the 2009 recession. However, other sectors have also benefited from this dynamism and the growth in activity has had a favourable impact on the labour market. Unemployment peaked at 4.2%, significantly below our fears. It has since fallen back to a level of 3.5%. Moreover, Swiss GDP has surpassed its pre-crisis level, which is an almost unique case among developed economies. For 2010, we estimate that real GDP will grow by about 3 2.5%, mainly due to the performance achieved in the first half of this year. However, the strong appreciation of the Swiss franc, coupled with the weakening of global growth, should act as a powerful brake and lead to a marked slowdown in growth in the second half of this year and early next year. As a result, we expect next year to perform significantly lower than this year. What about inflation? We believe that it is under control (see Figure 1). Under the assumption of an unchanged three-month Libor rate, the SNB expects an inflation rate of 0.7% in 2010, 0.3% in 2011 and 1.2% in 2012. We cannot rule out that inflation may be temporarily negative in early 2011. However, these forecasts are questionable because of the current great uncertainty in the global economy. I would also like to add that if the downside risks to the economy materialise and result in a danger of deflation, the SNB will then take all necessary measures to ensure price stability. It has already done so over the past two years using unconventional monetary policy measures, which I would now like to present to you. Unconventional monetary policy measures As you are no doubt aware, unconventional monetary policy measures have been the hot topic in the world of central bankers in recent quarters. They are still in the most important monetary areas at the global level. These measures arose from the impossibility for central banks to lower their key interest rates below zero. They aim to inject liquidity directly into the economy and/or apply downward pressure on long-term rates without using the traditional tool of the short-term policy rate. 4 Unconventional measures have been an important part of Swiss monetary policy since October 2008 and have had a significant impact on our balance sheet (see Chart 2). They consist of cross-currency swaps, long-term repo operations, purchases of private bonds and foreign exchange market interventions. Cross-currency swaps made up the bulk of unconventional measures in 2009. This is no longer the case as swaps have been phased out of the balance sheet as their expiry date matured when their renewal was no longer justified. Long-term rest operations have disappeared for the same reasons. Purchases of private bonds peaked a year ago, in September 2009, at a nominal value of just over 3 billion Swiss francs. By this time, the credit market in Switzerland had stabilized and risk premia had returned to normal levels. As a result, procurement operations were interrupted. The SNB benefited from favourable credit market conditions and the market appetite for private bonds evident in the summer of 2010. It thus liquidated its portfolio of domestic bonds, which was the result of non-conventional transactions. Interventions in the foreign exchange market were the last and most discussed of the unconventional measures used by the SNB. The first interventions took place in March 2009. At the time, the SNB had reduced its Libor target band to between 0.0% and 0.75% with the objective of the lower part of this interval. The room for manoeuvre of the Libor rate, which is the traditional instrument of monetary policy, was therefore concretely exhausted. The purchase of foreign currency was then an alternative instrument to combat the risk of deflation. Before judging the effectiveness of interventions in the foreign exchange market, I would like to stress, ladies and gentlemen, that this assessment must necessarily be made in terms of the SNB's mandate. The latter consists in guaranteeing price stability. In the context of the economic crisis, guaranteeing price stability meant avoiding the risk of deflation! 5 This mandate has been fulfilled through our expansive monetary policy. We have not seen deflation in Switzerland and inflation forecasts indicate that prices will be stable in the coming quarters. In addition, the current health of the Swiss economy can be considered satisfactory when compared with the situation of our neighbours or with the scenarios that concerned us last year. The facts therefore provide us with prima facie evidence that unconventional monetary policy measures have been successful. Going further in the analysis requires moving from concrete facts to unobserved hypotheses. In other words, to answer the question: what would have happened if the SNB had not intervened? Let me just tell you that this step can only be taken with great modesty because we have only a very partial knowledge of the functioning of the economy in general and the foreign exchange market in particular. The most visible consequence of our interventions in the foreign exchange market is the increase in our balance sheet, in particular our foreign exchange reserves. This increase implies significantly higher exchange rate risks for the SNB. It is true that market developments have led to significant accounting losses on foreign exchange positions for the SNB at this time of year. However, the SNB is not a commercial bank whose performance must be measured by its ability to generate profits. Again, a central bank must be assessed for its ability to fulfil its mandate, which is to ensure price stability. For a commercial bank, losses are "negative profits"; for a central bank, losses are costs that may be the consequence of fulfilling its mandate. The greatest contribution to the overall well-being that a central bank can make is to ensure price stability. With regard to costs, it is important to reiterate that the monthly or quarterly assessment of our foreign exchange reserves provides little information content. It is as futile to criticize interventions on the basis of monthly or quarterly losses as it would be to celebrate them on the basis of gains at the end of a month or a month. 6 quarter. It is clearly in the medium and long term that we can properly assess the financial consequences of our interventions. Interventions that are, I repeat once again, motivated solely by the conduct of monetary policy and our mandate to ensure price stability, not by financial considerations. Unconventional monetary policy measures have therefore enabled the SNB to fulfil its mandate. However, they have also led to the injection of a significant amount of liquidity into the economy. This influx of liquidity changed the situation for the SNB and led it to use new instruments for the conduct of monetary policy. It is on these new instruments and their goals that Sebastien Kraenzlin will come back in more detail after my speech. Development of measures to deal with the problem "too big to fail" Ladies and gentlemen, to conclude my presentation, I would like to say a few words about one of the latest actions in which the SNB has actively collaborated in order to adapt to the new global economic situation: the development of measures to deal with the problem of so-called "too big to fail" institutions. These measures are intended to reduce the risks that systemically important banks pose to the Swiss economy. The SNB therefore wants these measures to be adopted as soon as possible. Indeed, as the recent global financial crisis has clearly shown, the failure of one of our two major banks would pose a major risk to the Swiss economy. Such a failure would jeopardize the stability of the financial system and indirectly affect all branches of the real economy. In the event of a crisis, the State could not afford to let disappear an actor whose systemically important functions are not guaranteed. As you know, the problem of "too big to fail" is particularly acute in Switzerland. Indeed, the balance sheets of the two major banks are still about four times the national GDP. The measures proposed by the expert group, of which the SNB was a member, concern four areas: equity, organisation, liquidity and the distribution of 7 Risks. Firstly, the expert group proposes to significantly increase the capital of systemically important banks. It proposes to divide this capital into three "layers": the first to maintain the normal activities of banks, the second to absorb possible losses and the third for crisis management and to encourage banks to reduce their systemic importance. One of the innovations proposed by the group of experts is to allow the use of contingent convertible bonds or "CoCo bonds". These securities constitute bonds in the traditional sense of the term but they have the particularity of being transformed into equity capital at the time when the latter falls below a minimum threshold. The first layer of equity will have to be composed of shares with 4.5% of risk-weighted assets, the second with 5.5% of shares and 3% of CoCos and the last layer of 6% of CoCos. That is a total of 19% of equity divided between 10% of shares and 9% of Cocos (see Figure 3). The second measure proposed by the expert group concerns the organisation of the large banks. It requires the adoption of organisational measures to ensure the essential services of banks, even in times of crisis. These services cover the areas of payments, deposits and credits. In the event that a bank takes organisational measures that exceed the authorities' expectations, it could benefit from a capital discount. These two main requirements are complemented by stricter liquidity requirements as well as a limitation of interdependencies and risk concentration in the financial sector. In the event of a crisis, i.e. if a bank falls below a minimum of capital, the latter would then be reorganized to guarantee the essential services. CoCos bonds would be transformed into shares to guarantee the necessary capital for new entities. I will conclude by saying that the proposed measures are in line with the international standards prescribed by the Basel Committee. However, they go beyond 8 standards decided in Basel this summer, which did not yet take into account the problem of "too big to fail". As this is particularly acute in Switzerland, it is natural that our country should impose stricter measures to further reduce the risks and potential costs of the problem posed by "too big to fail" institutions. We are convinced that the measures proposed by the expert group, in which the major banks themselves were represented, are reasonable and likely to significantly reduce the problem posed by "too big to fail" institutions in Switzerland. The solution envisaged is innovative, coherent, and based on impeccable logic. In particular, it has the merit of involving creditors. In the event of bankruptcy, creditors are normally called upon. In return, they can be expected to play a supervisory role in the company they are financing. The impossibility of letting an institution fail "too big to fail" is above all an "undue" advantage granted to creditors who, assured of not being involved, lose all interest in monitoring and disciplining the company they finance. Coco bonds correct this major flaw in banking governance while providing the necessary funds to enable the maintenance of the bank's essential functions in the event of difficulties. The presence of these funds relieves the State and taxpayers all the more. But the incentive part of the proposed solution implies that the expected effect goes beyond this substitution effect alone. All in all, the effect on the economy will be positive, as both the real economy, the public sector and the financial sector should benefit from greater stability among the major Swiss banks. 9 Chart 1 10 Chart 2 11 Chart 3 New Capital requirements 6% CoCos 8.50% Max. 3% CoCos 4.50% Swiss Finish Progressive component Buffer Basis 12

Title: The new procedure for implementing monetary policy and how it is affecting the money market (summary)
text: Zurich, 24 March 2011 The new implementation of monetary policy and its impact on the money market (summary) Dewet Moser, Deputy Member of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank, Money Market Aperitif of the Swiss National Bank, Zurich, 24.03.2011 Since its inception, the Swiss National Bank (SNB) has implemented monetary policy by providing temporary liquidity. The banking system has traditionally been in a liquidity deficit vis-a-vis the SNB. By providing only temporary liquidity, the SNB forced banks to continuously request new liquidity. The SNB controlled the money market via the amount of liquidity injected and its interest rate. As part of the foreign exchange purchases from March 2009 to June 2010, the banking system was provided with unlimited liquidity totalling CHF 191 billion (see Figure 1). As a result, the liquidity deficit of the banking system resulted in a massive liquidity surplus (see Fig. 2). Banks' demand for liquidity gradually declined and came to a standstill in May 2010. Banks cannot independently reduce the excess liquidity present in the system. Only the SNB is in a position to manage overall liquidity. The existing excess liquidity required a new procedure for implementing monetary policy. No changes have been made to the monetary policy concept itself, with the definition of price stability, the inflation forecast and the setting of a target range for the three-month Libor. Maintaining price stability is and remains the primary objective. The new method for controlling interest rates is based on liquidity-absorbing open market operations (issuance of SNB bills and repo transactions) and was introduced in summer 2010 (see Fig. 3). The issuance of SNB Bills pursues the goal of tying up a large part of liquidity. As a result, the current balances of domestic banks can be reduced. Thanks to the chosen auction method (interest rate tender with American allocation method), pricing is left to the market. Interest rate management is therefore not in the foreground of the SNB Bills. The repo operations also siphon off liquidity (see Fig. 4), but at a fixed price specified by the SNB (volume tender). The repo operations therefore serve, as under the previous monetary policy procedure, to control the three-month Libor. In addition, the SNB carries out fine-tuning operations if necessary in order to smooth out excessive fluctuations in the overnight money rate. Meanwhile, the outstanding volume of liquidity-absorbing operations amounts to a total of CHF 140 billion. Despite this high amount, the three-month Libor is still below 25 basis points. In order to bring the Libor to the target value within the target range, the excess liquidity would have to be reduced (see Fig. 5). However, the extent of the remaining excess liquidity is not known exactly. This depends on the liquidity cushion that banks want to hold in addition to the reserve requirement. If interest rates rise and uncertainties on the financial markets diminish, banks are expected to reduce their liquidity cushions. SarON (Swiss Average Rate Overnight) is a good indicator of Zurich, 24 March 2011 the extent of the excess liquidity. As long as SARON is close to zero, excess liquidity is likely to exist. In May 2010, current account balances peaked at a weekly average of CHF 104 billion. Since then, they have been reduced to around CHF 25 billion as a result of levy measures (see Figure 6). The SNB Bills are issued in different maturities. SNB Bills with a maturity of one month are issued weekly. At the same time, SNB Bills with a maturity of three, six or twelve months are offered alternately. The outstanding volume of the SNB Bills reached over CHF 100 billion within a few months. Initially, the outstanding volume consisted almost entirely of SNB bills with a maturity of one month. In the course of the year, however, the share of longer-term SNB bills was increased to two-thirds. Meanwhile, the banking system has become accustomed to liquidity absorption. This is also reflected in the fact that the interest rates of the SNB Bills are now below the respective Libor rates in all maturities. With the SNB Bills, the previously created unlimited liquidity was partially tied up again. This created the conditions for the gradual normalisation of conditions on the money market. In terms of monetary policy, however, the levy measures are insignificant as long as excess liquidity is not completely reduced and interest rates remain close to zero. As a result, the issuance of SNB Bills has so far had little effect on monetary policy. In the current interest rate environment, SNB bills and current balances can almost be regarded as substitutes. The new implementation of monetary policy has brought about some changes in the money market. The SNB is no longer available as a source of funding. The SNB's circle of counterparties now consists primarily of domestic banks that want to invest their excess liquidity. Banks that need liquidity must procure it on the market. Thus, a liquid and efficient interbank market is essential for the liquidity management of banks. Liquidity can only be obtained from the SNB at a special rate to bridge unforeseen liquidity bottlenecks in the short term via the bottleneck financing facility. In the last two years, the trading volume on the repo interbank market has decreased significantly due to high excess liquidity and low interest rates (see Fig. 7). However, activity never came to a standstill, and daily sales averaged CHF 7 billion. Turnover on the unsecured money market suffered a major decline due to the loss of confidence and has not reached the level of before the crisis. Trading volume on the secured money market has recovered more strongly than on the unsecured money market. This can be attributed to the partial transfer from the unsecured to the secured money market and speaks for the efficiency of the repo system. Accordingly, the importance of the Swiss Reference Rates based on the repo business has increased. The repo business has thus proven itself for the liquidity management of banks even in the turbulent times of recent years. To sum up, the money market has become accustomed to the changed environment and to the SNB's liquidity-absorbing operations. Thanks to the flexibility of the toolbox, the procedure for implementing monetary policy could be easily adapted to the new liquidity situation. Conditions on the money market have gradually returned to normal. Mrz 2011 Die neue Umsetzung der Geldpolitik und ihre Auswirkungen auf den Geldmarkt (Zusammenfassung) Dewet Moser, Stellvertretendes Mitglied des Direktoriums der Schweizerischen Nationalbank, Geldmarkt-Apro der Schweizerischen Nationalbank, Zrich, 24.03.2011 Die Schweizerische Nationalbank (SNB) setzte seit ihrem Bestehen die Geldpolitik durch Zufhrung befristeter Liquiditt um. Das Bankensystem befand sich traditionell gegenber der SNB in einem Liquidittsdefizit. Durch die Zufhrung von lediglich befristeter Liquiditt zwang die SNB die Banken, laufend neue Liquiditt nachzufragen. ber die zugefhrte Liquidittsmenge und deren Zinssatz steuerte die SNB den Geldmarkt. Im Rahmen der Devisenkufe von Mrz 2009 bis Juni 2010 wurde dem Bankensystem unbefristete Liquiditt von insgesamt 191 Mrd. Franken zugefhrt (siehe Abb. 1). In der Folge entstand aus dem Liquidittsdefizit des Bankensystems ein massiver Liquidittsberschuss (siehe Abb. 2). Die Nachfrage der Banken nach Liquiditt bildete sich schrittweise zurck und kam im Mai 2010 zum Erliegen. Die Banken knnen die im System vorhandene berschussliquiditt nicht eigenstndig abbauen. Einzig die SNB ist in der Lage, die Gesamtliquiditt zu steuern. Die vorhandene berschussliquiditt erforderte ein neues Verfahren zur Umsetzung der Geldpolitik. Am geldpolitischen Konzept an sich mit der Definition der Preisstabilitt, der Inflationsprognose und der Festlegung eines Zielbandes fr den Dreimonats-Libor wurden keine nderungen vorgenommen. Der Erhalt der Preisstabilitt ist und bleibt das oberste Ziel. Das neue Verfahren zur Zinssteuerung beruht auf liquidittsabschpfenden Offenmarktoperationen (Ausgabe von SNB Bills und Repo-Geschfte) und wurde im Sommer 2010 eingefhrt (siehe Abb. 3). Die Emissionen von SNB Bills verfolgen das Ziel, einen Grossteil der Liquiditt zu binden. Dadurch knnen die Giroguthaben der inlndischen Banken reduziert werden. Dank des gewhlten Auktionsverfahrens (Zinstender mit amerikanischer Zuteilungsmethode) wird die Preisfindung dem Markt berlassen. Die Zinssteuerung steht somit bei den SNB Bills nicht im Vordergrund. Mit den Repo-Operationen wird ebenfalls Liquiditt abgeschpft (siehe Abb. 4), jedoch zu einem von der SNB vorgegebenen fixen Preis (Mengentender). Die Repo-Operationen dienen folglich, wie unter dem bisherigen geldpolitischen Verfahren, der Steuerung des Dreimonats-Libors. Daneben fhrt die SNB bei Bedarf Feinsteuerungsoperationen durch, um allzu grosse Schwankungen im Tagesgeldsatz zu gltten. Mittlerweile betrgt das ausstehende Volumen der liquidittsabschpfenden Operationen insgesamt 140 Mrd. Franken. Trotz dieses hohen Betrags liegt der Dreimonats-Libor nach wie vor unter 25 Basispunkten. Um den Libor auf den innerhalb des Zielbandes angestrebten Wert zu fhren, msste die berschussliquiditt abgebaut werden (siehe Abb. 5). Der Umfang der noch vorhandenen berschussliquiditt ist allerdings nicht genau bekannt. Dieser hngt vom Liquidittspolster ab, das die Banken zustzlich zum Mindestreserveerfordernis halten wollen. Steigt das Zinsniveau, und nehmen die Unsicherheiten an den Finanzmrkten ab, werden die Banken ihr Liquidittspolster voraussichtlich reduzieren. Der SARON (Swiss Average Rate Overnight) stellt als Referenzsatz fr das Tagesgeld einen guten Indikator fr Zrich, 24. Mrz 2011 das Ausmass der berschussliquiditt dar. Solange der SARON nahe bei Null ist, drfte berschussliquiditt vorhanden sein. Im Mai 2010 verzeichneten die Giroguthaben im Wochendurchschnitt einen Hchststand von 104 Mrd. Franken. Seither wurden sie durch Abschpfungsmassnahmen auf zuletzt rund 25 Mrd. Franken abgebaut (siehe Abb. 6). Die Emission der SNB Bills erfolgt in verschiedenen Laufzeiten. Wchentlich werden SNB Bills mit einer Laufzeit von einem Monat emittiert. Parallel dazu werden alternierend SNB Bills mit einer Laufzeit von drei, sechs oder zwlf Monaten angeboten. Das ausstehende Volumen der SNB Bills erreichte innert einiger Monate ber 100 Mrd. Franken. Anfangs bestand das ausstehende Volumen fast vollstndig aus SNB Bills mit der Laufzeit von einem Monat. Im Verlauf des Jahres konnte der Anteil der lngerfristigen SNB Bills indes auf zwei Drittel erhht werden. Inzwischen hat sich das Bankensystem an die Liquidittsabschpfung gewhnt. Dies zeigt sich auch daran, dass sich die Zinsstze der SNB Bills in allen Laufzeiten inzwischen unter den jeweiligen Libor-Stzen bewegen. Mit den SNB Bills wurde die zuvor geschaffene unbefristete Liquiditt teilweise wieder gebunden. Dadurch wurde die Voraussetzung zur allmhlichen Normalisierung der Verhltnisse am Geldmarkt geschaffen. Geldpolitisch sind die Abschpfungsmassnahmen jedoch unbedeutend, solange die berschussliquiditt nicht vollstndig abgebaut wird und die Zinsen nahe Null bleiben. Somit hatten die Emissionen von SNB Bills bislang kaum eine geldpolitische Wirkung. Im aktuellen Zinsumfeld knnen SNB Bills und Giroguthaben nahezu als Substitut betrachtet werden. Die neue Umsetzung der Geldpolitik hat am Geldmarkt einige Vernderungen bewirkt. Die SNB steht nicht mehr als Refinanzierungsquelle zur Verfgung. Der Kreis der Gegenparteien der SNB besteht neuerdings primr aus inlndischen Banken, die ihre berschussliquiditt anlegen wollen. Banken, welche Liquiditt bentigen, mssen diese am Markt beschaffen. Somit ist ein liquider und effizienter Interbankenmarkt essentiell fr die Liquidittsbewirtschaftung der Banken. Von der SNB kann Liquiditt nur zur kurzfristigen berbrckung unvorhergesehener Liquidittsengpsse ber die Engpassfinanzierungsfazilitt zum Sondersatz bezogen werden. In den letzten zwei Jahren verringerte sich das Handelsvolumen am Repo-Interbankenmarkt aufgrund der hohen berschussliquiditt und des tiefen Zinsniveaus deutlich (siehe Abb. 7). Die Aktivitt kam jedoch nie zum Erliegen, und der tgliche Umsatz betrug durchschnittlich 7 Mrd. Franken. Der Umsatz am unbesicherten Geldmarkt erlitt aufgrund des Vertrauensverlustes einen grsseren Rckgang und hat das Niveau von vor der Krise nicht mehr erreicht. Das Handelsvolumen am besicherten Geldmarkt hat sich strker erholt als am unbesicherten Geldmarkt. Dies kann auf die teilweise Umlagerung vom unbesicherten auf den besicherten Geldmarkt zurckgefhrt werden und spricht fr die Effizienz des Repo-Systems. Entsprechend hat sich die Bedeutung der auf dem Repo-Geschft basierenden Swiss Reference Rates vergrssert. Das Repo-Geschft hat sich somit auch in den turbulenten Zeiten der letzten Jahre fr die Liquidittsbewirtschaftung der Banken bewhrt. Zusammenfassend lsst sich festhalten, dass sich der Geldmarkt an das vernderte Umfeld und an die liquidittsabschpfenden Operationen der SNB gewhnt hat. Dank der Flexibilitt des Instrumentariums konnte das Verfahren zur Umsetzung der Geldpolitik problemlos der neuen Liquidittssituation angepasst werden. Die Verhltnisse am Geldmarkt haben sich allmhlich normalisiert. Zur Bewirtschaftung der Liquiditt drften die Banken auch knftig Zrich, 24.
