They also expect the Swiss franc to weaken further. A look at the currency movements of recent weeks shows that conditions on the foreign exchange market have obviously not yet normalized. That is why I would like to conclude by saying that the SNB never sleeps and is still operationally ready to intervene at any time if necessary. I firmly expect conditions on the foreign exchange market to return to normal. More on this at the latest at the Money Market Apero 2016. I would now like to invite you all to the convivial part of our traditional event, thank you for your interest and attention and wish you stimulating conversations, committed discussions and exciting encounters. In der Praxis ergibt sich bei der Absicherung allerdings eine Diskrepanz, weil der mit dem Swap abgesicherte Zinssatz, der Zins auf Kundeneinlagen, bei null bleibt. Mit diesem sogenannten Basisrisiko gehen die Banken unterschiedlich um. Eine Mglichkeit ist, weiterhin die Swapkurve fr die Zinsabsicherung von Hypotheken zu verwenden und die zustzlichen Absicherungskosten auf den Kunden zu berwlzen. Eine andere Option ist, die Laufzeiten der Aktiv- und Passivseite besser aufeinander abzustimmen und so das Zinsrisiko zu reduzieren. Banken knnen z.B. eigene Anleihen emittieren und dadurch die Fristigkeit der Passiven verlngern. Sie sehen an diesem Beispiel der Absicherung: Auch in einem Negativzinsumfeld besteht ein grosser Bedarf an reprsentativen und verlsslichen Referenzgrssen. Entsprechend tatkrftig und ausdauernd wirkt die SNB mit an den Reformbestrebungen bei den Referenzzinsstzen, die seit dem Bekanntwerden der Manipulationen des Libors in verschiedenen Whrungen Seite 9/10 2012 im Gange sind (Abbildung 22). Auf internationaler Ebene verffentlichte das Financial Stability Board (FSB) vergangenes Jahr dazu einen Bericht. Dieser nimmt eine Beurteilung der unbesicherten Geldmarktstze vor, der sogenannten Ibor-Stze, zu denen auch der Libor gehrt. Das FSB empfiehlt, zum einen die bestehenden Ibor-Zinsstze weiter zu verbessern. Zum anderen sollen aber auch risikofreie Zinsstze entwickelt werden. Wie Sie wissen, verfgt unser Markt bereits seit 2009 ber eine ausgewachsene Familie solcher Indikatoren fr den besicherten Geldmarkt, die Swiss Reference Rates. In der Schweiz hat die SNB im April 2014 Daten zum Frankengeldmarkt erhoben. Das Resultat zeigt, dass unsere Referenzzinsstze weiterhin nicht ausschliesslich auf Transaktionen basieren knnen, wie dies grundstzlich erstrebenswert wre, weil es an Liquiditt mangelt. An der morgigen Repo-Tagung werden wir Ihnen weitere Ergebnisse dieser Umfrage vorstellen, die wir brigens auf Anregung aus Marktkreisen durchgefhrt haben. Schlussbetrachtungen Die SNB beobachtet und analysiert nicht nur das Geschehen am Geldmarkt intensiv. Sie schenkt dem Devisenmarkt weiterhin ihre volle Aufmerksamkeit  und dies auch nach Aufhebung des Mindestkurses. Deshalb mchte ich meine Betrachtungen auch mit einem Blick auf den Devisenmarkt abschliessen. Auf Abbildung 23 sehen Sie in rot den Franken auf handelsgewichteter Basis, mit einem krassen berschiessen, das unverkennbar mit der Aufhebung des Mindestkurses in Verbindung steht. In den letzten zwei Monaten hat der handelsgewichtete Franken fast die Hlfte des Ausschlags wieder wettgemacht, bleibt aber insgesamt noch erheblich berbewertet. Wie geht es weiter? Wir erwarten, dass sich der Franken ber die Zeit deutlich abschwchen wird. Die gestrichelte Linie bezieht sich allerdings nicht auf unsere Erwartung, sondern auf den Median der Schtzungen der Bankanalysten. Auch diese rechnen damit, dass sich der Franken weiter abschwcht. Ein Blick auf die Whrungsbewegungen der letzten Wochen zeigt, dass sich die Verhltnisse am Devisenmarkt offensichtlich noch nicht normalisiert haben. Darum meine Botschaft zum Schluss: Die SNB schlft nie und ist weiterhin auch operativ jederzeit bereit, bei Bedarf einzugreifen. Ich rechne fest damit, dass sich die Verhltnisse am Devisenmarkt wieder normalisieren. Mehr dazu sptestens beim Geldmarkt-Apro 2016. Ich darf Sie jetzt alle zum geselligen Teil unseres traditionellen Anlasses einladen, danke Ihnen fr Ihr Interesse und Ihre Aufmerksamkeit und wnsche anregende Gesprche, engagierte Diskussionen und spannende Begegnungen. Title: Swiss National Bank - Independent and firmly anchored
text: Speech Embargo 24 April 2015, 10 am Swiss National Bank  independent and firmly anchored 107th Ordinary General Meeting of Shareholders of the Swiss National Bank Jean Studer President of the Bank Council Swiss National Bank Berne, 24 April 2015 , Zurich (speech given in German and French) Page 1/8 Dear Shareholders Ladies and Gentlemen Dear Guests I am delighted to be able to welcome you to the Swiss National Banks (SNB) 107th General Meeting. Today, for the first time in the long history of this event, we also have the pleasure of welcoming a group of secondary school students to attend our proceedings. The students  who join us from two schools, one in Liestal and one in Petit-Lancy  were selected from no fewer than 50 interested classes on the strength of their study of our institution and the way we operate as well as the quality of their application documents. So, let me once again extend a particularly warm welcome to you, dear students! Who knows, perhaps you will feel so inspired by our unique institution that you will one day buy an SNB share yourselves, thereby helping to rejuvenate our shareholder base? Perhaps you will even apply to work for the SNB as an economist or in some other position in the future? My remarks today will revolve around two topics, both of which will, I trust, be as interesting for secondary school students as for shareholders. First, I shall speak about the institutional role of the SNB in our democracy and society. In doing so, I intend to answer some of the questions that have arisen on this score in recent months. I shall sketch the legislative framework within which the SNB operates, focusing in particular on the interplay between independence and accountability. The second part of my speech will be devoted to a subject that was at the heart of my remarks this time last year, namely the rules governing the calculation and distribution of SNB profits. Substantially more interest in institutional matters As we all know, interest in a range of institutional questions relating to the SNB has increased palpably  and not just since the discontinuation of the minimum exchange rate against the euro on 15 January of this year. The gold initiative, for instance, springs to mind. With its rigid provisions on the composition of currency reserves, this initiative, which the Swiss people and cantons thankfully rejected by a clear margin last November, would have massively restricted the SNBs room for manoeuvre. Signatures are still being collected for another initiative known as the Vollgeldinitiative (plain money initiative), which aims to effect a fundamental reform of our financial and banking system. However, let us return to 15 January 2015  the corollary of 6 September 2011, the day the SNB introduced the minimum exchange rate. The minimum exchange rate was one of many exceptional measures adopted by the SNB and most other central banks over the last eight years in response to the financial crisis and its far-reaching consequences. It is quite understandable that this policy of active crisis management on the part of the central banks has triggered a broad public debate on the mandate, independence, responsibility and accountability of such institutions. I shall limit my remarks to Switzerland. As President of the Bank Council, my goal today is to contribute to a reasoned debate about the mandate and Page 2/8 role of the SNB and its institutional anchoring in our political system. You will hear more on current monetary policy and the decision to discontinue the minimum exchange rate from the Chairman of the Governing Board  the body officially entrusted with setting monetary policy according to the National Bank Act (NBA). Let us start by looking at the SNBs mandate. Via its Federal Constitution, the Swiss electorate stipulates that, as an independent central bank, the SNB must pursue a monetary policy that serves the overall interests of the country. The legislature  that is, parliament  sets out this mandate as follows: It [the SNB] shall ensure price stability. In so doing, it shall take due account of the development of the economy. The SNB has defined price stability, which it equates with a rise in the national consumer price index of less than 2% per annum, but not below zero. The SNB aims to keep inflation within the range of price stability or to bring inflation back within the range of price stability over the medium term following a disturbance. It should be noted that exchange rate and oil price shocks in particular may have a major impact on inflation in Switzerland in the short term and that temporary deviations from the price stability range may be unavoidable. As mentioned, the legislature also requires the SNB to take account of economic developments in formulating its monetary policy. What does this mean in practice? Here, it is important to be realistic about what the SNB can and cannot do. While the SNB cannot be expected to provide fully comprehensive insurance cover for Switzerlands economy, shielding it against all risks and crises, it can be expected to factor in the impact of its monetary policy decisions on the countrys economy. In this connection, the SNB has always explicitly highlighted the limits as well as the possibilities of monetary policy. As is well known, the Switzerlands economy is both open and highly interconnected with Europe and the rest of the world. This means that not just Switzerlands prices but its overall economic performance is invariably highly dependent on international developments. When setting monetary policy, the SNB must always be guided by the long-term interests of the country as a whole. This may include making difficult tradeoffs. The SNB cannot turn a blind eye to realities, even if these do not always look the way we would like at first glance. A central bank that wears blinkers cannot act in the long-term interests of the country. Naturally, the legislature has the right to amend the SNBs mandate at any time. Even back when the relevant articles of the Constitution or legislation were first being debated, politicians wrangled long and hard over the wording. At the time, not only did the legislature give the SNB a clear mandate but, in a far-sighted move, it also gave it considerable freedom within this framework to define the how and the when. The decision was far-sighted because this freedom is essential if the SNB is to be able to fulfil its mandate, especially over the long term. To this end, the legislature makes a broad spectrum of monetary policy instruments available to the SNB, which it may then deploy as it sees fit. I believe this operational flexibility with respect to monetary policy implementation has proved its worth, Page 3/8 particularly during the recent, difficult years. Equally, the SNB has shown that it can use this freedom in a prudent, responsible and targeted fashion. The SNBs independence: a means to an end The SNBs independence is a topic that has also attracted increasing attention of late. As already noted, this independence is rooted in the Constitution  a reflection of just how important its drafters considered the issue to be. As with its mandate, the SNBs independence is defined in detail in the NBA. In fulfilling its mandate, the SNB may not seek or accept instructions of any kind from outside entities. The legislature has also built in certain safeguards  for instance, the banks status as a special-statute joint-stock company  to ensure that the SNB remains independent in practice. You, dear shareholders, are the representatives of this unique institutional structure. Other independence safeguards include the ban on state financing via the central banks printing press and the relatively long, six-year term of office for Governing Board members. Notwithstanding this, the SNB remains firmly anchored in our political system. The independence argument should not be used to inflate the importance of our institution; rather it is purely a means to an end  ensuring that we are in a position to fulfil our mandate as effectively as possible. These institutional arrangements are informed by the experience that, in the long term, independent central banks achieve the goal of price stability set by the legislature more effectively than central banks that are obliged to obey political instructions. The counterweight to this independence is the duty of accountability laid down in the NBA. The SNB bears considerable responsibility, as monetary policy decisions  think of the minimum exchange rate  may have profound consequences for each and every one of us. It is only right that those who bear such responsibility should be expected to explain their decisions and their choice of instruments, and that they should be held accountable for their action(s) or inaction. The SNB thus submits a comprehensive accountability report to the Federal Assembly annually. It is called upon to justify its decisions before the relevant parliamentary committees several times a year and holds regular discussions with the Swiss government. The SNB also regularly informs the public about its monetary policy and monetary policy intentions. Our annual General Meeting at which we outline our concerns and put forward motions to our valued shareholders  and at which the Chairman of the Governing Board has another opportunity to explain the SNBs monetary policy  also forms part of our wider accountability obligations. It is not by chance that our shareholders are often described as the trustees of the SNBs independence  a phrase that neatly encapsulates the linkage between independence and accountability. This brings me to the question of whether the Governing Boards decisions are sufficiently broad-based. It is right that the committee elected by the Federal Council should consist of just three members, but in my view three points require clarification here. Firstly, the Governing Board is a committee of experts, not a government agency in which political currents must be represented. This focus on expertise is articulated in the NBA, which Page 4/8 requires candidates for the Governing Board to have an impeccable reputation and a recognised knowledge of monetary, banking and financial issues. Secondly, the SNBs staff analyse and supply the Governing Board with a vast amount of data and submit assessments that are potentially relevant to the decision-making process. This data includes first-hand information from Swiss companies from a wide range of industries and regions. Such a procedure ensures that multiple viewpoints are factored into the equation; these are then evaluated and weighed up by the Governing Board. The members of the Governing Board do not live in an ivory tower and do not rely exclusively on information and analysis from within their own ranks. They regularly interact with the public, engage directly with citizens and cultivate relationships with decision makers and representatives of the business, political and academic communities, both in Switzerland and abroad. The impressions gathered from all these meetings round out the overall picture. At the same time, the compact size of the Governing Board is conducive to intense and productive discussions. Only when all this input has been weighed up does the committee take its decision. The Governing Board does not reach its conclusions in a vacuum; on the contrary, its decisions are based on a wide range of information sources. This process allows the SNB to use its independence in matters of monetary policy to full effect. Furthermore, SNB monetary policy outcomes over the long term do not suggest that the institutional framework is in urgent need of reform. In recent decades, not only has the SNB successfully managed monetary policy in the interests of Switzerland as a whole but, in particular, it has successfully maintained price stability. The SNB undoubtedly has a strong track record in this field and its performance compares favourably with that of other central banks. Nothing in this world is so good that it cannot be improved, and this holds true for the SNBs institutional framework as well. The purpose of my remarks today is not to idealise the current system  as President of the Bank Council it is not my business to instruct the legislature; I simply want to lay out my thoughts in the spirit of a reasoned and productive debate. So let us remind ourselves once again of the advantages of the existing institutional framework: it defines the SNBs mandate precisely and grants it the freedom necessary for fulfilment. The independence the SNB enjoys is a means to an end; it does not give it carte blanche to make arbitrary decisions nor does it imply that monetary policy decisions are reached in isolation. The duty of accountability plays an important role in ensuring that the SNB is firmly anchored in our political system and it allows the relevant parties to assess accurately whether the mandate is being fulfilled. Last but not least, the SNBs record speaks for itself. Unequal treatment of shareholders versus the cantons and Confederation Allow me to move on to my second topic: the rules governing the calculation and distribution of SNB profits. These rules are also part of the institutional framework within which we operate and are extremely important as they ultimately help secure the SNBs freedom to act Page 5/8 in the long term. Understandably, some questions have arisen in relation to these rules, too. It is logical that shareholders in particular should ask: why is the SNB paying a CHF 1 billion supplementary distribution to the Confederation and the cantons for 2014 over and above the ordinary distribution of CHF 1 billion, while shareholders are merely to receive a dividend of CHF 1.5 million? Given that, for the first time in the SNBs history, there was no dividend payout for 2013, it is entirely legitimate that investors should ask this question. This then prompts another, related question: how can the granting of a supplementary distribution be reconciled with the fact that the discontinuation of the minimum exchange rate two weeks after the publication of the annual financial statements could significantly impair the 2015 result? And thirdly: at our General Meeting a year ago, I emphasised that the legislature attaches great importance to ensuring sufficient equity capital in order to guarantee the SNBs room for manoeuvre in the long term. Does the supplementary distribution suddenly invalidate this statement? Before answering these questions, let me remind you that in recent years the SNBs balance sheet total has increased five-fold to approximately CHF 570 billion today. This balance sheet expansion is a result of the monetary policy measures the SNB had to adopt in order to tackle the strong Swiss franc and fulfil its mandate against a backdrop of multiple crises. We currently hold currency reserves of CHF 560 billion, at least 90% of which is in foreign currency investments, the rest in gold. While one of the goals of our investment policy is to invest in safe assets and diversify as broadly as possible, there is inevitably considerable risk associated with a portfolio of this size. Exchange rate risk  which, for monetary policy reasons, the SNB is unable to hedge  and changes in the gold price are the most notable. However, fluctuations in interest rates and stock prices can also quickly lead to substantial absolute valuation changes. Having said this, the SNBs large portfolio of currency reserves may not only be associated with large losses, but potentially also with large gains. This was impressively illustrated in 2014 when the SNB reported a profit of CHF 38 billion. How is this profit allocated? Here, the provisions of the NBA are key. They ascribe great importance to the accumulation of sufficient equity capital, which acts as a buffer against financial risks of all kinds. Crucially, having enough equity capital allows the SNB to maintain its ability to conduct monetary policy over the long term. This explains why the legislature gives allocations to provisions (i.e. the creation of equity capital) priority over dividend payments and distributions. Thus, almost CHF 2 billion of the profit is first being allocated to provisions. A further CHF 6.8 billion is going towards balancing out the distribution reserve, which was negative due to the 2013 loss and had thus become a loss carried forward. From the remaining profit, once again a legally stipulated maximum dividend of CHF 1.5 million can be paid to shareholders, and a distribution of CHF 1 billion can be made to the Confederation and the cantons. As per NBA, the distribution amount is based on the profit distribution agreement between the Federal Department of Finance (FDF) and the SNB. Under this agreement, a supplementary distribution may be made, provided the distribution reserve exceeds CHF 10 billion. As this Page 6/8 was the case at the end of 2014, the FDF and the SNB agreed on a supplementary payment of CHF 1 billion. Not possible to catch up on unpaid dividends retroactively In answer to the first question: unfortunately, it is not possible to catch up on an unpaid dividend at a later date as there is no legal basis for making such a claim. The maximum dividend is fixed in the NBA. This in no way detracts from the fact that we hold our shareholders in the highest esteem; indeed, we regard our General Meeting as the highlight of our financial year. Nonetheless, the Confederation and the cantons are legally entitled to receive all profit remaining after the allocation to provisions and the payment of the dividend. As to the second question regarding potential losses due to the discontinuation of the minimum exchange rate: the calculation and distribution of profits is always based on the result of the previous financial year; the rules exclude taking account of events in the current year. Indeed, doing so would be quite impractical, as the result can fluctuate very substantially in a very short space of time depending on developments on the financial markets; there have been years in which the last couple of weeks proved crucial in determining whether the SNB closed with a profit or a loss. This is one of the reasons why the SNB does not issue earnings forecasts in the course of the year. There is  and this brings me to the third question  no contradiction between the supplementary distribution and my words at the last General Meeting. Irrespective of performance, provisions are always set up first; any remaining profit is allocated to the distribution reserve. A distribution per se is only possible if this reserve is in positive territory. Moreover, when profits are as high as they were in 2014, only a relatively small proportion of the total will be distributed; the bulk of what remains is held back in the distribution reserve, which, like provisions, qualifies as equity capital and may thus be used to absorb future losses. Generally speaking, the distribution of the previous years profits via the distribution reserve influences how profit is calculated for the current year. Whatever was distributed in the previous year is no longer available for the coming year. The Bank Council bears considerable responsibility on this score. It approves the level of provisions and monitors the investment and risk management process. Rather like the Governing Boards duties in monetary policy, the Bank Council must take account of the realities with which it is confronted. As early as 2009, for example, it passed a resolution, which has proved far-sighted in light of subsequent developments. In the context of building up provisions given incipient balance sheet expansion and the associated risks, the Bank Council decided at that time to take a figure of twice Switzerlands GDP growth (rather than simple GDP growth) as its indicator for economic development. Page 7/8 Outlook and concluding remarks Dear shareholders, cantonal representatives and students: I started by exploring the monetary policy mandate conferred upon the SNB by the Swiss legislature. This mandate ensures that the SNB faces reality head-on and cannot shrink from taking the requisite measures. The fact that the legislature grants the SNB considerable flexibility in monetary policy implementation in order to fulfil its mandate has proved invaluable. This independence is essential if the SNB is to conduct monetary policy successfully and fulfil its mandate; however, the SNB also has a duty to inform the public about its monetary policy decisions at all times and to account for its actions. Independence and accountability are two sides of the same coin. Only if the SNB is accountable can stakeholders gauge to what extent the SNB is fulfilling its mandate and pursuing a monetary policy that serves the interests of the country as a whole. The institutional framework ensures that the SNB is making proper use of its independence, that it is firmly anchored, and that it never loses touch with developments in the real economy. It is right and important that these questions are discussed regularly and openly. Equally, it is right and important that we debate issues rationally; we must weigh potential reform proposals carefully and ask ourselves whether these are really necessary and constructive. In this speech, I have also tried to explain the legal framework governing dividend payments. I hope you will appreciate that there is no scope for the SNB to change its position on this matter. I can, however, assure you that the Bank Council will continue to do everything in its power to maintain a healthy balance sheet, thereby guaranteeing the SNBs ability to conduct monetary policy over the long term. In doing so, we ensure that our institution remains on a solid footing in fulfilling the mandate bestowed on it by the legislature. On behalf of the entire Bank Council, may I once again thank you sincerely for the trust you have placed in us. I would also like to thank the Governing Board, with whose members we maintain a close and productive dialogue. Lastly, I should like to express my gratitude to the SNBs staff who work tirelessly in the service of our institution. Thank you for your attention. Page 8/8

Title: Monetary policy challenges currently facing the SNB
text: Report Embargo period 8 May 2015 11:00 Challenges of the current monetary policy of the SNB ASIP General Assembly Dewet Moser Alternate member of the Governing Board* Swiss National Bank Zurich, 8 May 2015 (c) Swiss National Bank, Zurich, 2015 * The speaker would like to thank Vincent Crettol, Peter Kuster, Sandro Streit and Martin Weder for their support in the preparation of this presentation. Page 1/11 Dear Sir or Madam, It is a great honour for me to attend your General Assembly today and to speak about the current monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and the associated challenges. The economic environment in Switzerland has undoubtedly become more difficult in recent months. This also has a lot to do with our monetary policy decision of 15 January 2015. This had obvious effects - especially for the pension funds. Nevertheless, it must be warned against overestimating the importance of monetary policy and thus also of this decision. Monetary policy must never be considered in isolation, but must always be placed in the context of international developments, the course of the economy, the situation on the financial markets and economic policy. For eight years, the international environment has been characterized by major imbalances, adjustment processes, uncertainties and recurring disruptions. Monetary policy cannot escape these unedifying realities. Or to put it another way: behind monetary policy decisions are difficult trade-offs; sometimes it's about choosing the lesser evil. In my presentation, I would first like to go into more detail about the background to the abolition of the minimum exchange rate and the introduction of negative interest rates. In a second step, I will shed light on the associated challenges for the economy and investors. The third and final part focuses on the low interest rate environment with the consequences for Swiss pension funds. Abolition of the minimum exchange rate - in the overall interest of the country I am sure you can all remember this well: on 15 January this year, the SNB abolished the minimum exchange rate (Figure 1). At the same time, the monetary policy reference rate, the three-month Libor, was lowered by 0.5 percentage points to -0.75%. This surprising decision has caused a sensation worldwide. Why did we act in this way? In the course of the past year, there have been growing signs that the us is approaching an exit from the very expansionary monetary policy. At the same time, monetary policy in the eurozone has been greatly eased in several steps. If the assessment of interest rate developments and the monetary policy orientation for two major currency areas differ so widely, this almost inevitably has an impact on the currencies. While the US dollar appreciated significantly on a trade-weighted basis, the euro continued to depreciate (Figure 2). This dynamic also affected the Swiss franc. The prospect of continued weakness in the euro put the Swiss franc under increasing upward pressure against the euro. Accordingly, the volume traded in the euro-franc currency pair also increased significantly (Figure 3). Towards the end of the year, the SNB had to intervene in the foreign exchange market for the first time since autumn 2012 in order to enforce the minimum exchange rate. The SNB was more and more the only buyer in the euro franc. In January, intervention amounts increased against the backdrop of the expected additional easing by the European Central Bank (ECB) and rising uncertainty over the elections in Greece. Page 2/11 massively (Figure 4). Ever larger sums were needed to enforce the minimum exchange rate. There was no end in sight to the interventions, quite the opposite. The SNB's willingness to buy euros against Swiss francs at a fixed rate could increasingly have been used as a vehicle in the huge global foreign exchange market to sell euros on relatively favourable terms. In retrospect, the ECB's decision of 22 January 2015 to buy securities totalling EUR 1140 billion by September 2016 confirmed our assessment. A further adherence to the minimum exchange rate would have led to an uncontrollable expansion of our balance sheet. The associated risks would have been disproportionate to the benefits for the Swiss economy. The expansion of the balance sheet would have severely reduced our ability to act in monetary policy. In the long term, we would have jeopardised the fulfilment of our mandate, namely to maintain price stability while taking account of economic developments. After careful consideration of the goods, it was therefore clear that we had to abolish the minimum exchange rate in order to be able to conduct a monetary policy in the overall interest of our country in the future. The SNB would have jeopardised its credibility if it had stuck to the minimum exchange rate and turned a blind eye to the changed international realities. Assessment and outlook for the economy With the abolition of the minimum exchange rate and the subsequent appreciation of the Swiss franc, the framework conditions for the Swiss economy have deteriorated. In December 2014, we still expected growth of 2% for the current year. We are now expecting just under 1%. A significant slowdown is to be expected, especially in the first half of the year, as the KOF Economic Barometer or the Purchasing Managers' Index in the manufacturing sector impressively suggest (Figure 5). In the short term, there is likely to be a significant underutilization of production capacities and a moderate increase in unemployment. This assessment by the SNB is broadly in line with that of other institutions. The risks to the forecast include an escalation in the debt dispute with Greece and an intensification of geopolitical tensions. Of course, the further development of the Swiss franc exchange rate is also important for our economy. At this point, I would like to emphasise that the end of the minimum exchange rate does not mean that the SNB is only passively watching events on the foreign exchange market. On 15 January, we stated unequivocally that we would continue to take account of the exchange rate situation when shaping our monetary policy. If necessary, the SNB will continue to be active in the foreign exchange market in order to influence the monetary environment. Overall, the Swiss economy is in much better shape than in 2011. It has survived the crisis years comparatively well and achieved respectable average growth of around 2% (Figure 6). This was due to the fact that, unlike many industrialised countries, Switzerland is not converging with an ailing banking system or with a significant price correction on the real estate market. Page 3/11 was fronted. Thanks to sound public finances, unlike in several European countries, no drastic consolidation measures were necessary. Exports proved resilient thanks to increasing specialisation and wider regional diversification. At the same time, monetary policy has also reacted quickly to the international upheavals and provided temporary stability and planning security with the minimum exchange rate, thus giving the Swiss economy time to adjust. Today, Switzerland's most important trading partners, above all the eurozone, are also in a better position than they were just four years ago (Figure 7). However, we are aware that our economy is undoubtedly facing a Herculean task due to the abrupt appreciation of the Swiss franc. The Swiss franc is still significantly overvalued almost four months after the abolition of the minimum exchange rate. On a trade-weighted basis, it is currently around 20% above its long-term average. However, the performance of Swiss companies in the past is also a reason for optimism. In recent years, they have impressively shown that they are extremely adaptable and innovative. This is also reflected again and again in the numerous international rankings on competitiveness and innovative strength, in which Switzerland has occupied top positions for years. In the inflation outlook, the marked appreciation of the Swiss franc is also noticeable, with the collapse of the oil price being added here (Figure 8). Last year, the average inflation rate as measured by the consumer price index was close to zero. This year, the inflation rate will fall significantly into negative territory. Accordingly, we lowered our inflation forecast for 2015 in March from -0.1% to -1.1%. Prices are likely to fall again slightly next year. We expect inflation to rise by -0.5%. Inflation will therefore not be back in positive territory until the beginning of 2017. Importantly, this is a temporary effect. The Swiss franc is likely to weaken somewhat over time, and the effect of the lower oil price will expire. A persistent negative inflation or even a deflationary spiral - i.e. a self-reinforcing interaction between the economic downward trend and falling price levels - is not to be expected. Price stability will thus be maintained in the medium term. Negative interest rate: rule-based and nationwide Let's go back from the middle term to January 15. How did the financial markets react to our decision? Experience has shown that they react much faster and more violently to unexpected changes in monetary policy than the real economy and the price level. That was also the case this time. For example, the abolition of the minimum exchange rate has caused an uproar in the foreign exchange market in the short term (Figure 9). Temporarily one euro was quoted at 85 centimes. The Swiss franc appreciated by 22% on a trade-weighted basis until January 16. Other markets were also affected by volatility. Swiss equities, for example, as measured by the SPI, have lost 14% in value within two days. These strong reactions were not intended by the SNB, but had to be accepted because the Page 4/11 Inevitably, the minimum exchange rate could only be abolished abruptly and surprisingly. Tempers have cooled down since then. However, the Swiss franc is currently still valued almost 14% higher than before the abolition of the minimum exchange rate. A new and important instrument in the fight against upward pressure is the negative interest rate on current account balances at the SNB. It makes investments in Swiss francs less attractive, thus counteracting the strength of the Swiss franc and loosening monetary conditions. Negative interest rates have quickly spread to the entire range of money and capital market interest rates (Figure 10). The three-month Libor has been in negative territory since the announcement and has since reached a low of -0.96%. As a result, part of the traditional interest rate differential with foreign countries, which had melted sharply in the crisis years, could also be restored (Figure 11). Long-term interest rates have also fallen again. More than half of the outstanding Swiss federal bonds currently no longer yield a positive return. It is understandable that such extraordinary conditions meet with little enthusiasm among investors. It is therefore important to us that the SNB's considerations are understood. The SNB conducts a monetary policy in the overall interest of the country. Without negative interest rates, the Swiss franc would be even stronger - with the corresponding effects on growth and prices. The negative interest rate is thus a monetary policy instrument to cushion the effects of the abolition of the minimum exchange rate on the Swiss economy. In designing the instrument, we rely on a robust monetary and legal procedure with clear rules. The allowances are therefore based on the minimum reserves that banks are required to hold by law (Figure 12). The allowance shall be twenty times this reserve requirement. With a minimum reserve target of just under CHF 15 billion, the allowances are currently around CHF 300 billion - this for sight deposits of almost CHF 450 billion. To ensure that the negative interest rate can produce the desired monetary policy effect, we have opted for a comprehensive solution with as few exceptions as possible. On April 22, 2015, we further reduced the list of exceptions. The current accounts of companies close to the federal government are now also subject to negative interest rates. The snb pension fund account is no longer an exception. In addition, the accounts of the cantons of Geneva and Zurich as well as the city of Zurich were dissolved. By charging all current account balances of all banks and other financial market participants with the negative interest rate, we are following the principle of equal treatment. In this context, it should be made clear that the negative interest rate is only charged on balances held by the SNB itself. Apart from the Confederation's pension fund, the SNB therefore does not directly burden the pension funds. From the point of view of monetary policy, however, it is quite desirable for the banks to pass on the negative interest rate to large investors, because this is the only way this instrument can unfold its full effect. How high the burden of the Page 5/11 Negative interest rates and the allowances vary from institution to institution and are outside the sphere of influence of monetary policy. The SNB is aware that a solid old-age provision is crucial for our country. Nevertheless, we have had to answer the request of your industry association to open interest-bearing current accounts for pension funds. What were our reasons? The first is more of a principled nature: exceptions run counter to our desire to treat all account holders equally. Granting an exception to one group of investors makes it more difficult to deny it to another group. Secondly, pension funds are not part of the SNB's business circle, i.e. they are not counterparties to our business and therefore do not have access to the SNB's accounts. Thirdly, monetary policy reasons also clearly militate against an exemption for a large proportion of institutional assets in Switzerland. In recent years, not only foreign investors have been responsible for the appreciation pressure on the Swiss franc, as a look at the balance of payments shows. Since the outbreak of the financial crisis, Switzerland's private capital flows have reversed. While the accumulated current account surplus of around CHF 400 billion in the period from 2002 to 2008 was offset by private capital exports of the same amount, these flows were replaced by the SNB's interventions in the foreign exchange market during the minimum exchange rate phase (Figure 13). Risk appetite in Switzerland has fallen sharply. The domestic private sector is now reluctant to invest abroad. In addition, part of the high level of international investment was repatriated to Switzerland, which contributed to the strength of the Swiss franc. Domestic investors are therefore also responsible for the strong franc. As is well known, these include pension funds. The various statistics on the foreign investments of pension funds suggest that the Swiss franc share of total pension assets has tended to increase since the beginning of the financial crisis. As a result, the average hedging ratio of foreign currency investments has also increased. This should have led to net purchases of Swiss francs. Even with a stable hedging ratio, the increase in the value of foreign currency investments alone can make it necessary to buy Swiss francs. The pension fund sector also accounts for its share of the strength of the Swiss franc. I do not want to make any accusations against this, as the pension funds, as franc-based investors, have acted with foresight in the interests of their policyholders and have comprehensively hedged their currency risks. Conversely, from a monetary policy point of view, however, there is no justification for preferential treatment. Reasons for the persistently low interest rate environment The negative interest rate in Switzerland is ultimately the result of exceptionally low interest rates, which have emerged as a continuation of a global trend of more than 30 years (Figure 14). Both nominal and real interest rates have fallen steadily in the industrialized countries since the early 1980s. A significant part of this decline can be explained by the significant fall in inflation rates over the same period (Figure 15). The Page 6/11 In the 1970s, due to the end of the Bretton Woods system, the two oil price shocks and the expansionary monetary and fiscal policy in many places, inflation rates were still characterized by high inflation rates. Since then, not least thanks to an independent and credibly price stability-oriented monetary policy, it has been increasingly successful in keeping inflation low and narrowing its fluctuation range. As volatility has declined, so have the inflation risk and maturity premiums that investors are demanding as compensation. Economic growth and the changed growth outlook are also likely to have contributed to the decline in real interest rates. While growth rates of up to 8% were recorded in the major industrialized countries in the 1960s and more than 10% in the case of Japan, today those of 4% are considered exceptionally high. The OECD estimates, for example, that the potential growth of the G-7 countries has more than halved since the beginning of the 1970s from around 4% to 1.5% last year. Behind this is lower population growth as well as lower productivity growth. The persistent real economic and structural problems seem to contribute to companies investing little. Despite low interest rates, the possibility and willingness to take out and invest additional loans, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises, are still limited. The supply side also contributes to this: the clean-up of legacy assets and the greater reluctance of banks have led to a decline in lending in many countries. Due to the increased uncertainty, the lack of investment demand is also offset by a tendency to increase the supply of savings capital, which also caused interest rates to fall. In addition, the demand for safe investments such as government bonds is high on the part of important investor groups. The measures taken by the major central banks to combat the crisis are also likely to have played a role (Figure 16). After the key interest rates were lowered to a level close to zero in a first step, the subsequent unconventional measures, such as the extensive purchase of various securities, led to additional downward pressure on interest rates. As a result, central bank balance sheets have grown strongly. Without these central bank measures, however, the recession would have been much deeper and the recovery would probably have been even more sluggish. So there are a few reasons why interest rates are currently very low or negative. However, it should be noted that negative nominal interest rates are not a normal state. We expect the economy to continue to recover and interest rates around the world to rise again. With regard to the international situation, however, it is also clear that the interest rate in Switzerland cannot be higher than in the rest of the world, because otherwise large inflows into the Franc would threaten. Challenges for investors and pension funds Investing in an environment characterized by exceptionally low interest rates remains challenging. In Switzerland, the negative interest rate is an additional challenge. Page 7/11 From a monetary policy point of view, the instrument is necessary for the reasons mentioned, but it makes it more difficult for investors who have to hold Swiss francs to find interest-bearing safe investments at all. This includes, in particular, pension funds and other institutional investors who have to achieve a certain minimum nominal interest rate in order to finance their obligations. However, negative yields on government bonds are not a purely Swiss phenomenon, but an international phenomenon (Figure 17). In Switzerland, however, it is particularly pronounced due to the small size of the capital market and the negative yields that temporarily even affected 13-year federal bonds. Another investment segment that is likely to be of particular interest to you as a pension fund manager is the Swiss real estate market. The SNB also follows developments in this market very closely, although not like you as an investor. Rather, we take the perspective of financial stability. The imbalances in the real estate market have not increased further in recent months. With the negative interest rate, however, real estate and real estate investments have become even more attractive. Real estate prices and construction could therefore be additionally stimulated, which can entail corresponding risks to financial stability. Due to the high proportion of real estate by international standards and the now very high valuation of real estate funds, there could also be dangers lurking here for Swiss pension funds. In the discussion about negative or low interest rates, it should not be forgotten that from the point of view of savers, it is not the nominal interest rate that is decisive, but the real interest rate. In the case of negative inflation, as we can currently observe, the real interest rate is above the nominal interest rate. Measured against Swiss federal bonds in the 5- to 10-year range, the real interest rate is currently still in positive territory (Figure 18). Unlike many other countries, the real interest rate on government bonds - with one small exception in autumn 2008 - has always been positive over the past 30 years. In historical comparison, however, there have always been phases with negative real interest rates. Against this background, the current constellation is still extraordinary, but not unique. It should also not be forgotten that the decline in nominal interest rates and the bull market on the stock exchanges have brought investors considerable valuation gains in recent years. A certain cushion should therefore be available for future fluctuations. What does the difficult investment environment mean for Swiss old-age provision? On the one hand, Switzerland's three-pillar system - consisting of AHV, occupational and private pensions - is praised both at home and abroad for its balance and resistance to crises. On the other hand, there is a broad consensus that the current system needs adjustments. However, the majority of these have failed to materialise in recent years. Since the referendum on the 10th AHV revision in 1995, voters have rejected all changes on the benefit and financing side. With the 2020 pension reform, the Federal Council is now seeking to maintain the current level of benefits and at the same time to maintain the financial balance of the AHV and the Page 8/11 occupational pensions. Let me therefore make a few observations on the role played by low or negative interest rates. In the first pillar, the pay-as-you-go AHV, assets amounting to just under CHF 30 billion are comparatively small in relation to the annual expenditure of over CHF 40 billion. In contrast to pension funds, investment income thus plays a smaller role. If, as in the previous year, the pay-as-you-go result is negative, above-average returns in the medium and long term are not sufficient to secure financial equilibrium. In the second pillar, a distinction must be made between low interest rates and negative interest rates on the one hand, and between the short and long term on the other. Let's start with the SNB's negative interest rate. As described, this is passed on to major customers by the financial institutions to varying degrees. Both the allowances and the interest rates vary. The negative interest rate therefore does not apply to all pension funds and only affects part of the liquidity. Cash and cash equivalents, on the other hand, account for only a small proportion of total assets under management (Figure 19). According to various surveys, the share of liquidity is usually between 5% and 8%. Under the very conservative assumption that there are no allowances, that all pension funds are equally affected and that the liquidity share remains unchanged, this results in a total burden of a maximum of CHF 400 million per year. This is not a small sum, but it corresponds to only a few basis points of assets under management, and is on the same scale as the daily changes in the capital and foreign exchange markets. The effective burden of negative interest rates on pension funds is therefore limited. Pension funds, like other investors, have been able to benefit from the advantages of low or declining interest rates in recent years. The returns achieved on the two main asset classes, equities and bonds, have been attractive in recent years (Figure 20). According to Pictet's frequently used BVG indices, the average annual return over the last ten years has ranged from 4% to 5%, depending on the proportion of shares. These returns are within the scope of what must be achieved at a conversion rate of 6.8% and the current life expectancy (especially since significantly lower conversion rates are applied in the non-mandatory area). The ASIP performance comparison also shows an annualized median return of 4.68% for the same period. However, further valuation gains on bonds are becoming less and less likely. Therefore, the return prospects are much more modest. The long-term trend since the beginning of the MANDATORY BVG system is also clearly pointing downwards. With each bond expiring, the question arises again and again as to how the dry spell can be bridged and how long it will last. The scale of the various crises and the extremely hesitant upswing still required more extensive measures by central banks - the normalisation of monetary policy and thus of interest rates has thus shifted. Page 9/11 postponed further into the future. For the time being, the return to be achieved on risk-free investments is likely to remain extremely low or even negative. At the same time, good diversification of asset classes and currencies can continue to generate a positive return. For example, the SNB also invests its currency reserves, which by definition are held in foreign currencies and gold and cannot be hedged, broadly. This can lead to large fluctuations, but is a promising long-term strategy. Currency diversification has not paid off for franc-based investors in recent years (Figure 21). But in the long term, the hedging costs of investments abroad in most currencies exceed the historical appreciation of the Swiss franc. Investments abroad generate higher returns in Swiss francs and without hedging than those in Switzerland (Figure 22). Therefore, for risky, longer-term investors, especially those who expect a gradual weakening of the Swiss franc, there are also reasons against a high or even complete hedging of currency risks. Even though negative interest rates and the low interest rate environment have dominated the headlines as the tip of the iceberg in recent weeks and months, one thing should not be forgotten in the discussion about the future of old-age provision: A large part of the challenges facing pension funds is of a regulatory or demographic nature (Figure 23). The focus on negative interest rates and the low interest rate environment therefore falls short. The return on investment is an important influencing factor. However, as pension fund managers, you know all too well that the financing of the second pillar is far more complex and multi-layered than the analysis could be limited to that alone. In addition, the average achievable return is largely outside the sphere of influence of politics, pension funds and the SNB. On the other hand, important parameters such as the retirement age, the amount and type of financing sources or the promised benefits are controllable. In this respect, a minimum interest rate and a conversion rate that take demographic and financial realities into account are crucial for the future soundness of occupational pensions. Schlussbetrachtungen Let me conclude my remarks. The SNB's monetary policy decision of 15 January has far-reaching implications. In times of extreme upheaval, the minimum exchange rate has served Switzerland as an extraordinary and temporary measure for more than three years. It was repealed because the costs and benefits of holding on were no longer in a reasonable relationship to each other. The high and increasing foreign exchange interventions necessary for further enforcement have led to an uncontrollable expansion of the SNB's balance sheet. This would have severely restricted our room for manoeuvre in monetary policy in the longer term and thus jeopardised the fulfilment of the statutory mandate. With the negative interest rate and our willingness to Page 10/11 In order to be active in the foreign exchange market, we continue to have the instruments to ensure price stability in the medium term. Ladies and gentlemen, monetary policy can do many things, but by no means everything. In particular, it cannot generate long-term growth or fix structural problems. It cannot and should not relieve market participants of risks in the medium and long term. If it nevertheless tries to do so, there is a risk that it will lose sight of its legal mandate of price stability. With a monetary policy focused on price stability, a central bank makes an important contribution to a healthy foundation that enables economic growth and prosperity. A central bank like the SNB sometimes has to make difficult decisions that incur costs and can be unpopular if they are necessary in the overall interest of the country. The decision of 15 January undoubtedly belongs in this category. The overall context is also important with regard to the challenges for occupational pensions. The persistently low interest rate environment is a global phenomenon and only partly due to the actions of central banks. Careful diversification in terms of asset classes and currencies continues to enable positive returns. However, the pressure for reform has undoubtedly increased in recent years. The SNB cannot guarantee a minimum interest rate or absorb demographic changes. However, she is aware of how important a solid retirement provision is for our country. Thank you for your attention.
